units.la: GRAVIS alicujus ac serii scripti, nullum unquam vidi titulū qui mihi magis videbatur mirus, quam qui est apud Redoanum, Navarrum, & Azorium, de spoliis clericorum. Quid illud esset quod hac appellatione designabatur, apud homines istos praesertim qui de clero papali nil hiscere solent mali, non potui certè non primo aspectu mirari: penitius verò inquirens, interpretationem inveni quae expectationi meae vocisque vi haud adeò congruere
units.tr: Of all the titles of serious works I have seen, none has struck me as more odd than the one that Redoanus, Navarrus and Azorius give their books: de spoliis clericorum, "on the spoils of the clergy." At first sight I could not help wondering what this phrase meant, especially among those men, who are usually silent about the evils of the Papal clergy. On closer inquiry I found an interpretation that seems not quite to fit my expectation or the force of the words

units.la: (:) ij gruere videtur: per spolia scilicet clericorum nihil aliud intelligere istos quàm ea bona clericorum jam vita functorum, quæ ut malè parta, Romani pontificis fiscus ad sese rapit. Opima sunt fateor illa spolia quæ ex reditibus & fructibus ad ecclesias earumque præfectos pertinentibus, per multa jam sæcula, pontifices illi maximi, aliique minores tulerunt. Ex quatuor enim portionibus illis, quibus per canones & consuetudinem veterem, ecclesiastica bona inter Episcopum, ministros, edificia, & pauperes, divisa fuisse legimus, ecclesijs reliquis (ab eorum cathedralibus si discesseris aulis) vix tantum invenies relictum quantum uni ministro sufficiet. reliquum absorpsit pontificalium hominum & heredum ipsorum luxus. Clericorum hæc spolia sunt, eaq; memoranda: sed magis ampla magisque cruenta sunt illa spolia, que ex spiritualibus ecclesiæ bonis ijdem pontifices & episcopo-satrapæ, qua arte, qua vi jamdudum retulere. Sic olim ecclesia queque incedebat ornata, sicut sponsam Christi decebat: peplo inprimis velata, Christum solum habens pro operimento oculorum apud omnes quibuscum agebat, claves domes ejus gestans quasi cingulo pendentes à latere dextro, & à sinistro virgam qua filios suos materno corrigebat more. Hæc inter alia ornamenta illa aurea fuere quibus instar auroræ spectata fuit jamprimum enascens ecclesia. Sed (ô facinus & scelus indignum) invenientes eam custodes vel qui sub custodum titulo dominantur cleris, percusserunt eam, vulnerarunt eam, abstulerunt ipse velim, claves & virgam extorserunt è manibus, exutam denique ornamentis hiscefæreque nudam sub jugum suum jusserunt eam ire, & ex nutu suo pendere, potestatem omnem sibimet vindicantes, & vix aut ne vix quidem vel nomen ipsum ecclesiæ, Christiano cætui relinquentes. Hij veri χλῆροι fuerunt (sic enim Aristoteles favorum pestes in alvearibus appellat) hęc vera spolia clericorum. Qui verò ex amisis sponsi aut fidis ejus servis fuerunt, rapinam istam sine ingente dolore & indignatione, nisi ferrei fuissent, non potuerunt videre. Induxerunt igitur in animos qui inter eos fortiores fuerunt, non lachrymis tantum & luctu quasi funus ecclesiæ prosequi, sed raptores ipsos legitimis armis adoriri, ut prædam ipsam (adspirante Deo) recuperare possint, & ecclesiæ suum pri-stinum reddere statum. Inter cæteros verò quibus Deus hunc animum indidit, eximius hic extitit Christi servus & fidelis ecclesiæ minister, Robertus Parkerus, qui post lachrymas profusas, præces ardentissimas, & conciones innumeras potentiam divinam spirantes, quibus matrem ecclesiam adjuvare studebat, quamvis nimia verecundia diu nimis præpeditus à scribendo fuerat, tandem tamen vinci se permisit à bonorum votis, ac surrexit alacer tanquam alter David, & Jehovam consuluit, dicens, num & ego persequar turmam hanc? Et responsum accepit, persequere: ô utinam & Deus noster bonus apponeret etiam & cætera quæ Davidi spopondit olim, assequuturus es, & eripiendo erepturus. Sed ex eventu pendere nec fortis est nec fidelis. Successum igitur divinæ providentiæ commendans, calamum arripuit, & certamen aggressus est, in Deo sese confirmans, cujus causam agebat. Sic verò actionem suam instituit, ut primo servitutis insignia removenda contenderet ab ecclesiis Christi: tum verò postea id ageret, ut è manu oppressorum emitti possint, ac justæ libertatis tam usum quam fructum habere.
units.tr: ...namely that by "the spoils of the clergy" these men mean nothing more than the goods of clergymen who have died, which the fiscus of the Roman pontiff seizes for itself as ill-gotten. I admit those spoils are rich, the revenues and fruits belonging to churches and their rulers, which for many centuries the supreme pontiffs and their lesser officials have carried off. For we read that church goods were divided, by the canons and ancient custom, into four shares: for the bishop, the ministers, the buildings, and the poor. Yet in the other churches (if you leave out the cathedral halls) you will scarcely find left enough for one minister. The luxury of the pontifical men and their heirs has swallowed the rest. These are the spoils of the clergy, and they deserve to be recorded. But far larger and more bloody are the spoils that the same pontiffs and bishop-satraps have long since taken from the spiritual goods of the Church, by one trick or another, by force. Once the Church walked adorned as the bride of Christ ought to be: veiled above all with a veil, having Christ alone as the covering of her eyes before all with whom she dealt, carrying the keys of her house hanging from a belt at her right side, and at her left the rod with which she corrected her sons in a mother's manner. Among her other ornaments were those golden ones, by which the Church, when first born, was seen like the dawn. But (O deed and shameful crime!) her guardians, or those who ruled over the clergy under the name of guardians, found her, struck her, wounded her, and took from her, I would say, the keys and the rod; and at last, stripped of her ornaments and left naked, they ordered her to go under their yoke and hang on their nod, claiming all power for themselves, and leaving to the Christian assembly scarcely, or hardly even, the very name of Church. These were the true clergy [χλῆροι] (for so Aristotle calls the pests of the hives), and these were the true spoils of the clergy. But those who were of the bride's friends or faithful servants could not see that plunder without enormous grief and indignation, unless they were made of iron. So among those who were stronger, they resolved not only to follow the Church with tears and mourning, as at a funeral, but to attack the plunderers themselves with lawful arms, so that they might recover the prey (with God breathing upon them) and restore the Church to her former state. Among the others in whom God put this spirit, the outstanding one was this servant of Christ and faithful minister of the Church, Robert Parker. After tears poured out, most fervent prayers, and countless sermons breathing divine power, by which he eagerly sought to help mother Church, he had long been hindered from writing by excessive modesty. At last, however, he allowed himself to be overcome by the wishes of good men, and he rose eagerly like another David and consulted Jehovah, saying, shall I too pursue this troop? And he received the answer, Pursue; and would that our good God would also add the rest that he once promised David: you shall overtake them, and by pursuing you shall recover all. But to depend on the outcome is neither brave nor faithful. Therefore, commending the success to divine providence, he took up the pen and engaged in the contest, confirming himself in God, whose cause he was pleading. He arranged his action in such a way that first he would press for the removal of the marks of servitude from the churches of Christ; then afterwards he would work toward the Church's being released from the hand of her oppressors, and having both the use and the fruit of a just liberty.

units.la: In priore causæ parte, de signo crucis præcipuè agebat, quod (nominis valorem superans) non signum tantum est crucis,
units.tr: In the first part of his cause he dealt chiefly with the sign of the cross, which (exceeding the value of its name) is not merely a sign of the cross,

units.la: {:} 3 crucis, sed planè crux ecclesias & ministros multos tam graviter crucians ut non sint ferendo. Hanc autem accusationem tam efficaciter peregit, & iniquitatem rei tam liquidè simul & copiosè monstravit, ut nisi turpe quidam haberent vel ab ipsa veritate vinci, isthoc certè gravamine jamdudum ecclesias levassent. Ad alteram verò curam cum se accincturus esset, quam concalefacto jam brachio, expeditius absolvere potuisset, Samfordus interpellat primo, & per omnia obtestatur sacra, ut, qui solus ferè potuit, perficiendum susciperet quod incepisset ille De Descensu Christi ad Inferos. Huic autem incumbentè studio, quod satis improbi fuit laboris, sic eum Hierarchica tempestas urgebat per scriptum illud de cruce vel excitata vel accelerata, ut nisi per fugam sibimet prospexisset, quam singularis etiam providentia Dei juvabat, à calce ac carcerem reducendus fuisset, ibique ad mortem usque indubiè detinendus. Turbinem istum cum evasisset, & Samfordi telam pertexuisset, tum voti sui memor, ad Hierarchiam totam examinandam, & veram ecclesiæ politeiam ex veris principijs demonstrandam, serò quidem nimis, sed seriò tamen suum animum applicavit. Sed quod monuit olim poëta, vitæ summa brevis spem nos vetat incohare longam, id in isthoc Dei viro cum summo nostro mærore, valuisse vidimus. Nam in medio cursu (sex enim libros instituit, & tres tantum absolvit) requiescere jussus à laboribus suis, ad puriorem illam ecclesiam transferrebatur in cœlis, cujus tantum imaginem quærebat in terris: fœliciter hoc ipsi quàm hæc translatio cesserit, & ipso die quo exspectabat, dubitari non potest ab eo qui finem hujus libri viderit, cujus ultima verba sunt anhelantis ad alteram vitam animæ, & quasi exeuntis in occursum sponsi, superest (inquit) ut nosmet sanctè præparemus, ut quando apparuerit, coram ipsius tribunali pu-ri sistamur & inculpati, fidam actuum omnium nostrorum rationem reddentes, ut ita cum eo aeterna lætitia perfruamur: quod pro immensa sua misericordia, Pater misericors largiatur, per D. NOSTRUM JESUM CHRISTUM. O beatum servum illum, quem cum venerit Dominus ejus, invenerit sic facientẽ. Nostrum tamen si spectemus commodum, im-maturus videtur discessus ejus & plane intempestivus. Non eo solo nomine quod reliquos tres libros jam desiderare cogimur: sed & exinde quod multo limatius, instructius, & ex omni parte apparatius edidisset nobis istos, si modo secundam suam in eos impendisset curam. Sicut enim liberi nostri curantur fidelius à matribus, quam nutricibus: ita libri ab authoribus prodeunt rectius atque emaculatius, quam ab eorum hæredibus. Atque adeo quidem imperfectum authori videbatur quod operis hujus jam effecisset, ut vix dignum haberet quod videret lucem. Sed hoc modestię & humilitati ejus (qua tam se quam sua demittere semper solebat) ab amicis quibusdam adscribebatur: quibus religio certè fuit thesaurum hunc ipsis commissum occultare sub terra. Visum est eis igitur, solo Deo patrono, hunc incomptum posthumum, sed veram patris pietatẽ, judicium & doctrinã spirantes, publici juris (idq; fideliter) facere: & lectorem orare, ut vitiligationes omnes relinquens, rẽ ipsam & argumenta æquâ lance perpendat. Hoc si fecerit: Nihil dubito, quin tantã lucem exinde percipiet, ut se nec operam nec oleum perdidisse dicet. Vis enim rerum ecclesiasticarũ principia, subjectum & columnas intueri? Hic si alicubi reclduntur. vis de eisdem controversias Anglicanas penitius notas habere? audias iam primũ latine loquentes; imò totius Europę protestantis viscera fraterna commoventes. Vis Hierar-
units.tr: but is plainly a cross, grievously tormenting the churches and many ministers, so that they cannot bear it. He pursued this accusation so effectively, and showed the injustice of the matter so clearly and so fully, that unless some people were too shameful to be beaten by the truth itself, they would long since have relieved the churches of this burden. When he was about to take up the second task, which he could have finished more quickly once his arm was warmed, Samford first interrupted him and by every sacred means entreated him to take up and complete what that man had begun, On the Descent of Christ into Hell, since he was almost the only one who could do it. But while he was devoting himself to this, which was a tremendous labor, the hierarchical storm so pressed him, roused or accelerated by that writing on the cross, that unless he had provided for himself by flight, which God's special providence also helped, he would have been dragged back from the chalk line to the prison, and there undoubtedly kept until death. When he had escaped that whirlwind and finished Samford's web, then, mindful of his vow, he applied his mind, though too late, but seriously, to examining the whole Hierarchy and demonstrating from true principles the true polity of the Church. But what the poet once warned, the brief sum of life forbids us to begin a long hope, we have seen to be true in this man of God, to our great sorrow. For in the middle of his course (he planned six books and finished only three), ordered to rest from his labors, he was transferred to heaven, to that purer Church whose image alone he sought on earth. How happily this transfer turned out for him, and that it occurred on the very day he was expecting, cannot be doubted by anyone who has seen the end of this book, whose last words are those of a soul panting for the other life, and as it were going out to meet the bridegroom: it remains (he says) for us to prepare ourselves holily, so that when he appears we may stand pure and blameless before his tribunal, rendering a faithful account of all our deeds, so that we may thus enjoy eternal joy with him; which may the merciful Father grant through his immense mercy, through OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST. O blessed servant, whom his Lord, when he comes, will find so doing. Yet if we look to our own advantage, his departure seems premature and altogether untimely. Not only for the reason that we are already forced to miss the remaining three books, but also because he would have given us these in a much more polished, more instructed, and in every way better-furnished form, had he devoted a second care to them. For just as our children are looked after more faithfully by mothers than by nurses, so books come forth more rightly and more correctly from their authors than from their heirs. Indeed, the author himself thought the work he had already completed so imperfect that he hardly considered it worth seeing the light. But this was ascribed by some friends to his modesty and humility, by which he always used to lower both himself and his own things. For them it was a matter of conscience to keep this treasure entrusted to them hidden underground. It therefore seemed good to them, with God alone as patron, to make this unpolished posthumous work, yet breathing the true piety of its father, its judgment and learning, public property (and to do so faithfully), and to beg the reader to set aside all cavilling and weigh the matter and the arguments with an even balance. If he does this, I doubt not that he will receive so much light from it that he will say he has lost neither labor nor oil. For do you wish to see the principles, the subject, and the pillars of ecclesiastical affairs? If they are hidden somewhere here, do you wish to have the English controversies known more thoroughly? You will hear them now speaking Latin for the first time; indeed, stirring the fraternal bowels of all Protestant Europe. Do you wish to see the Hierarchy...

units.la: Hierarchicum occæcantem fastum sævientemque tyrannidem in scenam produci? Sparsim perspicies in controversiis Hierarchicis prosequendis, multaque hujusmodi Hierarchiam Romanam spirantia. Sed non adeo promissis detinendus es ac dimittendus ad vindemiam ipsam. Opus ejus, messis tua est, si perlegas, releges, & fructum colliges, hoc si feceris, & fruaris, optatis etiam fruimur: utere igi-tur, fruere & Vale.
units.tr: Do you wish to see the blinding pride and raging tyranny of the hierarchy brought onto the stage? You will catch glimpses of it as you pursue the hierarchical controversies, and many things of this kind breathing the Roman hierarchy. But you should not be held too long by these promises, nor sent off to the vintage itself. The work is its harvest, and yours if you read it through, read it again and gather its fruit; if you do this and enjoy it, we too enjoy what we wished for. Use it, then, enjoy it, and farewell.

units.la: DE POLITEIA ECCLESIASTICA, LIBER PRIMVS.
units.tr: ON ECCLESIASTICAL POLITY, BOOK ONE.

units.la: De ejus Natura & Præstantia. De ejus Definitione.
units.tr: On Its Nature and Excellence. On Its Definition.

units.la: POstulat ratio, ut de Politeia Ecclesiastica verba facturi, ab eiusdem definitione auspicemur: ut ita Suteli-vio satisfiat, eam persæpe omissam esse, in nostrarum partium scriptis conquerenti. Ea autem qualis esse debeat, elicietur facillimè, ex iustiam [?] alijs, quibus humanæ & Christianæ Societates expoliuntur. Quid igitur œconomia? Ordo ille, quo dirigitur familia, per media domestica, ad felicitatem suam domesticam consequendam, 1.Reg.10.5. Quid Politeia Civilis? Ordo ille, quo respublica, per media civilia, ad felicitatem civilem provehitur, Deut.4.5. Id quod Aristotelis visum: Politeia est ordo (inquit) inhabitantium civitatem. Quidni autem, ad harum exemplar, Politeia Ecclesiastica definiatur? Velut ordo ille quo dirigitur coetus Ecclesiæ per media Ecclesiastica, ad felicitatem suam publicam, in Domo & Civitate Dei, sanctorumq; communione? Certè ita eam definivisse Paulus ipse videtur; cum Col.2.5. eam appellat ordinem, 1.Tim.3.15. ordinem illum, quo docentur fidelium ordines omnes, quomodo illis in Ecclesia, quæ est domus Dei vivi, versandum sit. Harum autem definitionum singularum explicata enucleatio, tum demum habebitur, quum in earum unaquaque hæc tria distinctè internoscuntur: primò Subiectum, deinde Finis, postremò Media, quibus hic finis in subjectum introducitur. In œconomia subjectum familia est: finis, actio sancta & beata domestica: media Regere & Parere, sicut domesticæ societati conveniens est. In Politeia Civili, subjectum respublica est: finis, actio sancta & beata civilis: media, Regere & Parere, sicut ad civilem felicitatem numeris omnibus absolvendam est accommodatissimum. In Politeia Ecclesiastica, subjectum coetus Ecclesiae est: finis, actio sancta & beata publica in sanctorum communione: media, Regere & Parere, sicut ad sanctorum congregationes summè beandas à Christo totius Ecclesiae principe, & descriptum & praescriptum est.
units.tr: Reason requires that, in speaking of ecclesiastical polity, we begin with its definition, so that we may satisfy Sutcliffe, who complains in the writings of our side that it has so often been left out. What it ought to be will be readily drawn out from the other things by which human and Christian societies are ordered. What then is economy? It is that order by which a household is directed, through domestic means, to its own domestic happiness (1 Kings 10:5). What is civil polity? It is that order by which a commonwealth is advanced, through civil means, to civil happiness (Deut. 4:5). This was also Aristotle's view: "Polity is the order of those who inhabit a city." Why then should ecclesiastical polity not be defined on the model of these? It would be: the order by which the assembly of the Church is directed, through ecclesiastical means, to its public happiness, in the house and city of God and the communion of the saints. Indeed Paul himself seems to have defined it this way, when he calls it order (Col. 2:5), and in 1 Timothy 3:15 he speaks of that order by which all the orders of the faithful are taught how they ought to conduct themselves in the Church, which is the house of the living God. Now a clear unfolding of each of these definitions will be reached only when, in each of them, three things are distinctly recognised: first the Subject, then the End, and last the Means by which this end is introduced into the subject. In economy the subject is the household; the end is holy and blessed domestic action; the means are to rule and to obey, as suits domestic society. In civil polity the subject is the commonwealth; the end is holy and blessed civil action; the means are to rule and to obey, as is most fitting for bringing civil happiness to completion in every respect. In ecclesiastical polity the subject is the assembly of the Church; the end is holy and blessed public action in the communion of the saints; the means are to rule and to obey, as they have been both described and prescribed by Christ, the prince of the whole Church, for the greatest blessing of the congregations of the saints.

units.la: Atquè de subiecto quidem nihil est, quod hoc in loco attinet dicere, de fine fortè quaerat quispiam, cur salutis animarum, qui finis huius politeias ultimus esse videtur, mentio praetermissa sit. Verùm non est, quod hoc quenquam remoretur: haec quidem salus finis isque ultimus huius politeias est: in definitione omittendus tamen videbatur, quia non proprius huius politeias est, sed tum Oeconomiae Christianae, tum civili politeiae communis, ut quae in id incumbant utraeque, ut non in hac vitâ solùm, sed maximè in futura & domesticorum & civium quisque beatus sit. Sed in fine hoc politeiae Ecclesiasticae proprio herebit fortè scrupulus, quod actionis beatae publicae in Ecclesiâ solâ mentio fiat, praetermissâ actione ethica, Oeconomia, civili, quae tamen omnes à politeia Ecclesiastica dirigi, informari, corrigi, & denique perpoliri videntur. Verum quidem hoc est, sed politeiae Ecclesiasticae primò & per se non videtur convenire, verùm illi accedere potius ex illo eminenti gradu, quo praepollet practicis singulis, in easque dominatur, quod suo loco fusiùs docebitur. Tertium quod attinet, cum politeias Ecclesiasticae medium unicum duntaxat non sit, regere scilicet, sed duo potius, Regere nempè & Parere: si tam morosi esse vellemus, ut Matheus Sutclivius est in definitionibus nostrorum scriptorum penè singulis arrodendis, haberemus profectò quod Thomae Bilsono impingeremus, quòd de politeia ecclesiastica librum scripturus, eam in ipsius titulo nuncuparit duntaxat gubernationem. Verum absit ut in illum hoc nomine iniquiores esse velimus: cum constet politicorum plerosque, de Gubernatione sola praecepta tradere solitos esse, de parendi autem ratione plerumque parum dicere, quòd illius praecepta absque ullo majori negotio, ex correlati sui praeceptis innotescere soleant. Æquanimitate vero ista Matheus Sutclivius indigens prorsus est, qui postquam singulas nostrorum hominum definitiones, non sine atro felle conspuerat: novam tandem de suo substituit, pede isto hunc in modum, claudicantem. Dicimus disciplinam Ecclesiae, externum ordinem esse, partim in verbo Dei, partim à Christiano Magistratu, at si is à religione alienus sit, à praecipuis ecclesiae ministris, juxta verbi divini regulas praescriptum, pro gubernatione ecclesiae totius, & membri cujusq, qua ad ecclesiam pertinet. Vitia huius definitionis cætera, ut pro presenti quiescere sinam, de medii politeias Ecclesiasticae secundi (quod nunc nobis præ manibus est), obdienti scilicet, omissione, cum saltem vel Hadrianus Serabia monere poterit, ut consultum fuit [?] de politeia civili scripturo, titulum praefigere. figere, non solū de imperandi authoritate, verum etiā de obedientia Christiana. Atquè controversia de politeia ecclesiastica, quæ inter nos Anglos agitatur, hæc prima est: de illius nempè Definitione.
units.tr: Now as to the subject, there is nothing that pertains to this place to say. Someone may perhaps ask about the end, why mention of the salvation of souls, which seems to be the ultimate end of this polity, has been passed over. But there is no reason for anyone to be held up by this. Indeed that salvation is the end of this polity, and its ultimate end; yet it seemed to be left out of the definition because it is not proper to this polity but common both to Christian economy and to civil polity, since both aim at this: that each person be blessed not only in this life but chiefly in the life to come, both as a member of a household and as a citizen. But a doubt may perhaps cling to this end, which is proper to ecclesiastical polity, namely that mention is made only of public blessed action in the Church, while ethical, economic and civil action is passed over, although all of these seem to be directed, shaped, corrected and finally refined by ecclesiastical polity. This is true, but it does not seem to belong to ecclesiastical polity first and in itself; rather it accrues to it from that eminent rank by which it excels all particular practices and rules over them, as will be taught more fully in its proper place. As for the third point, since ecclesiastical polity does not have only one means, namely to rule, but rather two, to rule indeed and to obey: if we wished to be so fault-finding as Matthew Sutcliffe is, nibbling at almost every definition of our writers, we would certainly have something to fling at Thomas Bilson, because in writing a book on ecclesiastical polity he named in its very title only government. But God forbid that we should be more unfair to him on this account, since it is established that most writers on polity are accustomed to deliver precepts about government alone, and usually say little about the manner of obeying, because its precepts are commonly known, without any great difficulty, from the precepts correlative to them. Yet Matthew Sutcliffe is entirely lacking in this evenness of temper: after he had spat upon each definition of our men with no little bitterness, he at last put forward a new one of his own, and it limps in this way: We say that the discipline of the Church is an external order, partly in the Word of God, partly by the Christian magistrate; but if he is alien to religion, by the principal ministers of the Church, prescribed according to the rules of the divine Word, for the government of the whole Church and of each member who belongs to the Church. I will let the other faults of this definition rest for the present. The omission of the second means of ecclesiastical polity, which is now before us, namely obedience, is one that Hadrian Saravia at least could warn against, as it was advisable for one who was to write on civil polity to set in the title not only the authority of ruling but also Christian obedience. And so the controversy about ecclesiastical polity, which is being waged among us English, begins here: with its very definition.

units.la: Politeia Ecclesiastica est pars Regni Christi.
units.tr: The ecclesiastical polity is a part of the kingdom of Christ.

units.la: SEcunda quæstio de illius præstantia est, quæ tria capita continet, quorum primum de illius Dignitate quærit, secundum de Vtilitate pugnat, tertium & ultimum de illius Necessitate controversatur. Ad Dignitatem illa quæstio pertinet: utrum politeia Ecclesiastica, pars regni Christi censenda sit? Nunquid verò qui sint inquies, qui de hoc dubitant? Qui dubitant autem? imò verò sunt, qui hoc sannis excipiunt: sic enim Richardus Bancroftus, Archiepiscopus nuper Cantuariensis. Ausim dicere subrisuros vos si id contingeret, ut consistoriani ministri omnes substituti Christi esse velint, quæ rex ecclesiæ est. Certè dicere cogor id ipsum ab illis fieri. Risum vero vos amici quæso teneatis tantisper, dum sententiam nostram audiveritis, quam ita ponimus. Prophetia Christi, illius meditationis pars ea est, qua Ecclesiam docet: sacerdotium quâ redimit & reconciliat: regnum, pars ea, quâ prophetiæ & sacerdotij electis efficaciter applicando spiritualiter Ecclesiam suam gubernat, ad perniciem omnium inimicorum, & perfectam suorum gloriam.
units.tr: The second question concerns its excellence, and it has three parts. The first asks about its dignity, the second disputes its usefulness, and the third and last deals with its necessity. The question concerning its dignity is this: is the ecclesiastical polity to be regarded as a part of the kingdom of Christ? You may ask, who are those who doubt this? Some do indeed doubt it, and indeed some greet it with scorn. So did Richard Bancroft, the late Archbishop of Canterbury: I would venture to say that you would laugh if it happened that all the consistorian ministers wished to be substitutes of Christ, who is the king of the Church. Certainly I am forced to say that this is in fact being done by them. But I beg you, my friends, to restrain your laughter for a while, until you have heard our view, which we state as follows. The prophecy of Christ is that part of his mediatorial office by which he teaches the Church; the priesthood is that part by which he redeems and reconciles; the kingdom is that part by which he governs his Church, effectively applying prophecy and priesthood to the elect, to the destruction of all his enemies and the perfect glory of his own.

units.la: Ejus partes duę sunt: spiritualis administratio in mundo: & in mundi consummatione judicium ultimum. Spiritualis administratio ecclesiam in mundo congregat, & ad ultimum judicium conservat. Hujus partes similiter duæ: interna operatio quę est spiritus, per media externa intus agens: & ipsius externę Ecclesiasticę administratio, quâ externa media diriguntur & benedicuntur ad internam operationem efficiendam. In hâc Christus solus Dominus est, in rebus divinis administrandis Dominium absolutum exercens: administri vero superiores in Ecclesia illi, qui juxta præscriptam à Domino suo rationem, rerum divinarum oikonomoi sunt, potestate servi, non autem domini dominatu. Quid hîc chachinnis subsannandum ac non verendum lector dixeris nisi prorsus ... fueris? A Bancrofto vero ipso quærendum, sub quo officio, politeias ecclesiasticæ ministros collocabit. Num eos Christi ut prophetæ vicarios dicet? Nequaquam: ad verba enim illa, I. B. de polit. pag. 68. Ministri, Christi vicarij sunt duntaxat, ut Propheta est, respondet. Nunquid autem quis ita dixit? certe quantum memini nemo. At si neque à Christo rege pendeant, nec à Christo propheta, verendum ne à Christo ullo modo sint. Minimè vero respondet, Communis retroactti temporis & recepta sententia est, Christum Christam Apostolos & Discipulos adiunxisse sibi in sacerdotali officio suo, quo praedicabat & docebat: unde adversus Papistas disputatum semper est, ministrum quemque vicarium Christi esse, perinde ac Papa ipse est, & dum praedicat, sacramenta administrat, & pro populo orat, ita excipiendum esse velut Christi legatum, ac si ipse in terris praesens Christus haec omnia perageret. Dissimilis huic in sua quidem, quod ad ipsam summam similitudinis, Thomae Bilsoni sententia est. Christus (inquit) qui plenitudo & caput Ecclesiae est, velut Propheta, Sacerdos, & Rex, eandem regit & administrat, ad cuius imaginem, omnis publica in Ecclesia gubernatio, Prophetica, sacerdotalis, & regalis est, Doctores Propheticam, Pastores sacerdotalem, Magistratus regalem obtinent. Hanc thesin Bilsoni primo apertam contradictionem, deinde inextricabilem absurditatem continere dico. Ministros Ecclesiae, Christi Prophetae Vicarios esse, inauditum esse dicit Bancroftus, quos tamen, qua docent, Christo ut prophetae subjicit Bilsonus. Hoc dum facit, reliqua tantum a Bancrofto commemorata, nempe Sacramentorum administrationem, & publicarum precum recitationem, a Christi sacerdotio pendere putat.
units.tr: Its parts are two: the spiritual administration in the world, and the final judgment at the consummation of the world. The spiritual administration gathers the Church in the world and preserves it for the last judgment. Of this there are again two parts: the inward operation, which is of the Spirit, working inwardly through external means; and the external ecclesiastical administration, by which the external means are directed and blessed so as to bring about the inward operation. In this, Christ alone is Lord, exercising absolute dominion in the administration of divine things. The superior ministers in the Church are those who, according to the manner prescribed by their Lord, are stewards of divine things, with the power of servants and not the lordship of masters. What, reader, could you call here worthy of mockery and laughter, unless you had altogether... been? But Bancroft himself must be asked under what office he will place the ministers of the ecclesiastical polity. Will he call them vicars of Christ as prophet? By no means: for to those words, Bilson, On Polity, p. 68: Ministers are only vicars of Christ, as he is Prophet, he replies: But did anyone say this? Certainly, as far as I remember, no one did. But if they depend neither on Christ the King nor on Christ the Prophet, there is reason to fear that they are in no way subject to Christ. Yet he does not answer that it is the common and received opinion of the past age that Christ joined the apostles and disciples to himself in his priestly office, by which he preached and taught; whence it has always been argued against the Papists that each minister is a vicar of Christ, just as the Pope himself is, and while he preaches, administers the sacraments, and prays for the people, he is to be received as the legate of Christ, as if Christ himself, present on earth, were performing all these things. Bilson's view, though in its own way unlike this, is similar in its main point: Christ (he says), who is the fullness and head of the Church, rules and administers it as Prophet, Priest, and King; and after his image every public government in the Church is prophetic, priestly, and kingly: the teachers hold the prophetic office, the pastors the priestly, the magistrates the kingly. I say that this thesis of Bilson contains first an open contradiction, and then an inextricable absurdity. Bancroft says it is unheard of for the ministers of the Church to be vicars of Christ as Prophet; yet Bilson subjects them to Christ as Prophet, in so far as they teach. In doing this, he thinks that the other things mentioned by Bancroft, namely the administration of the sacraments and the recitation of public prayers, depend on the priesthood of Christ alone.

units.la: Hinc inextricabilis difficultas enascitur sub quo officio Iesu Christi, jurisdictio Ecclesiastica ponenda sit. In ordinatione ea ponitur, & in excommunicatione: in quibus cardo quaestionis illius vertitur, quae inter nos de ἀρχιερωσύνη Episcopali agitatur. Annon pulchre hos homines laborasse dixeris, si hanc de qua tantopere digladiantur jurisdictionem, exclusam penitus & obducto pessulo foribus totam expulsam videres? Certe quantum ego assequor, Thamar ista quam tantopere deperibant, ab ipsis suis amatoribus si non despecta, neglecta tamen exulat. Nam neque illam ausus est Bancroftus dicere a sacerdotio Christi pendere, certe inter ministrorum munera, a sacerdotio Christi pendentia, eam non recensuit; & non video, quo modo eam, a ministris ad magistratum Bilsonus totam ablegarit. C. Scultingius ita: Musculus in locis communibus, cap. 10. de ministrorum officiis, officium Seniorum negligit, in capite autem de magistratibus, pluribus verbis refellit: & Gualtherus Tigurinus arte in illud invehitur in comment. in 1. Cor. 5. Anglo-Calvinistae vero defendunt in locum horum Seniorum magistratum civilem successisse. Gualtheri error in aperto est; ita enim ille Seniores sustulit, ut & excommunicationem & jurisdictionem Ecclesiasticam una sustulerit: ut miraculi instar sit, adeo in Gualthero Hierarchicos gloriari, qui jurisdictionem Episcopalem, per quam a reliquis ministris differunt, & de qua tantopere gloriantur, ad magistratum ablegarit. Hoc Hadriano Serravia perspectum satis, qui ita loquitur. Sunt qui omnem disciplinam morum magistratui committendam opinantur, & soli eâq; nudâ praedicatione verbi Dei, & Sacramentorum administratione, Evangelij ministerium includunt: quod cum neq; verbo Dei, neq; ullo maiorum exemplo possit doceri, mirum Theologis talem opinionem venire in mentem potuisse. isse. Imò & Banrofto ipsi hoc ipsum displicet.Sunt(inquit)in transmarinis partibus, (ut videtur) non nulli,qui affirmant potestatem Ecclesiæ spiritualem tantùm esse, ac non externum aliquod exercitium iurisdictionis, quo Lambertus Danæus non immerito commoluetur. Sed quid si hoc in partibus cismarinis fiat? quid si ab ipsis Hierarchicis ? quinimò a Bancrofto ipso? Anglo-Calvinistæ(dicit Scultingius) in locum Seniorum successisse dicunt Magistratum : Whitgiftum intelligit: qui nomine hoc ipso jurisdictionem Ecclesiasticam,ab his Senioribus,in Ecclesiâ primâ exercitam, ad Magistratum relegavit etiam. Neque enim dici potest in locum Seniorum Magistratum successisse, nisi in Seniorum potestatem successerit etiam. Sed si Whitgiftius sub conditione hâc dixerit, si Seniores in Ecclesiâ pris-câ aliqui fuerint(licet non eo sensu Scultingius eum interpretetur uri nec interpretandus est, ut suo loco demonstrabitur) quâ autem viâ Gualtheri & Erafti scopulum declinare Bilsonus poterit, ergo sanè non video. Nullus (inquit) locus Senioribus est, quia Doctores propheticum, pastores sacerdotale, Magistratus regale Christi munus obtinent. Quid ni addatur ex Gualthero & Erafto, ergo nec jurisdictioni ecclesiasticæ Episcopali,locus ullus reliétus est?Non enim sub prophetiâ Christi est, quia non docet(ipsorum judicio) ratione eâ, quâ doctores Ecclesiæ docent: Non sub sacerdotio Christi est,illud enim nunc dierû intercedit tantùm: aut ergo sub regno Christi est, aut exterminium patitur. Eodem in luto hæret Banrofius: Non potestas Ecclesiæ spiritualis tantùm est ( inquit ) sed externum quoddam jurisdictionis exercitium, ac proinde sub regno Christi non est, quia spirituale illud est. Quasi sacerdotium Christi duntaxat spirituale non sit adæquè ac regnum? ita exercitium iurisdictionis si adeo externum sit ut spirituale non sit, nec sub sacerdotio Christi, sed plane nullum erit. Vtcunque sit, dum regalem Christi authoritatem, a qua iurisdictio Ecclesiastica tota pendet, Magistratui Hierarchici totam adjudicant, ab Episcopis ipsis , perinde ac ministris reliquis, eam abjudicant. Sequitur Lours, qui ita suam sententiam explicat. Christus spiritus sui afflatu,ita errantes instruit, ut externum docendi munus aliis comittat,ita pascit ut alios in pascendo versari velit:ita deniq; gubernat ut alios veru ecclesiasticarû gubernatores constitui, præcipiat.Hoc cum ab illo adferatur ut Archiepiscopalé in Ministros authoritatem suffulcire:ita distinguere doctorum,& pastorum munus a regimine Episcopali videtur,ut ministri in docendo & pascendo, Christo subsint velut Prophetæ,&sacerdoti,Episcopi verò in ecclesiæ gubernatione, ab eo quasi rege & gubernatore pendeant. Hoc si ita fit, & Bancrofto & Bilsono contradicit : qui dum Christum Regere contendunt quia ut Propheta docet,& ut sacerdos pascit, rem nunquam ante anditam promunt. A quo etenim regimen nisi a rege? At Regere inquit Ecclesiasticum non nisi docere & pascere est. Respondeo primò ➤ in docenda & pascenda Ecclesia
units.tr: Hence arises an inextricable difficulty as to under which office of Jesus Christ ecclesiastical jurisdiction is to be placed. It is placed under his office in ordination and in excommunication, and in these the crux of that question turns, which among us is debated concerning the episcopal high-priesthood [ἀρχιερωσύνη]. Would you not say these men have laboured well, if you saw this jurisdiction, for which they struggle so eagerly, shut out entirely, the bolt drawn across the doors and the whole of it thrust out? Certainly, so far as I can make out, this Tamar, for whom they so eagerly pined, is exiled, if not despised, at least neglected, even by her own lovers. For Bancroft did not dare to say that it depends on the priesthood of Christ; certainly he does not list it among the ministers' functions, which depend on the priesthood of Christ; and I do not see how Bilson has banished it entirely from the ministers to the magistrate. Scultingius says this: Musculus in his Common Places, chapter 10, on the duties of ministers, passes over the office of the elders, but in the chapter on magistrates he refutes it at greater length. And Gualther of Zurich attacks it cleverly in his commentary on 1 Corinthians 5. The Anglo-Calvinists, however, defend that the civil magistrate has succeeded in the place of these elders. Gualther's error is plain; for he removed the elders in such a way that he removed excommunication and ecclesiastical jurisdiction together with them. It is a kind of miracle that the hierarchists boast of Gualther, when he has transferred to the magistrate the episcopal jurisdiction by which bishops differ from the other ministers, and of which they boast so greatly. Hadrianus Saravia saw this clearly enough, who speaks thus: There are some who think that all discipline of morals is to be committed to the magistrate, and who include in the ministry of the Gospel only bare preaching of the Word of God and administration of the sacraments; since this cannot be taught either by the Word of God or by any example of our forebears, it is strange that such an opinion could ever have entered the minds of theologians. Indeed, Bancroft himself dislikes this same view: There are (he says) in the lands beyond the sea (as it seems) some who affirm that the power of the Church is only spiritual, and not some external exercise of jurisdiction, with which Lambert Danaeus is not unjustly angry. But what if this happens on this side of the sea? What if it is done by the hierarchists themselves? Nay, by Bancroft himself? Scultingius says that the Anglo-Calvinists say the magistrate has succeeded in place of the elders: he means Whitgift, who by this very word also relegated to the magistrate the ecclesiastical jurisdiction exercised by those elders in the primitive Church. For it cannot be said that the magistrate succeeded in the place of the elders unless he also succeeded to the elders' power. But if Whitgift said this under this condition, that there were some elders in the primitive Church (although Scultingius does not interpret him in that sense, nor is he to be so interpreted, as will be shown in its place), then by what way Bilson will be able to avoid the rock of Gualther and Erastus, I certainly do not see. He says: There is no place for elders, because the teachers hold the prophetic, the pastors the priestly, and the magistrates the kingly office of Christ. Why should it not be added, from Gualther and Erastus, that therefore no place is left even for episcopal ecclesiastical jurisdiction? For it is not under the prophecy of Christ, because (in their judgment) it does not teach in the way in which the teachers of the Church teach; it is not under the priesthood of Christ, for that now intervenes only in name; so either it is under the kingdom of Christ, or it suffers extinction. Bancroft sticks in the same mire: The power of the Church (he says) is not only spiritual, but is an external exercise of jurisdiction, and therefore is not under the kingdom of Christ, because that is spiritual. As if the priesthood of Christ were not spiritual only, just as much as his kingdom is! So if the exercise of jurisdiction is so external that it is not spiritual, it will be neither under the priesthood of Christ, but will plainly be nothing at all. However that may be, while they assign the whole royal authority of Christ, on which all ecclesiastical jurisdiction depends, to the magistrate of the hierarchists, they deny it to the bishops themselves, just as to the other ministers. Lours follows, who explains his opinion thus: Christ by the breath of his Spirit instructs the erring, so that he commits the external office of teaching to others; he feeds them so that he wishes others to be occupied in feeding; and finally he governs them so that he commands others to be appointed as true governors of the Church. Since this is brought forward by him to support the archiepiscopal authority over the ministers, he seems to distinguish the office of teachers and pastors from episcopal government in such a way that the ministers, in teaching and feeding, are subject to Christ as Prophet and Priest, but the bishops, in governing the Church, depend on him as on a king and governor. If this is so, it contradicts Bancroft and Bilson, who, while they maintain that Christ rules because as Prophet he teaches and as Priest he feeds, put forward something never heard before. For from whom does government come, if not from the king? But, he says, ecclesiastical ruling is nothing but teaching and feeding. I answer first: in teaching and feeding the Church, two things are to be considered: the word itself of teaching and feeding, and the administration of the word, which implies the reason not only of teaching but also of ruling. From the word itself, simply considered, there flows only the act of teaching, which proceeds from Christ as Prophet; from the word...

units.la: Qurimen. Eccles.1. 148. duo consideranda esse, verbum ipsum docens & pascens, & administrationem verbi, quae rationem non docendi solum, sed & regendi infert: ex verbo ipso simpliciter considerato actus tantum docendi profluit, qui a Christo tanquam Propheta dimanat: ex verbi vero administratione actus regendi etiam emergit, & hic a Christo Rege est.
units.tr: Quaeritur (Eccles. 1. 148): two things are to be considered, the word itself, teaching and feeding, and the administration of the word, which implies a rationale not only of teaching but also of ruling. From the word considered simply, there flows only the act of teaching, which comes from Christ as Prophet. From the administration of the word, however, the act of ruling also arises, and this comes from Christ as King.

units.la: Secundò, dico Ecclesiasticam jurisdictionem quae in morum censura versatur, diversum quid esse, ab illa docendi & pascendi ratione, quae Doctori & Pastori propria est. Annon idem & adversarij docent? ex eo enim probant presbyteros duntaxat gubernantes, Act. 20. 28. non intelligi: quia gubernatio presbyterialis non pascit Ecclesiam ea ratione, qua presbyteri praedicantes eandem pascunt. Atque sane hoc ipsum, dicere eos, necesse est: si modo salvum suum regimen Episcopale velint, quum vel ipsis concedentibus in ipso docendi & pascendi munere, minister nihil a ministro differat. Imò & amplius addam: non solùm a Christo Rege regimen illorum in reliquos ministros authoritas mutuari opus habet, sed & regni etiá regimen: quum illud œconomi & servi quod est, tam late fimbrias non extendat. Par etenim ratio quae inter ministros licita est, & ejus qui Petri esse dicitur inter reliquos Apostolos: quam ut transformaret Sixtus Senensis ad primatum illicitum probandum, rejecta superioritate Apostolatus & Episcopat°, in quibus Apostolos pares fuisse Hieronymus docet, tertiam quandam confingit, quam appellat Regni, qua Petrum electum prae caeteris Apostolis eorumq; caput factum fuisse, Hieronymum affirmare, dicit. Sic aut regimen etiam regni a Christo Rege a Senensi fingendum est, aut corruit Episcopale regimé in pares ministros, aut Archiepiscopale saltem in Episcopos quos vel ipsi pares esse confitentur.
units.tr: Secondly, I say that ecclesiastical jurisdiction, which is concerned with the censure of morals, is something different from that method of teaching and feeding which belongs to the teacher and the pastor. Do not our opponents also teach this? For from it they prove that the elders who only govern are not meant in Act. 20. 28, because presbyterial government does not feed the Church in the same way that the elders who preach feed it. And indeed they must say exactly this, if they wish to keep their episcopal rule intact, since, even by their own concession, in the very office of teaching and feeding a minister differs in nothing from a minister. I will add more: their authority over the other ministers needs to borrow its rule not only from Christ the King, but also the government of the kingdom, since that which belongs to the steward and servant does not stretch its fringes so widely. For the reasoning that is lawful among ministers is the same as that of the one who is said to be Peter's among the other apostles. Sixtus of Siena, in order to turn this into a case for an unlawful primacy, rejected the superiority of the apostolate and episcopate, in which Jerome teaches that the apostles were equals, and invented a third kind, which he calls royal, by which he claims that Peter was chosen above the other apostles and made their head, and says that Jerome affirms this. Thus either the royal government must also be feigned by Sixtus as coming from Christ the King, or the episcopal rule over equal ministers collapses, or at least the archiepiscopal rule over bishops, whom they themselves confess to be equals.

units.la: CAP. 3. In quo sententia adversariorum ventilatur. Et primo eorum fucus detergitur.
units.tr: CAP. 3. In which the opponents' view is examined, and first their pretence is stripped away.

units.la: HVC usque de Hierarchicorum nostrorum cum contradictione, tum absurditate diximus, in sua ipsorum sententia explicanda: jam verò haec ipsa eorum sententia ventilanda nobis est. Hîc primo eorum fucus & detegendus & detergendus, quo causam suam larvare, nostram autem gravare solent. Secundò, arcana eorum denudanda, quibus ad eam suscipiendam adducti sunt. Tertiò, eorum sophistice refellenda, qua eandem tuentur. Quod ad primum: dependentiam Politeiae Ecclesiasticae suam a Christo tanquam sacerdote, Bancroftus hoc nomine ornat, quòd papistis maximè infesta sit, utpote ex qua doceatur, ministros omnes adæque Vicarios Christi esse, ac Papa ipse est.
units.tr: Hitherto we have shown the contradiction and absurdity of our Hierarchists in setting out their own view. Now this view itself must be examined. Here, first, their pretence must be uncovered and stripped away, the pretence they habitually use to disguise their own cause and burden ours. Second, their hidden motives, which led them to adopt the view, must be laid bare. Third, the sophistries by which they defend it must be refuted. As to the first point: Bancroft decorates the dependence of the Ecclesiastical Polity on Christ as priest with this label, because it is especially hostile to the Papists, since from it is taught that all ministers are equally Vicars of Christ, just as the Pope himself is.

units.la: Primo
units.tr: First.

units.la: Primò, si hoc sequatur, cur non & illud nostrũ sequetur itidé: omnes ministros adæq; Christi Vicarios esse, ac ipse Domin9 Archiepiscopus Episcopusve? Secundo, non in hac dependentia a Pontificijs Hierarchici ita dissentiunt, vt non eis maximè gratificentur.
units.tr: First, if this follows, why should not the following also follow from our view in the same way: that all ministers are equally Vicars of Christ, and the Lord Archbishop or Bishop himself is one? Second, the Hierarchists do not differ from the Papists on this dependence so far that they would not especially please them.

units.la: Tuentur illi, dices, Papæ primatum a Christo rege: sed non a Christo sacerdote etiam, idque præcipuè? Legatur Hardingus, Quod ad Christi regnum, id in illius sacerdotio inclusum erat (inquit) ac proinde cum de regno Christi loquimur, illud etiam in cruce fuisse diximus, vbi regnavit a ligno Deus. Eundem in sensum quod Moses regnum sacerdotale, id verbis inflexis Petrus sacerdotium regale appellat. Tantum igitur abest, vt a Pontificijs Bancroftus dissentiat, vt eundem planè lapidem cum eis voluat: nimirum contendunt vtrique, a Christo sacerdote regimen Ecclesiæ ascitum esse, vt omne duntaxat ad sacerdotes exclusis senioribus derivetur: Detrahunt etiam de regno Christi vtrique, sed dispari ratione: pontificij illud sacerdotio subordinant, Hierachici vero ab Ecclesiæ externo regimine penitus exterminant. Atque hic eorum fucus est, quo suam causam ornant: sequitur jam ille, quo nostram infamant? vbi primò statum quæstionis invertunt, larvasque fingunt, quibus cum tutò luctari queant.
units.tr: Those men, you will say, defend the Pope's primacy from Christ as king, but not from Christ as priest as well, and that especially? Let Harding be read: As for the kingdom of Christ, that was included in his priesthood, he says, and therefore when we speak of the kingdom of Christ, we say that it was also on the cross, where God reigned from the tree. To the same effect, what Moses called a kingdom of priests, Peter, with the words reversed, calls a royal priesthood. So far is Bancroft from disagreeing with the Papists that he turns over exactly the same stone with them. Both contend that the government of the Church was assumed from Christ as priest, so that all of it passes solely to priests, the elders being excluded. Both also detract from the kingdom of Christ, but for different reasons: the Papists subordinate it to the priesthood, while the Hierarchists utterly banish the external government from the Church. This is the pretence by which they adorn their cause. Now follows the device by which they defame ours. Here they first invert the state of the question and feign masks behind which they can safely wrestle.

units.la: Hoc a Bilsono imprimis factum, qui ita loquitur, Minimè omnium debemus ista nescio quæ consistoria tanti æstimare, vt pro dimidiata parte iustissimi & gloriosissimi regni Christi censeantur. Et quinam quæso ista faciunt? Ego sanè qui dimidiatam Christi regni partem, disciplinam presbyterialem dixerit, novi neminem; nobis quidem certè, eam regni Christi partem aliquam esse affirmare satis est: vt qui probè intelligamus, partem Christi regni in terra maius quiddam & augustius esse, quàm vt hanc externam parte dimidiatam appellari sinat, Age verò inquis at magnam tamen esse vociferamini, quod sine præcipiti & inconsulto fervore quodã dici non potest. Sed tu vide sis Bilsone, ne fervore nostrũ in furorẽ proprium converteris: si adeo tenuiter, vel de infima regni parte sentias, vt eam non magnã putes. Apud Isaiam certè, regnum Christi velut magnum, vel ex eo amplificatur, quòd universa domus supellex illi sit concredita, etiam ad vasa minima, cap. 22. verf. 24.
units.tr: This was done above all by Bilson, who speaks thus: We ought least of all to hold those I know not what consistories in such high esteem as to count them a half part of the most just and glorious kingdom of Christ. And who, I ask, does these things? I indeed know no one who called presbyterial discipline a half part of Christ's kingdom. It is enough for us to affirm that it is some part of Christ's kingdom, since we rightly understand that the part of Christ's kingdom on earth is something greater and more august than to be called an external half part. Come now, you say, but you shout that it is great, which cannot be said without some hasty and ill-considered heat. But see to it, Bilson, that you are not turned from our zeal into your own madness, if you think so meanly of the lowest part of the kingdom that you do not consider it great. Certainly in Isaiah the kingdom of Christ is magnified as great, partly from the fact that the whole household's furniture, even the smallest vessels, is committed to him: ch. 22, verse 24.

units.la: Secundo, causam nostram ex eo odiosam, si non & ridiculam facere nituntur, Bancroftus , Bilsonus , Downamus, quòd presbyteria nostra, Tribunalis, solij, sceptrique cælestis insignibus ornemus: quod politeiam Ecclesiasticam, regnum Dei, sceptrum Christi, eiusq; tribunal nuncupemus: quod denique presbiterij executionem, restaurationem regni Christi appellemus. Verum non est, quod nos horum pudeat: non ita raro in sacris paginis hæc occurrunt, vt oculato Theologo tam monstri loco habeantur, Vt thronus gloriosus exaltatus, is est domus sanctuarij nostri, Ierem. 17. 12. In diebus illis vocabitur Ierusalem solium domini. Ierem. 3. 17. Agnus qui in medio throni est, pascit eos, Apocalyp. 7. 17. Sceptrum regni tui sceptrum iustitiae est, & thronus tuus in seculum durat, Psal. 45. 6. Emittet sceptrum potestatis suae ex Zione, Psal. 110. 2. Sceptro oris sui terram percutiet, Isa. 11. 4.
units.tr: Second, they try to make our cause odious, if not also ridiculous. Bancroft, Bilson and Downame object that we adorn our presbyteries with the insignia of tribunal, throne and heavenly sceptre; that we call the Ecclesiastical Polity the kingdom of God, the sceptre of Christ and his tribunal; and finally that we call the execution of the presbytery the restoration of the kingdom of Christ. But we are not ashamed of this. These expressions occur so often in the sacred pages that a sharp-eyed theologian would not regard them as monstrous: As a glorious throne exalted from the beginning, it is the place of our sanctuary, Jer. 17:12. In those days Jerusalem shall be called the throne of the Lord, Jer. 3:17. The Lamb which is in the midst of the throne shall feed them, Rev. 7:17. The sceptre of your kingdom is a sceptre of righteousness, and your throne endures for ever, Ps. 45:6. He shall send forth the sceptre of your power out of Zion, Ps. 110:2. He shall smite the earth with the sceptre of his mouth, Isa. 11:4.

units.la: At quid haec pro presbyteriis inquient? Vel maximè. Nam cum in Ecclesia visibili tanquam in throno regnet Christus, ut per verbi administrationem suum sceptrum quatiat: cur disciplina presbyterialis parte huius honoris omni abjudicaretur, nulla ratio subest: cum & verbi sanctio sit, & regni Christi externi pars, & per Ecclesiae administros, in ipso nomine Christi Regis exerceatur. Quinimo clavis tantidem solium & sceptrum est, quum per clavem ipsius Iesu Christi regnum adumbretur, Isa. 22. 23. 24. disciplina autem presbyterialis, distinctis verbis ab ipso Christo, clavis nomine condecoratur, Math. 16. 19. Haec ita cum sint, quàm illa Richardi Bancrofti iniqua? Memini (inquit) effati illius Bezaei: presbyterium quodcunque ipsius Christi tribunal esse. De presbyter. pag. 124. quod fere idem est cum illa Parasitastrorum Papalium quorundam adulatione, quòd Papa & Christus unum & idem consistorium habeant.
units.tr: But what will they say these passages prove for presbyteries? Very much. For since Christ reigns in the visible Church as on a throne, shaking his sceptre through the administration of the Word, there is no reason why presbyterial discipline should be stripped of a share of this honour. It has the sanction of the Word, it is a part of the external kingdom of Christ, and it is exercised through the ministers of the Church in the very name of Christ the King. Indeed the key is just as much a throne and sceptre, since the kingdom is foreshadowed through the key of Jesus Christ himself, Isa. 22:22-24. Yet presbyterial discipline, in words distinct from Christ himself, is adorned with the name of key, Matt. 16:19. Since these things are so, how unfair is that of Richard Bancroft? I remember, he says, that saying of Beza: that the presbytery is whatever tribunal of Christ himself. On the Presbytery, p. 124. This is nearly the same as that flattery of certain Papal parasites, that the Pope and Christ have one and the same consistory.

units.la: Primò quorsum haec spectant ego non video, nisi ut evacuetur bilis: quum neminem lateat, quantum inter Bezae mentem, & Canonistarum sensum intersit. Secundò, non tribunal nominat tamen, quod quasi odiosum hoc in loco exagitare Bancroftus voluit: sed consistorium: sic ut Episcopale proprium consistorium quam reformati presbyterij tribunal, haec verba attingant. Tertiò, consistorium Papae Thronus Sathanae est. Apoc. 2. 13. Presbyterium reformatum Thronus Christi, Apocal. 4. 6. Haec commiscuisse minimè Bancroftum puduit. Neque tribunalis thronique nomen hoc in Apocalypseos loco defugere, quoquo pacto poterit: quum Ecclesia visibilis hoc in capite describatur, & visibilis ipsius administratio per Christum regem delineatur: a qua quo longius Bancroftus refugit, eo propinquius ad thronum ipsum sathanae accedit: id est ad Papale consistorium quoddam, cujus imago, utinam in Anglia nulla jam hodie superesset. Atque haec de Hierarchicorum fuco, quo suum ornare, causam verò nostram dehonestare satagunt.
units.tr: First, I do not see to what these things pertain, except to vent bile, since it is known to everyone how much difference there is between Beza's mind and the sense of the Canonists. Second, he does not name a tribunal, which Bancroft wanted to attack here as odious, but a consistory; so these words touch the proper Episcopal consistory rather than the tribunal of the reformed presbytery. Third, the consistory of the Pope is the throne of Satan, Rev. 2:13. The reformed presbytery is the throne of Christ, Rev. 4:6. Bancroft was not ashamed to confuse these. Nor will he be able in any way to escape the name of tribunal and throne in this passage of the Apocalypse, since the visible Church is described in this chapter and its visible administration through Christ the King is outlined. The further Bancroft flees from this, the nearer he draws to the very throne of Satan, that is, to a certain Papal consistory, whose image would that none now survived in England. And so much for the pretence of the Hierarchists, by which they strive to adorn their own cause and dishonour ours.

units.la: CAP. 4. Adversariorum arcana denudantur.
units.tr: CHAPTER 4. The secrets of our opponents are laid bare.

units.la: ACCEDO jam ad Arcana illa quibus permoti, hanc Politeias a Christo velut sacerdote dependentiam, potissimùm sibi amplexandam existimarunt. Mirabitur forte lector, cur tam solicitè Hierarchici hanc Politeias Ecclesiasticae a regno Christi dependentiam, tanquam scopulum fugiant, praesertim cum
units.tr: I now come to those secrets which led them to think that this dependence of the polity on Christ, as on a priest, was the one they should above all embrace. The reader may well wonder why the Hierarchicals so anxiously shun this dependence of ecclesiastical polity on the kingdom of Christ, as if it were a rock, especially since ACCEDO ...

units.la: Cap. 24. p. 280. cum Richardus Bancroftus confiteatur, amplissimam hinc praerogatiuam, ad omnes Ecclesiae Christi ministros derivari. Atque quidem huius praerogatiuae se satis cupidum pro se fert: sic ut eam repudiando, nihil aliud quàm amore veritatis, secutus videatur.Sed (quod aiunt) sublatet anguis, aliaque res agitur: vulnera quaedam hic praevidit suae causae secutura: quae medicina σπουδαῖα opus habebant.
units.tr: Chap. 24, p. 280, where Richard Bancroft admits that a very great prerogative is derived from this to all the ministers of Christ's Church. Indeed he professes himself very eager for this prerogative on his own behalf, so that in rejecting it he seems to have acted from nothing but love of the truth. But, as they say, the snake is not dead yet and another matter is at hand: he foresaw certain wounds that would follow for his cause, and these called for a serious [σπουδαῖα] remedy.

units.la: Primò cum praevidisse puto, quod si Politeiaa Christo pendeat tanquam a Rege, exactam quandam illius formam in Euangelio ab ipso Christo mandatâ fuisse: quum verisimile nullo modo sit, aut authoritate suam Christum in legibus condendis Ecclesiae arbitrio remisisse, aut eum in hoc regio munere fuisse negligentem. Hoc ut praecidatur, perdere Christum necesse est ius suum externum regium in Ecclesia gubernanda, & Thomas Cartwrightus reus sit oportet, quòd Christum ut regem formam disciplinae in verbo suo, eamque exactam praescripsisse asseveret. Quaero vero numnam concessurus sit aliquas saltem externas leges pro Politeia sanxisse Christum, & si aliquas (quod multi fatentur, alioqui enim authoritas illa episcopalis in suos Symmistas & collegas, quae eorum Helena est, divino iure non niteretur) num sit dicturus id a Christo non Rege factum, sed sacerdote? videtur enimvero a Christo Propheta aut sa, cerdote, eas leges sancitas esse quae sanciuntur; non autem rege. At repugnat Hadrianus Saravia, qui Philonem citat, vt probet, Legesferre principis esse. Repugnat Matheus Sutclivius. Et regis (inquit) & summi est principis & moderatoris leges ferre——longe aliter ergo Ecclesia regitur, aliter regnum & respublica. Repugnat tota natio Politicorum, quibus legu condendarum potestas adeo Monarchę propria est, ut inter regalia ipsius jura recenseatur. Quid multis? Richardus Bancroftus ipse fatetur, necnon Downamus, Genevensem rempublicam idcirco Democraticam esse, quòd legum condendarum potestas inter regalia jura sit, quae ibi penes populum est. Ex ore tuo te judicabo: hoc enim cum Bancroftus dicit, reum se peragit, quòd regali jure quodam Christi regnum spoliarit: quum legum condendarum potestatem illi surripuerit. Homerus antiquos principes legum-latores appellare solet. Legum-latio (inquit Aristoteles) ad dignitatem regiam pertinet. Hinc principes populi Dei in sacris ipsis Legum-Latores nuncupantur, Genes. 49.10. quod nomen sacerdotibus in tota lege non tribuitur. Postremò si leges a Christo prodeant tanquam sacerdote, cur non Aaron illius typus quâ erat sacerdos legumlator Israelitarū fuit, sed Moses, qui non sacerdos, sed princeps tantū politicus erat. Probat hoc fuse contra Bozium, Georgius Carleton, qui cum contrā attulisset Bozius Psal. 99.6 Moses & Aaron inter illius sacerdotes, respondet, verbum Cohanim tam civilibus magistratibus, quam sacerdotibus commune esse: unde Dauidis filij Cohanim dicuntur, 1. Sam. 8.18. qui tamen non sacerdotes, sed tantum
units.tr: First, I think he foresaw that if the polity depends on Christ as on a King, then some precise form of it must have been laid down in the Gospel by Christ himself. It is in no way likely that Christ, with his authority, left the making of laws for the Church to the judgement of men, or that he was negligent in this royal office. To avoid this, one must strip Christ of his external royal right in governing the Church, and Thomas Cartwright must be guilty for asserting that Christ, as King, prescribed in his word a form of discipline, and a precise one. But I ask whether he will concede that Christ at least laid down some external laws for the polity. If he does (as many admit; otherwise that episcopal authority over their fellow ministers and colleagues, which is their Helen, would have no basis in divine right), will he say that this was done by Christ not as King but as priest? It seems that the laws which are enacted are enacted by Christ as Prophet or Priest, not as King. But Hadrian Saravia objects, who cites Philo to prove that it is the prince's business to make laws. Matthew Sutcliffe objects: "It belongs to the king and the supreme prince and ruler to make laws." So the Church is governed quite differently from the kingdom and the commonwealth. The whole nation of politicians objects too, for whom the power of making laws is so much the proper right of a monarch that it is counted among his royal rights. What more? Richard Bancroft himself admits it, and Downame too, that the Genevan commonwealth is for this reason democratic, because the power of making laws is among the royal rights, and there it rests with the people. I will judge you out of your own mouth: for when Bancroft says this, he convicts himself of having robbed Christ's kingdom of a certain royal right, since he has taken from him the power of making laws. Homer is accustomed to call the ancient princes law-givers. Law-giving (says Aristotle) belongs to royal dignity. Hence the princes of God's people are called law-givers even in the sacred writings, Gen. 49.10, a title which is not given to priests anywhere in the law. Finally, if laws proceed from Christ as priest, why was it not Aaron, the type of Christ, who was priest, but Moses, who was not a priest but only a political prince, who gave laws to the Israelites? George Carleton proves this at length against Bozius, who had objected, citing Ps. 99.6, that Moses and Aaron were among his priests. Carleton replies that the word Cohanim is common to civil magistrates as well as to priests; hence the sons of David are called Cohanim, 1 Sam. 8.18, who were nonetheless not priests but only ...

units.la: C diebus illis vocabitur Ierusalem solium domini. Ierem. 3. 17. Agnus qui in medio throni est, pascit eos, Apocalyp. 7. 17. Sceptrum regni tui sceptrum iustitiae est, & thronus tuus in seculum durat, Psal. 45. 6. Emittet sceptrum potestatis suae ex Zione, Psal. 110. 2. Sceptro oris sui terram percutiet, Isa. 11. 4.
units.tr: In those days Jerusalem shall be called the throne of the Lord, Jer. 3.17. The Lamb which is in the midst of the throne shall feed them, Rev. 7.17. Your sceptre, O King, is a sceptre of righteousness, and your throne endures for ever, Ps. 45.6. He shall send forth the sceptre of his power out of Zion, Ps. 110.2. With the rod of his mouth he shall strike the earth, Isa. 11.4.

units.la: At quid haec pro presbyteriis inquient? Vel maximè. Nam cum in Ecclesia visibili tanquam in throno regnet Christus, ut per verbi administrationem suum sceptrum quatiat: cur disciplina presbyterialis parte huius honoris omni abiudicaretur, nulla ratio subest: cum & verbi sanctio sit, & regni Christi externi pars, & per Ecclesiae administros, in ipso nomine Christi Regis exerceatur. Quinimo clavis tantidem solium & sceptrum est, quum per clavem ipsius Iesu Christi regnum adumbratur, Isa. 22. 23. 24. disciplina autem presbyterialis, disertis verbis ab ipso Christo, clavis nomine condecoratur, Math. 16. 19. Haec ita cum sint, quàm illa Richardi Bancrofti iniqua? Memini inquit effati illius Bezani: presbyterium quodcunque ipsius Christi tribunal esse. De presbyter. pag. 124. quod fere idem est cum illa Parasitorum Papalium quorundam adulatione, quòd Papa & Christus unum & idem consistorium habeant.
units.tr: But what will they say that these passages have to do with the presbyteries? Very much indeed. For since Christ reigns in the visible Church as on a throne, so that by the administration of the Word he may wield his sceptre, there is no reason why presbyterial discipline should be deprived of its share of this honour, since it is both a sanction of the Word and a part of the external kingdom of Christ, and is exercised in the name of Christ the King through the ministers of the Church. Indeed the key is just as much a throne and a sceptre, since through the key of Jesus Christ himself the kingdom is foreshadowed, Isa. 22.22–24; and presbyterial discipline is expressly honoured by Christ himself with the name of key, Matt. 16.19. Since this is so, how unjust is that saying of Richard Bancroft's? "I remember," he says, quoting Beza, "that a presbytery is whatever tribunal of Christ himself." On the Presbytery, p. 124. This is nearly the same as the flattery of certain Papal parasites, that the Pope and Christ have one and the same consistory.

units.la: Primò quorsum haec spectant ego non video, nisi ut evacuetur bilis: quum neminem lateat, quantum inter Bezae mentem, & Canonistarum sensum intersit. Secundò, non tribunal nominat tamen, quod quasi odiosum hoc in loco exagitare Bancroftus voluit: sed consistorium: sic ut Episcopale proprium consistorium quam reformati presbyterij tribunal, haec verba attingant. Tertiò, consistorium Papae Thronus Sathanae est. Apoc. 2. 13. Presbyterium reformatum Thronus Christi, Apocal. 4. 6. Haec commiscuisse minimè Bancroftum puduit. Neque tribunalis thronique nomen hoc in Apocalypseos loco defugere, quoquo pacto poterit: quum Ecclesia visibilis hoc in capite describatur, & visibilis ipsius administratio per Christum regem delineatur: a qua quo longius Bancroftus refugit, eo propinquius ad thronum ipsum sathanae accedit: id est ad Papale consistorium quoddam, cuius imago, utinam in Anglia nulla jam hodie superesset. Atque haec de Hierarchicorum fuco, quo suum ornare, causam verò nostram dehonestare satagunt.
units.tr: First, I do not see to what these remarks tend, except to vent bile, since it is well known how far Beza's mind differs from the meaning of the canonists. Second, he does not name a tribunal, which Bancroft wished to attack in this place as if it were hateful, but a consistory, so that these words touch on the episcopal consistory as its own, rather than the tribunal of the reformed presbytery. Third, the consistory of the Pope is the throne of Satan, Rev. 2.13. The reformed presbytery is the throne of Christ, Rev. 4.6. Bancroft was not ashamed to mix these together. Nor will he be able, by any means, to escape the word tribunal or throne in this passage of the Apocalypse, since the visible Church is described in this chapter and its visible administration is portrayed as ruled by Christ the King. The further Bancroft flees from this, the nearer he draws to the very throne of Satan, that is, to a certain Papal consistory, whose image, would that no trace of it survived in England today. And this is enough of the Hierarchicals' smoke-screen, by which they labour to adorn their own cause and disgrace ours.

units.la: CAP. 4. Adversariorum arcana denudantur.
units.tr: Chapter 4. The secrets of the opponents are laid bare.

units.la: ACCEDO jam ad Arcana illa quibus permoti, hanc Politeias a Christo velut sacerdote dependentiam, potissimùm sibi amplexandam existimarunt. Mirabitur forte lector, cur tam solicitè Hierarchici hanc Politeias Ecclesiasticae a regno Christi dependentiam, tanquam scopulum fugiant, praesertim cum Richardus Bancroftus confiteatur, amplissimam hinc prærogatiuam, ad omnes Ecclesiæ Christi ministros derivari. Atque quidem huius prærogatiuæ se satis cupidum præ se fert: sic ut eam repudiando, nihil aliud quàm amore veritatis, secutus videatur. Sed (quod aiunt) sublatet anguis, aliaque res agitur: vulnera quædam hic prævidit suæ causæ secutura: quæ medicinâ ἀπομαλακτικὴ opus habebant.
units.tr: I now come to those secrets which led them to think that this dependence of polity on Christ as priest was above all to be embraced by them. The reader may well wonder why the Hierarchists so anxiously shun the dependence of ecclesiastical polity on the kingdom of Christ, as though it were a rock, especially since Richard Bancroft admits that a very great prerogative is derived from it to all the ministers of Christ's Church. Indeed he shows himself so eager for this prerogative that, in rejecting it, he seems to have done nothing but follow his love of truth. But (as they say) the snake is hidden under the grass, and another matter is at stake: he foresaw certain wounds that would follow for his cause, and these needed a softening remedy [ἀπομαλακτικὴ].

units.la: Primò cum prævidisse puto, quod si Politeia a Christo pendeat tanquam a Rege, exactam quandam illius formam in Euangelio ab ipso Christo mandatâ fuisse: quum verisimile nullo modo sit, aut authoritate suam Christum in legibus condendis Ecclesiæ arbitrio remisisse, aut eum in hoc regio munere fuisse negligentem. Hoc ut præcidatur, perdere Christum necessum est ius suum externum regium in Ecclesia gubernanda, & Thomas Cartwrightus reus sit oportet, quòd Christum ut regem formam disciplinæ in verbo suo, eamque exactam prescripsisse asseveret. Quæro verò numnam concessurus sit aliquas saltem externas leges pro Politeia sanxisse Christum, & si aliquas (quod multi fatentur, alioqui enim authoritas illa episcopalis in suos Symmistas & collegas, quæ eorum Helena est, divino jure non niteretur) num sit dicturus id a Christo non Rege factum, sed sacerdote? videtur enim vero a Christo Propheta aut sacerdote, eas leges sancitas esse quæ sanciuntur; non autem rege.
units.tr: First, I think he foresaw that if polity depended on Christ as King, a precise form of it would have been laid down in the Gospel by Christ himself. It is in no way likely that Christ, by his authority, left the enacting of laws for the Church to human judgment, or that he was negligent in this royal office. To cut off this objection, Christ must be stripped of his external royal right in governing the Church, and Thomas Cartwright must be found guilty, since he asserts that Christ as King prescribed the form of discipline in his word, and an exact form at that. But I ask whether he will concede that Christ laid down at least some external laws for the polity (as many admit; otherwise that episcopal authority over their fellow ministers and colleagues, which is their Helen, would have no basis in divine right). And if he concedes some, will he say that this was done by Christ not as King but as priest? For it seems rather that those laws which are enacted were enacted by Christ as Prophet or priest, and not as king.

units.la: At repugnat Hadrianus Saravia, qui Philonem citat, ut probet, Leges ferre principis esse. Repugnat Matheus Sutclivius. Et regis (inquit) & summi est principis & moderatoris leges ferre——longe aliter ergo Ecclesia regitur, aliter regnum & respublica. Repugnat tota natio Politicorum, quibus legum condendarum potestas adeo Monarchę propria est, ut inter regalia ipsius jura recenseatur. Quid multis? Richardus Bancroftus ipse fatetur, necnon Donnamus, Genevensem rempublicam idcirco Democraticam esse, quòd legum condendarum potestas inter regalia jura sit, quæ ibi penes populum est. Ex ore tuo te judicabo: hoc enim cum Bancroftus dicit, reum se peragit, quòd regali jure quodam Christi regnum spoliarit: quum legum condendarum potestatem illi surripuerit. Homerus antiquos principes legum-latores appellare solet. Legum-latio (inquit Aristoteles) ad dignitatem regiam pertinet. Hinc principes populi Dei in sacris ipsis legum-latores nuncupantur, Genes. 49. 10. quod nomen sacerdotibus in tota lege non tribuitur. Postremò si leges a Christo prodeant tanquam sacerdote, cur non Aaron illius typus quâ erat sacerdos legumlator Israelitarum fuit, sed Moses, qui non sacerdos, sed princeps tantùm politicus erat. Probat hoc fuisse contra Bozium, Georgius Carletonus, qui cum contrà attulisset Bozius Psal. 99. 6 Moses & Aaron inter illius sacerdotes, respondet, verbum Cohanim tam civilibus magistratibus, quam sacerdotibus commune esse: unde Dauidis filij Cohanim dicuntur, 1. Sam. 8. 18. qui tamen non sacerdotes, sed tantùm civiles magistratus erant, 1. Chron. 18. 17. Quod si verò Moses hic sacerdos vocetur, id tamen eo respectu tantummodo dicitur, quod sacerdotis more pro populo oraret, ut Iohannes Piscator in suis scholijs adnotavit.
units.tr: But Hadrian Saravia objects, who cites Philo to prove that to bring in laws belongs to the prince. Matthew Sutcliffe objects: It belongs to the king and the supreme prince and governor to make laws; so the Church is ruled quite differently from the kingdom and commonwealth. The whole nation of politicians objects, for whom the power of enacting laws is so much the monarch's own that it is counted among his royal rights. Why say more? Richard Bancroft himself admits, and Donellus too, that the commonwealth of Geneva is for this reason democratic, because the power of enacting laws, which there rests with the people, is among the royal rights. Out of your own mouth I will judge you: for when Bancroft says this, he convicts himself of having despoiled Christ's kingdom of a certain royal right, since he has taken from him the power of enacting laws. Homer is accustomed to call the ancient princes lawgivers. Lawgiving (says Aristotle) pertains to royal dignity. Hence the princes of God's people are themselves called lawgivers in the sacred writings, Gen. 49. 10, a name that is nowhere given to priests in the whole law. Finally, if laws come from Christ as priest, why was it not Aaron, who was the type of Christ as priest, who was the lawgiver of the Israelites, but Moses, who was not a priest but only a political prince?
