George Carleton proves this against Bozius. When Bozius had objected Ps. 99. 6, Moses and Aaron among his priests, Carleton replies that the word Cohanim is common to civil magistrates as well as to priests; whence the sons of David are called Cohanim, 1 Sam. 8. 18, though they were not priests but only civil magistrates, 1 Chron. 18. 17. But if Moses is here called a priest, he is so called only in this respect, that he prayed for the people as a priest does, as John Piscator noted in his scholia.

units.la: Secundò prævidit Bancroftus, si Politeia Ecclesiastica sub Christo Rege administraretur, Seniores & Diaconos nostros satis ad eam commodè admoveri, quamquam non sint sacerdotes. Hi igitur ut extra numerum sint, rerumque summa penes sacerdotes sit, ijque soli (ut cum sancto Ambrosio loquar,) aliquid esse videantur: non a Christo rege administrabitur disciplina, sed a Christo sacerdote. Hoc arcanum ab ipso Bancrofto satis certo indicio proditur: quum ex eo arguit in Christi politeia Ecclesiastica locum senioribus nullum esse, quòd neque sub Christo propheta sint, quia non sint prophetæ, neque sub Christi sacerdotio quia non sunt sacerdotes. Atqui hoc argumento inquam & magistratus regimen etiam Ecclesiasticum amputat: nam si Ecclesiæ gubernatio a Christi sacerdotio sit, & nemini locus in ejusdem parte aliqua residuus sit, qui non similiter sit sacerdos, & magistratus perinde atque seniores, sacerdotes non sint: consequitur profecto falcem suam in alienam messem haud minùs immittere eos quam seniores, qui res Ecclesiæ regunt.
units.tr: Secondly, Bancroft foresaw that if ecclesiastical polity were administered under Christ the King, our elders and deacons could easily and fittingly be admitted to it, although they are not priests. So then, that they may stand outside the number, and the chief power may rest with priests, and these alone (to speak with holy Ambrose) may seem to be something, discipline will be administered not by Christ the King but by Christ the priest. This secret is betrayed by Bancroft himself with fairly certain evidence, since from it he argues that in Christ's ecclesiastical polity there is no place for elders, because they are not under Christ the prophet, since they are not prophets, nor under Christ's priesthood, since they are not priests. But by this argument, I say, he cuts off even the ecclesiastical government of the magistrate. For if the governance of the Church belongs to Christ's priesthood, and no place remains in any part of it for anyone who is not likewise a priest, then magistrates, just as elders, are not priests; it follows that they thrust their sickle into another's harvest no less than the elders who manage the affairs of the Church.

units.la: Tertium Bancrofti arcanum hoc est. Politeias Ecclesiasticæ ministros proprie ille sacerdotes esse vult: idcirco Politeia sub sacerdote Christo futura est, non sub Rege, quia in regno Christi externo ministris tantum & servis locus est, non proprie autem sacerdotibus. At inquam in Novo Testamento disputat noster Whitakerus sacerdotis nomen, Evangelij ministris non attribui: cumque obiecisset Durenus Scotus, Patres tamen eos sacerdotes appellasse: respondet, id ex consuetudine natum fuisse, impropriamque locutionem fuisse, a qua cum Apostoli abstinuerint, & nobis quoque abstinendum esse. Quid quòd Patres diu hoc nomine abstinuerint vel ipso fatente Bellarmino: scilicet Tantisper dum Evangelij ministros a Iudeis sacerdotibus tum florentibus distingui opus erat. Ità nec consuetudo patrum pro Bancrofto quicquam facit; cum eadem jam hoc nomen abolédi necessitas sit, nempè ut Evangelij ministri a papisticis sacerdotibus discriminentur. Atque hæc arcana illa sunt, cur Ecclesiasticam Politeiam Hierarchici a Christi regno arceant.
units.tr: This is Bancroft's third secret. He wants the ministers of ecclesiastical polity to be priests in the proper sense; therefore polity will be under Christ the priest, not under the King, because in Christ's external kingdom there is room only for ministers and servants, not properly for priests. But, I say, our Whitaker argues in the New Testament that the name of priest is not attributed to ministers of the Gospel. When Durenus the Scot objected that the Fathers nevertheless called them priests, Whitaker replies that this arose from custom and was an improper way of speaking, from which the apostles abstained and from which we too should abstain. What if the Fathers long refrained from this name, even by the admission of Bellarmine himself: namely, only for as long as it was necessary to distinguish the ministers of the Gospel from the Jewish priests, who were then flourishing? Thus the custom of the Fathers does nothing for Bancroft either, since there is now the same necessity to abolish this name, namely, that the ministers of the Gospel be distinguished from papal priests. And these are the secrets for which the Hierarchists keep ecclesiastical polity away from the kingdom of Christ.

units.la: CAP. 5. Adversariorum Sophistice refellitur & primo tria Bancrofti argumenta.
units.tr: CHAPTER 5. The sophistries of our opponents are refuted, and first the three arguments of Bancroft.

units.la: Tertio jam loco de argumentis adversariorum videndum est: vix id forte fieri absque nausea poterit; non est tamen committendum, ut silendo victa veritas videatur. Primò ex eo arguit Richardus Bancroftus Christum quasi Regem, Ecclesiam in externis nullam gubernare, sed in internis electos tantum regere: quia affirmante Pezelio nostro consistoriano, Christus caput electorum tantùm est, & ut Ecclesia corpus Christi dicitur, ita electos solos significat. Facilis hic & expedita responsio est; corpus & caput dupliciter dici: primò propriè pro capite & corpore naturali, secundò figuratè pro corpore & capite Politico. Quid igitur est? ut Christus similitudinem capitis naturalis gerit, & Ecclesia corporis naturalis: ita electorum tantùm Rex & caput Christus est, quia in eos tantùm vitalem spiritus virtute infundit: & vicissim corpus Christi electi soli sunt, quia soli Christo tanquā a capite naturali spiritualiter vegetantur. Quemadmodum verò capitis Politici, ita quoscunque in Ecclesia externè regit, ac non electos solùm. Quid minus? cum & gentium caput etiam sensu isto a patre Christus constitutus sit, Psal. 18.44. & Angelorum, qui ne dum de Ecclesia redempta sint, Col.2 10. imo & singularum personarum sive de Ecclesia sint, sive non sint 1. Cor.11.3.
units.tr: Third, we must now look at the arguments of our opponents. This will perhaps hardly be possible without nausea, but we must not let the truth seem defeated through our silence. First, Richard Bancroft argues that Christ, as King, governs the Church in external matters not at all, but rules only the elect in internal matters. He grounds this on the claim of our consistorian Pezel that Christ is the head of the elect alone, and that, just as the Church is called the body of Christ, so it signifies the elect alone. The answer here is easy and ready. Body and head are spoken of in two ways: first properly, of a natural head and natural body; second figuratively, of a political body and political head. How then does it stand? As Christ bears the likeness of a natural head, and the Church the likeness of a natural body, so Christ is king and head of the elect alone, because he pours vital spirit into them alone; and conversely the body of Christ is the elect alone, because they alone are spiritually nourished by Christ as by a natural head. But as a political head, Christ governs externally all whom he rules in the Church, and not the elect only. What could be less surprising? For Christ has also been appointed by the Father in this sense as head of the nations, Ps. 18.44, and of the angels, who are not only of the redeemed Church, Col. 2.10; indeed also of single persons, whether they belong to the Church or not, 1 Cor. 11.3.

units.la: Hæc distinctio si non observetur, pugnare videbuntur quæ in authoribus subinde occurrunt, quæ tamen inter se cohærent. Exempli gratia, sic Whitakerus. Regere Ecclesiam in externis, Christo non convenit ut capiti. Rursus, Christus non aliter caput est, quam ut Ecclesiæ vitam præbet. Quis non hic putat & Hierchicorum partes agere Whitakerum? verùm non agit. Non regit Ecclesiam in externis Christus ut caput, id est in persona sua non regit externè. Christus non alter caput est (naturale nempe) quam qua Ecclesiæ vitā præbet. Quod vero Christus qua Politicum caput est, & quatenus rex, Ecclesiā in externis regat, ostendit idem alibi. Christus semper in suo regno præsens adest ut nullus Rex verius in suo regno esse possit. Facit ille verissimè ut reges solent, & curat omnes regni sui partes, & præstat sedulo quicquid a præsente Rege requiritur. Quid enim faciunt reges quod Christus non facit? Defendunt illi suos subditos, eosdemque legibus gubernant: non ne hæc similiter Christus facit?
units.tr: If this distinction is not observed, there will seem to be contradictions in the authors that occur from time to time, although they cohere with one another. For example, thus Whitaker: To govern the Church in external matters does not belong to Christ as head. And again: Christ is head only in that he gives life to the Church. Who would not think here that Whitaker is taking the side of the Hierarchists? But he is not. Christ does not govern the Church in external matters as head; that is, in his own person he does not govern externally. Christ is head (namely natural head) only in that he gives life to the Church. That Christ, however, as political head and as king, governs the Church in external matters, the same author shows elsewhere: Christ is always present in his kingdom, so that no king could be more truly present in his own kingdom. He does this most truly, as kings are wont to do: he takes care of all the parts of his kingdom and diligently supplies whatever is required of a present king. For what do kings do that Christ does not? They defend their subjects and govern them by laws. Does not Christ do these things likewise?

units.la: Secundum argumentum etiam Richardi Bancrofti est, qui ita disputat. In eo quod Ecclesiæ externum regimen, partem regni Christi statuitis, Genevensem papatum quendā & regalitatē in Ecclesias invehitis, imò seniores presbyteriales quoscunq; vestros facitis regulos. Atqui hoc nulla nulla connexione sequi dicimus: quid (inquit) non Christus Reges omnes eos facit quibus ut Rex praficitur? Expecto rationem cur regnum Christi Reges non faceret, perinde ac prophetia ejus prophetas, & sacerdotium sacerdotes, efficit? Respondeo nec prophetiam Christi mundanos & politicos Prophetas, nec sacerdotium mundanos sacerdotes & politicos quosvis facere, ut regnum Christi mundanos quosdam & politicos reges effecturum ex sententia nostra supponis, quum Politeiam Ecclesiae ideo a regno non pendere argumentaris, quod tum reguli quidam politici mundaniq; emersuri sint, qui authoritati magistratuum offendiculo essent.
units.tr: The second argument is also Richard Bancroft's, who reasons thus: In that you make the external government of the Church a part of Christ's kingdom, you introduce a certain Genevan papacy and royalty into the churches; indeed you make all your presbyterial elders petty kings. But this does not follow by any connection, we say. Why (he asks) does Christ not make kings of all those over whom he is set as King? I await a reason why the kingdom of Christ would not make kings, just as his prophetic office makes prophets and his priesthood makes priests. I answer that neither the prophecy of Christ makes worldly and political prophets, nor does his priesthood make worldly priests or any political priests, just as you suppose that the kingdom of Christ will bring forth certain worldly and political kings, since you argue that the polity of the Church does not depend on the kingdom for the reason that certain petty political and worldly kings would then emerge, who would be an obstacle to the authority of the magistrates.

units.la: Sed remora haec de mundanis remota, quid tum ad argumentum respondebis inquiet, Superest adhuc remora alia de politicis: aio enim ethicos tantum prophetas prophetiam Christi facere, & sacerdotium duntaxat ethicos sacerdotes, qua ratione & regnum Christi internum, reges quosque fideles efficit, sed ethicos solummodo, politicos non item. Prophetia Christi fidelibus omnibus communicatur, non tamen omnes publico prophetandi munere, in Ecclesiae Politeia fungi debent. Sic sacerdotium in fideles omnes influit, non tamen omnes ad sacerdotium in Ecclesia publicum, manus admovere debent. At prophetia Christi prophetas quosdam, quosdam etiam sacerdotes sacerdotum, & publicos & politicos praebet, cur non & regnum etiam ejusmodi regulos nobis proferet eos, qui ad Ecclesiam gubernandam vocabuntur? Nego prophetiam prophetas publicos, sacerdotium sacerdotes politicos ullos facere: qui enim in Ecclesia prophetarum sacerdotumque (ut loquimini) publico munere defunguntur, ij ab externo Christi regno quo author Politeiae est toti pendent, non a prophetia nec sacerdotio. Fac inquies: quum tamen regnum Christi internum reges ethicos faciat, cur non externum & politicum, externos adaeque & politicos nobis reges subministrabit? Quia ipsius regni externi natura adversatur.
units.tr: But setting aside this hindrance of worldly kings, he will say, what will you reply to the argument? There remains another hindrance, concerning political kings. For I say that the prophecy of Christ makes only ethical prophets, and the priesthood only ethical priests; and by the same reasoning, his inner kingdom makes faithful kings, but only ethical ones, not political ones likewise. The prophecy of Christ is communicated to all the faithful, yet not all must discharge the public office of prophesying in the polity of the Church. So the priesthood flows into all the faithful, yet not all must lay hands on the public priesthood in the Church. But the prophecy of Christ furnishes some prophets, and some priests of priests, both public and political. Why will his kingdom not also furnish us with such petty kings, who will be called to govern the Church? I deny that prophecy makes public prophets, or that priesthood makes political priests. For those who in the Church discharge the public office of prophets and priests (as you put it) depend wholly on the external kingdom of Christ, of which he is the author in the polity, and not on prophecy or priesthood. Suppose, you will say: since Christ's inner kingdom makes ethical kings, why will it not likewise supply us with external and political kings? Because the very nature of the external kingdom is opposed to it.

units.la: Accedit etenim hic principatus ad naturam Monarchiae, cujus vis cum nimine communicabilis sit, ipsa Monarchia esse desinit, nisi ipse Monarcha Rex sit solus, ita ut subditis privatis parere tantum, publicis autem regni sui administratoribus, inservire duntaxat servorum more, absque omni regum titulo relinquatur. Observatum hoc ab ipso Loo est, qui Theodoro Bezae concedit regem in Ecclesia neminem appellari debere nisi Christum solum; hac addita ratione: si regem se diceret, supremam sibi dignitatem vendicaret: si secundarium se appellaret, eo ipso fatetur se non esse Regem. Recte Poeta quisquis fuit: Esse sat est servus; iam nolo vicarius esse, qui rex est regum Maxime non habeat. Haec ita cum sint, tantum abest, quod haec Bancrofti ratiocinatio causae nostrae officiat, ut eam potius vel maxime confirmet. Regulos in Politeia Ecclesiastica detestaris. Recte tu quidem: Monarchica etenim Christi regalitas in Ecclesia externa, communicabilis minime est, dicit Lous. Quo loco igitur misera vestra jurisdictio Episcopalis monarchica est: quo jure instar regulorum Prælati (quos dicitis) in Ecclesijs dominantur? qua fronte denique author iste contra Bezam, nomen ἀρχιπίμην Archiepiscopis communicable esse contendit? Potestas monarchica incommunicabilis? nomina tamen monarchalia communicabilia? Vocem etenim ἀρχιπίμων monarchicam Christi authoritatem designare, quisquis non videt, cum ego ad Anticyras navigare suaderem.
units.tr: For this principality belongs to the nature of monarchy. Since the power of monarchy cannot be communicated without loss, monarchy itself ceases to exist unless the monarch himself is king alone, so that he is obeyed by private subjects while his public administrators are left to serve him merely as slaves, without any title of king. This was noticed by Loos himself, who concedes to Theodore Beza that no one in the Church ought to be called king except Christ alone, adding this reason: if a man called himself king, he would claim the supreme dignity for himself; if he called himself secondary, by that very fact he confesses that he is not king. Rightly said the poet, whoever he was: It is enough to be a servant; now I do not wish to be a vicar, who does not have the greatest King of kings. These things being so, this reasoning of Bancroft's is so far from harming our cause that it rather especially confirms it. You condemn petty kings in the ecclesiastical polity. Rightly so: For Christ's monarchical royalty in the external Church is by no means communicable, says Loos. In what respect, then, is your wretched episcopal jurisdiction monarchical? By what right do prelates, like the petty kings you speak of, lord it over the churches? By what brazenness, finally, does that author contend against Beza that the name archipoimen [ἀρχιποίμην] is communicable to archbishops? Monarchical power is incommunicable, yet monarchical names are communicable? For who does not see that the word archipoimen designates the monarchical authority of Christ? I might as well be advising a voyage to Anticyra.

units.la: Tertium argumentum adhuc Richardi Bancrofti est, ex illo sermone Domini nostri ad Pilatum: Regnum meum non est ex hoc mundo: Quod cum contra Episcopos ingeatur a vobis, cur igitur (inquit( pariliter non valebit, adversus hosce regulos nostros consistorianos? Quod ad comparationem Episcoporum & Seniorum, cecus est qui cernere nequit, spiritualiter tantum gubernare Seniores, cum imperium Episcopale mundanum a nobis dicatur, nec immerito quia a mundo & hominibus inventum, quia mundi typhum redolet, quia mundanae Monarchiae simile: quibus de causis ejsque solis regnu suum de hoc mundo esse, Pilato de regno Romano mundano moueti negavit Christus. Nullus igitur hujus argumenti Bancroftiani nucleus est, ideo scilicet regnum Christi, ad externu Ecclesiæ regimen se non extendere, quia tum mundanu esset, quia externum. Quæso mi domine cum sacerdotium Christi, a qua externu Ecclesiæ regimen pendere dicis, mundanum dixeris (externum enim est?) num etiam regimen Episcopale vestrum, mundanum concedes? externum siquidem est quid hic respondeat ego sane non video, nisi hoc forte: Munus Episcopale mundanum dici posse ut interim Christi regnum mundanum non sit, quia a sacerdotio hoc munus pendet non a regno. Ita salua res est, & Dominus Episcopus in portu navigat, ut qui regimen suum mundanum teneat, non a Christi regno quod mundanum non est, sed a Christi sacerdotio, quod mundanum dici posse credit, idcirco quia externum est. Atq; hic error hujus argumenti primus est, quod externum & mundanum confundat, ac si unum idemq; essent.
units.tr: The third argument is again Richard Bancroft's, from that saying of our Lord to Pilate: My kingdom is not of this world. Since you urge this against the bishops, why (he says) will it not likewise hold against these petty consistorian kings of ours? As for the comparison of bishops and elders, he is blind who cannot see that the elders govern only spiritually, since we call the episcopal government worldly, and not unjustly: it was devised by the world and by men, it smells of worldly pride, and it is like a worldly monarchy. For these reasons Christ denied, when Pilate was moved by the worldly Roman kingdom, that his kingdom was of this world, and his alone. There is therefore no kernel in this Bancroftian argument, namely that the kingdom of Christ does not extend to the external government of the Church because that government would be worldly, because it is external. I ask you, my lord: since you say that the priesthood of Christ, on which the external government of the Church depends, is worldly (for is it not external?), will you also concede that your episcopal government is worldly? For it is external. What he may answer to this I certainly do not see, except perhaps this: The episcopal office can be called worldly, while the kingdom of Christ is nonetheless not worldly, because this office depends on the priesthood and not on the kingdom. So the matter is safe, and the lord bishop sails into harbour, since he holds his worldly government not from the kingdom of Christ, which is not worldly, but from the priesthood of Christ, which he believes can be called worldly simply because it is external. And indeed the first error of this argument is that it confuses the external with the worldly, as if they were one and the same.

units.la: Secundus in eo latet, quod supponat Christum ipsum externum Ecclesiæ regem futurum, si modo qua rex, Ecclesiam in externis regat. Atqui hoc minime consequi dico; quodsi vero consequatur sequitur etiam ex adversariorum dependentia sacerdotali, eum sacerdotem etiam Ecclesiæ externum esse, quia (ut illi) qua sacerdos, Ecclesiam gubernat in externis. Distinguendum nempe in utroque cum regno tum sacerdotio inter ipsum Christum, & illius administros est: cum minime eodem modo dicuntur hi vel sacerdotes in veteri fædere, vel in novo Pastores, quomodo ille sacerdos & Pastor est, ut recte Whitakerus. Hoc Romanenses cum non intelligant, eodem modo monarcham Papam dici volunt quo ipse Christus Monarcha est: & quia Christus jam ipse absens, ideo Papam & visibilem Monarcham requirunt. Huic ut respondeat Whitakerus noster, negat externam gubernationem Ecclesiae Christo competere: sed moderationem spiritualem & invisibilem. Hoc dum explicat negat Christum aut Monarcham visibilem quoad regimen externum in Ecclesia fuisse, quum in terris versaretur: aut jam futurum esse, si in imis esset. Non enim inquit haec externa procuraret: non crearet Episcopos, non conferret ordines, non synodos congregaret, non reliqua ejusmodi faceret. Videri posset Whitakerus nobis contradicere qui negat Christum Monarcham esse quoad regimen externum: sed secus est; negat etenim pariliter eum Episcopum & Pastorem esse quoad regimen externum: eo modo quo Episcopi & Pastores sint. Quid igitur est? quaecunque Politeias dependentia a Christo sit, non sequitur ipsum Christum quoad personam suam externum Regem aut Pastorem esse, etsi Ecclesiam per Pastores externe gubernat: sed retinenda haec distinctio aliter atque aliter Christum & ministros rectores dici, quod hi externi rectores sint, Christus vero non sit.
units.tr: The second error lies hidden in this, that it assumes Christ himself will be the external king of the Church, if indeed he rules the Church in external matters as king. But I say this does not follow at all; yet if it did follow, it would also follow from the Papists' own sacerdotal dependence that he is the external priest of the Church, since (as they say) he governs the Church in external matters as priest. Indeed, in each case, both kingship and priesthood, a distinction must be drawn between Christ himself and his ministers, since these are not called priests in the same way in the old covenant, or pastors in the new, as he is priest and pastor, as Whitaker rightly observes. The Romanists, not understanding this, want the Pope to be called monarch in the same way that Christ himself is Monarch; and because Christ is already absent, they require a visible Monarch, the Pope. To answer this, our Whitaker denies that external government of the Church belongs to Christ, but rather spiritual and invisible moderation. In explaining this, he denies that Christ was a visible Monarch as to external government in the Church while he dwelt on earth, or that he would be one now if he were on earth. For, he says, he would not provide these external things: he would not create bishops, confer orders, convene synods, or do other such things. Whitaker might seem to contradict us, since he denies that Christ is Monarch as to external government; but it is otherwise. For he likewise denies that Christ is Bishop and Pastor as to external government, in the way that bishops and pastors are. What then is the case? Whatever the dependence of the polity on Christ may be, it does not follow that Christ himself, in his own person, is an external King or Pastor, even though he governs the Church externally through pastors. This distinction must be retained: Christ and the ministers who rule are called rulers in different ways, because these are external rulers, but Christ is not.

units.la: CAP. 6. Duo argumenta Bilsoni solvuntur.
units.tr: CHAPTER 6. Two arguments of Bilson are answered.

units.la: QVARTVM argumentum est Thomae Bilsoni: qui cum praemisisset Ecclesiae gubernationem duplicem esse, spiritualem & externam: infert deinceps externum Ecclesiae regimen ad Christi regnum non pertinere, quod illud & caeleste & spirituale sit; nempe quod ut ante Bancrofto omne regimen Ecclesiae externum mundanum fuit; ita jam Bilsono, minime caeleste aut spirituale. Sic spirituale Christi regnum, & externum Ecclesiae regimen apud Whitgiftum & Bancroftum opponuntur ubique. Atqui externam Ecclesiae faciem caelestem appellat confessus vel ipso Bilsonus est pagina proxime antecedenti: ubi sic loquitur. Externa species Ecclesiae ubi boni cum improbis per verbum & Sacramenta congregantur & commiscentur regnum caelorum aliquoties appellatur. Bene est? Ecclesia visibilis etenim si caelestis sit quamquam externa, imo ad regnum Christi caeleste pertineat, cur non & ejusdem Politeia etsi externa, & regni Christi caelestis erit? Nonne Iohannis ministerium externum, & tamen a coelo, ac proinde coeleste? Matth. 21.25. Nonne Ecclesia visibilis a suis rectoribus gubernata coelum dicitur etiam per totam Apocalypsim, nominatim vero cap. 4.2, Nunquam aut verbum sacerdotij aut Evangelium sacerdotij audimus, sed verbum regni & Evangelium regni, Matth. 4. 13. Marc. 1, 14. Matth. 13.19. Neque Evangelij externa praedicatio & politica administratio, sacerdotium unquam coeleste dicitur, sed regnum coelorum, regnumque caeleste, Mat. 3.2 & 11. 12. & 13.24. &c. Postremo
units.tr: The fourth argument is that of Thomas Bilson. He first lays down that the government of the Church is twofold, spiritual and external, and then infers that the external government of the Church does not belong to the kingdom of Christ, because that kingdom is heavenly and spiritual. Just as, before Bancroft, all external government of the Church was worldly, so now, according to Bilson, it is in no way heavenly or spiritual. Thus, among Whitgift and Bancroft, the spiritual kingdom of Christ and the external government of the Church are everywhere set against each other. Yet Bilson himself, in the page immediately preceding, confesses that the external aspect of the Church is heavenly, and speaks thus: "The external appearance of the Church, where good and bad are gathered and mingled together through the Word and the Sacraments, is sometimes called the kingdom of heaven." Is that right? If the visible Church is heavenly, although external, and indeed belongs to the heavenly kingdom of Christ, why should not its polity also be heavenly and part of the heavenly kingdom of Christ, even though it is external? Is not the external ministry of John also from heaven, and therefore heavenly? Matt. 21.25. Is not the visible Church, governed by its rulers, called heaven throughout the whole Apocalypse, and especially in chapter 4.2? We never hear of a priestly word or a priestly gospel, but of the word of the kingdom and the gospel of the kingdom: Matt. 4.13; Mark 1.14; Matt. 13.19. Nor is the external preaching of the Gospel and the political administration ever called a heavenly priesthood, but the kingdom of heaven and the heavenly kingdom: Matt. 3.2, 11.12, 13.24, etc. Finally,

units.la: mo mò Politeias Ecclesiasticæ administri nunquam ministri sacerdotij dicuntur, sed ministri regni, imo ministri Christi in regno cœlorum, Math. 11. 11 Atque ut cæleste externum regimen Ecclesiæ est, & ad regnum Christi cœleste, ita spirituale etiam, & ad regnum Christi spirituale pertinens, quod ad efficiens. Administratio illius a spiritu proficiscitur, spiritusque donis perficitur, 1. Cor. 12. 1. Ergo spirituale. Quòd ad finem, datur ad ædificationem spiritualem, Eph. 4. 12. Ergo spirituale. Quòd ad materiam, verbum & Sacramenta quæ administrat spiritualia sunt. 1. Cor. 10. 3. 4. Ergo spirituale. Quòd ad formam agendi, per evidentiam spiritus agit, 1. Cor. 2. 4. 13. Ergo spirituale. Quòd ad objectum, spiritus & animas hominum respicit, Heb. 13. 17. Ergo spirituale. Quòd ad media; operatur per arma spiritualia, 2. Corinth. 10. 4. Ergo spirituale. Quòd ad effectum, ministerium spiritus est, 2.Cor.3. 6. Ergo spirituale est.
units.tr: finally, the ministers of the administration of the ecclesiastical polity are never called ministers of the priesthood, but ministers of the kingdom, indeed ministers of Christ in the kingdom of heaven: Matt. 11.11. And just as the external government of the Church is heavenly and pertains to the heavenly kingdom of Christ, so it is also spiritual and pertains to the spiritual kingdom of Christ. As to its efficient cause, its administration proceeds from the Spirit and is brought to completion by the gifts of the Spirit: 1 Cor. 12.1. Therefore it is spiritual. As to its end, it is given for spiritual edification: Eph. 4.12. Therefore it is spiritual. As to its matter, the Word and the Sacraments which it administers are spiritual: 1 Cor. 10.3-4. Therefore it is spiritual. As to the manner of acting, it acts through the demonstration of the Spirit: 1 Cor. 2.4, 13. Therefore it is spiritual. As to its object, it regards the spirits and souls of men: Heb. 13.17. Therefore it is spiritual. As to its means, it works through spiritual weapons: 2 Cor. 10.4. Therefore it is spiritual. As to its effect, it is the ministry of the Spirit: 2 Cor. 3.6. Therefore it is spiritual.

units.la: Quintum argumentum etiam Thomæ Bilsoni est, qui etsi presbyteria nostra a Christo instituta esse concederentur, eorum tamen tribunalia ad regnum Christi minimè pertinere dicit, quia illud ipsius majestati proprium est. Cujus argumenti vim vix attigisse m ni meminissem a Iohanne Whitgifto scriptum, gubernationem Ecclesiæ duplicem esse, spiritualem & externam: in illa Christum Pastorem solum esse, in hac vero sub se Pastores habere substitutos. Ex hac collatione intelligere promptum est, regnum Christi adeo illi majestati proprium esse Bilsoni judicio, ut nullos habeat substitutos. Accipit hoc forte lucem a Gulielmo Whitakero. Christus (inquit) ut doctor multos vicarios reliquit non unum: in regno vero nullum vicarium reliquit. Et si velimus Christo vicarios aliquos in regno substituere, potius reges & principes esse debent, qui legibus & armis Ecclesiam muniunt, quam Papa qui destruit. Quo sensu, aut quam verè hæc dicantur, non jam disputabo: rem meam agere mihi pro præsenti satis erit: quod ut fiat, quos Whitgiftus substitutos, Whitakerus vicarios, eos ego servos & administros voco. Dico igitur regnum Christi quanquam Christo proprium sit, sub se tamen servos habere & administros, per quos regnum in externis administrat. Hoc mihi Bilsonus si non concesserit, magistratum ipsum excludet, quem alibi tamen regalem Christi authoritatem obtinere affirmavit, uti supra ostensum est. Regnum Christi sub se in republica servos habebit, per quos externe regit? In Ecclesia vero non habebit? Imo ut mihi quidem videtur multo magis: nam regalis Christi efficacia Ecclesiæ administratoribus præsentius adest, quam principibus hujus sæculi: & internum illius regnum cum suorum ministerio in Ecclesia arctius conjungitur, quam in republica. Hoc ita cum sit, audiendum potius Bilsono erat illud Christi: Quæ Deus coniunxit homo ne separet. Math. 19. 6. quàm ita scribendum. Quorundam nostræ ætatis præceps & inconsultus feruor facit, ut in externa disciplina Ecclesiæ separanda diutius hæreamus, donec eam ab interno illo & vero Christi regno diligenter & exquisite sejunxerimus. Intelligo quid dicis: separatio & sejunctio ea à te instituitur, ut internum Ecclesiæ regimen ad Christi regnum: externum vero ad illius sacerdotiū pertineat tantum, at non ad regnum. Affinis huic quadantenus Sta-pletoni ni fallor, aliorumque Papistarum seiunctio est: Capitis (inquit) duo officia sunt: primum interna est, ut sit principium vitalis influxus, & sic Christus caput est: alterum externum, ut dirigat suo imperio externas functiones corporis, & sic Papa est caput. Ad hæc respondens Iohannes Reynoldus, Primò (inquit) ex duobus capitis officijs nos duo capita excudere non debemus. Similiter Bilsono respondendum: ex unius Christi capitis duob° officijs, interno scil: & externo, duo regiminū capita efformare non licet: regnū nempe quod interne vegetet, & sacerdotiū, quod externè dirigat. Secundò, gubernare externas (inquit) actiones corporis, principale officium capitis est, & illi soli conveniens qui internum corpori influxum præbet, Similiter Bilsono respondendum: Gubernare Ecclesiam in externis principale officium officij illius in Christo est, quo Ecclesiæ caput & Rex est: externaquè directio ab eodem fonte fluit, a quo interna vegetatio, imo uno eodemque actu ac proinde uno eodemque officio, & externè dirigitur Ecclesia, & interne vegetatur. Tertio (inquit) internum influxum & externum gubernationem separantes, de Dei domo magnopere detrahitis, quia hac ratione pastores & doctores externis tantum corporis functionibus dirigendis præficientur, qui tamen à Christo dati sunt ad plenum consummationem sanctorum, Eph.f.4.12. Idem jam prorsus Bilsono respondendum: Pastorum etenim externum regimen, dum ab interno & (ut vocat) spirituali regimine Christi separat, externum tantùm illis in corpora administrationem relinquit: cum interim in intimas spiritus medullas eorum ministerium impenetraret, regali Christi potestate cooperante, næ ille (quod ipse agnoscit) suos cooperatores Christus non agnovisset, 1.Cor.3.9. Atq; hæc quidè què ego animadvertere possum aaversario ù argumenta singula sunt. Deus bone quam frivola? nostris certe infirmiora, quæ, quantum fieri potest breviter, deinceps subjungenda sunt.
units.tr: The fifth argument is also that of Thomas Bilson, who, even if our presbyteries were granted to have been instituted by Christ, nevertheless says that their tribunals do not pertain at all to the kingdom of Christ, because that belongs to his own majesty. I would scarcely have grasped the force of this argument, were I not reminded that John Whitgift wrote that the government of the Church is twofold, spiritual and external: in the former Christ alone is pastor, but in the latter he has pastors as substitutes under him. From this comparison it is easy to see that, in Bilson's judgment, the kingdom of Christ is so proper to that majesty that it has no substitutes. Perhaps this receives some light from William Whitaker: "Christ, as teacher, left many vicars, not one; but in his kingdom he left no vicar. And if we wish to appoint some vicars to Christ in the kingdom, they ought rather to be kings and princes, who defend the Church with laws and arms, than the Pope, who destroys it." In what sense, or how truly, these things are said, I shall not now dispute; it will be enough for my purpose to carry on my own business. To do this, I call servants and administrators those whom Whitgift calls substitutes and Whitaker calls vicars. I say, therefore, that the kingdom of Christ, although it is proper to Christ, nevertheless has servants and administrators under him, through whom he administers the kingdom in external matters. If Bilson does not grant me this, he will exclude the magistrate himself, whom elsewhere he affirmed holds the royal authority of Christ, as has been shown above. Will the kingdom of Christ have servants under it in the commonwealth, through whom it rules externally, and yet not have them in the Church? Indeed, as it seems to me, far more so: for the royal efficacy of Christ is more immediately present to the administrators of the Church than to the princes of this age, and his inward kingdom is joined more closely with the ministry of his servants in the Church than in the commonwealth. Since this is so, it was rather Bilson who ought to have heeded that saying of Christ, "What God has joined together, let not man put asunder," Matt. 19.6, than to write thus: "The rash and ill-advised zeal of some in our age makes us persist too long in separating the external discipline of the Church, until we have carefully and exactly sundered it from that inward and true kingdom of Christ." I understand what you mean: the separation and division which you make is such that the internal government of the Church pertains to the kingdom of Christ, but the external pertains only to his priesthood, not to the kingdom. This separation is, if I am not mistaken, somewhat akin to that of Stapleton and other Papists: "The office of the head is twofold. The first is internal, that it be the source of vital influx, and so Christ is head; the second is external, that by its command it directs the external functions of the body, and so the Pope is head." Answering these points, John Reynolds says: "First, from the two offices of the head we ought not to fashion two heads." Similarly, Bilson must be answered: from the two offices of the one head Christ, namely the internal and the external, it is not lawful to form two heads of government, one kingdom which quickens internally and one priesthood which directs externally. "Secondly, to govern the external actions of the body is the principal office of the head, and it belongs only to the one who gives inward influx to the body." Similarly, Bilson must be answered: to govern the Church in external matters is the principal office of that office in Christ, by which he is the head and King of the Church; and external direction flows from the same source from which inward quickening does. Indeed, by one and the same act, and therefore by one and the same office, the Church is both externally directed and inwardly quickened. "Thirdly, by separating internal influx from external government, you greatly detract from God's house, because in this way pastors and teachers are set over merely the external functions of the body to direct, though they were given by Christ for the full perfecting of the saints," Eph. 4.12. The same must now be answered entirely to Bilson. For when he separates the external government of pastors from the internal and (as he calls it) spiritual government of Christ, he leaves them only an external administration over bodies, whereas their ministry penetrates into the innermost marrow of the spirit, with the royal power of Christ cooperating. Otherwise Christ would not have acknowledged them as his fellow workers, which he himself acknowledges: 1 Cor. 3.9. These are the things which I can point out against each of the adversary's arguments. Good God, how frivolous! Certainly weaker than ours, which, as briefly as possible, are to be set out next.

units.la: CAP. 7. Argumenta nostra proponuntur.
units.tr: CAP. 7. Our arguments are set forth.

units.la: IN illo officio Iesu Christi politeiâ Ecclesiasticâ fundari consentaneum est, quod & authoritatem mittendi, & potestatem benedicendi, & efficaciam operandi, & virtutem vires largiendi & gloriam denique remunerandi habet. Illud autem nec Prophetia Christi quæ duntaxat revelat, nec sacerdotium quod nunc dierum intercedit tantùm, sed regium illius munus illud, quo ista quę diximus,cum potentissimè,tum gloriosissimè præstantur omnia.
units.tr: It is fitting that the ecclesiastical polity be founded on that office of Jesus Christ which holds the authority of sending, the power of blessing, the efficacy of working, the strength of giving power, and finally the glory of rewarding. But that office is neither his prophetic office, which only reveals, nor his priesthood, which now only intercedes, but his royal office, by which all the things we have mentioned are performed both most powerfully and most gloriously.

units.la: Disputo primùm, a promissione politeias constituendæ,Mat.16. 19. Tibi dabo claves regni cælorum.
units.tr: I argue first from the promise to establish the polity, Matt. 16.19: "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven."

units.la: Primò etenim,jurisdictio ecclesiastica,non clavis sacerdotij his in verbis, sed clavis regni, distertissimè appellatur.
units.tr: First, in these words the power of ecclesiastical jurisdiction is called, most plainly, the key not of the priesthood but of the kingdom.

units.la: Secundò, non alludit ad clavem aliquam sacerdotis, his in verbis Christus; quænam enim illa obscero est? sed ad clavem patrisfamilias& urbis præfecti, quæ œconomo portarum custodi,in commisso tradi solet.
units.tr: Second, Christ in these words does not allude to some key of a priest; for what sort of key would that be? He alludes to the key of a head of a household and of a city prefect, which is usually committed to the steward who keeps the gates.

units.la: Tertiò, non clavis Aaronis sacerdotis, sed clavis Davidis regis, apellatur alibi, Apocal.3.7.
units.tr: Third, elsewhere it is called not the key of Aaron the priest but the key of David the king, Rev. 3.7.

units.la: Quartò, qui hanc clavem in typo gessit Eliachimus,non sacerdos, sed princeps erat, Isa.22.22.
units.tr: Fourth, the one who bore this key in type was Eliakim, who was not a priest but a prince, Isa. 22.22.

units.la: Quintò, per hanc clavem, administri politeias, magno pondere judicant,uti loquitur Tertullianus, cui Gregorius Magnus accedit. Cæli, Ecclesiæ Doctores dicti sunt, quia Dominus in eis præsidet, dum per eos iudicia sua exercet. Quibus namque regni cœlorum claves tribuit, per eos judicat. Iudicare autem adeo regi atque principi proprium est, ut Iudaici populi principes, idcirco Iudices agnominarentur.
units.tr: Fifth, through this key the ministers of the polity pass judgments of great weight, as Tertullian says, and Gregory the Great adds: "The teachers of the Church are called heavens, because the Lord presides in them while he exercises his judgments through them. For to whom he has given the keys of the kingdom of heaven, through them he judges. Now judging is so proper to a king and a prince that the princes of the Jewish people were for that reason called judges."

units.la: Disputo secundò, ab institutione Politeias Ecclesiasticæ generali, Math.28.19. Ite & prædicate,&c. Quid enim? Num sacerdotium suum hîc allegat Christus, ut politeia in eo fnndari censeretur? Minimè omnium: sed regiam suam authoritatem pro fundamento potius adfert: nam & ita præfatur.. Data est mihi omnis potestas in cælo & in terra: & ita postmodum concludit de regali efficacia sua,ego ero vobiscum usque ad consummationem seculi.
units.tr: I argue second from the general institution of the ecclesiastical polity, Matt. 28.19: "Go and preach, etc." For what? Does Christ here appeal to his priesthood, so that the polity might be thought to be founded on it? By no means; rather he puts forward his royal authority as the foundation. For he begins thus: "All power is given to me in heaven and on earth," and then concludes, about his royal efficacy: "I will be with you until the end of the age."

units.la: Tertio disputo, à narratione illa politeias constitutæ particulari, Ephes.4.11. Alios dedit Apostolos, alios Prophetas, alios Evangelistas, alios Pastores & Doctores. Hoc a Christo factum narrat Apostolus cum ascendit in altum captivam ducens captivitatem, & dona dans hominibus. v.8. Nullus hîc igitur tergiversandi locus est. Non eo tempore cōstituitur politeia,quo Christi sacerdotium regali muneri prævalebat, sed eo potiùs ,1 quo sacerdotium regali subjicitur:nam ascendebat Christus primariò ad regnum novum exercendum, ad sacerdotium non nisi secundariò, ut pars ejus illa quæ sola jam re-liqua liqua in intercessione est (quae etiam in politeia constituenda nihil habet negotij) & in gloria regij sui muneris exercetur & ab eadem ornaretur.
units.tr: Third, I argue from that narrative of the particular establishment of the polity, Eph. 4.11: "He gave some apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, some pastors and teachers." The apostle relates that Christ did this "when he ascended on high, leading captivity captive, and giving gifts to men" (v. 8). There is therefore no room for evasion here. The polity was established not at a time when Christ's priesthood prevailed over his royal office, but rather at a time when the priesthood was made subject to the royal office. For Christ ascended chiefly to exercise a new kingdom, and to the priesthood only secondarily, as that part of it which alone now remains, intercession (which has no business at all in establishing the polity), and which is exercised within, and adorned by, the glory of his royal office.

units.la: Quartò disputo, a praecisa politeiae institutione particulari. Habetur ea, Act. 1. 3. Conspectus est ab iis per spatium quadraginta dierum & locutus est ad eos de rebus quae pertinent ad Regnum Dei. Hic ego inter caetera, cur non praecepisse Christum dicerem de tota Ecclesiae politeia, exactamque illius formam praescripsisse, quam & regnum suum vocat? At haec vestra interpretatione dicit Bencroftus, consentitis cum Iesuitis, qui hunc locum de regno suo Antichristiano interpretatur, perinde ac vos de vestra regalitate Genevensi. Regalitas nostra Genevensis nulla est, regalitas vero vestra Episcopalis, eò magis hypocritica, quòd licet ad Antichristianam propius quàm oportuit accedat, regale tamen Christi munus subterfugit, ut ab omni regalitatis suspitione, sub illius sacerdotio delitesceret. Quod ad Iesuitas, oppono Augustini illa. Quae quum Dominus ipse tacuerit, quis nostrum dicat illa vel ista sunt? Quis est tam vanus & temerarius, qui sine ullo testimonio divino affirmet ea esse, quae tunc dicere Dominus voluerit. Ista ut Iesuitas iugulant, ita & Downnamum refellunt. Putare eos Christum hic dicere voluisse de primatu Papae cujusdam necne ac de superioritate Episcoporum, vanum est & temerarium dicit Augustinus quum ex nullo alio scripturae loco politeia huiusmodi probari queat. Annon similiter vanum est & temerarium, Georg. Downam disputare, Apostolos intendisse metrapolitas, etsi non expresserint: quum nullibi ex eorum scriptis pateat, hoc illos voluisse? De politeia vero Genevensi haec verba Christi interpretari cum ea in reliquo Actorum libro deinceps narretur, nec vanum est, Augustini iudicio, nec temerarium, sed quod ego addendum puto, necessarium: prorsus & consentaneum.
units.tr: Fourth, I argue from the precise particular institution of the polity. It is found in Acts 1.3: "He appeared to them during forty days and spoke to them about the things that pertain to the kingdom of God." Here, among other things, why should I not say that Christ gave instructions about the whole polity of the Church and prescribed its exact form, which he also calls his kingdom? But, Bancroft says, by this interpretation of yours you agree with the Jesuits, who interpret this passage of his antichristian kingdom, just as you do of your Genevan royalty. Our Genevan royalty is nothing; but your episcopal royalty is all the more hypocritical, because, although it comes closer to the antichristian than it ought, it nevertheless shuns the royal office of Christ, so that, free from all suspicion of royalty, it may lurk under his priesthood. As to the Jesuits, I set against them that saying of Augustine: "Since the Lord himself has been silent about these things, which of us dares to say that they are this or that? Who is so vain and rash as to affirm, without any divine testimony, that these are the things the Lord wished to say then?" As these words throttle the Jesuits, so they also refute Downame. To think that the Lord here wished to speak of the primacy of some pope or of the superiority of bishops is vain and rash, says Augustine, since such a polity cannot be proved from any other passage of Scripture. Is it not likewise vain and rash for George Downame to argue that the apostles meant metropolitans, though they did not express it, since nowhere in their writings does it appear that they wished this? But to interpret these words of Christ as concerning the Genevan polity, since it is afterwards narrated in the rest of the Acts, is neither vain nor rash by Augustine's judgment; it is, as I think should be added, necessary, and altogether fitting.

units.la: Obiectant adversarii: Incertum nobis ipsis esse, quo loco & tempore, Seniores nostri presbyteriales primo a Christo instituti sint:
units.tr: The adversaries object: it is uncertain even to us ourselves at what place and time our presbyterial elders were first instituted by Christ.

units.la: Respondeo, Saraviae ipsi incertum pariliter videri, quo loco & tempore presbyteri qui in verbo laborant instituti primitus fuerint: Habetur inquit eorum mentio primò, Act. 11. 30. Sed eos ante institutos fuisse consentaneum est, quo tamen tempore instituti fuerint ignoro. En vero tempus tibi inquit Lucas; spatium nempe illud quadraginta dierum: tum & presbyteros docentes, & Seniores Gubernantes, & Diaconos ministrantes praecepit Christus, de tota sui regni ratione & politeia locutus: non ex suo cerebro aut Presbyteros, aut Seniores, aut Diaconos ordinassent Apostoli, ni ipse Christus hoc ipso tempore, regni sui administratores eos speciatim nominasset. Manifesta igitur ratione adducimur, de sua politeia hic Christum Dominum prospexisse, quia alioqui praecipui regni administratores, prefpresbyteri nempe prædicantes, ignota origine laborâ- lunt. Neque sanè ratio ulla reddi potest, cur historiam primæ illorum ordinationis Lucas prætermiserit, nisi quia satis esse putabat, quod initio libri, his in verbis eorum institutione primùm descripsisset, sicut G. Whitac. notat, eû Act. 15 de convocatione Ecclesiæ per Apostolos nulla verba fecisse, qui satis esse putavit, quod ab initio, Apostolos Ecclesiam convocare solitos, semel dixisset, Actorum cap.6.2.
units.tr: I reply: it seems equally uncertain to Saravia himself at what place and time the elders who labour in the word were first instituted. He says their mention is found first in Acts 11.30. But it is fitting that they were instituted before that; at what time they were instituted, however, I do not know. Yet see the time that Luke gives you: that space of forty days. Then Christ, speaking of the whole plan and polity of his kingdom, gave instructions concerning teaching elders, governing elders, and serving deacons. The apostles would not have ordained elders, or deacons, out of their own heads, unless Christ himself at this very time had named them specifically as administrators of his kingdom. By clear reasoning, therefore, we are led to conclude that Christ the Lord foresaw here his own polity; for otherwise the chief administrators of the kingdom, namely the preaching elders, would have an origin unknown. Nor indeed can any reason be given why Luke omitted the history of their first ordination, unless because he thought it sufficient that he had described their institution at the beginning of his book, in these words, as G. Whitaker notes. In Acts 15 he made no mention of the convening of the Church by the apostles, since he thought it enough to have said once, at the beginning, that the apostles were accustomed to call the Church together (Acts 6.2).

units.la: Quinto disputo, a conservatione politeias ecclesiasticæ jam institutæ usque ad iudicium ultimum: quam regni Christi conservationem esse, ex illa precandi formula constat. Adveniat regnum tuum, Luc. 11. 2. Dici non potest, quantos hic clamores Hierarchici tollant, quòd in petitione ista, pro disciplina Ecclesiastica, inter cætera, precandum esse contendamus. Hinc etenim deridet Kingstonium quendam R. Banc. & præfatorem Demonstrationis disciplinariæ Georg. Down. flagellat: quod inter cæteras Christi regni partes, pro adventu disciplinæ ecclesiasticæ, in oratio-nis dominicæ particula ista, nos precari oportere existimarent. Absoluit vero nos ipse J.Bridgesius Episcop° Oxoniensis calcu-lo suo, qui de politeia Ecclesiastica, cum Anglicana, tum Ecclesiarum reformatarum, verba faciens ita subinfert. Det Deus ut in statu nostro seniorumque vicinorumque nostrum, necnon in omnibus aliis veræ Dei Ecclesiæ partibus (secundum quod in oratione dominica omnes dicimus, Adveniat regnū tuum) hæ Dei benedictiones, indies magis magisque augeantur.
units.tr: Fifth, I argue from the preservation of the ecclesiastical polity, once instituted, until the last judgment; and that this is the preservation of Christ's kingdom is plain from that form of prayer: "Thy kingdom come," Luke 11.2. It cannot be said what great outcries the hierarchs raise here, because we contend that in this petition we ought to pray, among other things, for ecclesiastical discipline. Hence he mocks a certain R. Bancroft Kingston, and lashes G. Downame, the preface-writer of the Demonstration of Discipline, because they thought that among the other parts of Christ's kingdom we ought to pray, in this clause of the Lord's Prayer, for the coming of ecclesiastical discipline. But J. Bridges, bishop of Oxford, absolves us with his own verdict, who, speaking of the ecclesiastical polity, both of the Anglican and of the reformed Churches, then adds: "May God grant that in our state, and in that of our neighbours, and also in all other parts of the true Church of God (according as in the Lord's Prayer we all say, 'Thy kingdom come'), these blessings of God be increased more and more, day by day."

units.la: Sextò, disputo a politeias Ecclesiasticæ cessatione, in ultimo judicio, quam regni Christi cessationem esse, illa demonstrant quæ habentur, 1. Cor. 15. 24. Tum erit finis, quando tradiderit regnum Deo, &c. Quod habetur Luc. 1. 32. 33. Dabit ei DEVS thronum patris Dauidis, & regnabit super domum Iacobi in perpetuum, & regni ejus non erit finis: ia inepte Franciscus Turrianus de visibili Ecclesiæ regimine interpretatur, quia hîc de illo regno Christi agitur, cujus finis non erit. Hoc mihi largienti largiendū etiā adversarijs videtur, de visibili Ecclesiæ regimine, 1.Cor.15.24. verba fieri: quia ex adverso, de eo regno ibi agitur, cujus tandem finis erit. Imò vero (inquit Bilsonus) de interno regno Christi in suos inimicos, peccatum, mortem, infernum, hoc totum intelligendum est, quod & æternum in Luca, & hic in Paulo æternum non est? æternum quidem quoad possessionem & fruitionem, cum mirifica quadam suavitate & felicitate coniunctum: non æternum autem quoad administrationem, quia morte, peccato, inferno tum debellatis huius administrationis usus tum nullus erit. Atqui hoc ipsum illud est, quod nos etiam dicimus, qui possessionem & fruitionem quam commemoras, expectamus æternam: cessationemque quam regni Christi narrat Paulus, de illius administratione duntaxat intelligimus.
units.tr: Sixth, I argue from the cessation of the ecclesiastical polity at the last judgment, which the following passages show to be the cessation of Christ's kingdom: 1 Cor. 15.24: "Then will be the end, when he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God, etc." And Luke 1.32-33: "God will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there will be no end." Francis Turrian foolishly interprets this of the visible government of the Church, because here it is treated of that kingdom of Christ whose end will not come. Granting this to me, it seems the adversaries must also grant that in 1 Cor. 15.24 the words concern the visible government of the Church; for on the contrary, there it is treated of that kingdom whose end will at last come. "Indeed," says Bilson, "all this must be understood of the inward kingdom of Christ against his enemies, sin, death and hell. Is it not that which is eternal in Luke, and here in Paul is not eternal? It is eternal indeed as to possession and enjoyment, joined with a wondrous sweetness and felicity; not eternal, however, as to administration, because when death, sin and hell have been vanquished, there will be no use for this administration." But this very thing is what we also say, we who await the eternal possession and enjoyment you mention; and the cessation which Paul describes of Christ's kingdom we understand only of its administration.

units.la: Atqui hec inquit administratio specialis est, in Christi inimicos spirituales; ideoq; de administratione ea duntaxat Paulus loquitur, quæ spiritualis est,& ad internum regnum Christi pertinet,non autem externum Ecclesiæ regimen. Semper hac chorda aberrat Bilsonus, quòd regimē Ecclesiæ externum,administrationem regni Christi minimè spiritualem putat: eam præsertim quæ spirituales Christi hostes destruit,peccatum,morte,infernum,diabolum,contrà quod Paulus apertissimè, 2. Cor. 10. 4. Arma militiæ nostræ carnalia non sunt,sed diuinitus ualidi & ad subuersionem munitionum, ratiocinationes euertendo, omnemq; sublimitatem, quæ extollitur aduersus cognitionem Dei, &c. Quid igitur est? De spirituali regni Christi administratione ea hic loquitur Paulus,concedente Bilsono,qua hostes spirituales debellat: ergo de externa etiā & Ecclesiastica administratione ex parte saltē loquitur:quia non solùm interna administratione intùs agente hostes suos debellat Christus:sed & externa,absq; qua etiam ordinariè ; internam nullam exerit. Hoc sensu patres accipiendi:qui externi regni administrationem aduersus hostes non exscludūt,etsi de ea speciatim nihil dicant,sicut dicunt neoterici,quorū ego unum tantum recensebo, nempè qui inter postremos scripsit, Bartholomæum Keckermanum. Quod dicitur,inquit, 1.Cor.15.28.Postquam subiecta ei fuerint omnia,tum & Filius ipse subjiciętur illi, qui subjecit sibi omnia, ut Deus sit omnia in omnibus: id intelligi debet respectu huius regiminis externi, non autem respectu interni, aut diuinæ quam Christus habuit maiestatis: Neque enim loquitur Apostolus,quod ex contextu apparet,de priuatione, aut depositione maiestatis,aut potestatis regiæ. Respectu enim huius Christus est Deus benedictus in sæculà, & rex gloriæ cujus regni non erit finis: sed agit de mutatione externi illius & ministerialis regiminis quod viget in Ecclesia militante, quam mediatè per suos ministros in hac vita gubernat,dum tandem post consummationem sæculi, sublato illo ministeriali regimine, cui tanquam mediator præerat, regnum traditurus sit patri,id est, Ecclesiam immediatè cum patre recturus, ut Deus sit omnia in omnibus,id est,ne amplius sit opus mediis externis, quibus Deus populum suum gubernet. Hæc illæ, quibus externam tantùm administrationem hic vult intelligi: non autem internam, quia illa semper durabit, licet absque externis mediis.
units.tr: "But," he says, "this administration is special, directed against Christ's spiritual enemies; so Paul speaks only of that administration which is spiritual and pertains to the inner kingdom of Christ, and not of the external government of the Church." Bilson always strays on this point, in that he thinks the external government of the Church is not at all spiritual, and he especially denies this of the administration of Christ's kingdom that destroys his spiritual enemies: sin, death, hell and the devil. Yet Paul says the very opposite, most plainly, in 2 Cor. 10:4: "The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds, casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God," etc. What then follows? Granting Bilson's point, Paul here speaks of the spiritual administration of Christ's kingdom by which he overcomes spiritual enemies. Therefore he speaks, at least in part, of the external and ecclesiastical administration as well. For Christ overcomes his enemies not only by the inward administration working inwardly, but also by the external one, without which he ordinarily exerts no inward power at all. The Fathers must be understood in this sense: they do not exclude an external administration of the kingdom against enemies, even though they say nothing about it in particular. The modern writers, however, do say so, and I will cite only one of them, the last of them to write, Bartholomew Keckermann. "What is said," he says, "in 1 Cor. 15:28, 'When all things shall be subdued unto him, then shall the Son also himself be subject unto him that put all things under him, that God may be all in all,' must be understood with respect to this external government, not with respect to the inward government or the divine majesty which Christ had. For the Apostle does not speak, as the context shows, of a deprivation or laying down of majesty or of royal power." For in respect of that majesty Christ is "God blessed for ever" and "the King of glory, whose kingdom shall have no end." But the Apostle speaks of the change in that external and ministerial government which prevails in the militant Church, which Christ governs mediately in this life through his ministers. Then, at last, after the consummation of the age, that ministerial government, over which he presided as Mediator, will be removed, and he will deliver the kingdom to the Father, that is, he will govern the Church immediately together with the Father, so that God may be all in all, that is, so that there will be no further need for external means by which God governs his people. These are the words by which he wishes only the external administration to be understood here, and not the internal one, because the latter will endure always, even without external means.

units.la: Atquè certè aliquid est quod dicit, sicut facilè perspici possit quantopere Bilsonus hallucinetur, cum internum tantùm regnum hîc Christicessaturum dicit,quod reverà manebit,id est inquit quoad fruitionem: imo inquam non solùm quoad fruitionem: sed etiam quoad ipsam internam administrationem. Hoc in charitate videre est quæ semper manet, 1. Cor. 13. 8. ab interni regni Christi efficacia, etiam in futuro sæculo electis omnibus subministrata: cessare tamen dici potest tribus modis. Primò respectu objecti, non tum adversus hostes pugnabit,quia hostes tum nulli erunt. Secundò respectu materiæ,non quasdã gratias tum administrabit,quas nunc, puta spem,patientiam, &c. Tertiò, respectu formæ administrandi quæ tum immediata criit, 1. Cor. 13. 8. quando Deus erit omnia in omni'us,cum in hoc sæculo non nisi per externa media ordinariè operetur.
units.tr: And certainly there is something in what he says which shows easily how greatly Bilson is mistaken, when he says that here Christ's inward kingdom alone will cease, which in fact will remain; that is, he says, as to enjoyment. Indeed I say not only as to enjoyment, but also as to the inward administration itself. This can be seen in charity, which always remains (1 Cor. 13:8), from the efficacy of Christ's inward kingdom, which will be supplied to all the elect even in the age to come. Yet it can be said to cease in three ways. First, with respect to its object: it will not fight against enemies then, because then there will be no enemies. Second, with respect to its matter: it will not then bestow those graces which it bestows now, such as hope, patience, and so on. Third, with respect to the form of administering, which then will be immediate (1 Cor. 13:8), when God will be all in all, since in this age he works ordinarily only through external means.

units.la: Septimo disputo à sententia Theologorum , quorum numerus infinitus cum sit, ego uno contentus ero, Martino Bucero. Is ad Eduardum sextum de politeia Ecclesiastica scribens, huic libro suo titulum præfigit, De Regno Christi,quod utique non fecisset, ni politeiam Ecclesiasticam regnum Christi censuisset. In ipso libro, eam regni Christi descriptionem tradit, quæ & externum Ecclesiæ regimen comprehendit, sic enim habet. Præstat regni Christi desinitionem subjicere postquam id cognoscitur à tam paucis. Est igitur illud, administratio & procuratio salutis æternæ electorum Dei, qua unigenitus Dei filius illos missò eis Evangelio suo, per dek&tos ad id à se ministros, & adspirato suo spiritu, colligit de mundo ad se, siqque colt &tos sibi, Ecclesiæ sanctæ suæ incorporat,atq; incorporatos regit,& gubernat ipse : utens ad id verbi sui,atque Sacramentorum per idoneos ministros dispensatione , ac vigilanti etiam disciplinæ suæ administratione.
units.tr: Seventhly, I argue from the opinion of the theologians. Since their number is endless, I will be content with one, Martin Bucer. Writing to Edward VI about ecclesiastical polity, he prefixes to this book of his the title On the Kingdom of Christ, which he certainly would not have done unless he thought ecclesiastical polity to be the kingdom of Christ. In the same book he gives that description of Christ's kingdom which includes the external government of the Church. For he says: "It is best to set down a definition of the kingdom of Christ, since it is known to so few. It is therefore the administration and procurement of the eternal salvation of God's elect, by which the only-begotten Son of God, sending to them his Gospel, through ministers appointed for this by him, and by breathing his Spirit, gathers them from the world to himself, and, having gathered them, incorporates them into his holy Church, and rules and governs them when incorporated, using for this his Word and the dispensing of the Sacraments through fit ministers, and also the vigilant administration of his discipline."

units.la: Accedo ad ipsos Hierarchicos , Matheus Sutelvius disputat, Christum ut Regem Ecclesiam suam gubernare, quanquam medium gubernandi diversum ab eo sit, quo reges terreni respublicas suas moderantur. Iohannes Bridgefius, Ecclesiasticam politeiam in Christi regno & monarchia fundari patitur, hic ita pro Episcopis disputat. Christi Monarchia intacta manere potest, intrim ut separatam quis à Christo authoritatem possideat in Ecclesiastica gubernatione. Qui enim partem aliquam authoritatis Monarchæ (idque non a suis sed Monarcham repræsentans) sibi habet commissam, non statim ipsum Monarchiam invadit Had.Saravia.Christũ vehit Regé ex- actam Ecclesiæ gubernandæ formam in Evangelio præscripsisse, & eandem quasi immutabilem ad ipsum usque sæculi finem mandasse affirmat. Nec ego plura addam : quid enim in meridie lucernâ opus? hic igitur quæstionis de politeiæ Ecclesiasticæ præstantia, primæ, quæ est de illius dignitate,finis esto.
units.tr: I come now to the hierarchical writers themselves. Matthew Sutcliffe argues that Christ governs his Church as King, although the means of governing differ from those by which earthly kings manage their commonwealths. John Bridges allows that the ecclesiastical polity is founded in Christ's kingdom and monarchy, and he argues for the bishops in this way: "Christ's monarchy can remain intact, while someone possesses a separate authority in ecclesiastical government from Christ. For he who holds some part of the monarch's authority committed to him (and that not from his own people but as representing the Monarch) does not at once invade the monarchy itself." Hadrian Saravia affirms that Christ the King prescribed the exact form of governing the Church in the Gospel, and that he commanded this form to remain, as it were, unchanged until the very end of the age. I will add nothing more: for why need a lamp at noon? Let this, then, be the end of the first question concerning the excellence of ecclesiastical polity, the question of its dignity.

units.la: CAP. 8.
units.tr: CHAPTER 8.

units.la: De Disciplina Ecclesiastica utilitate.
units.tr: On the usefulness of church discipline.

units.la: SECUNDA, de illius utilitate est, quæ præteriri non debet, quum commune in Anglia opprobrium sit, importunitatem eorum qui pro disciplina reformanda contenduunt exutsari non posse, propterea quod de tricis quibusdam controversiis moveant,et circa rem nullius ponderis aut momenti Ecclesias turbent. At disciplinæ magnam vim esse in utramuis partem,primò illius cum reliquis præceptis disciplinis collatio ostendet. Quod Plato de politica in genere, πολιτικὴ πολιτῶν ἐπιστήμη, & Aristoteles, πολιτικὴ ἐπιστήμη, & Plutarchus denique De disciplina politica homo perfectissimum non possidet, id de politeia Ecclesiastica a multo magis dici potest, cum & huic ipsi politiæ civili imperet, de qua hæc illi locuti sunt.Ethica & œconomica privata tantum curant, hæc publica: politica civilis publica procurat quidem, ideo ethicæ & œconomicæ disciplinæ præpollet, juxta illud, salus reipublicæ prima lex esto. huic tamen politeia qua de agimus Ecclesiastica ipsi præsidet, unde Nazianzenus Ecclesiasticos etiam regere, & quidem nobiliori regendi genere, atque ipse imperator, affirmat, qui & gregis dominici ovis est. Et Chrisostomus; Si Rex quispiam, si Consul, si is qui diademate ornatur indignū audeat, cohibe & coerce, tu illo majorem habes potestatem. Et Gelasius ad Anastasium; Licet præsideas humano generi dignitate rerum terrenarum, tamen præsulibus divinarum devotus colla submittis.
units.tr: The second point concerning its usefulness must not be passed over. It is a common reproach in England that the importunity of those who contend for the reform of discipline cannot be excused, because they stir up certain trifling controversies and trouble the churches about matters of no weight or moment. But that discipline has great power, for good or ill, will first be shown by comparing it with the other disciplines. What Plato says of politics in general, that it is the science of citizens (πολιτικὴ πολιτῶν ἐπιστήμη), and Aristotle, that it is political science (πολιτικὴ ἐπιστήμη), and finally Plutarch, that a man is not most perfect who lacks discipline in politics, can be said much more of ecclesiastical polity, since it governs that very civil polity about which they spoke. Ethics and household management care only for private matters, while this governs public ones. Civil politics indeed deals with public matters, and therefore excels the disciplines of ethics and economics, in accordance with the saying, "let the welfare of the commonwealth be the first law." Yet this ecclesiastical polity, of which we speak, presides over civil polity itself. Hence Nazianzen affirms that it rules even ecclesiastical persons, and in a nobler way of ruling than the emperor himself, who is also a sheep of the Lord's flock. And Chrysostom: "If some king, or consul, or one adorned with the diadem dares something unworthy, you restrain and check him; you have greater power than he." And Gelasius to Anastasius: "Although you preside over the human race in earthly dignity, nevertheless you, devout, submit your neck to the bishops of divine things."

units.la: Neque vero momentum minus elucet, si Politeia Ecclesiastica in sese consideretur. Quod enim Isocrates de politeia in genere ψυχὴ πόλεως ἡ πολιτική, tantam vim obtinens in republica, quantam in corpore anima, id ita ad politeiam Ecclesiasticam accommodat Scultingius, ut eam Ecclesiæ & animam & nervum & artum dixerit. Atque animam quidem Ecclesiæ politeiam esse ego non dicerem, nisi verbi respectu: nervum autem & artum quoad ipsum morum regimen, dicere non vereor, cum id ipsum & Lenis ipse dicat. Cum enim Th. Cartwrightus dixisset, Ecclesiam non minus sine disciplina, quam civitatē sine muro, sine macerie hortū consistere posse: imo inquit, recte disciplinam Ecclesiæ magis necessariam esse quam murum civitati aut maceriam horto dicendum arbitror: etiam artui & nervo eam coparat postea. Accedit huic Th. Bilsonus qui controversias Anglicanas disciplinarias, non de tricis quibusdam levibus, sed de gravissimis religionis negotijs esse, in quibus Ecclesiæ totius salus & concordia vertuntur, fatetur non invitus. Non solum ratione ordinis hoc accidit, quem tamen haud secus in Ecclesia disciplina confervat ac in acie ars militaris, de quo ista Nazianzenus, ἀντιπολιτεία: nisi forte ordinem illuni vis quem nominat Paulus Colossenses 2.5, in quo omnis vitæ puritas honestatque confervatur.
units.tr: Nor does its importance shine less if ecclesiastical polity is considered in itself. For what Isocrates says of polity in general, that the civic constitution is the soul of the city (ψυχὴ πόλεως ἡ πολιτική), holding as much power in the commonwealth as the soul in the body, Scultingius applies to ecclesiastical polity in such a way that he calls it both the soul and the sinew and bond of the Church. Now I would not call ecclesiastical polity the soul of the Church, except in respect of the word; but as to the government of morals itself, I do not hesitate to call it the sinew and bond, since Lensaeus himself says the same. For when Thomas Cartwright had said that the Church can exist no less without discipline than a city without a wall or a garden without a hedge, he went on to say: "Indeed I think it rightly said that the discipline of the Church is more necessary than a wall to a city or a hedge to a garden," and afterwards he compares it to the joint and sinew. Thomas Bilson agrees with this, and he admits, not unwillingly, that the English disputes about discipline concern not certain light trifles but the most grave matters of religion, on which the whole salvation and concord of the Church turn. This is not only because of order, which discipline preserves in the Church no less than the art of war preserves order in an army. Of this Nazianzen says, ἀντιπολιτεία [counter-polity]: unless perhaps you mean that very order which Paul names in Colossians 2.5, in which all purity and honesty of life is preserved.

units.la: Atque hinc perspicere promptum est, quantum jam hodie Anglicanorum Episcoporum peccatum sit, qui disciplinam ab ipso Christo institutam adulterando, non murum tantum vineæ Dei dejecerunt, quod tamen immane quiddam habet, Psalm.80.12.13. sed & artus & nervos Ecclesiæ etiam inciderunt, negotium illud in quo salus Ecclesiæ, & concordia vertitur, male administrarunt; ipsi u: ordinis denique, imo morum probitatis retinæ calum sustulerunt. Atque quam longe lateque (proh dolor) proftrpit hoc malum: accommodandum hic enim, illud Lamberti Danæi est. Nul-
units.tr: And from this it is easy to see how great the sin of the English bishops now is, who, by corrupting discipline instituted by Christ himself, have not only thrown down the wall of the vineyard of God, which is nonetheless a monstrous thing (Psalm 80.12-13), but have also cut off the joints and sinews of the Church. They have mismanaged that matter on which the salvation and concord of the Church turn; they have finally taken away the very mark of order and even the integrity of morals. And how far and wide (alas) this evil spreads! For here that saying of Lambert Daneau fits: Nul-

units.la: Orat. ad civ. Trimontis Percus. In Math. Hom. 83.
units.tr: Oration to the citizens of Trimontium, Percus. On Matthew, Homily 83.
Chapter 13, p. 515.

units.la: De Moderat. in disciplina. libi gravius ab hominib° peccatur & periculosius erratur quàm in politicis: quae integras Nationes, provincias, regna, publica politicorum errata peruadunt. Hoc cum in charissima Anglia per Episcopos jam hodie factum boni pijque lugeant: quis eos qui remedium suspirant levitataris arguat, ut ipse interim levis non sit? Naso hoc adunco suspendit R. Banc.qui Allo'rogico invento nostro inesse dicit(in quib ⁹ ab eis dissidemus) omnino nihil, quod momenti boni alicujus, aut substantiae sit. Plus vero fervet imo furit Lous. Invectam (inquit) a Puritanis disciplinam, ut impurum erroris & malitiae foetum, ut labem omnis ordinis, ut perniciem venustatis, ut charitatis pestem, & ut omnium quae in Ecclesia habentur sacra cladem at̨ ruinam detestari debemus. Horrendum quod dicis, sed cum horrenda experientia comprobatum non sit, nae ex horrendo odio potius, quam ulla alia horrenda causa dictum est.
units.tr: On moderation in discipline. Nothing is sinned against more grievously by men, and no error is more dangerous, than in political matters, which overwhelm whole nations, provinces, and kingdoms with the public errors of politicians. Since good and pious men now lament that this is done by the bishops in dearest England, who will accuse those who sigh for a remedy of levity, so long as he himself is not light? Richard Bancroft scorns this with a hooked nose, saying that our invention of an "Allo-logical" is (in which we dissent from them) wholly without any good or substantial moment. But Lewis Invectam [a bishop] rages even more fiercely, saying: "We ought to detest the discipline introduced by the Puritans as an impure brood of error and malice, as the stain of all order, as the destruction of beauty, as the plague of charity, and as the ruin and wreck of all the sacred things which are held in the Church." It is a dreadful thing you say, but since it has not been proven by dreadful experience, it was said out of dreadful hatred rather than from any other dreadful cause.

units.la: 2. Iam vero si in oculi Ecclesias reformatas circumferantur, ubiq; protestatur Deus, ut apud Michaiam olim 6. 3. quid fecit tibi hoc disciplinae institutum meum popule mi testificare contra illud. Quasi vero (inquit R. Bancroftus.) H.Bullingerus in Epistola sua quadam, data Mart. 10. Anno 1574. & Rodolphus Gualterus in literis ad Episcopa Lodinensem, & Elienfem, & Gantesius quidam alij oculati, fideq; digni testes de miserabili Ecclesiarum reformatarum conditione, & disciplinae presbyterialis quam invexit confusione, satis testificati non sint? Quid mihi aut Gualtherum aut Gantesium obtrudis, quum forte Hadrianus Saravia (ipse hostis) noster est? Quod ad Bullingerum, ex illius testimonio si modo verum sit, hoc tantum liquet, in Ecclesijs reformatis morum corruptelas esse: sed ad hoc probandum nullius quidem testimonio opus erat: quis enim dubitat? Apparet hinc tamen, inquis, non eos fructus ubi recipitur disciplinam vestram dare, quos nobis productueram esse si reciperetur tanto hiatu pollicemini, cum in Humili Motione, tum in vestra Disciplinae Ecclesiasticae Defensione. Quid tum postea? Sic nec Euangelium ipsum quod prositemur, eos luculentos fructus profert ubi recipitur, quos tamen adversus papistas sepositâ hominum vitiositate, naturaliter ab eo germinare dicimus.
units.tr: 2. Now indeed, if we look about in the reformed Churches, God protests everywhere, as once through Micah: "O my people, what have I done to you, or in what have I wearied you? Testify against it" (Micah 6.3). "As if indeed" (says Richard Bancroft) "Heinrich Bullinger in a certain letter of his, dated 10 March 1574, and Rudolf Gualter in letters to the bishops of Lincoln and Ely, and certain Ghent men, eyewitnesses worthy of faith, had not sufficiently testified to the wretched condition of the reformed Churches and the confusion of the presbyterial discipline which they introduced?" Why do you thrust Gualter or the Ghent men upon me, when perhaps Hadrian Saravia (himself our enemy) is on hand? As to Bullinger, from his testimony, if it is indeed true, this alone is clear: that there are corruptions of morals in the reformed Churches. But to prove this there was no need of anyone's testimony: for who doubts it? Yet you say that it appears from this that those fruits do not follow where your discipline is received, which you promised with such great boasting would follow if it were received, both in the Humble Motion and in your Defence of Ecclesiastical Discipline. What then?
