Thus neither does the very Gospel which we profess bring forth those splendid fruits where it is received, which yet we say naturally spring from it against the Papists, setting aside the wickedness of men.

units.la: Aliquos illud semper proferre, adversus papistas satis esse putamus: sed sic & disciplina etiam semper aliquos profert, cur non & hoc adversus illius adversarios satis idoneum responsum erit? Certe cum huc usque pares simus, quod papistis responderi a nostris assolet, personarum non fidei fructus illos amaros esse, quibus Euangelium aggravant quod profitemur: id ipsum Bancrofto eandem calumniam adversus disciplinam interquenti, quam adversus doctrinam illi, respondere promptum est, personis non ipsi disciplinae Ecclesiarum reformatarum labes correptelasque attribuendas. Atque hic illud Obedi prophetae meminisse aequum erat. Annon & nos vj estis, & ut peccata cum vobis sint, coram Deo Domino vestro, 2. Chron. 28.
units.tr: We think it is enough against the Papists to bring forward that some always bring forth fruits from it: but discipline too always brings forth some, so why will this not be a sufficiently fitting answer against its adversaries? Certainly, since we are equal so far, the reply our people usually make to the Papists, that those bitter fruits are the fault of persons, not of faith, by which they weigh down the Gospel we profess, can readily be given to Bancroft, who urges the same calumny against discipline as against doctrine: the blemishes and corruptions of the reformed Churches' discipline are to be attributed to persons, not to discipline itself. And here it was fitting to recall that saying of the prophet Oded: "Are not you also guilty before the LORD your God, you who are with you?" (2 Chron. 28.)

units.la: 10. Extorquet lachrimas inquit Bridgesius Ecclesiarum re-formatarum deformitas, prætextu, reformationis in eas inuecta: Ecclesia nostra multò melior. Lamia es ô bone senex. Imo verè [illegible, ~6 letters] Laodicenus ille, qui de Ecclesiæ suæ statu gloriatur, cum tamen maximè miserabilis sit, Apocalipsi. 3.17. Etenim Ecclesia sub papatu latitans, Pergami, Ecclesia a temporibus Wiclephi renascens, Thiatiræ, Lutherana, Sardicenæ, Helvetica & reformata, Philadelphiæ, Anglia vero Laodicea [illegible, ~6 letters] est, ut in Brightmano videre licet. Inspicienda igitur Laodicea quasi speculum est, quo maculas nostras deprehēdamus, sic & non aliter, quàm deformis Ecclesiæ nostræ facies sit, quàm Ecclesiarum reformatarum spiritus sancti judicio pulchra, intelligemus: nusquam etenim nisi ad verbi divini speculum facici maculæ internoscuntur, Iacob. 1.23. quid autem? In Philadelphia quasi [illegible, ~4 letters], Ecclesijs reformatis quasi [illegible, ~6 letters] nihil culpari invenimus, in Laodicea verò ac proinde in Anglia, omnia. Cur in reformatis nihil culpatur, cum in ijs corruptelas esse; satis manifestum sit? Ratio jam nuper reddita est, quia hæ personarum sunt, non doctrinæ aut disciplinæ. Cur in Anglia culpantur omnia? Non respectu doctrinæ, in Laodicea etenim sicut in Anglia fidelem se & veracem testem Christus exhibuit, Apocalyps. 3.14. Disciplina igitur Anglicana totum mali onus sustinet: Loquitur enim Spiritus Sanctus (ut rectè Brightmanus) de communi forma externaque facie Ecclesiæ, qualis nimirum est, non tam sui gratia, quàm administratione Angelorum, quæ sic quidè est instituta ut qui rem æquis oculis considerat, illi merito videatur ab omni virtute vacua & inanis. Desinat itaque Bridgesius Ecclesiarum reformatarum mala, quasi reformationis prætextu inuecta, effusis lachrimis deplorare, morbos verò intestinos Angliæ siccis oculis prætərire, quasi aut nulli essent, aut disciplinæ pharmaco leviores redditi: cum & gravissimos detegat Christus, & eos disciplinæ corruptioni ascribat. Desinat etiam Bancroftus, Ecclesiarum reformatarum næuos, disciplinæ imputare, quos non eis ipse imputat Spiritus Sanctus, ut qui a privatis personis duntaxat oriantur. Atquè sane utramque columniam, tum Bridgesianam tum Bancroftianum, Iohannes ille Bodinus refutat, vir [illegible, ~5 letters], & qui cum absque affectu scribit, Bartholomeo Keckermano, sanum quid & admirabile habere videtur. Ita is igitur de disciplina Genevensi. Quorum illud (inquit) laudabile est, si quid usquam gentium, quodque Rempublicam efficit, si non opibus & imperij magnitudine, certè virtute ac pietate florentem: illa nempe pontificum censura, quâ nihil maius aut divinius cogitari potuit ad coercendas hominum cupiditates, & ea vitia, quæ legibus humanis & judicijs emendari nullo modo possunt. Hæc tamen coercitio ad Christi normam dirigitur, latenter primùm & amicè, deinde paulò acerbiùs, tunc nisi pareas, sequitur interdictio sacrorum gravis & efficax, interdictionem animadversio Magistratus. Ita fit, ut quæ legibus nusquam vindicantur. [?]indicantur, illic sine vi ac tumultu coercentur. Igitur nulla meretricia, nulle ebrietates, nulla saltationes, nulli mendici, nulli otiosi in illa civitate reperiuntur. Haec ille: ex quibus constat, coruptelarū, disciplinam reformatam, inimicam non amicam, falsem non fautricem esse: quod si verum non esset, os tamen Bancrofto obthurat merito, corruptelarum in Anglia chaos illud, numero plurium, noxâ acriorum, quarum culpam disciplina Hierarchica ementita, reatumque sustinet.
units.tr: 10. Bridges says that the deformity of the reformed Churches extorts tears, under the pretext of a reformation introduced among them: "Our Church is much better." You are a bogey, good old man. Indeed, truly that [illegible] Laodicean, who boasts of the state of his own Church, though he is most wretched, (Revelation 3.17). For the Church hiding under the papacy is Pergamos; the Church reviving from the time of Wycliffe is Thyatira; the Lutheran is Sardis; the Helvetic and reformed is Philadelphia; but England is [illegible] Laodicea, as may be seen in Brightman. Laodicea, therefore, is to be examined as a kind of mirror, in which we may detect our stains; and thus, and in no other way, we shall understand how deformed the face of our Church is, and how beautiful the reformed Churches are in the judgment of the Holy Spirit. For nowhere except in the mirror of the divine Word are stains recognised (James 1.23). But what then? In Philadelphia, as it were, [illegible], we find nothing to blame in the reformed Churches; but in Laodicea, and therefore in England, everything. Why is nothing blamed in the reformed Churches, when it is sufficiently plain that there are corruptions in them? The reason has just been given: these are faults of persons, not of doctrine or discipline. Why is everything blamed in England? Not with respect to doctrine: for in Laodicea, as in England, Christ presents himself as the faithful and true witness (Revelation 3.14). So the English discipline bears the whole burden of evil. For the Holy Spirit speaks (as Brightman rightly says) of the common form and external face of the Church, which is such not so much for its own sake as for the administration of the angels; which indeed is so instituted that to one who considers the matter with an even eye it seems rightly empty of all virtue. Let Bridges therefore cease to lament with flowing tears the evils of the reformed Churches, as if introduced under the pretext of reformation, while passing over with dry eyes the inward diseases of England, as if they either did not exist or had been made lighter by the remedy of discipline; since Christ himself lays bare the most grievous of them and ascribes them to the corruption of discipline. Let Bancroft also cease to impute to discipline the blemishes of the reformed Churches, which the Holy Spirit does not impute to them, since they arise only from private persons. And truly John Bodin refutes both calumnies, Bridges' and Bancroft's, a man who, since he writes without partiality, seems to have something sound and admirable, and who, as Bartholomew Keckermann has it, writes thus of the Genevan discipline: "The first thing is praiseworthy, if anywhere among the nations there is something which makes a commonwealth flourish, if not in wealth and magnitude of empire, certainly in virtue and piety: namely that censure of the ministers, than which nothing more great or divine could be imagined for restraining human desires and those vices which can in no way be corrected by human laws and judgments." Yet this restraint is directed to the rule of Christ: "first secretly and in a friendly way, then somewhat more sharply; then, if you do not obey, there follows a grave and effective interdiction from the sacraments, and to the interdiction the punishment of the magistrate. Thus it comes about that those things which are nowhere punished by laws are there restrained without force or tumult. Therefore there are no prostitutes, no drunkards, no dancers, no beggars, no idlers in that city." So he; from which it is established that the reformed discipline is hostile to corruptions, not friendly, and not their supporter. But even if this were not true, the chaos of corruptions in England, more in number and more harmful in kind, whose blame and guilt is borne by the feigned hierarchical discipline, rightly stops the mouth of Bancroft.

units.la: 3. Superest scrupulus Hadriani Saravie vel augurium potius: exuta etenim Theologi persona, pro eo quod disputare debuerat, agit aurusipicem. Nuper admodum (inquit) haec nova gubernationis forma reiectis Episcopis introducta est: quid paritura sit, nondum sciri potest. Nulla ratio quid mali in ea lateat, & quàm sit adversus haereticos, factuosos, schismaticos, infirma, docere potest: stultorum experientiâ magistra opus est, quos illa, quae praeteritorum temporum est, nihil movet. Sed vereor ne sero doceat, quando accepto malo, frustra quaeretur remedium. Quod a me dictum non ita volo accipi, tanquam eam regiminis formam, quae in Ecclesiis reformatis conspicitur sublatam cupiam, nisi melior substituatur, sed eam utilem esse tantùm loco & tempori, sciri ab omnibus velim. Secundus a Calvino cum Beza Genevensem regit Ecclesiam in parva republica, quandiu in tranquillo statu degitur, omnia quidem bene se habent, &c. Audiat Lotus. Malè tu disciplinam reformatam quasi pestem execratus es: nulla hoc ratione adhuc doceri poterit, dicit Saravia. Audiat Bancroftus. Malè tu Genevensem disciplinam quasi corruptelarum idvectricem exagitasti; omnia adhuc Geneve se benè habere affirmat Saravia. Audiat denique Bridgesius. Absque causa Ecclesiarum reformatarum disciplinam deplorasti, eam loco & tempori harum Ecclesiarum utilem esse Saravia agnoscit. Quod verò de nescio quo malo fato divinatur Saravia pro futuro; respondemus cum Tertulliano. Iniquum est quum de manifestis condemnare non potestis, de occultis praedamnare. Quid quod hoc praedamnatio Saravica, aperto ipsius Spiritus Sancti vaticinio praedamnetur? Bene adhuc se omnia Geneve habere dicis, rectè tu quidem; sic enim omnia Geneve, quasi bene se habentia collaudat Christus, in Geneve Ecclesia nempè Philadelphiensi Apocalyps.3.8. Atqui idem Christus qui omnia adhuc optimè se ibi habere dicit; omnia quoque usque ad finem optimè se ibi habitura praenunciat. Non etenim hujus Ecclesiae corona marcescet unquam.v.11. Columna illa in domo Dei sui est,v.12. Nomenque in fronte sua nova Ierusalem inscriptum gerit, quò certior fiat, clavem quam Davidis gerit,v.7, id est non doctrinam tantummodo, verùm & disciplinam etiam, quae clavis nomine adumbrari in sacris solet, ad ipsam usque Iudaeorum Ecclesiam perduraturam, & unà cum eâ consociatam iri, Atquè observandum est hanc promissionem Ecclesijs reformatis propriam esse, ex quo conjicere promptum est, non tam eorum doctrinam, quàm disciplinam eâdem prænuniri. Conspirat in doctrinâ quidem cum Philadelphiensi Laodicea, & ως ἐν τῷ νῷ, cum Geneva Angliæ, sic ut ob disciplinam solam accidat, ut hujus participes non sit. Quid dixi? Imò ob corruptam disciplinam non solùm hujus promissionis expers Angliæ, sed & horrendæ comminationi contrariæ obnoxia, ni resipiscat. Fiet ut ex ore meo evomam te: id est, te desolatam reddam in perpetuum: non enim cogitandum, Christum unquam ad suum vomitum reversurum.. Videsis igitur Hadriane Saravia, mens tibi quàm levis fuerit: quum id disciplinæ Genevensi falsò ominatus sis, quod disciplinæ Anglicanæ tuæ eventurum, ipsemet prædicit Christus. Atquè de politeiâs Ecclesiasticæ præstantia secunda, nempè utilitate hæc satis dixisse sit.
units.tr: 3. There remains the scruple of Hadrian Saravia, or rather a kind of augury: setting aside the part of a theologian, he plays the soothsayer instead of arguing as he ought. Very recently, he says, this new form of government, with the bishops rejected, has been introduced. What it will bring forth cannot yet be known. Reason can show what evil lies hidden in it, and how far it is weak against heretics, factious and schismatic men; but experience of fools is needed as a teacher, and they are not moved by that which belongs to past times. But I fear it will teach too late, when the harm has been received and the remedy is sought in vain. What I have said I do not want taken as if I desired that form of government which is seen in the reformed Churches to be abolished, unless a better one be substituted; I only want everyone to know that it is useful for its place and time. Calvin's successor, Beza, governs the Church of Geneva in a small commonwealth; as long as it lives in a peaceful state, all things indeed go well, etc. Let Lotus hear this. You have cursed the reformed discipline badly, as if it were a plague; Saravia says that it cannot yet be shown to be so by any reasoning. Let Bancroft hear this. You have badly attacked the Geneva discipline as if it were a bearer of corruptions; Saravia affirms that all things are still going well at Geneva. Let Bridges finally hear this. You have lamented the discipline of the reformed Churches without cause; Saravia acknowledges that it is useful for these Churches in their place and time. But as for what Saravia foretells for the future, divining some evil fate that I know not what, we answer with Tertullian: It is unfair, when you cannot condemn what is manifest, to pre-condemn what is hidden. What of the fact that this Saravian pre-condemnation is itself pre-condemned by the plain prophecy of the Holy Spirit? You say that all things are still going well at Geneva, and you say rightly; for Christ praises all things at Geneva as going well, in the Church of Philadelphia, in the Apocalypse 3.8. Yet the same Christ who says that all things there are still going very well also foretells that they will go very well there up to the end. For the crown of this Church shall never wither (v.11). That pillar is in the house of his God (v.12), and bears on its forehead the name of the new Jerusalem, so that it may be made more certain that the key which he holds of David (v.7), that is, not doctrine only but also discipline, which is usually signified in holy writ by the name of key, will endure even to the Jewish Church itself, and will be joined with it. It must be observed that this promise belongs to the reformed Churches, from which it is easy to conjecture that it is foretold of their discipline, not so much of their doctrine. In doctrine indeed it agrees with the Philadelphian Laodicea, and as it were in mind [ὡς ἐν τῷ νῷ], with Geneva and England; so that only on account of discipline does it happen that England does not share in this promise. What have I said? Rather, on account of its corrupt discipline England is not only without a share in this promise, but also liable to the dreadful threat contrary to it, unless it repents. I will spew you out of my mouth (Apoc. 3.16), that is, I will make you desolate forever; for it is not to be thought that Christ will ever return to his vomit. See then, Hadrian Saravia, how light your mind was, since you foolishly prophesied for the Geneva discipline what Christ himself foretells will befall your Anglican discipline. And so, concerning the second excellence of the ecclesiastical polity, namely its usefulness, let enough have been said.

units.la: CAP. 9. De necessitate Disciplinæ Eccles. Thesis prima, eam non esse rem indifferentem.
units.tr: CAP. 9. On the necessity of Church Discipline. Thesis first, that it is not a matter of indifference.

units.la: SVPEREST tertia, Ecclesiasticæ politeias Necessitas, de quâ hæ sequentes Theses considerandæ. Primò, Ecclesiasticæ Politeias necessitatem negativè efferimus, sic ut necessaria sit, quâ τὸ ἀναγκαῖον τῆς ἀδιαφορίας [?] opponitur, id est, res indifferens non est, quæ tamen adversariorum alicubi videtur esse sententia. Iohannes Whitgiftus ita. Non in eo controversia vertitur, an multa à reformatoribus commemorata, commodè temporibus Apostolorum in usu fuerint, & quibusdam in locis commodè iam recipi possint; imò & commodè recipiantur etiam in quibusdam Ecclesijs reformatis. Nihil horum negatur, neque ut falso traducimur, nobis id arrogamus, ut Ecclesias alias, vel improbemus, vel condemnemus, in ordine illo, quem tanquam suo statui accommodatissimum receperunt. Rursus, de Pastoum selectionibus agens, quæ res in Politeiâ Ecclesiasticâ fundamentalis quædam est. Alias Ecclesias non condemnamus (inquit) quæ ordinem diversum in electionibus suis sequuntur. Dico nullam certam eligendi formam in Scripturis præscriptam esse: unde cuique Ecclesiæ id facere licet, quod sibi maxime esse convenienς judicabit. Georgius Dovvnamus ita. Non ita functionem episcopalem de jure divino esse teneo, quasi nullum aliud gubernationis genus legitimum esset: neque ordinationem ita ab Episcopo pendere, ac si in Ecclesijs reformatis ministri nulli essent. Iob. Bridgesius, in medio relinquit liberum, utrum disciplinam necessariam an indifferentem censeamus necnè: hic ita loquitur. Si necessariam statuamus, aut superioritas Episcoporum Episco[?]um agnoscenda est, aut patres primi condemnandi, qui illam ab ipsis Apostolorum temporibus exercuerunt. Si vero necessariam statuere non libet, sed rem indifferentem quae variari & mutari potest: nec conedemnare par est Ecclesias illas, aut vero etiam de eis male aut sentiri aut loqui, quae diversa gubernationis forma utuntur, nec illas vicissim nos.
units.tr: There remains a third thesis, on the necessity of ecclesiastical polity, which the following theses are to consider. First, we state the necessity of ecclesiastical polity negatively, so that it is necessary in the sense that it is opposed to the necessary as opposed to the indifferent [τὸ ἀναγκαῖον τῆς ἀδιαφορίας] [?]; that is, it is not a thing indifferent, though this seems to be the opinion of our opponents in some places. John Whitgift writes thus: The controversy does not turn on whether the many things commended by the reformers were fittingly in use in the times of the Apostles, and whether they can now fittingly be received in some places, indeed whether they are fittingly received in some reformed Churches as well. None of this is denied, nor do we, as we are falsely accused, arrogate to ourselves the right to disapprove or condemn other Churches for the order which they have received as most suited to their own state. Again, when speaking of the selection of ministers, a matter which is something fundamental in ecclesiastical polity: We do not condemn other Churches (he says) which follow a different order in their elections. I say that no fixed form of election is prescribed in the Scriptures; so each Church may do whatever it judges to be most suitable for itself. George Downame writes thus: I do not hold that the episcopal function is of divine right, as if no other lawful kind of government existed; nor that ordination depends so much on the bishop, as if there were no ministers at all in the reformed Churches. John Bridges leaves it open whether we should judge discipline to be necessary or indifferent, and speaks thus: If we hold it to be necessary, then either the superiority of bishops must be acknowledged, or the first fathers must be condemned, who exercised it from the very times of the Apostles. But if we do not wish to hold it necessary, but a matter of indifference which can be varied and changed, then it is not right to condemn those Churches which use a different form of government, nor to think or speak ill of them, nor they of us in turn.

units.la: Recte quidem disciplinam rem indifferentem esse agnoscit, si necessaria non sit, & si propter ejusdem variationem Ecclesiae aliae condemnandae non sint, quo & illa tendunt Panormitani: Continentia (inquit) non est in clericis saecularibus de substantia ordinis, nec de jure divino, quia alias Graeci peccarent, nec excusaret eos consuetudo, quia illa non valet contra legem divinam. Exultat Stapletonus & Cornelius Scultingius, quod Episcopi Anglicani, per annos 40. Catholicorum disciplinam retinuerint, invitis Puritanis & Ecclesijs reformatis: contra quam politeiam fremunt (inquiunt) nequicquam Genevenses, Heydelbergenses, aliique Puritani. Scelus igitur Episcoporum Anglicanorum hoc quantum est? Domi vineam domini vastarunt, tragedias horrendas excitarunt, pastoribus orbarunt Ecclesias, carceres servis Dei implerunt: mare denique Anglicanum, quod ante a Iohanne praedictum Apocal. 15. 2. miscueruut igni: foras vero & sinum Philistaeorum gaudio referserunt, & Ecclesias Iesu Christi reformatas suffuderunt pudore, fremitu inquietarunt: quum interim disciplinam illam pro qua tam atrociter saeviunt, rem mere indifferentem esse concedant, Ecclesias diversam sequentes, condemnandas non esse putent, regimen illud denique contrarium, pro quo miseros Puritanos ita divexant, legitimum fateantur.
units.tr: He rightly acknowledges that discipline is a matter of indifference if it is not necessary, and if other Churches are not to be condemned on account of its variation; to this the Panormitan also tends: Continence (he says) is not of the substance of the order of secular clergy, nor of divine right; otherwise the Greeks would sin, and custom would not excuse them, since custom does not avail against divine law. Stapleton and Cornelius Scultingius exult that the English bishops have for forty years retained the discipline of the Catholics, against the will of the Puritans and the reformed Churches: Against this polity (they say) the Genevans, the Heidelbergers, and other Puritans rage in vain. How great, then, is the crime of these English bishops? At home they have laid waste the Lord's vineyard, stirred up horrible tragedies, bereft the Churches of ministers, and filled the prisons with the servants of God. Finally, the English sea, which John had foretold in Revelation 15:2 as mingled with fire, they have indeed opened to the joy of the Philistines and to the shame and disquiet of the reformed Churches of Jesus Christ; and yet, while they rage so savagely for that discipline, they concede that it is a matter purely indifferent, they think that Churches which follow a different one are not to be condemned, and finally they confess that the contrary government, for which they so cruelly harass the wretched Puritans, is lawful.

units.la: At similia a vobis de disciplina etiam vestra coceduntur dicit Bancroftus. Theodorus siquidem Beza, a Iohanne Whitgifto, propter πολυπραγμοσύνη in re disciplinaria sua obiurgatus, ita tevrendi illius Antistitis animum mulcet, per literas ad eum datas Mart. 8. 1591. Non compellimus Ecclesias contrarium sentientes ad ordinem nostrum: nec de eis aliter sentimus, atque aut eorum pietas & dignitas, aut mutua fraternitas requirit. Procul absit a nobis arrogantia &c. Quis aliquod nobis in ullam Ecclesiam imperium tribuit? Procul absit ut putemus (servatis substantialibus) nihil concedendum antiquitati esse, nihil consuetudini, nihil circumstantiis locorum, temporum personarum, &c. Rursus in libro adversus Hadrianum Saravium postquam de tyrannide Episcoporum papalium locutus esset, hanc exceptionem subiungit, p. 126. Neque tamen propterea, huius tyrannidis, omnes Archiepiscopos seu Episcopos hodie vocatos accusamus. Quae enim fuerit haec arrogantia? Imo multos sic hodie appellatos, modo sanctissimorum illorum Episcoporum exemplum imitentur, & tam miserè deformatam domum Dei, ad amussim, ex verbi divini regulâ, pro viribus instaurent, ut Ecclesiae Christianae veros pastores, cur non agnoscamus? observemus? & omnia omni reverentia prosequamur? nedum, ut, (quod salsissime & impudentissime, nonnulli nobis objiciunt) cuiquam usquam Ecclesiae sequendum nostrum peculiare exemplum praescribimus, imperitissimorum illorum similes, qui nihil, nisi quod ipsi agunt, rectum putant. Et ad eundem sensum paulo ante pag. 111. Quod si nunc Anglicanae Ecclesiae instauratae, suorum Episcoporum & Archiepiscoporum authoritate suffultae persistant: quemadmodum hoc illi nostra memoria contigit, ut huius ordinis homines non tantum insignes Dei martyres, sed etiam praestantissimos pastores ac doctores habuerit: fruatur same ista singulari Dei beneficentia, quae utinam ut sit perpetua. Citat & ista Bancroftus alibi, ubi confitetur, non nisi sub conditione, Dominum Bezam haec locutum fuisse: sic enim habet, Venia Bezae danda est, ut suum SI interponat. Quod si nunc inquit Anglicanae Ecclesiae, &c.
units.tr: But Bancroft says that similar concessions are made by you about your own discipline. For Theodore Beza, rebuked by John Whitgift for his meddlesomeness [πολυπραγμοσύνη] in disciplinary matters, soothes the spirit of that reverend prelate in a letter sent to him on 8 March 1591: We do not compel Churches that think otherwise to our order, nor do we think of them otherwise than either their piety and dignity or mutual brotherhood requires. Far be arrogance from us, etc. Who has granted us any power over any Church? Far be it from us to think (the substantials being preserved) that nothing should be conceded to antiquity, nothing to custom, nothing to the circumstances of places, times, persons, etc. Again, in a book against Hadrian Saravia, after speaking of the tyranny of the papal bishops, he adds this qualification, p. 126: Yet we do not on account of this tyranny accuse all those who are today called archbishops or bishops. For what arrogance would that be? Indeed, let the many so called today imitate the example of those most holy bishops, and with all their might restore the house of God, so miserably deformed, to the plumb line, by the rule of the divine Word, so that we may acknowledge, observe, and with all reverence follow them as the true ministers of the Christian Church. Why should we not? Nor, as some most saucily and shamelessly object to us, do we prescribe to any Church that our own peculiar example must be followed, like those most unskilled men who think nothing right except what they themselves do. And to the same effect a little earlier, p. 111: But if now the English Church, restored and supported by the authority of its bishops and archbishops, persists, just as it has happened in our memory that this order of men has had not only remarkable martyrs of God, but also most excellent ministers and teachers, let it enjoy this singular beneficence of God, which I wish may be perpetual. Bancroft also cites these words elsewhere, where he admits that Dr. Beza spoke them only under a condition: for the text reads, Beza's pardon is to be granted, if he inserts his IF. But if now, he says, the English Church, etc.

units.la: Atque hae sunt illae concessiones Bezianae de quibus tanquam victores triumphant Bancroftus, Bilsonus, Saravia, Downamus, advetsarijque reliqui, ut in quibus causam totam sibi a Beza tributam esse jactitant. At quid si istas pares illis esse quas nuper citavimus, concederemus? Ecquid lucrarentur aliud, quam Bezam suis parem esse? Bezam in hisce concessionibus, causam ipsam sibi concessisse dicunt: videant igitur illos suos nuper commemoratos, Whitgiftu, Downamu, Bridgesium & causam suam concessisse nobis. Atque sane si Beza per modum approbationis haec locutus fuisset, ut sua locuti sunt illi vestri, & sibi contradixisset (quod criminatur Bancroftus) & totam causam tradidisset, (quod caesatur Bilsonus) sicut & illos ucstros aut sibi aut suis contradixisse, & totam causam nobis tradidisse dicimus. At quam longum intervallum? Nusquam enim Beza Angliam, quod ad factum temeratae disciplinae, condemnandam esse negat. Nusquam Hierachiam Anglicanam legitimam esse concedit. Nusquam denique rem disciplinariam aut appellari a quoquam permittit indifferentem. Non compellendas Ecclesias dicit ad ordinem Genevensem, nempe quia Geneuensis est. Non peculiare exemplum suum aliis Ecclesiis praescribere affirmat, ut illud eis sequendum sit: nempe quia suum, & sibi peculiare est. Non condemnat eos qui aliter atque Genevenses agunt: nempe ad morem imperitissimorum eorum, qui actum suum qua suum est ita urgent, ut nihil praeterea rectum existiment. Quid ni? Imperium enim in Ecclesias alias Geneva nullum habet? & arrogantes Dei servos esse non oportet, ut eis imperare velint, in quos imperium a Deo concessum nullum habent. Cedendum aliquid antiquitati dicit, & pecem fraternam cum eis qui contra sentiunt colendam, & pios Episcopos tanquam fideles pastores reverendos affirmat, eisque obediendum esse. Quid ni? Indulgere etenim eis modestia Christiana movet, qui antiquitatatis errore licet abripiantur, in aliis fundamentalibus tamen orthodoxi sunt: & suadet charitas pacis vinculum rumpendum nonesse propter nævos nonnullos, quandiu catholici fidei unitas integra manet; & ad postremum iubet pietas reverendos illos esse, & ut pastoribus obediendos, qui revera se fideles præbent in domo Dei ædificandâ, aut locum pastorum obtinent, licet Archiepiscopatum aut Episcopatum illegitimum, illegitimè unâ possideant, errore occæcati. Dicit postremo: Fruatur per me Anglia, singulari Dei beneficentia, licet Archiepiscopali & Episcopali authoritate suffulta. Quidni? Non enim dicit fruatur hâc disciplinâ, sed fruatur hâc Dei beneficentiâ; si de disciplina non dicit, per me approbetur, sed per me frui toleretur, penes quem nec authoritas exauthorandi, nec potestas emendandi residet. Hoc dum facit, tantum abest quòd approbet, ut etiam tecte condemnet: quòd si tecte non vetaret, dum disciplinam Genevensem præfert, dissuadet saltem Anglicanam. Tertullianus sic! Quod permittitur, spontaneam habet permissionis suæ causam. Non propterea appetenda sunt quædam, quia non vetantur, etsi quodammodo vetantur, cum alia aliis præferantur. Præiatio enim superioris, dissuasio est inferiorum. Hactenus de thesi prima de politeiæ necessitate.
units.tr: These then are those Bezan concessions over which Bancroft, Bilson, Saravia, Downame, and the rest of our opponents triumph as victors, boasting that they have won the whole cause from Beza. But what if we were to concede that those passages which we have just cited are equal to them? What would they gain, except that Beza is equal to their own men? They say that in these concessions Beza conceded the cause itself to them; let them therefore look to it that their own Whitgift, Downame, and Bridges, whom we have just mentioned, have conceded their cause to us. And indeed, if Beza had spoken these words by way of approval, as your men spoke their own words, and had contradicted himself (which Bancroft charges) and had surrendered the whole cause (which Bilson complains of), we would say that your men too contradicted themselves and their own side, and surrendered the whole cause to us. But how great is the distance! For Beza nowhere denies that England is to be condemned for the fact of violated discipline. Nowhere does he concede that the English hierarchy is lawful. Nowhere, finally, does he allow anyone to call disciplinary matter indifferent. He says that Churches are not to be compelled to the Genevan order, namely because it is Genevan. He affirms that he does not prescribe his own peculiar example to other Churches so that it must be followed, namely because it is his own and peculiar to him. He does not condemn those who act otherwise than the Genevans do, namely in the manner of those most unskilled men who press their own action so insistently, because it is their own, that they think nothing else right. Why not? For does Geneva have no authority over other Churches? And God's servants ought not to be arrogant, so as to wish to command those over whom they have no authority granted by God. He says that something must be yielded to antiquity, that fraternal peace is to be cultivated with those who think otherwise, and he affirms that pious bishops are to be revered as faithful ministers, and that they are to be obeyed. Why not? For Christian modesty moves us to be indulgent toward those who, though carried away by the error of antiquity, are nonetheless orthodox in other fundamentals; and charity urges that the bond of peace is not to be broken on account of some blemishes, so long as the unity of the Catholic faith remains entire; and finally piety bids us revere and obey those ministers who in truth show themselves faithful in building the house of God, or hold the place of ministers, even if, blinded by error, they hold an archbishopric or bishopric illegitimately. Lastly he says: Let England, through me, enjoy this singular beneficence of God, though it is supported by archiepiscopal and episcopal authority. Why not? For he does not say, let it enjoy this discipline, but let it enjoy this beneficence of God; if he does not say of the discipline, let it be approved through me, but let it be tolerated through me, since he holds neither the authority to deauthorize nor the power to amend. In doing this, he is so far from approving that he even condemns covertly; and if he did not forbid it covertly, then, while he prefers the Genevan discipline, he at least dissuades from the English. Tertullian puts it thus: What is permitted has a spontaneous cause for its permission. Some things are not to be desired merely because they are not forbidden, even if in some way they are forbidden, since some things are preferred to others. For the preference of the superior is the dissuasion of the inferior. So far on the first thesis concerning the necessity of polity.

units.la: CAP. 10. Thesis secunda, quod Disciplina præcipitur in verbo.
units.tr: CAP. 10. Second thesis: that discipline is prescribed in the Word.

units.la: Secunda sequitur. Quum politeia Ecclesiastica res indifferens non sit: sequitur necessitatem præcepti & iuris illi tribuendam esse, eam nempe, quam ita describit Tertullianus. Quod præcipitur imperatur, quod imperatur necesse est fieri, si non fiat, pœnam habet. Ubi consilium datur, offerentis arbitrium est, ubi præceptum, necessitas est servientis. Atque huiusmodi necessitatem politeiæ inesse suo loco demonstrabitur libet hic tantum quasi de loco illo suscitari qui habetur, Heb. 6. 2. ubi principia religionis Christianæ sex recensentur, fides, pœnitentia, baptismus, impositio manuum, resurrectio à mortuis, & iudicium æternum. Quæritur quid hæc manuum impositio sibi velit? Sunt è nostris, qui electionem notari dicunt, ac per eam synecdochicè totam politeiam Ecclesiasticam insinuari opinantur. Hoc si verum sit, & de politeiâ doctrina quædam in scriptura tradita sit (id enim hic in ipsa manuum impositione dici videtur) & inter necessaria religionis Christianæ capita, ea recensetur. Id ipsum sequetur ex interpretatione Hierarchicorum, qui eam referunt ad Episcopalem quæ jam viget, adultorum confirmationem. At non etiam hæc confirmatio res disciplinaria quædam est? certe si hæc necessaria, & reliquæ partes disciplinariæ necessariæ etiam erunt. Neque quicquam hac interpretatione, Episcopali authoritati accedet: cum Bilsonus ipse confitetur, confirmatio
units.tr: The second thesis follows. Since ecclesiastical polity is not a matter of indifference, it follows that it must be ascribed the necessity of precept and law, namely the kind that Tertullian describes thus: What is prescribed is ordered; what is ordered must be done; if it is not done, there is a penalty. Where counsel is given, it is the choice of the one offering; where a precept is given, it is the necessity of the one serving. That such necessity belongs to polity will be shown in its proper place; here I wish only to raise, as it were in passing, the passage which is cited, Heb. 6. 2., where six principles of the Christian religion are listed: faith, repentance, baptism, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. The question is what this laying on of hands means. Some of our people say that election is signified, and they suppose that by this synecdoche the whole ecclesiastical polity is hinted at. If this is true, and some doctrine concerning polity is handed down in Scripture (for this seems to be spoken of here in the very laying on of hands), then it is counted among the necessary heads of the Christian religion. The same would follow from the interpretation of the hierarchists, who refer it to the episcopal confirmation of adults which now prevails. But is not this confirmation itself a certain disciplinary matter? Certainly, if this is necessary, the other disciplinary parts will be necessary too. Nor will this interpretation add anything to episcopal authority, since Bilson himself confesses that this confirmation belongs to the bishop by human right alone.

units.la: {y} Marginal fragments are illegible. firmationem istam, jure tantùm humano, Episcopo propriam esse. Atque sane jus istud humanum, injustum est: cum nulla hîc alia confirmatio stabiliatur, quàm quae Ecclesijs in reformatis ubique obtinet, in quibus adulti per presbyterium examinantur, populi consensu approbantur, & à tota Ecclesia speciali modo ut membra suae communionis recipiuntur,& ita quasi confirmantur, priusquam ad coenam Domini admittantur, mihi verò meaeque causae, istâ Hierarchicorum interpretatione accedunt alia duo.
units.tr: {y} Marginal fragments are illegible. Indeed that human right is unjust, since no other confirmation is established here than that which obtains everywhere in the reformed churches, in which adults are examined by the presbytery, approved by the consent of the people, and received by the whole Church in a special manner as members of its communion, and so are, as it were, confirmed before they are admitted to the Lord's Supper. But for me and for my cause, two other points follow from this interpretation of the hierarchists.

units.la: Primò, infirmum esse Georgi Downami [?] argumentum adversus Seniores Presbyteriales, si in nullo alio scripturae loco, Presbyter hujusmodi Seniorem notaret, quàm 1. Timoth. 5. 17. Quid enim? An ullo alio scripturae loco praeterquam in isto, confirmatio adultorum docetur, quam tamen necessariam dicitis? Secundò, arenosum esse non Georg. Downami solùm,sed & reliquorum Hierarchicorum fundamentum, ideo patribus in re disciplinaria credendum esse, quia per trecentos fere annos nihil mutarunt, nihil in disciplina corruperunt, quod ab Apostolis haberent acceptum. Quid enim? Annon hanc confirmationem quam hîc ab Apostolo traditam dicitis, adeo in ipsius Ecclesiae primordijs mutarant patres,ut haec manuum impositio infantibus daretur in ipso baptismo suo, sicut liquet ex illis testimonijs quae condensantur in Censura orientalium Ecclesiarum? Sed ut unde progressa est revertatur oratio,concludendum omnino ex Paulino loco isto, quo demumcunque sensu intelligatur, rem disciplinariam necessitate praecepti & iuris necessariam esse.
units.tr: First, the argument of George Downame against the presbyterial elders is weak, if the word presbyter does not denote an elder in any other passage of Scripture than 1 Tim. 5. 17. For what? Is confirmation of adults taught in any other passage of Scripture besides this one, which yet you call necessary? Second, the foundation not only of George Downame but also of the rest of the hierarchists is sandy, namely that the Fathers are to be believed in disciplinary matters because for nearly three hundred years they changed nothing and corrupted nothing in discipline that they had received from the Apostles. For what? Did not the Fathers so change this confirmation, which you say was handed down here by the Apostle, even in the very beginnings of the Church, that this laying on of hands was given to infants in their very baptism, as is clear from those testimonies which are gathered together in the Censure of the Eastern Churches? But that my discourse may return to where it set out, we must conclude from this Pauline passage, in whatever sense it is understood, that disciplinary matter is necessary by the necessity of precept and law.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CAP. II.

units.la: Argumenta adversariorum ab absurdo contra Thesim secund. primum,quod tum disciplina esset de fide,& pars Evangelij.
units.tr: The opponents' arguments from absurdity against the second thesis: first, that discipline would then be a matter of faith and a part of the Gospel.

units.la: ATqui ex hoc dogmate vestro (arguunt Hierarchici) multa absurda consequuntur. Quae nam obsecro? Primo (inquit Whitgiftus) hinc sequeretur disciplinam & de fide esse, & Evangelij partem esse, quod enim necessarium est obligat ad fidem. Quis hoc dubitat? nisi in dubium vocet quis, concertationes Theologorum de fide necne sint,quas adversus papatum instituunt, quil nonne quaeso disciplinaria res quaedam est? Certe primatus universalis,quem Iohannes Constantinopolitanus affectavit, universalis tantum Episcopatus erat,non qualis emersit,postea papatus: is enim adhuc caput non exercerat de quo tamen Gregorius Magnus non veretur affirmare. In isto scelesto vocabulo consentire, nihil est aliud quàm quàm fidem perdere. Rursus. Pacem nobis cum habebitis si prophani nominis superbiam declinatis juxta quod magister gentium dicit, ô Timotheé, depositum custodi, devitans profanas vocum novitates. Rursus, Non solus ego sed tota turbatur Ecclesia: quia piæ leges, quia venerandæ Synodi, quia ipsa Domini nostri Iesu Christi mandata super verbi atque pompatici cujusdam sermonis inventione turbantur. Rursus, In hac causa Evangeliorum ac canonum statuta humilitatis atque certitudinis virtute defendo. Rursus, Vos eandem causam illam dicere non debetis, quia si hanc æquanimitatem portamus, universæ Ecclesiæ fidem corrumpimus. Rursus, Pastorali constantia atque Apostolica authoritate suffulti, prædonem, irruentemque lupum excludite, & in dissipationem Ecclesiæ sævienti non cedite. Et quorsum tam multa ex Gregorio inquis? Quasi hæc singula causam nostram non intimè attingant? Iohannes Whitgift in Cartwrighto tanquam novum quid & inauditum explodit, quòd disciplinam de fide esse affirmarit, ideo quòd nulla certa aliqua regiminis Ecclesiastici forma in verbo præscripta sit. Imò Whitgifte eam regiminis formam in Timothei depositò contineri, in mandatis Christi reperiri, in Evangeliorum statutis tradi, Apostolica authoritate suffulciri Gregorius affirmat, quæ Archiepiscopatum tuum, & reliquam Anglicanam Hierarchiam subvertit funditus. Neque enim genere, sed gradu tantùm Constantinopolitanus & Anglicanus Episcopatus distat: usurpat uterque in collegas pares; tantum in hoc discrimen est, quod ille Universalis, hic Provincialis aut Diocesanus sit. Atqui quantitas iurisdictionis differentiam nullam specificam infert, dicit Sarabia; tam ille pater est qui unum, quam qui multos liberos habet; tam ille rex qui urbi quàm qui nationi imperat: ac proinde ex adverso, tam ille tyrannus qui in civitatem, quàm qui in regionem imperium affectat injustum.
units.tr: "But from your doctrine," the hierarchists argue, "many absurdities follow." "What are they, I beg you?" "First," says Whitgift, "it would follow from this that discipline is both a matter of faith and a part of the Gospel, for whatever is necessary binds us to faith." Who doubts this, unless someone would question whether the disputes of theologians against the papacy concern faith or not? Yet, I ask you, is not that dispute itself some matter of discipline? Certainly the universal primacy which John of Constantinople aspired to was only a universal episcopate, not the kind of papacy that later emerged; for he had not yet exercised that headship, which nonetheless Gregory the Great does not hesitate to affirm. "To consent to that wicked word is nothing other than to lose the faith." Again: "You will have peace with us if you avoid the pride of the profane name, as the teacher of the Gentiles says: O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding the profane novelties of words." Again: "Not I alone, but the whole Church is troubled, because the pious laws, because the venerable Synods, because the very commands of our Lord Jesus Christ are disturbed by the invention of a certain pompous word." Again: "In this cause I defend the statutes of the Gospels and of the canons by the virtue of humility and certainty." Again: "You ought not to say that the same cause is at stake, for if we bear this with equanimity, we corrupt the faith of the whole Church." Again: "Supported by pastoral constancy and apostolic authority, shut out the robber and the wolf who rushes in, and do not yield to him as he rages toward the scattering of the Church." And why, you ask, do you bring up so much from Gregory? As if these individual points did not touch our cause closely! John Whitgift, in his attack on Cartwright, rejects as something new and unheard of the claim that discipline is a matter of faith, on the ground that no fixed form of church government is prescribed in the Word. Yet Gregory affirms that this form of government is contained in Timothy's deposit, is found in Christ's commands, is delivered in the statutes of the Gospels, and is upheld by apostolic authority; and this overthrows your archbishopric and the rest of the English hierarchy from the foundations. For the Constantinopolitan and the English bishoprics differ not in kind but only in rank: each claims authority over colleagues who are equals. The only difference is that the one is universal, the other provincial or diocesan. But the extent of jurisdiction, says Sarabia, introduces no specific difference: a man who has one child is a father just as much as one who has many; a king who rules a city is a king just as one who rules a nation; and conversely, one who seeks unjust rule over a city is as much a tyrant as one who seeks it over a region. Apocalyp. 13. 6.

units.la: Quid quod rationes Gregorij, quas adfert plurimas, tam Episcopum Anglicanum iugulant, quàm Constantinopolitanum? sic ut fere nullum Timothei depositum, mandatum Christi nullum, nullum statutum Evangelij, Apostolicam authoritatem nullam proferat: quæ perinde adversus Anglicanum atque Constantinopolitanum Episcopatum non faciat. Quod vero Evangeliorum statutum nominat, in eo Stapletonio contravenit, qui fusè disputat, disciplinam (nostram saltem) Evangelij partem dici non posse, quia cum Evangelij proprietatibus non communicat. Puerile; Evangelij siquidem pars est, si in Evangelio tradita: neque magis disciplina nostra, quàm vestra exercitium mortis est: excommunicat quidem, sed nonne & vestra excommunicat etiam? Atque ut excommunicat impoenitentem, ita & poenitentem solvit: quo saltem respectu ut Evangelij proprie dicti sanctio est, ita & laetum illud (quod tu objectas) Evangelij nuncium affert.
units.tr: Moreover, do Gregory's many arguments, which he brings forward, not destroy the English bishop just as much as the Constantinopolitan? So that he produces almost no deposit of Timothy, no command of Christ, no statute of the Gospel, no apostolic authority, which does not bear equally against the English bishopric as against the Constantinopolitan. As for what he calls a statute of the Gospel, in this he goes against Stapleton, who argues at length that discipline (ours at least) cannot be called a part of the Gospel, because it does not share the properties of the Gospel. This is childish. It is a part of the Gospel if it is delivered in the Gospel; nor is our discipline more an exercise of death than yours is: it does excommunicate, but does not yours excommunicate too? And just as it excludes the impenitent, so it also absolves the penitent; in this respect at least, just as it is a sanction of the Gospel properly so called, so it also brings that joyful message of the Gospel which you object to.

units.la: Ridicula illius reliqua omitto, indigna enim sunt quæ refellantur. imò quæ recensentur quidem: cujus generis licet Bancrosti atque Dowbnami non tam argumenta quam ludibria sint, non tamen prorsus prætereunda. Pro eo quòd disputare debuerant ludificantur & irrid١ isti, quanquam è duobus multò modestior Georgius Dowbnamus est. Accepimus Presbyterialem Disciplinam vestram essentialem esse (inquit) si non & articulum fidei vestræ. Huc citat Bancrostum, qui in effectu disciplinam nostram articulum quendam Symboli nostri evasisse rotundè asserere non veretur. Animadvertendum autem est, ironiæ hujus Dowbnamum ipsum puduisse; Annon enim cernis quomodo corrigit? Primò etenim apponit S I: deinde, pro articulo symboli nostri, ponit articulum fidei nostræ, quòd aliquantò levius est: quum verò vocabula ista articulus fidei, ab ipso Dowbnamo plus satis odiosè ponantur, quum censeat verba illa Guilielmi Traversij (quibus hæc tota ludificatio nititur) nihil aliud implicare quàm disciplinam ita articulum fidei esse, perinde ac reliqua in verbo tradita, articuli fidei dici debent. Ita confessio Gallica: Credimus quòd Ecclesia gubernanda sit, politeia & disciplina eâ, quam Dominus noster Jesus Christus instituit, videlicet ut in ea Pastores & Seniores, & Diaconi sint. Ita confessio Ecclesiarum Belgicarum: Credimus, quod hæc Ecclesia regi oportet spirituali politeia illa, quam nos Deus in verbo suo edocuit, sic ut in eâ Pastores & Seniores & Diaconi sint, qui Ecclesia presbyterium constituant. In has ita Gualterus Traversus, Animadversione haud indignum est, quòd Ecclesiæ istæ necessarium iudicarint, in confessione suâ, quâ fidem suam declarant, articulum de Ecclesiæ disciplina inserere; quodque in ejusdem descriptione, non quod opinantur, sed quod credunt posuerint, eodem verbo usi, quo in articulis fidei & doctrinæ usi sunt. Quid hîc vel Momus ipse reprehendat? Reprehendit tamen illustres hasce Christi Ecclesias Richardus Bancroftus, eorumque fidem, præsertim si sensu Traversiano intelligantur, Fidem Carbonarij appellat, quod credunt quod Beza credit, quantumvis quid Beza hac in re credit, nec illæ, nec ipse Beza, sciant. Implete mensuram sociorum vestrorum, qui blasphemant tabernaculum Dei, & sanctos qui in eo habitant, Apocalyp. 13. 6. Atque hoc, ad absurdum primum.
units.tr: I pass over the rest of his ridiculous remarks, for they are unworthy of refutation; yet they must at least be mentioned. Although the arguments of Bancroft and Dowbnam are more mockeries than arguments, they should not be passed over altogether. Instead of arguing, as they ought to have done, they ridicule and mock; though of the two, George Dowbnam is far more restrained. "We have heard," he says, "that your Presbyterial discipline is essential, if not also an article of your faith." He cites Bancroft, who in effect does not hesitate to assert flatly that our discipline has become a certain article of our creed. It must be noted, however, that Dowbnam himself was ashamed of this irony. Do you not see how he corrects himself? First he adds an "S I" (as if to say, "if I may be allowed"); then, instead of "article of our creed," he puts "article of our faith," which is somewhat milder. Yet since Dowbnam himself uses the phrase "article of faith" quite invidiously, although the words of William Traverse, on which this whole mockery rests, mean nothing more than that discipline is an article of faith in the same way as the other things delivered in the Word ought to be called articles of faith. So the French Confession: "We believe that the Church is to be governed by the polity and discipline which our Lord Jesus Christ instituted, namely that in it there be pastors, elders and deacons." So the Confession of the Belgic Churches: "We believe that this Church ought to be ruled by that spiritual polity which God has taught us in his Word, so that in it there are pastors, elders and deacons, who constitute the eldership of the Church." On these texts Walter Traverse remarks: "It is not unworthy of note that these Churches judged it necessary to insert in their confession, by which they declare their faith, an article on the discipline of the Church; and that in its description they set down not what they opine but what they believe, using the same word they used for the articles of faith and doctrine." What could even Momus himself find to blame here? Yet Richard Bancroft reproaches these illustrious Churches of Christ, and especially their faith when understood in Traverse's sense, calling it "the faith of the Carbonari," because they believe what Beza believes, though neither they nor Beza himself know what Beza believes on this point. Fill up the measure of your fellows, who blaspheme the tabernacle of God and the saints who dwell in it. Apocalyp. 13. 6. And this is enough on the first absurdity.

units.la: CAP. 12. Absurdum secundum, quod tum damnantur qui eam non recipiant.
units.tr: CHAPTER 12. The second absurdity: that those who do not receive it are condemned.

units.la: Secundum ita ponit Mattheus Sutclivius. Quod si disciplina vestra necessaria sit, & in verbo tradita, obligaret ad obedientiam: unde sequetur, quotquot eam non recipiunt, eo ipso damnatos omnes esse. Similiter Bancrostus, qui Bezam æquiparat Boni-
units.tr: Matthew Sutcliffe puts forward this second point as well. For if your discipline is necessary and handed down in the Word, it would bind men to obedience. It would follow that all who do not receive it are thereby condemned. Bancroft likewise, who puts Beza on a par with Boni-

units.la: [illegible, ~40 letters] ter tot aculeatas contumelias, ne rationem vel unam adjecerit? At forte alibi adjicit inquies. Neque id quidem, nisi infirmam, puerilem, intolerabilem, absurdam, insensatam & ridiculam dixeris. Ita enim arguit: Si disciplina vestra necessaria sit, tum sequetur, eas non esse veras Ecclesias, quae istam Christi ordinatione non recipiunt: nam oves Christi illius vocem audiunt. Ioan. 10. In quo nonne vocem ego Pelagiani, Donatistae, Anabaptistae, Brownistae, Papistae vere audio? Num fallor? quid? Nulla auditio vocis Christi nisi perfecta: nulla ovis Christi nisi quae perfecte audit? non, nisi fundamentum istud verum sit, quod absurde nobis absurdum objectas, absurdius probas. Anglia scilicet Ecclesia non erit, si vel in una ordinatione Christum non audiat, ea nempe quam de disciplina sanxit, id est, societas nulla Ecclesia est, quae non in omnibus perfecte Christum audit. Quid hoc est aliud quam cum antiquis Pelagianis & hodiernis Anabaptistis conspirare, qui eam perfectam sanctitatem in Ecclesijs requirebant, ut societates omnes Ecclesias negarent, in quibus vel minima imperfectio sive interna sive externa reperiebatur? Quid hoc est aliud quam cum antiquis Donatistis, eas omnes societates ex Ecclesiarum albo expungere in quibus aliqua, aperta saltem immundities se ostendit? Quid hoc est aliud, quam Brownistam prorsus agere? nonne eundem textum adferunt, eodem modo argumentantur: oves Christi vocem ejus audiunt, Ioan. 10. Anglia vocem Christi in disciplina non audit, ergo vera Christi Ecclesia non est. Quid denique hoc aliud est, quam Papisticam illam phrenesin revocare, quam tam multis consutat Iohannes Gerson? nihil scilicet aberrans in Ecclesia esse posse vel quoad doctrinam vel quoad disciplinam; quia Ecclesia errare non potest supra petram aedificata.
units.tr: ...ter with so many stinging insults, and did he not add a single reason? You will say perhaps that he adds one elsewhere. Not even that, unless you call it weak, childish, intolerable, absurd, senseless and ridiculous. For he argues thus: If your discipline is necessary, then it follows that those churches which do not receive it by Christ's ordinance are not true churches, for Christ's sheep hear his voice (John 10). In that case, do I not truly hear the voice of the Pelagians, Donatists, Anabaptists, Brownists, Papists? Am I mistaken? What then? Is there no hearing of Christ's voice except a perfect one, and no sheep of Christ except one that hears perfectly? Unless that foundation is true, which you absurdly object to us, you prove it more absurdly. So England will evidently not be a Church if it does not hear Christ in a single ordinance, namely the one he has sanctioned concerning discipline. That is to say, no society is a Church which does not hear Christ perfectly in every respect. What is this but to conspire with the ancient Pelagians and today's Anabaptists, who required such perfect holiness in the churches that they denied the name of Church to every society in which even the least imperfection, internal or external, was found? What is this but to agree with the ancient Donatists, who struck from the roll of churches all societies in which some open uncleanness showed itself? What is this but to play the part of the Brownist entirely? Do they not bring forward the same text and argue in the same way: Christ's sheep hear his voice (John 10); England does not hear Christ's voice in discipline; therefore it is not a true Church of Christ? Finally, what is this but to revive that Papist frenzy which John Gerson refutes in so many places: that nothing erroneous can exist in the Church, either in doctrine or in discipline, because the Church, built upon the rock, cannot err.

units.la: Tenendum vero adversus Matthaeum Sutclivium atque hostes suos gregales omnes est: sicut privatim fidelis quis verum membrum Ecclesiae esse potest, etsi perfecte Christum non audiat, etsi plene non obediat, etsi in omnibus Evangelij praeceptis secundum officium suum non faciat: ita & publica societas quaeque vera Ecclesia esse potest, etsi omnes sanctiones Evangelicas perfecte non adimpleat. Scribit ad Ecclesiam Sardicensem Christus. Opera tua non sunt plena coram Deo, Apoc. 3. 2. quam tamen Ecclesiam agnoscit, quam Ecclesiam appellat, ad quam velut ad Ecclesiam scribit. Audiat Sutclivius, audiat Brownista, audiat Anabaptista quisque: Sardis vera Ecclesia est, etsi vocem Christi plene non audiat, etsi illius obedientia plena non sit, etsi ad plenum sicut oportuit ab Ethnicismo non fuerit reformata. Quid quod de Ecclesia Lutherana, quasi Ecclesiae Sardicensis arriva haec dicta esse Thomas Brightmanus probet? Ita & ea Ecclesia erit, etsi non tam audiat vocem Christi atque audit Anglia, etsi non tam plene a Papismo repurgetur.
units.tr: But against Matthew Sutcliffe and all his fellow enemies this must be maintained: just as a faithful individual can be a true member of the Church privately, even if he does not hear Christ perfectly, even if he does not obey fully, even if he does not fulfil all the precepts of the Gospel according to his duty, so too any public society can be a true Church, even if it does not perfectly fulfil all the evangelical ordinances. Christ writes to the Church at Sardis: "I have not found your works perfect before God" (Rev. 3.2). Yet he acknowledges it as a Church, calls it a Church, and writes to it as to a Church. Let Sutcliffe hear this, let the Brownist hear it, let every Anabaptist hear it: Sardis is a true Church, even though it does not hear Christ's voice fully, even though its obedience is not complete, even though it has not been reformed from heathenism as thoroughly as it ought to have been. What of the Lutheran Church, which Thomas Brightman proves to be the Sardis of our time, and to which these words are said? So that Church too will be a Church, even though it does not hear Christ's voice as fully as England does, and even though it has not been purged from Popery as thoroughly.

units.la: Secundo, sicut aberratio in disciplina Anglicana Ecclesiae natu-ram tam minimè tollit, quia non est totalis, sed partialis tantùm: ita etiam quia non est fundamentalis, sed ejusmodi, quæ licet graviter peccet propter præcepti juris̈q; divini prævaricationem, a Christo tamen Ecclesiæ capite ἀπὸ non separat, ipsúve ecclesiæ fundamētū aut subruit protin̄ aut subvertit. Errores fundamentales tantùmodo Ecclesiam destruere adversariorum doctissimus Richardus Feyldus docet: percurrat verò velim Matth. Sutclivius quos ille fundamentales recensèt: aberrationem in disciplina, qualis hæc Anglicana est; inter eos numeratam nusquam reperiet. Nec mirum: etenim vel ipse Stapletonus etsi acriter contendat doctrinam fidei idoneam Ecclesiæ notam non esse, quâ externè dignoscitur: largitur tamen fidem veram Ecclesiæ vitam esse: hæc vita in Ecclesiâ Anglicana disciplinam respuente adhuc viget: non igitur eam demortuam esse, non vitâ orbatam, non animam suam exhalasse censendum est. Videantur exempla: corripitur Ecclesia Ephesina ob neglectam disciplinam, Apoc. 2.4. ea tamen Ecclesia appellatur. In Ecclesia Corinthiaca adeo disciplina jacet, 1.Cor. 5.1. ut Hadrianus Saravia putet nullos illic disciplinæ administratores adhuc constitutos fuisse: ea tamen disertis verbis Ecclesia nominatur, 1.Cor. 1.1. Quid multis? Laodicea certè ipsa Ecclesia dicitur: licet disciplinam ušque adeo corrupisset, ut miserabilis, pauper, nuda, cæca, tepidaque sit, mediaque pendeat quidem inter Christianismum & Ethnicismum, ut Anglia inter Ecclesias reformatas, & Papismum.
units.tr: Secondly, just as the deviation of the English Church in discipline does not in the least take away its nature, because it is not total but only partial, so also, because it is not fundamental but of such a kind that, although it sins gravely through the transgression of a divine precept and law, it nevertheless does not separate the Church from Christ its head [ἀπὸ], nor does it at once undermine or overthrow the foundation of the Church. Our most learned adversary Richard Field teaches that only fundamental errors destroy the Church. But I would like Matthew Sutcliffe to run through the fundamental errors which Field lists: he will nowhere find a deviation in discipline, such as this English one, counted among them. Nor is this surprising. For even Stapleton, though he strongly contends that the doctrine of faith is not a fitting mark of the Church by which it is recognised outwardly, nevertheless concedes that true faith is the life of the Church. This life still flourishes in the English Church, which rejects discipline. It must therefore be judged that the Church is not dead, not deprived of life, and has not breathed out its soul. Let us look at examples. The Church of Ephesus is rebuked for neglecting discipline (Rev. 2.4), yet it is called a Church. In the Church of Corinth discipline lay so neglected (1 Cor. 5.1) that Hadrian Saravia thought no administrators of discipline had yet been appointed there, yet it is named a Church in plain words (1 Cor. 1.1). What need of more? Laodicea is certainly called a Church itself, although it had so corrupted discipline that it was wretched, poor, naked, blind and lukewarm, and hung halfway between Christianity and heathenism, just as England hangs between the reformed Churches and Popery.

units.la: Tertio, sicut aberratio Anglicana in disciplinâ, Ecclesiæ naturam minimè tolit, quia non est totalis, nec fundamentalis, ita etiam quia non est pertinax & obstinata. Probat Bellarminus veritatem doctrinæ insparabilem Ecclesiæ notam non esse, quia Ecclesia Galatharum Ecclesia erat, quamvis in Mosaicæ legis necessitate fundamentaliter aberraverit. Huic argumento ecquid aliud habet Feyldus quod respondeat, quàm Ecclesiam etiam in fundamento aberrante tamdiu Ecclesiâ remanere, quamdiu non sit pertinax: Ecclesiâ vero Galatharum adhuc non fuisse obstinatâ? Iudaica ecclesia ad eundē modū in fundamēto aberrabat: nō tamē ab ea velut à nō ecclesiâ seperabant Apostoli, nisi tū, quū obstinatione suâ prodiderat, Act. 13. 45. 46. 47. Hoc ita cum sit, quo velamento errot Sutcliuy & Brodnitaum cooperietur: qui Ecclesiam Anglicanam, Ecclesiæ velamento spoliant, in violatione disciplinæ duntaxat, multò levius quâ Galathiana, aut Iudaica, aberrantē: quū illæ Ecclesiæ aliquandiu quidem remanserint, quanquā in ipso fundamento aberrantes?
units.tr: Thirdly, just as the English deviation in discipline does not destroy the nature of the Church, because it is neither total nor fundamental, so also it does not do so because it is not stubborn and obstinate. Bellarmine proves that the truth of doctrine is not an inseparable mark of the Church, because the churches of Galatia were churches, although they had gone astray fundamentally on the necessity of the Mosaic law. Has Field anything else to answer this argument, except that a Church which errs even in a foundation remains a Church for as long as it is not obstinate, and that the Galatian Church had not yet been obstinate? The Jewish Church likewise erred in the foundation, yet the Apostles did not separate from it as from a non-Church until it had revealed itself by its obstinacy (Acts 13.45-47). Since this is so, with what veil will Sutcliffe and the Brownist cover their error? They strip the English Church of the name of Church for a deviation only in the violation of discipline, a deviation far lighter than that of the Galatians or the Jews, since those Churches remained Churches for some time, although they were erring in the very foundation.

units.la: Atqui huic nutanti Mat. Sutclivio Separistarumque argumento fert Lons suppetias. Anglia peccati admonita non audit, hominum pie consulentium postulata contemnit, invectam a reformatoribus discipli-nam constanter oppugnat: ita si disciplina Evangelij pars sit, eam, illa non solùm non utens, sed illam etiam plane contemnens fidelis Christi (ponsa) haberi non debet. Respondet R. Feyldus, Pertinacie gradus quosdam
units.tr: But Lorinus brings aid to this wavering argument of Matthew Sutcliffe and the Separatists: England, when warned of sin, does not listen; it despises the requests of men who consult its piety; it constantly attacks the discipline introduced by the reformers. So if discipline is a part of the Gospel, a faithful bride of Christ should not be considered one who not only does not use it but plainly despises it. Field replies that there are certain degrees of obstinacy

units.la: [illegible, ~40 letters] spondent hæc, ad objectionem illam: ex parte illa in Anglia quæ impugnat disciplinam, Anglia ipsam metiendam esse, quia ea & maior & potentior est, & rerum summa potitur: non tamen ex parte ea quæ à disciplina stat, quoniam & pusilla admodum est, & nullo numero nec authoritate pollens. Quid enim? Si ex maiori parte Sardicensis Ecclesia æstimetur, nè quidem Ecclesia omnino erit: nam quòd ad hoc ipsum dicitur, nomen habes quod vivis, sed mortua es, Apocalyps. 3.1. Quæro si mortua Sardiniæ, quomodo Ecclesia, quæ non nisi viventium est? Certè hic nodus quantum ego assequor, solvi non potest, nisi ut superius respondeatur, non metiendam Sardiniæ esse ex parte maiori quæ mortua, sed ex parte illa minori, quæ viva; cujus gratia, Ecclesia Sardiniæ reputatur. Palea pars ea major est quæ in area prævaleat: appellatur tamen non cumulus palææ sed cumulus tritici, uti habet Angustinius, quia tritici unus licet minor quantitate, pars tamen cum multi dignitate præstantior est. Quoties prophetæ societatem Israeliticam Ecclesiam agnoscunt, gratiâ paucarum reliquiarum, quas in ea sibi Deus reservaverat? Ecclesiam apud Papistas fuisse fere usque ad Concilium Tridentinum dicit Feyldus, orthodoxorum illorum gratia qui ibidem agebant, licet numero tam pauci, ut interiori atrio à Spiritu sancto assimilantur, Apocalyps. 11.1.2. quod ad versa in illa Ecclesia pontificiorum factio, velut atrium quoddam exterius, quam longissimè superabat. Nonne atrium exterius pars tabernaculi & templi erat? atrio igitur exteriori, cum Papistas antiquos æquiparet Spiritus Sanctus, videntur & illi de Ecclesia quadantenus fuisse: nempe ut loquitur Feyldus, potentissima quædam in Ecclesia factio. Pergamus ad societates alias, uxor pars œconomiæ inferior est, maritus potior & præstantior multò: uxor tamen fidelis si sit, maritum ipsum, liberos, & societatem totam œconomicam sanctificat, ut habet Paulus, 1 Cor. 7.14.
units.tr: ...to this objection, as follows. On that side of England which opposes discipline, England itself must be measured, because it is both larger and more powerful and holds the chief control of affairs. But it must not be measured on the side which stands for discipline, since that side is very small and possesses neither number nor authority. For what follows? If the Church of Sardis were judged by its greater part, it would not be a Church at all. For what is said to it, "You have a name that you live, but you are dead" (Rev. 3.1), would then apply. I ask: if Sardis is dead, how can it be a Church, since a Church consists only of the living? Certainly this knot, so far as I can follow it, cannot be untied unless, as was answered above, Sardis is judged not by its greater part, which is dead, but by that smaller part which is alive, for whose sake the Church of Sardis is reckoned a Church. Chaff is the greater part, which prevails on the threshing floor, yet the heap is called not a heap of chaff but a heap of wheat, as Augustine has it, because one grain of wheat, though smaller in quantity, is more excellent in worth than much chaff. How often do the prophets acknowledge the Israelite society as a Church for the sake of the few remnants whom God had reserved for himself in it? Field says that the Church existed among the Papists almost until the Council of Trent, for the sake of those orthodox men who acted there, though so few in number that they are compared to the inner court by the Holy Spirit (Rev. 11.1-2), while that Papist faction, as an outer court, far exceeded them. Was not the outer court part of the tabernacle and the temple? Since the Holy Spirit compares the ancient Papists to the outer court, they too seem in some measure to have been part of the Church, namely, as Field puts it, a certain very powerful faction within the Church. Let us go on to other societies. The wife is the lesser part of an household, the husband is far the more excellent; yet if the wife is faithful, she sanctifies the husband, the children and the whole household, as Paul says (1 Cor. 7.14).

units.la: Ad postremum: objiciebant Pelagiani, qui nullam Ecclesiam nisi ab omni peccato liberam agnoverunt, illud Cant. 4.7. Ephes. 5.27. ubi Ecclesia sine macula & sine ruga esse dicitur: quid ad hoc quod respondeant habuere unquam orthodoxi, quam Ecclesiam hoc attribui non quia omnes vel plures numero tales sint, sed quod optima & principalis Ecclesiæ pars talis sit, in hac vita quidem per imputationem, per sanctificationem in futura? Atque hæc, ad absurdum tertium.
units.tr: Finally: the Pelagians, who acknowledged no Church except one free from all sin, used to object that passage from the Song of Songs (4:7) and Ephesians 5:27, where the Church is said to be without spot and without wrinkle. What answer have orthodox writers ever given to this? That these things are attributed to the Church not because all, or even most, of its members are such, but because the best and principal part of the Church is such: in this life indeed by imputation, but in the future life by sanctification. And so much for the third absurdity.
