units.la: Argumentum quartum, quod tum esset separandum ab Ecclesijs eis quae excommunicationem non recipiunt.
units.tr: The fourth argument: that one must then separate from those Churches which do not admit excommunication.

units.la: QVARTVM ita proponit Iohannes Whitgiftus; aliquam regiminis formam adeo esse necessariam ut mutari nequeat, nibimet persuadere nequeo. Ratio una est quia excommunicatio quae genus quoddam gubernationis est, necessaria si esset, liceret ab Ecclesijs eis quae ea non utuntur separare, quod nunc contra esse videmus. Scripsit hec ille ante natā separationē nostrā (quę utinā ō utinam nata nunquam fuisset) sin minus aliter in hoc proculdubio unguem fixisset, sicut nuperi Hierarchici omnes figunt. Ita siquidem Matheus Sutcliuius. Si disciplina vestra pars Evangelij sit tam justam causam dissessionem faciendi & semetipsa nobis separandi Barrowistae habent: quibuscum in Ecclesiâ Anglicanâ infamandâ conspirastis. Similiter Lous Quid tandem reformatores nostri Barrowvum tam vehementer oppugnant, quid insectantur impuros Greenvv.fœtus: vel enim minuät oportet quae de suae sanctitate disciplinae toties perscribunt, vel hominum pacis & concordiae vincula disrumpentia puditissimos defendat conato. Nisi sciibisma approbetur, disciplina ista corruet. Eundem lapidem volvit Tho. Bellus. Presbyterij Anglici patroni (inquit) illud essentialem partem Evangelij faciunt, tam ad salutem necessariam, ut nulla absque ea Ecclesia esse possit. Quid facias homini tam impudenter mentienti? Sed pergat porro. Probo secundò (inquit) quia, ea in Ecclesia manere licet, quae excommunicatione destituta est, quod proculdubio facere non possemus, si excommunicatio pars Evangelij Christi esset, & necessaria ad salutē; ab ea enim Ecclesia fugere oportet, quae aliqua re ad salutem necessaria caret. Ita cum reliquis conspirat Bellus, ob defectum disciplinae separandum ab Anglia esse, si modo ea necessaria sit.
units.tr: John Whitgift proposes the fourth argument as follows: "I cannot persuade myself that any form of government is so necessary that it cannot be changed." One reason is this: if excommunication, which is a kind of governance, were necessary, it would be permitted to separate from those Churches which do not use it, and yet we see the opposite. He wrote this before our separation was born (would that it had never been born!), or otherwise he would undoubtedly have driven the nail home in this matter, as all the recent Hierarchists do. So too Matthew Sutcliffe: "If your discipline is a part of the Gospel, the Barrowists have as just a cause for dissension and for separating themselves from us as you have for conspiring with them to defame the English Church." Similarly Lous: "Why then do our reformers so vehemently attack Barrow, why do they harass the impure offspring of Greenwood? For they must either weaken what they so often write about the holiness of their discipline, or defend with the most shameless effort the bonds of peace and concord that it breaks." "Unless the schism is approved, this discipline will fall." Thomas Bell turns the same stone: "The patrons of the English Presbytery (he says) make it an essential part of the Gospel, so necessary to salvation that no Church can exist without it." What can one do with a man who lies so shamelessly? But let him go on. "I prove secondly (he says) that one may remain in a Church which lacks excommunication, which we could not do if excommunication were a part of the Gospel of Christ and necessary to salvation; for one must flee from a Church that lacks something necessary to salvation." So Bell agrees with the others that, because of the lack of discipline, one must separate from England, if indeed discipline is necessary.

units.la: Ita satis illis non erat, disciplinam corrumpendo separationi ansam praebere, nisi etiam à se excitatam indies foverent: imò nec hoc ipsis satis, nisi culpam etiam transferant in eos, quorum disputationes & dimicationes notiores sunt, quàm ut oratione indigeant. Pulchrae sanè adversus schismaticos dimicationes vestrae sunt (inquit Bancroftus) quum ex Epistola Greenvvoddi quaedam intercepta appareat, sed sua istud nihil aliud esse, quam ex vestro dogmate consequentiam, apponendo scilicet propositiones minores ad vestras majores. Dimicatio igitur vestra fortè pulchrior, hoc fundamento scilicet innixa. Nulla disciplinae forma in verbo Dei praescripta est: ergo separatio propter disciplinā faciendā nulla est. Hęc illa vestra Brovvnistarū debellatio est, tanti estimata, ut T.B. se cōtinere non potuerit, quin nobis diceret, assertionem suam de minime recta & in verba praescripta eligendi forma per suffragia populi, utile esse ad Brovvnistas cōfutandos, qui nullos apud nos ministros ministros esse volunt, propterea quod per vota plebis non elīguntur. Sed nullas Troia spes habes, si tales habes? tantum abest, quod hoc telo feriantur Brownistæ, ut eo armentur potius, idq; apponendo propositiones minores easq; veras ad majores vestras fallas. Si disciplina necessaria sit, & in verbo velut immutabilis tradita, tum ob illius corruptionem separatio facienda est: Ita Whitgiftus. Apponunt jam illi minorem veram: At disciplina necessaria est, & in verbo Dei velut immutabilis tradita, ergo ab Ecclesia Anglicana tandem corrumpente, separatio est facienda. Si disciplina necessaria sit & Evangelij pars, tum justam causam Barrowistæ habent, ut semel ab Ecclesia nostra separent: ita Sutclivius. Apponunt jam illi minorem veram: At disciplina necessaria est, & Evangelij pars: ergo justam causam habemus ab Ecclesia Anglicana separandi. Aut minuenda reformatorum elogia de sanctitate disciplinæ suæ, aut schisma approbandum: ita Lous. Apponunt jam illi minorem veram: At reformatorum elogia de sanctitate disciplinæ suæ minuenda non sunt: ergo separatio nostra approbanda. Schisma consequentia est ex disciplina illa quam reformatores petunt: ita Bancroftus. Apponunt jam illi minorem veritatem: At disciplina quam reformatores petunt vera est & a Christo institua & a vero nihil nisi verum consequitur: ergo separatio nostra pro veritate divina pugnat. Minores igitur ealque veras eis submittistratis vos; nos nullas omnino: deducere quidem conantur illi ex majoribus nostris minores quasdam, sed & absurdas, & inconsequentes.
units.tr: Yet it was not enough for them to give occasion for separation by corrupting discipline, unless they also fostered it day by day after they had stirred it up. Nor is even this enough for them, unless they also shift the blame onto those whose disputes and quarrels are too well known to need explanation. "Your battles against the schismatics are indeed fine" (says Bancroft), since some intercepted letter of Greenwood appears, but this is nothing other than a consequence of your own doctrine, namely by adding minor premises to your major ones. Your battle, then, is perhaps finer, resting on this foundation: No form of discipline is prescribed in the Word of God: therefore separation for the sake of establishing discipline is no separation. This is your refutation of the Brownists, so highly valued that T.B. could not restrain himself from telling us that his assertion concerning the least correct form of choosing ministers, prescribed in the words, by the votes of the people, is useful for refuting the Brownists, who want no ministers among us to be ministers, because they are not chosen by the votes of the common people. But you have no hope of Troy, if you have such hopes! So far is it from being true that the Brownists are struck by this weapon, that they are rather armed by it, and this by adding true minor premises to your false major ones. If discipline is necessary, and handed down in the Word as something unchangeable, then separation must be made on account of its corruption: so Whitgift. They now add the true minor premise: But discipline is necessary, and handed down in the Word of God as unchangeable; therefore separation from the English Church, which at last is corrupt, must be made. If discipline is necessary and a part of the Gospel, then the Barrowists have a just cause to separate once and for all from our Church: so Sutcliffe. They now add the true minor premise: But discipline is necessary and a part of the Gospel: therefore we have a just cause for separating from the English Church. Either the praises of the reformers concerning the holiness of their discipline must be diminished, or schism must be approved: so Lous. They now add the true minor premise: But the praises of the reformers concerning the holiness of their discipline must not be diminished: therefore our separation is to be approved. Schism is a consequence of that discipline which the reformers seek: so Bancroft. They now add the true minor premise: But the discipline which the reformers seek is true, and instituted by Christ, and nothing but truth follows from the truth: therefore our separation fights for divine truth. So you submit true minor premises to them, while we submit none at all; they try indeed to draw from our major premises some minor ones, but these are absurd and inconsequential.

units.la: Neque enim si necessaria disciplina sit & in verbo Dei tradita, idcirco separatio, sicubi corrumpatur, facienda statim est: uulla connexionis vi hoc porisma sequitur. Liquet hoc ex Johanne Calvino: censet is disciplinam in verbo Dei quod ad substantialia pertinet scriptam esse: satis solidis tamen argumentis probat, propter eiusdem corruptionem, discessionem facere, Novatianum & Donatistas cum esse: idem & T. Cartwrightus ipse adversus Harrisonum praefti-tit: cujus rationes frustra Sutclivius infirmas vocat & puerilis: cum Bancroftus eas non solum citet, verum etiam approbet. Approbat vero? quid igitur sibi ad respondendum relinqui fecit? Hoc nempe, quod hac a Cartwrighto, Harrisoni refutatio, ipsi Cartwrighto contraria est: quandoquidem hic disciplinam contendat non ad esse necessariam, sed tantum ad bene esse necessariam esse: quum alibi eam ad ipsum ipsius Ecclesiæ esse necessariam dicat. Vbi vero? in cœtu Cobentriensi inquit, qui anno Domini 1588. celebratus a Puritanis est: ubi formam disciplinæ tum approbarant, appellat in sua subscriptione essentialem. Essentialem vero cui? Non Ecclesiæ essentalem dixit, sed te ipso referente, essentialem disciplinæ veritatem & a Christo præscriptam, sic enim narras. Subscripserunt Cartwrighto præsente, formam illam disciplinæ tum exaratam, essentialem formam disciplinæ esse, & omnibus temporibus necessariam: in
units.tr: For even if discipline is necessary and handed down in the Word of God, it does not follow that separation must be made at once wherever it is corrupted; this conclusion follows from no force of connection. This is clear from John Calvin: he thinks that discipline, as far as its substance is concerned, is written in the Word of God; yet he proves with fairly solid arguments that, because of its corruption, one should withdraw, and that the Novatians and Donatists were of this kind. The same was also maintained by T. Cartwright himself against Harrison, whose arguments Sutcliffe calls weak and childish in vain, although Bancroft not only cites them but even approves them. Does he approve them? What, then, has he left himself with which to reply? Namely this: that the refutation of Harrison by Cartwright is contrary to Cartwright himself, since here he maintains that discipline is necessary not for being but only for well-being, whereas elsewhere he says that it is necessary to the very being of the Church itself. Where? At the Coventry gathering, he says, which was held by the Puritans in the year of the Lord 1588, where they approved the form of discipline then, and called it essential in their subscription. But essential to what? He did not say it was essential to the Church; rather, as you report it, he said it was the essential truth of discipline, also prescribed by Christ; for thus you narrate: They subscribed, with Cartwright present, that the form of discipline then drawn up was the essential form of discipline, and necessary in all times: in

units.la: quo minimè hallucinatus Cartwrightus est. Neque enim verum est, quod Iohannes Whitgiftus objicit, rixas nos movere de accidentalibus disciplinæ tantum, non autem de substantialibus, quia materia tantum disciplinæ, verbum nempe & sacramenta substantialia, sola sint, ut quæ sola in verbo præcisè tradita. At quis unquam materiam essentialem, absque forma etiam essentiali somniavit? Certè non H. S. qui formam etiam gubernationis, disciplinæ essentialem pertinet ad Ecclesiam, tat sic enim habet: Hoc ad ἀποστολικὴν essentiā pertinet, ut sint qui imperent, sint etiam qui pareant. Forma gubernationis autè nulla melior tradi potest quàm exemplo suo tradidit Apostolus. Ita salva Cartwrightı sententia est, & ad Harisonum confutandum firma formam disciplinæ reformatæ, essentialem disciplinæ esse; Ecclesiæ vero ipsi minimè, ut quæ ad bene esse Ecclesiæ duntaxat necessaria sit, non autem ad ipsum esse, instar muri ad civitatem.
units.tr: in which matter Cartwright was by no means mistaken. For it is not true, as John Whitgift objects, that we stir up quarrels only about the accidental features of discipline and not about its substance, because only the matter of discipline, namely the Word and the sacraments, is substantial, as these alone are handed down in the Word precisely. But who ever dreamed of an essential matter without an essential form as well? Certainly not H. S., who holds that the form of government also belongs essentially to discipline and to the Church; for thus he has it: This pertains to the apostolic [ἀποστολικὴν] essence, that there be some who rule and some who obey. Yet no better form of government can be handed down than the Apostle handed down by his example. So Cartwright's opinion stands safe, and to refute Harrison, a firm form of reformed discipline is essential to discipline; but not to the Church itself, since it is needed only for the well-being of the Church, not for its being, like a wall to a city.

units.la: 2. Occurrit hic nobis D. Cobquotus, qui in concione sua ad crucem Paulinum, anno 1584. ex eo probat negare nos Anglicam Ecclesiam esse, quòd disciplinam nostram adeque necessariam ad Ecclesiam esse dicamus, ac murus necessarius est ad civitatem. Atqui mi-lerum hunc vel uno ictu confodit Lous. Qui civitatem absque muro esse posse, multis demonstrat. Neque tamen ille in eo lanus, quod civitatem ut Spartam olim, non solum esse absque muro, sed etiam bene esse posse, imo & florere docet: quum miseram illam civitatem scriptura prædicet quæ absque muro est, Prov. 25, 28, quòd si vero florere etiam Ecclesia potest absque disciplina, quemadmodum civitas absque muro, non illius necessitatem ita Cartwrightus forte attigit, quum eam duntaxat Ecclesiæ murum facit? Certè inquit: Recta etenim disciplina plus est ad Ecclesiam, atque murus ad civitatem.
units.tr: 2. Here D. Cobquotus comes to meet us; in his sermon at St Paul's Cross, in the year 1584, he proves from this that we deny the English Church to be a Church, because we say that our discipline is as necessary to the Church as a wall is necessary to a city. But Lous strikes this wretched man down with a single blow, demonstrating at length that a city can exist without a wall. Nor is he silent on this point, that he teaches a city, like Sparta of old, can not only exist without a wall, but can even be well-off and flourish; whereas Scripture calls a city without a wall a miserable one, Prov. 25.28. But if the Church too can flourish without discipline, just as a city without a wall, has Cartwright perhaps not touched upon its necessity when he makes discipline only a wall of the Church? Certainly, he says: For right discipline is to the Church what a wall is to a city.

units.la: Ecce igitur Hierarchicos plus necessitatis in disciplina ponentes quàm ipse Cartwrightus; ac proinde ad dogma Bibliorum de illius essentialitate accedentes aliquanto propius, qui eam ecclesiæ duntaxat murum statuit. At si murus inquies, duntaxat sit, cur adeo contenditis? Quasi ingens illud Dei beneficium non sit, Murò cu-cumdedit. Isa. 5. 2. Ac proinde ingens calamitas, Illius murum demoliar. Isa. 5. 5, & sic postrem ingens in Anglia Episcoporum peccatu, qui hanc calamitatem in Ecclesiam invexerunt. Neque tamen est, quod hujus muri ipsorum culpa in Anglia ruentis crepitus adeo Brovvinistas perterrefaciat, ut alio sibi fugiendum putent, novasque sedes quæ-rendas. Quo etenim fugitis? præterquam cum Anglia v. ... rba vitæ æterna habeat? Ioan. 6. 68. Certè muri civitatis Iuæ demolitionem ita luxit Nehemias olim Neh. 2. 3. ut ex oris longinquis ad eundem restaurandum advolarit. Atque hoc vestrum officium fuit, iuxta illa Augustini, qui pios admonuit, ut corripiant quod possunt, quod non possunt, patienter ferunt, ut in dilectione & gemant & lugeant, donec aut emendet Deus & corrigat, aut in messe eradicet zizania, & palea.
units.tr: Behold, then, the Hierarchicals, who place more necessity in discipline than Cartwright himself does, and so come somewhat closer to the teaching of the Bible on its essentiality, since Cartwright makes it only a wall of the Church. But you will say, if it is only a wall, why do you contend so hard? As if that great gift of God were not, "He fenced it with a wall" (Isa. 5.2). And so the great calamity, "I will break down its wall" (Isa. 5.5), and thus the great sin of the English Bishops, who brought this calamity upon the Church. Nor is there any reason why the cracking of this wall, falling in England through their fault, should so terrify the Brownists that they think they must flee elsewhere and seek new seats. For where are you fleeing? Except that England has the words of eternal life? (John 6.68). Nehemiah certainly so mourned the demolition of the walls of Jerusalem (Neh. 2.3) that he flew from distant lands to restore them. And this was your duty, according to Augustine's words, which admonish the godly to correct what they can, to bear patiently what they cannot, and in love both to sigh and to mourn, until either God amends and corrects, or at the harvest uproots the tares and the chaff.

Quantum ad disciplinâ Christus ex parte foris stat, Apocal. 3.20. intrat quidem ad suos, non tamen patente porta, ut in Ecclesiis Helveticis, aliisque Philadelphiensis χριστιανοῖς reformatis, Apocal. 3.8. in quibus clavis Davidis viget, versf. 7. id est disciplina illa, quæ ostium apertum Christo introituro reserat: sed ostio quasi semi-occluso, quia in Anglia, clavigera disciplina ista ex magna parte deest. Atque hæc de Thesi secunda, politeiam scilicet necessariam esse, necessitate præcepti & juris.
units.tr: ...(the doors having been broken through) Christ presents himself familiarly. As far as discipline goes, Christ stands outside in part, Rev. 3.20; he indeed enters to his own, but not with the door open, as in the Helvetic Churches and the other reformed Philadelphian [χριστιανοῖς] Christians, Rev. 3.8, in whom the key of David is in force, verse 7, that is, that discipline which unlocks the open door for Christ about to enter. But the door is as though half-shut, because in England that key-bearing discipline is largely lacking. And this is what I have to say about the second thesis, namely that polity is necessary by the necessity of precept and of law.

units.la: CAP. 15. Thesis tertia, quod disciplina est in substantialibus immutabilis.
units.tr: CHAP. 15. Third thesis, that discipline is immutable in its essentials.

units.la: EX hac emergit tertia: quòd si erenim politeia Ecclesiastica res indifferens non sit, sed in verbo juris divino præcepta & statuta, sequitur eam in substantialibus immutabilem esse, id quod etiam verbis diserte Apostolus Paulus contestatur. Denuncio tibi coram Deo & Iesu Christo (inquit) ut serves mandatum hoc sine macula & reprehensione, usque ad revelationem Iesu Christi, 1.Timoth.6,13. In hanc ita Thom. Bilsonus commentatur, ut nostram plane de politeiæ immutabilitate thesim istam ita confirmet, Ut Timotheus hanc observaret usque adventum Christi in gloria nullo modo fieri poterat: moriendum ei multo ante fuerat. Itaq; præcepta hæc non ei solum, sed aliis, in ejus locum ad finem sæculi successuris tradita sunt. Citat porro Ambrosium, Magna vigilantia atq; providentia præcepta dat rectori Ecclesiæ. In ejus enim persona salus Ecclesiæ consistit; non solicitus de cura Timothei tam circumspectus est, sed propter successores ejus, ut exemplo Timothei Ecclesiæ ordinationem custodirent. Atque his verbis elucescit, non solum ordinationem pro regenda Ecclesia immutabilem a Christo & Apostolo sancitam esse; sed a quo puncto temporis etiam, hujus immutabilitatis æra petenda sit. Non inutilis hæc cura est, hoc in loco ab Ainl rosso tradita: ad Pontificios præsertim refutandos, & ad Hierarchicis respondendum. Probat Sutclivius, formam regiminis nunc esse mutabilem, quia olim a tempore Christi mutabatur: nam monarchica erat cum Christus in terris versabatur: & Apostoli Christo immediate succedentes, jam cessarunt. Nicolaus Sanderus ex adverso hinc probat, Monarcham in Ecclesia semper perpetuò esse debere, ac proinde Papam, quia Christus Monarcha erat dum vixit, & forma regiminis quæ illius tempore erat, immutabilis sit. Tho. Bilsonus, & Had. Saravia immutabilitatem a Christi tempore, repetendam esse negant, ne Papam admitterent: eam tamen a regimine Apostolorum incepisse dicunt, quorum authoritatem in Episcopos perpetuam esse asserunt. At vero uno eodemque ictu & istos sterniit Whitakerus, & Sanderum, dum ad idem Bellarmini argumentum respondet. Nona a tempore Christi (inquit) immutabilis disciplina fuit, nam primo regebatur Eccle- sia fiía a rectoribus extraordinariis, Apostolis, Evangelistis, Prophetis, qui iam sublati sunt: at nunc per pastores & doctores tantùm. Addit Staple-tonum ipsum fateri, aliam fuisse formam regiminis tempore Apostolorum, aliam nunc: Princip. Doctrinal. lib.6. cap.15. Concidit igitur papa, concidit etiam Episcopus: alia nunc regiminis forma esse debet, quàm quæ tempore regiminis Apostolorum fuit, multò magis quam quæ tempore regiminis Christi erat: sic ut immutabilitatis æra, neque à tempore regiminis Christi, neque a tempore regiminis Apostolorum petenda sit. Imò inquit Mat. Sutclivius a nullo tempore omnino, quia non ab his temporib9. Contra ex Paulo Ambrosius, Tempus quoddam est, inquit, a quo forma regiminis Ecclesiastici cœpit immutabilis esse: illud nempe, quo ordinatio Ecclesiæ, id est certus regendæ Ecclesiæ ordo ordinarius, ab Apostolis statutus est. Hic ille est, quem in epistolis tradit Paulus, quem in Actis Apostolorum narrat Lucas ab Apostolis quibusdam observatum fuisse, quàm primùm Ecclesiæ constituebantur. Hunc vero specialius Gulielmus Whitakerus cum delineare voluit, citat loco supra notato, ex Hieronymo. Primò Ecclesia communi consilio presbyterorum regebatur. Ea mandatum de regendâ Ecclesiâ, quod sine macula & reprehensione ad adventum usque Christi servandum esse denunciat Paulus: ut Episcopis Anglicanis cumprimis providendum sit, quomodo de monarchica sua, in statutâ à Christo regendi formam, per presbyteros aristocraticâ, usurpatione, eidem venienti ad judicium sint responsuri.
units.tr: From this emerges the third thesis: for if ecclesiastical polity is not a matter of indifference, but its precepts and ordinances are contained in the divine law of the Word, it follows that it is immutable in its essentials, which the Apostle Paul also plainly attests in words: "I charge you before God and Jesus Christ," he says, "that you keep this commandment without spot and blameless until the appearing of Jesus Christ" (1 Tim. 6.13). Thomas Bilson comments on this in such a way as to confirm exactly our thesis on the immutability of polity: "Timothy could in no way keep this until the coming of Christ in glory; he had to die long before. Therefore these precepts were given not to him alone, but to others who were to succeed him in his place until the end of the age." He further cites Ambrose: "Great vigilance and providence give precepts to the ruler of the Church. For the safety of the Church rests in his person; he is not so careful about Timothy's care, but on account of his successors, that by the example of Timothy they might keep the ordering of the Church." And by these words it is made clear not only that the ordering for governing the Church was established as immutable by Christ and the Apostle, but also from what point in time the era of this immutability is to be sought. This account, given here by Ainlerosso, is not useless, chiefly for refuting the Papists and for answering the Hierarchicals. Sutcliffe proves that the form of government is now mutable, because it was changed from the time of Christ: for it was monarchical while Christ dwelt on earth, and the Apostles who succeeded Christ immediately have now ceased. Nicholas Sander, on the contrary, argues from this that a monarch must always and perpetually be in the Church, and therefore the Pope, because Christ was the monarch while he lived, and the form of government that existed in his time is immutable. Thomas Bilson and Hadrian Saravia deny that immutability is to be traced from the time of Christ, lest they admit the Pope; yet they say it began with the government of the Apostles, whose authority they assert to be perpetual over the Bishops. But Whitaker strikes down both these and Sander at one blow, when he answers the same argument of Bellarmine: "Discipline was immutable from the time of Christ, for at first the Church was governed by extraordinary rulers, Apostles, Evangelists, Prophets, who have now been removed; but now only by ministers and teachers." He adds that Stapleton himself admits that the form of government in the time of the Apostles was different from the present one (Principles of Doctrine, book 6, chapter 15). So the Pope falls, and the Bishop falls too: the form of government now must be other than that which existed in the time of the Apostles' government, much more than that which existed in the time of Christ's government; so that the era of immutability is to be sought neither from the time of Christ's government nor from the time of the Apostles' government. Indeed, Matthew Sutcliffe says it is from no time at all, because it is not from these times. On the contrary, Ambrose, following Paul, says: there is a certain time from which the form of ecclesiastical government began to be immutable, namely that in which the ordering of the Church, that is, the fixed ordinary order for governing the Church, was established by the Apostles. This is the one which Paul hands down in his epistles, and which Luke relates in the Acts of the Apostles was observed by certain Apostles as soon as Churches were constituted. But William Whitaker, when he wished to outline this more specifically, cites from Jerome, in the place noted above: "First the Church was governed by the common counsel of the elders." That is the charge concerning the governing of the Church which Paul declares must be kept without spot and blameless until the coming of Christ; so the English Bishops above all must take care how they will answer to the same Christ coming to judgment, for their monarchical usurpation of the form of government which Christ prescribed, by aristocratic elders.

units.la: 2. Certè qui in eo responsionis suæ fiduciam collocant, quòd forma regiminis prima mutabilis sit; vel suorum calculo, quasi condemnationis tum futuræ præjudicio quodam condemnantur: sic ut in eis si non illa Christi locum habeant: Filij vestri, at similia tamen, Socij vestri erunt vestri judices. Ita Iohannes Whitgiftus, Fundamentum Puritanorum putridum hoc est, eandem disciplinam retinendam jam esse, quæ fuit temporibus Apostolorum. Et Mattheus Sutclivius Exemplum & usus Apostolicorum temporum in Ecclesiæ regimine, ol servanda jam non sunt. Contra Ha.Saravia. Non est arrogata illa regendæ Eccl. siæ forma quâ sunt usi Apostoli & Apostolorum viri. Non ignoraverunt Apostoli, homines plus moveri exemplis quàm præceptis: & citius imitaturos quos post se reliquebant Ecclesiarum rectores, quod viderant, quàm quod tradidissent, & ab eis audissent: ut si quid fuit necessarium clare & perspicue disertis verbis posteritati testatum relinqui, hoc imprimis fuerit necessarium. Ita Iohannes Whitgiftus, Vna certa Ecclesiæ gubernandæ forma in verbo præscripta non est, quæ ex necessitate perpetuo observari debet. Contra Ha.Saravia Nulli genti Deus unquam ullam certam ac perpetuam imperij formam dedit, quam propter loci aut temporum mutari non liceret. Sed regiminis ecclesiastici diversa est ratio: quoniam enim proximè à Deo est profecta, eam pro arbitrio suo homines mutare non possunt. Ita Iohannes Whitgiftus, Diversitas quæ est inter Apostolorum tempora & nostra diversam ruptę superatis) se Christus familiarę præbet. Quantum ad disciplinā Christus ex parte foris stat, Apocal. 3. 20. intrat quidem ad suos, non tamen patente porta, ut in Ecclesijs Helveticis, aliisq; Philadelphiensis reformatis, Apocal. 3. 8. in quibus clavis Davidis viget, verf. 7. id est disciplina illa, quæ ostium apertum Christo introituro referat: sed ostio quasi semi-occlusō, quia in Anglia, clavigera disciplina ista ex magna parte deest. Atque hæc de Thesi secunda, politeiam scilicet necessariam esse, necessitate præcepti & juris.
units.tr: 2. Certainly those who place their confidence in this answer, that the first form of government is mutable, are condemned by their own reckoning, as if by a kind of prejudgment of the condemnation to come: so that, if they do not have the place of Christ in them, nonetheless, "your sons, and likewise your companions, will be your judges." Thus John Whitgift: "This is the rotten foundation of the Puritans, that the same discipline must now be retained which was in the times of the Apostles." And Matthew Sutcliffe: "The example and practice of the Apostolic times in the governing of the Church are no longer to be observed." Against Saravia: "That form of governing the Church which the Apostles and the men of the Apostles used was not arrogated. The Apostles did not fail to know that men are moved more by examples than by precepts, and that the rulers of Churches whom they left behind would more quickly imitate what they had seen than what they had handed down and heard from them; so that if anything needed to be clearly and plainly attested to posterity in express words, this above all would have been necessary." Thus John Whitgift: "There is no one certain form of governing the Church prescribed in the Word, which must necessarily be observed perpetually." Against Saravia: "God has never given any nation one certain and perpetual form of rule which could not be changed on account of place or time. But the ecclesiastical form of government is different in its reasoning: since it has come forth most immediately from God, men cannot change it at their pleasure." Thus John Whitgift: "The difference that exists between the times of the Apostles and ours..."

units.la: Thesis tertia, quod disciplina est in substantialibus immutabilis.
units.tr: Thesis third: that church discipline is immutable in its essentials.

units.tr: From this arises a third thesis. If ecclesiastical polity is not an indifferent matter, but is prescribed and established in the Word by divine right, it follows that it is immutable in its essentials. The Apostle Paul affirms this expressly in words: "I charge you before God and Jesus Christ" (he says) "that you keep this commandment without spot or blame, until the appearing of Jesus Christ", 1 Tim. 6:13. Thomas Bilson comments on this as follows: "That Timothy should keep this until the coming of Christ in glory could in no way be done; he had to be warned long before. Therefore these precepts were given not to him alone, but to others who were to succeed him in his place until the end of the age." He further cites Ambrose: "With great vigilance and providence he gives precepts to the ruler of the Church. For the welfare of the Church consists in his person. He was not so careful for Timothy's sake, but for his successors, so that by Timothy's example they would keep the ordering of the Church." From these words it is clear not only that the ordering for governing the Church was established by Christ and the Apostle as immutable, but also from what point in time the era of this immutability is to be sought. This passage, set out here by Almrosius, is not an unhelpful one, especially for refuting the Papists and for answering the hierarchists. Sutcliffe argues that the form of government is now mutable, because it was changed in former times from the time of Christ: for it was monarchical while Christ dwelt on earth, and the Apostles, who immediately succeeded Christ, have now ceased. Nicholas Sander, on the other hand, argues from this that a monarch must always and perpetually be in the Church, and therefore the Pope, because Christ was monarch while he lived, and the form of government that existed in his time is immutable. Thomas Bilson and Hadrian Saravia deny that immutability is to be traced from the time of Christ, lest they should admit the Pope; yet they say it began with the government of the Apostles, whose authority over the bishops they assert to be perpetual. But Whitaker, in answering Bellarmine's same argument, strikes down both these and Sander with one and the same blow: "Discipline was not immutable from the time of Christ, for at first the Church was governed

Rursus Iohannes Whitgiftus Temporibus Apostolorum status Ecclesiae democraticus erat, quia tum nullus erat magistratus, non sic hodie. Contra Saravia Accedente magistratu mutari Ecclesiastici regiminis formam necesse non est. Nam sic eam temperavit divina sapientia, ut nulli civilis regiminis formae adversetur. Quando autem tota aliqua respublica facta est Ecclesia, gubernatio quidem mutationem aliquam recepit, sed quae naturam ipsius non mutat. Ita Iohannes Whitgiftus Archiepiscopi politeias gratia solummodo alterabiles sunt. Contra Saravia. Authoritas Archiepiscopi & Episcopi, Apostolatus est ἀμετάβλητος & immutabilis, Ita Lous. Nullam prescripserunt Apostoli regiminis Ecclesiastici formam, quam perpetuam esse mandarunt. Et Matthaeus Sutclivius Apostoli cessarunt, & usus Apostolicus iam non observandus est. Contra G. C. Sequitur profecto quos gubernatores in Ecclesia Apostoli constituerunt, perpetuo in Ecclesia remanere debere, quia ad usus perpetuos instituti sunt. Ita Iohannes Bridgesius Deus regimen Ecclesiae aut non expressit, aut ita expressit, ut nos eidem in perpetuum non obligaret. Contra Hadrianus Saravia Nullus hominum in ullam disciplinae mutationem consentire potest, absque peccato. Ita G. Dounamus Ordinatio & iurisdictio solummodo perpetuae a Paulo dicuntur, 1. Timoth. 6. 13, non vero officium Episcopale illud, per quod Titus & Timotheus ordinationem & iurisdictionem exercuerunt. Contra Thomas Bilsonus Efficacia sunt verba, vehemens obtestatio, mandata usque ad adventum Domini duratura, nec Titi aut Timothei morte finienda: personae ergo ad quos Apostolus scripsit Episcopi fuerunt. Quibus recte perpensis, episcopalem in his causis potestatem supra presbyteros velut dictante Spiritu, iussu divino sancitam esse nemo sanus inficiabitur. Atque hic mihi Christiane lector impense rogandus es, ut animum diligenter attendas: ex hoc enim pendet Episcopalis muneris & potestatis extructio, si probationes nostrae stabiles & firmae fuerint: contra eiusdem eversio & ruina, si responsio illorum satis in hac re ponderis habuerit. Plane enim hoc si defecerit, Episcopis suam authoritatem Ecclesiae consuetudine vendicare liceat: divino aliquo iure, aut scripturarum testimonio non licebit. At pro Episcopali authoritate nihil hic locus facit, dicit Georgius Dounamus, subversum igitur ius divinum iurisdictionis episcopalis funditus est. Ita Matthaeus Sutclivius Forma Gubernationis Ecclesiae non est semper una & eadem. Contra Hadrianus Saravia. Apostoli & evangelistae exemplum & legem nobis perfecti regiminis ecclesiastici reliquerunt quod perpetuo observandum est. Ita Mat. Sutclivius Magistratus gubernatores Ecclesiae mutare potest. Contra Thomas Bilsonus Principibus Ecclesiae administratio commissa est, non ut disciplinam ipsius, arbitratu suo mutent, aut moveant, sed ut diligenter ea, ad Ecclesiae & populi commodum utantur. Ita Matthaeus Sutclivius Forma regiminis Ecclesiasticum veteri & novo foedere non ea conditione statuta est, ut sit perperpetua. Contra Hadrianus Saravia Ut demus quicquid Deus constituit, non eâ forte conditione, ut perpetuum esset, tamen ea gubernationis ratio quæ ætate Apostolorum fuit, ea conditione constituta fuit, ut perpetua esset. Rursus Institutum Apostolorum de regimine Ecclesiastico mutari non potest, ut decretum Dei de sacerdotio Aronico mutari non potuit. Ita Mattheus Sutclivius: Leges de regimine Ecclesiastico non sunt in perpetuum perdurabiles. Contra Thomas Bilsonus: Leges quas Paulus in Epistola ad Timotheum posuit de regimine ecclesiastico sunt inviolatæ. Ita Mattheus Sutclivius: Non obligamur neque ad gubernatores neque ad leges temporum Apostolicorum. Contra Thomas Bilsonus. Paulus in Epistola ad Timotheum leges tulit in omnem posteritatem valituras.

Matthew Sutcliffe has the same words, on account of the arrival of the magistrate. Again John Whitgift: "In the times of the Apostles the state of the Church was democratic, because there was then no magistrate; it is not so today." Against this, Saravia: "When the magistrate arrives, it is not necessary for the form of ecclesiastical government to change. For divine wisdom so tempered it that it is opposed to no form of civil government. But when some whole commonwealth has become Church, the government indeed undergoes some change, but one which does not alter its nature." Thus John Whitgift: "The polities of archbishops are alterable only by favour." Against this, Saravia: "The authority of archbishop and bishop is an apostolate, and is unchangeable and immutable." So Lous.: "The Apostles prescribed no form of ecclesiastical government which they commanded to be perpetual." And Matthew Sutcliffe: "The Apostles have ceased, and Apostolic practice is no longer to be observed." Against G. C.: "It certainly follows that the governors whom the Apostles appointed in the Church must remain in the Church perpetually, because they were instituted for perpetual uses." So John Bridges: "God either did not express the government of the Church, or expressed it in such a way that it does not bind us to it forever." Against this, Hadrian Saravia: "No one can consent to any change in discipline without sin." So G. Downame: "Ordination and jurisdiction are called perpetual only by Paul, 1 Tim. 6:13, but not that episcopal office by which Titus and Timothy exercised ordination and jurisdiction." Against Thomas Bilson: "The words are forceful, a vehement adjuration, commands that will last until the coming of the Lord, and not to end with the death of Titus or Timothy: therefore the persons to whom the Apostle wrote were bishops." When these things are rightly weighed, no sane person will deny that episcopal power over the presbyters in these matters, as if dictated by the Spirit, has been sanctioned by divine command. And here, Christian reader, I must earnestly ask you to give your attention carefully: on this depends the building up of the episcopal office and power, if our proofs are stable and firm; but if their answer has had enough weight in this matter, then the overthrow and ruin of the same. For plainly, if this fails, bishops may claim their authority by the custom of the Church, but not by any divine right or the testimony of Scripture. But nothing in this passage supports episcopal authority, says George Downame; therefore the divine right of episcopal jurisdiction has been utterly overthrown. So Matthew Sutcliffe: "The form of the government of the Church is not always one and the same." Against this, Hadrian Saravia: "The Apostles and Evangelists left us, as an example and law of perfect ecclesiastical government, something that is to be observed perpetually." So Matthew Sutcliffe: "The magistrate can change the governors of the Church." Against Thomas Bilson: "The administration has been committed to the princes of the Church, not so that they may change or alter its discipline at their pleasure, but so that they may use it diligently for the benefit of the Church and the people." So Matthew Sutcliffe: "The form of ecclesiastical government in the Old and New Covenant was not established on the condition that it be perpetual." Against this, Hadrian Saravia: "Grant that whatever God established was perhaps not established on the condition that it be perpetual; nevertheless that mode of government which was in the age of the Apostles was established on the condition that it be perpetual." Again: "The arrangement of the Apostles concerning ecclesiastical government cannot be changed, just as God's decree concerning the Aaronic priesthood could not be changed." So Matthew Sutcliffe: "The laws concerning ecclesiastical government do not endure forever." Against this, Thomas Bilson: "The laws which Paul laid down in his Epistle to Timothy concerning ecclesiastical government are inviolable." So Matthew Sutcliffe: "We are bound neither to the governors nor to the laws of the Apostolic times." Against Thomas Bilson: Paul, in his Epistle to Timothy, enacted laws that were to be valid for all posterity.

units.la: Hunc in modum hoc uno in capite inter se consentiunt adversarij, qui in nobis nescio quas contradictiones tam acerbè exagitant. Desinat ergo M. Sutclivius nos quasi Cadmeios fratres serpentino semine natos incusare: & ad suos reflectat oculos, qui inter se quasi Cadmeij digladiantur. Atq; hæc huic loco sufficiant, de thesi tertia, politeiam nempe Ecclesiasticam, necessitate immutabilitatis necessariam esse.
units.tr: In this manner, on this one point, our adversaries agree among themselves, though they so harshly harass us for I know not what contradictions in us. Let Matthew Sutcliffe therefore cease to accuse us, as if we were the Cadmean brothers born of the serpent's seed, and let him turn his eyes to his own people, who, like the Cadmeans, fight among themselves. And let these things suffice for this place, concerning the third thesis: that ecclesiastical polity is necessary, by the necessity of its immutability.

units.la: CAP. 16.
units.tr: CHAP. 16.

units.la: Thesis quarta, quod disciplina sit necessaria necessitate finis, quæ triplex est.
units.tr: Thesis fourth: that discipline is necessary by the necessity of its end, which is threefold.

units.la: THesis quarta sequitur. Quòd si etenim politeia Ecclesiastica res indifferens non sit, sed in verbo Dei mandata, idque ut sit perpetua & immutabilis: sequitur necessitatem finis eidem tribuendam esse, sic ut medium quoddam a Deo institutum necessarium sit, ad finem perquam necessarium. Hic autem finis, ita contradicentium fumis abnubilatur, ut triplex nodus hic nobis dissolvendus sit; quorum primus de necessitate ad Ecclesiæ externam subsistentiâ est: secundus de necessitate ad Ecclesiam notandâ & judicandâ: tertius & ultimus de necessitate politeiæ ad Ecclesiæ salutem & beatitatem. Quod ad primam: approbat Ricardus Feyldus illud Stapletoni: Dici potest Christianorum societas vera Ecclesia esse, vel quia solum veram naturam & essentiam Ecclesiæ habet, vel etiam quia præter hanc omnia etiam ea habet, quæ ad Ecclesiæ integritatem & plenitudinem pertinent. Iuxta hanc verè mihi posse dici videtur, finem doctrinæ tantummodo necessariam esse absolute ad essentiam Ecclesiæ solam constituendam: disciplinam tamen secundum quid ad illius integritatem & plenitudinem. Hoc ita explico: essentia Ecclesiæ vel absolutè consideratur quâ Ecclesia est; & sic doctrina & fides ad illius essentiam necessaria est: aut secundum quid, quâ Ecclesia visibilis est: & sic disciplina ad illius essentiam necessaria est. Non contemnenda hæc distinctio est; eam & Iohannes Whitgiftus habet qui ita scribit. Et si gubernatio vel quoddam genus gubernationis pars Ecclesiæ esse possit, quod ad externam formam & perfectionem: non tamen pars pars ejusmodi est ipsius essentiae, quum Ecclesia Christi esse possit, aut sine hoc vel illo genere gubernandi. Cur igitur tantopere apud Bancroft. toto c. 34. vapulamus, quod disciplinam modo isto necessariam dicimus ad externam Ecclesiae subsistentiam: aut cur Theodorus Beza flagellatur, a nobis & sibimetipsi si contradiceret, quum de presbyter. pag. 199. ita scriptum erat? Doctrina tantummodo ad essentiam Ecclesiae absolute necessaria est. Tota Ecclesia in deserto, Sacramento circumcisionis carebat, non cessabat tamen Dei populus esse. Idem multo magis de Ecclesiastica disciplina dici potest: videlicet Ecclesiae ut illa careant, tamen Ecclesias vere pias & Christianas esse posse, si doctrinam praecipuorum dogmatum puram ac sincerum habuerint. Haec Beza, haec omnes reliqui qui de disciplina scripserunt: qui honoratius (ut Bancrofti vocabulo utar) de disciplinae essentialitate locuti unquam sunt, quam aut ipse Johanes Whitgiftus nuper, aut Hierarchici scriptores reliqui loqui solent. Quid enim Tomas Bilsonus, In Ecclesia perpetuo permanere debent, potestas annunciandi verbum & dispensandi Sacramenta, recta clavium administratio, manuumque impositio. Haec res, quamdiu manet Ecclesia, deficere non debent: nam si vel una horum defecerit, Ecclesiae nomen vix constabit. Quid Johannes Bridgesius, Citat ille & approbat ex Ignatio illa. Sine coetu presbyterorum, electa Ecclesia non est, nec sanctorum coetus, nec congregatio sancta. Epist. ad Trallianos. Quid Hadrianus Saravia. Ecclesia nulla esse potest, ubi nec ullum Christi Sacramentum, nec ministerium Ecclesiae perspicitur. Quid Georgius Downnamus? Authoritas quam Titus & Timotheus habuerint ordinaria est & perpetuo necessaria, non solum ad bene esse, sed etiam ad esse visibilium Ecclesiarum. Rursus, In omni regimine haec quinque consideranda sunt: potestas, ordo, forma, vel modus, titulus sive applicatio potestatis ad personam & usus. Ex his illa duo priora, ut scilicet gubernandi potestas sit, in eaque ordo, essentialia & perpetua sint tanquam immutabilia Dei statuta: quum ex illius instituto Ecclesiae societas ordinata esse debeat, & ut sapiens loquitur, tanquam acies ordinata, Cant.6.3,9. Haec Bancrofte, cum apud tuos reperiantur; cur in nos tam atrociter saevis, quod disciplinam ad existentiam Eccl. sic visibilis necessariam existimemus? Num tu Ecclesiam Cyclopicam turbam esse vis: ubi [illegible, ~12 letters]? Num politicis refragabaris, qui coetum latronum, non rempublicam, societatem eam volunt esse, ubi nulla politeia, ubi ordo nullus est? At video ad quem lapidem offendis, vel ad quem potius nos offendisse mundo persuadere cupis. Ita disputas, ac si plenam illam & perfectam quam in Ecclesia Anglicana deesse dicimus disciplinam, ad visibilis Ecclesiae existentiam externam, necessariam existimaremus. At hoc nobis inmentem nunquam venit, quorum sententia perspicue haec est, quod doctrinam & disciplinam Ecclesia perfectam habet, ea perfecta Ecclesia est; quae disciplinam imperfectam, imperfecta; quae vero nullam disciplinam vel minimam ex parte habet, ea nec Ecclesia ulla cen-
units.tr: THESIS FOURTH follows. For if ecclesiastical polity is not an indifferent matter, but is commanded in the Word of God, and that to be perpetual and unchangeable, it follows that the necessity of an end must be ascribed to it, so that a certain means instituted by God is necessary for an end that is itself most necessary. Now this end is so clouded by the smoke of our opponents that three knots must be untied here: the first concerns its necessity for the external subsistence of the Church; the second, its necessity for noting and judging the Church; the third and last, the necessity of polity for the salvation and blessedness of the Church. As to the first, Richard Field approves that saying of Stapleton: "The fellowship of Christians may be called the true Church either because it alone has the true nature and essence of the Church, or also because, besides this, it has all those things which pertain to the integrity and fullness of the Church." In accordance with this, it seems to me that it may truly be said that doctrine alone is absolutely necessary to constitute the essence of the Church, but discipline is necessary in a certain respect for its integrity and fullness. I explain this thus: the essence of the Church is considered either absolutely, as that by which the Church is the Church, and so doctrine and faith are necessary to its essence; or in a certain respect, as that by which the Church is visible, and so discipline is necessary to its essence. This distinction is not to be despised, and John Whitgift also holds it, who writes thus: "Even if government, or some kind of government, can be a part of the Church, as regards its external form and perfection, yet it is not a part of the essence itself, since the Church of Christ can exist without this or that kind of governing." Why, then, are we so severely lashed by Bancroft throughout chapter 34, for saying that discipline is necessary in this way to the external subsistence of the Church? Or why is Theodore Beza whipped, as if he contradicted both us and himself, since on page 199 of his work on the presbyters it was written thus: "Doctrine alone is absolutely necessary to the essence of the Church. The whole Church in the desert lacked the sacrament of circumcision, yet the people of God did not cease to be the people of God. The same can be said much more of ecclesiastical discipline: that the Churches may lack it and yet be truly pious and Christian Churches, if they have pure and sincere doctrine of the chief dogmas." This is Beza's view, and it is the view of all the others who have written about discipline; none of them ever spoke of discipline's essentiality more honourably (to use Bancroft's word) than John Whitgift recently did, or than the other Hierarchical writers are accustomed to speak. For what does Thomas Bilson say? "In the Church there must perpetually remain the power of announcing the Word and of dispensing the sacraments, the right administration of the keys, and the laying on of hands. These things must not fail as long as the Church remains; for if even one of them fails, the name of Church will hardly stand." What does John Bridges say? He cites and approves from Ignatius: "Without a gathering of presbyters there is no elect Church, nor holy assembly, nor holy congregation" (Epistle to the Trallians). What does Hadrian Saravia say? "No Church can exist where neither any sacrament of Christ nor the ministry of the Church is seen." What does George Downame say? "The authority which Titus and Timothy had is ordinary and perpetually necessary, not only for the well-being but also for the very existence of visible Churches." Again: "In every government these five things must be considered: power, order, form or manner, title or the application of power to a person, and use. Of these, the first two, namely that there be power of governing and order in it, are essential and perpetual, as unchangeable statutes of God, since by his ordinance the society of the Church ought to be ordered, and, as the wise man says, like an army set in array (Song of Songs 6.3,9)." You say this, Bancroft, since these views are found among your own people; why then do you rage so fiercely against us, because we think discipline is necessary to the existence of the visible Church in this way? Do you wish the Church to be a Cyclopean mob, where [illegible]? Do you not oppose the politicians, who want that society to be a gang of robbers and not a commonwealth, where there is no polity and no order? But I see which stone you strike against, or rather which stone you wish to persuade the world that we have struck against. You argue as if we considered the complete and perfect discipline which we say is lacking in the English Church to be necessary to the external existence of the visible Church. But this has never entered our minds; our view is clearly this: a Church that has perfect doctrine and discipline is a perfect Church; one that has imperfect discipline is an imperfect Church; but one that has no discipline, or only the smallest part of it, is not to be counted as any Church at all.
