units.la: [illegible, ~60 letters] esse, nec Beza, nec Cartwrightus dicit: addo etiam nec Bancrofti propositum fuisse, ut hanc (de qua accusat Downamus) essentialitatem, vel ex Beza probaret, vel ex Cartwrighto: sicut haec proximè subiecta verba docent. Videte necessitatem disciplinae illorum, nunc illius essentialitatem advertite: unde videre cuivis promptum, inter necessitatem & essentialitatem Bancroftum distinguere, atque illam quidem ex Cartwrighto & Beza patere, istam non item. Matheus Sutclivius quanquam adversariorum acerrimus: non hoc nobis (quod Downamus) impingit, nos disciplinam nostram essentialem Ecclesiae notam statuere, sed tantùm quòd inseparabilem: Nempe vidit, quod doctè Feyldus demonstrat, non solum illas necessarias Ecclesiae notas esse quae Ecclesiam à priori constituunt, sed etiam quae à posteriori, & ab Ecclesiae essentia fluunt, velut propria illius accidentia. Hoc ita cum sit quàm futilis Bancroftus, qui essentialitatem disciplinae ex nostris authoribus probaturus, nullam aliam rationem adducit, quàm nostrum quosdam unà cum verbo & Sacramentis, disciplinam ut Ecclesiae notam recensere? Quasi quicquid cum verbo ut Ecclesiae nota recensetur, adaeq; ac verbum essentiale eo ipso asseratur?
units.tr: [illegible passage] be, nor does Beza nor Cartwright say so. I add also that it was not the purpose of Bancroft to prove this essentiality (of which Downame accuses him), either from Beza or from Cartwright, as the words that immediately follow show: "See the necessity of their discipline; now notice its essentiality." Hence anyone can easily see that Bancroft distinguishes between necessity and essentiality, and that the former is evident from Cartwright and Beza, but the latter is not. Matthew Sutcliffe, although among our most bitter opponents, does not charge us, as Downame does, with setting up our discipline as an essential mark of the Church, but only as an inseparable one. He saw, as Field learnedly demonstrates, that not only those marks are necessary which constitute the Church a priori, but also those which flow a posteriori from the essence of the Church, like its proper accidents. Since this is so, how futile is Bancroft, who, intending to prove the essentiality of discipline from our authors, adduces no other reason than that some of us list discipline together with the Word and sacraments as a mark of the Church? As if whatever is listed along with the Word as a mark of the Church were asserted to be as essential as the Word itself!

units.la: Quaeso mi Domine, nonne & vos Ecclesiae notas describentes, unà cum verbo sacramenta recensere soletis? cum sacramenta tamen perinde ac verbum essentialia non sint, ut sine quibus Ecclesia esse possit? Multo verò pejùs sequitur, disciplinam idcirco essentialem perinde ac verbum à nobis statui, quia unà cum verbo Ecclesiae notam, eam faciamus; cum à nobis sacramentis postponatur. Atqui hoc ipsum Bancrofto disciplicet, quòd disciplinam ad verbum & Sacramenta, quasi tertiam Ecclesiae notam quomodocunque adjicimus: praesertim cum Calvinus, Bertrandus de Loques, Philippus Mornaeus, Petrus Martyr, Augustinus Marloratus, Nicolaus Galisus, imò & ipse Beza inter notas Ecclesiae verbum duntaxat & sacramenta numerent, disciplinae mentionem omittentes. Verba ipsa Bezae quae citat, apponenda videntur, utpote in quibus responsio ad haec testimonia cetera, idonea satis contineatur. Beza (inquit) in colloquio Pictaviensi Anno 1561. haec protulit. Ecclesiae notae duae sunt, purum Dei verbum & sincera sacramentorum administratio. Sunt qui Ecclesiasticam disciplinam addunt; sed nos duabus il is erimus contenti.
units.tr: I ask you, my Lord, do you not also, when describing the marks of the Church, usually list the sacraments together with the Word, although the sacraments are no more essential than the Word, in the sense that the Church could exist without them? Much worse follows from the claim that we set up discipline as essential just as the Word is, because we make it a mark of the Church together with the Word; when by us it is placed after the sacraments. Yet this very thing displeases Bancroft, that we add discipline to the Word and sacraments as a third mark of the Church in any way at all; especially since Calvin, Bertrand de Loques, Philippe Mornay, Peter Martyr, Augustine Marlorat, Nicolas Gallasius, and indeed Beza himself, count among the marks of the Church only the Word and the sacraments, omitting any mention of discipline. Beza's own words, which he cites, seem worth setting down, since they contain a sufficient answer to these other testimonies. Beza, he says, put forward the following at the Colloquy of Poitiers in the year 1561: "There are two marks of the Church: the pure Word of God and the sincere administration of the sacraments. Some add ecclesiastical discipline; but we shall be content with those two."

units.la: Quid igitur est? Non hi theologi eos condemnant (ut Bancroftus) qui disciplinam Ecclesiae notam tertiam faciunt: sed adversus Papistas disputantes, satis habent verbum tantùm & sacramenta exprimere, disciplinam in verbo & sacramentis includentes, ut quae illorum appendix sit. Neque vero nos condemnant, ut Bancroftus, Hierarchici omnes reliqui. D. Copquotus hac quidem in re totus noster est: qui in concione sua ad crucem Paulinam post impressa, diserte asserit, tres Ecclesiae notas esse, verbum, sacramenta, disciplinam. Quum & noster etiam Richardus Feyldus est: quo nemo accu
units.tr: What then is the position? These theologians do not condemn (as Bancroft does) those who make discipline a third mark of the Church; but when disputing against the Papists they are satisfied to express only the Word and the sacraments, including discipline within the Word and the sacraments, as its appendix. Nor do all the other Hierarchical writers condemn us, as Bancroft does. Dr. Cosin, in this matter, is wholly on our side: in his sermon at Paul's Cross, printed afterwards, he expressly asserts that there are three marks of the Church: the Word, the sacraments, and discipline. And our own Richard Field is also on this side, than whom no one...

units.la: De Eccles. lib. 2. cap. 2. & 4.
units.tr: On the Church, bk. 2, chs. 2 and 4.

units.la: Registrum. p. 519. De eccles. l. 2. cap. 2. accuratius aut limatius de Ecclesiæ notis scripsit. Notæ (inquit) Ecclesiæ, quæ sunt inseparabiles, perpetuæ & absolutè proprie, tres sunt: Verbi professio, usus Sacramentorum, & unio in hac professione, usuque, sub legitimis pastoribus, ad homines in viis salutis dirigendos. Quid hæc ad propositum vestrum inquies? vel maximè. Advertendum enim est, non verbum & sacramenta simpliter nominasse Feyldum: sed eorum administrationem, etiam atquè usum, inter notas Ecclesiæ posuisse, quæ res disciplinariæ nonnè sunt? Vnio etiam per disciplinam & conservatur, & exercetur; & pastores idonei, quos ad notandam Ecclesiam requirit, per disciplinam & dijudicantur & eliguntur: eorum directio denique in viis salutis, & externa & disciplinaria est. Frustra igitur sententiam nostram vellicant adversarij, de politeias necessitate ad Ecclesiam indicandam...
units.tr: Registrum, p. 519. In De Ecclesia, bk. 2, ch. 2, he wrote more exactly and precisely about the marks of the Church: "The marks of the Church, which are inseparable, perpetual and absolutely proper, are three: the profession of the Word, the use of the Sacraments, and union in this profession and use, under lawful ministers, for directing men in the ways of salvation." What will you say this has to do with your point? Quite a lot. For it must be noted that Field did not simply name the Word and the sacraments. He placed among the marks of the Church their administration and even their use. Are these not matters of discipline? Union too is both preserved and exercised through discipline, and the suitable ministers whom he requires for marking the Church are both examined and chosen through discipline. Finally, their direction of men in the ways of salvation is external and disciplinary. Therefore the adversaries pluck at our view in vain, regarding the necessity of polity for indicating the Church...

units.la: CAP. 18. De finis necessitate tertia, disciplinam necessariam esse ad Ecclesiæ salutem.
units.tr: CAP. 18. On the third necessity of the end: that discipline is necessary for the salvation of the Church.

units.la: SVperest necessitas finis tertia: ubi quæritur, an disciplina necessaria sit, ad Ecclesiæ salutem. Hujus quæstionis Thomas Cartwrightus partem affirmativam cum asseruisset, illius doctrinam, miram, novam, inauditam, ita exclamat Iohannes Whitgiftus, ac si totam viciniam, imò Theologorum scholam in eum concitare vellet. Quærit verò ab illo duo. Primùm, utrum intelligat necessitatem absolutam, sine qua nemo salvari potest: vel necessitatem secundum quid, ut disciplina sit duntaxat necessarium medium, & ordinarium adjumentum, sine quo non ita facilè Ecclesiæ salus obtineri possit. At hac inquisitione opus non erat, quum necessitatem tantùm generis secundi Thomas Cartwrightus se intellexisse, tum hujus capitis divisione proximâ, tum capitis tertij divisione secunda, satis manifestè docuisset.
units.tr: There remains the third necessity of the end, namely whether discipline is necessary for the salvation of the Church. When Thomas Cartwright had affirmed the positive side of this question, John Whitgift cried out at his doctrine as strange, new and unheard of, as if he wished to stir up the whole neighbourhood, indeed the whole school of theologians, against him. He asks him two things. First, whether he means an absolute necessity, without which no one can be saved, or a necessity in a qualified sense, so that discipline is only a necessary means and ordinary aid, without which the salvation of the Church cannot be obtained so easily. But there was no need for this inquiry, since Thomas Cartwright had made it quite plain, both in the immediately preceding division of this chapter and in the second division of the third chapter, that he meant only the second kind of necessity.

units.la: Quærit secundò, an regimen intelligat in genere necessarium esse, an hoc vel illud regiminis genus, quod sit immutabile? Primum concedit necessarium esse, secundo necessitatis genere: unum autè certum regiminis genus, necessarium esse ad Ecclesiæ salutem, vel secundo quidem necessitatis gradu negat. At affirmat Thomas Bilsonus qui concedit in quæstione de disciplina Anglicana (ea autem de uno certo regimine est, eoque immutabili Bilsoni sententiâ) ecclesiæ totius salutem verti. Affirmat Georgius Dovvnamus, Nulla necessitas absoluta est (inquit) ut Episcopalis functio in perpetuum retinenda sit, necessitate tamen expedientiæ & convenientiæ retinenda semper est.
units.tr: Second, he asks whether Cartwright means that government in general is necessary, or that this or that form of government, which would be unchangeable, is necessary. Cartwright grants that government is necessary in the second kind of necessity, but he denies that any one definite form of government is necessary for the salvation of the Church, even in the second degree of necessity. Thomas Bilson, however, affirms it. He concedes, in the question about English discipline (and this is about one definite government, and an unchangeable one in Bilson's view), that the salvation of the whole Church turns on it. George Downame affirms: "There is no absolute necessity," he says, "that the episcopal function be retained for ever; yet by the necessity of expediency and fitness it must always be retained."

units.la: Hanc verò necessitatem, necessitatem finis interpretatur ad salutem Ecclesiæ alibi, nempe ubi verba Hieronymi premit Salus Ecclesiæ in... in Episcopi dignitate consistit. Ita unam certam regiminis formam ad Ecclesiae salutem necessariam esse & immutabilem, necessitate & immutabilitate convenientiae & expedientiae docet Downamus adversus Whitgiftum: licet per errorem pro nostra quam vocat presbyteriali, suam illam episcopalem reposuerit, quam nunquam instituit Iesus Christus, velut necessariam, per quam homines ad salutem dirigerentur, Neque obstat Hieronymus.
units.tr: But this necessity, the necessity of the end, that is, of the salvation of the Church, he interprets elsewhere, namely where he presses the words of Jerome: "The salvation of the Church consists in ... in the dignity of the bishop." So Downame teaches, against Whitgift, that one definite form of government is necessary and unchangeable for the salvation of the Church, by the necessity of fitness and expediency. He does this although, through an error, he has put in place of our form, which he calls presbyterial, his own episcopal form, which Jesus Christ never instituted, as necessary for directing men to salvation. Nor does Jerome stand in the way.

units.la: Primò etenim non de Ecclesiae salute verba facit, quum in Episcopali functione Ecclesiae salutem consistere dixit, sed de externa salute tantummodo quae in pace Ecclesiae externa ponitur.
units.tr: For first, Jerome was not speaking of the salvation of the Church when he said that it consists in the episcopal function. He was speaking only of an external salvation, which is placed in the external peace of the Church.

units.la: Secundò non jure divino, aut Apostolicâ ordinatione hanc Episcopalem authoritatem statuminat Hieronymus, ut Downamus; sed jure humano tantùm: nempe politicum inventum existimavit (ut loquitur Iuellus) adversus schismata, quod pro Episcopo Anglicano nihil facit. Regimé Episcopale suo tempore invaluerat, politicū inventum bonum putabatur, ut schismatum plantaria evellerentur: nostro tempore contrarium accidit, cum schismatum seminarium evasit: ratio igitur diversa cum sit, & politici inventi istius jus etiam omne cessat.
units.tr: Second, Jerome did not ground this episcopal authority on divine right or apostolic ordinance, as Downame claims; he grounded it only on human right. He thought it a political invention (as Jewel puts it) against schisms, which does nothing in favour of the English bishop. The episcopal government had prevailed in his own time, and the political invention was thought good so that the seeds of schisms might be uprooted. In our time the opposite has happened, since it has become a seedbed of schisms. The reason is therefore different, and the right of that political invention ceases altogether.

units.la: Tertiò, nullam Anglicanam in Episcopo sui temporis somniavit Hieronymus authoritatem: praesidentiam tantùm ad ordinem conservandum approbavit ille, ut illa demonstrant, quando ait, Petrum Apostolis praepositum fuisse ut schismatū occasio tolleretur: ex quibus recte Iohannes Reynoldus colligit, qualis inter pares est, ad ordinem servandum sufficere concludit, ut pax Ecclesiae conservetur, & schismata praecidantur. Ne experientia quotidiana comprobatum ubique hoc, in Ecclesijs reformatis; quae nonne quaeso per praesidem suum pace dulciori & uberiori perfruuntur, quàm Anglia per Dominum Episcopum suum, Archipiscopumvè? Quod vero acclamat Conradus Vorstius, nullas in Belgia vires esse ad haereses tollendas, propter defectum Episcoporum, nihil est. Quid etenim Episcopus in Belgia adversus haereses praestare potuit plus (si modo illic extitisset) quàm quod à classi absq; Episcopo huc usque datum est: praesertim in republica ea, ubi promiscuae religionis libertatem concedendam ipse magistratus censet? Tantum vero abest ut retroactis temporibus Episcopatus utilis fuisset ad haereses in Belgia subvelendas: ut nihil Episcopatu ad eaedem sufflamandas & propagandas accomodatius fuisse putem. Quis etenim (pròut res nunc sunt) ad Episcopatum priùs ascendisset, quàm ipse tu Vorsti socijque tui, tuaeque haereseos sanè periculosissimae interpolatores? qui etiam hodie de Episcopatu in Belgia surrigendo non adeo cogitarent, si id rebus suis commodum, non arbitrarentur. Quartò, praesidentiam ad ordinem conservandum, in uno quidé Episcopo perpetuum, juxta sui saeculi consuetudinem approbat Hieronymus, sed non necessariā, sed ut illis temporibus duntaxat utilem. Hoc illud est quod Durœo respondet Guil. Whitakerus. Defendit Hieronymus (inquit) unius patoris in ecclesia superioritatem non tanquam necessariam sed tanquam conuenientem: & eodem ipse quem citat contra Iouinianum libro primo, Ecclesiam super omnes Apostolos fundatam esse dicit, & unamquamq; Ecclesiam pariliter claues regni caelorum ab eisdem recepisse.
units.tr: Third, Jerome never dreamed of the authority that the English bishop has in his own time. He approved only a presidency for keeping order, as those words show when he says that Peter was set over the Apostles so that an occasion for schism might be removed. From these words John Reynolds rightly draws the conclusion that such a presidency among equals is enough to keep order, so that the peace of the Church is preserved and schisms are cut off. Does not daily experience prove this everywhere in the reformed Churches, which, I ask, enjoy through their president a sweeter and more fruitful peace than England enjoys through its Lord Bishop or Archbishop? As for what Conrad Vorstius cries out, that there is no strength in Belgium to root out heresies because of the lack of bishops, it is nothing. For what could a bishop in Belgium have done more against heresies (had one existed there) than what has been given so far by the classis without a bishop? Especially in a commonwealth where the magistrate himself judges that freedom of mixed religion should be granted? Indeed, so far is the episcopate from having been useful in past times for checking heresies in Belgium, that I think nothing could have been more suited to fostering and spreading those same heresies. For who (as things now stand) would have risen to the episcopate before you yourself, Vorstius, and your companions, and the most dangerous corrupters of your heresy? Who would today not even be thinking of setting up a bishopric in Belgium, if they did not judge it convenient for their own affairs? Fourth, Jerome approves a presidency for keeping order that is perpetual in one bishop, according to the custom of his age, but he does not call it necessary; he calls it useful only in those times. This is what William Whitaker answers to Durán: "Jerome defends the superiority of one pastor in the Church not as necessary but as fitting. And in the same book, the first against Jovinian, which he cites, he says that the Church was founded upon all the Apostles, and that each Church likewise received the keys of the kingdom of heaven from them."

units.la: Quintò, Episcopalem functionem ne quidem simpliciter utilem censuit Hieronymus, sed respectu duntaxat uno, nempe ad supprimenda schismata. At non minus tyrannidi, quàm schismati via praecludenda est, in quam post Hieronymi tempora, Episcopatus degeneravit. Hanc ille non vidit, ut videmus nos: quòd si vidisset haud minus quàm nos de Episcopo abolendo laborasset, id quod Danieli Chamiero visum, qui Bellarmino pro uno Papa (perinde ac Hierarchicis pro uno Episcopo) argumentanti, ciuitatem unam non nisi ab uno regi posse, ita respondet. Tum Apostoli accusandi qui plures in eadem ciuitate Episcopos constituerunt, Putarunt quidem homines melius & facilius ab uno unam Ecclesiam regi, cum unius Episcopi inuecta est consuetudo, sed non est consequens, quod videtur melius, ideo sit necessarium. Deinde nè id quidem visum est melius absolutè, sed duntaxat ad vitanda schismata, teste Hieronymo. Simili autem modo nos ἰσοτιμίαν id est, æqualitatem inter pastores, possumus dicere esse ἀρχιτ meliorem, nempe ad vitandam paucorum in reliquos fratres tyrannidem, quam experientia tandem ostendit, quantum sit malum, & quàm opportuna ei sit aperta janua, ex hujusmodi φιλαρχίας ambitione. Atq; de praestantia politeias Ecclesiasticae tertiâ, necessitate nimirum, hic finis esto.
units.tr: Fifth, Jerome did not think the episcopal function useful even in a simple sense, but only in one respect, namely for suppressing schisms. Yet the way must be closed no less to tyranny than to schism, into which the episcopate degenerated after Jerome's time. He did not see this as we see it. But if he had seen it, he would have laboured no less than we do to abolish the bishop. This was seen by Daniel Chamier, who, when Bellarmine argued for one Pope (just as the hierarchists argue for one bishop) that a city can be ruled only by one, answers thus: "The Apostles would have to be accused who appointed several bishops in the same city. Men have indeed thought that one Church is ruled better and more easily by one, since the custom of a single bishop was introduced; but it does not follow that what seems better is therefore necessary." Then, even this was not seen as better in an absolute sense, but only for avoiding schisms, as Jerome testifies. In a similar way we may say that equality among pastors, that is, isotimia, is better than monarchy [ἀρχίαν], namely for avoiding the tyranny of a few over the other brethren, which experience has at last shown how great an evil it is, and how open a door is thrown wide to it by ambition of this kind of philarchia [φιλαρχίας]. And so let this be the end of the third point on the excellence of the ecclesiastical polity, namely its necessity.

units.la: CAP. 19.
units.tr: CAP. 19.

units.la: Visus praedictorum, quod cujusq; Ecclesiae sit exactam reformationem instituere,
units.tr: Of the view of these writers, that every Church ought to institute a thorough reformation of itself

units.la: ACCEPIMUS politeias Ecclesiasticae praestantia quanta sit: vidimus dignitatem, utilitatem conspeximus, expositumus denique necessitatem. Ex his jam porro hoc νῆμα emergit: in officio cujusque Ecclesiae esse, ut exacta illius reformatio instituatur; sic ut avito atq; pristino suo niteat. Quò magis dolendum in Anglia jam hodie usu venire illud, quod suo saeculo Gerardus Lorichius conquestus est: Sunt pseudocatholici qui reformationem Ecclesiae quoquo modo remorari non verentur: verum etiam quod tempore Hezechiæ, Leuitae promptiores erant se sanctificare quàm sacerdotes, 2. Chron. 29. 34. quod tempore Nehemiae etiam. Qui magni erant colla sua ad opus apponere recusarunt. Neh. 3. 5. Qui etenim in Anglia velut antesignani reliquis fratribus praeire debuerunt: hos ipsos fratres remorantur imo persequuntur, ipsumq; reformationis opus non tantùm collo subducto deserunt, sed quasi collo obdurato pro virili impediunt.
units.tr: We have seen how great the excellence of ecclesiastical polity is: we have considered its dignity, observed its usefulness, and at last set out its necessity. From these things there now emerges this thread [νῆμα]: it is the duty of every Church that a thorough reformation of it be undertaken, so that it may shine in its ancient and original state. All the more is it to be lamented that what Gerard Lorichius complained of in his own age now happens in England today: There are pseudo-Catholics who do not hesitate to delay the reformation of the Church in any way. Indeed, in the time of Hezekiah, the Levites were more ready to sanctify themselves than the priests, 2 Chron. 29.34; and so also in the time of Nehemiah, those who were great refused to put their necks to the work, Neh. 3.5. For those who in England ought to go before their brethren like standard-bearers, these very brethren they hold back, or rather persecute; and they abandon the work of reformation not merely by drawing back the neck, but, as with a stiff neck, they resist it with all their might.

units.la: Primò verò ita arguunt, eorum nonnulli saltem, ac si Euangelio quoad doctrinam restituto, non esset multùm de disciplina laborandum. Interrogant etenim, Annon hoc bene est? Mariae temporibus hæc vobis libertas gratissima fuisset; jam ipso Euangelio per Elizabetham restituto contenti esse non potestis? Benè quidem hoc esse dicimus, de eo gaudemus, de eo summas divinæ clementiæ gratias agimus: est tamen quod lætitiam nostram diminuat, quòd cum illis Iudeæ Senioribus. Ezræ 3.2. ita domus Dei fundamenta jacta cernimus, ut Ecclesiæ illius primæ puritatem & gloriam, in multis desiderare cogamur. Non etenim absq; causa fuit quod ad Magnam Elizabetham scribens Beza, restare adhuc disciplinę instaurationem admonuit, templis nostris non exactè purgatis, excelsis verò nonnullis stantibus, quę abolenda essent.
units.tr: First, some of them at least argue as if, the Gospel having been restored as to doctrine, there were no need to labour much over discipline. For they ask: "Is this not good? In Mary's time this freedom would have been most welcome to you; now that the Gospel itself has been restored through Elizabeth, can you not be content?" We indeed say that this is good; we rejoice at it and give the highest thanks to the mercy of God. Yet there is something that diminishes our joy: that, like those elders of Judah, Ezra 3.2, we see the foundations of the house of God laid in such a way that we are forced to lack in many respects the purity and glory of that first Church. Not without cause did Beza, writing to the great Elizabeth, warn that the restoration of discipline still remained to be done: our temples were not thoroughly cleansed, and some high places were still standing which ought to be abolished.

units.la: Neq; sanè video cur hanc Bezæ monitionē tantopere Bancroftus exagitaret: nisi aut solam doctrinę restitutionem sufficere putet, aut disciplinam jam satis restitutam existimet: quorum utrumvis si sòniare instituerit, audiat illâ I.Reynold, viri sicut doctissimi, ita temperatissimi refutatione luculentam. Is reformationis Ezechiane postquâ mentionem fecisset, subjicit: in regno nostro, religioni reformandæ, multo minori zelo studeri, præsertim in eis quæ pertinet ad officia & partes Levitarum: ac proinde Deū a nobis ardentib° precib° obsecrandū esse dicit, & homines obtestationib°, hortationib°, admonitionib° modis deniq; omnibus urgendos esse, ut in omnibus quæ pertinent ad purgandam & reformandam Ecclesiam, princeps gratiosissima, senatus nobilesq; omnes, atq; adeo totus populus, sui officij erga Iehovam, cum grata animi testificatione dies noctesq; perpetuo meminerint.
units.tr: Nor indeed do I see why Bancroft harassed this admonition of Beza so greatly, unless he thinks that the restoration of doctrine alone is sufficient, or considers discipline already sufficiently restored. If he undertakes to maintain either of these, let him hear the clear refutation of J. Reynolds, a man as learned as he is moderate. After mentioning the Hezekian reformation, he adds: In our kingdom much less zeal is applied to reforming religion, especially in those matters which pertain to the offices and duties of the Levites; and therefore we must besiege God with ardent prayers, and urge men by entreaties, exhortations, admonitions, and finally by every means, so that in all things which pertain to purging and reforming the Church, the most gracious prince, the senate, all the nobles, and indeed the whole people may with grateful acknowledgment of mind remember day and night, continually, their duty toward Jehovah.

units.la: Videre hinc licet, nihil a Bezâ admonitum fuisse, quod monendum non sit; nihil in reformatione Anglicana desideratum, quod non a singulis usque desiderari debeat. At magis illud Bancroftum urit, quòd D.Beza in Epistola 69. Anno 1572. ad nobilem quendam in Anglia scripserit, Ecclesias non multò meliori conditione esse propter reformatam doctrinam, nisi ad puritatem disciplinæ etiam adjungendam aspiretur. Atquè qui de priori Epistola tacuit Georgius Downamus hoc tamen in Bezā vellicat, non solùm ut quiddam inconsideratum, sed in Deum ingratum etiam. Atqui non hæc Dominus Beza locutus est, quasi doctrinæ reformatio admirabile Dei beneficium non esset: sed quòd hoc beneficium absque disciplinæ adminiculo diu conservari nequeat. Hoc sensu solùm Ecclesiarum conditionem non multo meliorem dixit propter doctrinam reformatam: quia exulante disciplina, hæc multo melior Ecclesiarum conditio, non ita multo obtineri tempore possit. Sed missô Bezâ, ita nos jam hodie Hierarchici adoriuntur. Siccine verò Elizabetha vere matris Israelis reformationem formationem deturpatis, Quasi vero Iosiæ regis illam multo nostrâ illustriorem reformationem, præter officium Zephaniæ deturparit: quòd quasdâ illû Baalis, reliquias reliquisse diceret, quæ è medio tollendæ erant, cap. 1. verf. 4. Neq; aliquam Asanæ reformationi labem se immeritò aspersurum credidit Iehosaphat: quando adhuc amplius animum leuavit ad Iehouam, & quæ supererant reformanda perpurgavit, 2. Chron. 17. 6. Perfecit Constantinus quæ inchoauit Philippus, dicit Baronius: certè quod reliquit non reformatum Constantinus, perfecit Theodosius, habet Ruffinus: neque tamen Constantini reformationem dehonestavit: sed exemplo suo præivit potiùs, ut incumbant singuli argenteam Ecclesiam relinquere, quam lateritiam invenerint: & quod Salomon, invento parieti, pallatium argenteum superstruere, Cant. 8. 9. Hæc ita cum sint, immerito in Anglia hodie vapulant servi Dei sub reformatorum nomine, quod Ezechiæ, Iosiæ, Malachiæ, ipsius deniq; Iesu Christi exempla secuti, non de doctrina reformanda tantùm, sed & de vicib' Levitarum ordinandis, de cortuptelis sacerdotum emendandis, de templi profanationibus amoliendis laborandum esse censent.
units.tr: From this it can be seen that Beza admonished nothing that ought not to be admonished; nothing is found wanting in the English reformation that ought not to be wanted by each one. But what galls Bancroft more is that Dr Beza, in Epistle 69, in the year 1572, wrote to a certain noble in England that the churches were not in a much better condition because of the reformed doctrine, unless they also aspired to add purity of discipline. George Downame, who was silent about the earlier epistle, nonetheless carps at Beza on this point, calling it not only something rash but even ungrateful toward God. Yet Dr Beza did not say this as if the reformation of doctrine were not a wonderful benefit of God, but because this benefit cannot long be preserved without the support of discipline. In this sense alone did he say that the condition of the churches was not much better because of the reformed doctrine: because, with discipline absent, this much better condition of the churches cannot be kept for long. But setting Beza aside, this is how the hierarchs attack us today: Thus indeed, Elizabeth, do you spoil the reformation of the true mother of Israel? As if Josiah's reformation, far more illustrious than ours, were spoiled by the office of Zephaniah, in that he said some remnants of Baal were left which had to be removed from the midst, ch. 1 v. 4. Nor did Jehoshaphat believe that any stain would justly be cast on Asa's reformation, when he "lifted up his heart further to Jehovah" and thoroughly purged what remained to be reformed, 2 Chron. 17.6. Constantine completed what Philip began, says Baronius; certainly what Constantine left unreformed, Theodosius completed, says Rufinus. Yet Constantine did not dishonour the reformation; rather, by his example he went before, so that each should strive to leave a silver church rather than find a brick one, and as Solomon, having found a wall, built a silver palace, Song 8.9. These things being so, the servants of God in England today are unjustly beaten under the name of reformers. They, following the examples of Hezekiah, Josiah, Malachi, and finally of Jesus Christ himself, judge that labour must be spent not only on reforming doctrine but also on ordering the offices of the Levites, on correcting the corruptions of the priests, and on removing the profanations of the temple.

units.la: Certè ad exemplum Christi flagello templum perpurgantis, disciplinam sui temporis reformandam esse, Nicolaus de Clemangis, ut apud D. Mornæum videre est: & ad exemplum Iosiæ collapsam disciplinam sibi restituendam Carolus Magnus existimavit: qui etiam ad hanc rem Anno. 813. concilium Moguntiacum congregavit. Hujus verò ipsius exemplo ita Carolus & Ludovicus reformandæ disciplinæ invigilarunt, ut in pastoribus præsertim pellendis & loco movendis, qui Evangelium prædicare, aut noluerunt sedulò, aut omninò non potuerunt, opus nos habeamus jam in Anglia cum Platina vovere: O Ludovice! utinam nunc viveres. Iohannes Rupescissanus vixit ad Annum 1350. is clarè indicavit fore, ut Clerus repurgaretur, sacerdotes pauperes, pios, & fideliter gregem Domini pascentes haberet Ecclesia, bonis superfluis Ecclesiasticis ad Laicos reversis. Proh prorsus Puritanum. Hanc reformationem benignissimâ Dei clementiâ, in Ecclesijs quibusque reformatis restitutam, quoad disciplinam deformare in Anglia jam Episcopi satagunt, sanctos hosce pastores ablegando, ornatum papisticum illum in divitijs & mundana pompa positum præligendo, & gaudium sanctorum denique inquietando, qui sanctis pastoribus suis decorati exultabant. Neque ego plura addam; præsertim cum hisce exemplis pateat, reformationem disciplinæ exactiorem, sanctis semper necessariam visam esse, quàm quæ in Anglia obtinet. Atque hæc de reformationis remora prima.
units.tr: Certainly, following the example of Christ cleansing the temple with a whip, Nicolaus de Clemangis held that the discipline of his own time must be reformed, as can be seen in Dr Mornay. Following the example of Josiah, Charles the Great thought that the collapsed discipline must be restored to its place, and for this very matter he gathered the council of Mainz in the year 813. By the example of this same man, Charles and Louis so watched over the reform of discipline that, especially in driving out and removing from their posts those ministers who either would not preach the Gospel diligently or could not do so at all, we in England now have cause to vow with Platina: O Louis! Would that you were living now! John of Rupescissa, who lived to the year 1350, clearly indicated that the clergy would be purged, and that the Church would have poor and pious priests faithfully feeding the flock of the Lord, with superfluous ecclesiastical goods returned to the laity. Oh, a true Puritan! This reformation, restored by the most gracious mercy of God in all the reformed churches, the bishops in England now labour to deform as regards discipline: by sending away these holy ministers, by choosing that papistical adornment placed in riches and worldly pomp, and finally by disturbing the joy of the saints, who once rejoiced, adorned by their holy ministers. I will add no more, since by these examples it is plain that a more exact reformation of discipline has always been seen as necessary by the saints than the one that obtains in England. And this is the first obstacle to reformation.

units.la: CAP. 20. Remora secunda, disciplinam non convenire his temporibus.
units.tr: CAP. 20. The second obstacle: that discipline does not suit these times.

units.la: Secundum adversariorum genus est, qui non tam ipsam reformationis in disciplinâ necessitatem impugnant, quàm istis temporibus convenientiam. In his Doctor Somius noster ita loquitur. Libenter scirem, an possibile veltutum sit in hac terra disciplinam plantare, antequam sacrosancta Dei veritas solidè & doceatur & accipiatur, & idonei rectores Ecclesiastici, aptuq; populus, ad disciplinam exercendum, reperiantur. Atqui libenter ego scirem ex adverso, annon haec ipsissima procrastinatio Iudaeorum sit, quam Haggeus reprehendit: Tempus adhuc non est ut domus Dei aedificetur, cap. 1. vers. 2. ipsissimaque ignavia illa quam in agricola non ferendam Salomon censet, Ecclesiast. 11. 4. qui sementem elabi è manibus finit, dum commodiorem tempestatem praestolatur? Vae illis qui opus Domini negligenter faciunt, non est in Dei negotijs lente agendum, sed imitandi Apostoli potiùs, qui Ecclesias nunquam plantarunt, quin in ipsis incunabulis, disciplinam unà cum doctrina absque mora stabilierunt, Act. 14. 20. Tit. 1. 5. Quibus haec solertia & prudentia spiritus in initijs Ecclesiarum negligitur; nae illi in posterum introducendae disciplinae tempus commodius frustra expectant; vulnus interim infligentes, quod aut nunquam aut nimis serò sanari poterit. Non ineptè siquidem Homerus, Ἄτη quae damna infert mortalibus, Deam pennatam & velocem facit, λιταὶ vero, quibus haec damna resarcire in officio est, non nisi lento gradu, incedentes & longo intervallo a tergo sequentes introducit.
units.tr: The second kind of opponents does not so much deny the necessity of reformation in discipline as deny that it suits the present times. Our Doctor Somius speaks thus: "I would gladly know whether it is possible, or even fitting, to plant discipline in this land before the most holy truth of God is both taught and received, and before suitable rulers of the Church and a people fit for exercising discipline can be found." But I would gladly ask in return whether this is not the very delay which Haggai rebuked: "The time is not yet come that the house of God should be built" (Hag. 1.2), and the very sloth which Solomon judges intolerable in a farmer (Eccles. 11.4), who lets the seed slip from his hands while he waits for a more convenient season? "Woe to them that do the work of the Lord negligently" (Jer. 48.10). In God's affairs one must not act slowly, but rather imitate the Apostles, who never planted churches without establishing discipline together with doctrine, at once, at their very beginnings (Acts 14.23; Titus 1.5). Those who neglect this skill and prudence of the Spirit at the beginnings of the Churches vainly wait for a more opportune time to introduce discipline later, meanwhile inflicting a wound which can never be healed, or can be healed only far too late. Homer aptly made [Ἄτη], Ruin, which brings harm upon mortals, a winged and swift goddess, while [λιταί], Prayers, which are the duty to repair these harms, come on with a slow step and follow far behind at a distance.

units.la: Sanè experientia omnium temporum quam hoc in disciplinae reformatione protelandâ, sit metuendum, comprobavit. Vrget Cesar Sigismundus disciplinae reformationem in concilio Constantiensi. Respondet Papa, vehementer ejus consilium sibi probari, summaque se id ope adjuturum: sed jam tantùm temporis non restare, quantùm ad rem tantam opus sit. Majora esse, quae prius perficienda essent; quibus transactis, se huiusce reformationis, memorem futurum. Quid fit? eluditur pius Imperator, pij frustrantur, & prodit in posterum ridiculus mus. Convenerant principes reformationis ergo Noribergae Anno 1523, ad eos ita scripsit Adrianus papa VI. Nemo mirari debet si non statim omnia errata & abusus omnes emendatos viderit. In veteratus mimium morbus est, nec simplex, sed varius & multiplex: pedetentim in ejus curâ procedendum est, & prius graviora magisque periculosi occurrendum, ne omnia pariter reformare volentes, omnia perturbemus. Fumum hîc Papa vendidit: certe procrastinatione ista, omnia piorum principum consilia, quae de Ecclesia reformanda volutabant, tum in fumos abierunt. Carnalis igitur haec prudentia humana est, & minimè ferenda. Desunt idonei rectores (inquit) & populus aptus ad disciplinam exercendam. Quid post tot annos? Cur desint rogo? Unde etiam est, quòd post Evangelium longo tempore praedicatum, ejusdem veritas adhuc nec solidè recipiatur nec doceatur? Annon quia deest disciplina illa, per quam Evangelij praedicatio efficax redditur? Penitentur diligenter illa, quae Christus ipse, ad Angliam nostram in sua Apocalipsi scribit, qua Ecclesiae Laodicea àrvuv est, Apoc. 3. 14. 15, &c. veracem etenim testem sese in Anglia praebuisse dicit, & hoc tantùm conqueritur, quod doctrinâ receptâ, disciplina ita exulet, ut non nisi tepida quaedam reformatio facta sit, quae media pendeat, inter Romam, & Ecclesias reformatas. Atque haec ad reformationis in disciplina remoram secundam.
units.tr: Indeed the experience of all ages has shown how much one must fear this postponement of reformation in discipline. Emperor Sigismund urged the reform of discipline at the Council of Constance. The Pope replied that he greatly approved of this counsel and would help with his utmost effort, but that there was not yet as much time as so great a matter required: greater things had first to be accomplished, and once these were done he would be mindful of this reformation. What happened? The pious Emperor was mocked, the pious were frustrated, and in the end the ridiculous mouse came forth. The princes who had gathered at Nuremberg for reformation in the year 1523 were written to by Pope Adrian VI in these terms: "No one ought to be surprised if he does not at once see all errors and all abuses corrected. The disease is too inveterate, and it is not simple but varied and manifold; one must proceed gradually in its cure, and deal first with the graver and more dangerous matters, lest in wishing to reform everything at once we throw everything into confusion." The Pope sold smoke here: certainly by this delay all the plans of the pious princes, which they had been turning over for reforming the Church, then vanished into smoke. This prudence, then, is merely human and by no means to be tolerated. "There are no fit rulers," he says, "and no people apt for exercising discipline." What after so many years? Why are they lacking, I ask? Is it not because that discipline is lacking, through which the preaching of the Gospel is made effective, that the truth of the Gospel, though preached for a long time, is still neither firmly received nor taught? Let us carefully consider what Christ himself writes in his Apocalypse to our England, where the Church is Laodicea, "the beginning" (Rev. 3.14, 15, etc.). For he says that he has shown himself a faithful witness in England, and he complains of only this: that while doctrine has been received, discipline is so banished that only a lukewarm reformation has been made, which hangs between Rome and the reformed Churches. And this is the second obstacle to reformation in discipline.

units.la: CAP. 21 Remora tertia, disciplinam jam in Anglia perfectam esse, removetur: primo morbum ejus ostendendo.
units.tr: CAP. 21. The third obstacle, that discipline is already perfect in England, is removed: first by showing its disease.

units.la: Tertia omnium impeditissima est. Multi ad perfectionem (dicit quidam) perventient, nisi jam se pervenisse crederent: ad perfectionem verò reformationis se jam pervenisse, plurimi de nostris credunt: quo fit, ut perventuros aliquando fore desperandum sit. Atq; hunc φλαυλιας morbum Ecclesiae nostrae, satis ostendunt Hierarchicorum ipsorum scripta. Quum enim in colloquio Hamptoniensi, rem reformationis proposuisset Rex, prosilijt in medium Jo. White, & procidens in genua, sanctè in suam animam recepit, in Ecclesia Anglicana nihil tum fuisse, quod reformandum esset. Ri. Baner. ita, Regimen nostrum in Anglia Ecclesiasticum vere Apostolicum est, & multis gradibus omni regimini anteferendum, quod usquam in tota Christianitate, jam hodie usurpatur. Ita Georg. Downamus; Nulla sub sole Ecclesia est, quae in doctrinae substantia, disciplinae & forma, ad exemplar primae, Apostolicae & Ecclesiae tam prope accedit, atq; ha nostrae, quae vestro gratioso sub iacent imperio. Itane verò? Tantumne Adonie; quanta caecitas in egentissima paupertate? Imo vero (inquit Georgius Downamus) disciplina Ecclesiarum reformatarum argentum tantum est: nostra vero Anglicana aurum: vere aureum somnium. Expergiscere etenim; audias Christum aureum disciplinam suam [in Anglia Laodicea àrvuv] deesse conquerentem, & dices postquam evigilaveris, ecce somnium erat.
units.tr: The third is by far the most hindering. "Many would attain to perfection," as someone says, "unless they believed they had already attained it." Yet very many of our people believe that they have already reached perfection in reformation, and so it comes about that one must despair of their ever attaining it. The writings of the Hierarchs themselves sufficiently show this disease of our Church, this [φλαυλίας], complacency. When the King had proposed the matter of reformation at the Hampton conference, John White sprang forward into the midst, and falling on his knees solemnly declared upon his soul that in the English Church at that time there was nothing that needed reforming. Richard Bancroft says: "Our government in England in Church matters is truly apostolic, and is to be preferred by many degrees to every government which is anywhere in all Christendom used today." So too George Downame: "There is no Church under the sun which in the substance of doctrine, in discipline and in form comes so near to the pattern of the first, apostolic Church as ours, which lies under your gracious rule." Is it so, Adonis? What blindness in the most abject poverty! "Nay indeed," says George Downame, "the discipline of the reformed Churches is only silver, but our English discipline is gold: a truly golden dream. For wake up, and you will hear Christ complaining that his golden discipline is lacking in England, the Laodicean [beginning], and when you are awake you will say: behold, it was a dream."

units.la: Neque illud ratione ullâ a te dicitur, quum disciplina Anglie aurea sit, contrariam in Ecclesijs reformatis argenteam esse posse. Jœnum etenim & stipulam illam disciplinam esse necesse est, quae per fundamentum, absque verbi divini ullo fundamento ædificatur, 1. Cor. 3. 12. quòd si vero hoc de Ecclesijs reformatis dicere veteris, cur auream disciplinam Angliæ dicere non veteris? præsertim cum illa pauper esse non poterit, si disciplinam in qua deficit, auream haberet. At vero illa non aureram nec argenteam disciplinam habet? cum vel te ipso confitente ex verbo divino præscripta non sit, quæ cujusque rectæ & legitimæ reformationis norma unica est,uti Zanchius attestatur. Is etenim de reformatione Ecclesiæ ad D. Knollum scribens: introducit tanquam ipsius regulam, illam hominis orthodoxi vocem apud Theodoretum. E'χεί μὴν πιστευ-ρον τε θεια χαρα. Descendit deinde ad reformationem disciplinæ specia-tim, de qua sic habet. Ecclesiæ sunt reformandæ ad formam eius optimam. Melior Ecclesiæ forma inveniri aut excogitari non potest eâ, quam Christus per se & per suos Apostolos, Ecclesiæ initio constituit & confirmavit. Et paulo post. Omnia cultus & disciplinæ dogmata, non ad Lesbyam regulam humani iudicij, sed ad lapidem Lydium verbi divini examinanda. Huic autem regulæ reformatio Anglicana respondere quî potest, Dolunami præsertim aliorumque judicio, qui disciplinam mutabilem iuxta Lesbiam regulam humani judicij esse volunt: quique Lydium in verbo lapidem nullum esse affirmant, ad quem disciplina examinaretur. Atque hic defectus reformationis Anglicanæ primus est.
units.tr: Nor can you say with any reason that, since English discipline is golden, the contrary discipline in the reformed Churches can be silver. For that discipline must necessarily be hay and stubble which is built upon the foundation without any foundation in the divine Word (1 Cor. 3.12). But if you say this of the reformed Churches, why do you not say that English discipline is golden? Especially since it could not be poor if it had golden discipline in which it is deficient. Yet does it have neither golden nor silver discipline, since, by your own confession, it is not prescribed by the divine Word, which is the only rule of any right and lawful reformation, as Zanchius attests? For writing to Mr. Knollys about the reformation of the Church, he introduces as its rule that saying of an orthodox man in Theodoret: [ἔχει μὲν πιστευρον τε θεια χαρα]. He then descends to the reformation of discipline in particular, of which he says: "Churches are to be reformed according to their best form. A better form of the Church cannot be found or devised than that which Christ himself and through his Apostles established and confirmed at the beginning of the Church." And a little later: "All the dogmas of worship and discipline are to be examined not by the Lesbian rule of human judgement, but by the Lydian touchstone of the divine Word." But how can the English reformation answer to this rule, especially by the judgement of Dolunami and others, who want discipline to be changeable according to the Lesbian rule of human judgement, and who affirm that there is no Lydian stone in the Word by which discipline might be tested? And this is the first defect of the English reformation.

units.la: CAP. 22. Secundo, ad normam primitivæ Ecclesiæ revocando.
units.tr: CHAPTER 22. Secondly, to be brought back to the norm of the primitive Church.

units.la: SECVNDVS, adversus secundam illam regulam Zanchianam peccat quam deinceps proponit de Ecclesiæ primitivæ imitatione, non tam reipsa forte, quam ratione à prima diversam. Qualis fuit (inquit) illa veteris & Apostolicæ Ecclesiæ forma tempore Christi & Apostolorum liquidò & certò apparet ex libris Evangelistarum & Apostolorum: probabiliter autem ex reliquis post Apostolos, antiquissimis Ecclesiasticis scriptoribus. Ad illam igitur Ecclesiæ formam quæ in sacris literis traditur, deinde ad illam quæ in antiquissimis scriptoribus conspicitur, quatenus ista cum illa non pugnat, disciplina reformanda est: juxta illud Isaiæ primo: Excoquam ad purum scoriam tuam, & auferam omne stannum tuum, & restituam iudices tuos sicut fuerunt primi, & seniores tuos sicut antiquitus, & post hæc vocaberis civitas iusticiæ, civitas fidelis. Similiter Ier. 6. 16. Hæc dicit Dominus. State in viis & circumspicite, & interrogate de semitis antiquis, quænam via bona sit. Et Christus denique Math. 19. reformaturus matrimonium, Iudæos ad primam matrimonij institutionem revocavit, dicens. A principio autem
units.tr: Secondly, he offends against that second rule of Zanchius, which he then sets out concerning the imitation of the primitive Church, a rule that perhaps differs from the first not so much in fact as in its reasoning. "Such (he says) was that form of the old and Apostolic Church at the time of Christ and the Apostles, as is clear and certain from the books of the Evangelists and Apostles; but probably from the rest, the most ancient ecclesiastical writers after the Apostles." Discipline is therefore to be reformed according to that form of the Church which is handed down in the sacred letters, and then according to that which is seen in the most ancient writers, so far as these do not conflict with the former; in accordance with that saying of Isaiah 1: "I will purge away your dross as with lye, and take away all your tin, and I will restore your judges as at the first, and your counsellors as at the beginning; afterward you shall be called the city of righteousness, the faithful city." Likewise Jer. 6.16: "Thus says the Lord: Stand in the ways and look, and ask for the old paths, which is the good way." And finally Christ, Matth. 19, about to reform marriage, called the Jews back to the first institution of marriage, saying: "But from the beginning..."

units.la: De Matthæo Sutclivio non opus est dicere: cum totum caput decimum tertium eò destinarit, ut probet Ecclesiæ regimen mutabile esse, quòd nulla ejusdem certa regula, vel ex verbo, vel ex primæ Ecclesiæ exemplo peti possit. Richardus Bancroftus non tam disputat, quàm suo more deridet & calumniatur. In ea ætate vivimus (inquit) qua ingeminari solet prima institutio, Institutio prima: Verba bona sunt si accommodentur bene. Sed aliquid nimis tectum erat in sacerdotis illius applicatione, quando inter rebellem domesticorum multitudinem exclamavit dicens: Quando teram fodiebat Adam, & telam Eva ducebat, ubi tum generosus erat? In his testimonijs largior fui, ne injuriam Hierarchicis à me illatam quis putaret, quòd Ecclesiæ primitivæ in politeiis Ecclesiasticæ reformatione imitationem, ab is negatam, aut quod magis est, impugnatam dicam: quanvis autem ea recitasse satis refutasse sit: error tamen adhuc amplius rationum nonnullarum appositione detegendus videtur.
units.tr: There is no need to speak of Matthew Sutcliffe, since he devotes the whole thirteenth chapter to proving that the government of the Church is changeable, because no certain rule for it can be drawn either from the Word or from the example of the primitive Church. Richard Bancroft does not so much argue as mock and slander, after his manner. "We live (he says) in an age in which the phrase 'first institution, first institution' is wont to be repeated. Good words are fine if they are fitted well. But something was too much hidden in that priest's application, when, among the rebellious crowd of household servants, he cried out: 'When Adam dug the earth, and Eve span the thread, where then was the gentleman?'" I have been rather full in these testimonies, lest anyone think that I charge the Hierarchicals with an injury, as if I were saying that they deny, or what is worse, attack, the imitation of the primitive Church in the reform of ecclesiastical polity. Although to have recited these is enough to refute them, the error nevertheless seems to need to be exposed further by the addition of some arguments.

units.la: CAP. 23. Adversarij Montanismi arguuntur: & disciplinam ad normam Primitivæ Ecclesiæ formandam esse probatur.
units.tr: CHAP. 23. The opponents of Montanism are refuted, and it is shown that church discipline must be shaped by the norm of the Primitive Church.

units.la: DICO igitur, primò Montanismo velificari, hanc Ecclesiæ primitivæ impugnationem: indeque suspicionem minimè levem suboriri, eam rudiorem & imperfectiorem fuisse, quàm ut Ecclesiæ ad maturitate jam perductæ illius infantiam imitari teneantur. Declinat quidem hujus hæreseos suspicionem Whitgiftus sedulò, ideò infert. Nulla derogatio est ab Apostolica Ecclesia, ut ejusdem ordinationes nonnullis in rebus immutentur: quanquam enim illi tempori expediebant non tamen huic ætati in qua nos vivimus, sicut forma Apostolicæ Ecclesiæ perfecta & absoluta fuerit, licet nunc admittat in quibusdam circumstantijs alterationem. Sed similiter pro se Montanista responderc potuit, Ecclesiam quidem Apostolicam perfectam suisse pro sua ætate infantili & puerili, licet in comparatione ad ætatem sequentem virilem & maturam, imperfectam. Atque sanè Montani principia hostes nostros plus satis olere, vel eo conjicere licet, quòd ad Tertullianum eo in loco confugere Whitgiftus veritus non sit, ubi Montanismi sui non leviter pressa vestigia prodit: probat etenim adversùs Cartwrightum disciplinam mutabilem esse, ex illo testimonio Tertulliani, in quo sic loquitur. Regula fidei manente, cevera disciplina & conversationis admittunt novitatem correctionis, operan do scilicet ad perficiente usque ad finem gratia Dei.
units.tr: I say, then, first, that this assault on the Primitive Church sails with the wind of Montanism, and from it there arises a suspicion by no means slight: that the Primitive Church was too rough and imperfect to be the infancy which the Church, now brought to maturity, is bound to imitate. Whitgift, indeed, takes care to avoid the suspicion of this heresy, and therefore he argues: There is no disparagement of the Apostolic Church in that its ordinances are changed in some matters. For although they were suited to that time, they are not suited to this age in which we live. Just as the form of the Apostolic Church was perfect and complete, so it now admits alteration in certain circumstances. But the Montanist could have answered in the same way on his own behalf: that the Apostolic Church was indeed perfect for its own infantile and childlike age, though imperfect in comparison with the following age, which is manly and mature. And indeed that the principles of Montanus smell strongly of our enemies may be inferred from this, that Whitgift has not been ashamed to take refuge with Tertullian in the very place where he betrays the traces of his own Montanism, not lightly pressed. For he proves against Cartwright that discipline is changeable from that testimony of Tertullian's, in which he speaks thus: The rule of faith remaining, the other matters of discipline and conduct admit the novelty of correction, working, namely, toward perfecting by the grace of God until the end.

units.la: En fundamenta Hierarchicorum quibus probant, regulam quidem fidei immutabilé esse, disciplinæ non item. Annon etenim hoc Tertulliani, Montanicum prorsus est? annon ipsum caput Montanisti tangit, quum uberiorem Dei gratiam somniat subsequentibus sæculis, quàm quæ temporibus Apostolorum effusa erat? Verbis vero proximis comparat Ecclesiam Apostolicam, arbori germinanti, quæ per adventum paracleti ad maturitatem perducenda erat, quoniam humana mediocritas omnia simul capere non potuit, ad persectam disciplinam tempore sequenti perduceretur, ab illo vicario domini Spiritu sancto: quæ aperte Montanica sunt.
units.tr: Behold the foundations of the Hierarchists, by which they prove that the rule of faith is indeed unchangeable, but discipline is not likewise. Is this not entirely the Montanist doctrine of Tertullian? Does it not touch the very head of Montanism, when it dreams of a more abundant grace of God in the following centuries than that which was poured out in the times of the Apostles? In the words that follow, moreover, he compares the Apostolic Church to a germinating tree, which was to be brought to maturity by the coming of the Paraclete, since human mediocrity could not take in everything at once; it would be led to perfect discipline in a later time by that Holy Spirit, the vicar of the Lord. These are plainly Montanist notions.

units.la: Secundò, Ecclesiam primitivam ita perfectam extitisse, vt tempora omnia subsecutura ad eandem disciplinæ formam obligarit; ex ipsis sacris apparet luculeter. Quorsum enim consuetudine Ecclesiarum primarum urgeret Paulus, si ad imitationem non obligarent? 1.Cor.11.16.Nullam eiusmodi consuetudinem Ecclesiæ Dei habent.1.Cor. 14.33. sicut videmus in omnibus Ecclesijs sanctorum. 2 Tim. 3, 14. Tu nosti conversationem meam in Ecclesijs. Quid ut a tergo rejiceret? imo addit continuò: permaneto in eis quæ didicisti. Sic Philip. 4, 9. in mandato dat, ut ea curarent, quæ vidissent in eo, aut de eo audi-visset. Sanè ostendunt hæc singula manifestè, non præceptum tantummodo Apostolorum, sed & exemplum etiam, una cum exemplo primarum Ecclesiarum in rebus a I disciplinam pertinentibus obligare in perpetuum. Apocal. 2. 5. mandatur Ecclesiæ Ephesinæ, eiusque antitypo Ecclesiæ primæ propè annum 300, deficienti.
units.tr: Secondly, that the primitive Church was so perfect that it bound all subsequent times to the same form of discipline, appears clearly from the sacred writings themselves. For why would Paul urge the custom of the first churches, if they did not bind to imitation? 1 Cor. 11.16: We have no such custom, nor have the churches of God. 1 Cor. 14.33: as we see in all the churches of the saints. 2 Tim. 3.14: Thou hast known my manner of life in the churches. What, so to speak, would he cast behind his back? Nay, he adds at once: continue in those things which thou hast learned. So in Philip. 4.9 he commands them in a mandate to observe those things which they had seen in me, or had heard from me. Indeed these single passages clearly show that not only the precept of the Apostles but also their example, together with the example of the first churches, binds in perpetuity in matters pertaining to discipline. In Apocal. 2.5 the Ephesian Church is commanded, and its antitype, the Primitive Church of about the year 300, which was failing.

units.la: Fac priora opera. Quid hinc concluditur inquis? Nempe primitivam gubernationem omnium temporum & locorum communem esse, in Ecclesia reformanda ad prima principia recurrendum esse, eandem disciplinam esse totius orbis & unius urbis, tam sub Christiano magistratu, quàm cum magistratus deerat. De disciplinæ etenim correctione hic agitur, & quanquam in Ephesi antitypo præ foribus iam Constantinus erat, Imperator Christianus gubernacula capessurus: pristinam tamen Ecclesiæ primæ disciplinam urget Christus, quam per Apostolos instituerat. Ap. 3,3. Memento quomodo acceperis & audieris, & observa & reservato. Annon monet hic Sardensis Christus, ut a primam institutionem recurrant, & res collapsas ad illius solium normam emendent? Quod si verò Lutherana Ecclesia ut Brighamnno videtur, hujus Sardicensis antytipos sit: eòdem recurrit reformationis ratio. Quæ enim prius à Luthero accepit Ecclesia Lutherani, ad primam restitutionem efformata singula erant, ut ex illa ipsius Lutheri contestatione liquet. Contestatos eos esse volo, me prorsus nullius quam tamlibet sancti patris authoritate cogi velle, nisi quatenus iudicio divinæ scripturæ fuerit probata. Apocal.12.describitur Ecclesiæ status qui aut Constantinum, & sub Constantino, & post Con-stanstantinum erat. Quero igitur. Num status ecclesiæ qui sub Constantino incepit imitandus a Spiritu sancto proponitur? Nequaquam vero, tum enim Ecclesia in solitudine fugari coepit.Cap.6.& 14. Sed nec Ecclefiæ pars illa posterior quæ Constantinum proximè antecessit, imitanda nobis est,quæ à Dracone suo ope impugnata erat, quæq; caudâ draconis partem tertiâ stellarum à cælo in terram dejectâ habuit: v.4.sed pars illa prima tantummodo quæ adornata duodecim suis stellis erat: id est Apostolis, & veritate à Christo tradita quasi solæ collucebat,c.1. Hæc illa Ecclesia est,quæ Ap.2.7.paradisus Dei dicitur:quo illa Bancrofti ratio(si ratio sit)refellitur, quâ supra tetigimus.Quemadmodû etenim ad primâ illâ Adami & Euæ fœlicitatem aspirare oportet:ita carduos & spinas ætatum sequentium,in omni Ecclesiæ reformatione defalcari par est,ut prima illa Ecclesiæ puritas,integritas,amœnitas reuocetur.
units.tr: Do the former works. What is concluded from this, you say? Namely, that primitive government is common to all times and places; that in reforming the Church one must return to first principles; that the same discipline belongs to the whole world and to a single city, as much under a Christian magistrate as when the magistrate was lacking. For the matter here is the correction of discipline, and although Constantine, the Christian Emperor about to take up the helm, was already at the doors in the antitype of Ephesus, nevertheless Christ urges the former discipline of the Primitive Church, which he had instituted through the Apostles. Apocal. 3.3: Remember how you have received and heard, and observe and hold fast. Does not Christ here, speaking to Sardis, admonish them to return to their first institution and to amend fallen matters by the norm of that? But if indeed the Lutheran Church, as it seems to Brightman, is the antitype of this Sardis, the same method of reformation applies. For those things which the Lutheran Church first received from Luther were each shaped to the first restoration, as is clear from Luther's own testimony: I want them to be called to witness that I by no means wish to be compelled by the authority of any saint, however holy a father, except insofar as it has been proved by the judgment of divine Scripture. In Apocal. 12 is described the state of the Church which was before Constantine, under Constantine, and after Constantine. I ask, therefore: is the state of the Church which began under Constantine set before us by the Holy Spirit for imitation? By no means; for then the Church began to be driven into the wilderness (Apocal. 6 and 14). Nor is that later part of the Church which immediately preceded Constantine to be imitated by us, which was attacked by its Dragon and had the third part of the stars cast from heaven to earth by the dragon's tail (v. 4). But that first part, which was adorned with its twelve stars, that is, the Apostles, and shone alone, as it were, with the truth handed down by Christ (c. 1): this is that Church which is called the paradise of God in Apocal. 2.7. By this, the reasoning of Bancroft (if it is reasoning), which we touched upon above, is refuted. For just as one must aspire to that first happiness of Adam and Eve, so in every reformation of the Church the thistles and thorns of the following ages must be cut away, so that that first purity, integrity and pleasantness of the Church may be recalled.

units.la: CAP. 24.
units.tr: CAP. 24.

units.la: Idem confirmatur testimoniis veteribus.
units.tr: The same is confirmed by testimonies of the ancients.

units.la: TErtiò, ad normam Ecclesiæ primitivæ recurrendum esse docent patres,& ætatum omnium regionum omnium, literati scriptores omnes.Tertullianus in præscriptionibus adversus hæreticos in eo totus est,ut probet ad primos fontes recurrendū esse,ac proindepotiori jure orthodoxos esse,quòd hæredes sint Apostolorū, quòd ab initio fuerint,quòd antiquos terminos non commoverint. Adversus Marcionē ita.In summa,si constat id verius quod prius,id prius quod ab initio,id ab initio quod ab Apostolis: pariter ut qui constalit id esse ab Apostolis traditum,quod apud Ecclesias Apostolorum fuerit sacrosanctum. Cyprianus similiter.Si canalis aquæ quæ copiosè primo & surgiter prosluebat subito deficiat,nonne ad fontem pergitur? Hoc & nunc sacere oportet Dei Sacerdotes,præcepta divina seruantes,ut in aliquo si mutaverit & vacillaverit veritas,ad originem Dominicam, atque Apostolicam traditionem reuertamur,ut inde surgat ortus nostri ratio, unde & ordo & origo surrexit. Hujus ad exemplum Ecclesiæ primitivæ,Hieronymus Lucillus revocat: quidni & eos Hierarchicos etiam? De disciplina etc-nim peræq: ac doctrina hæc Cyprianum intellexisse,vel ex eo solo constat,quod diaconos alibi revocet,ad illa primâ.Act. 6. diaconorum institutionem,cujus etiam eos meminisse jubet.Vincentius Liri-nensis librum scripsit adversus prophanas hereticorum novitates,cujus hæc summa est; quo quicquid recens est magis, & ab orthodoxo illo piæ antiquitatis consensu plùs recedens,hoc minus esse veritati congruum. Ne verò hæc de patribus dixisse illum, aut Papistæ aut Hierarchici putêt,quasi recipiendi illi essent authoritate aliqua sua : non pigebit illius verba quædam supponere. Depositū custodi,inquit Apostolus: in deposito autem Timothei disciplinam latere & Bisonis & Saravia docent. Quid est depositum? Id quod tibi creditum est,non quoda te inventum: quod accepisti,non quod excogitasti: rem non ingenij sed doctrinæ: non usurpationis privatæ,sed traditionis publicæ: rem ad te perperductam, non a te prolatam: in qua non auctor debes esse, sed custos: non institutor, sed seruator: non ducens, sed sequens. Aurum accepisti, aurum redde: nolo mihi pro alijs alia subijcias: nolo pro uno impudenter plumbum aut fraudulenter ornamenta supponas, nolo auri speciem, sed naturam plane. Isidorus Pelusiota, rem nostram propius attingit: ex eo etenim Hierarchem defendit Episcopatus refugiente, quod a simplicitate primitiuae Ecclesiae, Episcopatus degenerarit. Hinc ita loquitur. Illud fortasse ignorare videmini, leuitatis ac manifestudinis dignitatem in tyrannidem transisse. Nam si hoc ostendere potestis, vtrorum pasceudi gregis rationem nunc quoque vigere, maxime quidem eum qui se huic negotio imparem esse arbitratus est, a vobis laudari aequum est. Sin vero res in contrarium cessit, tab eo poena minime expetentur &c. Bernardus ad primam Ecclesiae primae puritatem, simplicitatem, integritatem, disciplinam Ecclesiae suo seculo collapsam, revocare ubique nonne studet? Quis mihi det, inquit, antequam moriar, videre Ecclesiam Dei, sicut in diebus antiquis, quando Apostoli laxabant retia in capturam, non in capturam auri vel argenti sed in capturam animarum. Quam cupio illius te haereditare vocem, cuius adeptus es fidem: pecunia inquit tua sit tecum ad perditionem. Alibi: Vbi aliquando quispiam Apostolorum iudex sederit, aut diuisor terminorum, aut distributor terrarum? Stultisse lego Apostolos iudicandos, sed disse iudicantes non lego. Alibi, Tu pastor procedis deauratus, &c. Hoc sic facitabat Petrus? sic Paulus ludebat? Alibi, Fuerunt ante te quifc totos ouibus pascendis exponerent. Vbi nunc quaeso consuetudo haec? Subijt dissimilis valde, longe in aliud mutata sunt studia, & vtinam non in peius. Quid haec ad Angliam? inquis, Quasi in Anglia videre Ecclesiam Dei, sicut erat in diebus antiquis, nunquam hodie contingat? Quasi praeter morem primitiuae Ecclesiae Episcopi Anglicani etiam in terrenis non sedeant iudicantes? Quasi lucrum, pompa, praedicandi Evangelij negleotu: non obtineat: consuetudo primitiuae Ecclesiae in peius mutata non sit. Quidni etiam Waldenses imitandi? Illi vero ad exemplar primitiuae Ecclesiae omnia reuocanda in disciplina censuerunt, ut pluribus Clytreus demonstrat.
units.tr: Thirdly, the Fathers teach, and all the literate writers of every age and every region, that we must return to the standard of the primitive Church. Tertullian, in his Prescription against Heretics, makes it his whole aim to prove that we must go back to the first sources, and that therefore the orthodox have the stronger right, because they are the heirs of the Apostles, because they existed from the beginning, and because they have not moved the ancient boundaries. Against Marcion he writes thus: In sum, if that is shown to be truer which is earlier, and that earlier which is from the beginning, and that from the beginning which is from the Apostles, then likewise that is shown to have been handed down by the Apostles which was held sacred in the churches of the Apostles. Cyprian similarly: If the channel of a water-course, which at first flowed abundantly and copiously, suddenly fails, does one not go to the spring? This too we priests of God must do, keeping the divine precepts: so that if truth has changed and wavered in any point, we may return to the Lord's and the Apostolic tradition as its origin, so that the reasoning of our practice may rise from the same source from which its order and origin arose. Jerome summons Lucillus to the pattern of the primitive Church. Why not also those advocates of hierarchy? That Cyprian understood this doctrine to apply to discipline as well as to doctrine is clear from this alone, that elsewhere he calls deacons back to that first institution of deacons in Acts 6, and bids them remember it. Vincent of Lérins wrote a book against the profane novelties of heretics, whose summary is this: the more recent a thing is, and the further it departs from that orthodox consensus of holy antiquity, the less it agrees with truth. Lest anyone think that he said these things about the Fathers as Papists or hierarchists do, as if they had some authority of their own, I will not hesitate to quote some of his words. Guard the deposit, says the Apostle; and Bison and Saravia teach that in the "deposit" discipline lies hidden as well as doctrine. What is a deposit? That which has been entrusted to you, not what has been found by you; what you have received, not what you have devised; a matter not of genius but of doctrine; not of private usurpation but of public tradition; a thing brought to you, not put forward by you; in which you ought to be not the author but the keeper, not the founder but the guardian, not the leader but the follower. You have received gold, give back gold: I do not want you to substitute one thing for another; I do not want you to pass off lead shamelessly for gold, or fraudulently to pass off ornaments; I want not the appearance of gold but its very nature. Isidore of Pelusium comes closer to our matter: for he defends the hierarch who shrinks from the episcopate on the ground that the episcopate has degenerated from the simplicity of the primitive Church. He speaks thus: Perhaps you seem not to know that the dignity of lightness and openness has passed into tyranny. For if you can show that the rule of feeding the flock still holds good among you, then he who judged himself unequal to this task deserves to be praised by you. But if the matter has turned out the other way, then he should by no means be punished, etc. Bernard, does he not everywhere strive to call back the Church of his own age, fallen from the first purity, simplicity, integrity and discipline of the primitive Church? Who will grant me, he says, before I die, to see the Church of God as it was in the ancient days, when the Apostles let down their nets for a catch, not a catch of gold or silver, but a catch of souls. How I wish to inherit that voice of his whose faith you have obtained: "Let your money perish with you." Elsewhere: Where has any of the Apostles ever sat as judge, or divider of boundaries, or distributor of lands? I read that the Apostles were stoned, but I do not read that they sat in judgment. Elsewhere: You, pastor, come forth gilded, etc. Did Peter do this? Did Paul act so? And elsewhere: There have been before you men who gave themselves wholly to feeding sheep. Where now, I ask, is this custom? It has fallen into great unlikeness; their pursuits have been changed far in another direction, and would that it were not for the worse. What has this to do with England, you ask? As if in England it could never happen today to see the Church of God as it was in the ancient days? As if, contrary to the custom of the primitive Church, the English bishops do not sit as judges even in temporal matters? As if the gain, the pomp, the neglect of preaching the Gospel had not taken hold, and the custom of the primitive Church had not been changed for the worse? Why should the Waldenses not also be imitated? They judged that everything in discipline should be called back to the pattern of the primitive Church, as Clytraeus shows at length.

units.la: Nicolaus Orem, in concione coram Papa habita, de primitivae Ecclesiae integritate revocanda multa habet. Non es recordata dierum adolescentiae tuae scilicet de statu primaevo, Erat namque futurum ut non vererentur praelati venerandam pudicitiam primitivae Ecclesiae infamari. Durandus Mimatensis de concilio celebrando scripsit, iussu Clementis Quinti, paulo ante concilium Viennense: qui omnia ad typum Ecclesiae primitivae reformanda ita censet. Sane recolentes quomodo haec sacra plantatio Ecclesiae fuerit instituta, dolentes dicere possumus quod et sinon ab omnibus, neque in omnibus & plerisque, tamen in pluribus ab illa sancta institutione primitiue Ecclesiae, in tantum discessum videatur, ut aliqui ex nobis primae institutionis videantur oblitti. Nilus Thessalonicensis quem Nicolaum Cabasilam multi putant, contra primatum Papae scribens, cum ubique hoc argumento confecit, quod ab usu Ecclesiae primitivae deflexerit. Petrus Damianus acerrimus discipli-
units.tr: Nicolaus Orem, in a sermon preached before the Pope, has much to say about restoring the integrity of the primitive Church. You have not remembered the days of your youth, namely the primeval state; for it was going to happen that the prelates would not hesitate to bring disgrace upon the venerable chastity of the primitive Church. Durandus of Mende wrote on holding a council, at the command of Clement V, shortly before the Council of Vienne; he judges that everything must be reformed according to the type of the primitive Church. Indeed, recalling how this holy planting of the Church was instituted, we can sadly say that although not by all, nor in all, and in most places, yet in many a departure has been made from that holy institution of the primitive Church, so far that some of us seem to have forgotten the first institution. Nilus of Thessalonica, whom many think to be Nicholas Cabasilas, writing against the primacy of the Pope, makes his whole case by the argument that he has departed from the practice of the primitive Church. Peter Damian, a most fierce champion of discipline,
