units.tr: Epist. 223.

units.la: næ, ad exemplar Ecclesiæ primitivæ assertor erat. Princeps Apostolorum, Petrus, inquit querela subditorum non ex potestate restitit, sed ob suum ad Gentiles ingressum postulatus, rationem reddendo humiliter satisfecit: quod adversus Episcopos Anglicanos dicitur, qui presbyteris suis subjici nolunt. Rodormus Zomorensis sub Paulo secundo vixit & in speculo vitæ humanæ quod scripsit, primitivam Ecclesiam, quasi reformationis speculum proponit. In primitiva Ecclesia, inquit multi floruerunt veri sancti: verissimum illos speculum puto perfectæ sanctæque vitæ. Ioannes Gerson multa pro reformatione Ecclesiæ scripsit, quod autem eam ad formam primitivæ Ecclesiæ reduci voluerit, vel ex his verbis solis constat. Maior fuit Ecclesiæ primitivæ authoritas quam Ecclesiæ quæ nunc est? Non enim est in potestate Papæ aut Concilij aut Ecclesiæ mutare traditiones doctas ab Evangelistis & a Paulo, sicut quidam delirant. Videat hic sibi Downamus, & quotquot alij, qui Apostolicas de disciplina institutiones, mutabiles contendunt. Petrus Aullicus iussit Sigismundi, Constantiensi Concilio, de Ecclesia reformanda, articulos obtulit: quem ad exemplum institutionis primæ omnia revocanda censuisse, vel ex eo patet, quod ad eos inclinet qui Cardinalium ordinem tollendum existimarent: quod neq; a Christo, neq; ab Apostolis institutii esset. Idem scripsit eodem tempore Nicolaus de Cusa: primum gradum ad Ecclesiam reformandam hunc ponens, ut Cardinalium authoritate sublata, ad eum statum redigatur Ecclesia, quo erat ab initio: quod illi de Cardinalibus id nobis de Episcopis disputare jam hodie licet. Gregorius Hamburgensis ad annum 1434. de Ecclesiæ reformatione ita scripsit, ut exemplar primitivæ Ecclesiæ per annos fere trecentos imitandum esse censeat. Budeus duo agit: primo deplorat degenerationem Ecclesiæ à prisca Ecclesia ita: Canonum cantitas vel caries potius nulli jam usui est, sed velut anus delira è foro explosa est: de ponte enim jam diu comitiorum paracleti, dicta est disciplina Canonica, ut annis sexaginta maior, atque etiam sexcentis &c. Secundo, disciplinam à Christo perfectè descriptam putat, quam etiam reverendam censet ita: Navis nobis disciplinæ à fornatore relicta est, Ecclesiæ conditore, quæ cautico, ministerio, instrumento, miraculis, instructa fuit ab ipso aut ejus auspiciis. Flarum etiam à puppi pollicitus est, ad exoptatum locum vectores perlaturum, si clavum rectum tenere, si vela spiritui afflaturo, pandere Ecclesia porrexisset. Veniamus ad modernos. Nic. Sanderus ita? Non potest rectior norma secundum quam Ecclesia gubernata est, ex nulla re alia peti, quam ex Christi factis & institutis, Universa Christianæ gubernationis regula et ab uno Christo pendet, & a visibili externo exemplo illius temporis pendet. Hadrianus Saravia politicam primitivæ normam immutabilem esse ubique affirmat: a qua si defecatur, non reformationem, sed potius Ecclesiæ deformationem fieri affirmat. Est tamen in quo & hic & Sanderus peccat, nempe quod immutabilitatis regulam hic à Christi, ille ab Apostolorum regimine ipso petendam putet, sicut ante demonstratum. Guilielmus Whitakerus ita: Concilii, Act. 15. celebrati reliquorum omnium norma esse debet: huic reliqua omnia similia esse oportet. I. Reinoldus spiritus judicandos esse docet, ex consensu Ecclesiarum, unde sermo Dei profectus est, & ad quas in Ecclesia prima pervenit ex 1. Cor. 14. Falluntur ergo Hierarchici, qui reformationem ad typum Ecclesiae primae, necessario faciendam negant. Atq; haec de reformationis Anglicanae in disciplina defectu secundo: nempe quòd ex adversariorum quorundam saltem confessione, ad exemplar primitivae Ecclesiae efformata non sit.
units.tr: ...pline, was a champion after the pattern of the primitive Church. The prince of the Apostles, Peter, he says, did not resist the complaint of his subordinates by authority, but when he was called to account for his entry among the Gentiles, he humbly satisfied them by giving his reasons. This is said against the English bishops, who are unwilling to be subject to their elders. Rodormus of Zamora lived under Paul II, and in his Mirror of Human Life he sets forth the primitive Church as a mirror of reformation. In the primitive Church, he says, many true saints flourished; I count them the most true mirror of perfect and holy life. John Gerson wrote much for the reformation of the Church, and that he wished it to be brought back to the form of the primitive Church is clear from these words alone: Was the authority of the primitive Church greater than that of the Church which now is? For it is not in the power of the Pope, or of a Council, or of the Church, to change the traditions taught by the Evangelists and by Paul, as some rave. Let Downame look to himself here, and all others who maintain that the Apostolic institutions concerning discipline are changeable. Peter of Ailly offered to the Council of Constance, at the command of Sigismund, articles on reforming the Church; that he judged everything should be called back to the pattern of the first institution is clear from this, that he inclines to those who thought the order of Cardinals should be abolished, because it was instituted neither by Christ nor by the Apostles. Nicholas of Cusa wrote at the same time, setting this as the first step toward reforming the Church: that with the authority of the Cardinals removed, the Church should be brought back to the state in which it was from the beginning; what he argued about Cardinals, we may today argue about Bishops. Gregory of Hamburg, writing about the reformation of the Church under the year 1434, judges that the pattern of the primitive Church, followed for nearly three hundred years, should be imitated. Budé does two things: first he laments the degeneration of the Church from the ancient Church, thus: The number of canons, or rather their decay, is now of no use at all; like a crazy old woman, it has been thrown out of the forum; for the bridge of assemblies has long been the place of the Paraclete, and canonical discipline has been called, as if it were sixty years older, or even six hundred... Second, he thinks that discipline was perfectly described by Christ, and he judges it to be revered thus: The ship of discipline has been left to us by its builder, the founder of the Church, equipped by him or under his auspices with the rule, the ministry, the instrument, and the miracles. He also promised a fair wind from the stern, to carry the passengers to the desired place, if the Church should hold the helm straight and spread the sails to the breathing of the Spirit. Let us come to the moderns. Nicholas Sander says thus: No more correct rule, according to which the Church has been governed, can be sought from anything other than the deeds and institutions of Christ. The whole rule of Christian government depends on Christ alone, and depends on the visible outward example of that time. Adrian Saravia affirms that the political pattern of the primitive Church is everywhere unchangeable; if one departs from it, he affirms, there is not reformation but rather a deformation of the Church. Yet there is something in which both he and Sander go wrong, namely that they think the rule of immutability is to be sought here from Christ, there from the very government of the Apostles, as was shown before. William Whitaker says: The council celebrated in Acts 15 ought to be the norm of all the rest; all other things ought to be like it. J. Reynolds teaches that spirits are to be judged by the consensus of the Churches from which the word of God went forth, and to which it came in the first Church, from 1 Cor. 14. The hierarchists are therefore mistaken, who deny that the reformation must necessarily be made according to the type of the primitive Church. And this is said concerning the second defect of the English reformation in discipline: namely, that by the confession, at least, of some of its adversaries, it has not been shaped after the pattern of the primitive Church.

units.tr: Chapter 25.

units.la: Tertius in Anglia Defectus est quod Fermentum Romanum omne non expurgaverit.
units.tr: The third defect in England is that it has not purged out all the Roman leaven.

units.la: TErtius sequitur, qui in eo vertitur, quòd fermentum Romanum omne non expurgaverit. Reformatio etenim Ecclesiae a Papatu Resurrectio quaedam, ab ipso Spirtu sancto dicitur. Ap. 20.5. Quemadmodum igitur Christus resurgens sepulchrales exuvias omnes abjecit: ita reformatio Deo probatur nulla, nisi a Papisticis sordibus ita resurgat ut omnes Romanae Apostasiae reliquias, procul amandari faciat. Hoc in Ecclesia Anglicana fieri quî potest? Hadrianus etenim Saravia qui disciplinam immutabilem statuit, divinum Episcopale regimen per Episcopos in Ecclesia Romana jam usque remanere asseruit: sic ut Romana Ecclesia vera Dei Ecclesia sit, totumque illius regimen Deo probatum, exceptâ solâ Papae ipsius Monarchiâ. Iohannes contra Whitgiftus disciplinam statuit mutabilem: jam verò is politeiam Ecclesiae indifferentem statuens, abusus tam Romani regimis emendandos esse dicit, regimen autem ipsum, quanquam mutari posse concedit, non tamen mutari utile esse multis contendit. Fundamentum (inquit) Cartwrighti putridum secundum hoc est, non esse retinenda quae in Papatu in abusum conversa sunt. Quid igitur de Hieronymo Zanchio, qui de Ecclesiae reformatione ad Dominum Knollum scribens, hanc regulam ponit: Illa quae licet suapte natura mala non sint, neque inutiliter in Ecclesia diu obtinuerunt, tamen post ea longo abusu in superstitiones & idolatrias versa sunt, ista inquam nolle vel penitus exemplo Ezechiae & Iosiae tollere, vel saltem exemplo aliorum piorum regum ita emendare & purgare, ut omnis Idololatriae & superstitionis occasio tollatur, pertinacia est, nullo modo probanda.
units.tr: The third defect follows, which consists in this: that it has not purged out all the Roman leaven. For the reformation of the Church from the Papacy is called a certain resurrection, by the Holy Spirit himself (Rev. 20.5). Just as the risen Christ cast off all the grave-clothes, so a reformation is approved by God only if it rises from Papistical filth in such a way that it removes far away every remnant of Roman apostasy. How can this happen in the English Church? For Hadrian Saravia, who holds that discipline is unchangeable, has asserted that the divine episcopal government through bishops has remained in the Roman Church even until now, so that the Roman Church is a true Church of God, and its whole government is approved by God, except only the monarchy of the Pope himself. John Whitgift, on the other hand, holds that discipline is changeable. Yet he, while regarding the polity of the Church as indifferent, says that the abuses of the Roman government are to be corrected, but that the government itself, although he concedes it can be changed, is not useful to change, as he strongly contends. The foundation of Cartwright (he says) is rotten, according to this: that those things which have been turned into abuse in the Papacy are not to be retained. What then of Jerome Zanchius, who, writing to Lord Knollys about the reformation of the Church, lays down this rule: Those things which, though not evil in their own nature, and which have not for a long time held their place uselessly in the Church, have nevertheless after long abuse been turned into superstitions and idolatries; to be unwilling to remove these entirely, in the example of Hezekiah and Josiah, or at least to correct and purge them in the example of other pious kings, so that every occasion of idolatry and superstition is removed, I say, is obstinacy and is in no way to be approved.

units.la: At Angliae ea pertinacia est ut superstitionis Papisticae occasiones non sustulerit. Verùm ne hic latebras quaerant; omnino tollenda, Ezechiae exemplo, quae in abusum versa sunt; Stephanus olim Episcopus ipse Romanus censuit: [Ezechias dissipavit excelsa, & contrivit statuas, & succidit lucos, & fregit serpentem aeneum quem fecit Moses. Ac per hoc magna authoritas est habenda in Ecclesia; nonnulli ex praedecessoribus [?] {a}& maioribus nostris fecerint aliqua, quae tempore illo potuerunt esse sine culpa, & postea vertuntur in errorem & superstitionem, sine tarditate aliqua, & cum magna authoritate a posteris destruantur. Hanc tollendi necessitatem à Stephano positam etiam in eis quae ab antecessoribus bene sunt inventa, approbat Juellus. Nae ergo longe ab illo dissidet Iohannes Whitgiftus, qui non solum res in abusu versas, quae primo bene institutae erant, retinendas defendit, sed etiam eas, quae male primo ab ipso Papa adinventae fuerunt. Haec etenim illius thesis est, quam fuse tractat. Res impiae inventae bonum usum habere possunt. Atqui inquam etsi bonum usum habere possint, id est utilem, de quo tamen dubito: malum tamen usum habere ut plurimum solent, id est in abusum verti: quae ut praecidantur, ne uti quidem eis licet in Ecclesia, vel ipso Tertulliano judice. Nulla distantia est abutendi, cum veritas cessat utendi: Quomodo quis abutatur, cum non habeat quo utatur? Nobis autem abuti apud Apostolum non licet, facilius, non uti docentem. Hadrianus Saravia, cum objecisset Dominus Beza nomen Archiepiscopi a Papa primitus inventum fuisse, ita respondet; Nihili est ista quam nonnulli inferunt conclusione ineptius. Hoc Antichristus invenit, ergo malum, nisi addatur, aut intelligatur, id esse contra verbum Dei. Atqui cum regimen Ecclesiasticum in verbo Dei praescriptum sit, vel teipso confitente: annon contra verbum Dei nomen praecipuorum rectorum erit, ideo quod in verbo praescriptum non sit? Itaque sane Anglicanum regimen per Archiepiscopos & Episcopos, non solum in eo peccat, quod fundamento verbi Dei omni careat: sed in eo etiam, quod alieno fundamento superstruatur, isto nempe, quod ab inimico Christi, ipso Antichristo, in re disciplinaria mutuatum sit. De hujus sceleris indignitate ita Tertullianus. Divino operi, Satanae ingenia superinducere quam scelestum est? Servi nostri ab inimicis nostris nihil mutuantur, milites ab hoste Imperatoris sui nihil concupiscunt. De adversario enim cujus in cujus manu sit, aliquid usu postulare transgressio est, Rursus: Nobis etsi quaerendum esset adhuc & semper, ubi tamen quaeri oportet? Apud haereticos, ubi omnia extranea & adversaria nostrae veritati? ad quos vetamur accedere? Quis servus cibaria ab extraneo, ne dicam ab inimico domini sui sperat? Quis miles ab infoederatis, ne dicam ab hostibus regibus, donativa & stipendia cupiat, nisi plane desertor & transfuga, & rebellis? Nemo inde strui potest, unde destruitur. Nemo ab eo illuminatur, unde contenebratur. Quaeramus ergo a nostro, & a nostris, & de nostro, idque duntaxat quod salva regula fidei, potest in quaestionem devenire.
units.tr: But England shows such obstinacy that it has not removed the occasions of Papistical superstition. Yet, lest they seek hiding-places here: things which have been turned into abuse must be removed altogether, in the example of Hezekiah. Stephen, once Bishop of Rome himself, judged this: [Hezekiah broke down the high places, and shattered the statues, and cut down the groves, and broke the bronze serpent which Moses made. And therefore great authority is to be had in the Church; some things which our predecessors and elders have done, which at that time could have been without fault, and afterwards are turned into error and superstition, are to be destroyed by their successors without any delay, and with great authority.] Juel also approves this necessity of removal, stated by Stephen, even in those things which were well devised by predecessors. Far indeed does John Whitgift differ from him, who not only defends the retention of things turned to abuse which were at first well instituted, but also those which were at first badly devised by the Pope himself. For this is his thesis, which he treats at length: Impious things when invented can have a good use. Yet, I say, even if they can have a good use, that is a useful one, about which I nevertheless have my doubts; still they are wont for the most part to have a bad use, that is, to be turned into abuse; and that these should be cut off, it is not even lawful to use them in the Church, according to the judgment of Tertullian himself. There is no difference between abusing when the right of using has ceased: how can someone abuse what he has no right to use? But for us it is not lawful to abuse, according to the Apostle, but it is easier not to use, as the teacher says. When Lord Beza objected that the name of Archbishop was first invented by the Pope, Hadrian Saravia answered thus: That conclusion which some draw is more foolish than nothing. Antichrist invented this, therefore it is evil, unless it is added, or understood, that it is against the word of God. But since ecclesiastical government is prescribed in the word of God, as you yourself confess, will not the name of the chief rulers be against the word of God, because it is not prescribed in the word? Therefore the English government by archbishops and bishops sins not only in this, that it lacks any foundation in the word of God, but also in this, that it is built upon a foreign foundation, namely that it was borrowed in disciplinary matters from the enemy of Christ, Antichrist himself. Concerning the shamefulness of this wickedness, thus Tertullian: How wicked it is to bring the devices of Satan upon the divine work! Our servants borrow nothing from our enemies, soldiers desire nothing from the enemy of their emperor. For to ask for anything from an adversary, in whose hand it lies, is a transgression. Again: Although we ought still and always to seek, where ought we to seek? Among heretics, where everything is foreign and hostile to our truth? To whom are we forbidden to come? What servant hopes for food from a stranger, not to say from the enemy of his master? What soldier from the treaty-breakers, not to say from the enemies of his king, desires largesse and pay, unless he is plainly a deserter, a runaway and a rebel? Nothing can be built up from that by which it is destroyed. No one is enlightened by him by whom he is darkened. Let us therefore seek from our own, and from our own people, and about our own things, and that only which, with the rule of faith preserved, can come into question.

units.la: 2. Hoc Iohannes Calvinus percitus (Bancrofto referente) quum ad Genevae disciplinam reformandam accessit, non domum Papalem pristinam stare permisit (quod tamen fieri oportuit, dicit Bancroftus) quasi resarciri posset; sed eam totam demolitus est, ipsamque veterem regiminis formam prorsus & penitus immutavit: ad quod necessitate quadam se esse adactum profitetur. Hanc Calvini in Eccle-sia {a} Decret. p. 1. dist. 63. c. 28. sia reformanda rationem asperè quidem Bancroftus exagitat: reprehendit etiā Hadrianus Saravia,sed aliquanto leviùs. Dico primis Ecclesiarū reformatoribus inquit, accidisse,quod caduceas ædes resarcituris solet: qui cum undique pleraque putrida & vitiata conspiciant, quamvis intra ædes,pulchra conclavia & plures necessario partes sint,quas servatas vellent, tamen quia cohærent putridis & labantibus,quæ emendatione habent opus, diruì & emendari posse diffidunt, nisi simul omnia demoliantur.
units.tr: 2. John Calvin, moved by this (as Bancroft reports), when he came to reform the discipline at Geneva, did not allow the old Papal house to stand (which, however, Bancroft says ought to have been done), as if it could be patched up; but he demolished the whole of it, and changed the ancient form of government itself utterly and entirely; to which he professes that he was driven by a certain necessity. This method of Calvin in reforming the Church Bancroft indeed criticises harshly; Saravia also finds fault with it, but rather more gently. I say, he writes, that what happens to those who are about to repair a ruinous building happened to the first reformers of the Churches: when they see that most parts on every side are rotten and corrupted, although within the building there are beautiful rooms and many parts which they would wish to be preserved, yet because they cohere with the rotten and tottering parts, which need correction, they despair that they can be restored and corrected unless everything is pulled down at once. (Decretum, p. 1, dist. 63, c. 28.)

units.la: Atqui regimen Hierarchicum ipso Calvino protestante, nunquam illi pulchrum conclave visum est, quod ille servatum vellet: partem ipsam putridam & labantem esse putabat,quæ imprimis demolienda erat. Loco hujus demolitionis,resarcinationem quandam (ut ita loquar) cum Bancroftus, tum Saravia requirit, quæ nonne illa ipsa rerum heterogeniarum contemperatio & conglutinatio quæso est: quæ illi separationi quæ a Deo mandata est ex diametro adversatur? pretiosum etenim à vili seperandum est, non cum vili commiscendum Ier.15..19.& in quaque reformatione stannum excoquendum est,non cum argento contemperandum Isa.1.25. exite ab ea populo mi,Apoc. 18.4. quid; ut mores Babylonis unà nobiscum reportemus; imo qui mores orientalis Babylonis in Ecclesia ferre non potuit, occidentalis qui jam ferat? Certè gressu corporali ut a Roma exeamus, hic putat mādari Nicolaus de Clemangis:quòd vero affectu saltè exeundū sit,vel illud Augustini docet,quòd separatio à corruptelis etiam à cujusque veræ Ecclesiæ quoad affectum, mandatur a Paulo ipsius judicio. 2. Cor.6.17. prosequitur multis hanc separationem Ioannes Iuellus etiam in rebus indifferentibus, ex Tertulliano, Beato Rhenano, Origene denique, cujus ista verba adfert. Quærendum est quid hoc sit. Ne fiant ei reliquiæ: Ne aliqua inquit rescindatis, Chaldæorum aliqua reservetis,ob id jubet ne pusillum quidem relinquatur in ea.
units.tr: Yet with Calvin himself a protestant, the Hierarchical government never seemed to him a fine room which he would wish to be kept; he thought that the very part which was rotten and tottering was to be demolished first of all. In place of this demolition, both Bancroft and Saravia require a kind of patching (so to speak), which is surely nothing other than that very mixing and gluing together of heterogeneous things, which is diametrically opposed to that separation which God has commanded. For the precious must be separated from the vile (Jer. 15.19), not mixed with the vile; and in every reformation the tin must be smelted out, not blended with silver (Isa. 1.25). Come out of her, my people (Rev. 18.4). What, that we may bring back the manners of Babylon along with us? Nay, if the manners of eastern Babylon could not be borne in the Church, how can those of western Babylon now be borne? Certainly Nicholas of Clamanges thinks that bodily departure from Rome is commanded; but that departure must at least be made in affection, the saying of Augustine teaches, since separation from corruptions, even as far as affection goes, is commanded by Paul in his own judgment (2 Cor. 6.17). John Jewel pursues this separation in many matters, even in indifferent things, from Tertullian, Beatus Rhenanus, and finally Origen, whose words he cites: It must be asked what this means. Lest remnants be left to it: lest, he says, you should leave any of the Chaldeans, lest you keep any of them, for this reason he commands that not even the smallest part be left in it.

units.la: Tantùm verò abest ut ne pusillum quidem Chaldæorum spiritualium reformatio Anglicana reliquerit, ut de eadem dicere Spiritus sanctus adigatur,quæ de Laodicea est. Nolbi opera tua, id est, te neq; frigidum esse, neq; ferv[idum]: id est, neq; papistam, neq; reformatam, sed tepidam quendam temperaturam quasi inter utramque mediam. Hoc scilicet meretur prudens illa & politica commoderatio Bancroftiini: nam [ qui Christum & ethnicissimum conjungunt, neutrum retinent, alicubi Ludovicus Vives ] & dum Judæi esse volunt (inquit Hieronymus) & Christiani, neque Judæi sunt neque Christiani. ] Sequitur in reprehensione Anglicana,utinam frigidus esses aut fervidus, non quod Papistam esse melius sit in se, sed quòd in Angelis Anglicanis minus esset peccatum nescientes, papistas esse, quàm hujusmodi doctos cōmoderatores. Rursus: Ecclesiæ nunquam exactè reformatæ (qualis jam nostra Anglia est (aut à prima reformatione sua in deterius post relapsæ,aves per medium cœlū volantes appellantur Ap.19.17. Ratio in promptu est, Ecclesiæ reformatæ ubique cœlum appellantur, societas Antichristiana terra: ideoque Anglia neque coelum dicitur, quia non reformata, neque terra, quia non Antichristiana: sed verè quasi avis, in medio volans. Commoderatio itaque Bancroftiana, quid aliud quàm coelū terraq; miscet, in quo ne nonnulli glorientur, videant in coelo volare Anglia ita ut Ecclesia sit, licet ad supremū coelū Ecclesiarū reformatarū nō pertingat, quātopere tamē nō nisi in coelo infimo volatᵍ Angliæ Deo displiceat, vel in Gregorio cernere licet, ejusdéq; sęculi pastoribᵍ reliquis: qui Angeli nō nisi in medio coelo volantes audiunt Ap. 8. 13, quòd plus satis terrenę sordis propter suam ad papismum inclinationem tum Ecclesiæ contraxissent: videre hoc ipsum & in Wiclepho est Apo. 14.6. qui licet Euangelium ęternum apportet, in hoc tamen minùs Deo ptobatur, quod per medium tantummodo coelum illud portet, à terrenis scilicet papismi sordibus non satis perpurgatum. Quòd si verò tam malè audiat Gregorij sęculum ad papismum tum inclinans, & ætas Wiclephi à papismo nisi jam renata: quomodo Anglia excusabitur; quę annis supra 50. grandis, coram medio coelo ita volat sciens prudensque, ut luce totas ubiq: Ecclesias collustrante non moveatur? quòd si verò hęc medietas Anglicana denegetur, Martinus Bucerus audiatur, qui Ian. 12. anno 1550, ad amicum quendam suum Cantabrigiæ scribens, ita ait. Sunt qui humanissima sapientia & evanescentibus cogitationibus, velint fermento Antichristi conglutinare Deum & Belial. Quin & audiatur Georgius Dolbnamus, qui in ipsa epistolę suę dedicatorię fronte ad Angliam aeconmodat illa Thucydidis.
units.tr: So far is the Anglican reformation from leaving not even a remnant of the spiritual Chaldeans that the Holy Spirit is compelled to say of it what he said of Laodicea: I know your works, that is, you are neither cold nor hot. That is, England is neither Papist nor reformed, but a certain lukewarm mixture, as it were halfway between the two. This is surely what that prudent and political moderation of Bancroft deserves. For [those who join Christ and the most heathen hold neither; somewhere Ludovicus Vives says so], and while they wish to be Jews (says Jerome) and Christians, they are neither Jews nor Christians. Next comes the Anglican rebuke: I wish you were cold or hot. This is not because being a Papist is better in itself, but because among the Anglican angels there would be less sin in those who do not know they are Papists than in such learned moderators. Again: churches never exactly reformed (such as England now is, or such as have relapsed for the worse since their first reformation) are called birds flying through the midst of heaven (Rev. 19.17). The reason is ready to hand. Reformed churches everywhere are called heaven, and the Antichristian society is called earth. Therefore England is called neither heaven, because it is not reformed, nor earth, because it is not Antichristian, but is truly like a bird flying in the middle. What, then, does Bancroft's moderation do but mix heaven and earth? Let no one boast of this: let them see that England flies in the heavens, so that it is a church, although it does not reach the highest heaven of the reformed churches. Yet how greatly God is displeased that England flies only in the lowest heaven may be seen in Gregory and the other ministers of his age, who, as angels flying only in the middle of heaven, are heard (Rev. 8.13) to have contracted more than enough earthly filth in the Church because of their inclination toward Popery. The same can be seen in Wycliffe (Rev. 14.6), who, although he brings the eternal gospel, is in this respect less approved by God, that he carries it only through the middle heaven, not sufficiently purged of the earthly filth of Popery. But if the age of Gregory, inclining toward Popery, and the age of Wycliffe, not yet reborn from Popery, fare so badly, how will England be excused? It has flown for more than fifty years, a great thing, in the sight of the middle heaven, knowing and consciously, and is not moved though the light of the Church shines everywhere. But if this Anglican middle position is denied, let Martin Bucer be heard, who, writing on 12 January 1550 to a certain friend of his at Cambridge, says: There are some who, with most refined wisdom and fading thoughts, wish to cement God and Belial together with the leaven of Antichrist. Indeed, let George Dolbeny also be heard, who, on the very front of his dedicatory epistle, applies to England those words of Thucydides.

units.la: Propterea qnòd media Anglia sit (ut ipse loquitur) inter Romanenses & Novatores, id est, Ecclesiarum reformatarum approbatores. Neque verò medietas ista illud poetę audire meretur, quod apponitur in margine. Medium tenuere beati: sed idipsum potiùs quod ipse textus què ex Thucydide, citat: qui nullos alios medianos, quam Metios Suffetios intellexit. Atque sic quidem hodie Anglia in medio est quòd ad disciplinam spectat, id est neutrarū partium est: quod sęviente præsertim in Ecclesias Christi tyranno Romano, quā sit ignobile quamq; indignum judicetur ex Solone, qui in republica hujusmodi Neutrales minimè ferendos existimavit, & ex politicorum placito illo, quod idem plane statuit, ut in Althusio, & Keckermanno videre est. Cessęt igitur Anglia medietatē suā, quæ mera quaedam Neutralitas est, sub titulo prudentiæ & moderationis palliare: audiat potiùs hortantem Christum Ap. 3. 19. Eerue & resipisce, id est zelo eorum flagres, quos pro nimis fervidis condemnas. Alludit etenim vocabulum istud ad ollam præ fervore ebullientem: sic ut resipiscere Anglia nequeat, nisi spumam Romæ vniuersam ejiciat. Atque hic defectus reformationis Anglicanæ tertius est: quòd fermentum Romanum totum (quod oportuit) non expurgaverit: neque à sordibus papatus omnibus, uti decuit, respurgaverit.
units.tr: Because England is (as he himself says) midway between the Romanists and the Innovators, that is, between the approvers of the reformed churches. Yet this middle position does not deserve that line of the poet which is placed in the margin: "The blessed have held the middle." Rather it deserves the very thing the text itself quotes from Thucydides, who understood no other middle men than the Mettii Suffetii. And so indeed today England is in the middle as far as discipline is concerned, that is, it belongs to neither party. That this is ignoble and unworthy, especially when the Roman tyrant rages against the churches of Christ, is judged from Solon, who thought that neutrals of this kind should by no means be tolerated in a commonwealth, and from that maxim of politicians which plainly lays down the same thing, as may be seen in Althusius and Keckermann. Let England therefore cease to cloak its middle position, which is pure neutrality, under the name of prudence and moderation. Let it rather hear Christ exhorting it (Rev. 3.19): Be zealous and repent, that is, burn with the zeal of those whom you condemn as too fervent. For that word alludes to a pot boiling over with heat. So England cannot repent unless it casts out the whole scum of Rome. And this is the third defect of the Anglican reformation: that it has not purged away the whole Roman leaven (as it ought to have done), nor thoroughly cleansed itself of all the filth of Papacy, as it should have.

units.la: CAP. 26. Quartus defectus quod Anglia vitiat disciplinam, eam ad politeiam civilem conformando.
units.tr: CHAPTER 26. The fourth defect, by which England corrupts church discipline by conforming it to the civil polity.

units.la: QVARTVS sequitur, qui in eo ponitur, quòd disciplinam vitiare Anglia non veretur, eam ad civilem politeiam conformando. Posuerat Cartwrightus, gubernationem civilem ad regimen Ecclesiæ potiùs reformandam esse, quàm gubernationem Ecclesiæ ad regimen civile. Hoc Whitgiftus exagitare videtur tanquam Anabaptisticum, & in omnem Monarchiam, qualis jam in Anglia viget, pernitiosum, In hunc sensum Whitgiftum citat Georgius Downamus, qui ita hac de re sententiam suâ ponit. A judicio Regis in tanto discrepant (Puritani) ut quando Rex sentit Ecclesiam conformari posse ad rempublicam: illi regimen civile ad regimen Ecclesiasticum attemperare deberi dicunt. Ecclesiam vero ad civilem politeiam formare idem esse docent, ac si quis aulam suam ad aulæa, non autem quod debuit, aulæa potius ad aulam accommodare vellet. Non igitur est, quod in Cornelium Scultingium, iniquior quis sit, qui hoc sensu Whitgiftum interpretatur. Imo quod absurdius est, (inquit) Anglo-Calvinistæ, politeiam Ecclesiasticam juxta reipublicæ politeiam formari atque componi volunt. Atque absurditas quidem hujus sententiæ, ipsius Whitgifti conscientiam pulsasse videtur: quanquam enim positio Cartwrightiana quam impugnat, ista sit, Regimen Ecclesiasticum non est conformandum ad regimen civile: Id quod à Whitgifto defendi dicit: is Whitgif. tamen, qui aut negare hoc à se defendi debuisset, aut contrarium probare, alio suâ oratione convertit: atq; hoc tantū agit, magistratui licitū esse, disciplinâ mutare ad statū Ecclesiæ. Hinc ita loquitur. Quandoquidem Magistratus suprem Ecclesiæ gubernator est: consentaneū non est ut aliter Ecclesiæ gubernentur, quâ prout illi expedire videbitur præsenti ipsorum statui. Rursus: Ordo ille inter ministros seruandus est, qui statui Ecclesiæ maxime convenit. Rursus: Non potest gubernari Ecclesia sub magistratu, ut sub tyranno: in toto regno, sicut in una civitate, qui non diversitatē gubernationis admittit pro statu Ecclesiæ diversitate, nō ædificat sed confundit. Sed utrū conscientia Whitgifti eū prohibuerit necne, apertis verbis sententiam suam de Ecclesia reipublicæ conformanda profiteri: hoc tamen & certū est,& ex illius verbis liquet, expedientiæ velo tegi, conformitatem in Anglia istam, qua factum est, ut ad ideam Monarchiæ quæ in Anglia viget, monarchalis correspondens gubernatio in Episcopis nata sit. Adversus autem expedientiæ colorem istum ita Whitakerus. Disputat Bellarminus contentionem inter Romam olim & Carthaginensem Ecclesiā in eo tantum positam fuisse, quod illa primatum Papæ expedire, hæc vero non expedire putaret. Atqui non est iudicandum, respondet Whitakerus, adeo absurde sensisse Carthagi-
units.tr: The fourth follows, which lies in this: England does not hesitate to corrupt church discipline by conforming it to the civil polity. Cartwright had laid down that the civil government should be reformed to fit the government of the Church, rather than the government of the Church to fit the civil government. Whitgift seems to attack this as Anabaptistical and as harmful to every monarchy, such as now flourishes in England. Georgius Downame, citing Whitgift to this effect, sets out his opinion on the matter as follows: The Puritans differ from the King's judgment so far that, when the King thinks the Church can be conformed to the commonwealth, they say the civil government ought to be adjusted to the ecclesiastical government. They teach that to shape the Church to the civil polity is the same as if someone wished to fit his hall to the hangings, rather than, as he ought, fit the hangings to the hall. There is therefore no reason to think that anyone is being unfair to Cornelius Scultingius when he interprets Whitgift in this sense. Indeed, what is more absurd (he says), the Anglo-Calvinists want the ecclesiastical polity to be formed and arranged according to the polity of the commonwealth. And the absurdity of this opinion seems to have struck Whitgift's own conscience. For although the Cartwrightian position which he attacks is this, The ecclesiastical government is not to be conformed to the civil government, which he says he defends, nevertheless Whitgift, who ought either to have denied that he defended it or to have proved the contrary, turns his speech to another matter, and only argues that it is lawful for the magistrate to change the discipline to suit the state of the Church. He speaks thus: Since the magistrate is the supreme governor of the Church, it is not fitting that the Church should be governed in any other way than as he sees fit for their present condition. Again: That order is to be kept among the ministers which best suits the state of the Church. Again: The Church cannot be governed under a magistrate as under a tyrant. In the whole kingdom, as in a single city, whoever does not admit a diversity of government according to the diversity of the Church's state does not build up but confuses. But whether Whitgift's conscience forbade him from openly professing his opinion that the Church should be conformed to the commonwealth, this at least is certain and clear from his words: under the cover of expediency, that conformity in England was brought about, so that a monarchical government, corresponding to the idea of monarchy which flourishes in England, arose in the bishops. Against this colour of expediency Whitaker argues as follows. Bellarmine contends that the dispute between the Church of Rome and the Church of Carthage was only that the former thought the primacy of the Pope was expedient, while the latter did not think it expedient. But it is not to be judged, Whitaker replies, that the Carthaginian Church so foolishly thought that its government ought to be changed because of expediency. The reasons which he brings forward mostly favour us. Why, he asks, was it expedient then, and now not expedient? How was it not expedient to be governed by the power which Christ himself instituted? Did they know better than Christ what was expedient for the Church? Would Augustine so have opposed the institution of Christ? Therefore, what they judged not to be expedient, they certainly declared that they believed it was not sanctioned by divine right. For if it had been sanctioned by divine right, what else would that have been but calling divine wisdom into doubt and overturning the order instituted by Christ? What then is the case? Since the form of governing the Church has been prescribed by Christ (as will be shown in its place), to change it under the colour of expediency to suit the civil state is, in Whitaker's judgment, the act of a man who calls into question the stone of Christ, as if some magistrate knew better than Christ himself what form of government would be expedient.

units.la: Respons. ad admonit. p. 114. thaginensem Ecclesiam, ut gubernationem Ecclesiæ mutandam censuerit propter expedientiam. Rationes quas adfert, pro nobis pleræque faciunt: quare tunc inquit expediebat, & nunc non expedit? cum quomodo non expediebat ut nicè potestate quam Christus ipse instituit? Quid, illine Christo melius sciebant quid Ecclesiæ expediret? Siccine Augustinus Christi instituto se opponeret? Ergo quod existimarunt non expedire, declararunt certe se satis credere, non esse hoc jure divino sanctum. Nam si jure Divino sanctum esset, quid hoc aliud fuisset, quasi divinam sapientiam in dubium vocare, & ordinem à Christo institutum evertere? Quid igitur est? Cum forma regendæ Ecclesiæ à Christo præscripta sit (ut suo loco demonstrabitur) eam sub colore expedientiæ, ad statum civilem immutare, hominis est, Whitakeri judicio, Christi lapidem in dubium vocantis, quasi melius ipso Christo, quæ forma regiminis expediret, magistratus quispiam sciret.

units.la: 2. Sed agamus punctim. Primò regimina hæc duo à se subsistunt divisim & seorsim: neutrum ab altero dependet, sed utrumque a DEO immediate authoritatis suæ originem trahit. Hinc licet nobis cum doctissimo Fyldo disputare. Nemo hominum immutandi rem aliquam potestatem habet, nisi ille tantummodo cui gradu eminenti inest, & à quo illa originaliter derivatur: regimen ergo Ecclesiasticum quà Ecclesiasticum cum magistratu non infit, neque ab eo originaliter dependeat, ab eodem immutari, & ad civile regimen, flecti minime potest. Secundo, utrumque regimen suo genere alterum altero præstantius est: pari igitur dignitate cum sint, nêpe suo genere præstantissima, quomodo alterum in alterum jus mutandi, aut ad sese conformandi competere potest? Quò I si vero de generis ipsius præstantia cogitatur, longe regiminis Ecclesiastici gen, civile præstantius est: sic ut ad Ecclesiâ respublica potius, quàm ad rempublicam civilem Dei Ecclesia temperari debeat. Probat hoc ex Thoma Waldensi Fildui (Spirituali, inquit & civilis potestas in rebus ad se pertinentibus altera altera præstantior est, & quælibet independens, quanquam illa spiritualis simpliciter civili perfectior & excellentior sit.) Similiter Gregorius Nazianzenus, Chrysostomus, Petrus Blesensis, Hugo de Sancto Victore, regimen Ecclesiæ propter obiectum & effectus civili præstantius statuunt, in eo in tantum præstantius, quantum anima corpus, & vita spiritualis terrenam vitam superat: quòd si igitur conformatio hic aliqua locum haberet, ut regimen civile quod minus excellit, ad regimen Ecclesiæ quod est præstantius, non autem hoc ad illud ut accommodetur, æquum est. Tertiò, politeia civilis medium est, quod regimen Ecclesiasticum velut finem suû respicere debet, quâ illud rempublicâ ad gradum eminentem perducit. Quanquam etenim (ut docent Politici) terrenâ fœlicitate rempublicam beet à sese politicia civilis; supernaturali tamen beare eam à sese non potest, nisi ad opem confi-giat. giat politeias Ecclesiasticæ, quâ ut fruatur, illam quærit, illam fovet, illi paret, ab illâ se regi permittit: illi denique & ancillatur & obsecundat. Hinc Isa. 49. 23. Reges nutrii Ecclesiæ sunt, non immutatores, & pulverem pedum lingunt, id est, Ecclesiæ fovendæ inserviunt. Quid igitur est? Politeia Ecclesiastica si ad civilem temperari possit, & finis ipse ad suum medium conformari. Quartò politeia Ecclesiastica certa est, à Deo præscripta, & immutabilis: politeia civilis verò ab hominibus ordinata (ad hoc vel illud regimen quod attinet) mutabilis, varia, & pro diversitate regionū & temporum alia atque alia. De hoc Whitakerus ita,Tot possunt esse humanarum politeiôn formæ quot ipsi homines voluerint; sed Ecclesia regi debet non ut humano ingenio arriserit, sed ut Christo Ecclesiæ Domino solùm, principi placet: quam ergo Christus formam instituit, ea servari atque optima judicari debet, & nepte faciunt qui ex Philosophorum sententijs aut humano judicio statuunt quam formam regendæ Ecclesiæ Christus præscripserit, qui politeias non prescripsit. Quinto politeia Ecclesiæ & civilis res à se invicem distinctæ sunt, sic ut regiminis Ecclesiastici inflexio ad politeiam civilem, ea confundat quæ Deus seperata manere vult, quæque copulari prohibet. Tangit hanc rationem Thomas Bilsonus, qui adversùs Iesuitas ita disputat Quanquam Ecclesia & respublica distincti statūs sunt, quod negari non potestis, utramque tamen regere vos concupiscitis. Ita confunditis quæ a se invicem distinxisse videri vultis. Quòd si autem distinctio illa quæ inter duo hæc regimina esse debet, tum confunditur, cum ab eisdem utrumque geritur & gubernatur: quanto tum magis, cum uni eidemque magistratui potestas conceditur, utrumque formare, instituere, in essentialibus immutare, imò utriusq; similitudinem adaptare. Sextò, politeia civilis & Ecclesiastica non solùm distinctæ & separatæ sunt, verùm etiam tota regione à se invicem distantes, interque sese admodum dissimiles: sic ut ad civilem attemperari politeia Ecclesiastica nequeat, nisi res dissimiles simul conglutinentur, & sic androgynes regendi formæ inducantur. Habet Matheus ipse Sutclivius, quæ ad hanc rem apprimè faciunt. Bellarminus, ipsius iudicio ut Papæ Monarchiam stabiliret, arguit à Monarchia civili, hoc fundamento nitens, quòd una & eadem sit reipublicæ & Ecclesiæ administrandæ ratio. Hoc dum ille convellere nititur, multas dissimilitudines recenset, quæ inter civilem & Ecclesiasticam politeiam intercedunt: in quarum tertiâ, ita pro nobis disertissimè disputat, Sicut unus est Ecclesiæ summus princeps Iesus Christus: sic una est Ecclesia vera & essentialis forma. At rerum publicarū ut variæ sunt Magistratūs sic variæ reperiuntur formæ: nā hæc a Rege, illa ab optimatibus, alia a potentioribus & locupletioribus de populo regitur: omnesq; istæ formæ bonæ sunt. At sec fit in Ecclesia: nā & unus est summus Ecclesiæ rex, & una est Ecclesiastica politeiæ ratio: a qua qui discedunt, in labem gubernationis Ecclesiæ incidunt, & Christi leges transgrediuntur. Quære hîc an verè à Papistis in Anglia jactatum illud sit, Episcopos dum adversus Papistas disputan puritanos esse: dum vero cum puritanis contendunt, se velut Papistas gerere. Dum etenim hic adversus Papistas Sutclivius disputat, quantum ab illo mutatus est, quando adversus Puritanos disputavit? Nulla illic quemadmodum hic disciplinae regula à Christo praescripta: neque illic, quemadmodum hoc loco, immutabilis disciplina, sed varia & ambulatoria, idque ipsius Ecclesiae, aut Magistratus arbitrio. Pergit porrò ita. Ineptissime faciunt adversarij, qui in Ecclesiae forma constituenda, a rebuspublicis humanis exemplar capiunt, & politicis principiis insistunt, & ad humanas leges formam Ecclesiae exigunt, quae nullo humano consilio erigitur, nec legibus humanis subiacet. Quum haec aperte conformationem politeias Ecclesiasticae ad civilem consutent, apparet Georgium Downamum reliquosque qui contrarium statuunt, in ipsa Papistarum castra transvolare, & eorum argumenta adversus suos corroborare. Paulo post; Magna insania est & non modo stultitia, formam reipublicae certis terminis & finibus locorum & temporum circumscriptam, Ecclesiae, quae nullis limitibus definitur, nullis personis certis alligatur, aptare. Quidni pari ratione, formam Ecclesiastici regiminis, civili? Postremo, Non Aristotelicam sed Apostolicam quaerimus Ecclesiae formam: nec magnopere laborandum censemus, quid homines politici de rebuspublicis, sed quid Christus de Ecclesia suâ praecepit. At Aristotelica hominumque politicorum Ecclesiae regendae forma ut introducatur necesse est: si hominibus politicis potestas datur, ut eam mutent ad rempublicam, quae praeceptis Aristotelicis, & arbitrio politicorum gubernatur.
units.tr: 2. But let us go through the points one by one. First, these two governments stand apart and separately from each other: neither depends on the other, but each derives the origin of its authority immediately from God. Hence we may argue with the most learned Fyldo: no one has the power to change anything unless he is one who holds a higher rank, and from whom that power is originally derived. Therefore the ecclesiastical government, as ecclesiastical, does not inhere in the magistrate, nor does it depend originally on him, so it cannot at all be changed by him or bent to the civil government. Second, each government is, in its own kind, more excellent than the other. Since they are equal in dignity, each being most excellent in its own kind, how can either have a right to change the other or to conform it to itself? Moreover, if we think about the excellence of the kind itself, the ecclesiastical government is far more excellent than the civil. So the commonwealth ought to be fitted to the Church, rather than the Church to the civil commonwealth. Thomas Waldensis of FiU proves this: "The spiritual and the civil power, each in matters pertaining to itself, are superior to the other, and each is independent; although the spiritual power is simply more perfect and excellent than the civil." Likewise Gregory Nazianzen, Chrysostom, Peter of Blois, and Hugh of Saint Victor hold that the government of the Church is more excellent than the civil, by reason of its object and its effects, and it is more excellent by as much as the soul is above the body, and spiritual life above earthly life. If, then, any conformity could have a place here, it would be fair that the civil government, which is less excellent, be adjusted to the ecclesiastical government, which is more excellent, and not the reverse. Third, the civil polity is a means, to which the ecclesiastical government ought to look as its end, since it brings the commonwealth to a lofty level. For although (as the Politicians teach) civil polity can make a commonwealth happy with earthly felicity, it cannot make it happy with supernatural felicity of itself, unless it assists the ecclesiastical polity. The civil polity seeks it, that it may enjoy it; it cherishes it, obeys it, permits itself to be ruled by it; and finally it serves and obeys it. Hence Isaiah 49:23: Kings shall be nursing fathers to the Church, not its changers, and they shall lick the dust of its feet, that is, they serve to cherish the Church. What then is the case? If the ecclesiastical polity could be adjusted to the civil, the end itself would be conformed to its means. Fourth, the ecclesiastical polity is certain, prescribed by God, and unchangeable; but the civil polity is ordained by men (as far as this or that government is concerned), changeable, varied, and different according to the diversity of regions and times. Whitaker says of this: There can be as many forms of human polities as men themselves may wish; but the Church ought to be governed not as it pleases human ingenuity, but as it pleases Christ alone, the Lord and Prince of the Church. Therefore the form which Christ instituted is to be kept and judged the best; and they act foolishly who, from the opinions of philosophers or human judgment, determine what form of governing the Church Christ has prescribed, since they have not prescribed civil polities. Fifth, the polity of the Church and the civil affair are distinct from each other, so that bending the ecclesiastical government to the civil polity confuses what God wills to remain separate and forbids to be joined. Thomas Bilson touches on this reason, disputing against the Jesuits thus: Although the Church and the commonwealth are distinct estates, which you cannot deny, you nevertheless desire to rule both. Thus you confound what you wish to seem to have distinguished from each other. But if that distinction which ought to exist between these two governments is confounded when both are carried on and governed by the same persons, how much more so when power is granted to one and the same magistrate to form both, to institute them, to change them in essentials, and indeed to adapt the one to the likeness of the other. Sixth, the civil and the ecclesiastical polity are not only distinct and separate, but also wholly different in region, and very dissimilar to each other. So the ecclesiastical polity cannot be adjusted to the civil unless dissimilar things are glued together and thus hybrid forms of government are introduced. Matthew Sutcliffe himself offers things that bear most directly on this matter. Bellarmine, in his own judgment, in order to establish the monarchy of the Pope, argues from civil monarchy, resting on this foundation, that there is one and the same method of administering the commonwealth and the Church. While Bellarmine strives to overturn this, Sutcliffe recounts many dissimilarities which lie between the civil and the ecclesiastical polity. In the third of these he disputes most eloquently for our side: As Jesus Christ is the one supreme prince of the Church, so there is one true and essential form of the Church. But the forms of commonwealths are various, as magistracies are various: for one is ruled by a king, another by the nobles, another by the more powerful and wealthy of the people; and all these forms are good. But it is not so in the Church: for there is one supreme king of the Church, and one method of ecclesiastical polity; those who depart from it fall into the ruin of the government of the Church and transgress the laws of Christ. Here one may ask whether the Papists in England have truly boasted of this: that the bishops, when they dispute against the Papists, are Puritans, but when they contend with the Puritans, they act like Papists. For when Sutcliffe disputes here against the Papists, how far has he changed from what he was when he disputed against the Puritans? There, as here, there is no discipline prescribed by Christ as a rule; nor is the discipline there, as here, unchangeable, but varied and shifting, and this at the discretion of the Church itself or of the magistrate. He goes on thus: Our adversaries act most foolishly, who, in constituting the form of the Church, take their pattern from human commonwealths and rely on political principles, and who fit the form of the Church to human laws, when it is set up by no human counsel and is not subject to human laws. Since these words plainly contend against conforming the ecclesiastical polity to the civil, it appears that George Downame and the others who hold the contrary have flown over to the very camp of the Papists and strengthened their arguments against their own side. A little later: It is great madness, and not merely folly, to fit the form of a commonwealth, circumscribed by fixed limits of places and times, to the Church, which is defined by no boundaries and bound to no fixed persons. Why not, by the same reasoning, fit the form of ecclesiastical government to the civil? Finally: We seek not the Aristotelian but the Apostolic form of the Church; nor do we judge that we must labour much over what political men think about commonwealths, but over what Christ has commanded concerning his Church. But an Aristotelian form of governing the Church, drawn from political men, must necessarily be introduced if political men are given the power to change it to suit the commonwealth, which is governed by the precepts of Aristotle and the judgment of politicians.

units.la: 4. Septimò, Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo, inquit Christus Ioh. 18.36. ergo regnis hujus mundi adaptari non debet. Eludunt hunc locum adversarij, quòd de regno interno duntaxat intelligitur, sic ut ad regimen Ecclesiae externum omninò non pertineat. Sed nupera haec distinctio est, & ante inaudita, nullo scripturae fundamento nititur, à nostris denique impugnatur. Gulielmus Whitakerus & de externo Ecclesiae regimine verba ista interpretatur; quum ex eo, externam Papae monarchiam ita convellit. Regnum Christi non est de hoc mundo, at omnis visibilis Monarchia de hoc mundo est. Ergo monarchia Papae visibilis (quidni & Episcopalis etiam) Christi non est. Distinguit hic Christus regnum suum ab externis regnis. Externa habent visibiles reges, Christus rex coelestis est: in externis regnis subditi civiliter gubernantur, Christus suos regit spiritualiter: externa regna instituta sunt propter externa huius vitae commoda, Christi regnum in spiritu & bonis internis versatur. Non requiro meliorem quam Ambrosium interpretem, qui dicit non esse de hoc mundo regnum suum, ostendit esse supra mundum ita & erat regnum & non erat: non erat in saeculo, supra saeculum erat. Quid igitur est? Regimen Ecclesiae spirituale est: civile mundanum, Ecclesia supra saeculum, civile saeculare: at ita regnum Christi à regno terreno distat, dicit Ambrosius, ut mundanum & saeculare esse nequeat: at quũ civili cõformatur,nonne quæso terreno simile, mundano conforme ; atque ita quodammodo seculare evadit? Richardus Bancrofius, nos hæc verba ad externum Christi regnum accómodantes,ita ludificatur. Dicent forte inquit,regnum Christi etsi non sit ex hoc mundo, tamen esse in hoc mundo& quid ni ita diceremus? Certe ipse tuus Georgius Carletonus id ipsum dicit,qui unà nobiscum de externo Christi regno, hæc dicta esse dicit; verba ista sunt. Regnum Christi quod non est ex hoc mundo ipsius Ecclesia est, quæ in hoc mundo est, sed non ex hoc mundo: & statum civilem assecurat his verbis Christus, ex regimine Ecclesiæ suæ, damnum nullum in respublicas exoriturum. Observandũ etenim est non pro se tantummodò hic Christum spondere, sed etiam pro Ecclesia sua: non enim dicit, ego non sum de hoc mundo, sed regnum meum: sic ut statum civilem ab omni periculo assecuret, non solùm quòd ad suam personam sed etiam quòd ad Ecclesiam suam quamdiu hic mundus durat.
units.tr: Seventhly, Christ says, "My kingdom is not of this world" (John 18.36); therefore it ought not to be adapted to the kingdoms of this world. Our opponents evade this passage by saying that it refers only to the inner kingdom, so that it does not pertain to the external government of the Church at all. But this distinction is recent and previously unheard of. It rests on no foundation in Scripture, and our own writers finally refute it. William Whitaker also interprets these words of the external government of the Church, and from them overthrows the external monarchy of the Pope: "The kingdom of Christ is not of this world, but every visible monarchy is of this world. Therefore the visible monarchy of the Pope (and why not the episcopal too?) is not Christ's. Here Christ distinguishes his kingdom from external kingdoms. External kingdoms have visible kings; Christ is a heavenly king. In external kingdoms subjects are governed civilly; Christ governs his own spiritually. External kingdoms were instituted for the external advantages of this life; Christ's kingdom lies in spirit and inner goods. I need no better interpreter than Ambrose, who says that his kingdom is not of this world, showing that it is above the world: thus it both was and was not a kingdom. It was not in the age; it was above the age." What then is it? The government of the Church is spiritual, civil government is worldly; the Church is above the age, civil government is secular. But, says Ambrose, the kingdom of Christ is so far distant from an earthly kingdom that it cannot be worldly or secular. Yet when it is conformed to civil government, is it not, I ask, made like the earthly, conformed to the worldly, and so in some measure becomes secular? Richard Bancroft, applying these words to the external kingdom of Christ, makes sport of them: "They will perhaps say," he says, "that the kingdom of Christ, although it is not of this world, is nevertheless in this world." And why should we not say so? Certainly your own George Carleton says the same thing, though he agrees with us that these words refer to the external kingdom of Christ. His words are these: "The kingdom of Christ which is not of this world is the Church itself, which is in this world but not of this world; and by these words Christ secures the civil state against any harm arising to commonwealths from the government of his Church." For it must be observed that Christ here vouches not only for himself but also for his Church: he does not say, "I am not of this world," but "my kingdom," so as to secure the civil state from every danger, not only as regards his own person but also as regards his Church, for as long as this world lasts.

units.la: Octavò, Reges gentium dominantur eis, vos autem non sic,Luc.22.25. 26. Quibus verbis nonne Monarchiam civilem ab Ecclesiastico regimine suo ita Christus eliminat,ut omnem cum illa conformariam similitudinem evitare debeat?Loquatur vel ipse Matthæus Sutclivius. Quid disertius(inquit)dici potuit adversus monarchiam(non quod Whitgiftus adversariique reliqui tyrannidem solum)quæ species est regiminis politici, apud Ethnicos,maximè usitata? Respondent adversarii non omnem dominationem Apostolis prohiberi, sed illam tantùm qua Gentiles utuntur,& quæ ad exemplum est regum Ethnicorum:quasi vero non hujusmodi Monarchiam Petro ascribant & in Ecclesiam introducere conentur? Similiter Johannes Reynoldus probat Mat. 20.26. interdici eam similitudinem Monarchiæ terrenæ quæ in Papæ Monarchia reperitur,quid ni & in Monarchia Episcoporum etiam? quòd si etenim omnis similitudo gubernationis terrenæ, in politeiá Ecclesiasticâ prohibeatur: constabit certè & omnem ejusdem ad terrenam gubernationem conformationem prohiberi itidem:quia nulla conformatio absque similitudine vel cogitari quidem possit. Certè in conformatione Anglicana, ea ipsa Monarchiæ similitudo reperitur, quæ hic interdicitur: pro qua tuendâ quid tandem afferri potest, quod non & Romanæ patriarchæ (seponamus Papæ tyrannidem) Monarchiam unâ tuebitur? Vel ipsa Petri Monarchia in Apostolos reliquos pares, Sutclivio hic interdici videtur: at Ministros omnes pares esse suo loco docebitur;sic ut Episcopalis Monarchia Anglicana, hic etiam,una condemnetur. Sed de hoc suo loco plura. Nero Apocalyps. 13. 14. Reprehendit Spiritus sanctus in politeia Romana quod ad imaginem bestiæ conformatur: ergo regiminis Ecclesiastici ad civile conformatio omnis, ubique gentium illicita est. Quid enim? Annon imperium Romanum quod hic per bestiam adversariorum judicio intelligitur regimen licitum erat? aut imago civilis regiminis liciti in Roviana tantum Ecclesia illicita erit, in cæteris nō item?Respondet Hadrianus Saravia, imaginem bestiæ in doctrina solùm positam esse,non item in politeia: reprehendique hoc in loco Romanam Ecclesiam dicit,non quòd Politeias imaginem, sed quòd veteris Idololatriæ in Romā Ethnica olim usurpatæ simulachrum retinuerit.Primò,si imago doctrinæ Ethnicæ in Ecclesia Romana sit, & imago Politeias Ethnicæ multo erit major: hanc majorem similitudinem prætermisisse Spiritum sanctum, ut minorem tantummodò poneret, quomodo verisimile fiet? Secundò si doctrinæ solius imitationem reprehendisset Spiritus sanctus, pontifices Ethnicos nominasset:nunc Bestiam id est civile imperium nominans, similitudinem politicam quandam & gubernatoriam, eam inclusisse in aperto est.
units.tr: Eighthly, "The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, but you shall not be so" (Luke 22.25–26). Does not Christ by these words so exclude civil monarchy from his ecclesiastical government that one must avoid any likeness or conformity to it? Let Matthew Sutcliffe speak: "What could be said more plainly against monarchy (I do not mean only the tyranny that Whitgift and the rest of our opponents oppose), which is the kind of political government most commonly used among the heathen?" Our opponents reply that the apostles are not forbidden all lordship, only that kind which the Gentiles exercise and which is modelled on heathen kings. As if they did not ascribe such a monarchy to Peter and try to introduce it into the Church! Likewise John Reynolds proves from Matthew 20.26 that the likeness of earthly monarchy found in the papal monarchy is forbidden. Why not also in the monarchy of bishops? For if every likeness of earthly government is forbidden in the ecclesiastical polity, it will surely follow that every conformity to earthly government is likewise forbidden, since no conformity can even be conceived without some likeness. Certainly in the Anglican settlement that very likeness of monarchy is found which is here forbidden. What can at last be advanced in defence of it that will not also defend a monarchy of the Roman patriarchs (leaving aside the tyranny of the Pope)? Even Peter's monarchy over the other apostles, who were equals, seems to be forbidden here by Sutcliffe; but it will be shown in its proper place that all ministers are equal, so that the Anglican episcopal monarchy too will be condemned here. But more on this in its place. Again, Apocalypse 13.14. The Holy Spirit rebukes the Roman polity in Revelation because it is conformed to the image of the beast. Therefore every conformity of ecclesiastical government to civil government is unlawful everywhere among the nations. For what? Was not the Roman empire, which by the opponents' judgement is meant here by the beast, a lawful government? Or will the image of lawful civil government be unlawful only in the Roman Church, and not in the others? Hadrian Saravia replies that the image of the beast lies only in doctrine, not in polity; and he says that the Roman Church is rebuked here not because of an image of polities, but because it has kept the likeness of the old idolatry once practised at heathen Rome. First: if the image of heathen doctrine is in the Roman Church, then the image of heathen polity will be much greater. How likely is it that the Holy Spirit would pass over this greater likeness and mention only the lesser? Second: if the Holy Spirit had rebuked only the imitation of doctrine, he would have named heathen pontiffs. Now, by naming the beast, that is the civil empire, he has plainly included some political and governmental likeness.

units.la: Tertiò de imagine politeias, hunc locum Matheus Sutclivius intelligit, cujus ista verba sunt. Non Petro successit in prædicando Papa, sed Constantino in sede imperiali: reddens vitam bestiæ quæ mortua videbatur, & Romæ erigens imaginem veteris imperij, Sed de hoc loco susiùs alibi.
units.tr: Thirdly, Matthew Sutcliffe understands this passage of the image of the polity, and his words are these: "The Pope did not succeed Peter in preaching, but Constantine in the imperial see, restoring life to the beast which seemed dead, and setting up in Rome the image of the old empire." But more fully on this passage elsewhere.

units.la: Decimo,non desunt,qui Politeias Ecclesiasticæ conformationem ad civilem apertis verbis jugulant. Primatum affectabat Iohannes Constantinoplitanus prætextu imperialis maiestatis Constantinopoli degentis: ideoque Episcopo Constantinopolitano primatum deberi arguebat: quòd Ecclesia rempublicam sequi debeat. Hoc ita cum sit, eodem fundamento Episcopatus Constantinopolitanus apud Iohannem nitebatur, quo hodie apud Whitgiftum Anglicanus. Non igitur adversus Iohannem solummodo, verùm etiam Whitgiftum valet illa antiqua Leonis & Gelasij refutatio: quorum ille ita. Alia est ratio rerum sæcularium, alia divinarum; hic vero ita: Alia potestas est regni sæcularis, alia Ecclesiasticarum distributio dignitatum. Sic olim ad Episcopos Constantinus. Vos quidem eorum quæ intus sunt in Ecclesia agenda, ego vero eorum quæ extra hanc sunt Episcopus a Deo sum constitutus. Eusebius de vita Constantini. Lib.4. c.34. In his verbis (inquit Carleton9) Ecclesiastica & politi a potestate ita disterminavit Constatin°,ut illa de internis tantu, hæc tantum de externis sit. Hoc sensu extra Ecclesiam Magistratus cum sit, potestate Ecclesiæ transmutandi nullam habet: nedum internum illius regimen,ad suum externum conformandi. Idem Ambrosij judicium erat, nullam scilicet Magistratui potestate competere in res sacras,ut eas immutare possit:quod si sit verum nec disciplinam quidem immutare ei licebit. Verba illius ad Valentinianum ista sunt. Noli te gravare, Imperator, ut putes te in ea quæ divina sunt, aliquod imperiale ius habere. Politicorum tibi munerum jus commissum est, non sacrorum. Ita de Hierarchicorum Anglicanorum conformatione Cornelius Sculingius speciatim. Observandum Anglo Calvinistas (inquit) contra puritanos fortiter defendere, quod officia Eccl. si istica pro temporum & locorum varietate Ecclesiæ constituere possit, sed perquam absurde. Volunt enim singulas provincias eam politiæ formam
units.tr: Tenthly, there are not lacking those who in plain words cut the throat of the conformity of ecclesiastical polity to civil. John of Constantinople claimed primacy under the pretext of the imperial majesty dwelling at Constantinople, and therefore argued that primacy was owed to the bishop of Constantinople because the Church ought to follow the commonwealth. Since this is so, the see of Constantinople rested on John's foundation in the same way as the Anglican episcopate rests today on Whitgift's. Therefore that ancient refutation by Leo and Gelasius applies not only against John but also against Whitgift. Leo says: "The reasoning of secular affairs is one thing, that of divine affairs another." Gelasius says: "The power of the secular kingdom is one thing, the distribution of ecclesiastical dignities another." So Constantine once said to the bishops: "You indeed have charge of what is within the Church; I indeed have been appointed by God as bishop of what is outside it." (Eusebius, Life of Constantine, book 4, chapter 34.) "In these words" (says Carleton) "Constantine so divided ecclesiastical and political power that the one is concerned only with inner matters, the other only with external ones." In this sense, since the magistrate stands outside the Church, he has no power to change the Church, much less to conform its inner government to his external one. This was also the judgement of Ambrose, that the magistrate has no power over sacred things to alter them; and if that is true, he may not even alter discipline. His words to Valentinian are these: "Do not burden yourself, emperor, with the notion that you have any imperial right in things divine. The right of political duties has been committed to you, not of sacred ones." Thus, specifically concerning the conformity of the Anglican hierarchy, Cornelius Scultingius writes: "It must be observed that the Anglo-Calvinists strongly defend against the Puritans that ecclesiastical officers can constitute the church's polity according to the variety of times and places, but quite absurdly. For they want each province to adopt the form of polity

units.la: Hierarchic. Anacrysh. l.10.col.69 formam assumere, quæ pio magistratui & ipsius provinciæ statui magis videbitur convenire. Sed quorsum Scultingius producitur in scenam inquies? quasi in scena Hierarchica is ante non fuerit, Hierarchiæ Anglicanæ partes anges: Neque mitior Hadrianus Saravia Scultingio est. Tuetur is certam & immutabilem regiminis Ecclesiastici formam ab ipso Christo mandatam esse: Hinc contra conformationem istam ad regimen civile, quâ de agimus, ita disputat. Nulli genti Deus unquam ullam certam & perpetuam imperii formam dedit, quam pro varietate loci & temporum mutari non liceret. Sed hujus regiminis de quo disserimus diversa est ratio: quoniam enim a Deo proxime est profecta, eam pro arbitrio suo homines mutare non possunt, nec necesse est. Nam sic eam temperavit divina sapientia, ut nulli civilis reginiis formæ adversetur. Quando autem tota aliqua respublica facta est Ecclesia, gubernatio quidem mutationem aliquam recipit, sed quæ ipsius naturam non mutat. Rursus, Quamvis Ecclesiastica gubernatio recepto Evangelio nonnihil (quantum per verbum Dei licet) ad rempublicam statum inflectenda sit, cavendum tamen est, ne ipsius mutetur substantia: cælestis quidem doctrina universalis est, & huiusmodi ut ab hominibus suscipi possit: proinde non est tanquam lesbia quædam regula inflectenda ad hominum mores, utpote qui ad illam fixam & immotam reducendi sint. Hæc ille pro regiminis episcopalis quidem immutabilitate disputans: quod tamen dicit verum est: aliàs regimen episcopale ut concidat necesse est, in rebuspublicis omnibus, quæ aut Aristocraticæ aut Democraticæ sunt. Ita reformationis Anglicanæ in disciplina defectus quartus iste, conformatio nempe politeiæ Ecclesiasticæ ad civilem, & apertis scripturis prohibetur, & ab ipsis Hierarchicis refutatur.
units.tr: Hierarchic. Anacrysh. l. 10, col. 69: to adopt the form which will seem more fitting to a godly magistrate and to the condition of the province itself. But you will ask why Scultingius is brought onto the stage? As if he had not played his part on the hierarchical stage before, acting the parts of the Anglican hierarchy! Nor is Hadrian Saravia any milder than Scultingius. He maintains that a fixed and unchangeable form of ecclesiastical government was commanded by Christ himself, and so against that conformity of ecclesiastical to civil government under discussion he argues thus: "God never gave any nation a certain and perpetual form of empire which could not be changed according to variety of place and time." But the case of the government we are discussing is different. Since it has come most immediately from God, men cannot change it at their pleasure, nor is there any need to. For divine wisdom has so tempered it that it opposes no form of civil government. "But when some whole commonwealth has become a Church, its government indeed receives some change, which does not alter its nature." Again: "Although ecclesiastical government, once the Gospel is received, must be bent somewhat toward the condition of the commonwealth (as far as the Word of God permits), care must be taken that its substance is not altered. The heavenly doctrine is universal and of such a kind that men can receive it; therefore it is not to be bent like a Lesbian rule to men's morals, since men are rather to be brought back to it, fixed and unmoved." He argues this for the unchangeability of episcopal government, and what he says is true; otherwise episcopal government must necessarily fall in all commonwealths that are aristocratic or democratic. Thus this fourth defect of the Anglican reformation in discipline, namely the conforming of ecclesiastical polity to civil, is both forbidden by plain Scripture and refuted by the hierarchists themselves.

units.la: CAP. 27. Defectus in Anglia quintus, quòd non adhibuit adhuc malorum fonti remedium.
units.tr: CHAPTER 27. The fifth defect in England: that no remedy has yet been applied to the source of evils.

units.la: Vintus sequitur, in eo peccans, quòd ipsi malorum in Ecclesiâ Anglicanâ omnium fonti, remedium adhuc nullum adhibitum sit. Rectè etenim admonet Petrus Martyr, in Ecclesiâ reformanda Elizæi exemplum imitandum esse: & fontem ipsum ante omnia sanandum: a quo contagio labes, omnis manat. Conqueritur Lo-us pro disciplinâ Anglicana scribens, Ecclesiæ statum in deterius semper prolabi, & videre cuivis licere, in deterius omnia ruere: de quo, ipsis videndum est, qui gloriosum Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ statum plenis buccis prædicare solent. Nos quidni Deum glorificemus, vaticinio suo fidem facientem, idque ex utraque parte. In illis etenim jactabundis impletum cernimus, quod de Angliæ Angelo prædicitur Apocal.3. 17. dicis, dives sum, & nullius egeo; in hac verò querimonia justissimâ, quod de eodem Angelo dicitur, miserabilis es & erumnosus: cerumnosius: præsertim cum addat Lous, Ecclesiā quasi ruinis oppressam jacere, & ita iacere, ut nec auxilij spem, nec miseriæ solatiū reperire possit. Addit vero non tam ab externis hostibᵒquam domesticis & intestinis hoc accidisse: in quo ut illi maximè cōsentio, ita hoc nomine reformationem & urgendam vehementius & citius inchoandam dico. Hoc etenim illud est quod Iohannes Picus Mirandulanus ad Maximilianum Imperatorem olim scripsit: Concutitur ab externis hostibus Ecclesia, ab internis laceratur: & Iesu Christi sanguine circumseptam & consecratum ovile, peius multo perpessum est, indi(que patitur a lupis sub ovina quam sub proprii pelle grassantibus. Age igitur jam Cæsar optime, & Christo regum omnium regi, oves suas tam ab hostilibus quam a perfidis pastoribus, iam iam liberaturo, te fidum ministrum exhibe. Quid igitur inquies? Num quosdam de nostris plus damni Ecclesiæ dedisse dices, quàm ipsas Papistas? Si mihi non credas, Leo saltem tuo credas: deinde rationem redde, cur lupi pelle ovina contecti periculosiores non jam sint, quàm qui aperti hostes habentur, sicuti olim Christus admonuit Matth. 7. 15. & Cypriano etiam respondet, qui plus nocere simulatum hostem, quàm inimicum apertum docuit. Verba ista sunt: Plus metuendus & cavendus est inimicus cum latenter obrepit: ea est diaboli astutia, ut sub ipso Christiani nominis titulo fallat incautos. Rationem reddit in causa simili Poeta tragicus: Odia (inquit) professa perdunt vindictæ locum: ita & hostes etiam professi perdunt nocendi modum. Hoc ita cùm sit evigilandum cuique est, & solicitè inquirendum, quinam illi lupi in Anglia sint, qui pelle ovinâ tecti, columnæ quidem Ecclesiæ putantur, sed eam subruunt & subvertunt tamen. Non temerè columnas memini: nam pastores, quòd sint, non laici, & ratio ipsa & omnium temporum experientia testata convincit. Hugo Cardinalis, sæculi sui mala unde orta fuerint ostendere conatur ex Dan.3. Egressa est iniquitas a senioribus. Nicolaus Orem, coram Urbano 5.de illius sæculi miseriis disserit: quarum caput repetit ex illo Ieremiæ loco Thren.4. propter iniquitatem sacerdotum ejus. Franciscus Picus coram Leone decimo, in Concilio Lateranensi, pro reformatione orationem elegantem habuit: ubi malorum omnium fontem perscrutatus, inter alia hæc habet: Malum omne de templo Ioannes Chrysostomus censet, & Hieronymus scribit se invenisse neminem, qui seduxerit populos præterquam sacerdotes. Chrysostomi verba ista sunt. Sicut de templo omne bonum progreditur: ita etiam de templo omne malum procedit. Hieronymi vero hæc: veteres historias scrutantes invenire non possum, aliquos alios scidisse Ecclesiam, & de domo Domini populos seduxisse, præter eos qui sacerdotes a Deo positi sunt, & Prophetæ, id est speculatores. Isti ergo vertuntur in laqueum tortuosum, in omnibus locis ponentes scandalum. A sæculorum igitur omnium experientiâ discedimus, si Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ mala ab alio fonte, quàm ab ipsis sacerdotibus repetamus: qui cùm aut Hierarchici sint aut Reformatores, quos vulgus hominum Puritanos appellat: inquirendum quirendum deinceps est, in utrum horum sacerdotum genus culpa omnis cudenda sit.
units.tr: The fifth defect follows, and here too the reformers err: no remedy has yet been applied to the source of all the evils in the Anglican Church. Peter Martyr rightly warns that in reforming the Church one should imitate the example of Elisha, and that the fountain itself must be healed before all else, since from it contagion flows and every stain spreads. Lous, writing about the discipline of the Anglican church, complains that the state of the Church always slides toward the worse, and that anyone may see that everything is collapsing for the worse. Those who are wont to proclaim the glorious state of the Anglican Church with full cheeks must look to this themselves. Why should we not glorify God, whose prophecy makes good on both sides? For in the boasters we see fulfilled what is foretold of the Angel of England in Rev. 3:17, "You say, I am rich, and I need nothing"; and in this most just complaint, what is said of the same Angel, "you are wretched and miserable," is fulfilled as well, especially since Lous adds that the Church lies as if crushed under ruins, and lies in such a way that it can find neither hope of help nor any solace for its misery. He adds, moreover, that this has come about not so much from external enemies as from domestic and internal ones. In this I wholly agree with him, and for this reason I say that reformation must be pressed more vehemently and begun more quickly. For this is what Giovanni Pico della Mirandola once wrote to the Emperor Maximilian: "The Church is shaken by external enemies and torn apart by internal ones; and the fold encircled and consecrated by the blood of Jesus Christ has suffered far worse, and more unworthily, from wolves prowling under sheep's skin than from those prowling under their own skin. Come then, best of Caesars, and show yourself a faithful minister to Christ, King of all kings, who is about to free his sheep both from enemies and from faithless shepherds." What then, you will say? Will you claim that some of our own people have done more harm to the Church than the Papists themselves? If you will not believe me, at least believe Leo. Then give an account of why wolves covered with sheep's skin are not now more dangerous than those held to be open enemies, as Christ once warned in Matt. 7:15, and as Cyprian also answers, teaching that a pretended enemy does more harm than an open one. His words are: "An enemy is more to be feared and guarded against when he creeps in secretly; such is the cunning of the devil, that under the very title of the Christian name he deceives the unwary." A tragic poet gives the reason in a similar case: "Hatreds professed, he says, lose the opportunity for revenge; so enemies too, once professed, lose the means of harming."
