Since this is so, each person must keep watch and diligently inquire who those wolves in England are, who, covered with sheep's skin, are thought to be pillars of the Church, and yet undermine and overthrow it. I do not recall calling them pillars rashly, for that they are ministers and not laymen is proved both by reason and by the experience of all times. Hugo the Cardinal tries to show from Dan. 3 where the evils of his age arose: "Iniquity has come out from the elders." Nicholas of Orem, speaking before Urban V, discusses the miseries of that age, and traces their head to that passage of Jeremiah in Lam. 4: "because of the iniquity of her priests." Francesco Pico, before Leo X in the Lateran Council, gave an elegant speech for reformation. Searching out the source of all evils, among other things he says: "Chrysostom judges that every evil comes from the temple," and Jerome writes that he had found no one who led the peoples astray except the priests. The words of Chrysostom are these: "As all good proceeds from the temple, so also all evil comes forth from the temple." Those of Jerome are these: "Searching the ancient histories, I cannot find that anyone has split the Church and led the peoples astray from the house of the Lord, except those who are set in place by God as priests and prophets, that is, watchmen. These, then, are turned into a twisted snare, placing stumbling-blocks in all places." We therefore depart from the experience of all ages if we derive the evils of the Anglican Church from any source other than the priests themselves. Since these are either Hierarchs or Reformers, whom the common people call Puritans, it must next be inquired to which of these two kinds of priests all the blame is to be assigned.

units.la: 2. Arbitrum se hic ingerit Georgias Dormamus. Certissimum est, inquit, Episcoporum contemptum si non omnis mali, (quod Chrysostomus tamen in 2. Timoth. Homil. 2. affirmare videtur) at ultro maximi mali tamen, inter nos causam esse. Atqui inquam Episcopum Anglicanum Chrysostomus numquam novit, alius tum Episcopatus, atq; nunc est; ut taceam, Episcopos nullos Chrysostomi sensu à nobis unquam contemptos fuisse. Fallaciam etenim accidentis committis: quum contemptus Episcoporum Chrysostomo mali causa sit, non quâ illius superioritas in reliquos ministros ex verbo Dei impugnatur, sed quâ illi authoritas potius in gregem Domini, recta docens, unitatem colens, morum puritati invigilans, per homines impios & rebelles in contemptum adducitur. Ita Sancti Chrysostomi censura nullam nobis notam inurit, quorum (quem vocas) contemptus hodie Episcoporum, nihil revera aliud est, quam adhibitio medicinæ illius, illius collirij atque auri, id est reformationis in disciplina illius, quam ad curandum Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ & morbum, & cæcitatem, & paupertatem ipse Spiritus sanctus & expeditissimam & efficacissimam esse dicit, Ap. 3. 18, Verè nos de Anglia, morbo Babylonico adhuc laborante contestari possumus, quod Ieremias de Babylone ipsâ olim.[ Curare voluimus Babilonem, sed ea noluit curari: ] Ier. 51. 9. ut quæ ne morbum quidem suum agnoscat, imò ab eo agnoscendo tantum absit, ut de eis etiam conqueratur, quæ illius vulnera quoquomodo tangere præsumpserint. Audiat uero qui aures habet, expeditam nostram ex Hieronymo defensionem: Non indignentur nobis hæc exponentibus, sed Dominum deprecentur, ut studiosè agant, ne de sacerdotibus, qui violant sancta Domini, esse mereantur. Æquâ etenim ulla nostra unquam culpa alia fuit quàm quòd exposuerimus quænam illa Ecclesiæ politeia sit, quæ in Verbo præscripta est: quamque fœda sanctorum Domini violatio illorum sacerdotum sit, qui ab eâdem deflexerunt; Nulla quidem nos vulnera infliximus, sed inflicta ab Hierarchicis curare voluimus, sic ut malí totius causa (quod Dominus calumniatur) esse nequeamus, nisi forte sanare, vulnerare sit. Quâm præposterè igitur in Anglia factû, ubi de nulla reformatione aliusmodi cogitatur, nisi ut (loqui sic vulgus solet) ipsi reformatores extirpetur; siccine fieri debuit? Vrgéti quódâ reformationé Sigis. ãdo Imperatori dictû ab Episcopis fertur: Incipiendũ esse à Minoritis. Imò verò, respódit Sigism. nô à minoritis, sed à majoritis incipiedum potiº est. Atqui in Anglia reformatores & pauci & minoritæ sunt: quid si igitur in his esset, quod reformatione opº haberet; dum Episcopi maioritæ nô reformátur, fôte ipso malorû nôdû curato, nunquâ manare mala cessabunt. Vidit vero Sigis. sicut malum Eccle.nô tâ ab externis hostibº quâ internis, & inter hos, non tam á laïcis, quâ à sacerdotibus promanare, ita inter sacerdotes, capita malorum cos esse, qui
units.tr: 2. Here Georgius Dormamus thrusts himself in as arbiter. "It is most certain," he says, "that contempt for bishops, if it is not the cause of every evil (which Chrysostom nevertheless seems to affirm in his second homily on 2 Timothy), is at least among us the cause of a very great evil." But I reply: Chrysostom never knew an English bishop of the kind that existed then and exists now, not to mention that bishops were never despised by us in Chrysostom's sense. For you commit the fallacy of accident. Contempt for bishops is the cause of evil in Chrysostom's sense not because their superiority over the other ministers is attacked on the authority of the Word of God, but because their authority, which rightly teaches the flock of the Lord, cultivates unity and watches over the purity of morals, is brought into contempt through wicked and rebellious men. Thus the censure of St Chrysostom brands us with no mark. The contempt for bishops that you speak of today is in reality nothing other than the application of that medicine, that eye-salve and gold, that is, the reformation of discipline, which the Holy Spirit himself declares to be the most ready and most effective remedy for the sickness, the blindness and the poverty of the Anglican Church (Rev. 3:18). Truly we may bear witness concerning England, still labouring under a Babylonian disease, what Jeremiah once said of Babylon itself: [We would have healed Babylon, but she would not be healed] (Jer. 51:9). She does not even recognise her own disease; nay, so far is she from acknowledging it that she complains about those who have presumed in any way to touch her wounds. Let him who has ears hear our defence, drawn ready from Jerome: "Let them not be indignant with us for setting these things forth, but let them pray to the Lord that they may act diligently, so that they do not deserve to be among the priests who violate the holy things of the Lord." For our only fault has been that we set forth what that polity of the Church is which is prescribed in the Word, and how foul is the violation of the holy things of the Lord by those priests who have turned aside from it. We have inflicted no wounds, but we have wished to cure those inflicted by the Hierarchs, so that we cannot be the cause of the evil (as the Lord is slandered), unless perhaps to heal is to wound. How preposterously, then, has this been done in England, where no reformation of any kind is contemplated except (as the common people are wont to say) that the reformers themselves be rooted out. Ought it to have been done so? When pressed for a certain reformation, it is said that the bishops told the Emperor Sigismund: "One must begin with the Minorites." But no, Sigismund replied, one must begin not with the Minorites but with the Majorites. Yet in England the reformers are both few and minorities. What if there were something in them that needed reforming, while the bishops, the majorities, are not reformed, the source of the evils not yet being cured? The evils will never cease to flow. Sigismund, however, saw that the evil of the Church flows not so much from external enemies as from internal ones, and not so much from laymen as from priests; and that among the priests, those who are the heads of the evils are the ones who

units.la: In Epist. dedicat.
units.tr: In the Epistle Dedicatory.

units.la: In Sophon. cap. 3. qui caput & arcem rerum tenent. Quod tandem saeculum? quae regio? ubi miserrimâ experientiâ hoc non testatum? Sic Canon: Totum corpus incipit morbus invadere, si languor non fuerit curatus in capite. Sic Concilium Toletanum. Quia nequaquam recte subditos judicat, qui non seipsum prius iustitiae censura castigat; expedibile nobis visum est ante nostris excessibus imponere modum, & sic errata corrigere subditorum. Durandus Mirapensis de Ecclesiae reformatione scribens eam inchoandam a Praelatis Ecclesiae dicit, & ab ipsa Romana curia de quibus populus universus inficitur. Wenceslaus miseriam sui saeculi deplorans, eam arcessit a capite: narrat etenim Ecclesiam in visione cuidam dixisse, Ex his quae vides in capite perpendere potes corruptelam & dolorem meum in reliquis membris. Habetur hoc apud Dominum Morneum, qui etiam refert, Roberto Gillo in visione ostensum, unde miseria Ecclesiae fluat, nempe ex capite acido & macilento, ac si ligneum esset. Apud eundem Luithpertus Archiepiscopus Moguntinus, totius mali fontem ex eo petit, quod morbus in capite paulatim per membra diffundatur. Sic Adrianus papa 6. Dices nos ingenue fateri, quod Deus hanc persecutionem Ecclesiae suae inferri permittit propter peccata hominum, maxime sacerdotum & Ecclesiae praelatorum. Clamant Scripturae peccata populi derivari a peccatis sacerdotum, propterea (aut ait Chrysostomus) Salvator noster curaturus infirmam civitatem Hierosolymam, ingressus est prius templum, ut peccata sacerdotum prius castigaret, instar boni medici, qui morbum a radice curat. Nec mirum si aegritudo a capite in membra, a summis Pontificibus in alios Praelatos inferiores descenderit. Qua in re quod ad nos attinet, polliceberis nos omnem operam adhibituros, ut primum Curia haec, unde forte omne malum hoc processit, reformetur: ut sicut inde corruptio in omnes inferiores emanavit, ita etiam ab eadem sanitas & reformatio emanet. Quid igitur est? Clamant Scripturae malum omne a summis sacerdotibus esse. Non audiunt Hierarchici? Dicit ratio, morbu capitis, totum corpus pessundare, a pedibus ortum malum omne esse volunt Hierarchici. Testatur experientia omnium temporum suos Praelatos fontem totius mali esse, in Anglia contra accidisse, Hierarchici protestantur. Ingenue fatetur vel Papa ipse, curiam suam totius mali causam esse: duriori fronte jam Hierarchici Anglicani sunt. Atne in abusus culpa omnis derivetur, audiatur Christus ipse judex: qui in corruptum Angliae regimen culpam omnem transfert totius illius tepiditatis; quae nisi citius emendetur, vindicé eum Angliae Angelus expectaturus est, quem hucusque per Puritanos (ut vocantur) & medicum benignum & benevolum admonitorem habuit, nec immerito: grassarentur etenim in Anglia tot mala intimaque Ecclesiae viscera depascerent, si salutare Iesu Christi regimen, sicut in Ecclesiis reliquis, ibi obtinuisset? Atque hic defectus Anglicanae reformationis quintus est, quod ipse fons omnium malorum non reformetur.
units.tr: In Zeph. 3. who hold the head and citadel of affairs. What age, what region, where has this not been attested by the most wretched experience? So the Canon says: The disease begins to invade the whole body, if the weakness is not cured in the head. So too the Council of Toledo: Since a man does not judge his subjects rightly if he does not first chastise himself with the censure of justice, it has seemed right to us to set a limit first to our own excesses, and so to correct the errors of our subjects. Durandus of Mirepoix, writing on the reformation of the Church, says that it must be begun by the prelates of the Church, and by the Roman court itself, from which the whole people is infected. Wenceslaus, lamenting the misery of his age, traces it back to the head: for he tells how the Church said to a certain man in a vision, From what you see in the head you can gauge my corruption and my pain in the other members. This is found in Lord Morneus, who also reports that Robert Gillo was shown in a vision where the misery of the Church flows from: namely from a sour and wasted head, as if it were made of wood. In the same author, Luithpert, Archbishop of Mainz, seeks the source of all evil in this, that the disease in the head gradually spreads through the members. So too Pope Adrian VI: You will say that we frankly confess that God permits this persecution to be inflicted on his Church because of the sins of men, chiefly of the priests and prelates of the Church. The Scriptures cry out that the sins of the people are derived from the sins of the priests; therefore (or, as Chrysostom says) our Saviour, about to cure the sick city of Jerusalem, first entered the temple, so that he might first chastise the sins of the priests, like a good physician who cures a disease at its root. Nor is it surprising if the sickness has descended from the head into the members, from the highest Pontiffs into the lower prelates. In this matter, so far as concerns us, you will promise that we shall take every care that this court first be reformed, from which perhaps all this evil has proceeded, so that just as corruption has flowed from it into all the lower ranks, so also soundness and reformation may flow from the same source. What then is the position? The Scriptures cry out that all evil comes from the chief priests. Do the Hierarchists not hear? Reason says that a disease of the head destroys the whole body; yet the Hierarchists want all evil to arise from the feet. The experience of every age bears witness that their prelates are the fountain of all evil; the Hierarchists protest that in England it is the other way round. The Pope himself frankly admits that his own court is the cause of all evil; the English Hierarchists are now more brazen-faced still. And if all blame for abuses is to be traced elsewhere, let Christ himself, the judge, be heard: he lays all the blame for that lukewarmness on the corrupt government of England, and unless it is quickly amended, the Angel of England will surely await the avenging, whom until now he has had, through those called Puritans, as a kindly and benevolent physician and admonisher, and not undeservedly: for would so many evils rage in England and devour the innermost vitals of the Church, if the wholesome government of Jesus Christ had prevailed there as in the other Churches? And this is the fifth defect of the English reformation: that the very fountain of all evils has not been reformed.

units.la: CAP. 28. Defectus in Anglia sextus & ultimus, quòd Hierar- chici disciplinam reformatarum Eccl- esiarum insectentur.
units.tr: CAP. 28. The sixth and last defect in England: the Hierarchists attack the discipline of the reformed Churches.

units.la: Extus & ultimus in eo est, quòd Ecclesiarum reformatarum zelum in disciplinâ restituendâ, tantum abest, quòd Hierarchici imitentur, ut eum etiam acriter & amarulenter insectentur. Postquam exemplū sui temporis Ecclesiarū propositsset Tertullianus, ita infert: Quid observabimus? quid elegemus? Non possumus respuere consuetudinem quam damnare non possumus, utpote non extraneam, quia non extraneorum, cum quibus scilicet communicamus jus pacis & nomen fraternitatis. Sed quod non potuit Tertullianus, possunt jam nostri: licet Ecclesiarum reformatarum disciplinā damnare se non posse dicant, eam respuunt tamen, quasi extraneam, quanquam extraneorum non sit: illam interim observantes & eligentes quasi domesticam, quæ verè extraneorum est, quos & condemnant, & quibuscum jus nullum pacis (à disciplina si discesseris) nomenque fraternitatis colunt. Quid schisma ab Ecclesiis facere, si hoc non sit; imo quid hoc aliud quam a fratribus in hostium castra aperta luce transvolare? Absque hoc si fuisset: quod tota per orbem frequentat Ecclesia, inquit Aug. hoc quin ita faciendum sit disputare, insolentissimæ insaniæ est: id quod non citat solum, verùm etiam approbat Thomas Bilsonus, Quid ni igitur, quod per totam Europam Ecclesiæ reformatæ faciunt, id Hierarchicos non facere, insolentiæ aut stultitiæ fuerit? At fallimini, respondent, aut alios fallitis, dum vel totas reformatas Ecclesias aut earum majorem partem, à vobis stare salsissimè iactitatis. Richardus Bancroftus postquam Ecclesias plurimas recensuisset, censuram Martini Iunioris nobis omnibus communem facit, quà dicit has Ecclesias mancas & imperfectas esse. Infert post, impugnationes nostras adæq; has Ecclesias impetere, ac ipsam Angliam: & ad postremum concludit, nos nullam in toto Christiano orbe Ecclesiam reformatam, pro legitima Ecclesia agnoscere & amplecti, & cui (ni schismati presbyteriali forte faveat) nos submittere velimus. At quomodo hæc coherent? nos has Ecclesias imperfectas dicere, & tamen legitimas Ecclesias negare? nam qui Ecclesias imperfectas dicit, eo ipso ecclesias legitimas agnoscit. Imperfectio, numnam Bancrofto terminus destruens Ecclesiam est? Non ita sane Iohanni Whitgifto visum, qui Anabaptismi Cartwrightum condemnat, quòd politeiam Ecclesiæ quoad generalem constitutionem, etiam in hac vita perfectam esse posse dixerat. Atqui utrumque, disciplina peræque ac doctrina ipsa perfecta esse potest (ut verè à Cartwrighto dictum) nunquam tamen à nostris quis perfectionem disciplinæ, vel in doctrina vel in disciplina somniavit: ut injuriam eum fecisse putet, Ecclesiæ quamvis perfectissimæ
units.tr: The sixth and last defect lies in this: far from imitating the zeal of the reformed Churches in restoring discipline, the Hierarchists attack it so bitterly and savagely. After Tertullian had set forth the practice of the Churches of his own time, he goes on: What shall we observe? What shall we choose? We cannot reject a custom which we cannot condemn, since it is not foreign, because it is not of foreigners, with whom of course we share the right of peace and the name of brotherhood. But what Tertullian could not do, our people now can. Although they say they cannot condemn the discipline of the reformed Churches, they nonetheless reject it as if it were foreign, though it is not foreign at all. Meanwhile they observe and choose as if it were domestic what is truly foreign to them, and they condemn those whom they hold in no right of peace and no name of brotherhood once you have departed from discipline. What is this, if not schism from the Churches? Indeed, what is it other than fleeing from brothers into the enemy's camp in broad daylight? If it were otherwise, which the whole Church throughout the world practises, says Augustine, to argue that it is not to be done is the height of insolent madness: which Thomas Bilson not only cites but also approves. Why, then, would it be insolence or folly for the Hierarchists not to do what the reformed Churches do throughout all of Europe? But you are mistaken, they reply, or you deceive others, when you boldly boast that the reformed Churches as a whole, or most of them, stand with you. Richard Bancroft, after listing very many Churches, makes Martin Junius's judgement common to all of us, by which he says these Churches are maimed and imperfect. He then adds that our objections attack these Churches equally, and England itself. At last he concludes that we acknowledge and embrace no reformed Church in the whole Christian world as a legitimate Church, and to which we are willing to submit (unless perhaps we favour the presbyterian schism). But how do these claims fit together? That we call these Churches imperfect, and yet deny that they are legitimate Churches? For whoever calls Churches imperfect thereby acknowledges them as legitimate. Is imperfection, then, for Bancroft a term that destroys a Church? Not so, indeed, did it seem to John Whitgift, who condemns Cartwright as an Anabaptist because he had said that the polity of the Church, as to its general constitution, can be perfect even in this life. Yet both doctrine and discipline can be perfect (as Cartwright rightly said), and yet none of our people has ever dreamed of a perfection of discipline or of doctrine, so that he would think he had wronged any Church, however most perfect,

units.la: {a} Tertull. de virg. velland c. 2. fectissimæ, qui eam imperfectam dicit: Nos quidem Genevan Ecclesiam omnium perfectissimam existimamus: veniam tamen petimus, ut eam in nonnullis ad disciplinā pertinentib⁹,imperfectā dicere liceat. Verūm ut Genevan à nobis stare affirmamus,quanquam in omnibus non satisfaciat: ita & Ecclesias reformatas reliquas etiam, quanquam plura in eis quùm in Ecclesia Genevensi desiderem̄us. Atqui hoc modo & ab Anglis etiam illæ stabunt ( inquit Bucerus) cùm adæquè Ecclesiis hisce adversamini,ac ipsi Anglicæ.Dico, nihil hoc potuisse salsius dici.Concordant Ecclesiæ istæ cum Anglis; aut verò nobis adversantur? Quidni inquit G. Downamus. *Multò maior Ecclesiarum reformatarum pars, ab Episcopis & superintendentibus gubernatur, quàm à disciplinā presbyteriali. Iterum, ‡ Sicut in numero doctorum hominum inferiores non sumus: ita in Ecclesiarum mo-lernarum multitudine, quæ seniores laicos non admittunt, sumus multo superiores.
units.tr: {a} Tertull. de virg. velland c. 2. most perfect, by calling it imperfect. We indeed consider the Genevan Church the most perfect of all, yet we beg pardon, so that we may be allowed to call it imperfect in some matters pertaining to discipline. But just as we affirm that we stand with Geneva, although it does not satisfy in all things, so also with the other reformed Churches, although we desire more in them than in the Genevan Church. Yet in this way the Anglicans too will stand with them (says Bucer), since you are as opposed to these Churches as the English Church itself. I say nothing could have been said more absurdly. Do these Churches agree with the English, or are they opposed to us? Why not, says G. Downame: "A much greater part of the reformed Churches is governed by bishops and superintendents than by presbyterial discipline." Again: "Just as we are not inferior in the number of learned men, so in the multitude of modern Churches, which do not admit lay elders, we are far superior."

units.la: Rursus. Vt de Ecclesiis Europæis tantū loquamur,annon in aperto est,multo earum maiorem partem ab Episcopis gubernari,& qui cum Episcopis idem sunt, a superintendentibus? His ut distinctè respondeatur,dico Downamum fœdissimè in duobus lapsum fuisse: Primo, quòd superintendentes,Seniores & disciplinam presbyterialem excludere afferat: Secundo, quòd eandem superintendetis authoritatem esse somniet cum ea quæ hodie Episcoporum in Anglia est. A superintendentibus Ecclesiæ quæ gubernantur, eæ (inquit) Downamus) seniores non admittunt, neque disciplinā presbyteriali regi solent: quanquā istarum Ecclesiarum ocularis inspectio , quam hoc sit falsum ad oculum monstret:nonnulla tamen afferenda sunt ex doctorum hominum scriptis, ut discat lector confidentiæ Dovvnamianæ non temere fidere.
units.tr: Again. To speak only of the European Churches, is it not plain that a much greater part of them is governed by bishops, and those who are the same as bishops by superintendents? To answer these points distinctly, I say Downame fell most shamefully into two errors. First, he asserts that superintendents exclude elders and presbyterial discipline. Second, he dreams that the authority of the superintendents is the same as that of the bishops in England today. Churches governed by superintendents, he says, do not admit elders, nor are they usually governed by presbyterial discipline. Yet an eyewitness inspection of these Churches shows how false this is. Nevertheless, some things must be cited from the writings of learned men, so that the reader may learn not to trust Downame's confidence rashly.

units.la: 2 Primò igitur, eo ipso in loco, qui postremus citatur, Comitatum Palatinatus presbyteriali disciplinā gubernari concedit: quanquam eam sub minoritate principis introducētam ex Bucero affirmat: p.149.At nulla huius labes disciplinæ magis quàm ipsi doctrinæ accrescit: uno enim eodemque tempore obtentæ utræque sunt,quo tempore regio Palatinensis à fermento Lutheranico purgata fuit. Quæro autem,nunmam ignotum tibi Dovvname, in comitatu Palatinatus, Superintendentem præsse talem, qualis in Ecclesiis reliquis Germanicis jam hodie visitur? Certè qui superintendentes Germaniæ reliquos paritati Bigicæ obijcit, Cornelius Scultingius, ac si veri Episcopi essent, is & Palatinensem non solùm speciatim nominat sed etiam in eo ipecatim instat. velut paritatis illius quæ in Bigi est, præcipuè subversore. Neque vero inter istum reliquosque Germaniæ Superintendentes, differentia ulla est, idem munus, eadem authoritas, præsidentia in singulis eadem est, Infra speciatim in Comitatu Hannoviæ, quem a Comitatu Palatinensi, quod ad disciplinam presbyterialem, qua tandem fide, quo fundamento, aut Bucerus aut Dovvnamus separavit; Comitatus Hanoviæ, inquiunt, nquiunt, a superintendente regitur, non a disciplina presbyteriali: Quòd i a Balione quodam dictum fuisse, aliter exciperem: nunc hoc tanüm respondeo, ipsimet oculi mei contrarium edocuerunt. Non st opus Ecclesias reliquas protestantes percurrere: ex hac una quivis iscere omnes poterit. At superintendens Lutheranicus forte Senires excludit. Ne id quidem: id quod ex Iohanne Bridgesio patet, Herbrandum Lutheranum citante, qui postquam superintendentem Tubingensem descripsit, ita infert de presbyterio. Hinc alij solerti & electi viri, tam Ecclesiastici, quam politici, additi, supremum Ecclesiae statum constituunt. Accedo ad Richardum Bancroftum, qui idem ipsum ex Zanchio docet. Postquam etenim Zanchium induxisset, p. 137 superintendentes Germanicos approbantem; pagina sequenti. 138. confitetur, quòd utrumque Episcopos & superintendentes Zanchius approbet, requirat tamen sub eisdem presbyterium, disciplinamque presbyterialem eousque unà approbat, ut idem cum Zanchio se entire Beza dicere non vereatur. Idipsum denique docet Saravia in Ecclesia peregrina Londini agente, temporibus Edwardi Regis sexi. Habuit illa Ecclesia Episcopum inquit, id est Dominum Alasco: recte superintendentem eam habuisse dicit Zepperus: quod adnotare diligenter lectorem suum Scultingius jubet. Sed quorsum? Id enim & nos etiā adnotari diligenter cupimus: ut perspiciatur non domestico quidē experimento caruisse Dolnamum, cum Germanico superintendenti bene stare posse, ex senioribus conflatum presbyterium. Neq; ego plura addam: nemini vel lippo & tonsori, in his oris ignotum est, superintendentes Germanicos disciplinae presbyteriali non obesse, sed praefesse: tantumque abesse quòd eidem adversentur, ut potius ejusdem maxime soliciti custodes sint.
units.tr: First, then, in that very passage which is cited last, he concedes that the Palatinate is governed by presbyterial discipline, although he affirms from Bucer that it was introduced during the minority of the prince (p. 149). But no stain of this kind attaches to discipline more than to doctrine itself: both were obtained at one and the same time, when the region of the Palatinate was purged of Lutheran leaven. I ask, however, whether you, Downame, do not know that in the Palatinate there presides a superintendent such as is seen today in the other German Churches. Certainly Cornelius Scultingius, who objects to the other German superintendents as if they were true bishops, opposing them to the Belgic parity, names the Palatinate not only specifically but also insists on it in particular, as the chief subverter of that parity which exists in the Belgic Churches. Nor indeed is there any difference between him and the other superintendents of Germany: the same office, the same authority, and the same presidency in each. Further, specifically in the county of Hanau, which Bucer or Downame separated from the Palatinate as regards presbyterial discipline, by what faith, and on what foundation? "The county of Hanau," they say, "is governed by a superintendent, not by presbyterial discipline": which I would otherwise take as said by a certain Balio. Now I answer only this: my own eyes have taught me the contrary. It is not necessary to run through the other Protestant Churches; anyone can learn all from this one. But perhaps a Lutheran superintendent excludes elders? Not even that, as is clear from John Bridges, citing the Lutheran Herbrand, who, after describing the superintendent of Tübingen, adds this about the presbytery: "Hence other able and chosen men, both ecclesiastical and civil, being added, constitute the supreme state of the Church." I come to Richard Bancroft, who teaches the same thing from Zanchius. For after introducing Zanchius approving the German superintendents (p. 137), on the following page (138) he confesses that Zanchius approves both bishops and superintendents, yet requires a presbytery under them, and approves presbyterial discipline so far that he does not hesitate to say that Beza agrees with Zanchius. Finally, Saravia teaches the same thing, when the foreign Church was acting at London in the time of King Edward VI. That Church, he says, had a bishop, that is, Lord Alasco; Zepperus rightly says it had a superintendent, which Scultingius bids his reader carefully note. But to what end? For we too wish this to be carefully noted, so that it may be seen that Downame, though lacking domestic experience, did not realise that a presbytery of elders can stand well alongside a German superintendent. I shall add no more: to no one, not even one who is bleary-eyed or a barber, in these parts is it unknown that German superintendents do not hinder presbyterial discipline but preside over it. They are so far from opposing it that they are rather its most anxious guardians.

units.la: 3 Atq; ex hoc vel solo patefit Georgij Dolnami commentum secundum: nam cum Superintendens Germanicus non alius quam inspector & praeses sit, atque ut Zepperus docet presbyterio subjiciatur, sequitur omnino non eundem eum cum Anglicano Episcopo esse, neq; parilé authoritate in ministros exercere. Quā igitur Dolnamus vanus, cum Superintendentem & Episcopum Anglicanum idem esse diceret? quam Bancroftus ineptus, cum Zanchium Episcopum Anglicanum approbasse assereret, cui Episcopus nullus alius placet, quam qualis Superintendens est, ordinis tantum conservandi causa praesidens? quam denique frivolus Hadrianus Saravia: Nonnulli inquit retenta re mutarunt nomina: & pro Episcopis crearunt Superintendentes, & pro Archiepiscopis, generales aut provinciales Superintendentes: quasi de nominibus non autem de ipsa re, iusta sit controversia? Vocabulorum cum arbitraria sit significatio, quando de re constat, inanis est de illis digladiatio. Quo spiritu ista? annon papistico? Eadem etenim Cornelij Scultingij verba sunt. Lutherani (inquit) retenta re nomina mutarunt, & pro Episcopis crearunt Superintendentes, & pro Archiepiscopis Generales sive Provinciales Superintendentes, quasi solum de nominibus bus non de re ipsa fierct controversia. Inanis est λογομαχία quando de re constat. Aut igitur in eadem verba uterque incidit, aut haec ex Saravia transcripsit Scultingius, quod omnino improbabile non est: nam tela Scultingio submin istrasse Hadrianum Saravium, vel ex eo liquet, quod ad librum Hadriani Saraviae, tanquam Hierarchiae papisticae egregiè patrocinantem, nos alibi Cornelius Scultingius remittit. Advertendum vero est, in ista papistis velificatione suâ, non suis solùm, verumetiam sibimetipsi Hadrianum Saravium contradixisse: cum non nomine tantùm, verum & reipsa etiam, ab Episcopo Anglicano discrepare Superintendentem ipse alibi confitetur. Sic enim scribit: De Germanicarum Ecclesiarum superintendentibus nihil dicam: ex eorum libris peti poterit quae sit apud Germanos Ecclesiae regendae ratio: Forma autem regiminis Anglicanae Ecclesiae in aliquibus ab illa discrepat. Quid dicis vero? in aliquibus discrepat; Ergo non nomina tantum, re retenta mutata sunt: sed non nomine tantum a superintendente Episcopus Anglicanus differt, sed etiam re, imo rebus: non enim dicis in aliquo, sed in aliquibus. At haec res aliquae forte leviusculae sunt: imo ipsi essentiae authoritatis Episcopalis institutae atque infixae, id quod vel ex hoc ipso loco colligere promptum est. Contemplare etenim Anglicanum Episcopum prout a Saravia ipso hic describitur, non ordinis gratia, sed ipso gradu, non directionis ergo sed authoritatis imperio in reliquos ministros dominantem: & ausim juraturum te, huiusmodi Episcopus in oris transmarinis sicubi reperiatur, impunè a quoquam eum occidi posse. Atque ad hunc Germaniae superintendentem pertinent quę alibi de inspectore Saravia adfert: cum superintendens iste communiter inspector dicitur, ut a Guilielmo Zeppero accepimus, & ad ipsum Germaniae superintendentem ipse respexisse videtur: quis enim alius quaeso inspector nominari aut solet aut debet? quod si vero huc non respexerit, eo pro nobis quę adfert omnia fortius faciunt: quādoquidem nullū ille aliū ex exemplo Timothei & Titi Episcopū elicere & effingere potuerit, quam qui inspector sit, qualis jam Germanicus superintendens est, quemlab episcopo Anglicano in tribus rebus essentialibus differre dicimus. Primò, inspector iste ordine & gradu a reliquis Verbi ministris non differt, ut differt Episcopus Anglicanus. Secundò, imperium & authoritatem nullam in collegas habet, ut habet Episcopus Anglicanus. Sextò, Inspector pro tempore synodus congregatae duntaxat praesidet, extra synodum nullam praerogativam exercet, ut exercet Episcopus Anglicanus. Ad haec singula respondere Saravia nititur: Sed quàm friuole! Quod ad primum hoc tantum dicit: Gradum nonnihil quiescere sinam. Siccine tu in Scholis Saravia, quiescendo respondere didicisti? sed bene se habet, quamdiu discrimen hoc in gradu positum quiescere sinis, discrimini ipsi acquiescis, ut & acquiescere necesse est. Episcopum etenim à presbytero ordine & gradu ipso differre diserte Bilsonus & Dob-
units.tr: 3 And from this alone it is plain that the second fiction of George Dolnamus is false. For since the German superintendent is nothing other than an overseer and president, and, as Zepper teaches, is subject to the presbytery, it follows entirely that he is not the same as the English bishop and does not exercise the same authority over the ministers. How empty, then, was Dolnamus, when he said that the superintendent and the English bishop were the same! How silly was Bancroft, when he asserted that Zanchius approved of the English bishop, to whom no bishop pleases except one such as the superintendent is, presiding only for the sake of preserving order! Finally, how frivolous is Hadrian Saravia: "Some," he says, "while keeping the thing, have changed the names, and in place of bishops have created superintendents, and in place of archbishops, general or provincial superintendents, as if the controversy were about names and not about the thing itself. Since the meaning of words is arbitrary, when the thing is agreed upon, the fighting over the words is empty." What spirit is this? Is it not a papist one? For these are the very words of Cornelius Scultingius. "The Lutherans," he says, "while keeping the thing, have changed the names, and in place of bishops have created superintendents, and in place of archbishops general or provincial superintendents, as if the controversy were only about names and not about the thing itself. A war of words [λογομαχία] is empty when the thing is agreed upon." Either both have fallen into the same words, or Scultingius copied these from Saravia, which is by no means improbable: that Hadrian Saravia supplied weapons to Scultingius is clear even from this, that Cornelius Scultingius refers us elsewhere to the book of Hadrian Saravia, as one that brilliantly defends the papal hierarchy. But it must be noted that in this sailing of the Papists, Saravia has contradicted not only his own colleagues but also himself. For he himself elsewhere admits that the superintendent differs from the English bishop not only in name but also in fact. For he writes thus: "I shall say nothing of the superintendents of the German churches; their books will show what plan of governing the church is used among the Germans. But the form of government of the English Church differs from that in some respects." What do you say, then? It differs in some respects. Therefore it is not only the names that have been changed while the thing has been kept; the English bishop differs from the superintendent not only in name but also in substance, indeed in matters (plural). For you do not say "in one respect" but "in some respects." But perhaps these matters are rather trivial? No indeed; they touch the very essence of the episcopal authority as instituted and fixed, which can readily be gathered from this very passage. For consider the English bishop as Saravia himself describes him here: ruling the other ministers not by the grace of order but by rank itself, not for the sake of direction but by the command of authority; and I would venture to swear that, if such a bishop were found anywhere in the lands beyond the sea, he could be killed with impunity by anyone. And to this German superintendent belongs what Saravia elsewhere brings forward about the overseer; for this superintendent is commonly called an overseer, as we have learned from William Zepper, and Saravia himself seems to have had in view the German superintendent; for what other overseer, I ask, is or ought to be named? But if he did not have him in view, then everything he cites works even more strongly for us, since he could not draw out and fashion from the example of Timothy and Titus a bishop other than one who is an overseer, such as the German superintendent now is, whom we say differs from the English bishop in three essential respects. First, this overseer does not differ from the other ministers of the Word in order and rank, as the English bishop differs. Second, he has no power or authority over his colleagues, as the English bishop has. Third, the overseer presides only over a synod when it is gathered, and outside the synod exercises no prerogative, as the English bishop does. Saravia strives to answer each of these points; but how frivolously! To the first he says only this: "I will let the rank rest somewhat." Did you learn to answer by resting, Saravia, in the schools? But it is well: as long as you allow this difference to rest in rank, you acquiesce in the difference itself, as you must also acquiesce. For Bilson and Dowsing [Dob-] clearly maintain that the bishop differs from the presbyter in order and rank itself.

units.la: Lib.10. p.65. Dominus tuentur: quum Inspector Germanicus ordine & gradu reliquis ministris superior non sit, id quod & Cornelius ipse Scultingius agnoscere videtur, qui tamen ex inspectore isto Episcopum Hierarchicum efformare ubique conatur. Sic enim habet. Nono, tametsi Lutherani omnes & Calvinistæ quidam, ut Zepperus pastor Herbornensis & alii, Superintendentes constituunt: tamen isti adeo inter se dissident, ut nemo alteri velit cedere. Decimo, inter Episcopum & sacerdotes nihil omnino statuunt discriminis. Quod ad secundum, authoritate scilicet in reliquos ministros Episcopum Anglicanum habere, Inspectorem Germanicum non item: hoc tantum Hadrianus Saravia regerit. At nihil sine consilio & consensu collegarum inspector agit: similiter nec Episcopus nec Archiepiscopus, quicquam sine legum iurisque praescripto possunt. Quasi, inquam, Monarcha quicquam sine legum iuris & præscripto agere possit: qui tamen authoritate propria absque consensu subditorum agit; Atque sane Episcopi Anglicani ut ex legum iurisque præscripto omnia agunt, ista tamen monarcharum more agunt: quod inspector nec agere solet nec debet, qui legum iurisque præscriptum non ulla authoritate sua, sed maiori parte suffragiorum, in presbyterio administrat & moderatur. Hoc ex Guilielmo Zeppero liquet: qui non obstante Superintendentis præsidentia nullum tamen ministrorum altero maiorem authoritatem, vel in verbi & Sacramentorum ministerio, inque disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ usu, obtinere aiit. Addit etiam de ipso Superintendente, quòd in disciplinæ ipsius ratione aliis subiectus sit: quod illius præsidentiæ hoc tantum munus sit, quòd Ecclesiæ suæ classi operam suam plus aliis ministris omnibus impendere teneatur: quod causas difficiliores ad Consistorij legitimam cognitionem & dijudicationem devoluere debeat: quod deniq; ministri & seniores earum Ecclesiarum quibus præest, de eo statuere, de eo iudicare, eum punire, imo etiam quemadmodum eligebant primum, ita etiam deponere & destituere possint. Idipsum de Lutheranis Superintendentibus dicendum est: Seniores enim agnoscit Nicolaus Himingius: ita Episcopo atque Superintendenti suo, nihil aliud relinquit, nisi illam in consistorio, quam nuper descripsimus præsidentiam: id quod etiam ex ipsius verbis liquet, quæ citantur à Bridgesio, ad authoritatem Episcopalem Anglicanam confirmandam. Ita enim inter cætera habet. Qui labore & donis reliquos antecedit, is ab Ecclesia præfertur: non ut dominium super cæteros exerceat sed ut eos regat sapientia & consilio. In testimonio vero Herbrandi ab eodem citato, apparet istud adhuc luculentius: diserta etenim verba Herbrandi allegat, in quibus dicit, Superintendentem, nullam in cæteros potestatem habere. Accedo ad discrimen tertium, ad quod respondens Hadrianus Saravia, ita loquitur: At inspector redibit postea ad suam particularem Ecclesiam: præstaret in vigilia mansisse, quam semel suscepērat, Hic discrimen ipsum agnoscis, ut quod te nulla fronte negare potuisse videras: Inspector Germanicus particularis alicujus duntaxat Ecclesiæ pastor est, Episcopus vero Anglicanus totius dioecesis pastor habetur, particularis vero gregis cuiam nullam gerit: Hoc tu præfers quidem dem, quam prudenter suo loco videbitur: nos interim ab Infpectore ad Episcopum, insulse arguisse te ex tuis ipsius verbis evicimus. Verumtamen invero in hoc tertio discrimine refiduu adhuc quiddā est, in quo diutius inhærendum: istud nempe, quod quanquam præses Synodorum & classium inspector Germanus perpetuus sit: jus tamē ipsius cesser cessante Synodo, sic ut extra classem atq; synodum nihil omnino à reliquis diff.rat, ut qui ad Ecclesiam suam illorum more redeat: Hoc ita cum sit, quām exiguum quæso intervallum inter Ecclesias eas Belgicæ, quæ superintendentes relg. uunt, & superioris Germaniæ Ecclesias illas quæ superintendentes habent? Tantosne clamores Sulcingianos merctur seperatio tam tenui discreta freto? Nulla etenim major superintendentis, quam præsidis Belgici authoritas est, imò neque perpetuitas authoritatis omnimodo major: cessat etenim jus inspectoris cessante synodo, quemadmodum & in præside Belgico lit: in hoc tantum discrimen est, in Ecclesijs Belgicis novus semper eligitur, in superiori verò Germania, idem semper ad solitam sibi præsidentiam redit: Tantine hoc est, ut propterea Scultingius Lutheranos & Calvinianos superintendentales distinguendo à Belgicis, hos planè ἀντίφωνος diceret, illos non item: Habent siquidem Belgici ejusdem authoritatis Caput, licet de novo electum: quod Lutherani & Calviniani superintendentes habent.
units.tr: Lib. 10, p. 65. Dominus tuentur: since the German overseer is not superior to the other ministers in order and rank, which Cornelius Scultingius himself seems to acknowledge, although he everywhere tries to shape from this overseer a hierarchical bishop. For he says thus: "Ninthly, although all Lutherans and some Calvinists, such as Zepper, minister of Herborn, and others, appoint superintendents, nevertheless they so disagree among themselves that no one is willing to yield to another. Tenthly, they establish no difference whatever between the bishop and the priests." As to the second point, namely that the English bishop has authority over the other ministers, which the German overseer does not, Hadrian Saravia alone replies to this. But an overseer does nothing without the counsel and consent of his colleagues; likewise neither the bishop nor the archbishop can do anything without the prescription of laws and right. "As if, I say, a monarch could do anything without the prescription of laws and right, when yet he acts by his own authority without the consent of his subjects! And indeed the English bishops, although they do everything according to the prescription of laws and right, nevertheless act in the manner of monarchs; which the overseer neither does nor ought to do, since he administers and governs according to the prescription of laws and right not by any authority of his own, but by the greater part of the votes, in the presbytery." This is clear from William Zepper, who, notwithstanding the presidency of the superintendent, nevertheless maintains that no minister has greater authority than another, either in the ministry of the Word and sacraments or in the practice of ecclesiastical discipline. He adds also of the superintendent himself that in the matter of discipline he is subject to the others; that the only duty of his presidency is that he is bound to give his labour to the classis of his church more than all the other ministers; that he ought to refer the more difficult cases to the lawful examination and judgement of the consistory; and finally, that the ministers and elders of those churches over which he presides can decide about him, judge him, punish him, and indeed, just as they first chose him, so also depose and remove him. The same must be said of the Lutheran superintendents: for Nicolaus Himingius acknowledges elders, and so leaves to the bishop or superintendent nothing except that presidency in the consistory which we have just described; which also is clear from his own words, which are cited by Bridgeman [Bridgesius] to confirm the English episcopal authority. For among other things he says thus: "He who surpasses the rest in labour and gifts is preferred by the Church, not that he may exercise dominion over the others, but that he may rule them by wisdom and counsel." In the testimony of Herbrand, cited by the same author, this appears even more clearly: for he quotes Herbrand's own words, in which he says that the superintendent has no power over the others. I come now to the third difference, to which Hadrian Saravia replies thus: "But the overseer will afterwards return to his particular church; it would be better to have remained in the watch which he had once undertaken." Here you acknowledge the difference itself, so that you could not have denied it with any face: the German overseer is the pastor of some particular church only, whereas the English bishop is regarded as the pastor of the whole diocese, and has no particular flock of his own. You bring this forward indeed, how prudently will be seen in its place; meanwhile we have shown that you argued foolishly from overseer to bishop, from your own words. Nevertheless, in truth there is still something in this third difference on which we must dwell longer: namely, that although the German overseer is the perpetual president of the synods and classes, yet his right ceases when the synod ceases, so that outside the classis and the synod he differs in no way at all from the others, since he returns to his own church in their manner. This being so, how small, I ask, is the interval between those Belgic churches, which have presidents, and the churches of upper Germany which have superintendents? Does such a separation, divided by so thin a strait, deserve the great outcries of Scultingius? For the authority of the German superintendent is no greater than that of the Belgic president; indeed neither is his authority perpetual in every way greater: for the right of the overseer ceases when the synod ceases, just as it does with the Belgic president. The only difference is that in the Belgic churches a new one is always elected, whereas in upper Germany the same man always returns to his customary presidency. Is this so great a matter that Scultingius, by distinguishing the Lutheran and Calvinist superintendents from the Belgic ones, should call the latter plainly "contrary-voiced" [ἀντίφωνος] and the former not so? For the Belgic churches have a head of the same authority, though newly chosen, which the Lutheran and Calvinist superintendents also have.

units.la: 4. Huc usque ad generalem de Ecclesiis superintendentalib9 objectionem responsum est: sequitur jam specialis enumeratio Ecclesiarū quæ velut adversæ nobis citari solent. Hic ita se Bancroft & Dorma. gerunt, ac si (ut ille Atheniensis) in pyreo starent, navesq; quas vident, si non omnes, saltem plurimas suas esse prædicarent. Catalogum enim bene longum conficiunt, Ecclesiasq; recensent, quasi suas, in Dania, in Suevia, in Sixonia, in ducatu Brunsuicensi, Lauiburgensi Magdaburgensi, Wirtenburgensi : in Marchionatu Brandeburgensi, Badensi : in Comitatu Henneberg ensi, Zwartzenbergensi, Lemin-gensi, Atingensi, Mansfeldensi, Stalbergensi, Glichensi, Rhinstar-nensi, Leonstinensi : in Baronatu Limpurgensi, Schemburgensi, Weildensildensi : in civitatibus denique liberis 34. vel 35. cum sibi adjunctis territoriis. Hinc inquis, exhaustam totam majorem credo: noli tamen expavescas. M. Cicero. cum aliquando dixisset Scamandrum probatum esse patrono, responsum sibi memorat: At patronus ipse cui probatus? Liem hic mihi respondere promptum: multas Ecclesias recenset Doamamus, & eas patronos suos esse dicit. Falsum hoc quidem has Ecclesias Angli o regimini Hierarchico patrocinari, sicut ante ostensum est: sed detur illud probari hisce patronis, patroni hi quæso ipsi quibusnam tandem probantur? Neque enim hæ Ecclesiæ reformatæ sunt, sed pl. rɛque salten. deformatæ, Lutherane (scil. non tam re quam nomine viventes: sicut earum judex pronuntiat in earum typo Sardicensi. Nomen habes quod vivas, sed mortua es: Apoc. 3,1. Hoc ita cum sit, næ ille à mor-tuus cuis consilium capturus est, qui ex illis disciplinam mutandam putat: quarum etiam pleraeque disciplinam nullam omnino habent. Viuere id licet in Ecclesijs Bremensibus, qui à fæce Lutherana non ita adhuc emerserunt, ut vel excommunicationem, vel morum censuram ullam exercuerint. Scribere quidem de excommunicatione Lutherani jam pridem inceperunt: sed hi unà presbyterium vbi deest erigendum etiam censent.
units.tr: 4. So far I have answered the general objection about the superintendent churches; now comes the specific list of churches which our opponents usually cite as being against us. Here Bancroft and Downame behave like that Athenian who, standing in the Piraeus, declared that the ships he saw, if not all of them, at least most of them, were his own. They draw up a fairly long catalogue and enumerate churches as if they were theirs: in Denmark, in Swabia, in Saxony, in the duchies of Brunswick, Lauenburg, Magdeburg and Württemberg; in the margraviates of Brandenburg and Baden; in the counties of Henneberg, Schwarzenberg, Lemingen, Ahlten, Mansfeld, Stolberg, Gleichen, Rheinstein and Leiningen; in the baronies of Limpurg, Schömberg and Weiltingen; and finally in thirty-four or thirty-five free cities, together with the territories attached to them. You will say that I am about to exhaust the whole of this greater catalogue; yet do not be alarmed. When Cicero once said that Scamander had been approved by a patron, he records the reply made to him: "But whom has the patron himself been approved by?" Here I can readily give the same answer to Downame: he lists many churches and says that they are his patrons. It is false, indeed, that these churches favour the Hierarchical government of the English, as has been shown above. But suppose it were proved by these patrons; I ask you, by whom are these patrons themselves approved? For these churches are not reformed; rather, most of them are deformed Lutheran churches, living in name rather than in reality, as their judge pronounces about them in the type of the church at Sardis: "You have a name that you are alive, but you are dead" (Rev. 3:1). Since this is so, he is certainly not taking counsel from a dead man who thinks that discipline should be changed by reference to those churches, most of which have no discipline at all. Indeed, this may be seen in the churches of Bremen, which have not yet risen out of the dregs of Lutheranism so far as to have exercised either excommunication or any censure of morals. The Lutherans have indeed long since begun to write about excommunication, but they also think that a presbytery should be set up where it is lacking.

units.la: Ita in Ecclesiis Lutheranis venditandis peccarunt adversarij: venio jam ad illas Helveticas, quæ Lutheranis in eo cognatæ sunt, quòd excommunicationis usum omnem repudiarunt. In Zuricensi & Helveticis aliis disciplinam nostram presbyterialem minimè stabilitam esse jactat Downamus. Quid, vestra rogo in eis stabilita est? Non id quidem audient dicere, licet multum Bancroftus suo more ausus sit. Invehitur is in nostrum quendam, quòd Ecclesias Zuricenses, Bernenses, Schaffusianas, S. Galli, Rhetbicenses, Millie-nenses, Bieunenses, Hungaricas, denique & Polonicas Ecclesias disciplinam nostram presbyterialem approbasse dixerat, in suâ ad consessionem Helveticam secundam subscriptione. Nihil, inquit in illa confessione de disciplina Genevensi habetur: quod dicitur de disciplina a viris probis & prudentibus administranda, id de ministris tantum intelligitur: quod ex eo liquet, quod in nullis Helveticis Ecclesiis disciplina Genevensis ad hunc usque diem recipiatur. Primò nullam excommunicationem morum vel censuram has Ecclesias exercere confiteris: quanquam igitur in doctrina Ecclesiis Lutheranis præstent, in disciplina tamen non magis quàm illæ imitandæ nobis sunt. Secundò Anglicanum hæc Ecclesiæ regimen jugulant, non enim à viro uno, Episcopo scil. sed à viris probis, & prudentibus, disciplinam administrari volunt. Tertio, quòd hi viris probi & prudentes, ministri tantum sint, id nulla quidem fronte dicitur: nam Schaffusianam per senatum politicorum duntaxat regi & gubernari Iosias Simlerus docet: & in Tigurina, ministros eligi a viris partim Ecclesiasticis, partim politicis, vel tute alibi confiteris. Quarto, quòd Ecclesiam Helveticam nullam disciplinam Genevensem ad hunc usque diem recepisse dicis, id mihi mirandum potius videtur, quàm confutandum. Certè Ecclesias Helveticas nonnullas, non solum Genevensibus, verum & Puritanis in Anglia etiam associat Cornelius Seultingius: Sic enim habet? Verum hodie nostrorum hereticorum saltem Ministrarum Genevensium & Helveticorum quibus tenaciter adhærent puritani in Anglia singularis error est, quod Episcopi vel superintendentes, vel pastoris quem vocant, nullius gradus est vermicens seu fixus a presbyteri officio distinctus, sed mutabilis tantum & temporarius. Ita in ipso controversiæ totius capite, Hierarchica nempe Episcopi unius jurisdictione, nec nullæ saltem Helveticæ Ecclesiæ nobiscum sentiunt.
units.tr: Thus our opponents have failed in their advertising of the Lutheran churches. I come now to those Helvetic churches, which are akin to the Lutherans in this respect, that they have rejected all use of excommunication. Downame boasts that our presbyterial discipline has not been established in the Zurich churches or the other Helvetic ones. What, I ask you, is your own discipline established in? They will not, indeed, dare to say this, although Bancroft, after his manner, has ventured much. He attacks a certain one of our number because he had said that the churches of Zurich, Bern, Schaffhausen, St Gall, Graubünden, Mülhausen, Biel, the Hungarian churches and finally the Polish churches had approved our presbyterial discipline, in his subscription to the Second Helvetic Confession. "Nothing," he says, "is found in that confession about the Genevan discipline. What is said about discipline being administered by upright and prudent men is to be understood of ministers only; and this is clear from the fact that the Genevan discipline has to this day been received in no Helvetic church." First, you admit that these churches exercise no excommunication or censure of morals; therefore, although they excel the Lutheran churches in doctrine, in discipline they are no more to be imitated by us than those are. Second, these churches undermine the English government, for they want discipline to be administered not by one man, namely a bishop, but by upright and prudent men. Third, that these upright and prudent men are ministers only is not asserted with any shame; for Josias Simler teaches that the Schaffhausen church is governed and directed only by the senate of civil magistrates; and you yourself admit elsewhere that in the Tigurine church the ministers are chosen by men partly ecclesiastical and partly civil. Fourth, your statement that the Helvetic Church has never received the Genevan discipline to this day seems to me a matter for wonder rather than for refutation. Certainly Cornelius Schultingius reckons some Helvetic churches as associated not only with the Genevans but also with the Puritans in England. For thus he writes: "Today the singular error of our heretics, at least of the Genevan and Helvetic ministers to whom the Puritans in England cling stubbornly, is that a bishop or superintendent, or what they call a pastor, is of no fixed or permanent rank distinct from the office of presbyter, but is merely changeable and temporary." Thus, on the very heart of the whole controversy, namely the sole jurisdiction of a Hierarchical bishop, not even the Helvetic churches, at least, agree with us.

units.la: §. Quoad reliqua, memini de Farello, & Viretu, Richardum Bancroftum pronunciasse, per aliquod tempus eos Genevæ simpliciter quadam dam Ecclesiastica gubernatione contentos fuisse, quia meliorem, magistratu obnitente, adipisci non potuerunt. Fieri potest in Helveticis Ecclesiis nonnullis idem accidisse, sic ut difficultates similes adhuc superare nequeant: quod si ita sit, non tam voluntati earum defectus, quam necessitati deputandus est. Imo vero (inquit Bancroftus & Downamus) hoc de defectu Anglicani regiminis in Ecclesiis reformatis dicendum est: volient illae ad regimen nostrum propius accedere, sed iniquitate rerum & temporum impediuntur. Probat primo ex confessione Augustana, cui Calvinus ipse interfuit, ubi protestantur Ecclesiae, se necessitate adactas esse, ut Episcopos (tum Papistas) removerent: quod eis in Ecclesia obtinentib°, spes nulla reformationis superesset. Atq; hoc eventu declararunt: quamprimum enim facultas illis concessa est, nominibus alijs superintendentium, Episcopos & Archiepiscopos restituerant. Respondeo, hunc eventum declarare non illos Episcopos Anglicanos voluisse nunquam, sed superintendentes Germanicos tantum, quos toto caelo a nostris distare, jam ante demonstravimus. Succedit Ecclesia Genevensis particularis, ubi status reipublicae democraticus, inquit Downamus, iurisdictionem Episcopalem non permittebat: Calvinus etenim presbyterium ministrorum stabilire in animo habuit, sed Democraticus civitatis status eorum loco seniores laicos requirebat. Beza etiam cuidam mihi toto dixit, sibi plurimum placuisse, si in restaurationE Evangelii, Episcoporum authoritas intacta remansisset: Atqui Beza in vita Calvini, cum de Calvino, tum de seipso contrarium prorsus tradit: sic ut haec fabulae eodem mihi loco sint, cum illa Bancrofti, qua scribit Bezam, in inclinante vita, Archiepiscopum se fieri concupivisse: & Scultingii illa, qua dicit Calvinum Episcopi Primatum ambivisse, quem cum assequi non potuerat, graviter de repulsu apud suum Farellum & Viretum conquestum fuisse: cum illo denique cujusdam Scoti, qui Ioannem Knoxum conciones plurimas eo destinasse dicit, ut in Regem Scotiae eligeretur. Sequitur Ecclesia Gallica, de qua refert Downamus sibi a fide dignis hominibus narratum fuisse, doctissimos in Gallijs, ad Episcopalem jurisdictionem recipiendam pronos & paratos esse, si modo illud Galliae status non praepediret. Atqui de hujusmodi fama sic Tertullianus. Nemo sapiens credit incerto praesertim cum certo constet, confessionem Gallicanam, idcirco disciplinam presbyterialem recepisse, quod eam a Christo mandatam & institutam esse crederet, sicut supra demonstravimus, & eorum nupera scripta (ut in Daniele Tileno videre est) contestantur. Agmen claudunt Ecclesiae Belgicae, quarum necessitate utitur Downamus, tum ad nos incusandos, tum ad seipsum excusandum. Nos incusat ita. In his Ecclesijs ubi orthodoxi Episcopi obtineri non potuerunt, presbyteria prudenter erecta & stabilita sunt: sed inconsiderate a Novatoribus Ecclesiae nostrae obtruduntur, ubi Episcopi Evangelium sincere profitentes collocati sunt. Seipsum vero ita excusat. Quanquam regimen Episcopale Apostolica institutio sit, & forma politiciae optima, non dubitamus tamen C.8.p.139 140. ubi ea obtineri non potest, quin alia admitti possit, neque negamus quin argentum bonum sit, licet aurum melius: quod eo dico, ut earum Ecclesiarum existimatio salva tecta conservetur, in quibus disciplina presbyterialis recepta est. Sed vacillat Dominus in utrisque, cum & nobis necessitas immineat eam in Anglia disciplinam vrgere, quae a Christo instituta est: Ecclesiarum vero Belgicarum necessitas sit nulla, quin Episcopalem iurisdictionem recipere possunt, si eam a Christo institutam crederent. Verum a Christo institutam illi non credunt, sed sicut ante ostensum est, presbyterialem quam exercent disciplinam, illam ipsam esse sciunt quae in verbo mandata est. Scribit ad ministros Belgicos Hadrianus Saravia: ille vero voluntarium illis errorem objicit: nec immerito, si modo regimen Episcopale Apostoli ipsi instituissent: Certum etenim Saravie est exactam disciplinae formam in Evangelio & exaratam & mandatã esse: sic ut haec aurum, contraria argentum esse nequeat (quod satis ineptè à Downamo dictum) sed aut Anglicana aut Belgica, fænum & stipula ut sit necesse est. Iam fænum & stipulam aedificare Belgicos, necessitas quaeso excusabit? Audiatur Tertullianus. Nulla necessitas excusat quae potest non esse necessitas: dicam, nos omnes Deus ita voluit esse dispositos, ut ubique sanctiones ejus obeundi sit disciplina. Atque ut Belgicos necessitatem non excusare dicit Tertullianus; sic necessitatem disciplinae obeundae inter reliquas Dei sanctiones nos excusare dicit alibi: quanquam adversus Dominos Episcopos per leges Angliae stabilitos (quod objicit Downamus) eam urgeamus: Respondere etenim cum illo possumus jure optimo, Cum ad omnia occurrit veritas nostra, postremo legum adstruitur authoritas adversus eam, ut aut nihil dicatur retractandum esse post leges, aut ingratis necessitas obsequij praeferatur veritati. Atque hucusque adversus exceptionem adversariorum primam: Ecclesias nempe reformatas, aut à nobis non stare, aut si à partibus nostris sint, id necessitate fieri.
units.tr: §. As for the rest: I recall that Richard Bancroft has stated that Farel and Viret were for some time at Geneva content with a simple sort of ecclesiastical government, because, the magistrate resisting, they could not obtain a better one. It may be that the same has happened in some Helvetic churches, so that they are still unable to overcome similar difficulties; and if that is so, their defect is to be ascribed not so much to their will as to necessity. "On the contrary," say Bancroft and Downame, "this must be said of the defect of the English government in the reformed churches: they would wish to come nearer to our government, but are hindered by the unfairness of circumstances and times." First, Downame proves this from the Augsburg Confession, at which Calvin himself was present, where the churches protest that they were driven by necessity to remove the bishops (who were then Papists), since, while these remained in the Church, there was no hope of reformation. And they showed this by the outcome: as soon as the opportunity was granted to them, under other names of superintendents, they restored bishops and archbishops. I reply that this outcome shows not that they ever wished for the English bishops, but only for the German superintendents, who, as I have already demonstrated, are as far from ours as heaven is from earth. Next comes the particular church of Geneva, "where the democratic condition of the commonwealth", says Downame, "did not permit episcopal jurisdiction: for Calvin indeed intended to establish a presbytery of ministers, but the democratic state of the city demanded lay elders in their place." Beza also told a certain friend of mine that he would have been very pleased if the authority of the bishops had remained untouched in the restoration of the gospel. Yet Beza, in the life of Calvin, hands down the exact opposite both about Calvin and about himself; so these stories are of the same worth to me as that of Bancroft, who writes that Beza, in his declining years, longed to become an archbishop; and that of Schultingius, who says that Calvin sought the primacy of a bishop, and, when he could not attain it, complained bitterly to his own Farel and Viret of the rebuff; and finally that of a certain Scot, who says that John Knox sent very many sermons there with the aim that he should be elected King of Scotland. Next comes the Gallican Church, about which Downame reports that he had been told by men worthy of belief that the most learned men in France are inclined and ready to receive episcopal jurisdiction, if only the state of France did not stand in the way. But concerning such rumour Tertullian speaks thus: "No wise man believes an uncertain report, especially when it is certain that the French Confession received the presbyterial discipline because it believed it to have been commanded and instituted by Christ, as we have shown above, and their recent writings (as may be seen in Daniel Tilenus) bear witness to this." The line is closed by the Belgic Churches, whose necessity Downame uses both to accuse us and to excuse himself. He accuses us thus: "In those churches where orthodox bishops could not be obtained, presbyteries have been prudently set up and established; but they are carelessly thrust upon our church by innovators, where bishops who sincerely profess the gospel have been placed." But he excuses himself thus: "Although the episcopal government is an apostolic institution and the best form of polity, we do not doubt that where it cannot be obtained, another may be admitted; nor do we deny that silver is good, although gold is better: which I say so that the good esteem of those churches in which presbyterial discipline has been received may be kept safe and sound." But the Lord wavers in both cases, since necessity presses us to urge in England* that discipline which was instituted by Christ, whereas the Belgic churches have no necessity at all not to receive episcopal jurisdiction, if they believed it to have been instituted by Christ. But they do not believe it was instituted by Christ; rather, as was shown above, they know that the presbyterial discipline which they exercise is that very discipline which is commanded in the Word. Adrian Saravia writes to the Belgic ministers; and he charges them with a voluntary error, and not undeservedly, if indeed the apostles themselves had instituted the episcopal government. For it is certain, according to Saravia, that the exact form of discipline is both set down and commanded in the Gospel; so that this cannot be gold and that silver (which Downame said quite foolishly), but either the English or the Belgic must necessarily be hay and stubble. Now, will necessity, I ask, excuse the Belgians for building with hay and stubble? Let Tertullian be heard: "No necessity excuses that which can fail to be a necessity: I say that God so ordained us all that the observance of his ordinances should be everywhere the discipline." And just as Tertullian says that necessity does not excuse the Belgians, so elsewhere he says that necessity of observing discipline excuses us, among the rest of God's ordinances, although we press it against the Lord Bishops established by the laws of England (which Downame objects). For we can answer him with the best right in the words: "When our truth meets everything, and finally the authority of the laws is brought against it, either nothing is to be reconsidered after the laws, or necessity of obedience is preferred to truth, against the will." And so far against the first objection of our adversaries: namely, that the reformed churches either do not stand with us, or, if they are on our side, they are so out of necessity.

units.la: CAP. 29 Exceptio aduersariorum secunda, quòd Anglia non tenetur Ecclesias reformatas imitari.
units.tr: CAP. 29. The second objection of our opponents: that England is not bound to imitate the reformed Churches.

units.la: SEquitur, adversus trãsmarinæ reformationis in disciplina imitationé, exceptio secunda: quâ vinculo Angliã teneri nullo dicitur, ut Ecclesias reformatas imitetur: etsi detur politeiam Anglicanã eis minimè probatam esse. Ita Io. Whitgiftus, Anglia non tenetur ad exemplum vel Galliæ vel Scotiæ: utinam utraque (si ita Deo placeret) quod ad religionem attinet, eo statu & conditione essent, quo Anglia est. Ita I. Bridgesius: Legibus vivitur, non exemplis: nos exemplo primitivæ Ecclesiæ non tenemur, nedum earum reformatarum, quae primitivam sequuntur. Ne in singulis immorer; ita sententiam Hierarchicorum Thomas Brightmanus succinctè ponit: Non videmus, cur Ecclesiæ
units.tr: Next, against the imitation of the foreign reformation in discipline, comes the second objection. They say England is under no obligation to imitate the reformed Churches, even granting that the English polity has not been approved by them. Thus John Whitgift: England is not bound to the example either of France or of Scotland. I wish that both of them, if it pleased God, were in regard to religion in the same state and condition in which England is. Thus J. Bridges: We live by laws, not by examples. We are not bound to the example of the primitive Church, much less to that of the reformed Churches, which follow the primitive one. I will not dwell on individual writers. Thomas Brightman sums up the opinion of the hierarchists briefly: We do not see why the Churches

units.la: In Apol. c. 100. ecclesiae reformatae nostram potius in regimine formam imitari non debeant, quàm nos illas, cum nulla re illis simus inferiores. Quanquam non ad plenum eorum sententiam his verbis Brightmanus complexus est: addendum etenim eos non Angliam solummodo praeferre reliquis reformatis solere, sed & ita praeferre etiam, ut prae ceteras omnes tantum non condemnare praesumunt, quanquam id dissimulent strenuè & contrarium prae se ferant. Dum etenim Georgius Downamus reformationem presbyterialem, labis Arianae ream facit, quam haereticam esse & verbo Dei contrariam dicit: nonne Ecclesias reformatas quasi haereticas eo ipso condemnat, & in verbum Dei rebelles? Habet Gul. Whitakerus, Quod si ab Episcopo presbyteri, tum nullum jurisdictionem habent presbyteri in Eccl. suis reformatis. Quid ad haec Downamus. Certè quod respondere solidè possit nihil habet, unde alicubi Ecclesias reformatas, suas res sibi habere jubet. Sic enim loquitur. Necessitate excusentur reformatae Ecclesiae, quod earum ministri ab Episcopo non vocentur & ordinentur: quod si minus arrideat, ego causae meae praejudicare nolo, se ipsis Ecclesiae reformatae defendant. Absit autem, ut aut gloriationem Angliae istam bonam ego dicerem: aut reformatarum Ecclesiarum vel condemnationem istam, vel desertionem saltem, non magnopere condemnandam.
units.tr: In his Apology, chapter 100, the reformed Churches ought rather to imitate our form of government than we theirs, since we are in nothing inferior to them. Yet Brightman did not fully express their view in these words. It must be added that they not only usually prefer England to the other reformed Churches, but prefer it so far that they presume to condemn all the others, though they dissemble this vigorously and profess the contrary. For when George Downame makes the presbyterian reformation guilty of the Arian stain, calling it heretical and contrary to the Word of God, does he not thereby condemn the reformed Churches as heretical, and as rebels against the Word of God? William Whitaker holds: If presbyters derive their power from the bishop, then presbyters have no jurisdiction in their reformed Churches. What does Downame reply to this? Certainly he has nothing solid to answer with, so he bids the reformed Churches look after their own affairs somewhere else. For he speaks thus: Let the reformed Churches be excused by necessity, because their ministers are not called and ordained by a bishop. But if this does not please you, I do not wish to prejudge my cause; let the reformed Churches defend themselves. Far be it from me to call this boast of England good, or to think that the condemnation of the reformed Churches, or at least their desertion, is not greatly to be condemned.

units.la: Primo etenim in Laodicea Angliae hoc diserte condemnatur, quòd se nullis indigentem putet: sicut hic fit, cum nullius Ecclesiae imitatione se opus habere praedicat.
units.tr: First, in Laodicea, that very thing is plainly condemned in England: that it thinks itself in need of nothing. So here too, it declares that it has no need to imitate any Church.

units.la: Secundo, in Philadelphia Ecclesiarum reformatarum, reprehenditur nihil, sed commendantur omnia, inter caetera, disciplina, quae per clavem Davidis insinuatur. Ap. 3, 7. cum in Anglia ex adverso qua Laodiceae proptér corruptam disciplinam, reprehendantur omnia nulla laudis mentione facta, nisi quod in doctrina, Christus se ibi fidelem testim & veracem exhibuerit. Tertio, cum ad septimi Angeli clangorem reformatur Anglia Apoc. 11. 15. in ea animalium mentio nulla reperitur; praeter morem hoc sit: in Ecclesiis etenim bene institutis aliis cap. 4. 9. & 5. 8. & 7. 11, imò in Ecclesiis reformatis ipsis de quibus agimus, cum de earum reformatione agitur, animalia suis nominibus inducuntur velut in caelo c. 14. 3. & 19. 4. Quaero igitur in reformatione Anglicana cur non nominantur, sed viginti quatuor seniores tantum, qui sanctum fidelium coetum repraesentant? An quia gerunt animalia typum ministrorum eorum, qui Deo probantur? nostri autem Anglicani a divino instituto adeò aberrat, ut cõsultò fugerit spiritus sanctus, animalium nomen eis tribuere? quicquid sit, defectus certè hic aliquis in Ecclesia Anglicanâ insinuari videtur, quae in Ecclesiis reformatis caeteris non reperitur.
units.tr: Second, in the case of Philadelphia, the reformed Churches are not rebuked at all; rather, everything is commended, including their discipline, which is hinted at through the key of David (Rev. 3:7). Whereas England, on the contrary, like Laodicea on account of its corrupt discipline, is rebuked in everything, with no mention of praise, except that Christ showed himself there as a faithful and true witness in doctrine. Third, when England is reformed at the sound of the seventh angel (Rev. 11:15), no mention is found there of the living creatures. This is contrary to custom, since in well-ordered Churches the living creatures are introduced by name (Rev. 4:6-9; 5:8; 7:11), indeed in the very reformed Churches of which we speak, when their reformation is under discussion, they are introduced by name as in heaven (Rev. 14:3; 19:4). I ask, therefore, why in the English reformation they are not named, but only the twenty-four elders, who represent the holy assembly of the faithful? Is it because the living creatures are a type of those ministers who are approved before God? Or do our English so far depart from the divine institution that the Holy Spirit deliberately avoided giving them the name of living creatures? Whatever the reason, some defect certainly seems to be hinted at here in the English Church, which is not found in the other reformed Churches.

units.la: 4 Quatt̀o, observetur progressus reformationis quem Spiritus ipse suggerit. Citharaedorum vox quae habetur Ap. 14: 2. mulieris est jamjamque quidem egressurae ex solitudine, sed adhuc tamen nondum dum egressæ: ponens ante oculos restitutionem illam quæ à tempore Wiclephi, ad tempora Lutheri & paulo ultra decurrebat: quando confessio Augustana, Argentoratensis, Basiliensis, Helvetica, Saxonica, Carolo quinto adhuc vivo suavé concentum & harmoniam instar vocis citharædorum personabat. Citharædorum vero vox illa quæ habetur, Apoc. 15. 12. & cytharas habet Dei id est præstantissimas, & in bestiam victoriam apertam celebrat, idque ad instar Israelitarum ad mare rubrum, postquam Carolus quintus mortuus, Papaque jam ex bona parte velut alter Pharaoh debilitatus erat. Significat autem citharædorum vox hæc confessiones illas, quæ post annum 1558. editæ sunt: confirmationesque illas quæ in Anglia, Scotia, Gallia, aliisque regionibus circa id tempus contigerunt. Quandoquidem autem mare doctrinam significat c. 4, 6. ignis vero contentiones Luc. 12. 49. mare vero vitreum ad quod hæ Ecclesiæ reformatæ stant, mistum sit igni Ap. 15. 2. significatur apertè earum Doctrinam respectu gratiæ à Christo partæ pellucidam, partim hæresi Lutheranorum partim disciplina Hierarchicorum, velut igne incendiario, & decoloratam & dedecoratam fore. Neq; mireris Hierarchicum in Anglia regimen hic ignem esse: cum Hierarchiæ erectio in Ecclesia prima mons ardens igne appelletur c. 8, 8. videat ergo Anglia de suo regimine Episcopali, cessetque erynnis illa, quæ tanquam elephantes efferatos Episcopos, ad suos conterendos extimulat, idque ad ipsum quasi mare rubrum: Pharaone Papa nondum penitus, aut submersò aut extincto. Extinguatur hic ignis, mare nostrum purum reddatur: cogitetur denique schismati ab Episcopis excitato, ascribi hic a Spiritu sancto, ignem contentionem illam, quæ per media Angliæ viscera jam debachatur.
units.tr: Fourth, let the progress of the reformation which the Spirit himself suggests be observed. The voice of the harpers, which is found in Rev. 14:2, belongs to a woman who is indeed about to come out of the wilderness but has not yet come out; it sets before our eyes that restoration which ran from the time of Wycliffe to the times of Luther and a little beyond, when the Augsburg, Strasbourg, Basel, Helvetic and Saxon confessions sounded a sweet concord and harmony like the voice of harpers, while Charles V was still alive. But the voice of those harpers which is found in Rev. 15:2, who have the harps of God, that is, the most excellent ones, and who celebrate open victory over the beast, comes in the manner of the Israelites by the Red Sea, after Charles V had died and the Pope was already in large part weakened, like another Pharaoh. The voice of these harpers signifies those confessions which were published after the year 1558, and the confirmations which took place in England, Scotland, France and other regions about that time. Since the sea signifies doctrine (Rev. 4:6), fire signifies contentions (Luke 12:49), and the glassy sea on which these reformed Churches stand is mixed with fire (Rev. 15:2), it is clearly signified that their doctrine, pellucid with respect to the grace obtained by Christ, will be darkened and disfigured, partly by the heresy of the Lutherans, partly by the discipline of the hierarchists, as by an incendiary fire. Nor should you wonder that the hierarchical government in England is here called fire, since the erection of the hierarchy in the primitive Church is called a burning mountain with fire (Rev. 8:8). Let England therefore look to its Episcopal government, and let that Fury cease, which goads on the bishops, like maddened elephants, to crush their own people, and that at the Red Sea itself, while the Pharaoh, the Pope, is not yet wholly drowned or extinguished. Let this fire be put out and our sea be made pure. Finally, let it be considered that this contention which now rages through the very bowels of England is here ascribed by the Holy Spirit to the schism stirred up by the bishops.
