units.la: 2 Quinto, Angelus Ecclesiarum reformatarum stat in sole Ap. 19, 17. utpote filius genuinus primitivæ Ecclesiæ, mulieris scilicet amictę sole Apoc. 12, 1. cum incolæ Ecclesiarum minime ad plenum reformatarū, Lutheranarū puta, & Anglicarū non nisi in medio cælo volent, ut qui duntaxat ex parte media reformentur, Ap. 19. 17.
units.tr: Fifth, the angel of the reformed Churches stands in the sun (Rev. 19:17), as the true son of the primitive Church, namely of the woman clothed with the sun (Rev. 12:1). But the inhabitants of Churches that are not fully reformed, Lutheran ones for example, and the English, will fly only in the midst of heaven, since they are reformed only in part (Rev. 19:17).

units.la: Sexto, Ecclesiæ reformatæ sicut mons decoris, mons ecclesiarum Christi. Apoc. 16: 16. collisque pretiosorum fructuum, de quo Brightmanus consulendus.
units.tr: Sixth, the reformed Churches are like the mount of beauty, the mountain of the Churches of Christ (Rev. 16:16), and the hill of precious fruits, on which Brightman should be consulted.

units.la: Septimo, Ecclesiarum typus Ecclesia Philadelphiensis est: ea vero coronam suam tenere jubetur: Apoc, 3. 11. quod igitur Ieremie olim dictum, hic locum habet. c. 15, 19. Revertantur aliæ Ecclesiæ adte, tu autem ad eas me, vertaris.
units.tr: Seventh, the type of the Churches is the Church of Philadelphia, and she is ordered to hold fast her crown (Rev. 3:11). Therefore what was once said of Jeremiah has its place here: Let them return to you, but do not you return to them (Jer. 15:19).

units.la: Octavo, Ecclesiæ reformatæ, Genevensis inprimis, in Christo ante Angliam fuerunt, cuius horum quæ Tamen exiguus non est. A vobis verbum Domini venit, 1. Thes. 1, 8, Anne a vobis audiens. Quid processit? 1. Cor. 14. 36. Matrices Ecclesiæ quasi Metropolitanas, reliquas regere Dominum volunt: certè matrices ecclesiæ hoc ergo prosequentes esse omnes consentiunt: quieni igitur quasi matres imitandas
units.tr: Eighth, the reformed Churches, especially Geneva, were in Christ before England, and this is not a small matter. From you the word of the Lord came (1 Thess. 1:8). Or did it come unto you only? (1 Cor. 14:36). What follows? The mother Churches, as it were metropolitan, all agree that they are to be followed by the others, since the Lord wishes them to rule the rest; surely the mother Churches, pursuing this, agree that all others are to be imitated as mothers. Those to whom England refers the Gospel of Christ and the word of God as their source, should be imitated by England as mothers.

units.la: P. 63 Brightmanus consulendus. tandas censeret Anglia, quibus Evangelium Christi, verbumque Dei acceptum refert: Num pudebit matris suae dives Laodicea, quod paupercula sit? At cogitet secum haud minus à turrita Pergamo (Roma scilicet) quòd ad externa, superari sese: quàm ab illa Philadelphia superatur. Quòd si autem regerant, Galliam & Belgiam, post Ecclesiam Anglicanā ad fidē accessisse: cogitét Corinthijs à Paulo imitandas non solum Ecclesias eas proponi, a quibus verbum Dei primo profluxit, verùm & eas etiam ad quas pervenit: 1. Cor. 14. 29. sicuti doctissimus Reynoldus noster observavit. Quid quòd de hic verè dici illud Christi possit, multi primi erunt qui erant ultimi, Matth. 20. 16. non eâ obstâte quam Bridgesius obijcit, externa afflictione, quam in quaestionibus veritatis in quaestionem vocandam non esse, monet Salomon: Cantic. 1. 5. Nolite me aspicere, quòd nigra sim.
units.tr: P. 63, Brightman to be consulted. Should England think that these mothers are to be imitated, from whom it received the Gospel of Christ and the word of God? Will rich Laodicea be ashamed that she is poor, her mother being so? Let her consider that the turreted Pergamum (that is, Rome) is surpassed by her in external matters no less than Philadelphia surpasses her. But if they reply that France and the Low Countries came to the faith after the English Church, let them consider that Paul ordered the Corinthians to imitate not only the Churches from which the word of God first flowed, but also those to which it came afterwards (1 Cor. 14:29), as our most learned Reynolds has observed. What of the fact that the saying of Christ can truly be applied here: Many who are first will be last, and the last first (Matt. 20:16)? This is not hindered by the external affliction which Bridges objects, which Solomon warns is not to be called into question in matters of truth: Do not look at me because I am dark (Song 1:5).

units.la: Nono, Ecclesias in eo quod bonum est imitandas esse concedit Whitgiftus: jam verò in causa disciplinae, contestari illae possunt adversus corruptum in Anglia regimen, quòd Abyjah olim adversus illud Icroboanicum 2 Chron. 13. 9. Annon sacerdotes Domini populistis, & sacerdotes constituistis similes sacerdotibus nationum aliarum? Sed nos ad Dominum pertinemus, Dominique Dei nostri vigiliam observamus: Apud nos sacerdotes filij Aaronis Domino Deo nostro ministrant, & Levitae iuxta vices suas. Objicit Bellarminus nullam apud nos finiendarum controversiarum regulam esse, sed privatum spiritum suum sequi omnes, eamq; inter nos superbiam regnare, ut nulla Ecclesia alteri cedere obstringatur. Quas vires calumniae huic jam Anglia ministret majori parti Ecclesiarum cedere renuens, judicet aequus: hoc certum est, ab Anglia funditus labefectari quae Fyldus ad respondendum adfert, Quid enim? Communione inquit privatur ille apud nos, qui confessioni us fidei cedere nolit, ab Ecclesiis illis publicatis, quae nostrae communionis sunt. Est in hac responsione quod Episcopos obligat, ut Ecclesiis eis cedant, earumq; maiori numero quae nostrae communionis sunt: si modo regulam sequi illam velint, quae sola, controversiam disciplinariam dirimere potest, ipsorum iudicio.
units.tr: Ninthly, Whitgift concedes that the Churches should be imitated in what is good. Now, in the matter of discipline, those Churches can bear witness against the corrupt government in England, just as Abijah once did against that Jeroboamite regime, 2 Chron. 13. 9: Have you not cast out the priests of the LORD, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites, and made priests for yourselves like the priests of the other nations? But as for us, we belong to the LORD, and we have not forsaken him; the priests who minister to the LORD are the sons of Aaron, and the Levites attend to their duties. Bellarminus objects that among us there is no rule for ending controversies, but that everyone follows his own private spirit, and that pride reigns among us so that no Church is bound to yield to another. Let a fair judge decide how much force this calumny now gains from England, which refuses to yield to the greater part of the Churches. This much is certain: what Fyldus brings forward in reply undermines England from its foundations. For he says: Communion is denied among us to anyone who will not yield to the confession of faith of those published Churches which belong to our communion. There is in this reply something that binds the bishops to yield to those Churches, and to the greater number of those that belong to our communion, provided only that they are willing to follow that rule which alone can settle a disciplinary controversy, by their own judgment.

units.la: Decimò, multa in Ecclesiâ Anglicana tam a Verbo manifestè aberrant, ut eam ab Ecclesiis reformatis condemnari necesse sit, nisi citiùs emendentur. Nihil aliud expectandum inquit Bridgesius, quàm tumultus a papistis, inter nos incendia intestina, si haec disciplina recipere-tur: Doctorum ministrorum in singulis parochiis procuratio impossibilis est. Ad ministros doctos in singulis parochijs alendos sustentatio deest, nec illa ulla possibilitas obtineri in Anglia potest: Atqui inquam si in Ecclesias reformatas circumferantur oculi, disciplinam absque sonitu stabilitam cernent, doctos ministros & procuratos & sustentatos videbunt ubique, ut hac ex parte haud minùs Angliam in die judicij illae condemnaturae sint, atque olim Noah sua obedientia veterem mundum condemnavit, Hebr. 11. 7. Atque haec adversus exceptionem nem secundam, reformatarum nempe Ecclesiarum exemplum nihil pensi habendum, si secus atque Anglia sentiant.
units.tr: Tenthly, many things in the English Church so clearly stray from the Word that it must be condemned by the reformed Churches unless they are quickly amended. Nothing else is to be expected, says Bridges, than tumults from the Papists and internal fires among us, if this discipline were received. The provision of learned ministers in individual parishes is impossible. The maintenance needed to support learned ministers in individual parishes is lacking, nor can any such possibility be obtained in England. But I say: if one turns one's eyes to the reformed Churches, one will see discipline established without any uproar, and learned ministers provided for and maintained everywhere. In this respect, then, those Churches will condemn England on the day of judgment no less than Noah, by his obedience, condemned the old world of old, Heb. 11. 7. And these things are to be set against the second exception, namely that the example of the reformed Churches is to be counted for nothing if they think otherwise than England does.

units.la: CAP. 30. Exceptio tertia, quòd perverso modo disciplina introducta sit in Ecclesias reformatas.
units.tr: CAP. 30. The third objection: that discipline was introduced into the reformed churches in a perverse way.

units.la: Tertia, a modo disputat quo disciplina in Genevensem Ecclesiam primò, deinde ab illa in alias Ecclesias introducta est: quem vaferrimæ seductionis, perversissimæque æmulationis plenum esse, ipsi omnium hominum perversissimi vociferantur. Exagitat Bezam Richardus Bancroftus, quòd Evangelium Genevæ mirabiliter restitutum dixerat, atque hujus miraculi memoriam diutius novem dierum spatio duraturam comminatur. Intelligit perpetuam ignominiæ notam Genevæ inustam hac ratione fuisse, quam sibi displicere affirmat, perinde ac cæterorum Helvetiorum tyrannorum ejectionem, utpote in qua non solum ( quod Melancthon ) excessit medicina modum, sed etiam excessit medicina malŭ. Negat tamen de civilibus iudicium suum se velle interponere: hoc tantum se non posse non damnare dicit, quòd mutatio reipublicæ Genevensis (Bodino teste, & Calvino in epistola ad Sadoletum) ex domini Farelli aliorumque ministrorum prædicatione initium sumpserit, quâ docebant, civilem in Episcopis iurisdictione Verbo divino interiectâ esse. Respondeo primò, culpâ mutatæ in Genevâ reipublicæ siqua sit, in doctrinam, non disciplinam cudendam omnem esse: præsertim cùm disciplina Genevensis non ante sancita fuerit, quàm post Episcopi ejectionem & status civilis mutationem, sicut & res ipsa clamat, & Bancroftus confitetur. Neque verum est ex Farelli prædicatione disciplinaria contra civilem in Episcopis iurisdictionem, sed prædicatione Evangelicâ protinus adversus papismum, ansam mutandæ reipublicæ oblatam fuisse: hæc enim diserta Iohannis Bodini verba sunt: ex studio mutandæ religionis, communitandæ reipublicæ oblatam occasionem arripuerunt. Idem docet Iohannes Calvinus (vel citante Bancrofto) in Epistola ad Sadoletum, ubi dicit, Genevenses paratos fuisse Episcopi authoritati civili perpetuò obedire, si modo illis libertatem Evangelij permittere voluisset. Quid opus est multis? Peleus ipse qui inflixit hoc vulnus, sanat, sic enim Bancrof Contentio inquit inter Episcopū & populū hinc orta est, quod ex prædicatione Farelli, pertinuit tædere cœperunt, & ad religionis reformationem inclinarunt, ad vicinarum exemplar civitatum, quibus unum fœdere conjuncti erant.
units.tr: Third, he disputes about the manner in which discipline was first introduced into the Church of Geneva and then from that Church into other churches. They loudly declare that this manner is full of the most cunning deception and the most perverse rivalry, and they are the most perverse of all men. Richard Bancroft censures Beza because he had said that the Gospel was wonderfully restored at Geneva, and he threatens that the memory of this miracle will last for nine days. He understands that a lasting mark of infamy was branded on Geneva in this way, which he says displeases him, just as the expulsion of the other Helvetian tyrants does, inasmuch as in it not only (as Melanchthon says) the remedy exceeded its measure, but also the remedy exceeded the evil. Yet he says he does not wish to interpose his judgment on civil matters; he only says that he cannot help condemning the fact that the change of the Genevan commonwealth (on the testimony of Bodin, and of Calvin in his letter to Sadoleto) began from the preaching of Master Farel and other ministers, in which they taught that the civil jurisdiction of bishops was contrary to the divine Word. I answer first: if there is any fault in the change of the commonwealth at Geneva, it must be laid to doctrine, not to discipline. This is especially so since the Genevan discipline was not enacted until after the bishop's ejection and the change of the civil state, as the thing itself cries out and Bancroft confesses. Nor is it true that from Farel's preaching an occasion for changing the commonwealth was offered by preaching about discipline against the civil jurisdiction of bishops; it was offered by evangelical preaching straight against Popery. For these are the plain words of John Bodin: they seized the occasion offered by their zeal for changing religion, to alter the commonwealth. John Calvin teaches the same (or, citing Bancroft) in his letter to Sadoleto, where he says that the Genevans were ready to obey the bishop's civil authority perpetually, if only he had been willing to allow them the liberty of the Gospel. Why need there be many words? Peleus himself, who inflicted this wound, heals it. For thus Bancroft's Contention says: the strife between the bishop and the people arose from this, that from Farel's preaching they began to grow weary and inclined to the reformation of religion, following the example of the neighbouring cities to which they were bound by one covenant.

units.la: Secundò, non ausus est ipse Bancroftus dicere, stabilitam ullam authoritatem civilem Episcopum Genevensem in illam urbem unquam habuisse; inde est, quòd iudicium Zanchianum de obedientiâ Episcopo in civilibus præstandâ postquam in actum perduxisset, ante pugnam dimiserit tamen: meminit siquidem quae in hanc partem a se ante allegata fuerant, Genevam scilicet inter civitates illas fuisse, de quarum permissio e se contra Imperatorem disputare noluerat. Franciscus Bonivardus, ut ex Munstero constat, dicit ad annum 1224. ab Imperatore Friderico primo, Episcopum Genevensem impetrasse ut Genevae principatum solus ipse obtineret, quo Hymo tum dejectus erat, qui cum eo de imperio civitatis contendebat: non acquievisse tamen Subaudiae Duces, vel usque ad nostra tempora. Imo nec ipse populus Genevensis huic Episcopi sui regimini acquievit: dicit enim Josias Simlerus, quanquam largis privilegiis Episcopatus Genevensis potiretur, populum tamen studiose semper conservasse, cum illas perpetuas cum Episcopo conditiones, tum libertates suas, quas a patribus accepissent. Atque ad harum conservationem inquit Bidinus, cui & Bancroftus ipse assentitur, foedus cum Bernatibus & Friburgensibus inierunt, tandemque eo devenerunt, ut vel Ducis Subaudiei, vel Episcopi sui legibus se nolle astringi attestarentur. Atque haec omnia sub Papismo facta sunt, sicut nulla fronte eum esse oportear, qui Evangelicam Genevensem reformationem, aut quod ad doctrinam, aut quod ad disciplinam, perduellionis condemnare voluerit.
units.tr: Second, Bancroft himself did not dare to say that the Bishop of Geneva ever had any settled civil authority in that city. Hence it is that Zanchi, after he had brought his judgment on obedience to bishops in civil matters into practice, nevertheless dismissed it before the battle; for he recalls what had been alleged by himself earlier on this side, namely that Geneva was among those cities whose permission he had not wished to dispute against the Emperor. Franciscus Bonivard, as is clear from Münster, says that about the year 1224 the Emperor Frederick I granted to the Bishop of Geneva that he alone should hold the principality at Geneva, from which Aymon, who then contested rule of the city with him, had been ousted; but the Dukes of Savoy did not acquiesce, even down to our own times. Indeed, the people of Geneva themselves did not acquiesce in this rule of their bishop either. For Josias Simler says that although the bishopric of Geneva held broad privileges, the people had always zealously preserved both those perpetual conditions with the bishop and the liberties which they had received from their fathers. For the preservation of these, says Bodin, with whom Bancroft himself also agrees, they made a covenant with the Bernese and the Fribourgers, and at last came to the point of declaring that they were unwilling to be bound by the laws either of the Duke of Savoy or of their bishop. And all these things were done under Popery. Therefore he ought to have no face who would wish to condemn the evangelical reformation of Geneva as treason, whether in doctrine or in discipline.

units.la: Tertio adnotandum, Bancrofti calumnias supra commemoratas, vel suis displicere: Johannes siquidem Bridgesius Deum laudandum esse dicit, quod Episcopus papismo addictus & reformationem impediens ex Geneva expulsus sit, quod ipsius tyrannidem meruisse, contestatur. Qui & addit insuper, quanquam Episcopi Ecclesiarum regimen retinere Geneuenses debuissent: si tamen nunc (quod ad disciplinam) agnoverit se in ordine & consuetudine aliqua Apostolica quiescere posse, bene id fit, inquit, Deusque hoc nomine benedicatur: non invidemus illis, neque eorum in hac Apostolica consuetudine quietem interturbamus, neque vice versa praescribere illi nobis possint, aut vero etiam praescribunt. Similiter Hadrianus Saravia: Episcopus Geneuensis cum suo clero vano timore perterriti stationem suam deseruerunt. Mala conscientia saepe facit ut sugiat impius nemine persequente. Unde accidit ut in eorum vacua loca fideles Christi servi succederent. Quod si Episcopus Geneuensis suscipere Filii Dei Evangelium voluisset, nunquam sua sede ejectus fuisset, &c. Ita nulla culpa disciplinae fuit in civilis Genevensis status immutatione.
units.tr: Third, it must be noted that the calumnies of Bancroft mentioned above displease even his own side. For John Bridges says that God is to be praised that the bishop, addicted to Popery and hindering the reformation, was expelled from Geneva; he testifies that the bishop had deserved this tyranny. And he adds moreover: although the Genevans ought to have kept the government of the churches by bishops, yet if now (as far as discipline is concerned) they have recognised that they can rest in some apostolic order and custom, it is well done, he says, and God is blessed for this; we do not grudge them, nor do we disturb their rest in this apostolic custom, nor can they prescribe to us in turn, or indeed they do prescribe. Similarly Adrian Saravia: the Bishop of Geneva, together with his clergy, terrified by vain fear, deserted their station. A guilty conscience often makes the impious flee when no one is pursuing. Whence it came about that faithful servants of Christ succeeded into their empty places. But if the Bishop of Geneva had been willing to receive the Gospel of the Son of God, he would never have been cast out of his see, etc. Thus there was no fault of discipline in the change of the Genevan civil state.

units.la: CAP. 31.
units.tr: CAP. 31.

units.la: Reformatio Geuevensis a Calumniis vindicatur.
units.tr: The Genevan Reformation is vindicated from calumnies.

units.la: Accedendum jam est ad status Ecclesiastici alterationem, qua Episcopali regimine spreto, Aristocratica politeia, juxta verbi divini regulam, consensu totius civitatis tandem stabilita fuit: contra quam tria praecipue a Bancrofto objecta video. Primo
units.tr: We must now turn to the change in the ecclesiastical order, by which, with episcopal government rejected, an aristocratic polity was at length established by the consent of the whole city, according to the rule of the divine Word. I see that Bancroft has raised three main objections against it. First

units.la: Primò, Senatus resistentiam inculcat, quæ quorsum inculcanda sit, ego tamen non video, cùm doctrina Euangelij ipsa, non sine ingenti malorum hominum resistentia, ubique terrarum introita sit, vt malos eos fuisse, qui disciplinæ restiterunt, vel præcipuorum Syndicorum horrendus exitus manifestè declarat, qui à Beza in vita Calvini memoratur.
units.tr: First, he presses the resistance of the Senate. I do not see why this should be pressed, since the teaching of the Gospel itself has made its way everywhere in the world, and not without great resistance from wicked men. The dreadful end of some of the chief syndics, which Beza records in the life of Calvin, clearly shows that those who resisted the discipline were wicked men.

units.la: Secundò, vafritiem Calvino objicit, cui etiam insignem calliditatem Richardus Hookerus impingit, ac si in disciplina procuranda, nihil propemodum ab impostore Calvino distaret: Epistolis verò quas Beza edidit uterque nititur, ac quasi verisimile esset, Calvinum adeo dementem fuisse, ut se stultum proclamaret: Eccles. 10. 3. perlegantur Epistolæ, quid in eis tandem æquus lector reperiet, quod non serpentinam prudentiam quidem sed cum simplicitate columbina conjunctam spirat? Vtinam, ò Vtinam innotuissent mundo artes illæ quibus Episcopi Anglicani Hierarchiæ suæ tyrannidem ad hæc usque tempora perduxerunt. Quod etenim Firmilianus in causa male pro Cypriano, tanquam impostore à Stephano Romano accusato respondeat olim, id iam nos in causa vera, pro Calvino verius respondere possumus: præbenit ut alteri ea per mendacia objicerent, quæ ipse ex merito, audire deberet.
units.tr: Second, he charges Calvin with craftiness, and Richard Hooker imputes to him remarkable cunning as well, as if in pursuing discipline he differed hardly at all from an impostor such as Calvin. Both rely on the letters that Beza published, and they argue as if it were likely that Calvin was so mad that he proclaimed himself a fool. Let the letters be read through (Eccles. 10. 3.). What will a fair reader finally find in them that does not breathe a prudence that is not serpentine, but joined with dovelike simplicity? Would that, oh, would that the arts had become known to the world by which the Anglican bishops have carried the tyranny of their hierarchy down to the present times! For just as Firmilian, once answering on behalf of Cyprian in a bad cause, when Stephen of Rome accused him as an impostor, so we can now answer far more truly on behalf of Calvin in a true cause: he allowed others to bring against him, by lies, those things which he himself ought to have heard for his own desert.

units.la: Tertiò, Calvinum dicit Bancrof. incautos Genevenses circumvenisse, cum illis nihil minùs suspicantibus authoritatem Episcopali æquivalentem superinduxeri, quam etiam sibi ipsi attraxit, etsi strenuè interim prorsus contrarium præ se ferret. Hujus calumniæ Hadrianus etiam Saravia reus est. Verum est illud, inquit, Naturam expellas furcâ licet, usque recurret. Constat enim Bezam collegis suis esse longe superiorem, & Iohannes Calvinus dum vixit plus authoritatis in suos collegas habuit, quam hodie Angliæ primas in suos coepiscopos exercet: nota loquor, ut impudentis fuerit negare, quod & res ipsa clamat, & eorum scripta testantur. Falsum quidem quod notum dicit, ac ut impudentiæ fuerit dicere; contra quod & res ipsa clamat, & eorum scripta testantur: sed fac ita fuisse, maiorem tamen authoritatem in reliquos ministros Episcopum in Anglia jam exercere confiteberis spero, atque Calvinus & Beza in suos collegas exercuerunt. Imo inquit alibi, Scire vultis qui concordiam Genevæ hactenus tantum inter pastores aluerit & alii? Habent quem negant, & quem nolunt, unum tantum Episcopum. Nam quicquid scribat dominus Beza aut sentit, nunquam mundo persuadebit, cum in collegio & in deliberationibus, & in tota Eccl. sua gubernatione, authoritate & pondere sententiæ suæ aliis collegis sit is cedere, sicuti loco præsidentiæ. Eaque habetur de pie recordationis Io. Calvino opinio. Quod nec Zanchius dissimulavit, quando suam sententiam de Ar. bispiscopis & Episcopis exposuit. Sed vt etiam (inquit) neq; vetera illa bona Græca, neque hæc nova male Latina verba obtinent, id tamen solent esse aliquot pri marij, p.nes quos ferè tota est authoritas, &c. Videtis quomodo ipsos nos naturæ vis reducit, unde fugimus? Scribat dominus Beza quicquid vult, Geneva, nec alius quivis locus, duos Bezas, aut duos Calvinos in una Ecclesia dissentientes unquam ferre poterit. Respondendum primo de Zanchio est: qui Episcopum Anglicanum nunquam approbavit, quem ille à patribus antiquitus constitutum Episcopum credidit, non alium quàm Superintendens Germanicus erat, sicut ipsa oratonis series demonstrat. Dixit sibi rationem habendam esse earum Ecclesiarum quae Episcopos haberent, inter quas Angliam cum non intellexisse ex eo liquet, quòd verbis proximis eas Ecclesias describens quas intellectas esse vellet, praeterita Angliae mentione in Ecclesiis tantummodò Germanicis instat, quae Superintendentes habent. Quid quòd licet eos agnosceret antiquos illos Episcopos esse: quiddam tamen in eis videbat quod adeo vel desideravit, vel improbavit: ut Praesidentiam Superintendentalem saepe à fratribus sibi oblatam constanter repudiarit, quo factum est, ut ordinarius tantùm Doctor, & vixerit, & consenuerit, & expirarit. Probaret ille Episcopum Anglicanum, qui ne Germanicum Superintendentem per omnia probavit? quòd verò Geneve authoritatem fere penes unum dixerat: de authoritate praesidentiae intelligitur: praesidebat etenim per totam vitam Iohannes Calvinus, praesidebat etiam Beza diu, nempe donec Daneus Genevam appulerat, ut ipse Geo. Dovnamus narrat. Sic igitur est. In eo tantùm Germanicus Superintendens à Genevensi praeside distabat, quòd hic mutabilis, ille immutabilis statuebatur: cum verò non mutetur, tamen inquit Zanchius apud Genevenses quis alius in effectu quam Germanicus Superintendens Geneva praesidet?
units.tr: Third, Bancroft says that Calvin deceived the unwary Genevans, since, when they suspected nothing, he slipped in an authority equal to episcopal authority, which he also drew to himself, although meanwhile he openly displayed the very opposite. Hadrianus Saravia too is guilty of this calumny. It is true, he says, that though you drive out nature with a pitchfork, it will keep coming back. For it is established that Beza is far superior to his colleagues, and John Calvin, while he lived, had more authority over his colleagues than the Primate of England today exercises over his fellow bishops. I speak of things well known, so that it would be shameless to deny what the facts themselves cry out and their writings bear witness to. What he calls well known is false, and it would be shameless to say it; the facts themselves cry out against it, and their writings bear witness. But grant that it was so: you will, I hope, confess that the bishop in England now exercises greater authority over the other ministers than Calvin and Beza exercised over their colleagues. Indeed, he says elsewhere, do you want to know who has hitherto kept up concord among the ministers at Geneva, and others too? They have one bishop whom they deny and do not want, and that is one only. For whatever Mr. Beza writes or thinks, he will never persuade the world, since in the college, in deliberations and in the whole governance of his Church, by authority and weight of opinion, he yields to his other colleagues, just as in the place of presidency. And this is the opinion held of John Calvin of pious memory. Zanchius did not conceal this either, when he set out his opinion about archbishops and bishops. But, he says, although neither those old good Greek words nor these new bad Latin words hold, nevertheless there are usually some leading men, in whose hands almost all authority lies, etc. Do you see how the force of nature brings us back to where we are fleeing from? Let Mr. Beza write whatever he wishes; Geneva, or any other place, will never be able to bear two Bezas or two Calvins disagreeing in one Church. I must reply first about Zanchius. He never approved of the English bishop, whom he believed to have been constituted a bishop by the Fathers of old; he was none other than the German superintendent, as the very sequence of his discourse shows. He said that account must be taken of those Churches that have bishops, among which it is clear that he did not understand England, because in the words immediately following, describing the Churches he wished to be understood, he mentions England in passing and dwells only on the German Churches, which have superintendents. Moreover, although he acknowledged that those were ancient bishops, he saw in them something that he either so much desired or disapproved of, that he constantly refused the superintendent's presidency, which the brethren often offered him; and so it came about that he lived, grew old and died only an ordinary teacher. Would he approve the English bishop, who did not approve the German superintendent in every respect? As for his saying that at Geneva authority lay almost in the hands of one man, this is understood of the authority of presidency: John Calvin presided throughout his whole life, and Beza also presided for a long time, namely until Danaeus came to Geneva, as George Downame himself relates. So it is. The German superintendent differed from the Genevan president only in this: the one was set up as changeable, the other as unchangeable. But since he is not changed, nevertheless, says Zanchius, who else at Geneva in effect presides, other than the German superintendent?

units.la: Secundò, quam authoritatem Calvinus Bezae habuit, ea tantùm meriti erat, non potestatis; hanc nos Episcopis Anglicanis non invidemus, potestatis jugo quo premimur, sublato, Calvini & Bezae evadere si possunt, Calvini & Bezae existimatione perfruantur. Atqui ego inquit Saravia, mallem Bezam legitimum habere Episcopum, quam collegam tyrannum. Cujus calumniae iniquitatem, vobis à simili patefaciam. Nicolai Sanderi De visibili monarchia libri quinti capitis quarti hic apud Scultingium titulus est. Ne daemoniorum quidem conspirantem factionem, multoque minus Lutheranorum & Calvinianorum Synagogam, a(i) unius pastoris alteriusque generis visi illi primatu stare ac florere posse. In capite verò ipso, Lutherum regem planè Saxonicum & quasi Papam egisse affirmat: quod & de Superintendentibus, & Episcopis Anglicanis dicit. Calvinus & Beza Episcopos legerunt dicit Saravia, adeò Episcopatus necessarius est ad unitatem conservandam. Lutherus & Episcopi Anglicani primatus Papalis imaginem gerunt, dicit Sanderus: adeò hic primatus necessarius est ad unitatem conservandam. Quanta hîc obsecro differentia est? Pudeat igitur Calvino & Bezae id objicere, quod vobis obiectum in summam injuriam deputatis; ausim enim dicere, tam prope ad tyrannidem accedere Episcopos Anglicanos, quàm longe Beza & Calvinus. dinus ab eadem abfuerunt: sic ut hac Saravinâ insimulatione nihil iniquius esse possit. Verùm ut hic locus concludatur: ab omni ea moli mali suspicione, quam Bancroftus obiectavit, Calvinum & Bezam Hadrianus ipse liberat alibi, quam sibi constanter, lector judicet. Verba ista sunt: Divinæ providentiæ permissione factum arbitror, ut gravissimi aliqui viri, omnem Episcoporum ordinem sublatum cuperent, & tollendum censerent. Præstat enim nullos in Ecclesia esse Episcopos, quam pro Episcopis habere lupos, & illa monstra pati quæ nobis peperit Romana Ecclesia. Hic error ab omni ambitionis suspitione doctores liberat per quos Deus doctrinæ veritatem restituit: eos nemo accusare potest verum novandarum studio permotos fuisse, ut in dignitates & opes Episcoporum ipsi succederent. Sed postquam innocentia & sincerus eorum candor, qui si nullas opes, nullos honores, nihil denique præter veræ pietatis restitutionem propositerunt, luce clarius, omnibus videre volentibus apparuit, &c. Ita reformatio in Geneuensi sua innocentia salva recta conservatur.
units.tr: Second, the authority that Calvin had over Beza was only of merit, not of power. We do not begrudge this to the Anglican bishops. If they can escape the yoke of power by which we are oppressed, let them enjoy the esteem of Calvin and Beza. But I, says Saravia, would rather have Beza as a lawful bishop than as a tyrannical colleague. I shall show you the unfairness of this calumny by a parallel. The title of the fourth chapter of the fifth book of Nicolas Sander's De visibili monarchia is here, as cited by Scultingius: Neither the conspiring faction of demons, much less the synagogue of the Lutherans and Calvinists, could stand and flourish by the primacy of one pastor and another kind of visible ministry. In the chapter itself, he asserts that Luther acted quite as a king of Saxony and as almost a Pope, which he also says of the German superintendents and the Anglican bishops. Calvin and Beza chose bishops, says Saravia, so necessary is episcopacy for preserving unity. Luther and the Anglican bishops bear the image of papal primacy, says Sander, so necessary is this primacy for preserving unity. What a great difference here, I beg you! Let it therefore be a shame for Calvin and Beza to bring up what you count as a very great wrong done to you. For I dare say that Anglican bishops come as close to tyranny as Beza and Calvin were far from it. So that there can be nothing more unfair than this insinuation of Saravia. But, to conclude this point: the reader may judge how consistently Hadrianus himself, elsewhere, frees Calvin and Beza from every suspicion of that wicked scheme which Bancroft raised. His words are these: I think it was by the permission of divine providence that some very serious men wished, and thought it should be done, that the whole order of bishops be abolished. For it is better to have no bishops in the Church than to have wolves in the place of bishops, and to suffer those monsters which the Roman Church has brought forth for us. This error frees from all suspicion of ambition those teachers through whom God restored the truth of doctrine; no one can accuse them of having been moved by a zeal for innovation so that they might themselves succeed to the dignities and riches of the bishops. But after their innocence and sincere candour, which proposed no riches, no honours, nothing at all except the restoration of true piety, appeared clearer than light to all who wished to see, etc. Thus the Reformation at Geneva, with its innocence preserved, is kept upright.

units.la: CAP. XXXII. Ecclesiæ reliquæ reformatæ a calumnia vafritiei & κακοζηλίας vindicantur.
units.tr: CHAP. XXXII. The other reformed Churches are vindicated from the calumny of craftiness and misguided zeal [κακοζηλία].

units.la: SVpereft ut damna resarciamus, quæ detractorum virulentia, Ecclesiarum reliquarum reformationibus intulit. His omnibus præpostera κακοζηλία Genevensium imputatur: absque quâ si suisset, presbyterialem disciplinam, Gallia, Scotia, Belgia, Ecclesiæque reformatæ reliquæ non recepissent. Hinc Saravia ita: Turpe eis videtur a magistris dissentire. Tanta est authoritas, tanta reverentia magistri ut plus simplex unius affectio persuadeat, quàm omnium sæculorum scriptores. Hoc præjudicium viam præcludit ad veritatem. Non temerè fuit, quòd verus magister nos vetuit mortalem hîc in terris deligere magistrum: unus est enim magister in cœlis, ab eo nos edoceri oportet. Primò criminationem retorqueamus: non ita nos Calvinum & Bezam ut Hierarchici Whitgiftam & Bilsonum venerantur, sic ut cum Tertuliano respondere liceat: magistrum neminem habemus nos nisi Deum solum: Cetera quos tu putas tibi magistros, homines sunt. Secundò, nosti hoc ipsum à Papistis in doctrinæ ipsius reformationem intorqueri, ut quam Ecclesias nostras amplexatas fuisse dicant, præcipiti Lutheri admiratione abreptas, quem nos ut etiam nostrum Apostolum celebrare affirmant, vel ipsi Paulo præferendum. Revocant hæc ultima mihi in memoriam Bancrofii illa, qui probaturus præ nimia Calvini admiratione disciplinam Genevensem in Ecclesias reliquas inundasse, instat in quodam Genevensi, qui, etsi Paulus Genevæ pulpitum ascensurus esset, se tamen ad Calvinum aucturum abiturum dixit. Atqui hæc in doctrinam ipsam recidunt, at non in disciplinam solùm: id quod vel Hadriani solius Saraviæ exemplo emplo demonstrari potest. Cur non etenim Gretzerus illum quod ad doctrinam Calvinistam appellaret, perinde ac Saravia nos quod ad disciplinam Calvinistas appellat?
units.tr: It remains that we make good the losses which the virulence of detractors has inflicted on the reformations of the other Churches. All of these are charged to the Genevans as a perverse, misguided zeal, without which, they say, France, Scotland, the Low Countries and the other reformed Churches would never have received presbyterial discipline. Hence Saravia says: It seems shameful to them to dissent from their masters. Such is the authority, such the reverence for a master, that the single affection of one man persuades more than all the writers of all the ages. This prejudice closes the way to the truth. It was not without reason that the true Master forbade us to choose a mortal master here on earth: for one is our Master in heaven, and by him we must be taught. First, let us turn the accusation back. We do not venerate Calvin and Beza as the hierarchs venerate Whitgift and Bilson, so that we might answer with Tertullian: We have no master but God alone; the others whom you think to be your masters are men. Second, you know that this very charge is turned by the Papists against the reformation of doctrine itself. They say that our Churches embraced it, carried away by a headlong admiration for Luther, whom we, they affirm, celebrate as our own Apostle, to be preferred even to Paul. These last words recall to my mind that charge of Bancroft, who, wishing to prove that the Genevan discipline had flooded into the other Churches from excessive admiration for Calvin, presses against a certain Genevan who said that, although Paul was about to mount the pulpit at Geneva, he would nevertheless go away to Calvin. But these charges fall back upon doctrine itself, and not upon discipline alone; this can be shown even from the example of Hadrian Saravia alone. For why would not Gretser call him a Calvinist in respect of doctrine, just as Saravia calls us Calvinists in respect of discipline?

units.la: Tertio, quod Gretzerus Saravia, id nos Saravie. Quibus tandem argumentis colligis nos Calvinistas esse, aut disciplinam illius gratia deamasse? quod pro argumento aff. ut Bancroftus, literas undiquaque a Dominum Bezam missas fuisse rei ab ipso Saravia refutatur. Non dispu. d, inquit, consultum fuisse Dominum Bezam in re gravissima: Num cariplicet vero? quo igitur loco Bancroftus habendus, qui huius rei gratia Calvinum & Bezam duos Patriarchas fuisse dicit: imo duos protestantium patres, talis, qualem si Papa vendit it suis Patriis. Annon putet calumniae? In promptu etenim nobis est Saravie verbis ad Gretzerum respondere. Nobis nec Calvinus nec, Lutherus, nec Beza Patriarcha est. Scito Ignatiane Anglicanam Ecclesiam, nemmem habere magistrum nisi Christum solum. Quod ai Calvinum & Bezam ipsum Nomine Calvinum virum excellentem fuisse fateris ipse? & quis prohiberet in re gravissima virum consulere excellentem? At de Calvino hoc dixit inquies, doctrinae intuitu, non disciplinae. Forte: Sed si excellens in doctrina, cur non & in disciplina etiam? liceat igitur Tertulliani illud argumentum retorquere. O Apologeticum in consideratam, testimonium sapientiae red actis vero, qui negabat Deos esse. Loquitur de Socrate; quin tamen idem nos de Calvino? Atque haec ad calumniam eam generalem, qua Ecclesiae reformatae omnes tangunctur.
units.tr: Thirdly, what Gretser says of Saravia, that we say of Saravia. By what arguments, finally, do you infer that we are Calvinists, or that we have loved his discipline for its own sake? As for the argument Bancroft urges, that letters were sent from every quarter to Mr Beza, this is refuted by Saravia himself: "I do not dispute," he says, "that Beza was consulted in a matter of the greatest weight: does that please anyone?" By what standard, then, is Bancroft to be regarded, who says that Calvin and Beza were two patriarchs for this purpose, nay, two fathers of the Protestants, such as the Pope would sell to his own people? Does he not seem to be slandering? For we have Saravia's words ready at hand in reply to Gretser: for us neither Calvin, nor Luther, nor Beza is a patriarch. Know, Ignatian, that the English Church has no master but Christ alone. But do you yourself admit that Calvin was an excellent man? And who would forbid consulting an excellent man in a matter of the greatest weight? But you will say he spoke of Calvin with regard to doctrine, not discipline. Perhaps so; but if he was excellent in doctrine, why not in discipline too? Let us therefore be permitted to turn Tertullian's argument back. In his Apologeticus, considering the testimony of wisdom drawn from the very truth, he who denied that there were gods... He speaks of Socrates; why should we not say the same of Calvin? And so much for that general calumny by which all the reformed Churches are touched.

units.la: 2 Sequuntur speciales quaedam. De Gallis nihil particulare objicitur nec de Belgis: de Anglis Bancroftus ita. Confitentur B zyn per literas Puritani, cui is in tractatu, particulares coetus mihi & fureas factiones per fuerationes plurimae factae sunt. Respondemus cum Tertullino: Haec ea tio Christianorum meritos sanctae iniuriatur, si illis itis par, merito damnanda si quis de ea queratur, o titulo, quod sationibus quaerela est. In cuius perniciem aliquando conveniunt? Hoc fumus cogregati quod & dispersi hoc universi, quod inguli, nemine Ledantes, nemine extra stantes: quum probi, cum boni coeunt, cum pij, non est factio dicenda, sed curia. Quod ad calumnias Bancroftii reliquas, quibus nos Hypocritas vocit. Cuiusmodi ille H. N. serpentes, locustas, Edomitas, Aldoditas, & Samaritas, carnules denique sed vitiosos, qui apud Iudam gubernationes contemnunt, & mali lucunt eis qui in authoritate positi sunt, nihil aliud respondio, quam regerendum in illum ipsum esse, quod nobis impingit alibi. Linguae eorum suae sunt, linguas grandi loquentes dominus excindet. Psal. 12. Transmigrandum deinceps in Scotiam est: ubi à lohanne Knoxo populari tumultu stabilitam primo disciplinam fuisse Bancroftus objicit. At nonne eadem quaeso in doctrinam ipsam recidunt? Doctrina quidem olim erat quae Papistas accusantibus Scotorum tumultuum crimen sustinebat: nunc disciplinae onus omne imponitur ab ipsis Protestantibus; liberatur autem defensione ea (nequo (neque enim alia opus) quam pro doctrina adornat Iuellus contra Hardingum, & Thomas Bilsonus contra Alanum Cardinalem: Iuellus ita: De regno Scotiae nihil dicam. Regna mundi varios pactiones & compositiones habent: Nobiles seu populus ibi, neque gladios evaginarunt, neque violenti im adversum principem attentarunt: Continuationem tantum indubitatae veritatis divinae quaesiverunt: & adversus barbaras crudelissimas invasiones, vitarum propriarum defensionem. Praeter alia movendi signa, Vassiacae vestrae immanitatis meminerunt, ubi fratrum suorum in gentes multitudinem, inter precandum, in ipso templo palmas innocentes ad coelum tendentes, & nomen Dei invocantes, ex inopinato trucidatae sunt. Nobiles isti a Petro didicerunt: Melius est Deo obtemperare quam hominibus, &c.
units.tr: 2. Some particular charges follow. Nothing special is objected against the French or the Belgians. Against the English, Bancroft says this: they confess, through the letters of the Puritans, that many particular assemblies and factions have been formed by the Puritans, and in his treatise he speaks of "private gatherings and furious factions." We answer with Tertullian: this is the reason why the Christians are unjustly harmed, and a complaint about it is deservedly to be condemned if anyone complains of the name rather than of the crime. For what is the harm they have ever done? We are gathered together, but we are also scattered; we are all one, and each of us is single; we harm no one, we stand apart from no one. When the upright, the good, and the pious come together, it is not to be called a faction but a senate. As for Bancroft's remaining calumnies, by which he calls us hypocrites, of what sort are they? He calls us serpents, locusts, Edomites, Ammonites, Samaritans, and finally carnal but vicious men, who despise governments in Judah and speak evil of those who hold authority. I answer only that what he hurls at us elsewhere should be thrown back at himself. Their tongues are their own; the Lord will cut off all tongues that speak great things (Ps. 12). We must next cross over into Scotland, where Bancroft objects that discipline was first established there by the popular tumult stirred up by John Knox. But are not these charges, I ask, again referred back to doctrine itself? Formerly it was doctrine that bore the charge of Scottish tumults when the accusers were the Papists; now the whole burden of discipline is laid upon them by the Protestants themselves. Yet that charge is relieved by the defence which Jewel prepares, not only for discipline but for doctrine, against Harding, and Thomas Bilson against Cardinal Allen. Jewel says: "I will say nothing about the kingdom of Scotland. The kingdoms of the world have various pacts and compositions. The nobles or the people there have neither drawn their swords, nor have they violently attacked their prince; they have sought only the continuance of the indubitable truth of God, and the defence of their own lives against barbarous and most cruel invasions. Besides other signs of stirring, they recall your monstrous massacre at Vassy, where, while their brothers were praying in the temple and stretching innocent hands to heaven, invoking the name of God, the multitude of them was suddenly slaughtered among the nations. Those nobles learned from Peter: It is better to obey God than men, etc."

units.la: Bilsonus vero tumultus omnes Scoticos Papistis imputat, tam doctrinae quam disciplinae obnitentibus, ipsisque, & regis necem, & Iacobi in utero materno tollendi conatum, totum ipsis asscribit. Disciplinam vero aeque ac doctrinam, omnes papistarum tumultuantium conatus tandem superasse, vel ipse Banerostus diffiteri nequit, tantum nescio quid doli insinuare videtur, quum videre in Scoticis Chronicis cuivis licere dicit, quomodo Actu Parlamentario sancita disciplina fuerit. Quid hoc, quomodo, aut quid accusationi tam generali respondeas? Nobis quidem satis est, quod modo satis licito, non solum actu Parlamentario, sed & omnium ordinum juramento etiam, disciplina stabilita sit: verba mandati haec sunt.
units.tr: Bilson, however, imputes all the Scottish tumults to the Papists, who resisted both doctrine and discipline, and ascribes to them the whole attempt both on the king's life and on James's removal while still in his mother's womb. That discipline, as much as doctrine, finally overcame all the attempts of the tumultuous Papists, even Bancroft himself cannot deny; he only seems to insinuate some sort of trickery, when he says that anyone may see in the Scottish chronicles how discipline was sanctioned by act of Parliament. What do you say to this, how, or what answer will you give to so general an accusation? For us, indeed, it is enough that discipline was established not only by act of Parliament but also by the oath of all the orders, and in a fully lawful way. The words of the mandate are these:

units.la: Secundo Martij anno 1581. in aedibus sanctae crucis mandatum Regiae Majestatis est editum, quo omnibus mandatariis & nominatim verbi ministris injunctum fuit. Quum Rex ipse omnesque ipsius domestici, praedictae confessioni subscripsissent, ut omnes pastores hanc confessionem ab omnibus suis parœciis exigerent, & recusantes ministris domus Regiae deferrent, idque sub multa 40. florenorum, ab ipsorum stipendiis detrahendorum. & ratio additur in illo mandato cur tales recusantes erant deferendi: nimirum (inquit) ut nos ex Senatus nostri consilio ejusmodi Dei, & legum nostrarum contemptores in ordinem cogamus. Hoc mandatum chyrographo & sigillo Regio est subsignatum, loco & tempore quae antea sunt nominata: Verba etiam juramenti haec sunt:
units.tr: On 2 March 1581, in the house of the Holy Cross, a royal mandate was issued, by which it was enjoined upon all officers, and by name upon the ministers of the Word, that since the King himself and all his household had subscribed the aforesaid confession, all the pastors should require this confession from all their parishes, and should report those who refused to the ministers of the royal household, under a fine of 40 florins to be deducted from their stipends. And a reason is added in that mandate why such refusers were to be reported: namely, (he says) that we, by the counsel of our Senate, may bring to order such contemners of God and of our laws. This mandate is signed with the royal signature and seal, in the place and at the time named above. The words of the oath are also these:

units.la: Promittentes & solemniter jurantes per magnum illud Nomen Domini Dei nostri, nos persuaderaos in doctrina & disciplina hujus Ecclesiae: quod pro vocatione et facultate nostra eadem defendemus omnibus diebus vitae nostrae sub poena omnium maledictionum in lege contentarum, & periculo corporis & animae, in die tremendi illius judicij Dei.
units.tr: Promising and solemnly swearing by the great Name of the Lord our God, that we will persevere in the doctrine and discipline of this Church, and that according to our calling and ability we will defend the same all the days of our life, under the penalty of all the curses contained in the law, and at the peril of body and soul in the day of that dreadful judgment of God.

units.la: At Iacobus Rex, inquit Becanus, plus fidei in Papistis, imo in efferis latronibus reperisse se dicit, quam in puritanis. At non omnes qui vel in Scotia vel in Anglia pro disciplina reformata stabant se intellexisse, in praefatione editionis posterioris idem aperte protestatur. At in praefatione monitoria inquis, qui pro reformatione in Anglia stat, Puritanos appellat. Quid omnes? qui in Scotia factiosos quosdam duntaxat intellexit: cur non & in Anglia fanaticos tantum quos putat, quosdam intellexisse censendus est? Certè qui omnes hac censura involvit, audire necesse habet, quod in jus canonicum ex Hieronymo relatum est. [Priusquam audias ne judicaveris quempiam, quia non statim qui accusatur reus est, sed qui convincitur criminosus.] Insto in sancto Chrysostomo: qui ab Arcadio imperatore piissimè multa iniqua, indigna multa innocenter passus est. Atsi nos omnes criminosi, non tamen ipsa pro qua stamus disciplina criminosa est: quam ante nos Calvinus & Beza, reliquæq: Ecclesiæ reformatæ amplexæ sunt, quas ex catalogo Puritanorum, monitorio particulari ad id instituto, eadem majestas Regia expungit. Nec igitur illius velamento tegi immodestia in Anglia eorum potest, qui in Calvinum, Bezam Ecclesiarumq; reformatarum nutritios reliquos è suggestis & Cathedris tanquam in Puritanos impurissimè debacchantur. Atque hæc ad exceptionem tertiam quæ adversus Ecclesiarum reformatarum imitationem adferri solet: earum scilicet, aut vafritiem aut κοινωνίαν qua presbyterialem disciplinam superinduxisse perhibentur.
units.tr: But King James, says Becanus, claims to have found more faith in the Papists, indeed in savage robbers, than in the Puritans. Yet in the preface to the later edition he openly protests that he did not understand all who stood for reformed discipline either in Scotland or in England. But in the admonitory preface you say that whoever stands for reformation in England he calls Puritans. What of "all"? He understood only certain factious persons in Scotland; why should he be thought to have understood only certain fanatics whom he judges to be such in England? Surely whoever includes all under this censure must hear what is quoted from Jerome in the canon law: "Before you hear, do not judge anyone; for not he who is accused at once is guilty, but he who is convicted of a crime." I insist on holy Chrysostom, who, at the hands of the Emperor Arcadius, most piously suffered many unjust and undeserved things though innocent. And if we are all criminals, yet the discipline for which we stand is not itself criminal; it was embraced before us by Calvin, Beza, and the rest of the reformed Churches, and the same royal majesty strikes them off the catalogue of Puritans in a particular admonitory edict drawn up for that purpose. Therefore the excessive license of those in England who rage most foully from pulpits and chairs against Calvin, Beza, and the other nurses of the reformed Churches, calling them Puritans, cannot be covered by his cloak. And so much for the third objection which is usually brought against the imitation of the reformed Churches: namely, that they are said to have introduced presbyterial discipline either by craftiness or by collusion.

units.la: CAP. 33. Quarta Calumnia adversariorum, disciplinam esse malorum fontem, diluitur.
units.tr: CAP. 33. The fourth calumny of our adversaries, that discipline is the source of evils, is refuted.

units.la: QVartò, adversus reformationem ipsam introductam excipit Lous, quam tanquam malorum omnium in Ecclesia fontem, inunstatis labem, ordinis perniciem, detestandam esse clamat. Atqui Hierarchiam Anglicanam potius, tanquam totius tepiditatis fontem fugiendam esse Spiritus sanctus innuere videtur, cùm ex adverso ad Angliam clamat, Qui habet aures ad audiendum audiat, quid Spiritus sanctus ad Laodiceam, ipsius Anglicanæ Ecclesiæ dicit. Ap. 3, 22. Hoc ut fiat, obthurandæ aures sunt, adversus clamores Hierarchicos quosque, qui adversus unicum Angliæ remedium disciplinæ nempe reformationem horrenda multa ejaculantur. Quid Calvinus? Calvinus in causa disciplinæ tanquam Ixion alter cum errorum nube ingressus est, inquit Lous: & cum Synedrium tribunal Christi vocat, Papatum & plus erigit. Quid Beza? Beza in causa disciplinæ quasi Circæo populo mutatus est, habet idem: quem etiam Saravia inter eos ponere videtur, qui ad turbandam Ecclesiam Anglicanam nati sunt.
units.tr: Fourthly, Lous attacks the reformation itself as introduced, crying out that it is the source of all evils in the Church, the stain of disorder, the ruin of good order, to be detested. Yet the Holy Spirit seems rather to point to the English hierarchy as the fount of all lukewarmness that is to be shunned, since on the other side He cries out to England: He who has ears to hear, let him hear. This is what the Holy Spirit says to Laodicea, that is, to the very English Church (Rev. 3:22). To bring this about, one must stop one's ears against all the hierarchical outcries, who hurl many dreadful charges against the one remedy of England, namely the reformation of discipline. What of Calvin? Calvin entered the cause of discipline like another Ixion, wrapped in a cloud of errors, says Lous; and when Calvin calls the Consistory the tribunal of Christ, he even raises up the papacy. What of Beza? In the cause of discipline Beza has been changed, like the people of Circe, he says; and Saravia seems to count him too among those born to disturb the English Church.

units.la: Quid reliqui? qui disciplinæ in Anglia reformationem expetunt? Reformatio by stra ab orco. Pergit Puritana lues. Puritanus furor, l trant Aery catuli. Ex nemine vero alio apertius quam ex Cornelio Scultingio apparet, quàm indignis modis, Pel teiæ Ecclesiasticæ reformatio excepta sit. Consistorii senigrum inquit, ex cerebro Calvini, Genevæ nati.
units.tr: What of the rest, who seek the reformation of discipline in England? Reformation... from the pit of hell. The Puritan plague goes on. Puritan madness: the airy puppies bark. Yet nowhere is it clearer, than in Cornelius Scultingius, with what unworthy abuse the reformation of ecclesiastical discipline has been received. A consistory-nightmare, he says, born from the brain of Calvin, of Geneva.

units.la: Cens.4.8.c. 5. sunt anno Domini 1541. tam ex Laicis, quam ex ministris coagmentata, monstrum, absurdum, infame, ingens, seditionum Gallicarum flabellum & fomentum, non solum a Catholica Ecclesia ut profana novitas, rejectum, damnatum, anathamatizatum, sed etiam ab aliis Novatoribus & sectarijs egregiè exagitatum, a Zanchio contra Calvinum, ab Erasto contra Bezam, a Petro Ramo contra utrumque, qui illud Thalmum Sabaudicum nominans, acerrime contra invehitur, ab Ecclesiis omnibus Germanicis & Helveticis procacissime repudiatum, lacerantibus illud, scriptisque publicis condemnantibus in Loc. Com. Musculo, cap. de Magistratu, in Comment. 1. Cor. 5. Gualtero, in defensione contra Puritanos, Iohanne Whitgifto Cantuariensi Pseudo-archiepiscopo. Qui & alios politeiae reformatae hostes addit alibi. Ipsorum conventus & consistoria inquit, placidi & pacifici Calvinistae, ut Carpentarius To. 4. praefat. Confessionis Hieronymi, & alij execrantur, quod in eis consilia capiantur, ad evertendos omnes Catholicos principes, etiam & reges: unde Dominus F. Costerus in Sica Tragica c. 8. ostendit Calvinistas esse sanguinarios, sanguine Catholicorum sitire, & talia consilia in eorum consistorijs agitari quotidie: hinc eorum consistoria extiterunt flabella tot seditionum & bellorum tot annis in Gallia, Cap. 11. docet ex historia Caroli Noniregis Galliarum, & ex insidijs eidem per Calvinistas structis, ipsos esse regum in suis consistorijs interfectores. Brochtomus in epistola ad doctissimum virum Nicolaum Serrarium asserit, rabiem Genevensem prorumpere in Cyclopicam immanitatem, nullam fovere lenitatem, neque placide disserere, unde accidit ut pacifici cum seditiosis in unam mentem coalescere non possint. Idem ait Calvinistas, sine fine bella accendere, ut sic omnia vastescant, censet eos Turcae fenestram aperire ad occupandum Germaniam & Christianitatem. Sed nec adhuc hostes politeias reformatae omnes habemus, addit enim alibi & alium sed omnibus turpitudinis notis injustum insignemque Apostatam, qui postquam ministros reformatos quosdam in Americam adduxisset, disciplinam immutavit primo, deinde doctrinâ ipsam, ac papismum repente coloniae imponens persecutione crudelissima excitavit, ut videre est, in commentarijs regni Gallici: in Carolo Nono. De hoc verò Scultingius ita.
units.tr: (Cens. 4.8, c. 5.) It was put together in the year of the Lord 1541, from laymen as well as ministers: a monster, absurd, infamous, huge, a fan and fuel of French seditions. It has been rejected, condemned and anathematized not only by the Catholic Church as a profane novelty, but also has been thoroughly harried by other innovators and sectaries: by Zanchius against Calvin, by Erastus against Beza, and by Peter Ramus against both, who, calling it the Savoyard Thalmus, attacks it most bitterly. It has been shamelessly repudiated by all the German and Helvetic Churches, which tear it apart and condemn it in public writings: in Musculus's Loci communes, chapter on the magistrate; in Gualter's commentary on 1 Corinthians 5; in the defence against the Puritans; and by John Whitgift, the Pseudo-archbishop of Canterbury. He adds elsewhere other enemies of the reformed polity. Their assemblies and consistories, placid and peaceable Calvinists, as Carpentarius (vol. 4, preface to the Confession of Jerome) and others curse, because plans are made in them to overthrow all Catholic princes, even kings. Hence Dom F. Coster, in his Sica Tragica, chapter 8, shows that the Calvinists are bloodthirsty, thirst for Catholic blood, and that such plans are daily debated in their consistories. Hence their consistories have become the fan of so many seditions and wars in France for so many years. Chapter 11 teaches, from the history of Charles IX, king of France, and from the plots laid against him by the Calvinists, that they are the murderers of kings in their consistories. Brochtomus, in a letter to the most learned man Nicolas Serrarius, asserts that the Genevan rage breaks out into Cyclopean savagery, fosters no gentleness, and does not argue calmly; whence it happens that peaceable and seditious men cannot coalesce into one mind. The same man says that the Calvinists kindle wars without end, so that everything is laid waste; he thinks they open a window for the Turk to occupy Germany and Christendom. But we do not yet have all the enemies of the reformed polity: he adds elsewhere another apostate, unjust and marked with every stain of disgrace, who, after he had brought certain reformed ministers into America, first changed the discipline, then the doctrine itself, and suddenly imposed Papism on the colony, stirring up a most cruel persecution. This may be seen in the commentaries on the French kingdom, under Charles IX. But Scultingius speaks thus about him.

units.la: Nicolaus Villagnon inquit, Eques auratus, lib. 1. c. 8. contra articulos Richeri, ita habet: Non defuit nobis in rebus plurimis discordiae occasio, cum funditus Ecclesiasticam disciplinam, ei tui ministri evertere abolereque contenderent. Tradunt in Ecclesia neminem authoritate reliquis antecellere, quod omnes Christiani regale sint sacerdotium, sibi omnes persuadent, se esse religionis scientiâ praeditos antequam litteras didicerint, quod eam dominus parvulis revelaverit, nõ sapientibus. Sunt ꝛ omnes perfecti Theologi absque literis & doctrina. Richardus Bancroftus ut Raмum & Carpentarium sibi patronos asciscit: ita eis adjungit Baldwinum & Hessusinum, quos viros doctos apellat: mirum, quod non Staphylum etiam & Bolsecum adiecerit. Vides jam disciplinae reformatae hostes praecipuos quosdam falsò, quosdam verè nominatos minatos, de quorum plerisque nihil nos aliud respondisse fumus, quàm Siculus ille apud Ciceronem. Cum Scipio prætor patronum sibi dedisset hospitem suum, virum nobilem sed admodum stultum: quæso inquit prætor, adversario meo da iustum patronum, interim mihi deueris nemunem. Ita nos patronos hujusmodi adversarijs libenter largiturfumus,ut ipsi interim habeamus neminem: Ejusmodi etenim plerique sunt, ut causæ nostræ nihil plus officiant, quam famæ Origenis illi, de quibus Socrates. Detractiones illorum, famam Origenis, meo quidem iudicio, existimationemque adauxerunt: Nitescet etenim disciplina magis,quû horû hominû criminationes,quâ sint vanæ intelligatur,quod vt fiat, ad particulares illas maculas descendendum jam nobis est, quas eidem in genere nonnulli asperserunt.
units.tr: Nicolas Villagnon, says a knight of the golden spur, book 1, chapter 8, against the articles of Richer, has the following: We have not lacked occasions for discord in many matters, since your ministers have striven to overturn and abolish ecclesiastical discipline from its foundations. They teach that no one in the Church excels the rest in authority, since all Christians are a royal priesthood, and they persuade themselves that they are endowed with knowledge of religion before they have learned letters, because the Lord has revealed it to little ones, not to the wise. And all of them are perfect theologians without letters and learning. Richard Bancroft takes Ramus and Carpentarius as his patrons, and joins to them Baldwin and Hesshusius, whom he calls learned men. It is a wonder he did not add Staphylus and Bolsec too. You see now the chief enemies of reformed discipline, some falsely, some truly named, of most of whom we have replied nothing more than that Sicilian in Cicero did. When Scipio, as praetor, had given his host, a noble but very foolish man, as patron, the praetor said: I beg you, give my adversary a fair patron; meanwhile give me none at all. So we gladly grant such patrons to our adversaries, so that for ourselves we may have none at all. For most of them are of such a kind that they harm our cause no more than the reputation of that Origen of whom Socrates speaks: Their detractions, in my judgment, have increased the fame and esteem of Origen. Indeed discipline will shine the brighter when the accusations of these men are understood to be empty. To make this happen, we must now descend to those particular stains which some have cast upon it in general.

units.la: 2 Prima Koranifmi est:sic enim Bancroftus. Mundus ad libertatem totus aspirat: singulos fere reperias eorum spiritu prædītos, quibus quennquam supra congregationem præponi, agere est. Num. 16, Hadrianus Saravia ita. Quod quidam omnis imperij impatientes sicut Chore & Dathan, qui cōtra Mosem & Aaronē insurrexerunt,nescio cujus tyrānidis Episcopos insimulant, sunt mere calumniæ: nisi parere bonis legibus, & fungi officia suo tyrānidem vocent. Respondeo primò cōmune Evangelio ipsi impro-perium istud esse: Sic enim apud Iuellum Papistæ. Sicut Dathan & Abiram adversus Mosem & Aaronem olim conspirarunt: Ita & vos Episcopo Romano nuncium misistis, & communem Ecclesiæ pacem perturbastis. Non est igitur quod calumniâ istâ commoveamur: cujus disciplina non magis rea, quam ipsa doctrina est.
units.tr: 2. The first is Korahism; so Bancroft calls it. The whole world aspires to liberty; you may find nearly every one of them endowed with that spirit, to whom it is absurd to set anyone above the congregation. (Num. 16.) Hadrianus Saravia says this: That certain men, impatient of all rule, like Korah and Dathan, who rose up against Moses and Aaron, accuse the bishops of I know not what tyranny, is pure calumny, unless they call it tyranny to obey good laws and to perform their duties. I answer, first, that this reproach is common to the Gospel itself. For thus the Papists speak in Jewel: Just as Dathan and Abiram once conspired against Moses and Aaron, so you have sent a messenger to the Roman bishop and have disturbed the common peace of the Church. There is therefore no reason to be moved by this calumny, whose discipline is no more guilty of it than doctrine itself.

units.la: Respondeo secundo, quod in hac conspiratione τὰ•Θίνκα erat,nos minimè attingit:voluerunt enim illi ministerium nullum, ideoque populum omnem adæque sanctum proclamarunt : id quod Eyldus observavit. Quod verò in eadem Ϙιπκα est, id hoștes attingit, quorum peccatum,nescio an quibusdam gradibus, hoc Korahano gravius sit.Sine vocatione se ingessit Chorah: ita sine vocatione Episcopalem in Ecclesias authoritatem Hierarchici arripuerunt: Disturbavit Chorah disciplinam, hi sustulerunt: latravit ille, hi mordent: parem superioribus se facit ille,hi semetipsos superiores suis paribus faciût nullam ille injuriam spirauit, hi carcere multant, bonis exuunt, laribus exterminant: parem ille locum veris Dei ministris non invidebat, hi eisdem plane nullum, nec in ministerio, nedum in Dei Ecclesia concedunt. Atque si peccatum sub Evangelio, peccato sub lege gravius sit, uti Apostolus docere videtur,Heb.10. gravius certè peccare Hierarchicos necesse est, qui adversus Evangelicam à Christo Domino,quam Corahanos qui adversus legalem à Mose servo institutam disciplinam insurgunt, pari certè peccato obstringi eos par est, qui adversus disciplinæ antistites insurgunt, pari authoritate præditos: jam verò ministris Evangelicis datum est: Apocalypf. 11. 5. ut ignis exeorum ore prodeat ad inimicos devorandos, quemadmodum Mosis denuntiatione factum olim, ut ignis egressus sit à facie Iehovæ ad Corab consumendum. Quidni? Ignem minimè sanctificatum Corab minimè sanctificatus altari admovit: annon Hierarchici pariliter faciunt? Montem enim igne ardentem, id est Episcopatum minimè à Deo sanctificatum, ipsi etiam non vocati aut ad hoc munus sanctificati in Ecclesiam protecerunt. Apoc. 3..
units.tr: Second, I answer that the point in this conspiracy which [τὰ•Θίνκα] was does not touch us at all. For those men wanted no ministry at all, and therefore proclaimed the whole people equally holy; this is what Hildus observed. But what in the same conspiracy is [Ϙιπκα] touches our enemies, whose sin is perhaps, by some degrees, graver than Korah's. Korah thrust himself in without a call; so the hierarchical men seized episcopal authority over the churches without a call. Korah disturbed discipline; these men have overthrown it. He barked; these men bite. He made himself equal to his superiors; these men make themselves superiors to their equals. He breathed no injury; these men fine, imprison, strip of goods and banish from their homes. He did not begrudge equal standing to the true ministers of God; these men concede to them plainly nothing at all, neither in the ministry, much less in the Church of God. And if sin under the Gospel is graver than sin under the Law, as the Apostle seems to teach (Heb. 10), then the hierarchical men must surely sin more gravely, who rise against the discipline instituted by Christ the Lord in the Gospel, than Korah's followers, who rose against the discipline of the Law instituted by Moses the servant of God. And those who rise against the ministers of discipline, endowed with equal authority, must surely be bound by equal guilt. Now the power has been given to the ministers of the Gospel (Rev. 11:5) that fire should come out of their mouth to devour their enemies, just as it once came to pass by Moses's declaration that fire went out from the face of Jehovah to consume Korah. Why not? Korah offered unsanctified fire at an altar not sanctified: do not the hierarchical men do the same? For they have thrust into the Church, without being called or sanctified for this office, a mountain burning with fire, that is, an episcopacy not sanctified by God (Rev. 3).

units.la: 3 Secunda macula quam disciplinæ reformatæ aspergunt adversarij Novatianismi, Donatismi, & Puritanismi denique est. Cartwrightum etenim velut hujus sæculi Novatum depingit Louis: & disciplinæ reformationé nostram Novatum sapere affirmat Bridgesius, qui sub prætextu simili puriotis reformationis, puritanismi doctor evasit: Denique Iohannes Whitgiftus puritanos nos & καλωμους merito appellat longis logis probare nititur. Atqui his alibi à nobis responsum abundè est: Iam igitur hoc tantum urgeo, iniquè eos qui Episcopatum aboleri volunt, homini eo æquiparari, qui præ amore Episcopatus, Ecclesiam Dei scidit. Nullo igitur colore hæredes Novati reformatores dicuntur, qui illud diruunt quod Novatus ædificabat, illud tollunt quod Novatus deperibat: annon Hierachici potius, quiscisma in Ecclesia majus, in causa eadem excitarunt: cum ob retinendum Episcopatum insaniant hodie, ut ille olim ob adipiscendum insaniebat. Similis nobis à Barloe Episcopo Lincolniensi iniuria fit: qui nos Theobatis successores esse vult, qui propter repulsam Episcopatus (quem nos è medio sublatum cupimus) Ecclesiam Hierosolymitanam primus corrupit, non (quod ille) Episcopalem authoritatem, ut post Aerius, impugnando, sed sermone adulterato, inquit Eusebius, id est doctrinâ falsâ.
units.tr: 3 The second stain that the adversaries cast upon the reformed discipline is that of Novatianism, Donatism, and Puritanism. Louis portrays Cartwright as a Novatus of this age, and Bridges affirms that our reformation savours of Novatus, since he, under the pretext of a similar reformation of purity, became a doctor of Puritanism. Finally, John Whitgift calls us Puritans and [καλωμους] with good reason, and labours to prove it in long arguments. But we have answered this abundantly elsewhere. So I press only this: it is unjust to equate those who wish Episcopacy abolished with that man who, out of love for Episcopacy, tore the Church of God. Reformers can therefore be called heirs of Novatus on no pretext, when they demolish what Novatus was building and remove what Novatus was destroying. Are not the prelatists rather those who have stirred up the greater schism in the Church, in the same cause? They now rage to keep Episcopacy as Novatus once raged to obtain it. A similar wrong is done us by Barlow, Bishop of Lincoln, who wants us to be successors of Theudas. Theudas, because his bid for Episcopacy was rejected (and we wish Episcopacy removed from the midst), was the first to corrupt the Church of Jerusalem. He did this not, as Aerius later did, by attacking episcopal authority, but with adulterated speech, says Eusebius, that is, with false doctrine.

units.la: 4 Tertia macula quam disciplinæ reformatæ aspergunt adversarij, Aerianismi est: ubi breviores jam esse volumus, quia de Aerio alius nobis dicendi locus futurus est. Accusatio hîc ipsa ita à Loo iustituitur. Sed quod potissimum reformationis genus in Anglia stabilire contendit Dæmon? non aliud quam quod inchoavit olim per Aerium & hac ætate in multis Europæ partibus ad incredibilem pietatis iacturam collocavit,
units.tr: 4 The third stain that the adversaries cast upon the reformed discipline is that of Arianism. Here we wish to be briefer, since there will be another place to speak of Aerius. The accusation itself is framed by Loo in this way: But what kind of reformation does the Demon chiefly strive to establish in England? Nothing other than what he began long ago through Aerius, and in this age has placed in many parts of Europe, to incredible loss of piety.

units.la: Primò, si disciplina in multis Europæ partibus hæretica & dæmoniaca sit, & Aeriana: quomodo eam legitimam agnoscit Dominus? quomodo eam argeuto comparat? aut quo ore Whitgiftus adversariique reliqui reformatas Ecclesias se non condemnare dicunt?
units.tr: First, if discipline is heretical and devilish in many parts of Europe, and Arian, how does the Lord acknowledge it as legitimate? How does He buy it with silver? Or with what face do Whitgift and the other adversaries say that they do not condemn the reformed Churches?

units.la: Secundò, disciplinam in multis Europæ partibus stabilitam Aerianam esse negat ipse Scultingius, cujus ista verba sunt; Aerij hæresis à præsenti hæresi differt: Ille enim per omnia Episcopum & presbyterum parem esse voluit, tum honore, & gradu, & ordine, adeoque presbyterum posse manus imponere, tum ordinare dixit: nostri hodie aliter: Superintendens enim Germaniæ manus solus imponit, & pastor apud Genevenses, quem Decannm classis vocant, imponit manus nus etiam solus. Quod si autem præses ordinis conservandi causa præsidens & manus reliquorum nomine imponens soluis, ab hæresi Arianâ salvat: abstersa penitus hæc macula est, cum nemo reformatorum sit cui hoc displiceat. Hæc enim ratione inità, negavit Arius, ipsam unius præsidentiam, quæ est ad ordinem conservandum, quam Ecclesiæ reformatæ precisè retinendam putant.
units.tr: Second, Scultetus himself denies that the discipline established in many parts of Europe is Arian. His words are these: The heresy of Aerius differs from the present heresy. For he wished the bishop and presbyter to be equal in all things, both in honour, rank and order, so that a presbyter could both lay on hands and ordain. Ours today are otherwise: for the superintendent of Germany lays on hands alone, and the minister among the Genevans, whom they call the Dean of the classis, lays on hands also alone. But if the president, for the sake of preserving order, presiding and laying on hands alone in the name of the rest, saves them from Arian heresy, then this stain is wiped away entirely, since there is no reformer who would object to it. For on this principle Arius denied the very presidency of one man, which serves to preserve order, and which the reformed Churches think must be strictly retained.

units.la: Tertiò, hoc in Aerio reprehendere tantùm videtur Fyldus, Willetus, & alij quòd Episcopi superioritatem ex iure humano tum introductam, non utilem Ecclesiæ existimaret, sed ausu temerario, præsenti Ecclesiæ consuetudini se opponere non dubitaret: nam alioquin manus imponendi authoritatem iure divino præsbytero competere, libenter largiuntur. Atque certè hanc viam inire eos necesse est, qui Episcopalem authoritatem iure tantùm humano, aut non divino immutabili pendere putant, & tamen reformatores Arianos esse volunt. Quid enim? non hi Arium accusare possunt, quòd iure divino Episcopum & presbyterum eundem censeret: cùm idem ipsi sentiant: in quo igitur ab Ario differunt? aut in quo tandem cum Ario peccamus nos? Nempe differunt illi ab Ario, quòd Episcopatum jure humano utilem censeant, quod ille negavit: peccabimus verò nos, quòd Ecclesiæ consuetudini Episcopatum tanquam utilem approbanti, sicut ille, obnitamur. Atqui inquam, qui in Ecclesijs reformatis vivunt, consuetudini Ecclesiæ parent: Episcopatum enim Anglicanum Ecclesiæ omnes reformatæ abjecerunt: quòd verò ad nos qui in Anglia vivimus, etsi consuetudini Anglicanæ obnitamur, non tamen cnm Ario consuetudini Ecclesiarum uniuersò: Imo cum majorem partem sequamur, ne quidem velut refractarij in Ecclesiæ consuetudinem omnino dici possumus.
units.tr: Third, Fulke, Willet and others seem to blame in Aerius only this: that he thought the superiority of the bishop, introduced by human law, was not useful to the Church, and with rash daring did not hesitate to oppose the present custom of the Church. For otherwise they willingly grant that the authority to lay on hands belongs to the presbyter by divine right. Certainly those must take this path who think that episcopal authority depends on human law alone, or at least not on immutable divine law, and yet want us to be called Arian reformers. For what? Can they not accuse Arius of thinking that bishop and presbyter were the same by divine right, when they themselves think the same? In what, then, do they differ from Arius? Or in what, finally, do we sin with Arius? They differ from Arius in that they judge Episcopacy, by human law, to be useful, which he denied. We would sin, however, by resisting the custom of the Church, which approves Episcopacy as useful, as he did. But I say that those who live in the reformed Churches obey the custom of the Church: all the reformed Churches have cast off the Anglican Episcopacy. As for us who live in England, although we resist the Anglican custom, we do not resist the custom of the Churches universally, as Arius did. Indeed, since we follow the greater part, we cannot even be called refractory toward the custom of the Church at all.

units.la: Quartò, quòd iure divino nullum inter Episcopum & presbyterum discrimen esse Arius dixit: in eo, vel Medina teste, antiquos patres adstipulatores habuit. Hinc Guilelmus Whitakerus noster ita. Michael Medina non dubitat affirmare hac in re hæreticum esse Hieronymum, & idem plane cum Ario sensisse. Sensit sane cum Ario Hyeronimus, quò minus curandum est, toties nobis obyci Arium ab insulsis bominibus. Si fuit hac in re hæreticus Arius, faciunt hæreses Hieronymum habuit, nec illum modò, sed alios etiam veteres patres, Græcos pariter & latinos, quemadmodum Medina confitetur. Videlne te insulsum hominem esse Whitakeri judicio, nisi Arium in Ecclesias reformatas objectare desistas? Simile etiam Iohannis Reynoldi judicium est: Cum enim Richardus Bancroftus pro concione ad crucem Paulinam, Puritanos hæreticos pronunciasset, quòd idem cum Ario sentirent: rogavit per literas Iohannem Reynoldum vir illustrissimus, & reginæ Consiliarius Franciscus Knollys, vt judicium suum de re tibi exponeret: Responsum verò Iohannis Reynoldi jam extat impressum: Arium defendit: Puritanos hæreseos crimine purgat.
units.tr: Fourth, that Arius said there is no distinction by divine right between bishop and presbyter: in this, Medina being witness, he had the ancient fathers as supporters.
