Hence our William Whitaker says: Michael Medina does not hesitate to affirm that in this matter Jerome is a heretic, and felt entirely the same as Arius. Jerome did indeed feel with Arius, and so much the less is it to be cared about that Arius is so often thrown at us by silly men. If Arius was a heretic in this matter, then the heresies Jerome held were not his alone, but those of other ancient fathers too, both Greek and Latin, as Medina confesses. Do you see yourself, by Whitaker's judgement, to be a silly man, unless you cease to object Arius to the reformed Churches? John Reynolds has a similar judgement. When Richard Bancroft, in a sermon at St Paul's Cross, had pronounced the Puritans heretics because they thought the same as Arius, that most illustrious man, Francis Knollys, councillor of the queen, asked John Reynolds by letter to set out his judgement on the matter. Reynolds's reply is now extant in print: he defends Arius and purges the Puritans of the crime of heresy.

units.la: {Cont. 4. q. 1, 3. f. 30 p. 105 t} gat: jure denique divino Episcopum & presbyterum eundem esse docet. Imo quid si Hadrianus Saravia ipse hac in parte nos tueatur? Certè diserta hæc illius verba sunt. Quod objici solet ex Hieronymo Hieronymi opinionem confirmantem cum Ærio, & verba Dei contrariam. Rursus. Error Hieronymi & Aerii ne scitur ex vocabulorum presbyteri & Episcopi, generalis & promiscuo usu, qui tunc temporis fuit. Quid igitur est? Non Aerij pudere nos decet, hac quidem in causa, nisi & ipsius Hieronymi etiam pudere lubet. Atque hæc ad abstergendam maculam tertiam.
units.tr: {Cont. 4. q. 1, 3. f. 30 p. 105 t} he lastly teaches that by divine right bishop and presbyter are the same. Indeed, what if Adrian Saravia himself defends us on this point? His words are certainly explicit: What is usually objected from Jerome, that Jerome's opinion agrees with Aerius and is contrary to the words of God. Again: The error of Jerome and Aerius is known from the general and promiscuous use of the words presbyter and bishop, which prevailed at that time. What then is the matter? It becomes us not to be ashamed of Aerius in this cause, unless we also wish to be ashamed of Jerome himself. And so much for wiping away the third stain.

units.la: § Quarta macula quam disciplinæ reformatæ aspergunt adversarij Acephalismi est: sic enim Georgius Dovvnamus. In quaque Diœcesi Clerici omnes, Episcopo suo diœcesano subjecti erant: Cui sic ad-do; A prima institutione Episcoporum, quæ Apostolorum temporibus fuit, ad nostram usque ætatem aliter nunquam fuit: sed clerici quicunque sic se a subjectione Orthodoxi Episcopi sui separabant sibi schismatici habebantur, et sic sub Episcopo nullo vivebant, vocabantur Acephali, sicut patet ex Burchardo lib. Decret. c. 126. qui Concilium Parisiense citat. Hoc illud est quod apud Gratianum hodie legitur. Nulla ratione Clerici aut sacerdotes habendi sunt, qui sub nullius Episcopi disciplina & providentia gubernantur: Tales enim acephalos, id est, sine capite, prisca Ecclesiæ con-suetudo nominavit,
units.tr: § The fourth stain that the adversaries cast upon the reformed discipline is that of Acephalism, as George Downame calls it. In every diocese all the clergy were subject to their diocesan bishop. To this I add: from the first institution of bishops, which was in the time of the Apostles, to our own age it was never otherwise. But whatever clergy separated themselves thus from the subjection of their orthodox bishop were regarded as schismatics, and, living under no bishop, were called Acephali, as appears from Burchard, Decretals book, chapter 126, who cites the Council of Paris. This is what is read today in Gratian: On no account are clergy or priests to be held who are governed under the discipline and providence of no bishop. For the ancient custom of the Church named such men acephali, that is, without head.

units.la: Primò, nomen ipsû Clericorum infertû, hanc (de qua Cõcilium Parisiense loquitur) consuetudinem priscam ultra non ascendere docet, quàm ad tempus, quo primò Clerus institutebatur: quod longè post tèporaApostolorû contigisse Historiæ omnes clamát: quid igitur? qui ante Clerum institutū vixerunt ἀκέφαλοι erât? liceat ita ἀκέφαλος esse: neque enim quicquam optatius, quam ut fœlicia tempora prima renoventur. Atque nonne vel hinc cernis Dovvname, Episcopi caput quando emersit? non Anglicanæ Episcopû dico, qui multa post sæcula exortus est, sed priscû illû Clericorû, id est iuvenû ad sacrum ecclesiæ ministerium destinatorum educatoré? Ne hic quidem Episcopus temporaApostolorum vidit quando sumptibus Ecclesiæ caruit, quibus scholæ alerentur: tantum abest ut Episcopus Anglicanus ea viderit, qui scholarum longa post tempora reditus ad sese attraxisse dicitur.
units.tr: First, the very name clergy that has been introduced shows that this ancient custom (of which the Council of Paris speaks) does not reach back further than the time when the clergy was first instituted. All histories proclaim that this happened long after the times of the Apostles. What then? Were those who lived before the clergy was instituted acephali [ἀκέφαλοι]? Let it be so, to be headless [ἀκέφαλος]: for nothing is more to be wished than that the happy times of the first age be renewed. And do you not see from this, Downame, when the head of the bishop emerged? I do not mean the Anglican bishop, who arose many centuries later, but that ancient bishop of the clergy, that is, the educator of the young men destined for the sacred ministry of the Church. Not even this bishop was seen in the times of the Apostles, when the Church lacked the funds with which schools were maintained. So far is it from being true that the Anglican bishop saw those times, who is said to have drawn the revenues of the schools to himself long afterwards.

units.la: Secundò, educationem clericalem, tum eandem fuisse quæ nunc Academica est. aduersariorum nonnulli confitentur. Priscæ hujus consuetudinis quam meminit Concilium Parisiense hic tantum sensus est: qui in aliquo Clero sub ejusdê rectore non educatur, Clericus is habendus non est, sic ut nec hodie Academicus, qui in nulla Academia educatus est. Quid hoc ad Episco. Diœcesanû? Episcopû Zanchius talé esse oportere docet, qualis rector in universitate ant in collegio præsidens; certe ejusmodi Episc. & non alios antiqua illa te-
units.tr: Secondly, some of our opponents admit that the clerical education of that time was the same as what is now academic. The only sense of that ancient custom, which the Council of Paris mentions, is this: whoever is not educated under some clergy under the direction of a rector is not to be regarded as a cleric, just as today no one is considered an academic who has not been educated in some university. What does this have to do with the diocesan bishop? Zanchius teaches that a bishop should be such as a rector presiding in a university or college; certainly such bishops, and not others, that ancient time

units.la: O 2 porā pora tulerunt,non extensive Dioecesanos,non intensive Anglicanos; ad morem etenim rectoris in universitate,praesidentis in Collegio, maiori parti suffragiorum subjecti erant.
units.tr: bore, not diocesan in extension, not Anglican in intension; for, according to the custom of a rector in a university or a president in a college, they were subject to the vote of the greater part.

units.la: Tertiò,quod in Clericis sub Episcopo non viventibus reprehendit Concilium Parisiense, ἀνωφηγίαι tantùmmodo amor est: sic ut illius iudicio, illa tantùm ἀνιφθαλία illicita fit, quæ anarchica est. Hoc perspexisse Cornelius Scultingius visus est: qui satis non habuit paritatem ministrorum Belgicam ἀνιφθαλίαν dicere, nisi etiam addidisset eam ἀνηρχίαν esse. Hoc sensu Episcopi hodie Anglicani ἀνιφθαλοι sunt: quia gubernationem presbyterialem excusserunt, & illos Ecclesiæ superiores rejecerunt, quibus ipsos parere ex Christi mandato decuit. Nonne illi ἀνιφθαλοι qui Christum pro capite minimè habent? quiq; capita Ecclesiarum sustulerunt, quibus eos subesse Christus iussit.
units.tr: Thirdly, what the Council of Paris reproves in clerics who do not live under a bishop is merely a love of lawlessness [ἀνωφηγία]. So in its judgment only that acephaly [ἀνιφθαλία] is unlawful which is anarchic. Cornelius Scultingius seems to have perceived this: he was not content to call the equality of the Belgic ministers an acephaly [ἀνιφθαλία], unless he had also added that it is anarchy [ἀνηρχία]. In this sense the Anglican bishops today are acephali [ἀνιφθαλοι], because they have cast off presbyterial government and rejected those superiors of the Church to whom they ought to submit by Christ's command. Are not those acephali who by no means hold Christ as their head, and who have removed the heads of the churches to whom Christ commanded them to be subject?

units.la: Quarto, ita jus canonicum. Acephalos dicit, id est sine capite: nullus enim eorum reperitur author à quo exorti sunt. Desumptum ab Ifiodoro hoc, qui eos Eutychianorum hæreticorum genus quoddam fuisse dicit: adversus quos Concilium secundum Hispalense coactum fuisse historiæ tradunt, anno vigesimo quarto Heraclij, sub Schisbuto rege. Hic ego ad Episcopos Anglicanos verbis Tertulliani clamo: Edant originem suam: nam si nullus justus saltem eorum author reperiatur, quidni ἀνιφθαλοι dicendi sunt? Num à Christi capite sunt? Nugæ. Num ab Apostolis? ad populum Phaleras. Num à prisca Ecclesia? Ne id quidem, nisi eam prisçam Ecclesiam dixeris, quâ primùm bestia exoriri cœpit: nam in illius utero Episcopatus Anglicanus primùm omnium formatus est velut Embryo quidam papatus illius quem postea peperit, sicuti ex Apocalypsi Iohannis suo loco demonstratur.
units.tr: Fourthly, canon law calls them acephali, that is, without a head, for no author of theirs can be found from whom they arose. This term is taken from Isidore, who says they were a certain kind of Eutychian heretics; against them the histories report that the Second Council of Seville was held in the twenty-fourth year of Heraclius, under King Sisebut. Here I cry out to the Anglican bishops in the words of Tertullian: "Let them produce their origin; for if no just author of theirs at least can be found, why should they not be called acephali?" Are they from the head of Christ? Nonsense. From the Apostles? Fine trappings for the crowd. From the ancient Church? Not even that, unless you mean that ancient Church in which the beast first began to arise; for in its womb the Anglican episcopate was first of all formed, like a certain embryo of that papacy which it afterwards brought forth, as is shown in its place from the Apocalypse of John.

units.la: Quintò, non est quòd tua calumnia ista magis nos Dolname commoveat,quàm tete commovet Nicolai Sanderi similis illa, !qui & te ἀκλησιος & ἀνιφθαλον vocat, quòd non sub Papa, suo (ut putat) Ecclesiæ capite vivas. Narrat Carolus Sigonius Ravennam olim ἀνιφθαλον dictam, quòd imperium Romanum & Papale excutere aniza fit: Hujusmodi ἀνιφθαλίας te pudebit Dolname? Nostra autem alia non est: cum illicitum illud Episcopale regimen fit,quod à nostris cervicibus propulsare, omni modo legitimo nitimur. At hoc ἀνιφθαλια dum tu accusas,in Papistarum caltra apertè transfugis: sic etinim Scultingius Calvinismos omnes qui Superintendentes minimè habent, ἀνιφθαλια vocat. Quâ ratione verò? Quis,inquit,in Synodis pares omnes minis- stros & equales faciunt. At præsidente in Synodis habent, eádem cum Superintendente prærogativa fruentem. Cur igitur ἀνιφθαλοι Calviniani; qui Superintendentes agnoscunt non item? cum in sola temporis perpetuitate differentia sit? Ita dilutum est quod de reformatæ disciplinæ Acephalismo dicitur.
units.tr: Fifthly, there is no reason why this calumny of yours should move us about Downame more than Nicolas Sander's similar one moves you, who calls you both acleisios [ἀκλησιος] and acephalos [ἀνιφθαλον], because you do not live under the Pope, the head of the Church, as he thinks. Carolus Sigonius relates that Ravenna was once called acephalous, because it was eager to shake off the Roman and Papal empire. Will you be ashamed of such acephaly, Downame? Our case is no different, since we strive by every lawful means to drive from our necks that illicit episcopal government. But while you accuse this acephaly, you openly desert to the camp of the Papists; for thus Scultingius calls all the Calvinists who by no means have superintendents acephali. And on what ground? "Who," he says, "make all ministers in synods equal and alike?" But the president in synods enjoys the same prerogative as the superintendent. Why then are the Calvinists who acknowledge superintendents not acephali, when the only difference is the permanence of the office? Thus what is said of the acephalism of the reformed discipline is answered.

units.la: 6 Quinta macula, quam disciplinæ reformatæ aspergunt adversarij Anabaptismi est: Sic enim Iohannes Whitgiftus, Anabaptismus in Ecclesia Anglicana magnopere formidandus est, imò Anabaptismum Admonitores fere apertè profitentur. At primò {a}quàm hic sibilus serpentinus sit, vel ex eo conjicere promptum, quòd teste Calvino doctrina ipsa reformata in Gallia olim eâdem contumeliâ impetebatur, ubi & Evangelium Anabaptismus,& ejusdem Martyres & confessores Anabaptistæ appellabantur. Quòd si verò Calvini fides apud adversarios vacillet: Thomæ tamen Bilsono suo credendum illis est. Is citat Bezam,non eis credendum esse affirmantem, qui doctores Evangelicos cum Anabaptistis consociant: in quo & Anabaptismum doctrinæ ipsi à Papistis objectum fatetur: & Bezam approbando, nos etiam approbat, sive in doctrina,sive in disciplina,quid enim nos alind quàm Bezâ sapimus, quem etiam tanquam magistrum sequi, accusamur.
units.tr: 6 The fifth stain which our opponents smear upon the reformed discipline is Anabaptism. For so John Whitgift says: Anabaptism is greatly to be feared in the Church of England; indeed the Admonitioners almost openly profess Anabaptism. But first, how serpentine this hiss is may easily be gathered from this: that, as Calvin testifies, the reformed doctrine itself was once assailed with the same insult in France, where the Gospel too was called Anabaptism, and its martyrs and confessors were called Anabaptists. But if Calvin's authority wavers with our opponents, they must still believe their own Thomas Bilson. He cites Beza, affirming that those who associate evangelical teachers with the Anabaptists are not to be believed; in which he also confesses that Anabaptism is objected to the doctrine itself by the Papists; and in approving Beza he also approves us, both in doctrine and in discipline. For what else do we think than Beza does, whom we are accused of following even as a master?

units.la: Secundò, nemo magis contra Anabaptistas depugnavit,quam ipse Calvinus: id quod Bancroftus ipse agnoscit: supra omnem fidem igitur est, eum in disciplina constituenda Anabaptistam reperiri.
units.tr: Secondly, no one fought more strongly against the Anabaptists than Calvin himself, as Bancroft himself acknowledges. Beyond all belief, then, is it that he should be found an Anabaptist in constituting discipline.

units.la: Tertiò, adeo colore omni hîc adversarij destituuntur,ut tanquam falsi illi testes qui Christum Dominum accusarunt, sibi mutuò contradicant.Eisdem cum Anabaptistis vestigijs insistimus(inquit Whitgiftus) eundem malleum terimus, eundem cursum tenemus: Atqui contra Iohan. Bridgesius. Non hoc eo dico, quasi reformatores Anabaptismum redolerent, aut Anabaptismo consulto faverent. Absit, Æqualitas inter ministros Cartwrighti,Anabaptisticum somnium est: Sic Richardus Bancroftus. At contra Whitgiftus: Non eos accuso de doctrina Anabaptistarum.
units.tr: Thirdly, our opponents are so wholly destitute of any colour here that, like those false witnesses who accused the Lord Christ, they contradict one another. "We tread the same path as the Anabaptists," says Whitgift, "we wear down the same hammer, we keep the same course." And yet against this, John Bridges: "I do not say this as if the reformers smelt of Anabaptism, or deliberately favoured Anabaptism. Far from it. Equality among Cartwright's ministers is an Anabaptist dream." So Richard Bancroft. But on the contrary Whitgift: "I do not accuse them of the doctrine of the Anabaptists."

units.la: Quartò, Postquam Whitgiftus nos cum Donatistis comparasset, ita ad postremum se excusat. Non loquor de omnibus eorum opinionibus,sed de eis in quibus hi nostri eis similes esse videntur. Similia, uti nostris,non conveniunt in omnibus, satis est si in eis conveniant in quibus comparantur. At hâc nos excusatione freti & Episcopos ipsos Anabaptismi accusare merito possumus: nam & seniores impugnant eisdem argumentis Anabaptistæ, quibus Hierarchici: ut ex Iohanne Smitho liquet: & quoddam genus Anabaptistarum, Episcopos habere quosdam,harum regionum lippis & tonsoribus notissimum est.
units.tr: Fourthly, after Whitgift had compared us with the Donatists, he finally excuses himself thus: "I do not speak of all their opinions, but of those in which our people seem to be like them. Similar things, like ours, do not agree in all respects; it is enough if they agree in those respects in which they are compared." But relying on this very excuse, we too may rightly accuse the bishops themselves of Anabaptism: for the elders attack the hierarchists with the same arguments that the Anabaptists use, as is clear from John Smyth; and that a certain kind of Anabaptists have certain bishops is well known to the bleary-eyed and the barbers of these regions.

units.la: Quintò, æqualitas Anabaptistarum Anarchica est: nullum etenim illi regimen admittunt,neque vel pastores apud illos authoritatem ullum exercent: æqualitas autem ministrorum quam nos tuemur, Aristocratica est, & optimam regiminis formam, Aristocraticam agnoscunt omnes: nos etiam eam esse ipsam dicimus, quam ipse Christus pro regenda Ecclesiâ suâ & mandavit & commendavit. Imò nec Dollnamo assentiri possim,qui Democraticam illam quam exercent Separatores Democratici,Anabaptisticam esse dicit.Quantum etenim inter Democraticam & Anarchiam intervallum ? Cum Anabaptista primi pili homine mihi aliquando colloqui contigit: à quo didici tam exolum sectæ suæ Seniorum in Ecclesia nomen esse, atque in republica magistratus. At Seniorum officium agnoscunt. SeparatoSeperatores Democratici: qui cum Anabaptistæ dici nequeant, quantò minùs nos, quos per contemptum, consistoriales appellare consuescunt? Atque ita macula ista quinta eluitur, nullo negotio.
units.tr: Fifthly, the equality of the Anabaptists is anarchic: for they admit no government, and their pastors exercise no authority among them. But the equality of ministers which we defend is aristocratic, and all acknowledge aristocracy to be the best form of government; we too say that it is precisely the form which Christ himself both commanded and commended for governing his Church. Indeed I cannot even agree with Downame, who says that the democratic form practised by the Democratic Separatists is Anabaptist. For how great is the gap between democracy and anarchy? When I once happened to talk with a leading man among the Anabaptists, I learned from him that the name of Elders in their sect's Church is as empty a title as that of the magistrate in the commonwealth. But they acknowledge the office of Elders. The Democratic Separatists, who cannot be called Anabaptists, how much less are we, whom they are accustomed to call Consistorians by way of contempt? And thus this fifth stain is washed away with no trouble at all.

units.la: 7 Sexta & ultima papismi est. Ain vero inquis, Anabaptismi & Papismi simul disciplinam reformatam Hierarchicos insimulare? Certè: sic enim Ioh.Whitgiftius.Isti homines cum Papistis plane se coniungunt. O nos ergo miseros qui in Scyllam & Charybdin simul idque uno naufragio incidimus. O miseras etiam reformatas Ecclefias quæ horrendum monstrum ex tam contrarijs religionibus consarcinatum, velut illam simplicem à Christo Iesu institutam disciplinam exosculantur. Certè vel ab illa anabaptismi, vel ab hac papismi accusatione abstinuisse se Whitgiftium, consultissimum fuerat: jam disciplinæ reformatæ utrumque simul impingendo, occasionem lectori præbet, illa Salomonis in memoriam revocare: Eccles. 10. 13. prioremque cum anabaptistis similitudinem sultitiæ, hanc posteriorem cum papistis, insaniæ deputare. Atque sanè non intelligere, nos nulla alia in Hierarchicis quàm Papistica impugnare, nefcire est,& cæcutire: qui verò Papistica duntaxat impugnant, eos pro Papistis habere, annon hoc est prorsus insanire? Ex adverso, colore nullo à Papismi affinitate Hierarchicos se purgare posse, vel ipse Georgius Downamus m onstrat:qui ad objectionem de Papismo, hoc tantum respondet alibi, honestius se Episcopos defendentem cum Bellarmino, quàm nos eosdem impugnantes, cum Aerio conspirare. At alibi tamen inquies, differentiam allegat, nempe quòd Papistæ Episcopum jure divino immutabilem tueantur, cum Hierarchici Anglicani ita jure divino Episcopum stabiliant, ut tamen mutabilem consiteantur.
units.tr: 7 The sixth and last is Papism. "What, really?" you say. "Do you charge the hierarchists at once with Anabaptism and with Papism?" Certainly: for so John Whitgift says, "These men plainly join themselves with the Papists." O us wretches, then, who have fallen at once into Scylla and Charybdis, and in one shipwreck! O wretched also the reformed Churches, which embrace a horrible monster patched together from such contrary religions, as if it were that simple discipline instituted by Christ Jesus! Certainly it would have been most prudent for Whitgift to abstain from one or the other accusation, Anabaptism or Papism; by hurling both at once against the reformed discipline he gives the reader occasion to recall that saying of Solomon, Eccles. 10.13, and to count the former resemblance to the Anabaptists as folly, the latter to the Papists as madness. And indeed, not to understand that we attack nothing in the hierarchists except what is Papistical is to be ignorant and blind; but to regard those who attack only what is Papistical as Papists, is not this utterly to rave? On the other hand, that the hierarchists can by no means clear themselves of affinity with Papism is shown by George Downame himself, who, answering the objection about Papism, says only this elsewhere: that he defends the bishops more honourably with Bellarmine than we who attack them conspire with Aerius. But elsewhere, you will say, he alleges a difference: namely, that the Papists defend the bishop as unchangeable by divine right, whereas the Anglican hierarchists establish the bishop by divine right in such a way that they nevertheless confess him to be changeable.

units.la: At parum sibi constans in jure Episcopi mutabili Georgius Downamus est: & juris divini ullâ mutabilitatem somniare delirare est,ut suo loco demonstrabitur: & Thomas Bilsonus, Hadrianus Saravia, pluresqs alij Episcopatum jure divino imutabilem esse opinantur. Differimus tamen à Papistis, dicit Saravia, cujus ista verba sunt: Romanæ jactantiæ est, quod se Petri & Pauli successores tenem, unus Romanus Episcopus gloriatur. Hunc Romanæ Ecclesiæ errorem frustra D. Beza allegare videtur, contra nos, qui cum veteribus credimus, omnes Catholicos Episcopos successores Petri aut Pauli esse, æque atque Romanus ullus unquam fuit, aut ostitui potuit Episcopus. Atqui inquam defensione ista, parte tantum corporis non toto corpore è cœno Papistico emersistis, ut nos emersimus, qui non omnes Episcopos solum, sed & omnes ministros, Apostolorum parili modo successores esse dicimus. Ipsum jugulum Antichristi hoc dogmate Beza dissecat: vestro autem parum læditur: ita enim disputabitur. Episcopos solos præ cæteris ministris, Apostolis successisse dicitis: bene se habet: hinc etenim sequetur, sicut Petrus inter Apostolos,ita & unum quendam inter Episcopos præsidere oportere: qui nonne per omnem antiquitatem Romanus quasso fuit? Atque ut argumentis vestris Papa, ita & nullis Anglicanus Episcopus
units.tr: But Georgius Downamus is himself inconsistent about the mutability of the bishop's office, and to dream of any mutability in divine right is folly, as will be shown in its place. Thomas Bilson, Hadrianus Saravia and several others hold that episcopacy is unchangeable by divine right. Saravia says, "We differ from the Papists," and his words are these: "It is Roman boasting that they are the successors of Peter and Paul; one Roman bishop glories in it. D. Beza seems to cite this error of the Roman Church in vain against us, who with the ancients believe that all Catholic bishops are successors of Peter or of Paul, just as much as any Roman bishop ever was or could have been." But I say, with that defence you have come out of the Papist mire only in part, not in whole, as we have come out, who say that not only the bishops but all ministers alike are successors of the Apostles. Beza cuts the throat of Antichrist with this doctrine, but your position is hardly harmed by it. For the argument runs thus: you say that bishops alone, before other ministers, succeeded the Apostles. Very well: from this it will follow that, just as Peter presided among the Apostles, so one man must preside among the bishops. Has not this man been the Roman pope throughout all antiquity? And so, by your arguments, the English bishop is as much a pope as the Papists' own.

units.la: Lib.1 p.7.
units.tr: Lib.1 p.7.

units.la: De Triplic. Episcopus quàm Papisticis stabilitur: quod objectum Georgio Downa me no cum esset, non tam ille loco supra commemorato refutavit, quàm id honestè fieri posse disputavit. Confugiet scio ad Augustini illud: Non debet ovis pellem suam deponere, quod ea se lupus aliquando contegat. Quasi pellis ovina sit, non lupina, quam à Papistis mutuati estis? Christus ipse judex esto. Certè tepidam illam in Anglia pellem, quam à Papistis Angelus Angliæ est mutuatus, adeò ille in Angliæ tamen Laodicea abominatur, ut optet: Utinam esses frigidus potius: id est, utrinam Hierarchici Anglicani Papistas potius se esse aperte prositerentur. Non igitur vestra, sed nostra, illa Augustini defensio est: quod papistas aliquando, ut Paulus poetas & ethnicos, allegemus, non tamen papisticis principiis initimur, prout Hierarchici calumniatur. Papistæ fundamentis inniuntur, puritani. Sic Bancrofius: & a papistis argumenta mutuantur: papisticis argumentis niuntur: inquit Bilgel. Reformatores sic ut Ejus voce in ei sub habitu laico ingeniose liceat. Ita denique; Johannes Whitgiftus: Admonitorum & Cartwrighti argumenta papistica sunt. Quod de principiis papisticis dicitur calumnia est? Num Sathanæ regnum in papatu adeò divisum, ut nobis nihil alimentum mutuantur, quàm ejusdem demolitionem, principia submi-nistret? Quòd verò argumenta contra se nonnunquam ministret, id veritatis quàm tuetur inclusam firmitatè potius, quàm cum papistis affinitatem aliquam prodit. Quidni à Philistæis arca repetatur? Quidni in capite de resurrectione cum Pharisæis conspiret Paulus? Quidni denique (quod Augustinus) ovis suam pellem à lupo repostulet? Mutuatur Iohannes Reynoldus nostrer argumenta, nunc à Bellarmino contra Medinam, nunc à Medina contra Bellarminum, cujus facti fui rationem ita reddit: Ut Hannibal apud Ennium sitante Cicerone, cohortans suos pronuntiat: Hostem qui ferit mihi Cartha-ginensis erit, quisquis erit: ita quisquis erit qui veritatem d fendit, eorum refutarit, mihi ex numero Protestantium erit. Trot Tyrias sive mihi nullo discrimine agitur. Omninò rectè hoc: quòd etenim ad veritatem, inter papistas & protestantes ecclesiæ nullum est: nulla hæresis unquam fuit, quæ principia quædam vera non retinuerit. verùm ea hæreseos minimè sunt, sed veritatis. Ita quando cum Papistis in principiis quibusdam veris convenimus, principia tamen à papistis non mutuamur, quia ea papistica non sunt. At ludos facitis papistis saltem (cisputat Whitgiftus) dum contentiones in Ecclesia excitantes quibus illi lætantur, quæ in rem suam vertunt: Quasi contentione intra castra oberrant, lætentur hostes de earum fortitudine, qui in vallo fortiter nimicant, ac non de illis fœderatis potiùs, qui intra vallum de litescentes, ipsorum partes promovent. Ij verò in nostris castris Anglicanis Hierarchici sunt: qui & contentionem excitarunt, & pro regimine papisticâ excitarunt, in quâ non leviter gaudent papistæ & lætantur: catholi à cau-sam In Whitgift, in libro adversus Cartwrightum suo tutaus est, ut it Guildelinus Reynoldus Iesuita, Ioannis Reynoldi uterinus frater: Colloquium Hamptonienſe a Barloo Episcopo Lincolnienſi editum in sermonem Gallicum Pariſienses converterunt: librum q; nuper Thomae Bilſoni excuderunt denuo, ut pro se maximè facientem. In Hadriano Saravia & Matheo Sutclivio Episcoporum in civilibus authoritatem defendentibus, exultat & triumphat Gretzerus Iesuita: Cornelij Scultingij ista sunt. Defensio disciplinae Ecclesiasticae in Anglia, nostrae etiam Catholicae disciplinae propugnationem continet: cum Anglo-calvinistae nobiscum fere in causa disciplinae conveniant: quem librum obtare Latine extare, sicut in Anglia Anglicè prostat. Rursus: Puritani in plenis comitijs, admonitiones suas porrexerunt, reformationem & correctionem variam Ecclesiarum Anglicanarum postulantes. Admonitionibus istis respondit Ioannes Whitgiftus: & adversus Whitgiftum replicat Cartwrightus, alteramque Whitgifti defensionem secunda replica convellit. Unde prodierunt in Anglia duo egregij & utiles libri pro politeia & disciplina nostra, editi a primarijs viris, hujus nostrae disciplinae suis patronis. Primus liber inscribitur, Defensio disciplinae Ecclesiasticae per Ioannem Whitgiftum; alter vocatur Examen praetensae disciplinae (intelligit Survegium Ricardi Bancrofti) Londini, anno 1593, ut adnotat Stapletonus in Antidotis in Acta sol. 409. Si Latine ista extarent profecto ad confutationem Puritanorum & harum Synodorum, vix quicquam amplius desideraremus. Postremo, Anglo-calvinistae de Consistoriali disciplina & politeia und nobiscum judicant: ipsa pro nostra veteri disciplina condensant patrum testimonia. Ita de quibus laetantur papistae, quique papistis ludos faciunt quae denique causa papistas uicinos habet, jam liquidè constat. Proclamari fecit Themistocles, aedes suas commodas esse, quia bonum vicinum habuerant: nos ex adverso Hierarchiam Anglicanam suspicari debemus, quòd Hierarchiae papisticae pessimae, non solùm vicina, sed etiam contigua sit. Atque ita tandem abstersis maculis universis, splendore proprio, disciplina reformata nitescit.
units.tr: On the threefold matter: how the bishop is established more by Papist principles than by ours. Since this objection was made to George Downame, he did not so much refute it in the passage cited above as argue that it could honestly be done. I know he will take refuge in the saying of Augustine: "A sheep should not put off its skin because a wolf sometimes covers itself with it." As if it were a sheep's skin and not a wolf's, which you have borrowed from the Papists! Let Christ himself be judge. Certainly that lukewarm skin which the "Angel of England" borrowed from the Papists is so detested by him in the Laodicea of England that he wishes: "Would that you were cold rather": that is, would that the English prelates openly professed themselves Papists rather. Therefore the defence of Augustine is not yours but ours: that we sometimes cite Papists, as Paul cited poets and heathens, yet we do not lean on Papist principles, as the prelates slander us. The Papists rest on foundations; the Puritans rest on... Thus Bancroft: "and they borrow arguments from the Papists; they rest on Papist arguments," says Bilson. The reformers, as far as it is lawful for them to speak in her voice under a layman's guise, act cleverly. Finally, John Whitgift: "The arguments of the Admonitioners and of Cartwright are Papist." Is it slander to say this of Papist principles? Is Satan's kingdom in the papacy so divided that it supplies us with no nourishment except principles for its own demolition? That it sometimes furnishes arguments against itself shows rather the firmness of the truth it defends than any kinship with the Papists. Why should the ark not be recovered from the Philistines? Why should Paul not agree with the Pharisees on the chapter about the resurrection? Why should the sheep not reclaim its skin from the wolf, as Augustine says? John Reynolds borrows our arguments, now from Bellarmine against Medina, now from Medina against Bellarmine, and gives the reason for this in these words, as Hannibal in Ennius, with Cicero listening, encourages his men and declares: "Whoever strikes the enemy will be a Carthaginian, whoever he is; so whoever defends the truth and refutes them will be, to me, one of the Protestants, whoever he is." Here the matter is at stake with no distinction. Quite rightly so: for in truth there is no church, between Papists and Protestants, and no heresy has ever existed that did not retain some true principles. But these are not marks of heresy but of truth. So when we agree with the Papists on certain true principles, we do not borrow those principles from the Papists, because they are not Papist principles. "But you at least make sport for the Papists," says Whitgift, "while you stir up contentions in the Church, in which they rejoice and which they turn to their own advantage." As if, when strife breaks out inside the camp, the enemy rejoiced at its strength, rather than at those allies who, hidden inside the rampart, advance their cause, while the enemy fights bravely outside the wall. But these are the English prelates in our Anglican camp, who have both stirred up the contention and, for the sake of Papist government, stirred it up, in which the Papists rejoice and exult not lightly. The Catholics defend their cause in Whitgift's book against Cartwright, as Guillelmus Reynoldus the Jesuit, the uterine brother of John Reynolds, shows. The Parisians have translated into French the Conference at Hampton, edited by Barlow, Bishop of Lincoln, and have reprinted Thomas Bilson's book, since it serves their cause greatly. Over Hadrianus Saravia and Matthew Sutcliffe, who defend the authority of bishops in civil matters, the Jesuit Gretser exults and triumphs. These are the words of Cornelius Schultingius: "The Defence of Ecclesiastical Discipline in England also contains a defence of our Catholic discipline, since the Anglo-Calvinists agree with us almost entirely on the question of discipline; I wish this book existed in Latin as it circulates in English." Again: the Puritans presented their Admonitions to Parliament, demanding various reformation and correction of the English Churches. John Whitgift answered these Admonitions, and Cartwright replied against Whitgift, and by a second reply overthrew Whitgift's second defence. From this there came forth in England two excellent and useful books on our polity and discipline, published by leading men, the patrons of our discipline. The first book is entitled The Defence of Ecclesiastical Discipline by John Whitgift; the other is called The Examination of the Pretended Discipline (meaning Richard Bancroft's Survey), London, 1593, as Stapleton notes in his Antidotes, on Acts 409. If these were available in Latin, we would hardly need anything more to refute the Puritans and these Synods. Last, the Anglo-Calvinists judge with us concerning consistorial discipline and polity, and they gather the testimonies of the Fathers in support of our old discipline. Thus it is now clear what it is that the Papists rejoice in, who make sport of them, and why the Papists have such neighbours. Themistocles had it proclaimed that his house was a good one because he had a good neighbour; so we, conversely, ought to suspect that the English hierarchy is not only near to, but even contiguous with, the most wicked papal hierarchy. And so, at last, with all stains wiped away, reformed discipline shines with its own splendour.

units.la: CAP. 34. Ex praemissis infert, primò Magistratuum esse disciplinam restituere.
units.tr: CAP. 34. From the foregoing he infers, first, that it is the duty of the magistrates to restore discipline.

units.la: Quod si verò disciplina reformata adeò splendida sit, adeòprae-adeo necessaria: quis non videt in officio magistratibus esse ut ex veterno excitati, de eâdem restituendâ serìò cogitêt? Huius officij Edwardum sextum Martinus Bucerus ita admonuit, ut Sculingius dixerit, Eum Anglo-calvinistas exagitasse, qui Puritanis meliores sunt. Quod si verò Episcopale regimen sub Edwardo sexto magistratui reformandum erat, quantò nunc magis? quando minimè omnium audiendus Hosius est, qui Ecclesiae reformationem ad magistratum minimè pertinere dicit, sed ad Episcopos? Deploranda etenim expe-rientia zientiâ jam satis didicimus, Episcopos eos ipsos esse, quos maximè reformari oportet: cujus intuitu, in medijs papismi tenebris, qui oculatiores extiterunt, magistratus semper opem implorabant. Nam & Theodoricus à Nyem ad status Ecclesiastici reformationé Imperatoré advocavit: ut Franciscus Zabarellus Imperatoris esse descripsit concilium contra Papam cogere, ne Ecclesia periclitaretur: & Iohannes Picus denique Maximilianum Imperatorem cohortatus est, ut pro impositio sibi munere, curam Ecclesiæ reformandæ in se suscieperet. Atque hæc ultima, errorem etiam illum perstringunt, qui illo errore pontificio jam diu explosó, vel per supinam negligentiam, vel per rerum divinarum contemptum, apud Evangelicos ipsos succrevit, haud minus, quàm ille, Ecclesiæ Dei perniciosus. Quanquâ etenim reformandi jus suum jam principes probè sciant: officio tamè probè se defunctos putant, si in Episcopos quos pios putant à se delectos, totam Ecclesiæ reformandæ curam ablegent. Non ita olim Ioas Rex, qui cunctantes sacerdotes non solùm increpat dicens: Quare non restauratis domum Dei? 2. Reg. 12. 7. verùm & ejusdem restaurandæ curam in seipsum recipit. Ita Leo Episcopus ad Leonem imperatorem; Debes imperator incunctanter advertere, regiam potestatem non solum ad mundi regimen, sed maximè ad Ecclesiæ præsidium tibi collatam. Ex quibus apparet, haud magis Ecclesiæ curam ad alios demandandam esse, quàm reipublicæ. Similiter Isidorus: Cognoscent principes sæculi, Deo debere se rationem reddere, propter Ecclesiam quam à Deo tuendam suscipiunt. Nam sive servetur pax & disciplina Ecclesiæ, sive solvatur: ille rationem ab eis exiget, qui eorum potestati Ecclesiam suam credidit. Ita Augustinus: Miran-tur quia commoventur potestates Christianæ contra àssipatores Ecclesiæ destructos: Sed si non commoverentur, quomodo rationem redderent de imperio suo Deo? Intendat charitas vestra quid dicam, quia hoc ad reges sæculi pertinet, scilicet Christianos, ut temporibus suis semper velint pacatam Ecclesiam matrem suam habere, unde spiritualiter nati sunt. Ostendunt hæc rationem principi de rebus Ecclesiasticis perinde ac civilibus Deo reddendam: per se igitur, ac non per Episcopos earum reformatio correctioque curanda est. Sed nihil hinc inquies reformationi quam postulamus nostræ accrescit; quam ut arceant principes, Lous; ut suprimant, extirpentque, Iohannes Whitgiftus cohortatur: Sed nullis illi rationibus nituntur, quàm quibus ante responsum est: Synedrium Papatu deterius est, inquit Lous & quæ Zuinglius contra Anabaptistas, ea omnia condensat Whitgiftus, ut animos magistratuum concitet adversus disciplinam illam, quæ tantopere à Papali tyrannide distat, & ab Anabaptistica confusione, quantopere Christus ab Antichristo, & apum alvearia (ut cum Tertulliano loquar) à vesparum favis differunt. Atque qui hisce auscultant principes, vereor ne in totius Ecclesiæ jacturam, in Theodosij errorem incidant: qui Imperator cæteroquin piissimus erat. Admonent Episcopi, ut tyrannidem Flaviani compesceret. iniquum enim esse, ut spirituales tyrannides
units.tr: But if reformed discipline is so splendid and so very necessary, who does not see that it is the duty of magistrates to rouse themselves from their slumber and give serious thought to restoring it? Martin Bucer admonished Edward VI of this duty so strongly that Sculingius said he had harassed the Anglo-Calvinists, who are better than the Puritans. But if the episcopal government under Edward VI had to be reformed by the magistrate, how much more must it be done now, when Hosius is by no means to be heard, who says that the reformation of the Church does not pertain to the magistrate at all but to the bishops? For we have learned well enough from deplorable experience that the bishops themselves are the very men who most need to be reformed. Because of them, in the midst of the darkness of popery, those who were more clear-sighted always implored the help of the magistrate. For Theodoric of Niem called upon the Emperor for the reformation of the ecclesiastical estate; Francis Zabarella described it as the Emperor's business to convene a council against the Pope, lest the Church be endangered; and John Pico at last exhorted the Emperor Maximilian to take upon himself, as the office laid on him, the care of reforming the Church. And this last point also strikes at that error which, now that the papal error has long been exploded, has grown up among the Evangelicals themselves, through either supine negligence or contempt for divine things, and is no less ruinous to the Church of God than that one. For although princes now know well their own right to reform, they think they have discharged their duty if they hand over the whole care of reforming the Church to bishops whom they regard as pious and have chosen. This was not so in the past. Joash the king not only rebuked the hesitant priests, saying Why do you not repair the house of God? (2 Kings 12.7), but also took upon himself the care of repairing it. So Leo, bishop, wrote to Leo the emperor: You ought, Emperor, to attend without delay that royal power has been conferred on you not only for the government of the world but chiefly for the protection of the Church. From these things it appears that the care of the Church is no more to be committed to others than the care of the commonwealth. Likewise Isidore: The princes of the world will know that they must render an account to God on account of the Church, which they undertake to protect for God. For whether the peace and discipline of the Church is preserved or broken, he will demand an account from those who entrusted his Church to their power. So Augustine: They marvel that the Christian powers are stirred against the destroyers of the Church. But if they were not stirred, how would they render account to God for their rule? Let your charity attend to what I say, because it pertains to the kings of the world, namely the Christians, that in their times they always wish their mother, from whom they were spiritually born, to have the Church at peace. These passages show that a prince must render account to God for ecclesiastical affairs just as for civil ones; therefore the reformation and correction of the Church must be looked after by the prince himself, and not through bishops. But you will say that nothing hence accrues to the reformation we demand, which Lous urges princes to keep off, and John Whitgift to suppress and root out. But they rest on no arguments other than those already answered: the Synedrion is worse than the Papacy, says Lous; and whatever Zwingli said against the Anabaptists, all that Whitgift gathers together, in order to stir the minds of magistrates against that discipline which differs from papal tyranny as much as Christ differs from Antichrist, and from Anabaptist confusion as much as beehives differ from the honeycombs of wasps (to use the words of Tertullian). And I fear that princes who listen to these men may fall, to the loss of the whole Church, into the error of Theodosius, who was otherwise a most pious emperor. The bishops admonished him to restrain the tyranny of Flavian, for it was unjust that he should suffer spiritual tyrannies

units.la: Cato’sg. Iestin. m.p. 1857. nos ferret in Ecclesia grassantes illè, qui civiles à cervicibus reipub-licæ propulsaverat. Sed cùm respondisset ille, se Flaviani patrocini-um suscepisse, Flavi ini causam, suam causam esse, quæ objiciebān-tur Flaviano, sibi etiam objecta esse: contristatus est eos quos Letificare, letiscavit autem eos, quos contristare debuit. Horreo dictum: sed quid quibusdam in Ecclesiis jam hodie geritur, notius est, quàm ut dici sit necesse. Dolenda interim hæc humana infirmitas est; quòd qui tyrannos in republica facilè internoscunt, ij tyrannos in Ecclesia spirituales nonnisi seriùs dignoscant: sed Theodesij ad instar, hanc tyrannidem probari sibi & demonstrari petunt, probatam verò & demonstratam credere non possunt. Atque ut ad tyrannidem Episcopalem dignoscendam tardi, ita ad luxum, pompam, superbiamque coercendam ita ferè negligentes sunt, ut locum hodie ferè ea habeant, quæ de sæculi sui temporibus Bossardus conquestus est. Scio quidem deiecturos, inquit, super hisce rebus posteros, & Ecclesiam in talem turbationem delabi, aut dilapsam durare tandiu posse. Sed hæc plaga fuit a Deo missa, quæ Ecclesiastico ordini ob oculos considerandum exhi-beret pomposum statum & luxum quem usurpabant, sed plures nullam ejus rei habebant curam aut rationem. Sed principes sæculares à quibus bona primum venere ad Ecclesiam, nihil aliud quam ridebant & ludebant, eo tempore quo condebam hæc Chronica, anno salutis 1500. Siccine hac tempestate fieri decet? Audiant Principes Christum Regem regum: Apoc. 19. non ob nihilum se indigitasse, sed ut notum Regibus faceret, non illos, sed illum in Ecclesia Regem supremum esse, reges verò nonnisi illius servos esse sic ut ejus dicto audientes esse debeant, in politeia Ecclesiæ illâ, quam fovendam, non arcendam; propugnandam, non extirpandam; eorum curæ fideique commisit. Nam hæc verò Laodiceæ [illegible, ~6 letters] Anglicana est; Imò cùm per eam stet, ut Christus ex parte, ostio quasi semiocclufo foris stet Ap. 3.20. in Anglia certè quòd ad disciplinam, iam locum illa Davidis habent: Attollite portas principes ut Rex gloriæ ingrediatur: Psal. 24. 7. Non erat igitur quòd D. Bezam Richardus Bancroftus ita flagellaret, quòd ad Sarnicium epist. 14. scriberet: quandoquidem doctrinæ atque disciplinæ idem author sit; ideò absq; fructu doctrinam recipi, quandiu disciplina deest: erat potius quòd Petrus Martyr idipsum urgeret verbis istis gravissimis. Consulo præterea ut disciplinam quantò ocius fieri poterit, in vestras Ecclesias omnino invebatis, nam si ab initio non recipiætur, cum homines Evangelij cupiditate ferveant, non facile cum postea (ut fit) aliquod srigus obresperit, admittitur. Ut vero absque illa frustra la-boretur, Ecclesiæ quam plurimæ vobis possunt esse exemplo, quæ à suæ instaurationis fundamentis, cum hoc tam salutare jugum subire noluerint, numquam deinde quoad mores & vitam, justâ ulla regula potuerunt in or-dinem redigi, quod jit (quod magno cum dolore dico) ut omnia propemodum p.rum firma sint, & undique ruinam minantur. Est igitur grave dam-num & certa Ecclesiarum pernicies, si nervus discipiinæ illi ademptus fuerit: neque que vere solideque habere, ac profiteri Evangelium ille dicendæ sunt, qui disciplina vel carent, vel illam contemnunt, nullove studio ejus tenentur, Certe in Evangelijs & Apostolicis Epistolis, cum tanta diligentia tradatur, illam oportet fateri non minimam Christianæ religionis partem. Quod fit, ut Evangelium ab eis videatur negligi, qui tam præclaram ejus portionem a seipsis ablegarunt.
units.tr: Justin's Cato, m.p. 1857, that he should bear with the spiritual tyrants raging in the Church, he who had driven civil tyrannies from the neck of the commonwealth. But when Theodosius replied that he had undertaken the patronage of Flavian, that the cause of Flavian was his own cause, and that the charges brought against Flavian had been brought against himself as well: he grieved those whom he ought to have gladdened, and gladdened those whom he ought to have grieved. I shudder at the saying; but what is done today in some churches is better known than that it need be told. Meanwhile this human weakness is to be lamented: those who readily recognise tyrants in the commonwealth recognise spiritual tyrants in the Church only late; and, like Theodosius, they ask that this tyranny be proved and demonstrated to them, and when it has been proved and demonstrated they cannot bring themselves to believe it. And as they are slow to discern episcopal tyranny, so they are almost as negligent in curbing luxury, pomp and pride, so that today they hold roughly the position which Bossard lamented in the times of his own age. I know indeed, he says, that posterity will find fault with these things, and that the Church will fall into such turmoil, or, once fallen, will endure so long. But this plague was sent by God, to set before the eyes of the ecclesiastical order the pompous state and luxury which they usurped; but many had no care or regard for this. Yet the secular princes, from whom the goods first came to the Church, did nothing but laugh and play at the time when I was writing these chronicles, in the year of salvation 1500. Should it be so in this age? Let princes hear that Christ is King of kings (Rev. 19). He did not give himself this title for nothing, but to make known to kings that he, not they, is the supreme King in the Church, and that kings are only his servants, so that they ought to obey his word in that polity of the Church which he committed to their care and faith to cherish, not to exclude; to defend, not to extirpate. For the English Church is indeed that Laodicean church [illegible]; nay, since it is through her that Christ stands outside, as it were with the door half-closed (Rev. 3.20), in England, at least as far as discipline is concerned, those words of David now apply: Lift up your gates, princes, that the King of glory may come in (Ps. 24.7). There was therefore no reason for Richard Bancroft to lash Beza so, writing to Sarnicius (Epist. 14) that since doctrine and discipline have the same author, doctrine is received to no profit as long as discipline is lacking. Rather it was Peter Martyr who urged the same thing in these weighty words: I advise moreover that discipline be introduced into your churches as quickly as possible, for if it is not received from the beginning, while men glow with zeal for the Gospel, it is not easily admitted later, when (as happens) some coldness has crept in. But that without it labour is in vain, very many churches may serve you as an example: they, from the foundations of their restoration, when they were unwilling to undergo this so salutary yoke, could never afterwards be brought into order by any sound rule as regards morals and life. This comes about (I say it with great grief) so that almost everything is weak and threatens ruin on every side. It is therefore a grave loss and a certain destruction of the Churches if the sinews of discipline are taken away. Nor are those to be said truly and solidly to hold and profess the Gospel who lack discipline or despise it, or are held by no zeal for it. Certainly in the Gospels and the Apostolic Epistles, since it is handed down with such diligence, we must acknowledge it to be no small part of the Christian religion. Hence it happens that the Gospel seems to be neglected by those who have cast away so excellent a portion of it.

units.la: Atque hoc resultat ex disciplinæ reformatæ cum pietate tum necessitate ad magistratus potisma primum.
units.tr: And from this there follows, chiefly and first, the necessity of reformed discipline for the magistrates, both for its piety and for its necessity.

units.la: CAP 35.
units.tr: Chapter 35.

units.la: Porisma secundum, Episcopis non sola possessione certandum esse, ne pertinaces, impatientes, superbos, perniciosos & persequutores se probent.
units.tr: Second conclusion: the bishops should not rely on mere possession, lest they prove themselves stubborn, impatient, proud, pernicious and persecutors.

units.la: Ecundum Episcopos ipsos affatur, eorumque fautores, qui disciplinæ reformandæ adversi maxime infensique sunt. Hos jubet primò ut possessione certare desinant: quod malorum semper hominum & mos & morbus fuit: Displicuit siquidem Tito Livio, quòd Dionisius senior de tyrannio dixit: eum non equo insedentem, sed pedibus tantummodo tractum de Regno solere cedere. Displicuit Roberto Capitoni Episcopo Lincolniensi, quòd Ecclesia sui temporis ab Ægyptiaca servitute Papæ & prelatorum, nisi in ore gladij cruentandi, liberari nequiret. Displicet jam hodie Florentino nobili cuidam, quod in præfatione sua ante Guicciardini Paralipomena de Paulo tertio refert: Simpliciter magis inquit & ingenue quam caute Paulus tertius, quum de sua illius potestate aliquando inter familiares sermo in iderat videre illos solitus erat, ut scholasticos & rerum rudes, qui a Christo eam tam anxie repeterent, cuius se possessionem vel solam optimum & firmissimum titulum habere dicebat. Leo decimus eiusdem cum Paulo tertio sententiæ fuit, simplicitatis verò minus: ut qui possessione sola certare maluerit, quam eam solam apertè profiteri: Sic etenim Whitakerus noster: Vno anno, inquit, ante Lutherum à Leone 10. in Concilio Lateranensi, Sess. 11. cavetur ne prædicatores de adventu Antichristi prædicent: sed si Dominus quibusdam revelaverit quoddam, quod per Amos se promittit factursum, non debere hos antea eadem divulgare, quam Apostolica sedes examinabit, aut, si id commode fieri non poterit, Episcopus cum aliis; qui contra fecerit excommunicantum esse.
units.tr: Next he addresses the bishops themselves and their supporters, who are most opposed and hostile to reforming the discipline. He first bids them stop contending by possession, which has always been the custom and the disease of wicked men. Livy was displeased that Dionysius the elder said of a tyrant that he is wont to give up his kingdom not when sitting on a horse but only when dragged on foot. Robert Capito, bishop of Lincoln, was displeased that the Church of his time could not be freed from Egyptian servitude to the Pope and the prelates except by bloodying the edge of the sword. Today a certain Florentine nobleman is displeased, who in his preface to Guicciardini's Paralipomena on Paul III reports: "Paul III spoke more simply and frankly than cautiously, when talk arose among his familiars about his power; they were accustomed to see him treat such men as schoolboys and ignorant of affairs, who so anxiously demanded from Christ that power, of which he said that possession alone was the best and firmest title he had." Leo X was of the same opinion as Paul III, but less simple: he preferred to contend by possession alone rather than openly profess it. For so says our Whitaker: "One year before Luther, under Leo X, in the Lateran Council, session 11, it was provided that preachers should not preach about the coming of Antichrist; but if the Lord has revealed to some something which he promises to do through Amos, these men must not publish it before the Apostolic See has examined it, or, if that cannot conveniently be done, before the bishop with others; whoever acts otherwise is to be excommunicated."

units.la: Quid hæc ad Episcopos Angli-anos, inquies? Vel maximè. Sunt qui cum Paulo tertio simpliciores & ingenui sunt, non enim illi à Christo Episcopatum repetunt, sed jure humano & præscriptione solâ certant: Sunt qui licet Episcopatum ab ordinatione Apostolicâ repetant, quia tamen mutabilem statuunt, posse sionem præcipuè urgere solent, ut in Downamo cernere est, qui ex eo audaciam nostram intolerabilem esse arguit, quòd Episcopos eo in regno mutari velimus, ubi in possessione Episcopi sunt, per regni legis stabilita. In Leonis vero X attibus conspirant ferè omnes: neq; enim vel quid à Domino ejusq; verbo revelatum cuiquam à quoquam in vulgus vel verbo vel scripto proferri sinunt: quod non dico Antichristianismi suspitione in eorum regimen, sed vel peccati reprehensione in eorum abusus redolere possit: sic ut ipsam non resi lentiam pro concione taxare, tacitam papistarum tolerationem deplorare, novitatem falsitatis a quoquam alio prædicatam refutare, nisi prius Episcopo hæc delata, & ab eodem aprobata sint, censura dignū sit, Quid quod disputationem æquissimis conditionibus a ministris oblatam superbè recusarunt? Quid quòd ad curias suas citatis, non eos ad scholas ut disputent, sed a tribunal ut judicentur accitos esse, dicere soleant? Quid quòd locis moveant, bonis exuant, carceribus multent, excommunicationibus feriant, quotquot eorum voluntati non obsecundantur?
units.tr: What has this to do with the English bishops, you will ask? Very much. There are some who are more simple and frank, like Paul III: for they do not derive the episcopate from Christ, but contend by human law and prescription alone. There are some who, though they derive the episcopate from apostolic ordination, because they hold it to be changeable, are wont to press chiefly the argument from possession, as can be seen in Downame, who argues from this that our boldness is intolerable, since we want bishops changed in that kingdom where they are in possession, established by the laws of the realm. Indeed, almost all conspire in the manner of Leo X: for they allow nothing revealed by the Lord and his word to be brought before the people by anyone, either by word or in writing, which might smell not merely of suspicion of Antichristianism in their rule, but even of rebuke for sin in their abuses. So much so that it is worthy of censure to rebuke in a sermon even their non-resistance, to deplore the tacit toleration of the Papists, or to refute a novelty of falsehood preached by anyone else, unless these matters were first referred to the bishop and approved by him. What of the fact that they proudly refused a disputation offered by the ministers on the fairest conditions? What of the fact that, when they summon men to their courts, they are wont to say that these were called not to the schools to dispute but to the tribunal to be judged? What of the fact that they remove from their places, strip of their goods, fine with prisons, and strike with excommunications all who do not comply with their will?

units.la: Annon hoc dotins possessione certare est, quam ratione? Sed video nimis verum esse quod in jus Canonicum relatum est ex Augustino, Quomodo potest esse humilitas ubi regnat falsitas? præsumtum cum ita comparatum sit, ut fraude coparatus f perhibetur, non nisi superbo superciliosimo & bracchio defendi possit. Verùm enim verò cum nemo periculosius peccet, quàm qui vel verbo peccata defendit, ut habet Pius: & non verbo modo, sed & elata manu pariter peccatum suum fuerat periculosissimè isti defendere moliantur, Hieronymi verbis admonendum, ut ad opus istud corrigendum, quod libitur, cavite. Hoc quo commodius fiat, consiiderent velim cum animis suis, quàm indigna res sit, ut Ecclesiæ columnæ haberi qui volunt, mercantur cum Anaxagora Ciceronis audire illud: Nesio quomodo plerique errare malunt quam sententiam quam semel amplexi sunt, derelinquere. Dixit olim Aristoteles: Aequum est veritatis retinendæ causa, vel nostra etiam ipsorum dogmata ebertare, præsertim cum sumus Philosophi. Nam cum utraq; chara sint, tamen praeclarum est, pluris æstimare veritatem. Venit hic in mentem illud Tertullciani: Sitante consideratione paganus vir fuit, quanto magis nos qui sacerdotes dicimur; Movebatur siquidem ille quòd philosophus esset, nos quòd Christiani simus, nec Christianorum sacerdotes, non commovebimur? Apage pertinacium: nullus pudor est ad meliora transire, dicit Ambrosius: imo Augustinus recte: Magnæ sapientiæ est revocare hominem, quæ ante male locutus est.
units.tr: Is this not to contend by possession rather than by reason? But I see that what is brought into canon law from Augustine is only too true: "How can there be humility where falsehood reigns?" Presumption, since it is so constituted that it is said to be obtained by fraud, can be defended only by a haughty brow and a strong arm. But since no one sins more dangerously than he who defends sin even by word, as Pius says, and since they strive not only by word but also with a raised hand to defend their sin equally dangerously, let them be admonished in the words of Jerome to take care in correcting this work which they undertake. So that this may be done more conveniently, I would have them consider in their own minds how unworthy a thing it is that men who wish to be held pillars of the Church should buy with Anaxagoras the hearing of Cicero's words: "I know not how most men prefer to err than to abandon an opinion once embraced." Aristotle once said: it is fair, for the sake of retaining the truth, even to overthrow our own dogmas, especially since we are philosophers; for though both are dear, it is noble to esteem truth more highly. The saying of Tertullian comes to mind: "If a pagan man was moved by reflection, how much more we who are called priests? For he was moved because he was a philosopher, we because we are Christians; and shall we, who are not even priests of Christians, not be moved?" Away with the obstinate: there is no shame in passing over to better things, says Ambrose; and Augustine rightly: it is a mark of great wisdom to recall a man from what he has said badly before.

units.la: Secundo, si uti certandi ratio ea quæ supra commemorata est, pertinaciam in Episcopis spirat: ita & impatientiam illam quam Episcopis rectoribus indignissimam esse Barnardus olim testatus est: Dissimulamus inquit de prælatis & Magistris Ecclesiæ. Sic nimirum, si plures ipsi, ut chaduit nunc humana judicia, beniatque grave judicium his quæ præsunt, & potentes patiuntur tormenta potenter. An Episcopis Anglicanis hæc merito accommodantur? Fertur Scapulam tantum aufuisse quod
units.tr: Second, if the manner of contending just mentioned breathes obstinacy into bishops, so too does that impatience which Bernard once declared most unworthy of bishops and rulers: "We dissemble, he says, about prelates and teachers of the Church. Thus, if many of them, as human judgments now run, are placed over those who are in authority, and the powerful suffer powerful torments..." Do these things rightly apply to the English bishops? It is said that Scapula only removed what was...

units.la: {b} Ibid. Epist. 9. Ser. 62. Eth. l. c. 6. quòd scripto Tertulliani leniretur, ut eodem potiùs exacerbatus atrociùs in Christianos desæviret. Hoc ipsum jam in Anglis fit, adeo molles Episcoporum aures sunt, ut irritatiores semper eva-lâat,quandocunq; eas vel verbo quis, vel scripto vellicaverit. His rectè olim Leodienſes ad Pilchalum remoto Romanæ ambitionis typho: Cur de gravibus & manifestis non reprehendantur Romani Episcopi? Qui reprehendi & corrigi non vult, Psudo est, sive Episcopus sive clericus, Mutent igitur se Episcopi Anglicani oportet, ad Petri exemplum illud, de quo Cyprianus pulchrè. Nam ea est de consuetudine præscribendum, sed ratione vincendum. Nam nec Petrus, quem primum Dominus elegit, & super quem Ecclesiam ædificavit suam, quum secum Paulus de circumcisione postmodum disceptaret, vindicavit sibi aliquid insolenter, aut arrogant-er assumpsit, ut diceret se primatum tenere & obtemperari a novellis & posteris sibi oportere?
units.tr: {b} Ibid. Epist. 9. Ser. 62. Eth. l. c. 6. ...that by Tertullian's writing he was softened, so that, rather exasperated by it, he raged more savagely against the Christians. This very thing now happens among the English: so soft are the ears of the bishops that they are always made more irritated whenever anyone, whether by word or in writing, plucks at them. The Leodienses rightly said once to Pilchalus, with Roman ambition's pride set aside: "Why are the Roman bishops not rebuked for grave and manifest faults? Whoever does not wish to be rebuked and corrected is proud, whether bishop or cleric. Let the English bishops therefore change themselves, after the example of Peter, of which Cyprian speaks beautifully: 'For custom is to be pleaded against, but overcome by reason. For neither Peter, whom the Lord first chose and upon whom he built his Church, when Paul afterwards disputed with him about circumcision, claimed anything for himself insolently, or assumed arrogantly, so as to say that he held the primacy and that novices and successors ought to obey him?'"

units.la: Tertio, certatio Episcoporum Anglicanorum supra commemora-ta, superbiam non in collegas presbyteros modo, sed in Christum ip-sum pariter, eamque haud levem spirat. Caput Iobi Caligulum substulisse ferunt, & suum illius loco posuisse: pari modo, disci-plinam a Christo institutam hi substuletunt, suam supposuerunt, & presbyterorum capitalem authoritatem aboleverunt, quos Christus Ecclesiæ capita constituit, ut ipsi soli pro summis & præcipuis Ecclesiæ capitibus haberentur. Nota sunt illa tritaque. Quid in meo facitis non uti? Quis posuit id solum hoc in domo mea? Leviusculum vobis videtur, in Christi Ecclesia locum gradumque, invito Christo, usurpare? Rectè Chrysostomus. Qui non utitur sacra Scriptura, sed assendit alia via, hic non pastor est, sed fur. Atque in Chrisium ipsum recidit, quod sibi presbyteros subjugarunt, nisi forte Hieronymum aberrasse sentiamus. Sic enim ille, Qui non vult presbyteros facere quæ iubentur a Deo, dicat quis major est Christo: Iubentibus nobis, o immitissimi sacerdotes, solum presbyteri nomen habet presbyter, plenitudinem & perfectionem, quæ consecratione eius competit non retentat. Ipsi presbyteri ut legimus, Episcopi nunc supantur, secundum quod scriptum est, qui vos posuit Episcopos, regere Ecclesiam Dei, sed oderunt hoc sacerdotes superbi in presbyteris nomen, qui nolunt esse hoc quod Christus, qui discipulorum pedes lavit. Similia habet ex analogia Gregorius Magnus, quum adversus Episcopatum illicitum Constantinopolitanum disserit. Quid tu Christo (inquis) universali Ecclesiæ capiti, in extremi iudicii responsurus es examine, qui cunctta eius membra tibimet conaris universilis appellatione subjicere? Nihil aliud affectabat Iohannes (ut rectè Eyldus) quàm ut omnes a se pendere & ordinationes suas a se dimanare ministri & Episcopi crederent. Hoc dum in ministros Anglicanos Episcopi Anglici assectent: annon membra Christi sibi subjiciunt præter Christi voluntatem? nihil ergo habebunt Gregorij judicio, quod in die judicij Chri-sto respondere possint.
units.tr: Third, the contention of the English bishops mentioned above breathes pride not only against their fellow presbyters but against Christ himself, and no slight pride. They are said to have removed the head of Job and put Caligula's in its place; in the same way these men have removed the discipline instituted by Christ, put their own in its place, and abolished the chief authority of the presbyters, whom Christ appointed as heads of the Church, so that they alone might be regarded as the chief and principal heads of the Church. Those sayings are well known and worn: "Why do you do what is not lawful in my house? Who appointed you to this alone in my house?" Does it seem a small matter to you to seize, against Christ's will, a place and rank in Christ's Church? Rightly Chrysostom: "He who does not use holy Scripture, but climbs in by another way, is not a shepherd but a thief." And it falls back upon Christ himself, that they have subjected the presbyters to themselves, unless perhaps we think Jerome was mistaken. For he says: "Let him who does not want presbyters to do what God commands say who is greater than Christ. When we command, O most savage priests, the presbyter has only the name of presbyter; he does not keep the fullness and perfection which belongs to his consecration. The presbyters themselves, as we read, were placed above the bishops, according to what is written: who set you bishops to rule the Church of God? But proud priests hate this name of presbyter; they do not wish to be what Christ was, who washed the feet of his disciples." Gregory the Great has similar things by analogy, when he disputes against the unlawful episcopate of Constantinople: "What will you answer to Christ, the universal head of the Church, at the examination of the last judgment, you who strive to subject all his members to yourself under the title of universal?" John aimed at nothing else (as Eyldus rightly says) than that all ministers and bishops should believe they depend on him and that their ordinations flow from him. While the English bishops pursue this same aim over the English ministers, do they not subject the members of Christ to themselves against Christ's will? They will therefore have nothing in Gregory's judgment with which they can answer to Christ on the day of judgment.

units.la: Quarto. Certatio Episcoporum Anglicanorum supra commemo-
units.tr: Fourthly, the contention of the English bishops, mentioned above, has inflicted on our Church a vast harvest of evils and a ruin that can never be lamented enough.

units.la: {y} Con. Tom. 2 rata, ingentem malorum messem, & nunquam satis deplorandam cladem, Ecclesiæ nostræ intulit. Quæ Episcopalis authoritatis commoditas maximè prætendi solet, ea pacis & unitatis conservatio est. Quid igitur pa… & unitate in ecclesia Anglicana ista conservavit: Imo Eccl…sii nominato illâ, ubi plures rixæ, plures cōtentiones plura Schismata, plura cuiusq; generis dissidia jam hodie glif…ūt; quæ etiam ex hac ipsa usurpata authoritate, tanquam ex Pandoræ pixide, quasi ad cœlos, terras, maria turbâda, vndiquaq; provolitarūt. Sed fac in Anglia unitatē, hanc præservasse: quid hæc ad mala alia, quæ invexit innumera? quorū utuitu regerere ex Canone possumus.
units.tr: {y} Con. Tom. 2 The advantage of episcopal authority that is most often pleaded is the preservation of peace and unity. But what has this authority preserved of peace and unity in the English Church? Indeed, in that Church, where quarrels, contentions, schisms and every kind of dissension now flourish in abundance, which, drawn from this very usurped authority as if from Pandora's box, have flown out on every side, as if to stir up heaven, earth and sea. But suppose it has preserved unity in England: what does this matter against the countless other evils it has brought in? Against these we could answer with the canon.

units.la: Abjicenda sunt falsa remedia quæ veris & manifestis perieculis sunt grauiora. Nec non ex Augustino illud: Non vult Deus tale lucrum comp…nsari tali damno. Quid enim ego de Angliæ tepiditate dicerem? nam hæc ab Angliæ Angelo Laodiceno, vel ipso judice Christo potissimum introducta est? Quid de canum mutorum & cæ orum speculatorum & multitudine & insciitia dicerem? nam hæc quasi exercitus lo…ustarum Apocalypticarum quidâ ex ordinatione solis Episcopis scilicet, reservata, tanquam ex equo Troiano prorupit? Quid de morum turpitudine dicerem, nullo discipline freno coercita? nam hæc Episcopis haud minùs hodie, quam illa similis Leonis temporibus deputanda est. Is ad Episcopos Bavaricæ apud Aventinum ita scribit, ut nostros unâ Anglicanos luculenter depinxerit. Christi ut, inquit, in vestris provinciis authoritus Episcopis invitem imponunt. Ultra modum sumptu & magnificentiâ ne ciram luxu, æ ificando egregij sanè Pastores Christiani gregis prodeunt. Gravissimus solet esse morbus qui à capite diffunditur.
units.tr: False remedies must be rejected when they are more serious than the true and obvious dangers. Hence also the saying of Augustine: God does not wish such gain to be bought at such a loss. For what should I say of the lukewarmness of England, which was introduced chiefly by the Laodicean angel of England, or by Christ himself as judge? What should I say of the multitude and ignorance of the dumb dogs and blind watchmen, which, reserved for ordination by the bishops alone, has burst forth like a swarm of apocalyptic locusts, as from the Trojan horse? What should I say of the baseness of morals, restrained by no curb of discipline? For this must be imputed to the bishops today no less than it was to the times of that similar Leo. He writes to the bishops of Bavaria, as reported by Aventinus, in such a way that he has vividly depicted our English bishops too. "The authority of Christ," he says, "is imposed on your provinces by bishops who are sluggish. Beyond measure they go forth in expense and magnificence, in luxury and building, as truly remarkable pastors of the Christian flock. The disease that spreads from the head is always the most grievous."

units.la: Quintò, decertatio Episcoporum Anglicanorum suprà commemorata, persecutionem excitavit eam, quæ satis verbis cōmemorari non poterit. Exclamavit olim Bernardus: Heu heu Domine Deus, quia ipsi sunt in persecutione tua primi, qui videntur in Ecclesia tua primatum diligere, gerere principatum. Quid ita? Impedit (inquit) salutem est persequi salutarem: & quid amplius est? Dantur (inquit) sic i gradus in ordinationem turpis lucri, ut quæstum æstiment pietatem: Copiosissimè si quidem pietatem invenirunt, in susceptionem, imo a cipiendo magis animarum cura: sed hæc apud eos cura minor, & de animarum salute novissima cogitatio est. Atqui hanc omnem Christi persecutionem eos qui principatum in Anglia gerunt excitasse, sæus est qui non videt, curus qui non deplorat. Quod ibi quæstus aut upium? quæ ad sacros or i-nes promotio indignorum? quæ salutis animarum injuria? qui effi-ij adimplendi negl ctus? quæ pseudo-regimen Episcopale non solum tolerat, verumetiam fovet: nec tolerantibus interim nedum favenclibus Ecclesijs refor matis eis, quæ r & Christi disciplina gubernatur. Sed hæc persecutio præ illa ignotior, quæ nec in sensus omnium incurrit, & tuisque lo i omnes infestat, nempe sacrorum Verbi ministrorum degravati, & laicorum, vestimenta sua ab Ecclesiæ Angl. glicane corruptelis pura servantium, divexatio. Episcoporum ambitiones, contentiones, tyrannides, simultates, persecutionem Dioclesiani attraxisse dicit Eusebius. Quis pius judicium simile prae foribus stare non veretur, idque ob Episcoporum in Anglia ambitiones, superbias, crudelitates, impiasque; in pessimos Christi servos conspirationes. Haec Hieronimus si vidisset nonne excandesceret, qui Ecclesiam suo tempore episcopos gravissime afflixisse coqueritur, in eo vel solo, quod presbyterum in praesentia Episcopi praedicare prohiberent? Audiantur ipsius verba ut Episcopale in Anglia regimen quam sit tyrannicum intelligatur. Quis inquit hic rego o sacerdotes honor vester est, ut dominium gibbi inferatis, quoniam cum pastoribus per potentiam vestram aufertur Deo digna diligentia, contagium quoddam & calamitas excesit in gregibus, ac dominici patrimonij damna conquiritis, dum soli vultis in Ecclesia potentari, propterea haec scribo ut si praeteriti temporis error non potest jam revocari, vel ad praesens in Ecclesiis servetur humilitas. Presbyteri Hieronymi tempore pastores Ecclesiarum erant; jam Episcopus in Anglia, Dioeceseos totius pastor est, presbyteri tantum illius delegati, & coadjutores sunt. Episcopos in Ecclesia solos potentari Hieronymi saeculo monstrum erat: potentantur jam soli in Anglia Episcopi, non solum in eo, quod presbytero absque illorum licentia praedicare non liceat, (quod tamen solos potentari Hieronymi est:) sed quod exclusso presbytero (quod tempore Hironymi nondum factum) gubernant ipsi soli. Calamitatem in gregibus per Episcopos crescere, dominicumque patrimonii damnum pati censuit Hieronymus, quod presbytero diligentia praedicandi ablata esset in praesentia Episcopi: & damnosi multo magis Episcopi in Anglia jam hodie non sunt qui ducentis, & amplius Ecclesiis pastoribus suis nuper spoliatis, homines maximam partem aut indoctos, aut leves, aut vitae minus probatae, aut non residentes, negligentes certe & stertentes, substituerunt? Atque hic disciplinae reformatae ad Episcopos Anglicanos sermo primus est, ut pro possessione sua modo supra commemorato, certare desinant.
units.tr: Fifthly, the contention of the English bishops mentioned above has stirred up a persecution that cannot be described adequately in words. Bernard once cried out: "Alas, alas, Lord God, they are the first in your persecution who seem to love the first place in your Church and to hold the principate." Why so? "It is a sin," he says, "to persecute the saviour of souls; and what is worse?" "Steps are given," he says, "into ordination for base gain, so that they regard godliness as a source of income. Indeed they find godliness very abundantly in the receiving, or rather in the taking up, of the care of souls; but this care is smaller with them, and the thought of the salvation of souls is last of all." Now, that all this persecution of Christ has been stirred up by those who hold the principate in England, only one who does not see is blind, only one who does not lament is heartless. What gain or profit is there there? What promotion of the unworthy to the sacred orders? What injury to the salvation of souls? What neglect of fulfilling the duties of office? What pseudo-episcopal government not only tolerates these things but actually cherishes them, while meanwhile the Churches reformed in the other way, which are governed by the discipline of Christ, are not merely tolerated but even favoured. But this persecution is less known than that one, which does not fall under the senses of all and does not infest everyone; namely, the harassment of ministers of the Word who are burdened, and of laymen who keep their garments pure from the corruptions of the Anglican Church. Eusebius says that the ambitions, contentions, tyrannies and enmities of the bishops brought on the persecution of Diocletian. What pious man does not fear that a similar judgment is at the gates, on account of the ambitions, pride, cruelties and impious conspiracies of the bishops in England against the worst servants of Christ? If Jerome had seen these things, would he not have burst into anger, he who complains that the Church in his own time was most grievously afflicted by bishops, in this one thing alone, that they forbade a presbyter to preach in the presence of a bishop? Let his own words be heard, so that it may be understood how tyrannical the episcopal government is in England. "Who," he says, "is this ruler? Your honour as priests is this: that you impose lordship on the flock. For since, through your power, the ministers have been deprived of the diligence owed to God, a certain contagion and calamity has gone out among the flocks, and you complain of the losses of the Lord's patrimony, while you alone wish to hold power in the Church. Therefore I write these things, so that if the error of past times cannot now be recalled, humility may at least be kept in the Churches for the present." In Jerome's time the presbyters were the pastors of the Churches; now in England the bishop is the pastor of the whole diocese, and the presbyters are merely his delegates and assistants. For bishops alone to hold power in the Church was a monstrous thing in Jerome's age; in England now bishops alone hold power, not only in that a presbyter may not preach without their licence (which nevertheless is "bishops alone holding power" in Jerome's sense), but because, the presbyter being shut out (which was not yet done in Jerome's time), they alone govern. Jerome judged that calamity grows among the flocks through bishops, and that the Lord's patrimony suffers loss, because the presbyter's diligence in preaching was taken away in the bishop's presence; and how much more damaging are the bishops in England today, who have replaced the homes of the flocks, lately stripped of their own pastors, with two hundred and more churches, and with men for the most part unlearned, or frivolous, or of less approved life, or non-resident, certainly negligent and drowsy?
