And this is the first word of reformed discipline addressed to the English bishops, that they should cease to contend for their possession in the manner mentioned above.

units.la: Porisma tertium; Episcopis de possessione cedendum esse.
units.tr: Third corollary: the bishops must yield their possessions.

units.la: Vperest secundus sermo, qui de possessione sua cedere eos argumentis gravissimis cohortatur. Quid enim? Annon schisma jam excitant ob Episcopatum retinendum, quemadmodum Novatus ob adipiscendum? Novati Episcopatum condemnavit Cornelius, quod a Deo illi concessum non esset: at multo magis condemnandus Episcopatus Anglicanus, quod is nemini quidem supernè a Deo concessus sit, ut suo loco demonstrabitur. Quibus igitur rationibus Novatum valuit. vatum persuasit Dionysius Alexandrinus: eisdem jam nos uti licet, ut Episcopatui Hierarchico suo, Anglicani abrenuncient. Quidvis potius pati vos decet, quàm ut Ecclesia discindatur: vos Episcopatus illiciti damnum pati non vultis? Martyrio æquivalebit damnum hoc licet pusillum, quia in cómodum totius Ecclesiæ cedet: compensabit insuper pristinum peccatum vestrum, & famam vestri nominis illustrabit: illud non imputabitur, hoc verò commendabitur: Animas postremò vestras perire non sinetis. Gregorij verò Nazianzeni resignatio illustre admodum exemplar est, atque imitatione dignum: de qua Gregorius presbyter, in vita ipsius ita narrat: Quum contentioneminter Episcopos propter suam electionem coortam vidisset, fortiter sapienterque in concilium prodijt, atque ita locutus est: Viri collegæ & compastores sacrosancti gregis Christi, turpe fuerit prorsus & a vobis alienum, si qui picis documenta aliis præbetis, intestinum ipsi bellum inter vos exciteti. Quonam enim modo alios ad concordiam adduxeritis, ipsi circa sententias vestras & decreta disrepantes? Ac vos per Trinitatem etiam obsecro ut mutua vestra negotia, præclarè & pacifice constituatis. Quod si vobis ullo modo dissidij causa fuit, Ionam Prophetam vitæ integritate non supero, projicite me in mare, ut cessèt a vobis hæc turbulenta tempestas: Quicquid vobis visum fuerit, tametsi a culpa immunis, libentur perpetiar, siquidem hac ratione concordia vestra reprehendi & resarciri possit. Throno exturbate, urbe ejicite, tantum veritatem & pacem amate: Hæc Theo. Bilsonus postquam posuisset, ita subjnngit: Ut Christianum viro dignum erat, Ecclesiæ unitatem propria salute chariorem habuit, vitamque privatam in quiete & solitudine, honori dignitatique tam tumultuose prætulit. Atqui inquam si Ionam Prophetam sibi imitandum duxit Nazianzenus, quum à culpa immunis erat, ut ita schisma excitatum ab aliis extingueretur, atque in eo ut viro Christiano dignum erat, sese gesserit: quomodo viris Christianis digne se hodie Hierarchici gerent, si tam culpæ ipsius rei, atque ipse Ionas erat, vitam non privatam, sed pastoralem, sanctam, honori suo usurpato non prætulerint, ut ita schisma non ab aliis sed a seipsis excitatum sopiatur? Regimen Episcopale rem indifferentè & legitimè mutabilem plurimi fatentur, regimen Ecclesiæ reformatum legitimum esse largiuntur: his ritè petpensis, Ecclesiæ unitatem Nazianzeni ad instar charam habere nunquam possunt, qui indifferentem honorem suum, tantarum tempestatum flabellum, adversus regimen Ecclesiarum reformatarum, ut illi, legitimum, ut nos, necessarium, opstinatè tuentur. Sed ut istud Hierarchicos Nazianzeni exemplum quàm proximè attingit, ita Hieracis illud ab Isidoro Pelusiota & complobatum & collaudatum, Hierarchiam ipsam iugulat. Ad Episcopatum electus Hierax; detrectabat: cum vero calumniis varijs impeteretur, ita illius patronum agit Isidorus: Illud fortasse ignorare videmini, lenitatis & mansuetudinis dignitatem, in tyrannidem transfijle: Nam si hoc ofiédere potestis, veterem pascendi gregis rationem nunc quoq; negere maximè. maxime quidem tum qui se huic inegotio impacem esse arbitratus est, ut propterea in fugam se dedit, a nobis laudari aquum fuerit. Sed res in contrarium cessit, ab eo pœnæ minime expectantur: Tunc enim [salutis su]um causa mortem oppetebant, nunc autem pastores ovibus mortem inferunt, non corpora jugulantes (levius enim hoc malum esset) verum animis offensiones afferentes. Tum iniquis corpus cassigabant, nunc autem ut luxu ac deliciis exultent, efficiunt. Tum bona sua egentibus distribuebant: nunc autem pauperum bona in rem suam vertunt. Tum virtutem colebant, nunc virtutum cultores proscribunt & eliminant. Verum cum ostendam quamtum inter vetus ministerium, & præsentem tyrannidem interfit; quæ tamen causa est. quamobrem æqualitatis amantes, coronis non redimitis ac prædatis? quod eo nomine Hierarcem Isidorus celebret, quod præ æqualitatis amore Episcopatum recusarit, id ad alium locum pertinet, ac proinde jam non vrgeo: illud tantum pro præsenti adnoto, nulla conscientia Episcopatum in Anglia Isidori judicio retineri posse, ubi lenis & manuosa Pastoris dignitas in fastuosam ut ille loquitur, tyrannidem abiit, vetus pascendi gregis in Episcopis ratio cessavit, ubi luxu & deliciis Episcopatus exultat, ubi salus animarum offensionibus Episcopatus impeditur, ubi servi Dei ab Episcopis depauperantur & bonis exuuntur, ubi denique virtutum cultores ab Episcopis proscribuntur & eliminantur. Quod contra Dominamus affert, subfstantiam Episcopi se duntaxat defendere, personales abusus huic subfstantiæ præjudicare non debere: id nihil est: quum Isidoro aliter visum sit, idque recte, & subtilis ista distinctio tum locum non habeat, cum Episcopatus ipse ita degeneravit, ut abusus supra commemoratos insitos sibi & infixos, intimeque adhærentes habeat, Iam vero ne Hierax sanctissimus quis, vitijs supra positis vacare poterit, qui strictissimè juxta Canones Anglicanos, absque ullo personali abusu, Episcopatum exercere voluerit. Quid enim? Annon luxus & deliciæ episcopatui Anglicano adeo tenaciter jam hodie adhærent, ut caulsentur Episcopi pompam & splendorem suum ad tuendam loci sui dignitatem necessarium esse? Annon Johannes Whitgiftus juramento episcopali suo se obstringi dicit, ut ministri non conformantes, quanquam doctì, sancti, in Evangelio prædicando diligentes, exauthorentur? Annon ex officio suo esse Officiales protestantur, ut excommunicent, bonis exhaurant, censuris exagitent, sive ministros sive laicos, quos curiæ suæ inquisitionis decretis minus obsequentes reperierint? Absque his si fuisset, ipsa tamen experientia iam diu clamavit, de sede Episcopali Anglicana verum id esse quod de aulâ dixit quidam, eam bonos sæpe recipere, nunquam facere: ni etiam addendum, eam cum ante bonos receperit. eos deinceps facere malos. Quotusquisque; etenim est, quantum doctus, pius, in prædicando diligens, qui accepta infula Episcopali, cum Ænea Sylvio iam Papa facto non adeo de repente mutatur, ut opus habeat prioris zeli palinodiam, ut ille canere? units.tr: There remains a second argument, which urges them to give up their possessions on the strongest grounds. For what? Do they not already stir up schism in order to keep the episcopate, just as Novatus did in order to obtain it? Cornelius condemned the episcopate of Novatus, because it had not been granted to him by God; but the English episcopate deserves far more to be condemned, since it has been granted by God to no one at all, as will be shown in its place. So the arguments by which Dionysius of Alexandria persuaded against Novatus may now be used by us, to persuade the English bishops to renounce their hierarchical episcopate. You ought to suffer anything rather than let the Church be torn apart. Will you not bear the loss of an unlawful episcopate? This loss, though small, will be like a martyrdom, because it will turn to the advantage of the whole Church. Moreover, it will make up for your former sin and will bring lustre to your name: the one will not be imputed to you, and the other will be commended. Finally, you will not allow your souls to perish. The resignation of Gregory Nazianzen, however, is a most illustrious example and worthy of imitation. Gregory the presbyter, in his life, relates it as follows: when he saw a quarrel arising among the bishops over their election, he came forward into the council bravely and wisely, and spoke thus: "Colleagues and fellow-shepherds of the holy flock of Christ, it would be utterly shameful and unworthy of you, if you who give lessons to others in peace should stir up civil war among yourselves. For how will you bring others to concord, when you yourselves disagree about your opinions and decrees? And I beg you by the Trinity to settle your mutual business clearly and peacefully. But if there is any cause of dissension among you, I am not superior to the prophet Jonah in integrity of life: throw me into the sea, so that this turbulent storm may cease from you. Whatever you decide, I will gladly endure, though I am free from fault, provided that your concord can in this way be restored and repaired. Drive me from the throne, cast me out of the city, only love truth and peace." After setting out these words, Theodore Beza adds: "As was worthy of a Christian man, he valued the unity of the Church above his own safety, and he preferred a private life of quiet and solitude to honour and dignity, which were full of tumult." But I say: if Nazianzen took the prophet Jonah as his model, although he was free from fault, so that the schism stirred up by others might be extinguished, and if he conducted himself in this as was worthy of a Christian man, how will the hierarchical men today conduct themselves worthily as Christian men, if, though they are guilty of the very fault, and are themselves Jonah, they do not prefer a pastoral and holy life, not a private one, to the honour they have usurped, so that the schism may be quieted not by others but by themselves who have stirred it up? Very many admit that episcopal government is a thing indifferent and lawfully changeable; they grant that the reformed government of the Church is lawful. Having weighed this rightly, they can never hold the unity of the Church dear as Nazianzen did, who stubbornly defend their indifferent honour, that fan of such great tempests, against the government of the reformed Churches, which they call lawful and we call necessary. But while this example of Nazianzen's bishops touches so closely upon the matter, that passage of Isidore of Pelusium, which praises and commends Hierax, ruins the hierarchy itself. Hierax, though chosen to the episcopate, refused it; but when he was assailed with various slanders, Isidore defends him thus: "You perhaps seem not to know that the dignity of gentleness and meekness has passed into tyranny. For if you can deny this, you must especially deny the old manner of feeding the flock. Indeed, it would be right for us to praise him above all, since he thought himself unfit for this business and therefore took to flight. But the matter turned out otherwise, and punishments are by no means to be expected from him. For then men faced death for the sake of salvation; but now the pastors bring death to the sheep, not slaughtering their bodies (for that evil would be lighter), but inflicting offences on their souls. Then they chastised the wicked with the body; now they bring it about that they exult in luxury and pleasures. Then they distributed their goods to the needy; now they turn the goods of the poor to their own use. Then they cultivated virtue; now they banish and eliminate the cultivators of virtue. But since I will show how much the old ministry differs from the present tyranny, what is the reason why men who love equality, not crowned and plundered...?" As for the fact that Isidore praises Hierax for this, namely that out of love of equality he refused the episcopate, that belongs to another place, and so I do not press it now. I note only this for the present: in Isidore's judgment, the episcopate in England cannot be kept with any clear conscience, where the gentle and meek dignity of the pastor has passed, as he puts it, into haughty tyranny; where the old way of feeding the flock has ceased among the bishops; where the episcopate exults in luxury and pleasures; where the salvation of souls is hindered by the offences of the episcopate; where the servants of God are impoverished and stripped of their goods by the bishops; and where, finally, the cultivators of virtue are banished and eliminated by the bishops. As for the objection the Dominicans bring, that they defend only the substance of the bishop and that personal abuses should not prejudice this substance: that is nothing. Since it has seemed otherwise to Isidore, and rightly so, this subtle distinction has no place when the episcopate itself has so degenerated that it has the abuses mentioned above implanted and fixed in itself and closely cleaving to it. Now indeed, however holy a man Hierax may be, he cannot be free from the vices stated above, if he wishes to exercise the episcopate most strictly according to the English canons without any personal abuse. For what? Do not luxury and pleasures cling so tenaciously to the English episcopate today, that the bishops claim that pomp and splendour are necessary for defending the dignity of their office? Does not John Whitgift say that he is bound by his episcopal oath to have non-conforming ministers, though learned, holy, and diligent in preaching the Gospel, deprived of their office? Do not the officials declare that it is their duty to excommunicate, drain men's goods, and harass with censures, whether ministers or laymen, whomever they find less compliant with the decrees of their court of inquisition? Even without these things, experience has long cried out that what someone said of the court is true of the English episcopal see, "that it often receives good men, but never makes them good": indeed it should be added that, having once received good men, it afterwards makes them bad. For how few are there, however learned, pious, and diligent in preaching, who, once the episcopal mitre is accepted, change so suddenly, like Aeneas Sylvius after he became Pope, as to need a palinode of their former zeal, as he sang? units.la: Sect. 65 ite Aeneam, suscipite Pium? Haec certe graviora sunt eis, propter quae tamen Iohannes olim Beverlaius, Archiepiscopatui Eboracensi renunciaiuit. Bede is praeceptor erat, Evangelium praedicare ad animarum salutem dulcissimum duxit: sed certamina & jurgia de ceremoniis exteris exorta inter Ecclesiasticos detestatus, & affectus tandem taedio tumultuum ab eisdem in Ecclesia excitatorum, cessit officio, Beverlaium se conferens, ubi in magna spiritus constantia vitam finivit, anno 721. Praedicare Evangelium e suggestu dulcissimum Beverlaio fuit: vos Evangelij Praedicatores suggestu pellere non cessabitis? Detestatus ille est certamina inter Ecclesiasticos excitata de ceremoniis externis: vos certamina de ceremoniis excitare, ad certissimam Ecclesiae perniciem non desistetis? Cessit ille officio, quando certamina se non potuisse componere viderat: vos illo ossicio cedere non vultis, per quod stat, ut difficilia Anglicana componi non possint? quo vero sublato, apertissimus ad concordiam aditus patefactus erit? Hoc ex Gregorio Magno liquet, qui eandem quod ad genus nobiscum causam egit: quandoquidem Episcopatus Constantinopolitanus gradu tantum ab Anglicano differebat, ut alibi dementrum. Locum igitur hic illa habent. Ille coercendus est qui Ecclesiae injuriam facit, qui corde tumet, qui gaudere de nomine singularitatis appetit, qui honori quo, imperij vestri se super ponit. Ecce omnes hae de re scandalum patimur. Ad viam ergo rectam revertatur auctor scandali, & omnia sacerdotum jurgia cessabunt. Videsnum viam ad pacem compendiariam esse, ut Episcopi Anglicani de suo primatu decertari desinant: spem vero pacis nullam esse dum injuriam Ecclesiae faciunt, ministris caeteris scandalum inferunt, honori eorum sese superponunt, & nomen singularitatis (id enim pro Episcopo speciatim Bilsonus urget) appetunt? Facessat igitur superba Episcopalis, & lites omnes cessabunt: serveretur humilitas, & redibit pax: Christus ipse audiatur, qui ad pacem suos cohortans, contentiones de primatu suas, eos missas facere jubet. Marc. 9.34. 35.50. Quum jam patefactum esset, Aristocraticum Israelis regimen in Monarchicum commutatum a Deo esse, magistratum libenter abdicavit Samuel, & ad privatam vitam transijt: 2. Sam. 12. 1. Quidni hujus ad instar Episcopatu jam se exuerat Anglicanus Episcopus, quum Monarchicum Ecclesiae per Episcopos regimen, lux veritatis ubique jam exorta damnet, & Aristocraticum in ministris singulis pari potestate praeditis, amare Christum constet? Atque hoc ad Episcopos portima secundum est, quod a disciplinae reformatae, cum pietate tum necessitate oritur, ut Episcopi scilicet eandem persequentes, & de possessione sua certare desinant, & de eadem cedant.
units.tr: Sect. 65 ject Aeneas, receive Pius? Certainly these are more serious matters than those for which John of Beverley once renounced the archbishopric of York. He was a teacher of Bede; he thought it sweetest to preach the Gospel for the salvation of souls. But, detesting the quarrels and disputes about external ceremonies that arose among churchmen, and at last worn out with weariness of the tumults stirred up in the Church by them, he gave up his office, withdrew to Beverley, and there ended his life in great steadiness of spirit, in the year 721. For Beverley, preaching the Gospel from the pulpit was sweetest: will you not cease to drive the preachers of the Gospel from the pulpit? He detested the quarrels stirred up among churchmen over external ceremonies: will you not cease to stir up quarrels over ceremonies, to the most certain ruin of the Church? He gave up his office when he saw that he could not settle the quarrels: will you not give up that office, through which it stands that the difficulties of the English cannot be settled? And once that office is removed, will not the most open way to concord be laid open? This is clear from Gregory the Great, who dealt with the same cause, in kind, as ours: since the episcopate of Constantinople differed from the English only by a degree, as he says elsewhere. So those words apply here. That man must be restrained who does injury to the Church, who swells in heart, who desires to rejoice in the name of singularity, who sets himself above the honour of others. Behold, we all suffer scandal on this account. Let the author of the scandal therefore return to the right path, and all the quarrels of the priests will cease. Do you see that the way to a short-cut to peace is for the English bishops to cease contending over their primacy; but that there is no hope of peace while they do injury to the Church, bring scandal upon the other ministers, set themselves above their honour, and seek the name of singularity (for Beza especially urges this of the bishop)? Let the bishop's pride therefore depart, and all strife will cease; let humility be preserved, and peace will return. Let Christ himself be heard, who, exhorting his people to peace, bids them let go their contentions over primacy. Mark 9:34, 35, 50. When it had already been made plain that God had changed the aristocratic government of Israel into a monarchical one, Samuel gladly gave up the magistracy and passed into private life: 2 Sam. 12:1. Why should the English bishop not likewise strip himself of the episcopate in the manner of Samuel, since the light of truth, now everywhere risen, condemns the monarchical government of the Church through bishops, and it is agreed that Christ loves the aristocratic government in single ministers endowed with equal power? And this is the second duty of the bishops, which arises from the reformed discipline, both from piety and from necessity: namely, that the bishops, pursuing the same, should cease to contend over their possessions and should yield them up.

units.la: Porisma quartum; Episcopis non Puritanis dissidium Anglicanum imputandum esse.
units.tr: Fourth corollary: the dissension in England is not to be imputed to the bishops who are not Puritans.

units.la: TErtium defensionem porrigit sanctorum in Anglia servorum Dei, qui in causa reformatae disciplinae patiuntur: Hos pro haereticis habet Bancroftus, pro schismaticis Hierarchici omnes, usque adeo ut schismatis seperatistarum etiam, authores eos patresque decantent. Huic calumniae ut respondeatur, sciendum primo non unius generis omnes esse, qui Episcopale in Anglia regimen impugnarunt: sed alios Ecclesiae communionem sancte colere, alios eandem publice deserere, qui vulgari nomine separatistae appellantur. His ego idem accidisse dicerem, quod Tertulliano, si Hieronymo crederem: sic enim ille. Hic cum usque ad mediam aetatem in Ecclesia presbyter remansisset, invidia postea & contumeliis Romanae Ecclesiae ad Montani dogma dilapsus est. Refragatur hac in re Hieronymo Caesar Baronius: quod si vero in re historica adeo labilis Baronij judicio Hieronymus sit, cur illius authoritatem quasi necessariam credendam urget, si modo alicubi dixerit Episcopatum a Marci tempore Alexandriae institutum fuisse? Sed ad rem. Contumeliis Cleri Romani, si modo Hieronimus verus, divexatus Tertullianus, in schisma incidit: sic isti schismatici hodie, persecutione Episcopali in schisma suum prolapsi sunt. Idem & Audio accidit, apud Epiphanium: Multa ille ab Episcopis passus est, propterea quod in eorum luxum atque superbiam inveheretur, adeo haec natio & fastu turgida, & reformationis impatiens, & monitoribus aspera, & ad superbiam luxumque denique, vel ab ipso ortu prona fuit. Sed praestat Epiphanij verba ipsa subtexere. Audius clarus in patria sua propter sinceritatem vitae & zeli, conspicatus ea quae in Ecclesiis fiebant, in faciem Episcoporum & presbyterorum se opponebat, & redarguebat, velut vir veritatis studiosus & exactam vitam vivens. Si quem ex Clero videbat Episcopum vel presbyterum pecuniae studiosum, aut in voluptatibus & deliciis viventem, non ferebat: Et erat hoc grave admodum eis qui vitam approbatam non vivebant. Atque hac de causa contumeliis afficiebatur, contradictiones sustinebat, odio habebatur, agitarique ac protrudi & ignominia affici tolerabat, ad multum tempus in Ecclesia simul degens, donec quidam potenter in ipsum irruentes, virum expellunt propter talem causam: ipse vero non sustinebat se expelli, sed magis nitebatur ut veritatem diceret, & a vinculo Ecclesiae non discedebat. Cum vero verberaretur saepe tum ipse tum sodales ejus, & gravia paterentur valde, ingemiscens consiliarius sibi sumit in iuriarum[?] necessitatem. Nam seipsum ab Ecclesia separat, & multi cum eo discedunt, & sic divisionem fecit, etsi nihil haberet in fide diversum. Habes hic lector quasi in scena huius saeculi mores, omni ex parte, quasi ad vivum repraesentatos. Quando ea legis quae
units.tr: The third defence is offered by the servants of God in England who suffer for the cause of a reformed discipline. Bancroft counts these men heretics, and all the high churchmen call them schismatics, so much so that they even name them the authors and fathers of the schism of the separatists. To answer this calumny, it must first be understood that not all who have opposed the episcopal government in England belong to one kind. Some hold the communion of the Church in holy reverence, while others openly desert it; these are commonly called separatists. I would say that what happened to these men is what happened to Tertullian, if I may believe Jerome. For Jerome says this: Tertullian, though he had remained a presbyter in the Church until middle age, afterwards fell away to the teaching of Montanus, out of envy and because of the insults of the Roman Church. Caesar Baronius contradicts Jerome on this point. But if Jerome is so unreliable in matters of history by Baronius's judgment, why does Baronius insist that his authority must be believed as if it were necessary, whenever Jerome says somewhere that the episcopate was instituted at Alexandria from the time of Mark? But to the point. If Jerome is truthful, Tertullian, harassed by the insults of the Roman clergy, fell into schism; so today these schismatics have fallen into their schism through episcopal persecution. The same thing happened, according to Epiphanius, to Audius. He suffered much from the bishops, because he inveighed against their luxury and pride. This nation, puffed up with arrogance, impatient of reform, harsh toward its admonishers, and inclined from its very origin to pride and luxury, was of such a kind. But it is better to set out Epiphanius's own words. "Audius, famous in his own country for the sincerity of his life and for his zeal, when he saw what was done in the churches, opposed the bishops and presbyters to their faces and rebuked them, like a man devoted to truth and living an exact life. If he saw a bishop or presbyter of the clergy eager for money, or living in pleasures and delights, he did not bear it; and this was very grievous to those who did not live an approved life. For this reason he was subjected to insults, he endured contradictions, he was hated, and he suffered himself to be harassed, thrust out and disgraced, for a long time remaining in the Church together with others, until certain men, rushing upon him with power, drove the man out for such a cause. Yet he would not suffer himself to be expelled, but strove the more to speak the truth, and did not depart from the bond of the Church. But when he and his companions were often beaten and suffered very grievously, he, groaning, took counsel and resolved on separation out of the necessity of injuries. For he separated himself from the Church, and many left with him, and so he made a division, although he held nothing different in faith." Here, reader, you have the manners of this age, as it were on a stage, represented in every respect, as if to the life. When you read what is written there, Epiphanius speaks of the bishops: imagine you are seeing the English bishops, hating, insulting, tearing apart, harassing, and trampling down the wretched Puritans with contradictions, and finally, rushing in with power, driving them from their homes, their functions, and the Church itself. When you see what Epiphanius reports of Audius, imagine you are seeing Puritans in England, famous for the sincerity of their life and their zeal, rebuking the faults they see in the English Church, as men devoted to truth and living an exact life ought to do; and although they suffer all those dreadful things already mentioned at the hands of the bishops, they do not depart from the bond of the Church, nor do they suffer themselves to be expelled, but strive the more that the cause of truth they have taken up may be left safe to posterity. What remains in Epiphanius touches the separatists, who are the more inexcusable because they do not imitate the patience of the Puritans, who suffer all the same things and yet have never shaken themselves free from the bosom of the Church. Nor do I fear that any fair-minded person will not praise them for this, that though they suffered so much they did not violate fraternal charity and the bond of peace. And as for the accusation of viperous brood, let the bishops remember that those who tear the Church asunder, even though they do not depart from its communion, are also called vipers by Christ. Matthew 23:33. Hugo of Saint Cher explains this thus: "Many clerics are the offspring of vipers: for the young kills the mother when it is born, because the mother bursts; and many who have been born in the Church persevere against the Church and against Christ the Father, and, as far as in them lies, kill it." Therefore those bishops and clergy who persecute the holy servants of God in the Church cannot even allege against the schismatics that famous secession of Menenius Agrippa to the Aventine, nor could Pope Hadrian the Fourth, of whom we read thus in John of Salisbury: "Rebuked for luxury, avarice, sloth, and the plundering of the Church, he confessed that the prelates of the Church might seem to be bellies, which devour much, yet not wholly idle, since they supply the body with the irrigation and vegetation it needs." But Scripture is accustomed to compare ministers not to the belly but rather to the head, the eyes, and the nostrils, 1 Cor. 12. And a bishop, insofar as he is a bishop, supplies no necessary irrigation to the body, and a bishop who persecutes the holy servants of God is to be called a viper in the belly rather than the belly itself, since he causes the belly to burst. However that may be, the ministers in England who suffer for the reformed discipline are so far from being vipers that I may fairly say they sustain a common cause with all the holy servants of God who have contended vigorously and bravely against the corruptions of their own times, at whatever time they lived. Basil was displeased by the pride of the western bishops, just as the English are displeased by the pride of theirs; and they do not usually threaten harshly, as he did, that it is not fitting to press those who have been humbled and afflicted by temptations, nor that such a sin, even if it stood alone, would suffice to establish enmity against God. In

units.la: Tom. 2. epist. 281. hic Epiphanius de Episcopis, cogita te videre Episcopos Anglicanos, miseros Puritanos odio habentes contumeliis afficientes, contradictionibus lacerantes, agitantes, protrudentes, injuriis divexantes, & ad postremum potenter irruendo, eos laribus, functionibus, Ecclesiâ ipsâ expellentes. Quando quæ de Audio refert cernis, cogita te videre Puritanos in Angliâ, propter vitæ sinceritatem zelumque claros, quæ in Ecclesia Anglicana vitiosa fieri vident redarguentes, prout viros studiosos & exactam vitam viventes decet, & quanquâ omnia ea dira, quorum mentio jam facta est, ab Episcopis patiantur, a vinculo Ecclesiæ non discedentes, neque se expelli sustinentes, sed eo magis adnitentes, ut quàm suscéperunt veritatis causam, relinquant salvam posteris. Quæ vero reliqua apud Epiphanium sunt, ea separatistas attingunt, eo magis inexcusabiles, quòd patientiam Puritanorum non imitentur, qui eadem omnia patiuntur, & Ecclesiæ gremio tamen semet minimè excusserunt: Neq; verò, vereor, quin quisq; æquus eos hoc nomine collaudaturus sit, quòd tanta passi, fraternam tamen charitatem, pacisque vinculum non violarint. Et quòd ad viperinam accusationem attinet, meminisse Episcopos & uiperas etiam audire eos apud Christum, qui interstitin us Ecclesiam lacerant, etsi ab illius communione non discedent. Math. 23, 33, Hoc ab Hugone de sancto Charo explicatum ita. Multi Clerici sunt progeniés viperarum: Fœtus enim interficit matrem quando nascitur, quia mater crepat: & multi ex quo nati sunt in Ecclesia, perseveruntur contra Ecclesiam, & Christum Patrem, & quantum in ipsis est, interficiunt. Qui igitur sanctos in Ecclesia servos Dei Episcopi & Clerici perseguuntur: ne illud quidem Menonij Agrippæ in Aventino discessione contra schismaticos causari possunt, sicut nec Hadrianus Papa quartus potuit, de quo ita legimus apud Iohannem Sarisburiensem: Reprehensus illæ, ob luxum, avaritiam, inertiâ, & Ecclesiæ delapidatione, confessus est Prælatos Ecclesiæ ventres videri posse, qui multa devorarent, sed non penitus ignavos tamen, mihi agentes, ut qui necessaria corpori irrigationi, vegetationemq; tribuerent. At non ventri pastores copararē Scripturæ solet, sed capiti potius, oculis, naribus, 1, Cor. 12. & Episcopus qua Episcopus necessariam corpori irrigationem nullam tribuit, & Episcopus sanctos Dei servos persequens, vipera in ventre potius, quàm ipse venter dicendus est, ut qui ventrem crepare faciat. Vtcunq; sit, ministri in Anglia pro disciplina reformata patientes, tantum abest ut vperæ sint, ut communem eos causam sustinere merito dixerim, cùm sanctis quibusque servis Dei, qui adversus sui temporis corruptelas, quoquo tempore strenuè & fortiter decertarunt. Displicuit Basilio Episcoporum occidentalium superbia, perinde ac his Anglicanorum, neque hi duris denuntiare solent, quam denunciauit ille, non decere premere eos qui per tentationes humiliati sunt, & afflicti, neque cum id peccati vel solum ad constituendam adversus Deum inimicitiam sufficiat. units.tr: Epiphanius, Letter 281, vol. 2. Here Epiphanius speaks of bishops; think that you see the English bishops hating and insulting the wretched Puritans, tearing them with contradictions, harassing, thrusting out, troubling them with injuries, and at last, rushing in with power, driving them from their homes, their functions, and the Church itself. When you see what he reports of Audius, think that you see Puritans in England, famous for the sincerity of their life and their zeal, rebuking what they see done amiss in the English Church, as is fitting for men devoted to truth and living an exact life; and although they suffer from the bishops all those dire things already mentioned, they do not depart from the bond of the Church, nor do they suffer themselves to be expelled, but strive the more that the cause of truth they have undertaken may be left safe to posterity. What remains in Epiphanius touches the separatists, who are the more inexcusable because they do not imitate the patience of the Puritans, who suffer all the same things and yet have never shaken themselves out of the bosom of the Church. Nor, I fear, will any fair-minded person fail to praise them on this account, that though they suffered so much they did not violate fraternal charity and the bond of peace. And as for the viperous accusation, let the bishops remember that those too are called vipers by Christ who tear the Church from within, even though they do not depart from its communion. Matthew 23:33. Hugo of Saint Cher explains this thus: "Many clerics are the offspring of vipers: for the young kills the mother when it is born, because the mother bursts; and many who have been born in the Church persevere against the Church and against Christ the Father, and, as far as in them lies, kill it."

units.la: In eadem etiam causa patiuntur in qua Hieronymus passus est, in quem quod liberius & locutus esset & scripsisse, Clerum Romanum coniurasse Baronius ipse non diffitetur: unde in Palaestina se recipere cogebatur: Haec autem libertas ea fuit, quae jam Anglicana est, Ecclesiae suae Hierarchicam impetere visus est, inquit Dominus Mornaeus, verba vero illius ea citat, quae & ministrorum sunt, & in Episcopos Anglicanos recidunt. Est ibi (inquit) sancta Ecclesia, id ipsum de Anglia jam ministri confitentur. At sane ambitio (inquit) & potentia, luxuria etiam ventris & gutturis, quae subvertere nititur fortitudinem cujus vexillum auferitas sustulerat praedicationis. At nunquam Hieronymo videre contigit divexationas praedicantium crucé eas, quas jam in Anglia videre est: ubi austera praedicatio crucis omnis videtur, quae adversus vitia fortis est: ita ambitio, potentia, luxuriaque praevaluerunt. Concilium Ephesinum Canonem edidit contra Episcopos alienam provinciam invadentes: primo ne sub praetextu sacerdotij potestatis factus in Ecclesiam irreperet: secundo, ne libertas amittatur, quam nobis Christus dedit. Quas rationes citat & approbat Whitakerus: Duplici igitur nomine ministri in Anglia exeusandi jam sunt: primo qui sciunt Episcoporum Anglicanorum in reliquos collegas usurpationem, potestatis factum redolere: secundo, quia standum pro libertate putant, quam pastori unicuique Christus dedit, quae multo magis ab usurpatione Episcopali Anglicana jam periclitatur, quam ab invasione ea, quam concilium Ephesinum condemnavit. Quum Iohanes Constantinopolitanus Episcopus Universalis fieri voluit: non solum Gregorius ipsi restituit, sed ad alios scripsit etiam, ut communem sacerdotum dignitatem tuerentur. Rationes vero easdem fere quas Concilium anno Ephesinum affert. Primo, quod Luciferi superbiam imboleat, supra Episcopos, qui nubes & stellae sunt, se exaltare.
units.tr: They suffer in the same cause in which Jerome suffered, against whom Baronius himself does not deny that the Roman clergy conspired, because he had spoken and written too freely; on account of this he was forced to withdraw into Palestine. This freedom is the very freedom that the English now have. He seemed to attack the hierarchical rule of his own Church, says Lord Mornay, and he quotes his words, which belong to the ministers and fall back upon the English bishops. "There is," he says, "a holy Church," and the ministers in England already confess the same thing about England. "But truly ambition," he says, "and power, and also the luxury of belly and throat, which seek to undermine the strength whose banner the enemy had lifted up, that of preaching." But it never fell to Jerome's lot to see the harassments of those who preach the cross which are now to be seen in England, where the austere preaching of the cross seems to be all that is strong against vices. Thus ambition, power, and luxury have prevailed. The Council of Ephesus issued a canon against bishops who invade a province not their own: first, lest under the pretext of priestly power a faction should creep into the Church; second, lest the liberty which Christ has given us be lost. Whitaker cites and approves these reasons. Therefore the ministers in England must now be excused on a double ground: first, because they know that the usurpation of the English bishops over their fellow colleagues smells of the faction of power; second, because they think they must stand up for the liberty which Christ gave to each pastor, which is now far more endangered by the English episcopal usurpation than by that invasion which the Council of Ephesus condemned. When John, bishop of Constantinople, wished to be made universal bishop, Gregory not only rebuked him but also wrote to others that they should defend the common dignity of priests. The reasons he gives are almost the same as those the Council of Ephesus gave in its time. First, because it imitates the pride of Lucifer, to exalt himself above the bishops, who are clouds and stars.

units.la: Secundo, quia dum privatum aliquid datur uni, honore debito sacerdotes spoliantur universi. Duplici igitur nomine ministri in Anglia rursus excusandi sunt. Primo, quod sciant ministros omnes Episcopos esse, & nubes Dei, & stellas Christi, quas ille in manu sua tenet: sic ut Luciferiana superbia turgeant Anglicani Episcopi sit necesse, qui supra eos se exaltant. Secundo quod videant, si privatum illud & singulare quod jam Episcopi sibi vendicant, illis tribuerent, honore debito ministros verbi Dei reliquos spoliarent. Iam vero hujus Gregorij tepore appulit in Anglia Augustinus monachus qui mille ducentos Bangorenses neci tradi procuravit, quod sium pro suo Archiepiscopo recipere noluerant. Quidni igitur hodie imitatores ministros dicerem, etsi usq; ad sanguinem, sicuti illi, adversus Episcopos Archiepiscopos adhuc non restituerunt; Imo vero, inquies, refert Galfridus Monumetensis, septem ex Episcopatus, & Archiepiscopatum unum habuisse. Sed quaeo, quales? Quum ad Synodum anno 602, inquit Bales, authoritate regia vocarentur: consu- lucerunt luerunt virum gravem quendam & prudentem,qui Augustinum proArchiepiscopo recipiendum non fuisse suasit, nisi ipsis assurgeret, praesertim numero pluribus, & signa sodalitatis praeberet. Quid fit? Accedunt Bangorenses & Augustinum ambitose in scilla sedentem vident, & neque eis assurgentem, neque signa aliqua familiaritatis praebentem.Quid illi?Mori potius maluerunt,quam hujusmodi Archiepiscopo patriamque Ecclesiamque subiugatam videre. Quam illi virtutem ne admitteretur Episcopatus Hierarchicus ostenderunt, annon jam ut profligaretur ostendere eorum posteros? Vide Anglia quinā tui prisci Archiepiscopi fuerint,& ob amissam libertate ingemisce.In sella sedere olim Archiepiscopū, ambitiosū putabatur: non collegis assurgere,non signa omnia familiaritatis, socijs praebere, numero pluribus eorumq; maiori parti subiectum non esse : tyrannicū, impudens,superbū habebatur. Atq; hanc societatē quam Bangorenses in Augustino expectabant,non in Episcopos solum, verū & ipsis patriarchis requisivit Bernard. de qua amissa, ita jam ministri in Anglia illius verbis conqueruntur.Vides omnem Ecclesiasticum zelum ferveré pro sola dignitate tuenda: Honori tantum datur;sanctitati nihil,aut parum: Si causa requirente paulo summissius agere,aut socialius te habere tentaveris, absit inquiunt, non decet, tempori non congruit, majestati non convenit, quam geras personam attendite:De placito Dei ultima mentio est,pro justura salutis nulla cunctatio,quod sublime est hoc salutare putamus, & quod gloriam redolet, id justum . . . . Hic, hic, non parco tibi, ut parcat Deus. Vides non nunc primo inter omnes verbi ministros socialitatem desiderari: non nunc primo in Anglia, hic graphice depictum Episcopalem fastum coargui, zelumque illum qui in Episcopis Anglicanis fervere jam solet,pro sola dignitate tuenda, reprehendi.
units.tr: Secondly, when something private is given to one man, all the priests are robbed of their due honour. The ministers in England may therefore be excused again on two counts. First, they know that all ministers are bishops, clouds of God and stars of Christ, which he holds in his hand, so it is inevitable that the English bishops, who exalt themselves above them, should swell with Luciferian pride. Second, they see that if the bishops were to grant to them that private and singular status which the bishops now claim for themselves, the remaining ministers of God's Word would be robbed of their due honour. Indeed, in the time of this Gregory, Augustine the monk landed in England and brought it about that twelve hundred Bangorians were put to death, because they had refused to receive him as their archbishop. Why, then, should I not call the ministers today their imitators, even if they have not yet, as those did, resisted bishops and archbishops even to the point of bloodshed? But you will say that Geoffrey of Monmouth reports that Britain had seven bishoprics and one archbishopric. But I ask, what sort of men were they? When they were summoned by royal authority to a synod in the year 602, as Bale says, they consulted a certain grave and prudent man, who advised that Augustine was not to be received as archbishop unless he rose to greet them, especially since they were more in number, and showed signs of fellowship. What happened? The Bangorians came up and saw Augustine sitting ostentatiously in a chair, neither rising to them nor showing any sign of familiarity. What did they do? They preferred to die rather than see their country and church subjected to such an archbishop. By that courage they showed that a hierarchical episcopate should not be admitted; should not their descendants now show that it be overthrown? Look, England, at what sort of archbishops your forebears were, and groan over your lost liberty. In former times an archbishop who sat in a chair was thought ambitious; not to rise to his colleagues, not to show them any sign of familiarity, and not to submit to the greater number and to the greater part of them, was held to be tyrannical, shameless and proud. This fellowship, which the Bangorians looked for in Augustine, Bernard sought not only in bishops but in the patriarchs themselves; and since it has been lost, the ministers in England now complain in his words: "You see all ecclesiastical zeal glowing only to defend dignity. Honour alone is given; holiness nothing, or very little. If, when the cause requires, you try to act a little more humbly, or to behave more sociably, they say, 'Far be it; it is not fitting, it does not suit the time, it does not agree with majesty; consider the person you bear.' The will of God is mentioned last; for the sake of salvation there is no hesitation. What is sublime we think salutary, and what smells of glory, that is just... Here, here, I do not spare you, so that God may spare you." You see that fellowship has not been missed for the first time now among all ministers of the Word; and not for the first time in England is episcopal pride here vividly depicted and rebuked, and that zeal which now customarily glows in the English bishops, for defending dignity alone, reproved.

units.la: Operaepretium vero est ea interere, quae de novo Bernardo Otho Frisingensis refert. Praefuit ille Sinodo in Iulliis, Pictaviae habitae, in qua Gilbertus Porretanus ejus loci Episcopus, de Trinitate male sentiens, damnatus est, composito symbolo, in quo quid erat eā de re sentiendum probatur. Hinc Cardinales vociferantur. Quid fecit Abbas ille tuus, & cum eo Gallicana Ecclesia? Qua fronte, quo ausu, cervicem contra Romanæ sedis primatum & apicem erexit? Hæc est enim sola qua claudit & nemo aperit, aperit, & nemo claudit. Ipsa sola de fide Catholica disputare habeas, à nullo etiam absens, in hoc singulari honore praejudicium pati non potest. His Eugenius irritatus,novitatem tantam severio vindicandum putat: unde, Romam accitus Bernardus, se humiliter purgat, & symbum Gallicum, quanquam bonum rescissum est. Vrebat vero & illud, quod Bernardus inter disputandum, quaedam verba liberiora protulisset:ad quae cum Gilbertus Porretanus dixisset, scribatur; & hoc, respondit Bernardus: Ita quidem & stylo fereo & ungue admanitio. Revocetur hic Iurisperitorum placitum illud. De similibus sumus est judicium: & in Ecclesia Gallicana Ecclesias reformatas,in Bernardo ministros Anglicanos, in cardinalibus libus Anglicanos Episcopos repræsentari affirmo. In Ecclesiis reformatis Synodus celebrant, de rebus fidei in Synodis judicant, & Synodis præsident, authoritate communi & in singulis pari. Pro quâ libertate Ecclesiasticâ revocanda, ministri Anglicani contendunt: Exclamant Episcopi, cervicem hoc modo erigi in primatum & apicem dignitatis Episcopalis, eamque in suo singulari honore præjudicium non ferendum pati; Episcoporum etenim proprium esse judices sedere, excommunicationemq; ad eos soles pertinere, ut nemo præterea, aut claudere, aut aperire nisi eorum licentiâ possit: factiosum deniq; cœtum unumquemq; in Anglia Puritanicum esse, ubi ipsis insciis formæ disciplinæ exarantur, aut res aliæ Ecclesiasticæ agitantur. Nihil igitur novi in Anglia fit, libertas ministrorum, libertas Bernardiana fuit: singularis Episcoporum honor, honor ille erat, pro quo Romani Cardinales contra Bernardum dimicabant: At sicuti quæ Bernardus pro libertate ecclesiastica à Cardinalibus patiebatur, pro ministris in Anglia patientibus sunt: ita etiam & illa, quæ à Bernardo AlbingensES. Quum enim ille externam eorum conversationem damnari non posse intellexit, ut nec ministrorum damnare jam hodie Episcopi possunt; hypocrisin scilicet illis objecit, sed verbis eis, quæ ex pulpitis jam detonare in ministros Hierarchici solent: Hi ovec sunt habitu, astu vulpes, crudelitate lupi, hi sunt qui boni videre, non esse mali non videri & esse volunt. Quinetiam Episcopum Anglicanum egit? quum multitudinem ad eos confluentem ægrè tulit: quemadmodū multitudines ad ministros confluentes ferre jam nequeunt Hierarchici Anglicani: Atq; sanè has ut cohibeant, similia ferè cum Bernardo vociferantur: Basilicæ sine plebibus, plebes sine sacerdotibus, sacerdotes sine reverentia, & sine Christo deinde Christiani. Ecclesiæ hac ratione Synagogæ reputantur: Atque hos quidem Albingenses, Bernardus in Cantica, per contemptum Apostolicos vocat, quem ad morem, & ministri Anglicani jam à nonnullis traducuntur, quod nullum illis regimen Ecclesiæ, nisi Apostolicum placeat.
units.tr: It is worth inserting what Otto of Freising reports about Bernard. He presided over the synod held at Iulliis in Poitou, in which Gilbert of Poitiers, bishop of that place, thinking ill about the Trinity, was condemned, and a creed was drawn up in which what was to be thought on that matter was set out. Hence the cardinals cry out: "What has that abbot of yours done, and with him the Gallican Church? With what brow, with what daring, has he raised his neck against the primacy and summit of the Roman see? For this is the one that shuts and no one opens, that opens and no one shuts. It alone has the right to dispute about the Catholic faith, and it cannot suffer prejudice in this singular honour, even in its absence." Angered by this, Eugenius thought such novelty should be punished more severely; hence Bernard was summoned to Rome, humbly cleared himself, and the Gallican creed, though sound, was annulled. What also galled them was that Bernard, in the course of the debate, had uttered some rather free words; and when Gilbert of Poitiers said, "Let it be written down," Bernard replied: "Indeed, let it be written with an iron stylus and a point of adamant." Let that legal maxim be recalled here: concerning like things the judgement is the same. I affirm that in the Gallican Church the reformed churches are represented, in Bernard the English ministers, and in those cardinals the English bishops. In the reformed churches they hold synods, they judge matters of faith in synods, and they preside over synods, with common authority and equal standing for each member. For the recovery of this ecclesiastical liberty the English ministers contend; the bishops cry out that the neck is thus raised against the primacy and summit of episcopal dignity, and that such prejudice to their singular honour must not be borne. For it is proper to bishops to sit as judges, and excommunication belongs to them alone, so that no one else may shut or open except by their leave; and every assembly in England is a factious Puritan one, where forms of discipline are drawn up or other ecclesiastical matters are discussed without their knowledge. Nothing new, then, is happening in England: the liberty of the ministers was Bernardine liberty, and the singular honour of the bishops was that honour for which the Roman cardinals fought against Bernard. But just as what Bernard suffered at the hands of the cardinals for ecclesiastical liberty is suffered by the ministers in England, so too are those things which Bernard [did] against the Albigensians. For when he understood that their outward way of life could not be condemned, just as bishops today cannot condemn ministers, he charged them with hypocrisy, in words such as hierarchs are wont to thunder from the pulpits against ministers today: "They are sheep in habit, foxes in cunning, wolves in cruelty; these are the ones who wish to seem good, not to be evil, and not to seem evil while being so." Did he not also act like an English bishop, when he took it badly that crowds flocked to them? Just as English hierarchs can no longer bear crowds flocking to ministers, so too, to restrain these crowds, they cry out much as Bernard did: "Churches without people, people without priests, priests without reverence, and then Christians without Christ. By this reasoning churches are reckoned as synagogues." Bernard, in his sermons on the Canticles, scornfully calls these Albigensians "Apostolics"; and in this manner some now malign the English ministers too, because they approve of no church government except an apostolic one.

units.la: Horum vero successores Waldenses, Cathari audiebant, sicut nunc ministri in Anglia, Puritani: idque eandem ferè ob causam, uti ex eis liquet, quæ Reinerius Pisanus objicit: Quid enim ille? Male nempe cum habet, quòd affirment Ecclesiam à Sylvestri tempore degenerasse, quòd lentiant Episcoporum dotationes per Constantinum, venenum in Ecclesiam effundisset quod denique cruce-signationes & ceremonias Ecclesiæ reliquas abolcant, quæ primævam simplicitatem redolere non viticbantur. Quòd si porro hæc sequentia Reinerij verba tecum recolas, Episcopum Anglicanum in Puritanos detonantem te audire putabis. Inter omnes sectas (inquit) non est permissior quam Leonistarum (puritanorum:) quia omnes aliæ (papisticæ præsertim) immanitate blasphemiarum horrorem inducunt: hæc vero magnam habent speciem pietatis, eo quod coram bonimibus juste vivant, & sine omnia de Deo credant, & omnes articulos qui in Symbolo continentur.
units.tr: The successors of these were the Waldenses and Cathari, who heard the same things as the ministers in England, the Puritans do now; and this for almost the same reason, as is clear from those charges which Reinerius of Pisa brings: for what does he say? He is angry, of course, that they assert the Church has degenerated since the time of Sylvester, that they lament the endowments of bishops from Constantine, that Constantine poured poison into the Church, and that they finally abolish the sign of the cross and the other ceremonies of the Church, which did not seem to smell of primitive simplicity. But if you go over with yourself the following words of Reinerius, you will think you are hearing an English bishop thundering against the Puritans: "Among all sects (he says) none is more tolerable than that of the Leonists (that is, the Puritans), because all the others (the Papistical especially) bring horror by the enormity of their blasphemies; but this one has a great appearance of piety, because they live justly before men, believe everything about God, and believe all the articles contained in the Creed."

units.la: Serm. in Cantic. 66.
units.tr: Serm. in Cantic. 66.

units.la: Epist. 240.
units.tr: Epist. 240.

units.la: Histor. Pal. p. 329.
units.tr: Histor. Pal. p. 329.

units.la: P. 328. tinentur: Ioannem Rothanam (Anglicanam) Ecclesiam blasphemant & ode- runt, cui multitudo facilis est ad credendum (adeo scilicet popularem Puritani sunt) Ad haec vero Waldensium tempora Iohannes Sarisburiensis prope accedit, circa annum 1160: qui adeo graphice reformatorum in Anglia conditionem describit, ut nihil supra. Qui pro veritate fidei inquit aut pro sinceritate morum aliquid loquitur, aut superstitiosus est, aut invidus, aut quod capitale est, principis inimicus. Si quid dixeris contra dominatores fidei, bene tecum agetur, si non mutilatus retundaris in carcerem, aut in exilium propellaris: undique conclamaberis: & tam ambitiosi quam fautores eorum, extremae damnationis in te non verebuntur ferre sententiam: unum autem remedium tibi Dominus procurabit, quod cuiusque sapientis & timentis Deum conscientia consonat verbis tuis. Inde est quod sententia eorum de te, non semper obtinet: Si enim ipsis creditum fuerit, quasi lese maiestatis reus, hostis publicus iudicaberis. Diceris quippe publica evacuare iudicia, & dum professionis propriae zelator, Ecclesiasticam erigis libertatem, sapientum subvertis principum, cosque quasi stultos & contemptibiles reddere machineris.
units.tr: P. 328. are contained: they blaspheme and hate the (Anglican) Church, to which the crowd is easily persuaded (so popular, indeed, are the Puritans). Near to the times of the Waldenses comes John of Salisbury, about the year 1160, who describes the condition of the reformers in England so vividly that nothing could be added. "Whoever speaks anything for the truth of the faith or for the sincerity of morals, he says, is either superstitious, or envious, or, what is worst, an enemy of the prince. If you say anything against the lords of the faith, it will go well for you if you are not mutilated, and beaten back into prison or driven into exile. From every side you will be cried down; and the ambitious, as well as their supporters, will not hesitate to pronounce on you the sentence of utter damnation. But the Lord will provide one remedy for you: that your words agree with the conscience of every wise man who fears God. Hence it is that their judgement about you does not always prevail; for if they are believed, you will be judged guilty of treason, a public enemy. You will be said to overturn public judgements; and while you zealously profess your own cause and raise up ecclesiastical liberty, you are plotting to subvert the wise princes and to make them seem foolish and contemptible."

units.la: Matte igitur virtute o fratres fortissimi, non vos patribus vestris meliores estis: qui eadem ut hic videtis, passi sunt, facem vobis praeferentes: ex invidia Hierarchiam reprehendere dicimini, ita & de illis dictum. Professionis quasi propriae zelatores stulti quidem si non insani habimini: haud minus illis singularitatis amantes, & zelo plus nimium fervido sententiarum propriarum sectatores habebantur. Libertatem Ecclesiasticam quaerere vobis iam probri loco est: ita & illis etiam eandem exercere: presbyterialem disciplinam erigendo, regiam maiestatem laedere, & publica iudicia evacuare conclamamini: ita & de illis conclamatum erat: principis sapientiam in quaestione vocare vos, ut eiusdem potestatem contemptibile reddere obiicitur hodie: ita illis obiectum olim. Cogitate porro criminationes quas ad horum instar sustinetis, carceres quibus mancipamini, exilia in quae pellimini: ab eisdem ambitiosis, eisdem dominatoribus fidei, eisdem adulatoribus iam provenire, a quibus olim similia intentata sunt, testimonium interim vobis perhibente, cuiusque Deum timentis viri conscientia, imo Christo ipso quasi agonotheta, vos inspectante, coronamque; vobis immarcescibilem in caelo praeparante.
units.tr: Take courage then, O most brave brothers. You are no better than your fathers, who suffered the same things, as you see here, and who carried the torch before you. You are said to rebuke the hierarchy out of envy, and this was said of them too. As zealots for your own profession you are considered fools, if not madmen. They were regarded no less as lovers of singularity and as followers of their own opinions with a zeal that burned too hotly. To seek ecclesiastical liberty is now a reproach to you, and they were likewise shouted down for exercising that same liberty by setting up presbyterial discipline, injuring royal majesty, and overturning public judgments. It was likewise cried out against them that they called the wisdom of the prince into question so as to make his authority contemptible, which is now objected to you and was objected to them of old. Consider further the accusations you endure like these, the prisons into which you are thrown, and the exiles into which you are driven. These have come from the same ambitious men, the same lords of faith, and the same flatterers, by whom similar things were once directed against them. Meanwhile the conscience of every man who fears God bears witness for you, and Christ himself, as it were the judge of the games, watches you and prepares for you an unfading crown in heaven.

units.la: 9 Pergamus ad alios: Adelbertus, Clemens, Sampson, Sidonius, Virgilius sive Vergilius, cur quaeso a Papa Zachariá excommunicati, quidam etiam incarcerati sunt? Non ut haeretici sed ut schismatici, revera ut Puritani Anglicani: Bonifacio etenim Romani Episcopi authoritate iactitanti reiterunt, principio isto puritanico, Omnes veros doctores Apostolorum successores esse. Quaeso te quisquis es, si omnes doctores Apostolorum successores sint adaeq; ac ipse Papa; cur non adaeq; ac ipse Dominus Archiepiscopus Episcopusque? Neq; lepidum illud de Virgilio apud Aventinum, extra hanc causam nostram est: praedicasse scilicet Virgilium esse Antipodas, ob eamque causam de gradu deiectum.
units.tr: 9 Let us pass on to others. Adelbert, Clement, Sampson, Sidonius, Virgil or Vergil: why, I ask, were they excommunicated by Pope Zachary, and some of them even imprisoned? Not as heretics but as schismatics, indeed as English Puritans. For they repeated, against the boastful authority of the Roman bishop, that Puritan principle that all true teachers are successors of the Apostles. I ask you, whoever you are: if all teachers are successors of the Apostles, are they equal to the Pope himself? If so, why are they not equal to the Lord Archbishop and Bishop? Nor is that witty story about Virgil in Aventinus relevant to our cause, namely that Virgil taught that there were Antipodes and for that reason was deposed from his rank.

units.la: Salum tent. 14. c. 30. §1. 32. jectum, quòd alium mundum, alium œcumenicum pontificem, alium solem docere videretur: Nam ut quaelibet monstra fabricatus tum Bonifacius est, cum primatui papali quid detractum videbatur: ita ex nostra pro reformata disciplina defensione haud minùs vera, mirabilia quaedam somniant Episcopi, mundi scilicet totius innovationem, imò mundi cujusdam novi fabricationem, novos Papas, novos Pontifices, novas regulas, novum certè regimen, solemque etiam Ecclesiæ novum, quia spirituali radio tantùm, non autem externo hoc Hierarchico collucentem: Atque ut hisce succedunt jam ministri in Angliâ, ita & aliis viris haud minori sanctitate claris.
units.tr: ...Salum tent. 14. c. 30. §1. 32. ...he was ejected, because he seemed to teach another world, another ecumenical pontiff, and another sun. For Boniface was just as much a fabricator of monsters whenever anything seemed to be taken from papal primacy. So too, from our defence of the reformed discipline, which is no less true, the bishops dream up certain marvels: namely a renewal of the whole world, indeed the fabrication of some new world, new Popes, new pontiffs, new rules, certainly a new government, and also a new sun of the Church, because it shines only with a spiritual ray and not with this external hierarchical one. And just as these things now befall the ministers in England, so they also befell other men of no less distinguished holiness.

units.la: Quid ego de Arnulpho dicerem? Non etenim ob haeresim aliquam Honorij tempore, aut odio habitus ille, aut clanculùm à Romano Clero interfectus: sed illius temporis Puritanus cum esset, quòd Episcoporum inertiam, luxum, superbiam, delicatioris{q} vitae amorem liberius reprehenderet. Non multùm ab hujus tempore Arnoldus Brixiensis distabat, ab Haeriano 4. haereseos damnatus, quòd civilem administrationem in clero damnaret, quô nomine in Anglia & hodie ministri patiuntur. Puritanus etiam ad annum 1250. Robertus Capito Episcopus Lincolniensis erat, ob assertiones tum Puritanicas, & vexatus multis modis, & excommunicatus, & excomunicatione tandem mortuus. In epitaphio, Praelatorum correptor, & Presbyterorum director celebratur: nimirum à luxu, pompa, superbiaque ea abfuit, quibus jam praelati Anglicani laborant: prout illa tempora ferebant, ad puritanicam dumtaxat presbyterorum directionem accedebat. Quam verò puritanicè in concione ea quam commemorat Io. Hus, coram Papa; contra Episcopos, indoctos pastores & negligentes, jam in Anglia non tolerantes modò, sed pariter approbantes detonabat?
units.tr: What should I say about Arnulf? He was not hated, nor secretly killed by the Roman clergy, on account of any heresy in the time of Honorius. He was a Puritan of his own time, because he reproved more freely the sloth, luxury, pride and love of soft living among the bishops. Not much different from this time was Arnold of Brescia, condemned as a heretic by Hadrian IV because he condemned civil administration by the clergy, a charge for which ministers in England even today suffer. Also a Puritan, up to the year 1250, was Robert Grosseteste, Bishop of Lincoln, because of his Puritan assertions. He was harassed in many ways, excommunicated, and died under excommunication. On his epitaph he is celebrated as corrector of prelates and director of presbyters. Clearly he was free of that luxury, pomp and pride with which English prelates now labour. As those times allowed, he came close only to the Puritan direction of presbyters. But how Puritanically did he thunder, in that sermon which John Hus mentions, before the Pope, against bishops, and against pastors who were ignorant and negligent, and who in England now not only tolerate such men but also approve of them!

units.la: Lugendae inquit coarctationis ac imminutionis, ac per hoc dilationis complementi regni Christi causa in promptu est, bonorum scil. pastorum defectio, & malorum multiplicatio. Unius enim una est causa, & oppositorum causae oppositae: unde cùm boni pastores, & potestatis pastoralis libertas causa fuerunt dilatationis fidei & religionis Christianae: necessariò contra coarctationis & immutationis ejusdem fidei & religionis causae, sunt pastores mali, & eorum multiplicatio, & potestatis pastoralis repressio. Et quia boni corruptio est oppositi mali generatio, necessario mali pastores sunt causa infidelitatis, schismatis, haereticae pravitatis, & vitiosae conversationis per omnem orbem. Ipsi enim sunt secundum vocem Prophetarum, portionis dominicae desiderabilis in desertum solitudinis datores, omnis terrae desolatores, gregis Domini dispersores, dilaceratores & dissipatores vineae Domini, depastores & demolitores, & pollutionis super omnem terram effusores. Sed quae est hujus mali tanti prior & originalis causa, fons & origo? Causa, fons, & origo hujus est haec Curia: non solum ex eo quod haec non dissipat: & has abominationes non purgat, cum ea sola haec maxime possit & ad hoc summe teneatur, sed eo amplius, quod ipsa per suas provisiones, dispensationes, & collationes, curae pastoralis talis, quaVt prætassi sint pastores, imo mundi proditores, in oculis solis bujus constituit. Hæc ille, in quibus causam nostram agit multis modis.
units.tr: "Lamentable," he says, "is the cause of the restriction and diminution, and so of the delayed completion of the kingdom of Christ, namely the failure of good pastors and the multiplication of bad ones. For one cause has one effect, and opposite causes have opposite effects. Hence, since good pastors and the freedom of pastoral power were the causes of the spread of the faith and the Christian religion, the causes of the restriction and diminution of that same faith and religion must necessarily be bad pastors, their multiplication, and the repression of pastoral power. And since the corruption of the good is the generation of the opposite evil, bad pastors are necessarily the cause of unbelief, schism, heretical depravity and vicious conduct throughout the whole world. For they are, according to the voice of the prophets, the givers of the Lord's desirable portion to the desert of solitude, the desolators of all the earth, the scatterers of the Lord's flock, the tearers and wreckers of the Lord's vineyard, the devourers and destroyers, and the pourers-out of pollution over all the earth. But what is the prior and original cause of so great an evil, its source and origin? The cause, source and origin of it is this Curia: not only because it does not scatter these abominations or purge them, although it alone could most of all do this and is most bound to do so, but further because, through its provisions, dispensations and grants, it so arranges the pastoral care that the prelates who are pastors are, indeed, betrayers of the world, in the eyes of this Curia alone." Thus he speaks, and in these words he argues our cause in many ways.

units.la: Primò, pastoralis potestatis repressionem, totius in Ecclesia mali originalem causam ponit: mali igitur in Episcopos culpa jam omnis conferenda, quia & libertatem pastoralem, dum prædicant, diminuunt miserè, & pastores permultos qui diligentissimè prædicabant, à prædicando depellunt.
units.tr: First, he puts the repression of pastoral power as the original cause of all evil in the Church. So all the blame must be laid on the bishops, because they wretchedly diminish pastoral liberty while they preach, and drive away from preaching many pastors who preached most diligently.

units.la: Secundò, malorum omnium origo in Ecclesia, Lincolniensis judicio, malorum pastorum multiplicatio est; non igitur papistarum hæretica pravitas nobis deputanda est, sed Episcopis: per quos hæc mala multiplicatio & toleratur, & approbatur.
units.tr: Second, the origin of all evils in the Church, in the judgment of the Bishop of Lincoln, is the multiplication of bad pastors. Therefore the heretical depravity of the Papists is not to be attributed to us, but to the bishops, through whom this multiplication of evils is both tolerated and approved.

units.la: Tertiò, Curiam illam Facultatem, canonesque illos damnat Lincolniensis, a quibus per Episcopos pluralitates aliarumq; abominationes & dispensationes & approbationes prodeunt ad totam terram desolandam.
units.tr: Third, the Bishop of Lincoln condemns that Curia, that Faculty, and those canons from whom pluralities and other abominations, dispensations and approvals come through the bishops, to desolate the whole earth.

units.la: Sequitur Petrus de Corbaria & Michael Sisenas, qui ob Puritanismum Anglicanum, propria bulla in extravagantib Iohannis 22. quæ incipit, Dudum ab audientia &c. & damnati & excommunicati sunt. Hæc enim illa capita sunt, propter quæ patiebantur. Primò, Petrum non fuisse magis caput Ecclesiæ, quam quilibet Apostolorum. Secundò, sacerdotes omnes cujuscunq; gradus existunt, esse æqualis authoritatis, potestatis, & iurisdictionis ex institutione Christi.
units.tr: Next follow Peter of Corbière and Michael Sisenas, who, on account of English Puritanism, were condemned and excommunicated by the bull of John XXII in the Extravagants, which begins "Dudum ab audientia," etc. For these are the chapters on account of which they suffered. First, that Peter was no more the head of the Church than any of the Apostles. Second, that all priests of whatever rank are of equal authority, power and jurisdiction by the institution of Christ.

units.la: Sequitur Iohannes de Poliaco, qui anno 1322. floruisse fertur ob id damnatus in extravagantibus canonibus, quod dixerit pastores & Episcopos habere suam potestatem immediatè à Christo ejusque Apostolis, & discipulis, & non à Papa, eoque Papam eorum jus & potestatem nec posse nec debere minuere. Hoc planè puritanicum erat: utpote ex quo sequitur, à nullo Episcopo jus & potestatem prebyterorum, quòd ad iuridistionem & exercitium, minui posse, quod eam habeat presbyteri non mediatè ab Episcopis, sed ab ipso Iesu Christo immediatè. Quanta Zisca nobilis ille Bohemus pertulerit, notum est; in cuius Epitaphio inter cætera legitur Visus sum mihi sfurientium iustissima causam, adversus delicatos, pingues, & bene saginatos sacerdotes egregiè egisse, & ob hoc Dei auxilium sentisse.
units.tr: Next follows John of Pouilly, who is said to have flourished in 1322. He was condemned on that account in the Extravagant canons, because he said that pastors and bishops have their power immediately from Christ and his Apostles and disciples, not from the Pope, and that therefore the Pope neither can nor ought to diminish their right and power. This was plainly Puritan, since it follows from it that the right and power of presbyters, as far as jurisdiction and its exercise go, cannot be diminished by any bishop, because they have it not mediately from bishops but immediately from Jesus Christ himself. How much the noble Bohemian Zizka suffered is well known. On his epitaph, among other things, it is read: "I seemed to myself to have pleaded most justly the cause of the furious against the delicate, fat and well-fed priests, and on that account to have felt the help of God."

units.la: Atqui inquam Puritanorum in Anglia, jam hodie justissima hæc causa est, sic ut Dei auxilium in eadem defenseda merito expectare possint.
units.tr: But, I say, the cause of the Puritans in England is today most just, so that they may rightly expect God's help in defending it.

units.la: Sequitur testimonium Civitatensis, de piorum suo sæculo viventium vexatione, quæ eadem quæ mimistrorum erat.
units.tr: Next follows the testimony of the Civitatensis, concerning the persecution of pious men living in his age, which was the same as that of the ministers.

units.la: [O error cæcus, inquit: Nam si subdui intelligentes prælatorum ac rectorum leviter saltem negligentias & vitia tetigerent, ac sacrorum canonum ac divinorum eloquiorum testimonia adduxerint, totmdiretis iucrepationibus, depressionibus, humiliationibus, iniuriis grabaminibus & contumeliis afficiuntur: imo tanquam fanatici, & cauteriatas erroneasque conscientias habentes, contemni, & non audiri dicuntur: quod etiam ex hoc pro humana injurimis interdum commouentur se defendendo, a quo cau-
units.tr: "O blind error," he says. For if wise subjects merely touched lightly on the negligences and vices of prelates and rulers, and adduced the testimonies of the sacred canons and divine oracles, they are assailed with so many reproofs, oppressions, humiliations, injuries, burdens and insults. Indeed they are said to be like fanatics, with cauterised and erroneous consciences, to be despised and not listened to. And because of this, stirred by human injury, they are sometimes moved to defend themselves, from which...

units.la: Mi. trà Prælati sibi occasionem suscipiunt, eosdem quasi juste deprimendi & humiliandi. O nimis stupendi & vere culpanda vesania. Quid pernitiosius? quidve a salute remotius, quam illos detestari qui eos situgant ad salutem adducere, & se lethaliter vulneratos sanos æstimare? Tales sunt prælati & rectores, qui sibi ipsi aliorum vitia reprehendunt, sed cum ipsis vel leviter resistitur, mox ad hæreticorum ructum, qui (secundum Origenem) reprehensores suos persequuntur, se convertunt, & tanquam carnales, dissensiones fructificant.
units.tr: Yet the prelates seize upon this as an occasion to depress and humiliate those men, as if it were just. O most astonishing and truly blameworthy madness! What is more pernicious, or further from salvation, than to detest those who try to bring them to salvation, and to think themselves sound when they are mortally wounded? Such are the prelates and rulers: they rebuke the faults of others, but when they are resisted even slightly, at once they turn to the vomiting of heretics, who (according to Origen) persecute their reprovers, and, like carnal men, bear the fruit of dissensions.

units.la: Non est igitur quod ministrorum perpessiones quis condemnet, etsi nonunquam lapsi fuerint præ humana infirmitate in seipsis defendendis: agnoscenda potius in Episcopis ars vetus est, qui inde prætextum quærunt, ac si iuste affligerentur. Non est credendum eos fantasticos esse, & conscientias erroneos habere, ut calumniantur: vetus hæc prælatorum criminatio semper fuit adversus eos, qui eorum vitia vel leviter tetigerunt. Non est fidendum jactationi Anglicanæ, quæ gloriosam Ecclesiam nostram prædicare solet: sic olim factum, prælatis sanos se æstimantibus etiam quando læthaliter vulnerabantur. Non est denique dissensionum in Anglia culpa in ministros conferenda, sanare hi (ut olim pij) & ad salutem reducere conantur: reverendum potius in Episcopis divinum iudicium est, quod hanc erroris Hierarchici mercedem eiusdem patronis retribuerit, ut fructus in eis hominum errantium aperte appareat, persequutio nempe, & in suos reprehensores dissensionum fructificatio. Apponendum vero adhuc de sæculo suo Francisci Petrarchæ, testimonium est. Simplicitas (inquit) amentiæ, malitia sapientiæ nomen habet, virique boni usque adeo irridentur ut fere nullus qui irridere possit appareat. Quis oculatior in hac tabulâ non ipsa.n iam Angliam descriptâ videt? evanescit etenim morû simplicitas, quia quæ residua in piis & puritanis erat, pro fatuitate habetur: languescit zelus, quod qui reliquus in piis & puritanis erat, irrisioni habetur; increbrescit è contra morum malitia quod ij soli sapientes habeantur, qui se tempori ita accommodant, ut à contempto illo piorum & puritanorum grege se quam longissimè segregent. Atque iam videre est, quam magni & quam multi viri, ministris in Anglia patientibus præiverunt.
units.tr: There is therefore no reason for anyone to condemn the sufferings of the ministers, even if they have sometimes slipped, through human weakness, in defending themselves. Rather, the old craft of the bishops must be recognised, for they seek a pretext there, as if they were justly afflicted. We must not believe that these men are fanatics and have erroneous consciences, as the bishops slander them; this old charge of the prelates has always been levelled against those who have touched even lightly on their faults. We must not trust the boasting of the English, who are wont to proclaim our Church glorious; so it was done of old, when the prelates considered themselves sound even while they were mortally wounded. Nor, finally, is the blame for the dissensions in England to be laid on the ministers, who (like the godly of old) strive to heal and bring back to salvation; rather, the divine judgement is to be revered in the bishops, which has repaid the patrons of this hierarchical error with its own wages, so that the fruit of erring men appears openly in them: namely persecution, and the bearing of dissensions against their reprovers. Moreover, the testimony of Francis Petrarch from his own age should also be added. "The simplicity of folly," he says, "bears the name of wisdom, and malice the name of wisdom; and good men are so mocked that hardly anyone appears who could mock them." What more keen-sighted observer, in this picture, does not see England itself described? For the simplicity of manners is fading away, since what remained of it among the godly and Puritans is held to be foolishness; zeal is growing faint, since what remained of it among the godly and Puritans is held up to ridicule; on the contrary, the malice of manners is increasing, so that only those are held wise who accommodate themselves so to the times that they separate themselves as far as possible from that despised flock of the godly and Puritans. And now one can see how many great and numerous men have gone before the ministers in England in suffering.

units.la: CAP. 38. Macula generales diluuntur.
units.tr: CAP. 38. The general blemishes are wiped away.

units.la: Diluendæ iam maculæ generales quædam sunt: brevissimè tamen, quia de plerisque separatus dicendi locus est.
units.tr: Some general blemishes must now be wiped away, though only very briefly, since most of them will be treated separately in their own place.

units.la: Prima est, quod ministros tribunalia Anglicana cum forensia tum Ecclesiastica condemnarint: cui nihil aliud respondendum, quam illu Gelasij: Neminem gravare debet iniqua sententia: Neq; est, quod sparsa hinc in vulgus communi infamia quis commoveatur, sed in memoriam revocandum quod de Paulo Gregorius Doctor Gentium se in prædicatione currere testatur, per infamiam, & bonam famam, qui etiam dicit ut seductores & tamen veraces. Secunda, de causæ ievitate est, quæ nova non est: sic enim à Mauritio Imperatore Gregorio objectum olim, cum de re frivola contentionem in Ecclesia excitare, quum de nomine tantum Episcopi universalis controversaretur. At quod ille Episcopatum Constantinopolitanum impugnans, id nos contra Anglicanum perinde illicitum contendentes, respondere jam possumus: Quædam frivola sunt & innoxia, quædam frivola & noxia: etsi frivolum quis esse dixerit quod Dei est: quodque totam Ecclesiam turbat? Rursus igitur cum Gregorio. Non mea causa sed Dei est, pompatici cujusdam sermonis inuectione tota turbatur Ecclesia. Rursus: Vos eandem causam nullam esse dicere non debetis, quia si hanc æquanimitatem portamus, universæ Ecclesiæ fidem corrupimus. Sic & unitatem etiam; de hac etenim ita Cyprianus: Hanc unitatem firmiter tenere & vendicare debemus, maximè Episcopi qui in Ecclesiâ præsidemus, ut Episcopatum quoque ipsum unum & indivisum probemus. Hæc adfert Iuellus noster, contra Papæ primatum, sed valent etiam adversus primatum Episcopalem Anglicanum, cum Episcopi nomen hic generaliter à Cypriano usurpatum esse pro quovis Ecclesiæ præside (sicut ipsemet interpretatur) & res ipsa clamat, & suo loco demonstrabitur. Idipsum demonstrat locus ille Cypriani alter, unà à Iuello citatus: Ecclesia invicem sibi cohærentium sacerdotum glutino copulatur. Quid igitur est?
