Non per unius Episcopi præsidentiam Anglicanæ Ecclesiæ unitas; sed pastorum omnium concordiâ potius, quasi glutino quodam conservatur, quæ cum inter pares maximè vigeat, ita a ministris jam Anglicanis colenda est, ut ministerium omnium unum & indivisum (juxta consilium Cypriani) contra Anglicanam Episcoporum usurpationem una ab ipsis defendatur.
units.tr: The first is that the English courts, both civil and ecclesiastical, have condemned the ministers. To this nothing else need be replied than the saying of Gelasius: an unjust sentence ought not to burden anyone. Nor should anyone be moved by the common infamy spread abroad among the people, but we should recall what Gregory the Doctor of the Gentiles says of Paul, that in preaching he runs through infamy and good report, and that he is called a deceiver and yet true. The second objection concerns the triviality of the cause, which is not new. Long ago the Emperor Mauritius objected this to Gregory, saying that he stirred up contention in the Church over a trifling matter, since the dispute was only about the name of universal bishop. But we can now answer as Gregory answered him, when he opposed the bishopric of Constantinople, and as we contend against the English bishopric, which is equally unlawful: some things are trifling and harmless, some trifling and harmful. Or will anyone call trifling what belongs to God, and what disturbs the whole Church? So again with Gregory: "The cause is not mine but God's; the whole Church is thrown into turmoil by the bringing in of a showy word." Again: "You ought not to say that this same cause is nothing, for if we bear this with equanimity we corrupt the faith of the whole Church." So too with unity. Cyprian says of this: "We ought firmly to hold and maintain this unity, especially we bishops who preside in the Church, so that we may also prove the episcopate itself to be one and undivided." Our Jewel brings this forward against the papal primacy, but it holds also against the English episcopal primacy, since the word bishop is here used by Cyprian in a general sense for any president of a church (as he himself explains), and the matter itself cries out for it, and it will be shown in its own place. That other passage of Cyprian, also cited by Jewel, demonstrates the same: "The Church is joined together by the glue of priests cohering with one another." What then follows? The unity of the English Church is preserved not by the presidency of one bishop, but rather by the harmony of all the ministers, as by a certain glue. This unity, since it flourishes most among equals, must now be cherished by the English ministers, so that the ministry of all, one and undivided (according to Cyprian's counsel), may be defended by them together against the English usurpation of the bishops.

units.la: Superest macula tertia: in quâ ministris hoc non parum præjudicare quibusdam videtur, quòd non contra exteros, sed fratres suos, hæc lis eorum intendatur. Atqui pollicitationem illam Ap. 14:13. Beati qui postremis temporibus adversus Bestiam, adæque ac illi qui contra Ethnicos Imperatores in primâ Ecclesiâ, patiuntur, ad ipsos pertinere dico: Bonitas etenim causæ est, secundum quam servorum suorum patientiam metiri Deus solet: hostium inæqualitas inæqualitatem si inferret non adeò beati martyres qui à Papa Christianum nomen profitente, quàm qui ab Ethnicis Imperatoribus, ab eodem alienis, occisi sunt. Quid quòd ministri Anglicani pro nullo alio jam à fratribus patiuntur quàm quod papale est? Addam etiam & amplius, prout certamen majus illud est, quod contra fratres servi Dei sustinere adiguntur: ita & uberiorem gloriæ segetem continere semper solet: id quod vox illa Spiritus sancti insinuare videtur. Hic est tolerantiæ sanctorum: Ap. 14:12. ac si dixisset: Hic experimentum fortitudinis Christianæ eo luculentius, quòd non jam adversus Ethnicos, sed professos Christianos, certamen subeundum sit. Intuea- mur
units.tr: There remains a third blemish, in which it seems to some to prejudice the ministers not a little that this dispute is directed not against outsiders but against their own brethren. Yet I say that the promise in Revelation 14:13, "Blessed are they who in the last times suffer against the Beast," applies to them, just as it applies to those who suffered in the early Church under the heathen emperors. For the goodness of the cause is that by which God is wont to measure the patience of his servants; and the inequality of the enemies would not make the martyrs more blessed if they were killed by a Pope who professes the Christian name than if they were killed by heathen emperors who were alien to him. What of the fact that the English ministers now suffer from their brethren for nothing other than what is papal? I will add even more: the greater the struggle that the servants of God are compelled to undergo against their brethren, the richer the harvest of glory it usually contains. This is what that voice of the Holy Spirit seems to suggest: "Here is the patience of the saints," Revelation 14:12, as if he had said: here is the proof of Christian fortitude, all the more clear because the struggle must now be undertaken not against heathens but against professing Christians.

units.la: Lib.4. epist. 32. Lib.6. epist. 24. De Simplic. prælat. Artic.4. Lib.4. epist. 9. mur Christum authorem & consummatorem salutis nostræ, qui non tam propter apertos hostes, quàm domesticos, qualis Iudas erat, (ut olim David propter Achitophelem) commotus est: Psal. 55: 12, 13. cui jam qui conformantur, verè eis cum Cypriano dicere licet: Nobis ignominia non est pati à fratribus quod passus est Christus: neque vobis gloria est facere, quod fecit Iudas. Pertinet huc quod Ecclesiæ Smyrnensi scribit Christus Ap. 2:9. Tulit gravissimas calamitates Ephesus, illiusque ἐλλιπῶν primitiva Ecclesia, sed ab Ethnicis hominibus. quod aliquod lenimentum erat doloris: sed Smyrna, Ecclesiaque illi ἐλλιπῶν, à Constantino ad Gratianum usque; decurrens, à suis ultima quæque passa est, à suis inquam, qui se Iudæos & germanos Christianos profitebantur. Hinc omittit minas Spiritus sanctus, qui ad has Ecclesias scribit, & consolatur quantum potest, idque solamine eo, quod jam in Anglia languescentes confirmare merito potest: Novi afflictionem tuam, ut eam justam esse, hostes tui vociferentur: novi paupertatem, despiciunt te turgidi, contemnunt superbi, sed coram me dives es: ne metue quæ passurus es, nam & hæc quæque quantumvis à Iudæis illata, quantumvis ab eis qui se orthodoxos haberi volunt, in præmium tibi cedent. Hoc ita cùm sit, ne fatiscant animo jam in Anglia patientes, sed pergant porro, & ad singulos gressus (quod mater illa Lacedæmonia) virtutis masculæ, & (quæ Spartanâ multo potior est) Christianæ recordentur: robore increscant insuper, juxta illa Iohannis, qui justus est, justificetur adhuc: Ap. 22.11 vestimenta denique sua à subscriptione Anglicanâ impolluta conservent: ita enim Christo suo dealbati incedent, pariter ut illi qui in Sardicensi ἐλλιπῶν Ecclesiâ Lutherana, à subscriptione libri concordiæ se impollutos servaverunt: Ap. 3. Atque hoc porisma tertium est, quod ex disciplinæ reformatæ cum sanctitate tum necessitate oritur, ministros in Anglia qui pro eadem patiuntur, laudandos non condemnandos, coronis potiùs redimendos quàm pœnis affligendos esse,
units.tr: Let us look to Christ, the author and finisher of our salvation, who was moved not so much by open enemies as by domestic ones, such as Judas was, as David once was on account of Ahithophel (Psalm 55:12–13). To him, whoever are conformed now may say with Cyprian: "It is no shame to us to suffer from brethren what Christ suffered, nor is it any glory to you to do what Judas did." To this belongs what Christ writes to the church at Smyrna (Revelation 2:9): "Ephesus endured very grievous calamities, and the primitive church of that city, but from heathen men; which was some relief of the pain. But Smyrna, and the church of that city, from Constantine down to Gratian, suffered the last afflictions of all from its own people, from its own, I say, who professed themselves Jews and true Christians." Hence the Holy Spirit, who writes to these churches, omits threats and comforts as far as he can, and with a comfort which he may rightly give to those who are now languishing in England: "I know your affliction, though your enemies cry out that it is just; I know your poverty, though the proud despise you and the haughty scorn you; but before me you are rich. Do not fear what you are about to suffer." For all these things, however much they are inflicted by Jews, however much by those who wish to be held orthodox, will turn to your reward. Since this is so, let those who now suffer in England not lose heart, but press on, and at every step remember that manly virtue of which the Spartan mother spoke, and (far better than Spartan virtue) the Christian kind; let them grow strong in the words of John, "He who is righteous, let him be righteous still" (Revelation 22:11). Finally, let them keep their garments undefiled by the English subscription; for thus they will walk clothed in white with their Christ, just as those in the church at Sardis who, from subscription to the Lutheran book of concord, kept themselves undefiled (Revelation 3:4). This is the third corollary, which arises from the holiness and the necessity of the reformed discipline: that the ministers in England who suffer for the same cause are to be praised, not condemned, and are to be redeemed with crowns rather than afflicted with punishments.

units.la: CAP 39. Porisma quintum, fratribus non esse silendum in causa disciplina, etsi Episcopi ea conditione conniverent,
units.tr: CAP 39. The fifth conclusion: that the brethren must not keep silent in the cause of discipline, even if the bishops connive at them on that condition.

units.la: QVartum, ministros tacentes respicit: de quibus sciendum est, solere Episcopos ad nonnullos connivere nonnunquam, præsertim ruri constitutos (in locis. n. celebribus non ita id facilè ferent) quos aut populi gratia, aut potentum dominorum patrocinio, florere vident. Hic autem hanc viam ineunt: spondebunt pro sua parte ministri de quæstione disciplinæ, tum in concionibus, tum in publicis coram populo orationibus, se tacituros: hac conditione recepta, promittent illi vicissim, à quæstione abstinere se velle tantisper, dum nulla de his querela deferatur: ita nemine accusante, sub isto silentio, & praedicare nonnulli permiuntur, nec conformantes, nec subscribentes, & satis quiete agere. Similis ista quo ad Episcopos indulgentia quae illa Traiani olim erga Christianos fuit, quam ita exagitat Tertullianus: Atqui invenimus inquisitionem quidem in nos prohibitam: Plinius enim secundus cum provinciam regeret, multitudine Christi morum perturbatus, consulit Trajanum Imperatorem, cui Trajanus rescripsit: Hoc genus inquirendos quidem non esse, oblatos vero puniri oportere. O sententiam necessitate confusam. Negat inquirendos ut innocentes, & mandat puniendos ut nocentes. Parcit & saevit, dissimulat & animadvertit. Quid temetipsum censura circumvenis? Si damnas, cur non inquiris? Si non inquiris, cur non a solvis; Latronibus vestigandis per universas provincias militaris statio sortitur, & ad socios, ad conscios usque inquisitio extenditur. Solum Christianum inquiri non licet, offerri licet, quasi aliud esset actura inquisitio quam oblatio? Damnatis ergo oblatum, quem nemo voluit requisitum, qui puto non jam incurrit poenam, quia nocentes sit, sed quia non requirendus inventus est. Haec ille, quibus & innocentiam nostram ab Episcopis contestatam, & Episcopos censura propria circumventos esse luculenter demonstrat. Non ego igitur ab Episcopis rogabo quo loco Whitgifti excusatio habenda sit, qui juramento Episcopali obstrictam se fuisse dixit, ut ministri non conformantes exauthorentur: neque eorum conscientias pulsabo, qui quocunque juramento non obstante quosdam tulerant, etsi astutam sub pedore vulpem in eo gerere videantur, quod ut Pharisaei olim, in populi gratiam, nonnullis parcant: dum in alios saeviunt, vel haec una Tertulliani expostulatio fatis erit. Non magis Traianus Christianis faveret quam latronibus, nisi conscius esset Christianos velut latrones maleficos non esse: sic non magis ad ministros non conformantes conniverent jam Episcopi, quam ad maleficos, si non dictaret conscientia, eos homines nequaquam esse. Subesse igitur syntheresis quaedam conscientiae videtur, quae de horum hominum probitate Episcopos admonet: praesertim cum exacte urgeat canon subscribendi necessitatem. Baronius de libellis indulgentiae & concessionis agens citat ex Vlpiano libellum ejusmodi etiam quoad causarum cognitiones illicitum esse, quod edicto contravenit: Vti decretu necessarium est, inquit Vlpianus, per libellum i I Consul expedire non potest: Omnia enim quaecunque causae cognitionem desiderant per libellum expedire non possunt. Sed utrum haec cognitionis & inquisitionis omissio, canone prohibita, Episcopis licita necne sit, non magni refert: illud minis-tros attingit propius, utrum hic libellus quasi indulgentiae, ab illis licite, ab Episcopis accipi posset. Dubium hoc facit eorum sententia, qui libellaticos eos olim dictos putant, qui pecunia se redemerant. Citant hi in hanc sententiam haec Cipriani, qui in persona libellatici ita loquitur: Ergo prius legeram idolis sacrificandum non esse, & idcirco hoc facerem quod non licebat ad magistratum vel veni vel alio eunte mandavi, Christianum me esse, sacrificare mihi non licere, dare me ob hoc pretium. sium, ne quidnon licet faciam. Verba haec quanquam plana sint, inquit Baronius, semper tamen Tertulliani dogma illud, non licere Christiano se à vexationibus Gentilium pecuniâ redimere,pro Montanico habitû est,& à Petro Alexandrino condemnatum. Allegat verò exemplum Iasonis,quem pecuniâ se redemisse dicit: Act. 17, 9. sed falsò: non etenim satis pecuniae à Iasone magistratus accepisse dicitur,sed &c. id est, vel responsionem talem quae ipsis satisfacere bat, vel, ut Budeus hanc phrasin interpretari solet, satisfactionem, ut se legitimo judicio, si opus esset, sisterent. At quid si pecuniâ se Iason redemisset, annon Pauli exemplum merito praeponderare debeat qui se pecunia redimere noluit? Act. 24. 27.
units.tr: Fourthly, it concerns ministers who keep silent. Concerning them it must be known that bishops are wont sometimes to connive at some of them, especially those settled in the country (for in the more famous places they do not so readily bear it), whom they see flourishing either through the favour of the people or the patronage of powerful lords. Here these men take the following course. The ministers promise, for their part, that they will keep silent about the question of discipline, both in sermons and in public prayers before the people. On this condition being accepted, the bishops in turn promise that they will refrain from the question for as long as no complaint about these matters is lodged. Thus, with no one accusing them, under this silence, some are permitted to preach, neither conforming nor subscribing, and to get on quite quietly. This indulgence of the bishops is like that which Trajan once showed toward the Christians, which Tertullian thus assails: But we have found that inquiry against us is indeed forbidden: for Pliny the Younger, when he governed a province, troubled by the multitude of Christians, consulted the Emperor Trajan, who replied: This class of people is indeed not to be sought out, but if they are brought forward they must be punished. O sentence confused by necessity. It forbids them to be sought out as innocent, and orders them to be punished as guilty. It spares and it rages, it dissembles and it punishes. Why do you entrap yourself by your own judgment? If you condemn, why do you not inquire? If you do not inquire, why do you not acquit? For the hunting down of robbers a military post is assigned throughout all the provinces, and the search extends even to accomplices and abettors. Only the Christian may not be sought out, but he may be brought forward; as if inquiry would do anything other than bring forward! You condemn, then, the one who was brought forward, whom no one wished to be searched for; who, I think, does not now incur punishment because he is guilty, but because he was found not to be one to be sought. So he writes, and he clearly shows both that our innocence was attested by the bishops and that the bishops were entrapped by their own judgment. I therefore will not ask the bishops in what place Whitgift's excuse should be held, who said that he was bound by his episcopal oath to deprive the non-conforming ministers; nor will I trouble the consciences of those who, in spite of whatever oath, have allowed some to stand, even though they seem to carry a cunning fox under their cloak in that they spare some, as the Pharisees once did for the sake of the people, while they rage against others. Tertullian's single complaint will suffice on this point. Trajan would not have favoured the Christians any more than robbers, unless he knew that Christians were not evildoers like robbers. So too the bishops would not now connive at the non-conforming ministers any more than at evildoers, if conscience did not dictate that these men are by no means such. Therefore some inward sense of conscience seems to lie beneath, which admonishes the bishops about the integrity of these men, especially since the canon on the necessity of subscription presses strictly. Baronius, discussing libels of indulgence and concession, cites from Ulpian that a libel of this kind is also unlawful as regards the hearing of causes, because it contravenes the edict: As it is necessary by decree, says Ulpian, the consul cannot dispatch it through a libel: for all matters that require a hearing of the case cannot be dispatched through a libel. But whether this omission of hearing and inquiry, forbidden by the canon, is lawful for the bishops or not does not greatly matter. What touches the ministers more closely is whether this libel, as if of indulgence, could be lawfully received by them from the bishops. This is made doubtful by the opinion of those who think that the so-called libellatici were those who had redeemed themselves with money. In support of this view they cite these words of Cyprian, who speaks in the person of a libellaticus: Therefore I had earlier read that one must not sacrifice to idols, and so I did what was not permitted: I sent word to the magistrate, either by going myself or by another going, that I am a Christian, that it is not lawful for me to sacrifice, and that I give money for this, lest I do anything not permitted. Although these words are plain, says Baronius, nevertheless Tertullian's doctrine, that it is not lawful for a Christian to redeem himself from the persecutions of the Gentiles with money, has been regarded as Montanist and was condemned by Peter of Alexandria. He cites, however, the example of Jason, whom he says redeemed himself with money: Acts 17.9, but wrongly. For it is not said that the magistrates received enough money from Jason, but &c., that is, either such a reply as would satisfy them, or, as Budaeus is accustomed to interpret this phrase, a satisfaction, that they would present themselves to legitimate judgment if there were need. But what if Jason had redeemed himself with money? Should not the example of Paul, who was unwilling to redeem himself with money, rightly outweigh it? Acts 24.27.

units.la: Postremò, quid si pecunia se redimere licitum sit? aliud est se pecunia; aliud promissione silentij se redimere, quod à nullo Christiano factum in prisca Ecclesia legimus.
units.tr: Lastly, what if it were lawful to redeem oneself with money? It is one thing to redeem oneself with money; it is another to redeem oneself by a promise of silence, which we read was done by no Christian in the early Church.

units.la: 2. Quid igitur de ministris Anglicanis sentiendum qui promissione silentij se ab Episcoporum vexationibus redimere solent? Certè ut socios suos in eadem causa patientes non condemnant illi quos interno Spiritus motu in arenam protractos judicant, quem in semet se non sentire dicunt: ita nec ego vicissim eos temerè condemnandos putarem, praesertim cum singulari Dei providentia hinc datum videam Ecclesijs nonnullis, ut prosperetum jam sit, qui verbi aliter beneficio privarentur. Hanc ob causam non ego durius cum eis agam, imò ne multis quidem, tantùm breviter quaedam addam ad ea quae alibi à me olim scripta sunt,ut capita rerum perstrinxisse potius, quàm solidam disputationem instituisse videar.
units.tr: 2. What then should be thought of the Anglican ministers who are accustomed to redeem themselves from the bishops' harassments by a promise of silence? Certainly, just as they do not condemn their fellows who suffer in the same cause, those whom they judge to have been dragged into the arena by an inward motion of the Spirit, which they say they do not feel in themselves, so I too would think they should not be rashly condemned in turn, especially since I see that by a singular providence of God some churches have thereby been given the advantage that they might prosper even though they were deprived of the benefit of the Word otherwise. For this reason I will not deal with them more harshly, nor even with many, but will briefly add a few things to what I have written elsewhere, so that I may seem to have touched on the heads of the matter rather than to have set out a solid disputation.

units.la: Primùm igitur magno hic & serio conscientiae examine opus esse dico, sic ut intimi animi recessus excutiantur, latebrae omnes explorentur, propterea quòd promissio silentij ista, silentiumque ipsum, speciem ejusdem abnigatae vel ludificatae confessionis praesefferre videatur. Absit claudicatio. 1 Reg. 18. 21. absit secreta confessio Nicodemitica. Iohan. 3. 2. absit tepiditas: Ap. 3. 16. absit pudor verborum Christi coram natione adultera & prava: Marc. 8. 38. absit timor perdendi: Ap. 21. 8. absit denique amor acquirendi: cauda etenim draconis haec fuit, qua stellae de caelo ad terram dejici confuerunt. Apocal. 12. 4.
units.tr: First, then, I say that a great and serious examination of conscience is needed here, so that the innermost recesses of the mind are searched out and all hiding places explored, because this promise of silence, and silence itself, seems to present the appearance of a denied or mocked confession. Let there be no halting: 1 Kings 18.21. Let there be no secret confession of the Nicodemites: John 3.2. Let there be no lukewarmness: Rev. 3.16. Let there be no shame at the words of Christ before an adulterous and perverse generation: Mark 8.38. Let there be no fear of loss: Rev. 21.8. Let there be, lastly, no love of gain: for this was the tail of the dragon, by which the stars were wont to be cast down from heaven to the earth: Rev. 12.4.

units.la: Secundò, Anglicanas corruptelas in Anglia tum Laodicaea postquam Christus reprehenderat,hoc subjungit Epiphonema: Qui habet aures ad audiendum audiat: Apo. 3. ult. Ex his verbis perspicere cuivis promptum, singularem illis affulsisse gratiam. Dei, quorum aures referravit, ut Ecclesiae Anglicanae corruptelas & discernere & fugere queant. Hoc ita cum sit, nonne gratitudo postulare videtur, ut hac gratiâ utamur, ad Dei honorem à quo misericorditer data est? Verum est, respondetis: idque à nobis optimè fit, nefmet etenim puros servamus ut Ecclesiae corruptelis non communicemus, & si silemus,eò silemus ut praedicando Evangelium Filij sui Deum gloglorificemus. Atqui intelligendum, non in nostri duntaxat gratiam hoc donum dari, sed etiam ut proximus ædificetur: Omnis manifestatio Spiritus data est ad ædificationem, inquit Paulus 1. Cor. 12.7. Claudicat igitur hæc defensio; quòd hac gratiâ utimini ad vosmetipsos purgandos: bene est, sed dum siletis de disciplina, non jam proximus ædificatur: & quod Evangelium prædicatis bene etiam est, sed talentum interim de disciplina, quòd ad alios lucrandos & instruendos, sub terra defoditur. Math. 25.18.
units.tr: Secondly, concerning the Anglican corruptions in England, after Christ had rebuked Laodicea, he adds this epiphonema: He who has ears to hear, let him hear: Rev. 3, last. From these words it is plain to anyone that a singular grace of God shone upon those whose ears he opened, so that they might both discern and flee the corruptions of the Anglican Church. Since this is so, does not gratitude seem to require that we use this grace, to the honour of God from whom it was mercifully given? True, you reply, and we do this very well: for we keep ourselves pure so as not to share in the corruptions of the Church, and if we are silent, we are silent so that by preaching the Gospel of his Son we may glorify God. But it must be understood that this gift is given not for our sake alone, but also that our neighbour may be built up: Every manifestation of the Spirit is given for edification, says Paul, 1 Cor. 12.7. This defence therefore limps: that you use this grace to purge yourselves, well and good; but while you keep silent about discipline, your neighbour is not built up. And that you preach the Gospel is also well; but meanwhile the talent of discipline, which should be used to gain and instruct others, is buried in the ground. Matt. 25.18.

units.la: Tertiò, disciplinam reformatam Evangelij partem esse cognoscitis: at partem debiti Deo subtrahere quàm sit iniquum in Ananias cernere est Act. 5, 2. & ut unam Evangelij partem prædicetis, aliam clam habere, quàm Deo ingratum, vel eo conjicere licet, quod oderit ille sacrificium vel minima ex parte mutilum: Levit. 22.22. Loquere ad illos omnia quæ præcepi tibi. Ierem. 1: 17. Docentes eos observare omnia, quæcunque præcepi vobis. Matth. 28.20. Quomodo totum consilium Dei nobis patefecerim, & nihil subtraxerim Act. 20.20. At additur, inquies, nihil nobis utile. Quasi disciplina utilis non sit, aut disciplinam Ephesi non constituisset Paulus, 1. Tim. 5:17, sic ut eam inter res utiles eum his verbis numerasse necesse sit? At inter doctrinam & disciplinam gradus tamen sunt, illa etenim utilior. Quasi in utilioris gratiam, pars Evangelij minus utilis altera, aut perdenda, aut prodenda sit? At nostrum silere, neque perdere neque prodere est: est tamen subtrahere, quod præter officium censet Paulus. Gregorio etiam Magno, & perdere & prodere videbatur. Eadem Episcoporum usurpatio in ministros, atque Iohannis Constantinopolitani erat: in hoc tantum discrimen est, quod illa in totam, hæc in partem duntaxat Ecclesiæ peccet: utcunque fit, res disciplinaria erat, non doctrinalis. Ita tamen ille: Tam scelesto vocabulo consentire, nihil est aliud quàm fidem perdere. At silere nostrum consentire non est. Gregorij judicio prorsus: nam & Mauritio Imperatori eum quiescere iubenti (sic & piissimi magistratus ambitioni Episcopali plus satis velificari volent) hoc nomine purgat sese quod silere nequiret, quia tam scelesto vocabulo consentire non posset: & alios ad resistendum incitat, quia quiescere & consentire, fidem perdere erat. Patet hoc ex loco alio, ubi & æquanimiter ferre prohibet. Si hoc æquanimiter portamus, inquit, universæ Ecclesiæ fidem corrumpimus. Æquanimiter vero jurisdictionem Episcopalem si non feratis vos, æquanimius tamen fertis, quàm quod æquanimiter veritas feret: de qua rectè Tertullianus: Nihil veritas erubescet nisi tantùmodo abscondi: abscondit autem lucernam sub modulo: Matth. 5. 15. sicut interpretibus constat, qui modulum statuit (idem de eis sentiendum qui modulum observant) quousque ministris prædicandum sit, ultra quod non progrediendum.
units.tr: Thirdly, you acknowledge that discipline is part of the reformed Gospel. But how wicked it is to withhold part of what is owed to God is seen in Ananias, Acts 5:2. That you preach one part of the Gospel while secretly keeping another is ungrateful to God, as one may gather from the fact that he abhors a sacrifice even slightly maimed, Lev. 22:22. Speak to them all that I have commanded you, Jer. 1:17. Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you, Matt. 28:20. How I have declared to you the whole counsel of God and kept back nothing, Acts 20:20. But, you will say, it is added, nothing useful to us. As if discipline were not useful, or as if Paul had not established discipline at Ephesus, 1 Tim. 5:17, so that he must have counted it among useful things by these words? But there are degrees between doctrine and discipline, since the former is the more useful. As if, for the sake of the more useful, the less useful part of the Gospel must either be lost or betrayed! Yet our keeping silent is neither losing nor betraying; it is, however, withholding, which Paul judges to be beyond duty. Gregory the Great also seemed both to lose and to betray. The same usurpation of ministers by bishops was that of John of Constantinople. The only difference is that the former sins against the whole Church, the latter against a part only. However it is, the matter was disciplinary, not doctrinal. Thus he wrote: To consent to so wicked a word is nothing else than to lose the faith. But keeping silent is not consenting, to the judgment of Gregory entirely. For when the Emperor Maurice bade him be quiet (so the most pious magistrates, too, want to sail more than enough with the episcopal ambition), he excuses himself on this ground: that he could not keep silent, because he could not consent to so wicked a word. And he urges others to resist, because to keep quiet and consent was to lose the faith. This is clear from another passage, where he also forbids bearing it with equanimity: If we bear this with equanimity, he says, we corrupt the faith of the whole Church. But if you do not bear the episcopal jurisdiction with equanimity, you bear it more calmly than the truth will bear it with equanimity. Of this Tertullian rightly says: Truth blushes at nothing except being hidden; but it hides its lamp under a bushel, Matt. 5:15. As the interpreters agree, who set up the bushel (the same is to be thought of those who keep the bushel) as the limit to which ministers may preach, and beyond which they must not go.

units.la: Quarto, fidem disciplinæ reformatæ deberi, vos ipsi agnoscitis: ac quomodo fides atq; silentium commorari simul, cohabitareque possint, ego sanè non video. Plenus sum sermonibus: Coarctat me spiritus ventris. ventris mei: aeteterter meus ut vinum, cui non aperitur, sicut alres nol finderentur Iob, 32. 32. 18. 19. Credidi, ideo locutus sum: Psal. 116. 10.
units.tr: Fourthly, you yourselves acknowledge that faith is owed to the reformed discipline; and how faith and silence can remain together and cohabit, I certainly do not see. I am full of words; the spirit within me constrains me. Behold, my belly is like wine which has no vent, Job 32:18–19. I believed, and therefore I have spoken, Ps. 116:10.

units.la: 2. Cor. 4. 13. Est in animo meo, quasi ignis ardens inclusus ossibus meis, & defetiscor sustinendo, nec possum amplius: Ictem 20, 9.
units.tr: There is in my mind as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary with forbearing, and I cannot any longer, Jer. 20:9; cf. 2 Cor. 4:13.

units.la: Quinto,taciturnitas haec vestra,tacita quadam cum Episcopis collusio est, dum eorum technis atque artibus velificatur, ut ... et enim illicitis occurendum est jubet Paulus Eph. 4.14. 2 Cor. 2: 11,& bellatorum placitum est, Nec tuae occasioni defis, nec suam hosti des.
units.tr: Fifthly, this silence of yours is a certain tacit collusion with the bishops, since it favours their tricks and arts. For Paul bids us withstand the wiles of the wicked, Eph. 4:14; 2 Cor. 2:11, and the saying of warriors is: Do not fail your own opportunity, nor give your enemy his.

units.la: Datis vero vos Episcopis occasionem quam quaerunt suam. Docetis religionem & obedientiam, inquit Whitgiftus, de disciplina rixari quiscite: ita dum de disciplina filetis religione tantum & obedientiam (ut loqui solent) praedicatis, cuniculos illos promovetis quibus disciplinae veritate subruere machinatur. Quid quod taciturnitate hanc vestram, concessione causae quanda interpretantur? quo respectu insidiatoribus locu illum datis, quem a Gregorio damnatum legimus. Hortor at ... fidedeo, inquit, ut nullus vestrum hoc nomen aliquando recipiat, nullus ad id consentiat, nullus scribat, nullus ubi fuerat scriptura admittat, ... subscriptionem suam adjiciat, sed sicut omnipotentis Dei ministros decet, integrum se ab hujusmodi venenata infectione custodiat, & insidiatori in se locum non praebeat, quoniam hoc in totius Ecclesiae injuriam & disclusionem, & sicut dixi, in omnium vestrum desperatum fuit. Ad haec, taciturnitas haec vestra, technam illam Episcoporum promovet, qua moderationis atque clementiae auram captant, quasque mundo perfuadere nituntur, se factiosos tantum percequi, imo furiosos, certe homines plus nimio fervidos; patienter autem ferre eos qui sobrie sapiunt, quantumvis ipsis in disciplina contrarium sentiant. Ad postremum, Episcopis ipsis scandalo est, dum eos induratis, eorum superbiam augeris, eoque mollitie vestra, in miniistros qui hunc in modum cedere nesciunt, ferociores redditis. Ita Gregorius Magnus: Inter nos & coepiscopum Cyriacum, sicut beatitudo vestra novit, propter appellationem profani nominis, est gravis discordia. Meus vero Diaconus, cum praedicto fratre nostro Cyriaco, missarum solemnia celebrare non debet: qui per prophanum vocabulum culpa superbiae aut crimisit aut sequitur, ne si (quod absit) procedat, ei in tali elatione posito, vanitas? stultis nominis confirmare videatur. Eundem vero fratrem admonere studui ut se a tali elatione corrigat, quia si hanc non correxerit, pacem nolisum nullo modo habebit.
units.tr: But you give the bishops the very opportunity they seek. You teach religion and obedience, says Whitgift, and do not quarrel about discipline. So, while you keep silent about discipline and preach only religion and obedience (as they are wont to say), you advance those mines by which they plot to undermine the truth of discipline. Why do they interpret your silence as a kind of concession of the cause? By this attitude you give the ambushers that place which we read was condemned by Gregory: I exhort you, in the faith of God, that none of you ever accept this name, that none consent to it, that none write it, that none admit it where it has been written, nor add his subscription, but, as becomes ministers of almighty God, that each keep himself whole from this poisonous infection and give no place to the ambusher against himself, since this has been done to the injury and disgrace of the whole Church, and, as I have said, to the despair of all of you. Besides, this silence of yours promotes that trick of the bishops by which they catch at the breeze of moderation and clemency, and try to persuade the world that they pursue only the factious, indeed the frenzied, certainly men more than enough fervent, while they patiently bear with those who think soberly, however much they feel contrary to them in discipline. Finally, it is a scandal to the bishops themselves, while you harden them by your yielding and increase their pride; and by your softness you make ministers, who know not how to give way in this manner, more fierce. Thus Gregory the Great: Between us and my fellow bishop Cyriacus, as your blessedness knows, there is serious discord because of the appellation of a profane name. My deacon, indeed, ought not to celebrate the solemnities of the Mass with our aforesaid brother Cyriacus, who, through the profane word, either commits or follows the fault of pride; lest, if (which God forbid) it proceeds, vanity seem to be confirmed in the foolish name by one set in such elation. I have, however, tried to admonish the same brother that he correct himself from such elation, because if he does not correct it, he will by no means have peace with us.

units.la: Superbiae crimen Anglicanos Episcopos in sua prophana usurpatione committere, vobis certum est: hoc posito, superbiam eorum Gregorij judicio confirmatis, dum silentij sponsione viam precludi- tis quo minus eos, vrgere, refutare, reprehendere, & denique admonere possitis. Haec praeterita a nobis satis bene sunt (dicetis) cum nostram illis de Episcopatu illegitimo sententiam ab initio testatam fe- cimus. Annon Ieremias postquam Hananiam reprehendisset, ab eo decessit & deinceps non admonuit? Ier, 28. 11, Atqui ratio dissimilis est, Ieremie rem extraordinarie revelatam semel patefecisse satis erat, *ut disciplina rationibus è verbo petitis probanda jam est: Ac proinde ora contradicentium obthuranda: Tit.1.10. neque cessandum, donec aut evincantur Episcopi, aut convertantur. Hoc Gregorio perspectum nuper, qui Cyriacum admonendum censuit, donec ab elatione sua sese, correxerit, aut si incorrigibilis repertus fuerit, à pace Ecclesiæ abstinueretur.
units.tr: It is certain to you that the English bishops commit the crime of pride in their profane usurpation. Granted this, you confirm their pride by Gregory's judgment, while by your promise of silence you close off the way by which you could urge, refute, rebuke, and finally admonish them. These matters, you will say, are sufficiently dealt with by us, since we declared our opinion from the beginning concerning the illegitimate episcopate. Did not Jeremiah, after he had rebuked Hananiah, depart from him and admonish him no further? Jer. 28:11. But the case is not similar. It was enough for Jeremiah to make known once a matter revealed in an extraordinary way; discipline, however, must now be proved by reasons drawn from the Word, and therefore the mouths of gainsayers must be stopped, Titus 1:10. Nor must one cease until either the bishops are convicted or converted. Gregory perceived this recently, who judged that Cyriacus should be admonished until he corrected his elation; or, if he were found incorrigible, he should be kept from the peace of the Church.

units.la: Prima igitur Episcoporum admonitio vestra, tepida illa Eli objurgatione levior est: non instatis donec corriguntur, in scandalum igitur (ut olim Hophni & Phinees Eli) eos ruere finitis, & plus ipsos quam Deum vestrum honoratis: 1.Sam 3.13. Thyatira typus Ecclesiæ in Papatu latitantis erat, quæ à Wiclepho ad Lutherum usque decurrit. Fidelibus vero hujus Ecclesiæ comminatur Christus, si adversus eos venturum, quod Iezabelem, id est, quod Romam ferrent: Ap. 2. 20. Non quin sub hoc tempore reprehensa semper Roma fuerat, sed quia remissius & indulgentius egerunt sanctì, & non ita atque decuit vehementer intonabant. At vereor ne plus adversus Iezabelem illi, quam vos jam hodie adversus superbiæ Iezabeliticæ fucum, in Episcopis Anglicanis adhuc superstitem, excanduerint. Atque ex Pergamo patet vos nulla temporum difficultate excusari: nam si sanctis intonandum in Pergamo, ubi thronus Satbanæ erat, Ap, 2.13. quanto jam magis in Anglia vobis, ubi thronus Christi est. At undiq; tamen conclamamur. Quasi id Amos pariter non accideriti; Conspiravit contra te Amos. Terra verba ipsius ferre non poterit, Hæc est domus regia. Ne prophetes Bethele. Propheras tamen: sic ut nulla difficultate temporum, nulla asperitate hominum, nulla potentia adversantium, remissus & pusillus animus in Ecclesiæ corruptelis reprehendis excusetur. Difficilium quidem (ut habet Tertullianus facilis est venia: sed turpe tamen ut (habet idem) Christianos Pastores, non in prælio Leones, sed potius cervos esse, Quid autem est Leonem esse? respondeat Solomon, Non retrogreditur metu cujusquam: Proverb. ca. 30.30. Qui hæc non audiunt, vel poetæ illius voce pudefiant.
units.tr: Your first admonition of the bishops, therefore, is lighter than that lukewarm rebuke of Eli. You do not press on until they are corrected; so, like Hophni and Phinehas with Eli, you let them rush into scandal, and you honour them more than your God, 1 Sam. 3:13. Thyatira was a type of the Church hiding in the Papacy, which ran from Wycliffe to Luther. Christ threatens the faithful of this Church, that if they go over to her, as to Jezebel, that is, to Rome, Rev. 2:20. Not that Rome had not always been rebuked during this time, but the saints acted more mildly and indulgently, and did not thunder as vehemently as they ought. But I fear that those men were more inflamed against Jezebel than you today against the Jezebelian pride's paint that still survives among the English bishops. And from Pergamos it is plain that you are excused by no difficulty of the times: for if the saints had to thunder at Pergamos, where the throne of Satan was, Rev. 2:13, how much more now must you in England, where the throne of Christ is. Yet we are shouted down on every side. As if the same had not happened to Amos: Amos has conspired against you; the land cannot bear his words. This is the king's house, Amos 7:10 (of Bethel's prophet). Yet he prophesied: so that no difficulty of the times, no harshness of men, no power of opponents excuses a faint and timid spirit in rebuking the corruptions of the Church. Easy is pardon for difficult things, as Tertullian says; but it is shameful, as he says too, for Christian pastors to be not lions in battle but rather stags. What is it to be a lion? Let Solomon answer: He does not turn back for fear of anyone, Prov. 30:30. Whoever does not hear these things should be shamed by the voice of that poet.

units.la: Tunc cede malis, sed contra audentior ito.
units.tr: Then yield to misfortunes, but go forward against them with greater boldness.

units.la: Quintò, charitas in Ecclesiam Dei, illius amantem neminem silere finit. Patet hoc ex Esaia 62.6.7. Super muros tuos præficio custodes tota die, & tota nocte jugiter, non tacituros: qui commemoratis Iehovam, ne silentium esto vobis: Et ne permittatis silentium esse de illo, donec stabilitat & donec disponat Ierusalem laudem in terra. Nonne disciplinæ stabilitor Ecclesia, ut laudem in terra habeat? Nonne ex adverso disciplinæ in Ecclesia Anglicana perturbatio, & ordinem Christi pulcherrimum remoratur: & horrendas deformitates parit, quæ interitum appropinquantem comminantur. locum nempe hïc habeant illa, quibus quasi stimulis Gregorius Magnus, sacerdotes excitavit, ut illicito Episcopatui Constantinopolitano obviam irent: ne quid Ecclesia detrimenti caperet. Non solus ego (inquit) sed tota turbatur Ecclesia, quia ipsi Domini nostri Iesu Christi mandata superbi atque pontifici patiti. patici uulsfdam sermonis inuectione spernuntur. En Ecclesiæ jam nostræ statum: mandatum Christi est ne superbus & pompaticus Episcopatus super eos qui pares sunt, in Ecclesiam, invehatur: invehunt jam in Anglham Episcopi, perinde ut Iohannes olim Constantinopolitanus in Ecclesiam universam: Quæ hinc turbæ quæ tempestates? In navem etenim Ecclesiæ nostræ una Eurusque Notusque ruunt, imò quasi ex utre Æoli per Episcopos reserata, omnis in eam ventorum omnium vis incumbit: at nos interim otiosi complesis manibus sedemus in littore? Atque Gregorius sanè ex Episcopatu Constantinopolitano adventantem Antichristum odorari potuit, cujus ille præambulo erat: vos ex Episcopatu Anglicano jampridem plusquam unquam ante & sæviente & superbiente, de Antichristi in patriam reditu nihil suspicamini? præsertim cum ab ipsa nupera tempestate Episcopali, quantum Papistæ aucti sint, quæ cornua sumpserint, quid machinati fuerint, & quid etiamnum indies machinantur,eis omnibus notum sit, quibus ipsa Anglia nota. Revocentur igitur, altoque animo reponantur, quę tum ille: Adversarius diabolus contra humiles fœviens, sicut leo rugiens circuit, quærens quem devoret: Non jam,ut cernimus,caulas circuit,sed ita valide in quibusdam necessariis Ecclesiæ membris dentes figit, ut nulli sit dubium, quia nisi unanimiter favente Domino, cunctorum providastorum turba concurrat ,omne (quod absit)citius ovile dilaniet. Quanta nuper in humiles Puritanos Episcoporum sævitia? quam leoninus Hierarchicorum rugitus? quanta caularum non circuitio,sed dissipatio? Hęc cernitis,nisi ceci, non concurritis tamen, ut providi, quid igitur nisi vota supersunt, ne totum, idque citiùs, ovile ipsum dilanietur? Occlamo igitur vobis fratres, verbis sequentibus paulo post, State fortes, state securi : oportet enim ut constanter & sine præjudicio servetis ut (a Christo) acceptistis Ecclesias, & nihil sibi in nobis, hæc tentatio diabolicæ usurpationis adscribat. Rursus :Nunquid,si ex superbo & profano vocabulo, meus non in modico vulneratus animus est, tantæ indiscretionis esse potui, ut nescirem quid unitati fidei, quid concordiæ Ecclesiasticæ deberem? Nimis mihi fuerat despuisse, sic facere. Medici ecclesiæ Anglicanæ omnes pro viribus esse debemus: profanâ Episcoporum usurpatione,imo & sævitia, ea jam hodie vulneratur:qui igitur medicâ manum adhibere cessant, aut despiunt nescientes,aut salutem Ecclesiæ,ut perfidi, produnt.
units.tr: Fifthly, love for the Church of God does not allow anyone who loves her to keep silent. This is clear from Isaiah 62.6-7: Upon your walls I have set watchmen all day and all night continually, who shall never hold their peace. You that make mention of the LORD, keep not silence, and give him no rest, till he establish, and till he make Jerusalem a praise in the earth. Does not the Church need the establishing of discipline, so that she may have praise in the earth? On the contrary, does not disorder in discipline in the English Church delay the most beautiful order of Christ, and bring forth horrible deformities that threaten impending ruin? Surely those words apply here, with which Gregory the Great roused the priests, as with goads, to resist the unlawful episcopate of Constantinople, so that the Church might suffer no harm. I alone (he says) am not troubled, but the whole Church is troubled, because the commands of our Lord Jesus Christ are despised by the proud and the pompous, and are set aside by the insolence of their speech. Here is the state of our own Church now: the command of Christ is that the proud and pompous episcopate should not lord it over those who are equals, in the Church. Now the bishops are attacking England, just as John of Constantinople once attacked the whole Church. What storms and what tumults arise from this? For a wind from the east and a wind from the south rush upon the ship of our Church together, indeed, as if the bags of Aeolus had been opened by the bishops, the full force of all the winds bears down on her; and meanwhile are we sitting idle on the shore with folded hands? Gregory could indeed sniff out the Antichrist coming from the episcopate of Constantinople, whose forerunner that bishop was; will you, who have long seen the English episcopate raging and swelling prouder than ever before, suspect nothing of the return of Antichrist to our country? Especially since everyone who knows England itself knows how much the Papists have grown since the recent episcopal tempest, what horns they have raised, what they have plotted, and what they still plot day by day. Let these things be recalled, and taken to heart with a high spirit, as he said then: The adversary the devil, raging against the humble, goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. Now, as we see, he does not go about the sheepfolds, but so fiercely fastens his teeth in certain necessary members of the Church that there is no doubt that, unless the Lord favours us with one accord and a crowd of all the prudent gathers together, he will tear the whole flock to pieces, (which God forbid) all the more quickly. How great was the recent cruelty of the bishops against the humble Puritans? How lion-like the roaring of the hierarchs? How great the scattering, rather than the going about, of the sheepfolds? You see these things, unless you are blind, yet you do not gather together as the prudent do. What then remains but prayers, lest the whole flock itself be torn apart, and that more quickly? Therefore I cry out to you, brothers, in words that follow shortly after: Stand firm, stand secure; for you must constantly and without prejudice keep the Churches as you received them (from Christ), and let this temptation of diabolical usurpation ascribe nothing to itself in us. Again: Could I, if my spirit had not been wounded in no small measure by a proud and profane name, have been so lacking in judgement as not to know what I owed to the unity of faith and to ecclesiastical concord? It would have been too much for me to spit upon that, to act in such a way. We who are physicians of the English Church must all do what we can: the Church is now wounded by the profane usurpation, indeed by the cruelty, of the bishops. Therefore those who cease to apply the physician's hand either despise it through ignorance, or betray the salvation of the Church like traitors.

units.la: 5. Sextò, cùm libertas Ecclesiastica, gratia sit non contemnenda imò etiam donum Dei singulare: eam deserere ingratum, Episcopis eandem opprimentibus adulari abjectum,socios pro ea patientes negligere perfidum, Ecclesiam ejusdem amissione turbatam contemnere, proditorium esse dico. Non papatum affectabat Iohannes Constantinopolitanus, sed Episcopatum duntaxat talem in omnes qualem jam in Anglia Hierarchici possident, in suos pares collegas Anglicanos. Ecce igitur ad quem zelum Gregorij exemplo excitatur. Absit à Christianorum cordibus (inquit) nomen hoc blasphemiæ,
units.tr: 5. Sixthly, since ecclesiastical liberty is a grace not to be despised, indeed a singular gift of God, I say it is ungrateful to desert it, base to flatter those who oppress it with bishops, treacherous to neglect fellow sufferers who suffer for it, and treacherous to scorn a Church troubled by its loss. John of Constantinople did not aim at the papacy, but only at such an episcopate over all as the hierarchs now hold in England over their fellow colleagues, the English equals. Behold, then, the zeal with which Gregory's example stirs us. Far from the hearts of Christians (he says) be this name of blasphemy,

units.la: § 3 in quo omnium sacerdotum honor adimitur, dum ab uno sibi dementer arrogatur. Ille coercendus est qui sanctae universali Ecclesiae injuriam facit, qui corde tumet, qui gaudere de nomine iungluniatis appetit, qui honori quoque imperij nostri se per privatum vocabulum superponit. Rursus: Perpende rogo quia in hac praesumptione temeraria, pax totius turbatur Ecclesiae & gratiae contradicitur communiter omnibus effusae. Rursus: Cognoscat fraternitas vestra, Iohannem contra Deum, contra pacem Ecclesiae, in omnium despectum & injurium sacerdotum, modestiae ac mensurae suae terminos excessisse. Ita Gregorij, Durandus Mildensis, adversus oppressionem suo loculo libertatis Ecclesiasticae accomodare veritas non est? quidni ego pariter adversus eandem jam in Anglia per Episcopos agitatam? Annon etenim in omnium ministrorum Anglicanorum despectum Episcopatus Anglicanus est, praesertim cum in eos quos pro paribus habere debuerat, principetur? Anno honor adimitur omnibus, dum uni Episcopo arrogatur, qui omnibus communis est? Annon nomen singularitatis (sic enim Bilsonus loquitur) authoritati pastorum omnium superponitur? Annon gratiae omnibus pastoribus communiter effusae contradicitur, sic ut scandalum patiantur omnes? Quid quod ipsa Durandi verba haec suo saeculo accomodata, in Anglia jam recidant? Monet etenim sui saeculi sacerdotes ex Gregorio, ne nimium Papae subjecti essent, ne eorum vitia venari compellantur, modo vero assumendum esset quod sic Romano honoretur Ecclesia ut aliis honor nullus debitus negaretur. Bene se habet: quae Gregorius adversus Iohannem attulit, ea non solum Iohannem refutant, sed & omnes eos, qui Episcopatui alicui illicito nimis addicti sunt, quique unam ecclesiam ita honorant, aut honorari volunt, sic ut aliis honor debitus denegetur. Refutaturdicirco a Gregorio ministri in Anglia illi, qui Episcopis nimium subjecti sunt, qui Cathedralem Episcopalemque sedem prae aliis Ecclesiis honorari velint, Anglicani denique Episcopi ipsi, qui Ecclesiis honorem debitum negant, dum eas sibi metipsis subjiciunt, quas pro paribus revereri oportuerat. Pergamus ad alios. Anno 1555. editus quidam liber est, qui Aureum Speculum dicitur, ubi post oppressionis Ecclesiae per Papam factae mentionem, hoc subjungitur: Omnes quidem intus murmurant, nulli autem clamant. Haec si pudenda ignavia sit, quis illis in Anglia excusationis locus superest, qui perinde faciunt? certunt etenim est advetsus Episcopos murmurare intus quidem plurimos, clamare autem paucos. Conqueritur Gregorius Hamburgensis, in usurpatione Potestatis Ecclesiasticae & totius mundi inquietudine, nullos aulos fuisse contradixerunt, alii tacentibus ob spem promotionis ad beneficia, alii, per metum peridencia jam adepta. Hoc inde provenisse dicit, quod liberius esset a multis annis de potestate Dei quam Papae praedicare & disputare. Muta Papae in Episcopi nomen, & quis veterum temporum jam modo in Anglia non cernit effigiem? Dinitcavit acriter pro libertate Ecclesiastica in Concilio Basiliensi Ludovicus Arelatensis, ad quam quam constanter ruendum extimulat alios, verbis illis Hieronymi {x}ymi ad Iohannem Episcopum Hierosolymitanum. Quomodo ego te habeam pro consule, qui me non habes pro Senatore: Dictum illud, ad quod ni fallor Hieronymus allusit, ita loquebatur: Quomodo me habere pro Imperatore, quum tu me non habeas pro Senatore: sic ut de Episcopis loquens, Imperatoris in consulis nomen, consulto mutarit Hieronymus. Nullam ergo in Episcopo sui saeculi imperandi authoritatem agnovit: tantum illi consulis in Senatu praerogativa adjudicat, ut suffragia colligat, secundum majorem partem pronunciet, & reliquas actiones humanas moderetur. Non ita jam hodie Episcopi nostri, qui ipsum Senatum, non modo presbyterorum Senatoriam authoritatem sustulerunt: Imperatoriam vero & monarchicam authoritatem sibimetipsis asciverunt, ut illi soli (exclusis presbyteris,) Ecclesiarum rectores, rerum iudices, Canonum custodes & executores videantur. Huic tyrannidi in uno Johanne Hierosolymitano tum gliscenti, & quasi per rimulas erumpenti, cumprimis sibi resistendum Sanctus Hieronymus iudicavit: vos eidem in Episcopis Anglicanis, pestifera flamma omnia undiq; circumlambenti & corripienti jam resistendum non putabitis? Nae tum dignissimi qui audiatis Apostoli illud, 2. Cor. 11: 20. permittitis si quis vos in servitutem redigat, si quis se super vos exaltet, si quis in facie percutiat. Num etenim se praedicatores Corinthiaci tum exaltabant, ut nunc se in Anglia exaltant Episcopi? aut in eam servitutem redegerunt, in quam & collegas pares suos, non plebem modo, jam Episcopi redigunt?
units.tr: § 3 by which the honour of all priests is taken away, while it is madly claimed for himself alone by one man. He must be restrained who does injury to the holy universal Church, who swells in heart, who desires to rejoice in the title of universal, who by a private title also sets himself above the honour of our empire. Again: Consider, I beg you, that by this rash presumption the peace of the whole Church is disturbed, and the grace poured out in common upon all is contradicted. Again: Let your brotherhood know that John, against God, against the peace of the Church, to the contempt and injury of all priests, has exceeded the limits of his modesty and measure. Thus Gregory. Is it not true that what Durandus of Mende says against the oppression of ecclesiastical liberty may be applied, with the same force, to the oppression now stirred up in England by the bishops? Is not the English episcopate, indeed, to the contempt of all English ministers, especially since it rules over those whom it ought to have regarded as equals? Is not honour taken from all, while it is claimed for one bishop who is common to all? Is not the name of singularity (for so Bilson speaks) set above the authority of all pastors? Is not the grace poured out in common upon all pastors contradicted, so that all suffer offence? What of the fact that these very words of Durandus, adapted to his own age, now apply again in England? For he admonishes the priests of his age, following Gregory, not to be too subject to the Pope, lest they be compelled to hunt out his faults; but now it must be assumed that the Roman Church is so honoured that no due honour is denied to others. It is well: what Gregory brought against John refutes not only John, but also all those who are too much devoted to some unlawful episcopate, and who so honour one church, or wish it to be honoured, that due honour is denied to others. Therefore, by Gregory's refutation, those English ministers who are too subject to bishops are refuted, those who wish the cathedral and episcopal see to be honoured above other churches, and finally the English bishops themselves, who deny due honour to churches while subjecting to themselves those whom they ought to have reverenced as equals. Let us proceed to others. In the year 1555 there was published a certain book called the Golden Mirror, where, after mention of the oppression of the Church by the Pope, this is added: All indeed murmur within, but none cry out. If this is shameful cowardice, what excuse remains in England for those who act in the same way? For it is certain that against the bishops very many murmur within, but few cry out. Gregory of Hamburg complains that, in the usurpation of ecclesiastical power and the unrest of the whole world, there were no few who contradicted, some keeping silent through hope of promotion to benefices, others through fear of losing what they had already obtained. He says this arose from the fact that for many years it had been freer to preach and dispute about the power of God than about the power of the Pope. Change "Pope" into "bishop", and who of the ancient times does not now see its likeness in England? Ludovicus of Arles vigorously defended ecclesiastical liberty at the Council of Basel, and urged others to fight as constantly for it, using those words of Jerome to John, bishop of Jerusalem: How can I count you as consul, when you do not count me as senator? That saying, to which Jerome, if I am not mistaken, alluded, ran thus: How can I count myself as emperor, when you do not count me as senator? Speaking of bishops in this way, Jerome deliberately changed the title of emperor to that of consul. He therefore recognised no authority of ruling in a bishop of his own age; he grants him only so much prerogative of a consul in the Senate that he may collect votes, announce the decision of the greater part, and moderate the other human actions. Our bishops today are not like this, who have removed not only the authority of the presbyters, the Senate itself; and they have claimed for themselves an imperial and monarchical authority, so that they alone (with the presbyters excluded) appear to be rulers of the Churches, judges of affairs, and guardians and executors of the canons. Against this tyranny, which was then swelling in the single John of Jerusalem and breaking out as if through cracks, Saint Jerome judged that resistance was above all required. Will you not think that resistance must now be offered to the same tyranny in the English bishops, who with a pestilential flame lick round and seize everything on every side? Indeed, you would be most worthy to hear that word of the Apostle, 2 Cor. 11.20: you suffer it, if anyone brings you into bondage, if anyone exalts himself over you, if anyone strikes you on the face. For did the Corinthian preachers then exalt themselves as the bishops now exalt themselves in England? Or did they reduce to that bondage into which the bishops now reduce not only the people, but also their own fellow equals?

units.la: Septimo, socios commilitonesque vestros in die belli, certe tempore difficillimo diseruistis, quod quam sit turpe; ex his scripturae locis patet: An fratres vestri procederent in bellum, & vos hic consisteretis? Imo quasi rumpitis animum filiorum Israelis, ne transeant in terram illam quam dat eis Iehova? Num. 32. 9. 7. Maledicite Merozo, inquit Angelus Iehovae, indesinenter maledicite habitatoribus ejus: quia non advenerunt ad auxilium Iehovae, ad auxilium Iehovae inter fortes. Iud. 5: 23. cur desideres inter duas illa sarcinas audiendo sibila gregum: magni profundis cogitationibus animi ad partes Reubinis: Gilehad ultra Iordanem habitans, & Dan quare degeret apud naves? Ascher quare desideret ad portum marium & in praeruptis suis habitaret? Zebulun & Naphtali populus est, qui abjecit scipsum ad moriendum in editis locis agri. Iud. 5: 16, 17, 18. Dixit Uria ad Davidem, Arca ipsa & Israel ac Iehuda manent in tugurtis & Ioab Dominus meus, ac servi domini mei in superficie agri castra habent, & ego ingrederer domum meam? 2. Sam. 11: 11. In prima mea defensione nemo mihi adfuit, sed omnes me deseruerunt: ne illis imputetur. 2 Tim. 4: 16. Certe hi Scripturae loci non unum vobis crimen fratres imputare videntur, ut qui Dominum adjuvare inter fortes detractastis, segniter decubuistis, dum quasi sibila arietum aures vestras circumsonarent, profundas cogitationes inter vosmet volvistis, constitistis quasi trans Iordanem, & non in bellum processistis, animos sociorum debilitastis, quosdam etiam exemplo vestro languescere
units.tr: Seventhly, you have deserted your comrades and fellow soldiers on the day of battle, at the most difficult time, and how shameful that is is clear from these passages of Scripture: Will your brothers go out to war while you sit here? Why do you discourage the hearts of the children of Israel, so that they will not cross into the land which Jehovah gives them? Num. 32. 9. 7. Curse Meroz, said the Angel of Jehovah; curse its inhabitants bitterly, because they did not come to help Jehovah, to help Jehovah among the mighty. Judg. 5: 23. Why did you remain between the two saddlebags, listening to the whistling of the flocks? The men of Reuben had great deliberations of heart. Gilead dwelt beyond the Jordan, and why did Dan stay with the ships? Asher remained at the seashore and dwelt in his creeks. Zebulun and Naphtali are a people who risked their lives to die on the high places of the field. Judg. 5: 16, 17, 18. Uriah said to David, The ark and Israel and Judah abide in tents, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are encamped in the open field; and shall I go into my house? 2 Sam. 11: 11. At my first defence no one stood by me, but all deserted me; may it not be laid to their charge. 2 Tim. 4: 16. Certainly these passages of Scripture seem to charge you brothers with more than one fault: that you refused to help the Lord among the mighty, lay idle, while the whistling of the rams sounded about your ears like a voice, turned over profound thoughts among yourselves, stood as if beyond the Jordan and did not go forth to battle, weakened the spirits of your comrades, and by your example caused some of them to grow faint

units.la: Ante Sil. degest. concilii Basilens. guescere fecisti, domi constitistis dum servi Dei sub castris erant, & in defensione pro veritate ejus eosdem deseruistis, forte etiam ita deseruistis, ut magnam quae sequuta est calamitatis partem attraxisse videamini. Quis enim scit, si operas virésque vestras, una cum reliquis adhibuisset, an a porta pugnam avertissetis? nam ut paucitate animari hostes solent, ita deterreri multitudine: certè multitudo hominum ad martyrium convolantium Edessam servavit olim, & persecutoris impetum retundit: & Valentem Imperatorem ab Alexandria se temperasse idem Socrates narrat, quòd multos ibi comperisset, qui cum sancto Athanasio in causa fidei vitam profundere parati erant. At ex adverso dum colla sua subtrahunt quidam, subest ignavia discordiaque, quâ fit ut conjunctis animis corruptelae Ecclesiasticae non impugnentur: eae autem non unanimiter impugnatae & crescere & confirmari solent, ut quondam Probo Episcopo Tullensi visum. Quousque, inquit, collegae charissimi mei, Romulei illi vultures patientia nostra, ne dicam stultitia, abutentur? quousque eorum flagitia, avaritiam, superbiam, luxum tolerabimus? Non cessabit hoc genus ArchiSynagogi pessimum, nisi omnes ad egestatem & servitutem durissimam redegerit. Discordia nostra hocce malum crevit: discordia nostra nebulones illi visi sunt: Non unquam quum diu illi salvi fuerint, Christianis sanctam pacem servare, ab armis feriari, pietatem inter se colere licebit. Atque hîc ego me reprimam. Consideratè, fratres, quae dixi & Deus det vobis intelligentiam in omnibus, Certe mihi ejusmodi haec videntur, ut temerè contemnenda non sint, nisi rationibus validioribus praeponderentur, quas ego nullas scio: non quasi me lateat quae à vobis adferri solent, sed quia eas nullius ponderis ac momenti esse video.
units.tr: You caused some to grow faint. You remained at home while the servants of God were in the camp, and you deserted them in their defence of the truth; you may even have deserted them in such a way that you seem to have brought on a large part of the calamity that followed. For who knows whether, had you added your efforts and strength along with the rest, you would have turned the fight away from the gate? For as enemies are usually encouraged by the smallness of a force, so they are deterred by its size. Certainly the great number of men who flocked together to martyrdom once saved Edessa and repulsed the attack of a persecutor; and the same Socrates relates that the Emperor Valens refrained from Alexandria because he found there many who were ready to lay down their lives with holy Athanasius in the cause of the faith. On the other hand, while some withdraw their necks, sloth and discord lie beneath, with the result that the corruptions of the Church are not attacked with united minds; and those corruptions, when they are not attacked unanimously, are wont to grow and become established, as once seemed to Probus, bishop of Toul. How long, my dearest colleagues, will those Roman vultures abuse our patience, not to say our folly? How long shall we tolerate their shameful deeds, their greed, their pride, their luxury? This most wicked kind of archsynagogue will not cease unless it reduces everyone to poverty and the harshest slavery. Our discord has made this evil grow; our discord made those scoundrels appear. Since they have been safe for so long, will it ever be permitted to Christians to keep holy peace, to rest from arms, and to cultivate piety among themselves? And here I will restrain myself. Consider carefully, brothers, what I have said, and may God give you understanding in all things. Certainly these things seem to me to be of such a kind that they should not be lightly despised, unless they are outweighed by stronger reasons; and I know of none. Not as if I did not know what is usually brought forward by you, but because I see that those arguments are of no weight or moment.

units.la: CAP. 40.
units.tr: CHAP. 40.

units.la: Rationes sponsentium silentium tolluntur.
units.tr: The arguments of those who favour silence are overturned.

units.la: PRimò illud Salomonis citare soletis, tempus silendi perinde ac loquendi esse: Eccles. 3.7. Quod quàm parum vobis faveat, ex eodem loco liquet, vers. 7. ubi tempus pacis nullum esse in tempore belli dicitur. In militia siquidem nostra spirituali, silentium paci, confessio bello respondet: sic ut tempus jam loquendi pro disciplina maxime sit, quando bellum de disciplina, ut nostis, magnum geritur: 1. Cor. 16.9. Ita Paulus. Ostium mihi apertum est magnum & efficax, & adversarij multi: idcirco permanebo Ephesi usque ad Pentecosten: quasi tum maximè in statione permanendum, & dimittendum sit, quando per multos adversarios ipsa veritas impugnatur. Ita alibi: Sunt multi refractarij, quibus oportet os obturare: Tit. Cap. 1. verf 10. 11. quasi tum maximè servo Dei loquendum sit, quando se maximè refractarij veritati opponunt: horum ora obturari posse vestri oris silentio creditis, ac non aperiri potiùs? Sic Deus ipse: Nemo est qui clamet pro justitiâ, & nemo qui disceptet pro fide: Isai. cap. 59. verf. 4. Non in fide invalescunt in terra: Ierem. cap. 9. 3. Nullus fuit adjutor, obstupui quòd nullus fulciret: Isai. cap.93. 5. nonne ex his singulis liquet, quantopere displiceat Deo secordia hominum, quæ laboranti veritati suppetias non fert? Rectè jus Canonicum ex Augustino.Cum totius Ecclesiæ salus queritur, fides impugnatur, necesse est ut ex adversò prælati ascendant, & in die belli seipsos murū opponant pro domo Domini,& animos suos ponant pro ovibus suis,ut exemplo passionis eos accendant, quos sermone doctrinæ diutius confirmare non valent. Quàm hæc apposita adversus eos qui se disciplinæ corruptelis non opponunt. Secundò, exemplum Pauli allegare soletis, quem Ephesi per triennium de verbis illius idololatriæ tacuisse dicitis, ut occasionem prædicandi Iudæis lucraretur.
units.tr: First, you are accustomed to cite Solomon's saying that there is a time for keeping silent just as there is a time for speaking: Eccles. 3.7. How little this favours you is clear from the same passage, verse 8, where it is said that there is no time of peace in a time of war. In our spiritual warfare, silence corresponds to peace and confession to war. So the time for speaking is above all the time for church discipline, when, as you know, a great war is being waged over discipline: 1 Cor. 16.9. Thus Paul: A great and effective door has been opened to me, and there are many adversaries; therefore I will remain at Ephesus until Pentecost. It is as if one must especially remain at one's post and not depart when the truth itself is being assailed by many adversaries. Elsewhere: There are many refractory men, whose mouths must be stopped: Titus 1.10-11. It is as if the servant of God must especially speak when the most refractory men set themselves against the truth. Do you believe that their mouths can be stopped by the silence of your mouth, rather than opened? So God himself: There is no one who cries out for justice, and no one who contends for the faith: Isaiah 59.4. They do not grow strong in the earth in faith: Jer. 9.3. There was no helper; I was astonished that no one upheld: Isaiah 63.5. Does it not clearly appear from each of these passages how greatly the apathy of men displeases God, when they do not bring help to the truth as it labours? The Canon Law rightly cites Augustine: When the salvation of the whole Church is sought and the faith is assailed, it is necessary that prelates come forward from the opposite side and, in the day of battle, set themselves as a wall for the house of the Lord and lay down their lives for their sheep, so that by the example of their suffering they may inflame those whom they cannot confirm for long by the word of doctrine. How apt these words are against those who do not set themselves against the corruptions of discipline. Secondly, you are accustomed to allege the example of Paul, who, you say, kept silent for three years at Ephesus about the matters of that idolatry, in order to gain an opportunity of preaching to the Jews.

units.la: Primò, prædicandum Iudæis primo loco Evangelium erat, deinde Gentibus: quòd si igitur abstinuerit aliquantisper sese Paulus à Gentilibus Ephesiis, donec Iudæos prius instruxisset, non tamen silentio vestro favet, quibus nulla ejusmodi dispensatio commissa est.
units.tr: First, the Gospel had to be preached to the Jews in the first place and then to the Gentiles. If, therefore, Paul for a while refrained from speaking to the Gentile Ephesians until he had first instructed the Jews, he still does not favour your silence, since no such dispensation has been committed to you.

units.la: Secundò, tam de omnibus papisticis idolomanijs taceri posse, quàm de disciplinâ, ex istâ ratiocinatione sequitur.
units.tr: Secondly, from this same line of reasoning it would follow that one could keep silent about all the papistical idolatries just as about discipline.

units.la: Tertiò, cum pro idololatria Ephesina contentio orta esset, non tum cum bestiis Ephesinis pugnare Paulus detrectabat: 1.Cor.15:32. Act. 19. 30. Cum igitur contentio de disciplina in Anglia acris sit, cunctandi vobis tempus non est, si Pauli exemplum imitari volueritis,
units.tr: Thirdly, when the contention over Ephesian idolatry arose, Paul did not shrink from fighting with the Ephesian beasts at that time: 1 Cor. 15.32; Acts 19.30. Therefore, since the contention over discipline in England is fierce, there is no time for you to delay, if you wish to imitate Paul's example.

units.la: Quartò, Paulum tam diu de Ephesina Idololatria tacuisse falsum est, quod dicit Scriba, Act, 19: 37. hi homines in Deam vestram contumeliosi non sunt, politicum pseudos erat, ut tumultus sedaretur, cui ipse Demetrius contradicit Act. 19.26. Auditis & spectatis Paulum, non solum Ephesiam sed prope totius Asiæ multam turbam persuadendo avertisse, quod dicat Deos illos non esse, qui manibus fiunt.
units.tr: Fourthly, it is false that Paul was silent for so long about Ephesian idolatry. The town clerk says in Acts 19.37 that these men are not blasphemers of your goddess, but this was a political pretence, so that the tumult might be calmed. Demetrius himself contradicts it, Acts 19.26: You hear and see that Paul has turned away, by persuading, a great crowd not only at Ephesus but almost throughout all Asia, saying that those are not gods which are made with hands.

units.la: Quintò, quid servis Dei faciendum sit, docet suo exemplo Paulus Act 17:16. cujus Spiritus Athenis irritabatur in ipso,quamprimùm conspexisset urbem idolis deditam esse: cui adjungendus Samson est, quem incessit Spiritus Iehovæ, quamprimum sonitus vociferantium in suum occursum Philistæorum auribus suis percepisset: Iudic. 14: 15. Annon docent ista vel ipsum conspectum temeratæ in Anglia disciplinæ spiritus vestros irritare, ipsam Hierarchicorum adversus eandem vociferationem, Spiritum in vobis Dei exsuscitare oportuisse?
units.tr: Fifthly, Paul teaches by his own example what the servants of God must do: Acts 17.16, where his spirit was stirred within him at Athens as soon as he saw the city given over to idols. To this should be added Samson, upon whom the Spirit of Jehovah came as soon as the shouting of the Philistines reached his ears: Judges 14.15. Do not these things teach that even the mere sight of discipline violated in England ought to stir your spirits, and that, against that same clamour of the hierarchy, the Spirit of God ought to be roused in you?

units.la: Tertiò, vos vestro de disciplina silentio, occasionem doctrinæ Evangelicæ prædicandæ lucrari obtenditis: quod parum ab illa Pilati versutiâ distare dico, qui in corpore flagellandum Christum censuit, ut illius vitā pacatis Iudæis lucraretur: Ioh.19:1.Potuit Moses populum lucrari, si de bestiis Pharaoni cederet, sed ille ne de ungula una cedendum sibi existimavit: Exod.10:26. Potuit Daniel tempus longius
units.tr: Thirdly, you put forward as an excuse for your silence about discipline that you gain an opportunity of preaching the Gospel. I say this differs little from the cunning of Pilate, who judged that Christ should be scourged in his body, so that he might win Christ's life by pacifying the Jews: John 19.1. Moses could have won over the people if he had yielded to Pharaoh about the beasts, but he thought he must not yield so much as a hoof: Exod. 10.26. Daniel could have gained time longer,

units.la: T giùs lucrari, quo Ecclesiæ prodesset, si vel per pauxillum temporis ab orando Deo suo abstinere voluisset :-sed & fenestram conclavis sui aperiendam sibi censuit, quò clariorem pietatis suæ confessionem edere posset: Dan: 6: 11. potuit Iohannes Baptista occasionem Evangelij diutiùs prædicandi lucrari, si ab Herode reprehendendo sibi temperare voluisset: Marc. 6.18. sed hujusmodi carnalem prudentiam ille longè à se facessere jussit. Neque ipse Dominus Iesus Christus eidem Herodi parcere voluit, ut ita liberiùs Evangelium prædicaret, sed in Providentia Patris recumbens ( quod & vos fecisse oportuit) profecti, inquit, dicite vulpi illi, me hodie & eras, & perindie iter facturum, quousque consummatus fuero: Luc.13.32.33. Ita de Meletio Socrates: Meletius, inquit, Antiochiæ per aliquod tempus negotiis fidei se non immiscuit, sed auditoribus ea tantum tradidit quæ ad mores pertinebant: tandem tamen clausulam unius substantiæ aperuit, atque ita se in exilium relegari passus est: pertæsus igitur prudentiæ vestræ Meletius tandem est.
units.tr: by which he might have benefited the Church, if he had been willing to abstain from praying to his God even for a little while; but he thought fit to open the window of his room, so that he could make a clearer confession of his godliness: Dan. 6.11. John the Baptist could have gained the opportunity of preaching the Gospel for longer if he had been willing to refrain from rebuking Herod: Mark 6.18. But he ordered such carnal prudence to be far from himself. Nor did the Lord Jesus Christ himself wish to spare the same Herod, so that he might preach the Gospel more freely; rather, resting on the providence of the Father (which you too ought to have done), he said: Go and tell that fox: behold, I shall perform cures today and tomorrow, and on the third day I shall be perfected: Luke 13.32-33. So Socrates says of Meletius: Meletius, for some time at Antioch, did not meddle in matters of faith, but delivered to his hearers only those things which pertained to morals; at last, however, he opened the clause about one substance, and so allowed himself to be relegated into exile. Therefore Meletius at last grew weary of your prudence.

units.la: Quartò, eos operam ludere dicitis, qui hodie de disciplina prædicant, & planè laterem lavare. Laterem verò? quid si & Æthiopem etiam? recte etenim Augustinus: Haud minus mercedis tonsori debetur quam Aethiopem lavat, quanquam eum nigriorem, quam cum Græcum quem tamen candidiorem reddit. Atque quam multa adversus istam objectionem responderi possent, vos minimè latet: ego interim intra hujus causæ pellem me continebo. Occurrit igitur huic objectioni sanctus Bernardus, qui ad Eugenium hanc ipsam ob causam Evangelizare detrectantem, ita loquitur. Dracones (inquis) me mones pascere, & scorpiones: propter hoc inquam magis aggredere eos. Alludit ad illud Ezechiel.2.6. Tu autem fili hominis ne timeto ab istis, quod refractarij & spinei sint in te, & apud Scorpiones habites, a facie eorum ne consternator, quod domus rebellis sit. Coegit olim Regino burgi conventum quendam, contra Iohannem Papam, Ludovicus Imperator, in quo ita ab Episcopis contra istam objectionem decretum est: Semmystas ferunt, cum sint nuncij Antichristi. Eos inexplebilis honoris, potentiæ, pecuniæ sitis, atque luxus, avaritia, fastus, quæ in proverbium venere, producunt. Ingenue fatemur, tempora nostra censuram non ferunt: Iampridem corruptis moribus simplicitas Christiana sordet, longinquior consuetudo potentior veritate vicit: tamen indignatio silentium rumpit. In altissima humanarum rerum specula cælitus positi, tacere non possumus, ne canes muti juxta sacrum vatem qui latrare non possunt, simus. Et si lupos pelle ovina tectos abigere, ob infelicitatem temporum non valemus, non resistere tamen hujusmodi, prodere munus nostrum est: Quamvis tantundem ut volumus non possumus tamen non assequutis voluisse abundè pulchrum & magnificum est. Similia illa Civitatensis Episcopi sunt: Quid dicam aut ultrà adjiciam de statu Clericorum? Nam ut video, populus iste durae cervicis est & in iniquitatibus suis venditus, & in scelleribus suis pertinax: Vocavi eum & non erat qui audiret Is. 63. Si vero luxuriam, avaritiam, superbiam, simoniam [illegible, ~20 letters] vim, ac cætera Clericorum vitia profundius tractare præsumpsero, fantastiçus ac præsumptuosus totaliter promulgabor, atque de mendacio arguar, & effundam sermonem (contra doctrinam sapientis) ubi non est audi-tus.
