Sed ue mihi, Isaia teste si tacuero: populus enim iste, ordo scili-cet sacerdotalis & clericalis ad iracundiam provocans est, & filij mendaces, nolentes audire verbum Dei, qui dicunt videntibus, nolite videre, & aspicientibus, nolite aspicere nobis ea quæ recta sint, loquamini nobis placentia, videte nobis errores, cessit a facie vestra sanctus Israel. Propterea quia reprobasti verbum meum, & sperastis in tumultum, erit vobis iniquitas hæc, sicut interruptio cadens de muro excelso, quoniam subito dum non speratur veniet contritio eius, ut comminuatur sicut conteritur lagena figuli contritione valida. Hæc quantumuis longiora, exscribere non sum veritus, quia non solum munus pastorale vestrum fratres, ante oculos ponunt, quanquam proficiendi spes nulla sit: sed etiam quia rationes urgent, quibus tantisper dum siletis, satis facere non potestis. Eadem enim mala jam Anglie imminent, ob corruptam clericalis ordinis disciplinam, quæ hic commemorantur: nam & qui communicant in peccato, ommunicabunt in pœnâ, & de Anglia comminatur Christus speciatim, in illius vrbe Laodicea, illius Angelus nisi ferveant & resipiscant, ex ore suo se vomiturū: Ap.3.16. Quæ igitur viscera vestra fratres, si ad ipsū distinctum ensem, instar illius naturalis matris non commovemini? Quæ fides, si hostem in portis considentem tubam non sonatis? Quæ denique animas proprias liberandi cura, si de exitio jam instanti patriam vestram non monueritis; Atque hoc, ex reformatæ disciplinæ cum sanctitate tum necessitate, ad ministros in Anglia tacentes porrisma quartum est.
units.tr: Fourthly, you say that those who preach about discipline today are wasting their effort and are plainly washing a brick. A brick? What if also an Ethiopian? Augustine rightly says: No less wage is owed to the barber who washes an Ethiopian, though he makes him blacker, than to one who washes a Greek whom he makes whiter. How many things could be answered to that objection, you are not unaware; meanwhile I shall keep myself within the bounds of this cause. The holy Bernard meets this objection, speaking to Eugenius, who for this very reason shrank from preaching the Gospel: You warn me, you say, that I am to feed dragons and scorpions; for this very reason, I say, attack them all the more. He alludes to Ezekiel 2.6: But you, son of man, do not fear them, because they are refractory and thorny toward you, and you dwell among scorpions; do not be dismayed at their face, because it is a rebellious house. Once Regino of the burgh convened a certain assembly against Pope John, at the command of the Emperor Ludwig, in which the bishops decreed against this same objection as follows: They call them Semmystae, since they are messengers of Antichrist. They produce the insatiable thirst for honour, power, money, luxury, avarice and pride, which have passed into a proverb. We frankly confess that our times do not bear censure: Christian simplicity has long been despised as morals have been corrupted, and longer-standing custom has prevailed over truth more strongly. Yet indignation breaks silence. Placed by heaven on the highest watchtower of human affairs, we cannot be silent, lest we be dumb dogs, as the sacred prophet says, which cannot bark. And if, because of the unhappiness of the times, we are unable to drive away the wolves clothed in sheep's skin, nevertheless not to resist such things is to betray our office. Although we cannot achieve as much as we wish, yet to have wished for what we have not attained is abundantly fine and great. Similar to these are the words of the Bishop of Civitas: What shall I say, or add further, about the state of the clergy? For, as I see, this people is stiff-necked and sold under its iniquities, and persistent in its wickednesses: I called them, and there was no one who would hear (Is. 63). If indeed I should presume to treat more deeply of luxury, avarice, pride, simony [illegible in the scan] and the other vices of the clergy, I shall be entirely published as fanciful and presumptuous, and shall be convicted of falsehood, and I shall pour out speech (contrary to the teaching of the wise man) where there is no one to listen. But woe to me if I keep silent, Isaiah being witness: for this people, that is, the sacerdotal and clerical order, is a provoker of wrath, and lying sons, unwilling to hear the word of God, who say to those who see, "Do not see," and to those who look, "Do not look at what is right for us; speak to us what is pleasing, see errors for us; the Holy One of Israel has withdrawn from your face." Because you have rejected my word and trusted in tumult, this iniquity will be for you like a breach falling from a high wall, which suddenly, when it is not expected, comes to its ruin, so that it is crushed as a potter's jar is shattered by a violent blow. I have not hesitated to transcribe these passages, however lengthy, because they set before your eyes, brothers, not only your pastoral duty, although there is no hope of advancing, but also because they press the reasons which, while you keep silent, you cannot satisfy. For the same evils that are recorded here now threaten England, on account of the corrupted discipline of the clerical order. For those who share in sin will share in punishment, and Christ threatens England specifically, in its city of Laodicea, saying that unless its angel grow fervent and repent, he will vomit him out of his mouth: Rev. 3.16. What, then, brothers, are your bowels, if you are not moved, like that natural mother, when the very sword is at hand? What faith is yours if you do not sound the trumpet when the enemy sits in the gates? And what care for saving your own souls is yours if you do not warn your country of the destruction now at hand? This is the fourth porism, concerning the necessity of reformed discipline, both in its sanctity and its necessity, addressed to the ministers in England who are silent.

units.la: CAP 41. Porisma sextum, notitia disciplinæ est populo necessaria.
units.tr: CAP 41. Sixth corollary: knowledge of discipline is necessary for the people.

units.la: SExtum ad populum Anglicanum pertinet, cujus auram nos captare tritum jam & obsoletum improperium est. Quod etenim ad conciones nostras confluere populus etiam ex longinquo soleret: hinc seductores multitudines post nos trahentes: Act. 20.30. ab Hierarchicis accusati sumus: Quasi Albingenses seductores quòd Bernardo conquerente ingens ad eos concursus fuerit? Quasi Waldenses seductores quòd accusante Reinerio, facilis eis ad credendum multitudo erat? Quasi Ambrosius seductor, quòd populi multitudine se circumvallere potuisset? Quasi Chrysostomus seductor,quòd populum in se adeò propensum haberet, ut clam ex urbe discedere coactus sit, ut tumultum popularem præveniret? Quid ego in his insto? Dominus ipse Iesus Christus eandem calumniam
units.tr: The sixth concerns the English people, and the charge that we court their favour is a stale and worn-out reproach. People used to flock to our sermons even from far away, so we are called seducers who draw crowds after us (Acts 20:30), and the hierarchs have accused us of this. Were the Albigenses seducers because, as Bernard complained, huge crowds gathered to them? Were the Waldenses seducers because, as Reinerius accused, the multitude was easily persuaded by them? Was Ambrose a seducer because he could surround himself with a crowd of people? Was Chrysostom a seducer because the people were so well disposed towards him that he was forced to leave the city secretly, to head off a popular uprising? Why do I labour these points? The Lord Jesus Christ himself faced the same calumny.

units.la: Cathol. Tert. lib.19.p. 1039. mali sunt actus nostri, & operamur malignum in conspectu Domini, dan- tur nobis principes secundum cor nostrum, sicut ait Dominus: Fecerunt si-bi regem, & non per me, & principes, & non per consilium meum. Tale ergo aliquod intelligamus etiam in Ecclesiis fieri: quod pro meritis populi aut in verbo & opere potens a Deo tribuitur rector Ecclesiae: aut si malignum faciat populus in conspectu Domini, talis Ecclesiae judex datur sub quo famem & sitim populus patiatur, non famem panis neque sitim aquae, sed famem audiendi verbum Domini.
units.tr: Cathol. Tert. lib.19.p. 1039. Our deeds are evil, and we work wickedness in the sight of the Lord; princes are given to us according to our own heart, as the Lord says: "They have made themselves a king, but not by me, and princes, but not by my counsel." Let us understand that something like this also happens in the Churches: the ruler of the Church is granted by God as a reward for the people's merit, powerful in word and deed; or, if the people does evil in the sight of the Lord, a judge of the Church is appointed under whom the people suffer hunger and thirst, not hunger for bread nor thirst for water, but hunger for hearing the word of the Lord.

units.la: Ad postremum, invalescente morum malitia, non est Ecclesia, inquit Petrus Alliacus, digna regi, nisi a reprobis. Quid igitur est? peccatum populi Anglicani malos pastores tanquam caecia nubes attraxit. Peccatum populi regimen reprobum, id est, a Deo in verbo suo reprobatum, ad hunc usque diem continuavit: Peccatum populi denique reformationem Anglicanae Ecclesiae huc usque remoratum est: Ignoretur igitur disciplina, & morbi isti & eorum causa ignorabuntur: his ignoratis poenitentia nulla intercedit, poenitentia nulla intercedente, festinabit vindicta divina, ad totam terram desolandam.
units.tr: Finally, "when the malice of morals grows, the Church is not worthy to be ruled except by the reprobate," says Pierre d'Ailly. What then is the cause? The sin of the English people has drawn bad ministers upon them like a blinding cloud. The sin of the people has kept up to this day a reprobate rule, that is, one reprobated by God in his word. The sin of the people, in short, has held back the reformation of the English Church up to now. Discipline is therefore ignored, and these diseases and their causes will be ignored too. With these things ignored, no repentance intervenes; and with no repentance intervening, divine vengeance will hasten to lay waste the whole land.

units.la: Tertio, notitia rectae disciplinae necessaria populo est, ad officia pietatis: utpote qua ignorata nec pro malis Ecclesiae ingemiscere, nec pro ejusdem debita pace precari populus potest. Particula illa orationis Dominicae adveniat regnum tuum. ostendit populo in officio esse pro disciplinae restitutione, ad Deum clamare, juxta illa Iohannis Reynoldi nostri: Non Zorobabel modo & Ioshua, inquit, aedificare domum Dei studere debent, & lapides redivivos e rudetibus aptare aedisicio, sed & cunctus populus, cui in officio esse dicit, ut instet Deo cum Dan. 9. 17. ut facies Dei super desolatum sanctuarium luceat: & zelum illum ab Esaia expressum imitetur: 62. 3. propter Zionem non taceamus, & propter Ierusalem ne quiescamus, donec prodeat ut splendor, justitia ejus, & salus, ejus, ut lampas ardens. Cum haec fronti libri sui praeposuisset Cartwrightus, quas ille calumnias a Bancrofto non passus est? Sed immerito: eadem etenim per Episcoporum usurpationem jam in Anglia difficultas est, quae olim Gregorii tempore, per Episcopatum Constantinopolitanum erat: in qua preces ita ille praescribit: Magnopere orandum est, & omnipotens Deus assiduis precibus implorandus, ut hoc ab unitate atque humilitate Ecclesiae malum superbiae & confusionis amoveat. Si Gallieni tempore pax Ecclesiae concessa sit, id a precibus fidelium erat: nihil enim dat Deus nisi precibus: Apocalyps. 6, 10. Quid igitur? Nullus persecutionis Episcopalis finis erit? nunquam ministros suos exauthoratos rursus audiet Anglia? nunquam pace videbit? Certe nunquam, nisi in corde fidelium indiderit Deus, ut a peccatis suis quiescant, Deum vero prae oradi assiduitate quiescere non sinant: quo magis jam populo Anglicano imitandus Nicolaus Clemangius est: O quantum, inquit, a Christi institutione, ab Apostolorum traditione, a ritu & forma primaevae Ecclesiae, nostra teterrimas tempora defluxerunt. Expurga Domine vineam tuam, sen-tibu
units.tr: Third, knowledge of right discipline is necessary for the people for the duties of piety, since, if it is ignored, the people can neither groan over the evils of the Church nor pray for her due peace. That petition of the Lord's Prayer, "Thy kingdom come," shows that it is the people's duty to cry out to God for the restoration of discipline, in line with the words of our John Reynolds: "Not only Zerubbabel and Joshua," he says, "ought to labour to build the house of God and to fit the living stones from the rubble into the building, but the whole people too, whom it is their duty to urge on God, that the face of God may shine upon the desolate sanctuary" (Dan. 9:17), and to imitate that zeal expressed by Isaiah (62:3): "For Zion's sake we will not keep silent, and for Jerusalem's sake we will not rest, until her righteousness goes forth as brightness, and her salvation as a burning lamp." When Cartwright prefaced this to his book, what calumnies did he not suffer from Bancroft? But undeservedly: for the same difficulty that once existed in Gregory's time through the Constantinopolitan episcopate now exists in England through the usurpation of the bishops. In that matter Gregory prescribed prayers in this way: "It must be prayed for earnestly, and almighty God must be implored with constant prayers, that he may remove this evil of pride and confusion from the unity and humility of the Church." If peace was granted to the Church in the time of Gallienus, it came from the prayers of the faithful, for God gives nothing except to prayers (Rev. 6:10). What then? Will there be no end to episcopal persecution? Will England never again hear her ministers restored? Will she never see peace? Certainly not, unless God puts it into the hearts of the faithful to cease from their sins, and they do not let God rest by their unceasing prayer. All the more, therefore, the English people must imitate Nicolaus Clemangius: "O how much," he says, "have our most foul times fallen away from the institution of Christ, from the tradition of the Apostles, from the rite and form of the primitive Church! Cleanse, Lord, your vineyard, sen-

units.la: T. 3 {ibus undique & labruscis oppletam: fac, ut olim flagellum de funiculis, & de templo tuo sancto numularios expelle, vendentes eijce, ementes exturba, eunctos impios mercatores, nisi poenitentiam egerint, Giezitas lepra percute, Simonitas altè volantes, Sathanaeque minustros in excelsum elevatos allide ac dejice, quoniam non est qui eos deponat, nisi tu solus.
units.tr: T. 3 {ibus undique & labruscis oppletam: make it so that, as once with a whip of cords, you drive the moneychangers out of your holy temple, throw out the sellers, drive out the buyers, and expel all impious merchants unless they have repented. Strike the Gehazites with leprosy, cast down and crush the Simonists who fly so high, and the ministers of Satan lifted up on high, since there is no one who can depose them except you alone."

units.la: Quarto, notitia rectae disciplinae necessaria populo est ab obedientiam erga quosque superiores sanctificandam: quae aliter duobus vitiis praecipue laborabit.
units.tr: Fourth, knowledge of right discipline is necessary for the people so that obedience toward superiors may be sanctified. Otherwise, this obedience will suffer chiefly from two vices.

units.la: Primo ex conscientia subjici nos jubet Paulus: Rom. 13 : 5. quae in causa disciplinae nulla erit, si ignoretur. Id siquidem in schismate jam Anglicano accidit, quod in Papali accidisse olim Aeneas Sylvius conquestus est. Non video Clericos qui velint pro ipsa vel illa parte tyrium ferre: omnes eam fidem habemus quam nostri principes, qui si colerent idola & nos & jam cohemus. Et non solum Paulam, sed Christum ipsum negaremus saeculari potestate urgente: quia refrigui charitas, & omnis interijt. Non ego dicam Christum ipsum negaturos plurimos, dicam tamen Episcopos sane negaturos, pro quibus jam dimicant, si saecularis potestas urgeret: martyrium saltem non terrent, imo nec illa dira, quae pro adversa veritate Puritani fortiter constanterque sustinuerunt. Atque sane vel istinc patet causae ipsius inter utrosque differentia: nam si veritas penes Hierarchicos esset, nonne eorum obedientiam sanctificaret, perinde ac puritanorum sanctificavit? At illi obedientiam nullam praestant, inquiens cum Iucllo respondendum est: Objicit Hardingus Evangelium doctrinam in principes rebellem tradere: id quod ex Scoticis tumultibus probat. Respondet Iuellus: Non sibi derogatum principes putare debet, quod ante se, Deo obediri videat: non etenim Deus est, sed minister Dei. Leo dicit: Christus; quae Dui sunt, Deo; quae Caesaris sunt Caesari reddenda constituit. Hoc est vere non impugnare Caesarem, sed juvare.
units.tr: First, Paul bids us to be subject for conscience's sake (Rom. 13:5), and in the cause of discipline there will be no such conscience if discipline is ignored. This has indeed already happened in the English schism, as Aeneas Sylvius once complained had happened in the Papal one: "I do not see clergy who are willing to bear tyranny for this or that side. We all hold the faith our princes hold; if they worshipped idols, we too would already be worshipping them. And not only Paul but Christ himself we would deny, with secular power pressing on us, because charity has grown cold and all of it has perished." I do not say that very many would deny Christ himself, but I do say that the bishops, for whom they now fight, would certainly deny him if secular power pressed them. They do not fear martyrdom, nor even those dreadful sufferings which the Puritans have borne bravely and steadfastly for the unpopular truth. And certainly from this alone the difference between the two sides of the cause is plain. For if the truth lay with the hierarchs, would it not sanctify their obedience, just as it sanctified that of the Puritans? But they render no obedience at all. To the objection that must be answered with Jewel. Hardingus objects that the Gospel delivers a doctrine rebellious against princes, and he proves this from the Scottish tumults. Jewel replies: "Princes should not think they are belittled because they see God obeyed before them; for he is not God, but the minister of God." Leo says: "Christ established that what belongs to God is to be rendered to God, and what belongs to Caesar to Caesar." This is truly not to attack Caesar, but to help him.

units.la: Secundum obedientiae vitium quod ex disciplina ignorata proficiscitur, caecitas illa mentis est, qua, splendore regiminis Hierarchici abrepti homines, quod in hac causa verum est, videre non possunt. Atque hinc rursus patet causae inter utrasque partes differentia: quis etenim putabit regimen Ecclesiae Christum ejusmodi constituisse, quod rationi, sensui, & carnali hominis naturalis judicio abblandiretur? Sevocat Johannem Angelus in solitudinem, ut mysterium Babylonicum intelligeret: Ap. 17 : 3. quod ob causas fere easdem cum populo jam faciendum est: populum etenim meretricium, quod Babylon propinat, si ideo (quod interpretibus constat) aureum dicatur, quod pompa, antiquitate, consensu, multitudine, potentia, prosperitate, splendoreque externo populum ad credendum facilem inebriet: illud jam ex parte Episcopi Anglicani porrigunt, sic ut in controversia disciplinaria veritatem nunquam assequetur populus, nisi a frequentia & celebritate abalienentur, nisi ab omni hujusmodi glaucomate atque larva ablactentur, in solitudinem denique quasi puripuritanicam abducantur, ubi veri Ecclesiastici regiminis videndi duntaxat copia est. Quis etenim alioquin Hierarchici regiminis splendorem & pompam non miraretur, cùm eam in Roma elucentem Iohannes ipse miratus sit? Ap. 17:6. Vtinam verò ita Hierarchicam miraretur populus, ut Iohannes miratus est, sic ut erroris efficaciam per splendorem hunc externum operantem detestaretur. Iam hanc efficaciam dum non advertit,annon periculum est, ne prae ejusdem admiratione in genua procidat ad adorandum, quod eis accidisse videmus, qui ad bestiae potentiam & magnificentiam obstupuerunt? Ap. 13.4.8. Hanc adorationem qualis suo saeculo erat, ita describit Theodoricus Niemensis: Sicut sacerdotes Iudaeorum ad eam devenerunt dementiam, ut dicerent, regem non habemus nisi Caesarem: eodem modo jam diu timui & timeo, quod nostri sacerdotes dicere possint, regem non habemus, nisi pontificem. Quàm igitur timeo ego, ne bestiae imago in Anglicana superstes Hierarchia plus nimio adoretur, cùm eo jam deventum sit, ut spreto Christi Regis verbo, & instituto, id solum attendant plurimi quid reverendis Ecclesiae patribus Episcopis placeat, ac si illos solos reges haberent? Communicat hoc modo populus cum omnibus peccatis Episcoporum, malorumq; omnium se reos faciunt, quae ab eorum pseudoregimine exorta sunt: secundùm illa Ieremiae, 5:30, 31. Res stupenda & horrenda fit in terra hac: prophetae ipsi prophetarant falso, & sacerdotes dominatum exercent, horum opera & populus meus ita amant: quid autem facturi estis tandem?
units.tr: The second vice of obedience, which arises from ignored discipline, is that blindness of mind by which men, carried away by the splendour of hierarchical rule, cannot see what is true in this cause. And hence again the difference between the two sides is plain. For who would think that Christ established a government of the Church of such a kind as would flatter reason, the senses and the natural judgement of carnal man? The angel carried John away into the wilderness so that he might understand the Babylonian mystery (Rev. 17:3). The people must now be dealt with for nearly the same reasons. For if the cup of harlotry which Babylon offers is called golden (as interpreters agree) because by its pomp, antiquity, consent, multitude, power, prosperity and outward splendour it easily intoxicates the people into believing, then the English bishops now hold out the same thing on their side. Thus in the disciplinary controversy the people will never reach the truth unless they are drawn away from crowds and celebrity, unless they are weaned from every such cataract and mask, and finally led off into a solitude, as it were purely Puritan, where there is the opportunity only of seeing true ecclesiastical government. For who otherwise would not marvel at the splendour and pomp of hierarchical rule, since John himself marvelled at it shining forth in Rome? (Rev. 17:6). Would that the people marvelled at the hierarchy as John marvelled, so as to detest the power of error working through this outward splendour! But while they do not notice this power, is there not danger that, in admiration of it, they will fall on their knees to worship, as we see happened to those who were astonished at the power and magnificence of the beast? (Rev. 13:4, 8). Theodoric of Niem describes such worship as it was in his own age: "As the priests of the Jews came to such madness that they said, 'We have no king but Caesar,' in the same way I have long feared, and still fear, that our priests may say, 'We have no king but the pontiff.'" How much, then, do I fear that the image of the beast, surviving in the English hierarchy, is worshipped to excess, since it has come to this: that, with the word and institution of Christ the King spurned, most people attend only to what pleases the reverend fathers of the Church, the bishops, as if they had only these as kings! In this way the people share in all the sins of the bishops, and make themselves guilty of all the evils that have arisen from their false government, according to those words of Jeremiah (5:30–31): "A stupendous and horrible thing is done in this land: the prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests rule by their own authority, and my people love it so. But what will you do in the end?"

units.la: 3 Quintò, notitia disciplinae populo necessaria est ad opera charitatis: quae eo magis jam in Anglia necessaria sunt, quò magis saevitia Episcoporum servi Dei afflictantur: redierunt etenim tempora illa de quibus Sylvius conquestus est: Lusus jam Ecclesia est quaedem de pila fieri videmus dum huc atque illuc impellitur lusorum ictibus percussa: Quid enim? Annon pilae in morem Episcoporum ictibus percussi sancti, cùm ministri tum laici, huc & illuc impelluntur? annon bonis exuuntur? carceribus mancipantur? mala denique quaeque perpetiuntur? Hic Episcopis Anglicanis benedicere, quia divites sunt, stupidum: Iac.2:16. Ministros innocentes condemnari, iniquum: Mat.12.7. in causa veritatis patientes non sublevare, perfidum; 3 Ioh. 8: veritatem ipsam laborantem non defendere proditorium, Matth. 12:30. Non Pharisaeis Christum blasphemantibus sese populus adjunxit: quid tum? in eo quòd litigantes eos quibus audivit, & Christum ab eisdem exagitatum non defendebat, audire merebatur; qui non est mecum, adversus me est, & qui non cogit mecum, spargit.
units.tr: 3 Fifthly, knowledge of church discipline is necessary for the people for the works of charity. These are now all the more necessary in England, because the cruelty of the bishops afflicts the servants of God the more. For those times of which Sylvius complained have returned: The Church is now a kind of game; we see it made like a ball, struck hither and thither by the blows of players. For are not holy men, both ministers and laymen, struck and driven hither and thither like balls in the manner of the bishops? Are they not stripped of their goods, consigned to prisons, and made to suffer every kind of evil? To bless the English bishops because they are rich is foolish: James 2:16. To condemn innocent ministers is unjust: Matt. 12:7. Not to relieve those who suffer for the cause of truth is faithless: 3 John 8. Not to defend truth itself when it is in trouble is treacherous: Matt. 12:30. The people did not join themselves to the Pharisees who blasphemed Christ; what then? In that they did not defend Christ when they heard him assailed by those who were quarrelling with him, they deserved to hear: He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters.

units.la: Sextò, notitia rectae disciplinae populo necessaria est, ut praeparetur pro suis partibus ad eandem excolendam non solùm in liberorum educatione, sed etiam in consensu suo, in electionibus & excommunicationibus, caeterisque negotijs Ecclesiasticis pretractandis. Sic Tertullianus: Nonne & laici sacerdotes sumus? Differentiam inter ordinem & plebem, constituit Ecclesiæ authoritas & honor per ordinis concessum sanctificatus a Deo: Nisi laici ea observent, per quæ adlegantur presbyteri, quomodo erunt presbyteri qui a laicis adleguntur? Non igitur Tertulliani tempore regimen Hierarchicum obtinebat: Regit jam Ecclesiam Episcopus, at tum ordinis concessus, id est presbyterium. Iam ex Laicis ut eligatur presbyter, pro absurdo habetur; non ita Tertulliani tempore: Tum ab electionibus cæterisque negotiis Ecclesiasticis, non penitus populus, ut jam hodie, exclusus est: neque notitia disciplinæ interdicebatur, sed ad eandem pro sua parte digne excolendam extimulabatur. Vide igitur insignem Episcoporum calliditatem. Populo cum rebus disciplinariis nihil negotij esse debet: quid ita? quia rudis, ineruditus, ineptus ad negotia Ecclesiastica vel aliquatenus pertractanda. Hoc si verum sit, culpa eo major, quod in eo instruendo & edocendo vos negligentiores præbuistis. Quanquam quid ego negligentiam voco, quæ dolus ipse malus est: in ignoratione rei disciplinaris populus scilicet detinendus est, ut sic Episcopi dominentur soli clerisque solus potentetur in æternum. Hoc ni ita fit, cur pro Episcopali authoritate concionibus ferè singulis, aures populi obtunditis? Vos pro disciplina vestra absque popularitate concionari coram populo potestis, nos pro disciplina Christi non possumus? Atque hoc ex disciplinæ reformatæ cum sanctitate tum necessitate de populo, porisma sextum est.
units.tr: Sixthly, knowledge of right discipline is necessary for the people, so that they may be prepared, each in his own part, to cultivate it, not only in the education of their children but also in their consent, in elections and excommunications, and in the other ecclesiastical business to be dealt with. So Tertullian: Are we not also priests, we laymen? The distinction between order and the people has been established by the authority of the Church and by the honour sanctified by God through the grant of order. Unless laymen observe those things through which presbyters are chosen, how will those be presbyters who are chosen from among the laity? Therefore in Tertullian's time the hierarchical rule did not prevail. The bishop now governs the Church, but then there was the grant of order, that is, the presbytery. Now it is regarded as absurd for a presbyter to be chosen from the laity; it was not so in Tertullian's time. Then the people were not wholly excluded from elections and the other ecclesiastical business, as they are today; nor was knowledge of discipline forbidden to them, but they were stirred up to cultivate it worthily in their own part. See, then, the remarkable cunning of the bishops. The people ought to have nothing to do with disciplinary matters. Why so? Because they are rough, unlearned and unfit to handle ecclesiastical business even in some small degree. If this were true, the fault would be the greater, because you have been the more negligent in instructing and teaching them. Yet why do I call it negligence, which is in itself an evil trick? The people must evidently be kept in ignorance of disciplinary matters, so that the bishops alone may rule and the clergy alone may hold power for ever. If this is not so, why do you almost at every sermon batter the ears of the people with your episcopal authority? Can you preach before the people for your discipline without popular support, and we cannot for the discipline of Christ? This is the sixth corollary, concerning the holiness and the necessity of the reformed discipline on the part of the people.

units.la: CAP 42. Porisma septimum.
units.tr: CAP 42. Seventh corollary.

units.la: SEptimum Ecclesias transmarinas respicit, quas de Anglicana tempestate Hierarchici solicitas esse vetant: Nam & dominum Bezam propter suam in Anglia πνευματικὴν Whitgiftus objurgavit: & virulenter eundem exagitat Richardus Bancroftus, quod a Puritanis Anglicanis consultus, consilium suum illis suppeditarit. Quod vero dixisset Episcopos Evangelium impedire, respondet: Quidam disciplinam inordinatè urgentes apud nos exauthorati sunt, sed quid hoc ad illum? Vel maximè: Imitandus siquidem cuique Christiano Apostolus Paulus est: Absque iis quæ extrinsecus eveniant, urget agmen illud in me quotidie conspurgens; id est solicitudo de omnibus Ecclesiis. Quis affligitur, quin ego affligar? quis offenditur quin ego uror? 2. Cor: 11, 28. Absit igitur ut gravissimus turbinibus jactati in Anglia servi Dei, cum tepiditatem in ejusdem fidei fratribus transfmarinis experiantur, quam orientalis quondam Ecclesia in occidentali exoerta est. Adnos respexminus fratres venerandissimi (inquit Basilius) quos in præsenti tribulationum tempore, ad nos frequenter venturos speravimus. Verum spe ista frustrati ipsi quoque nobis illud occiniimus: expectavimus qui simul contristaretur & non fuit, & qui consolaretur & non inveni. Non ita ipse Basilius Nicæna etenim Ecclesia ejectos non solum ac-cessit.
units.tr: The seventh concerns the churches overseas, which the Hierarchists forbid us to be anxious about because of the English storm. Whitgift rebuked Beza for his spiritual [πνευματικὴν] conduct in England, and Richard Bancroft attacks him bitterly because, when the English Puritans consulted him, he gave them his advice. As for the charge that the bishops hinder the Gospel, Bancroft replies that some who urged discipline without order have been deprived among us, but what is that to the point? Indeed, the best answer is this: every Christian should imitate the Apostle Paul, who says: "Apart from those things which come from outside, there is the daily pressure on me, the care of all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is offended, and I do not burn?" (2 Cor. 11.28). Far be it, then, that the servants of God, tossed by the most severe storms in England, should find among their brethren overseas the lukewarmness which the Eastern Church once showed toward the Western. We have looked upon you, most venerable brethren (says Basil), whom we hoped would often come to us in this time of tribulation. But disappointed in that hope, we ourselves sing to you that lament: we waited for one who would grieve together with us, and there was none; and for one who would comfort us, and I found none.

units.la: Epist. in add. cessit consolaturus, sed etiam pro eis ad Valentem legatum & intercefforem interposuit. Non ita Georgius Laodicenus qui literas ad Synodum misit, ut Ecclesiarum laborantium rationem haberent : Non ita Synodus Ariminensis, quae pro expulsis Episcopis Constan- tino supplicavit: Exulat Liberius Roma? ex officio suo esse putant E- pifcopi occidentales, ut pro eo apud Constantium per literas interce- derent. Exulat Athanasius Alexandrin? non solum pro eo Constantium interpellandum fuisse censuit Julius : sed & suam etiam autho- ritatem interponendam Occidentales Episcopi reliqui, qui cum eti- am ad fe fugientem benigne susceperunt, & honore prosecuti sunt. Postremò exulat Constantinopoli Iohannes Chrysostomus? intercedentes dum sibi censuit Innocentius Romanus, pro eo scribendum, & qua- qua ope eum sublevandum existimavit.Quid causae est fratres? quidni in causa veritatis ministri in Anglia jam miserè pressi, similem à vobis consolationem expectarent? Nummam illud quod à Gallo miniftro quodam responsum audivi, scandalum fore, fi discordia Anglicana papistis innotesceret, & ea usque ad exteras Ecclesias dilataretur? Atqui Christiano indignam hanc vocem dico. Rectè etenim Bernardus: Melius est scandalum oriatur, quàm ut veritas relinquatur : verùm fi scandalum hic Papistis praebeatur, illud à vestra afflictorum fratrum desertione apertè praebetur,utpote de qua tanquam discordia vestrâ quadam, aut fi in eadem veritate concordatis, in eadem tamen tuenda, socordia,vel maximè glorientur. Liquet hoc in Gretzero Papistisque reliquis : qui vel id vobis objiciunt (quàm meritò non dicam) quòd librum illum magno applausu denuò excudistis, in quo (vos ipsi Puritani) disciplina vestra velut Puritanica condemnatur. Quod verò dicitur, discordiam Anglicanam apud Philisftheos & Gathanos hàc ratione promulgari, id ipso nihilo minus est; cum refponfio illa Bernardina hic locum habeat : Non retego veritas, sed inveretundi confutio —Nunc cernente mundi orbe fabulam, foli tacebimus? Major erit confusio, vobiffe celare, etem celari nequiverit. Sed hevent forte in quibusdam suspiciones nescio quae, ac fi non fatis sobriè fe ministri in Anglia prudenterque gesserint: Arqui hoc afflictis afflictionem (nescio etiam an more Nabalitico. 1. Sam. 25. 10.) addere est. Certè cum Basilio profeffari nobis licet, Miserum statum necftrum toto orbe cognitum ignorare cos impossibile est, quorum tamen baetenus lrmen nullum sentimus. Quòd fi igitur & conversatio nostra nota non fit, vercor ne idem jam nobis accidérit quod olim eidem Basilio accidit,qui ita conqueri aladus est. Quicquid veri fit neque sciunt neque diftrat, sed fallis fubfitionis ut praecoccpantur. Neque verum confirmari, fit autem fi uti, neque illam per quam instruerentur admittunt —non ... ad ... memoriae... didicerunt, morosiores in Anglia videntur ij, qui ad nutum magistratus Papisticas reliquias nonnullas tolerare nescvery iuriunt. Atqui disparem Longè conditio est: non Anabaptistas ceu Papistas ministri reformati approbare coguntur, aut subscriptione errores eorum confirmare, imo ne silere tenentur, quo minus eos è suggestu refutare & veritatem ex verbo Dei praedicare possint. In Anglia secus est: tolerare ministri semper paratissimi erant, sed hoc habetur pro nihilo: aut approbandum illis est,& suo chirographo confirmandum, silendum insuper; aut bonis, laribus, functionibus, ipsâ denique Ecclesiâ exeundum. Quid nobis hîc faciendum censetis?Certè Dominum Bezam olim ab initio consuluimus, atque consilium hoc retulimus.
units.tr: Basil did not act in this way. The Church of Nicaea did not merely come to comfort the exiles, but also interposed its intercession on their behalf with Valens the legate. Nor did Georgius of Laodicea act so, who sent a letter to the Synod so that they might take account of the suffering churches. Nor did the Synod of Ariminum act so, which petitioned Constantius on behalf of the bishops who had been expelled. When Liberius is exiled from Rome, the Western bishops think it is their duty to intercede for him with Constantius by letter. When Athanasius of Alexandria is exiled, Julius judged that not only should Constantius be petitioned on his behalf, but that the other Western bishops should also interpose their authority; they also received him kindly when he fled to them and honoured him. Finally, when John Chrysostom was exiled from Constantinople, Innocentius of Rome thought that letters should be written on his behalf and that he should be relieved by whatever help was possible. What is the reason, brethren? Why should the ministers in England, now miserably oppressed in the cause of truth, not expect a similar consolation from you? Is it that I heard from a certain French minister the remark that it would be a scandal if the English discord became known to the Papists and spread even to foreign churches? Yet I say that this word is unworthy of a Christian. For Bernard rightly says: It is better that a scandal arise than that the truth be abandoned. But if a scandal is here given to the Papists, it is openly given by your desertion of your afflicted brethren, since they will glory in it as if it were some discord among you, or, if you agree in the truth, a sloth in defending that same truth. This is plain in Gretser and the other Papists, who object to you (I will not say how justly) that you have reprinted with great applause that book in which your discipline, which is Puritan, is condemned by you yourselves, O Puritans. As for the claim that the English discord is being spread abroad among the Philistines and Gittites in this way, that is no less true, since Bernard's reply applies here: Truth is not exposed, but the refutation of error is hidden. Now, while the whole world is watching the spectacle, shall we alone keep silent? The confusion will be greater if we try to conceal from you what cannot be hidden. But perhaps some suspicions arise in certain people, as if the ministers in England have not acted with sufficient sobriety and prudence. But to add affliction to the afflicted is indeed (I know not whether in the manner of Nabal, 1 Sam. 25.10) to do so. Certainly, with Basil we may declare: It is impossible that those should not know of our miserable state, known throughout the whole world, yet we perceive no help from them so far. If, then, our conduct is not known, I fear that the same thing has now happened to us that once happened to Basil, who was moved to complain thus: Whatever the truth is, they neither know nor care, but they are led astray by false reports as they are prejudiced. Neither do they admit the truth to be confirmed, nor the means by which they might be instructed ... they have learned ... by memory. Those seem to be more obstinate in England who, at the nod of the magistrate, refuse to tolerate some Papist remnants. Yet the condition is far from similar: the reformed ministers are not compelled to approve Anabaptists as if they were Papists, or by subscription to confirm their errors; indeed they are not even bound to keep silent, so that they cannot refute them from the pulpit and preach the truth from the Word of God. In England it is otherwise: the ministers have always been most ready to tolerate, but this counts for nothing; they must either approve and confirm with their signature, and besides keep silent, or leave their goods, homes, offices, and finally the Church itself. What do you think we should do here? Certainly we consulted Lord Beza long ago, from the beginning, and reported this counsel.

units.la: Quod si à vobis requiratur non solum ut tolercetis, sed etiam ut chirographo tanquam recta comprobetis, quid aliud restat, quàm ut de innocentia vestra testati, & omnia remedia in timore Domini experti, manifestae violentiae cedatis: sed melius de Angliâ speramus. Quod speravit Beza fore id vos jam forte esse putatis: sed ne decipiamini. Constantinus pius imperator erat, in Eusebium suum aulicum tamen, quam in Athanasium reliquosque Orthodoxos propensior. Theodosius pius imperator erat, Flavius tyrannidi tamen adversus reliquos Orthodoxos Episcopos, plus aequo favit. Arcadius pius imperator erat, sed in sanctum Chrysostomum iniquior tamen. Mauritius pius imperator erat, primatum tamen Constantinopolitanum adversus Gregorium nimis promovebat: quòd ad splendorem imperij sui eum conducere existimavit. Ethelbertus denique rex pius erat, sed in Archiepiscopatu Hierarchico stabiliendo adversus Bangorenses durior. Atque hoc ex disciplinae reformatae cum sanctitate tum necessitate, ad Ecclesias reformatas porisma septimum & ultimum est, in quo etiam de Politeiae Ecclesiasticae praestantia, Finis esto.
units.tr: But if you are asked not only to tolerate but also to approve by your signature as right, what remains but that, having testified to your innocence and having tried every remedy in the fear of the Lord, you yield to manifest violence? But we hope better things of England. What Beza hoped would happen, you perhaps now think has happened; but do not be deceived. Constantine was a pious emperor, yet he was more partial to his courtier Eusebius than to Athanasius and the other orthodox. Theodosius was a pious emperor, yet Flavian favoured the tyranny of the orthodox bishops more than was right. Arcadius was a pious emperor, yet he was more unjust toward the holy Chrysostom. Maurice was a pious emperor, yet he promoted the primacy of Constantinople too much against Gregory, because he thought it would serve the splendour of his empire. Finally, King Ethelbert was a pious king, yet he was harsher against the Bangorians in establishing a hierarchical archbishopric. And this, from the sanctity and necessity of reformed discipline, is the seventh and last corollary for the reformed Churches, in which also the excellence of the Ecclesiastical Polity is treated. Let this be the end.

units.la: Libri Primi Finis.
units.tr: End of the First Book.

units.la: DE POLITEIA ECCLESIASTICA LIBER SECUNDUS.
units.tr: ON ECCLESIASTICAL POLITY, BOOK SECOND.

units.la: De ejus Principijs. CAP. I. De eius Iudice.
units.tr: Of its Principles. Chapter I. Of its Judge.

units.la: RVSTRA de Politeia Ecclesiastica disceptabitur, nisi ante omnia de Iudice constet, cujus sententiâ lis sopienda, controversia tota dirimenda sit. Hunc ego si scripturam solam statuero, semotis patrum & cuiusq; antiquitatis humanae calculis, neutiquam quidem certè a veritate aberrauero, non a vestigiis antiquorū. Bonaventurae saeculo multū Philosophiae tribuebatur: quam ut a finib9 Theologiae eliminaret, ad solas Scripturas veritatis studiosos quantum potuit, revocabat. Sic enim de eo Iohan. Gersom, Bonaventura recidit a curiositate quantum potest, non immiscens positiones extraneas, vel doctrinas saeculares, dialecticas aut philosophicas terminis theologicis obumbratas more multorum: Unde factum est ut ab indevotis scholasticis, quorum (prob dolor!) major est numerus, ipse minus exiterit frequentatus. Sequentibus temporibus, Scholasticorum subtilitas palmam ferebat, quam de ponte dejicere, piorum hominum prima cura fuit: ut ita Scriptura sola in tribunali collocaretur. Videre hoc est in Iocchio Puppero Mechlinienfi, de quo D. Morneus ita: Omnibus Sophistarum & Scholasticorum glossis explosis, soli sacrae Scripturae & in articulo justificationis Paulo nominatim inhaerendum esse docuit; quas vulgo interpretationes assumunt a verbo Dei alienas plane esse, &c. Sed supererat postea, de antiquis Patribus molestior labor: quos de tribunali ut deturbaret Huldrichus Zwinglius, ante disputationem Tiguri habendam, palam professus est, se solâ Scripturâ absque patribus disputaturum: quo factum est, ut praecipuo illius antagonista clam noctu aufugiente, hora disputationis jam adventante, nemo esset repertus, qui contrà in arena auderet descendere. Hanc rationem optimo consilio a majoribus institutam, immutant jam hodie Hierarchici Anglicani: de quibus Daniel Chemnicus non immerito ita scribit: Fidei solum fundamentum Scriptura est, unde improbare cogor non in papistis tantum qui patribus libenter tribuunt illud Pythagoricum ἀὐτὸς ἔφα, sed et quorundam (appellate sanè Papistas) importunam antiquitatis a limitationem, qui hiis ceteri ius ita se contraversiarum arbitros faciunt, ut non prorsus ex scriptura praefiniti Ecclesiam velint reformari, sed potius adducere in medio quod quod ipsi sibi confinxerunt, ex fabulis, ut videri volunt utinam illam jam sit antiquitatis cognitione: quorum conatus, misi compesceat Deus, horrendum ne id perficiatur, non ut Papistae sint correctiores, sed ut nos sumus corrupti ... Hic ego a clarissimo viro Isaaco Casaubono veniam peto, si huic culpae affinem putem: quod duo ... posuerit, quibus modernae controversiae finirentur, verbum Dei & antiquitatem. Hoc enim id ipsum ni fallor est, quod Georgius olim Cassander Semipapista verbis magis papisticis, id est, veris & apertis tradidit: duo esse quae in omnibus controversiis Christianis sibi proponere debet, Canonica authoritas & Catholica traditio.
units.tr: OUR discussion of the ecclesiastical polity will be unresolved unless it is first settled who the judge is, by whose sentence the dispute is to be quieted and the whole controversy decided. If I set Scripture alone as this judge, with the reckonings of the Fathers and of all human antiquity set aside, I would certainly not stray from the truth, though I would not be following the footsteps of the ancients. In the age of Bonaventure, much was attributed to philosophy. He, wishing to remove it from the bounds of theology, called earnest lovers of truth back to Scripture alone as far as he could. For thus John Gerson says of him: Bonaventure withdraws from curiosity as far as he can, not mixing in foreign positions or secular doctrines, dialectical or philosophical, obscured with theological terms in the manner of many. Hence it came about that he was less frequented by the irreverent scholastics, whose number (alas!) is greater. In later times the subtlety of the Scholastics bore the palm, and it was the first care of pious men to cast it down from the bridge, so that Scripture alone might be placed on the tribunal. One may see this in Jodocus Pupper of Mechlin, of whom D. Mornay speaks thus: Having cast out all the glosses of the Sophists and Scholastics, he taught that one must cleave to holy Scripture alone, and in the article of justification especially to Paul; those interpretations which they commonly adopt are plainly alien to the word of God, etc. But afterwards there remained a more troublesome labour concerning the ancient Fathers. To thrust them from the tribunal, Huldrych Zwingli, before the disputation to be held at Zurich, openly professed that he would dispute with Scripture alone, without the Fathers. As a result, when his chief antagonist secretly fled by night, and the hour of disputation was already at hand, no one could be found who would dare to descend into the arena against him. This method, instituted by our forefathers with the best counsel, the English Hierarchs now change today. Of them Daniel Chemnitz writes not undeservedly thus: "The sole foundation of faith is Scripture, whence I am compelled to disapprove not only of the Papists, who willingly ascribe to the Fathers that Pythagorean saying, ipse dixit [αὐτὸς ἔφα], but also of the importunate limitation of antiquity by certain men (rightly called Papists), who make themselves arbiters of the controversies in such a way that they do not wish the Church to be reformed wholly from Scripture, as previously defined, but rather to bring into the midst what they have themselves fashioned from fables, as they wish to appear, and would that they now had knowledge of antiquity. Their endeavours, unless God restrains them, are a horror, lest this be accomplished; not so that the Papists may become more correct, but so that we may be corrupted..." Here I beg pardon of the most distinguished man Isaac Casaubon, if I think he is akin to this fault, in that he laid down two things by which modern controversies would be ended: the word of God and antiquity. For this, unless I am mistaken, is the very thing that Georg Cassander, once a semi-Papist, delivered in more papistical words, that is, in true and plain ones: that there are two things which he must set before himself in all Christian controversies, canonical authority and Catholic tradition.

units.la: Hanc Catholicam traditionem non ullo ille alio sensu quam quo nostri requirit: scripturam etenim solam sufficere putat, sed tamen ex Vincentio Lirinensi antiquitatem adhibendam (quemadmodum nostri) constat, ad scripturam interpretandam, tum praesertim, cum ab haereticis in verus sensus distrahatur. Imo traditiones nō tam urgere Cassander videtur, atq; urgent Hierarchici: cum displicere videantur Cassandro, duplex Clementis Alexandrini agricultura scripta & non scripta, & duplicia Basilij dogmata ... quae Guil. Barclaius plane probare videtur. Sed hanc cum Cassandro collatione missa faciamus: & ipsos Hierarchicos hac de re sententia suam explicantes audiamus, Celebris apud eos omnes Hieronomi Zanchij positio est: quit) nititur cumprimis & simpliciter Verbo Dei: deinde nonnihil etiam communi totius veteris catholicae Ecclesiae consensu, si ille cum sacris Literis non pugnet: Credo enim quae a piis patribus in nomine Domini congregatis, communi omnium consensu, citra ullam sacrarum literarum contradictionem, definita & recepta fuerunt, ea etiam (quamquam haud ejusdem cum sacris literis authoritatis) a spiritu sancto esse, Haec cum ab omnibus citantur, Dominamo imprimis & Saravia: liquet sententiam Hierarchicorum, in tribus turpiter hallucinari. Primo eorum sententia contradictoria est. Nam si simpliciter eorum fides verbo Dei niteatur: certè nihil omnino, gradu aliquo, authoritate humanae antiquitatis niti potest. Secundo eorum sententia papistica est: licere hominibus putant verbo Dei addere, dummodo id cum scriptura non pugnat: cum Protestantibus omnibus ex adversō constet, non solum contra scripturam, sed etiam & praeter scripturam, addendum nihil esse. Postremò sententia eorum hypocritica est: injuriam quam {scripscripturæ inferunt, hoc velo palliant, quod præcipuè & cumprimis fides eâ innitatur: cum honor scripturæ [?] esse nequeat, nisi eâ fides nitatur sola: sic ut nec præcipue n[?] minus præcipue, patres a se ut loquitur Iuellus, aut seli abssque luce nisi divini præeunte, audiendi sint. Quid quòd rerum praxis reclamat? nam quando multo plures in eorum scriptis citationes patrum, quàm scripturarum (imo in infinitum plures) reperiuntur, quis non ait et eos, præcipue patribus, minus autem præcipue reuera scripturis nixi? Id ipsum ex modo ciranci liquet. Richardus Eyldus postquam pro Episcopis Anglos septem Ecclesiarum citasset, obij-cit ex persona nostra, [?] ordinis Episcopo deberi tantum non autem potestatem. Quid ille ad hoc: Nempe cum Angelos Ecclesiarum superiores autem potestatis nulla textus circumstantia comprobare animadvertisset: cò tantum descendit ut antiquitate sola pugnaret: hoc enim respondet solum. Hanc nobis praesidentiam approbare non possumus: quia in tota antiquitate, nullum hujusmodi Episcopi aut præsidentis exemplum reperimus: sed ejusmodi nobis Episcopum describunt patres, qui eminentem & exortem potestatem haberet, sine cujus consensu nihil agere presbyteri deberent. Similiter Georgius Dounamus Apostolos Metropolitanas civitates intendisse affirmat: siccitamur unde ejusmodi intentio liquere possit: respondet, eam ex prima Ecclesia communi praxi liquidissime apparere. An hoc præcipue ex scriptu-ris disputare est, minus autem præcipue ex patribus? imo hæc probatio ex scripturis nihil pendet, prorsus nihil: sed tantummodo, omnino, prorsus ex patribus. Est etiam quando non solum sine scripturis, ex patribus prorsus pugnant: sed etiam patres scripturis anteponunt: Thomas siquidem Bilsonus postquam Matth. 18. 20. Dic Ecclesiæ de civili tribunali, idque (ut ipse quidem putat) ex circumstantiarum consideratione, interpretatus fuisset, permittit ad postremum, in patrum gratiam, ut de Ecclesiastico (si modo vestigiis patrum insistere cuiquam placeat) intelligatur. Atqui hoc scripturam sub jugum patrum mittit: etsi enim ille in conscientia sua hanc interpretationem veram putat: eam deberi tamen permittit potius quam patrum authoritati vel minimum derogetur. Quid de nobis interim fit, qui pro scriptura sola pugnamus, & ex scriptura sola (patribus semotis) in unaquaque controversia Theologica disputandum omnimodo existimamus? Nempe quoda Cornelio Scultingio Protestantes omnes audiunt, quod Soli Scripturarij sint, id jam nos ab ipsis protestantibus Hierarchicis, quod nihil legerimus, patres nescianus, antiquitatem contemnamus, denique quod soli Scripturarij sumus. Huic calumniæ & errori medicinam facient Thesis sequentes.
units.tr: Cassander did not mean this Catholic tradition in any other sense than ours does. It is clear that he thinks Scripture alone is sufficient, yet following Vincent of Lérins he also admits that antiquity must be used (as we do) to interpret Scripture, especially when it is pulled into false senses by heretics. Indeed Cassander does not seem to press traditions as hard as the Hierarchs do; the twofold written and unwritten teaching of Clement of Alexandria, and the twofold dogmas of Basil, seem to displease Cassander, though William Barclay seems plainly to approve them. But let us set aside this comparison with Cassander, and hear the Hierarchs themselves explaining their view on this matter. The position of Jerome Zanchius is famous among them all: it rests first and simply on the Word of God, and then to some extent also on the common consensus of the whole ancient catholic Church, provided that it does not conflict with the holy Scriptures. "For I believe that those things which were defined and received by the pious Fathers gathered in the name of the Lord, by the common consent of all, without any contradiction of the holy Scriptures, are also from the Holy Spirit, though not of the same authority as the holy Scriptures." Since these words are cited by all, Dominamo above all, and by Saravia, it is clear that the opinion of the Hierarchs goes astray shamefully in three respects. First, their opinion is self-contradictory. For if their faith rests simply on the Word of God, then certainly nothing whatever, to any degree, can rest on the authority of human antiquity. Second, their opinion is Papist: they think it is lawful for men to add to the Word of God, provided it does not conflict with Scripture; whereas all Protestants agree on the contrary that nothing is to be added, not only against Scripture, but even beside Scripture. Lastly, their opinion is hypocritical: they cover over the injury which they inflict on Scripture with this veil, that faith rests chiefly and above all on it, since the honour of Scripture cannot be maintained unless faith rests on it alone. Thus, as Jewel says, the Fathers are to be heard neither chiefly nor least of all, apart from the light of the divine and without its going before. What of the fact that practice cries out against this? For when far more citations of the Fathers than of Scripture (indeed infinitely more) are found in their writings, who would not say that they lean chiefly on the Fathers, and only least of all on Scripture? This is clear from the practice of the English themselves. Richard Field, after citing the seven churches of Asia for the bishops of the English, objects in our person that the order of bishop is owed only the title, not the power. What does he reply to this? Having noticed that no context of the text proves that the angels of the churches had superior power, he descends only so far as to fight from antiquity alone, for he answers only this: "We cannot approve this presidency for us, because in all antiquity we find no example of such a bishop or president; but the Fathers describe such a bishop for us, who would have an eminent and unique power, without whose consent the elders ought to do nothing." Similarly George Downame affirms that the Apostles intended metropolitan cities, and when asked how such an intention could be made clear, he answers that it appears most plainly from the common practice of the first Church. Is this to dispute chiefly from Scripture, and only least of all from the Fathers? Rather, this proof depends on Scripture not at all, absolutely nothing, but only, entirely and wholly, on the Fathers. There is also the case where they not only argue without Scripture, purely from the Fathers, but even set the Fathers before Scripture. Thomas Bilson, after he had interpreted Matthew 18:20, "tell it to the Church," of a civil tribunal, and that on the basis of consideration of the circumstances (as he himself thinks), finally yields, for the sake of the Fathers, that it may be understood of an ecclesiastical tribunal, if anyone is pleased to follow the footsteps of the Fathers. But this puts Scripture under the yoke of the Fathers. For although he thinks in his conscience that his own interpretation is true, he nevertheless allows that it should be given up rather than the least derogation be made from the authority of the Fathers. What, meanwhile, becomes of us, who fight for Scripture alone, and think that every theological controversy must be disputed from Scripture alone, with the Fathers set aside? Surely all Protestants hear from Cornelius Schultingius that they are Scripturists alone; now from the Protestant Hierarchs themselves we hear that we read nothing, know nothing of the Fathers, despise antiquity, and finally that we are Scripturists alone. The following theses will provide a remedy for this slander and error.

units.la: Thesis ix. quibus confirmatur Scripturam solam esse judicem.
units.tr: Thesis ix. By which it is confirmed that Scripture alone is the judge.

units.la: PRimò, sola scriptura fidem fundat: sic ut ad ipsam ( ut rectè Alliacus ) fiat ultima resolutio Theologici discursus: & ex ea primo singulæ conclusiones Theologicæ deducantur. Hoc ia Thoma Bilsono ipso adversario datum, imo & comprobatum etiam. Rom. 10. fides (inquit) ex auditu est, auditus autem ex verbo Dei, unde colligimus, fidem neque absque verbo neque præter verbum, ullam esse posse. Citat deinde Basilium. Si omne quod ex fide non est, peccatum est, ut ait Apostolus, fides autem ex auditu, auditus autem per verbum Dei: sine dubio quicquid extra divinam scripturam est, quum ex fide non sit, id peccatum est. Similiter Hilarius. Fidem quæris imperator? Audi eam non ex novis chartulis, sed ex Dei libris: Audi rogo quod à Christo scriptum est, ne eorum prætextu quæ non sunt scripta, prædicentur. Sic Tertullianus: Aliunde loqui nos de rebus fidei non posse docet, nisi ex literis fidei: Quum credimus, nihil desideramus ultra credere: hoc enim primum credimus, non esse quod ultra credere debeamus. Ita Augustinus: Titubabit fides, si divinarum scripturarum vacillet authoritas. Sic Chrysostomus: Si quid dicitur absque scriptura claudicat auditorum cogitatio. Postremo audiatur ipse Matheus Sutclivius, Fides supra verbum Christi: Rom. 10. & Ecclesia super fundamentum Prophetarum & Apostolorum structa est, sic ut nisi ex Apostolorum scriptis docere possint totâ hanc suâ fide adversarij super arenam fundatâ esse fateatur necesse est: Ipsi enim fatentur fidem niti revelatione divina, & non alibi fundari quàm in verbo Christi. Thom. Sum. p. 2. q. 1. art. 1, 2. 6. Vanum igitur est, quod ab Hierarchicis ponitur, fidem quidem cumprimis verbo Dei niti, sed nonnihil tamen ex consensu antiquitatis.
units.tr: First, Scripture alone founds faith, so that to it (as Alliacus rightly puts it) the final resolution of theological reasoning is brought, and from it first the individual theological conclusions are derived. This is granted even by Thomas Bilson, our adversary, indeed he also confirms it. Rom. 10: faith (he says) comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God; whence we gather that faith can be neither without the word nor beyond the word. He then cites Basil: If everything that is not of faith is sin, as the Apostle says, and faith is by hearing, and hearing through the word of God, then undoubtedly whatever lies outside divine Scripture, since it is not of faith, is sin. Similarly Hilary: Do you seek faith, emperor? Hear it not from new little papers but from the books of God. Hear, I beg you, what has been written by Christ, lest under the pretext of things that are not written they be preached. So Tertullian: That we cannot speak of matters of faith from anywhere but from the letters of faith teaches us. When we believe, we desire to believe nothing further; for this we first believe, that there is nothing further we ought to believe. So Augustine: Faith will totter if the authority of the divine Scriptures wavers. Thus Chrysostom: If anything is said without Scripture, the thought of the hearers limps. Finally let Matthew Sutcliffe be heard: Faith rests upon the word of Christ: Rom. 10. And the Church is built upon the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles, so that unless they can teach from the writings of the Apostles, the adversaries must admit that their whole faith is founded on sand. For they themselves admit that faith rests on divine revelation, and is founded nowhere but in the word of Christ. Thom. Sum. p. 2. q. 1. art. 1, 2. 6. It is therefore vain what is put forward by the hierarchical party, that faith indeed rests above all on the word of God, but yet in some measure on the consent of antiquity.

units.la: Secundò Scriptura sola αυτάρκης est, & à se authoritatem habet quod a Guilielmo Whitakero adversus Bellarminum aliisque nostris adversus eundem, & Stapletonum fusissimè demonstratum est. Quemadmodùm igitur rem calidam esse ex hoc solo probatur, quòd ab igne participet, qui a se calidus est: ita in quæstionib° Theologicis, rem veram esse nullo alio modo probari potest, quam ratiocinado eam a Scripturis robur accipere, quæ solæ a se veritatem continent. Quantiuntur hoc ariete testimonia adversariorum omnia ex patribus producta, quæ ratione nullâ adferùt ex scripturis: liberamur verò nos ab omni arrogantiæ & impudetiæ suspicione, cum nudam patrum authoritate, à se, absq; ratione à scripturis depromptâ loquente, rejicendâ existimamus. Si nos etenim hoc nomine arrogantes & impudétes simus: arrogans sanè & impudés Augustinus fuit, cujus ista vox est, Alios autem ita lego, ut quantalibet sanctitate doctrinaq; præpolleant: non idcò verum putem quia ipsi ita senserunt, sed quia mihi vel per illos authores thores Canonicos vel probabili ratione quod a veritate non abhorreat, persua-dere potuerunt. Arrogans & impudens Athanasius, qui provocantib9 ad patres ita respondet: Si bene fidunt suae sectae, ostendant, si quid pro ea defendenda vel ex sacris literis vel ex aliqua humana saltem ratione pia deducere possunt, aut si non possunt, taceant. Arrogans denique & impudens Guilielmus Whitakerus noster. Desinat ( inquit ) nuda Patrum testimonia nobis objicere, & scripturas potius, vel argumenta saltem solida afferant. Quod si autem arrogantiae morbo aliquo hac de causa laboraremus: consultum tamen adversariis esset, de illo Poetae monito cogitare. Loripedem rectus derideat, Aethiopem albus. Nam quum praecise jubeamur. 1. Pet. 4. 11. Nulla nisi domini verba loqui: videant quam ipsi arrogantes sunt, qui nuda hominum testimonia, non loquirantur, verum & personare audeant. Non ita ipsi sancti patres arrogates: Sic etenim Origenes: Necesse est Scripturas sanctas in testimonium vocare: nam sine his testibus enarrationes nostrae non habent fidem. Sic Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus: Necesse est non sine sacris scripturis quicquam tradere: neque mihi haec dicenti simpliciter credas, nisi demonstrationem horum ex sacris literis accipias. Sic Hieronymus. Omne quod loquimur debemus affirmare de scripturis sanctis. Sic denique Clemens Alexandrinus: Si non satis est solum absolutè dicere, quod visum est, sed oportet etiam probare quod dictum est, non expectamus testimonium quod datur ab hominibus, sed quod voce Domini probatur, quaeritur. Ex his omnibus confirmatur, quum à se Scriptura solâ authoritatem habeat, frivola esse omnia ea, quae ab adversariis producuntur testimonia patrum, quae nuda sunt, & rationem per se nullam ex sacris Scripturis afferunt.
units.tr: Second, Scripture alone is self-sufficient [αὐτάρκης] and has authority from itself. This has been most fully demonstrated by William Whitaker against Bellarmine, and by others of ours against the same man, and against Stapleton. Just as a thing is proved to be hot from this alone, that it partakes of fire, which is hot of itself, so in theological questions a thing can be proved true in no other way than by reasoning that it receives its strength from the Scriptures, which alone contain truth from themselves. Thus all the testimonies of our adversaries produced from the Fathers, which bring no reason from Scripture, are battered by this ram. We are freed from any suspicion of arrogance and impudence when we judge that a bare authority of the Fathers, speaking from itself without a reason drawn from the Scriptures, is to be rejected. For if we are arrogant and impudent on this account, then Augustine was certainly arrogant and impudent, whose words these are: I read other writers in such a way that, however much they excel in holiness and learning, I do not therefore think something true because they thought so, but because they could persuade me, through those canonical authors or by probable reasoning, that it does not depart from the truth. Athanasius was arrogant and impudent, who answers those who appeal to the Fathers thus: If they trust well in their sect, let them show it. If they can deduce anything in its defence either from the sacred letters or from some human but at least pious reason, let them do so; if they cannot, let them be silent. Finally, our own William Whitaker was arrogant and impudent: Let them cease, he says, to object to us bare testimonies of the Fathers, and let them bring Scriptures, or at least solid arguments. But even if we were suffering from some disease of arrogance for this reason, it would still be wise for our adversaries to think on that saying of the poet: Let the straight-legged mock the crooked-legged, the white man the Ethiopian. For since we are strictly commanded, 1. Pet. 4. 11: Let no one speak but the words of the Lord, let them see how arrogant they themselves are, who dare not merely to bring forward bare human testimonies, but even to sound them forth. The holy Fathers themselves were not so arrogant. Thus Origen: It is necessary to call the holy Scriptures as witnesses, for without these witnesses our expositions do not have credibility. Thus Cyril of Jerusalem: It is necessary to hand down nothing without the holy Scriptures; and do not simply believe me when I say these things, unless you receive a demonstration of them from the sacred letters. Thus Jerome: Everything we say we ought to affirm from the holy Scriptures. And finally Clement of Alexandria: If it is not enough merely to say absolutely what seems right, but it is necessary also to prove what has been said, we do not look for a testimony given by men, but ask for what is proved by the voice of the Lord. From all these it is confirmed that, since Scripture has authority from itself alone, all those testimonies of the Fathers which the adversaries produce, being bare and bringing no reason from the holy Scriptures themselves, are frivolous.

units.la: Tertiò, Scriptura sola docet: Unus etenim tantummodo Doctor est: Math. cap. 23. verf. 8. 10. qui semel docuit: sic ut jam non dico patres sed & Angeli ipsi rejiciendi à nobis sunt: Gal. 1. 8. non solùm si contra, sed etiam si praeter Scripturam sacram doceant. Iugulatur hoc telo fides Hierachica illa, quae consensu antiquitatis nititur, quando Scriptura non contradicit, aut eadem cum Scriptura minimè pugnat. Qua in re vel ad ipsum Thomam Bilsonum adversarium provoco: Neque pastor neque consiliam, inquit, imo neq; Angelus in rebus fidei recipiendus est: non dico solum contra Scripturas (videant hîc de Zanchio suo Hierarchici) sed etiam absque Scripturis, vel praeter Scripturas. Citat huc Hilarium super Psalm. 86: Quicquid praeterea est abscindatur. Tertullianum de praescript. Nihil aliud credendum. Irenaeum lib. 3. 3. C. 1: A nullis aliis, nisi ab Apostolis. Cyrillum, De recta fide, ad Regin. lib. 2: In nullo a sacris Scripturis. Augustinum De pastoribus, cap. 11. Quicquid praeter est repudia, & contra literas Petil. lib. 3. cap. 3. Praeterquam quod ——— anathema sit. Isidorum denique Cauf. 11. q. 3. Con. 5. is qui praeest: Praeter id quod evidenter in Scripturis praeceptum est. Provoco etiam ad Hierarchicum alium, Thomam nempe Mortonum praesertim in illa altera pronuntiati Zanchiani parte, ubi
units.tr: Third, Scripture alone teaches: For one is your Teacher, Matt. 23, vers. 8, 10, who taught once for all. So that now, I say, not only the Fathers but even the Angels themselves are to be rejected by us, Gal. 1. 8, not only if they teach against it but even if they teach beside sacred Scripture. That Hierarchical faith, which rests on the consent of antiquity, is struck down with this weapon, when Scripture does not contradict it, or at least does not clash with Scripture at all. In this matter I challenge even the adversary Thomas Bilson himself: Neither minister nor counsellor, nay, not even an angel, is to be received in matters of faith. I do not say only against the Scriptures (let the Hierarchists here look to their Zanchius) but also without the Scriptures, or beside the Scriptures. He cites here Hilary on Psalm 86: Whatever is beyond this is to be cut off. Tertullian, On Prescription: Nothing else is to be believed. Irenaeus, lib. 3. 3. C. 1: From no others except the Apostles. Cyril, On Right Faith, to Regin., lib. 2: In nothing apart from the holy Scriptures. Augustine, On Pastors, cap. 11: Whatever is beyond it, reject, and against the letters. Petil. lib. 3. cap. 3: Except that ... let him be anathema. Finally Isidore, Causa 11, q. 3, Con. 5, on the one who presides: Beyond what is evidently commanded in the Scriptures. I also challenge the other Hierarchist, Thomas Morton, especially in that second part of the Zanchian proposition where

units.la: Epist. cont. Arian dicit a Spiritu sancto profecta esse quae sancti patres de disciplina quantum-vis praeter Scripturam sacram, tradiderunt. Dixit Petrus à Soto olim: Non est Spiritus Evangelici Scripturis solis intentum esse: Quocum quàm proximè sese Zanchius conjunxerit judicet aequus: Ego Spiritum diabolicum eos sequi potius, qui extra Scripturas Spiritum quaerunt, ex illo testimonio Theophilii me probaturum posse puto, quod citat Morinus: Diabolicum est extra divinarum Scripturarum authoritatem aliquid divinum putare. Simile illud est quod adversus Iiardingum affert Iuelius ex sancto Chrysostomo. Dixerat ille id quod Zanchius, Spiritum sanctum in sanctis patribus loqui: regerit Iuelius, finire: Spiritum sanctum aliquae authoritate Scripturarum vendidari: quo hoc tendunt Chrysostomi, inquit, Si quis eorum qui dicuntur habere Spiritum sanctum dicat aliquid a se ipso, & non ex Evangeliis, non credite: Si quis sequitur dicta Christi Spiritum sanctum habet. Ex quo non legit haec scripta, sed a seipso loquitur, manifestum est quod non habet Spiritum sanctum, Huc pertinent quae à Bilsono & Mortono adferuntur etiam, ex Psalm. 119:105. 2 Pet. 1. quod Scriptura sola, lucerna & lux sit: sic ut qui patres aut mortales ullos, praeter eam audiant, in tenebras incidere necesse sit. Hinc Chrysostomus: Quod lumen est oculo, id Scriptura mentis est: quod & habent Hieronymus in Isa. 8.20. Ambrosius in Psal. 118. Serm. 14. Augustinus in Luc. c.16. Neque ego plures addam: qui plures desiderat, Mortonum consulat: quorum ille authoritates ita recapitulat: Nihil sine, nihil extra nihil praeter, nihil ultra divinam Scripturam admittendum esse contestatur: ut non necesse sit nobis amplius (seu obtritis Gibeonitarum calceis) traditionibus putridis & vetustatis fuco ementitis decipi.
units.tr: in the Epistle against the Arians he says that what the holy Fathers handed down about discipline, however much beside the holy Scripture, proceeded from the Holy Spirit. Peter à Soto once said: It is not the spirit of the Gospel to be intent on Scripture alone. Let the fair-minded judge how closely Zanchius has joined himself with him. I think I can prove from that testimony of Theophilus, which Morinus cites, that those who seek the Spirit outside the Scriptures rather follow a diabolical spirit: It is diabolical to think anything divine outside the authority of the divine Scriptures. Similar to this is what Jewel brings against Hardinge from holy Chrysostom. Hardinge had said what Zanchius says, that the Holy Spirit speaks in the holy Fathers. Jewel replies that the Holy Spirit is bound to the authority of the Scriptures. Chrysostom's words to this effect, he says: If any of those who are said to have the Holy Spirit says something from himself, and not from the Gospels, do not believe him. If anyone follows the sayings of Christ, he has the Holy Spirit. Since he does not read these writings but speaks from himself, it is manifest that he does not have the Holy Spirit. To this belong also the arguments which Bilson and Morton adduce from Psalm 119:105 and 2 Pet. 1, that Scripture alone is lamp and light, so that whoever hears the Fathers or any mortals apart from it must necessarily fall into darkness. Hence Chrysostom: What the light is to the eye, Scripture is to the mind. Jerome has this on Isa. 8.20, Ambrose on Psalm 118, Sermon 14, and Augustine on Luke, chap. 16. I will add no more. Whoever wants more, let him consult Morton, who sums up their authorities thus: he testifies that nothing is to be admitted without, nothing outside, nothing beside, nothing beyond divine Scripture, so that we need no longer (the Gibeonites' shoes being worn out) be deceived by putrid traditions falsely painted over with the veneer of antiquity.

units.la: 4 Quartò, Scriptura sola ad fidem faciendam probat: unde solemne Prophetis fuit: Hoc dicit Dominus; & Christus solum adversus ea quae ab antiquo dicta essent, afferre solet: Ego dico vobis: Matth. 5. Perspici hinc potest, quàm audax Hierarchicorum probatio illa sit: Hoc dicit Tertullianus, hoc dicit Cyprianus: quae & ipsa Thomae Mortono quantumvis adversario displicet, qui illud Augustini & citat & approbat: Scriptum est; Audi quid dicit Dominus, non, quid dicit Donatus, aut Vincentius, aut Hilarius, aut Augustinus. Ruri-us: Non audiamus, Haec dico, haec dicis, sed audiamus, Haec dicit Dominus: Sunt certè libri Dominici quorum authoritati u igue consenti-mus ... illi discutiamus causam nostram, Iterum. Nemo mihi dicat quid dixit Donatus, aut Parmenianus, aut Pontius, aut quilibet eorum: Quia nec Catholicis Episcopis consuetudinem est, sicubi forte fallantur, ut ca-nonicas Dei Scripturas aliquid sentiant: Excellunt vero a ne-strum propositum illa Hieronymi, qui eandem calumniam quam jam nos, expertus est, quod solâ Scripturae authoritate fiat, veteres patres à se loquentes repudiavit: Non juxta Pythagoram, inquit, f-cijudis, praejudicata doctoris opinio, sed doctrinae ratio pondus ei: Omnis probate, quod bonum est tenete: & esse probati numinum, ut si quis nummulus adulter est, & figuram Cæsaris non habet, nec signatus est, moneta publica reprobetur: qui autem Christi faciem claro lumine præfert, in cordis nostri marsupium recondatur. Cur me lacerant amici mei & adversum silentem crassæ sues grunniunt? quarum omne studium est, imo scientiæ supercilium aliena carpere, & sic veterum perfidiam defendere, ut perdant fidem suam. Meum propositum est antiquos legere, probare singula, retinere quæ bona sunt, & a fide Ecclesiæ Catholicæ non recedere. Quem non moveret tam sancta hominis pij contestatio? quem non terreret calumniantem tam moderata defensio? quæ etiam & nostra est. Patres nos legimus, sed probamus; non contemnimus, examinamus tamen. Pythagoræ loco nobis solus Christus est, ut qui Pastor solus, Eccles.12:11. magister solus, Matth. 23. solus Propheta Ecclesiæ sit, Act.7.37. patres vero, utcunque ad fidem illustrandam testes approbativi esse possunt: ad fidem tamen faciendam, tantùm abest ut judices, ut ne quidem testes probativi esse queant: sic enim Christus Ioh. 5:34. Ego ab hominibus testimonium non accipio.
units.tr: 4 Fourthly, Scripture alone is what establishes faith. Hence it was the prophets' customary formula: "Thus says the Lord." And Christ, when setting himself against what had been said of old, regularly uses only: "But I say to you" (Matt. 5). From this one can see how bold that Hierarchical appeal is: "Tertullian says this, Cyprian says this." Even Thomas Morton, however much an opponent, dislikes it, for he both cites and approves Augustine's saying: "It is written; hear what the Lord says, not what Donatus says, or Vincentius, or Hilary, or Augustine." Again: "Let us not listen to 'I say this, you say this,' but let us listen to 'Thus says the Lord.' There are indeed the books of the Lord, whose authority we consent to. Let us discuss our cause by them." Again: "Let no one tell me what Donatus said, or Parmenian, or Pontius, or any of them. For it is not the custom even of Catholic bishops, if they should perhaps be mistaken, to think anything contrary to the canonical Scriptures of God." Those words of Jerome also bear directly on our proposition. He, having met the same calumny that we now meet, rejected the old fathers speaking on their own authority, because the matter is settled by the authority of Scripture alone: "Not according to Pythagoras, he says, is the prejudged opinion of the teacher, but the weight of reason counts. Prove all things, hold fast what is good, and be approved money-changers: as, if a counterfeit coin is not stamped with Caesar's image, it is rejected as currency; but whoever bears the face of Christ in clear light is to be stored in the purse of our heart. Why do my friends tear me to pieces, and why do the silent swine grunt against me? Their whole zeal is to carp at what belongs to others, indeed to show the arrogance of learning, and so to defend the faithlessness of the ancients, so that they lose their own faith. My purpose is to read the ancients, to test each thing, to keep what is good, and not to depart from the faith of the Catholic Church. Who would not be moved by such a holy protestation of a godly man? Who would not be frightened by a calumniator at so moderate a defence? And this defence is ours too. We read the fathers, but we test them; we do not despise them, yet we examine them." In place of Pythagoras, Christ alone is for us, as the one "Shepherd" (Eccles. 12:11), the one "Master" (Matt. 23), the one "Prophet of the Church" (Acts 7:37). The fathers, however far they may serve as witnesses that approve and illustrate the faith, are so far from being judges of the faith that they cannot even be proving witnesses for establishing it.
