For Christ says thus (John 5:34): "I do not receive testimony from men."

units.la: 5 Quintò, Scriptura sola refutat, id quod in Christo videre est, qui nullis Rabinorum scriptis (ut habet Reynoldus) sed solis Scripturæ testimoniis, diabolum repulit: Matth. 4. & in Apostolis, qui adversus Iudæos sacras Scripturas recipientes, nullius nisi Scripturæ sacræ testimonijs disputabāt. Hoc nobis jam in officio esse docet vel ipse adversarius Bilsonus ex 2. Tim. 3. 16, 17. Scriptura divinitus inspirata dicitur, ut vir Dei perfectus esset in redarguendo, id est, errores refutando, idque in causa disciplinæ: nam de disciplinâ Ecclesiastica, vel ipsis fatentibus adversariis, illa ad Timotheum epistola Pauli tractat: Non immerito igitur concludit Bilsonus Apostolos quæ prædicarent ideò scriptis mandasse, ut tanquam lydius lapis Scriptura posteris relinqueretur, per quam veritas probanda & examinanda esset. Concludit idipsum ex Christi exemplo Tomas Mortonus adversarius alius, illa Stellæ approbans: Non aliter impios hæreticos perfrictæ frontis possumus convincere, nisi sacros habeamus codices, ex quibus clara veritas elucesfit, Iohannes Iuellus postquam hoc Christi exemplum, & illum ad Timotheum locum protulisset, subjungit: Ita & patres nullis aliis viribus contra hæreticos olim pugnarunt quam sacris Scripturis. Rursus, cum indignaretur Haraingus, (ut hodie Hierarchici) se ad solas Scripturas revocari, respondet in hæc verba: Nos te semper ad Scripturas revocare duxis; Non tam gravis hæc, spero, culpa est: Ita faciendum esse jubet Christus; Scrutamini (inquit ille) Scripturas. Iohannes Reynoldus, cum ad patres Hartus provocasset, admonet in Scripturis solis acquiescendum potius esse, ut quæ solæ ille lapis lydius sint, quo veritas diiudicatur: Quid ille? Deridet nempe fere eisdem cum Richardo Bancrofto verbis illorum hypocrisin, qui licet verbo tenus honorifice de patribus loqui soleant, cum tamen ad rem deventum sit, ad Scripturas solas confugiunt: Gravis hæc accusatio erat & mordax sarcasmus: nihil tamen ille aliud respondendum putavit quàm perperam haberi
units.tr: 5 Fifthly, Scripture alone refutes, as we see in Christ, who repulsed the devil not with the writings of the rabbis (as Reynolds has it), but with the testimonies of Scripture alone (Matt. 4); and in the Apostles, who, when disputing with the Jews who accepted the holy Scriptures, argued with the testimonies of holy Scripture alone. Even our adversary Bilson teaches us that this is our duty, from 2 Tim. 3:16–17, where Scripture is said to be "divinely inspired," "that the man of God may be perfect in refuting," that is, in refuting errors, and this in the matter of discipline. For that epistle of Paul to Timothy deals with ecclesiastical discipline, as even our adversaries admit. Not undeservedly, therefore, does Bilson conclude that the Apostles committed to writing what they preached so that Scripture might be left to posterity as a touchstone, by which truth was to be tested and examined. Thomas Morton, another adversary, concludes the same from Christ's example, approving that of Stella: "We cannot otherwise convict impious heretics of brazen brow, unless we have the holy codices, from which clear truth shines forth." John Jewel, after he had brought forward this example of Christ and that passage to Timothy, adds: "So also the fathers never fought against heretics in former times with any other weapons than the holy Scriptures." Again, when Harding was indignant at being recalled to Scripture alone (as the Hierarchists do today), Jewel replies in these words: "I have always thought it right to recall you to the Scriptures. This fault, I hope, is not so grave. Thus Christ commands that it be done: 'Search the Scriptures,' he says." John Reynolds, when Hart had appealed to the fathers, admonishes that one should rather rest in the Scriptures alone, since these alone are the touchstone by which truth is judged. What did Hart do? He mocked, in nearly the same words as Richard Bancroft, the hypocrisy of those "who, though they are accustomed to speak honourably of the fathers in words, yet when it comes to the matter, flee to the Scriptures alone." This was a grave accusation and a biting sarcasm, yet he thought nothing else needed to be answered than that it was "wrongly held" (to be) a man unduly dutiful toward men who is dutiful toward God.

units.la: X {a}habere se contra homines inofficiosum, qui officiosus erga Deum esset. Superest Gul. Whitakerus, cui cum à Dureo (quod iam nobis objectum esset, miseram illum causam esse, qui armis patrum, conciliorum, Ecclesiae, interdictis, Scriptura sola pugnare vellet, ita respondet: Non hic armis quibuslibet utendum, sed quae in hoc certamine genere legitima sola sunt: ea autem ex armentario Scripturae solo petenda. Quam tu igitur causam meliorem putas: an nostram, quae Scriptura sola tuta est, an vestram, quae si Scripturis solis agatur, salva nequit consistere? Opus R. Nymoldi Henrici Pareus Episcopus Glocestrensis ex Anglico Latinum, opus vero Whitakeri ex Latino Anglicum Richardus Stockius fecit: annon igitur vel adversarios ipsos suffragatores hac in causa habemus, Scripturis nempe Dei sacris, eisque solis pugnandum esse? Cur hanc sanctissimam aequissimamque disputandi aleam fugerent adversarii, nisi ob eam quam reddit Augustinus causam? Odit aegrotus medicinam. Quam vero sibi ipsis hoc consilio pessime consulant, docet sanctus Chrysostomus: Ex quo haeresis impia, quae est exercitus Antichristi obtinebit Ecclesias, nulla probatio poterit esse vera, neque refugium poterit esse Christianorum aliud, nisi Scripturae divinae. Qui ergo vult cognoscere quae sit Ecclesia vera, unde cognoscit nisi tantum modo per Scripturas: Sciens ergo Dominus tantam confusionem futuram, mandat ut Christiani ad nullam rem fugiant, nisi ad Scripturas: Alioqui, si ad alia respexerint, scandalizabuntur et peribunt, non intelligentes quae sit vera Ecclesia: et per hoc incident in abominationem desolationis, quae stat in sanctis Ecclesiae locis. Impletum in oculis nostris hoc vaticinium hodie est. Deturpavit disciplinam Antichristus et abominationem in sanctis Ecclesiae locis collocavit. Scripturis solis adhaerentes reformati hanc et discernunt et detestantur: cum ad patres confugientes Hierarchici (qui quanquam nescientes, Antichristum tamen in ementita Hierarchia promovebant) in disciplinam nothan inciderunt, et ab Antichristo mutuatam, et ut sanctus Chrysostomus loquitur, volentes, prudensque scandalizantur.
units.tr: Finally, there is William Whitaker, to whom, when Durus (as had already been objected to us) said that he was a wretched advocate who wished to fight with the weapons of the fathers, councils, the Church, and interdicts, but with Scripture alone, he replies thus: "Here one must not use just any weapons, but only those that are lawful in this kind of contest; and these are to be sought from the armoury of Scripture alone. Which cause, then, do you think the better: ours, which is safe with Scripture alone, or yours, which cannot stand safe if the matter is pursued with Scriptures alone?" The work of R. Nymold was made into Latin by Henry Parey, Bishop of Gloucester, from English, and the work of Whitaker was made from Latin into English by Richard Stock. Do we not then have even our adversaries themselves as supporters in this cause: that we must fight with the holy Scriptures of God, and with them alone? Why would the adversaries shun this most holy and most equitable hazard of disputation, unless for the reason that Augustine gives: the sick man hates the physician? How gravely they ill-serve themselves by this counsel is taught by St. Chrysostom: "From the time when the impious heresy, which is the army of Antichrist, shall hold the Churches, no proof can be true, nor can there be any other refuge for Christians but the divine Scriptures. Whoever wishes to know which is the true Church, from what does he know it, except only through the Scriptures? The Lord, therefore, knowing that such great confusion will come, commands that Christians flee to nothing but the Scriptures. Otherwise, if they look to other things, they will be scandalized and perish, not understanding which is the true Church, and through this they will fall into the abomination of desolation, which stands in the holy places of the Church." This prophecy has been fulfilled before our eyes today. Antichrist has defiled the discipline and set up the abomination in the holy places of the Church. Reformed men, adhering to Scripture alone, both discern and detest this; but the Hierarchists, fleeing to the fathers (who, though unknowingly, nevertheless advanced Antichrist in their fabricated hierarchy), have fallen into a discipline that is a sham, borrowed from Antichrist, and, as St. Chrysostom says, are scandalized willingly and knowingly.

units.la: Sexto, Scriptura sola iudicat et definit. Fixum hoc ratumque Theo. Bisfino, vel adversario nostro est, qui huc illa ex capite Isaiae 8 citat: Nonne populus a Deo suo consilium capere debet? Ad legem et ad testimonium: qui non secundum hoc verbum loquitur, ideo est, quia lumen nullum habet. Ratum hoc etiam adversario alteri, Thomae nempe Morton, qui exemplum Constantini Magni urget, sacrum codicem in medio Concilii Nicaeni proponentis, cum his verbis: Evangelici et Apostolici libri plane nos instruunt quid de divinis sentiendum sit, proinde hostili posita discordia, ex variis divinitus inspiratis sumamus quaestionum explicationem. Constat hinc quod ex Libero in responsione sua ad Constantium affert Thomas Bisfinus, qui in Synodo timorem Domini, et insectationem Apostolorum, ad omnia sufficere dixit: Iam vero in Synodis tantummodo codex Dei quasi iudex proponendus? imo vero inquit Augustinus: Vicunque locus ad disputandum constitutus fuerit, faciamus
units.tr: Sixthly, Scripture alone judges and defines. This is fixed and settled even for Thomas Bilson, or for our adversary, who cites from Isaiah 8: "Should not a people seek counsel from their God? To the law and to the testimony: if they do not speak according to this word, it is because they have no light." It is equally settled for the other adversary, Thomas Morton, who urges the example of Constantine the Great, who placed the holy codex in the midst of the Council of Nicaea, with these words: "The Gospel and apostolic books plainly instruct us what is to be thought about divine things; therefore, setting aside hostile discord, let us take the explanation of questions from the various divinely inspired books." From this, what Thomas Bilson brings from Liberius in his reply to Constantius is established, who said that in the Synod the fear of the Lord and the teaching of the Apostles were sufficient for all things. Indeed, should the codex of God be put forward in the Synods only, as a judge? Nay, says Augustine: "Wherever a place is appointed for disputation, let us have the canonical codices ready at hand, and, setting aside the rest, let us bring so great a matter to the end of inquiry by whatever evidence can be produced on each side."

units.la: Cont. Bur. p. 4. (marginal references in left margin) faciamus codices Canonicos presto esse, & si quae proferri possunt ex utraque parte documenta, postpositis caeteris rem tantam ad inquisitionis terminum perducamus: Eodem pertinent quae ex Chrysostomo citat Mortonus.Cum habeamus omnium exactissimam regulam ex divinarum Scripturarum assertione, ito vos omnes ut relinquatis, quid huic, quid illi videatur, & de bis a scripturis, haec omnia inquirite: At haec patres non excludunt, inquis. Quid, nonne excluduntur, cum postponi & relinqui jubentur? Sed planus Thomas Mortonus alibi est, illa Bellarmini probans: Patres exponunt Scripturas non more iudicum sed more doctorum: id est, supremi iudices non sunt, possunt tamen quasi secundarij esse. Apage has nugas: Ita Scriptura pro solo judice agnoscenda, ut patres penitus removendi sint, vel ipso Johanne Juello judice: qui ad hanc rem Augustinum adducit: Auferantur e medio quae adversus nos invicem, non ex divinis canonicis libris, sed aliunde recitantur. Quaeret fortasse aliquis, cur vis ista auferri de medio? Quia nolo humanis documentis, sed divinis oraculis Ecclesiam sanctam demonstrari. Rursus: Auferantur de medio chartae nostrae, procedat in medium codex Dei, audi Christum dicentem, audi veritatem loquentem. En seipsos de medio prorsus auferendos ipsi Patres docent, ut in controversiis Theologicis terminandis solis sacrae divinaeque Scripturae relinquatur locus. Postremo prodeat in medium adversarius tertius Isaacus Casaubonus: Quid in libris patrum, inquit, occurrit frequentius quam haec verba? ὅτι διδάσκειν ἐν τῷ γραφῇ quae docentur in Ecclesia Dei e verbo Dei peti debent: aut haec ... judicium de controversiis in causa religionis penes Scripturam esto locus integer: Non putamus justum esse obtinentem apud ipsos consuetudinem legem & regulam facere rectae doctrinae. Igitur Scriptura divinitus inspirata judex a nobis constituatur, & apud quos inveta fuerint dogmata divinis sermonibus concordantia, huic omnino etiam veritatis suffragium accedat. Simile illud est quod habet Henricus Pareus adversarius quartus, in sua Johannis Reynoldi versione. Quaerendi sunt aliqui hujus controversiae judices: In terrenis de hac re nullum reperiri potest judicium: de caelo quaerendus est judex; sed ut quid pulsamus ad caelum cum habeamus hic in Evangelio Testamentum? &c. Sic Augustinus: Haec controversia judicem requirit, & quis erit judex? judicet Christus: judicet cum illo & Apostolus, quia in Apostolo ipse loquitur Christus. Rursus: Sedeat inter nos judex Apostolus Johannes: Citat & ista Thomas Martonus: pag.2. lib. 5. c.11. Septimo, Scriptura sola interpretatur. Contra hanc thesin contrariam iniquissime allstruunt passim Hierarchici: patres nimirum ut Scripturae interpretes credendos esse: quorum sententiam vel unus ex Saravia locus ita patefecit: De verbo Dei, inquit aut de ejus authoritate nulla inter nos est controversia, quin ei tanquam certissimae regulae parendum sit: sed id nos cogitare oportet, veteres, qui proxime a temporibus Apostolorum praefuerunt Ecclesiae, verbo Dei non fuisse destitutos, nec omnes pariter Ecclesias simul a verbo Dei potuisse deficere. Si quis contra
units.tr: Cont. Bur. p. 4. Let us have the canonical books at hand, and if any proofs can be brought forward from either side, let us set aside everything else and bring so great a matter to the end of inquiry. The same applies to what Morton cites from Chrysostom: Since we have the most exact rule of all, namely the assertion of the divine Scriptures, go, all of you, and leave off what seems to this one or that one, and inquire about all these things from the Scriptures. "But," you say, "the Fathers are not excluded by this." What? Are they not excluded, when they are ordered to be set aside and left behind? Yet Thomas Morton elsewhere plainly approves Bellarmine's words: The Fathers expound the Scriptures not in the manner of judges but in the manner of teachers; that is, they are not supreme judges, yet they can be, as it were, secondary ones. Away with these trifles! Scripture must thus be acknowledged as the sole judge, so that the Fathers are to be utterly removed, even by the judgment of John Jewel himself. He brings forward Augustine on this matter: Let those things be taken out of the way which are recited against us, not from the divine canonical books but from elsewhere. Someone may perhaps ask why this authority should be taken out of the way. Because I do not wish the holy Church to be shown by human documents, but by the divine oracles. Again: Let our papers be taken out of the way; let the book of God come forward into the midst; hear Christ saying it, hear the truth speaking. Behold, the Fathers themselves teach that they must be wholly removed from the midst, so that in the ending of theological controversies room is left to the holy and divine Scripture alone. Lastly, let the third adversary, Isaac Casaubon, come forward: What, he says, occurs more often in the books of the Fathers than these words, that the things taught in the Church of God must be sought from the word of God [ὅτι διδάσκειν ἐν τῷ γραφῇ], or these: the judgment on controversies in matters of religion must rest wholly with Scripture? We do not think it right that a custom held among themselves should make a law and rule of sound doctrine. Therefore let the Scripture inspired by God be set up by us as judge, and wherever doctrines agreeing with the divine words have been found, let the witness of truth also wholly attach itself to them. Similar is what Henry Pareus, our fourth adversary, says in his version of John Reynolds: We must seek some judges of this controversy. In earthly matters no judgment on this can be found; the judge must be sought from heaven. But why do we knock at heaven, when we have here the Testament in the Gospel? etc. So Augustine: This controversy requires a judge, and who will be the judge? Let Christ judge; let the Apostle judge with him, because in the Apostle Christ himself speaks. Again: Let the Apostle John sit between us as judge. Thomas Morton also cites these words, p. 2, book 5, ch. 11. Seventh, Scripture interprets itself alone. Against this contrary thesis the Hierarchists everywhere most unjustly maintain that the Fathers are to be believed as interpreters of Scripture. Their opinion one passage from Saravia has laid bare: Concerning the Word of God, or its authority, there is no controversy among us, but that it must be obeyed as the most certain rule. But we must consider that the ancients who most nearly followed the times of the Apostles were not destitute of the Word of God, nor could all the churches together have failed at once from the Word of God. If someone argues against this

units.la: {x} Lib. 2. c. 49. tra contendat, atque adeo amore sui, suaeque aetatis caecus est, ut sibi nostra tantum aetas sapere videatur, fruatur ille per me sapientia sua: ego illud iudico & admittendum primarum Ecclesiarum morem & usum universalem Interpretem obscurorum locorum qui dubij sunt & controvertuntur, arbitror.
units.tr: {x} Book 2, ch. 49. and is so blind through self-love and the bias of his own age that our age alone seems wise to himself, let him enjoy his wisdom through me. For my part I judge that the custom and universal practice of the earliest churches is to be admitted, and I hold it to be the interpreter of obscure passages which are doubtful and disputed.

units.la: Primo, huic papistico dogmati minùs assentiendum putabit, qui secum consyderat, quàm illius fundamentum blasphemum sit; Scripturam nempe ex sola Scriptura interpretandam non esse, quia muta, quia obscura, quia non perfecta: ut apud Iuellum videre est, Defens. Apolog. cap. 9. Divis. 1. Ecclesiae vero praxim ad opem ferendam advocare quam iniquum? Recte enim Guilielmus Whitakerus quum Hierarchicorum more objecisset Bellarminus: Consuetudo Ecclesiae subsequentis optima est interpres Scripturarum, ita respondet: Imo consuetudo semper habita est pessima Scripturarum interpres: a Tertulliano, & Cypriano, & ab Augustino: Ita illi cum partibus non consentiunt.
units.tr: First, whoever considers it will think less of assenting to this Papist doctrine, when he sees how blasphemous its foundation is: that Scripture is not to be interpreted from Scripture alone, because it is mute, because it is obscure, because it is not perfect, as may be seen in Jewel, Defence of the Apology, ch. 9, div. 1. And how unjust it is to call in the practice of the Church to lend its aid! For when Bellarmine, after the manner of the Hierarchists, had objected that the custom of the later Church is the best interpreter of Scripture, William Whitaker rightly answers: Nay, custom has always been held the worst interpreter of Scripture, as Tertullian, Cyprian and Augustine show. Thus those men do not agree with their own side.

units.la: Secundò, aperta testimonia praesto sunt, Scripturam non nisi ex ipsa Scriptura interpretandam esse; nam & Levitae Neh. 8:8. dabant intelligentiam per Scripturam ipsam, & Christus Scripturae vitiatae a Diabolo, sensum verum ex Scripturarum aliarum collatione elicuit, Mat. 4. & nullo alio adminiculo quàm diligenti comparatione veteres Prophetas in suis epistolis interpretati Apostoli sunt: Act. 9 : 29. & Apostolorum lucem clariorem cum illa Prophetarum obscuriore conferre nos jubet Sanctus Petrus: 2. Pet. 1. 19. & consilium Tridentinum denique Ap. 11. c. 8, Scripturas occidisse dicitur, & in cadaver merum vertisse: quum earum interpretatio ipsis esset adempta, & humano judicio emancipata: de quo Brightmannus consulendus est, p. 296.
units.tr: Second, clear testimonies are at hand that Scripture is to be interpreted only from Scripture itself. For the Levites in Nehemiah 8:8 gave understanding from Scripture itself, and Christ, when Scripture had been corrupted by the Devil, drew out the true sense by comparing other Scriptures, Matthew 4; and the Apostles interpreted the old Prophets in their epistles with no other aid than careful comparison, Acts 9:29; and St Peter bids us compare the clearer light of the Apostles with the darker words of the Prophets, 2 Peter 1:19. Lastly, the Council of Trent is said, Rev. 11. c. 8, to have killed the Scriptures and turned them into mere corpses, since their interpretation was taken away from them and surrendered to human judgment. On this Brightman should be consulted, p. 296.

units.la: Tertiò, rationes suppetunt ex Scripturis manifestae: Nam cum Scriptura non in verbis sed in sensu, non in superficie, sed in medulla, non in sermonum foliis, sed in radice rationis consistat, ut rectè Hieronymus: petatur jam interpretatio Scripturae ex scriptis humanis: & domini in fidem homines erunt, 2 Cor. 1, 24. fides humana authoritate nitetur, non divina: 1. Cor. 2 : 5, Scriptura privatae interpretationis erit: 2. Pet. 1, 20. Patres aequalis cum Scripturis authoritatis erunt (ut recte Whitakerus) vel etiam majoris, quia patrum interpretatio non illud erit, propter quod, quidque verum aestimabitur.
units.tr: Third, reasons plainly drawn from the Scriptures are at hand. For since Scripture consists not in words but in sense, not in the surface but in the marrow, not in the leaves of speech but in the root of reason, as Jerome rightly says, let the interpretation of Scripture now be sought from human writings; and men will become lords over faith, 2 Cor. 1:24; human faith will rest on human authority, not divine, 1 Cor. 2:5; Scripture will be of private interpretation, 2 Pet. 1:20. The Fathers will have authority equal to Scripture (as Whitaker rightly says), or even greater, because the interpretation of the Fathers will be that by which whatever is true is judged.

units.la: Quartò, consulantur testimonia ipsorum patrum, quae a nostris condensantur, ut probetur Scripturam non nisi per ipsam Scripturam interpretandam nobis esse: apud Iuel. Defen. Apolo p. 1. c. 9. divis. 1. Joh. Reynoldum collat. cnm Hart. c. 1. Diuis. 2, Guil. Whitakerum cont. 1. q. 5. c. 13. Thomam deniq; Mortonum Apolog. Catholic. p. 2. lib. 5. c. 9. ex toto acervo, sufficiat nobis adversus eam, quae est in Anglia Hierarchiam illa Tertuliani appellatio. Surge veritas: ipsa scripturas tuas
units.tr: Fourth, let the testimonies of the Fathers themselves be consulted, which our men have gathered together, to prove that Scripture is for us to be interpreted only by Scripture itself: in Jewel, Defence of the Apology, part 1, ch. 9, div. 1; John Reynolds, collated with Hart, ch. 1, div. 2; William Whitaker, controversy 1, q. 5, ch. 13; and finally Thomas Morton, Catholic Apology, part 2, book 5, ch. 9. From this whole heap it will suffice for us against the hierarchy which exists in England to cite that appeal of Tertullian: Arise, truth; interpret your own Scriptures yourself

units.la: De uelandi- ung. tuas interpretare: quam consuetudo non novit, nam si nosset non esset. Frustra quidem, quia falso universam Ecclesiae antiquae praxin obtendunt Hierarchici: sed quid si ea Hierarchiam Anglicanam recepisset? num inde sequitur eam approbandam esse, aut Scripturis consentaneam? Minime vero: ipsa etenim Scripturarum veritas, scripturas interpretari debet, non consuetudo: quia ea cujusmodi esse potest, quae si Scripturas nosset, omnino non esset: Id quod de ista consuetudine Hierarchica verissime dici potest.
units.tr: On the Veiling of Virgins: which custom does not know, for if it knew them it would not exist. Indeed, the Hierarchists allege the whole practice of the ancient Church in vain, since it is falsely alleged. But what if that practice had received the English hierarchy? Does it follow from this that the hierarchy is to be approved, or that it agrees with the Scriptures? By no means. For the truth of Scripture itself ought to interpret Scriptures, not custom; because custom can be of such a kind that, if it knew the Scriptures, it would not exist at all. This may be said most truly of this Hierarchical custom.

units.la: Quinto, non desunt huic veritati vel ipsa quidem, ipsorum adversariorum testimonia, qui cum papistis decertantes, Scripturam per solam Scripturam interpretandam esse liberrime protestantur. Sic Thomas Bilsonus Frustra illius sensum & interpretationem in Ecclesia quaeritis, quod nusquam in Scripturis reperitur. Sic Richardus Fyldus, qui Cajetanum & Andradium contra Canum defendit; licere contra torrentem patrum, & communem antiquitatis consensum, cuius ratione manifesto Scripturam sacram interpretari. Matheus Scutelivius ita. Iurisconsulti dicunt principis esse summi, qui leges condidit, eas interpretari: sic Scripturas cum non ediderit Pontifex, nec edere possit, nec eas interpretari debet. Thomae Mortoni haec adversus Pontificios positio est: Scriptura eam studiose perscrutantibus, est sui interpres. Hadrianus Saravia adversus Gretzerum: Quicquid disputatur ad Scripturae insufficientiam demonstrandam, nisi Papae accedat interpretatio, ad injuriam Spiritus sancti & Domini nostri Iesu Christi ex eo pertinere probat, quod in Scriptura omne Dei consilium traditum sit. At valet haec ratio, tam adversus interpretationes patrum quam Papae, id quod dilucidius perspicietur, si addantur quae ipse subijcit: Omnes haereses ex SOLIS Scripturis convincendas esse veteres Orthodoxi docuerunt: idque juxta Dei verbum: Scriptura divinitus inspirata est——ut integer sit Dei homo, ad omne opus bonum apparatus.
units.tr: Fifth, the very testimonies of our adversaries themselves are not lacking to support this truth, men who, contending with the Papists, most freely protest that Scripture must be interpreted by Scripture alone. Thus Thomas Bilson: In vain do you seek its sense and interpretation in the Church, which is nowhere to be found in the Scriptures. Thus Richard Field, who defends Cajetan and Andradius against Cano: It is lawful, against the torrent of the Fathers and the common consensus of antiquity, by whose reasoning the sacred Scripture is manifestly interpreted. Matthew Scutelivius says: The lawyers say that it belongs to the supreme prince who made the laws to interpret them; so since the Pontiff has not published the Scriptures, he can neither publish them nor ought he to interpret them. This is the position of Thomas Morton against the Papists: Scripture is its own interpreter for those who study it diligently. Adrian Saravia against Gretser: Whatever is argued to demonstrate the insufficiency of Scripture, unless the interpretation of the Pope be added, proves that it pertains to the injury of the Holy Spirit and of our Lord Jesus Christ, because in Scripture the whole counsel of God has been delivered. But this reasoning holds against the interpretations of the Fathers just as much as against the Pope's; which will be seen more clearly if we add what he himself subjoins: The ancient orthodox taught that all heresies are to be refuted from Scripture ALONE, and that according to the word of God: Scripture is divinely inspired ... that the man of God may be complete, furnished for every good work.

units.la: Octavo, Scriptura sola conscientiae satisfacit. Mihi satisfecit. inquit Dovvnamus, quod Ambrosius Archippum Episcopum appellarit. Vide quantum distamus: mihi etenim e contra satisfacit, quod eum Paulus minime Episcopum Hierarchicum vocitarit, quodq; hujus muneris in literis sacris nullibi aliâs mentio fiat: Non enim oportet supra id quod scriptum est sapere 1 Cor. 4. 6, unde recte Ambrosius aliter; Sanctis Scripturis non loquentibus quis loquetur? Non abludit Gregorius magnus: Qui vere loqui desiderat e sacris sumere debet quid loquatur: ut omne quod loquitur, ad divinae authoritatis fundamentum revocet: quae cum Thomas Mortonus citet, Donnamum condemnat, qui absque ullo textus Paulini fundamento, Episcopum Archippum dicere ausus est, Episcopum nempe qualis jam in Anglia Hierarchicus viget. Citat & illa praecedentia ex Ambrosio alibi, cui addit Basilium: Quodcunque verbum vel factum corroborandum est divinae Scripturae testimonio, ad plerophoriam bonorum, & confusionem malorum: quasi absque Scripturae testimonio plerophoria nulla esse possit, quae conscientiam satisfaciat.
units.tr: Eighthly, Scripture alone satisfies the conscience. It satisfied me, says Downame, that Ambrose called Archippus a bishop. See how far apart we are: for me, on the contrary, it is satisfying that Paul never called him a hierarchical bishop, and that no mention of such an office is made anywhere else in the sacred writings. For we ought not to think beyond what is written (1 Cor. 4:6). Hence Ambrose rightly says otherwise: If the holy Scriptures are not speaking, who will speak? Gregory the Great does not disagree: whoever truly wishes to speak must take from the sacred writings what he says, so that everything he says is traced back to the foundation of divine authority. Thomas Morton cites these words and condemns Downame, who dared, without any foundation in Paul's text, to call Archippus a bishop, namely a bishop of the sort that now flourishes hierarchically in England. He also cites the earlier passage from Ambrose elsewhere, and adds Basil: Whatever word or deed needs to be confirmed by the testimony of divine Scripture, for the full assurance of the good and the confusion of the wicked; as if, without the testimony of Scripture, there could be no full assurance that satisfies the conscience.

units.la: Conf. Apol. p. 4. p. 547. De Eccles. li. 4. c. 2. & 16 De Pontif. Rom. l. 4. c. 2. p. 283. Apolog. p. 2. lib. 5. c. 9 Con. Gretz. p. 347.
units.tr: Conf. Apol. p. 4. p. 547. De Eccles. li. 4. c. 2. & 16 De Pontif. Rom. l. 4. c. 2. p. 283. Apolog. p. 2. lib. 5. c. 9 Con. Gretz. p. 347.

units.la: falsificat. Hinc Theodoretus: Non audeo dicere aliquid quod tacuit divina Scriptura. Tenerior scil. Theodoreto conscientia fuit, audacior Downamo, cujus praesumptionem in citandis patribus, reliquorumque Hierarchicorum confidentiam, ita refutat Augustinus: Vbi de re obscurissima ma disputatur, non adjuvantibus divinarum Scripturarum certis clarisque documentis, cohiberi se debet humana praesumptio. A Downamo ad Bancroftum transeamus, qui cum illud Carlwrighti de patribus exagitet, periculosum est super homines Ecclesiae politicam fundare: nonne aperte super homines absque periculo fidem disciplinarum fundari posse docet? Quam vero hoc absone ab eo dictum, demonstrat ustitata Apostoli phrasis, qui cum aliquid falsibiliter dictum efferre vellet, id secundum hominem dictum appellat: Roma. 3 : 5. 1 Cor. 9 : 8. Ratio in aperto est, Solus Deus verax, omnis autem homo mendax: unde recte Ambrosius: Ad illum doctorem Prophetam contendit, qui solus est magister verus. Quomodo enim potest quasi verum docere quod nesciat, cum ipse sit mendax? Et quidni Bancroftus Hierarchicos ipsos ponam alios, imprimis vero Thomam Bilsonum: qui ex Augustino statuit, Scripturas solas montes illos Israel esse, ubi TANTVN pascua saluberrima sunt, nihil autem venenosum, nihil alienum: sic ut quicquid extra eas est, refuendum nobis sit. Consonat huic quod alibi habet Augustinus: Per scripturas divinas multo tutius ambulatur: quas cum scrutari volumus, aut hoc inde exit, quod non habet controversiam, aut sit habet, ex eadem scriptura ubicunque inventis, atque adhibitis ejus testibus terminetur. Sequitur Thomas Mortonus Hierarchicus alius, qui ex Augustino scripturam solam stateram infallibilem, humanum vero quodcunque judicium dolosum probat. Non afferamus, inquit Augustinus, stateras dolosas, ubi appendamus quod volumus, & quomodo volumus pro arbitrio nostro, sed stateram divinam de Scripturis sanctis: in illis quid sit gravius appendamus, vel potius a Domino appensa recognosc amus. Adjungendum huic quod habet alibi: Recurro ad illam stateram dominicam, ubi non ex humano sensu sed ex authoritate divina, rerum momenta pensantur. Quid igitur? cum scriptura sola infallibilis sit, ex scriptura sola lux affulget, pax quieq, conscientiae, quae in dolosis patrum scriptis non reperitur. Concludendum igitur cum Iustino Martyre: Dixi tibi sedulo te operam dare debere (TV TVS ut sis in omnibus) ut Scripturis adhaereamus. cum Hilario: Bene habet ut sis TANTVM quae scripta sunt CONTENTVS sis. ad postremum cum Theodoreto: Decet te ACQUIESCERE Apostolicis & Prophetiis demonstrationibus.
units.tr: falsifies. Hence Theodoret: I do not dare to say anything that divine Scripture has passed over in silence. Theodoret's conscience was clearly more tender, and Downame's more bold; his presumption in citing the Fathers, and the confidence of the other hierarchical writers, is refuted thus by Augustine: Where a very obscure matter is being disputed, and without the help of the certain and clear documents of divine Scripture, human presumption ought to be restrained. Let us pass from Downame to Bancroft, who, while he assails Cartwright's saying about the Fathers, It is dangerous to found the polity of the Church upon men, does he not plainly teach that the faith of church disciplines can be founded upon men without danger? How absurd this statement of his is, the customary phrase of the Apostle shows, who, when he wished to state something in a fallible way, calls it spoken according to man (Rom. 3:5; 1 Cor. 9:8). The reason is obvious: God alone is true, but every man is a liar. Hence Ambrose rightly says: He appeals to that Teacher and Prophet who alone is the true master. For how can he teach as if it were true what he does not know, since he himself is a liar? And why should I not set against Bancroft other hierarchical writers, above all Thomas Bilson, who, following Augustine, lays down that the Scriptures alone are those mountains of Israel where there are the most wholesome pastures and nothing poisonous or foreign, so that whatever lies outside them must be rejected by us. This agrees with what Augustine says elsewhere: Through the divine Scriptures we walk far more safely; when we wish to examine a matter, either it comes out of them that there is no controversy, or, if there is one, it is to be settled from the same Scripture, wherever it is found, and by applying its witnesses. Thomas Morton, another hierarchical writer, follows him, and from Augustine proves that Scripture alone is the infallible balance, while any human judgment whatsoever is deceitful. Let us not bring, says Augustine, deceitful balances, on which we weigh what we want and how we want, as we please; but the divine balance drawn from the holy Scriptures: in them let us weigh what is weightier, or rather recognise what has been weighed by the Lord. To this should be added what he says elsewhere: I have recourse to that Lord's balance, where the weight of things is weighed not by human sense but by divine authority. What then? Since Scripture alone is infallible, it is from Scripture alone that light shines forth, and the peace of the conscience, which is not found in the deceitful writings of the Fathers. We must therefore conclude with Justin Martyr: I told you that you must diligently take pains (that you yourself may be in all things) to cling to the Scriptures. With Hilary: It is well that you should be content with ONLY what has been written. And finally with Theodoret: It becomes you to ACQUIESCE in the Apostolic and Prophetic demonstrations. [Ἐγὼ δὲ μόνῃ πιστεύω τῇ θείᾳ γραφῇ] — I believe in the divine Scripture alone.

units.la: Nono, scriptura sola conscientiam obligat: Vnus siquidem legislator est Iesus Christus in verbo suo edicta sua omnia proponens, qui solus potest salvare & perdere: Iac. 4 : 12. ac proinde interim legate & solvere, quae Matheus Sutclivus ad externam Ecclesiae politeiam accommodasse repertus est. Quod ad pastores autem, recte a Mortono Hierarchico approbatum Hieronymi illud: Quod de scripturis sanctis non non habet authoritatem, eadem cum facilitate contemnitur, quia probatur. Sic Lactantius: Nihil habent ponderis humana praecepta, quae authoritate majori, id est divina carent. Sic Augustinus: Quia non est Canonicum, non me astringit. Rursus: In hominem quemlibet liber sum. Rursus: Nec ego Arimimensis concilij authoritate, nec tu Nicaeni decineris. Rursus: In opusculis posteriorum liberum habet lector auditorum judicium, quo vel approbet, vel improbet: non cum credendi necessitate, sed cum judicandi libertate, legenda sunt.
units.tr: Ninthly, Scripture alone binds the conscience: For there is one lawgiver, Jesus Christ, who sets out all his commands in his word, and who alone is able to save and to destroy (Jas. 4:12). Accordingly, whatever Matthew Sutcliffe has been found to have adapted to the external polity of the Church, let them be bound and loosed by no one for the time being. As for the ministers, that saying of Jerome, approved by the hierarchical Morton, is rightly applied: What lacks authority from the holy Scriptures is despised with the same ease with which it is asserted. So Lactantius: Human precepts have no weight, since they lack a greater authority, that is, a divine one. So Augustine: Because it is not canonical, it does not bind me. Again: I am free with respect to any man whatever. Again: I am bound neither by the authority of the Council of Arminum nor by you by the decrees of Nicaea. Again: In the writings of later authors the reader has a free judgment of the hearers, by which he may either approve or disapprove; they are to be read not under compulsion to believe, but with freedom to judge.

units.la: Multa ejusmodi testimonia proferri possunt: sed properandum ad extremum hujus orationis est: breviter igitur sententias eas patrum proponam, quibus solam scripturam in omni controversia Theologica valere volunt, seclusis hominum quorumcunque authoritatibus. Ita Irenaeus: Polycarpus docuit quae ab Apostolis didicerat quae & Ecclesia tradit & SOLA sunt vera. Ita Clemens Alexandrinus: Non satis est solum absolute dicere quod visum est, sed oportet etiam probare... ex voce Domini, quae est magis fide digna quam quaevis demonstratio, vel potius quae est SOLA demonstratio, &c. Ita Cyprianus: Si SOLUS Christus audiendus est, non debemus attendere quid aliquis ante nos faciendum putaverit, sed quid (qui ante omnes est) Christus prior fecerit: nec enim hominis consuetudinem sequi oportet, sed Dei veritatem. Ita Lactantius: Sola scriptura sanctis opus est. Rursus: Doctrina caelestis SOLA sapientia est. Iterum: Cypr. captus eximia cognitione sacrarum literarum ut eis SOLIS contentus esset, quibus constat fides. Ita Gregorius Nyssenus: Dei verbum, UNICA vitae norma. Ita Ambrosius: Christus est solus quem nemo deserere debet, nemo mutare: cui bene dicitur, Domine ad quem ibimus? verba vitae aeternae habes. Ita Augustinus: Ego solis eis scripturarum libris qui jam Canonici appellantur, didici hunc timorem honoremque deferre, ut nullum eorum authorem scribendo aliquid erravisse firmissime credam. Alios autem ita lego, ut quantalibet sanctitate doctrinaque praepolleant, non video verum puteum, quia ipse senserunt, sed quia mihi vel per illos authores canonicos, vel ratione probabili persuadere potuerunt. Ita Vincentius Lyrinensis: SOLVS scripturae canon sibi ad universa sufficit: & ante apertius: SOLVS Canon scripturae ad omnis satis superque sufficit. Ita August. rursus: In quorumlibet hominum scriptis sum liber: quia SOLIS Canonicis debeo sine ulla recusatione consensum. Ita Chrysostomus: Nullo modo cognoscitur Ecclesia, nisi solummodo per scripturas. Ita Iohannes Cassianus: SOLA ad dictorum confirmationem, rerum sufficit demonstratio, quando probatio in authoritate dicentis est. Ita Origenes: Vide quam proximi periculis fiant by qui exerceri in divinis literis negligunt, ex quibus solis hujusmodi examinationis agnoscenda discretio est. Accedant his vel ex ipsis Hierarchicis nonnulli. Isaacus Casaubonus etsi ante duo constituisset, verbum DEI & antiquitatem, Pag. 25. ad postremum tamen nempe Pagina 33. ita scribit. Dogmata fidei a sola scriptura sacra peti debent, neque a quorumvis mortalium authoritate pendent. sed a verbo Dei duntaxat, quo suam ipse nobis voluntatem per Spiritum Sanctum declaravit. Patribus enim & Ecclesiae veteri, fidei articulos cliciendia sacra scriptura & explicandi ius fuisse, novos articulos commi-niscendi nullum jus fuisse. Thomae Mortoni Hierarchici alterius, haec thesis est adversus traditiones posita. Quemadmodum verbum scriptum iudicij Ecclesiastici principium verum esse liquet: sic idem quoque vivum esse demonstrabimus. Approbat alibi illud Cajetani: Solis scripturis reservata est haec authoritas, ut ideo id ita esse credamus, quia ita scripserunt. In eandem sententiam concedit Henricus Pareus Episcopus Gloceftrensis in sua versione Reynoldiana. Exprobrat Bristous Castellum protestantium solius scripturae infirmum & mentitium esse: Mot. 48, respondet Reynoldus, castellum hoc scripturae solius validius esse, quam ut portae tenebrarum adversus illud praevalere possint. Accedit postremo Hadrianus Saravia. Citat etenim ex Hieronymo Zanchio & probat illam apud Theodoretum, in Arpinn Christiani hominis vocem Ἐγὼ δὲ μόνῃ πιστεύω τῇ θείᾳ γραφῇ[?]. Ego solis scripturae fido. Ex his luce clarius constat, & ipsis patribus & sibi ipsis Hierarchicos bellum indicere, si nos de patrum contemptu fuggillare non desistant, ipsi nuda sanctorum patrum testimonia promere minimè cessent: totam hanc denique disciplinariam quaestionem, ex solis scripturae authoritate, sepositis patrum quorumcumque calculis, terminari non patiantur,
units.tr: Many testimonies of this kind can be produced, but I must hasten to the end of this discourse; I will therefore briefly set out those sayings of the Fathers by which they wish Scripture alone to be valid in every theological controversy, with the authority of all men set aside. Thus Irenaeus: Polycarp taught what he had learned from the Apostles, which both the Church hands down and which ALONE is true. Thus Clement of Alexandria: It is not enough merely to state absolutely what seems right, but one must also prove it... from the voice of the Lord, which is more worthy of belief than any demonstration, or rather which is ALONE the demonstration, etc. Thus Cyprian: If Christ ALONE is to be heard, we ought not to consider what someone before us thought should be done, but what Christ, who is before all, did first; for we ought to follow not human custom but the truth of God. Thus Lactantius: Scripture alone is needed by the saints. Again: Heavenly teaching is ALONE wisdom. Again: Cyprian, having been taken up with an outstanding knowledge of the sacred letters, so that he was content with THOSE ALONE on which the faith rests. Thus Gregory of Nyssa: The word of God is the SINGLE rule of life. Thus Ambrose: Christ is the only one whom no one ought to forsake or change, to whom it is rightly said: Lord, to whom shall we go? Thou hast the words of eternal life. Thus Augustine: I have learned to pay this fear and honour ONLY to those books of Scripture which are now called canonical, so that I most firmly believe that none of their authors erred in writing anything. But the other writers I read in such a way that, however much they excel in holiness and learning, I do not regard them as the true well, because they themselves thought so, but because they were able to persuade me by means of those canonical authors or by probable reasoning. Thus Vincent of Lérins: The canon of Scripture ALONE is sufficient for all things; and earlier, more openly: The canon of Scripture ALONE is more than sufficient for all things. Thus Augustine again: I am free in the writings of any men whatever, because I owe my assent without any refusal ONLY to the canonical books. Thus Chrysostom: The Church is known in no way except ONLY through the Scriptures. Thus John Cassian: For the confirmation of what is said, ALONE the demonstration of things suffices, when the proof rests on the authority of the speaker. Thus Origen: See how near to danger those are who neglect to exercise themselves in the divine letters, from which ALONE the discernment of such an examination is to be recognised. To these let me add some of the hierarchical writers themselves. Isaac Casaubon, though he had earlier laid down two things, the word of God and antiquity (p. 25), nevertheless at last, namely on p. 33, writes thus: The dogmas of faith ought to be sought from holy Scripture alone, and do not depend on the authority of any mortals whatever, but from the word of God only, by which he himself has declared his will to us through the Holy Spirit. For it was lawful for the Fathers and the ancient Church to draw out the articles of faith and explain them from holy Scripture, but it was not lawful to devise new articles. This thesis of another hierarchical writer, Thomas Morton, is laid down against tradition: Just as the written word is clearly the true principle of ecclesiastical judgment, so I will demonstrate that the same is also living. Elsewhere he approves that saying of Cajetan: This authority is reserved to the Scriptures alone, so that we believe a thing to be so because they have written it so. Henry Parry, Bishop of Gloucester, agrees with this opinion in his version of Reynolds. Bristow reproaches the Protestants' stronghold of Scripture alone as weak and fictitious (Mot. 48); Reynolds replies that this stronghold of Scripture alone is too strong for the gates of hell to prevail against it. Last of all comes Adrian Saravia. For he cites from Jerome Zanzius and proves it from Theodoret, where a certain Christian man says in Arpinum: [Ἐγὼ δὲ μόνῃ πιστεύω τῇ θείᾳ γραφῇ] — I trust in Scripture alone. From these things it is clearer than light that the hierarchical writers both wage war on the Fathers and on themselves, if they do not cease to stigmatise us for despising the Fathers; if they do not cease to put forward the bare testimonies of the holy Fathers; and, finally, if they do not allow this whole question of discipline to be settled from the authority of Scripture alone, with the reckonings of any Fathers whatever set aside.

units.la: CAP 3. Adversariorum argumenta, & primò ab antiquitate
units.tr: CAP 3. The arguments of our opponents, and first from antiquity

units.la: Oppount tamen firmamenta alia, varia quidem, sed Papistica omnia: sic ut in eis verum sit quod Tertullianus: Auferab haereticis, quae cum Ethnicis sapiunt, ut de scripturis solis quaestiones suas sistant, & stare non poterunt.
units.tr: They do, however, set up other defences, various in kind but all of them Papist, so that what Tertullian says holds true of them: Let the heretics, who savour of the heathen, be taken away, so that they may base their questions on Scripture alone, and they will not be able to stand.

units.la: Primum autem omnium, generali nomine Antiquitas est: cujus fundamentum Hierarchicum ita ponit [Hadrianus Saravia: Antiqui Patres sunt interrogandi de semitis antiquis, movendi enim non sunt termini quos constituerunt Patres. Hesterni enim nos sumus & ignoramus: quoniam sicut umbra dies nostri supra terram: Iob: 8. 9,
units.tr: First of all, under the general heading of antiquity, the Hierarchists lay their foundation thus [Hadrian Saravia]: The ancient Fathers are to be asked about the ancient paths; for the boundaries which the Fathers set are not to be moved. For we are of yesterday and know nothing, since our days upon earth are as a shadow. Job 8.9.

units.la: Primo dividendi hic Hierarchici sunt: quorum prima classis Hierarchiani, non jure divino sed humano statuminant. Horum ab antiquitate argumentum nullum esse potest, nisi forte istud: Quanquam in verbo Episcopatus introductus non sit, rejiciendus tamen minimè est, quia ab antiquo rationabiliter introductus. Atqui haec ipsissima Constantiensis Concilij ab omnibus jamdiu explosa cantilena est. Etiamsi a Christo caena sub utraque specie administrata sit: quum tamen diversa consuetudo ab Ecclesia & sanctis patribus rationaliter introducta & diutissime obseruata sit, habenda iam est pro lege. Qui vero Apostolicam ordinationem prætendunt; Ignatium scriptorum antiquissimum citare solent, qui semiporibus Iohannis Apostoli posterioris vixit: sic ut Episcopos ab Apostolis, Iohanne præsertim approbatos fuisse, necesse sit. Atqui hæc ipsissima C. Cæsaris Baronij, pro Ecclesiasticis ordinibus cæteris, Exorcistis, Acolutis &c. ratiocinatio est: sic enim habet. Licet trium tantum, Episcoporum, presbyterorum & Diaconorum in scripturis mentio fiat: Ignatius tamen plures commemorat, ita tum temporibus Apostolorum, ab eis approbatos fuisse necesse est.
units.tr: First, the Hierarchists must be divided. The first class, the Hierarchians, maintain their office not by divine right but by human institution. From antiquity they can have no argument for this, except perhaps this one: although the word "episcopate" is not introduced in Scripture, it is by no means to be rejected, because it was introduced long ago and for good reason. Yet this very song of the Council of Constance has long since been hooted down by everyone. Even though Christ administered the Lord's Supper under both kinds, yet since a different custom was reasonably introduced by the Church and the holy Fathers and has been observed for a very long time, it is now to be held as law. Those who put forward apostolic ordination usually cite Ignatius, the most ancient writer, who lived in the later days of the Apostle John, so that bishops must have been approved by the Apostles, and especially by John. Yet this very reasoning is that of Caesar Baronius concerning the other ecclesiastical orders, exorcists, acolytes and so on. For thus he says: Although mention is made in Scripture of only three orders, of bishops, presbyters and deacons, Ignatius nevertheless mentions more; therefore in the times of the Apostles they must have been approved by them.

units.la: Secundò, Antiquitas revera pro nobis est; qui cum Tertulliano contestari possumus. Antiquior omnibus est veritas, hoc mihi proficit. Antiquitas præstructa divinâ literaturâ: ac tum etiam adversus hostes hanc antiquitatem plane divinam violantes contestari. Laudatis semper antiquitatem & nova de die vivitis, per quod ostenditur, dum a bonis maiorum institutis deceditis, ea vos retinere & custodire quæ non debuistis, cum quæ debuistis non custoditis. Atque hanc solam antiquitatem quæ divinâ literaturâ præstructa est sequendam vel ipsi Hierarchici demonstrabunt. Quid Guilielmus Barlow Episcopus Lincolniensis? Quod ad antiquitatem (inquit) attinet, eam iudicium postulamus dum modo ea sit, ad quam provocat Ignatius. Quid M. Sutclivius? Christus inquit nobis ut olim, Ignatio sola (audi) antiquitas esse debet: & ut recte Auctor Quæst. nov. & vet. Testament. 144. adversus Paganos religionis suæ antiquitatem objicientes, antiquitas & consuetudo non præjudicant veritati. Vtitur etiam testimonio Arnobij: Religionis authoritas non tempore æstimanda est, sed numine. Neque enim quo die sed quid colere cœperis invenieris conuenit: quod verum est, prius non est. Prodeat postremò in medium Richardus Eyldus Hierarchicus alius, qui totam hanc rem limâte & accuratè, pro nobis disputat. Antiquitas, inquit, primaria est, vel secundaria. Primaria est primæva cuiusque rei origo, & hæc nota bonitatis & perfectionis est iuxta illud Tertulliani: Veritas in omnibus imaginem antecedit, posterior similitudo sequitur. Rursus: Id verum quodcumque primum, id adulterum quodcumque posterius. Secunda is antiquitas est eorum quæ diu ante cæperunt, & a quorum prima origine, longus temporis decursus fluxit: & hæc antiquitas veritatis nota non est, iuxta Cyprianum: Non debemus attendere quid aliquis ante nos fecerit, aut faciendum vel ubi erit, sed quid qui ante omnes est Christus prior fecerit. Neque enim bonitatis coniunctum ... Hac bonitas dei: Patroni... non debemus est consuetudine præscribendum, sed ratione vincendum. Et rursus: Consuetudo sine veritate vetustas erroris est. Quid igitur? Vel ipsis Hierarchicis iudicibus, antiquitate scripturaria sola pugnandum est: Episcopatus Anglicanus Hierarchicus hac destitutus, adulteratus Episcopatus est, & veri imago tantum, si tamen imago: Hierarchia Anglicana nihil eo melior est, quod sit antiqua, quædam enim antiquitas
units.tr: Second, antiquity is truly on our side, and we can call it to witness with Tertullian: Truth is older than all things; this profits me. Antiquity is prestructured by divine writings, and it is to be invoked also against enemies who violate this antiquity, which is wholly divine. You always praise antiquity and live by the novelties of the day, by which it is shown that, while you depart from the good institutions of your ancestors, you retain and keep those things which you ought not, and do not keep those which you ought. And that the only antiquity to be followed is that which is prestructured by divine writing, the Hierarchists themselves will demonstrate. What does William Barlow, Bishop of Lincoln, say? As to antiquity, he says, we demand that it be judged, provided it is that to which Ignatius appeals. What does M. Sutcliffe say? Christ, he says, to us as once to Ignatius: antiquity alone (listen) ought to be the rule. And as the author of the Quaestiones novi et veteris Testamenti rightly says (144), against the pagans who object the antiquity of their religion, antiquity and custom do not prejudice truth. He also uses the testimony of Arnobius: The authority of religion is not to be judged by time but by the divine will. For it is not the day on which you began to worship that matters, but what you began to worship; that is true, and what is earlier is not thereby truer. Lastly, another Hierarchist, Richard Field, comes forward, who argues this whole matter carefully and accurately on our side. Antiquity, he says, is either primary or secondary. Primary is the first origin of each thing, and this is a mark of goodness and perfection, according to that saying of Tertullian: Truth goes before the image in all things; the likeness follows later. Again: Whatever is first is true; whatever is later is adulterated. Secondary antiquity is that of things which began long ago and from whose first origin a long course of time has flowed; and this antiquity is not a mark of truth, according to Cyprian: We ought not to attend to what someone did before us, or what ought to be done or where it will be, but to what Christ, who is before all, did first. For goodness is not joined to ... by custom, but is to be conquered by reason. And again: Custom is not to be prescribed by [the rule of] truth, but overcome by reason. Custom without truth is only the antiquity of error. What then? Even by the Hierarchists' own judgement, the battle must be fought with antiquity drawn from Scripture alone. The English Episcopate, destitute of this, is a corrupted episcopate, and only the image of the true one, if indeed it is an image. The English Hierarchy is no better for being ancient, for there is some antiquity

units.la: {y} [illegible, ~3 letters] quitas, vetustas tantummodo erroris est: Postremo iniquè contemptum antiquitatis reformatis ministris obiiciunt: cum non consuetudine præ-scribendum, sed ratione sola a sacris petita vincendum sit.
units.tr: {y} [illegible, ~3 letters] quitas, mere age is only the age of error. Lastly, they charge the reformed ministers with unjustly despising antiquity, since it must be overcome not by custom which prescribes, but by reason alone, drawn from the sacred writings.

units.la: Tertiò, antiquitatem patrum nostrorum sequi in rebus divinis, peccatum est, & a spiritu sancto vetitum: id quod Thomas Bilsonus ipse Hierarchicus non præterijt, De obiectione etenim papistarum quæ ab antiquitate ducitur verba faciens, ita respondet: Quid vobis in mentem venit, cum de religione judicadi viam præscribere, quam Deus in verbo suo prohibuit? Ne ambuletis in statutis patrum vestrorum. Ego sum Dominus Deus vester: in statutis meis ambulate: Ezech. 20. Accedamus ad hanc ipsam causam propius. Gregorius Hamburgensis ita: Papæ vinum prostitutionis affuefactione Sophisticarum propinat: quæ, prava non dico consuetudine sed corruptela, inebriati, putant omnem talem prostitutionem, ex divina institutione ortam. Rectè hic vinum meretricium: Ap. 17.24. interpretatur. Quid enim aureum poculum illud, quàm species ementita antiquitatis & successionis, qua creditur esse, prostitutam Antichristi authoritatem, ex divina institutione ortam fuisse? Nonne igitur verentur Hierarchici, antiquitatem vendere? muta enim nomen Papæ in nomen Episcopi, & verè etiam de Hierarchia Anglicana narratur hæc Gregorij fabula: factum scilicet jam esse, prava antiquitatis opinione ut ex divina institutione fluxisse putetur. Ap. 13.2. Papatus assimilatur Pantheræ: quid ita togo? quia Pantheræ ad instar capitis torvitatè in vepreto aliquo occultantis, corpus verò in propatulo collocantis, ut illius pulchritudine & odore allliciantur bestiæ; terrorem tyrannidis suæ quantum potest palliat, velo antiquitatis & successionis: quarum specie, quasi doctrina quadam, illecti & capti incautiores, ab intuenda fœditate illa quæ intus est oculos avertunt. Pudeat homines Evangelicos hujus turpitudinis: ac proinde tyrannicam dominationem suam, cessent Hierarchici, antiquitatis fuco tinire; sapiant vero, quibus mentem Deus indidit, ne hujusmodi Pantherino odore aliquo decipiantur: Ap.13.12. Facit ut terra & ipsius incolæ adorent illam bestiam cujus curata fuerat plaga lethalis. & v.14. faciat imaginem bestiæ, quæ gladio vulnerata fuit, sed revixit & v.deniq; 15. Datum ei est ut animaret imaginem bestiæ, ut etiam loquatur imago bestiæ & faciat ut quicunque non adorarint imaginem bestiæ, occidantur. Quid hæc? cur primam bestiam adorari jubet? Antichristus, nisi ut emeritò antiquitatis nomine se commendaret, quasi nihil sibi novum venditaret, sed primam illam tantùm dignitatem revocaret, quæ nupero vulnere plagaque sua, intercisa fuisset? Neq; aliud quicquam imago primæ & antiquæ bestiæ & facta & animata, quàm Papatus ementito antiquitatis nomine, & erectus & potens factus, hoc colore: quòd nihil novi obtrudatur, sed imago tantùm illius & umbra revocetur, cujus veritas prioribus temporibus extitit. Nihil igitur antiquitatem eandem venditando agunt Hierarchici, nisi ut de eis dicatur: qualis mater, talis filia: scilicet ut ortus Episcopatus Hierarchici Antichristiani ita & progressus etiam eiusdem artificiis statuminatur & illinc Antichristus, & hic Episcopus Anglicanus: non nisi primâ bestia ille, non hic alius quàm Episcopus priscus esse vult: ille imago haberi cupit antiquorum Pontificum Romanorum, hic antiquorum Episcoporum, qui in Ecclesia primitiva floruerunt.
units.tr: Third, to follow the antiquity of our fathers in divine matters is a sin, and forbidden by the Holy Spirit. Thomas Bilson, himself a Hierarchist, did not pass this over; speaking of the Papists' objection drawn from antiquity, he answers thus: What has come into your mind, to prescribe a way of judging religion which God has forbidden in his word? "Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers. I am the Lord your God: walk in my statutes." Ezek. 20. Let us come closer to this very matter. Gregory of Hamburg says: The Pope gives the wine of prostitution to drink through the habituation of sophistries, and those who are drunk on it, not on bad custom I say but on corruption, think that every such prostitution arose from divine institution. He rightly interprets this as the wine of the harlot: Ap. 17.24. For what is that golden cup but the counterfeit appearance of antiquity and succession, by which the prostituted authority of Antichrist is believed to have arisen from divine institution? Do the Hierarchists not fear, then, to sell antiquity? Change the name Pope into the name Bishop, and this tale of Gregory is told truly of the English Hierarchy as well: namely, that by a corrupt opinion of antiquity it has already come about that it is thought to have flowed from divine institution. Ap. 13.2. The Papacy is compared to a panther. Why so? Because the panther hides its head in some thicket with a fierce look, but places its body in the open, so that beasts are lured by its beauty and smell. The Papacy veils the terror of its tyranny as far as it can with the veil of antiquity and succession. By the appearance of these, as if by some teaching, the more incautious are enticed and captured, and they turn their eyes away from looking at that foulness which lies within. Let Evangelical men be ashamed of this baseness; and therefore let the Hierarchists cease to disguise their tyrannical domination with the paint of antiquity. Let those to whom God has given minds be wise, lest they be deceived by any such panther-like odour. Ap. 13.12. It makes the earth and its inhabitants worship that beast whose deadly wound had been healed. And v. 14, it makes an image of the beast which was wounded by the sword but revived. And finally v. 15: It was given to it to animate the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast also speaks, and causes whoever does not worship the image of the beast to be killed. What is this? Why does it order the first beast to be worshipped? Would Antichrist not commend himself under the name of antiquity, as if deservedly, so that he sells nothing new but merely recalls that first dignity which had been cut off by its recent wound and blow? Nor is the image of the first and ancient beast, both made and animated, anything other than the Papacy, raised up and made powerful under the false name of antiquity, with this colour: that nothing new is thrust upon us, but only its image and shadow is recalled, whose truth existed in earlier times. Therefore, by selling this same antiquity, the Hierarchists do nothing other than deserve to have it said of them: Such a mother, such a daughter. That is, just as the origin of the Antichristian Hierarchical episcopate is established by such devices, so is its progress; and thence Antichrist, and here the English Bishop. The former wishes to be taken for nothing other than the first beast, the latter for nothing other than the ancient bishop. The former wishes to be held the image of the ancient Roman Pontiffs, the latter the image of the ancient bishops who flourished in the primitive Church.

units.la: Quartò, antiquitas (inquit Matheus Sutclivius) veritatis nota esse non potest, quia separatur, & falsis sectis convenit: Atque hoc eodem argumento. Thomas Mortonus Hierarchicus, hoc ab antiquitate argumentum Papisticum confodit. Eo usque (inquit) est, mulier Samaritana adversus Christum. Patres nostri adorarunt in monte hoc: Ioan. 4. nec falso: nam referente Carolo Sigonio prius in Zilo quàm in Ierusalem invocatum Dei nomen est. Pharisaei etiam (inquit) hoc argumento antiquitatis adversus Christum usi sunt, unde ipsius Christi illud, Math. 5. Dictum est vobis ab antiquo, at ego contrarium huic emendo antiquitati doceo. Symachus etiam (inquit) hoc argumento antiquitatis, Ethnicissimum suum apud Theodosium, confirmavit. Servanda est tot saeculis fides nostra, & sequendi sunt maiores nostri, qui secuti sunt felicitèr suos. Respondet Ambrosius: Reprehendit messem quia sera fœcunditas est: reprehendit vindemiam quia in anni occasu est: reprehendit olivam quia postremus est fructus. Messis nostra fides est quæ ab ortu mundi manebat in sanctis: explosa igitur ea opinione quæ ante convaluit, id quod erat verum iure prælatum est. Iure inquit Ambrosius, Christiana religio quanquam quasi messis sero & in anni quasi occasu renovata est apud Gentiles, quia quanquam Ethnicismus adversus eandem convaluisset, antiqua tamen erat & quæ in ipso mundi exortu constituta. Quid ni de Senioribus idem ratiocinari liceat? Prævaluit error adversus disciplinam presbyterialem: quid tum? in ipso exortu Evangelij à Christo institutâ est: ita antiqua satis est, dignaque, quæ etsi sero, & quasi messis in anni occasu revocetur: Sed ad rem. Patres sanctissimi (inquit Lotus) nobis aperte favent & non solùm quæ suis quisque libris privatim scripserunt, sed quæ decreverunt in Synodis communi consensu, in subsidium nobis militant: At ista de Patribus antiquis iactantia Papistis communis est, quorum clamores ut retundantur consulatur Iuellus, qui ostendit, communes eos iam ante haereticis plurimis fuisse. At falsè, inquies, illi patres ingeminarunt, quod & nunc Papistæ. Quid, Origenis libros prorsus false allegarunt Ariani? Quod ad Papistas, in nonnullis nonnunquam adæque ac ipsi Hierarchici patres citant: & in nonnullis adæq; hi atq; illi falso. Sed quid semper verè? Vere etenim Whitakerus: Urgent contra nos quanta contentione possint patres. Quid si essent nobis infesti, nec eis res, ondere possimus? non tamen hoc latere causam nostram debent: quia fides nostra, non ex patribus, sed ex scripturis pendet.
units.tr: Fourthly, antiquity (says Matthew Sutcliffe) cannot be a mark of truth, because schismatics and false sects also lay claim to it, and it is the same argument again. The Hierarchist Thomas Morton demolishes this Papist argument from antiquity. "So far," he says, "was the Samaritan woman against Christ: 'Our fathers worshipped on this mountain' (John 4)." Nor is this untrue, for, as Carolus Sigonius reports, the name of God was invoked at Silo before it was invoked at Jerusalem. The Pharisees also, he says, used this argument from antiquity against Christ, and hence Christ's own words in Matthew 5: "It was said to you of old," but I teach the contrary to that ancient view. Symmachus too, he says, confirmed his plea for the pagan altar before Theodosius by this argument from antiquity: "Our faith must be kept for so many centuries, and we must follow our ancestors, who followed happily." Ambrose replies: "He finds fault with the harvest because its fruitfulness is late; he finds fault with the vintage because it comes at the end of the year; he finds fault with the olive because it is the last fruit. Our harvest is the faith which remained in the saints from the beginning of the world. So when that opinion which grew strong earlier has been cast out, what was true has rightly been preferred." Rightly, says Ambrose, the Christian religion, though renewed among the Gentiles late, as it were in the harvest, and as it were at the end of the year, is nevertheless ancient, since although paganism had grown strong against it, it was established at the very beginning of the world. Why, then, should we not reason the same way about the elders? The error against presbyterial discipline has prevailed; so what? It was instituted by Christ at the very beginning of the gospel. So it is ancient enough and worthy, even if it is recalled late, like a harvest at the year's end. But to the point. "The most holy Fathers," says Lotus, "clearly favour us, and not only what each has written privately in his own books, but what they have decided in councils by common consent, fights on our side." But this boasting about the ancient Fathers is common to the Papists, whose clamours are to be beaten back by consulting Jewel, who shows that many heretics had already made the same claims before them. "But falsely," you will say, "those Fathers were repeated, as the Papists now repeat them." What then? Did the Arians not cite the books of Origen quite falsely? As for the Papists, they sometimes cite some things just as the Hierarchist Fathers do, and in some cases both sides cite falsely alike. But what is always true? Truly Whitaker says: "They press against us with as much contention as they can muster. What if they were hostile to us, and we could not refute them? Yet they ought not to conceal from themselves that our cause does not stand: for our faith depends not on the Fathers but on the Scriptures."

units.la: Quinto, antiquitas nota veritatis esse non potest, quia (ut rursus Matheus Matthæus Sutcliffius) obscura est: multa enim videntur nova & inaudita, quæ revera antiqua sunt: Celso & Paganis religio Christiana nova videbatur: neque aliud nomine Iudæos Hamah in odium adducere conabatur, quàm quòd novas quasdam haberent leges: Heft. 3. & Christi doctrinam Pharisæi ut novam despexerunt: & Paulus denique apud Athenienses novitatis convicio exceptus est: quo igitur evanuerunt clamores Hierarchici illi, quas adversus Reformatos ciebant, de novitate nescio qua, & Innovatione? Certè ubi novitatem maximè exagitat Puritanorum Cornelius Scultingius, non tam novitatis studio, quàm Romani Pontificis odio tribuit quòd omnem penitus primatum abolendum exi-stimemus: & H. Saravia: luce clarius omnibus videre volentibus constare dicit, primos Ecclesiarum reformatores nullo rerum novarum studio permotos fuisse, sed sincero candore, solum veræ pietatis restitutionem sibi in animo propositum esse. De re ipsa verò in promptu nobis cum Arnobio respondere. Sed quod nos agimus novum est, quod hoc, prisum. Et quid hoc aut vos juvat aut causam nostram contristat? Religionis authoritas non est tempore metienda, sed numine: sed ne bonam causam prodere videamur, Omnipotens Deus novella res est? Sic Tertullianus: Hæreses non tam novitas quam veritas revincit: quodcunque contra veritatem sapit hæresis est, etiam vetus consuetudo. Sic deniq; Bernardus: Novitatem dico propter linguas hominum impiorum, qui cum maniféstum lumen obmubilare non queunt, de solo novitatis nomine cavillantur. Sed hæc novitas non est novella vanitas: res est enim antiquæ religionis: &c. Vereor ne hunc reatum Georgius Domnanus sibi attraxerit, qui cum disciplinam reformatam Genevæ primum constituitur fuisse affirmat anno 1541. & nondum annos 70. vidisse: quam propè accedit, ad illam similem papistarum calumniam, ad quam ita respondet Eyilius? Magna vanitas illius inepta objectionis est qui Ecclesiam nostram non Hierosolymis ortam dicunt, sed Wittenbergæ & Genevæ, in hac ætate mundi ultima. Eadem nempe utriusque calumniæ ratio est: tam justè illa disciplinæ, quam doctrinæ hæc impingitur: & perinde doctrinæ atque disciplina Genevæ noviter restituta est, neque ob id aliter nova tamen, quàm mandatum de charitate novum dicitur: Iohan. 13. Quia de novo redintegratum. Ad magistratum primò ista pertinent: cui ob oculos proponendum quod in jus Canonicum relatum est ex Augustino. Quum Deus aliquid contra morem jubet, etsi ibi nunquam factum est, tamen faciendum est, & si omissum est, restaurandum est: & si statutum non erat, instituendum est. Rufus: Si consuetudinem fortassis opponas, advertendum est, quod Dominus dicit, Ego sum via, veritas, & vita: non dixit, ego sum consuetudo, sed veritas. Certè ut beati Cypriani utamur sententia, quæ licet consuetudo, quantumvis vetusta, quantumvis vulgata veritati omnino est postponenda, & usus qui veritati est contrarius est abolendus. Pertinent hæc secundo ad advetarios, quibus regerendum Tertulliani illud. Fiderint, quibus novum um est quod sibi est vetus: nec non quod Gratianus habet ex Augustino: Frustra qui ratione convincuntur obiiciunt consuetudinem, quasi consuetudo sit major ratione. Pertinent postremò ista ad populares Anglicanos: ut clamoribus de novitate disciplinae reformatae Hierarchicis minimè perterreantur: sed serio considerent, quod monet Augustinus. Hic est mos Diabolicus, ut per antiquitatis traducem commendetur fallacia. Ægrè forte vobis est, quod disciplina reformari nequeat, ni evanescant magnifica Episcoporum Palatia, egregius praelatorum splendor violescat, abalienentur denique in usus alios pinguissimi reditus illi, quibus, tanto majorum vestrorum sumptu, Cathedrales Ecclesiae dotatae sunt. Sed nunquid res istiusmodi admiramini, dicit Christus? Luc.21.6. Male vos cepit parietum amor, habet Hilarius.
units.tr: Fifthly, antiquity cannot be a mark of truth, because (again, as Matthew Sutcliffe says) it is obscure: many things that are really ancient seem new and unheard of. To Celsus and the pagans the Christian religion seemed new; and Haman sought to bring the Jews into hatred for no other reason than that they had certain new laws (Esther 3). The Pharisees also despised Christ's doctrine as new; and Paul, finally, was met among the Athenians with the charge of novelty. Where, then, have those clamours of the Hierarchists gone, which they raised against the Reformed about I know not what novelty and innovation? Certainly where Cornelius Scultingius inveighs most against the novelty of the Puritans, he attributes it not so much to a zeal for novelty as to hatred of the Roman Pontiff, because we think all primacy must be abolished. And H. Saravia says that it is clearer than light to all who wish to see that the first reformers of the Churches were moved by no zeal for new things, but by sincere candour, and that they had in view only the restoration of true piety. As to the thing itself, we can answer in the words of Arnobius: what we do is new, what they do is old. And how does this help you, or trouble our cause? The authority of religion is not to be measured by time but by the divine will. But lest we seem to betray a good cause, is Almighty God a new thing? So Tertullian: "Heresies are refuted not so much by novelty as by truth: whatever savours against the truth is heresy, even if it is an old custom." So finally Bernard: "I say 'novelty' because of the tongues of impious men, who, since they cannot obscure the manifest light, carp only at the name of novelty. But this novelty is not a new vanity: it is the matter of the ancient religion," and so on. I fear that George Domnanus has incurred this charge, who affirms that the reformed discipline was first set up at Geneva in 1541, and that it has not yet seen seventy years. How closely does this come to that similar calumny of the Papists, to which Eyilius replies thus: "Great is the vanity of that foolish objection of those who say that our Church did not arise at Jerusalem but at Wittenberg and Geneva, in this last age of the world. The reasoning of the two calumnies is the same: the one is charged against discipline just as justly as the other against doctrine. And just as doctrine and discipline were newly restored at Geneva, they are not for that reason any the less new than the commandment of love is called new (John 13), because it was renewed." These things pertain first to the magistrate, before whose eyes must be set what canon law has taken from Augustine: "When God commands something against custom, even if it was never done there, it nevertheless must be done; and if it has been omitted, it must be restored; and if it was not established, it must be instituted." Rufus says: "If perhaps you should oppose custom, it must be noted that the Lord says, 'I am the way, the truth, and the life'; he did not say, 'I am custom,' but 'truth.'" Certainly, to use the sentence of blessed Cyprian, custom, however old, however widespread, must altogether give way to truth, and a practice contrary to truth must be abolished. These things pertain secondly to adversaries, to whom must be returned Tertullian's saying: "Let those believe who find new what is old to them." So too what Gratian has from Augustine: "Those who are refuted by reason object custom in vain, as if custom were greater than reason." Finally, these things pertain to the English people, so that they may not be terrified by the Hierarchists' clamours about the novelty of the reformed discipline, but may seriously consider what Augustine warns: "This is the devilish custom, that a fallacy is commended through the stock of antiquity." Perhaps it grieves you that discipline cannot be reformed unless the magnificent palaces of the bishops vanish, the splendour of the prelates grows dim, and, finally, those very rich revenues with which your ancestors at such great expense endowed the cathedral churches are alienated to other uses. But does Christ say you marvel at such things? (Luke 21:6). "The love of walls has ruined you," as Hilary has it.

units.la: Postremò videndum est ne cum Paganis consociemini de quibus Xavierius. Indi ne Christiani fierent, causam hanc afferebant, se à majoribus suis semper cultores extitisse, sacerdotibus suis Bontiis plurima largitos esse, sedes & domicilia excitasse, itaque se jam ad Christum si transferrent, omnem superioris vitae fructum, perdituros. Atque haec de extraneo firmamento Hierarchico primo, nempe antiquitate.
units.tr: Finally, you must see that you do not associate with pagans, of whom Xavier speaks. When the Indians were asked why they did not become Christians, they gave this reason: that they had always been worshippers from their ancestors, had given many gifts to their bonzes, and had built seats and homes; so if they now turned to Christ, they would lose all the fruit of their former life. And this is the first extraneous support of the Hierarchy, namely antiquity.

units.la: CAP 4.
units.tr: CHAP. 4.

units.la: Argumentum secundum adversariorum a visibili perduratione,
units.tr: The second argument of our opponents, from visible perpetuity.

units.la: Secundum à papistis perinde mutuatum est: Visibilis nempe perduratio, à qua Ricardus Bancroftus ratiocinatur, quum ex eo probat disciplinam reformatam à Christo nunquam iustitutam fuisse, quia nunquam in usu recepta est: sed gubernatio Episcopalis per annos plenos 1500. ad hodierna usq; tempora perduravit. Primò nihil hîc objicitur nobis, quàm quod Waldensibus majoribus nostris occinibatur. Num igitur majores nostri tamdiu erraverunt? tam multi hallucinati sunt. Hos nobiscum in disciplina conspirasse suo loco demonstrabitur: quod igitur Reynerius Pisanus de illis testimonium tulit id pro nostra etiam perduratione facit: Sic autem ille: Non est pestilentior secta quàm Leonistarum: Primò quia est diuturnior. Quidam dicunt, quòd duraverit a tempore Sylvestri, alij dicunt quòd a tempore Apostolorum. Non igitur à tempore Apostolorum Episcopus semper Anglicanus perduravit: sed à nonnullis forte etsi latentius, ut a Waldensibus, impugnatus potius est. Episcopum Anglicanum cum dico, eum secundum praxin Ecclesiae Anglicanae æstimo, quae hodie obtinet, cujus respectu, vere in eum recidunt quae Alexander Fabritius olim de Papalibus Episcopis scripsit: Superbi sacerdotes & praelati contra doctrinam & exemplum Iesu Christi, quasi reges gentium dominantur nantur : traditionibus superfluis, & constitutionibus iniquis suos opprimunt — humiles Christi servos persequuntur, & incarcerant — quia eorum voluptates reprehendunt. Quid igitur est? Contra exemplum & doctrinam Iesu Christi Episcopus iam hodie Anglicanus cùm apertè delinquat, verisimile nullo modo fuit eum temporibus Apostolorum perdurasse.
units.tr: The second argument has been borrowed from the Papists in the same way: namely, visible perpetuity, from which Richard Bancroft reasons. He argues that the reformed discipline was never instituted by Christ, because it was never received into use, whereas episcopal government has endured for a full 1500 years down to the present day.
