First, nothing is objected to us here except what was once chanted against our forefathers, the Waldenses: Have our forefathers, then, erred for so long? Have so many gone astray? That these men agreed with us in discipline will be shown in its proper place. What Reinerius of Pisa bore witness to concerning them also supports our own perpetuity. He writes: No sect is more pestilent than that of the Leonists. First, because it is of longer standing. Some say it has lasted from the time of Sylvester, others say from the time of the Apostles. Therefore the episcopate in the Anglican sense has not persisted from the time of the Apostles. Rather, it has been opposed, perhaps somewhat more quietly, by some, as by the Waldenses. When I say the Anglican bishop, I judge him by the practice of the Anglican Church that prevails today. With respect to this practice, what Alexander Fabritius once wrote about the Papal bishops falls precisely upon him: Proud priests and prelates, against the teaching and example of Jesus Christ, lord it over the nations as kings; they oppress their people with superfluous traditions and unjust constitutions; they persecute and imprison the humble servants of Christ, because they rebuke their pleasures. What then? If the Anglican bishop today openly sins against the example and teaching of Jesus Christ, it is in no way probable that he has persisted from the times of the Apostles.

units.la: Secundò, Bellar. probaturus religionem pontificiam veram, quia haereses nullae tamdiu durant, quamdiu illa duravit: causam suam his communit argumentis: 2Tim.3:9. Non proficient amplius, nam eorum amentia manifesta erit omnibus. Cypr. Systematici semper initio fervent, incrementa vero habere non possunt, sed statim prava sua aemulatione deficiunt. Augustinus : Non vos terreant fratres quidam fluvij qui vocantur torrentes : decurrit aqua, ad tempus strepit, mox cessabit : Multae haereses iam emortuae sunt, concurrent in rivis suis quantum potuerunt, decurrerunt, siccati sunt rivi, vix eorum memoria, vel quod fuerint. Quid ad haec nostri? respondent? Haec de omnibus haeresibus verum non esse, sed de quibusdam tantum : nam Mahometismus iam mille annos duravit, Arianismus mille ducentos. At haec extra Ecclesiam haereses grassabantur : in ipso gremio Ecclesiae tamdiu errorem aliquem duraße ostendi non potest, quamdiu Hierarchia Anglicana perduravit. Imò potest, idque altius repetito principio. Insto primo in errore liberi arbitrij, qui à Iustino Martyre incipiens, in patrum scriptis, ad tempus usque religionis reformatae perduravit. Quod Augustinus ei restiterit nihili est, duravit tamen : sic & Episcopo Hierarchico (quoad jus divinum praesertim) à patribus nonnullis restitum fuisse suo loco demonstrabitur. Insto secundò in errore de visione Dei : fusè etenim demonstrat Iohannes Reynoldus patres omnes uno consensu per quaque aetates credidisse, Animas sanctorum non videre in gloria faciem Dei, ante diem judicij. Insto tertiò in errore Millenario : nunquam etenim ante nostra tempora intellectus ille Iohannis de mille annis locus est, sed Chilliastarum somnium, per quaeque saecula perduravit. Atque si in hisce mihi fides non habeatur, audiatur Whitgiftus: Ferè omnes patres errore Millenariorum infecti fuerant. Fere omnes scriptores Graeci, Latini etiam pro majori parte doctrinis liberi arbitrij, Meriti, Invocationis sanctorum, & hujusmodi aliis, commaculati sunt. Insto postremò in errore de Antichristo : qui hanc ipsam causam nostram intimè attingit. Exaestuat Richardus Bancroftus, quod Patres multa ineptè & ridiculè de Antichristo scripsisse Cartwrightus dixerat. Quid igitur? Num ille negare potest, nugare Patres in doctrina de Antichristo, imò prorsus somniare, quinetiam caelo toto aberrare? addo etiam (quanquam nescientes) Antichristo viam communire, aditum patefacere? Iam vero Episcopatus Hierarchicus, Antichristi ovum erat : quid igitur mirum, si in Episcopo Hierarchico, quemadmodum in ipso Antichristo, antiqui Patres aberraverint? Operari vero coepit hoc mysterium iniquitatis etiam tempore
units.tr: Second, Bellarmine, wishing to prove the Papist religion true because no heresies last as long as it has lasted, fortifies his case with these arguments: 2 Tim. 3:9, They shall proceed no further, for their folly will be manifest to all. Cyprian: Heretical systems always burn fiercely at the beginning, but they cannot attain growth; they soon fail through their own perverse rivalry. Augustine: Let not certain streams called torrents frighten you, brethren. The water runs down, roars for a time, and soon ceases. Many heresies are already dead; they rushed along in their channels as hard as they could, they ran down, the channels dried up, and scarcely is there any memory of them, or even that they existed. How do our people answer this? They reply that this is not true of all heresies, but only of some: for Mahometanism has lasted a thousand years already, Arianism a thousand two hundred. But these were heresies running wild outside the Church. It cannot be shown that any error has lasted so long within the very bosom of the Church as the Anglican hierarchy has lasted. Indeed it can be shown, and by a principle traced from further back. I press first the error concerning free will, which, beginning with Justin Martyr, persisted in the writings of the Fathers down to the time of the reformed religion. That Augustine resisted it is of no account; it nonetheless persisted. So too, that the hierarchical bishop (especially as to divine right) was opposed by several Fathers will be shown in its proper place. I press secondly the error concerning the vision of God. For John Reynolds has demonstrated at length that all the Fathers, in one agreement through every age, believed that the souls of the saints do not see the face of God in glory before the day of judgement. I press thirdly the Millenarian error. For that interpretation of John's passage about the thousand years never existed before our times; it was the dream of the Chiliasts, and it persisted through every century. And if you do not give me credit in these matters, let Whitgift be heard: Almost all the Fathers had been infected with the error of the Millenarians. Almost all the Greek writers, and for the most part the Latin too, were stained by the doctrines of free will, of merit, of the invocation of saints, and other such things. I press lastly the error concerning Antichrist, which touches our very cause most closely. Richard Bancroft fumes that Cartwright had said the Fathers wrote many foolish and ridiculous things about Antichrist. What then? Can he deny that the Fathers trifled in the doctrine of Antichrist, indeed dreamed utterly, and even wandered wide of the whole heaven? Shall I add that, though unknowingly, they paved the way for Antichrist and opened his entrance? Now the hierarchical episcopate was the egg of Antichrist. What wonder, then, if the ancient Fathers went astray about the hierarchical bishop, just as they did about Antichrist himself? For this mystery of iniquity began to work even in the time

units.la: Whitak. c.2 q.5.6.4.
units.tr: Whitak. c.2 q.5.6.4.

units.la: Ceus. Apoc. Praesat.1.
units.tr: Ceus. Apoc. Praesat.1.

units.la: Surv.c.27. pag.343. pore Apostolorum, & cessare non debuit, donec homo peccati revelaretur: qui non ante tempora religionis reformatæ consumendus:
units.tr: Surv.c.27. pag.343. of the Apostles, and it ought not to have ceased until the man of sin was revealed, who was not to be destroyed before the times of the reformed religion.

units.la: 2. Thess. 2:8. En igitur apertam [?] error de Antichristo à primis temporibus per quæque sæcula perduravit. En etiam refutationem de Episcopo Hierarchico luculentam: perduravit ille; verum èst, sed ut mysterium iniquitatis perduravit: cujus fundamentum in hujusmodi Episcopatu positum & collocatum erat.
units.tr: 2 Thess. 2:8. Behold, then, an open [?] error about Antichrist, from the earliest times, has lasted through every century. Behold also a splendid refutation of the hierarchical bishop: he has lasted, that is true, but he has lasted as the mystery of iniquity, on whose foundation such an episcopate was laid and fixed.

units.la: Tertiò,cum visibilitatem Ecclesiæ suæ per omnia sæcula perdurantem urgent Papistæ, responderi à nostris solitum, de Ecclesia prædictum esse, eam in solitudinem fugatam iri: sic ut Ecclesia Romana vera esse non poterit, si modò semper visibilis extiterit,& nunquam in abdito delituerit. Hoc nomine consultiores multo Hierarchici fuissent, si hoc de visibili Hierarchiæ præduratione argumentum omisissent. Perpetuo perduravit Episcopatus dignitas, inquit Saravia: nam & in ipso Papatu verus semper Episcopus remansit. Itane vero? Ergo inquam, vera Christi disciplina, Hierarchia Episcopalis minimè est, quæ interrumpenda erat. Quid enim? Abdita in latiLulo Ecclesia ipsa est: Ap. 11.2? Ecclesiæ disciplina interim minimè abdita? Fugit Ecclesia ipsa in solitudinem Ap.12.6? Ecclesiæ disciplina non unà fugit? Sed & aliud quiddam est,quod hic urgendum. Si enim præcise agendum sit, dicendum omnino, corruptionem disciplinæ, per introductionem Episcopatus, causam unam inter cæteras extitisse, cur Ecclesia sese abdiderit,& in solitudinem avolarit. Quo enim tempore latebras Ecclesia circumspexit, nisi quando à tempore Constantini Episcopi grassari in Ecclesiæ libertatem inceperunt? id quod suo loco docebitur fusius. Tantum igitur abest quòd duratio non interrupta Reformatos lædat: ut nihil causam plus nostram juvet. Hinc enim perspicitur disciplinam reformatam veram esse, Episcopalem vero falsam: quòd illa unà cum muliere in solitudinem fugata sit: hæc pro sua parte mulierem fugarit, sic ut ejus pertæsa, latebras quærere cogeretur.
units.tr: Third, when the Papists press the visibility of their Church, which endures through all ages, our people are accustomed to answer that it was foretold of the Church that she would be driven into solitude, so that the Roman Church cannot be the true Church if she has always been visible and never hidden herself in concealment. On this count the hierarchists would have been far wiser had they omitted this argument from the visible perpetuity of the hierarchy. The dignity of the episcopate has endured without interruption, says Saravia, for even in the Papacy the true bishop always remained. Is that so? Then, I say, the true discipline of Christ is not the episcopal hierarchy, which ought to have been interrupted. For what? Is the Church herself hidden in the wilderness? Ap. 11.2? Is the discipline of the Church meanwhile not hidden at all? Does the Church herself flee into the wilderness, Ap. 12.6? Does the discipline of the Church not flee along with her? But there is also something else to press here. For if we must speak with precision, we must say without qualification that the corruption of discipline, through the introduction of the episcopate, was one cause among others why the Church hid herself and flew off into the wilderness. For at what time did the Church look about for hiding-places, if not from the time when bishops began to rage against the liberty of the Church, from the time of Constantine? This will be taught more fully in its proper place. So far, then, is uninterrupted duration from harming the Reformed, that nothing helps our cause more. For from this it is seen that the reformed discipline is true and the episcopal discipline false: the former fled into the wilderness together with the woman, while the latter, for its part, drove the woman away, so that, weary of her, it was compelled to seek hiding-places.

units.la: Quartò,affirmat Downamus, sicut Episcopi huc usque durarunt, ita alicubi ad finem sæculi duraturos,quod verum vigilantis somnium est ex illo Senecæ ortum. Quod nimis miseri volunt, id facile credunt. Ap. 18. 17. Prædicit Iohannes Hierarchiam Papalem desolatam iri: cujus partes enumerat. Primo prælatos majores (inter quos Episcopi) quos navium gubernatores appellat; secundò ordines inferiores quos nautas & remiges nuncupat. Intelligit, inquis, Episcopos quâ Papales. Quasi consideret ullibi Spiritus Sanctus Episcopos Hierarchicos, ut minime Papales? Intuere hujus vaticinij complementum: ex illo etenim quæ mens fuerit Spiritus sancti facillime innotescet. Circumferto oculos in Ecclesias reformatas, quæ Antichristum prorsus & penitus profligarunt, an in earum aliqua retinetur Episcopus Hierarchicus quasi minimè Antichristianus esset? Certè in singulis unà cum ipso Antichristo, quasi Antichristianus anus Episcopus Hierarchicus exulat. At contra in Anglia apparet, inquis. At inquam in Anglia hoc Iohannis vaticinium non adhuc adimpletum est: neque Antichristum Anglia prout debuit, omni ex parte profligavit. Quando adimplebitur vero, tam (quod de Angelo Laodicea, quæ Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ τυπος est, prædicit Iohannes, Episcopus in Anglia ex ore Christi evometur. Hæc de extraneo firmamento Hierarchico secundo, Visibili nempe perduratione.
units.tr: Fourth, Downame asserts that just as the bishops have lasted until now, so in some places they will last until the end of the age. This is a waking man's dream, derived from that saying of Seneca: What wretched men wish, they readily believe. Ap. 18.17. John foretells that the Papal hierarchy will be made desolate, and he enumerates its parts: first, the greater prelates (among whom are the bishops), whom he calls the masters of ships; second, the lower orders, whom he names sailors and oarsmen. You say he means the bishops insofar as they are Papal. As if the Holy Spirit anywhere considers hierarchical bishops as not at all Papal! Look at the fulfilment of this prophecy: from it the mind of the Holy Spirit will most easily become known. Let me cast my eyes over the reformed Churches, which have utterly and completely overthrown Antichrist. Is the hierarchical bishop retained in any of them, as though he were in no way Antichristian? Certainly in each of them the hierarchical bishop, as though Antichristian, has been banished together with Antichrist himself. But on the contrary, you say, it appears in England. But I reply: in England this prophecy of John has not yet been fulfilled, nor has England wholly overthrown Antichrist as it ought. When it is fulfilled, then (as John foretells of the Angel of Laodicea, who is the type of the Anglican Church) the bishop in England will be vomited out of the mouth of Christ. These things concerning the second external support of the hierarchy, namely visible perpetuity.

units.la: CAP. 5.
units.tr: CHAPTER 5.

units.la: Firmamentum tertium a perpetua successione Episcoporum refutatur.
units.tr: The third foundation, the perpetual succession of bishops, is refuted.

units.la: TErtium sequitur, à papistis similiter mutuatum. Successio nempe Episcoporum, ad hæc nostra usq; tempora continuata. Hadrianus siquidem Saravia, vocationem nullam extraordinariam agnoscens, & ordinationem solis Episcopis competere credens: successionem istam Episcoporum, non solùm extitisse dicit, sed & necessario extitisse: absque qua si fuissent Mart. Lutherus, Huld. Zwinglius, cæterique primi Evangelij reformatores, legitimè vocari nullo modo potuissent. Quid igitur sentiendum de ministris reformatis qui ab Episcopis non ordinantur? fortasse in casu necessitatis licere presbytero ordinare: de quo in præsenti nihil dicam, nisi quod Whitakerus: qui ita respondet Bellarmino, ex hoc Hadriani Saraviæ dogmate disputanti. Respondeo (inquit) Lutherum & reliquos illos nostros præclaros & nobiles heroas, fuisse presbyteros—ac proinde jure divino Episcopos: ergo quicquid ad Episcopos pertinet idem ad illos quoque jure divino pertinebat: nam quòd Episcopi postea presbyteris prælati sunt, is ordo humanus fuit ad schismata tollenda, ut historiæ testantur.
units.tr: The third comes next, likewise borrowed from the Papists: the succession of bishops, continued down to our own times. Hadrian Saravia, who acknowledges no extraordinary calling and believes that ordination belongs to bishops alone, says that this succession of bishops not only existed but necessarily existed, and that without it Martin Luther, Huldrych Zwingli and the other first reformers of the Gospel could in no way have been lawfully called. What then is to be thought of reformed ministers who are not ordained by bishops? Perhaps in a case of necessity it is lawful for a presbyter to ordain. On this I will say nothing at present, except what Whitaker says, who thus answers Bellarmine, arguing from this doctrine of Hadrian Saravia: I answer (he says) that Luther and those other famous and noble heroes of ours were presbyters, and therefore by divine right bishops. So whatever pertains to bishops pertained by divine right to them too. For that bishops were afterwards set above presbyters is a human arrangement, made to remove schisms, as the histories bear witness.

units.la: 2 Post Saraviam prodeat in medium loco jam secundo Thomas Bilsonus. Confitenti Harto successionem localem solidum argumentum non esse, nisi doctrinæ successio adjungatur: regessit Iohannes Reynoldus noster: Quid tum sibi volunt successionis Catalogi illi, quos Bristous & Rishtonus ad nos per mare transmiserunt; Dixerat olim Thomas Bilsonus: Successio nullius ponderis est nisi addatur doctrinæ veritas (& proinde ex pari disciplinæ etiam) & pura vitæ conversatio. Quid tum rogo sibi volunt (liceat enim Iohannem Reynoldum imitari) tam longi Episcopalium successionum in plurimis Ecclesiis catalogi illi quos alibi colligis, ac si abunde probata dignitas Episcopalis esset, quòd successio Episcoporum ex historijs ostendi potest? Rationem fortassis redditam dicis in verbis eis quæ hisce Catalogis subjunguntur: Iure successionis singulari ab Apostolicis usque temporibus Episcopi semper a presbyteris distincti fuerunt, quod certissimè omnibus eis qui non veritatem voluntati suæ mancipatam esse volunt, certissimo argumento potest. est esse, primum Apostolorum supra presbyteros institutionem vere fuisse Apostolicam.
units.tr: 2 After Saravia, Thomas Bilson comes forward in second place. When Harte admitted that local succession is not a solid argument unless the succession of doctrine is joined to it, our John Reynolds replied: What do those catalogues of succession mean to them, which Bristow and Rishton sent across the sea to us? Thomas Bilson had once said: Succession is of no weight unless the truth of doctrine is added (and therefore the truth of discipline too) and a pure manner of life. What then, I ask, do those long catalogues of episcopal successions in many churches, which you gather elsewhere, mean? (For I may imitate John Reynolds.) It is as if episcopal dignity were sufficiently proved because the succession of bishops can be shown from histories. Perhaps you say a reason is given in the words that accompany these catalogues: By the singular right of succession, from Apostolic times bishops have always been distinguished from presbyters, which can be shown by a most certain argument to all who do not want the truth to be subject to their own will. That is, namely, that the Apostles' first setting of bishops above presbyters was truly apostolic.

units.la: Primò, certissimum argumentum vocas subsequentis Ecclesiæ praxim? revoca hoc dictum, temerè namque evolavit: certissimum nihil est, nisi quod a Deo profectum, in sacris literis reperitur.
units.tr: First, do you call the later practice of the Church a most certain argument? Retract this saying, for it slipped out rashly. Nothing is certain except what comes from God and is found in the sacred writings.

units.la: Secundò, jus successionis supereminentius nominas? Profer tabulas. Quo sacrarum literarum loco hoc jus statuitur? Certè si omnino fuit, jure humano aut nullo, hæc in Ecclesia prisca supereminens successio fuit: quod si velint sibi sumant Episcopi, dum nostris presbyteris relinquant divinum.
units.tr: Second, do you call it a more eminent right of succession? Produce your documents. In what passage of the sacred writings is this right laid down? Certainly if it existed at all, it was a right of human law or of none, this more eminent succession in the ancient Church. But if the bishops want to take it for themselves, let them do so, while leaving the divine right to our presbyters.

units.la: Tertiò, successione supereminenti gravisos fuisse primos Episcopos usq; a temporibus Apostolorum salsissimum est, ab omni non modo veritate, sed & veritatis specie etiam derelictum. Congerit nonnulla Bilsonus ex patrum scriptis, quę & Downamus, sed eadem, aut ejusdem generis, quæ Bellarminus, ad quæ ita respondet Guilielmus Whitakerus. In his omnibus petiit principium & quod probandum erat, non probavit. Idem hisce respondendum prorsus est: Probanda etenim illis erat successio Episcoporum talis quæ in reliquos ministros potestatem Anglicanam exerceret: hoc vere in nullo testimonio dicitur eorum omnium quæ protulerunt. Conglomerantur quidem loca quædam in quibus successio Episcoporum ab Apostolis commemoratur, sed quales hi Episcopi fuerint, aut quòd potestatem Hierarchicam (quæ jam in Anglia nostra obtinet,) exercuerint, id minimè dicitur: sic ut in manifestam petitionem principii incidant, tales Episcopos & non alios olim fuisse, atq; nunc in Anglia falsissimè præsumentes. Sed de hac re alias.
units.tr: Third, it is utterly absurd that the first bishops, from the times of the Apostles, were burdened by a more eminent succession, and it is abandoned by every semblance not only of truth but even of the appearance of truth. Bilson gathers some things from the writings of the Fathers, as does Downame, but they are the same things, or things of the same kind, as those of Bellarmine, to which Guilielmus Whitaker replies thus: In all these he assumed the principle and what was to be proved, and did not prove it. The same must be answered to these men altogether. For they had to prove a succession of bishops such as would exercise the Anglican power over the other ministers. This is truly not said in any of the testimonies they have produced. Certainly some passages are heaped together in which the succession of bishops from the Apostles is mentioned, but what kind of bishops they were, or that they exercised the hierarchical power which now prevails in our England, is by no means said. So they fall into a manifest petitio principii, presuming most falsely that bishops of this kind, and no others, existed of old as they do now in England. But of this matter, elsewhere.

units.la: Tertio in loco loquatur Downamus, qui postquam huius Episcoporum in primis Ecclesijs successionis mentionem fecisset, ita subinfert. Atque hæc moderato Christiano commendatio functionis Episcopalis sufficiens videri posset, etsi nihil aliud pro eadem posset dici. Heu spiritum prorsus Scultingianum: sic enim ille: Tametsi ne syllaba quidem vel apex de dictis officijs in sacra scriptura extaret, tamen oportebat nos sequi ordinem traditionis Ecclesiasticæ: Constat enim iam inde ab Apostolorum temporibus istorum officiorum mentionem fieri in singulorũ sæculorum patribus, in historiis Ecclesiasticis & Conciliis, quæ Iohannes Whitgiftus in Defensione, & Censor in examine (Bancroftum intelligit in Surveggio) & illustrissimus Cardinalis Baronius in Annalibus magno cumulo & a. crbo profiunt. Baronium hic medium, inter Whitgiftum & Bancroftum sedere, quam pulchrum: Ex eorum societate se Whitakerus segregavit, qui a successione ad scripturâ provocari posse dicit, & licere nobis successionem reicere, & clarum aliquod ex scripturis testimonium requirere. Hæc enim est constans omnium patrum Catholicorum sententia, Nihil esse in religione recipiendum aut approbandum quod scripturæ testimonio non nitatur, quodque ex Scriptuis probari & confirmationem potest. Et merito quidem cum scriptura sit absoluta & sufficiens veritatis regula. Hinc pro successione quasi veritatis nota quum Augustinum protulisset Bellarminus Epistol. 161. reperit ille quod in eadem Epistola reperitur: Quanquam nos non tam de istis documentis praesumimus, quam de sacris Scripturis. Sic igitur est. Praesumunt Hierarchici de minime idoneo documento, cum per successionem, Episcopalem dignitatem satis comprobatam putant: scripturis sanctis agendum illis erat: sanctae vero Scripturae argumentu nobis solidu suppeditant, quo hoc documento de successione episcopali jugulatur? praedicit etenim subingressurâ in Ecclesiâ Hierarchiam ementitam, quae specie antiquitatis & successionis, quasi aureo meretricis poculo mentes hominum dementaret? Ap. 17, sic ut successionem Hierarchicam adversarij dum premunt nihil aliud agunt quàm ut Episcopalem Hierarchiam suam meretriciam prodant & Antichristianam esse. Atque revera ut primis saeculis Antichristi embryo erat, ita nostris temporibus illius cauda quaedam est: de quo concludo cum Whitakero: Apostasia operabatur diebus Apostoli, & quantumvis Apostoli ista & Christus clarissime praedixerunt, tamen multi non credunt mutari Ecclesiae e statu potuisse, & perpetuum successionis argumentum urgent, quoniam imperiti homines fallantur, quasi nihil ejusmodi futurum esset.
units.tr: Third, let Downame speak, who, after mentioning this succession of bishops in the first churches, adds: And this might seem a sufficient commendation of the episcopal office to a moderate Christian, even if nothing else could be said for it. Alas, a thoroughly Scultetian spirit! For he says: Although not a syllable or a dot about those offices stood in holy scripture, yet we ought to follow the order of ecclesiastical tradition. For it is established that from the times of the Apostles mention of these offices is made in the writings of the Fathers of each century, in ecclesiastical histories and councils, which John Whitgift in his Defence, and the Censor in his Examination (he means Bancroft in the Survey), and the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius in the Annals, set forth in great heaps and in abundance. What a fine thing that Baronius sits here in the middle, between Whitgift and Bancroft! Whitaker separated himself from their company, who say that one may appeal from succession to Scripture, that we are free to reject succession, and that we should require some clear testimony from the Scriptures. For this is the constant opinion of all the Catholic Fathers: that nothing is to be received or approved in religion which does not rest on the testimony of Scripture, and which cannot be proved and confirmed from the Scriptures. And rightly so, since Scripture is the complete and sufficient rule of truth. Hence, when Bellarmine had brought forward Augustine, Epistle 161, in support of succession as a kind of mark of truth, that man found what is found in the same epistle: Yet we do not presume so much on these documents as on the holy Scriptures. So it is. The hierarchists presume upon a very unsuitable document when they think episcopal dignity is sufficiently proved by succession; they should have dealt with the holy Scriptures. But what solid argument do the holy Scriptures supply by which this document of episcopal succession is throttled? Do they not foretell that a counterfeit hierarchy would enter the Church, which by the appearance of antiquity and succession would drive men's minds mad, like the golden cup of the harlot? Ap. 17. So when our opponents press hierarchical succession, they do nothing else than expose their episcopal hierarchy as harlot-like and antichristian. And indeed, just as in the first centuries it was the embryo of Antichrist, so in our times it is a certain tail of him. With Whitaker I conclude: Apostasy was already at work in the days of the Apostle, and however clearly the Apostles and Christ foretold these things, many still do not believe that the Church could be changed from its state, and they press the perpetual argument of succession, since ignorant men are deceived, as if nothing of the kind were going to happen.

units.la: Quarto in loco, locus Bancrofto dandus est: Dixit Cartwrightus quosque ministros Apostolorum successores esse qua Apostolorum doctrinam praedicant, & Antonius Sadeel fideles item quousque, quâ Apostolorum doctrinam retinent, & Apostolicis vestigiis insistunt: & id solum voluisse patres quum successio Apostolicam commendarunt. Quid ille ad haec? Ita personalis successio (inquit) penitus excluditur: hanc vero patrum interpretationem talem postea esse affirmat, qualis illa est psalmi Mat. 4, Angelis suis mandavit de te. Quid igitur? personali successioni tribuit quod Pontificij? Sic quidè videtur: neq; obstat quod ante ab eo dicitur, bene a nostris responderi Papistis, personalem successionem nihili esse ad probandam veritatem religionis: nam eodem loco concludit, Episcopalem successionem valere ad probandum eorum originem ab Apostolis, licet ad caput aliquod fidei probandum non valeat, nisi & successio verae doctrinae adjungatur. Atqui ego putarem, perinde requiri in successione veritatem disciplinae, ad probandam quaestionem disciplinariam, atque requiritur veritas doctrinae, ad probandam quaestionem doctrinalem. Hoc posito, nulla argumenta proferunt nostri adversus personalem successionem in causa fidei: quae non pariter valent adversus personalem successionem in causa disciplinae.
units.tr: Fourth, the place must be given to Bancroft. Cartwright said that ministers are successors of the Apostles so far as they preach the doctrine of the Apostles, and Antonius Sadeel likewise that the faithful are so far as they retain the doctrine of the Apostles and tread in the Apostolic footsteps; and that the Fathers wanted only this when they commended Apostolic succession. What does Bancroft reply to these? Thus personal succession (he says) is utterly excluded. But he afterwards affirms that this interpretation of the Fathers is of the same kind as that of the psalm, Mat. 4: He has given his angels charge concerning you. What then? Does he attribute to personal succession what the Papists do? So it seems indeed. Nor does it stand in the way that he says earlier that our men rightly answer the Papists that personal succession is nothing for proving the truth of religion; for in the same place he concludes that episcopal succession is valid for proving their origin from the Apostles, although it is not valid for proving any article of faith unless the succession of true doctrine is joined to it. But I would think that in succession the truth of discipline is required for proving a question of discipline, just as the truth of doctrine is required for proving a question of doctrine. Given this, our men put forward no arguments against personal succession in a matter of faith which do not equally hold against personal succession in a matter of discipline.

units.la: 5 Primo, personalis successio (disputant nostri) in causa fidei solidum argumentum non est, quia haereticis competit: ad eundem modum Episcopalis successio, (disputamus nos) in causa disciplinae solidum argumentum non est, quia extraneis officiis competit, quae in verbo minime fuisse constituta constat. Patet hoc ex Cornelio Scultingio supra citato: vere etenim affirmat, in singulorum saeculorum patribus, historijs Ecclesiasticis & conciliis, mentionem fieri diaconorum Episcopo ministrantium, Accoluthorum, Exorcistarum, Lectorum, Cantorum, &c. mentionem fieri, perinde & ipsorum Episcoporum, Diaconos nisi eleemosynarios non agnoscit scriptura, Acoluthos & Exorcistas non omnino agnoscit: successionem tamen personalem, adaeque ac Episcopi, in patribus historiis, conciliis, habent: personalis igitur successio minimè probat Episcopos Hierarchicos in verbo Dei institutos fuisse. Quod igitur dicit, T. Mortonus Hierarchicus successionem personae pompae aptiorem esse quàm pugnae, id hac in causa locum habet. Citat Nazianzen. Successio sedis est nomine tenus successio nisi fidei habeat veritatem: sic successio Episcopalis est nomine tenus successio, nisi probetur eam habere disciplinae veritatem. Citat Ambrosium: Non habent haereditatem Petri qui Petri fidem non habent: sic non habent haereditatem Apostolorum Episcopi, nisi probetur, eos eandem potestatem habere quam Apostoli ecclesiae ministris tradiderunt. Postremò Tertull. ita; Non ex personis fidem, sed ex fide personas probare oportet: sic non ex personis Episcoporum disciplinaria veritas, sed ex disciplinaria veritate in verbo Dei patefacta Episcoporum personae probandae & examinandae sunt.
units.tr: 5 First, personal succession (our opponents argue) is not a solid argument in matters of faith, because heretics also possess it. Likewise, episcopal succession (as we argue) is not a solid argument in matters of discipline, because it belongs to offices outside the Word, which are plainly not established in the Word. This is clear from Cornelius Schultingius, cited above. He truly affirms that in the Fathers, the ecclesiastical histories and the councils of every age there is mention of deacons who serve the bishop, of acolyths, exorcists, readers, cantors, and so on. Just as there is mention of the bishops themselves, so Scripture recognises only almoners as deacons and does not recognise acolyths and exorcists at all. Yet the Fathers, the histories and the councils have personal succession for these offices just as they do for bishops. Personal succession therefore does not prove that hierarchical bishops were instituted in the Word of God. So what T. Morton, the hierarchist, says, that succession of person is better suited to display than to battle, applies in this case. He quotes Nazianzen: The succession of a see is a succession in name only, unless it holds the truth of faith. So episcopal succession is a succession in name only, unless it is shown to hold the truth of discipline. He quotes Ambrose: They do not have the inheritance of Peter who do not have Peter's faith. So bishops do not have the inheritance of the Apostles unless it is shown that they have the same power which the Apostles handed on to the ministers of the Church. Last, Tertullian says: Persons must be proved by faith, not faith by persons. So the disciplinary truth is not to be proved from the persons of bishops; rather the persons of bishops must be proved and examined by the disciplinary truth revealed in the Word of God.

units.la: 6 Secundò, personalis successio (disputant nostri) in causa fidei solidum argumentum non est, quia Apostasia in fide contigit, sicut scripturae praedixerunt, sic ut successiorum eadem fides non fuerit, quae majorum suorum erat: eundem in modum personalis successio in causa disciplinae (disputamus nos) solidum argumentum minimè est, quia mutatio disciplinae contigit, sicut scripturae praedixerunt, sic ut successorum disciplina eadem non fuerit, quae fuerat majorum. R. Eyldus Hierarchicus illa Nazianzeni citat & approbat, quę in laudibus Athanasij scribit: Neque qui per vim irrupit successor habendus est, sed qui vim perpessus, nec qui contrariam sententiam tuetur, sed qui eadem fide praeditus est, nisi quis fortassis ita successurè dicat, quemadmodum morbum saitati, tenebras luci, tempestatem tranquilitati, prudentiae dementiam succedere dicimus. Sic qui vim jam presbyteri perpetiuntur, veri veterum Episcoporum successores habendi sunt, quia veteré Episcopalem & nen aliam potestatem revocant: sed Episcopi Hierarchici qui contrariâ vendicant, successores non sunt: quia mutata per illas disciplina veteri, non aliter, veteribus Episcopis succedunt, quam quomodo luci succedere tenebrae solent. Quod quum Eusebius: (disputat Dovvnamus) sequentium Episcoporum successiones recensfit eosdem eos cum veteribus facit. At Eusebio aureus ille calamus defuit, sui saeculi unda abrepto, qui nostrorum temporum historiographis datus est Apoc. 11. 2. ut intervalla temporum, discrimina morum, Ecclesiarum inclinationes, Hierarchiae denique Antichristianae incrementa & progressus metirentur: quae Eusebius paulatim irrepentia, & non ut postea conspicua facta, non denique, ut nostro tempore, ad suum usque fastigium perducta, non ita dilucidè observare potuit. Est tamen ubi vestigium reliquit, vetustissimæ disciplinæ, eo nempe in loco, quem Bellarminus de successione istâ disputans, incautius allegavit. Nomen (inquit) presbyteri commune erat olim presbyteris & Episcopis, ut patet ex Epistola Irenæi ad Victorem quæ est apud Eusebium Histor. lib. 5. c. 24. Vbi Romanos Pontifices, Victorem, Anicetum, Pium, Telesphorum, Xystum, appellat presbyteros. At nihil hoc inquies facit, ut probetur veteres Episcopos, non alios quam presbyteros fuisse. Falsus igitur Guilelmus Whiakerus, qui ita respondet Bellarmino: Fateor olim inter presbyterum & Episcopum discrimen nullum fuisse, non opus ergo fuit his testimoniis ad hoc probandum. Sed si hi presbyteri qui olim, & à quibus ordinatus erat Timotheus, tales Episcopi erant, quales nunc sunt in Ecclesia Romana, tunc plures erant unius urbis Episcopi, ut patet Act. 20: 17. ubi Paulus dicitur accersisse presbyteros & Episcopos Ephesinæ Ecclesiæ. Hi si Episcopi fuerunt tum unius Ecclesiæ Ephesinæ plures simul Episcopi fuerunt, Habet & hæc: Fuisse semper tales Episcopos in Ecclesia quales nunc sunt Pontifices, salsissimum est, nec unquam probari potest. Erant quidem in initio in singulis Ecclesiis Episcopi, id est pastores, non tales quales nunc sunt in Ecclesia Romana.
units.tr: 6 Second, personal succession (our opponents argue) is not a solid argument in matters of faith, because apostasy in faith has occurred, as the Scriptures foretold, so that the successors did not hold the same faith as their predecessors. In the same way, personal succession in matters of discipline (as we argue) is by no means a solid argument, because a change of discipline has occurred, as the Scriptures foretold, so that the successors did not keep the same discipline as their predecessors. R. Hooker, the hierarchist, cites and approves those words of Nazianzen which he writes in praise of Athanasius: Neither is he to be counted the successor who has forced his way in, but he who has suffered violence; nor he who defends the contrary opinion, but he who is endowed with the same faith; unless perhaps someone would say that they succeed in the way we say that sickness succeeds to health, darkness to light, a storm to calm, madness to prudence. So those who now suffer violence at the hands of the presbyters are to be considered the true successors of the ancient bishops, because they recall the ancient episcopal power and no other; but the hierarchical bishops, who claim the contrary, are not successors, because, with the discipline changed by them, they succeed the ancient bishops no differently than darkness customarily succeeds light. When Eusebius (Downame argues) recounted the successions of the later bishops, he made them the same as the earlier ones. But that golden pen was lacking to Eusebius, carried off by the wave of his own age. It has been given to the historians of our times (Rev. 11. 2), so that they may measure the intervals of time, the differences of morals, the inclinations of the Churches and, finally, the growth and progress of the antichristian hierarchy. Eusebius could not observe these as clearly, since they crept in gradually, were not yet conspicuous as they later became, and were not yet carried, as in our time, to their full height. Yet he has left a trace of the most ancient discipline in the very place which Bellarmine, when disputing about this succession, cited too carelessly. The name (he says) of presbyter was once common to presbyters and bishops, as is clear from the letter of Irenaeus to Victor, which is in Eusebius, History, book 5, chapter 24. There he calls the Roman pontiffs Victor, Anicetus, Pius, Telesphorus and Xystus presbyters. But you will say that this proves nothing, since it is not shown that the ancient bishops were none other than presbyters. Therefore William Whitaker is wrong, who answers Bellarmine thus: I admit that once there was no difference between presbyter and bishop, so there was no need for these testimonies to prove this. But if those presbyters who once ordained Timothy, and by whom he was ordained, were bishops such as are now in the Roman Church, then there were several bishops of one city, as is clear from Acts 20:17, where Paul is said to have summoned the presbyters and bishops of the Church of Ephesus. If these were bishops, then several bishops at once existed in the one Church of Ephesus. He also says this: That there have always been bishops in the Church such as the Pontiffs are now is most absurd and can never be proved. At the beginning there were indeed in each Church bishops, that is pastors, but not such as are now in the Roman Church.

units.la: Tertiò, ut Papæ à nostris omnibus objicitur, eum Apostolorum successorem non esse, quia opera eorum non exercet, non docet, non gregem curat &c. ita & nobis jam Episcopis Anglicanis occinere licet, eos veterum Episcoporum successores appellandos non esse, quia ambitione, luxu, negligentiâ, sævitiâ impia & tumidâ potentiæ suæ ampliatione, Episcoporum priscorum humilitatem, frugalitatem, diligentiam, & cum suis collegis socialitatem polluerunt, profanarunt, dehonestarunt. Dixit olim Symacus Petrum perennem meritorum dotem cum hereditate innocentiæ transmisisse ad posteros, ut si desint bona acquisita per merita, sufficiant quæ à loci prædecessore præstantur. Tantum verò abest, quòd hoc verum sit, ut ex adverso condemnentur successores eò magis, quo magis successionem ostentant eorum à quorum pietate degenerarunt. Sic condemnat Moses Judæos degenerantes, quo magis Mosi fidunt, Ioh. 5: 45. & condemnat Abraham eos qui contrarium faciunt, quò magis se Abrahæ filios gloriantur: Ioh. 8: 39, 40.
units.tr: Third, as the Pope is objected to by all our side, that he is not a successor of the Apostles because he does not exercise their work, does not teach, does not care for the flock, and so on, so we too may now sing the same tune to the English bishops: they are not to be called successors of the ancient bishops, because by ambition, luxury, negligence, impious cruelty and the swelling expansion of their power they have polluted, profaned and dishonoured the humility, frugality, diligence and fellowship with their colleagues of the ancient bishops. Symmachus once said that Peter transmitted to posterity a perpetual dowry of merits together with the inheritance of innocence, so that if the goods acquired by merit are lacking, those supplied by the predecessor of the place suffice. But this is so far from being true that, on the contrary, successors are condemned all the more, the more they boast of a succession from those whose piety they have degenerated from. Thus Moses condemns the degenerate Jews, the more they trust in Moses (John 5:45), and Abraham condemns those who do the opposite, the more they glory in being sons of Abraham (John 8:39, 40).

units.la: Nonne eò Tyrannus sibi gravius accersit judicium, quò magis se Pij Principis successorem venditat? Citat Thomas Mortonus Hierarchicus illa Basilij: Non cathedræ sed religionis propriam successionem æstimare debemus: qui contrariam fidei doctrinam amplectitur, adversarius quoque in throno censeri debet. Contrariam de Episcopali dignitate sententiam Episcopi Anglicani jam sectantur: & per ambitionem, contraria veteribus Episcopis faciunt: non tantùm igitur non pro successoribus, sed & pro adversariis habendi sunt. Citat Guilelmus
units.tr: Does not a tyrant bring a heavier judgment on himself the more he presents himself as successor of a pious prince? Thomas Morton, the hierarchist, cites that saying of Basil: We ought to value not the succession of the throne but of religion: whoever embraces doctrine contrary to the faith must be regarded as an adversary even on the throne. The English bishops now follow an opinion about episcopal dignity contrary to the ancient one, and by their ambition they act contrary to the ancient bishops. They are therefore to be regarded not merely as not successors, but as adversaries. He quotes William

units.la: Apolog. Catholic. p. 1. 1, 6. 23. elmus Whitakerus illa Hieronymi apud Gratianum distinct. 40. c.6.non est facile : Non sanctorum loco sunt qui tenent loca sanctorum, sed qui exercent opera eorum. Sic ut operibus Episcoporum Anglicanorum longissime diversis, aperte pateat eos veterum Episcoporum succesfores minime esse.
units.tr: Apolog. Catholic. p. 1. 1, 6. 23. Whitaker also cites that saying of Jerome, found in Gratian, distinction 40, chapter 6, which is not easy: They are not in the place of the saints who hold the places of the saints, but those who perform their works. So, since the works of the English bishops are very far different, it is plainly clear that they are by no means successors of the ancient bishops.

units.la: Ad postremum, dixit olim Hieronymus ad Damasum : Facessat Romani culminis ambitio, ego veteri cathedrae confor. Similiter jam nos: Facessat Episcopi Anglicani ambitio: nobis humili Episcoporum antiquorum cathedrae consociari liceat.
units.tr: Finally, Jerome once said to Damasus: Let the ambition of the Roman summit go away; I will be joined to the ancient chair. Similarly we now say: Let the ambition of the English bishops go away; let us be permitted to be joined to the humble chair of the ancient bishops.

units.la: Quintò jam & ultimo loco, Downnamus rursus audiendus: qui hinc Seniores nostros presbyteriales jugulat, quòd eam successionem ostendere nequeant, quam ostendere Episcopi possunt. Respondemus ex nostrorum omnium communi sententia, linearis successionis interruptionem, successionis legitimae veritatem minimè tollere : sic ut quamvis Ecclesia nostra omninò intercisa fuisset, vera tamen Ecclesia fuisset, quandiu cum illa vetustissima conspirat & consentit.
units.tr: Fifth and last, Downame is to be heard again. He here slays our presbyterian elders because they cannot show the succession which bishops can show. We answer, following the common opinion of all our side, that an interruption of linear succession does not destroy the truth of lawful succession. So even if our Church had been wholly cut off, it would still have been a true Church, as long as it agrees and harmonises with that most ancient one.

units.la: Probat hoc ex instantia ipsius Christi Whitakerus : Vera & legitima successio potest esse interrupta : Christus enim Melchisedeco per multos annos successit. Sic nos dicimus, licèt successio per multos annos fuerit interrupta; si quis tamen veram doctrinam docet, eum Apostolis succedere. Quid igitur? Nullus inter Christum & Melchisedecum per annos quam plurimos, ejusdem ordinis rex & sacerdos linea- ri successione intercedebat: & tamen Christus verus Melchisedeç fuit successor erat : ita quid si nullus sententiarum senatus per multos annos extitit? non hoc impedit, quin moderni seniores illis Apostolicis verè successisse credantur.
units.tr: Whitaker proves this from the instance of Christ himself: a true and lawful succession can be interrupted, for Christ succeeded Melchizedek after many years. So we say that although succession was interrupted for many years, whoever teaches the true doctrine succeeds the Apostles. What then? No line of succession of the same order of king and priest stood between Christ and Melchizedek over very many years, and yet Christ was the true successor of Melchizedek. So if no senate of opinions has existed for many years, this does not prevent the modern elders from being believed to have truly succeeded those Apostolic men.

units.la: Accedit Thomas Mortonus Hierarchicus : Successio personae cum adest non est aspernanda, cum abest, modo ne desit Catholicae doctrinae successio, non est vehementius exigenda. Hinc illa Stapletoni probat: perso- nalem successionem nihil motamur, modò doctrinam nostram con- sentientem scripturis ostendere possimus : necnon illa Aenea Sylvij : Mihi nec laudi nec vituperio erit, dummodo verus Christianus sum, majorum meorum matutina aut vespertina conversio. Ita contra seniores plumbeo pugione pugnavit Downnamus, quamdiu veritas disciplinae illibata est, secundùm quam senioribus Apostolicis confirmantur : successio personalis urgenda non erat nec exigenda, illius defectum morari seniores non debent, nec vituperio illis danda est vespertina majorum suorum conversio, ad Senatum presbyterialem, juxta Dei institutum, restaurandum. Hæc, de extraneo firmamento Hierarchico tertio, successione.
units.tr: Thomas Morton, in his Hierarchicus, adds: "A personal succession is not to be despised when it is present; when it is absent, provided the succession of Catholic doctrine is not lacking, it is not to be demanded too insistently." Hence Stapleton's words also prove the point: "We do not object at all to personal succession, provided we can show that our doctrine agrees with the Scriptures." Likewise Aeneas Sylvius: "It will be neither praise nor blame to me that my forefathers were converted in the morning or the evening, so long as I am a true Christian." So Downame fought against the elders with a leaden dagger: as long as the truth of discipline remains unimpaired, by which the Apostolic elders are established, personal succession was not to be pressed or demanded. The elders need not be delayed by its absence, nor should their forefathers' conversion in the evening be held against them, when they seek to restore the presbyterial senate according to God's appointment. These are my remarks on the third, external support of the Hierarchical side, succession.

units.la: CAP 6. Firmamentum quartum ab unanimi consensu refutatur.
units.tr: CAP 6. The fourth prop, from unanimous consent, is refuted.

units.la: QVartum sequitur, à Papistis similiter mutuatum, Vnanimis consensus: nam quòd causa nostra traducatur accerrimè, quæ omnis quasi communem antiquitatis consensum infestum habeat, tragicæ illæ cum Bancrofii tum Downami vociferationes, non sinunt quenquam ignorare. Quin & Isaacus Casaubonus, nimium huic consensui unanimi attribuisse videtur, quum eo sublato controversias hodiernas finem nunquam πὶ καὶ ἀνθρώπους accepturas, neque ulla disceptatione terminandas fore dicit. Forte causam ponit in pervicatia papistarum: sed ita quid si secundum hominem sine hoc consensu litium finis sperandus non sit: secundum Deum tamen Scripturam habemus, absque hujus consensus adminiculo, absolutissimam dijudicatricem. Atq; sane hoc sensu, adeò consensum antiquitatis depereunt Hierarchici, ut vix quoad homines, hæc controversia disciplinaria ut unquam finiatur, sperandum sit. Quid tum? eorum error detegendus: neque tam leges hujus consensus (quod Isaacus Casaubonus) figendæ, quàm ipsius authoritas prorsus t. lenda, ut ita tandem ad Scripturæ solius limam res tota revocetur.
units.tr: Fourthly comes the argument, likewise borrowed from the Papists, from unanimous consent. That our cause is most bitterly misrepresented, as though all antiquity stood against it in one common agreement, is shown by the tragic outcries of Bancroft and Downame, which leave no one ignorant of it. Indeed Isaac Casaubon also seems to have attributed too much to this unanimous consent, since he says that without it the present controversies will never reach an end [πὶ καὶ ἀνθρώπους], nor be settled by any debate. Perhaps he places the cause in the obstinacy of the Papists; but what if, humanly speaking, no end of the dispute is to be hoped for without this consent? Yet with God we have Scripture, a most complete judge, without the aid of this consensus. And indeed in this sense the Hierarchists so deny the consent of antiquity that, as far as men are concerned, it is hardly to be hoped that this disciplinary controversy will ever be ended. What then? Their error must be exposed. Nor are the rules of this consensus to be fixed (as Isaac Casaubon would have it), but its authority is to be utterly removed, so that at last the whole matter may be brought back to the touchstone of Scripture alone.

units.la: Hoc ut fiat, sciendum est primo, appositè ad causam nostram Whitakerum affirmasse. Adversariorum vero humana media sunt: Nam praxis Ecclesiæ est consuetudo hominum, Patrum sententia, est opinio hominum, Conciliorum definitio, est judicium hominum. Hæc ita cum sint, robur totum unanimis consensus istius in eo ponitur, quòd multitudinem hominum consentientium ponit: cujus in rebus divinis ecquod quæso robur est? provoco hic ego ad Thomam Mortonum Hierarchicum, qui adversus istud argumentum Papisticum ab unanimi consensu ductum, pugnat, & ita pugnat, ut in medium producat Salmeronis illa. Contra hanc quam objectant multitudinem, respondemus ex verbo Dei, Exod. 23: 2. In judicio plurimorum non acquiesces sententiæ, ut à vero devies. Provoco deinde ad Henricum Paræum Episcopum Glocestrensem, in sua Iohannis Reynoldi versione. Quum unanimem consensum ursisset Hartus ex Vincentio Lyrinensi, respondet Reynoldus, Vincentium in eo supra petram ædificasse, quod scripturam solam ad controversias dirimendas adhibuisset: in hoc vero, quod unanimem consensum requisivisset, super arenam bum navum opinionum. Atq; huic Vincentio opponit Augustinum, qui & Scripturam solam pro fundamento ponit & scripturæ interpretationem ex ipsa scriptura sola sumendam dicit, non ex incertis hominum sensibus.
units.tr: To do this, it must first be noted that Whitaker rightly asserted what bears on our cause. But the adversaries' means are human. For the practice of the Church is the custom of men, the opinion of the Fathers is the opinion of men, and the definition of Councils is the judgement of men. Since this is so, the whole strength of this unanimous consent rests on its claim of a multitude of agreeing men. But what strength, I ask, does that have in divine matters? Here I appeal to Thomas Morton the Hierarchist, who fights against this Popish argument drawn from unanimous consent, and fights in such a way as to bring forward the words of Salmeron. Against this multitude which they object, we answer from the Word of God, Exod. 23: 2: "You shall not acquiesce in the judgement of the majority so as to turn aside from the truth." I appeal next to Henry Parry, Bishop of Gloucester, in his version of John Reynolds. When Hart had urged unanimous consent from Vincent of Lérins, Reynolds replies that Vincent built upon the rock in this, that he used Scripture alone to settle controversies; but in this, that he required unanimous consent, he built upon sand, the boat of opinions. And against this Vincent he sets Augustine, who both lays down Scripture alone as the foundation and says that the interpretation of Scripture must be taken from Scripture itself, not from the uncertain senses of men.

units.la: Secundò, argumentum hoc ab unanimi consensu ductum, incertum est: nullo etenim modo loquere potest, utrum antiqui in re aliqua consenserint necne. Ihò inquit Isaacus Casaubonus, duas regulas posuit Cardinalis Peronius, quae omnino recipiende videntur. Prior est ut tunc existimetur satis probatus esse consensus patrum, quando eminentissimi quique singularum nationum, in rei alicujus affirmatione consenserint, neque illis sese quisquam opposuerat, qui quidem orthodoxus censeretur. Posterior, quando Patres non ut doctores loquuntur, neque dicunt hoc aut illud sic esse credendum aut faciendum, sed tanquam testes eorum quae suis temporibus Ecclesia universalis credebat aut faciebat, dicunt banc esse fidem aut praxim Ecclesiae Catholicae per totum orbem terrarum; tunc eum honorem illis habendum esse, ut ad unanimem consensum Ecclesiae ejusmodi affirmatio satis credatur valere. Atqui inquam haec consensus indicia, ipsi Vincentio Lyrinensi, hujus consensus primo, aut primario saltem patrono, infirma visa sunt. Ille namque non alium consensum ad quaestiones determinandas adhibendum esse censet, quam quando omnes pariter uno consensu, idem manifestè, comiter, constanterque tenent, scribunt, docent. Atque hic ille est, quem dissimulato nomine perstringit Peronius, quando ait: Sententia eorum palam iniqua est qui de consensu patrum satis liquere non posse contendunt, nisi quando res eadem totidem verbis apud omnes patres reperitur. Miror igitur, maluisse se Isaacum Casaubonum, Peronium, Bellarminum, hujusq; farinae Papistas reliquos sequi, potius quàm Vincentium Lyrinensum, & scriptores protestantes, quorum eadem cum Vincentio sententia est. Guil. Whitakerus ita: Quomodo scimus reliquos non dissentire? nam multi libri patrum perierunt & multi patres nihil scripserunt: fieri potest ut illi dissenserint. Praeterea a patribus etiam nonnullis multa tradita sunt, quae vel Papistarum confessione non sunt Apostolica, a quibus tamen reliquos ab illis dissensisse non possunt ostendere. Similiter Iohannes Reynoldus necnon in illius versione Henricus Pareus: Cum eadem quae Peronius supra posuisset Hartus: Quando interpretatio a multis patribus fit, & non contradicunt reliqui, aut nihil omnino de eadem dicunt: tum eam unanimi consensu factam putamus. Regerit Reynoldus: Haec summa male colligitur: quia in scriptis Patrum, unus nonnunquam contra quam omnes reliqui scripturas exponit (quod & Sixto Senensi & Aloysio Lippomano constat (. & quia probabile est in patribus eis quos non habemus, diversam interpretationem traditam fuisse ab ea quae jam reperitur, in eis quorum monumenta extant. Subjungit deinde: Consensus via non est per quam tuto incedere licet, si viam veritatis quaerimus: nam & sitis enecabimur, sicut qui Timane aquas expectant, Iob. 6.38: 9. & quod peius est, pro limpida veritatis unda lutum & caenum propinabitu.
units.tr: Secondly, this argument from unanimous consent is uncertain. For in no way can it be known whether the ancients agreed on some matter or not. Isaac Casaubon says: "Cardinal Perron laid down two rules, which seem entirely acceptable. The first is that the consent of the Fathers is held to be sufficiently proved when the most eminent men of the individual nations agree in affirming something, and no one orthodox has opposed them. The second is that when the Fathers do not speak as teachers, nor say that this or that must be believed or done, but as witnesses of what the universal Church believed or did in their own times, and they say that this is the faith or practice of the Catholic Church throughout the world, then such honour is to be given to them that such an affirmation is sufficiently believed to hold as the unanimous consent of the Church." But, I say, these signs of consent seemed weak even to Vincent of Lérins himself, the first, or at least the chief, patron of this consent. For he judges that no other consent is to be used in deciding questions than when all alike, with one accord, manifestly, sincerely and constantly hold, write and teach the same thing. This is the man whom Perron touches on with his name concealed, when he says: "The opinion of those is plainly unjust who contend that there can be no sufficient clarity about the consent of the Fathers unless the same thing is found in the same words among all the Fathers." I wonder, therefore, that Isaac Casaubon, Perron, Bellarmine and the rest of that breed of Papists preferred to follow these men rather than Vincent of Lérins and the Protestant writers, whose opinion is the same as Vincent's. William Whitaker says: "How do we know that the rest do not dissent? For many books of the Fathers have perished, and many Fathers wrote nothing: it may be that they dissented. Moreover, many things have been handed down by some Fathers which, even by the confession of the Papists, are not apostolic, yet they cannot show that the rest dissented from them." Likewise John Reynolds, and Henry Parry in his version. Hart had put forward the same thing as Perron above: "When an interpretation is given by many Fathers, and the rest do not contradict it, or say nothing about it at all, then we think it was made by unanimous consent." Reynolds replies: "This conclusion is badly drawn, because in the writings of the Fathers one sometimes expounds Scripture against what all the others expound (as is clear to Sixtus of Siena and to Aloysius Lippomanus), and because it is probable that among those Fathers whose works we do not have, a different interpretation was handed down from the one now found among those whose writings survive." He adds: "The way of consent is not one on which it is safe to walk, if we are seeking the way of truth: for we shall be killed by thirst, like those who wait for waters at Timana, Iob. 6.38: 9. And what is worse, instead of the clear water of truth they will be given mud and filth to drink."

units.la: Tertiò, si unanimus consensus patrum ad dirimendas lites sufficiat, tum ad exitum profligata est haec quaestio disciplinaria. Quid etenim? Citat Thomas Mortonus Medinam verè affirmantem: Non dubito affirmare sanctum Hieronymum, Sedulium, Primasium, Theodoretum, Oecumenium, Theophylactum, cum Aerianis haereticis sensisse, quòd Episcoporum ac presbyterorum ordinem jure divino, eundem esse dicunt. Hæc de extraneo firmamento Hierarchico quarto, Vnanimi consensu.
units.tr: Thirdly, if unanimous consent of the Fathers is enough to settle disputes, then this disciplinary question is brought to an end. Indeed, Thomas Morton cites Medina rightly affirming: "I do not hesitate to say that St Jerome, Sedulius, Primasius, Theodoret, Oecumenius and Theophylact agreed with the Arian heretics, who say that the order of bishops and that of presbyters are the same by divine right." Thus far on the fourth external Hierarchical prop, unanimous consent.

units.la: CAP 7, Argumentum quintum ab Ecclesia universæ praxi solvitur.
units.tr: CAP 7. The fifth argument, from the universal practice of the Church, is answered.

units.la: Vintum sequitur, à Papistis iterum mutuatum: Vniversa nempe Ecclesiæ praxis: quam cum urgeret Bellarminus, supponit Ecclesiam in universa praxi sua minimè errare potuisse. Hucusque fortè Hierarchici non progredientur, ut Ecclesiam non potuisse errare dicant: dicunt tamen (quod eodem fere recidit) eam non erravisse, id quod dicere necesse est, ut huic argumento vis solida insit. Hinc Apostolicum illis est, quodcunque in Ecclesiæ subsequentis communem usum receptum est: quò Tertullianum citant: Constabit id esse ab Apostolis traditum, quod apud Ecclesias Apostolorum fuerit sacrosanctum. Respondeo, Videri mihi Tertullianum per Ecclesias Apostolorum eas tantùm intelligere, quæ Apostolorum tempore exiterunt: quo sensu verum est quod dicit.
units.tr: The fifth argument follows, again borrowed from the Papists: the universal practice of the Church. When Bellarminus pressed it, he assumed that the Church could not possibly have erred in its universal practice. Perhaps the Hierarchicals will not go so far as to say that the Church could not err, but they say (which comes to nearly the same thing) that it has not erred, and this they must say if the argument is to have any solid force. Hence for them whatever has been received into the common use of the later Church is apostolic. They cite Tertullian for this: It will be established that that was handed down by the Apostles which was held sacred among the churches of the Apostles. I reply that Tertullian, by "the churches of the Apostles," seems to me to mean only those that existed in the Apostles' own time, and in that sense what he says is true.

units.la: Primò etenim in hac citatione delumbata, si Ecclesias sequentes intellexisset, dixisset profectò quod apud Ecclesias Apostolorum est sacrosanctum, non quod fuerit: tempus etenim præteritum, non præsens, hæc verba notant.
units.tr: For, first, in this clipped citation, if he had meant the churches that followed, he would certainly have said what is held sacred among the churches of the Apostles, not what has been. These words denote past time, not present.

units.la: Secundo, scribetur locus integer. Si constat id verius quod prius, id prius quod ab initio, ab initio quod ab Apostolis; pariter utique constabit id esse ab Apostolis traditum, quod apud Ecclesias Apostolorum fuerit sacrosanctum. Initio respondent Ecclesiæ tantum quæ ab initio plantatæ sunt: & non dicit apud Ecclesias Apostolicas, sed apud Ecclesias Apostlorum quæ non nisi illæ esse poterant, quas Apostoli plantaverunt, aut saltem quæ eorum tempore plantatæ erant. Sequitur locus ille celebris ex Augustino, qui fere una cum isto Tertulliani citari ab Hierarchicis solet: Quod universa tenet Ecclesia, nec Conciliis institutum, sed semper retentum est, non nisi authoritate Apostolica traditum rectissime creditur. Hoc illud Achilleum Hierarchicorum argumentum est: quo miseros puritanos suffocatos putant: certè ab omnibus aut saltè coram pluribus magna contentione allegatur. Dolmanus etiam in fronte concionis posuit, tanquam eorum quæ sequerentur, omnium fundamentum. Neque Angelum septem Ecclesiarum, vel ex vocis significatione, vel ex ulla textus sui circumstantia, Episcopum Hierarchicum significare, probare nititur: sed hoc solo (quantum ego assequi possum) argumento pugnat. Ecclesia subsequens Episcopos Hierarchicos habuit: ergo hic Angelus Apocalypticus Episcopus Hierarchicus erat.
units.tr: Second, let the whole passage be written out. If that is more truly established which is earlier, and that which is earlier which is from the beginning, and that which is from the beginning which is from the Apostles; then in the same way it will be established that that was handed down by the Apostles which was held sacred among the churches of the Apostles. "From the beginning" refers only to the churches planted from the beginning. He does not say "among the Apostolic churches" but "among the churches of the Apostles," which could only be those the Apostles planted, or at least those planted in their time. There follows the famous saying of Augustine, which the Hierarchicals usually cite together with this one of Tertullian: What the whole Church holds, and what was not instituted by councils but has always been retained, is most rightly believed to have been handed down by apostolic authority alone. This is the Hierarchicals' Achilles' heel, by which they think they strangle the wretched Puritans. Certainly it is put forward by all of them, or at least by most of them, with great vehemence. Dolman even placed it at the head of his sermon as the foundation of everything that followed. Nor does he try to prove that the Angel of the seven churches signifies a Hierarchical bishop, either from the meaning of the word or from any circumstance of the text. He fights only with this argument, as far as I can make out: the later Church had Hierarchical bishops; therefore this Angel of the Apocalypse was a Hierarchical bishop.

units.la: Consequentiam argumenti probaturus, præfatur ex hoc Augustini [?]ini loco: Quod universa tenet Ecclesia, nec a Conciliis institutum, sed semper retentum est, nonnisi authoritate Apostolica traditum rectissimè creditur. De mente Augustini non controversatur: quanquam per semper retentum prima facie, id tantùm intelligere videtur, quod ab ipsis Apostolorum temporibus dimanavit. Sed verba sequentia, inquis, ostendunt, nec a Conciliis institutum, Augustinum intelligere omne id semper retentum esse, quod primum in Conciliis institutum non est ut exponit Bilsonus, aut ejus origo ignota est, ut Richardus Bancroftus, & Georgius Dolmanus interpretantur. Ostendunt sanè: neque ego hanc Augustini quam Hierarchici adferunt interpretationem rejiciam: tantum admoneo posterioris clausulae nuditatem folio ficulneo coopertam ab eis esse, ne ejusdem foeditas appareret. Rogo, quid illud sibi vult? ab Apostolica authoritate traditum? Intelligunt, inquit, id ab Apostolis in sacris literis scriptum esse, aut inde colligi posse: quod universa, postmodum Ecclesia tenuit. Apage φλυαρίας. Nihil certius est, quam traditiones non scriptas Augustinum hic somniasse in hunc sensum. Quod in universa Ecclesia praxi retentum est, si ejus origio aliàs, puta, per Concilia cognita non sit: ab Apostolis voce viva traditum censetur, etsi in eorum scriptis non reperiatur. Et nonne pudet Evangelicos praecipuum suae Hierarchiae fundamentum ex hujusmodi loco repetere, quod non scriptas Apostolorum traditiones tam fortiter spirat? Hanc enim Augustini mentem fuisse testantur alia ejusdem loca, quae una cum isto a Baronio copulantur: & etiam ab Hierarchicis allegantur.
units.tr: Intending to prove the consequence of the argument, he prefaces it with this saying of Augustine: What the whole Church holds, and what was not instituted by councils but has always been retained, is most rightly believed to have been handed down by apostolic authority alone. No one disputes Augustine's meaning, although at first sight by always retained he seems to mean only what came down from the very times of the Apostles. But, you say, the following words, not instituted by councils, show that Augustine means that everything always retained is something not first instituted in councils, as Bilsonus explains it, or whose origin is unknown, as Richard Bancroft and George Dolman interpret it. They certainly do show this, and I will not reject this interpretation of Augustine that the Hierarchicals bring forward. I only point out that they have covered the nakedness of the latter clause with a fig leaf, so that its foulness should not appear. I ask, what does it mean? handed down by apostolic authority? They understand, he says, that it was written by the Apostles in the Holy Scriptures, or can be gathered from them, since the whole Church later held it. Away with such nonsense [φλυαρίας]! Nothing is more certain than that Augustine here dreamed of unwritten traditions in this sense. What is retained in the universal practice of the Church, if its origin is not otherwise known, for instance through councils, is judged to have been handed down by the Apostles by the living voice, even if it is not found in their writings. And are not the Evangelicals ashamed to draw from such a passage the chief foundation of their Hierarchy, when it breathes so strongly of unwritten apostolic traditions? For that Augustine held this view is attested by other passages of his, which Baronius couples with this one, and which the Hierarchicals also cite.

units.la: Quam consuetudinem credo, inquit, ex Apostolorum traditione venientem, sicut multa non inveniuntur in literis eorum & tamen quia custodiuntur per universam Ecclesiam, nonnisi ab ipsis tradita & commendata traduntur. Disputatur locus à Iohanne Whitgifto, ut probet Patriarchas ab Apostolis descendisse, & Archidiaconos, Archiepiscopos Metropolitanos: de quibus sic habet: Quandoquidem origo & initium harum nominum reperiri non potest, ea horum antiquitas est, ut credendum sit ab Apostolis ipsis exorta fuisse: memini etenim Augustinum hanc habere regulam: Illa autem quae non scripta sed tradita ostendimus, quae quidem toto terrarum orbe observantur, datur intelligi, vel ab ipsis Apostolis vel plenariis Conciliis (quorum est in Ecclesiis salubberrima authoritas) commendata atque statuta RETINERI: sicuti quod Domini passio & resurrectio, & ascensio in caelum, & adventus de coelo Spiritus sancti, anniversaria solemnitate celebrantur, & si quid tale occurrerit, quod servatur ab universa quacunque se diffundit Ecclesia.
units.tr: I believe, he says, that this custom comes from apostolic tradition, just as many things are not found in their writings, and yet, because they are kept throughout the whole Church, they are handed down as having been delivered and commended by the Apostles themselves. John Whitgift argues from this passage to prove that patriarchs descended from the Apostles, and archdeacons and metropolitan archbishops too. Of these he says: Since the origin and beginning of these names cannot be found, their antiquity is such that it must be believed that they arose from the Apostles themselves. For I remember that Augustine has this rule: "Those things, however, which we show are not written but handed down, and which are observed throughout the whole world, are understood to have been commended and established either by the Apostles themselves or by plenary councils (whose authority in the Churches is most salutary), and to be RETAINED:" just as the Lord's passion, resurrection, ascension into heaven, and the coming of the Holy Spirit from heaven are celebrated with an annual solemnity, and whatever else of this kind occurs which is kept by the whole Church wherever it spreads.

units.la: Videte singulare Hierarchicorum artificium: Commemoratur ab antiquis Episcopus, ideo descendit ab Apostolis, quod testimonium ab antiquissimis scriptis habeat. Metropolitanus & Archiepiscopus è contra, in scriptis antiquis non reperitur, ideo originem ab Apostolis ipsis habebit, quia ejus origo aliàs ignota est. Quid ita? Nempe propter universam Ecclesiae praxim, cujus authoritas infallibilis est; in quam etiam sententiam allegatur à Bilsono, & Casaubono, ille alter Augustini locus: Non facere quod universa facit Ecclesia, insolentissimae insaniae est. Quàm autem parum solidi huic argumento insit, deinceps demonstrandum.
units.tr: See the peculiar craft of the Hierarchicals. A bishop is mentioned by the ancients, so he descends from the Apostles, because he has testimony from the most ancient writings. A metropolitan and an archbishop, on the other hand, are not found in ancient writings, so they will have their origin from the Apostles themselves, because their origin is otherwise unknown. Why so? Obviously because of the universal practice of the Church, whose authority is infallible. To the same effect Bilsonus and Casaubon cite that other saying of Augustine: Not to do what the whole Church does is the height of insolent madness. How little solid strength this argument has, I shall show in what follows.

units.la: 3 Compara Augustini locū cum quibusdam paribus & similibus. Baronius postquam sacerdotum apud omnes gentes authoritatem demonstrasset, ita infert: Recte Socrat. apud Xenophon. lib. 4. Quod ob omnibus gentibus observatum est, id non nisi a Deo sancitum esse, dicendum est. Quidni universa hominum praxis a Deo per lumen naturale: perinde ac universa Ecclesiae praxis ab Apostolis per lumen supernaturale? Bellarminus: Illud proculdubio est Apostolicum habendum & judicandum quod pro tali habetur in eis Ecclesiis in quibus est integra successio Episcoporum. Exploditur haec regula Bellarmini a Gulielmo Whitakero: quis tamen non videt, ex hac Augustini regula, robur eam lucemque accipere? Ita Melchior Canus: Credendum est ea Romanam Ecclesiam per traditionem a Deo recepisse, cujus authoritamentum nullum in verbo Dei reperitur. Exibilatur haec sententia a Richardo Fyldo, nec immerito: ex hypothesi tamen Romanam Ecclesiam veram Dei Ecclesiam esse, ex isto Augustini loco, quanquam absurdissimum, dogma istud omninò sequitur.
units.tr: 3. Compare Augustine's passage with certain similar ones. Baronius, after he had demonstrated the authority of priests among all nations, draws this conclusion: Socrates rightly says in Xenophon, book 4: "What is observed by all peoples must be said to have been sanctioned by God alone." Why not say that the universal practice of mankind comes from God through the natural light, just as the universal practice of the Church comes from the Apostles through the supernatural light? Bellarmine: That must without doubt be held and judged apostolic which is regarded as such in those churches in which there is an unbroken succession of bishops. This rule of Bellarmine is exploded by William Whitaker; yet who does not see that this rule of Augustine receives strength and light from it? So Melchior Cano: It must be believed that the Roman Church received by tradition from God something for which no warrant is found in the word of God. This opinion is hissed off by Richard Field, and not undeservedly. Nevertheless, on the hypothesis that the Roman Church is the true Church of God, this dogma follows entirely from that saying of Augustine, however absurd it is.

units.la: 4 Secundò, nihil pro Apostolico habendum nisi id tantummodo quod in scriptis Apostolorum reperitur: Falsum igitur (quod Augustinus) universam Ecclesiae praxim sufficere, ut quid probetur Apostolicum esse. Diserte Hieronymus: Quae absque authoritate & testimoniis scripturarum, quasi Apostolica traditione sponte reperiunt atque confingunt, percutit gladius Dei. Ita Cypr. Si aut in Evangelio praecipitur, aut in Apostolorum Epistolis & actibus continetur: observetur (alias non) haec divina traditio. Ita Theoph. Diabolicum est extra divinarum scripturarum authoritatem aliquid divinum putare: at divinum est quod Apostolicum est, non igitur illud extra scripturam quaerendum ubi.
units.tr: 4. Second, nothing is to be held apostolic unless it is found in the writings of the Apostles. Therefore it is false (as Augustine says) that the universal practice of the Church is enough to prove something apostolic. Hierome says plainly: Whatever they spontaneously discover and invent, without authority and testimony of the Scriptures, as if by apostolic tradition, is struck down by the sword of God. So Cyprian: If it is commanded in the Gospel, or contained in the Epistles and Acts of the Apostles, let this divine tradition be observed; otherwise not. So Theophylact: It is diabolical to think anything divine apart from the authority of the divine Scriptures; but what is divine is what is apostolic; therefore it is not to be sought outside Scripture.

units.la: Tertiò, si vera haec Augustini regula esset, nihil tamen pro Hierarchicis faceret, cum Episcopos a concilio sancitos primò constet. Superpositus etenim Episcopus fuit totius orbis decreto, inquit Hieronymus, statuente Concilio Ambrosius. At non nominat Ambrosius quo concilio, respondet Bilsonus, & totius orbis apud Hieronymum decretum ipsorum Apostolorum decretum erat: Regerit Dominamus: Adjicit rationem Hadrianus Saravia contra Bazam: Elegantior Hieronymus erat, quam ut consuetudinem decreti nomine signaret. At non nudam consuetudinem intellexit Beza: sed decretum per Ecclesias singulas in suis Synodis particularibus, per consuetudinem gradatim, & ut sese Hieronymus explicat, paulatim invalescens, de quo alius dicendi locus erit. Hoc sensu & ipse Augustinus, Episcoporum honorem secundum usum Ecclesiae invaluisse dicit. Respondet Saravia: Usus Ecclesiae, inquit Augustinus, obtinuit: quid hoc significat? Male Ecclesiae usus divinae institutioni opponitur: quum Augustino qui ita locutus est Ecclesiae universalis alicujus cuius rei usus, argumentum sit institutionis divinae ut traditionis Apostolicae. August. de Baptismo, cont. Donatist. lib. 4. c. 24. Quod universa tenet Ecclesia, nec Conciliis institutum, sed semper retentum est nonnisi Apostolica authoritate traditum rectissime creditur. Quo teneam vultus mutantem Protea nodo; Quod a Conciliis institutum est, a rebus Apostolicis hac sententia excipit Augustinus: & tamen quum Episcopum ex usu Ecclesiae in Conciliis & decretis suis introductum dicit, tum & quae a Conciliis sunt, hac ipsa in sententia includit.
units.tr: Third, even if this rule of Augustine were true, it would still do nothing for the Hierarchicals, since it is clear that bishops were first instituted by a council. For a bishop was set over the whole world by decree, says Hierome, the Council decreeing, Ambrose. But Ambrose does not name which council, replies Bilson, and the decree of the whole world in Hierome was the decree of the Apostles themselves. The Dominicans retort. Hadrian Saravia adds a reason against Beza: Hierome was too elegant to designate a custom by the name of a decree. But Beza did not understand a bare custom, but a decree made in individual churches in their particular synods, through custom gradually, and, as Hierome himself explains, growing strong little by little, about which there will be another place to speak.
