In this sense Augustine too says that the honour of bishops has grown strong according to the usage of the Church. Saravia replies: "The usage of the Church," says Augustine, has prevailed. What does this mean? Church usage is wrongly set against divine institution, since for Augustine, who spoke thus, the usage of some universal Church in any matter is a ground of divine institution just as of apostolic tradition. Augustine, On Baptism against the Donatists, book 4, chapter 24: What the whole Church holds, and what was not instituted by councils but has always been retained, is most rightly believed to have been handed down by apostolic authority alone. Where shall I hold the shape-changing Proteus with a knot? From what has been instituted by councils, Augustine excepts it from apostolic matters by this sentence; and yet, when he says that the bishop was introduced by the usage of the Church in its councils and decrees, he includes within this same sentence those things which come from councils.

units.la: Quarto, si vera haec regula Augustini sit, tum fides humana authoritate niteretur: nam ecclesiae praxis nonnisi humana consuetudo est, ut recte ante Whitakerus. Hoc respectu hanc ipsam Augustini regulam ab ipso Augustino rescissam dico, ut cum consuetudinem absque veritate & ratione nihil esse, imo in quaestione hac nostra de disciplina, ubi ratio, & veritas contra illucet, omnino rejiciendam docet. Sic enim habet: Quod anterius est inquiunt, falsum esse non potest, quasi antiquitas & vetus consuetudo praejudicet veritati? Rursus Veritate manifestata cedat consuetudo rationi — Plane quis dubitat veritati manifestae consuetudine cedere? Nemo consuetudini veritati & rationi, proponat, quia consuetudinem ratio & veritas semper excludit. Postremo: Qui contempta veritate, praesumit consuetudinem sequi, aut circa fratres invidus est, aut malignus, quibus veritas revelatur, aut circa Deum ingratus est, inspiratione cujus Ecclesia instruitur. Nam Dominus in Evangelio Ego sum, inquit, veritas, non dixit: Ego sum consuetudo, itaque veritate manifestata cedat consuetudo rationi. Atque ut Augustinus Augustino in his quae adversus consuetudinem scribit contrarius est: ita Bilsonus Augustino pro Ecclesiae praxi consentiens, adversatus Bilsono in eis quae contra consuetudinem disputat. In causis (inquit) religionis, non quid homines facere consueverunt, sed quid facere debuerunt respiciendum est. Tertullianus. Quodcunque adversus veritatem sapit hoc erit haeresis, etiam vetus consuetudo. & Concilium Carthaginense: Dominus in Evangelio dicit, Ego sum veritas, non ego sum consuetudo. Et Cypr. Consuetudo sine veritate vetustas erroris est. Dixit haec adversus universam Ecclesiae praxim Cyprianus: & licet in materia rebaptizationis erravit, in forma tamen argumentandi non erravit, Bilsono ipso teste. Quidni igitur nos absolvamur, etsi contra universam Ecclesiae praxim, veritate ejus jam manifestata, disciplinam reformandam esse existimamus? Atque ut in materia errans Cyprianus, in forma tamen contra universam Ecclesiae praxim disputandi non erravit, ut Thomae Bilsonae visum: ita vice versa, in materia non errans Stephanus Romanus in forma argumentandi ex universa Ecclesiae praxi erravit, uti Domino Morneo placet, qui ita hanc historiam penitus. Dixit Stephanus: Nihil innovetur nisi quod traditum est: respondet Cyprianus: Oportet Episcopum non solum docere, sed discere, quasi dicat, praestaret Stephanum communicato cum collegis consilio religionem discere, quam consuetudinis praetexta impotenter imperare: cum praesertim
units.tr: Fourthly, if this rule of Augustine were true, then human faith would rest on human authority, for the practice of the Church is nothing but human custom, as Whitaker rightly said before. In this respect I say that this very rule of Augustine has been annulled by Augustine himself, since he teaches that custom without truth and reason is nothing, and indeed that in this question of ours about discipline, where reason and truth shine against it, it must be wholly rejected. For he says: "They say, 'What was earlier cannot be false'; as if antiquity and old custom prejudiced truth? Again, when truth has been made plain, let custom yield to reason." — "Who can doubt that custom must yield to plain truth? No one should set custom against truth and reason, since reason and truth always exclude custom." Last of all: "Whoever, having scorned truth, presumes to follow custom, is either envious or malicious toward the brethren, to whom truth is revealed, or ungrateful toward God, by whose inspiration the Church is instructed." For the Lord in the Gospel says, "I am the truth," not "I am custom"; therefore, when truth has been made plain, custom must yield to reason. And just as Augustine is opposed to Augustine in what he writes against custom, so Bilson, agreeing with Augustine in defence of the Church's practice, is opposed to Bilson in what he argues against custom. "In matters of religion," he says, "what men have been accustomed to do is not to be considered, but what they ought to have done." Tertullian: "Whatever savours of something against the truth will be heresy, even if it is an old custom." And the Council of Carthage: "The Lord says in the Gospel, 'I am the truth,' not 'I am custom.'" And Cyprian: "Custom without truth is the antiquity of error." Cyprian said these things against the whole practice of the Church; and although he erred on the matter of rebaptism, he did not err in his method of arguing, as Bilson himself testifies. Why then should we not be excused, even if we judge that discipline must be reformed against the whole practice of the Church, now that its truth has been made plain? And just as Cyprian, erring in the matter, did not err in the form of arguing against the whole practice of the Church, as it seemed to Thomas Bilson, so conversely Stephen of Rome, not erring in the matter, erred in the form of argument from the whole practice of the Church, as it pleases Mr. Morney, who thus wholly recounts this history: "Stephen said: 'Let nothing be changed except what has been handed down.' Cyprian replies: 'A bishop ought not only to teach but also to learn,' as if to say it were better for Stephen, after taking counsel with his colleagues, to learn religion than to command powerlessly under the pretext of custom, especially since

units.la: A a 2 praesertim confusitudo absque veritatis veteribus erroris sit.
units.tr: A a 2 especially since custom without truth is the antiquity of error.

units.la: En sententiam in Stephanos nostros Anglicanos capitalem. Confuetudinis & universæ Ecclesiæ praxis praetextu impotenter collegis imperant: qui nonnisi communicato cum collegis consilio, quicquam agere debuerunt. Post hos Hierarchici ipsi consulendi. Ita Richardus Fyldus: Quanquam tota multitudo fidelium, uno tempore per totum orbem errare non potest pertinaciter & damnabiliter in falsa traditione recipienda: qui tamen in Ecclesia plurimum poterunt, errare omnes possunt. Quoniam haec, inquis; Nempe ut patet errorem tantum pertinacem & damnantem ab universa Ecclesiæ praxi excludi, non hunc nostrum disciplinarium, quem non ex pertinacia sed ignorantia, in re minimè absolutè salutem fidelium destruente, in universam Ecclesiam grassatum fuisse dicimus, si tamen in universam grassata sit.
units.tr: Here is the sentence, fatal to our English Stephens: they command their colleagues powerlessly under the pretext of custom and the whole Church's practice, when they ought to do nothing except after taking counsel with their colleagues. After these, the prelates themselves are to be consulted. So Richard Field: "Although the whole multitude of the faithful cannot, at one time throughout the whole world, stubbornly and damnably err in receiving a false tradition, yet all who have the greatest power in the Church can err." Why these things, you ask? Clearly so that only a stubborn and damnable error is excluded from the whole practice of the Church, not this disciplinary error of ours, which we say, if indeed it has spread through the whole Church, spread not from stubbornness but from ignorance, in a matter that does not absolutely destroy the salvation of the faithful.

units.la: Thomas Morton Hierarchicus illud Cani approbat: Infirmum est ex omnium patrum consensu argumentum, & contraria sententia potius probabiliter & piè defenditur. Hadrianus Saravia ita: Mos populi Dei ab omnibus Eccl. sis totius orbis receptus, inviolabilis quaedam lex est. Verisimile non est universalem consensum omnium Ecclesiarum & temporis, sine verbo Dei aut Apostolica traditione potuisse accidere. Tamen quia nullus consensus, nulla cosuetudo, nulla longi temporis praescriptio contra Dei verbum locu in Ecclesia Christi retinere debet: ponderandae sunt nobis rationes, & scripturae loca examinanda, quibus inducti patres illud regimen in Ecclesia receperant, quod nostra aetatis hominibus minime probetur, ut certo sciamus, illine, an nos erremus. En confessionem luculentam: ut omnia dicantur quae in laudem universae praxeos congeri possunt: non ea tamen à sese certos nos facere potest; sed ad verbum examinanda, & si absque ea, vel praeter eam, reperiatur, eliminanda.
units.tr: Thomas Morton, a prelate, approves that saying of Canus: "An argument from the consensus of all the Fathers is weak, and the contrary opinion may be defended as probable and pious." Hadrian Saravia says: "The custom of the people of God, received by all the Churches of the whole world, is a certain inviolable law. It is not likely that a universal consensus of all Churches and all times could have arisen without the Word of God or apostolic tradition. Yet, since no consensus, no custom, no prescription of long time ought to retain a place in the Church of Christ against the Word of God, we must weigh the reasons and examine the passages of Scripture by which the Fathers were led to receive that government in the Church, which is least approved by men of our age, so that we may know for certain whether they or we are in error." Here is a clear confession. Let everything be said that can be brought together in praise of the universal practice; yet it cannot make us certain of itself. It must be examined by the Word, and if it is found without the Word, or beside it, it must be cast out.

units.la: Quinto, ita hanc regulam Augustini interpretatus Desiderius acsi per Concilia, generalia Concilia tantùm intellexit, ita probat Episcopalem fun�tionem ab Apostolis descendisse, quia ante annos 300 exititit, quo tempore generale Concilium nullum celebratum est. Primum autem generale Concilium Nicaenum fuit: in quo tantum abfuit, quòd Episcopalis functio tum primum instituta fuerit, ut Patriarchalis etiam ab ipso Concilio agnoscatur, more antiquo, longè ante inolevisse. Respondeo primo, hinc sequi Augustini hanc regulam salvam esse, nisi statuatur pro fundamento, Ecclesiam in sua praxi minimè potuisse errare per annos 300, per quod temporis spacium, generale Concilium nullum extitit, quod quicquam in universam praxim inducere potuit, non ab Apostolis institutum. Vidit haec Bellarminus: Ecclesia, inquit, non magis operando quàm credendo errare potest, juxta Augustinum, qui ait, insolentissimè insaniè esse, disputare num id faciendum sit, quod tota die per orbem frequentat Ecclesia. Hoc autem quàm absurdum sit, ostendunt nostrorum scripta omnia, quibus Ecclesiam errare posse probant. Ego pro praesenti ipsius unico Augustini exemplo insistam. Disputabat contra Cypri[ani] rebaptizationem ex universa Ecclesiae praxi intra hos trecentos annos: & hoc argumento contra Donatistas uti noluit Augustinus, inquit Whitakerus noster: Quid ita? quia humanum documentum erat: at si humanum documentum erat universa intra annos 300. Ecclesiae praxis, & infirmum etiam ad rem quamlibet Apostolicam probandam erit. Imitentur igitur Augustini ipsius quo nituntur exemplum: de hac universa praxi in posterum sileant, scripturisque solis agant, cum eo denique dicant: Ne videar humanis argumentis id probare, ex Evangelio profero certa documenta. Certè hoc exemplo Augustini tolluntur opprobria illa quae ex superiori Augustini sententia, de insania insolentissima, nobis obiectari à Bilsono aliisque solent. Quid enim? humani argumenti certitudinem differri an insania insolentissima quaeso est? cum ipse hujusce sententiae author Augustinus, contra documenta & humana argumenta, quasi contraria opposuerit? Quanto justius nos insaniae Hierarchicos insimulare possumus, ex Chrysostomo. Sed quid si non credat scripturae? Tu ipsum adversperis velut furibundum & mente captum.
units.tr: Fifthly, Desiderius, interpreting this rule of Augustine as if he understood it only of general councils, proves that the episcopal function descended from the Apostles because it existed before three hundred years ago, at which time no general council was held. But the first general council was that of Nicaea, in which it was so far from being the case that the episcopal function was first instituted at that time, that even the patriarchal function is acknowledged by the council itself as having grown up long before, in the ancient manner. I answer first that it follows from this that the rule of Augustine stands safe, unless it is laid down as a foundation that the Church could in no way have erred in her practice for three hundred years, during which span of time no general council existed that could have introduced anything into the universal practice that had not been instituted by the Apostles. Bellarmine saw this: "The Church," he says, "can err no more in acting than in believing, according to Augustine, who says that it is most insolently mad to dispute whether that should be done which the Church throughout the world practises every day. How absurd this is, all the writings of our people show, by which they prove that the Church can err." For the present I will rest on this one example of Augustine himself. He disputed against the rebaptism of Cyprian from the whole practice of the Church within those three hundred years; and Augustine was unwilling to use this argument against the Donatists, says our Whitaker. Why so? Because it was a human argument. But if the practice of the whole Church within three hundred years was a human argument, it will also be weak for proving any apostolic matter whatever. Let them therefore imitate the very example of Augustine on which they rely: let them be silent from now on about this universal practice, and deal with Scripture alone, saying with him: "Lest I seem to prove this by human arguments, I bring forward certain proofs from the Gospel." Surely by this example of Augustine those reproaches are removed which are commonly thrown at us by Bilson and others from the earlier saying of Augustine, about most insolent madness. For what? Is the certainty of a human argument, I ask, the same as most insolent madness, since the very author of this saying, Augustine, has opposed human arguments and proofs as if they were contrary? How much more justly can we charge the prelates with madness, from Chrysostom: "But what if he does not believe Scripture? You treat him as one raving and out of his mind."

units.la: Secundò, respondeo hoc ipsum generale Concilium in quo insistit Georgius Downamus, hanc ipsam ex Augustino, ipsius regulam impugnare. Nihil nisi Apostolicum, inquit, in universa Ecclesiae praxi fuit ante concilium Nicaenum, quia nullum tum generale concilium extitit, quod universam praxim noviter introducere potuit. At conclamant ipsissima Concilij verba, quae etiam Downamus in margine appoluit, [illegible, ~3 words]: quae ad ea quae humano jure introducta fuerunt, vel ipse Downamus defert. Consequitur igitur eum ipsum fateri in universa Ecclesiae praxi, ante primum Concilium generale, quosdam mores fuisse, qui humano jure introducti, non Apostolica authotitate traditi fuerunt.
units.tr: Secondly, I answer that this very general council on which George Downame insists is itself an argument against this very rule of Augustine. "Nothing but what was apostolic," he says, "was in the universal practice of the Church before the Council of Nicaea, because no general council then existed which could newly introduce a universal practice." But the very words of the council cry out against this, which Downame himself noted in the margin, [illegible, about three words]: which he himself refers to those things that were introduced by human law. It follows, then, that he himself admits that in the universal practice of the Church, before the first general council, there were certain customs which, introduced by human law, were not handed down by apostolic authority.

units.la: Sextò, haec regula Augustini ab universa Ecclesiae praxi ducta, incerta est: sicuti de eadem adversus Bellarminum noster Whitakerus agens, verissimè asseveravit. Magnum, inquit, est Augustini nomen in Ecclesia Dei, & merito quidem. Sed meminisse debeamus hominem fuisse, ac proinde errare potuisse. Et licet hoc loco quidem videatur favere traditionibus, tamen aliis in locis scripturae perfectionem acerrime defendit. 2, probare non potuit traditiones ab Ecclesiis omnibus fuisse servatas. Neque enim narrat quid ab Ecclesiis aliis factitatum erat. Virine fortasse Ecclesiae hanc consuetudinem servarunt, & non dubium est, Hipponensem totam Ecclesiam servasse: sed non constabat illi similiter de omnibus aliis Ecclesiis. Dixit Waldensis olim, traditiones Apostolicas a puré Ecclesiasticis jam temporis vetustate discernere nescimus: Non agnovit igitur hanc regulam Augustinus de universa Ecclesiae praxi, utpote hanc Ecclesiae praxim despexit, quòd jam temporis vetustate confusa & ignorata sit.
units.tr: Sixthly, this rule of Augustine, drawn from the universal practice of the Church, is uncertain, as our Whitaker, arguing against Bellarmine about the same, most truly affirmed. "The name of Augustine is great in the Church of God, and rightly so. But we ought to remember that he was a man, and so could err. And although in this place he seems indeed to favour traditions, yet in other places he most vigorously defends the perfection of Scripture. Second, he could not prove that the traditions were observed by all the Churches. For he does not relate what was done by the other Churches. Perhaps the Church of Virinus kept this custom, and there is no doubt that the Church of Hippo as a whole kept it; but it was not clear to him that the same was true of all the other Churches. Waldensis once said that we cannot distinguish apostolic traditions from those which are purely ecclesiastical, now that they have been confused and lost by the antiquity of time." Augustine therefore did not recognise this rule about the universal practice of the Church, since he despised that practice because, by the antiquity of time, it had become confused and unknown.

units.la: Septimò, aut falsa haec regula Augustini est, aut nullae fuerint olim consuetudines latenter & paulatim irrepentes, quae neque ab Apostolis, neque à Conciliis introductae fuerunt. Hujusmodi autem consuetudines olim extitisse, haec Tertulliani fidem faciunt: Veritati nemo praescribere potest, non spatium temporum, non patrocinia personarum, non privilegium regionum. Ex his enim fere consuetudo initium ab aliqua ignorantia aut simplicitate sortita, in usum per successionem corroboratur & ita adversus veritatem vindicatur. Quod si regerant autem in consuetudinibus universa Ecclesiae praxi observatis, locum ista non habere: ab ipso Tertulliano alibi luculenter refutantur: recenset etenim exempla plurima, quae sine ullius scripturae instrumento, solius traditionis titulo, exinde consuetudinis patrocinio vindicantur. Nominat, renuntiationem, trinam mersionem, baptismi interrogationes, abstinentiam a lavacro per totam hebdomadam, oblationes pro defunctis, natalitia anniversaria, jejunium & geniculationem dominica die prohibitam, crucis signum fronti impressum, quaecunque veterum conversatio exerceret: quae nonne quaeso ab universa tum Ecclesia usurpata fuerunt?
units.tr: Seventhly, either this rule of Augustine's is false, or there have been, in former times, customs that crept in unnoticed and gradually, which were introduced neither by the Apostles nor by Councils. That such customs did exist is shown by this saying of Tertullian: no one can prescribe against truth; not the length of time, not the patronage of persons, not the privilege of regions. For from these, a custom that began from some ignorance or simplicity gains a lot, is strengthened in use by succession, and is thus defended against the truth. But if they reply that these things do not apply to customs observed in the universal practice of the Church, Tertullian himself refutes them clearly elsewhere. For he lists many examples which, without any written instrument of Scripture, are defended on the sole title of tradition and by the patronage of custom. He names renunciation, threefold immersion, the questions at baptism, abstinence from bathing throughout the whole week, oblations for the dead, anniversary birthday celebrations, fasting and kneeling prohibited on the Lord's day, the sign of the cross impressed on the forehead, and whatever else the conduct of the ancients practised. Were not these, I ask you, then used by the whole Church?

units.la: Octavo & ultimo, pessimam operam locare Ecclesiae Hierarchicos dico, qui de universa Ecclesiae praxi hanc Augustini regulam probant & complectuntur, imo & aliis etiam imponunt: ut quae data portaverunt in Ecclesiam, tanta fere traditionum papalium infesta agmina: Non enim absque causa Caesar Baronius, hanc regulam Augustini qua Apostolicum esse vult, quodcunque olim ab Ecclesia universa est observatum funiculum appellat, qui traditionum latitudinem metitur. Atque scire vis lector quam haec falsa regula sit? Percurre illas antiquas consuetudines omnes, quae in nullo concilio sancitae sunt, & ignotam originem habent, quaeque jam a Pontificiis pro Apostolicis obtruduntur: & non solum quam Augustinus falsus, sed etiam quam Papistici Hierarchici, facillime deprehendes.
units.tr: Eighthly and lastly, I say that the Hierarchs do a very bad service to the Church, who approve and embrace this rule of Augustine's concerning the universal practice of the Church, and even impose it on others, so that they bring in the things they have carried in, almost a hostile host of papal traditions. For not without cause Caesar Baronius calls this rule of Augustine, by which whatever the whole Church has observed is held to be Apostolic, a measuring cord, which measures out the breadth of tradition. And if you wish to know, reader, how false this rule is, run through all those ancient customs which were sanctioned in no council, have an unknown origin, and which the Papists now thrust forward as Apostolic. You will very easily discover not only how false Augustine is, but also how false the Papist Hierarchs are.

units.la: Primo, insto cum Sixtrando Lubberto in observatione Paschatis: de qua sic ille: Non quis statim inferat hoc vel illud Apostolicum esse, quoniam ab Ecclesia servabatur, inquirendum in illud paulo diligentius. Nemo tamen existimet haec in Augustinum ferri: ejus enim memoria est apud me in benedictione: sed tantum veritatis indagandae studio facio. Augustinus dicit observationem certi diei paschatis observari ab universa Ecclesia, ideo esse vel ab Apostolis vel a plenariis Conciliis profectam. Verum tempore Polycarpi & Aniceti, Apostoli nullum diem certum statuerant. Anicetus enim praetendebat Iohannem, & Polycarpus e contra majorum suorum morem contrarium, Eusebius Histor. lib. 5. c. 24. neque eo tempore in ullo Concilio de eo actum erat. Sequitur ergo certae diei paschae observationem non esse ab Apostolis profectam. Excipiet fortasse quis nullam tum fuisse diei paschatis observationem universam, quod falsum est: quanquam enim in ipso die differentia erat: in hoc tamen Ecclesiae omnes conspiraverunt, diem paschatis observandum aliquem esse. At qui nego hoc ab Apostolis profectum esse: nihil illi de festis diebus aliquibus, nedum de paschate tradiderunt: vel ex hac unica igitur universae Ecclesiae observatione constat, ex eo non sequi Apostolicum cum quid esse, quòd eo universa Ecclesia utatur. Atq; liceat hic mihi quod poëta admonere: Ex uno disce omnes. Fac Episcopatum ab universa Ecclesia pristina observatum; nonne illa in Episcopatu tanquam ab Apostolis tradito errare potuit, perinde ac in paschate?
units.tr: First, I press, with Sibrandus Lubbertus, on the observance of Easter, of which he speaks thus: One should not straightway infer that this or that is Apostolic because it was kept by the Church; it must be inquired into a little more carefully. Yet let no one think these remarks are directed against Augustine, for I hold his memory in blessing; I say this only from zeal for searching out the truth. Augustine says that the observance of a certain day of Easter was kept by the whole Church, and therefore that it came either from the Apostles or from full Councils. But in the time of Polycarp and Anicetus the Apostles had appointed no fixed day. For Anicetus claimed the authority of John, while Polycarp, on the other hand, the contrary custom of his elders; Eusebius, Church History, book 5, chapter 24. Nor at that time was anything decided about it in any Council. It follows, therefore, that the observance of a fixed Easter day did not come from the Apostles. Perhaps someone will object that at that time there was no universal observance of an Easter day, which is false. For although there was a difference about the day itself, yet in this all the churches agreed, that some day for Easter should be observed. But I deny that this came from the Apostles: they handed down nothing to them about any festival days, still less about Easter. From this single observance of the universal Church, therefore, it is clear that it does not follow that what the whole Church uses is Apostolic. And here allow me to recall the poet's words: From one, learn all. Suppose the episcopate was observed from early times by the whole Church; could not the Church have erred in the episcopate, as it did in Easter, though it was thought to be handed down by the Apostles?

units.la: Secundò, insto in Symbolo Apostolico, quod intra primos trecentos annos prodiisse Dominamus censet. Hoc quoad ipsam formam in nullo plenario Concilio sancitum est, sed origine ignota est, ab universa tamen Ecclesia usurpatum est: quid igitur, ab Apostolis quoad formam traditum? Imò negat ipse Fyldus: negabit sat scio Dominamus: certè negat ipse Augustinus: Illa verba, inquit, quae audivistis per divinas scripturas sparsa, sunt inde collecta & ad unum reducta. Nihil igitur apertius, quàm quiddam ab universa Ecclesia observatum fuisse, non sancitum in plenario Concilio, aut ab Apostolis traditum, ac proinde hanc regulam Augustin de universa Ecclesiæ praxi vacillare.
units.tr: Secondly, I press on the Apostles' Creed, which Dominamus thinks came out within the first three hundred years. As to its very form, this was sanctioned in no full Council, its origin is unknown, yet the whole Church has used it. What then? Was it handed down by the Apostles as to its form? Indeed Fyldus denies it; Dominamus will deny it, I know well; Augustine himself certainly denies it: Those words, he says, which you have heard scattered through the divine Scriptures, have been gathered from there and reduced to one. Nothing is clearer, then, than that something was observed by the whole Church which was neither sanctioned in a full Council nor handed down by the Apostles; and therefore this rule of Augustine's about the universal practice of the Church wavers.

units.la: Tertiò. insto in quadragesima, quam ab universa Ecclesia observatam, & ab omnibus patribus, non Ignatio prætermissò, pro Apostolica traditione habendam, ideoque ab Apostolis ipsis profectam, & semper cùm fusissimè tum salsissimè contendit Lous. Atque quidem ab Ignatio commemoratam quadragesimam esse, perinde ac Episcopum certum est: universam etiam Ecclesiam, quoddam ante pascha jejunium constanter observasse constat: quadragesima tamen, (cur non & Episcopus, quanquam ab Ignatio commemoratus, & ab vniversa Ecclesia receptus?) ab Apostolis tradita minimè erat, sed in ea lapsi patres sunt, (prout in Episcopo) quum eam traditionem Apostolicam existimârunt, ut Theologis nostris omnibus constat. Iohannes Iuellus Defen.Apolg.p.2.c.9.divis.1. Guili.Whitakerus cont 1.q.6.c.3. Sibrandus Lubbertus de princip. Christ. dogmat. lib. 7.c.5.& ut alios omittam, Thomas Mortonus Apolog.Cathol.p.lib.1. c.75.& 88.Observandum autem est cum quadragesima discrimen Episcopi à presbytero Iohannem Hardingum unà conjunxisse, sic ut necessum haberet Iuellus interrogare, utrum hoc discrimen ipsius judicio Traditio Apostolica esset: videant ergo Hierarchici quàm latam portam Traditionibus apperiant: consideret verò lector, hoc discrimen quanquam per universam Ecclesiæ praxim comprobatum, nihil aliud Iuelli iudicio, quam merum humanum inventum fuisse. Neq pro haeretico habendus est, inquit, qui hanc universa Ecclesiae praxim repudiarit: sic ut innocentiam hac in re nostram, adversus clamores Hierarchicos egregiè tueatur. Tantane haeresis est, inquit, Episcopum & presbyterum eundem esse, asseverare? vel Hardingus quo & ad quos extendit haeretici nomen, Hardingus intelligit? Certè Chrysostomus dicit inter Episcopum & presbyterum interesse fere nihil. Hieronymus, Apostolus perspicuè docet eosdem esse presbyteros, quos Episcopos Augustinus dicit, Quid est Episcopus nisi primus presbyter, hoc est summus sacerdos? Ambrosius dicit: Episcopi & presbyteri una ordinatio est: utrque enim sacerdos est, sed(1)
units.tr: Thirdly, I press on Lent, which Lous has always contended, both most fully and most wittily, was observed by the whole Church and by all the fathers, Ignatius not omitted, and is to be held as an Apostolic tradition, and therefore came from the Apostles themselves. And indeed it is certain that Lent is mentioned by Ignatius, just as the Episcopate is; it is also established that the whole Church constantly observed a certain fast before Easter. Yet Lent (why not the Episcopate too, though mentioned by Ignatius and received by the whole Church?) was by no means handed down by the Apostles; but in this the fathers erred (as with the Episcopate), when they thought it an Apostolic tradition, as is agreed by all our theologians. John Jewel, Defence of the Apology, part 2, chapter 9, division 1. William Whitaker, Contra 1, question 6, chapter 3. Sibrandus Lubbertus, On the Principles of Christian Doctrine, book 7, chapter 5; and, to omit others, Thomas Morton, Catholic Apology, book 1, chapters 75 and 88. It must be noted, however, that Hardingus joined the distinction between bishop and presbyter to Lent, so that Jewel was obliged to ask whether this distinction, in his judgment, was an Apostolic tradition. Let the Hierarchs see, then, how wide a gate they open to traditions. But let the reader consider that this distinction, although approved by the universal practice of the Church, was in Jewel's judgment nothing but a merely human invention. Nor, he says, is he to be held a heretic who has rejected this universal practice of the Church; so he defends our innocence in this matter excellently against the clamours of the Hierarchs. Is it such a heresy, he says, to assert that bishop and presbyter are the same? Or does Hardingus understand whom and how far he extends the name of heretic? Certainly Chrysostom says that there is almost no difference between bishop and presbyter. Jerome, the Apostle, teaches clearly that the presbyters are the same as the bishops. Augustine says: What is a bishop but the first presbyter, that is, the chief priest? Ambrose says: The bishop and the presbyter have one ordination; for both are priests, but (1)

units.la: In 2. Tim. Homil. 11. Ad cuagr. Quaest. vet. & non. Test. p. 101. irrepentia, & non ut postea conspicua facta, non denique, ut nostro tempore, ad suum usque fastigium perducta, non ita dilucidè observare potuit. Est tamen ubi vestigium reliquit, vetustissimæ disciplinæ, eo nempe in loco, quem Bellarminus de successione ista disputans, incautius allegavit. Nomen (inquit) presbyteri commune erat olim presbyteris & Episcopis, ut patet ex Epistola Irenæi ad Victorem quæ est apud Eusebium Histor. lib. 5. c. 24. Vbi Romanos Pontifices, Victorem, Anicetum, Pium, Telesphorum, Xystum, appellat presbyteros. At nihil hoc inquires facit, ut probetur veteres Episcopos, non alios quam presbyteros fuisse. Falsus igitur Guilelmus Biakeus, qui ita respondet Bellarmino: Fattor olim inter presbyterum & Episcopum distrimen nullum fuisse, non opus ergo fuit his testimoniis ad hoc probandum. Sed si hi presbyteri qui olim, & à quibus ordinatus erat Timotheus, tales Episcopi erant, quales nunc sunt in Ecclesia Romana, tunc plures erant unius urbis Episcopi, ut patet Act. 20: 17. ubi Paulus dicitur accersisse presbyteros & Episcopos Ephesinæ Ecclesiæ. Hi si Episcopi fuerunt tunc unius Ecclesiæ Ephesinæ plures simul Episcopi fuerunt, Habet & hæc: Fuisse semper tales Episcopos in Ecclesia quales nunc sunt Pontifices, salsissimum est, nec unquam probari potest. Erant quidem in initio in singulis Ecclesiis Episcopi, id est pastores, non tales quales nunc sunt in Ecclesia Romana.
units.tr: On 2 Timothy, Homily 11. Quaestiones veteris et novi Testamenti, p. 101. (The custom) crept in, and was not then as conspicuous as it later became, nor finally, as in our own time, brought up to its full height; so it could not have been observed so clearly. Yet it left a trace of the most ancient discipline, namely in that passage which Bellarmine, arguing about this succession, cited rather carelessly. The name (he says) presbyter was once common to presbyters and bishops, as is plain from the letter of Irenaeus to Victor, which is in Eusebius, Church History, book 5, chapter 24. There he calls the Roman Pontiffs, Victor, Anicetus, Pius, Telesphorus, Xystus, presbyters. But you will object that this proves nothing, so that it is shown that the ancient bishops were none other than presbyters. Therefore William Biake is wrong, who answers Bellarmine thus: It is granted that formerly there was no distinction between presbyter and bishop; there was no need therefore for these testimonies to prove it. But if those presbyters who once ordained Timothy, and by whom he was ordained, were bishops such as those now in the Roman Church, then there were several bishops of one city, as is plain from Acts 20:17, where Paul is said to have summoned the presbyters and bishops of the Church of Ephesus. If these were bishops, then there were several bishops of the one Church of Ephesus at the same time. He also holds: That there were always bishops in the Church such as the Pontiffs now are, is most false, and can never be proved. There were indeed at the beginning, in each church, bishops, that is ministers, but not such as they now are in the Roman Church.

units.la: Tertiò, ut Papæ à nostris omnibus objicitur, cum Apostolorum successorem non esse, quia opera eorum non exercet, non docet, non gregem curat &c. ita & nobis jam Episcopis Anglicanis occinere licet, eos veterum Episcopprum successores appellandos non esse, quia ambitione, luxu, negligentiâ, sævitiâ impia & tumidâ potentiæ suæ ampliatione, Episcoporum priscorum humilitatem, frugalitatem, diligentiam, & cum suis collegis sociálitatem polluerunt, profanarunt, dehonestarunt. Dixit olim Symmacus Petrum peremem meritorum dotem cum hereditate innocentiæ transfmisssse ad posteros, ut si desint bona acquisita per merita, sufficiant quæ à loco prædecessoro præstantur. Tantum verò abest, quòd hoc verum sit, ut ex adverso condemnentur successores eò magis, quo magis successionem ostentant eorum à quorum pietate degenerarunt. Sic condemnat Moses Iudeos degenerantes, quo magis Mosi fidunt, Ioh. 5: 45. & condemnat Abraham eos qui contrarium faciunt, quò magis se Abrahæ filios gloriantur: Ioh. 8: 39, 40.
units.tr: Thirdly, just as all our people object to the Pope that he is not the successor of the Apostles because he does not perform their work, does not teach, does not care for the flock, and so on, so we too may now sing the same tune about the English bishops: they should not be called successors of the ancient bishops, because by ambition, luxury, negligence, impious cruelty, and the swelling enlargement of their power, they have polluted, profaned, and dishonoured the humility, frugality, and diligence of the early bishops and their fellowship with their colleagues. Symmachus once said that Peter transmitted to posterity a perpetual dowry of merits together with the inheritance of innocence, so that if the goods acquired by merit are lacking, those that are supplied by the place of the predecessor suffice. But this is so far from being true that, on the contrary, successors are condemned all the more, the more they boast of a succession from those whose piety they have abandoned. Thus Moses condemns the degenerate Jews, the more they trust in Moses (John 5:45), and Abraham condemns those who do the opposite, the more they glory in being the sons of Abraham (John 8:39, 40).

units.la: Nonne eò Tyrannus sibi gravius accersit judicium, quò magis se Pij Principis successorem venditat? Citat Thomas Mortonus Hierarchicus illa Basilij: Non cathedræ sed religionis proprium successionem existimare debemus: ——jui contrarium fidei doctrinam amplectitur, adversarius quoque in throno censeri debet. Contrariam de Episcopali dignitate sententiam Episcopi Anglicani jam sedantur: & per ambitionem, contraria veteribus Episcopis faciunt: non tantum igitur non pro successoribus, sed & pro adversarijs habendi sunt. Citat Guli-
units.tr: Does not the tyrant bring a heavier judgment upon himself the more he advertises himself as the successor of a pious prince? Thomas Morton, in his Hierarchicus, cites those words of Basil: "We ought to regard as the proper successor not the one who holds the chair but the one who holds the religion; whoever embraces the contrary doctrine of the faith must be counted an adversary even on the throne." The English bishops now hold a view of episcopal dignity contrary to that of the Fathers, and by their ambition they act contrary to the ancient bishops. Therefore they must be regarded not merely as not successors, but even as adversaries. William Whitaker cites

units.la: {s} Apolog. Catholic. p. 1. lib. 1. c. 6. p. 284. elmus Whitakerus illa Hieronymi apud Gratianum distinct. 40. c.6.non est facile: Non sanctorum loco sunt qui tenent loca sanctorum, sed qui exercent opera eorum. Sic ut operibus Episcoporum Anglicanorum longissime diversis, apertè patet eos veterum Episcoporum successores minime esse.
units.tr: {s} Apolog. Catholic. p. 1, lib. 1, c. 6, p. 284. [it is not easy] the words of Jerome in Gratian, dist. 40, c. 6: "Those are not in the place of saints who hold the places of saints, but those who perform their works." Thus, since the works of the English bishops are very far different from those of the ancient bishops, it is plainly evident that they are by no means successors of the ancient bishops.

units.la: Ad postremum, dixit olim Hieronymus ad Damasum: Facessat Romani culminis ambitio, ego veteri cathedrae consocior. Similiter jam nos: Facessat Episcopi Anglicani ambitio: nobis humili Episcoporum antiquorum cathedrae consociari liceat.
units.tr: Finally, Jerome once said to Damasus: "Let the ambition of the Roman height depart; I associate myself with the ancient chair." Similarly, we now say: let the ambition of the English bishops depart; may it be lawful for us to associate ourselves with the chair of the ancient bishops in humility.

units.la: Quintò jam & ultimo loco, Downamus rursus audiendus: qui hinc Seniores nostros presbyteriales jugulat. quòd eam successionem ostendere nequeant, quam ostendere Episcopi possunt. Respondemus ex nostrorum omnium communi sententia, linearis successionis interruptionem, successionis legitimae veritatem minimè tollere: sic ut quamvis Ecclesia nostra omninò intercisa fuisset, vera tamen Ecclesia fuisset, quandiu cum illa vetustissima conspirat & consentit.
units.tr: Fifthly and lastly, Downame is to be heard again, who from this point cuts down our presbyterial elders, because they cannot show that succession which the bishops can show. We reply, from the common opinion of all of us, that an interruption of the linear succession does not remove the truth of a lawful succession; so that even if our Church had been wholly cut off, it would nonetheless have been a true Church, as long as it agrees and consents with that most ancient Church.

units.la: Probat hoc ex instantia ipsius Christi Whitakerus: Vera & legitima successio potest esse interrupta: Christus enim Melchisedeco per multos annos successit. Sic nos dicimus, licèt successio per multos annos fuerit interrupta; si quis tamen veram doctrinam docet, eum Apostolis succedere. Quid igitur? Nullus inter Christum & Melchisedecum per annos quam plurimos, ejusdem ordinis rex & sacerdos linearì successione intercedebat: & tamen Christus verus Melchisedec hi successor erat: ita quid si nullus seniorum lenatus per multos annos extitit? non hoc impedit, quin moderni seniores illis Apostolicis verè successisse credantur.
units.tr: Whitaker proves this from the instance of Christ himself: "A true and lawful succession can be interrupted; for Christ succeeded Melchizedek after many years." So we say that, although the succession was interrupted for many years, whoever nonetheless teaches true doctrine succeeds the Apostles. What then? For many years there was no linear succession between Christ and Melchizedek, a king and priest of the same order; and yet Christ was the true successor of Melchizedek. So too, even if no elder has been in the senate for many years, this does not prevent us from believing that the present elders have truly succeeded those Apostolic elders.

units.la: Accedit Thomas Mortonus Hierarchicus: Successio personae cum adest non est aspernanda, cùm abest, modo ne desit Catholicae doctrinae successio, non est vehementius exigenda. Hinc illa Stapletoni probat: personalem successionem nihil moramur, modò doctrinam nostram consentientem scripturis ostendere possimus: necnon illa Æneæ Sylvii: Mihi nec laudi nec vituperio erit, dummodo verus Christianus sum, majorum meorum matutina aut vespertina conversio. Ita contra seniores plumbeo pugione pugnavit Downamus, quamdiu veritas disciplinae illibata est, secundùm quam senioribus Apostolicis confirmantur: successio personalis urgenda non erat nec exigenda, illius defectum morari seniores non debent, nec vituperio illis danda est vespertina majorum suorum conversio, ad Senatum presbyterialem, juxta Dei institutum, restaurandum. Hæc, de extraneo firmamento Hierarchico tertio, successione.
units.tr: Thomas Morton in his Hierarchicus adds: "Where personal succession is present it is not to be spurned; where it is absent, provided the succession of Catholic doctrine is not lacking, it is not to be demanded too vehemently." Hence Stapleton's words prove this: "We do not dwell on personal succession, provided we can show our doctrine agreeing with the Scriptures"; and also those of Aeneas Sylvius: "It will be neither praise nor blame to me, so long as I am a true Christian, whether my forefathers' conversion was in the morning or in the evening." Thus, on the other side, Downame fought against the elders with a leaden dagger: as long as the truth of discipline, by which the Apostolic elders are established, remains unimpaired, personal succession was not to be pressed or demanded; the elders ought not to be held back by its lack, nor is the evening conversion of their forefathers to be held against them, in restoring the presbyterial senate according to God's institution. These things are said concerning the third, external Hierarchical support, succession.

units.la: CAP 6.
units.tr: Chapter 6.

units.la: Firmamentum quartum ab unanimi consensu refutatur.
units.tr: The fourth prop, from unanimous consent, is refuted.

units.la: QVartum sequitur, à Papistis similiter mutuatum, Vnanimis consensus: nam quòd causa nostra traducatur acerrimè, quæ omnis quasi communem antiquitatis consensum infestum habeat, tragicæ illæ cum Bancrofii tum Downami vociferationes, non sinunt quenquam ignorare. Quin & Isaacus Casaubonus, nimirum huius consensui unanimi attribuisse videtur, quum eo sublato controversias hodiernas finem nunquam πὰ καὶ ἀληθείας acceptuuras, neque ulla disceptatione terminandas fore dicit. Forte causam ponit in pervicacia papistarum: sed ita quid si secundum hominem sine hoc consensu litium finis sperandus non sit: secundum Deum tamen scripturam habemus, absque huius consensus adminiculo, absoluti ssimam dijudicatricem. Atq; sane hoc sensu, adeò consensum antiquitatis depereunt Hierarchici, ut vix quoad homines, hæc controversia disciplinaria ut unquam finiatur, sperandū sit. Quid tum? eorum error detegendus: neque tam leges huius consensus (quod Isaacus Casaubonus) figendæ, quàm ipsius authoritas prorsus ti lenda, ut ita tandem ad Scripturæ solius limam res tota revocetu.
units.tr: The fourth prop follows, likewise borrowed from the Papists: unanimous consent. That our cause is most bitterly misrepresented, as if all of antiquity were hostile to it, is made plain by those tragic outcries of Bancroft and of Downame alike. Isaac Casaubon also seems to attribute great weight to this unanimous consent, since he says that without it the present controversies will never be settled according to truth [πὰ καὶ ἀληθείας] and can never be ended by any debate. Perhaps he locates the cause in the obstinacy of the Papists. But suppose that, humanly speaking, there is no hope of an end to these disputes without this consent. Still, we have Scripture, the most absolute judge, without any support from such consent. Indeed, in this sense the Hierarchists so despair of the consent of antiquity that, as far as men are concerned, there is scarcely any hope this disciplinary controversy will ever be settled. What then? Their error must be exposed. The rule of this consent (as Isaac Casaubon has it) must not so much be fixed as its authority must be utterly rejected, so that at last the whole matter is referred back to the touchstone of Scripture alone.

units.la: Hoc ut fiat, sciendum est primo, appositè ad causam nostram Whitakerum affirmasse. Adversariorum vero humana media sunt: Nam praxis Ecclesiæ est consuetudo hominum, Paruum sententia, est opinio hominum, Conciliorum definitio, est judicium hominum. Hæc ita cum sint, robur totum unanimis consensus istius in eo poñtur, quòd multitudinem hominum consentientium ponit: cujus in rebus divinis ecquod quæso robur est? provoco hic ego ad Thomam Mortonum Hierarchicum, qui adversus istud argumentum Papisticum ab unanimi consensu dudum, pugnat', & ita pugnat, ut in medium producat Salmeronis illa. Contra hanc quam objectant multitudinem, responderemus ex verbo Dei, Exod. 23: 2. In judicio plurimorum non acquiescet sententiæ, ut à vero deviet. Provoco deinde ad Henricum Pareum Episcopum Glocestrensem, in sua Iohannis Reynoldi versione. Quum unanimem consensum urgisset Hartus ex Vincentio Lyrinensi, respondet Reynoldus, Vincentium in eo supra petram edificasse, quod scripturam solam ad controversias dirimendas adhibuisset: in hoc vero, quod unanimem consensum requisivisset, super arenam hum-anum opinionum. Atq; huic Vincentio opponit Augustinum, qui & Scripturam solam pro fundamento ponit & scripturæ interpretationem ex ipsa scriptura sola sumendam dicit, non ex incertis hominum sensibus.
units.tr: To bring this about, it must first be understood that Whitaker rightly affirmed, with reference to our cause, that the means of our opponents are human. For the practice of the Church is the custom of men; the opinion of the Fathers is the opinion of men; the definition of Councils is the judgment of men. Since these things are so, the whole strength of this unanimous consent lies in the fact that it appeals to a multitude of men agreeing together. But in divine matters, I ask, what strength is there in that? Here I appeal to Thomas Morton the Hierarchist, who for some time has been fighting against this Papist argument from unanimous consent, and fights in such a way that he brings forward the arguments of Salmeron. Against this multitude which they object, we would answer from the Word of God, Exod. 23:2: "You shall not follow a multitude to do evil, nor shall you bear witness in a dispute so as to turn aside after many to pervert justice." Next I appeal to Henry Parry, Bishop of Gloucester, in his version of John Reynolds. When Hart had urged unanimous consent from Vincent of Lérins, Reynolds replies that Vincent built on rock in that he used Scripture alone to settle controversies, but in that he demanded unanimous consent he built on the sand of human opinions. And he opposes to this Vincent, Augustine, who both lays down Scripture alone as the foundation and says that the interpretation of Scripture must be drawn from Scripture itself alone, not from the uncertain feelings of men.

units.la: Secundò, argumentum hoc ab unanimi consensu duƈtum, incertum est: nullo etenim modo loquere potest, utrum antiqui in re aliqua consenserint necne. Imò inquit Isaacus Cafaubonus, duas regulas posuit Cardinalis Peronem, quae omnino recipiendae videntur. Prior est ut tunc existimetur satis probatus esse consensus patrum, quando eminentissimi quique singularum nationum, in rei alicujus affirmatione consenserint, neque illis se quisquam opposuerat, qui quidem orthodoxus censeretur. Posterior, quando Patres non ut doctores loquuntur, neque dicunt hoc aut illud sic esse credendum aut faciendum, sed tanquam testes eorum quae suis temporibus Ecclesia universalis credebat aut faciebat, dicunt hanc esse fidem aut praxim Ecclesiae Catholicae per totum orbem terrarum; tunc eum bonorem illis habendum esse, ut ad unanimem consensum Ecclesiae ejusmodi affirmatio satis creditur valere. Atqui inquam haec consensus indicia, ipsi Vincentio Lyrinensi, hujus consensus primo, aut primario saltem patrono, infirma visa sunt. Ille namque non alium consensum ad quaestiones determinandas adhibendum esse censet, quam quando omnes pariter uno consensu, idem manifeste, comiter, constanterque tenent, scribunt, docent. Atque hic ille est, quem dissimulato nomine perstringit Peronius, quando ait: Sententia eorum palam iniqua est qui de consensu patrum satis liquere non posse contendunt, nisi quando res eadem totidem verbis apud omnes patres reperitur. Miror igitur, maluisse se Isaacum Casaubonum, Peronium, Bellarminum, hujusque farinae Papistas reliquos sequi, potius quam Vincentium Lyrinensum, & scriptores protestantes, quorum eadem cum Vincentio sententia est. Guil. Whitakerus ita: Quomodo sciemus reliquos non dissentire? nam multi libri patrum perierunt & multi patres nihil scripserunt: fieri potest ut illi dissenserint. Praeterea a patribus etiam nonnullis multa tradita sunt, quae vel Papistarum confessione non sunt Apostolica, a quibus tamen reliquos ab illis dissensisse non possunt ostendere. Similiter Iohannes Reynoldus necnon in illius versione Henricus Pareus: Cum eadem quae Peronius supra posuisset Hartus: Quando interpretatio a multis patribus fit, & non contradicunt reliqui, aut nihil omnino de eadem dicunt: tum eam unanimi consensu factam putamus. Regerit Reynoldus: Haec summa male colligitur: quia in scriptis Patrum, unus nonnunquam contra quam omnes reliqui scripturas exponit (quod & Sixto Senensi & Aloysio Lippomano constat (. & quia probabile est in patribus eis quos non habemus, diversam interpretationem traditam fuisse ab ea quae jam reperitur, in eis quorum monumenta extant. Subjungit deinde: Consensus via non est per quam tuto incedere licet, si viam veritatis quaerimus: nam & siti enecabimur, sicut qui Timane aquas expectant, Iob. 6.8: 9. & quod peius est, pro limpida veritatis unda lutum & caenum propinabitur. Tertiò, si unanimus consensus patrum ad dirimendas lites sufficiat, tum ad exitum profligata est haec quaestio disciplinaria. Quid etenim? Citat Thomas Mortonus Medinam verè affirmantem: Non dubito affirmare sanctum Hieronymum, Sedulium, Primasium, Theodoretum, Oecumenium, Theophylactum, cum Arianis haereticis sensisse, quòd Episcoporum ac presbyterorum ordinem jure divino, eundem esse dicunt. Haec de extraneo firmamento Hierarchico quarto, Vnanimi consensu.
units.tr: Secondly, the argument drawn from unanimous consent is uncertain: indeed, it can in no way be known whether the ancients agreed on some matter or not. Rather, as Isaac Casaubon says, Cardinal Perron laid down two rules which seem entirely acceptable. The first is that the consent of the Fathers is then considered sufficiently proved when the most eminent men of each nation agree in affirming some matter, and no one who would be regarded as orthodox has opposed them. The second is that when the Fathers do not speak as teachers, nor say that this or that must be believed or done, but as witnesses of what the universal Church believed or did in their own times, and say that this is the faith or practice of the Catholic Church throughout the whole world, then such an affirmation is to be accorded so much honour that it is believed to be sufficient to establish the unanimous consent of the Church. Yet, I say, these signs of consent seemed weak even to Vincent of Lérins himself, the first, or at least the chief, champion of this consent. For he holds that no other consent is to be used for determining questions than when all alike, with one consent, clearly, universally and constantly hold, write and teach the same thing. And this is the man whom Perron attacks, without naming him, when he says: "The opinion of those is plainly unjust who contend that the consent of the Fathers cannot be sufficiently clear unless the same thing is found in the very same words in all the Fathers." I wonder, then, that Isaac Casaubon, Perron, Bellarmine and the rest of that stripe of Papists preferred to follow these men rather than Vincent of Lérins and the Protestant writers, whose view is the same as Vincent's. William Whitaker says: "How shall we know that the rest do not dissent? For many books of the Fathers have perished, and many Fathers wrote nothing: it may be that they dissented. Moreover, many things have been handed down by some of the Fathers which, even by the confession of the Papists, are not apostolic, and yet they cannot show that the rest dissented from them." Likewise John Reynolds, and Henry Parry in his version, with the same point Perron had made above: Hart says: "When an interpretation is given by many Fathers, and the rest do not contradict it, or say nothing at all about it, then we think it was made by unanimous consent." Reynolds replies: "This conclusion is badly drawn: because in the writings of the Fathers one sometimes expounds Scripture contrary to all the rest (as is established both for Sixtus of Siena and for Aloysius Lippomanus), and because it is probable that among those Fathers whose works we do not have, a different interpretation was handed down from that which is now found among those whose monuments survive." He adds then: "The way of consent is not one on which it is safe to walk, if we seek the path of truth: for we shall be parched with thirst, like those who wait for waters at Timana, Job 6:18–19, and, what is worse, instead of the clear water of truth, mud and filth will be poured out for us." Thirdly, if the unanimous consent of the Fathers were sufficient to settle disputes, then this disciplinary question would be finished. For what then? Thomas Morton quotes Medina, who truly affirms: "I do not hesitate to affirm that Saint Jerome, Sedulius, Primasius, Theodoret, Oecumenius and Theophylact agreed with the Arian heretics in saying that the order of bishops and presbyters is the same by divine right." These things concern the fourth outside prop of the Hierarchists, unanimous consent.

units.la: CAP 7, Argumentum quintum ab Ecclesiae universae praxi solvitur.
units.tr: CAP 7, The fifth argument is answered from the practice of the whole Church.

units.la: Quintum sequitur, à Papistis iterum mutuatum: Vniversa nempe Ecclesiae praxis: quam cum urgeret Bellarminus, supponit Ecclesiam in universa praxi sua minimè errare potuisse. Hucusque forte Hierarchici non progredientur, ut Ecclesiam non potuisse errare dicant: dicunt tamen (quod eodem fere recidit) eam non erravisse, id quod dicere necesse est, ut huic argumento vis solida insit. Hinc Apostolicum illis est, quodcunque in Ecclesiae subsequentis communem usum receptum est: quò Tertullianum citant: Constabit id esse ab Apostolis traditum, quod apud Ecclesias Apostolorum fuerit sacrosanctum. Respondeo, Videri mihi Tertullianum per Ecclesias Apostolorum eas tantum intelligere, quae Apostolorum tempore exiterunt: quo sensu verum est quod dicit.
units.tr: The fifth argument follows, borrowed again from the Papists: the universal practice of the Church. Bellarmine presses it, assuming that the Church in its whole practice could not possibly err. Perhaps the Hierarchists will not go so far as to say that the Church could not err, but they say (which comes to almost the same thing) that she has not erred, and this they must say if the argument is to have any real force. Hence they hold that whatever has been received into the common use of the later Church is apostolic, and they cite Tertullian: It will be established that that was handed down by the Apostles which was held sacred among the churches of the Apostles. I reply that Tertullian seems to understand by "the churches of the Apostles" only those which existed in the Apostles' own time, and in that sense what he says is true.

units.la: Primò etenim in hac citatione delumbata, si Ecclesias sequentes intellexisset, dixisset profecto quod apud Ecclesias Apostolorum est sacrosanctum, non quod fuerit: tempus etenim praeteritum, non praesens, haec verba notant.
units.tr: For first, in this citation, if he had meant the churches that followed, he would certainly have said "what is held sacred among the churches of the Apostles," not "what has been held sacred"; these words denote past time, not present.

units.la: Secundo, scribetur locus integer. Si constat id verius quod prius, id prius quod ab initio, ab initio quod ab Apostolis; pariter utique constabit id esse ab Apostolis traditum, quod apud Ecclesias Apostolorum fuerit sacrosanctum. Initio respondent Ecclesiae tantum quae ab initio plantatae sunt: & non dicit apud Ecclesias Apostolicas, sed apud Ecclesias Apostlorum quae non nisi illae esse poterant, quas Apostoli plantaverunt, aut saltem quae eorum tempore plantatae erant. Sequitur locus ille celebris ex Augustino, qui fere una cum isto Tertulliani citari ab Hierarchicis solet: Quod universa tenet Ecclesia, nec Conciliis institutum, sed semper retentum est, non nisi authoritate Apostolica traditum rectissime creditur. Hoc illud Achilleum Hierarchicorum argumentum est: quo miseros puritanos suffltos putant: certè ab omnibus aut saltè coram pluribus magna contentione allegatur. Downamus etiam in fronte concionis posuit, tanquam eorum quae sequerentur, omnium fundamentum. Neque Angelum septem Ecclesiarum, vel ex vocis significatione, vel ex ulla textus sui circumstantia, Episcopum Hierarchicum significare, probare nititur: sed hoc solo (quantum ego asseque possum) argumento pugnat. Ecclesia subsequens Episcopos Hierarchicos habuit: ergo hic Angelus Apocalypticus Episcopus Hierarchicus erat.
units.tr: Second, let the whole passage be written out. If that is more truly established which came earlier, and that which came earlier is from the beginning, and that which is from the beginning is from the Apostles; then, surely, it will likewise be established that what was held sacred among the churches of the Apostles was handed down by the Apostles. At the beginning, the churches that answer are only those planted from the beginning; and he does not say "among the Apostolic churches" but "among the churches of the Apostles," which could only be those the Apostles planted, or at least those that existed in their time. There follows that famous passage from Augustine, which the Hierarchists usually cite alongside this one from Tertullian: What the whole Church holds, which has not been instituted by councils but has always been retained, is rightly believed to have been handed down by apostolic authority alone. This is that Achilles' heel of the Hierarchists' argument, by which they think the wretched Puritans are struck down; at any rate it is cited by everyone, or at least before many people, with great emphasis. Downame also placed it at the head of his sermon as the foundation of all that followed. Nor does he attempt to prove that the angel of the seven churches means a Hierarchical bishop, either from the meaning of the word or from any circumstance of the text; he fights only with this one argument, so far as I can see. The later Church had Hierarchical bishops; therefore this Apocalyptic angel was a Hierarchical bishop.

units.la: 2 Consequentiam argumenti probaturus, praefatur ex hoc Augustini {a}mini loco: Quod universa tenet Ecclesia, nec a Conciliis institutum, sed semper retentum est, nonnisi authoritate Apostolica traditum rectissime creditur. De mente Augustini non controversatur: quanquam per semper retentum prima facie, id tantùm intelligere videtur, quod ab ipsis Apostolorum temporibus dimanavit. Sed verba sequentia, inquis, ostendunt, nec a Conciliis institutum, Augustinum intelligere omne id semper retentum esse, quod primum in Conciliis institutum non est ut exponit Bilsonus, aut ejus origo ignota est, ut Richardus Bancrofus, & Georgius Dolmamus interpretantur. Ostendunt sanè: neque ego hanc Augustini quam Hierarchici adferunt interpretationem rejiciam: tantum admoneo posterioris clausulæ nuditatem folio ficulneo coopertam ab eis esse, ne ejusdem fœditas appareret. Rogo, quid illud sibi vult? ab Apostolica authoritate traditum? Intelligunt, inquit, id ab Apostolis in sacris literis scriptum esse, aut inde colligi posse: quod universa, postmodum Ecclesia tenuit. Apage φλυαρίας. Nihil certius est, quam traditiones non scriptas Augustinum hîc somniasse in hunc sensum. Quod in universa Ecclesia praxi retentum est, si ejus origio aliàs, puta, per Concilia cognita non sit: ab Apostolis voce viva traditum censetur, etsi in eorum scriptis non reperiatur. Et nomine pudet Evangelicos præcipuum suæ Hierarchiæ fundamentum ex hujusmodi loco repetere, quod non scriptas Apostolorum traditiones tam fortiter spirat? Hanc etenim Augustini mentem fuisse testantur alia ejusdem loca, quæ unà cum isto à Baronio copulantur: & etiam ab Hierarchicis allegantur.
units.tr: 2. To prove the consequence of his argument, he prefaces it with this passage of Augustine: What the whole Church holds, which has not been instituted by councils but has always been retained, is rightly believed to have been handed down by apostolic authority alone. No one disputes Augustine's meaning, although at first sight by always retained he seems to understand only what has come down from the very times of the Apostles. But the following words, you say, show that by not instituted by councils Augustine means that everything always retained is something not first instituted in councils, as Bilson explains it, or whose origin is unknown, as Richard Bancroft and George Downame interpret it. They certainly do show this, and I will not reject this interpretation of Augustine which the Hierarchists bring forward. I only warn that they have covered the nakedness of the latter clause with a fig leaf, so that its foulness should not appear. I ask, what does it mean? "Handed down by apostolic authority"? They understand, you say, that it was written in Holy Scripture by the Apostles, or can be gathered from it, since the whole later Church held it. Away with nonsense! Nothing is more certain than that Augustine here is not dreaming of unwritten traditions in this sense. What is retained in the practice of the whole Church, if its origin is otherwise unknown, that is, not known through councils, is judged to have been handed down by the Apostles by the living voice, even if it is not found in their writings. And are the Evangelicals ashamed to draw the chief foundation of their Hierarchy from such a passage, which breathes so strongly of unwritten apostolic traditions? Other passages of the same author, which Baronius couples with this one and which the Hierarchists also cite, testify that this was Augustine's mind.

units.la: Quam consuetudinem credo, inquit, ex Apostolorum traditione veniente, sicut multa non inveniuntur in literis eorum & tamen quia custodiuntur per universam Ecclesiam, nonnisi ab ipsis tradita & commendata traduntur. Disputatur locus à Iohanne Whitgifto, ut probet Patriarchas ab Apostolis descendisse, & Archidiaconos, Archiepiscopos Metropolitanos: de quibus sic habet: Quandoquidem origo & initium horum nominum reperiri non potest, ea horum antiquitas est, ut credendum sit ab Apostolis ipsis exorta fuisse: memini etenim Augustinum hanc habere regulam: Illa autem quæ non scripta sed tradita ostendimus, quæ quidem toto terrarum orbe observantur, datur intelligi, vel ab ipsis Apostolis vel plenariis Conciliis (quorum est in Ecclesiis salubberrima authoritas) commendata atque statuta RETINERI: sicuti quod Domini passio & resurrectio, & ascensio in cælum, & adventus de cælo Spiritus sancti, anniversaria solennitate celebrantur, & si quid tale occurrerit, quod servatur ab universa quacunque se diffundit Ecclesia.
units.tr: "I believe," he says, "that this custom comes from apostolic tradition, just as many things are not found in their writings and yet, because they are kept throughout the whole Church, are handed down only as having been delivered and commended by the Apostles themselves." This passage is cited by John Whitgift to prove that patriarchs descended from the Apostles, and archdeacons and metropolitan archbishops as well. Of these he says: Since the origin and beginning of these names cannot be found, their antiquity is such that it must be believed they arose from the Apostles themselves. For I remember that Augustine holds this rule: "Those things, however, which we show not to be written but handed down, and which are observed throughout the whole world, are understood to have been commended and established either by the Apostles themselves or by plenary councils (whose authority in the Churches is most salutary), and to be RETAINED"; just as the passion and resurrection of the Lord, and his ascension into heaven, and the coming of the Holy Spirit from heaven, are celebrated with an annual solemnity, and whatever similar thing occurs which is observed by the whole Church wherever it spreads.

units.la: Videte singulare Hierarchicorum artificium: Commemoratur ab antiquis Episcopus, ideo descendit ab Apostolis, quod testimonium ab antiquissimis scriptis habeat. Metroplitanus & Archiepiscopus è contra, in scriptis antiquis non reperitur, ideo originem ab Apostolis ipsis habebit, quia ejus origo aliàs ignota est. Quid ita? Nempe propter universam Ecclesiæ praxim, cujus authoritas infallibilis est; in quam etiam sententiam allegatur à Bilsono, & Casaubono, ille alter Augustini locus: Non facere quod universa facit Ecclesia, insolentissimae insaniae est. Quàm autem parum solidi huic argumento insit, deinceps demonstrandum.
units.tr: See the peculiar craft of the Hierarchists. A bishop is mentioned by the ancients; therefore he descends from the Apostles, because he has testimony from the most ancient writings. A metropolitan and an archbishop, on the other hand, are not found in ancient writings; therefore they will have their origin from the Apostles themselves, because their origin is otherwise unknown. Why so? Namely because of the universal practice of the Church, whose authority is infallible. To this same opinion Bilson and Casaubon also cite that other passage of Augustine: Not to do what the whole Church does is the most intolerable madness. How little solid strength this argument has, we shall show next.

units.la: 3 Compara Augustini locū cum quibusdam paribus & similibus. Baronius postquam sacerdotum apud omnes gentes authoritatem demonstrasset, ita infert: Recte Socrat. apud Zenophon. lib. 4. Quod ab omnibus gentibus observatum est, id non nisi a Deo sanctum esse, dicendum est. Quidni universa hominum praxis a Deo per lumen naturale: perinde ac universa Ecclesiae praxis ab Apostolis per lumen supernaturale? Bellarminus: Illud procul dubio est Apostolicum habendum & judicandum quod pro tali habetur in eis Ecclesiis in quibus est integra successio Episcoporum. Exploditur haec regula Bellarmini a Guilielmo Whitakero: quis tamen non videt, ex hac Augustini regula, robur eam lucemque accipere? Ita Melchior Canus: Credendum est ea Romanam Ecclesiam per traditionem a Deo recepisse, cujus authoramentum nullum in verbo Dei reperitur. Exibilatur haec sententia a Richardo Fylda, nec immerito: ex hypothesi tamen Romanam Ecclesiam veram Dei Ecclesiam esse, ex isto Augustini loco, quanquam absurdissimum, dogma istud omninò sequitur.
units.tr: 3. Compare Augustine's passage with some similar and parallel ones. Baronius, after demonstrating the authority of priests among all nations, concludes thus: Rightly Socrates, in Xenophon, book 4: "What is observed by all nations must be said to be holy only by God." Why should not the universal practice of men come from God through the natural light, just as the universal practice of the Church comes from the Apostles through the supernatural light? Bellarmine: Without doubt that must be held and judged apostolic which is regarded as such in those churches where there is an unbroken succession of bishops. This rule of Bellarmine is exploded by William Whitaker; yet who does not see that this rule of Augustine receives from it strength and light? So Melchior Cano: It must be believed that the Roman Church received by tradition from God what no authority for it can be found in the word of God. This opinion is hissed off by Richard Field, and not undeservedly; yet on the hypothesis that the Roman Church is the true Church of God, this dogma follows entirely from that passage of Augustine, however absurd it is.

units.la: 4 Secundò, nihil pro Apostolico habendum nisi id tantummodo quod in scriptis Apostolorum reperitur: Falsum igitur (quod Augustinus) universam Ecclesiae praxim sufficere, ut quid probetur Apostolicum esse. Disertè Hieronymus: Quae absque authoritate & testimonis scripturarum, quasi Apostolica traditione sponte reperiunt atque confingunt, percutit gladius Dei. Ita Cypr. Si aut in Evangelio praecipitur, aut in Apostolorum Epistolis & actibus continetur: observetur (alias non) haec divina traditio. Ita Theoph. Diabolicum est extra divinarum scripturarum authoritatem aliquid divinum putare: at divinum est quod Apostolicum est, non igitur illud extra scripturam quaerendum ubi.
units.tr: 4. Second, nothing is to be held apostolic except what is found in the writings of the Apostles. Therefore it is false (as Augustine says) that the universal practice of the Church is enough to prove something apostolic. Jerome plainly: Whatever things they spontaneously discover and invent, without the authority and testimony of the Scriptures, as if by apostolic tradition, the sword of God strikes down. So Cyprian: If it is commanded in the Gospel, or contained in the Epistles and Acts of the Apostles, let this divine tradition be observed; otherwise not. So Theophylact: It is diabolical to think something divine outside the authority of the divine Scriptures; but what is divine is what is apostolic; therefore it is not to be sought elsewhere than in Scripture.

units.la: Tertiò, si vera haec Augustini regula esset, nihil tamen pro Hierarchicis faceret, cum Episcopos a concilio sancitos primò constet: Superpositus etenim Episcopus fuit totius orbis decreto, inquit Hieronymus, statuente Concilio Ambrosius. At non nominat Ambrosius quo concilio, respondet Bilsonus, & totius orbis apud Hieronymum decretum ipsorum Apostolorum decretum erat: Regerit Dorman: Adjicit rationem Hadrianus Saravia contra Bezam: Elegantior Hieronymus erat, quam ut consuetudinem decreti nomine signaret. At non nudam consuetudinem intellexit Beza: sed decretum per Ecclesias singulas in suis Synodis particularibus, per consuetudinem gradatim, & ut sese Hieronymus explicat, paulatim invalescens, de quo alius dicendi locus erit. Hoc sensu & ipse Augustinus, Episcoporum honorem secundum usum Ecclesiae invaluisse dicit. Respondet Saravia: Usus Ecclesiae, inquit Augustinus, obtinuit: quid hoc significat? Male Ecclesiae usus divinae institutioni opponitur: quum Augustino qui ita locutus est Ecclesiae universalis ali-cujus cujus rei usus, argumentum sit institutionis divinae ut traditionis Apostolicae. Augustin. de Baptismo cont. Donatist. lib. 4. c. 24. Quod universa tenet Ecclesia, nec Conciliis institutum, sed semper retentum est nonnisi Apostolica authoritate traditum rectissime creditur. Quo teneam vultus mutantem Protea modo; Quod a Conciliis institutum est, a rebus Apostolicis hac sententia excipit Augustinus: & tamen quum Episcopum ex usu Ecclesiae in Conciliis & decretis suis introductum dicit, tum & quae a Conciliis sunt, hac ipsa in sententia includit.
units.tr: Third, even if this rule of Augustine were true, it would still do nothing for the Hierarchists, since it is first established that bishops were sanctioned by a council. For a bishop was set above (the others) by the decree of the whole world, says Jerome, the council decreeing, says Ambrose. But Ambrose does not name which council, answers Bilson; and in Jerome the decree of the whole world was the decree of the Apostles themselves. Dorman replies; Adrian Saravia adds a reason against Beza: Jerome was too elegant to use the word "decree" to denote a custom. But Beza did not understand a bare custom; he understood a decree made in the individual Churches in their particular synods, gradually through custom, and, as Jerome himself explains it, gradually gaining strength, about which there will be another place for discussion. In this sense Augustine himself also says: He says that the honour of bishops prevailed according to the usage of the Church. Saravia replies: "The usage of the Church," says Augustine, "prevailed": what does this mean? The usage of the Church is wrongly opposed to divine institution, since for Augustine, who spoke thus, the usage of some universal Church is a proof of divine institution, like apostolic tradition. Augustine, On Baptism against the Donatists, book 4, chapter 24: "What the whole Church holds, which has not been instituted by councils but has always been retained, is rightly believed to have been handed down by apostolic authority alone." How can I hold Proteus, changing his face in this way? What was instituted by councils, Augustine excepts from apostolic matters by this statement; and yet, when he says that the bishop was introduced by the usage of the Church in its councils and decrees, he includes within this same statement what came from councils.

units.la: Quartò, si vera haec regula Augustini sit, tum fides humana authoritate niteretur: nam ecclesiae praxis nonnisi humana consuetudo est, ut recte ante Whitakerus. Hoc respectu hanc ipsam Augustini regulam ab ipso Augustino rescissam dico, ut cum consuetudinem absque veritate & ratione nihil esse, imo in quaestione hac nostra de disciplina, ubi ratio, & veritas contra illucet, omnino rejiciendam docet. Sic enim habet: Quod anterius est inquiunt, falsum esse non potest, quasi antiquitas & vetus consuetudo praejudicet veritati? Rursus Veritate manifestata cedat consuetudine rationi — Plane quis dubitat veritati manifestae consuetudine cedere? Nemo consuetudini veritati & rationi, proponat, quia consuetudinem ratio & veritas semper excludit. Postremò: Qui contempta veritate, praesumit consuetudinem sequi, aut circa fratres invidus est, aut malignus, quibus veritas revelatur, aut circa Deum ingratus est, inspiratione cujus Ecclesia instruitur. Nam Dominus in Evangelio: Ego sum, inquit, veritas, non dixit: Ego sum consuetudo, itaque veritate manifestata cedat consuetudo rationi. Atque ut Augustinus Augustino in his quae adversus consuetudinem scribit contrarius est: ita Bilsonus Augustino pro Ecclesiae praxi consentiens, adversatus Bilsono in eis quae contra consuetudinem disputat. In causis (inquit) religionis, non quid homines facere consueverunt, sed quid facere debuerunt respiciendum est. Tertullianus. Quodcunque adversus veritatem sapit hoc erit haeresis, etiam vetus consuetudo. & Concilium Carthaginense: Dominus in Evangelio dicit, Ego sum veritas, non, ego sum consuetudo. Et Cypr. Consuetudo sine veritate vetustas erroris est. Dixit haec adversus universam Ecclesiae praxim Cyprianus: & licet in materia rebaptizationis erravit, in forma tamen argumentandi non erravit, Bilsono ipso teste. Quidni igitur nos absolvamur, etsi contra universam Ecclesiae praxim, veritate ejus jam manifestata, disciplinam reformandam esse existimamus? Atque ut in materia errans Cyprianus, in forma tamen contra universam Ecclesiae praxim disputandi non erravit, ut Thomae Bilsoni visum: ita vice versa, in materia non errans Stephanus Romanus in forma argumentandi ex universa Ecclesiae praxi erravit, uti Domino Morneo placet, qui ita hanc historiam ponit. Dixit Stephanus: Nihil innovetur nisi quod traditum est: respondet Cyprianus: Oportet Episcopum non solum docere, sed discere, quasi dicat, praestaret Stephanum communicato cum collegis consilio religionem discere, quam consuetudinis praetextu impotenter imperare: cum praesertim
units.tr: Fourthly, if this rule of Augustine were true, then human faith would rest on human authority, for the practice of the Church is nothing but human custom, as Whitaker rightly said earlier. In this respect I say that this very rule of Augustine is itself annulled by Augustine, since he teaches that custom without truth and reason is nothing, and indeed that in this question of ours about discipline, where reason and truth shine against it, it must be wholly rejected. For he says: "Are we to say that what is older cannot be false, as though antiquity and long-standing custom prejudged the truth? Again: when the truth has been made plain, custom must yield to reason. Who indeed doubts that custom must yield to manifest truth? No one should set custom against truth and reason, because custom is always excluded by reason and truth." Lastly: "Whoever, despising the truth, presumes to follow custom is either envious toward the brethren, to whom the truth has been revealed, or malicious, or ungrateful toward God, by whose inspiration the Church is taught." For the Lord says in the Gospel: "I am the truth," not "I am custom." Therefore, when the truth is made plain, custom must yield to reason. And just as Augustine is at odds with Augustine in what he writes against custom, so Bilson, agreeing with Augustine in defence of the Church's practice, is at odds with Bilson in what he argues against custom: "In matters of religion (he says) we must look not to what men have been accustomed to do, but to what they ought to have done." Tertullian: "Whatever savours of something against the truth will be heresy, even if it is an old custom." And the Council of Carthage: "The Lord says in the Gospel, 'I am the truth,' not 'I am custom.'" And Cyprian: "Custom without truth is the antiquity of error."
