Cyprian said this against the whole practice of the Church; and although he erred on the matter of rebaptism, he did not err in his manner of arguing, as Bilson himself bears witness. Why then should we not be excused, even though we judge that discipline must be reformed against the whole practice of the Church, now that its truth has been made plain? And just as Cyprian, though erring in the matter, did not err in the manner of disputing against the whole practice of the Church, as it seemed to Thomas Bilson, so conversely Stephen of Rome, not erring in the matter, erred in the manner of arguing from the whole practice of the Church, as Mr. Mornay holds, who presents the story thus: "Stephen said: 'Nothing is to be changed except what has been handed down.' Cyprian replies: 'A bishop ought not only to teach but also to learn,' as if to say: it would be better for Stephen, after taking counsel with his colleagues, to learn religion, rather than to rule imperiously under the pretext of custom, especially since

units.la: Cont. Apol. p. 4. p. 603. De virginit. Veland. praesertim consuetudo absque veritate vetustas erroris fit.
units.tr: Against the Apology, p. 4, p. 603; On the Veiling of Virgins. especially since custom without truth becomes the antiquity of error.

units.la: En sententiam in Stephanus nostros Anglicanos capitalem. Consuetudinis & universae Ecclesiae praxis praetextu impunter collegis imperant: qui nonnisi communicato cum collegis consilio, quicquam agere debuerunt. Post hos Hierarchici ipsi consulendi. Ita Richardus Fyldus: Quanquam tota multitudo fidelium, uno tempore per totum orbem errare non potest pertinaciter & damnabiliter in falsa traditione recipienda: qui tamen in Ecclesia plurimum polleant, errare omnes possunt. Quoniam haec, inquis; Nempe ut patet errorem tantum pertinacem & damnantem ab universa Ecclesiae praxi excludi, non hunc nostrum disciplinarium, quem non ex pertinacia sed ignorantia, in re minime absolute salutem fidelium destruente, in universam Ecclesiam grassatum fuisse dicimus, si tamen in universam grassata sit. Thomas Mortonus Hierarchicus illud Cani approbat: Infirmum est ex omnium patrum consensu argumentum, & contraria sententia potius probabiliter & piè defenditur. Hadrianus Saravia ita: Mos populi Dei ab omnibus Eccl. fidelis totius orbis receptus, inviolabilis quaedam lex est. Verisimile non est universalem consensum omnium Ecclesiarum & temporum, sine verbo Dei aut Apostolica traditione potuisse accidere. Tamen quia nullus consensus, nulla consuetudo, nulla longi temporis praescriptio contra Dei verbum locum in Ecclesia Christi retinere debet: ponderandae sunt nobis rationes, & scripturae loca examinanda, quibus inducti patres illud regimen in Ecclesia receperant, quod nostrae aetatis hominibus minime probetur, ut certo sciamus, illine, an nos erremus. En confessionem luculentam: ut omnia dicantur quae in laudem universae praxeos congeri possunt: non ea tamen a sese certos nos facere potest; sed ad verbum examinanda, & si absque ea, vel praeter eam, reperiatur, eliminanda. Quintò, ita hanc regulam Augustini interpretatus Dolmanus acsi per Concilia generalia Concilia tantum intellexit, ita probat Episcopalem functionem ab Apostolis descendisse, quia ante annos 300 exititit, quo tempore generale Concilium nullum celebratum est. Primum autem generale Concilium Nicaenum fuit: in quo tantum abfuit, quod Episcopalis functio tum primum institua fuerit, ut Patriarchalis etiam ab ipso Concilio agnoscatur, more antiquo, longe ante inolevisse. Respondeo primo, hinc sequi Augustini hanc regulam falsam esse, nisi statuatur pro fundamento, Ecclesiam in sua praxi minime potuisse errare per annos 300, per quod temporis spacium, generale Concilium nullum extitit, quod quicquam in universam praxim inducere potuit, non ab Apostolis institutum. Vidit haec Bellarminus: Ecclesia, inquit, non magis operando quàm credendo errare potest, juxta Augustinum, qui ait, insolentissime insanie esse, disputare num id faciendum sit, quod tota die per orbem frequentat Ecclesia. Hoc autem quàm absurdum sit, ostendunt nostrorum scripta omnia, quibus Ecclesiam errare posse probant. Ego pro praesenti ipsius unico Augustini exemplo insistam. Disputabat contra Cypri-ani ani rebaptizationem ex universa Ecclesiae praxi intra hos trecentos annos: & hoc argumento contra Donatistas uti noluit Augustinus, inquit Whitakerus noster: Quid ita? quia humanum documentum erat: at si humanum documentum erat universa intra annos 300. Ecclesiae praxis, & infirmum etiam ad rem quamlibet Apostolicam probandam erit. Imitentur igitur Augustini ipsius quo nituntur exemplum: de hac universa praxi in posterum sileant, scripturisque solis agant, cum eo denique dicant: Ne videar humanis argumentis id probare, ex Evangelio profero certa documenta. Certè hoc exemplo Augustini tol- luntur opprobria illa quae ex superiori Augustini sententia, de insania insolentissima, nobis obiectari à Bilsono aliisque solent. Quid enim? humani argumenti certitudinem diffiteri an insania insolentissima quaeso est? cum ipse hujusce sententiae author Augustinus, contra documenta & humana argumenta, quasi contraria opposuerit? Quanto justius nos insaniae Hierarchicos insimulare possumus, ex Chrysostomo. Sed quid si non credat scriptura? Tu ipsum adversperis velut furibundum & mente captum.
units.tr: Here is a sentence against our English Stephens, and a chief one: they rule imperiously over their colleagues under the pretext of custom and the universal practice of the Church, though they ought to do nothing except after taking counsel with their colleagues. After these, the bishops themselves are to be consulted. Thus Richard Field: "Although the whole multitude of the faithful cannot, at one time throughout the whole world, stubbornly and damnably err in receiving a false tradition, yet all of them, however greatly they prevail in the Church, can err." Why do you bring this up, you ask? Clearly, as is plain, only the stubborn and damnable error is excluded from the universal practice of the Church, not this disciplinary error of ours, which we say crept into the whole Church not from obstinacy but from ignorance, in a matter that by no means absolutely destroys the salvation of the faithful, if indeed it has crept into the whole Church. Thomas Morton, the bishop, approves that saying of Cano: "An argument from the consensus of all the Fathers is weak, and the contrary opinion may be defended with probability and piety." Hadrian Saravia says this: "The custom of the people of God, received by all the faithful churches of the whole world, is a certain inviolable law. It is not likely that a universal consensus of all churches and times could have arisen without the Word of God or apostolic tradition. Yet, because no consensus, no custom, and no prescription of long time ought to retain a place in the Church of Christ against the Word of God, we must weigh the reasons and examine the passages of Scripture by which the Fathers were led to receive that government in the Church, which is by no means approved by men of our age, so that we may know for certain whether they or we are in error." Here is a clear confession: though everything that can be gathered in praise of the universal practice is said, it cannot of itself make us certain; it must be examined by the Word, and if it is found without the Word, or beside it, it must be cast out. Fifthly, Dolman, interpreting this rule of Augustine as though by general councils he understood only councils, proves that the episcopal office descended from the Apostles because it existed more than 300 years ago, a time in which no general council was held. But the first general council was that of Nicaea, in which it was so far from being true that the episcopal office was first instituted then, that even the patriarchal office is acknowledged by that very council as having long before grown up by ancient custom. I reply, first, that it follows from this that the rule of Augustine is false, unless it is laid down as a foundation that the Church could in no way have erred in its practice for 300 years, during which span of time no general council existed that could have introduced anything into the universal practice that was not instituted by the Apostles. Bellarmine saw this: "The Church, he says, cannot err in practice any more than in belief, according to Augustine, who says that it is most insolent madness to dispute whether that should be done which the Church throughout the world practises every day." How absurd this is, however, is shown by all our writings, in which we prove that the Church can err. For the present I will rest on the one example of Augustine himself. He disputed against the rebaptism of Cyprian from the universal practice of the Church within these three hundred years; and Augustine, says our Whitaker, did not wish to use this argument against the Donatists. Why so? Because it was a human proof; but if the universal practice of the Church within 300 years was a human proof, it will also be weak for proving any apostolic matter whatever. Let them therefore imitate the very example of Augustine on which they rely: let them be silent henceforth about this universal practice and deal with Scripture alone, saying with him: "Lest I seem to prove this by human arguments, I bring forward certain documents from the Gospel." Certainly by this example of Augustine those reproaches are removed which Bilson and others are wont to throw at us from the earlier sentence of Augustine about the most insolent madness. For what? Is it, I ask, the most insolent madness to deny the certainty of a human argument, when the very author of this sentence, Augustine, has set up documents and human arguments against one another as though they were contrary? How much more justly can we charge the bishops with madness, from Chrysostom: "But what if Scripture does not believe it? You assail it as one raving and out of his mind."

units.la: Secundò, respondeo hoc ipsum generale Concilium in quo insistit Georgius Downamus, hanc ipsam ex Augustino, ipsius regulam impugnare. Nihil nisi Apostolicum, inquit, in universa Ecclesiae praxi fuit ante concilium Nicaenum, quia nullum tum generale concilium extitit, quod universam praxim noviter introducere potuit. At conclamant ipsissima Concilii verba, quae etiam Downamus in margine apposuit, κατὰ τὴν ἀρχαίαν παράδοσιν: quae ad ea quae humano jure introducta fuerunt, vel ipse Downamus defert. Consequitur igitur eum ipsum fateri in universa Ecclesiae praxi, ante primum Concilium generale, quosdam mores fuisse, qui humano jure introducti, non Apostolica authoritate traditi fuerunt.
units.tr: Secondly, I reply that this very general council on which George Downham relies is itself used to attack this rule of Augustine. "Nothing but what was apostolic," he says, "existed in the universal practice of the Church before the Council of Nicaea, because no general council then existed that could newly introduce a universal practice." But the very words of the Council cry out against this, which Downham also placed in the margin: "according to ancient tradition" [κατὰ τὴν ἀρχαίαν παράδοσιν]; and Downham himself refers that to those things which were introduced by human law. It follows, therefore, that he himself admits that in the universal practice of the Church, before the first general council, there were certain customs which were introduced by human law and not handed down by apostolic authority.

units.la: Sextò, haec regula Augustini ab universa Ecclesiae praxi ducta, incerta est: sicuti de eadem adversus Bellarminum noster Whitakerus agens, verissimè asseverat. Magnum, inquit, est Augustini nomen in Ecclesia Dei, & merito quidem. Sed meminisse debeamus hominem fuisse, ac proinde errare potuisse. Et licet hoc loco quidem videatur favere traditionibus, tamen aliis in locis scripturae perfectionem acerrime defendit. 2, probare non potuit traditiones ab Ecclesiis omnibus fuisse servatas. Neque enim narrat quid ab Ecclesiis aliis factitatum erat. Virine fortasse Ecclesiae hanc consuetudinem servarunt, & non dubium est, Hipponensem totam Ecclesiam servasse: sed non constabat illi similiter de omnibus aliis Ecclesiis. Dixit Waldensis olim, traditiones Apostolicas a puré Ecclesiasticis jam temporis vetustate discernere nescimus: Non agnovit igitur hanc regulam Augustinus de universa Ecclesiae praxi, utque hanc Ecclesiae praxim despexit, quòd jam temporis vetustate confusa & ignorata sit.
units.tr: Sixthly, this rule of Augustine's, drawn from the universal practice of the Church, is uncertain. Our Whitaker, arguing against Bellarmine on this very point, rightly asserts: "Augustine's name is great in the Church of God, and deservedly so. But we should remember that he was a man, and so could err. Although in this place he seems to favour traditions, in other places he very vigorously defends the perfection of Scripture. Second, he could not prove that the traditions were kept by all the Churches. For he does not relate what was done by the other Churches. Perhaps the Churches kept this custom; and there is no doubt that the whole Church of Hippo kept it, but he was not certain of the same for all the other Churches. Waldensis once said that we cannot, by the lapse of time, distinguish apostolic traditions from those that are purely ecclesiastical." Augustine therefore did not recognise this rule about the universal practice of the Church; and he despised that practice, because by the passage of time it had become confused and unknown.

units.la: Septimò, aut falsa haec regula Augustini est, aut nullae fuerint olim consuetudines latenter & paulatim irrepentes, quae neque ab Apostolis, neque à Conciliis introductae fuerunt, Hujusmodi autem cum quid esse, quòd eo universa Ecclesia utatur. Atq; liceat hic mihi quod poëta admonere: Ex uno disce omnes. Fac Episcopatum ab universa Ecclesia pristina observatum; nonne illa in Episcopatu tanquam ab Apostolis tradito errare potuit, perinde ac in paschate?
units.tr: Seventhly, either this rule of Augustine's is false, or there have been in former times customs that crept in secretly and gradually, introduced neither by the Apostles nor by Councils; and of this kind there surely are some, which the whole Church nonetheless uses. And here let me be allowed the poet's warning: "Learn all from one." Suppose that the Church of old observed episcopacy universally: would it not have been able to err in this regard, as if episcopacy had been handed down by the Apostles, just as it erred about Easter?

units.la: Secundò, insto in Symbolo Apostolico, quod intra primos trecentos annos prodiisse Dominamus censet. Hoc quoad ipsam formam in nullo plenario Concilio sancitum est, sed origine ignota est, ab universa tamen Ecclesia usurpatum est: quid igitur, ab Apostolis quoad formam traditum? Imò negat ipse Eyldus: negabit sat scio Dominus: certè negat ipse Augustinus: Illa verba, inquit, quae audivistis per divinas scripturas sparsa, sunt inde collecta & ad unum reducta. Nihil igitur apertius, quàm quiddam ab universa Ecclesia observatum fuisse, non sancitum in plenario Concilio, aut ab Apostolis traditum, ac proinde hanc regulam Augustin de universa Ecclesiæ praxi vacillare.
units.tr: Secondly, I press the Apostles' Creed, which Downame thinks came forth within the first three hundred years. As to its very form, it was enacted in no full Council; its origin is unknown, yet it was used by the whole Church. What then? Was it handed down by the Apostles as to its form? Indeed Eyld himself denies it; Downame, I am quite sure, will deny it; certainly Augustine himself denies it: "Those words," he says, "which you have heard scattered through the divine Scriptures, have been gathered from there and brought together into one." Nothing is clearer, then, than that something was observed by the whole Church which was neither enacted in a full Council nor handed down by the Apostles; and so this rule of Augustine's about the universal practice of the Church wavers.

units.la: Tertiò. insto in quadragesima, quam ab universa Ecclesia observatam, & ab omnibus patribus, non Ignatio praetermissò, pro Apostolica traditione habendam, ideoque ab Apostolis ipsis profectam, & semper cùm fusissimè tum salsissimè contendit Lotus. Atque quidem ab Ignatio commemoratam quadragesimam esse, perinde ac Episcopum certum est: universam etiam Ecclesiam, quoddam ante pascha jejunium constanter observasse constat: quadragesima tamen, (cur non & Episcopus, quanquam ab Ignatio commemoratus, & ab vniversa Ecclesia receptus?) ab Apostolis tradita minimè erat, sed in ea lapsi patres sunt, (prout in Episcopo) quum eam traditionem Apostolicam existmarunt, ut Theologis nostris omnibus constat. Iohannes Iuellus Defen. Apolg. p.2.c.9.divis.1. Guili.Whitakerus cont 1.q.6.c.3. Sibrandus Lubbertus de princip. Christ. dogmat. lib. 7.c.5.& ut alios omittam, Thomas Mortonus Apolog. Cathol. p. lib.1. c.75.& 88. Observandum autem est cum quadragesima discrimen Episcopi à presbytero Iohannem Hardingum unà conjunxisse, sic ut necessum haberet Iuellus interrogare, utrum hoc discrimen ipsius judicio Traditio Apostolica esset: videant ergo Hierarchici quàm latam portam Traditionibus apperiant: consideret verò lector, hoc discrimen quanquam per universam Ecclesiæ praxim comprobatum, nihil aliud Iuelli iudicio, quam merum humanum inventum fuisse. Nec pro haeretico habendus est, inquit, qui hanc universa Ecclesiae praxim repudiarit: sic ut innocentiam hac in re nostram, adversus clamores Hierarchicos egregiè tueatur. Tantane haeresis est, inquit, Episcopum & presbyterum eundem esse, asseverare? vel Hardingus quo & ad quos extendit haeretici nomen, Hardingus intelligit? Certè Chrysostomus dicit inter Episcopum & presbyterum interest fere nihil. Hieronymus, Apostolus perspicue docet eosdem esse presbyteros, quos Episcopos Augustinus dicit, Quid est Episcopus nisi primus presbyter, hoc est summus sacerdos? Ambrosius dicit: Episcopi & presbyteri una ordinatio est: utrque enim sacerdos est, sed. Sed Episcopus primus est. Ex quibus concludit: omnes hij aliique sancti patres una cum Apostolo Paulo, propter hanc sententiam Hardingi judicio pro haereticis habendi sunt.
units.tr: Thirdly, I press Lent, which Lotus has contended, always and most copiously and most sharply, was observed by the whole Church and by all the Fathers, not excepting Ignatius, and is to be regarded as an apostolic tradition, and therefore came from the Apostles themselves. That Lent is recorded by Ignatius is as certain as that there is a bishop; it is also established that the whole Church kept a certain fast before Easter. Yet Lent (why not also the bishop, although recorded by Ignatius and received by the whole Church?) was in no way handed down by the Apostles; rather the Fathers fell into error about it, since they thought it an apostolic tradition, as all our theologians know. John Jewel, Defence of the Apology, part 2, chapter 9, division 1; William Whitaker, Against Duraeus, question 1, chapter 3; Sibrand Lubbertus, On the Principles of Christian Doctrine, book 7, chapter 5; and, to pass over others, Thomas Morton, Catholic Apology, book 1, chapters 75 and 88. It must also be observed that Harding joined the distinction between bishop and presbyter together with Lent, so that Jewel was obliged to ask whether, in the judgement of Harding, this distinction was an apostolic tradition. Let the Hierarchics see how wide a gate they open to traditions! But let the reader consider that this distinction, though approved by the universal practice of the Church, was in Jewel's judgement nothing but a mere human invention. "Nor is he to be regarded as a heretic," he says, "who has rejected this universal practice of the Church." In this way he splendidly defends our innocence in this matter against the Hierarchical clamours. "Is it so great a heresy," he says, "to assert that bishop and presbyter are the same? Or does Harding understand to whom and how far the name of heretic extends? Certainly Chrysostom says that between bishop and presbyter there is almost no difference. Jerome, the Apostle clearly teaches that the presbyters are the same as the bishops. Augustine says: What is a bishop but the first presbyter, that is, the chief priest? Ambrose says: the ordination of bishop and presbyter is one; for both are priests, but" the bishop is first. From these things he concludes: all these and the other holy Fathers, together with the Apostle Paul, must be held heretics by Harding's judgement, because of this opinion.

units.la: Quartò, insto in antiquis Eucharistiae ritibus: quas ex regula August. Quod universa Ecclesia tenet &c. confirmat Baronius. Quod si vero dixeris, male hanc regulam istis ritibus accommodari: subiungit Baronius testimonium aliud ex August. quod rem totam conficit. Totum illum agendi ordinem insinuat Ecclesiae, quem per universum orbem servat, ab ipso (Paulum intelligit) ordinatum esse, quod nulla rerum diversitate variatur. Inter caetera, Eucharistiam à jejunis sumendam esse docet eodem argumento: sic enim habet. Nunquid calumniandum est universae Ecclesiae quod a jejuniis accipitur? Non calumniandum Ecclesiae quidem, affirmandum tamen est, etsi hoc ab universa Ecclesia observatum fuisset, non tamen ab Apostolis ipsis ordinatum, quod si esset & necessarium esset, & mutari ab Ecclesijs posterioribus hoc decretum non potuisset. Solebant veteres in Eucharistia sanctorum demortuorum nomina commemorare, & felicem eis resurrectionem precari, hinc suffragia pro mortuis papistica probat Baronius, supposita hac Augustini regula. Quod universa tenet Ecclesia, &c. Ma-le ille quidem hunc veterem ritum interpretatur: sed certe acceptum ab Apostolis prodiisse quis quaeso contendet? eum tamen in nullo Concilio primitus sancitum, ab universa Ecclesia observatum fuisse, ipse Bilsonus confitetur.
units.tr: Fourthly, I press the ancient rites of the Eucharist, which Baronius confirms on the basis of Augustine's rule, "What the whole Church holds," etc. But if you should say that this rule is wrongly applied to these rites, Baronius adds another testimony from Augustine which settles the whole matter. It indicates that the whole order of action which the Church keeps throughout the world was ordained by him (he means Paul), and is not varied by any difference of circumstances. Among other things, Augustine teaches by the same argument that the Eucharist is to be received by those who are fasting: for he says: "Is the Church, which receives it from those who are fasting, to be accused? The Church is not to be accused; yet it must be affirmed that, even if this was observed by the whole Church, it was not ordained by the Apostles themselves; for if it were, it would be necessary, and this decree could not have been changed by later Churches." The ancients used to commemorate the names of the saints who had died in the Eucharist, and to pray for them a happy resurrection; from this, on the supposition of that rule of Augustine's, "What the whole Church holds, etc.," Baronius proves the Papist suffrages for the dead. He certainly interprets this ancient rite badly; but who, I ask, will contend that it came forth from the Apostles? Yet that it was never first enacted in any Council, but was observed by the whole Church, Bilson himself confesses.

units.la: Quintò, insto in ritibus baptismi, quorum plurimos docuimus supra ex Tertulliano, & sola consuetudine introductos, quanquam ab universa tum Ecclesia observarentur. Vrget pro Chrismatis sacramento, hanc Augustini regulam Baronius, Quod universa tenet Eccle-sia &c: male quidem quòd ad sacramentum, moremque Papisticu: quòd ad sacrum usum olei tamen non inepte: hunc etenim ab universa Ecclesia observatum fuisse, antequam in Concilio ullo sanciretur adductae ab illo authoritates aperte probant.
units.tr: Fifthly, I press the rites of baptism, of which we taught very many above from Tertullian, introduced by custom alone, although they were then observed by the whole Church. Baronius urges this rule of Augustine's, "What the whole Church holds, etc.," in support of the sacrament of chrism. He does so badly, in that it bears on the sacrament and on the Papist custom; but it is not inappropriately applied to the sacred use of oil. For that this was observed by the whole Church before it was ever enacted in any Council is plainly proved by the authorities he himself adduces.

units.la: Sextò, insto in ritibus orationis: stabant etenim ex universa Ec-clesiae usurpatione diebus dominicis, & intra Pascha & Pentecosten sine ullo Concilio, ante Nicaenum: & versus orientem precabantur, & non nisi in Paschate & Pentecoste baptizabant: & haec pro Apostolicis habebantur ubique, quae tamen haud credo, vel ipsos Hierarchicos dicturos ab Apostolis descendisse.
units.tr: Sixthly, I press the rites of prayer: for by the universal usage of the Church, before Nicaea and without any Council, they stood on the Lord's days and between Easter and Pentecost, they prayed towards the east, and they baptised only at Easter and Pentecost; and these things were everywhere regarded as apostolic. Yet I do not believe that even the Hierarchics themselves will say that they descended from the Apostles.

units.la: Septimò, insto in diebus festis, Nativitatis, Ascensionis, Penteco-stis quos Augustinus speciatim nominat, ac si ab Apostolis traditi vel à Conciliis sanciti essent: idque ob hanc solam causam quia ab Ecclesia universa absque ulla variatione servabantur: Atque certè haec festa observata fuisse, idque ab universa Ecclesia, priusquam in Concilio ullo stabilita ex historijs liquet: quid igitur? ab Apostolis tradita? Negat Iuellus noster ex Socrate: l.15. c.22. Euangelium non imposuerat jugum sed hominesipsi suis quique locis, propter remissionem {a}in memoriam passionis, Paschæ & alios Dies festos, sicut voluerant, ex consuetudine quadam celebrarunt. Non enim hoc vel Salvator vel Apostoli lege aliqua observandum esse docuerunt.
units.tr: Seventhly, I press the festal days of the Nativity, the Ascension and Pentecost, which Augustine names specifically, as if they had been handed down by the Apostles or sanctioned by Councils; and this for the sole reason that they were kept by the whole Church without any variation. And certainly it is clear from histories that these festivals were observed, and by the whole Church, before they were established in any Council. What then? Were they handed down by the Apostles? Our Jewel denies it, on the authority of Socrates, book 5, chapter 22: "The Gospel had not imposed a yoke, but men themselves, in their several places, celebrated Easter and other festal days by a certain custom, as they wished, in memory of the passion. For neither the Saviour nor the Apostles taught that these were to be observed by any law."

units.la: Octavò, in jejunijs quartæ & sextæ feriæ apud Epiphanium necnon in iciunijs quatuor temporum, quæ observata sunt ab universa Ecclesia, antequam in Concilio ullo sanciebantur: & pro Apostolicis habebātur: neque ab Apostolis prodierunt tamen, sicuti nostris omnibus constat. Excipiendus hic solus Lotus Hierarchicus est, qui pro ieiunijs antiquis, diebusque festis clamores plane horrendos tollit. Vel minuantur oportet quæ tanta cum insolentia reformatores pro ieiunijs affirmant, vel solus à Christo passo, ad infelicia hæc tempora Aerius verum pervidisse judicetur. Cum ab Aerio abscesserunt haud unum ex omni antiquitate patrū reperiunt. Quid si singulas etiam Synodos à vero aberravisse affirmant & eo impudentiæ si prorepuerint, ad extremam impietatem hoc unum deest, ut Ecclesiæ suæ preces per multa sæcula Deum repudiasse, & solum delegisse Aerium quem familiarius doceret, impudenter affirment. Hos clamores qui audit, in re aperte falsa, (quis enim quadragesimam cæteraque jejunia propter universam Ecclesiæ praxim, aut Apostolica primo fuisse, aut nunc necessariò retinenda censebit:) minùs ut spero commovebitur, quum in causa Seniorum, aut Episcoporum, Tragicas illas Hierarchicorum vociferationes exaudierit. In causa Seniorum ita Scultingius: O cæcos hæreticos, ô impudentiâ singularem: Adeone vos primæ fidei propagatoribus & disseminatoribus auditis Leoninum dentem infigere, isdemque vos anteponere? Hæc præmittenda existimarim, ut conjecturam faciat Lector de spiritu simili Bancroftiano, qui pro Episcopis Hierarchicis ita declamat, Nulli docti extitere, antequam principia disciplinæ Genevensis edocti estis? Sapientia numnam mortua, priusquam vos nati? Quid Apostolorum temporibus facilitatum erat, vos meliùs scitis, quam qui Apostolis succedebant? Noverunt patres trium personarum in sacrosancta Trinitate distinctionem: & quod discrimen inter Episcopum & presbyterum, quoad regendam Ecclesiam suam reliquit Christus non noverunt? Tenebræ quas secum apportat superbia adeo lucidæ, lux vero patrum adeo tenebrosa evasit: ut Cartwrightus, Traversus, Fennerus (eruditionis vix quidem umbræ) adeo oculati censebantur: & Irnæus, Tertullianus, Cyprianus, Ambrosius, Hieronymus, Chrysostomus, Augustinus, Hilarius habeātur cæci. Miraris hæc stercorea lector? mirari desine. Universa Ecclesiæ praxis, & consensus patrum, unica Hierarchicorum mHi na est: quid igitur miri, si æstuant, fremant, indignentur, cum horum infallibilem authoritatem in dubium vocari videant? quæ in nobis superbia? quis veterum contemptus? qui quod merentur libenter tribuimus: atque hoc tantum eis denegamus, ne in throno ipsius Dei collocentur. An hæc loquor secundum hominem (inquit Apostolus) annon hoc i, sum dicit lex? 1. Cor 9. & Hæc nostra jam justissima defensio est: non nosmetipsos patribus præferimus, qui ex nobismetipsis minime loquimur: quod Scriptura dicit, id patribus præferimus, præferimus, quod vitio verti non debuisset. Nihil igitur illi clamores sunt: universa Ecclesiæ praxis à se certa minimè est: ex scripturis hæc causa discutienda: harum judicium qui declinat, Deum ipsum contemnit, qui his solis caulam suam sistere renuit, divinum tribunal pedibus proterit.
units.tr: Eighthly, I press the fasts of Wednesday and Friday mentioned by Epiphanius, and the fasts of the Ember days, which were observed by the whole Church before they were ever enacted in any Council, and were regarded as apostolic; yet they did not come from the Apostles, as is known to all our people. Here the only exception is the Hierarchic Lotus, who raises quite horrible clamours on behalf of the ancient fasts and feast days. "Either what the reformers affirm about fasts with such insolence must be diminished, or the one who alone saw the truth, from Christ crucified down to these unhappy times, must be judged to be Aerius." When they depart from Aerius, they find not one from all antiquity of the Fathers. "What if they affirm that even the single Synods have strayed from the truth, and if they have broken forth into such impudence, then, to complete the utmost impiety, only this remains: that they shamelessly assert that the prayers of their Church for many centuries have rejected God, and that God has chosen only Aerius, whom he might teach more familiarly." Whoever hears these clamours, in a matter plainly false (for who will judge that Lent and the other fasts were either apostolic at first, or must now be necessarily retained, on account of the universal practice of the Church?), will, I hope, be less moved when he hears those tragic outcries of the Hierarchics in the case of the elders or of the bishops. In the case of the elders Scultingius says: "O blind heretics, O singular impudence! Do you dare to fix the Lion's tooth upon the propagators and disseminators of the first faith, and to set yourselves above them? I think these things must be premised, so that the reader may form a conjecture about the spirit akin to Bancroft's," who declaims thus on behalf of the Hierarchical bishops: "Were there no learned men before you were taught the principles of the Geneva discipline? Was wisdom dead before you were born? What was made easy in the times of the Apostles, you know better than those who succeeded the Apostles? The Fathers knew the distinction of the three persons in the most holy Trinity, and did not know the difference between bishop and presbyter, which Christ left for the governing of his Church? The darkness that pride carries with it has become so bright, and the light of the Fathers has become so dark, that Cartwright, Travers, Fenner (scarcely even the shadows of learning) were thought so sharp-sighted, and Irenaeus, Tertullian, Cyprian, Ambrose, Jerome, Chrysostom, Augustine, Hilary are regarded as blind." Do you marvel at these filthy things, reader? Cease to marvel. The universal practice of the Church and the consensus of the Fathers is the Hierarchics' sole stronghold; what wonder, then, if they seethe, rage and are indignant, when they see the infallible authority of these men called into doubt? What pride is in us? What contempt of the ancients? We gladly give them what they deserve, and we deny them only this: that they be placed on the very throne of God. "Do I say these things according to man," says the Apostle, "or does not the law also say the same? 1 Cor. 9. And this is our now most just defence: we do not set ourselves above the Fathers, who do not speak from themselves; what Scripture says, that we set above the Fathers," we set above them, which ought not to be counted as a fault. Those clamours, therefore, are nothing: the universal practice of the Church is by itself by no means certain; this cause must be decided from the Scriptures; whoever shuns their judgement scorns God himself, and whoever refuses to bring his cause before these alone tramples the divine tribunal under foot.

units.la: CAP. 8.
units.tr: CHAPTER 8.

units.la: Argumentum sextum a praxi in prima post Apostolos periodo solvitur.
units.tr: Argument six is answered from practice in the first period after the Apostles.

units.la: DIximus de universa Ecclesiæ praxi in genere, jam ad periodos descendendum: & primò quidem de Ecclesia prima videndum est, quæ ipsis Apostolis immediatè succedebat, utrùm certa veritatis index, illius praxis censenda sit? Negamus nos, affirmant Hierarchici, idq; contentione summa. Sic enim Thom. Bilson. Ecclesiæ ab Apostolis plantatæ, quæque proxime ætatem eorum subsecutæ sunt, laicos aliquos presbyteros non agnoverunt, nedum in usu habuerunt. Quod mihi quidem certissimo argumento est, nullos hujusmodi ab Apostolis Ecclesiæ relictos esse. Quid enim? Num omnes totius orbis Ecclesiæ statim ab Apostolis hanc regendæ Ecclesiæ formam ab ipsis præscriptam & impositam uno impetu rejecerent, aliamque novam & insolitam nullo præcepto aut Apostolorum exemplo munitam inveherent? Quomodo alij in hac parte affecti sint nescio, ut universam Christi Ecclesiam protinus idque consulto in gravissimam incidisse Apostasiam existiment: de me autem profiteor, malle recentiorum quorundam conjecturis & opinionibus dissere, quam tot Apostolicos viros, tot doctrina & antiquitate reverendos patres, pro manifestis disciplinæ Apostolicæ contemptoribus, & acerrimis Antichristianæ tyrannidis & superbiæ propugnatoribus, ne dicam inventoribus, habere. Rursus: Quo propius ab Apostolorum temporibus aberant, eo melius eorum sensus attingere poterant. Omnes totius orbis Ecclesiæ simul in eadem gubernandi forma minime conspirassent, nisi ab Apostolis eorumque discipulis, veluti fidei Christianæ seminatoribus, tradita & præscripta fuissent. Ita Georgius Downamus: Incredibile est omnes sanctos patres, & Christi Ecclesiæ disciplinam a Christo & Apostolis institutam abolere voluisse: & impossibile omnino, ut gubernatio ab Apostolis non recepta, neque a Conciliis statuta, uno impetu in omnibus partibus Christiani orbis surrigeretur. Quæ de Apostasia consultò invecta, & patrum voluntaria disciplinæ Apostolicæ rejectione contemptuq; interseruntur: quæq; de disciplina, quasi uno impetu mutatâ garriunt, ea præter quæstionem sunt, ad invidiam conflandam, & verum quæstionis statum obscurandum excogitata. Non volentes, sed nescientes, non per Apostasiam aut contemptum sed per infirmitatem & ignorantiam, lapsi sunt patres, qui in disciplina aberrarunt: neque uno impetu disciplina statim tentata est, sed gradatim & paulatim: quæ defectio lectio in Ecclesia quidem ipsa Apostolorum aetati proxima, adeo coepit: ut argumento certo, nedum certissimo, illius universa praxis esse nequeat.
units.tr: We have spoken of the practice of the whole Church in general; now we must descend to the periods. And first we must consider the first Church, which immediately followed the Apostles themselves, and ask whether its practice is to be judged a certain index of truth. We deny it; the Hierarchists affirm it, and with the utmost vehemence. For Thomas Bilson says: The churches planted by the Apostles, and those which closely followed their age, did not acknowledge any lay elders, much less use them. This is to me a most certain argument that no such officers were left to the Church by the Apostles. For what? Would all the churches of the whole world at once, by one impulse, reject the form of church government prescribed and imposed by the Apostles themselves, and bring in another new and unusual form, supported by no precept or example of the Apostles? How others are affected in this matter I do not know, that they think the whole Church of Christ fell at once, and deliberately, into the gravest apostasy. As for me, I declare that I would rather argue from the conjectures and opinions of some recent writers than hold so many apostolic men, so many fathers reverend for their learning and antiquity, to be manifest despisers of apostolic discipline, and most fierce defenders, not to say inventors, of Antichristian tyranny and pride. Again: The nearer they were to the times of the Apostles, the better they could grasp their meaning. All the churches of the whole world would never have agreed in the same form of government, unless it had been handed down and prescribed to them by the Apostles and their disciples, as the sowers of the Christian faith. So George Downame says: It is incredible that all the holy fathers and the discipline of Christ's Church, instituted by Christ and the Apostles, wished to abolish it; and it is wholly impossible that a government not received from the Apostles, nor established by Councils, should rise up in one impulse in all parts of the Christian world. These things, which are deliberately brought in about apostasy and the fathers' voluntary rejection and contempt of apostolic discipline, are beside the point; and what they chatter about discipline as if it had been changed by one impulse is devised to stir up hatred and to obscure the true state of the question. The fathers who went astray in discipline fell not willingly but unknowingly, not through apostasy or contempt but through weakness and ignorance; nor was discipline attacked at once by one impulse, but gradually and little by little. And this defection began so early, even in the Church nearest to the age of the Apostles, that its universal practice cannot be a certain argument, much less a most certain one.

units.la: Primo etenim argumenta certa, ex solis scripturis hauriuntur: ita, ne Ecclesiae immediatae quidem quaquam universa praxis, nos certos reddere potest. Non interest (inquit) Tertullianus, quando qui sit, quod sub Apostolis non fuit: adulterum est quod ab Apostolis nominatum non est. Posterior res nostra non est: imo omnibus prior est: hoc erit testimonium veritatis ubique occupantis principatum. Quod ab Apostolis non damnatur, imo defenditur, hoc erit iudicium proprietatis. Quid igitur? Nihil interest, quando Hierarchia Episcopalis exoriebatur: sive anterius, sive serius satis hoc est ut adultera sit, quod ab Apostolis non nominetur. Disciplina e contra reformata quo tempore labefactata fuerit, sive in prima Ecclesia necne, sive tempore subsequente nihil refert: prior omnibus erat & ab Apostolis defensa: hoc satis est ad iudicium proprietatis, & veritatis testimonium. Eis etenim veritas adjudicanda est (ut subinfert Tertullianus) qui in ea regula incedunt, quam Ecclesia ab Apostolis, Apostoli a Christo, Christus a Deo tradidit. Constat ratio propositi, qui hanc pro se afferre potest: illi usque professio prior, quia origines firmas habet, ab ipsis authoribus quorum fuit res. Ad has origines Tertulliani adiunges illas Cypriani: Si ad divinae traditionis caput & originem revertamur: cessit omnis error humanus. Adiunge etiam illud Hilarij: Hoc proprium est Apostolicae doctrinae, Deum ex lege & Prophetis in Evangelijs praedicare. Haec adfert Iuellus ut probet, nullo modo quid Apostolicum sit cognosci a nobis posse: nisi ex ipsis Apostolorum originalibus: sic ut originalis illa Ecclesia quae Apostolis proxime successit, pro indice certa, recipienda non sit.
units.tr: First, certain arguments are drawn from Scripture alone; so the universal practice even of the nearest churches cannot make us certain. It makes no difference, says Tertullian, when a thing came in, if it was not under the Apostles: that is adulterous which was not named by the Apostles. Our later matter is not a later matter; rather it is prior to all: this will be the testimony of truth occupying the primacy everywhere. What is not condemned by the Apostles, but defended by them, will be the judgment of ownership. What then? It makes no difference when episcopal hierarchy arose; whether earlier or later, it is enough that it is adulterous if it was not named by the Apostles. Likewise, at what time the reformed discipline was overthrown, whether in the first Church or not, or in a later time, makes no difference: the earlier one was prior to all and was defended by the Apostles; this is enough for the judgment of ownership and the testimony of truth. For truth must be adjudged to those (as Tertullian adds) who walk in that rule which the Church handed down from the Apostles, the Apostles from Christ, and Christ from God. The reason of the proposal is clear for anyone who can offer this in his own defence: that profession is prior, because it has firm origins, from the very authors whose thing it was. To these origins of Tertullian you may add those of Cyprian: If we return to the head and origin of divine tradition, every human error gives way. Add also that of Hilary: It is proper to apostolic doctrine to preach God in the Gospels from the Law and the Prophets. Jewel brings these forward to prove that we can know nothing of what is apostolic except from the original documents of the Apostles themselves; so that the original Church which came closest to the Apostles is not to be received as a certain index.

units.la: Secundo, mutationem disciplinae ex parte coepisse in Ecclesia immediata, incredibile & impossibile (ut Downami utar verbo) videre quis potest? cum Ecclesiarum nonnullarum exempla praesto sint, quae si non uno impetu, cito tamen & celeriter defecerunt: nam recte Seneca: Quod cuiquam contingere potuit, cuivis potest: Exod. 32. 8. Recesserunt cito ab ea via quam praecepi illis Gal. 1. 6. Miror quomodo celeriter avers estis a Christo. Iudic. 27. Coluerunt quidem Iehovam populus omnibus diebus Iosuae & Seniorum qui prolongarunt dies post Iosuam, qui viderunt totum opus Iehovae quod fecerat Israel. Sed quum mortuus esset Iosua, & tota illa aetas aggregati essent ad majores suos, & surrexisset aetas altera post illos, qui non agnoscebat Iehovam, nec etiam opus illud quod fecerat Israelis, fecerunt filii Israelis malum in oculis Iehovae. 2. Chron. 12. 1. Reliquit Rehoboam Iehovam, & totus Israel cum eo. Defecit Ecclesia Israelitica cel. ritur in ipsam quidem Idololatriam: quam primum per Moysis absentiam cum sublatum existimarunt: & credibile non est in ignorantiam disciplinae ex parte aliquam, Ecclesiam Christianam incidisse, quum Apostoli e medio per mortem sublati erant? Defecit Ecclesia Israelitica etiam in ipsam idololatriam, statim a mor-
units.tr: Second, who can see it as incredible and impossible (to use Downame's word) that the change of discipline began in part in the immediately following Church, when there are examples of some churches which, if not by one impulse, yet quickly and speedily fell away? For Seneca rightly says: What has happened to anyone can happen to anyone. Exodus 32:8: They have turned aside quickly from the way which I commanded them. Galatians 1:6: I marvel how quickly you have turned away from Christ. Judges 2:7: The people served Jehovah all the days of Joshua and of the elders who outlived Joshua, who had seen all the work of Jehovah which he had done for Israel. But when Joshua was dead, and that whole generation was gathered to its fathers, and another generation arose after them which did not know Jehovah, nor the work which he had done for Israel, the children of Israel did evil in the eyes of Jehovah. 2 Chronicles 12:1: Rehoboam forsook Jehovah, and all Israel with him. Did not the Israelite Church fall into idolatry itself as soon as they thought Moses was gone during his absence? And is it not credible that the Christian Church fell into some ignorance of discipline when the Apostles had been removed from the midst by death?

units.la: {a} Mors. ce Iosue & Seniorum qui redemptionem ex Ægypto viderant: Et E elesiam Christianam statim a morte Apostolorum,nulla ex parte defiere potuisse consundum est? Defecit denique Israelitica Ecclesia tota etiam in ipsam idololatriam;statim ab illa illustrissima Davidis & Salomonis religionis institutione, & augustissima templi aedificatione: Ecclesiam vero Christianam, habem aliquam contraxisse, statim post Apostolorum Evangelij promulgationem, incredibile videtur? Apostolorum aetate in summa sanitas erat Ecclesiae: at ex aliquot sanitatis, periculosissimos in morbos cadus laesissime fieri, medici crauerunt. Apostolorum aetate in summum saltigium elatum Christi externum regnum erat: quod etsi non ruinae, mutationibus tamen variis expositum est: & confusum politi is est, ex summa regnorum celsitudine, ruinas celerrimas & citissimas perspicere experiri. Ne imperio ruinas immunes hi gradibus (inquit Seneca) q. ...
units.tr: {a} Death: after Joshua and the elders who had seen the redemption from Egypt. And that the Christian Church could in no part have fallen away immediately after the death of the Apostles, is to be considered absurd? Finally, the whole Israelite Church also fell into idolatry itself immediately after that most illustrious institution of religion by David and Solomon and the most august building of the temple. Is it incredible that the Christian Church should have contracted some such fault immediately after the proclamation of the Apostles' gospel? In the age of the Apostles the Church was in the highest health; but physicians have observed that from a state of good health men fall into the most dangerous diseases. In the age of the Apostles the external kingdom of Christ was raised to the highest summit; and although it was not exposed to ruin, it was nevertheless exposed to various changes; and it is confused with political affairs to see and experience swift and sudden ruins from the greatest height of kingdoms.

units.la: imperia ruinas immunes his gradibus (inquit Seneca) q. ad summa pervenitur: sepe inter fortunam maximam & minimam, interest. Cutrespondet Corn. Tac. lib. 2. Imperium capientibus habenda est, nihil medium inter praecipitia & summa. Non opus est multis: cum commune politicorum hoc placitum sit: Circumactio triennio anno plerumque aliqua mu- tatio solet fieri in imperiis: e statione sua accedentibus qui antea rebus communibus praefuerunt, & successoribus deinde novis, qui intra istos 30. annos adoleverunt, & mores novos sententiasque ad rem publicam attulerunt.
units.tr: Empires are not immune from ruin by those steps (says Seneca) by which one comes to the heights; often there is a great difference between the greatest and the least fortune. Cornelius Tacitus, book 2, agrees: For those who take up empire, there must be nothing between precipices and the highest summits. There is no need for many words, since this is the common opinion of political writers: every three years or so some change is usually made in empires, as those who previously presided over public affairs withdraw from their posts, and new successors then grow up within those thirty years and bring new manners and opinions to the commonwealth.

units.la: Tertio, ex ipsis Apostolorum temporibus conjecturam facere licet, mutationem disciplinae nonnullam in Ecclesia immediate subsequente, non solum possibilem,sed & probabilem etiam esse. Tenet hic etenim illa Mosis ratiocinatio: Deut 31. 27. Dum adhuc ego vivo vobiscum hodie, rebelles fuistis contra Dominum: quanto igitur magis post mortem meam? Credendum omnino Paulo Act. 20. 29. Ego illud scio, lupos graves & non parcentes gregi ingressuros esse in vos post discessum meum, & ex vobis ipsis exorturos, qui loquantur perversa ut discipulos post se trahant. Ne quis vero tempus longinquum somniet; audiatur Tertullianus: Haec est in titulo, non dico jam quae suturas haereses praenunciabat, sed de qua haereses prodierunt. Sed non fuerat ex illa, ex quo facta sunt adversus illam. Etiam de oliva nucleo multi & oleum & ne effari ab eo afferre ex oleastro exoriri: etiam de Papavere fici gratissima & suavissima, ventosa & vana capiuntur. Similiter Gilmar. Whitakerus: Si Paulo mortuo statim futurum erat, ut tales falsi doctores exurgerent, nonne temporis sui etiam praesciebat ...
units.tr: Third, from the very times of the Apostles it is possible to conjecture that some change of discipline in the immediately following Church was not only possible but also probable. For that reasoning of Moses holds here: Deuteronomy 31:27: While I am still living with you today, you have been rebellious against the Lord; how much more, then, after my death? We must certainly believe Paul, Acts 20:29: I know this, that grievous wolves will enter in among you after my departure, not sparing the flock, and from among yourselves men will arise speaking perverse things to draw away disciples after them. But lest anyone dream of a long interval, let him hear Tertullian: This is in the title, not only what heresies he foretold were to come, but from which heresies arose. But it was not from that which came after, but against it. Many also take oil from the kernel of the olive, and the wild olive arises from the fruit of the cultivated one; the sweetest and most pleasant figs are also caught from the poppy, windy and empty. Similarly Whitaker: If it was to happen immediately after Paul's death that such false teachers would arise, did he not also foreknow...

units.la: Quid tum? Evangelij claritas prohibere non potuit, quin etiam haereses craessimae & apertissimae exorirentur: quanto igitur probabilis, eam nec impedire etiam, quin errores subtilio- res & latentiores ad vitiandam politiciam seminari possent. Certe disciplina vel ipsa etiam Apostolis vitiis vitiata fuit: nam & in Ecclesia Corinthia a per supinam negligentiam disciplina iacuit 1. Cor. 5. & in Ecclesiis Asianis illis vigor exaruit Ap. 2. & 3. & ipso denique Iohanne vivo praeminentiam Episcopalem Diotrephes arripuit. 3. Ioh. Sed excellit ad propositum nostrum locus ille Paulinus 2. Thess. 2. Vbi mysterium iniquitatis, vel etiam ipsis diebus suis operari coepit ipse dicit: quia hoc mysterium non in vitiana doctrina tantum, verum etiam disciplina, positum fuisse, omnes nerunt. De hoc Whitakerus noster ita: Regnum Antichristianum quasi aetatis totum dicimus, cujus fundamenta temporibus Apostolorum jacta sunt: reliqua structura postea accessit. Si fundamentum sit pars aetatis illum regni Antichristiani pars eo tempore fuit. Quid igitur? aedificium primatus Romani, nunquam cessavit a quo incepit, donec ad fastigium summum perduceretur. Incepit vero Apostolorum tempore: non cessavit igitur in Ecclesia Apostolos subsequente. In haereticis, inquies, non cessavit: in onec in iis patribus: sic enim ibidem Whitakerus, imo sanctissimi patres licet nescirent, ut Beza ait sensit, Antichristi regnum adiuverunt.
units.tr: What then? The clarity of the Gospel could not prevent even the grossest and most manifest heresies from arising. How much more probable is it, then, that it did not prevent subtler and more hidden errors from being sown to corrupt the polity? Certainly discipline itself was corrupted even in the time of the Apostles. In the Corinthian church discipline lay dormant through supine negligence (1 Cor. 5), in the Asian churches its vigour withered (Rev. 2 and 3), and finally, while John was still alive, Diotrephes seized the episcopal pre-eminence (3 John). But that Pauline passage (2 Thess. 2) fits our purpose well, where he says that the mystery of iniquity had already begun to work, even in his own days. Everyone knows that this mystery lay not only in corrupt doctrine but also in discipline. On this our Whitaker writes: "We call the Antichristian kingdom, as it were, of the whole age, whose foundations were laid in the times of the Apostles; the rest of the structure was added later." If the foundation belonged to that age, then part of the kingdom of Antichrist was present at that time. What then? The edifice of Roman primacy never ceased from the point where it began until it was brought up to its highest pinnacle. But it began in the time of the Apostles; therefore it did not cease in the Church that followed the Apostles. "Among heretics," you will say, "it did not cease." Nor did it cease among those Fathers either, for Whitaker says in the same place: Indeed the most holy Fathers, although they did not know it, as Beza says, nevertheless felt that they helped the kingdom of Antichrist.

units.la: Quarto, ipsum Ecclesiae primae statum, quae immediate secuta est tempus Apostolorum inspiciamus, a quo ita disputat Iohannes Bridgesius Episcopus Oxoniensis. Adeo praecisus Polycarpus, ut ne diem quidem unum praevaricatus fuerit, quem ad Pascha bi celebrandum ab Apostolis traditum existimabat: ergo Episcopatum gerere noluerat, nisi Episcoporum superioritas ab ordinatione Apostolorum defluxisset. Anima evertenda primo verba Socratis sunt: Et sunt insuper presbyteri qui immediate Apostolis succedebant, inter se de Paschate variasse. Ausus? Polycarpus caeterique qui immediate successerunt Apostolis Episcopi, non dioecesani Episcopi erant sed Parochiales, id est, nihil aliud quam presbyteri fuerunt. Verumenimvero licet nihil aliud quam presbyteri essent, ad Episcopatum tamen Hierarchicum, quantum licebat, eorum nonnulli enisi sunt, ut in Victore Romano liquet, qui in hac de Paschate controversia ita se gessit, ut coactus Whitakerus sit de eo dicere. In istis quidem ecclesiae incunabulis, coepit in isto Victore ebullire spiritus ille Antichristi qui postea Ecclesiam misere vexavit et perturbavit. Atque in ista, de Paschate controversia, vel Polycarpus vel Victor erravit: quis igitur non videt, adversus Bridgesium ipsum valere, quod contra nos deducit argumentum? Quod si etenim universa Ecclesia prima, quae immediate Apostolos sequuta est, aliquid de Paschate ab Apostolis traditum servavit, qui nihil de hac re quicquam unquam statuerunt: quidni etiam Episcoporum Hierarchicum ab eis traditum opinari potuit qui traditus non fuit: liceat etenim mihi cum Constantino argumentari. Cum in hac re evidente veritatem non vident, quid mirum si in multis aliis errent?
units.tr: Fourthly, let us look at the state of the primitive Church itself, which immediately followed the time of the Apostles, on which John Bridgeman, Bishop of Oxford, argues thus: So exact was Polycarp that he did not depart from it by even a single day, the observance of Easter which he believed had been handed down by the Apostles; therefore he had been unwilling to hold the episcopate, unless the superiority of bishops had flowed down from the ordination of the Apostles. To overturn this, the first witness is the words of Socrates: And moreover there were elders who immediately succeeded the Apostles, and who differed among themselves about Easter. Would you dare? Polycarp and the others who immediately succeeded the Apostles as bishops were not diocesan bishops but parochial, that is, they were nothing other than presbyters. Yet although they were nothing but presbyters, some of them strove, as far as they could, for a hierarchical episcopate, as is clear in Victor of Rome, who in this controversy about Easter so conducted himself that Whitaker was compelled to say of him: In those cradle days of the Church, that spirit of Antichrist began to boil up in this Victor, which afterwards sorely vexed and disturbed the Church. And in this controversy about Easter, both Polycarp and Victor erred. Who then does not see that the argument he brings against us tells against Bridgeman himself? For if the whole primitive Church, which immediately followed the Apostles, kept something about Easter handed down by the Apostles, though the Apostles laid down nothing at all on this matter, why could it not likewise be thought that a hierarchical episcopate was handed down by them, though it was not handed down? For let me argue with Constantine: When they do not see the truth in this plain matter, what wonder if they err in many others?

units.la: 5 Accedamus ad errorem secundum, quem universa Ecclesia prima recepit, errorem nempe Chiliastarum: ubi ad ipsum Caesarem Baronium provocare non erubescet? Sic ille de Papia hujus erroris authore, primo, ex Eusebio. Papias recepit traditiones falsas a presbyteris (adverte rursus Episcopi primi non nisi Presbyteri vocantur) qui Apostolos viderant: fabulosa miracula ab eo tradita sunt, quae ab eisdem sese recepisse affirmavit: Irenaeus ab eo seductus est, prae antiquitatis specie. Quid? errare igitur in relationibus suis etiam immediate Apostolorum successores potuerunt? Imo & erraverunt (inquit:) ac proinde etiam immediatorum traditionum delectus habendus est. Bene est: hinc enim sequetur, Episcopatum Hierarchicum etiam examinandum esse: etsi ab Ecclesia prima comprobatum fuisse demonstrari posset. Quid ni? sed a l Ecclesiae universae praxim delectus (inquit) faciendus iste est: ut traditiones eas servandas putemus, quas universa tenet Ecclesia. Atqui inquam fallacem hanc regulam esse, vel haec ipsa res demonstrat. Quid enim? errorem istum de mille annis a Papia desseminatum, annon Justinus, Irenaeus, Tertullianus amplexati sunt, nemine interim dissentiente: quem consensum primi saeculi universum sufficere dicit Cardinalis Peronius, cui subscribit Casaubonus.
units.tr: 5 Let us come to the second error, which the whole primitive Church received, namely the error of the Chiliasts. To whom will Caesar Baronius himself not blush to appeal? Thus he writes of Papias, the author of this error, first from Eusebius: Papias received false traditions from the elders (note again that the first bishops are called only elders) who had seen the Apostles. Fabulous miracles were handed down by him, which he affirmed he had received from the same men. Irenaeus was seduced by him, on account of the appearance of antiquity. What then? Could even the immediate successors of the Apostles err in their reports? Indeed, they erred, he says, and therefore the choice of immediate traditions must also be made. Very well: from this it will follow that the hierarchical episcopate too must be examined, even if it could be shown to have been approved by the primitive Church. Why not? But this choice, he says, must be made from the practice of the universal Church, so that we think those traditions should be kept which the whole Church holds. Yet I say this rule is fallacious, and this very matter proves it. For did not Justin, Irenaeus, and Tertullian embrace that error concerning the thousand years, spread abroad by Papias, with no one dissenting in the meantime? This consensus of the first century, which Cardinal Perron says is enough for everything, Casaubon subscribes to.

units.la: Sequitur error hujus Ecclesiae primae tertius, quem & a Papia ortum putant doctores ex Eusebio: Babilonem nempe in Epistola Petri notare Romam, Petrum Romae fuisse, ibique mortuum: Marcum Evangelistam ipsius ibi auditorem, quae aut fabulosa fuisse aut incerta saltem esse suo loco demonstrabitur, utcunque ab Irenaeo, Tertulliano, caeterisque hujus aetatis doctoribus universis recepta fuerint.
units.tr: There follows a third error of this primitive Church, which the teachers, following Eusebius, also think arose from Papias: that in the Epistle of Peter Babylon denotes Rome, that Peter was at Rome and died there, and that Mark the Evangelist was his hearer there. These will be shown in their place to be either fabulous or at least uncertain, however generally they were received by Irenaeus, Tertullian, and all the other teachers of that age.

units.la: Error etiam hujus Ecclesiae quartus quidam est: ut in Irenaeo cernitur, nempe Christum per annos fere 50. vixisse: quod a presbyteris qui in Asia Iohannem viderant, narratum affirmat. Colligere hinc promptum, quam nulla certa fides, vel antiquissimis viris qui Apostolos vidisse dicuntur, vel Ecclesiis immediate succedentibus, qui salsissimis narrationibus fidem suam adjunxerunt.
units.tr: There is also a fourth error of this Church, as is seen in Irenaeus, namely that Christ lived almost fifty years, which he affirms was related by the elders who had seen John in Asia. From this it is easy to gather how little certain faith there was, both in the most ancient men who are said to have seen the Apostles and in the Churches immediately succeeding them, who attached their faith to the most absurd narratives.

units.la: Quinto, quomodo fides huic primae Ecclesiae pro certo adhiberi poterit: cum nec ea fidem certam scriptis ipsis Apostolorum adhibuerit? De Epistola etenim Iacobi & Iudae nulla apud hanc Ecclesiam mentio fuit, inquit Eusebius: sed suspectae fuerunt: epistola secunda Petri ab Ecclesia prima neutiquam approbata fuit: Epistola ad Hebraeos rejecta, cum Hermae pastor interim publice in Ecclesia legeretur: sicut & Clementis Epistola ad Corinthios. De duabus Iohannis posterioribus Epistolis,& Apocalypsi in hac Ecclesia dubitatum. Duo Iohannes in hac Ecclesia introducti, Iohannes Apostolus qui Evangelium scripsit & Iohannes Epistolam primam, & alius Iohannes Senior, qui Apostolo Ephesi successit, qui duas Epistolas Posteriores & Apocalypsin exaravit. Haec ne Ecclesia illa est, quae certum testimonium in causa disciplinaria praebitura nobis est? Quae Apocalypsin intra sacrum Canonem esse ignoravit, de progressu Antichristi qui ab Episcopatu Hierarchico initium sumpsit, in Apocalypsi declarato, pro certo dijudicare potuit? Audiatur Guilielmus Whitakerus de Iustino & Irenaeo ac proinde de hac ipsa Ecclesia prima & immediata. Videtis quemadmodum Patres opiniones quasdam superstitiosas perstitiosas amplexi sint, & non mirum sit si de Antichristo multa praeter scripturas finxerint. Rursus: Non est quod adversarij hic patrum testimonia in hac causa de Antichristo urgeant, quos toto coelo erravisse constat. Ergo inquam non est, quòd Ecclesiae immediatae testimonium in causa Hierarchiae adversarij urgeant: quum Antichristi in hac ipsa Hierarchia, fundamenta iacta sint.
units.tr: Fifthly, how can faith be placed with certainty in this primitive Church, since it did not place certain faith even in the very writings of the Apostles? For there was no mention in this Church of the Epistle of James and Jude, says Eusebius; but they were suspected. The second Epistle of Peter was by no means approved by the primitive Church. The Epistle to the Hebrews was rejected, while Hermas' Shepherd was meanwhile publicly read in the Church, as was also Clement's Epistle to the Corinthians. Concerning the two later Epistles of John and the Apocalypse there was doubt in this Church. Two Johns were introduced into this Church: John the Apostle, who wrote the Gospel and the first Epistle, and another John the Elder, who succeeded the Apostle at Ephesus and wrote the two later Epistles and the Apocalypse. Is this the Church which will furnish us with sure testimony in a disciplinary cause? Could a Church which did not know that the Apocalypse was within the sacred Canon judge with certainty about the progress of Antichrist, which is declared in the Apocalypse and which began from the hierarchical episcopate? Let William Whitaker be heard on Justin and Irenaeus, and therefore on this very primitive and immediate Church: You see how the Fathers embraced certain superstitious opinions, and it is no wonder if they invented much about Antichrist beyond the Scriptures. Again: There is no reason why the adversaries press here the testimonies of the Fathers in this matter about Antichrist, whom it is plain they erred utterly. Therefore, I say, there is no reason why the adversaries should press the testimony of the immediate Church in the cause of the hierarchy, since the foundations of Antichrist were laid in this very hierarchy.

units.la: Sextò, de degeneratione immediatae Ecclesiae, luculentum habemus apud Eusebium testimonium: quod Dominus Mornaeus ira ponit, cuius ego verba, quàm mea malim. Mysterium, inquit, iniquitatis iam pristem operatur: Pauli adeo ipsius tempora iam tum monstrum illud superbiae animo concipiebat Satan. Omnem impuritatem pro viribus praevenerunt Apostoli——At post Apostolorum decessum, non diu otiata est ambitio, quin primis vestigiis insisteret: ut quod nobis apud Eusebium Egesippus, non minus in hoc capite, quam in ceteris verum deprehenditur. Ad tempora usque Trajani Ecclesia integra & incorrupta permansit. At postquam sacer Apostolorum chorus varium vitae exitum & diversa mortis genera pertulerat: tum recta falsa & veteratoria impij erroris conspiratio exoratum coepit, idque illorum fraude & astutia qui doctrinam a veritate penitus alienam disseminare laborarent, quique, cum nemini Apostolorum vita suppeteret, iam nudo capite, sincero veritatis sermoni, falsam & commentitiam doctrinam ex adverso opponere pro viribus niterentur. Addit D. Mornaeus: Quae periodus in annum Domini incidit circiter centesimum: Id est: circiter ultimi Apostoli Iohannis mortem. Nullo igitur colore Cornelius Scultingius ex Baronio, hinc statum Ecclesiae usque ad Egesippi tempora integrum permansisse affirmat, id est ad tempora Hadriani. Downamus vero, ad annum 169. floruisse, ex Eusebio asserit: quo tempora & ipse Irenaeus floruisse ab Eusebio dicitur: Vult vero Downamus ad haec usque Egesippi tempora Ecclesiam castam atque integram permansisse: cui aperte Guilielmus Barlous Episcopus Lincolniensis contradicit, qui aperte ex testimonio Egesippi supra comemorato, Ecclesiam statim ab ipsa morte Apostolorum corruptam fuisse contestatur. Immeritò igitur flagellatur à Scultingio liber Raepellensis, quod diceret Irenaei tempore caepisse Ecclesiarum pastores & seniores in quibusdam ab Apostolorum tempore deflectere: praesertim cum adjiciat ipse Idem fere judicat Whitakerus contra Campianum & Duraeum, non diu nascentem Ecclesiam castam mansisse virginem. Atque certe in hac sententia Whitakerum fuisse certum est; sic enim alibi. Hegesippus apud Eusebium lib. 3.c. 32. Ecclesiam scribit quousque superstites Apostoli essent fuisse ... eis eriptis, mox infectam esse venenatis & pestiferis haereticorum doctrinis. Ita Maldonatus de Ecclesia prima tempore Tertullianj: Nondum adhuc satis culta Theologia, spinas aliquando proferebat. Recte quidem: Ecclesia etenim Apostolica sola paradysus est: Ap. 2. ab ea si discedas in spinas & tribulos aliquos, ut doctrinae, sic disciplinae ut incidas, necesse est. Ita Richardus Fyldus. Plures erro- { Ibid p.369 } res in scriptis patrum primitivae Ecclesiae reperiuntur, quam eorum qui ab illis primis exordiis remotiores exiterunt, quia falsis & incertis relationibus decepti sunt, quas homines illorum temporum avidis auribus hauriebant ab eis qui una cum eis vixerunt qui cum Apostolis vel eorum discipulis conversati fuissent. Ita Iohannes Whitus Hierarchicus. Quod nobis importune obiicitur. Verisimile esse plus vidisse doctores Apostolicis temporibus propinquiores, quam nos qui sumus remotiores: id a Dominico Bannes doctore suo denegatur: Necessarium non est, inquit, quo remotior a temporibus Apostolorum Ecclesia est, eo minus perfecta sit in mysteriis fidei cognitio: quia post Apostolorum tempora, non exiterunt doctissimi viri, qui in rebus fidei intelligendis et exponendis dexteritatem habuerunt. Quidni igitur cum Fulo ex Cypriano concludem: Non est consuetudine praescribendum sed ratione vincendum: nam cum consuetudo & universa praxis etiam primae illius Ecclesiae, quae immediate Apostolis successit, nullam certam fidem faciat: superest ut missa istius praxeos authoritate, ad solas scripturas confugimus.
units.tr: Sixthly, we have a clear testimony from Eusebius about the degeneration of the immediate Church, which Lord Mornay cites. I prefer his words to my own: "The mystery of iniquity," he says, "is already at work. Already in Paul's own time Satan was conceiving that monstrous pride. The Apostles forestalled every impurity as far as they could. But after the death of the Apostles, ambition was not long idle, but at once trod in their first footsteps, as what Hegesippus in Eusebius shows is found true in this chapter no less than in the others. Up to the times of Trajan the Church remained whole and uncorrupted. But after the sacred band of the Apostles had undergone diverse ends of life and various kinds of death, then a crafty and deceitful conspiracy of impious error began to be hatched, through the fraud and cunning of those who laboured to spread a doctrine utterly alien to the truth, and who, since none of the Apostles was left alive, now with bare head strove as far as they could to set against the sincere word of truth a false and fabricated doctrine." Mornay adds: This period falls in the year of the Lord about the hundredth, that is, about the death of the last Apostle, John. Therefore, by no colour does Cornelius Schultingius, following Baronius, affirm that the state of the Church remained whole down to the times of Hegesippus, that is, to the times of Hadrian. Downame, indeed, asserts from Eusebius that it flourished down to the year 169, when Irenaeus himself is said by Eusebius to have flourished. Downame wishes the Church to have remained chaste and whole down to the times of Hegesippus, but William Barlow, Bishop of Lincoln, openly contradicts him, maintaining from the testimony of Hegesippus cited above that the Church was corrupted from the very death of the Apostles. Justly, then, the book of Raepel is scourged by Schultingius, because it said that in the time of Irenaeus the pastors and elders of some churches began to depart from the time of the Apostles. Especially since he adds that Whitaker, against Campian and Duraeus, judges much the same: the Church, newly born, did not long remain chaste and virgin. And indeed it is certain that Whitaker held this opinion, for he says elsewhere: Hegesippus in Eusebius, book 3, chapter 32, writes that the Church remained whole as long as the Apostles survived ... once they were taken away, it was soon infected with the venomous and pestilential doctrines of heretics. So Maldonatus speaks of the primitive Church in Tertullian's time: Theology, not yet sufficiently cultivated, sometimes put forth thorns. Rightly so: the Apostolic Church alone is paradise (Rev. 2), and if you depart from it, you must fall into thorns and briars, as much in doctrine as in discipline. So Richard Field: More errors are found in the writings of the Fathers of the primitive Church than in those of men more remote from those first beginnings, because they were deceived by false and uncertain reports, which men of those times drank in with eager ears from those who lived together with them and had conversed with the Apostles or their disciples. So John White, the hierarchist. What is objected to us unfairly is this: it is probable that teachers nearer to the Apostolic times saw more than we who are further away. This their own teacher, Dominic Bañez, denies: It is not necessary, he says, that the further a Church is from the times of the Apostles, the less perfect is its knowledge of the mysteries of faith, for after the times of the Apostles there did not arise most learned men who had skill in understanding and explaining matters of faith. Why, then, should I not conclude with Fulgentius, from Cyprian: Custom is not to be prescribed, but to be overcome by reason. For since custom and the whole practice even of that primitive Church, which immediately succeeded the Apostles, makes no certain faith, it remains that, setting aside the authority of that practice, we take refuge in the Scriptures alone.

units.la: CAP. 9.
units.tr: CHAPTER 9.

units.la: Argumentum septimum de Ecclesiastica praxi in secunda periodo sohvitur.
units.tr: The seventh argument, concerning ecclesiastical practice, is answered as to the second period.

units.la: DE Ecclesiae periodo prima vidimus: jam ad secundam deveniendum, de qua non veretur Geor. Dotnumas affirmare, per annos a Christo trecentos, nihil in disciplina mutatum fuisse. Nullus color, inquit, solidae rationis reddi potest, ut superioritas & authoritas Episcoporum, quae dioecesani, maior esset in quarta centuria, quam in tertia, aut tertia, quam in secunda, aut in secunda quam in prima. Rursus, quasi universa & perpetua praxis omnium Ecclesiarum & consensus patrum primis annis trecentis sufficiens demonstratio non esset ad persuadendum homini judicioso, & bona conscientia praedito, quaenam illa doctrina, & praxis Apostolorum fuit. Quod si etenim quis dixerit, omnes Ecclesias Apostolicas, sanctos patres, gloriosos Martyres semper ab Apostolorum temporibus disciplinam & Ecclesiae regimen observasse illi contrarium, quod Apostoli praescripserant: de eo dicere non dubito eum ut modestis vacuum, ita & non multum judicij habere aut benestatis. Rursus, Reicit refutator Canonem Apostolorum, concilium Ancyranum & Arelatense, & Cyprianum, qui omnes de superioritate Episcopi testantur, quia intra annos 200 non vixerunt. Quasi omnis veritas illa periodo circumscriberetur: aut patrum nonnulli sequentes (nominatim Cyprianum) tantam quam illi fidem non mercantur? Cyprianus 40 vel 50 annis junior est. Concilium Ancyranum annis 50, vel 60 Cypriano posterius est. Non est dubium quin ingens alteratio in disciplina & regimine Ecclesiastico pretendi possit, ante tempus Constantini, dum sub cruce Ecclesia esset. Sed has authoritates quantum vult Refutator estimet: nemo modestus, & moderatus Christianus nullus est, qui horum affirmationem præsertim in materia facti, negationi mille refutatori similium præfert. Rursus, Regimen Ecclesiæ per trecentos a Christo annos, absque omni dubio Apostolicæ institutionis fuit: iuxta Augustinum de Baptis. cont. Donat. l. 4, 2:2,4. Quod universa tenet Ecclesia, & a conciliis institutum non est, sed semper retentum est, id ab Apostolis traditum certissimè creditur. Postremò, Quod communiter in Ecclesiis per trecentos annos receptum, antequam Concilium aliquod Generale erat, quod id definiret, absque omni dubio ab ipsis Apostolis profectum est. Quid facis homini tam apertè prævaricanti? Ego D. Dormamum virum doctum & pium agnosco, neque mihi cum persona, sed cum errore lis est: eum hic tamen apertissimè lapsum fuisse non possum non asserere.
units.tr: We have seen the first period of the Church; now we must come to the second, concerning which Geor. Dotnumas does not hesitate to affirm that for three hundred years after Christ nothing in discipline was changed. No plausible reason, he says, can be given for the superiority and authority of the bishops over their dioceses being greater in the fourth century than in the third, or in the third than in the second, or in the second than in the first. Again, as if the universal and constant practice of all the Churches and the agreement of the Fathers in the first three hundred years were not a sufficient proof to persuade a judicious man of good conscience what the doctrine and practice of the Apostles was! For if anyone should say that all the apostolic Churches, the holy Fathers and the glorious Martyrs had always, from the times of the Apostles, kept a discipline and government of the Church contrary to what the Apostles had prescribed, I do not hesitate to say that such a man is, to put it modestly, empty of judgment and lacking in good sense. Again, the refuter rejects the Canon of the Apostles, the Council of Ancyra and the Council of Arles, and Cyprian, who all bear witness to the superiority of the bishop, because they lived not within two hundred years. As if all that truth were confined to that period, or as if the testimony of some Fathers who followed (Cyprian by name) deserved no such credit as theirs! Cyprian is forty or fifty years younger. The Council of Ancyra is fifty or sixty years later than Cyprian. There is no doubt that a huge change in discipline and church government could be alleged for the time before Constantine, while the Church was under the cross. But let the refuter weigh these authorities as much as he likes: there is no modest and moderate Christian who would prefer the denial of a thousand men like the refuter to their affirmation, especially in a matter of fact. Again, the government of the Church during the three hundred years from Christ was, beyond all doubt, of apostolic institution, according to Augustine, On Baptism against the Donatists, book 4, chapter 24. What the whole Church holds, and what was not instituted by councils but has always been retained, is most certainly believed to have been handed down by the Apostles. Lastly, what was commonly received in the Churches for three hundred years, before any general council existed to define it, beyond all doubt proceeded from the Apostles themselves. What can one do with a man who so plainly prevaricates? I acknowledge Dormamus as a learned and pious man, and my dispute is not with the person but with the error; yet I cannot but assert that he has here very plainly fallen.

units.la: Primò verò cum à suis refutatum dico, ab eis nempe qui disciplinam mutabilem contendunt, quorum instituto parum hoc dogma Dormami uti convenit; ita & Dormamo ipsi: Ex eis etenim Dormamus est, qui disciplinam mutabilem docent: parum ver est universam praxim Ecclesiarum per annos trecentos adversam habere? Quis enim ausit disciplinam mutare, quam illi non mutandam sensuerunt? Consultiores ergo Dormamo, hujus opinionis reliqui sunt: nam ut mutabilitati disciplinæ viam muniant: communiter tradunt, & in primis Ecclesiis mutationes in disciplina contigisse. Ita Lous. Ecclesia jam inde ab Apostolorum temporibus, varias administrationum species admisit. Quæ de disciplinæ mutatione intelligit, aut ineptè disputat: nam infert hæc ut probet disciplinam mutari posse. Iohannes Whitgiftus, postquam probandum sumpsisset formam regiminis Ecclesiastici mutari posse, instat ex Ambrosio in Eph. 4. in mutatione, quam ab illo intra annos Dormami trecentos contigisse scribitur. Alteratio gubernationis & ordinum Ecclesiæ (inquit) bene ab Ambrosio ponitur. Ubi omnia loca circumplexa est Ecclesia, conventicula constituta sunt, & Rectores & cætera officia in Ecclesiis sunt ordinata: & cæpit alio ordine & providentia gubernari Ecclesia. Ideo non conveniunt per omnia scripta Apostoli, ordinationi quæ nunc in Ecclesia est, quia hæc inter ipsa primordia sunt scripta.
