En apertum testimonium à primordijs Ecclesiarum degeneratum fuisse: sic ut ordo Ecclesiæ minimè scriptis Apostolorum respondeat, idque intra annos trecentos: nam ante concilium Nicænum, hunc Ambrosium floruisse suo loco demonstrabitur: Accedo ad Iohannem Bridgesium, qui pro disciplinæ mutabilitate contendens, ita infert: Nonne Apostoli consultum putaverunt propter commodiorem Ecclesiæ gubernationem, nonnulla officia addere, quæ a Christo instituta non sunt? Verbis sequentibus adeo mutabilem disciplinam contendit, ut patres in Ecclesia primitiva succedentes, potiùs in eo offendere dicat, quod laborarint ordinationes quasdam & ossicia, ab Apostolis pro suo tempore institutas, retinere, & tanquam perpetua urgere. Intelligit proculdubio Seniores: utcunque sit, habet hic Dormamus, Ecclesiæ Apostolos succedentis universam praxim condemnatam, à socio suo, ab Hierarchico, ab Episcopo: idque in eo quòd. quòd in quibusdam non mutarit disciplinam. Erubescat deinceps igitur clamorum suorum, quos adversus Puritanos ciere solet. Aut concedendum refutatori est (inquit) Apostolicas Ecclesias hoc regimen per Episcopos, ab Apostolis recepisse: aut confitendum (secundùm consuetam modestiam suam, totius antiquitatis testimonium nihili æstimantem) omnes Ecclesias conspirasse, gubernationem mutare, quam Apostoli instituissent. Quam hic conspirationis accusationem appellat, etiam paulò post turpem imputationem nuncupat. Quam verò tu conspirationem narras? quam turpem imputationem? Mutare potuerant disciplinam ab Apostolis institutam (inquit Whigiftus,) absque conspiratione aliqua, aut turpis imputationis nota, imo & mutarunt etiam recte, legitime, pie, prudenter, commode. Ingens piaculum nos patribus aspergere dicis, quòd eos disciplinam immutasse dicamus? At Bridgesius in eo potiùs offendisse patres docet, quòd quædam non mutarent. Quid ipse? Annon disciplinam legitimè mutari posse contendis? pudeat igitur clamorum istorum, de conspiratione patrum, de turpi imputationis nota, de Apostasia, in quam Bilsonus, de contemptu Apostolicæ institutionis, in quam primas Ecclesias incidisse Bancroftus clamat, si modò Episcopale regimen subintroduxerint ab ipsis Apostolis non receptum. Quidni introducerent aiunt reliqui Hierarchici: veterem etenim Apostolorum disciplinam mutare peccatum non est.
units.tr: But first, when I say that he is refuted by his own side, namely by those who contend that discipline is changeable, to whose position this doctrine of Dormamus fits poorly, I say the same to Dormamus himself. For Dormamus is one of those who teach that discipline is changeable, and is it not a poor thing to have the whole practice of the Churches against him for three hundred years? For who would dare to change a discipline which they did not judge should be changed? The more careful of his fellow-thinkers are therefore left to Dormamus; for in order to pave the way for the mutability of discipline, they commonly teach that changes in discipline occurred even in the earliest Churches. Thus Lous. The Church, from the very times of the Apostles onward, admitted various forms of administration. Whoever understands this of a change in discipline either argues foolishly, for he adduces it to prove that discipline can be changed. John Whitgift, having undertaken to prove that the form of church government can be changed, presses the point from Ambrose on Ephesians 4, concerning the change which is written of as having occurred within those three hundred years of Dormamus. The alteration of government and of the orders of the Church (he says) is well stated by Ambrose. Where the Church spread over all regions, meeting-places were established, and rectors and other offices were ordained in the Churches, and the Church began to be governed by a different order and providence. Therefore the Apostles' writings do not agree in every respect with the order that now exists in the Church, because these were written in the very beginnings. Here is a plain testimony that from the beginnings of the Churches there was a decline, so that the order of the Church does not correspond to the writings of the Apostles, and this within three hundred years; for it will be shown in its place that Ambrose flourished before the Council of Nicaea. I come to John Bridges, who, contending for the mutability of discipline, infers thus: Did not the Apostles think it expedient, for a more convenient government of the Church, to add certain offices which Christ had not instituted? In the words that follow he so insists on a mutable discipline that he says the Fathers succeeding in the primitive Church rather offended in this, that they laboured to retain certain ordinances and offices which the Apostles had instituted for their own time, and to press them as perpetual. He doubtless means the elders. However that may be, Dormamus here has the whole practice of the Church succeeding the Apostles condemned by his own colleague, by a hierarchist, by a bishop; and that for this reason, that in some things they did not change discipline. Let him therefore be ashamed of the outcries he is accustomed to raise against the Puritans. Either the refuter must concede (he says) that the apostolic Churches received this government by bishops from the Apostles; or he must confess (according to his customary modesty, valuing the testimony of all antiquity at nothing) that all the Churches conspired to alter the government which the Apostles had instituted. What he calls an accusation of conspiracy he also soon names a shameful imputation. But what conspiracy do you speak of? What shameful imputation? They could have changed the discipline instituted by the Apostles (says Whitgift) without any conspiracy or mark of shameful imputation; indeed they also changed it rightly, lawfully, piously, prudently, and fittingly. Do you say that we heap a huge sacrilege on the Fathers when we say that they changed discipline? But Bridges teaches that the Fathers rather offended in this, that they did not change certain things. What about yourself? Do you not contend that discipline can be lawfully changed? Let him be ashamed, then, of those outcries about a conspiracy of the Fathers, about the mark of shameful imputation, about the apostasy into which Bilson, about the contempt of apostolic institution into which Bancroft cries out that the first Churches fell, if indeed they introduced episcopal government which had not been received from the Apostles themselves. Why should they not introduce it, the other hierarchists say? For to change the old discipline of the Apostles is no sin.

units.la: Secundò, ex ipsis sacris colligi potest haud obscurè, intra annos trecentos, Ecclesias plurimùm degenerasse, & quædam invexisse, quæ ab Apostolis non acceperant. Propositum Apocalips. primò Christum esse, juxta statum primæ Ecclesiæ, non erit, opinor, contra Brightmannum à quoquam dubitatum. Quid autem? Ap. 1,20. septem candelabræ integro typo Exod.25.11. respondent, ad demonstrandum florentissimum Ecclesiæ statum, quandiu lucebant in ea Apostoli, eorumque integri successores. At Constantini tempora quinque amissis, duæ tantùm remanent Ap. 11.4. ad demonstrandum luctuosum Ecclesiæ statum, quæ reliquarum detrimentum passa est. Quid? quinq; lucernæ uno impetu amissæ? Deesse tantùm in nobis quamquam fallo Hierarchici, ac si uno impetu Ecclesiam defecisse dicamus: quod hic meminisse operæ pretium est. Non enim uno impetu has quinque lucernas amissas fuisse Constantini tempore colore ullo dicere poterunt: sed post varias contractas sordes, idque gradatim, intra ipsos præcedentes trecentos annos. Deinde Ecclesia tempore Apostolorum in cælo est, ornata stellis: Apo.12.1.ad exitum verò trecentorum annorum, Sol factus est niger, ut saccus cilicinus & Luna tota facta est ut sanguis, & stellæ cæli ceciderunt in terram sicut ficus ubijcit grossos suos, quum vento magno concutitur: & cælum abscedit sicut liber qui convolvitur. Ap. 6.12: 13:14. Dicuntur hæc de misera Ecclesiæ uastitate sub Diocletiano & Maximiano: quando Sol, id est Scriptura ab Ecclesia auferebatur judicijs publicis: Luna, id est Ecclesiæ puritas ab hujus solis commercio seclusa Eclipsin passa est: stellæ, id est ministri ad primum impetum defecerunt: & cœlum, id est Ecclesia ipsa, illiusque facies externa, tam atra caligine operiebatur, ut nunquam ferè compareret.
units.tr: Secondly, it can be gathered quite clearly from Scripture itself that within three hundred years the Churches had greatly degenerated and had introduced some things which they had not received from the Apostles. That in the Apocalypse the first thing set forth is Christ, according to the state of the first Church, will not, I think, be doubted by anyone against Brightman. But what follows? Rev. 1.20: the seven candlesticks, according to the whole type of Exod. 25.11, correspond to show the most flourishing state of the Church, as long as the Apostles and their complete successors shone in it. But at the time of Constantine, five having been lost, only two remain, Rev. 11.4, to show the mournful state of the Church, which suffered the loss of the rest. What? Were five lamps lost at a single blow? Hierarchists, although I may be mistaken, are lacking in this, if we say the Church failed at a single blow; and it is worth remembering this here. For they will not be able to say with any colour that these five lamps were lost at one stroke in the time of Constantine, but after various defilements had been contracted, and that gradually, within those three hundred years immediately preceding. Furthermore, the Church in the time of the Apostles is in heaven, adorned with stars (Rev. 12.1); but at the end of the three hundred years: the sun became black as sackcloth, and the whole moon became as blood, and the stars of heaven fell to the earth as a fig tree casts its unripe figs when shaken by a great wind; and the heaven departed like a scroll that is rolled up. Rev. 6.12, 13, 14. These things are said of the wretched desolation of the Church under Diocletian and Maximian, when the Sun, that is Scripture, was taken away from the Church by public judgments; the Moon, that is the purity of the Church, cut off from commerce with this sun, suffered an eclipse; the stars, that is the ministers, fell at the first onset; and the heaven, that is the Church itself and its outward appearance, was so covered with such dark mist that it hardly ever appeared.

units.la: Ad hæc, Ephesus Brighmanni judicio, typus est Ecclesiæ veteris ad annos trecentos decurrentis: ea autem quasi ἔφυς dicta est, & prior opera non facit: quia ad postremum deficere quodammodo illa prima Ecclesia eo magis videbatur, quo magis ad exitum horum annorum trecentorum deveniebat. Sed fac Ecclesias Asianas πάντως non esse, cum omnes tamen, Philadelphia sola excepta, remissæ disciplinæ etiam intra Johannis tempora redarguantur: quomodo verisimile fiet posteriores Ecclesias per trecentorum annorum spacium non delineasse, multa mutasse, varias denique sordes contraxisse? Atque Epheso nominatim remotio candelabri denunciatur, quod pœnitentiâ non intercedente, proculdubio, non ita multo post adimpletum est, saltem ante 800 annos. Per candelabrum intelligitur Episcopalis dignitas, inquit Riberus, sed absurdè: intelligitur etenim Evangelij lux, & Ecclesiæ Ephesinæ puritas; unde ita disputo: Auferetur candelabrum Epheso ante annos 800. Episcopalis dignitas ante annos 800 ablata non est: Episcopalis igitur dignitas candelabri lucisque in eodem fulgentis pars nulla est, sed floret illa candelabro remoto, luce exincta, missa Ecclesiæ puritate.
units.tr: In the judgement of Brightman, Ephesus is a type of the ancient Church, which ran on to about three hundred years. It is called ephys [ἔφυς] as though by nature, and it does not do the earlier work. For that first Church seemed in some measure to fail the more it drew near the end of those three hundred years. But grant that the Asian Churches were not by all means [πάντως] that type. Still, all of them except Philadelphia alone are rebuked for slack discipline even within the times of John. How likely is it that the later Churches, over a space of three hundred years, did not go astray, did not change many things, and finally did not contract various defilements? Moreover, the removal of the lampstand is announced by name to Ephesus. Without repentance this was undoubtedly fulfilled not long afterwards, at least eight hundred years ago. Ribera says that the lampstand means the episcopal dignity, but absurdly so. It means rather the light of the Gospel and the purity of the Church of Ephesus. Hence I argue thus: the lampstand will be removed from Ephesus eight hundred years ago. The episcopal dignity was not removed eight hundred years ago. Therefore the episcopal dignity is no part of the lampstand, or of the light shining in it. Rather, it flourishes when the lampstand is removed, the light is quenched, and the purity of the Church is gone.

units.la: Tertiò, in doctrina intra annos trecentos multa mutata, vitiata multa sunt: quid ni pariter in disciplinâ? non minus in disciplinâ quàm in doctrina errare patres potuerunt? Sic quidem Io. Whitgifto videtur, qui cum neminem modestiæ & eruditionis virum, tempora annorum 500 eorumque ordinationes absque manifesta probatione condemnare velle dicit, præsertim in Ecclesiæ gubernatione: insinuare videtur minùs proclivem in disciplinâ quàm in doctrinâ ad errorem lapsum esse. Scultingius è contra doctrinam corrumpi non posse dicit propter Spiritus assistentiam: sed in disciplinâ semper fuisse defectus, modo magis, modo minus. Sed medium veritas iter inter hos duos facit: adæquè in disciplinâ atque in doctrinâ, errare quorumcunque temporum Ecclesia potest. Quanquam è duobus propiùs Scultingius ad metam collimavit. Si etenim aliqua disparitas danda sit, facilius quidem certè disciplina corrumpitur quàm doctrina: nam cum instar muri ad civitatem sit, quis non videt Sathanæ impetum primùm disciplinam sustinere debuisse? præterea mores corrumpi solent, etiam illabatâ doctrinâ: corruptio vero morum aut ex disciplinâ corrupta oritur, aut disciplinæ corruptionem secum trahere fere semper solet. Rectè etenim alicubi Matheus Sutclivius ex Plauto: Ubi mores deficiunt, non ibi murus centuplex sufficit. Hinc disciplinam intra annos trecentos corruptam fuisse, aut saltem corrumpi potuisse ex eo licet colligere: quòd mores hoc tempore depravatissimi fuerint: D. Mornæus pro degeneratione Ecclesiæ clesiæ in promovendo papatu, affert degenerationem morum. Quid ni & ego eandem adferrem pro degeneratione, in Episcopatu invehendo, in quo Romani primatus Antichristiani fundamenta jacta sunt. Vtcunq; sit, si in moribus degenerare intra annos trecentos Ecclesia potuit, in disciplina etiam potuit : res enim moralis disciplina est, ad mores proxime desccndit,& mores aut flectit, aut eifdem flectitur. Iam vero testimonia de morum intra annos trecentos corruptione, luculenta extant cum apud Cyprianum,tum apud Eusebium,quæ etiam D. Morneus recenset.
units.tr: Thirdly, within three hundred years many things in doctrine were changed and many were corrupted. Why not likewise in discipline? Could the Fathers not err in discipline as much as in doctrine? Indeed this seems to be the view of John Whitgift, who says that no man of modesty and learning would wish to condemn the times of five hundred years and their ordinations without clear proof, especially in the government of the Church. He seems to suggest that the Church was less prone to fall into error in discipline than in doctrine. Scultingius, on the contrary, says that doctrine cannot be corrupted because of the Spirit's help, but that in discipline there was always a failing, now greater, now less. But the truth takes a middle way between these two: the Church of any age can err in discipline just as much as in doctrine. Yet of the two, Scultingius has aimed more nearly at the mark. For if some difference must be granted, discipline is certainly corrupted more easily than doctrine. Since discipline stands like a wall about the city, who does not see that Satan's assault must first have been met by discipline? Moreover, morals are wont to be corrupted even when doctrine is unharmed. But the corruption of morals arises either from corrupted discipline, or almost always draws corrupted discipline along with it. Indeed Matthew Sutcliffe somewhere rightly quotes Plautus: Where morals fail, a wall a hundredfold will not suffice. From this it may be gathered that discipline was corrupted within three hundred years, or at least could have been corrupted, because morals were most depraved at that time. D. Mornay, to account for the degeneration of the Church in advancing the papacy, adduces a degeneration of morals. Why should I not adduce the same, to account for the degeneration in introducing episcopacy, in which the foundations of the Roman primacy, the Antichristian one, were laid? However that may be, if the Church could degenerate in morals within three hundred years, it could also degenerate in discipline. For moral discipline is a matter of morals, comes very near to them, and either bends them or is bent by them. Now clear testimonies to the corruption of morals within three hundred years exist, both in Cyprian and in Eusebius, which Mornay also recounts.

units.la: Ita Cyprianus : Non in sacerdotibus religio devota, non in ministris fides integra, non in operibus misericordia, non in moribus disciplina. Quin & Episcopi plurimi quos & ornamento esse oportet cæteris & exemplo, divina procuratione contempta, procuratores rerum sæcularium fieri, derelictâ cathedra, plebe desertâ, per alienas provincias oberrantes, negotiationis quæstuosæ nundinas aucupari, esurientibus in Ecclesia fratribus, habere argentum lingiter, velle fundos insidiosis fraudibus capere, usuris multiplicantibus fenus augere. Quid non perpeti tales pro peccatis hujusmodi merèrentur? Ita Eusebius. Episcopi in Episcopos irruerant ac populi contra populum seditiones moverant.—Alij alios sunt odio & contumelia prosequuti, & tantum non nosipsos per nosipsos armis ac telis verborum ubicunque contigit, impugnavimus :—Et qui pastores nostri videbantur, repulsa pietatis norma, mutuis inter se contentionibus fuerunt inflammati, & dum hæc sola, contentiones videlicet, minas, æmulationem, mutuum odium & inimicitiam exaggerant, & ambitionem suam quisque in morem tyrannidis studiose persequitur. Isaacus Casaubonus probat disciplinæ degenerationem in quarto sæculo, ex eo quod legantur passim apud pios patres, Basilium, Nazianzenum, Hieronymum, Chrysostomum, Augustinum,& alios, gravissimæ querelæ de vitijs Ecclesiarum suarum & varijs depravationibus. At si ita à degeneratione morum, ad degenerationem disciplinæ in quarto sæculo argumentum firmum petituri quanto magis intra trecentos annos degeneratio morum talis, quæ ambitiosorum Episcoporum typhum, imò & tyrannidem aperte spirat?
units.tr: Thus Cyprian: Religious devotion is not found among priests, sound faith is not found among ministers, mercy is not found in works, discipline is not found in morals. Nay, very many bishops, who ought to be an ornament and example to the others, despising divine care, have become managers of secular affairs. Abandoning their chair and deserting their people, they wander through foreign provinces, hunting out the markets of profitable trade. While brothers in the Church are hungry, they hold silver in abundance, wish to seize estates by deceitful frauds, and increase their money by multiplying usury. What might such men not deserve to suffer for sins of this kind? So Eusebius. Bishops had rushed upon bishops, and peoples had stirred up sedition against peoples. Some pursued others with hatred and insult, and we ourselves, as far as it happened anywhere, attacked one another with the weapons of words. And those who seemed to be our ministers, the rule of godliness being rejected, were inflamed with mutual contentions, and while these alone, namely contentions, threats, rivalry, mutual hatred and enmity, were magnified, each one zealously pursued his own ambition in the manner of tyranny. Isaac Casaubon proves the degeneration of discipline in the fourth century from the fact that everywhere in the pious Fathers, Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Jerome, Chrysostom, Augustine, and others, the most grave complaints are read concerning the faults of their Churches and their various corruptions. But if from the degeneration of morals one seeks a firm argument for degeneration of discipline in the fourth century, how much more so for a degeneration of morals within three hundred years, such as openly breathes the pride and even the tyranny of ambitious bishops?

units.la: 4 Quartò,quàm falsò à Downamo dictum sit, Nihil in disciplinâ intra annos trecentos mutatum esse: constabit ex ipsarum mutationum enumeratione : ubi de mutationibus silebo,quæ Episcopatui Hierarchico introducendo inserviebant : quia de eis alius erit nobis peculiaris dicendi locus. Quod ad reliquas, initio primo in decimis : quæ iure divino debitas esse, Richardus Fyldus, Georgius Carletonus, & plurimi alij Hierarchici dicunt. Aliquid igitur illorum iudicio de iure divino intra annos trecentos mutatum est : nam vel ipso Fyldo confitente voluntarijs contributionibus foliis per hæc tempora Ecclesiarum ministri alebantur : decimæ nullæ persolvebantur.
units.tr: Fourthly, how falsely Downame has said, Nothing in discipline was changed within three hundred years, will be clear from a list of the changes themselves. I shall keep silent about those changes that served to introduce the hierarchical episcopacy, because we shall have another special place to speak of them. As for the rest, first, in tithes, which Richard Field, George Carleton, and many other Hierarchists say are owed by divine right. Therefore something, by their judgement, concerning divine right was changed within three hundred years. For, even by Field's own admission, during these times the ministers of the Churches were supported by voluntary contributions, and no tithes were paid.

units.la: Secundo,initio in Diaconis: sic enim ipse Fyldus : Diaconi Act. 6. ex primâ intentione ad pauperum curam principaliter ordinati erant, positæ verò cum pauperibus aliter prospectum esset, speciales Episcoporum assisten- tes facti sunt, &c. Diaconos Episcopo speciales ministrantes intra annos trecentos extitisse, fatetur ipse Downamus: in Diaconis igitur à prima principali saltem Apostolorum intentione & ordinatione intra annos trecentos deviatum est.
units.tr: Secondly, concerning deacons. For thus Field himself: Deacons (Acts 6) were ordained at first principally for the care of the poor. But when the poor were otherwise provided for, they became special assistants to the bishops, &c. That deacons served bishops in a special way existed within three hundred years, Downame himself admits. Therefore, concerning deacons, a departure has been made within three hundred years at least from the first principal intention and ordinance of the Apostles.

units.la: Tertiò, insito in electione populari: nam Act. 14. & Tit. 2. Episcopos solos eligisse Hierarchici dicunt: intra annos trecentos tamen per universam Ecclesiæ praxim, ministri à populo eligebantur, ut ipsimet fatentur: velint igitur nolint, ipsorum iudicio, mutatio, hàc in parte intra annos trecentos facta est.
units.tr: Thirdly, concerning popular election. For the Hierarchists say that Acts 14 and Titus 2 show that bishops alone were chosen. Yet within three hundred years, through the whole practice of the Church, ministers were chosen by the people, as they themselves confess. Whether they wish it or not, then, by their own judgement a change was made in this respect within three hundred years.

units.la: Quartò, insito in Seniorum illa exclusione, quam refert Ambrosius, 1. Tim. 5. per doctorum sive ignaviam, sive superbiam, factam, dum soli videri vellent esse aliquid: nam intra trecentos annos hunc authorem vixisse suo loco constabit, & si non vixerit, tamen de temporibus præteritis scribit. Mutationem hîc factum esse vel ipse Hadrianus Saravia dat: cuius hæc verba sunt: Ceterum quod Ambrosium deplorasse ait D. Beza, non recte eum intellexit, qui ordinatione presbyteros nusquam abrogatos queritur: sed quod ætate, sapientia, & gravitate senes laici non eo loco haberentur ut olim, quando in rebus gravioribus in consilium adhibebantur. Quo tantum loco si haberentur ut deberent, qui hodie in Ecclesiis reformatis pastoribus adiunguntur, nihil repugnarem. En hic Seniores abrogatos; adeoque mutationem intra trecentos annos factam.
units.tr: Fourthly, concerning that exclusion of the elders which Ambrose reports on 1 Timothy 5: it was brought about by the sloth or the pride of the teachers, while they wished to seem to be something. For it will be clear in its place that this author lived within three hundred years, and if he did not live then, yet he writes of past times. That a change was made here Adrian Saravia himself grants, whose words are these: Moreover, as to what Beza says Ambrose lamented, he did not understand him rightly, who complains that presbyters were nowhere abrogated by ordinance, but that elders, lay men by age, wisdom and gravity, were not held in the place they once held, when they were called into council in weightier matters. If they were held in that place which they ought to have, those who today are joined with pastors in the reformed Churches, I would not object. Behold, here the elders are abrogated, and so a change was made within three hundred years.

units.la: Quintò, insito in Patriarchis, quos intra annos trecentos extitisse, Downamus ipse & reliqui Hierarchici docent. Quid igitur? Patriarchæ iuxta hanc regulam Downamianam ab Apostolis prodierunt? Apage has nugas Whitgiftianas: audiatur potius Matheus Sutclivius Primatus, inquit, Romani Pontificis qui multo est iunior quam papatus qui fuit ante Nicænum Concilium, a consuetudine populorum originem habuit: probat ex concilio Nicæno: Mos antiquus obtineat. Planior Georgius ipse Downamus: Negare non possum quin Patriarchæ fuerint supra Metropolitanos longe ante Nicænum concilium: quorum origo ab invento politico humano ut videtur (concil. Nicæn. c. 6.) ordebatur, sic ut eorum ratihabitio continuatioque antiquo mori adscribitur. Itane vero? Patriarcha longè ante Nicænum Concilium, & ex iure humano, & consuetudine? Ergo tuo te iudicio prodidisti: universa Ecclesiæ praxis latenter per consuetudinem irrepere potest, absque plenario concilio, & intra annos trecentos summum in Hierarchia fastigium nempe patriarchatus quanquam in universam Ecclesiarum praxim receptus, ab Apostolis tamen non descendebat. Si patriarcha iure humano, cur non & Metropolitanus, si Metropolitanus cur non Episcopus? donec ad presbyteros devenitur, quorum certa origo desumitur ab Apostolis.
units.tr: Fifthly, concerning the patriarchs, whom Downame himself and the other Hierarchists teach existed within three hundred years. What then? Did the patriarchs, according to this Downamian rule, come forth from the Apostles? Away with these Whitgiftian trifles! Let us rather hear Matthew Sutcliffe, Primacy, he says, of the Roman Pontiff, which is much younger than the papacy that existed before the Council of Nicaea, had its origin from the custom of peoples. He proves it from the Council of Nicaea: Let the ancient custom prevail. Clearer still is George Downame himself: I cannot deny that patriarchs existed above metropolitans long before the Council of Nicaea, whose origin, as it seems, was ordered by a human political invention (Council of Nicaea, canon 6), so that their ratification and continuance is ascribed to ancient custom. Is that really so? A patriarch long before the Council of Nicaea, and from human law and custom? Then by your own judgement you have betrayed yourself: the whole practice of the Church can creep in covertly by custom, without a full council, and within three hundred years the highest pinnacle of the hierarchy, namely the patriarchate, although received into the general practice of the Churches, nevertheless did not descend from the Apostles. If a patriarch is by human law, why not a metropolitan? If a metropolitan, why not a bishop? One comes down at last to presbyters, whose certain origin is derived from the Apostles.

units.tr: The eighth argument, from ecclesiastical practice, is answered in the third period.

units.la: Vidimus de periodo Ecclesiae secunda quae ad annum 300 desinit: de tertia jam, quae, à tempore Constantini ad annum 500 usque porrigitur, videndum est: Iohannes siquidem Whitgiftus Ecclesiam primitivam ad annum usque 500 extendit: de qua etiam ita habet: Nulla factio introducta est in Ecclesiam per totos 500 annos, a concilio generali, vel fide digno scriptore aliquo approbata, quae illis temporibus apta, & per Dei verbum approbata non est. R. Bancroftus in Cartwrightum invehitur quòd dixerat, tempora post Nicaenū concilium pura casta, minime fuisse, sed Ecclesiam tum in multis a simplicitate in qua Apostoli eam reliquerant, defecisse: exemplumque ab his temporibus, non absque periculo peti posse: sic ut hanc periodum castamque puramque censeat, in simplicitate Apostolica Ecclesiam perdurasse autumet: exempla denique ad firmandam disciplinam, tuto & absque periculo sumi posse opinetur. Praecipuè verò observanda hîc sunt, quae Georgius Downamus scripta reliquit: cuius verba ipsa ad majorem perspicuitatem quantumvis longiuscula exaranda videntur. Nullam rationem video, inquit, cur Ecclesia temporis Constantini, non pro exemplari ad imitandum proponi potius debeat Ecclesiis sub magistratu degentibus; paceque & prosperitate per Dei beneficium fruentibus: quam Ecclesiae ullae priorum temporum, quae in omnibus stabilitae non fuerunt, & pro voto firmatae, sed persecutione impediebantur: Tempore etenim persecutionis, gubernatio non semper talis erat, qualem optabant, sed quam assequi poterant: Atque nisi Ecclesiam semper velimus sub persecutione vivere, requirere ut in omnibus imitandae sint, insania prorsus esset. Quod vero generali censensu & in usum versum est, tempore pacis & prosperitatis: id ipsorum judicio fiendum tum erat, & nobis in eodem casu imitandum, Iam vero Constantini tempore, Episcopos in alios minisros gradu, potestate, & authoritate, superioritate habuisse, evidentissimum est. Neque crevit haec superioritas & authoritas Christiani magistratus accessione, sed decrevit potius: quandoquidem deficiente magistratu, defectum illum supplebant ipsi, & authoritate propria multa fecerunt, quae postea vel à magistratu facta sunt, vel ab ipsis per assistentiam magistratus. Neque color ullus rationis est superioritate Episcopali majorem fuisse in quarta centuria quam in tertia, in tertia quam in secunda, in secunda quam in prima. Iuxta haec verba adjicitur in margine: Forma gubernationis & authoritas Episcopalis per omnia tempora primitivae Ecclesiae eadem fuit: Ecclesiam vero primitivā quarta hic centuria circumscribere videtur: ita quintā quam addiderat Whitgiftus amputavit, vel neglexit saltem. Ac necessum non erat: aeque enim verè Scultingius, disciplinam Gregorij tempore incorruptam fuisse afferere potuit, & eandem politeiam quae sub Apostolis erat; atque aut in quarta centuria Romanus,aut in quinta Whitgiftus. Imo & annum 608 includere potest, ad annum 607 qui annus natalis Papae erat. Quae etenim mutatio? quae factionum additio, ante hoc tempus, ab ea quae fuerat centuria quarta, quintaque praecedente? Concilium Chalcedonense, in quo Patriarcha Romanus, & Constantinopolitanus, ita supra caeteros elati sunt, ut hic in oriente, ille in occidente patrimonium Christi invasisse videatur, intra annos 400 fuit. In hoc concilio nomen universalis Episcopi Pontifici Romano obtum fuisse dicit Whitgiftus: quod si verum sit, causam hanc pejorem multo atque deteriorem reddit: quid enim? Numnam tutum (quod ante Bancroftus) ab eis temporibus, Conciliis eis, formam gubernationis sumere, quae usque adeo depravata fuerunt, ut Papatui ipsi fenestram aperirent, & etiamnum aperuisset: ni ipsius Romani Pontificis modestia obstitisset? Sed ad rem? Cum nulla mutatio intra hanc periodum essentialis accideri, per novorum officiorum additionem: in Constantini tempore aeram nostram statuemus, a quo exemplar sumendum non esse, Episcopum Hierarchicum non diminutum sed auctum fuisse, disciplinamque Ecclesiasticam misere fadatam pollutamque fuisse, manifestissimis contra Dominum argumentis comprobabitur.
units.tr: We have seen the second period of the Church, which ends at the year 300. Now we must consider the third, which stretches from the time of Constantine to the year 500. John Whitgift extends the primitive Church as far as the year 500, and of it he says: No faction has been introduced into the Church through the whole of those 500 years that has been approved by a general council or some trustworthy writer, and that was not suited to those times and approved by the word of God. Richard Bancroft attacks Cartwright for saying that the times after the Council of Nicaea were not pure and chaste, but that the Church had then fallen away in many respects from the simplicity in which the Apostles had left her, and that examples cannot be drawn from those times without danger. So Bancroft holds that this period was chaste and pure, that the Church persisted in apostolic simplicity, and finally he thinks that examples for confirming discipline can be taken safely and without danger. Especially to be noted here are the things written by George Downame. Although they are rather long, I think they should be set down in full for greater clarity. I see no reason, he says, why the Church of Constantine's time should not rather be proposed as a model for imitation to churches living under the magistrate and enjoying peace and prosperity by the benefit of God, than any churches of earlier times, which were not established in all respects, nor confirmed according to their wish, but were hindered by persecution. For in a time of persecution the government was not always such as they wished, but such as they could obtain. And unless we always want the Church to live under persecution, it would be sheer madness to demand that she be imitated in all things. But what was done by general consent and put into practice in a time of peace and prosperity, that, in their judgment, was to be done then, and by us is to be imitated in the same case. Now, that in Constantine's time the bishops had superiority over the other ministers in rank, power and authority, is most evident. Nor did this superiority and authority grow through the addition of a Christian magistrate; rather it was established, since when the magistrate was lacking, the bishops themselves supplied that deficiency and by their own authority did many things, which were afterwards done either by the magistrate or by the bishops with the magistrate's help. Nor is there any reasonable ground for saying that episcopal superiority was greater in the fourth century than in the third, in the third than in the second, or in the second than in the first. In the margin, close to these words, is added: The form of government and episcopal authority was the same through all the times of the primitive Church. Yet here the fourth century seems to mark the limit of the primitive Church. So he has cut off, or at least neglected, the fifth century, which Whitgift had added. And there was no need: for Scultingius could just as truly assert that discipline was uncorrupted in the time of Gregory, and the same polity that existed under the Apostles, and that the Roman polity was so in the fourth century, or Whitgift's in the fifth. Indeed he could include even the year 608, since 607 was the year of the Pope's accession. For what change, what addition of factions, took place before this time, beyond what had existed in the fourth and fifth centuries before? The Council of Chalcedon, in which the Roman and Constantinopolitan patriarchs were so exalted above the rest that the one seems to have seized the patrimony of Christ in the East and the other in the West, took place within 400 years. Whitgift says that in this council the title of universal bishop was granted to the Roman Pontiff. If that is true, it makes the case much worse and more wretched. For what then? Is it safe (as Bancroft said before) to take a form of government from those times and those councils, which were so depraved that they would open a window to Papacy itself, and would still have opened it, had not the modesty of the Roman Pontiff himself stood in the way? But to the point. Since no essential change occurred within this period, except by the addition of new offices, we shall fix our era in Constantine's time. It will be proved, by the plainest arguments against the Lord, that his model is not to be taken as an example, that the hierarchical episcopate was not diminished but increased, and that ecclesiastical discipline was wretchedly deformed and polluted.

units.la: 2 Primo, disputo ab horum temporum typis: fidem etenim fecit mihi Thomas Brightmannus Ecclesias illas tunc Asiacas typos futurarum fuisse. Inter caetera, cum scribere ad has Ecclesias jubetur Iohannes: Ap. 1: 19. non tantum ea quae sunt, scriptis commendare jubetur, in his ipsis Ecclesiis scilicet: sed etiam quae futurae sunt, id est, futurarum Ecclesiarum delineationem, quae in his Ecclesiis adumbrantur: cum postea quando ab his particularibus Ecclesiis discessum est, & ad historiam generalem perscribendam devenitur, ea tantum jubetur scribere quae sunt futura: Ap. 4, 1. Neque tamen funem contentiosum traham: sed ut per me suo cuique sensu frui licet: ita per alios mihi etiam liceat, meo quoque frui. Meminisse igitur debemus priori Ecclesiae quae Constantinum antecessit, in Epheso ejusdem typo denunciatum a Christo fuisse: Ap. 2. 5. Venium adversum te cito, & movebo candelabrum tuum a loco suo nisi resipueris. Quid sibi vult hoc cito? Nomen quidem Ecclesiae Ephesus ipsa ad annos 800 tenuit: sic ut pollutionem illam hic intelligi necesse sit, quae priorem sinceritatem commaculaeret. Ecclesia vero Ephesina non resiput, sed ut ante ex Eusebio obtinuit, quo propius ad Constantini tempora accessit, eo magis ad fastum Episcopalem tyrannidemque anhelavit. Inflammatior hic spiritus a Constantino quam ante: sic ut manifesta experientia, exitusque rerum edoceamur, hanc citam Ecclesiae primae obscurationem, ante Constantini tempus inchoatam, a tempore vero Constantini indies adauctam, idque ex parte per disciplinae Hierarchicae promotionem.
units.tr: 2. First, I argue from the types of these times. For Thomas Brightman convinced me that those Asian churches were then types of things to come. Among other things, when John is ordered to write to these churches (Rev. 1:19), he is commanded to commend in writing not only the things that are, that is, in these very churches, but also the things that are to come, that is, the outline of future churches, which are foreshadowed in these churches. Later, when we have left these particular churches and come to write a general history, he is ordered to write only the things that are to come (Rev. 4:1). Yet I will not drag the rope into a dispute; just as I allow others to enjoy their own opinion, so let me enjoy mine. We ought therefore to remember that in the earlier church, which preceded Constantine, Christ announced its type in Ephesus (Rev. 2:5): I will come to you quickly, and will remove your candlestick out of its place, unless you repent. What does this quickly mean? The name of Church indeed Ephesus kept for about 800 years, so that it is necessary to understand here that pollution which stained the earlier purity. But the Church of Ephesus did not repent; as it had already obtained, according to Eusebius, the closer it came to the times of Constantine, the more it panted after episcopal pride and tyranny. This spirit was more inflamed under Constantine than before. So that by plain experience and the outcome of events we are taught that this swift darkening of the first Church began before Constantine's time, and since Constantine's time has increased daily, and this in part through the promotion of hierarchical discipline.

units.la: Secundo, Smyrna typus Ecclesiae quae a Constantino ad tempora usque que Gratiani decurrit, ostendit, quàm ea pro exemplari ad imitandum proponenda non sit. Ab Epheso versus Aquilonem tendit, propiusq; ad Pergamum Ecclesiae sub Papatu typum accedit, quae in Septentrione etiamnum ulterius ponitur. Hoc, quid aliud insinuatur, quâ post primę Ecclesię lucę obnubilatâ porrecturam horũ temporũ Ecclesiam quidè a Constantini seculo, in majores indies tenebras esse; donec tandem ad Pergamum, ultimam nempe tenebrarum metam peruentum esset. Atque misera Smyrnæ facies à Spiritu sancto depicta Ap. 2. 8. commodissimè respondet ad calamitosam Ecclesiam illam quæ & sub Constantino, & a Constantino extitit. Quàm pauci, quàm despecti, qui hoc tempore veritatem amplectebantur, quamque a falsis Iudæis, id est hypocritis Christianis, Arianis præsertim affligebantur; in exilium pellebantur, carcerib9 includebantur, variis iniurijs, contumelijs, imo & tormentis etiâ afficiebantur, Episcopi suorum contentionibus funestabantur, cum infinitis deniq; malis luctabantur? Constantinus ipse ad posttremum ab eis aversus, sic ut Athanasius & exilio vitam redimere & in exilio vitam finire cogerentur. Hanc ego Ecclesiam (quod Downamus) in pace & prosperitate floruisse: aut si floruerit, pro exemplari ad imitandum proponendam esse existimarem?
units.tr: Second, Smyrna, a type of the Church that runs from Constantine down to the times of Gratian, shows how that Church is not to be proposed as a model for imitation. It stretches from Ephesus toward the north and comes closer to Pergamum, the type of the Church under the Papacy, which is placed further in the north even now. What else is hinted at here, except that after the light of the first Church was clouded over, the Church of these times, from the age of Constantine, was going into ever greater darkness day by day, until at last it reached Pergamum, the final limit of darkness? And the wretched face of Smyrna, painted by the Holy Spirit (Rev. 2:8), corresponds most aptly to that calamitous Church which existed both under Constantine and from Constantine onward. How few and how despised were those who at that time embraced the truth, and how they were afflicted by false Jews, that is, Christian hypocrites, especially the Arians! They were driven into exile, shut up in prisons, and treated with various injuries, insults, and even tortures. Bishops were worn out by the quarrels of their own people, and at last they were struggling with endless evils. Constantine himself at last turned away from them, so that Athanasius was forced both to buy back his life with exile and to end his life in exile. Should I think that this Church (as Downame says) flourished in peace and prosperity, or, if it did flourish, that it should be proposed as a model for imitation?

units.la: 3 Secundò, disputo à sacræ scripturæ testimoniis, quæ hæc ipsa Constantini tempora concernunt, cum eis quæ subsequuta sunt.
units.tr: 3. Second, I argue from the testimonies of Holy Scripture, which concern these very times of Constantine together with what followed them.

units.la: Primò, tempore Constantini, quatuor Angeli ventos salutiferos tenent, ne in Ecclesiam spirare possint: Ap. 7: 1, sic ut coactus Constantinus sit consignare electos, ne communi peste lueque perderentur. Consignatio verò cum paucorum semper & latentium sit, ostendit non adeo fœlicem horum temporum ecclesiæ faciem fuisse, ut pro speculo serviat, ad quod Ecclesiæ reliquæ conponere sese debeant. Consignavit vero Ecclesiam Constantinus per concilium Nicænum: hoc enim pro remedio usus est, quo à lue Arianorum Ecclesia sanaretur. Atqui in Concilio Niceno ante aram stetisse Constantinus dicitur: Ap. 8. 3. quò planum est, ipsius tempore occultationem illam inchoatam esse, quia intra atrium interius Ecclesia coarctata est. Hæ angustiæ cum tempore Constantini Ecclesiæ acciderint: parùm movere illa Georgij Downami debent, quibus pacem externamque horum temporum prosperitatem in cœlum effert. Quid quòd hæc per semihorarium tantùm silentium appelletur: Ap. 8: 8. idque non immeritò: Nam & Licinius pace rupta intra triennium in Ecclesiam sævire cæpit: & intra ipsa Ecclesiæ viscera (bello civili multo asperius) Episcopis mutuo inter se exardescentibus, bellum intestinum erectum: de quo citat T. Bright. Aurel. Vict. de Cæsar. part. 2. Euseb. l. 10. 8, 9. & devit. Constant. lib. 1. ad finem: & lib. 2. ad initium.
units.tr: First, in the time of Constantine, four angels hold back the winds of salvation so that they cannot blow upon the Church (Rev. 7:1), so that Constantine was compelled to seal the elect, lest they should perish by the common plague and pestilence. But since a sealing always concerns a few and hidden people, it shows that the face of the Church in these times was not so happy that it could serve as a mirror to which the other churches should conform themselves. Now Constantine sealed the Church through the Nicene council, for he used it as a remedy by which the Church might be healed of the plague of the Arians. And yet it is said that Constantine stood before the altar at the Nicene council (Rev. 8:3). It is plain from this that the concealment began in his time, because the Church was confined within the inner court. Since these straits came upon the Church in the time of Constantine, they ought to move very little those men of George Downame who extol the peace and external prosperity of these times to the heavens. What of the fact that this period is called a silence of only half an hour (Rev. 8:1)? And that not undeservedly: for Licinius, once the peace was broken, began to rage against the Church within three years, and, with the civil war raging inside the Church's very bowels (far more bitterly than in war), bishops flared up against one another and an internal war was stirred up. Of this, T. Bright cites Aurelius Victor, De Caesaribus, part 2; Eusebius, book 10, chapters 8 and 9; and De vita Constantini, book 1 at the end, and book 2 at the beginning.

units.la: Secundò, tempore Constantini cæpit Angelus primus tuba clangere, contentio scilicet: unde imber grandinis & ignis exoritur: Ap. 8:5. qui & in ipsis medijs Concilij Nicæni patribus perstrepuit: & post Consilium lata damna dedit: unde Ap. 8. 5. narratur, contentionis ignem ab altari Concilij Nicaeni fuisse, & in terram projectum. Atq; haec contentio eo usque invaluit ut coactus Constantinus ipse fuerit in Synodo Tyri congregatis Episcopis exprobrare, quod nihil aliud agerent quam ut dissentiones & odia sererent, & ea quae spectant ad exitium humani generis. En scilicet tempora, quae ad immitandum Downamus proponenda putavit. Immitantur sane plus aequo haec tempora, Episcopi hujus temporis Anglicani, ut qui sub altero Constantino regnante, ignem contentionum accendunt, imbrem grandinis mittunt, & dios exagitando, dissidia excitando, mala innumera invehendo, charissimae simul & illustrissimae illius Ecclesiae (ni Deus eorum conatibus obstitat) exitium machinantur.
units.tr: Secondly, in the time of Constantine, the first angel began to sound the trumpet, namely contention, from which a storm of hail and fire arises (Rev. 8:5). This contention raged even in the midst of the fathers of the Council of Nicaea, and after the Council it inflicted heavy losses. Hence Rev. 8:5 relates that the fire of contention came from the altar of the Council of Nicaea and was cast upon the earth. This contention grew so strong that Constantine himself was compelled, at the Synod of Tyre with the bishops assembled, to reproach them that they did nothing but sow dissensions and hatreds, and things that lead to the ruin of the human race. Behold the times which Downamus thought should be set forth for imitation. Indeed, the bishops of this English age imitate these times more than is fitting. Under another Constantine they kindle the fire of contentions, send down a storm of hail, and, by harassing the godly, stirring up divisions and bringing in countless evils, they plot the ruin of that most dear and most illustrious Church (unless God stands in the way of their attempts).

units.la: 4 Tertio, Constantini tempore, clangere coepit Angelus secundus, Ambitio scilicet Ecclesiastica, quo factum est, ut mons ingens ardens igni, in Ecclesiam projiceretur: Ap. 8:8. Accedat velim ad hunc montem contemplandum Georgius Downamus: ut pudeat eum deinceps dicere, Episcopalem dignitatem a Constantini tempore diminutam fuisse, quum hic videmus ab exiguo quasi colle, in montem ingentem evasisse. Quid etenim hoc montis vocabulum sibi vult, nisi Ecclesiasticae dignitatis inane funestumque incrementum? quomodo elationem mons significat, If, 11: 14, 15. & aliis scripturae locis passim? Accedat etiam Iohannes Whitgiftus, qui nullam functionem Ecclesiasticam per annos 500 introductam in Ecclesiam dicit, quae verbo Dei consentanea non esset. Num hunc montem ardentem verbo Dei consentaneum dicet, quem hic diserte condemnatum videt? Accedat deniq; Richardus Bancroftus, qui superioritatem in ministros Episcopalem, in nullo scripturae loco damnatam asserit, imo ne a Iohan. quidem in Apocal. Si Iohan. in Apocal. tibi satisfacere poterit: En hic Iohannem Episcopalem superioritatem sub montis nomine condemnantem: Episcopalem dico superioritatem generaliter, quo sensu sumpta Episcopum, Archiepiscopum, & Patriarcham comprehendit. Dixerat supra D. Morneus paritatem ministrorum quasi adversus Antichristum alexipharmacum quoddam Apostolos pro virili praefervasse: sic ut Antichristum promoveat imparitas quaeque, quae hic mons dicitur, supra caeteras vineae donanicae aequales partes, suum verticem erigens. Primo etenim Sathanae conatu mons Episcopalis datus est: cui deinceps superpositus mons Archiepiscopalis: tertio mons Patriarchalis accessit, & qui summum cacumen occupat. Ne etenim dicat Bancroftus hunc montem Papatum significare, sciendum est, quatuor tubas priores, contentionem, ambitionem, haeresim, bellumque illud tantum significare, quae quatuor illi noxij Angeli supra memorati immiserunt a Constantini tempore, usque ad tubam quintam, id est usque ad Papatum circa annum 600: sic ut intra 500 illos annos Hierarchicos, hunc montem ortum fuisse necesse sit, idq; ante haeresum multiplicatam, sive Ariani. nam, sive Macedonianam, sive Nestorianam, sive Eutichianam: bellumque Constantinum aut Vandalicum. Papatus non nisi sub tuba quinta oritur, quæ ab Angelo alio clangitur, non ab ullo ex illorum quatuor, qui in tempore Constantini Ecclesiam Dei infensare dicuntur. Neque tubæ confundendæ sunt,ut unam & eandem rem sub tuba quarta, & tuba quinta Spiritum sanctum significare exi?stimemus: quæ ab eo confusio & tautologia longissime abest. Ita & intervallo temporum, & distinctione Angelorum, & tubarum diversitate liquidè constat, hunc montem ardentem Ecclesiasticam aliquam superioritatem significare, quæ intra annos 500 introducta in Ecclesiam est. Non sequitur, inquis, quia intra annos 500 & 600 projici in Ecclesiam potuit. Nomina igitur intra has centurias sublimitatem aliquam Ecclesiasticam de novo inventam quæ ante intra annos 500 non extiterat. At inquies, dicitur de Papatu sub quinta tuba, non quòd tum caderet, sed quòd ante reciderat: sic enim textus Græcus habet: Vidi stellam de cælo cecidisse in terram. Atqui hoc pro nobis facere dico: agitur de Romano Pontifice: si de clavibus interroges,eæ sub tuba quinta natæ sunt post annum 600: si verò de casu roges, quo de cœlo in terram recidit, id est,ex Episcopo divino, Episcopus humanus factus est, is sub tuba secunda incipit, quando Episcopus Hierarchicus Metropolitanus, Patriarcha denique in Concilio Nicæno, non primò factus quidem, sed primò tamen factus conspicuus est. Hæc ita cùm sint, nihil reliquì est ad respondendum, nisi dicatur, non functionem quidem Episcopalem ipsam hoc nomine montis damnari,sed ejusdem tantummodo abusum qui temporibus tubæ secundæ increbuerat. Quem tu mihi abusum nominare potest, nisi contentionem, & externam hæresim in Episcopis Christianis quidem, sed Ecclesiam Christianam hostium more infestantibus? At nihil hæc dico ad tubam secundam pertinere: contentio etenim tubæ primæ est, hæresis tertiæ: sic ut in monte secundæ tubæ non contentio, non hæresis, non abusus extraneus aliquis illiusque temporibus duntaxat proprius, sed ipsa Episcopalis superioritas necessariò intelligenda relinquatur.
units.tr: 4 Thirdly, in the time of Constantine, the second angel began to sound the trumpet, namely ecclesiastical ambition, as a result of which a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the Church (Rev. 8:8). I would have Georgius Downamus contemplate this mountain, so that he may be ashamed henceforth to say that episcopal dignity was diminished from the time of Constantine, when we see here that it has grown from a small hill, as it were, into a huge mountain. For what does this word "mountain" mean, if not an empty and baneful increase of ecclesiastical dignity? How does a mountain signify exaltation? (Isa. 2:14, 15, and in many other places of Scripture.) Let Iohannes Whitgiftus also be considered, who says that no ecclesiastical office introduced into the Church over the past 500 years is inconsistent with the Word of God. Will he say that this burning mountain is consistent with the Word of God, when he sees it expressly condemned here? Finally, let Richardus Bancroftus be considered, who asserts that episcopal superiority over ministers is condemned in no passage of Scripture, not even by Iohan. in the Apocalypse. If Iohan. in the Apocalypse can satisfy you, behold, here Iohannem condemns episcopal superiority under the name of a mountain. I say episcopal superiority in general, which in this sense includes bishop, archbishop and patriarch. D. Morneus had said above that parity of ministers was, as it were, a kind of antidote against Antichrist, which the apostles had zealously fostered. Thus every inequality, which here is called a mountain, promotes Antichrist, raising its summit above the other equal parts of the Lord's vineyard. For at the first attempt of Satan the episcopal mountain was given; upon it was afterwards placed the archiepiscopal mountain; thirdly the patriarchal mountain was added, which occupies the highest peak. Lest Bancroftus say that this mountain signifies the Papacy, it must be known that the four earlier trumpets signify only contention, ambition, heresy and war, which those four harmful angels mentioned above let loose from the time of Constantine up to the fifth trumpet, that is, up to the Papacy about the year 600. So within those 500 years of hierarchy this mountain must have arisen, and that before the multiplication of heresies, whether Arian, Macedonian, Nestorian or Eutychian, and before the war of Constantine or of the Vandals. The Papacy arises only under the fifth trumpet, which is sounded by another angel, not by any of those four who are said to have harassed the Church of God in the time of Constantine. Nor are the trumpets to be confused, as if we supposed that one and the same thing is signified by the Holy Spirit under the fourth trumpet and under the fifth; from such confusion and tautology this is far removed. Thus, by the interval of time, the distinction of the angels and the diversity of the trumpets, it is clearly established that this burning mountain signifies some ecclesiastical superiority which was introduced into the Church within 500 years. "It does not follow," you say, "because it could have been cast into the Church between 500 and 600." Then they say that within these centuries some new ecclesiastical loftiness was invented, which did not exist within the first 500 years. But you will say that it is said of the Papacy under the fifth trumpet not because it then fell, but because it had fallen before; for the Greek text reads: "I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth." Yet I say this makes for us, for it concerns the Roman Pontiff. If you ask about the keys, they arose under the fifth trumpet, after the year 600; but if you ask about the fall, by which he fell from heaven to earth, that is, when the divine bishop became a human bishop, this begins under the second trumpet, when the hierarchical bishop, metropolitan, and finally patriarch was seen at the Council of Nicaea, not indeed first made, but first made conspicuous. These things being so, nothing remains to answer except to say that it is not the episcopal function itself that is condemned under the name of this mountain, but only its abuse, which had grown up in the times of the second trumpet. What abuse can you name for me, except contention and external heresy among Christian bishops, who nonetheless assail the Christian Church like enemies? But I say these things do not pertain to the second trumpet at all: contention belongs to the first trumpet, heresy to the third. So in the mountain of the second trumpet, it must necessarily be understood that neither contention, nor heresy, nor some foreign abuse peculiar to those times alone is meant, but episcopal superiority itself.

units.la: Quarto, tempore Constantini cæpit Ecclesia se abdere in occulto, in interiori scilicet Templi sacrario: Ap.11:1, quo etiam obsignatio illa pertinet: c. 7. 1. quæ & paucorum & occultorum esse solet. Menses etenim illi 42. quibus latitat ecclesia nullo modo commodè iuxta si ripturæ analogiam cōputari possunt: nisi à Constantini tempore statuantur incipere,desinere vero in messe,vindemiaque illa reformationis quæ capite 14. commemoratur. Consulat lector Thomam Brightmannum illiusque rationes ad examen revocet, reperiet nullam habuisse causam Downamum cur Ecclesiam temporibus Constantini pro exemplari immitandam proponeret: eam in latibulum nempe conferentem, in quo delitesceret, usque ad tempora Eccle- siæ no?strae reformatæ. Quid Ecclesiæ pace fruentes, Ecclesias ante
units.tr: Fourthly, in the time of Constantine the Church began to hide herself in secret, namely in the inner sanctuary of the Temple (Ap. 11:1), to which that sealing also belongs (ch. 7, v. 1), which is usually said to be of few and hidden people. For those forty-two months during which the Church lies hidden cannot be reckoned in any way suitably according to the analogy of Scripture, unless they are held to begin from the time of Constantine and to end at the harvest and vintage of that reformation which is recalled in chapter 14. Let the reader consult Thomas Brightman and submit his arguments to examination; he will find that Downame had no reason for proposing the Church of Constantine's time as a pattern to be imitated, namely as a Church withdrawing into a hiding-place, in which she lay concealed until the time of our reformed Church.

units.la: Pd 2 Conftan & post Consilium lata damna dedit: unde Ap. 8. 5. narratur, contentionis ignem ab altari Concilij Niceni fuisse, & in terram projectum. Atq; haec contentio eo usque invaluit ut coactus Constantinus ipse fuerit in Synodo Tyri congregatis Episcopis exprobrare, quòd nihil aliud agerent quàm ut dissentiones & odia serrerent, & ea quae spectant ad exitium humani generis. En scilicet tempora, quae ad immitandum Downamus proponenda putavit. Immitantur sanè plus æquo haec tempora, Episcopi huius temporis Anglicani, ut qui sub altero Constantino regnante, ignem contentionum accendunt, imbrem grandinis mittunt, & pios exagitando, dissidia excitando, mala innumera invehendo, charissimae simul & illustrissimae illius Ecclesiae (ni Deus eorum conatibus obsistat) exitium machinantur.
units.tr: Constantine, and after the Council: what damage the Churches, enjoying peace, inflicted on Churches both before and after the Council. Whence Ap. 8. 5. relates that the fire of contention came from the altar of the Council of Nicaea and was cast upon the earth. And this contention grew so strong that Constantine himself was compelled to reproach the bishops gathered at the Synod of Tyre, because they did nothing but stir up dissensions and hatreds, and things that tend to the destruction of the human race. Behold, these are the times which Downame thought should be put forward for imitation. Surely these times are imitated more than is fitting by the bishops of our English time, who, while another Constantine reigns, kindle the fire of contentions, send down a hailstorm, and, by harassing the godly, stirring up discords, and bringing on countless evils, plot the ruin of that most dear and most illustrious Church (unless God resist their attempts).

units.la: 4 Tertio, Constantini tempore, clangere cæpit Angelus secundus, Ambitio scilicet Ecclesiastica, quo factum est, ut mons ingens ardens igni, in Ecclesiam, projiceretur: Ap. 8:8. Accedat velim ad hunc montem contemplandum Georgius Downamus: ut pudeat eum deinceps dicere, Episcopalem dignitatem à Constantini tempore diminutam fuisse, quum hic videmus ab exiguo quasi colle, in montem ingentem evasisse. Quid etenim hoc montis vocabulum sibi vult, nisi Ecclesiasticæ dignitatis inane funestumque incrementum? quomodo elationem mons significat, Is. 11:14, 15. & aliis scripturæ locis passim? Accedat etiam Iohannes Whitgiftus, qui nullam functionem Ecclesiasticam per annos 500 introductam in Ecclesiam dicit, quæ verbo Dei consentanea non esset. Num hunc montem ardentem verbo Dei consentaneum dicet, quem hic diserte condemnatum videt? Accedat deniq; Richardus Bancroftus, qui superioritatem in ministros Episcopalem, in nullo scripturæ loco damnatam asserit, imo ne à Ioban. quidem in Apocal. Si Ioban. in Apocal. tibi satisfacere potest: En hîc Iohannem Episcopalem superioritatem sub montis nomine condemnantem: Episcopalem dico superioritatem generaliter, quo sensu sumpta Episcopum, Archiepiscopum, & Patriarcham comprehendit. Dixerat supra D. Morneus paritatem ministrorum quasi adversus Antichristum alexipharmacum quoddam Apostolos pro virili præservasse: sic ut Antichristum promoveat imparitas quæque, quæ hîc mons dicitur, supra cæteras vineæ dominicæ æquales partes, suum verticem erigens. Primò etenim Sathanæ conatu mons Episcopalis datus est: cui deinceps superpositus mons Archiepiscopalis: tertiò mons Patriarchalis accessit, & qui summum cacumen occupat. Ne etenim dicat Bancroftus hunc montem Papatum significare, sciendum est, quatuor tubas priores, contentionem, ambitionem, hæresim, bellumque illud tantum significare, quæ quatuor illi noxij Angeli suprà memorati immiserunt à Constantini tempore, usque ad tubam quintam, id est usque ad Papatum circa annum 600: sic ut intrà 500 illos annos Hierarchicos, hunc montem ortum fuisse necesse sit, idq; ante hæresim multiplicatam, sive Arianam nam, sive Macedonianam, sive Nestorianam, sive Eutichianam: bellum- que Constantinum aut Vandalicum. Papatus non nisi sub tuba quinta oritur, quae ab Angelo alio clangitur, non ab ullo ex illorum quatuor, qui in tempore Constantini Ecclesiam Dei infensare dicuntur. Neque tubae confundendae sunt, ut unam & eandem rem sub tuba quarta, & tuba quinta Spiritum sanctum significare existimemus: quae ab eo confusio & tautologia longissime abest. Ita & intervallo temporum, & distinctione Angelorum, & tubarum diversitate liquidè constat, hunc montem ardentem Ecclesiasticam aliquam superioritatem significare, quae intra annos 500 introducta in Ecclesiam est. Non sequitur, inquis, quia intra annos 500 & 600 projici in Ecclesiam potuit. Nomina igitur intra has centurias sublimitatem aliquam Ecclesiasticam de novo inventam quae ante intra annos 500 non extiterat. At inquies, dicitur de Papatu sub quinta tuba, non quod tum caderet, sed quod ante recideret: sic enim textus Graecus habet: Vidi stellam de caelo cecidisse in terram. Atqui hoc pro nobis facere dico: agitur de Romano Pontifice: si de clavibus interroges, cae sub tuba quinta natae sunt post annum 600: si vero de casu roges, quo de coelo in terram recidit, id est, ex Episcopo divino, Episcopus humanus factus est, is sub tuba secunda incipit, quando Episcopus Hierarchicus Metropolitanus, Patriarcha denique in Concilio Nicaeno, non primo factus quidem, sed primo tamen factus conspicuus est. Haec ita cum sint, nihil reliqui est ad respondendum, nisi dicatur, non functionem quidem Episcopalem ipsam hoc nomine montis damnari, sed ejusdem tantummodo abusum qui temporibus tubae secundae increbuerat. Quem tu mihi abusum nominare potest, nisi contentionem, & externam haeresim in Episcopis Christianis quidem, sed Ecclesiam Christianam hostium more infestantibus? At nihil haec dico ad tubam secundam pertinere: contentio etenim tubae primae est, haeresis tertiae: sic ut in monte secundae tubae non contentio, non haeresis, non abusus extraneus aliquis illiusque temporibus duntaxat proprius, sed ipsa Episcopalis superioritas necessario intelligenda relinquatur.
units.tr: Fourth, in the time of Constantine, the second angel began to sound, namely ecclesiastical ambition, and as a result a great mountain burning with fire was thrown into the Church (Rev. 8:8). I would like George Downame to consider this mountain, so that he will be ashamed to say hereafter that episcopal dignity was diminished from the time of Constantine, since here we see it rise from a small hill, as it were, into a huge mountain. For what does the word "mountain" mean here, except the empty and baneful growth of ecclesiastical dignity? How does a mountain signify elevation, see Isa. 11:14, 15, and in many other places of Scripture? Let John Whitgift also come forward, who says that no ecclesiastical office introduced into the Church for 500 years was contrary to the Word of God. Will he say that this burning mountain is consistent with the Word of God, when he sees it expressly condemned here? Finally, let Richard Bancroft come forward, who asserts that episcopal superiority over ministers is condemned in no passage of Scripture, indeed not even by John in the Apocalypse. If John in the Apocalypse can satisfy you, behold here John condemning episcopal superiority under the name of a mountain. I say episcopal superiority in general, which, taken in this sense, comprehends the bishop, the archbishop and the patriarch. Dr Morney had said above that the parity of ministers had preserved the apostles, as a kind of antidote, against Antichrist, to the best of their power. Thus every inequality, which is here called a mountain, raising its summit above the other equal parts of the Lord's vineyard, promotes Antichrist. For first, by the endeavour of Satan the episcopal mountain was given; upon it was afterwards placed the archiepiscopal mountain; thirdly the patriarchal mountain was added, which occupies the highest peak. Lest Bancroft say that this mountain signifies the Papacy, it must be understood that the four earlier trumpets signify only the contention, the ambition, the heresy and the war which those four noxious angels mentioned above sent forth from the time of Constantine, down to the fifth trumpet, that is, down to the Papacy about the year 600. So within those 500 years of hierarchy, this mountain must have arisen, and that before the heresies multiplied, whether Arian, or Macedonian, or Nestorian, or Eutychian, and the war of Constantine or of the Vandals. The Papacy does not arise until the fifth trumpet, which is sounded by another angel, not by any of those four who are said to have harassed the Church of God in the time of Constantine. Nor are the trumpets to be confused, so that we should think one and the same thing is signified by the fourth trumpet and the fifth trumpet, the Holy Spirit; such confusion and tautology is far removed from it. Thus, both by the interval of time, and by the distinction of the angels, and by the diversity of the trumpets, it is clearly established that this burning mountain signifies some ecclesiastical superiority, which was introduced into the Church within 500 years. "It does not follow," you say, "because it could have been cast into the Church between 500 and 600." Therefore within these centuries some ecclesiastical eminence was newly invented, which had not existed before, within 500 years. But you will say that what is said of the Papacy under the fifth trumpet is not that it then fell, but that it had fallen back earlier; for the Greek text has it thus: "I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth." Yet I say this makes for us: the matter concerns the Roman Pontiff. If you ask about the keys, the keys under the fifth trumpet were born after the year 600; but if you ask about the fall, by which he fell back from heaven to earth, that is, when a divine bishop became a human bishop, this began under the second trumpet, when the hierarchical bishop, the metropolitan, and finally the patriarch became visible at the Council of Nicaea, not indeed the first, but nevertheless first made conspicuous. These things being so, nothing remains to be answered, except that it be said that the episcopal function itself is not condemned under this name of mountain, but only its abuse, which had grown up in the times of the second trumpet. What abuse can you name for me, except contention and external heresy among Christian bishops, who nevertheless attack the Christian Church in the manner of enemies? But I say these things do not pertain to the second trumpet at all: for contention belongs to the first trumpet, heresy to the third. So that on the mountain of the second trumpet, not contention, not heresy, not some foreign abuse peculiar to those times alone, but episcopal superiority itself must necessarily be understood.

units.la: Quarto, tempore Constantini caepit Ecclesia se abdere in occulto, in interiori scilicit Templi sacrario: Ap. 11: 1. quo etiam obsignatio illa pertinet: c. 7. 1. quae & paucorum & occultorum esse solet. Menses etenim illi 42. quibus latitat ecclesia nullo modo commodè iuxta scripturae analogiam coputari possunt: nisi à Constantini tempore statuantur incipere, desinere vero in messe, vindemiaque illa reformationis quae capite 14. commemoratur. Consulat lector Thomam Brightmannum illiusque rationes ad examen revocet, reperiet nullam habuisse causam Dominum cur Ecclesiam temporibus Constantini pro exemplari immitandam proponeret: eam in latibulum nempe conferentem, in quo delituisset, usque ad tempora Ecclesiae reformatae. Quid Ecclesiae pace fruentes, Ecclesias ante Constantinum imitarentur, inquit ille, quae sub persecutione vivebant? quid inquam ego Ecclesiae nostrae reformatae, caelo pristino restitutae, Ecclesiam à Constantino incipientem imitarentur, quae caelo pulsa fecerat in latibulum? Hoc eò dico, quia caelum prioris Ecclesiae quae Constantinum antecessit, ablevisse dicitur Apoc. 6, 14. anno 304, sub sigillo sexto, quod in tempore Constantini definit. Cum vero pristinae Ecclesiae sedes evanuissent, quid ni de novis cogitaret? In ista cogitatione vero, cum alios lites accendere, alios parandis honoribus inhiare, multos & parturire & parere haereses, omnes accumulandis superstitionibus incumbere, nihil denique sinceri & solidi suo loco consistere animadvertisset, prae mundi taedio a mundi conspectu sibi secedendum putavit, & sub alis Dei fui, intra interius ipsius sacrarium delitescendum. Dura haec de Constantini tempore dicta videntur? cur dura rogo? Neque enim Ecclesiae integritas, in gloria illa, pace illa, externa abundantia illa consistit, quibo temporibo Constantini & dotata & ditata floruit: sed in veritate, sinceritate, simplicitate, solida denique pietate: quibus eo magis indies decrescentibus quo magis pestes illae creverunt, quas recensuimus: quis mirabitur, secessionem Ecclesiae in latibulum Constantini tempore incepisse?
units.tr: Fourth, in the time of Constantine the Church began to hide herself in secret, in the inner sanctuary of the Temple (Rev. 11:1), to which also that sealing pertains (ch. 7:1), which is usually of a few and hidden persons. For those forty-two months during which the Church lies hidden cannot in any way be reckoned fittingly according to the analogy of Scripture, unless they are set to begin from the time of Constantine, and to end at the harvest and vintage of that reformation which is recorded in chapter 14. Let the reader consult Thomas Brightman and call his reasons to examination; he will find that the Lord had no cause for proposing the Church of the time of Constantine as an example to be imitated, namely, that she withdrew into a hiding-place, in which she lay concealed until the times of the reformed Church. Why, he says, should those enjoying the peace of the Church imitate the churches before Constantine, which lived under persecution? Why, I say, should our reformed Church, restored to her pristine heaven, imitate the Church beginning from Constantine, which, driven from heaven, had made itself a hiding-place? I say this because the heaven of the earlier Church, which preceded Constantine, is said to have vanished (Rev. 6:14) in the year 304, under the sixth seal, which ends in the time of Constantine. But when the seats of the pristine Church had vanished, why should it not think of new ones? Yet in this thinking, when it perceived that some were kindling strife, others gaping after honours to be got, many both in labour and in bearing heresies, all busying themselves with piling up superstitions, and finally that nothing sincere and solid stood in its place, out of weariness of the world it thought it must withdraw from the sight of the world, and hide itself under the wings of God, within its innermost sanctuary. Do these things said of the time of Constantine seem harsh? Why harsh, I ask? For the integrity of the Church does not consist in that glory, that peace, that external abundance, in which she flourished, endowed and enriched, in the times of Constantine*; but in truth, sincerity, simplicity and, finally, solid piety; these decreasing day by day the more those plagues grew which we have recounted. Who will wonder that the Church's withdrawal into a hiding-place began in the time of Constantine?

units.la: Quintò, tempore Constantini aufugit Ecclesia in solitudinem, Ap. 12, 6, 14: sic ut pro exemplari ad imitandum (quod Domnamus) proponenda non fit, nisi forte Ecclesias (vestigiis Domnami insisto) semper in solitudinem ablegari velint. Tria vero sunt quae fidem faciunt, hanc Ecclesiae solitudinem, ab ipso Constantino incepisse.
units.tr: Fifth, in the time of Constantine the Church fled into the wilderness (Rev. 12:6, 14). So that it is not to be proposed as an example to imitate (as Downame does), unless perhaps they wish churches (following in the footsteps of Downame) to be always banished into the wilderness. Now there are three things which make it credible that this solitude of the Church began from Constantine himself.

units.la: Primò, partus filij masculi Constantini ad imperium evectio est: affirmat vero spiritus sanctus v.6. mulierem statim postquam ad thronum Dei, id est, ad imperij fastigium, subvectus Constantinus esset, in solitudinem aufugisse, ubi haberet locum paratum a Deo. Pertinent huc illae duae aquilae alae, quae mulieri datae sunt ad fugam maturandam ver. 14. quemadmodum quatuor alae in dorso Alexandri Magni indices insignis pernicitatis sunt, Dan. 7, 6.
units.tr: First, the birth of the male child is the elevation of Constantine to empire; the Holy Spirit however affirms (v. 6) that the woman, immediately after Constantine had been raised to the throne of God, that is, to the summit of empire, fled into the wilderness, where she might have a place prepared by God. To this pertain those two wings of an eagle which were given to the woman to hasten her flight (v. 14), just as the four wings on the back of Alexander the Great are signs of his remarkable swiftness (Dan. 7:6).

units.la: Secundò, spatium per quod latuit mulier in solitudine quodnam quaeso? nempe 1260 dies: quod cum idem prorsus sit, cum tempore obligationis Cap. 7. & secessionis in interius atrium Cap. 11. Quis non videt has Ecclesiae latebras, per obligationem, sacrarii latibulum, & in solitudinem fugam adumbratas, a sexto sigillo una cum tubis inchoandas, quae ad tempus Constantini nos reducunt?
units.tr: Second, what, I ask, is the space during which the woman lay hidden in the wilderness? Namely 1260 days. Which is exactly the same as the time of the sealing in chapter 7 and the withdrawal into the inner court in chapter 11. Who does not see that these hiding-places of the Church, shadowed forth by the sealing, the sanctuary's hiding-place, and the flight into the wilderness, begin with the sixth seal together with the trumpets, and lead us back to the time of Constantine?

units.la: Tertiò, fugatur mulier in solitudinem a Draconé, plus jam quam ante seviente, postquam a caelo id est Ecclesia dejectus esset, per victoriam Constantini in Licinium v. 13. Sic igitur est. Tempore persecutionis in priori priodo Ecclesia in caelo fuit: contemnebat etenim ferrum, contemnebat equuleum, omnia Ethnicorum Imperatorum vel exquisitissima tormenta quaeque contemnebat: tempore vero Constantini, quum sub specie Christiani nominis, abusurpaclisg, Christistum per hæreses oppugnari, & salutem animarum periclirari vidisse non jam di utiùs morandum duxit, sed quàm celerimè avolandum. Discere hinc promptum, quàm inepte Donatus Constantini tempora propter pacem, potius quàm priora sæcula propter persecutionem, imitanda proponat: cum certum sit per pacis abusum plus damni Sathanam Ecclesiæ dedisse, quàm ante dederat per persecutiones Ethnicorum Imperatorum.
units.tr: Thirdly, the woman is put to flight into the wilderness by the Dragon, who now rages more than before, after he has been cast down from heaven, that is, from the Church, through Constantine's victory over Licinius (Rev. 12.13). So it is. In the time of persecution, in the earlier period, the Church was in heaven: for she despised the iron, despised the rack, and despised all the most exquisite tortures of the heathen emperors. But in the time of Constantine, when under the guise of the Christian name Christ was attacked through heresies and the salvation of souls was seen to be in danger, she thought she should no longer delay but must fly away as quickly as possible. From this it is easy to see how foolishly Donatus proposes the times of Constantine for our imitation on account of peace, rather than the earlier centuries on account of persecution, since it is certain that through the abuse of peace Satan did more harm to the Church than he had done before through the persecutions of the heathen emperors.

units.la: Sexto, sub tempore Constantini exorta Bestia est. Apo. 13, 1. sic ut parum causæ habuerit Donatus hæc tempora nobis ad imitandum proponere, nisi Bestiæ hujus reliquas (sicut proh dolor jam in Anglia) quoad regimen saltem Ecclesiasticum retineri semper in Ecclesiis perpetuarique velit.
units.tr: Sixthly, the Beast arose in the time of Constantine (Rev. 13.1). So Donatus had little reason to propose these times to us for imitation, unless he wishes the remnants of this Beast to be retained and perpetuated in the Churches, as far as ecclesiastical government is concerned, as (alas, now in England) they already are.

units.la: Primò, etenim Ap. 13. 5. tempus Bestiæ idem est quod mulieris in sacrario & in solitudine: illud à sexto sigillo quod ad Constantinum pertingit inchoandum: ergo & hoc etiam: nam conspectus bestiæ ille erat, ad quem mulier trepidabat, bestia erat quæ mulierem fugabat, bestia regnante, mulieri locus non erat, cadente verò, egreditur mulier & non ante, è latebris suis; quòd benignissima Dei clementiâ, hoc posteriori sæculo factum.
