units.tr: First, because in Rev. 13.5 the time of the Beast is the same as that of the woman in the sanctuary and in the wilderness: that which begins at the sixth seal and reaches to Constantine. Therefore this too: for the Beast was the sight at which the woman trembled; the Beast was what put the woman to flight. While the Beast reigned there was no place for the woman, but when it fell the woman came out of her hiding places, and not before. This was done in this latter age by the most gracious clemency of God.

units.la: Secundo, Ap. 17, 11. Antichristus septimum caput Bestiæ est, quod immediatè sexto succedit: sextum caput Imperatores ethnicos notat: Bestia hæc igitur Antichristiana, statim ab ethnicis Imperatoribus, à Constantino debellatis exurgere cæpit. Fateor hîc multa objici posse: de hoc igitur Thoma Brightmani argumento, liberum cuique judicium esto.
units.tr: Secondly, Rev. 17.11: Antichrist is the seventh head of the Beast, which immediately follows the sixth. The sixth head denotes the heathen emperors. This Antichristian Beast therefore began to rise immediately after the heathen emperors were overthrown by Constantine. I admit that many objections can be raised here; as to this argument of Thomas Brightman, let each judge as he thinks fit.

units.la: Tertiò, Bestia thronum accepit à Dracone Apo. 13, 2. id est à Diabolo quidem, sed a Diabolo in ethnicis Imperatoribus operante: nã ut tota Apocalypsis percurratur, per Draconem hostes aperti & ethnici: per bestiam, hostes interni & intestini intelliguntur. Quàdo Draco id est Imperatores ethnici per Constantinum debellati essent, tunc caput ex undis elevavit Bestia: Draco scilicet projectus è cœlo id est ecclesia Ap. 12.9. profperit sibi de hoc Vicario, qui eo absente res suas gereret. Hæc ita cum sint, necesse est Episcopatum Hierarchicum bestiam in scenam produxisse, & in propatulo collocasse. Agitur etenim hoc in loco, non de tempore, quo vitam & spiritum primò Bestia trahere cœpit: sed de tempore quo ex mari, id est ex corrupta cum doctrina tum disciplina ascendit, id est, conspicua facta est, sic ut conspici ab hominibus & facilè animadverti possit. Nemo se spiritu ipso sanctò acutiorem putet: Arcessit verò spiritus sanctus originem bestiæ, ab illa prima imparitate, quæ inter ministros, contra divinum institutum, introducta in Ecclesiam est. Peperit hæc impari tas Episcopum primò, post Archiepiscopum, ad postremum, Patriarchiam, idque ante Constantini tempora. Hi gradus imparitatis ipsius Papatus quasi embrio erant, a quibus ita ab initio animatus est, ut vivere quidem & spirare cœperit ante tempora Constantini, sed sub. sub undis tamen tanquam recens edita Balaena se′ continuerit. In Niceno vero Concilio in quo hij gradus imparitatis & sanciti & confirmati sunt: jam se ex undis effert Bestia, caput exerit, corpore emergit, & mundo se denique conspicuum praebet. Putabant quidem Nicaeni patres se paci Ecclesiae consuluisse,sed exitus docuit, quam haec ab eis opera pessime locata fit:trifteq; posteris documentu reliquerunt,quam periculosum fit, ratioini propriae, humanae prudentiae, carnis consilio iudulgere, & a divini verbi regula, vel tantillum deviare. Revera non doctrina tantum, sed & disciplina Ecclesiae etiam spiritualis est: unde est, ut spiritus Christi, disciplinam mitem, humilem, caelestem, spiritualem amet, ratio vero humana non nisi mundanam, & superbiam, typhum, fastum, pompam, primatum, redolentem. Hanc vero a concilio Niceno confirmatam, sub montis nomine condemnat Iohannes: Ap. 8. 8. quo perspicuum redditur,quam acclivem Bestiae aflenfum Concilium illud praeparaverat. Triplicem nempe montem, alterum alteri supernè politum erexerat, Episcopatum, Archiepiscopatum, & Patriarchatum: in horum montium summo cacumine Romanum Pontificem pofuerunt: sic unus tantum gradus superfuit, isque quidem ascensu facillimus: quàm enim proclivis, à primo & summo Patriarchatu, ad universalem,id est Papalem tranfcenfio erat?Clarissima à fe haec omnia: testimonijs tamen humanis non destituuntur. Ante Concilium Nicaenum (inquit Aeneas Sylvius:) Parvus respectus ad Ecclesiam Romanam habebatur: ac fi dixisset, concilium Nicaenum illud erat, quod viam Papatui praemuniebat. Accedit Socrates, qui tempore Celestini anno post Constantinum octagefimo, Romanum Episcopatum, ultra sacerdotij terminos ad principatum provectum,dicit: Idem habet & de Alexandrino: & tutum tamen utique Bancrofto videbitur, ab hisce temporibus exempla capere ad formandam disciplinam?
units.tr: Thirdly, the Beast received its throne from the Dragon (Rev. 13.2), that is, indeed from the Devil, but from the Devil working in the heathen emperors. For, to run through the whole Apocalypse, by the Dragon are understood open and heathen enemies, and by the Beast enemies inward and internal. When the Dragon, that is the heathen emperors, had been overthrown by Constantine, then the Beast lifted its head out of the waves. The Dragon, cast down from heaven, that is the Church (Rev. 12.9), provided for himself this vicar, who would manage his affairs in his absence. These things being so, it is necessary that the hierarchical episcopate brought the Beast onto the stage and set it in full view. For here the question is not of the time when the Beast first began to draw life and breath, but of the time when it ascended from the sea, that is from corrupt doctrine as well as corrupt discipline, that is, when it became conspicuous, so that it could be seen by men and easily noticed. Let no one think himself sharper than the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit, however, traces the origin of the Beast back to that first inequality which was introduced into the Church among the ministers, contrary to divine institution. This inequality gave birth first to the bishop, after him to the archbishop, and at last to the patriarch, and this before the time of Constantine. These degrees of inequality were, as it were, the embryo of the Papacy itself, and it was so animated by them from the beginning that it began to live and breathe before the time of Constantine, yet nevertheless kept itself under the waves like a newly born whale. But at the Council of Nicaea, at which these degrees of inequality were both sanctioned and confirmed, the Beast now rises out of the waves, raises its head, emerges with its body, and at last presents itself visibly to the world. The Nicene Fathers indeed thought they had provided for the peace of the Church, but the outcome showed how very badly this work of theirs turned out; and they left a sorrowful lesson to posterity of how dangerous it is to indulge one's own reasoning, human prudence and the counsel of the flesh, and to deviate even slightly from the rule of the divine word. Indeed, the discipline of the Church is spiritual, no less than its doctrine. Hence it is that the Spirit of Christ loves a discipline that is mild, humble, heavenly and spiritual, whereas human reason savours only of what is worldly: pride, haughtiness, pomp and primacy. This discipline, confirmed by the Council of Nicaea, John condemns under the name of a mountain (Rev. 8.8), which makes it plain how steep an ascent to the Beast that council had prepared. For they had raised a triple mountain, one placed above the other: the episcopate, the archiepiscopate and the patriarchate. On the highest peak of these mountains they set the Roman Pontiff. Thus only one degree remained, and that the easiest to climb: for how easy was the passage from the first and highest patriarchate to the universal, that is, the papal! All these things are clear in themselves, yet they are not without human testimonies. "Before the Council of Nicaea," says Aeneas Sylvius, "little regard was paid to the Roman Church": as if he had said that the Council of Nicaea was what paved the way for the Papacy. Socrates agrees, who, in the time of Celestine, eighty years after Constantine, says that the Roman bishopric was advanced beyond the limits of the priestly office to principality. He says the same of the Alexandrian bishop. And yet will it seem safe to Bancroft to take examples from these times for forming discipline?

units.la: Sequuntur iam nonulla testimonia extrinseca: quòd narrat Nauclerus Constantini tempore, auditam vocem de coelo fuisse, quae venenum sparsum in Ecclesiam diceret, in eo a nostris deridetur:quam mirito ipsi viderint. Dominus certe Mornaeus ita. Aucta tantis opibus affatim Ecclesia, sinistrum psis plerisque augurium fuit. Sylvestri legerunt da auditam hanc vocem de caelo tradunt: Hodie infusum est venenum in Ecclesiam.Citat etiam ad hanc rem alibi Albericum de Rozote, in hac verba. Audiij a magnis viris (de tempore Constantini loquitur) quod vox fuerit audita de caelo dicens, Hodie seminatum est venenum affidum in Ecclesia Dei, & dicunt hoc reperiri in antiquis authenticis scripturis, & etiam narrat dictus magister Iohannes Patifi:nfis in lib. de papatu. Papal. & Imperial. c. 21. Sic Guilielmus Whitakerus. Quin & ipsi qui fa-vent huic donationi, scribunt tamen auditam esse eo tempore vocem angelorum in aere dicentium, Hodie effusum est venenum in Ecclesiam.Sed quicquid de ista voce evenerit,rem quidem ipsam agnoscunt Waldenfes: hic etenim error primus est, quem illis Reynerius Pisanus impegit. impegit.Dicunt quod Ecclesia defecerit in Sylvestro quum venenum temporalium in Ecclesiam infusum esset. At certe nunc primum ditari Ecclesiam certum est: ad haec igitur tempora pertinent, lanctorum quaerelae subsequentes, etsi apertam Constantini mentionem nullam faciant. Ita Isidorus Pallusiota Florente Ecclesia & nondum morbo laborante, divinae gratiae circa eam velut chorus agebant, sancto Medicet spiritu res administrante, atque antistitum unumquemque incitante, ac Ecclesiam in caelum convertente. Quod autem postea quam ea morbo affecta est ac seditione laborarunt, haec omnia abolarint, nemini obscurum est. Vt alia omittam & unare caetera significem, Pacis nomen ubique est, sed autem ipsa nusquam, verum Ecclesia femina cuidam, quae ex antiqua felicitate excidit, & signa tantum habet, similis est; Ornamentorum enim suorum thecas & arculas habet: opibus autem spoliata est: non ob ejus qui eam primo exornavit merciam, sed ob eorum qui non ut convenit, res administrant, improbitatem. Sic Barnardus: Olim praedictum est & nunc tempus advenit. Ecce in pace amaritudo mea amarissima. Amara prius, in nece martyrum: amarior post, in conflictu haereticorum: amarissima nunc, in moribus domesticorum. Ideo in pace amaritudo amarissima est. Sed in qua pace? Et pax est, & non est pax. Pax a Paganis, & pax ab haereticis, sed non profecto in filiis, &c. Praefert utramque horum puriora illa Ecclesiae tempora quae Constantinum antecedebant: a quo externa pax quidem, sed Ecclesiae inutilis, imo noxia, invecta est. Respicit etiam haec tempora Elizabetha virgo Germana, Hildegardis familiaris, ad annum 1150 quum Episcopos Pompaticos Constantini tempore primum exorientes, ita alloquuta est. Occupastis principatum sanctorum meorum & neficiis, unde ascendistis turbare otile meum, & aggravare cor meum super filios meos, quos genui in amaritudine animae meae (sub persecutionibus Ethnicorum) in die laboris & angustiarum mearum? Author etatum Ecclesiae degenerationem ex eo incepisse dicit, quod amplissimis, principum donariis aucta sit: quo citat Gregorium: Religio peperit divitias, & filia devoravit matrem. Comparans vero Ecclesiae statum qui ante Constantinum fuit, cum eo qui subsecutus est, ita infert. Inde venit quod antiqua saecula ad ferreum redacta, divitias antiquas amiserunt, quia devotio decrevit & matrem extinxit filia. Ita Alanus Cartherius: Non statui vituperare bonos viros saeculares, qui ex perfecta devotione donarent Ecclesiae praedia: quia exonerarunt se ut ad Deum tanto expeditiores spiritu ascenderent, & ordo sacerdotalis tam magnam gravemque sarcinam humeris suis imposuit, ut ipsum plane in terram decurvet, ac impediat quo minus sursum in caelum possit aspicere. Mare cum vehit navem nimis graudem, veliscatur magno cum discrimine, neque ullum flumen extra suum alveum diu perdurat. Accomodat vero haec ad Constantinum spiciatim alibi. Et te quidem Dantes posta Florentinus si viveres etiamnum, materia haberes exclamandi contra Constantinum, quem etiam tempore bene absolutae religionis ausus es reprehendere, imputans ei in quodam tuo opere, quod in Ecclesiam ipse coniecisset venenum & toxicum, illaturum eidem pestilitatem & desolationem, id est nempe quia primus Ecclesiae donavit possessiones & praedia &c. Greg. Hamburg. gloriam primae Ecclesiae sub persecutione praefert, gloriae illi externae quam persecutione cessante assecuta est. Hujus (inquit) Ecclesiae gloria fuit, non purpura, non dignitatum acervus, non equus albus, non fastus, non dominatus: sed ecce nos reliquimus omnia & secuti sumus te Domine, sperantes ex hoc, non acquirere sedem temporalis eminentia, sed sedem iudicantium duodecim tribus Israel, juxta Christi promissum: Laurentius Valla disputans aversus donationem Constantini, ita loquitur. Melius summus Pontisex ab augendo Augustus diceretur, nisi quod dum temporalia auget spiritualia minuit. Negat gesta Sylvestri esse Apocrypha, in quibus dicitur vocem de caelo auditam esse, venenum a Constantino fuisse insusum in Ecclesiam. Ita Franciscus Duarenus: Puto majorem nostrorum satis animadvertisse, nihil Ecclesiae exitialius pestilentius esse, quam ministros ut ejus nimiam opulentiam. Res enim ipsa loquitur, immensam principum munificentiam utcumque, pius esset eorum affectus, tantum virus in Ecclesiam sparsisse, ut ex pixide illa pandorae a poetis decantata, non plus malorum inter homines & calamitatum exiisse videatur. Bonifacius Martyr aliquando interrogatus, an liceret ligneis calicibus in sacris uti, respondisse fertur. Olim aurei sacerdotes ligneis vasis, nunc lignei aureis utuntur: haud dubie sentiens immodicis opibus facile sacerdotes & gubernatores Ecclesiae corrumpi.
units.tr: Now follow some external testimonies. Naucler reports that in the time of Constantine a voice was heard from heaven saying that poison had been scattered into the Church. Our people deride this, though what they themselves made of it is their own affair. Certainly Mornaeus, the lord, writes thus: The Church, enriched so abundantly with wealth, was for most of them an ominous omen. They read in the Acts of Sylvester that this voice was heard from heaven, and they hand it down: Today poison has been poured into the Church. Elsewhere he also cites Alberic of Rozote for this matter, in these words: I heard from great men (he speaks of the time of Constantine) that a voice was heard from heaven saying, Today a deadly poison has been sown in the Church of God, and they say this is found in ancient authentic writings. The said master John of Paris also relates it in his book On the Papacy and the Empire, chapter 21. Thus William Whitaker. Moreover, even those who favour this donation write that at that time a voice of angels was heard in the air, saying, Today poison has been poured out into the Church. But whatever became of that voice, the Waldenses acknowledge the thing itself: for this is the first error with which Reinerius of Pisa charged them. They say that the Church fell away in the time of Sylvester, when the poison of temporal goods had been poured into the Church. Yet it is certain that the Church was first enriched at this time, and the lamentations of the saints that follow belong to these times, even though they make no open mention of Constantine. Thus Isidore of Pelusium: While the Church flourished and was not yet afflicted by disease, the grace of God danced about her as a chorus, the Holy Spirit governing the affairs and inciting each of the bishops, and raising the Church to heaven. That after she was struck by disease and laboured under sedition they destroyed all these things, is obvious to everyone. To omit other things and to indicate the rest in a word: the name of peace is everywhere, but peace itself is nowhere; the Church is like a certain woman who has fallen from her former happiness and has only the tokens left. She has cases and little chests of her ornaments, but she has been stripped of her wealth, not through the excellence of him who first adorned her, but through the wickedness of those who do not manage affairs as they ought. Thus Bernard: It was foretold long ago, and now the time has come. Behold, in peace my bitterness is most bitter. Bitter before, in the slaughter of martyrs; more bitter afterwards, in the conflict with heretics; most bitter now, in the morals of those within the household. Therefore in peace the bitterness is most bitter. But in what peace? There is peace and there is not peace: peace from the pagans, and peace from the heretics, but certainly not peace among the sons, &c. He prefers those purer times of the Church that preceded Constantine to both of these; by him external peace was indeed introduced, but it was useless to the Church, nay harmful. Elizabeth, the German virgin, a companion of Hildegard, also looks back to these times; in the year 1150, when the bishops of the pomp had only just arisen in the time of Constantine, she addressed them thus: You have seized the rule of my saints, and by your wiles, from where have you risen to trouble my rest and to weigh heavily on my heart against my sons, whom I bore in the bitterness of my soul (under the persecutions of the heathen) in the day of my labour and my distress? The author says that the degeneration of the Church began from the fact that she was enriched with the very ample gifts of princes; to which he cites Gregory: Religion brought forth riches, and the daughter devoured the mother. Comparing the state of the Church before Constantine with that which followed, he concludes thus: Hence it comes that the ancient ages, reduced to iron, lost their ancient riches, because devotion decreased and the daughter destroyed the mother. Thus Alan of Cartherius: I do not intend to blame the good laymen who, out of perfect devotion, gave lands to the Church, because they unburdened themselves so that they might ascend to God with greater ease of spirit; but the priestly order has laid such a great and heavy burden on its shoulders that it bends it right down to the earth and prevents it from looking up to heaven. When the sea carries a ship that is too large, it is tossed with great danger, and no river long endures outside its own channel. He applies these things specifically to Constantine elsewhere. And you, Dante of Florence, if you were still alive, would have cause to cry out against Constantine, whom you also dared to reprove in a time of well-ordered religion, charging him in a certain work of yours with having thrown poison and venom into the Church, which would bring pestilence and desolation upon it, namely, because he was the first to give possessions and lands to the Church, &c. Gregory of Hamburg prefers the glory of the first Church under persecution to that external glory which she obtained when persecution ceased. Her glory (he says) was not purple, not a heap of dignities, not a white horse, not pomp, not domination; but behold, we have left all things and followed you, Lord, hoping thereby not to acquire a seat of temporal eminence, but the seat of judging the twelve tribes of Israel, according to Christ's promise. Lorenzo Valla, arguing against the donation of Constantine, speaks thus: The highest Pontiff would more fittingly be called Augustus from increasing, were it not that while he increases temporal things he diminishes spiritual ones. He denies that the Acts of Sylvester, in which it is said that a voice was heard from heaven and that poison had been poured into the Church by Constantine, are apocryphal. Thus Francis Duaren: I think our elders have sufficiently observed that nothing is more destructive and more pestilential to the Church than the excessive opulence of its ministers. For the thing itself speaks: however pious the affection of princes may be in their immense munificence, it has poured such a poison into the Church that, out of that box of Pandora sung of by the poets, it seems not more evils and calamities have come forth among men. Bonifacius the martyr, when once asked whether it was lawful to use wooden chalices in sacred rites, is said to have replied: Once golden priests used wooden vessels; now wooden priests use golden ones, clearly perceiving that priests and governors of the Church are easily corrupted by immoderate wealth.

units.la: 9 Festino ad ipsos Hierarchicos. T. Bilsonus aperte Dominam contravenit. Dicit ille superioritatem Episcopalem a tempore Constantini non auctam sed diminutam fuisse: ac Episcopus Romanus (inquit Bilsonus) ut in opulentia crevit, ita etiam in potentia. Hoc in Romano cum verum sit, numnam probabile in Episcopis caeteris plane contrarium accidisse? nempe ut eorum potestas a tempore Constantini decrevit, quo magis opulentia crevit? Miror tanto ingenio, rem tam ridiculam prodire potuisse. Richardus Eyldus disputat, florere Ecclesiam in persecutione magis quam in prosperitate, & instat in Eccl. sia prima ante Constantinum, quam magis floruisse probat ex Augustino de civitate Dei: & ex Bernardo, qui in triplicia tempora Ecclesiam distinguens, primum sub ethnicis Imperatoribus, secundum in conflictu cum haereticis, tertium in pace ab utriusque, hoc postremum omnium amarissimum facit: Inducit enim Ecclesiam conquerentem. Amarissima amaritudo in pace mea, omnes amici, omnes inimici, omnes domestici, nulli pacifici, servi Christi serviunt Antichristo. Richardus Stockjus Hierarchicus Whitakerum transferens, hunc illius sermonem probat, quem etiam tanquam memoratu dignum in indicem retulit. Constantinus quidem, in temporibus tunc Ecclesiae turbulentissimis, eam pace donavit, & quibus potuit, possessionibus ornavit: & ab illis tempore ut in opulentia crevit ita decrevit in pietate: Affinia habet Gu. Whitak. alibi. Tandem pace in Ecclesia, ut Constantinum constituta, captum est de nova quaedam disciplinae forma excogitare, quae temporibus consentanea esset, &c. Illud verum esse constat quod Hieronymus scripsit & habetur in Gratiano. Ex quo in Ecclesiis sicut in imperio Romano, crevit aparitia, periitque ex defacerdote & visio de Propheta. Rufus: Ante Constantinum magnum, qui tyrannis & Ecclesiae persecutoribus in imperio successit, nihil in conciliis de primatu sancitum est. At ego pluris unum ejusmodi concilium facio, quam quaedam eorum, quae postea secuta sunt. Nam saeviente persecutione. Episcopi de Ecclesia, & religione magis solliciti erant: ea vero sublata, mox ambitio Ecclesiam invasit. Iterum. Olim Episcopi eis nominibus contenti erant, quae in Scripturis habentur, per annos trecentos dumrante persecutione titulis modestis usi sunt: at postea cum pax in Ecclesia constituta esset, ambitio paulatim irrepsit, & tum demum captum est de nominibus nomina cogitari, quorum etsi quaedam non mala fuerunt, tamen satius fuisset ab eis abstineri. Hadrianus Saravia ita: Quod contentiones inter Episcopos & presbyteros attinent, non leguntur ante Constantini tempora, & male conjunguntur cum Ignatij seculo. In quieta & otio sub Constantino, primum magnae illae contentiones, & exitiales Ecclesiae ceperunt. Ita Iohannes Bridgesius: Status Ecclesiae primitivae sub persecu-tione beatior erat, quam pace & prosperitate fruens, & eadem abutens: unde corruptiones & contentiones exortae sunt, quo nomine statu bic posterior non adeo beatus erat.
units.tr: 9 Let me now come to the Hierarchists themselves. T. Bilson openly contradicts him. He says that episcopal superiority was not increased but diminished from the time of Constantine, and that the Roman bishop (says Bilson) grew in power just as he grew in wealth. Granting this is true of the Roman bishop, is it probable that in the other bishops the opposite happened, namely that their power decreased from the time of Constantine in proportion as their wealth increased? I marvel that so great a mind could bring forth so ridiculous a thing. Richard Field argues that the Church flourished more under persecution than in prosperity, and he insists on the first Church before Constantine, which he proves to have flourished more from Augustine's City of God, and from Bernard, who, distinguishing the Church into three periods, the first under the heathen emperors, the second in conflict with heretics, the third in peace from both, makes this last the most bitter of all. For he introduces the Church complaining: Most bitter is the bitterness in my peace: all friends, all enemies, all of my household; none peaceable; the servants of Christ serve Antichrist. Richard Stock, a Hierarchist, translating Whitaker, approves this speech of his, which he has also listed in his index as worthy of being remembered. Constantine indeed, in the most turbulent times of the Church, gave her peace, and adorned her with such possessions as he could; and from that time, as she grew in wealth, so she declined in piety. Whitaker has similar remarks elsewhere. Finally, once peace had been established in the Church under Constantine, it was resolved to devise some new form of discipline suited to the times, &c. That is clearly true which Jerome wrote, and which is found in Gratian: From this, as in the Roman empire, so in the Churches pride grew, and the vision of the prophet perished, since the priest had gone astray. Rufinus: Before Constantine the Great, who succeeded the tyrants and persecutors of the Church in the empire, nothing concerning primacy was decreed in councils. But I value one such council more than some of those which followed afterwards. For while persecution raged, bishops were more anxious about the Church and religion; but when that was removed, ambition straightway invaded the Church. Again: Formerly bishops were content with those names that are found in the Scriptures; for three hundred years, while persecution lasted, they used modest titles; but afterwards, when peace was established in the Church, ambition gradually crept in, and then at last it was resolved to devise names for them, some of which, though not bad, it would have been better to abstain from. Adrian Saravia thus: As for the contentions between bishops and presbyters, they are not read of before the time of Constantine, and they are wrongly joined with the age of Ignatius. In quiet and leisure under Constantine, those great contentions and destructive troubles of the Church first began. Thus John Bridges: The state of the primitive Church was happier under persecution than when enjoying peace and prosperity and abusing them; whence corruptions and contentions arose, and this later state was not so happy.

units.la: Postremo G. Downamo, ex diametro se opponit If. Casaubonus, cusus ista verba sunt. Quod in hac observatione pluris videntur aestimari tempora post Constantinum quam anteriora: id vero Serenissimus rex valde miratur, & omnino haud probat. Fatetur rex quarti seculi Ecclesiam, gloria, splendore, opibus, ac doctorum virorum copia magis quam priora floruisse: at certitudine fidei quam ogdoadis vocant, aut incorrupte disciplinae sinceritate aut parem, aut etiam superiorem, priorem seculorum Ecclesia fuisse, dubitare posse putat rex mortalium neminem.—Neq; potest ambigi quo longius ab origine prima descedebatur, eo etiam longius, a primeva puritate & simplicitate esse recessum. Quare si de verenda & mundanda domo Dei serio cogitatur, cur ad Apostolorum tempora, aut Apostolicis proxima non potissimum respiciatur? Verum quidem est, partem multo maximam illius temporis, in tenebris, & squalore, propter continuas persecutiones pijs esse transfactam, sed hi tamen etiam atque etiam, ne in hac quoque re, meliuus fit ire ad domum lu-tus, quam ad domum conviviij. Pauperias & calamitas bonae mentis forores ad iunt: divitiae & gloria non eandem famam obtinent, &c. Ita tutum non est a temporibus post Constantinum exempla sumere, ut Bancroftus: multo minus tempora ipsa Constantini (quod vult Downamus) pro praecipuo exemplari ad imitandum proponi debent. Haec de extraneo firmamento Hierarchico quinto: nempe universa Ecclesiarum prisca praxi.
units.tr: Last of all, I come to Isaac Casaubon, who directly opposes John Downame, and whose words are these: "That in this observation the times after Constantine seem to be valued more than the earlier ones, the most serene King greatly wonders at this and does not approve it at all. The King admits that the Church of the fourth century flourished more than the earlier Church in glory, splendour, wealth and the number of learned men; but he thinks that no mortal can doubt that the Church of earlier centuries was equal, or even superior, to it in the certainty of faith which they call the ogdoad, or in the purity of uncorrupted discipline."—And it cannot be disputed that the further the Church moved from its first origin, the further it departed from its primeval purity and simplicity. So if we seriously think about cleansing and restoring the venerable house of God, why is it not chiefly looked to in the times of the Apostles, or those nearest to the Apostolic age? It is true that a very large part of that period was spent in darkness and squalor, because of continual persecutions, yet these men, again and again, lest in this matter too it be better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting. Poverty and calamity are the sisters of a good mind; riches and glory do not enjoy the same reputation, and so on. Thus it is not safe to take examples from the times after Constantine, as Bancroft does; much less should the times of Constantine himself (which Downame wishes) be put forward as the chief model to be imitated. These things concerning the fifth foreign support of the hierarchy, namely the universal ancient practice of the Churches.

units.la: CAP II. Firmamentum Hierarchicorum V I. a patrum authoritate solvitur.
units.tr: CAP II. The foundation of the hierarchists, V I., is overthrown by the authority of the Fathers.

units.la: SExtum sequitur, à Papistis pariliter mutuatum, Patrum scilicet & doctorum antiquorum authoritas: ubi tria mihi reprehendenda occurrunt: primo, quòd nimiam patribus authoritatem tribuant: secundo, quod patres fictitios & spurios producant: ter-tio, & ultimo,quod patres & scriptores antiquos recentibus Ecclesiæ reformatæ doctoribus anteponant. Quod ad primum, Papistarum calumniis velificantur,
units.tr: The sixth argument, likewise borrowed from the Papists, is the authority of the Fathers and the ancient teachers. Three things here call for my censure: (1) they ascribe too much authority to the Fathers; (2) they produce fictitious and spurious Fathers; and (3) above all, they put the Fathers and ancient writers before the recent teachers of the reformed Church. As to the first, they set their sails to the calumnies of the Papists.

units.la: Primo, errores imbibunt. Vitio nobis Puritanis vertit Cornelius Scultingius, quòd disciplinam ex solis scripturis hauriendam existimemus: & contra astruit.Non ex solis scripturis haurienda disciplina est. Non tantùm petenda ex scripturis disciplina, sed etiam ex salubberrimis sta-tutis sanctorum patrum. Non tantum ex sacris Scripturis, sed etiam ex antiquorum Canonum institutis, depromenda disciplina est, contra sententiam Puritanorum. Non ex puris & solis scripturis hauriendA disciplina, necesse est per posteriores Canones defectam supplere, non in Scripturis solis in specie omnis disciplina comprehenditur. Fontes disciplinæ etiam regulæ patrum, non sola Scriptura. In solis bibiljs sinistrè & male intellectis occupantur: in lectione sanctorum Patrum, Conciliorum, & antiquitatis Ec-clesiasticæ, rudes sunt & ignari. Vt Whitgiftus pro Episcopis & Archiepiscopis, veteris Ecclesiæ ritu, veterumque Patrum crebris testimonijs fortiter pugnat: sic in id maxime ex altera parte incumbit Cartwrightus, aliqʒ ejus sodales hoc argumentum pertractantes, ut Patrum consensum veluti Paleas, Ecclesiæ veteris exemplum ut putidas næmias audacissime rejiciant. Puritani perverse interpretantes scripturam in Politeiâ & disciplina sanctorum patrum, Conciliorum, traditionis Ecclesiæ authoritatem perperam penitus repudiant, quàm Anglo-Calvinistæ à nobis stantes, plurimi faciunt. Anglo-Calvinistæ pro nostra veteri disciplina & politeia condensant patrum testimonia & consensum antiquæ Ecclesiæ producunt de singulis partibus politeiæ: Puritanos veteris Ecclesiæ consensum & authoritatem repudiantes, graviter accusant & damnant. Dum Puritani à patribus ad scripturas appellant, regerunt optime, Patres antiquos melius scripturas ipsis intellexisse. Citat in margine Bancrofti Survegium, sub nomine examinis disciplinæ prætensæ, Londini, per Iohannem Woolffe ann. 1593. ex quo multa transcribit, pagina sequenti. Egregiè & pulchrè (inquit) declamitat censor iste contra Puritanos. An hactenus nunquam in Ecclesia viri docti extiterunt priusquam disciplinæ Genevensis axiomata, à vobis prodita sunt; Ante vos exortas sapientia omnis extincta iacuit? Rectius vos quid Apostolorum tempore creditum vel factum fuit intelligitis, quam patres illi Apostolorum successores? &c. Accedens deinde ad examinis minis Bancroftiani finem, Hæc omnia (inquit) author examinis, multo- que his plura se accumulasse scribit, ut hinc Dei judicia glorificentur, quando ex Barowviftarum adversus Puritanos criminationibus acerbifsimis adimplctum videmus quod Christus dixit, qua mensura mensi sueritis, eadem & remetietur vobis. Qua enim arrogantia, acerbitate, maledicentia, Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ politeiam Puritani criminati & calumniati sunt: ca lem vicissim Puritanorum consistoria, a Barowviftis calumniosa & acerbissima criminatione sedari. Hoc certe Dei judicium summa admonitione est dignum: sicut as istas, in una Anglia mutuas sibi penas tam strenuè dare, mutuisque vulneribus sese ita conficere.
units.tr: First, they swallow errors. Cornelius Scultingius finds fault with us Puritans for thinking that discipline is to be drawn from Scripture alone, and he argues the opposite: Discipline is not to be drawn from Scripture alone. Discipline is to be sought not only from Scripture but also from the most wholesome statutes of the holy Fathers. Discipline is to be derived not only from the holy Scriptures but also from the institutions of the ancient canons, contrary to the opinion of the Puritans. Discipline cannot be drawn from pure and Scripture alone; it is necessary to supply by later canons what is lacking, for not all discipline is comprehended in Scripture alone. The fountains of discipline are the rules of the Fathers as well as Scripture alone. The Puritans are busy with the Bibles alone, understood perversely and wrongly; in reading the holy Fathers, the Councils and the ecclesiastical antiquity they are rude and ignorant. As Whitgift fights stoutly for bishops and archbishops, after the rite of the ancient Church and with frequent testimonies of the ancient Fathers, so Cartwright especially presses hard on the other side, and some of his companions treating this argument, so that they most boldly reject the consent of the Fathers as chaff and the example of the ancient Church as stinking trifles. The Puritans, perversely interpreting Scripture, utterly and wrongly repudiate the authority of the holy Fathers, the Councils and the tradition of the Church in polity and discipline, whereas the Anglo-Calvinists, standing with us, value it very highly. The Anglo-Calvinists, for our old discipline and polity, gather the testimonies of the Fathers and bring forward the consent of the ancient Church on each part of polity, and they gravely accuse and condemn the Puritans who repudiate the consent and authority of the ancient Church. When the Puritans appeal from the Fathers to the Scriptures, they are answered rightly: the ancient Fathers understood the Scriptures better than they do. In the margin he cites Bancroft's Survey, under the title of the pretended Examination of Discipline, London, printed by John Wolfe, 1593, from which he transcribes much on the following page. Splendidly and beautifully (he says) does that censor declaim against the Puritans. Have there never until now been learned men in the Church before the axioms of the Geneva discipline were brought forth by you? Lay all wisdom extinct before you arose? Do you understand better than those Fathers, the successors of the Apostles, what was believed or done in the time of the Apostles? etc. Then, approaching the end of Bancroft's examination, The author of the Examination (he says) heaps up these and many more things, so that by this God's judgments may be glorified, since we see fulfilled from the most bitter accusations of the Barrowists against the Puritans what Christ said: with what measure you have measured, it shall be measured to you again. For with what arrogance, bitterness and slander the Puritans accused and calumniated the polity of the English Church, with the same in turn the consistories of the Puritans are being assailed by the slanderous and most bitter accusation of the Barrowists. Surely this judgment of God is worthy of the highest admonition: that in England alone they so vigorously inflict penalties on one another and so wound themselves with mutual wounds.

units.la: Secundò, Ex his ita positis hæc pauca breviter observari vellem.
units.tr: Second, with these things so laid down, I would wish a few points to be briefly observed.

units.la: Primò, in citandis patribus colludere Hierarchicos cum Papistis. Non negant inquies ex scriptura solâ petendam disciplinam esse. Quid ni, illi quidem qui disciplinam nisi ex parte, in verbo præscriptam negant: Coguntur hi certè verbis ipsis Scultingianis affirmare, defectum hac ex parte scripturæ, ex patribus supplendum esse. Quod ad reliquos, qui disciplinam exactè, quoad essentialia in verbo exaratam dicunt: disciplinam ex sola Scriptura examinandam ubi quæso dicunt? Dicunt perspicuè ex Scriptura & ex antiquitate, ex scriptura & usu Ecclesiæ, nempe, ut rem disciplinæ in Scriptura contineri concedant, hujus tamen rei interpretationem, non ex ipsa scriptura sola, sed ex patribus etiam petendam existimant.
units.tr: First, in citing the Fathers the hierarchists are colluding with the Papists. "They do not deny," you will say, "that discipline is to be sought from Scripture alone." Why not, since those who deny that discipline is prescribed in the Word except in part are certainly compelled, in Scultingius' own words, to affirm that the defect on the part of Scripture is to be supplied from the Fathers. As for the rest, who say that discipline is exactly set down in the Word as to its essentials: where, I ask, do they say that discipline is to be examined from Scripture alone? They say plainly: from Scripture and from antiquity, from Scripture and the practice of the Church. That is, they concede that the matter of discipline is contained in Scripture, but they think that the interpretation of this matter is to be sought not from Scripture alone but from the Fathers too.

units.la: Secundò, Hierarchici sua nimia erga patres honorificentiâ, Papistas indurant in sua erga solam Scripturam blasphemia, & patrum veterum ut ita dicam idololatria: ut ex ista Scultingij gloriatione videre est, ex eo desumpta, quòd Anglo-Calvinistæ, tâm acriter patres adversus Puritanos condensent & urgeant.
units.tr: Second, the hierarchists, by their excessive honour toward the Fathers, harden the Papists in their blasphemy against Scripture alone, and, so to speak, in the idolatry of the old Fathers. This can be seen from Scultingius' boast, drawn from the fact that the Anglo-Calvinists press the Fathers so fiercely against the Puritans.

units.la: Tertiò, præcipuos Ecclesiæ reformatæ columnas, Calvinum præ- sertim & Bezam, papistis deridendos proponunt, ut ex ista Scultingij illatione constat. Calvino indignantur Anglo-calvinistæ quòd vetera Concilia quoad doctrinam recipiat, & quoad Ecclesiæ gubernationem repudiet: sed Ecclesiæ veteris contemptus in Calvino ab una parte, ipsius Calvini contemptum ex altera parte peperit: idemque sibi circa Calvini consistoria & disciplinam soli Anglo-calvinistæ licere existimarunt, quod circa vetera Concilia licere sibi Calvinus voluit.
units.tr: Third, they propose our chief pillars of the reformed Church, Calvin especially and Beza, to be mocked by the Papists, as is clear from this inference of Scultingius. The Anglo-Calvinists are indignant with Calvin because he accepts the ancient Councils in doctrine but rejects them in the government of the Church. But contempt for the ancient Church in Calvin on the one hand has bred contempt for Calvin himself on the other; and they have thought that the same licence which Calvin wished for himself regarding the ancient Councils is allowed to the Anglo-Calvinists alone regarding Calvin's consistories and discipline.

units.la: Quartò, parum commovere debent, quæ objiciunt Hierarchici, Puritanis de patrum contemptu sicut parum commoventur Hierarchici, quod idem contemptus eis à Papistis objiciatur ut cum ex eodem principio separemus quoad disciplinam à Papistis nos, scripturæ soli scilicet innitendo, ex quo illi quoad doctrinam separarunt: non magis ab illis nos hoc nomine, quàm illi à Papistis exagitari debent. Pensitentur hic illa Scultingij verba, Anglo-Calumistæ & Puritani ex eisdem principiis (soli scilicet scripturæ adhærendo) sibi sua fecerunt illi in doctrina, ly in disciplina.
units.tr: Fourth, the objections which the hierarchists bring against the Puritans concerning contempt for the Fathers should move them little, just as they are little moved that the same contempt is objected to them by the Papists. If we separate ourselves from the Papists in discipline on the same principle, namely by resting on Scripture alone, on which principle they separated from them in doctrine, then we ought to be no more harassed by them on this account than they ought to be harassed by the Papists. Let those words of Scultingius be weighed here: the Anglo-Calvinists and the Puritans, by the same principles (namely by adhering to Scripture alone), have made their own those things which the Papists did in doctrine, but in discipline.

units.la: {Ec 4} Postremo Postremò, si glorificandum Dei iudicium (quòd Bancroftus) quòd eandem mensuram Barowista nobis remetiantur: glorificandum multò magis, quod eandem mensuram (de hoc patrem contemptu) Papistæ Hierarchicis remetiantur. Quid enim lucratus Bancroftus est invectiuâ illa sua,quà adeò Papistis gratificatur? Nempè ex ea ita infert Scultingius. Quantum (inquit) ad doctrinam fidei hæc ipsa in Calvino- Papistarum capita recidunt: in qua ipsi quoque vetere patres contemnunt. Plura & graviora sunt quæ contra totius antiquitatis consensum Calvinistica selta circa dogmata fidei violavit: quàm quæ Consistorium Genevense circa Politeiam Ecclesiasticam peccavit.
units.tr: Lastly, if the judgment of God is to be glorified (as Bancroft says) because the Barrowists measure back to us the same measure, it is to be glorified much more that the Papists measure back to the hierarchists the same measure (in this matter, contempt of the Fathers). For what has Bancroft gained by that invective of his, by which he so gratifies the Papists? Namely, from it Scultingius thus infers: As far as doctrine of faith goes, these very things fall back on the heads of the Calvino-Papists, in which they also despise the ancient Fathers. More and graver are the things which the Calvinistic sect has violated in the dogmas of faith against the consent of all antiquity than those which the Geneva Consistory sinned in regard to ecclesiastical polity.

units.la: Sequitur. Nimiâ suâ observantiâ erga patres Hierar.in patre patrum qui solus pater agnosci debuit, Math. 23, in filium ejus Iesum Christum, qui solus propheta audiendus est Heb.11. in spiritum sanctum, qui solus veritatem docet & scripturas interpretatur, 1.Ioh. 5. & ab his omnibus profectam scripturam injurii sunt: cui soli proprer authoritatem suam auscultare debemus, exclusis hominum omnium scriptis. Patet hoc ex Eccl. 12 : 11. Quæsivit Ecclesiastes æquè verba delectabilia & singula scripta rectè, verba fidelia: Verba sapientum similia aculeis & similia clavis infixis ad caulas, tradita à Pastore eodem. Potiùs inquam ex istis fili mi admonitus esto: faciendi libros multos nullus est finis, & lectio multorum fatigationi est carni. Quanquam autem hic patres exclusos videas, nosque ad scripturas sacras easque solas revocatos: authoritatem tamen quæ soli scripturæ debita est, communem patribus Hierarchici faciunt, ut in eorum antesignano Iohanne Whitgifto videre est. Probarat ille Timotheum solum ordinasse, ac proinde solum Episcopum ordinare debere, ex Ambrosio, Chrysostomo, & Hieronymo in illum locum. Replicarat inter alia Cartwrightus, omnes Whitgifti probationes per totum librum in hominum authoritatibus positas esse: quas Aristoteles non nisi ἀπὸ τῶν ἔξωθεν vocat. Quid hîc ille? Non negat probationes suas in humanis authoritatibus positas esse: sed hanc illius probandi viam ita ornat. Semper iudicium & opiniones piorum hominum plurimi fieri: & tum mihi rationem sufficientem habere videor, quando habeo authoritatem scripturarum & doctorum hominum. Locutus est Aristoteles de humanis scientiis quæ ratione nituntur: sed quam nos profitemur, ea in authoritate, non ratione fundata est. Atque mihi tibi velis toties mecum litigando, quòd authoritates doctorum scriptorum à me allegatæ sunt. Vt breviter respondeam. Existimo authoritatem in rebus divinis optimam rationem esse (in margine, optimum probationis genus) sive ea ipsarum scripturarum sit, sive doctorum hominum qui recte scripturas interpretantur. Iudicet hic lector, annon patres cum Scripturis conjungantur: annon eorum authoritas, etiam absque ratione, optimum probationis genus dicatur: annon denique nuda patrum authoritas à se his arguere & probare permittatur? Quod addit, scripturam rectè interpretantem, aut tergiversatio, aut mera ἀλογία est: addit hæc clausula.
units.tr: It follows. By their excessive observance toward the Fathers the hierarchists have wronged the Father of the Fathers, who alone ought to be acknowledged as Father (Matt. 23), and his Son Jesus Christ, who alone is to be heard as the prophet (Heb. 11), and the Holy Spirit, who alone teaches the truth and interprets the Scriptures (1 John 5), and they have wronged the Scripture which proceeds from all of these, to which alone we ought to listen by reason of its authority, with the writings of all men excluded. This is clear from Eccles. 12:11: The Preacher sought to find pleasant words, and what was written uprightly, words of truth. The words of the wise are like goads and like nails fixed in the sheepfolds, given by the one Shepherd. Rather, my son, be warned by these: there is no end to the making of many books, and much reading is a weariness to the flesh. Although here you see the Fathers excluded and we called back to the holy Scriptures and to them alone, the hierarchists nonetheless make common to the Fathers the authority which is due to Scripture alone, as can be seen in their standard-bearer John Whitgift. He tried to prove that Timothy alone ordained, and therefore that only a bishop ought to ordain, from Ambrose, Chrysostom and Jerome on that passage. Cartwright replied, among other things, that all of Whitgift's proofs throughout the book rest on the authorities of men, which Aristotle calls arguments from without [ἀπὸ τῶν ἔξωθεν]. What does he say to this? He does not deny that his proofs rest on human authorities, but he adorns this manner of proving thus: I always make much of the judgment and opinions of pious men, and I seem to myself to have sufficient reason when I have the authority of the Scriptures and of learned men. Aristotle spoke of human sciences, which rest on reason; but the faith we profess is founded on authority, not on reason. And I wish you would stop so often quarrelling with me because I have alleged the authorities of learned writers. To answer briefly: I hold that authority in divine matters is the best reason (in the margin, the best kind of proof), whether it be that of the Scriptures themselves or of learned men who interpret the Scriptures rightly. Let the reader judge whether the Fathers are not joined with the Scriptures, whether their authority, even without reason, is not called the best kind of proof, and finally whether the bare authority of the Fathers is not allowed to argue and prove these things by itself. As for what he adds, that Scripture rightly interpreted is either evasion or sheer unreason [ἀλογία]: he adds this clause.

units.la: §.10.p.66 — Tract.3.c.7. — p.1.p.200 (marginal references, left margin) clausula ad improprietatem sermonis, addit etiam ad absurditatem sensus: nam aut principium petit, recta semper doctorum hominum interpretationem esse, aut nihil hac clausula pro se, doctorum hominum authoritatem rationi praeponente, respondet.
units.tr: §.10.p.66 — Tract.3.c.7. — p.1.p.200 (marginal references, left margin) The clause is faulty in its wording, and it is also absurd in its sense. For either it begs the question, assuming that the interpretation of learned men is always correct, or it answers nothing in its favour, since it places the authority of learned men above reason.

units.la: Quid multis opus? Authoritatem patrum praevalere debere putat, contra quam Hieronymus: Nemo post Apostolos authoritatem habet, Argumentum a patribus ductum, optimum probationis genus dicit, contra quam Tho. Mortonus Hierarchicus: qui illud Cani approbat. Infirmum est ex omnium patrum consensu argumentum. Authoritatem deniq; patrum rationi praeferendam affirmat: contra quam idem ex Salmerone. Rationum efficacia omni authoritati praestare dignoscitur. Secundo, ideo scripturae interpretationem rectam esse probare Hierarchici solent, quod eam ita patres interpretati sint, etsi nullam suae interpretationis rationem afferant ex scripturis. Exempli gratia, locum 1: Tim.5. 17. de solis sacerdotibus intelligendum esse probat Bilsonus, quicquid docti homines recentiores sentiant, quia Patres ita dixerunt, & secum hunc locum intellexerunt. Recte Whitakerus in causa simili, Suam hanc expositionem consensu totius Ecclesiae comprobatam esse affirmat Iesuita. Ita mox a scripturis ad patres delabitur, nosque atria scribentes postico fallit. Perquam hoc tenue fuit a Scripturis argumentum: cumque nullum haberet aliud, reliquum fuit, ut fugeret ad commentarios sententiasque patrum.
units.tr: Why say more? He thinks the authority of the Fathers ought to prevail. Against this, Jerome says: No one after the Apostles has authority. Thomas Morton, the Hierarchist, calls an argument drawn from the Fathers the best kind of proof, and he is opposed by Jerome. He approves the saying of Cano: Cani: An argument from the consensus of all the Fathers is weak. Finally, he affirms that the authority of the Fathers is to be preferred to reason, and against this the same man quotes Salmeron: The force of reasons is known to surpass all authority. Secondly, the Hierarchists usually prove that their interpretation of Scripture is right because the Fathers interpreted it in that way, even though they give no reason for their interpretation from Scripture. For example, on 1 Tim. 5. 17, Bilson proves that it must be understood of priests alone, whatever learned men of more recent times think, because the Fathers said so and understood this passage in the same way. Whitaker rightly, in a similar case, says that the Jesuit affirms his exposition to be confirmed by the consent of the whole Church. Thus he slips from Scripture to the Fathers at once, and deceives us who write in the back courtyard. This argument from Scripture was very slight, and since he had no other, what was left was for him to flee to the commentaries and opinions of the Fathers.

units.la: Tertio, ex eo, interpretationem scripturae malam esse arguere Hierarchici solent, quod patrum suffragiis destituatur. Sic enim Bancroftus interpretationem nostram, Math.18. Die Ecclesiae, absurdam probat, quia nullus de patribus unquam ita hunc locum intellexit: & Georgius Downamus locum illum 1.Tim.5.17. de Senioribus nonstris minime intelligendum arguit: quia patres hunc locum de hujusmodi senioribus non intellexerunt: nam si unquam extitissent, eos patribus notos fuisse oportuit. Quid ego hic aliud responderem, quam scripturam non fore scripturam istis, nisi hominibus placeat: quemadmodum olim Tertullianus: Apud vos de humano arbitratu divinitas constitutur. Nisi homini Deus placuerit, Deus non erit: homo iam Deo propitius esse debebit. Oppono vero Richardum Eyldum Hierarchicum. Professus est Cajetanus se scripturam etiam contra torrentem patrum interpretari velle si ratio suppetat, reprehendit eum Canus, defendit contra Canum Andradium, cui accedit Eyldus. De terrestri Paradyso contordant omnes patres, Eugenius & Pererius adversantur omnibus, reprehendit eos Bellarminus, defendit Fyldus. Oppono deinde Thomam Mortonum Hierarchicum, qui Bellarminum & Maldonatum in eo approbant, quod Scripturam ex ratione interpretentur, etiam cum authorem neminem haberent. Ita patres Scripturae aequiparant Hierarchici,cum authoritatem eis a se tribuunt perinde ac Scripturae: anteponunt autem, quum eiusdem interpretationem ideo vera volunt, quia patres adstipulantur, aut falsam quia adversantur.
units.tr: Thirdly, the Hierarchists usually argue that an interpretation of Scripture is bad because it lacks the support of the Fathers. So Bancroft declares our interpretation of Matt. 18 (Tell it to the Church) absurd, because none of the Fathers ever understood this passage in that way. And George Downame argues that the passage 1 Tim. 5. 17 must not be understood of our elders, because the Fathers did not understand it of such elders; for if they had ever existed, they would have had to be known to the Fathers. What else should I reply here, than that Scripture will not be Scripture to them unless it pleases them? Just as Tertullian once said: With you, divinity is established by human judgement. Unless God pleases man, God will not be God; man will then have to be propitious to God. But I set against this Richard Hooker, the Hierarchist. Cajetan declared that he was willing to interpret Scripture even against the torrent of the Fathers, if reason supported him; Canus rebuked him, and Andrade defended him against Canus, and Hooker joins Andrade. All the Fathers agree about the earthly Paradise; Eugubinus and Pererius oppose all of them; Bellarmine rebukes them, and Hooker defends them. Next I set against this Thomas Morton, the Hierarchist, who approves Bellarmine and Maldonatus in this, that they interpret Scripture by reason, even when they have no author for it. Thus the Hierarchists make the Fathers equal to Scripture, when they attribute to them the same authority as to Scripture; yet they prefer the Fathers when they want the interpretation of Scripture to be true because the Fathers support it, or false because the Fathers oppose it.

units.la: 4 Hoc vero dum faciunt multiplici peccato se obstringunt. Primò, absurditate, cuius eos ita coarguit Chrysostomus. Quomodo aliorum sententiam simpliciter sequi non absurdum? quum habeamus omnium exactissimam trutinam & gnomonem, ac regulam, divinarum inquam legum assertionem.
units.tr: 4 By doing this, they bind themselves to many sins. First, to absurdity, for which Chrysostom rebukes them in this way: How is it not absurd to follow simply the opinion of others, when we have the most exact balance, rule and gnomon of all, I mean the declaration of divine laws?

units.la: Secundo, impietate in Deum, cuius eos ita idem coarguit. Quia progrediente tempore multi impegerunt, scripta sunt quae spiritus sanctus dictavit: vide quanti sit criminis non per istud auxilium velle proficere, Deum non putamus offendi quando ad alia convertimur.
units.tr: Secondly, to impiety towards God, for which the same writer rebukes them: Since many have stumbled as time went on, the things which the Holy Spirit dictated have been written down. See how great a crime it is to wish to make progress not by that help, and we do not think God is offended when we turn to other things.

units.la: Tertio, superbia, cuius eos ita coarguit Basilius. Quod si fidelis sit dominus fideliaque sint ejus mandata omnia, haud dubie, manifestissime a fide lapsus est, & crimen maximae superbiae vel a scripto residere, vel non scriptum admittere.
units.tr: Thirdly, to pride, for which Basil rebukes them: If the Lord is faithful and all his commands are faithful, then without doubt he has most manifestly fallen from the faith, and the crime of the greatest pride lies either in admitting what is written or in admitting what is not written.

units.la: Quarto, sacrilegio, cujus eos ita coarguit Isidorus sicuti citatur a Billono: Is qui praeest, si praeter voluntatem Dei, vel praeter quod in sacris scripturis evidenter praecipitur, vel dicit aliquid vel imperat, tanquam falsus testis Dei, & sacrilegus habeatur.
units.tr: Fourthly, to sacrilege, for which Isidore, as quoted by Billon, rebukes them: He who presides, if he says or commands anything contrary to the will of God, or contrary to what is clearly enjoined in the Holy Scriptures, is to be regarded as a false witness of God and a sacrilegious man.

units.la: Quinto, praesumptione, cujus eos ita coarguit Augustinus. Sancta Scriptura nostrae doctrinae regulam figit, ne audeamus sapere, plus quam oportet. Non sit aliud mihi te docere nisi verba tibi doctoris exponere. Alibi: Ubi de re obscurissima disputatur, non adjuvantibus divinarum scripturarum certis clarisque documentis, cohibere se debet humana praesumptio.
units.tr: Fifthly, to presumption, for which Augustine rebukes them: Holy Scripture fixes the rule of our teaching, so that we do not dare to be wiser than we ought. Let it not be for me to teach you anything except to expound the words of your teacher to you. Elsewhere: When a most obscure matter is disputed, and the sure and clear testimonies of the divine Scriptures are not helping, human presumption ought to restrain itself.

units.la: Sexto, garrulitate cujus eos ita coarguit Hieronymus: Sine scripturarum authoritas garrulitate non habet fidem.
units.tr: Sixthly, to garrulousness, for which Jerome rebukes them: The authority of Scripture without garrulousness has faith.

units.la: Septimò & ultimo, haeresi, cuius eos ita coarguit Alphonsus a Castro: Qui tam leviter de haeresi pronunciant, non expendentes de qua re loquuntur, saepe sua ipsorum sagitta feriuntur, inciduntque in eam foveam quam parabant aliis. Nam velle humanas scripturas in divinarum ordinem connumerare, hoc verius ego dixerim haeresim, quia humanis scriptis dissentire ineptum autumant, perinde ac divinis. Haeretici Puritani sunt (inquit Bancroftus) quod cum Aerio discrimen Episcopi & presbyteri tollant: at potius Bancroftus ipse haereticus, tam leviter de haeresi pronuncians, inquit Alphonsus, quod discrimen scripturae & patrum tollat: nam a patribus dissentire ineptum putat, perinde ac a scripturis. Accommodata etiam reliqua sunt ad clamores Hierarchicos reliquos refutandos. Quod enim nos absurdos clamant, superbos, arrogantes, sacrilegos, impudentes, quando nudas patrum authoritates repudiamus: id in eorum capita recidit, quum scriptura sola divina non contenti, patres accersendos autumant.
units.tr: Seventhly and lastly, to heresy, for which Alfonso a Castro rebukes them: Those who pronounce so lightly on heresy, without weighing what matter they speak of, are often struck by their own arrow, and fall into the pit which they prepared for others. For to wish to count human writings among the order of divine ones, that I would call heresy more truly, since they think it foolish to dissent from human writings just as from divine ones. Bancroft says: The Puritans are heretics, because with Aerius they abolish the distinction between bishop and presbyter. But rather Bancroft himself is a heretic, pronouncing so lightly on heresy, says Alfonso, because he abolishes the distinction between Scripture and the Fathers; for he thinks it foolish to dissent from the Fathers just as from Scripture. The remaining points are also suited to refuting the other clamours of the Hierarchists. For when they cry out that we are absurd, proud, arrogant, sacrilegious and shameless when we reject the bare authorities of the Fathers, that charge falls back on their own heads, since they, not content with divine Scripture alone, claim that the Fathers must be called in.

units.la: Tertio, sua hac honorificentia erga partes Hierarchici, & suam in certam produnt, & aliorum fidem in incertitudinem pellunt.
units.tr: Thirdly, by this honour of theirs towards their own side, they both reveal their own uncertainty and drive the faith of others into uncertainty.

units.la: § Recte olim Tertullianus. Fides in regula posita est, cedat curiositas fidei, cedat gloria saluti. Nihil ultra regulam scire, omnia scire est. Ultra regulam vero fidem progredi Hierarchici volunt; qui fidem patribus adhibendam ita urgent, ut qui eis fidem denegarit, vix pro Christiano fideli habeant. Videt hoc est in Gese. Dodm. qui in concione sua Lambethiana arguit pa: 19. Si omnis antiquitas Aerio excepto, superioritatem Episcoporum agnoscit: sum superiores Episcopi fuerunt. Negat Refutator hanc consequentiam firmam esse: quid ille? Nemo hoc faceret (inquit) qui faciem Theologi, sive etiam dixerim, Christiani gerit. Homines vero fidem omni antiquitati in materia facti, scriptura minime contradicente denegare, aperta demonstratio est, cum novitati & singularitati potius quam veritati additum esse. Testificatur omnis antiquitas unanimi consensu, Episcopos gradu in prima Ecclesia minstris reliquis superiores fuisse: & quis quam de nostris frontem habet, ut id verum esse deneget? Ligat vero haec omnia hoc conclusionis nodo. Hucusque de authoritate antiquitatis qua haec consequentia nititur. Quis non videt authoritatem hic patribus a se tributam? Fidem huic authoritati debitam requiri? quam qui denegat, non Christianus nisi impudentissimus habendus sit. Non impedit quod objicitur, scriptura minime contradicente: relinquitur adhuc etenim quaestio, ipsa scriptura contradicat necne, quam ille consensu antiquitatis ita praejudicatam vult, ut scripturam minime contradicere censendum sit, quando unanimis antiquitatis consensus concordat: relinquitur etiam fidem antiquitati necessario adhibendam esse, quando scriptura de re aliqua nihil dicit: non etenim in materia facti contradicere scriptura potest, quando nihil de eadem omnino dicit. Hoc vero quam absurdum dictu sit, a simili patefiet. Probat Bellarminus, Romanum pontificem Petri successorem esse a facto Petri, sedem Romae collocantis: hoc factum Petri (inquit) ab omni antiquitate comprobatur: nam & omnes patres affirmant Petrum Romae fuisse, & scriptura non contradicit: & ecquis frontem habet in materia facti, manimi antiquori n omnium consensui denegare fidem? Similiter H. Sarav. in facto primae Ecclesiae primatum Episcopatus Hierarchici ponit; ad hujus etenim probationem se accingens, ita inchoat. Episcopum reliquis ministris superiorem esse, facilime erit probatu, si hoc mihi primum detur, quod omnis dat antiquitas, Apostolorum successores esse. Vides hic omnia paria: eundem etenim consensum totius antiquitatis habet Bellarminus, Petrum Romae fuisse, atque Saravia Episcopos Apostolorum fuisse successores. Accomodata igitur ad utrosque Calvii. Whitakeri responsio est. Pontificia fides (sic Hierarchica) non potest esse Sacramentum cum fundamento patrum ita nitatur, & hujus principium sit non divina sed humana authoritas. Velim hoc quibus perpendant: nam in eo aliquid momenti est. Possunt sic ii dare conjectiones, non aut certa aliqua authoritas acquiescere. Quod de conjecturis dicitur, quam nullum fidei fundamentum praebeat, liquet vel ex ipso Aquinate, cujus ista verba sunt. Sacra doctrina philosophorum authoritatibus utitur tanquam extraneis & probabilibus: authoritate canonicae scripturae utitur, proprie ex necessitate argumentandi. Authoritatibus autem aliorum doctorum Ecclesiae utimur, non quasi argumento ex propriis, sed ex probabilibus. Initiatur fides nostra revelatione Apostolis Conf.4.q.3 stolis & Prophetis facta, qui canonicos libros scripserunt, non autem revelatione illa, si quae fuerat aliis doctoribus facta. Allegatur saepe a nostris Hi. Zanchius qui fidem suam aliquatenus antiquitate niti dicit: at hoc ita explicat ipse Zanchius alibi. Qualis fuerit illa veteris & Apostolicae Ecclesiae forma tempore Christi & Apostolorum, liquido & certo apparet ex libris Evangelistarum & Apostolorum: probabiliter autem ex reliquis post Apostolos antiquissimis Ecclesiasticis scriptoribus. Quid igitur est? Fides Hiero. Zanchij aliquatenus quidem antiquitate nititur, sed non quasi certo fundamento, sed probabili tantummodo conjectura: sic vel a Zanchio suo discere Georgius Downamus potuerit, frontem Christianam gerere posse hominem eum, qui toti antiquitati fidem suam non adiunxerit. Quid enim? Probabilibus tantum conjecturis ita tenemur, ut eis credendum sit? Imo testimonia patrum extranea sunt (inquit Aquinas; non propria) & probabilitatem tanquam inducunt: at fides probatilibus non nititur, sed illi soli revelationi quae scriptoribus canonicis facta est. Ἀναλογία igitur Zanchio Aquinas est: cujus fides aliquatenus antiquitate nititur, etiamsi ea tantum probabilis sit: multo magis Downamo, qui fidem fere necessario in materia saltem facti ei adhibendam esse clamat. Aliter Whitakerus, qui de facto Petri Romam accedentis verba faciens, ab antiquitate tota comprobato, ita habet. Nemo papisticam religionem fide retinere aut sequi potest sed opinione tantum & conjectura, quod hujus religionis fundamentum est, sub fidem non cadit. Rursus, Nititur hoc totum fide humana & ex historica veritate pendet; at fides & religio nostra certiori testimonio niti debet, nempe testimonio spiritus sancti.
units.tr: § Tertullian rightly said long ago: Faith is placed in the rule; let curiosity yield to faith, let glory yield to salvation. To know nothing beyond the rule is to know everything. But the Hierarchists want faith to advance beyond the rule; they press so hard that faith must be given to the Fathers, that whoever denies them faith can scarcely be regarded as a Christian believer. This can be seen in Gese. Dodm., who in his Lambeth sermon argues (p. 19): If all antiquity, Aerius excepted, acknowledges the superiority of bishops, then bishops were superior. The Refuter denies that this consequence is sound. What does he say? No one would do this (he says) who bears the face of a theologian, or I would even say of a Christian. But that men should deny faith to all antiquity in a matter of fact, when Scripture does not contradict it, is a plain demonstration that they prefer novelty and singularity to truth. All antiquity testifies with unanimous consent that bishops in the first Church were superior in rank to the other ministers; and which of ours has the face to deny that this is true? Yet he ties all of this together with this knot of conclusion: Thus far concerning the authority of antiquity on which this consequence rests. Who does not see that authority is here attributed by him to the Fathers? That faith due to this authority is required? Whoever denies it should be regarded as no Christian, unless he is most shameless. The objection that Scripture does not contradict it is no hindrance: for there remains the question whether Scripture itself contradicts it, which he wants so prejudged by the consent of antiquity that Scripture must be judged not to contradict it, whenever the unanimous consent of antiquity agrees. There also remains the point that faith must necessarily be given to antiquity whenever Scripture says nothing about a matter; for Scripture cannot contradict in a matter of fact when it says nothing about it at all. How absurd this is to say will become clear from a parallel. Bellarmine proves that the Roman pontiff is the successor of Peter from the fact that Peter fixed his see at Rome. This fact of Peter, he says, is confirmed by all antiquity: for all the Fathers affirm that Peter was at Rome, and Scripture does not contradict it; and who has the face to deny faith, in a matter of fact, to the unanimous consent of all antiquity? Similarly Hadrian Saravia places the primacy of the bishop in the fact of the first Church; for, preparing to prove it, he begins thus: That a bishop is superior to the other ministers will be very easy to prove, if this first is granted to me, which all antiquity grants, that the bishops are the successors of the Apostles. You see here that everything is alike: for Bellarmine has the same consent of all antiquity that Peter was at Rome, as Saravia has that the bishops were successors of the Apostles. Therefore Whitaker's reply, suited to both, is this: Papist faith (or Hierarchical faith) cannot be a sacrament, since it rests on the foundation of the Fathers, and its principle is human, not divine, authority. I would like them to consider this, for there is some weight in it. They can give conjectures in this way, but cannot rest on any certain authority. That faith rests on conjectures, which provide no foundation for faith, is clear even from Aquinas himself, whose words are these: Sacred doctrine uses the authorities of philosophers as external and probable; it uses the authority of canonical Scripture properly, from necessity of arguing. But we use the authorities of other teachers of the Church not as argument from proper sources, but from probable ones. Our faith is founded on the revelation made to the Apostles and Prophets, who wrote the canonical books, and not on that revelation, if any was made to other teachers. Our people often cite Hieronymus Zanchius, who says his faith rests in some measure on antiquity; but Zanchius himself explains this elsewhere: What the form of that old and Apostolic Church was at the time of Christ and the Apostles appears clearly and certainly from the books of the Evangelists and Apostles; but probably from the other most ancient ecclesiastical writers after the Apostles. What then follows? The faith of Hieronymus Zanchius rests in some measure on antiquity, but not as on a certain foundation, only on a probable conjecture; and Downame could have learned this from his own Zanchius, and could have seen that a man who has not joined his faith to the whole of antiquity can bear a Christian face. For why? Are we bound by merely probable conjectures so that they must be believed? Nay, the testimonies of the Fathers are external (says Aquinas; not proper), and they bring in probability as it were; but faith does not rest on probable things, only on that revelation which was made to the canonical writers. Therefore Aquinas is the analogy of Zanchius: his faith rests in some measure on antiquity, even if that antiquity is only probable; much more so Downame's, who shouts that faith must necessarily be given to it at least in a matter of fact. Otherwise Whitaker, speaking of Peter's coming to Rome, and having approved it by all antiquity, says this: No one can hold to or follow Papist religion by faith, but only by opinion and conjecture; and what is the foundation of this religion does not fall under faith. Again, this whole thing rests on human faith and depends on historical truth; but our faith and religion ought to rest on a more certain testimony, namely the testimony of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: 6 Atque haec si ita sint, inquies, authoritates patrum nè quidem omnino citandae erunt: cui obiectioni, respondet Daniel Chamierus De Oecumenico Pontifice in praefat: Guliel. Whitakerus cont. 1. q. 6. c. 12. & Iohannes Reynoldus Censur: Apocryphor: Tom. 1: praelect. 17. Quanquam itaque testimonia patrum nihil probent, aut afferre potuerint, ad fidem faciendam: non tamen probanda est (inquit Whitakerus) eorum sententia, qui patrum testimonia contemnenda ac rejicienda esse existimant.
units.tr: 6 "And if these things are so," you will say, "then the authorities of the Fathers should not be cited at all." To this objection, Daniel Chamier, De Oecumenico Pontifice, in his preface, William Whitaker, Contra 1, q. 6, c. 12, and John Reynolds, Censura Apocryphorum, Tom. 1, praelect. 17, give answer. Although, therefore, the testimonies of the Fathers prove nothing, or could offer nothing toward establishing faith, yet the opinion of those who think the testimonies of the Fathers are to be despised and rejected is not to be approved (says Whitaker).

units.la: Primò, inquit Whitakerus, Patrum scripta scire periti Theologi est: quamquam enim in foro contentioso eorum authoritas parum valeat, ignavia tamen quaedam est aut superbia ignorare, quid quique patrum senserint. Hinc illa Socratis criminatio adversus Nestorium: Hoc illi prae insigni inscitia & ignoratione contigit, Nam tametsi natura, lingua erat disserta, & propterea doctus putabatur, tamen revera imperitus fuit. Quinetiam veterum interpretum scripta perdiscere dedignatus est. Linguae enim volubilitate & elegantia insolenter se efferens, cum veteres prope neglexit, tum seipsum omnibus antecellere existimavit. ——Nestorius videtur veterum lucubrationes penitus ignorare, & ob eam causam banc vocem Deiparam (uti dixi) duntaxat insectatur.
units.tr: "First," says Whitaker, it is the business of a skilled theologian to know the writings of the Fathers; for although their authority carries little weight in a contentious court, it is a kind of sloth or pride to be ignorant of what each of the Fathers thought. Hence that charge of Socrates against Nestorius: This happened to him through remarkable ignorance and lack of knowledge. For although he was by nature eloquent in speech, and for that reason was thought learned, yet in truth he was unskilled. Moreover, he disdained to learn thoroughly the writings of the ancient interpreters. Puffing himself up insolently with fluency and elegance of speech, he all but neglected the ancients, and thought himself superior to everyone. ——Nestorius seems to have been wholly ignorant of the labours of the ancients, and for that reason he assails this term "Mother of God" (as I have said) alone.

units.la: Ioan. 3. etc. Secundo, quanquam patrum testimonia fidem non faciant, illustrant tamen inquit Whitakerus alibi: atq; ita citanda ex abundanti, sive ad cumulum ut loquitur Iohannes Reinoldus ex Augustino, de civitate Dei: lib. 18, c. 47.
units.tr: John 3, etc. "Secondly," says Whitaker elsewhere, "although the testimonies of the Fathers do not establish faith, they nevertheless illustrate it; and so they are to be cited in addition, or, as John Reynolds puts it, for the sake of heaping up," citing Augustine, De Civitate Dei, bk. 18, c. 47.

units.la: Tertio, quanquam patrum testimonia fidem non faciunt, citanda tamen sunt in infirmorum fratrum gratiam: de quo Iohannes Reynoldus ita: Verbellem quidem itidem liceret in refutando, scriptura divinitus inspirata tantum uti, quae quaestionum omnium longe perfectissima norma est. 1. Tim. 3. 16. Sed quoniam eorum infirmitas subleuanda est, quorum palato cibus caelestis non est satis gratus nisi conditur confessione bonum: idcirco patrum testimonia attexenda sunt, ad exemplar caetus Hierosolymitani, Actor. 15. 25, qui ad fratrum Antiochiae degentium fidem confirmandam, diuinae sententiae asscriberunt suam: Pauli, qui ad animos dissentientium facilius inflectendos, Ecclesias sanctorum proponit pro exemplo 1. Corin. 14. 33. & ad Paganos persuadendos, Aratí carmen citat, Actor. 17. 28.
units.tr: "Thirdly, although the testimonies of the Fathers do not establish faith, they are nevertheless to be cited for the sake of weaker brethren." On this, John Reynolds writes: "I could indeed in refuting them use Scripture alone, which is divinely inspired and is by far the most perfect rule of all questions (1 Tim. 3:16). But since their weakness must be relieved, those for whom heavenly food is not pleasant enough unless it is seasoned with a little human confession, therefore the testimonies of the Fathers are to be added, after the example of the council of Jerusalem (Acts 15:25), which, to confirm the faith of the brethren living at Antioch, attributed its own judgement to the divine sentence; and of Paul, who, to bend the minds of dissenters more easily, sets the churches of the saints forward as an example (1 Cor. 14:33), and to persuade the pagans cites a verse of Aratus (Acts 17:28)."

units.la: Quarto quanquam patrum testimonia fidem non faciant; quando tamen cum adversariis eis (Papistas intellige & Hierarchicos) res est, qui patribus pugnant, non solum expedit, sed etiam necessarium est ut allegantur, uti Reynoldo atq; Chamiero visum. Hic posterior ita, Facit ad disputationis magnificentiam quando veritati non tantum necessaria oftenduntur abundare, sed & ea quae ad elegantiam conferunt: facit etiam ad historiae cerebritudinem, quum his ipsis quibus impugnatur veritas repugnat, & animi excidij fui, bincit: quae verba sunt Hilarij, non invenusta. Quid vero hec proHierarchicis? qui praeterquam quod a patribus vitiose arguit ad fidem obligandam: in ipso citandi modo peccant, idq; non uno modo.
units.tr: "Fourthly, although the testimonies of the Fathers do not establish faith, when we have to do with adversaries (I mean the Papists and the hierarchs) who fight against the Fathers, it is not only expedient but even necessary that they be alleged, as Reynolds and Chamier thought. The latter says: 'It contributes to the magnificence of the dispute when there is abundance not only of what is necessary to the truth, but also of what contributes to its elegance. It also contributes to the vigour of history when the very people by whom the truth is attacked are opposed to it, and bind themselves by their own failings'; these are the words of Hilary, not inelegantly put." But what has this to do with the hierarchs? They not only argue poorly from the Fathers to bind the faith, but in the very manner of citing them they err, and not in one way only.

units.la: Primo, rariores in eorum scriptis scripturae sunt, patres frequentiores: ita illustramenta ipso fundamento illis potiora sunt, contra disertissimam Augustini regulam, qui in disputationibus, non ornamenta sed documenta quaerenda dicit.
units.tr: "First, Scripture is rarer in their writings and the Fathers more frequent; thus illustrations are preferred to the foundation itself, contrary to Augustine's most eloquent rule, who says that in disputations one should seek not ornaments but proofs."

units.la: Secundo, patres saepe solos citant, absq; praevia scripturae luce, contra communem patrum ipsorum antiquorum praxim, de qua recte Chamierus. Veteres non ante patres citarunt, quam postquam solidum fundamentum per scripturas iecissent: hoc postquam fecissent, tum demum augumenta ab authoritate in extrema disputatione exponebant: Sic Theodoretus in dialogis, Gelasius adversus Eutychem, Leo Romanus ad Leonem Augustum: sic reliqui plaerique omnes.
units.tr: "Secondly, they often cite the Fathers alone, without any prior light from Scripture, contrary to the common practice of the ancient Fathers themselves, about which Chamier rightly says: The ancients did not cite the Fathers before they had laid a solid foundation through the Scriptures; only after doing this did they then at last set forth additions from authority in the final part of the dispute. So Theodoret in his Dialogues, Gelasius against Eutyches, Leo of Rome to the Emperor Leo; so almost all the rest."

units.la: Tertio, varias patrum atque hominum opiniones (ut in Bilsono, 1. Tim. 3. 17. exponente videre est) proponunt, & lectorum ambiguum relinquunt, quaenam pro certo recipienda sint.
