Hoc non immerito reprehendit in scholasticis Antonius Sadeel: quia ad Academicam inducendam potius facit (ab Augustino iugulatam) quam ad generandam fidem: & Iovinianum imitatur, cui haec objecit sanctus Hieronymus, quod non decertasset.
units.tr: "Thirdly, they set out the varied opinions of the Fathers and of men (as may be seen in Bilson, expounding 1 Tim. 3:17) and leave readers in doubt as to which ones are to be received as certain. Antonius Sadeel rightly reproaches the scholastics for this, because it tends rather to introduce Academic doubt (which Augustine throttled) than to generate faith; and they imitate Jovinian, to whom St Jerome objected that he had not contended."

units.la: Quarto & ultimo: Nunquam fere Augustinus patres citat, nisi quando ab adversariis provocatus erat, ipsis ad patrem per aliquem provocantibus. Facit hoc reformatis licitum,ut citent patres adversus Hierarchicos,qui ad patres provocant: Hierarchicis vero illicitum adversus reformatos, qui a patribus ad scripturas easque solas provocare vellent. Mulier quid mihi et tibi est, dixit olim Christus: sic nobis,cum hominibus,quid quaeso in causis fidei,negotii est? Referetur patrum testimonia adversus papistas: adversus nos ne produci quidem possunt,nisi ea illis tribuatur authoritas,quam tribuunt papistae, ut os invitis obthurare possint, qui hortos scripturis solis debetur.
units.tr: "Fourthly and lastly: Augustine almost never cited the Fathers except when he was challenged by adversaries who appealed to a father against him. It is lawful for us reformed to cite the Fathers against the hierarchs, who appeal to the Fathers; but for the hierarchs it is unlawful to use them against the reformed, who would appeal from the Fathers to Scripture, and to Scripture alone. 'Woman, what have I to do with you?' Christ once said; so what business, I ask, do we have with men in matters of faith? The testimonies of the Fathers will be brought against the Papists; against us they cannot even be produced, unless to them is granted that authority which the Papists grant, so that they may stop the mouths of the unwilling, which is due only to the gardens of Scripture."

units.la: 7 Quarto, sua erga patres honorificentia Hierarchici libertatem Christianam tollunt,nosque hominum servos fieri jubent,contra Apostolum 1.Cor.7.23. Nolite fieri servi hominum. Nam cum de scriptis iudicare, & quae in eisdem disciplicent libere rejicere, semper in Ecclesia Dei liberum fuit,ad calculos patrum ita nos jam revocant isti, ut nisi eorum authoritate nos constringi patiamur, indignum nos moliri facinus vociferentur. Canon Scripturae constitutus est (inquit Augustinus) secundum quem,de caeteris literis fidelium iudicemus. Rursus Obycere nobis soletis Cypriani literas & concilium. Quis autem nescit Episcoporum literas, & per sermonem forte sapientiorem cujuslibet in ea re peritioris, & per aliorum Episcoporum gravitorem authoritatem, doctorumque prudentiam, & per concilia licere reprehendi, si quid in eis forte a veritate deviatum est. Rursus,alijs testibus & testimonijs extra divinas scripturas juibus aliquid credeđum esse suadetur,tibi credere vel non credere liceat,quantum meriti ea ad faciendam fidem, vel habere,vel non habere perpenderis. Rursus: Noli meis literis quasi Canonicis scripturis deservire: sed in illis et quae non credebas,quum invenieris,incunctanter crede: in istis aut e,quod certi nō habebas,nisi certi intellexeris,noli firmi tenere. Rursus De Hilario & Cypriano,& Agrippino loquens: Hoc genus literarum ab authoritate Canonica destinguendi est:non enim sic leguntur,tanquam ex eis testimonia ita proferatur ut citra fidem intelligere licet.
units.tr: 7 "Fourthly, by their honouring of the Fathers the hierarchs destroy Christian liberty and command us to become slaves of men, contrary to the Apostle, 1 Cor. 7:23: Be not made slaves of men. For to judge the writings, and freely to reject whatever in them is discordant, has always been permitted in the Church of God; but these men now call us back to the verdicts of the Fathers in such a way that, unless we allow ourselves to be bound by their authority, they cry out that we are attempting an unworthy crime. The canon of Scripture has been established (says Augustine), according to which we judge the other writings of the faithful. Again, you are accustomed to object to us the letters and council of Cyprian. But who does not know that the letters of bishops may be reproved, and by the discourse perhaps of someone wiser and more skilled in the matter, and by the greater authority of other bishops, and the prudence of teachers, and by councils, if anything in them has perhaps strayed from the truth? Again: when other witnesses and testimonies outside the divine Scriptures are urged as deserving belief, it is permitted for you to believe or not believe them, weighing how much merit they have for establishing faith, or lacking it. Again: Do not serve my letters as if they were canonical Scriptures; but in them, when you find things you did not believe, believe them without hesitation; and what you did not hold as certain, unless you understand it as certain, do not hold firmly. Again, speaking of Hilary, Cyprian and Agrippinus: This kind of letter is to be distinguished from canonical authority; for they are not read as if testimonies were drawn from them in such a way that one may understand without faith.

units.la: Cont. cref. Gram.l.2. c.32. Epist.126. ad evagr. Dialog.5. Apol. Cathol.p.2.1.2 s.18. Shrv.c.27. praeteà. Ist.p.144 ...
units.tr: Against the Crefeld Grammar, bk. 2, c. 32. Epistle 126 to Evagrius. Dialogue 5. Apology of the Catholics, p. 2, sec. 18. Shrove, c. 27. Moreover, Ist. p. 144...

units.la: Citat & alia Thomas Mortonus Hierarchicus, quibus nititur probare, libere legenda sanctorum patrum scripta esse, & rejicienda, quando cum veritate non consentiunt. Quid ni igitur cum Apostolo non argumentaretur? Nos soli libertatem non habemus, quam omnes habent 1 Cor. 9.6. Respondet Bancroftus & Downamus, nos hac abuti libertate: urgent patres (inquit) strenue cum eis favere videntur, et cum eorum libidini adversantur, tum eos nullo numero habent. At ex trivio Papistico acceptum istud convitium est. Dixerat Lutherus olim contestatos esse volo me prosus nullis, quantumvis sanctis patris authoritate cogi velle, nisi quatenus iudicio divinae Scripturae fuerit probatus. Si huic sententiae non subscribant Hierarchici, in papistarum castra transeunt: si subscripserint nos liberarunt, & hoc convitium in proprios humeros suscepepunt: Quid enim apud Papistas solem, qua nos patres nuncmagni facere, nunc nihili, pro haeresis nostrae comodo, & patres subfevulas nostras vocare pro libito nostros: nos denique patres pro semipatribus, tantum habere: quod non ut ipsi eos totos sequamur, eorum doctrinam (non alia ex parte admittentes, alia repudiantes) integram complectentes.
units.tr: The hierarch Thomas Morton also cites other things, on which he relies to prove that the writings of the holy Fathers are to be read freely and rejected when they do not agree with the truth. Why then should he not argue with the Apostle: We alone do not have the liberty which all have (1 Cor. 9:6)? Bancroft and Downame reply that we abuse this liberty: they press the Fathers vigorously (he says); when these seem to favour them, and when they oppose their lust, then they count them as nothing. But this insult is taken from the Papist crossroads. Luther once said: I want it to be witnessed that I am wholly unwilling to be compelled by the authority of any saints, however holy, except insofar as they have been proved by the judgement of divine Scripture. If the hierarchs do not subscribe to this opinion, they pass over to the Papist camp; if they subscribe, they have set us free, and have taken this insult upon their own shoulders. For what else is it among the Papists, to make the Fathers now of great account for us, now of no account, according to the advantage of our heresy, and to call the Fathers our sub-servants at pleasure, and at last to hold the Fathers as half-fathers, so much that we do not follow them wholly, embracing their whole doctrine (admitting some parts and rejecting others).

units.la: Quinto, prae sua erga patres honorificentia Hierarchici honoris quem fratribus debent, imo praecipuis Ecclesiae reformatae luminibus, oblivisci untur, ut in quos horrenda multa ejaculentur. Quod etenim Sculungius Puritani cum patribus omnem authoritatem adimunt sibi ipsis nullam relinquunt: id ab Hadriano Saravia hausit, cuius eadem verba sunt: Quisquis patribus omnem authoritatem admit ipse sibi nullam relinquit: quod multo tolerabilius est, quam illud Dovnami. Qui patribus fidem denegat ipse sibi nullam meretur. Fidem etenim scripturae soli conservant omnes: quam fidem historicam requirit Meridithus Hanmerus, eam libentur historicis damus, sub illa quam proponit, iudicandi libertate. Hanc tollit Dovnamus in re Episcopalis sic probabilibus conjecturis nos obstringit: probabilia etenim tantumodo patres dare possunt, quibus certitudo nulla subest, quia semper illud Philosophi axioma verum est. Quaedam falsa, sunt probabilitera, quil uf dam vera. Quod de Episcopo verissimum, Quod vero Saravia de authoritate omnia a nobis patribus ademta dicit: verum quidem est, nos cum Iohanne Iuello, non vereri affirmare: Iudicis patrum, a se, & sola, sine ulteriori authoritate, & verbi divini directione, non semper authoritamenta sufficientia sunt ad fidem nostram vel imperandam vel impetrandam. Probat ex ipsis patribus, qui scripturis solis fidem nostram pendere dicunt: quam solam authoritatem fi Scripturis Hierarchici admunt nullam certe nec sibi, nec patribus relinquunt, juxta illud in jure Canonico ab Augustino desumptum: Qui divina testimonia non sequuntur, pendus humani testimonij perdiderunt.
units.tr: Fifthly, in their great respect for the fathers, the hierarchists forget the honour of the hierarchy that they owe to their brethren, indeed to the chief lights of the reformed Church, and so they hurl horrible charges at them. Sculungius took the phrase The Puritans, by denying all authority to the fathers, leave themselves none from Adrian Saravia, whose words are Whoever grants the fathers no authority leaves himself none. This is much more tolerable than Dovnam's He who denies faith to the fathers deserves none himself. For everyone keeps faith in Scripture alone. The historical faith that Meredith Hanmer requires we willingly give to historians, under that liberty of judgment which he proposes. Dovnam, in the question of episcopacy, binds us to such probable conjectures, for the fathers can give only probable things, which have no certainty, since that saying of the Philosopher is always true: Some false things are probable, and some true things are probable. What he says of the bishop is most true. As for Saravia's claim that all authority has been taken from the fathers by us, it is true indeed, and we do not hesitate, with John Jewel, to affirm: The judgments of the fathers, taken by themselves and alone, without further authority and the direction of the divine word, are not always sufficient to impose or to obtain our faith. He proves this from the fathers themselves, who say that our faith depends on Scripture alone. If the hierarchists take this sole authority away from Scripture, they certainly leave neither themselves nor the fathers any, according to that saying taken into canon law from Augustine: Those who do not follow the divine testimonies have lost the support of human testimony.

units.la: Secundo, nos Iuliano haeretico aequiparat Bancroftus: adversus quem sic Augustinus Usque adeo permisit ima summis longus dies, tenebrae adeo in lucem & lux in tenebras verse sunt, ut videant Pelagius, Cclestius, Iulianus, & caeci sint Hylarius, Cyprianus, Ambrosius? Cont. Pelag. lib.2.c.10. Sed male in nos, nec superbos, nec errantes, sed a patribus ad scripturas provocentes hoc intorquetur: quod recte ab Augustino in Iulianum objectum est, scripturis adeque ac ipsis patribus destitutum: male etiam Augustini exemplo se retegunt Hierarchici, qui patres contra Iulianum non citavit, nisi postquam sententiam suam apertis Scripturis confirmasset. Spirat igitur hoc convitium, amarorem Papisticum illum, qui Lutherum profanitatis condemnavit, quod fi mille Cyprianos, mille Augustinos non curare dixerat. Defendit hac ex parte Lutherū Hierarchicus ipse Richardus Fyldus: quidni nos igitur in Luthero eandem veritatis causam agentes, ab hac Bann. rofti ac- cusatione plane eadem absolvamur?
units.tr: Secondly, Bancroft equates us with the heretic Julian, against whom Augustine says: So far has the long day made the lowest the highest, and the darkness so turned into light and the light into darkness, that Pelagius, Celestius and Julian see, while Hilary, Cyprian and Ambrose are blind? (Against Pelagius, book 2, ch. 10.) But this is wrongly twisted against us, who are neither proud nor erring, but who appeal from the fathers to the Scriptures. What Augustine rightly objected to Julian, that he was destitute of Scripture just as much as of the fathers, is not applicable to us. The hierarchists also reveal themselves wrongly by Augustine's example, since he did not cite the fathers against Julian until he had first confirmed his own opinion by plain Scriptures. This insult therefore breathes that Papist bitterness which condemned Luther for profanity because he said that he did not care about a thousand Cyprians or a thousand Augustines. Richard Field, the hierarchist himself, defends Luther in this respect. Why then should we, pursuing the same cause of truth in Luther, not be absolved entirely of this accusation of Bancroft's?

units.la: Tertiò, nos patres pro idiotis habere, nos ipsos solos doctos putare dicit Dovnamus: Refutator (inquit) illiusque soci, annis 1400. immo quod ad patrum nonnullos 1500. minores: patres tanquam idiotas condem- nant: quasi non vidissent quod ipsi scilicet docti videntur. Minor quia fronte, vel qua conscientia potius, haec dicere refutator potuit? Sed mirandum magis, non videre Dovnamum, Bernardum minime idiotam fuisse, quantumvis (ut in Proverbio dicitur) non viderit omnia. Atque hunc Bernardum, se solum doctum existimasse, quaeso sequetur, quod rivos commentariorum delpexerit, & ad scripturas interpretandas, in scripturis solis meditandis se exercuerit, nullis aliis magistris, prae- ter quercus & fagos, usus, Augustinus (inquit Iohannes Reynoldus) contra Hieronymum epist. 19. praefuisse multorum patrum testimonijs, ab eis omnibus provocat ad Paulum: Ab eis omnibus inquit qui aliud sentiunt, litterarum tractatoribus provoca ad ipsum Apostolum. Dent veniam quilibet aliud opinantes, ego magis credo tanto Apostolo juranti, ecce per Christum non mentior. Superbus jam Dovnamo Augustinus erit, & se solum doctum sentiens? certe durior hic quam ipse Torrensis apud eundem: qui licere dissentire a patribus, dummodo id modeste fiat: ita enim arguit ac si nulla a patribus dissensio fieri possit, nisi superba & immodesta.
units.tr: Thirdly, Dovnam says that we regard the fathers as idiots and think ourselves alone learned: "The Refuter (he says) and his fellows condemn the fathers, some 1400 years and more ago, as idiots, as if they had not seen that they themselves seem learned." With what forehead, or rather with what conscience, could the refuter say this? But it is more remarkable that Dovnam does not see that Bernard was by no means an idiot, however much (as the proverb says) he did not see everything. And if this Bernard thought himself alone learned, I ask, does it follow that he despised the streams of commentaries, and that he exercised himself in interpreting Scripture by meditating on Scripture alone, using no other teachers except oaks and beeches? Augustine, says John Reynolds, in his letter 19 against Jerome, though supported by the testimonies of many fathers, appeals to Paul against them all: "From all of them," he says, "who think otherwise, I appeal to the Apostle himself, the writer of the letters. Let anyone who thinks otherwise pardon me; I believe more the Apostle, who swears: Behold, before God, I do not lie." Will Augustine now be proud, to Dovnam, and feel himself alone learned? Certainly this is harsher than Torrensis himself, in the same place, who allows dissent from the fathers, provided it is done modestly. For he argues as if no dissent from the fathers could occur except a proud and immodest one.

units.la: 9 Quarto, objicit Dovnamus intollerabilem impudentiam. Observetur inquit, tanquam intollerabilis impudentiae indicium, in materia facti tam scriptura confusa (Titum nempe & Timotheum Episcopos fuisse.) quenquam fidem denegare, constanti, generali, perpetuoque consensui, antiquorum scriptorum, quorum nonnulli annos 1300. vel etiam 1400. ante annos dixerunt. Sed Titum & Timotheum Episcopos fuisse res non confusa sed scripturis contraria est, ut suo loco demonstrabitur: quo respectu si nos impudentes qui homines, quid tum Paulus, qui ne Angelos quidem audiendos existimavit? unde sic Chrysostomus: Etiam Angelis praeponit scripturas. Nam Angeli sunt servi, at Scriptura non a servis, sed a Domino Deo ipso venit ad nos. Consonat huic, quod habet Iuellus. Ad intelligendas scripturas, opus nonnunquam patrum pru- dentia habemus: sed non tamen major illis fides habenda est, quam quae expedit, aut quam ipsi oblatum, recipere vellent. Vere de eis omnibus quod Seneca olim in causa simili dicere possumus. Non sunt Domini, sed duces nostri.
units.tr: Fourthly, Dovnam objects to us "intolerable impudence." "Let it be noted," he says, "as a sign of intolerable impudence, that anyone, in a matter of fact so confused in Scripture (namely, that Titus and Timothy were bishops), should deny faith to the constant, general and perpetual consensus of the ancient writers, some of whom spoke 1300 or even 1400 years ago." But that Titus and Timothy were bishops is not a confused matter but one contrary to Scripture, as will be shown in its place. If we are impudent in this respect, what of Paul, who did not think even Angels should be heard? Hence Chrysostom: "He puts the Scriptures even before Angels. For Angels are servants, but Scripture comes to us not from servants but from the Lord God himself." What Jewel has is consistent with this: "For understanding the Scriptures we sometimes need the prudence of the fathers; yet no greater faith is to be placed in them than what is useful, or than they themselves would wish to receive when it is offered." Truly, of all of them we can say what Seneca once said in a similar case: "They are not our masters, but our guides."

units.la: Quinto, accusamur novitatis: sic enim Dovnamus: Hominem fidem omni antiquitati in materia facti denegare aperta demonstratio est, eum novitati potius & singularitati, quam veritati esse addictum. At Episcopum Hierarchicum ab initio fuisse, & ab Apostolis profectum, non obstante antiquitate, rem esse novam, absque novitatis studio iudicare liceat: nam & noua partes antiquos introducere potuisse, ostendit Vincentius Lyrinensis, qui authoritatem Cypriani, Caecilii Africani, aliorumque patrum qui fauebant rebaptizationi, ita reiecit: Quis fuit exitus illius disputationis? relicta est antiquitas, explosa novitas.
units.tr: Fifthly, we are accused of novelty, for Dovnam says: "That a man denies faith to all antiquity in a matter of fact is a clear demonstration that he is addicted to novelty and singularity rather than to truth." But that the hierarchical episcopate was there from the beginning and proceeded from the Apostles, despite antiquity, is a new thing, and one may judge this without any zeal for novelty. For that new parties could introduce things against the ancients is shown by Vincentius Lyrinensis, who rejected the authority of Cyprian, Caecilius of Africa and the other fathers who favoured rebaptism, thus: What was the outcome of that dispute? Antiquity was kept, novelty was driven out.

units.la: Sexto, intolerabilem nos esse exclamat Dominus & minime ferendos: sic enim habet, postquam generalem antiquitatis consensum pro Tito & Timotheo, Episcopis intulisset: Diuo intolerabilem audaciam & arrogantiam esse, contrarium afferre. At si temporibus ipsorum Patrum vixissset, inconsulta audacia ipse condemnatus fuisset, quod non scriptura sola contentus, partes & antiquitatem crepuerit: sic enim Iustinus Martyr: Dixi tibi sedulo te operam dare debere, tutus ut sis in omnibus, ut scripturis inhaereas. Aliis te dicentem non sustinuissemus.
units.tr: Sixthly, Dovnam cries out that we are intolerable and not to be borne. For he says, after having put forward the general consensus of antiquity for the bishops Titus and Timothy: It is an intolerable audacity and arrogance to bring forward the contrary. But if he had lived in the times of the fathers themselves, he would have been condemned for reckless audacity, because, not content with Scripture alone, he cried up parties and antiquity. Thus Justin Martyr: I told you earnestly that you ought to take pains to be secure in all things, to cling to the Scriptures. We would not have tolerated you saying otherwise.

units.la: Septimo, patres contemnere dicimur: ac si salua patrum honorificentia, non iam hodie, perinde ac olim, quae perperam patres scripserint, reici queant. Sic Augustinus: Neque quorumlibet disputationes quamuis Catholicorum & cordatorum hominum, belut scripturas canonicas habere debemus, ut nobis non liceat saluo honorificentia quae illis debetur hominibus aliquid in eorum scriptis improbare, & repuerre, si forte inuenerimus quod aliter senserant, quam veritas habet, diuino adjutorio, vel ab illis intellecta vel a nobis. Praecipuum in causa Hierarchica haec habent locum: quum Episcopatus enormem eminentiam plus videre nequiret, quam ipsum Antichristum, cuius embrio erat: qua in causa id iam dicimus, quod Whitakerus: Videmus patribus hac in re non esse multum tribuendum, qui tam incerta, futilia, absurda de Antichristo tradiderunt. Absit ergo ut illi hac in re nobis fucum faciant. Patribus quidem id tribuendum est, quod merentur, sed non dicendum ut ille. Malo cum patribus errare, quam cum aliis verum sentire.
units.tr: Seventhly, we are said to despise the fathers, as if, with their honour preserved, what they wrote amiss could not now be rejected any more than formerly. Thus Augustine: Nor must we hold the disputations of any men, however Catholic and wise, as if they were canonical Scripture, so that we may not, with the honour owed to those men, disapprove and reject anything in their writings, if perhaps we find that they thought otherwise than the truth is, whether it was understood by them or by us, with divine help. The hierarchists hold these points in the chief place in their cause: since the episcopate, unable to see its own enormous pre-eminence, could see no more than Antichrist himself, of whom it was the embryo. In this matter we say what Whitaker says: We see that little is to be attributed to the fathers in this matter, who handed down such uncertain, trifling and absurd things about Antichrist. Far be it, therefore, that they should impose on us in this matter. What is due to the fathers is indeed to be given them as they deserve, but not to be said as he says: I would rather err with the fathers than be right with others.

units.la: Octavo & ultimo, ecquid aliud aduersus nos habent Hierarchici quod objiciant, quam quod nuda sanctorum patrum testimonia, a scripturis destituta reiiciamus? Imo inquit Whitgiftus & Bancroftus: Patres comitio impetitnam dicit Cartwrightus, nos in fossis roftrare quando patres allegamus. Quid ni diceret, scripturas fontipatres in earum comparatione, fossis, & cisteris aequiparando, praesertim cum ad rem salsam comprobandam afferuntur? Certe monet Gregorius Nazianzenus: [illas in coeno immorari & luto adhaerescere, qui non contendunt ad purissimam scripturarum divinarum fontem.] Sic Lactantius: [Quoniam multae haereses extiterunt, determinanda nobis est veritas & in suo proprio domicilio collocanda: ut si quis aquam vitae cupiat haurire, non ad detritos lacus deferatur, qui non habent venam, sed uberrimum Dei noverit fontem, quo irrigatus, perenni luce potiatur.] Sic Ruffinus [Ex fontibus verbi Dei in libris Canonicis patefactis, haurienda sunt pocula.] Similiter Iebamus in Symbolo, Lucius.
units.tr: Eighthly and lastly, do the hierarchists have anything else to object against us, except that we reject the bare testimonies of the holy fathers, destitute of Scripture? Indeed, say Whitgift and Bancroft: Cartwright says that the fathers are a crowd of sorts; we stick in ditches when we cite the fathers. Why should he not say so, equating the fathers with ditches and cisterns in comparison with the fountains of Scripture, especially when they are brought forward to prove a false thing? Certainly Gregory Nazianzen warns: [those who do not strive towards the purest fountain of the divine Scriptures linger in mud and cling to the slime]. Thus Lactantius: [Since many heresies have arisen, the truth must be defined and placed in its own home, so that if anyone wishes to draw the water of life, he is not led to worn-out lakes, which have no vein, but may know the abundant fountain of God, by being watered from which he may enjoy perpetual light.] Thus Rufinus: [From the fountains of God's word, opened in the canonical books, the cups are to be drawn.] Similarly Iebamus in the Symbolo, Lucius.

units.la: Lib. 4. c. 4. fionis Synodus, ut universo Patrum consensui in materia facti fidem denegët? Certe, idque ea in Patres acerbitate, quae in nostrarum scriptis nullibi reperitur, ita enim habet. Incertum est an Petro ex urbe fugienti aperuerit Christus & ea dixerit quae narrat Egesippus. De excidio Hierosolym. lib. 3. cap. 2. Ambrosius, & Gregorius ut fortasse Athanasius fabulam ex Egesippo hauserunt. Rursus: Plerique patrum alia loquuntur, reliqui audita & fama recepta narrant, quae nihil probant praeter incertam famam. Irenaeus de Petro tantum quae fama divulgata dedit. Eusebius nihil praeter audita loquitur. Arnobius non aliter narrat quam alij, a quibus ea prius acceperat. Epiphanius de Petro traditionem deterrem memoriae pandit. Chrysostomus & Orosius, audita tantum narrant. Omitto reliqua: haec satis ostendunt non minus quam nos quandoque Hierarchicos patres rejicere: in hoc tantum discrimen est, cum a scripturis & veritate discedunt patres tum eos nos relinquimus, illi vero, cum vere sentiunt, & secundum scripturas docent. Atque hoc in citandis patribus, errarum Hierarchicum primum est, nempe quod patribus nimiam authoritatem tribuat.
units.tr: Lib. 4. c. 4. ...the synod, so as to deny faith to the unanimous consensus of the Fathers on a matter of fact? Certainly, and with such bitterness toward the Fathers as is found nowhere in our writings. For this is what they say: "It is uncertain whether Christ revealed himself to Peter as he fled from the city and said the things that Hegesippus recounts (De excidio Hierosolymitano, bk. 3, ch. 2). Ambrose and Gregory, and perhaps Athanasius, drew the story from Hegesippus." Again: "Most of the Fathers say other things; the rest relate what they heard and received by report, which proves nothing beyond an uncertain rumour. Irenaeus gives only what was spread abroad by report about Peter. Eusebius says nothing except what he heard. Arnobius relates no differently than others from whom he had earlier received it. Epiphanius sets out a tradition of Peter that is worse than tedious. Chrysostom and Orosius relate only what they heard." I pass over the rest. These examples sufficiently show that the Hierarchical Fathers are sometimes rejected by us no less than by them. There is only this difference: when the Fathers depart from Scripture and truth, we abandon them, but they, when they think rightly, teach in accordance with Scripture. And this is the first error of the Hierarchicals in citing the Fathers: that they attribute to the Fathers an excessive authority.

units.la: CAP 13. Erratum Hierarchicorum secundum quod patres fictitios reformatis obtrudunt.
units.tr: CAP 13. The error of the Hierarchicals, by which they foist fictitious Fathers on the Reformed.

units.la: Secundum sequitur: quod Patres fictitios in scenam producant. Dixit Adrianus apud Iurisconsultos: Testibus non testimonijs credendum est: quis igitur nobis difficilem laborem objectum negat, quibus non solum cum testimoniis falsis, verumetiam cum falsis testibus est conflictandum. Quanquam enim causam prodat famefica, umbras Patrum, instar patrum veterum, consectati: ea tamen Hierarchicorum audacia est, ut etiam falsis patrum nominibus imperitis imponere non verentur.
units.tr: The second follows: that they bring fictitious Fathers onto the stage. Hadrian said among the jurists: "One must believe witnesses, not testimonies." Who therefore denies that we face a difficult task, since we must contend not only with false testimonies but also with false witnesses? For although the deadly cause betrays itself, the Hierarchicals, pursuing the shadows of the Fathers as if they were old Fathers, have such audacity that they do not hesitate to impose false names of the Fathers even on the unlearned.

units.la: Primus autem, quo nituntur suppositus scriptor, author libri illius est, cui nomen inscribitur Canones Apostolorum, quem pro primate Episcoporum & Archiepiscoporum citat Thomas Bilsonus de perpet. Eccles. gubernat. cap. 14. pag. 385. Hadrianus Saravia cont. Bez. de diverti. minist. grad. c. 20. p. 192. & Georgius Domnanus Defens. Lib. 2. Pag. 13. & c. 7. p. 138. 139.
units.tr: The first writer on whom the spurious author relies is the author of the book entitled The Canons of the Apostles. Thomas Bilson cites it for the primacy of bishops and archbishops (De perpetua Ecclesiae gubernatione, ch. 14, p. 385), as do Hadrian Saravia (against Beza, On the Diversity of Ministerial Grades, ch. 20, p. 192) and George Downame (Defence, bk. 2, p. 13, and ch. 7, pp. 138–139).

units.la: Primo, huncine librum a Gelasio & 70. Episcopis in concilio Romano habito condemnatum fuisse, vel ipsi inficiari nequeunt: Respondet Saravia. Quod Gelasius titulum damnavit, nec habere titulum Apostolorum canones voluit, non idcirco singulos reiecit, cum ipsi inter suos canones, Patres inseruerit. Dovvnamus vero viros nostros aliquot iudiciosos, multum hallucinatos fuisse, quasi a iure Canonico, & ab Isidoro hoc canones condemnatos fuerint: cum distinctionis decimae sextae praecipuus scopus sit, verum Canonum auctoritatem quaerere, quanquam non ut scriptura. vum Canonicarum, tamen ut authenticorum Canonum: Vt de distinctione hac 16, nihil dicam: si hac distinctione non condemnentur, à jure tamen Canonico condemnantur. Quid enim de distinctione 15. dices? Titulus ibi tantum libri condemnatur, inquit Sarav a, non Canones ipsi: Inspiciantur igitur verba ipsa Gelasij. Quæ ab hæreticis vel a schismaticis, conscripta vel prædicata sunt, nulla tenus recipit Catholica & Apostolica Ecclesia Romana: è quibus pauca quæ ad memoriam venerunt & a Catholicis vitanda sunt, credimus esse subdenda. In enumeratione vero subsequenti, liber iste Canon. Apostol. inter cæteros condemnatur. Non igitur titulus solum libri sed & liber ipse rejicitur, contra Sarav. & rejicitur, tanquam non recipiendus, imò tanquam vitandus contra Down. qui hunc librum minime à jure Canonico condemnatum dicit, sed authoritatem authenticorum Canonum illi relictam esse affirmat. Quomodo quæso hoc fieri potest, ut authentica illius authoris authoritas sit, qui impudentissimè personam Apostolorum induit? Quodsi titulus libri aliunde acceptus esset, vereque asseruisset Bilsonus, hunc librum ab aliis Canonem Apostolorum appellatum fuisse, quòd cum Apostolorum doctrina consentiat, aliquid esset. Atqui secus est: author ipse sub nomine Apostolorum hos Canones edidit: ut hæc testantur Canone 85. Libri nostri, & Acta nostra, id est Apostolorum: quibus verbis nonne ipsos Apostolos loquentes inducit, at si hij canones ab ipsis Apostolis fuissent editi; Certe sanior Bils. atq; Sarav. vel Bellar. ipse est, qui hanc fraudem & impostura usq; eo abominatur, ut affirmare non dubitaret non sine causa Gelasium numerasse Canones Apostolorum inter Apocrypha. Sic Bessarion apud Iuellum, de Sacrament: Eucharist: Licet hæc Clementis verba inter Apocryphas scripturas commemorare solent: placet tamen eis in præsentiarum tanquam veris assentiamur. Nempe impudentiæ esse putavit hunc librum citare sub Apostolorum nomine falso conscriptum, nisi pro præsenti supponeretur, cum verum Apostolorum fœtum esse. Downamus è contra, fœtum Apostolorum fictitium agnoscit, & tamen non citat solum, sed ad alios etiâ obligandos citat. Quanto melius Leo apud Iuellum. Apocryphæ scripturæ quæ sub nominibus Apostolorum multarum habent seminarium falsitatem, non solùm interdicenda, sed etiam penitus auferendæ atque ignibus tradendæ sunt. Quod dicit Saravia, Gelasium ex hoc libro Canones non nullos sumpsisse, ac proinde librum ipsum non condemnasse, falsum est: canones hic nonnulli satis boni sunt. quid tum? num quisque liber recipiendus aut utendus, quia nonnihil veri continet? imo è contra, quia veris hic falsa commixta sunt, ideo librum ipsum vetandum Gelasius, ignibus tradendum rectè Leo censuit.
units.tr: First, that this book was condemned by Gelasius and seventy bishops in a Roman council, they themselves cannot deny. Saravia replies that although Gelasius condemned the title and did not want the canons to bear the title of the Apostles, he did not on that account reject each canon, since he himself inserted the Fathers among his own canons. But Downame and some of our judicious men were greatly mistaken, as if these canons had been condemned by canon law and by Isidore; for the chief aim of the sixteenth distinction is to seek the authority of the canons, not indeed as of Scripture, but as of authentic canons. I say nothing about this sixteenth distinction: even if it does not condemn them, canon law does. For what will you say about the fifteenth distinction? Saravia says that only the title of the book is condemned there, not the canons themselves. Let us then look at the words of Gelasius: "Whatever has been written or preached by heretics or schismatics the Holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church in no way receives; of these, a few that have come to mind and must be avoided by Catholics, we believe should be added." In the list that follows, this book, the Canons of the Apostles, is condemned among the others. Therefore it is not only the title of the book that is rejected, but the book itself, contrary to Saravia; and it is rejected as not to be received, indeed as to be avoided, contrary to Downame, who says that this book was by no means condemned by canon law, but affirms that the authority of authentic canons was left to it. I ask, how can it be that the authority of that author should be authentic, who most shamelessly puts on the person of the Apostles? If the title of the book had been received from elsewhere, and Bilson had truly asserted that this book was called by others the Canon of the Apostles because it agrees with the teaching of the Apostles, it would be something. But it is otherwise: the author himself published these canons under the name of the Apostles, as the eighty-fifth canon bears witness: "Our books and our Acts, that is, of the Apostles." By these words does he not bring in the Apostles themselves speaking? And if these canons had been published by the Apostles themselves, certainly Bilson, Saravia or Bellarmine would be the more sensible men. It is rather Gelasius himself who so abhors this fraud and imposture that he did not hesitate to affirm that Gelasius had not without cause numbered the Canons of the Apostles among the Apocrypha. So Bessarion, as cited by Jewel, On the Sacrament of the Eucharist: "Although these words of Clement are usually reckoned among the Apocryphal Scriptures, it pleases us for the present to assent to them as true." Clearly he thought it impudent to cite this book, falsely written under the name of the Apostles, unless it were assumed for the present to be a true offspring of the Apostles. Downame, on the contrary, acknowledges the offspring of the Apostles to be fictitious, and yet not only cites it but cites it to bind others as well. How much better is Leo, cited by Jewel: "Apocryphal writings which under the names of the Apostles contain the seeds of much falsehood must not only be forbidden but utterly removed and handed over to the flames." As for what Saravia says, that Gelasius took some canons from this book and therefore did not condemn the book itself, that is false: some of these canons are quite good. So what? Is every book to be received and used because it contains some truth? On the contrary, because true things are mixed here with false, Gelasius rightly forbade the book itself, and Leo rightly judged it to be handed over to the flames.

units.la: Secundo, multos subditicios Canones hic reperiri si inficientur, ipsis sane Papistis deteriores Hierarchici sunt: cum hoc fateatur Cæsar Baronius, fateatur Sixtus Senensis, fateatur Lindanus: qui etiam
units.tr: Second, if they deny that many spurious canons are found here, the Hierarchicals are certainly worse than the Papists themselves, since Caesar Baronius admits this, Sixtus of Siena admits it, and Lindanus admits it, who also

units.la: Cont. 1. 2. cap. 20. Act. 1. p. 7 4 Hoc vero dum faciunt multiplici peccato se obstringunt.
units.tr: (Contra, bk. 1, ch. 20, Act. 1, p. 74). But in doing this they bind themselves with many sins.

units.la: Primò, absurditate, cuius eos ita coarguit Chrysostomus. Quomodo aliorum sententiam simpliciter sequi non absurdum? quum habeamus omnium exactissimam trutinam & gnomonem, ac regulam, divinarum inquam legum assertionem.
units.tr: First, with absurdity, of which Chrysostom convicts them thus: "How is it not absurd to follow simply the opinion of others, when we have the most exact balance, standard and rule of all, namely the assertion of the divine laws?"

units.la: Secundo, impietate in Deum, cuius eos ita idem coarguit. Quia progrediente tempore multi impegerunt, scripta sunt quae spiritus sanctus dictavit: vide quanti sit criminis non per ipsum auxilium velle proficere, Deum non putamus offendi quando ad alia convertimur.
units.tr: Second, with impiety toward God, of which the same writer convicts them thus: "Because as time went on many have fallen into error, the things which the Holy Spirit dictated have been written. See how great a crime it is to wish to make progress not through that very help, and we do not think God is offended when we turn to other things."

units.la: Tertio, superbia, cuius eos ita coarguit Basilius. Quod si fidelis sit dominus fideliaque sint eius mandata omnia, haud dubie, manifestissime a fide lapsus est, & crimen maximae superbiae vel a scripto recedere, vel non scriptum admittere.
units.tr: Third, with pride, of which Basil convicts them thus: "If the Lord is faithful and all his commands are faithful, then without doubt he has most plainly fallen from the faith, and it is the greatest crime of pride either to depart from the written word or to admit what is not written."

units.la: Quarto, sacrilegio, cuius eos ita coarguit Isidorus sicuti citatur à Billono: Is qui praeest, si praeter voluntatem Dei, vel praeter quod in sacris scripturis evidenter praecipitur, vel dicit aliquid vel imperat, tanquam falsus testis Dei, & sacrilegus habeatur.
units.tr: Fourth, with sacrilege, of which Isidore convicts them, as cited by Bilson: "He who presides, if he says or commands anything against the will of God, or beyond what is plainly commanded in the holy Scriptures, is to be regarded as a false witness of God and a sacrilegious person."

units.la: Quinto, praesumptione, cuius eos ita coarguit Augustinus. Sancta Scriptura nostrae doctrinae regulam figit, ne audeamus sapere, plus quam oportet. Non sit aliud mihi te docere nisi verba tibi doctoris exponere. Ubi de re obscurissima disputatur, non adjuvantibus divinaris scripturarum certis clarisque documentis, cohibere se debet humana praesumptio.
units.tr: Fifth, with presumption, of which Augustine convicts them thus: "Holy Scripture fixes the rule of our teaching, so that we do not dare to be wiser than we ought. Let it not be my aim to teach you anything except to expound the words of your teacher. Where a matter most obscure is disputed, and without the help of the certain and clear documents of the divine Scriptures, human presumption must restrain itself."

units.la: Sexto, garrulitate cuius eos ita coarguit Hieronymus: Sine scriptu-rarum authoritas garrulitate non habet fidem.
units.tr: Sixth, with garrulousness, of which Jerome convicts them thus: "The authority of writings without Scripture has no credit with garrulity."

units.la: Septimò & ultimo, haeresi, cuius eos ita coarguit Alphonsus a Castro: Qui tam leviter de haeresi pronunciant, non expendentes de qua re loquuntur, saepe sua ipsorum sagitta feriuntur, inciduntque in eam foveam quam parabant aliis. Nam velle humanas scripturas in divinarum ordinem connumerare, hoc verius ego dixerim haeresim, quia humanis scriptis dissere ineptum autumant, perinde ac divinis. Haeretici Puritani sunt (inquit Bancroftus) quod cum Aerio aesirmen Episcopi & presbyteri tollant: at potius Bancroftus ipse haereticus, tam leviter de haeresi pronuncians, inquit Alphonsus, quòd discrimen scripturae & patrum tollat: nam a patribus dissentire ineptum putat, perinde ac a scripturis. Accommodata etiam reliqua sunt ad clamores Hierarchicos reliquos refutandos. Quod enim nos absurdos clamant, superbos, arrogantes, sacrilegos, impudentes, quando nudas patrum authoritates repudiamus: id in eorum capita recidit, quum scriptura sola divina non contenti, patres accersendos autumant.
units.tr: Seventh and last, with heresy, of which Alphonsus à Castro convicts them thus: "Those who pronounce so lightly about heresy, without weighing what they are talking about, are often struck by their own arrow and fall into the pit they had prepared for others. For to wish to number human writings among the divine ones, I would more truly call this heresy, since they think it foolish to dissent from human writings just as from divine ones. The Puritans are heretics" (says Bancroft) "because they remove the Bishops and presbyters together with Aerius. But rather Bancroft himself is a heretic, who so lightly pronounces about heresy" (says Alphonsus) "because he removes the difference between Scripture and the Fathers; for he thinks it foolish to dissent from the Fathers just as from Scripture." The rest also fit to refute the other Hierarchical clamours. "For when they cry out that we are absurd, proud, arrogant, sacrilegious, impudent, because we reject the bare authorities of the Fathers, that falls back on their own heads, since, not content with Scripture alone, they claim that the Fathers must be summoned."

units.la: Tertio, sua hac honorificentia erga partes Hierarchici, & suam in certam produnt, & aliorum fidem in incertitudinem pellunt.
units.tr: Third, by this honour of theirs toward their own party, they reveal their own faction, and they drive the faith of others into uncertainty.

units.la: 5 Recte olim Tertullianus. Fidei in regula posita est, cedat curiositas fidei, cedat gloria salutis. Nihil ultra regulam scire, omnia scire est. Vi-ta regulamvero fidem progredi Hierarchici volunt; qui fidem patribus adhibendam ita urgent, ut qui eis fidem denegarit, vix pro Christo Christiano fideli habeant. Vider e hoc est in Gerson. Dathn. qui in concione sua Lambethiana arguit pa: 29. Si omnis antiquitas Ario excepto, superioritatem Episcoporum agnoscit: cum superiores Episcopi fuerunt. Negat Refutator hanc consequentiam firmam esse: quid ille? Nemo hoc faceret (inquit) qui faciem Theologi, fere etiam dixerim, Christiani gerit. Hominem vero fidem omni antiquitati in materia facti, scriptura minime contradicente denegare, aperta demonstratio est, cum novitati & singularitati potius quam veritati additum esse. Testificatur omnis antiquitas unanimis consensu, Episcopos gradu in prima Ecclesia minoris reliquis superiores fuisse: & quis quam de nostris frontem habet, ut id verum esse deneget? Ligat vero haec omnia hoc conclusionis nodo. Hucusque de authoritate antiquitatis qua haec consequentia nititur. Quis non videt authoritatem hic patribus a se tributam? Fidem huic authoritati debitam requiri? quam qui denegat, non Christianus nisi impudentissimus habendus sit. Non impedit quod objicitur, scriptura minime contradicente: relinquitur adhuc etenim quaestio, ipsa scriptura contradicat necne, quam ille consensu antiquitatis ita praejudicatam vult, ut scripturam minime contradicere censendum sit, quando unanimis antiquitatis consensus concordat: relinquitur etiam fidem antiquitati necessario adhibendam esse, quando scriptura de re aliqua nihil dicit: non etenim in materia facti contradicere scriptura potest, quando nihil de eadem omnino dicit. Hoc vero quam absurdum dictu sit, a simili patefiet. Probat Bellarminus, Romanum pontificem Petri successorem esse a facto Petri, sedem Romae collocantis: hoc factum Petri (inquit) ab omni antiquitate comprobatur: nam & omnes patres affirmant Petrum Romae fuisse, & scriptura non contradicit: & ecquis frontem habet in materia facti, unanimi antiquori in omnium consensui denegare fidem? Similiter H. Saravia in facto primae Ecclesiae primatum Episcopatus Hierarchici ponit; ad hujus etenim probationem se accingens, ita inchoat. Episcopum reliquis minoribus superiorem esse, facillime erit probatu, si hoc mihi primum detur, quod omnis dat antiquitas, Apostolorum successores esse. Vides hic omnia paria: eundem etenim consensum totius antiquitatis habet Bellarminus, Petrum Romae fuisse, atque Saravia Episcopos Apostolorum fuisse successores. Accommodata igitur ad utrumque Calvini Whitakeri responsio est. Pontificia fides (sic Hierarchica) non potest esse ... cum fundamento patrum ita nisi tatur, & hujus primipium sit non divina sed humana authoritas. Velim hoc quibus perpendant: nam in eo aliquid momenti est. Possunt se ludere conjecturis non aute certa aliqua ... acquiescere. Quod de conjecturis dicitur, quem nullum fidei fundamentum entu praebeat, liquet vel ex ipso Aquinate, cujus ista verba sunt. Sacra doctrina philosophorum authoritatibus utitur tanquam extraneis & probabilibus: authoritate canonica fide tutus utitur, proprie ex necessitate argumentandi. Authoritatibus autem aliorum doctorum Ecclesiae utimur, non quasi argumentando ex propriis sed ex probabilibus. Initiatur fides nostra revelatione Apostolis ... stolis & Prophetis facta, qui canonicos libros scripserunt, non autem revelatione illa, si quæ fuerant aliis doctoribus facta. Allegatur sæpe a nostris Hi-Zanchius qui idem suam aliquatenus antiquitate niti dicit: at hoc ita explicat ipse Zanchius alibi. Qualis fuerit illa veteris & Apostolicæ Ecclesiæ forma tempore Christi & Apostolorum, liquido & certo apparet ex libris Evangelistarum & Apostolorum: probabiliter autem ex reliquis post Apostolos antiquissimis Ecclesiasticis scriptoribus. Quid igitur est? Fides Hiero. Zanchij aliquatenus quidem antiquitate nititur, sed non quasi certo fundamento, sed probabili tantummodo conjectura: sic vel a Zanchio suo discere Georgius Downamus potuerit, frontem Christianam gerere posse hominem eum, qui toti antiquitati fidem suam non adiunxerit. Quid enim? Probabilibus tantum conjecturis ita tenemur, ut eis credendum sit? Imo testimonia patrum extranea sunt (inquit Aquinas; non propria) & probabilitatem tanquam inducunt: at fides probabilibus non nititur, sed illi soli revelationi quæ scriptoribus canonicis facta est. ἑκάστῳ- ἐ& igitur Zanchio Aquinas est: cuius fides aliquatenus antiquitate nititur, etiamsi ea tantum probabilis sit: multo magis Dolmamo, qui fidem fere necessario in materia saltem facti ei adhibendam esse clamat. Aliter Whitakerus, qui de facto Petri Romam accedentis verba faciens, ab antiquitate tota comprobato, ita habet. Nemo papistiam religionem fide retinere aut sequi potest sed opinione tantum & conjectura, qua quod hujus religionis fundamentum est, sub fidem non cadit. Rursus, Niitur hoc totum fide humana & ex historica veritate pendet; at fides & religio nostra certiori testimonio niti debet, nempe testimonio Spiritus san-cti.
units.tr: 5 Tertullian long ago rightly said: The rule of faith is laid down; let curiosity give way to faith, let vainglory give way to salvation. To know nothing beyond the rule is to know everything. But the Hierarchicals want faith to advance beyond the rule. They press the Fathers so hard upon us that whoever denies them faith can scarcely be regarded as a Christian believer, let alone a faithful one for Christ. This can be seen in Gerson (Dathn.), who in his Lambeth sermon argues at p. 29: If all antiquity, Arius excepted, acknowledges the superiority of bishops, then bishops were superior. The Refuter denies that this inference is sound. What does he say in reply? "No one (he says) who bears the face of a theologian, I might almost say of a Christian, would do this." But that a man should deny faith to all antiquity on a matter of fact, where Scripture does not contradict it, is a plain demonstration of novelty and singularity rather than truth. All antiquity bears unanimous witness that in the earliest Church bishops were superior in rank to the other ministers, and which of us has the effrontery to deny that this is true? Yet he binds all of this together with a single knot of conclusion. So far, the argument rests on the authority of antiquity. Who does not see that authority is here ascribed to the Fathers, and that faith is required to be given to that authority, and whoever denies it must be regarded as nothing but a most shameless non-Christian? The objection that Scripture does not contradict it is no obstacle, for the question remains whether Scripture itself contradicts it, which he wants so prejudged by the consensus of antiquity that Scripture must be judged not to contradict it whenever the unanimous consensus of antiquity agrees. It also remains that faith must necessarily be given to antiquity whenever Scripture says nothing about a matter, for Scripture cannot contradict on a matter of fact when it says nothing at all about it. How absurd this is to say will be clear from a parallel. Bellarmine proves that the Roman pontiff is the successor of Peter from the fact that Peter fixed his see at Rome. This fact of Peter's (he says) is confirmed by all antiquity: for all the Fathers affirm that Peter was at Rome, and Scripture does not contradict it. And who has the face to deny faith to the unanimous consensus of all antiquity on a matter of fact? Similarly, H. Saravia places the primacy of the Hierarchical episcopate in the fact of the primitive Church. Setting himself to prove this, he begins thus: "It will be very easy to prove that a bishop is superior to the other lesser ministers, if this first point is granted me, which all antiquity grants, that bishops are the successors of the Apostles." You see here that all the cases are alike. Bellarmine has the same consensus of all antiquity that Peter was at Rome, and Saravia has the same that bishops were the successors of the Apostles. Therefore Calvin's and Whitaker's reply fits both equally: "Papist faith (or Hierarchical faith) cannot be ... when it rests on the foundation of the Fathers in this way, and its beginning is not divine but human authority." I would have people weigh this well, for there is some weight in it. They may amuse themselves with conjectures, not with anything certain ... to acquiesce. That conjectures, which provide no foundation of faith at all, are of this kind is clear even from Aquinas himself, whose words are these: "Sacred doctrine uses the authorities of the philosophers as external and probable; it uses the canonical authority with the certainty of faith, properly from the necessity of arguing. But we use the authorities of other teachers of the Church not as arguing from our own principles but from probable ones. Our faith is founded on the revelation made to the Apostles and Prophets, who wrote the canonical books, and not on that revelation, if any, made to other teachers." Our people often cite Hieronymus Zanchius, who says that his own faith rests in some measure on antiquity; but Zanchius himself explains this elsewhere: "What the form of the ancient and Apostolic Church was at the time of Christ and the Apostles is clear and certain from the books of the Evangelists and Apostles, but probably from the most ancient ecclesiastical writers after the Apostles." What, then, follows? The faith of Zanchius rests to some extent on antiquity, but not as on a certain foundation, only on a probable conjecture. From his Zanchius, George Downame could have learned this much, that a man who has not joined his faith to all antiquity can still bear a Christian face. For what? Are we bound by probable conjectures only, so that we must believe them? Nay, the testimonies of the Fathers are external (Aquinas says, not proper), and they bring in probability as it were; but faith does not rest on probabilities, only on that revelation which was made to the canonical writers. [ἑκάστῳ] Zanchius is therefore Aquinas's man, whose faith rests in some measure on antiquity, even if that antiquity is only probable. Much more is this so for Dolman, who cries out that faith must almost necessarily be given to antiquity at least on matters of fact. Whitaker speaks otherwise, when discussing Peter's coming to Rome, which is confirmed by all antiquity: "No one can hold or follow the Papist religion by faith, but only by opinion and conjecture, by which what is the foundation of this religion does not fall under faith." Again: "It rests on human faith and depends on historical truth; but our faith and religion ought to rest on a surer testimony, namely the testimony of the Holy Spirit."

units.la: 6 · Atque hæc si ita sint, inquies, authoritates patrum ne quidem omnino citandæ erunt: cui obiectioni, respondet Daniel Chamierus De Oecumenico Pontifice. in præfat: Guliel. Whitakerus cont. 1.q.6. c. 12. & Iohannes Reynoldus Censur: Apochryphor: Tom.1: præle&t.17. Quamquam itaque testimonia patrum nihil probent, aut afferre potuerint, ad fidem faciendam: non tamen probanda est (inquit Whitakerus) eorum sententia, qui patrum testimonia contemnenda ac rejicienda esse exi-stimant.
units.tr: 6 · And if these things are so, you will say, then the authorities of the Fathers are not even to be cited at all. Daniel Chamier, in the preface to On the Oecumenical Pontiff, answers this objection; so does William Whitaker, Contra 1, q. 6, c. 12; and John Reynolds, Censura Apocryphorum, vol. 1, lecture 17. Although the testimonies of the Fathers prove nothing, or could not be brought to make faith, yet (says Whitaker) the opinion of those who think that the testimonies of the Fathers are to be despised and rejected is not to be approved.

units.la: Primò, inquit Whitakerus, Patrum scripta scire perîti Theologi est: quamquam enim in foro contentioso eorum authoritas parum valeat, ignavia tamen quædam est aut superbia ignorare, quid quique patrum senserint. Hinc illa Socratis criminatio adversus Nestorium: Hoc illi præ infig-ni inscitia & ignoratione contigit, Nam tamsi natura, lingua erat diserta, & propterea de Itus putabatur, tamen revera imperitus fuit. Quinetiam veterum interpretum scripta perdiscere dedignatus est. Linguæ enim volubilitate & elegantia insolenter se efferens, cum veteres prope neglexit, tum seipsum omnibus antecessere existimavit.——Nestorius videtur veterum lucubrationes penitus ignorare: & ob eam causam banc vocem Deiparam (uti dixi) duntaxat insistatur. Secundo, quanquam patrum testimonia fidem non faciant, illustrant tamen inquit Whitakerus alibi : atq; ita citanda ex abundanti, sive ad cumulum ut loquitur Iohannes Rainoldus ex Augustino, de civitate Dei: lib. 18, c. 47.
units.tr: First, says Whitaker, to know the writings of the Fathers is the mark of a skilled theologian. Although their authority carries little weight in a contentious forum, it is a kind of laziness or pride to be ignorant of what each of the Fathers thought. Hence that accusation of Socrates against Nestorius: "This happened to him through remarkable ignorance and neglect. For although he was by nature eloquent in speech, and therefore was thought learned, he was in truth unlearned. Indeed he disdained to learn thoroughly the writings of the ancient interpreters. Proudly exulting in the fluency and elegance of his tongue, he neglected the ancients almost entirely, and thought himself superior to everyone." "Nestorius seems to have been completely ignorant of the labours of the ancients, and for that reason he insisted on this term Deipara (as I have said) alone." Secondly, although the testimonies of the Fathers do not make faith, they nevertheless illustrate, says Whitaker elsewhere; and so they are to be cited in abundance, or, as John Rainolds puts it, for the sake of accumulation, from Augustine, De civitate Dei, book 18, ch. 47.

units.la: Tertio, quanquam patrum testimonia fidem non faciunt, citanda tamen sunt in infirmorum fratrum gratiam: de quo Iohannes Reynoldus ita : Perbellem quidem itidem liceret in refutando, scriptura dispilds inspirata tantum uti, quae quaestionum omnium longe perfectissima norma est. 1. Tim. 3. 16. Sed quoniam eorum infirmitas subleuanda est, quorum palato cibus caelestis non est satis gratus nisi condiatur confinsione hominum : idcirco patrum testimonia attexenda sunt, ad exemplar caetus Hierosolymitani, Actor. 15. 25, qui ad fratrum Antiochiae degentium fidem confirmandam, diuinae sententiae asscripserunt suam; & Pauli, qui ad animos dissentientium facilius inflectendos, Ecclesias sancti orum proponit pro exemplo 1. Corin. 14. 33. & ad Paganos persuadendos, Arati carmen citat, Actor. 17. 28.
units.tr: Thirdly, although the testimonies of the Fathers do not make faith, they are nevertheless to be cited for the sake of weaker brethren. John Reynolds says of this: "I could indeed fittingly use only Scripture, inspired and alone, which is by far the most perfect rule of all questions, 2 Tim. 3.16. But since the weakness of those must be relieved whose palate does not find heavenly food pleasing unless it is seasoned with the opinions of men, therefore the testimonies of the Fathers are to be added, after the example of the assembly at Jerusalem, Acts 15.25, which, to confirm the faith of the brethren living at Antioch, added its own judgment to the divine sentence; and of Paul, who, to bend more easily the minds of dissenters, sets before them the churches of the saints as an example, 1 Cor. 14.33; and to persuade the pagans, quotes the poem of Aratus, Acts 17.28."

units.la: Quarto quanquam patrum testimonia fidem non faciant; quando tamen cum adversariis eis (Papistas intellige & Hierarchicos) res est, qui patribus pugnant, non solum expedit, sed etiam necessarium est ut allegantur, uti Reynoldo atq; Chamiero visum. Hic posterior ita, Facit ad disputationis magnificentiam quando veritati non tantum necessaria saepe abundare, sed & ea quae ad elegantiam conferunt: facit etiam ad historiae certitudinem, quum biis ipsis quibus impugnatur veritas repugnat, & animis excidii fui, vincit: quae verba sunt Hilarii, nō invenusta. Quid vero hec pro Hierarchicis? qui praeterquam quod a patribus vitiose arguit ad fide obligandam: in ipso citandi modo peccant, idq; non uno modo.
units.tr: Fourthly, although the testimonies of the Fathers do not establish faith, when we have to do with adversaries who oppose the Fathers (I mean the Papists and the Hierarchicals), it is not only expedient but necessary to cite them, as Reynolds and Chamier thought. The latter writes: "It serves the grandeur of a disputation when truth is abundantly supplied not only with what is necessary but also with what contributes to elegance. It also serves the certainty of history, since truth is contradicted by the very people it attacks, and, though it is wounded by its own weapons, it wins." These are the words of Hilary, and they are not without charm. But what do these words have to do with the Hierarchicals? Apart from the fact that they argue wrongly from the Fathers to bind faith, they err in the very manner of their citing, and in more than one way.

units.la: Primo, rariores in eorum scriptis scripturae sunt, patres frequentiores : ita illustramenta ipso fundamento illis potiora sunt, contra diversissimam Augustini regulam, qui in disputationibus, non ornamenta sed documenta quaerenda dicit.
units.tr: First, Scripture is rarer in their writings and the Fathers more frequent. So the illustrations are more important to them than the foundation itself, against the very different rule of Augustine, who says that in disputations one should seek not ornaments but proofs.

units.la: Secundo, patres saepe solos citant, absq; praevia scripturae luce, contra communem patrum ipsorum antiquorum praxim, de qua recte Chamierus. Veteres non ante patres citarunt, quam postquam fodidum fundamentum per scripturas iecissent: hoc postquam fecissent, tum denique augmenta ab authoritate in extrema disputatione exponebant: Sic Theodoretus in dialogis, Gelasius adversus Eutychem, Leo Romanus ad Leonem Augustum: sic reliqui plurimique omnes.
units.tr: Second, they often cite the Fathers alone, without any prior light from Scripture, contrary to the common practice of the ancient Fathers themselves, as Chamier rightly observes. The ancients did not cite the Fathers before they had first laid the foundation through the Scriptures. Only after they had done this did they at last bring forward the support of authority at the end of the disputation. So Theodoret in his Dialogues, Gelasius against Eutyches, and Leo of Rome to the Emperor Leo did, and so did all the rest, or nearly all.

units.la: Tertio, varias patrum atque hominum opiniones (ut in Bilsono, 1. Tim. 3. 17. exponente videre est) proponunt, & lectorum ambiguum relinquunt, quaenam pro certo recipienda sint. Hoc non immerito reprehendit in scholasticis Antonius Sadeel: quia ad Academicam inducendam potius facit (ab Augustino iugulatam) quam ad generandam fidem: & Iovinianum imitatur, cui haec objicit sanctus Hieronymus, quod non dpnsixxs decertasset. Quarto & ultimo: Nunquam fere Augustinus patres citat, nisi quando ab adversarijs provocatus erat, ipsis ad patrem per aliquem provocantibus. Facit hoc reformatis licitum,ut citent patres adversus Hierarchicos, qui ad patres provocant: Hierarchicis vero illicitum adversus reformatos, qui a patribus ad scripturas easque solas provocare vellent. Mulier quid mihi fecerit ut, dixit olim Christus: sic nobis,cum hominibus,quid quaeso in causis fidei,negotij est? Refertur patrum testimonia adversus papistas: adversus nos ne produci quidè possunt,nisi ea illis tribuatur authoritas,quam tribuunt papistae, ut os invitis obthurare possint, qui honos scripturis solis debetur.
units.tr: Third, they set out the varied opinions of the Fathers and of men (as may be seen in Bilson, expounding 1 Tim. 3.17), and leave the readers in doubt as to which are to be received as certain. Antonius Sadeel rightly criticised this in the scholastics, because it tends to introduce an academic scepticism (which Augustine had strangled) rather than to produce faith. They imitate Jovinian, whom St Jerome reproached because he had not fought with "Mulier quid mihi fecerit ut" [the Latin text is not reproduced here]. Fourthly and lastly: Augustine almost never cites the Fathers except when he was challenged by adversaries who appealed to a Father against him. This makes it lawful for the reformed to cite the Fathers against the Hierarchicals, who appeal to the Fathers, but unlawful for the Hierarchicals to do so against the reformed, who want to appeal from the Fathers to the Scriptures, and to the Scriptures alone. Christ once said, "Woman, what have I to do with you?" What, I ask, is the business of men, and of us, with questions of faith? The testimonies of the Fathers are brought forward against the Papists; against us they cannot even be produced, unless that authority is granted to them which the Papists grant, so that they may stop the mouths of the unwilling, an honour that is due to the Scriptures alone.

units.la: 7 Quartò, sua erga patres honorificentiâ Hierarchici libertatem Christianam tollunt,nosque hominum servos fieri jubent,contra Apostolū 1.Cor.7.23. Nolite fieri servi hominum. Nam cum de scriptis iudicare, & quae in eisdem disciplicent libere rejicere, semper in Ecclesia Dei liberum fuit,ad calculos patrum ita nos jam revocant isti, ut nisi eorum authoritate nos constringi patiamur, indignum nos moliri facinus vociferentur. Canon Scripturae constitutus est (inquit Augustinus) secundum quem,de caeteris literis fidelium iudicemus. Rursus Obycere nobis soletis Cypriani literas & concilium. Quis autem nescit Epistoporum literas, & per sermonem forte sapientiorem cuiuslibet in ea re peritioris, & per aliorum Episcoporum graviorum authoritatem, doctorumque prudentiam, & per concilia licere reprehendi, si quid in eis forte a veritate deviatum est. Rursus,alijs testibus & testimonijs extra divinas scripturas juibus aliquid credendum esse suadetur,sibi credere vel non credere liceat,quantum meriti ea ad faciendam fidem, vel habere,vel non habere perpenderis. Rursus: Noli meis literis quasi Canonicis scripturis deferbire: sed in illis & quae non credebas,quum invenieris,incunctanter crede: in istis auté,quod certū nō habebas,nisi certū intellexeris,noli firmū tenere. Rursus De Hilario & Cypriano,& Agrippino loquens: Hoc genus literarum ab authoritate Canonica destinguendū est: non enim sic leguntur,lunquā ex eis testimonia ita proferatur ut citra sentire non liceat subi forte aliter ahcubi fapuerunt quā veritas postulabat. Postremo,Ego hujus epistolae authoritate non teneor, qui literas Cypriani non ut Canonicas habeo sed ex Canonicis confidero,& quod in eis divinarum scripturarum authoritati convenit, cum ejus laude accipio, quod non congruit,cum ejus pace refuno. Hieronymus postquam patrum sententias de Melchisedecho collegerat,subjungit. Meum fuit citare thesis,tuum sit de fide testium judicare. Ad postremum, hortatur Theodoretus Eranisem: ut hortos patrum circumbulans, imitetur apes?quod bonum est, sumendo, quod noxim, relinquendo.
units.tr: 7 Fourthly, by their reverence for the Fathers the Hierarchicals take away Christian liberty and order us to become servants of men, contrary to the Apostle, 1 Cor. 7.23: "Be not made servants of men." For it has always been free in the Church of God to judge the writings and freely to reject whatever in them is discordant. Yet these men now call us back to the reckonings of the Fathers, so that, unless we allow ourselves to be bound by their authority, they cry out that we are attempting an outrageous crime. "The canon of Scripture has been established," says Augustine, "according to which we judge the other writings of the faithful." Again: "You are accustomed to throw in our face the letters and the council of Cyprian. But who does not know that the letters of bishops may be criticised, both by the wiser speech of anyone more skilled in the matter, and by the authority of other, weightier bishops, and by the prudence of teachers, and by councils, if anything in them has perhaps strayed from the truth?" Again: "Whether it is permitted to believe or not to believe other witnesses and testimonies outside the divine Scriptures, by which we are urged to believe something, you may weigh how much merit they have for making faith, whether to have it or not to have it." Again: "Do not bow down before my letters as if they were canonical Scripture; but in those things which you did not believe, when you have found them, believe without hesitation; in those, however, which you did not hold as certain, do not hold them firmly unless you have understood them to be certain." Again, speaking of Hilary, Cyprian and Agrippinus: "This kind of letters must be distinguished from canonical authority; for they are not read in such a way that testimonies are drawn from them so that it is not lawful to dissent from them, in case they perhaps thought otherwise elsewhere than truth required." Lastly: "I am not bound by the authority of this letter. I do not hold the letters of Cyprian as canonical, but I examine them by the canonical ones, and what agrees with the authority of the divine Scriptures I accept with praise of it; what does not agree I reject with its leave." Jerome, after he had gathered the opinions of the Fathers about Melchizedek, adds: "It was mine to cite the theses; let it be yours to judge the faith of the witnesses." Finally, Theodoret exhorts Eranistes: "Go round the gardens of the Fathers and imitate the bees; taking what is good, leaving what is harmful."

units.la: Citat & alia Thomas Mortonus Hierarchicus, quibus nititur probare, libere legenda sanctorum patrum scripta esse, & rejicienda, quando cum veritate non consentiunt. Quid ni igitur cum Apostolo non argumentaretur? Nos soli libertatem non habemus, quam omnes habent 1 Cor. 9. 6. Respondet Bancroftus & Downamus, nos hac abuti libertate : urgent patres (inquit) strenue cum eis favere videntur, at cum eorum lividini adversantur, tam eos nullo numero habent. At ex trivio Papistico acceptum istud convitium est. Dixerat Lutherus olim contestatus esse volo me profusissime nullis, quantumvis sanctis patris authoritate cogi velle, nisi quatenus iudicio divinae Scripturae fuerit probatus. Si huic sententiae non subscribant Hierarchici, in papistarum castra transeunt: si subscripserint nos liberarunt, & hoc convitii in proprios humeros suscepepunt: Quid enim apud Papistas solem, qua nos patres nunc magni facere, nunc nihili, pro haeresis nostra comodo, & patres subfervulas nostras vocare pro libito nostro: nos denique patres pro semipatribus, tantum habere: quod non ut ipsi eos totos sequamur, eorum doctrinam (non alia ex parte admittentes, alia repudiantes) integram complectentes.
units.tr: Thomas Morton, a Hierarchical, also cites other passages by which he tries to prove that the writings of the holy Fathers are to be read freely and rejected when they do not agree with the truth. Why then should he not argue with the Apostle: "We alone do not have the liberty which all have" (1 Cor. 9.6)? Bancroft and Downame reply that we abuse this liberty: "The Fathers press us hard," they say, "and seem to favour them; but when they oppose their own prejudices, they count them as of no account." But that insult is taken from the Papist crossroads. Luther once said: "I wish it to be solemnly declared that I by no means want to be compelled by the authority of any Fathers, however holy, except insofar as they have been approved by the judgement of divine Scripture." If the Hierarchicals do not subscribe to this opinion, they pass over into the camp of the Papists; if they do subscribe, they have set us free and have taken this insult upon their own shoulders. For among the Papists what else do we see but that they now make much of us Fathers and now nothing of us, according to the convenience of their heresy; that they call our Fathers sub-servants at their pleasure; and that, in short, they hold the Fathers as half-Fathers, so much that they do not follow them wholly, embracing their doctrine entire (not admitting some parts and rejecting others).

units.la: Quinto, praे sua erga patres honorificentia Hierarchici honoris quem fratribus debent, imo praecipuis Ecclesiae reformatae luminibus, oblivisci untur, ut in quos horrenda multa ejaculentur. Quod etenim Scultingius Puritani cum patribus omnem authoritatem adimunt sibi ipsis nullam relinquunt: id ab Hadriano Saravia hausit, cujus eadem verba sunt: Quisquis patrilus omnem authoritatem adimit ipse sibi nullam relinquit: quod multo tolerabilius est, quam illud Dovvnami. Qui patribus fidem denegat ipse sibi nullum meretur. Fidem etenim scripturae soli conservant omnes: quam fidem historicam requirit Meridithus Hanmerus, eam libentur historicis damus, sub illa quam proponit, judicandi libertate. Hanc tollit Dovvnamus in re Episcopali: sic probabilibus conjecturis nos obstringit: probabilia etenim tantum patres dare possunt, quibus certitudo nulla subest, quia semper illud Philosophi axioma verum est. Quaedam falsa, sunt probabilia, quaedam vera. Quod de Episcopo verissimum. Quod vero Saravia de authoritate omnia a nobis patribus ademta dicit: verum quidem est, nos cum Johanne Iuello, non vereri affirmare: Iudicia patrum, a se, & sola, sine ulteriori authoritate, & verbi divini directione, non semper authoramenta sufficientia sunt ad fidem nostram vel imperandam vel impetrandam. Probat ex ipsis patribus, qui scripturis solis fidem nostram pendere dicunt: quam solam authoritatem si Scripturis Hierarchici adimunt nullam certe nec sibi, nec patribus relinquunt, juxta illud in jure Canonico ab Augustino desumptum: Qui divina testimonia non sequuntur, pendus humani testimonij perdiderunt.
units.tr: Fifthly, in their reverence for the Fathers, the Hierarchicals forget the honour they owe to their brethren, indeed to the outstanding lights of the reformed Church, so that they hurl at them many horrible charges. For what Scultetus wrote, "The Puritans take away all authority from the Fathers and leave none for themselves," he drew from Adrian Saravia, whose very words these are: "Whoever takes away all authority from the Fathers leaves none for himself; which is far more tolerable than that of Downame: 'He who denies faith to the Fathers himself deserves none.' For all men preserve faith to Scripture alone." The historical faith which Meredith Hanmer demands, we readily give to historians, under that freedom of judgement which he proposes. Downame takes this away in the matter of episcopacy; thus he binds us with probable conjectures. For the Fathers can give only probable things, which have no certainty beneath them, since that axiom of the Philosopher is always true: "Some false things are probable, some true." This is most true of the bishop. As for Saravia's claim that all authority has been taken from the Fathers by us, it is indeed true that we, with John Jewel, do not hesitate to affirm: "The judgements of the Fathers, by themselves and alone, without further authority and the direction of the divine word, are not always sufficient grounds for imposing or obtaining our faith." He proves this from the Fathers themselves, who say that our faith depends on the Scriptures alone. If the Hierarchicals take this sole authority away from the Scriptures, they certainly leave nothing either for themselves or for the Fathers, in accordance with that saying taken by Augustine into the canon law: "Those who do not follow the divine testimonies have lost the weight of human testimony."

units.la: Secundò, nos Iuliano haeretico aequiparat Bancroftus: adversus quem sic Augustinus: Ut ad eo permisit ima summis longus dies, senebrae adeo in lucem & lux in tenebras versae sunt, ut videant Pelagius, Coelestius, Iulianus, & caeci sint Hilarius, Cyprianus, Ambrosius? Cont. Pelag. lib.2.c.10. Sed male in nos, nec superbos, nec errantes, sed a patribus ad scripturas provocentes hoc intorquetur: quod recte ab Augustino in Iulianum objectum est, scripturis adeque ac ipsis patribus destitutum: male etiam Augustini exemplo se retegunt Hierarchici, qui patres contra Iulianum non citavit, nisi postquam sententiam suam apertis Scripturis confirmasset. Spirat igitur hoc convitium, amarore Papisticum illum, qui Lutherum profanitatis condemnavit, quod si mille Cyprianos, mille Augustinos non curare dixerat. Defendit hac ex parte Lutherum Hierarchicus ipse Richardus Eyldus: quidni nos igitur in Luthero candem veritatis causam agentes, ab hac Bantrefti accusatione plane eadem absolvamur?
units.tr: Secondly, Bancroft equates us with the heretic Julian, against whom Augustine says: "As if the long day had been granted to him so that darkness has become so great, and light has been turned into darkness, that Pelagius, Caelestius and Julian see, and Hilary, Cyprian and Ambrose are blind?" (Against Pelagius, book 2, ch. 10). But this is twisted badly against us, who are neither proud nor erring, but who, while appealing from the Fathers to the Scriptures, do nothing of the kind; the charge was rightly brought by Augustine against Julian, who was destitute of Scripture just as much as of the Fathers. The Hierarchicals also badly reveal themselves by Augustine's example, since he did not cite the Fathers against Julian until he had confirmed his own opinion by plain Scripture. This insult therefore breathes that bitterness of the Papists who condemned Luther for profanity, because he had said that he did not care about a thousand Cyprians or a thousand Augustines. In this respect the Hierarchical Richard Field himself defends Luther. Why then should we, who are pursuing the same cause of truth in Luther's case, not be wholly absolved of this accusation of Bancroft?

units.la: Tertio, nos patres pro idiotis habere, nos ipsos solos doctos putare dicit Dovnamus: Refutator (inquit) illiusque socij, annis 1400. immo quod ad patrum nonullos 1500. minores: patres tamen idictas condemnant: quasi non vidissent quod ipsi scilicet docti viderent. Minor qua fronte, vel qua conscientia potius, hæc dicere refutare potuit? Sed mirandum magis, non videre Downamum, Bernardum minime idiotam fuisse, quantumvis (ut in Proverbio dicitur) non viderit omnia. Atque hunc Bernardum, se solum doctum exiitimasse, quæsto sequitur, quod rivos commentariorum despexerit, & ad scripturas interpretandas, in scripturis solis meditandis se exercuerit, nullis aliis magistris, praeter quercus & fagos, usus, Augustinus (inquit Iohannes Reynoldus) contra Hieronymum epist. 19. pressus multorum patrum testimonijs, ad eis omnibus provocat ad Paulum: Ab eis omnibus inquit qui aliud sentiunt, literarum tractatoribus provoca ad ipsum Apostolum. Dent venia quilibet aliud opinantes, ego magis credo tanto Apostolo jurandi, ecce per Christum non mentior. Superbus jam Downamo Augustinus erit, & se solum doctum sentiens? certe durior hic quam ipse Torrensis apud eundem: qui licere dicit dissentire à patribus, dummodo id modeste fiat: ita enim arguit ac si nulla a patribus dissensio fieri possit, nisi superbe & immodesta.
units.tr: Thirdly, we are said to regard the Fathers as laymen and to think ourselves alone learned, says Downame: "The Refuter (he says) and his fellow, by 1400 years, or rather by 1500 for some of the Fathers, are lesser; yet they condemn the Fathers as unlearned, as if they had not seen what they themselves, the learned, see." With what face, or rather with what conscience, could Minor say and refute these things? But it is more remarkable that Downame does not see that Bernard was by no means unlearned, though, as the proverb says, he did not see everything. And as to this Bernard, whom he thought himself alone learned, it follows, I ask, that he despised the streams of commentaries and trained himself to interpret Scripture by meditating on Scripture alone, using no other teachers except oaks and beeches. Augustine (says John Reynolds) against Jerome, Epistle 19, pressed by the testimonies of many Fathers, appeals to all of them to Paul: "From all of them," he says, "who think otherwise, appeal to the Apostle himself, the interpreter of the letters.
