Let anyone who thinks otherwise pardon me; I rather believe so great an Apostle, behold, I do not lie before Christ." Will Augustine now be proud towards Downame and thinking himself alone learned? Certainly Torrens, in the same place, is harsher than this, since he says it is lawful to dissent from the Fathers, provided it is done modestly. For he argues as if no dissent from the Fathers could be made except proudly and immodestly.

units.la: 9 Quarto, objicit Downamus intollerabilem impudentiam. Observetur inquit, tanquam intollerabilis impudentia indicium in materia facti tam scripturis consona (Titum nempe & Timotheum Episcopos fuisse) quenquam fidem denegare, consentanti, generali, perpetuoque consensui, antiquorum scriptorum, quorum nonnulli annos 1300. vel etiam 1400. ante annos vixerunt. Sed Titum & Timotheum Episcopos fuisse res non consona sed scripturis contraria est, ut suo loco demonstrabitur: quo respectu si nos impudentes qui homines, quid tum Paulus, qui ne Angelos quidem audiendos existimavit? unde sic Chrysostomus: Etiam Angelis præponit scripturas. Nam Angeli sunt servi, at Scriptura non a servis, sed a Domino Deo ipso venit ad nos. Consonat huic, quod habet Iuellus. Ad intelligendas scripturas, opus nonnunquam patrum prudentia habemus: sed non tamen major illis fides habenda est, quam quæ expedit, aut quam ipsi oblatum, recipere vellent. Vere de eis omnibus quod Seneca olim in causa simili dicere possumus. Non sunt Domini, sed duces nostri.
units.tr: 9 Fourthly, Downame objects to our "intolerable impudence". "Let it be observed," he says, "that it is a sign of intolerable impudence that anyone should deny faith, in a matter of fact so consonant with Scripture (namely that Titus and Timothy were bishops), to the agreed, general and perpetual consent of the ancient writers, some of whom lived 1300 or even 1400 years ago." But that Titus and Timothy were bishops is not a matter consonant with Scripture but contrary to it, as will be shown in its place. In that respect, if we are impudent men, what then of Paul, who did not think even angels should be heard? Hence Chrysostom says: "He places the Scriptures even above the angels. For angels are servants, but Scripture comes to us not from servants but from the Lord God himself." Jewel agrees with this, who says: "To understand the Scriptures we sometimes need the wisdom of the Fathers; yet they are not to be given greater trust than is useful, or than they themselves would wish to be offered." Truly, of all of them we can say what Seneca once said in a similar case: "They are not our masters, but our guides."

units.la: Quinto, accusamur novitatis: sic enim Downamus: Hominem fidem omni antiquitati in materia facti denegare aperta demonstratio est, eum novitati potius & singularitati, quam veritati esse addictum. At Episcopum Hierarchicum ab initio fuisse, & ab Apostolis profectum, non obstante antiquitate, rem esse novam, absque novitatis studio judicare liceat: nam & nova partes antiquos introducere potuisse, ostendit Vincentius Lyrinensis, qui authoritatem Cypriani, Cæcilij Africani, aliorumque patrum qui favebant rebaptizationi, ita reficit: Quis fuit exitus illius disputationis? retinita est antiquitas: explosa novitas.
units.tr: Fifthly, we are accused of novelty. For thus Downame: "That a man denies faith to all antiquity in a matter of fact is a clear demonstration that he is devoted to novelty and singularity rather than to truth." But that the episcopate was from the beginning and derived from the Apostles, and is not a new thing despite its antiquity, may be judged without any zeal for novelty. For that new things can introduce ancient ones, Vincentius Lyrinensis shows, who weakens the authority of Cyprian, Caecilius Africanus, and the other Fathers who favoured rebaptism, in this way: What was the outcome of that dispute? Antiquity was retained; novelty was driven out.

units.la: Sexto, intollerabiles nos esse exclamat Downame & minimè fe-rendos: sic enim habet, postquam generaliter antiquitatis confensum pro Tito & Timotheo, Episcopis intulisset: Diu intollerabilem audaciam & arrogantiam esse, contrarium afferre. At si temporibus ipsorum Patrum vixisset, impollerabilis audacie ipse condemnatus fuisset, quod non scripturæ sola contentus, partes & antiquitatem crepuerit: sic enim Iustinus Martyr: Dixi tibi sedulo te operam dare debere, tutus ut sis in omnibus, ut scripturis inhæreas. Aliis te dicentem non sustinuissemus.
units.tr: Sixthly, Downame cries out that we are intolerable and not to be borne. For thus he says, after he had set out the general consent of antiquity for Titus and Timothy as bishops: "It is intolerable audacity and arrogance to bring forward something contrary." But if he had lived in the times of the Fathers themselves, he would have been condemned for intolerable audacity, because he, being content with Scripture alone, rails against the Fathers and antiquity. For thus Justin Martyr: "I told you that you should diligently take care to be secure in all things, that you cling to the Scriptures. We would not have tolerated you speaking otherwise."

units.la: Septimo, patres contemnere dicimur: ac si salva patrum honorificentia, non iam hodie, perinde ac olim, quæ perperam patres scripserunt, rejici queant. Sic Augustinus: Nam quorumlibet disputationes quamvis Catholicorum & coæpatorum hominum, velut scripturas canonicas habere debemus, ut nobis non liceat salva honorificentia quæ illis debetur hominibus aliquid in eorum scriptis improbare, & repudiare, si forte invenerimus quod aliter senserunt, quam veritas habet, divino adjutorio, vel ab illis intellecta vel a nobis. Præcipuum in causa Hierarchica hæc habent locum: quum Episcopatus enormem eminentiam plus videre nequiret, quam ipsum Antichristum, cuius embrio erat: qua in causa id jam dicimus, quod Whitakerus: Videmus patribus hac in re non esse multum tribuendum, qui tam incertis, futilis, absurdis de Antichristo tradiderunt. Absit ergo ut illi hac in re nobis fucum faciant. Patribus quidem id tribuendum est, quod merentur, sed non dicendum ut ille. Malo cum patribus errare, quam cum aliis verum sentire.
units.tr: Seventhly, we are said to despise the Fathers, as if, with the honour of the Fathers preserved, what they wrote wrongly could not now be rejected, just as it could once. Thus Augustine: "For we ought to hold the disputations of any men whatsoever, even Catholic and learned men, as canonical Scripture, so that it is not lawful for us, with the honour due to those men preserved, to disapprove and reject anything in their writings, if perhaps we find that they thought otherwise than the truth holds, either understood by them or by us with the help of God." In the Hierarchical cause these points have particular place: since the episcopate could not see the enormous eminence of its own power, it saw nothing more than Antichrist himself, whose embryo it was. In this cause we say what Whitaker says: "We see that little credit is to be given to the Fathers in this matter, who handed down such uncertain, trifling and absurd things about Antichrist. Far be it, therefore, that they should deceive us in this matter." Credit is indeed to be given to the Fathers as they deserve, but not in the way he says. "I would rather err with the Fathers than think the truth with others."

units.la: Octavo & ultimo, ecquid aliud adversus nos habent Hierarchici quod objiciant, quam quod nuda sanctorum patrum testimonia, a scripturis deflituta rejiciamus? Imo inquit Whitgiftus & Bancroftus: Patres contra initio impetitum dicit Cartwrightus, nos in foßis roftrare quanquam patres allegamus. Quid ni diceret, scripturas fontipatres in earum comparatione, fossis, & cisterns æquiparando, præsertim cum ad rem falsam comprobandam afferuntur? Certe monet Gregorius Nazianzenus: [illas in cœno immorari & luto adhærescere, qui non contendunt ad purissimam scripturarum divinarum fontem.] Sic Lactantius: [Quoniam multæ hæreses exiterunt—determinanda nobis est veritas & in suo proprio domicilio collocanda: ut si quis aquam vitæ cupiat haurire, non ad detritos lacus deferatur, qui non habent venam, sed uberrimum Dei noverit fontem, quo irrigatus, perenni luce potiatur.] Sic Ruffinus [Ex fontibus verbi Dei in libris Canonicis patefactis, haurienda sunt pocula.] Similiter Iohannes Chrysostomus in Symbol. Lucas Iuellus, Hardingum à scripturis ad Ecclesiam confugientem, verbis Ieremiæ reprellit: [quod ita Deum fontem vivarum aquarum derelinquat, & fodiat sibi cisternas, non valentes continere aquam.] Postremò Guilielmus Barlæus, Episcopus Lincolniensis dicit: [Priscam Ecclesiam se post tempora Apostolorum corrupisse, quòd se ad purum scripturarum fontem absque omni mixtura non alligaret, sed præceptum illud Vegetij, lib. 3, c. 21. militibus datum violaret.] Non palustribus aquis utantur.
units.tr: Eighthly and lastly, have the Hierarchists anything else to object against us, except that we reject the bare testimonies of the holy Fathers, cut off from Scripture? Indeed, say Whitgift and Bancroft: "Cartwright, at the very beginning of the attack, says that the Fathers are against us; we, though we allege the Fathers, are digging in ditches." Why would he not say this, equating the Fathers with ditches and cisterns in comparison with the fountain of Scripture, especially when they are brought forward to prove a false thing? Certainly Gregory Nazianzen warns: "[They linger in mud and cling to slime, who do not hasten to the most pure fountain of the divine Scriptures.]" So Lactantius: "[Since many heresies have arisen, the truth must be determined by us and placed in its own proper home, so that if anyone wishes to draw the water of life, he is not led to broken cisterns, which have no vein, but may know the most abundant fountain of God, by being watered from which he may enjoy eternal light.]" So Rufinus: "[From the fountains of the word of God, opened in the canonical books, the cups must be drawn.]" Similarly John Chrysostom in his work on the Creed. Lucas Jewel, repelling Harding, who fled from the Scriptures to the Church, with the words of Jeremiah: "[because they forsake the Lord, the fountain of living waters, and hew out for themselves cisterns that cannot hold water.]" Finally, William Barlow, Bishop of Lincoln, says: "[The ancient Church corrupted itself after the times of the Apostles, because it did not bind itself to the pure fountain of Scripture without any mixture, but violated that precept of Vegetius, book 3, chapter 21, given to soldiers.]" Let them not use muddy waters.

units.la: CAP. 12, Quòd Hierarchici patres cum pro sua causa non faciunt, reijciant, utcunque eos simpliciter reformatis obtrudant.
units.tr: CAP. 12, That the Hierarchical fathers, when they do not support their cause, reject them, and yet in any case press them simply upon the Reformed.

units.la: VIdimus quàm rigidi censores in Reformatos Hierarchici sint, quòd nudis patrum testimonijs stare nolunt: jam, quid si ipsi vestem regalem qua patres induerunt, patribus denuo detrahant, Iudæorum more eos iudificantes? Certè nec ipsi, quando illis adversi sunt, antiquis patribus stare volunt: sed eorum placita rescindunt, authoritatem respuunt, interpretationes a tergo reijciant, Videatur Thomas ille Bilsonus, annon locum Math: 18. Dic Ecclesiæ de tribunali civili interpretatur, contra omnes patres qui eum de Ecclesiastico interpretantur; Richard. Fyldus eundem sensum sequitur, & nominatim in margine nos ad Erastum & Bilsonum remittit. Si nos unum de nostris, quanquam Erasto saltem præstantiorem universis patribus hunc in modù antepositissemus, quos quæso clamores non audivissemus? Locum Act. 6. de Diaconis Ecclesiasticis omnes patres intelligunt, ni unus forte Chrisostomus excipiendus, hunc tamè non de diaconis Ecclesiasticis sed civilibus nescio quib9 elimosinarijs procuratorib9, Bilson intelligit. Pro iure populi in electione ministrorum acriter disputat Cypr. Quid ad hunc Bilson9? Allegatio ista errore, si nō falsitate aspersa est. Nihil enim verborum in illo contextu, nihil rerum, cuiusmodi citat Cypr. reperitur. Et rursus, Teste quendam produxistis qui & suo more disertus, & in eo quod vult, accerrimus esse solet: sed deficit eum probatio, si errore manifesto non tenetur. Lousd hac ipsa re tractans, electionem populi affirmat esse contra jus. Quid igitur de universa Ecclesiæ primæ praxi dicemus? Non exemplis inquit sed regulis adhærere oportet, nec quid aliquando factum fuit, sed quid perpetuo fieri debet, perquirendum est, Ita universam Ecclesiæ praxin, non solùm repudiat, verumetiam condemnat, quod in nobis tantopere Hierar. abhorrinantur. Narrat Socrates circa annum 430, Episcopatum, non aliter atque Alexandrinum, quasi extra sacerdotij fines egressum, ad seculare principatum jam ante dilapsum fuisse. Quid ad hoc Whitgiftus? Socrates inquit Novatianus & Puritanus
units.tr: We have seen how strict the Hierarchical critics are against the Reformed, in that they refuse to rest on the bare testimonies of the Fathers. Now, what if they themselves strip the royal robe with which the Fathers were clothed and, in the manner of the Jews, condemn them again? Certainly they do not themselves wish to stand by the ancient Fathers when the Fathers are against them. They annul their decisions, reject their authority and cast their interpretations behind their backs. Let us look at Thomas Bilson, who interprets Matthew 18, "Tell it to the Church," of a civil tribunal, against all the Fathers who understand it of the ecclesiastical court. Richard Field follows the same sense and, in the margin, refers us by name to Erastus and Bilson. If we had put forward one of our own men in this way, though he were at least more distinguished than Erastus and than all the Fathers, what complaints would we not have heard? All the Fathers understand Acts 6 of ecclesiastical deacons, except perhaps Chrysostom alone, who must be excepted; yet Bilson understands it not of ecclesiastical deacons but of I know not what civil almoners and stewards. Cyprian argues vigorously for the right of the people in the election of ministers. What does Bilson say to this? "That allegation is stained with error, if not with falsehood. For nothing of the words in that context, nothing of the matter, such as Cyprian cites, is to be found." And again: "You have produced a certain witness who is, after his fashion, eloquent and most vehement in what he wants to say; but his proof fails, if he is not held in manifest error." Lowd, treating this very matter, affirms that the election by the people is contrary to right. What then shall we say of the whole practice of the primitive Church? "One must cling not to examples but to rules, and what ought always to be done must be sought, not what was once done." So he not only rejects the whole practice of the Church but even condemns it, which the Hierarchicals so greatly abhor in us. Socrates relates that about the year 430 the episcopate, not otherwise than the Alexandrian, as if it had gone beyond the limits of the priesthood, had already slipped into secular rule. What does Whitgift say to this? "Socrates," he says, "is a Novatian and a Puritan.

units.la: Defens. Apol. p.6.c.1.d.1 / Defens. Ant. relig. prokesl. p.20. / De perpet. Gubern. c.4 / De perpet. Gubern. c.7 / Ibid. c.15 p.407 / P.409 / Queri. eccles. p.216 / Histor. l.7. c.11. erat, & non magis contra hos Episcopos baptismo rebaptizandi, quam vos ipsi contra Episcopos hujus nostrae Ecclesiae, quorum authoritati invidetis, ex occasione simili. De Cyrillo Alexandrino ita ante Socrates: Cyrillus in sede Episcopali collocatus, maiorem principatum quam unquam Theophilus habuisset, pariter sibi assumpsit. Etenim ex illo tempore Episcopus Alexandrinus praeter sacri cleri dominatu, verum praeterea saecularium principatum acquisivit. Thomas Bilsonus de his utrisque Socratis testimonii una agit, qui quanquam ita modeste respondeat, ut Whitgiftium pudefaciat: non tamen ita Socratem probat, ut a nobis requirant Hierarchici ut patres approbemus. Quam iuste inquit hoc Cyrillo tribuit Socrates videriunt qui recte sapiunt. Quasi Socrati hoc in re minime sapuerit: Subjungit vero. Si ad aliam quam oportuit affirabesunt, absit ut ego cujusvis insolentiam extenuem aut defendam. Cassentur ergo, quaecunque a sanctitatem veterum Episcoporum ad Episcopatum Hierarchicum comprobandum, adferri solent argumenta. Ego nunquam credam, inquit Saravia, sanctas patres Ambrosium, Cyprianum &c, tyrannide gessisse voluisse Episcopatum, quem tyrannicum fuisse noverint: alias quis cedo mihi Cyrillo sanctior? quis doctior? invasit tamen & usurpavit (quod tyranni est) ut habet Socrates principatum saecularem. Sed pergamus ad alios. Hieronymus presbyterum exaequat Episcopo. Quid hic Dovvnamus? Hic nempe magister non tacetat: ita enim habet: Determinatio haec Hieronymi istius disputationis prorumpens tanti ponderis esse non debet: ac quod contra non agyrisa sed bymanos vel ’spiritus tradidit. Presbyter erat Hieronymus, & duo tant, quae in gradum gradus sui plus eum dicere provocare potuerunt, per contentionem, quam quod exacte ad veritatem respondeat.
units.tr: Defens. Apol. p.6.c.1.d.1 / Defens. Ant. relig. prokesl. p.20. / De perpet. Gubern. c.4 / De perpet. Gubern. c.7 / Ibid. c.15 p.407 / P.409 / Queri. eccles. p.216 / Histor. l.7. c.11. And he was no more (in the wrong) on this point against these bishops regarding rebaptism than you yourselves are against the bishops of this our Church, whose authority you begrudge, on a similar occasion. Of Cyril of Alexandria, Socrates says earlier: Cyril, placed in the episcopal see, took to himself a greater princedom than Theophilus had ever held; for from that time the Bishop of Alexandria acquired, besides the lordship of the sacred clergy, also a secular principate. Thomas Bilson deals with both of these testimonies of Socrates together. Although he answers so modestly as to shame Whitgift, he does not so prove Socrates that the Hierarchicals can require us to approve the Fathers. "How justly Socrates attributes this to Cyril, let those judge who think rightly." As if Socrates had been least wise in this matter! He adds, however: "If they were carried to what was not fitting, far be it from me to excuse or defend anyone's insolence." Let therefore be set aside whatever arguments are commonly brought forward to prove the Hierarchical episcopate from the holiness of the ancient bishops. "I shall never believe," says Saravia, "that the holy Fathers Ambrose, Cyprian, etc., wished to exercise a tyrannical episcopate, which they knew to be tyrannical. Otherwise, who, I ask you, is holier than Cyril? Who more learned? Yet he invaded and usurped (which is the act of a tyrant), as Socrates reports, a secular principate." But let us proceed to others. Jerome makes the presbyter equal to the bishop. What do the Downames say here? Here, certainly, the master is not silent, for thus he has it: "The determination of Jerome in this dispute, bursting forth, ought not to be of such weight as he gave it, since he did not hand it down as an accurate judgement of the matter but out of the heat of the argument." Jerome was a presbyter, and two things, which could provoke him more than to advance his own rank by contention, drove him to say more than accurate truth allowed.

units.la: Primum, quod sine Episcopi licentia, nec praedicare presbyteri nec baptizare potuerunt: alterum quod Diaconi Romae se presbyteris praetulerunt: ad quos confutandos, quantum potest presbyteros exstolle, sic ut eos plus quam veritas patiebatur. Episcopus adequare videbatur: cujus hoc solum fundamentum habet, quod nomen Episcopi & Apostoli Apostolorum tempore aliquandiu confunderetur: quod certe debile fundamentum est, & facile ex propriis illius scriptis refutari potest Hadrianus Saravia, adhuc plus incalescit: nam quod Episcopum non dominica dispositione, sed potius Ecclesiae consuetudine presbytero praelatum dicit: Hic (inquit) Hieronymus aperte Aerianus est.
units.tr: First, that without the bishop's licence neither presbyters could preach nor baptize; second, that the deacons at Rome preferred themselves to the presbyters. To refute these, he exalts the presbyters as much as he can, beyond what the truth allowed. He seemed to make the bishop equal to them. His only foundation for this is that the name of bishop and that of apostle were for some time confused in the age of the apostles. This is certainly a weak foundation and can easily be refuted from his own writings. Hadrian Saravia grows even warmer, for because Jerome says the bishop was set above the presbyter not by divine appointment but rather by the custom of the Church, "Here," he says, "Jerome is plainly an Arian."

units.la: Veniamus ad patres de materia facti testificantes, in qua intollerabiliter impudens dicitur apud Dowhamum, qui eis fide denegat. Verum igitur, ne ipse Dowhamus, intollerabilis & impudens inveniatur. Quid enim? Petrum Romae Episcopum fuisse, omnes patres asserunt, scribunt, praedicant, ne uno quidem dissentiente, & materia facti est: non credit Dowhamus ipse: Malebus tamen Sutclivius plus ultra progreditur: non enim solummodo negat Petrum Romae Episcopum fuisse, sed etiam Petrum Romae tunqua vidisse. Quid igitur adeo durae frontis
units.tr: Let us come to the Fathers testifying about matters of fact, in which Downame is said, intolerably and impudently, to deny them credit. Let us see, lest Downame himself be found intolerable and impudent. For what? That Peter was bishop of Rome, all the Fathers assert, write and preach, not one dissenting, and it is a matter of fact. Downame himself does not believe it. Yet Sutcliffe goes further, for he not only denies that Peter was bishop of Rome, but also that he ever saw Rome. What then of such hard-faced

units.la: Quid igitur adeo durae frontis fictionis Sanctorum, ut universo Patrum consensui in materia facti fidem denegat? Certe, idque ea in Patres acerbitate, quae in nostrarum scriptis nullibi reperitur, ita enim habet. Incertum est an Petro ex urbe fugiendi aperueris Christus & ea dixerit quae narrat Egesippus. De excidio Hierosolymi lib. 3. cap. 2. Ambrosius, & Gregorius & Fortasse Athanasius fabulam ex Egesippo hauserunt. Rufus: Plerique patrum alia loquuntur, reliqui audita & fama recepta narrant, quae nihil probant praeter incertam famam. Irenaeus de Petro tantum quae fama divulgarat dedit. Eusebius nihil praeter audita loquitur. Arnobius non aliter narrat quae aliij, a quibus ea prius acceperat. Epiphanius de Petro traditionem deterrem memoriae pandit. Chrysostomus & Orosius, audita tantum narrant. Omitto reliquas: haec satis ostendunt non minus quam nos quandoque Hierarchicos patres rejicere: in hoc tantum differimen est, cum a scripturis & veritate discedunt patres tum eos nos relinquimus, illi vero, cum vere sentiunt, & secundum scripturas docent. Atque hoc in citandis patribus, erratum Hierarchicum primum esse, nempe quod patribus nimiam authoritatem tribuat.
units.tr: What then of such hard-faced fiction about the saints, that he denies credit to the consensus of all the Fathers on a matter of fact? Certainly, and with that bitterness against the Fathers which is found nowhere in our writings, it runs thus: "It is uncertain whether Christ opened to Peter a way of fleeing from the city and said those things which Hegesippus narrates" (De excidio Hierosolymi, book 3, ch. 2). Ambrose, Gregory and perhaps Athanasius drew the fable from Hegesippus. Rufinus: "Most of the Fathers say other things; the rest narrate what they heard and received by report, which prove nothing beyond an uncertain rumour. Irenaeus gave only what rumour had spread about Peter. Eusebius speaks only of things heard. Arnobius narrates no differently than others from whom he had received them earlier. Epiphanius sets out a tradition of worse memory about Peter. Chrysostom and Orosius narrate only things heard." I pass over the rest. These sufficiently show that, no less than we, they sometimes reject the Hierarchical Fathers. In this there is only this difference: when the Fathers depart from Scripture and truth, we leave them behind; but they, when they truly think, teach according to Scripture. And so in citing the Fathers, the first error of the Hierarchicals is this: that it ascribes to the Fathers excessive authority.

units.la: CAP 13. Erratum Hierarchicorum secundum quod patres fictitios reformatis obtrudunt.
units.tr: CAP 13. The error of the Hierarchicals, in foisting fictitious Fathers upon the Reformed.

units.la: Secundum sequitur: quod Patres fictitios in scenam producant. Dixit Adrianus apud Turisconsultos: Testibus non testimonijs credendum esse: quis igitur nobis difficilem laborem objectum negetur, quibus non solum cum testimoniis falsis, verumetiam cum falsis testibus est confligendum. Quanquam enim causam prodat famelicam, umbras Patrum, instar patrum veterum, consectari: ea tamen Hierarchicorum audacia est, ut etiam falsis patrum nominibus imperitis imponere non verentur.
units.tr: The second error follows: that they bring fictitious Fathers onto the stage. Hadrian said among the jurists: "Witnesses, not testimonies, are to be believed." Who, then, could deny us a difficult labour, since we must contend not only with false testimonies but with false witnesses? For although they put forward a starving cause, pursuing the shadows of the Fathers as if they were the old Fathers, such is the audacity of the Hierarchicals that they do not hesitate to impose on the unlearned even with false names of Fathers.

units.la: Primus autem, quo nituntur suppositivus scriptor, author libri illius est, cui nomen inscribitur Canones Apostolorum, quem pro primate Episcoporum & Archiepiscoporum citat Thomas Bilsonus de perpet. Eccles. gubernat. cap. 14. pag. 385. Hadrianus Saravia cont. Beza de diversi. ministr. grad. c. 20. p. 192. & Georgius Downame Defens. Lib. 2. Pag. 13. & c. 7. p. 138. 139.
units.tr: The first writer on whom the spurious author relies is the author of the book entitled The Canons of the Apostles, which Thomas Bilson cites as the basis for the primacy of bishops and archbishops (On the Perpetual Government of the Church, ch. 14, p. 385), as do Hadrian Saravia (Against Beza, On the Different Grades of Ministers, ch. 20, p. 192) and George Downame (Defence, bk. 2, p. 13, and ch. 7, pp. 138–139).

units.la: Primo, hunc librum a Gelasio & 70. Episcopis in concilio Romae habito condemnatum fuisse, vel ipsi inficiari nequeunt: Respondet Saravia. Quod Gelasius titulum damnavit, nec habere titulum Apostolorum canones voluit, non idcirco singulos reiecit, cum ipsa inter suos canones, plures inseruerit. Dovnamus vero, viros nostros aliquos ludicrosos, multum hallucinatos fuisse, quasi a jure Canonico, & ab Isidoro hy canones condemnati fuerint: cum distinctionis decimae sextae praeceptus scopus sit, horum Canonum authoritatem asserere, quanquam non ut scriptura ruum rum Canonicarum, tamen ut authenticorum Canonum. Vt de distinctione hac 16, nihil dicam: si hac distinctione non condemnentur, à jure tamen Canonico condemnantur. Quid enim de distinctione 15. dices? Titulus ibi tantum libri condemnatur, inquit Sarava, non Canones ipsi: Inspiciantur igitur verba ipsa Gelasij. Quae ab haereticis vel a schismaticis, conscripta vel praedicata sunt, nulla tenus recipit Catholica & Apostolica Ecclesia Romana: è quibus pauca quae ad memoriam venerunt & a Catholicis vitanda sunt, credimus esse subdenda. In enumeratione vero subsequenti, liber iste Canon. Apostol. inter caeteros condemnatur. Non igitur titulus solum libri sed & liber ipse rejicitur, contra Sarav. & rejicitur, tanquam non recipiendus, imo tanquam vitandus contra Down. qui hunc librum minime à iure Canonico condemnatum dicit, sed authoritatem authenticorum Canonum illi relictam esse affirmat. Quomodo quaeso hoc fieri potest, ut authentica illius authoris authoritas sit, qui impudentissime personam Apostolorum induit? Quodsi titulus libri aliunde asceriptus esset, verèque asseruisset Bilsonus, hunc librum ab alijs Canonem Apostolorum appellatum fuisse, quòd cum Apostolorum doctrina consentiat, aliquid esset. Atqui secus est: author ipse sub nomine Apostolorum hos Canones edidit: ut haec testantur Canone 85. Libri nostri, & Acta nostra, id est Apostolorum: quibus verbis nonne ipsos Apostolos loquentes inducit, at si hi canones ab ipsis Apostolis fuissent editi; Certe sanior Bils. atq; Sarav. vel Bellar. ipse est, qui hanc fraudem & impostur am usq; eo abominatur, ut affirmare non dubitaret non sine causa Gelasium numerasse Canones Apostolorum inter Apocrypha. Sic Bessarion apud Iuellum, de Sacrament: Eucharist: Licet haec Clementis verba inter Apocryphas scripturas commemorare solent: placet tamen eis in praesentiarum tanquam veris assentiamur. Nempe impudentiae esse putavit hunc librum citare sub Apostolorum nomine falso conscriptum, nisi pro praesenti supponeretur, cum verum Apostolorum foetum esse. Downamus è contra, foetum Apolorum fictitium agnoscit, & tamen non citat solum, sed ad alios etiâ obligandos citat. Quanto melius Leo apud Iuellum. Apocryphae scripturae quae sub nominibus Apostolorum multarum habent seminarium falsitum, non solum interdicendae, sed etiam penitus auferendae atque ignibus tradendae sunt. Quod dicit Saravia, Gelasium ex hoc libro Canones non nullos sumpsisse, ac proinde librum ipsum non condemnasse, falsum est: canones hic nonnulli satis boni sunt. quid tum? num quisque liber recipiendus aut utendus, quia nonnihil veri continet? imo è contra, quia veris hic falsa commixta sunt, ideo librum ipsum vetandum Gelasius, ignibus tradendum rectè Leo censuit.
units.tr: First, that this book was condemned by Gelasius and seventy bishops in a council at Rome, they themselves cannot deny. Saravia replies that Gelasius condemned the title and did not want the canons to bear the title of the Apostles, but that he did not therefore reject each one of them, since he included several of them among his own canons. Downame, however, says that some of our men, who are rather playful, were greatly mistaken in supposing that these canons were condemned by the Canon Law and by Isidore. But the purpose of the sixteenth distinction is to assert the authority of these canons, though not as canonical Scripture, yet as authentic canons. I will say nothing about that sixteenth distinction: even if they are not condemned by it, they are condemned by the Canon Law. For what will you say about the fifteenth distinction? Saravia says that only the title of the book is condemned there, not the canons themselves. Let us then look at the words of Gelasius: "Those things which have been written or preached by heretics or schismatics the Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church in no way receives; of which the few that have come to mind and are to be avoided by Catholics we believe should be appended." In the list that follows, this book of the Canons of the Apostles is condemned among the others. Therefore it is not only the title of the book that is rejected but the book itself, against Saravia; and it is rejected as not to be received, indeed as to be avoided, against Downame, who says that this book was by no means condemned by the Canon Law, but affirms that its authority as authentic canons was left to it. How, I ask, can it be that the authentic authority belongs to that author who most shamelessly assumes the person of the Apostles? If the title of the book had been ascribed from elsewhere, and Bilson had truly asserted that this book was called the Canons of the Apostles by others because it agrees with the teaching of the Apostles, there would be some force in it. But it is otherwise: the author himself published these canons under the name of the Apostles, as Canon 85 bears witness: "Our books, and our Acts, that is, of the Apostles." By these words does he not introduce the Apostles themselves speaking? And if these canons had been published by the Apostles themselves... Certainly the more sound one is Bilson, or Saravia, or Bellarmine himself, who so abhors this fraud and imposture that he did not hesitate to affirm that Gelasius had not without reason numbered the Canons of the Apostles among the Apocrypha. So Bessarion, cited by Jewel, On the Sacrament of the Eucharist: "Although these words of Clement are usually reckoned among the Apocryphal writings, it pleases us for the present to assent to them as true." Indeed he thought it impudence to cite this book under the name of the Apostles when it was falsely written, unless for the present it were supposed to be a true offspring of the Apostles. Downame, on the contrary, acknowledges that the offspring of the Apostles is fictitious, and yet not only cites it but cites it to bind others too. How much better Leo, cited by Jewel: "Apocryphal writings which under the names of the Apostles hold a seedbed of many falsehoods are not only to be forbidden, but are also to be utterly removed and given to the flames." What Saravia says, that Gelasius took some canons from this book and therefore did not condemn the book itself, is false. Some of these canons are quite good. So what? Is every book to be received or used because it contains something true? On the contrary, because true things are mixed here with false, Gelasius rightly forbade the book itself, and Leo rightly judged that it should be given to the flames.

units.la: Secundo, multos subditicios Canones hic reperiri si inficientur, ipsis sane Papistis deteriores Hierarchici sunt: cum hoc fateatur Caesar Baronius, fateatur Sixtus Senensis, fateatur Lindanus: qui etiam
units.tr: Second, if they deny that many spurious canons are to be found here, the Hierarchicals are surely worse than the Papists themselves, since Caesar Baronius admits this, Sixtus of Siena admits it, Lindanus admits it, and they too

units.la: Cap. 20. Act. 1. p. 7. etiam diserte testatur; has constitutiones Apostolorum, ut haereticorum facibus adulteratas, à patribus repudiatas esse, En secundum argumentum, qua ne hic liber ab Hierarchicis citandus sit, nedum nobis obtrudendus. Authorem personatum in scenam producere sit leve: at librum talem huiusmodi authoris imperitis obtrudere, qui varie adulteratus sit, quis quaeso leve dixerit? Et repudiatus a patrib hic liber est, quia varia adulterata continet: authoritatem tamen authenticam habebit quae adversus adversarium valeat? Sed remedium forte adhibebunt, quo minus fallamur in delectu. Canones huius libri illi recipiendi pro veris sunt (inquit Baronius) quos post observavit Ecclesia. Eatenus solùm hi Canones (inquit Bilsonus) fidem merentur, quoad cum primi temporis historiis, & antiquorum Conciliorum decretis consentiunt. Qui huius libri Canones a patribus & conciliis citantur (inquit Downamus) tanquam authentici, extra omnem exceptionem sunt: ut qui tantam authoritatem habeant, quantam ulla alia Ecclesiastica scripta quaecunque. Et tu Downame dehinc fides lector: has putridas merces ita ornanti, quo venaliores essent? quod ad praxim Ecclesiae attinet, quam pro sua regula affert Baronius, ea satis certa non est, nam observati quidam Canones huius libri sunt ab antiqua Ecclesia, qui doctrinae Apostolicae adversantur, ut a Magdeburgensibus recte adnotatum est. Instant in Canone 17. qui secundas nuptias damnat, in Canone 27, qui nuptias in Presbyteris vetat, & Canone 68. qui ad jejunia quadragesimae, Paschae, feriae quartae, & Parasceves alligant conscientias. Respondent ista & Bilsono, annon etenim in sequentibus Conciliis stabilita sunt? Quod ad citationes attinet, vel ex hoc uno discere promptum, quam minime patrum juniorum testimonijs de saeculis ipsos antecedentibus, fidendum sit. Iob. Fiquidem Damasc. hos Canones Apostolorum inter ipsas sacras scripturas copulat. Confirmati sunt hi Canones in Trullo inquit Downamus his verbis. Can. 2. Placuit huic sanctae Synodo, ut modo confirmati & rati sint, Canon. Apostol. 85. c. qui a sanctis patribus qui nos praecesserunt suscepti ac confirmati sunt, atque adeo nobis etiam traditi sunt, sanctorum & gloriosorum Apostolorum nomine. Celebrata haec Synodus est ad annum. 675. Ad annum vero 1049. Leo nonus contra Epistolam Nicetae abbatis scribens, tantummodo 50 genuinos Canones esse dicit. Consulit iste horum Canonum authoritati, magis quam Downamus, qui Concilium in Trullo. & Canonem blasphemum illum 85. confirmatum citat: quem & Bancroftus abhominatur, & ipsemet Downamus quasi ab haereticis interpolatum rejicit.
units.tr: Cap. 20. Act. 1. p. 7. openly testify that these constitutions of the Apostles, adulterated as they are by the torches of heretics, were rejected by the Fathers. Here is the second argument, by which this book is not to be cited by the Hierarchicals, let alone forced upon us. To bring a fictitious author onto the stage is a light matter; but to foist on the unskilled a book of such an author, variously adulterated, who would call that a light matter? And this book was rejected by the Fathers because it contains many adulterated things: will it nevertheless have an authentic authority that can prevail against an adversary? But perhaps they will apply some remedy, so that we may not be deceived in the selection. "These canons of this book are to be received as true," says Baronius, "which the Church afterwards observed." "These canons merit belief only so far," says Bilson, "as they agree with the histories of the earliest times and the decrees of the ancient councils." "The canons of this book which are cited by the Fathers and councils," says Downame, "as authentic, are beyond all exception, since they have as great an authority as any other ecclesiastical writings whatever." And you, Downame, do you expect the reader to believe you, adorning these rotten wares so that they may sell better? As for the practice of the Church, which Baronius brings forward as his rule, that is not certain enough, for some canons of this book which the ancient Church observed are contrary to apostolic doctrine, as the Magdeburg men rightly noted. They press on Canon 17, which condemns second marriages; on Canon 27, which forbids marriage to elders; and on Canon 68, which binds consciences to fasts of Lent, Easter, Wednesday and Good Friday. They answer that these things were also established in later councils, and that is also to be said against Bilson. As for the citations, this one thing is enough to learn quickly how little the testimonies of later Fathers about the ages preceding them are to be trusted. For John of Damascus indeed joins these canons of the Apostles with the Holy Scriptures themselves. These canons were confirmed in Trullo, says Downame, in these words. Canon 2: "It has pleased this holy Synod that the Canons of the Apostles, 85 in number, which were received and confirmed by the holy Fathers who went before us, and have indeed been handed down to us under the name of the holy and glorious Apostles, be now confirmed and held." This Synod was held in the year 675. But in the year 1049, Leo IX, writing against the letter of Nicetas the abbot, says that there are only fifty genuine canons. This man is more careful of the authority of these canons than Downame, who cites the Council in Trullo and the blasphemous Canon 85 as confirmed; which Bancroft abhors, and Downame himself rejects as interpolated by heretics.

units.la: Tertiò, hos Canones Apostolorum dictos dicit ob duas causas, nempe propter magnam eorum antiquitatem & authenticam authoritatem. Sunt inquit qui Epiphanium primò horum mentionem fecisse dicunt, sed mihi alter videtur, nam citantur Concil. Nic. 8, 15. & 16, & Concil. Antioch. cap. 9. Primò oppono rationem Magdeburgensium, qui
units.tr: Third, he says that these are called the Canons of the Apostles for two reasons, namely on account of their great antiquity and their authentic authority. "There are some who say that Epiphanius was the first to mention them, but to me it seems otherwise, for they are cited at the Council of Nicaea, canons 8, 15 and 16, and at the Council of Antioch, canon 9." First I set against this the argument of the Magdeburg men, who
