units.la: L. 2. c. 7. p. 139. qui hinc probant hos canones antiquos non esse, quia nulla eorum mentio est apud Iustinum, Irenaeum, Tertullianum & caeteros prisco-s patres. Secundò, oppono rationem Caesaris Baronij. Magnum inquit impostura ...
units.tr: L. 2. c. 7. p. 139. Who from this argue that these canons are not ancient, because no mention of them is made by Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian and the other early Fathers. Secondly, I set against them the argument of Caesar Baronius: "Great," he says, "is the imposture

units.la: impostura, suspitionem facit canon. 65, quo excommunicatione plectendus statuitur laicus, depositione clericus, qui Sabbato ieiunaverit. Quando quidem tot tamque disertos antiquos patres canon ille praeterijt ut à nemine citatus reperiatur? vel quomodo observationem Romanae Ecclesiae contrariam omnium Apostolorum canoni Sabbati jejunij suscepisset, vel eorum Episcopus Clemens id fieri permisisset, qui quod statuissent Apostoli & ipsi scripsissent, quàm optimè novit? &c. Tertiò, oppono sententias & rationes Guiliel. Whitakeri & I. Reynoldi, Guil. Whitakerus ita. [Videtur iste liber consarcinatus & confutus ex actis aliorum Conciliorum praecipuè vero ex Concilio Antiocheno: multa enim leguntur in Antiocheno Concilio similia, Non verisimile vero est Antiochenos Patres, sumpsisse aliquid ex Canonibus. Si enim sumpsissent non dissimulassent sed potius indicassent ut majorem inde suis sanctionibus ac decretis authoritatem conciliarent. Sed nullam illi prorsus huius libri mentionem faciunt.] Ita vero Iohan. Reynoldus. [Canones Apostolorum in unum corpus collecti videntur circa tempora Constantini, post Concilium Antiochenum, cuius omnes Canones ibidem interseruntur. Neque enim verisimile est eos patres cosdem Canones, eisdem verbis tanquam suos promulgare voluisse, quos prius in Canonibus Apostolorum fuisse agnoverunt. Vt mihi videantur, quemadmodum Hieronymus monuit epistola ad Lycinium: quaeque provincia abundet in sensu suo, & praecepta maiorum leges Apostolicas arbitretur: ita veteres Graeci prisco-rum Synodorum decreta collegisse, & Apostolorum Canones maioris reverentiae causa appellasse.] Postremò, Tho. Bilsonus, non ausus est dicere Concilium Antiochenum hos Canones citasse: hic tantum dicit, Concilium Antiochenum, c. 9. eodem specatasse, quo hij Canones spectarunt.
units.tr: imposture, the canon 65 gives rise to suspicion, by which a layman who fasts on the Sabbath is condemned to excommunication and a cleric to deposition. For how is it that that canon has passed over so many and so clear ancient Fathers that it is found cited by no one? Or how could the Roman Church have adopted a practice contrary to the canon of all the Apostles on the fasting of the Sabbath, or how could its bishop Clement have allowed it, when he knew very well what the Apostles had laid down and had themselves written? And so on." Thirdly, I set against them the opinions and arguments of William Whitaker and John Reynolds. William Whitaker says this: [This book seems to have been patched together and refuted from the acts of other councils, especially from the Council of Antioch, for many things similar to those are read in the Antiochene Council. But it is not at all likely that the Fathers of Antioch took anything from these canons. For if they had taken it they would not have concealed it but would rather have pointed it out, so as to win greater authority for their own sanctions and decrees. But they make no mention of this book at all.] John Reynolds says this: [The Canons of the Apostles, collected into one body, seem to date from around the time of Constantine, after the Council of Antioch, all of whose canons are inserted in it. For it is not likely that those Fathers wished to promulgate as their own, in the same words, the same canons which they had already recognised as among the Canons of the Apostles. It seems to me, as Jerome warned in his letter to Lycinius, that every province abounds in its own opinion and regards the precepts of its elders as apostolic laws; so the ancient Greeks gathered the decrees of earlier synods and called them the Canons of the Apostles out of greater reverence.] Lastly, Thomas Bilson did not dare to say that the Council of Antioch cited these canons; he says only that the Council of Antioch, canon 9, looked to the same things to which these canons looked.

units.la: Author secundus fictitius, Clemens Romanus: sic Geor. Downamus. [Desinunt Acta Apostolorum in Pauli ad Romam accessu: nullam de eis rebus mentionem facientia, quae post per spacium 9. vel 10. annorum acciderunt. Quorum temporum Acta aliter cognosci non possunt, nisi ex illius epistolis, aut alijs antiquitatis monumentis, quam clausulam licet sub silentio praetericit refutator, opere pretium exi stimavi lectori in mentem revocare, ut multa sciat facta esse ab Apostolis, quae in alijs antiquitatis regestris narrantur, quanquam in Actis Apostolorum non narrantur, quae in eis rebus confiantur, quae annis 40. ante mortem Iohannis acciderunt. Iam vero Acta Apostolorum quae post Lucae historiam gesta sunt, ex parte narrantur per Egesippum & Clementem, & alios antiquos authores, qui testantur Paulum ordinasse Timotheum Ephesi Episcopum & Titum Cretae, aliosque alijs in locis Episcopos, ab Apostolis constitutos fuisse. {†} Quorum testimonijs quisquis recusat fidem adjungere, fidem ipsemet nullam meretur? Quid tibi videtur lector? Annon gratulandum Dorimamo est, quod supplementarios nobis dederit, tam egregios, tam necessarios, tam fide dignos, quo historiae sacrae defectus farciatur? Sistendus tamen hic Clemens est; ne forte circumforaneo aliquo impostore decipiamur. Quis igitur hic Clemens est? Procul dubio Clementem Romanum intelligit, verum Apostolorum discipulum. At vera tantum unica illius Epistola ad Corinthios est (inquit Eusebius) contra omnia quae Clementi ascribuntur suppositicia. Et in illa Epistola, qui novit Dorinam, quicquam ab eo de Titi & Timothei Episcopatu scriptum fuisse? Quid igitur? aut recognitiones, aut decretales Epistolas, aut Constitutiones Apostolorum, quae Clementi ascribuntur, intelligat Dorinamus necesse est. Ea veto affinitas est constitutionum Apostolorum, cum Canonibus Apostolorum, qui etiam Clementi a Bellarmino, Baronio, aliisque ascribuntur: ut eas potissimum respexisse Dorinamum credam. Neque obstat quod fateatur in Trullo condemnatum fuisse Canonem Apostolorum 85 qua Clementis constitutiones roborat: cur etenim has constitutiones quanquam ab haereticis adulteratas (neque enim aliam ob causam eas condemnat Concilium (non amplecteretur? atque Canones Apostol. amplectitur: quos tamen ab haereticis adulteratos confitetur? Quid igitur? Impostor iste, qui undique ab omnibus conclamatur, succedaneus Lucae erit in actis Apostolorum memoriae prodendis: imo sacrarum Pauli epistolarum supplementarius, author porro dignus tanta fide ut nullam fidem mereatur, qui ei fidem adhibere detrectaverit? Egone haec a Dorinamo expectabam? Egone, impudentiam impudentissimum non exclamassem, si quis alius praeter Dorinamum haec barritasset? Huccine iam tandem deventum est ut falsorium notabilem, a jure canonico vetitum, a Concilio in Trullo condemnatum, a Caesare Baronio ipso in quibusdam improbatum: a Iuelio, Whitakero, Reynoldo, Lubberto, Perkinso detectum, a Bilsono denique, Feyldo, Mortono, Hierarchicis ipsis consputum, conspurcatum, explosum, exhibitum: non solum pro vero Apostolorum discipulo, sed etiam digno Apostolorum in historia sacra pertexenda succedaneo amplecti necesse sit, ni fidem etiam nostram prodere velimus & prostituere? Atque vel ex hoc uno intelligere promptum, quam Dorinamus vanus sit, quum patres saeculo posteriores credendos affirmat, quando de prioribus foeculis in materia facti, testimonium ferunt. Nam ut Carolum Bovinum, Athanasius, & Eusebius deficiant, quos pro Clementis constitutionibus testes producit: Cyrillus tamen Hierosolymitanus, Epiphanius & Chrysostomus non deficient. Cyrillus etenim Catechif. 18. citat librum quintum sub his verbis: ut scribit Clemens, ut multi narrant; & Chrysostomus Homilia 53. in Matthaeum ita habet. Quomodo autem quidem sacerdotes ab hominibus ordinentur, manifestum est in libro octavo Canonum Apostolorum docetur. Epiphanius vero ita. Caeterum ad hoc afferunt suae idem Audiani Apostolorum constitutionem quae apud multos in ambigue est, sed non reprobata. Omnis enim regularis ordo in ipsa habetur, & nihil a fide adulteratum, neque a confessione, neque ab Ecclesiastico gubernatione & regula: Decernunt enim in eadem constitutione Apostoli, &c. Nihil mirum est, si Epiphanius contra Arium defendit Epiphanius, tanquam ab Apostolis constitutum: cum has Clementis constitutiones, tanquam ab Apostolis ipsis sanctas defendit: nihilque in eis quoad gubernationem Ecclesiae adulteratum esse dicat. Multa ad refutationem afferre non est opus: ipsa constitutio quam tuetur contra Audianos Epiphanius eiusmodi est: ut & Epiphanium refutare, & eandem explodere Carolus ipse Bovinus coactus sic. [Tantum (inquit) abest ut ea quae hoc capite legimus Apostoli statuerunt, ut etiam contraria horum ab ipsis praecepta videantur. Ipsa constitutio se prodit, & tantum non vocem emittens, clamat se novam esse. Ait enim aequinoctium fieri vigesima secunda Dystri-mensis, hoc est, Martij. Perspicuum est autem Christi tempore, aequinoctium fuisse vigesima quinta Martij. Quare nova est constitutio, fortasse edita post Concilium Nicenum in quo Pascha observatio, ad eam rationem redacta fuit, &c. Quid igitur est? Clemens ipse, verus ille Apostolorum discipulus non est: neque hic liber Constitutionum antiquus, sed post Concilium Nicaenum editus: neque authenticam authoritatem ullam habet ad Episcopatum Hierarchicum comprobandum.
units.tr: The second fictitious author is Clement of Rome, so says George Downamus. [The Acts of the Apostles end with Paul's arrival at Rome, saying nothing of those things which happened afterwards over a space of nine or ten years. The Acts of those times cannot be known otherwise than from his letters or other monuments of antiquity. I have thought it worth while to remind the reader of this clause, which the refuter passes over in silence, so that he may know that many things were done by the Apostles which are related in other records of antiquity, although they are not related in the Acts of the Apostles; and that things which happened forty years before the death of John are the subject of these records. Now the Acts of the Apostles that were done after Luke's history are told in part by Hegesippus and Clement, and other ancient authors, who testify that Paul ordained Timothy bishop of Ephesus and Titus of Crete, and that others were appointed bishops by the Apostles in other places. Whoever refuses to give credence to their testimonies, does he himself deserve any credence?] What do you think, reader? Ought we not to be thankful to Downamus that he has given us supplementary accounts so distinguished, so necessary, so worthy of belief, by which the defects of sacred history are filled? Yet we must pause here at Clement, lest perhaps we be deceived by some street-corner impostor. Who, then, is this Clement? Without doubt he means Clement of Rome, a true disciple of the Apostles. But (says Eusebius) there is only one genuine letter of his, the one to the Corinthians, and everything else ascribed to Clement is spurious. And in that letter, who that knows Downamus has found anything written by him about the episcopate of Titus and Timothy? What, then? Downamus must mean either the Recognitions, or the Decretal Epistles, or the Constitutions of the Apostles, which are ascribed to Clement. But the resemblance of the Constitutions of the Apostles to the Canons of the Apostles, which are also ascribed to Clement by Bellarmine, Baronius and others, is so close that I believe Downamus chiefly had these in view. Nor does it stand in the way that he admits the Canon 85 of the Apostles, which confirms the Constitutions of Clement, was condemned at the Council in Trullo. For why would he not embrace these Constitutions, though corrupted by heretics (for the Council condemns them on no other ground), and yet embrace the Canons of the Apostles, which he confesses were corrupted by heretics as well? What then? Is this impostor, who is cried down on all sides by everyone, to be a substitute for Luke in recording the memory of the Acts of the Apostles, or indeed a supplementer of the sacred Epistles of Paul, an author so deserving of credence that he deserves no credence at all, if anyone refuses to give him faith? Did I expect these things from Downamus? Would I not have cried out at the most shameless impudence if anyone other than Downamus had brayed such things? Has it come at last to this, that a notorious forger, forbidden by canon law, condemned by the Council in Trullo, disapproved in some points even by Caesar Baronius himself, exposed by Jewel, Whitaker, Reynolds, Lubbertus and Perkins, and finally spat upon, befouled, cast out and exhibited by Bilson, Feild, Morton and the Hierarchists themselves, must nonetheless be embraced not only as a true disciple of the Apostles but as a worthy substitute for the Apostles in weaving sacred history, unless we are willing to betray and prostitute our own faith? And from this one point alone it is easy to see how vain Downamus is, when he affirms that the Fathers of a later century are to be believed, when they bear witness about the earlier centuries in a matter of fact. For even if Athanasius and Eusebius fail, whom he produces as witnesses for the constitutions of Clement, Cyril of Jerusalem, Epiphanius and Chrysostom will not fail. For Cyril, in Catechesis 18, quotes the fifth book with these words: "as Clement writes, as many relate"; and Chrysostom, in Homily 53 on Matthew, says thus: "How priests are ordained by men is made plain in the eighth book of the Canons of the Apostles." But Epiphanius says this: "Moreover, the same Audians cite in support of their views a constitution of the Apostles, which is among many in doubt, but not rejected. For in it is found every regular order, and nothing is corrupted from the faith, neither from the confession nor from the ecclesiastical government and rule. For the Apostles decree in the same constitution, etc." It is no wonder if Epiphanius, when defending against Arius, Epiphanius, as established by the Apostles, since he defends these constitutions of Clement as holy and given by the Apostles themselves, and says that nothing in them concerning the government of the Church is corrupted. There is no need to bring much to the refutation: the constitution which Epiphanius defends against the Audians is of such a kind that Carolus Bovinus himself was compelled to refute Epiphanius and to explode it in the same breath, saying: [(he says) So far is it from being the case that what we read in this chapter was laid down by the Apostles, that their contrary precepts seem to be found there as well. The constitution itself betrays itself, and, scarcely uttering a voice, cries out that it is new. For it says that the equinox falls on the twenty-second of Dystrimensis, that is, March. But it is clear that in Christ's time the equinox was on the twenty-fifth of March. Therefore the constitution is new, perhaps published after the Council of Nicaea, at which the observance of Easter was reduced to that reckoning, etc.] What, then, is the result? Clement himself is not that true disciple of the Apostles; nor is this book of Constitutions ancient, but was published after the Council of Nicaea; and it has no genuine authority whatever for establishing the hierarchical episcopate.

units.la: 5 Tertius author suppositivus, Ignatius; de quo notum omnibus est, quantopere Hierarchiae gloriantur. Purissima Ecclesiae fa-cies (inquit S. Ultingius) in Ignatio est: Ignatij epistolae (inquit Baronius) ubi unico Ecclesiae, disciplinae, & traditionum sunt. Non Ecclesiae sed Synagogae Sathanae sunt, quae non conformant ad Ecclesiam tempore Ignatii. Hinc stomachantur nostri quod harum Epistolarum authoritatem in dubium vocari videant. Ita Lous: Epistolae Quam Ecclesiae tuas sanctissimi Ignati adulterinas esse contendunt. In idem impudentiae diversentur, si non se experiant, adulterata penitus & turpissimis fraudibus appositas, eorum doctrina habeatur. Richardus Bancroftus ita: Aut ad merum Genevensem Ignatius loqui debet: aut si plus quam volunt urgeat, parum precis antiquus patet ipsi, unquam fictiius, & homo unus iure rejicitur. His ut respondeatur, non ego hic disputabo pro nobis Ignatius in ea sit: sive sit, sive non sit perinde est. Fictitium etenim authoritatem habere est, absque impudentia affirmari potest: id quod in aliis argumentis fieri non potest.
units.tr: 5 The third spurious author is Ignatius, about whom everyone knows how greatly the Hierarchists boast. The purest face of the Church (says S. Ultingius) is in Ignatius. The epistles of Ignatius (says Baronius) are where alone the Church, discipline and traditions are. They are not the Church but the synagogue of Satan, since they do not conform to the Church of Ignatius's time. Hence our people are annoyed that they see the authority of these Epistles called into doubt. So Lous: They contend that the Epistles of the most holy Ignatius are adulterine. In the same impudence they will persist, unless they find that their doctrine is adulterated and fitted out with the most shameful frauds. Richard Bancroft says: Either Ignatius must speak in a purely Genevan way, or, if one presses more than they wish, it is plain that the old man was never anything but a fiction, and one man is rightly rejected. To answer these men, I shall not argue here for our side, whether Ignatius is genuine or not; it makes no difference. For to have a fictitious authority can be asserted without shamelessness, which cannot be done in the other arguments.

units.la: Primum in omnibus fere Epistolis satis copiosis (quod observarunt Magdeburgenses) occasio tentandi praetermittitur nec vel divinari licet, quam ac hanc aut illam Ecclesiam, potius quam ad aliam, litteras mittere Ignatius voluerit. Unde hoc? annon quia fingi occasiones ab interpolatore satis commode non potuerant?
units.tr: First, in almost all the fairly full Epistles (as the Magdeburg writers observed), the occasion for writing is left out, and one cannot even guess why Ignatius wished to send letters to this church rather than to that. Why is this? Is it not because the interpolator could not conveniently invent occasions?

units.la: Gg 3 Secunda
units.tr: Gg 3 Second

units.la: Secundò, refert Eusebius, scripsisse Ignatium a Smyrna & cum ultra Smyrnam esset, a Troade scripsisse: quod (ut rursus Magdeburgenses) itineris Ignatiani ratio & cursus non patitur. [Expende (inquiunt) quàm longum iter sit, Antiochiâ ad littus Ægæi pelagi se recipere, ibique rectâ sursum versus Septentrionem ascendere, & præcipuas civitates in littore sitas usque ad Troadem perlustrare: cum tamen iter ad Romam sit destinatum versus occasum. An decem illi Leopardi à quibus captivus ducebatur has illum ambages quaerere permittebant? aut per tot circuitus illi ancillatos fuisse verisimile est? aut fidem Christianam adeo illi diligebant, ut ad eandem terendam ad tot loca cum divertentem comitarentur? Humanius tractatus Pauli erat, quàm Ignatius quando Romam captivus abducebatur, qui tamen multò rectiori & breviori itinere traductus est.]
units.tr: Secondly, Eusebius reports that Ignatius wrote from Smyrna, and when he was beyond Smyrna, he wrote from Troas. This (again as the Magdeburg writers note) does not fit the route and course of Ignatius's journey. [Consider (they say) how long a journey it is to go from Antioch to the shore of the Aegean Sea, and then to climb straight northward and travel through the chief cities on the coast as far as Troas, when the journey was intended for Rome, which lies to the west. Did those ten leopards, by whom he was led as a captive, allow him to seek these detours? Is it likely that he was carried through so many windings? Or did they love the Christian faith so much that they accompanied him to so many places to spread it? The treatment of Paul was gentler than that of Ignatius, when he was led captive to Rome, and yet he was taken by a much straighter and shorter route.]

units.la: Tertiò, ea authoritate Ignatius erat, ut eum magis imitari Justinus & Irenæus, & Cyprianus ipse voluerit si modo illius Epistolæ illorum ætate extitissent, quam Tertullianum, qui eum tamen usque adeo imitatus est, ut prope quibusdam cum Tertulliano Montanizare videatur. Atque nulla apud hos patres Ignatij Epistolarum imitatio, imò ne citatio quidem reperitur, donec ad constitutiones Apostolorum deventum est, quas post Concilium Nicænum confectas esse dominus monstravimus supra. Multas sententias collegit Carolus Bovinus, quæ in Epistolis Ignatij & in constitutionibus Apostolorum, penitus eadem reperiuntur. Quid igitur sentiendum? aut Ignatius ex Clemente, aut Clemens ex Ignatio has sententias desumpsit. Si Ignatius ex Clemente, ut Carolo Bovino placet, tum post Concilium Nicænum & non ante, scriptæ hæ Epistolæ Ignatij sunt. Si Clemens ex Ignatio, rationem expecto, cur primò hic author sententias Ignatij ita condensaret? Justinus, Irenæus, Tertullianus, Cyprianus, Origenes, similiter non condensarent? Atqui certè à nemine horum, adeo frequenter citatum Ignatium fuisse constat: ego verò epistolas Ignatij à nemine unquam ante Concilium Nicænum, omnino citatas dico. Quod si citatus fuisset, non tamen inde sequeretur, epistolas hasce ab ipso Ignatio scriptas fuisse, quia citat Hermæ pastorem Irenæus, quem librum tamen à vero Herma quem Paulus meminit Roman. 16. scriptum non fuisse, sed sub persona Hermæ fictum agnoscunt omnes. Qui librum fictum citavit Irenæus, nonne Epistolas Ignatij veras multo magis citassert, si ante extitissent: præsertim cum ostendat Iohannes Reynoldus omnia undique testimonia etiam ex Ethnicis conquisivisse se Irenæum: & Iustinum Martyrem & Clementis Epistolam citavisse. Respondebis eundem Reynoldum dicere Irenæum Ignatium citasse hisce verbis. Quidam è nostris. At non Epistolam aliquam citare Irenæum dicit Reynoldus (quod & in aperto est) sed tantum Ignatij dictum quoddam. Verba sic se habent. Quemadmodum quidam de non-stris dixit, propter Martyrium in Deum adiudicatus ad bestias: quoniam frumentum sum Christi, & per dentes bestiarum molor, ut mundus panis Deo Deo inveniar. Cum Clementem citat, utitur hâc voce, scripsit: cum citat Iustinum: Bene inquit Iustinus in eo libro qui est ad Marcionem, &c. in hac autem citatione hoc tantum ait. Quidam è nostris dixit: adde quod nomina Clementis & Iustini ponat, cum quid ex eorum scriptis adfert: Ignatium verò circumscribit tantùm: quibus omnibus patet, non illius scriptam Epistolam aliquam, sed tantùm illius dictum quodpiam, quod vulgo tum circumferebatur, eum allegasse. Quo suspectior Eusebius, qui Epistolas Ignatij nullo alio argumento confirmare potuit, quàm hac Irenæi citatione.
units.tr: Thirdly, Ignatius had such authority that Justin, Irenaeus and Cyprian himself would have imitated him more, if his Epistles had existed in their time, rather than Tertullian, who nevertheless imitated him so closely that to some he seems almost to Montanize with Tertullian. Yet among these Fathers there is no imitation of Ignatius's Epistles, nor even any citation of them, until we come to the Constitutions of the Apostles, which, as I have shown above, were composed after the Council of Nicaea. Charles Bovinus has gathered many sentences that are found in the Epistles of Ignatius and in the Constitutions of the Apostles, entirely the same. What then should we think? Either Ignatius took them from Clement, or Clement took them from Ignatius. If Ignatius took them from Clement, as Bovinus pleases to hold, then these Epistles of Ignatius were written after the Council of Nicaea and not before. If Clement took them from Ignatius, I ask for a reason why this author would first have condensed the sentences of Ignatius in such a way. Would Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Cyprian and Origen likewise not have condensed them? And yet it is certain that by none of these was Ignatius cited so frequently; I say that his Epistles were cited by no one before the Council of Nicaea at all. But even if he had been cited, it would not follow that these Epistles were written by Ignatius himself, because Irenaeus cites the Shepherd of Hermas, a book which everyone acknowledges was not written by the true Hermas whom Paul mentions in Romans 16, but was fabricated under Hermas's name. If Irenaeus cited a fabricated book, would he not have cited the genuine Epistles of Ignatius much more, if they had existed earlier? Especially since John Reynolds shows that Irenaeus gathered every testimony from all sources, even from the Gentiles, and cited Justin Martyr and the Epistle of Clement. You will reply that the same Reynolds says Irenaeus cited Ignatius in these words: One of our people. But Reynolds says that Irenaeus did not cite any Epistle (which is also evident) but only a certain saying of Ignatius. The words are these: As one of the non-ours said, condemned to the beasts for martyrdom to God: I am the wheat of Christ, and I am ground by the teeth of the beasts, that I may be found pure bread for God. When he cites Clement, he uses the word wrote; when he cites Justin: Justin rightly says in that book which is against Marcion, etc. But in this citation he says only: One of our people said. Add that he names Clement and Justin when he brings something from their writings, but he merely circumscribes Ignatius. From all of this it is plain that he alleged not some written Epistle of his, but only some saying of his that was then commonly circulated. All the more suspect is Eusebius, who could confirm the Epistles of Ignatius by no other argument than this citation of Irenaeus.

units.la: Quartò, septem tantum Epistolas scripsisse refert Eusebius, quod Hieronymus confirmat, in Catalogo virorum illustrium, at nos iam duodecim habemus. Quid de Epistola Mariae ad Ignatium sentiendum: lectoris iudicio eum permittit Baronius, transfodit verò Suarez. An beata virgo aliquid scripserit (inquit) non constat: nam Epistola quædam ad Ignatium quæ nomine eius circumfertur, incertæ authoritatis est: si constaret eam à beata virgine scriptam, nemo ut existimo dubitaret, quin inter Canonicas scripturas esset numeranda. Quid etiam de Epistola Polycarpi quæ unà cum Epistolis Ignatij extat sentiendum est? Ita Eusebius: Polycarpus dicit se ab Ignatio per Epistolam rogatum esse ut Epistolà ferret ad Philippenses: at nihil huiusmodi in Polycarpi Epistola quæ nunc extat. Non rogabo etiam quid de ipsis septem Epistolis Ignatij reliquis sentiendum sit: ut omittam probabile esse, eas esse fictitias, quemadmodum hæ sociæ Epistolæ Mariae nempe & Polycarpi fictæ sunt: respondeo & eas antiquorum patrum citationibus ut nunc extant, non respondere. Theodoretus si quidem dialogo 3. affert testimonium ex Epistola Ignatij ad Smyrnenses, quod in hac nunc edita non reperitur. Idem Theodoretus dialog. 1. & Gelasius contra Eutychem, citat ex Epistola Ignatij ad Ephesios testimonium, quod in his nunc editis exemplaribus nusquam apparet.
units.tr: Fourthly, Eusebius reports that Ignatius wrote only seven Epistles, which Jerome confirms in the Catalogue of Illustrious Men; but we now have twelve. What should we think of the Epistle of Mary to Ignatius? Baronius leaves the judgment to the reader, but Suarez runs it through. It is not certain (he says) whether the blessed Virgin wrote anything, for a certain Epistle to Ignatius which circulates under her name is of uncertain authority. If it were established that it was written by the blessed Virgin, no one, I think, would doubt that it should be counted among the canonical Scriptures. What too should be thought of the Epistle of Polycarp which stands together with the Epistles of Ignatius? Thus Eusebius: Polycarp says that he was asked by Ignatius, through an Epistle, to carry a letter to the Philippians. But nothing of this kind is in the Epistle of Polycarp that now exists. I will not ask either what should be thought of the other seven Epistles of Ignatius; I will omit that it is probable they are fictitious, just as these companion Epistles, namely those of Mary and Polycarp, are fictitious. I answer that the other seven, as they now stand, do not match the citations of the ancient Fathers. Theodoret indeed, in his third Dialogue, brings a testimony from the Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, which is not found in the edition now published. The same Theodoret, in his first Dialogue, and Gelasius against Eutyches, cite a testimony from the Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, which never appears in the copies now published.

units.la: Postremò Hieronymus dialog.3. contra Pelagianos, testimonium citat ex Ignatij Epistolis,quod in his editis non habetur. Sed & scrupulus adhuc alius restat,in Ignatio non citando. De anno quo Christus baptizatus est dissentiunt à sese patres, Ignatius verò ab omnibus (inquit Baronius) Is anno 30. expleto baptizatum tradit: contra quam sententiam audacter insurgit Epiphanius? Hoc probabili argumento est, has Epistolas Ignatianas tum temporis non extitisse. Quid enim? Num tota antiquitas sese Ignatio opponerat? In re tantùm controversa, non Ignatium consulissent? non citassent? sine mentione omni præterijssent? si contrà sentirent,nonne illius authoritatem refutassent?
units.tr: Lastly, Jerome, in his third Dialogue against the Pelagians, cites a testimony from the Epistles of Ignatius which is not found in these published ones. But there remains yet another difficulty, in not citing Ignatius. The Fathers disagree among themselves about the year in which Christ was baptized, but Ignatius (says Baronius) agrees with all. He hands down that Christ was baptized when the thirtieth year was complete; against this opinion Epiphanius boldly rises up. This is a probable argument that these Ignatian Epistles did not exist at that time. For what? Did all antiquity set itself against Ignatius? In a matter that was merely disputed, would they not have consulted Ignatius, cited him? Would they have passed him over without any mention at all? If they had held the opposite view, would they not have refuted his authority?

units.la: Quintò,phraseis harum Epistolarum tempori Ignatiano non conveniunt,frequens etenim apud eum, sacerdotis, altaris, offerendi, sacerdotijq; mentio est, quæ nomina in prima Ecclesia non fuisse observata fatetur ipse Bellarm. qui veteres longo tempore, Iudeorum causa,ab his abstinuisse dicit.
units.tr: Fifthly, the phrasing of these Epistles does not agree with the Ignatian period. For there is frequent mention in him of priest, altar, offering and priesthood, which names, as Bellarmine himself admits, were not in use in the earliest Church, and he says that the ancients abstained from them for a long time because of the Jews.

units.la: Sextò, in Epistola ad Philippenses, eum esse socium eorum qui Christum occiderunt dicit, qui cum Iudæis Pascha celebrat: quo strepitu sorex se iste prodidit non Ignatium orientalem, sed hominem potiùs occidentalem, Romanumq; fuisse. Magna controversia de Pascha te inter Episcopos orientales & occidentales fuit: quorum illi Iohannis & Philippi exemplo freti, quartâ decimâ lunâ una cum Iudæis celebrandum Pascha censuerant: Orientales morem contrarium acriter tuebantur, qui post in Concilio Nicæno sancitus erat: sic ut post hoc Concilii scribens Epiphanius, ex Canone Apostolorum, quem citat, Orientales refutet. Quid igitur? contra Apostolorum Canonem, contra Orientales coepiscopos suos ivisse Ignatium,& in castra Occidentalium transfugisse verisimile est? Fac hoc verisimile, id tamen quomodo verisimile fuit, Victorem Romanum hanc Ignatij authoritatem prætermittere voluisse? cum orientalem contra Orientales citasse Ignatium præsertim tantæ authoritatisvirum, pro causa sua maximè fecit. Redolent certè ista Ignatij tempora illa, quæ Nicænum Concilium subsecuta sunt.
units.tr: Sixthly, in the Epistle to the Philippians he says that whoever keeps the Passover with the Jews is a companion of those who killed Christ. By this noise the mouse has betrayed himself: this Ignatius was not an Eastern but rather a Western man, a Roman. There was a great controversy about Easter between the bishops of the East and of the West. The former, relying on the example of John and Philip, judged that the Passover should be celebrated on the fourteenth day of the moon together with the Jews. The Easterners defended the opposite custom fiercely, and it was afterwards sanctioned at the Council of Nicaea. So Epiphanius, writing after this Council, refutes the Easterners from the Canon of the Apostles, which he cites. What then? Is it likely that Ignatius went against the Canon of the Apostles and against his Eastern fellow bishops, and deserted to the camp of the Westerners? Grant that this is likely. How is it likely, nonetheless, that Victor the Roman wished to pass over this authority of Ignatius? Citing an Eastern Ignatius against the Easterners, especially a man of such authority, would have served his cause most of all. Those times of Ignatius certainly smell of the period which followed the Council of Nicaea.

units.la: Septimo, qui Sabbato ieiunat, cum Christi occisorem esse dicit Ignatius in Epistola ad Philippenses: at jejunium Sabbati nunquam interdictum fuit in Ecclesia Orientali, ante tempora Marcionis, qui Sabbato jejunavit in odium Dei creatoris omnium. Canone 65. Apostolorum hoc jejunium interdictum est: sed Cæsar Baronius ipse fatetur, non ante tempora Marcionis hunc Canonem inventum & insertum fuisse. Quid ni igitur dicendum, hanc Epistolam Ignatij non nisi post tempora Marcionis scriptam?
units.tr: Seventhly, he who fasts on the Sabbath, Ignatius says in the Epistle to the Philippians, is a murderer of Christ. But the fast on the Sabbath was never forbidden in the Eastern Church before the time of Marcion, who fasted on the Sabbath out of hatred of God the Creator of all. Canon 65 of the Apostles forbids this fast; but Caesar Baronius himself admits that this canon was not invented and inserted until after the time of Marcion. Why, then, should we not say that this Epistle of Ignatius was written only after the time of Marcion?

units.la: Octavo, citat contra nos Dononamus, verba Ignatij in Epistola ad Philadelphienses: quibus insinuat separationem quorundam suo tempore ab Episcopo: contra quos ad unitatem cum Episcopo hortatur, a divisione vero ab Episcopo dehortatur. Ex his verisimile est, non nisi post Novati aut Donati tempora, has Epistolas Ignatij scriptas esse: quæ enim occasio tempore Ignatij horum quasi verborum fuit.
units.tr: Eighthly, Downame cites against us the words of Ignatius in the Epistle to the Philadelphians, in which he hints at the separation of certain people from their bishop in his day. Against them he urges unity with the bishop and dissuades from division from the bishop. From this it is probable that these Epistles of Ignatius were written only after the times of Novatus or Donatus, for what occasion for such words was there in the time of Ignatius?

units.la: Nonò, in Epistola ad Trullenses dicit se intelligere angelorum & Archangelorum ordines, multivarias diversitates, virtutum & dominationum differentias, sedium atq; potestatum distantias, thronorum magnificentias, Cherubim & Seraphim excellentis spiritus sublimatem: quæ Ignatij spiritum minimè sapiunt, imo ne tempora quidem redolent. Dicit Baronius Dionysium, hac in re Ignatium citasse, quod falsum est: quod si citaret vero, suspitio augeretur: redolent hæc quidem Dionysij tempora, quæ Ignatio multò posteriora sunt. Apponi hic possunt quæ habet de Ignatio Socrates. Iam vero dicamus unde consuetudo hymnorum, qui in Ecclesia alternis dicantantur, initium cœperit. Ignatius Antiochiæ quæ est in Syria, tertius à Petro Apostolo Episcopus, qui cum Apostolis ipsis multùm versatus est, visionem vidit Angelorum sanctam trinitatem hymnis alternis voce decantatis collaudantium Lib. 6. c. 8. dantium: & formam eaneudi in ea visione expressam Ecclesiæ Antiochenæ tradidit. Unde illa traditio in omnibus Ecclesiis recepta est: in quibus observandum contra Downamum, quàm parum patres juniores de Ecclesiis antecedentibus in materia facti, idonei testes sint. Quàm traditionibus & relationibus à manu in manum tradidis fidendum, quàm parum denique, quæ passim inculcat de universâ Ecclesiæ praxi firma sint. Mihi (inquit) sufficit testimonium quod citavi, Eusebij tempore, qui intra ducentos ab Ignatio annos vixit, suspectum non fuisse. Nam si Eusebius & qui illius tempore vixerunt, nullam causam noverunt, cur Epistola Ignatij ad Ephesios suspecta esset: nullam ego causam noscet cur pro suspecta refutator eam habere debeat. Sufficit igitur quòd Socratis testimonium illius tempore suspectum non fuit? certe tam verum hymnos alternos in tota Ecclesiæ primæ praxi usurpatos fuisse (quod tamen est salsissimum) eosque per visionem ab angelis acceptos Ignatium tradidisse, quam verum est, Ignatium Episcopum Hierarchicum fuisse: eumque epistolam illam scripsisse, quæ nunc extat, ad Ephesios.
units.tr: Ninthly, in the Epistle to the Trallians he says he understands the orders of angels and archangels, the manifold diversities, the differences of virtues and dominions, the distances of seats and powers, the magnificence of thrones, and the sublime excellence of the Cherubim and Seraphim. These things hardly savour of the spirit of Ignatius; indeed they do not even smell of his times. Baronius says that Ignatius was cited here by Dionysius, which is false; for if he had really cited him, the suspicion would only grow. Indeed these things smell of the times of Dionysius, which are much later than Ignatius. What Socrates says about Ignatius may be added here. "Now let us say whence the custom of hymns sung alternately in the Church began. Ignatius, bishop of Antioch in Syria, third from the Apostle Peter, who had much to do with the Apostles themselves, saw a vision of angels praising the holy Trinity with hymns sung alternately with voice, and handed down to the Church of Antioch the form of singing expressed in that vision. Whence that tradition was received in all the Churches." Book 6, chapter 8. In these matters, against Downame, it must be observed how little the later Fathers are trustworthy witnesses to facts about earlier Churches, and how little traditions and reports handed from hand to hand are to be trusted, and how little, in short, what he everywhere urges about the universal practice of the Church is firm. "For me (he says) the testimony which I have cited is enough, since in the time of Eusebius, who lived within two hundred years of Ignatius, it was not suspected. For if Eusebius and those who lived in his time knew no reason why the Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians should be suspect, I, a refuter, know no reason why I should hold it as suspect." Is it therefore enough that the testimony of Socrates was not suspected in his time? Certainly it is as true that alternating hymns were used in the whole practice of the early Church (which is nonetheless most absurd), and that Ignatius handed them down, having received them by vision from angels, as it is true that Ignatius was a hierarchical bishop and wrote that Epistle to the Ephesians which now exists.

units.la: 8 Decimò, quum traditionem quadragesimæ, jejunij quartæ feriæ, ordinum minorum, Acoluthorum, exorcistarum &c. nobis ex Ignatio objiciunt pontificij, quid aliud habent quod respondeant nostri, quàm hæc longo post tempore introducta, satis solido argumento esse, has Ignatij epistolas suppositicias esse? Undecimò, qualia illa quæso sunt quæ in epistola ad Magnesianos reperiuntur? Non presbyter, non Diaconus, non laicus sine Episcopo debet aliquid facere, sicut Christus sine patre nihil facit. Num hæc aut spiritum, aut etiam tempora Ignatij redolent? Quàm etiam illud ἀκυρον, quod de honorando rege et episcopo verba faciens, episcopum præponit regi. Duodecimò, cum in citando Ignatio Downamus tam multus sit, cur non rationes produxit, quæ fidem Ignatio afferre possint? Producit inquies: nam hæ epistolæ piæ & doctæ sunt inquit, & sufficiens probatio est, eas non esse fictitias quòd ab Eusebio memorentur. Negatur hanc probationem sufficientem esse: falli etenim potuit Eusebius de illis epistolis, æquè ac de illius hymnis Socrates, traditione tanta. Collegerat quis fortè dicta Ignatij ante tempus Eusebij, eaquè in formam epistolarum redegit: sed Ignatium ipsum epistolas scripsisse, non magis certum est ex Eusebij relatione, quàm certum est, epistolas Pauli ad Senecam, & Senecæ ad Paulum genuinas esse, quod memorentur ab Hieronymo in catalogo virorum illustrium, et tanquam genuinæ ab eodem approbentur. Accedo propius ad ipsum Eusebium: dicit ille, Ignatium septem epistolas scripsisse, quid tum? sic etiam dicit (ac non ille solum, sed universa prima Ecclesia) librum pastoris, verum Hermæ scriptum fuisse: quod tamen quàm falsum sit, iam omnes facilè internoscunt. Negatur secundò, has epistolas Ignatij quæ nunc extant, illas ipsas esse, quæ ab Eusebio commemorantur. At in epistola ad Ephesios inquis eadem verba reperiuntur quæ recitat Eusebb. Euseb. Quinq; has epistolas dolauit, & titulum & verba Eusebij imitari non potuerit? Extant inquis in epistola ad Ephesios eadem verba quae Eusebius recitat: at habuimus supra Theodoretum & Gelasium verba quaedam citasse ex epistola Ignatij ad Ephesios, quae in ista quae iam circumfertur, minimè extant.
units.tr: 8 Tenthly, when the Papists object to us from Ignatius the tradition of Lent, the fast on Wednesdays, the minor orders, acolytes, exorcists and so on, what else have our people to answer, except that these things were introduced long afterwards, which is a solid enough argument that these Epistles of Ignatius are spurious? Eleventhly, what sort of things, I ask, are those found in the Epistle to the Magnesians? "A presbyter, a deacon or a layman must do nothing without the bishop, just as Christ does nothing without the Father." Do these smell of the spirit or even of the times of Ignatius? Also that word ἀκυρον [unlawful], where, speaking of honouring the king and the bishop, he puts the bishop before the king. Twelfthly, since Downame is so lavish in citing Ignatius, why did he not produce reasons that could give credit to Ignatius? He produces some, you will say: these epistles are pious and learned, he says, and it is sufficient proof that they are not fictitious that Eusebius mentions them. This proof is denied to be sufficient. Eusebius could have been mistaken about those epistles, just as Socrates was about his hymns, by such tradition. Perhaps someone had collected the sayings of Ignatius before Eusebius' time and reduced them to the form of epistles. But that Ignatius himself wrote the epistles is no more certain from Eusebius' report than it is certain that the epistles of Paul to Seneca and of Seneca to Paul are genuine, which Jerome mentions in his catalogue of illustrious men and approves as genuine. I come closer to Eusebius himself. He says Ignatius wrote seven epistles; so what? So too he says (and not he alone, but the whole early Church) that the Shepherd was written by Hermas, which, however, everyone now easily recognises as false. Secondly, it is denied that the epistles of Ignatius which now exist are those very ones mentioned by Eusebius. But you say the same words are found in the Epistle to the Ephesians that Eusebius quotes. Could not someone who had fashioned these epistles have imitated Eusebius' title and words? You say the same words which Eusebius quotes are found in the Epistle to the Ephesians; but above we had Theodoret and Gelasius citing certain words from the Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, which are by no means found in the one that is now in circulation.

units.la: 9 Decimo tertiò & ultimò, doctorum virorum judicia, hac in re, a nobis sunt: fictitias etenim has Ignatij epistolas esse docent inter alios, Magdeburgenses Centur. 2. lib. 10. Gulielmus Whitakerus cont. 1. qu. 6. cap. 19. Sibrandus Lubbertus de princip. Christian. dogmat. lib. 7. cap. 10. & Gulielmus Perkins. in problem. quem ego quia unus de nobis est non citassem, nisi eum antè a Georgio Downamo citatum vidissem. Quid ipsi Hierarchici? Thomas Billonus in canonibus Apostolorum fidentior est, quàm in Ignatio. Canones (inquit) qui dicuntur Apostolorum, antiquioris disciplinae documenta sanè pervetusta sunt. Pagina verò proxima ita habet de Ignatio. Ejusdem hujus vocis usum in epistolis illis, quae Ignatij feruntur, semel atqz iterum invenio. Observa eandem notam inuisse Ignatio, quam canonibus, laudem verò vetustatis attribuisse Canonibus, quam Ignatij epistolis non attribuit. Quum dicit, Canones qui dicuntur Apostolorum, apertè innuit, eos ipsorum Apostolorum minimè esse, sicuti alibi apertè docet: pari ratione quum dicit, epistolae quae feruntur Ignatij, eas Ignatij minimè esse subinsinuat. Eadem ni fallor doctissimi Causaboni opinio est. Probandum illi erat, ad priscam Ecclesiae disciplinam demonstrandam potiora esse prioris saeculi, quàm quarti aut quinti testimonia. Instat autem in Cypriano solo. Vel unicus (inquit) Christi Martyr sanctissimus Cyprianus, primitivae Ecclesiae mores & disciplinam totam, melius nos docuerit, quàm multi alij qui in quarto saeculo vixerunt. Cur omisit Ignatium ergo, si cum genuinum existimasset? nam & multò antiquior est, & multi de disciplina habet, sic ut Baronius, ecclesiasticae disciplinae faciem purissimam in eo lucere dicat. Iohannes Bridgesius Episcopus Oxoniensis, multò apertissimus est. Quicunque (inquit) in Ignatij nomine illas epistolas scripsit: non enim audeo (tam audacter ut fratres) affirmare, eas ipsius Ignatij esse. Richardus Stochius, itâ in sua versione Whitakeriana. Authoritate Ignatij obrui veritas non debet, cujus fides exigua est, si tamen omnino blu: non te latent quae doctorum hominum omnium de illis Ignatij epistolis judicia sint. Gratianus ipse non multum huic Ignatio favet: multa in his epistolis reperiuntur, quae illius temporibus doceri incredibile est, qualis ista stricta quadragesimae observatio est: imò non nisi iam pridem hae epistolae impressae & publicatae sunt.
units.tr: 9 Tenthly, thirdly and last, the judgments of learned men in this matter are on our side. They teach that these Epistles of Ignatius are fictitious, among others the Magdeburg Centuriators, Century 2, book 10; William Whitaker, Controversy 1, question 6, chapter 19; Sibrandus Lubbertus, On the Principles of Christian Doctrine, book 7, chapter 10; and William Perkins in his Problems, whom I would not have cited, since he is one of us, had I not first seen him cited by George Downame. What do the Hierarchists themselves say? Thomas Bilson is more confident about the Canons of the Apostles than about Ignatius. "The canons which are called those of the Apostles are very ancient documents of an older discipline." But the next page says this about Ignatius: "I find the use of this word in those epistles which are attributed to Ignatius once and again." Notice that he gives the same mark of suspicion to Ignatius as to the canons, but he attributes the praise of antiquity to the canons and does not attribute it to the epistles of Ignatius. When he says "the canons which are called those of the Apostles," he plainly hints that they are not of the Apostles themselves, as he elsewhere plainly teaches; by the same reasoning, when he says "the epistles which are attributed to Ignatius," he subtly suggests that they are not Ignatius'. This, if I am not mistaken, is also the opinion of the most learned Casaubon. He had to prove that for demonstrating the ancient discipline of the Church, the testimonies of the earlier century are weightier than those of the fourth or fifth. He insists, however, on Cyprian alone: "Cyprian, the most holy martyr of Christ, alone (he says) taught us better about the customs and the whole discipline of the primitive Church than many others who lived in the fourth century." Why, then, did he omit Ignatius, if he had thought him genuine? For Ignatius is much older and has much to say about discipline, so that Baronius says "the purest face of ecclesiastical discipline shines forth in him." John Bridges, Bishop of Oxford, is far more open: "Whoever wrote those epistles under the name of Ignatius; for I do not dare (as boldly as brothers) to affirm that they are Ignatius' own." Richard Stock, thus in his version of Whitaker: "The truth must not be overthrown by the authority of Ignatius, whose faith is slight, if indeed it is sound at all. Nor are you unaware what the judgments of all learned men are about those epistles of Ignatius. Gratian himself does not much favour this Ignatius: many things are found in these epistles which it is incredible were taught in his times, such as this strict observance of Lent; indeed these epistles were not printed and published until lately."

units.la: 10 Quartus author fictitius qui ab Hierarchicis produci solet, Dyonisius Areopagita est. Iohannes siquidem Whitgiftus, interrogationes in baptismo ad infantes, in Ecclesia Anglicana hodie usurpatas, ita tuetur. Nova non sunt, nec nuper inventa, sed magna antiquitatis. Nam Dyonisius Areopagita earum meminit, &c. Quam autem indignum digrum dignum sit nos hoc fabulatore & circumforaneo prægravari, videre est in Gulielmo Whitakero Cont. 1. quæst. 6. cap. 12. Sibrando Lubberto de princip. Christianorum dogmat. lib. 7. cap. 10. Gulielmo Perkin, in problemat. Gulielmo Fulcone in respons. ad AngliRhemen. In Act. 17. Thom. Mortono Apolog. Catholic. q. 2. lib. 2. cap. 3. alijsque authoribus nostris, qui laruam huic Dyonisio egregiè detraxerunt.
units.tr: 10 The fourth fictitious author whom the Hierarchists commonly produce is Dionysius the Areopagite. John Whitgift, for example, defends in this way the questions put to infants at baptism, which are now in use in the English Church: They are not new, nor recently invented, but of great antiquity. For Dionysius the Areopagite mentions them, etc. How unworthy it is that we should be burdened by this storyteller and street-corner fabulist can be seen in William Whitaker, Contra 1, quaest. 6, cap. 12; Sibrandus Lubbertus, De principiis christianorum dogmatum, lib. 7, cap. 10; William Perkins, in Problemata; William Fulke, in Responsio ad Angli-Rhemenses, on Acts 17; Thomas Morton, Apologia Catholica, quaest. 2, lib. 2, cap. 3; and our other authors, who have excellently stripped this mask from Dionysius.

units.la: II Quintus author fictitius qui ab Hierarchicis produci solet, author epistolarum decretalium est, sub nomine Clementis, Anacleti, Aniceti, &c. Sed ecquis ullus Evangelicus, inquis, his epistolis decretalibus fidem adhibendam censebit? Quid ni, dummodo (ut est apud Comicum) ob rem. Richardus etenim Bancroftus, in capite eo, quo nostros in patres contemptus exaggerat, hos etiam patres inter reliquos a nobis reijci & repudiari indignissimè fert. Quando antiquitas & legitimus usus nominis Archiepiscopi, ex authoritate Clementis, Anacleti & Anaceti probatur, horum authoritatum citationem ipsius infirmi citationem appellant: hos omnes authores sub pedibus proterunt, Clemens, Anacletus, Anicetus, tanquam circumforanei notis Thaziciis comperti ab eis dimittuntur. Vide lector cum quo hominum genere nobis lis est: certè cum eis, qui vel ipsis papistis quibusdam longè deteriores sunt. Cæsar etenim Baronius fatetur epistolas Clementis quas nunc habemus, easdem non esse cum eis quas Ruffinus transtulit: & fusè disputat Nicolaus Cusanus contra harum Clementis et Anacleti epistolarum ligitimationem: et Antonius Cautius denique jurisconsultus doctissimus, has epistolas decretales veru transfigit. Hos citans Richardus Fyldus Hierarchicus, Philistæos proprio glado cadere (dicit) et se mutuis verberibus conficere. Omitto nomen Philistæorum, hoc tamen dico: dum ea quæ Philistæorum sunt Hierarchici satagunt, eos gladio proprio ad illum Philistæorum morem, non immeritò cadere. Primò etenim hic ipse Fyldus Hierarchicus, quasi gladio evaginato has decretales epistolas transverberat, ac proinde per ipsorum latus Richardũ Bancroftum vulnerat. Deinde Thomas Bilsouus Hierarchicus has epistolas decretales fictitias esse doctè disputat. Ad hæc, Thomas Mortonus Hierarchicus adversus decretales epistolas multa habet. Postremò, Iohannes Whitgiftus, citat ille quidem pro episcopatu et Archiepiscopatu comprobando Clementis epistolam: sed præ pudore aliud illi nomen indit, ex Polidoro Vergilio, Compendium scilicet Christianæ religionis, quin etiam hanc Clementis epistolam agnoscit fictitiam his verbis. Nemo negat quin epistolæ Clementis fictitiæ sint. Itane verò fictitiæ, & tamen ad comprobandum Archiepiscopatum presse? Certè Nicolai Cusani is candor erat, ut quanquam primatui Romanæ Ecclesiæ consultum pervellet: pet has epistolas decretales tamen, propterea quòd fictitiæ suut, consuli eidem nollet. Quo nomine laude dignus & Matheus Sutcliuius Hierarchicus: qui de epistolis decretalibus Clementis, Anacleti, &c. Verba faciens ita habet.Nec Pontificum Romanorum advocatus Bellarminus aut negare errores in eas irrepsisse, aut affirmare eas indubitatas esse ausus sit. Quid ergo eas nobis profert, aut cur vtitur testibus dubijs? Cur instrumenta producit falsa; num ex fonte erroris se veritatem probaturum putat?
units.tr: 11 The fifth fictitious author whom the Hierarchists commonly produce is the author of the decretal letters, published under the names of Clement, Anacletus, Anacletus' successor Anicetus, and others. But, you will say, what Evangelical would consider these decretal letters worthy of belief? Why not, provided (as the comic poet has it) there is a reason? For Richard Bancroft, in the very chapter in which he magnifies the contempt of our people for the Fathers, bitterly complains that these Fathers too are rejected and repudiated by us along with the rest: When the antiquity and lawful use of the name Archbishop is proved by the authority of Clement, Anacletus and Anaceus, they call the citation of these authorities a citation of the weak; they trample all these authors underfoot, Clement, Anacletus, Anicetus, and dismiss them as street-corner fabulists, known by their Thacian marks. Let the reader see with what sort of men we have our dispute: surely with men who are far worse than some of the Papists themselves. For Caesar Baronius admits that the letters of Clement which we now have are not the same as those which Rufinus translated; and Nicholas of Cusa argues at length against the legitimacy of these letters of Clement and Anacletus; and Antonius Cautius, a most learned jurist, plainly pierces these decretal letters. Citing these men, Richard Fyldes, a Hierarchist, says that the Philistines fall by their own sword, and destroy themselves with their own blows. I pass over the name of the Philistines, but I say this: while the Hierarchists busy themselves with what belongs to the Philistines, they are not unjustly falling on their own sword, in the manner of those Philistines. For first, this same Fyldes, a Hierarchist, as if with drawn sword, runs these decretal letters through, and so by their side wounds Richard Bancroft. Next, Thomas Bilson, a Hierarchist, learnedly argues that these decretal letters are fictitious. Besides, Thomas Morton, a Hierarchist, has much against the decretal letters. Lastly, John Whitgift, though he cites the letter of Clement to prove episcopacy and archiepiscopacy, out of shame gives it another name, taken from Polydore Vergil, namely a Compendium of the Christian religion; and indeed he acknowledges this letter of Clement to be fictitious in these words: No one denies that the letters of Clement are fictitious. Are they really fictitious, and yet pressed into service to prove archiepiscopacy? Certainly Nicholas of Cusa showed such candour that, although he wished to serve the primacy of the Roman Church, he would not on that account wish to be served by these decretal letters, because they are fictitious. Matthew Sutcliffe, a Hierarchist, also deserves praise on this score, who, speaking of the decretal letters of Clement, Anacletus and others, says: "Nor has Bellarmine, the advocate of the Roman Pontiffs, dared either to deny that errors have crept into them or to affirm that they are beyond doubt. Why then does he bring them forward to us, or why does he use doubtful witnesses? Why does he produce false documents; does he think he will prove the truth from a source of error?"

units.la: 11 Sextus author fictitius, qui ab Hierarchicis produci solet Egesippus est. De quo quid scriptum reliquit Downamus audivimus supra. Docet nempe hunc Egesippum abhibendum esse vt succedaneum sancti Lucae, ut intelligamus Acta ea Apposlolorum quae in libro Actorum non habentur ad mortem Iohannis fere per spatium quadragesimum annorum. Probat autem Titum & Timotheum episcopos fuisse, quia Egisippus dicit Paulum ordinasse Timotheum episcopum Ephesi, Titum Cretae: qua in re qui ei fidem non habet nullam sibi fidem mereri dicit. Sed vbi quaeso aut hoc scribit Egisippus, aut ad Lucam supplementa illa continuat quae memorasti? Dicit forte Eusebius, eum quinque libros scripsisse, in quibus sinceram Evangelicae praedicationis explicationem complexus est:Hieronimus afirmat hos libros continere historiam eorum quae gesta sunt a Christi Apostolis et episcopis ad sua usque tempora: Trithemius vero Egesippum ad annum 160 viventem scripsisse libros tradit ecclesiasticorum actuum a passione Domini ad suam usque aetatem: at quinque Egesippi libri, qui in Bibliotheca sanctorum patrum extant, minime de historia Ecclesiasticarum rerum tractant, sed de Machabeis, de bello Iudaico, de vrbis Hierosolymae excidio, & huiusmodi similibus. Dixit insuper hic author plures quam quinque libros scriptos lib. 3. c.5. Dicit etiam Antiochiam in quartum locum reiectam postquam excrevit Constantinopolis civitas Bizantiorum: quo manifestum sit non nisi post tempora Constantini hos quinque Egesippi libros scriptos fuisse: a quo primum huic civitati hoc nomen impositum est. Quid multis opus? Bellarminus ipse fatetur eos quinque libros non extare quae Egesippus scripsit: & quae Egesippi hodie extant fictitia esse testatur Gulielmus Whitakerus cont. 1. q. 6. c. 12. Sibrandus Lubbertus de princip. christianorum Dogmat. li. 7. cap. 10. Iohannes Bridgesius Episcopus Oxoniensis. Defens. gubernat. lib. 3. pag. 299. et Meredithus Hanmerus Hierarchicus in Chronolog. Eccles. anno 121. At vtcunque fictitius hic author sit, fidem tamen forte meretur. Qui id fieri potest cum novitius sit, post tempora Constantini prodiens, sic ut de seculis antecedentibus, praesertim de Titi & Timothei ordinatione in episcopatum testis idoneus esse nequeat? A Daniele Chamiero comprobatum hoc: qui Egesippum reijcit etiam in historia Simonis haeretici: quia multis seculis post eam rem gestam vixerit. Nam Egisippum illum inquit falso nonnulli putant esse Apostolis συνχρονον, quum vixerit post Constantinum magnum. Neque patitur eum de traditione Domine quo vadis testificari Gulielmus Whitakerus, cujus ista verba fuut,Haec omnis historia, seu potius fabula nititur fide Egesippi, cuius exigua sane fides & authoritas est. Matheus Sutclivius non magis animadvertisse videtur Egesippum quem nunc habemus adulterinum fuisse, atque ipse Downamus; non tamen eam fidem quam Downamus adhibendam esse censet. Incertum est (inquit) an Petro ex urbe fugienti apparuerit Christus, & ea dixerit quae narrat Egesippus. Ambrosius, Gregorius, & fortasse Athanasius fabulam ex Egesippo hauserunt, &c.
units.tr: 12 The sixth fictitious author whom the Hierarchists commonly produce is Hegesippus. We have heard above what Downame has left written about him. He teaches, to be sure, that this Hegesippus is to be used as a substitute for St Luke, so that we may understand those Acts of the Apostles which are not contained in the Book of Acts, down to the death of John, over a period of nearly forty years. He proves, moreover, that Titus and Timothy were bishops, because Hegesippus says that Paul ordained Timothy bishop of Ephesus and Titus of Crete; and in this matter he says that whoever does not trust him deserves no trust himself. But where, I ask, does Hegesippus write this, or does he continue those supplements to Luke which you have mentioned? Perhaps Eusebius says that he wrote five books, in which he comprised a sincere explanation of the Evangelical preaching. Jerome affirms that these books contain the history of what was done by the apostles and bishops of Christ down to his own times. Trithemius, however, hands down that Hegesippus, living to the year 160, wrote books of ecclesiastical acts from the passion of the Lord to his own age. But the five books of Hegesippus which exist in the Bibliotheca of the holy Fathers do not treat at all of the history of ecclesiastical affairs, but of the Maccabees, of the Jewish war, of the destruction of the city of Jerusalem, and of similar matters. This author, moreover, speaks of more than five books having been written, in book 3, chapter 5. He also says that Antioch was pushed back into fourth place after the city of Constantinople grew up among the Byzantines; by which it is clear that these five books of Hegesippus were written only after the times of Constantine, from whom this city first received this name. But why say more? Bellarmine himself admits that those five books which Hegesippus wrote are not extant; and that the Hegesippus which exists today is fictitious is attested by William Whitaker, Contra 1, quaest. 6, cap. 12; Sibrandus Lubbertus, De principiis christianorum dogmatum, lib. 7, cap. 10; John Bridges, bishop of Oxford, Defence of the Government, lib. 3, p. 299; and Meredith Hanmer, a Hierarchist, in his Chronology of the Church, year 121. But however fictitious this author may be, he perhaps deserves some trust? How can that be, since he is a newcomer, appearing after the times of Constantine, so that he cannot be a suitable witness about earlier centuries, especially about the ordination of Titus and Timothy to the episcopate? This is confirmed by Daniel Chamier, who rejects Hegesippus even in the history of Simon the heretic, because he lived many centuries after that event. For he says that some falsely think that this Hegesippus was contemporary [σύγχρονον] with the Apostles, since he lived after Constantine the Great. Nor does William Whitaker allow him to attest the tradition of Domine, quo vadis, whose words these are: This whole story, or rather fable, rests on the faith of Hegesippus, whose faith and authority are certainly slight. Matthew Sutcliffe does not seem to have noticed any more that the Hegesippus we now have is spurious, and so too Downame himself; yet he does not think it should be given the faith which Downame gives it. It is uncertain, he says, whether Christ appeared to Peter as he was fleeing the city, and said the things which Hegesippus relates. Ambrose, Gregory, and perhaps Athanasius drew the fable from Hegesippus, etc.

units.la: Septimus author supositititius ab Hierarchicis productus Dorotheus est. Hujus vitam collegit Meredithus Hanmerus Hierarchicus: cui dubium non est, quae nunc Dorothei Sinopsis extat, ab illo vero Dorotheo scriptam fuisse, quem multis laudibus ornat Eusebius lib. 7. cap. 31. & Demochares institut. Christian. relig. & quem martyrio sub Iuliano coronatum Petrus de Natalibus asserit. lib. 6. de sanctis. Atque hunc Dorotheum opponit Bellarmino Matheus Sutcliuius, ut probet non alium, sed Barnabam Ecclesiam Romanam primo fundasse. At etiamsi cum fictitium existimasset Sutclivius, melius tamen adversus Bellarminum cum ex parte amplexurum producere potuit, quam adversus nos Downamus, eundem penitus reijcientes & repudiantes. Probat is Apostolos Iacobum ordinasse episcopum Hierosolimitanum ex Dorotheo in Synopsi, sed eum loco penultimo citans, ante solum Augustinum. Alibi vero magnificentiori sede collocatur: citatur etenim loco primo ante Hieronimum & reliquos omnes, ut probetur Timotheum episcopum Ephesi Hierar. fuisse: ante omnes inquam eos, quos authores fide dignos Downamus affirmat. Quam vero parum fide dignus Dorotheus ipse sit, probat fusissime & eruditissime, ut alios omittam, Iohannes Reinoldus. Sane inquit Dorotheus ipse quisquis fuerit, synopsin hanc nescio an majori imperitia an impudentia fecerit ac ediderit: inepte, quia sine judicio, ea, quae ipse stultissime somniavit putaverit esse vera: impudenter, quia ea quae ipse sibi opinionis errore affinxerat, tanquam verissima scriptis commendavit. En authorem Downami fide dignum: quem mirandum non est si Timotheum fecerit Ephesi episcopum, quum in alios tam liberalis fuerit, ut (citante Reinoldo) Caesarem Philip. 4 22. commemoratum id est, Neronem imperatorem fecerit episcopum Dirrachij, & Priscillam uxorem Aquilae donarit episcopatu Colophonis. Addit insuper Reinoldus Celarem Baronium, qui fatetur nullum fuisse talem Dorotheum Episcopum Tyri, sed authorem hujus operis esse alium recentiorem cujus errores notat passim in Annalibus: nec non Bellarminum, qui ait Synopsin hanc falso Dorotheo adscribi: eamque plenam esse narrationibus confictis et mendacibus affirmat. Inter 72. Discipulos numerat Eunuchum Reginae Aethiopum, quem a Philippo conversum constat post ascentionem Domini: & Iuniam Episcopum facit, quam tamen faeminam fuisse certum est: Haec ita cum sint, miror Thomam Mortonum Hierarchicum asseruisse, Sixtum Senensem, hunc Dorotheum tanquam verum & genuinum agnovisse.
units.tr: Seventh, a supposititious author produced by the Hierarchists is Dorotheus. Meredith Hanmer, a Hierarchist, has gathered his life; and there is no doubt that the Synopsis of Dorotheus which now exists was written by that true Dorotheus whom Eusebius, book 7, chapter 31, adorns with many praises, and whom Demochares, in his Institutes of the Christian Religion, and Peter de Natalibus, in book 6 of On the Saints, say was crowned with martyrdom under Julian. And Matthew Sutcliffe sets this Dorotheus against Bellarmine, to prove that it was not another, but Barnabas, who first founded the Roman Church. But even though Sutcliffe thought him fictitious, he could have brought him forward against Bellarmine more effectively in part than Downame has against us, rejecting and repudiating him altogether. He proves from Dorotheus in the Synopsis that the Apostle James ordained the bishop of Jerusalem, but he cites him in second-last place, only ahead of Augustine. Elsewhere, however, he is placed in a more honourable seat: he is cited in first place, before Jerome and all the rest, to prove that Timothy was bishop of Ephesus. I say, before all those whom Downame affirms to be trustworthy authors. How little trustworthy Dorotheus himself is, John Reynolds proves most fully and learnedly, to pass over others. Indeed, Dorotheus himself, whoever he was, did not know whether he made and published this synopsis out of greater ignorance or greater impudence: ignorantly, because without judgement he took those things which he had foolishly dreamed up to be true; impudently, because he commended as most true in his writings those things which he had fabricated for himself through an error of opinion. Behold the author whom Downame deems trustworthy! It is no wonder if he made Timothy bishop of Ephesus, since he was so liberal towards others that (as Reynolds cites) he made Caesar, mentioned in Philippians 4:22, into Nero the emperor, and made bishop of Dyrrachium, and gave the bishopric of Colophon to Priscilla, the wife of Aquila. Reynolds adds further that Caesar Baronius, who admits that there was no such Dorotheus as bishop of Tyre, but that the author of this work was another, more recent man whose errors he notes throughout the Annals; and also Bellarmine, who says that this Synopsis is falsely ascribed to Dorotheus, and asserts that it is full of invented and lying narratives. Among the seventy-two disciples he counts the eunuch of the Queen of the Ethiopians, who is known to have been converted by Philip after the Lord's ascension; and he makes Junia a bishop, although it is certain that she was a woman. These things being so, I wonder that Thomas Morton, a Hierarchist, asserted that Sixtus of Siena acknowledged this Dorotheus as true and genuine.

units.la: De Pontif. Rom. l. 2. c. 11. etiam diserte testatur; has constitutiones Apostolorum, ut haereticorum facibus adulteratas, à patribus repudiatas esse, En secundum argumentum, qua ne hic liber ab Hierarchicis citandus sit, nedum nobis obtrudendus. Authorem personatum in scenam producere sit leve: at librum talem huiusmodi authoris imperitis obtrudere, qui variè adulteratus sit, quis quaeso leve dixerit? Et repudiatus a patrib9 hic liber est, quia varia adulterata continet: authoritatem tamen authenticam habebit quae adversùs adversarium valeat? Sed remedium forte adhibebunt, quo minus fallamur in delectu. Canones huius libri illi recipiendi pro veris sunt (inquit Baronius) quos post observavit Ecclesia. Eatenus solùm hi Canones (inquit Bilsonus) fidem merentur, quoad cum primi temporis historiis, & antiquorum Conciliorum decretis consentiunt. Qui huius libri Canones a patribus & conciliis citantur (inquit Dovvnamus) tanquam authentici, extra omnem exceptionem sunt: ut qui tantam authoritatem habeant, quantam ulla alia Ecclesiastica scripta quaecunque. Et tu Downame dehinc fides lector: has putridas merces ita ornanti, quo venaliores essent? quòd ad praxim Ecclesiae attinet, quam pro sua regula affert Baronius, ea satis certa non est, nam observati quidam Canones huius libri sunt ab antiqua Ecclesia, qui doctrinae Apostolicae adversantur, ut a Magdeburgensibus rectè adnotatum est. Instant in Canone 17.qui secundas nuptias damnat, in Canone 27, qui nuptias in Presbyteris vetat, & Canone 68. qui ad jejunia quadragesimae, Paschae, feriae quartae, & Parasceves alligant conscientias. Respondent ista & Bilsono, annon etenim in sequentibus Concilijs stabilita sunt? Quòd ad citationes attinet, vel ex hoc uno discere promptum, quàm minimè patrum juniorum testimonijs de saeculis ipsos antecedentibus, fidendum sit. Iob. siquidem Damasc. hos Canones Apostolorum inter ipsas sacras scripturas cōputat. Confirmati sunt hi Canones in Trullo inquit Downamus his verbis. Can. 2. Placuit huic sanctae Synodo, ut modo confirmati & rati sint, Canon. Apostol. 85. c. qui a sanctis patribus qui nos praecesserunt suscepti ac confirmati sunt, atque adeò nobis etiam traditi sunt, sanctorum & gloriosorum Apostolorum nomine, Celebrata haec Synodus est ad annum. 675. Ad annum vero 1049. Leo nonus contra Epistolam Nicetae abbatis scribens, tantummodo 50 genuinos Canones esse dicit. Consulit iste horum Canonum authoritati, magis quam Downamus, qui Concilium in Trullo. & Canonem blasphemum illum 85. confirmatum citat: quem & Bancroftus abhominatur, & ipsemet Downamus quasi ab haereticis interpolatum rejicit.
units.tr: In De Pontif. Rom. l. 2. c. 11. he also plainly testifies that these Constitutions of the Apostles, as corrupted by the torches of heretics, were rejected by the Fathers. This is the second argument by which this book should not be cited by the Hierarchicals, much less pressed upon us. To bring a fictitious author onto the stage is a light matter, but to press on unskilled people a book of this kind, by an author of this kind, which has been corrupted in various ways, who, I ask, would call that a light matter? And this book was rejected by the Fathers because it contains many corrupted passages. Will it nonetheless have an authentic authority that can prevail against an opponent? Perhaps they will apply a remedy, so that we are not deceived in the choice. These canons of this book are to be received as true (says Baronius), which the Church afterwards observed. So far only (says Bilson) do these canons deserve belief, insofar as they agree with the histories of the earliest times and the decrees of the ancient councils. The canons of this book which are cited by the Fathers and councils (says Downame) as authentic are beyond all exception, since they have as much authority as any other ecclesiastical writings whatever. And you, Downame, reader, how did you dress these rotten wares so that they would sell better? As for the practice of the Church, which Baronius brings forward as his rule, that is not sufficiently certain. For some canons of this book were observed by the ancient Church which are opposed to apostolic doctrine, as the Magdeburg writers have rightly noted. They press on canon 17, which condemns second marriages; canon 27, which forbids marriage for elders; and canon 68, which binds consciences to the fasts of Lent, Easter, Wednesday and Good Friday. Bilson's answer to these is that such things were established in later councils. As for the citations, one may easily learn from this one instance how little the testimony of later Fathers about the centuries before them is to be trusted. For Damascene counts these canons of the Apostles among the sacred Scriptures themselves. Downame says these canons were confirmed in the Trullan council, in these words: Canon 2. It has pleased this holy Synod that the canons of the holy Apostles, 85 in number, which were received and confirmed by the holy Fathers who went before us, and handed down to us in the name of the holy and glorious Apostles, be now confirmed and held as valid. This synod was held in the year 675. But in the year 1049, Leo IX, writing against the letter of Nicetas the abbot, says that only 50 canons are genuine. This man has more regard for the authority of these canons than Downame does, who cites the Trullan council and the blasphemous canon 85 as confirmed, which Bancroft abhors, and which Downame himself rejects as interpolated by heretics.

units.la: Tertiò, hos Canones Apostolorum dictos dicit ob duas causas, nempe propter magnam eorum antiquitatem & authenticam authoritatem. Sunt inquit qui Epiphanium primò horum mentionem fecisse dicunt, sed mihi alter videtur, nam citantur Concil. Nic. 8, 15. & 16, & Concil. Antioch. cap. 9. Primò oppono rationem Magdeburgensium qui hinc probant hos canones antiquos non esse, quia nulla eorum mentio est apud Iustinum, Irenaeum, Tertullianum & cæteros priscos patres. Secundò, oppono rationem Cæsaris Baronij.Magnum inquit impostura, suspitionem facit canon. 65, quo excommunicatione plectendus statuitur laicus, depositione clericus, qui Sabbato ieiunaverit. Quando quidem tot tamque diserte antiquos patres canon ille præterijt ut à nemine citatus reperiatur? vel quomodo observationem Romana Ecclesia contrari-am omnium Apostolorum canoni Sabbati ieiunij suscepisset, vel eorum Episcopus Clemens id fieri permisisset, qui quod statuissent Apostoli & ipse scripsisset, quàm optimè novit? &c. Tertiò, oppono sententias & rationes Guilielmi Whitakeri & I. Reynoldi. Guil. Whitakerus ita. [Videtur iste liber consarcinatus & confusus ex actis aliorum Conciliorum præcipuè vero ex Concilio Antiocheno: multa enim leguntur in Antiocheno Concilio similia, Non verisimile vero est Antiochenos Patres, sumpsisse aliquid ex Canonibus. Si enim sumpsissent non dissimulassent sed potius indicassent ut majorem inde suis sanctionibus ac decretis authoritatem conciliarent. Sed nullam illi prorsus huius libri mentionem faciunt.] Ita vero Iohan. Reynoldus. [Canones Apostolorum in unum corpus collecti videntur circa tempora Constantini, post Concilium Antiochenum, cuius omnes Canones ibidem interseruntur. Neque enim verisimile est eos patres eosdem Canones, eisdem verbis tanquam suos promulgare voluisse, quos prius in Canonibus Apostolorum fuisse agnoverunt. Ut mihi videntur, quemadmodum Hieronymus monuit epistola ad Lycinium: quæque provincia abundet in sensu suo, & præcepta maiorum leges Apostolicas arbitretur: ita veteres Græci priscorum Synodorum decreta collegisse, & Apostolorum Canones maioris reverentiæ causa appellasse.] Postremò, Theo. Bilsonus, non ausus est dicere Concilium Antiochenum hos Canones citasse: hic tantum dicit, Concilium Antiochenum, c. 9. eodem specatasse, quo hij Canones spectarunt.
units.tr: Thirdly, he says these canons are called the canons of the Apostles for two reasons: namely, because of their great antiquity and their authentic authority. Some say he says that Epiphanius first made mention of them, but to me it seems otherwise, for they are cited in the councils of Nicaea, canons 8, 15 and 16, and in the council of Antioch, chapter 9. First, I set against this the argument of the Magdeburg writers, who prove from this that these canons are not ancient, since there is no mention of them in Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian and the other early Fathers. Secondly, I set against it the argument of Caesar Baronius. It is a great deceit, he says, and it raises suspicion, that canon 65 lays down that a layman who fasts on the Sabbath is to be punished with excommunication, and a cleric with deposition. For how is it that such a canon was passed over by so many and such clear ancient Fathers, that it is found cited by no one? Or how could the Roman Church have adopted a practice contrary to the canon of all the Apostles about the Sabbath fast, or how could its bishop Clement have permitted it, who knew very well, and himself wrote, what the Apostles had laid down? etc. Thirdly, I set against it the opinions and arguments of William Whitaker and John Reynolds. William Whitaker says: [This book seems to have been patched together and jumbled from the acts of other councils, especially from the Council of Antioch. For many things similar to the Council of Antioch are read there. Nor is it likely that the Antiochene Fathers took anything from the canons. For if they had taken it, they would not have concealed it, but would rather have pointed it out, so as to win greater authority for their decrees and enactments. Yet they make no mention of this book at all.] And John Reynolds says: [The canons of the Apostles seem to have been collected into one body around the time of Constantine, after the Council of Antioch, all of whose canons are inserted there. For it is not likely that those Fathers wished to promulgate the same canons, in the same words, as their own, which they had previously recognised as in the canons of the Apostles. As it seems to me, just as Jerome warned in his letter to Lycinius, that a province which abounds in its own opinion thinks the precepts of its elders to be apostolic laws, so the ancient Greeks gathered together the decrees of the earlier synods and called them the canons of the Apostles out of a greater reverence.] Finally, Theophilus Bilson did not dare to say that the Council of Antioch cited these canons; he says only that the Council of Antioch, canon 9, looked to the same thing as these canons did.

units.la: Author secundus fictitius, Clemens Romanus: sic Geor. Dermanus. [Desinunt Acta Apostolorum in Pauli ad Romam accessu: nullam de eis rebus mentionem facientia, quæ post per spacium 9. vel 10. annorum acciderunt. Quorum temporum Acta aliter cognosci non possunt, nisi ex illius epistolis, aut alijs antiquitatis monumentis, quam clausulam licet sub silentio preterierit refutator, opere pretium exi stimavi lectori in mentem revocare, ut multa sciat facta esse ab Apostolis, quæ in alijs antiquitatis regestris narrantur, quamquam in Actis Apostolorum non narrantur, quæ in eis rebus confiuntur, quæ annis 40. ante mortem Iohannis acciderunt.
