Iam vero Acta Apostolorum quæ post Lucæ historiam gesta sunt, ex parte narrantur per Egesippum & Clementem, & alios antiquos authores, qui testantur Paulum ordinasse Timotheum Ephesi Episcopum & Titum Cretæ, aliosque alijs in locis Episcopos, ab Apostolis constitutos fuisse.
units.tr: The second fictitious author is Clement of Rome, so says George Dermann. [The Acts of the Apostles end with Paul's arrival at Rome, and make no mention of those things which happened afterwards over a space of nine or ten years. The acts of those times cannot be known otherwise than from his letters or from other monuments of antiquity. Although the refuter has passed over this clause in silence, I have thought it worth while to remind the reader that many things were done by the Apostles which are related in other records of antiquity, although they are not related in the Acts of the Apostles; and that those things which are feigned in these matters happened forty years before the death of John. Now indeed, the acts of the Apostles which were done after Luke's history are told in part by Hegesippus, Clement and other ancient authors, who testify that Paul ordained Timothy bishop of Ephesus and Titus of Crete, and that bishops were appointed by the Apostles in other places.]

units.la: § Quorum testimoniis quisquis recusat fidem adjungere, fidem ipsemet nullam meretur? Quid tibi videtur lector? Annon gratulandum Dowmamo est, quod supplementarios nobis dederit, tam egregios, tam necessarios, tam fide dignos, quo historiae sacrae defectus sarciatur? Sistendus tamen hic Clemens est; ne forte circumforaneo aliquo impostore decipiamur. Quis igitur hic Clemens est? Proculdubio Clementem Romanum intelligit, verum Apostolorum discipulum. At vera tantum unica illius Epistola ad Corinthios est (inquit Eusebius) contra omnia quae Clementi ascribuntur supposititia. Et in illa Epistola, qui novit Dowmam. quicquam ab eo de Titi & Timothei Episcopatu scriptum fuisse? Quid igitur? aut recognitiones, aut decretales Epistolas, aut Constitutiones Apostolorum, quae Clementi ascribuntur, intelligat Downamus necesse est. Ea vero assinitas est constitutionum Apostolorum, cum Canonibus Apostolorum, qui etiam Clementi a Bellarmino, Baronio, aliisque ascribuntur: ut eas potissimum respexisse Dowmamum credam. Neque obstat quod fateatur in Trullo condemnatum fuisse Canonem Apostolorum 85 quâ Clementis constitutiones roborat: cur etenim has constitutiones quanquam ab haereticis adulteratas (neque enim aliam ob causam eas condemnat Concilium) non amplecteretur? atque Canones Apostol. amplectitur: quos tamen ab haereticis adulteratos confitetur? Quid igitur? Impostor iste, qui undique ab omnibus conclamatur, successaneus Lucae erit in actis Apostolorum memoriae prodendis: imo sacrarum Pauli epistolarum supplementarius, author porro dignus tanta fide ut nullam fidem mereatur, qui ei fidem adhibere detrectaverit? Egone haec a Dowmamo expectabam? Egone, impudentiam impudentissimam non exclamassem, si quis alius praeter Dowmamum haec barritasset? Huccine iam tandem deventum est ut falsorium notabilem, a jure canonico vetitum, a Concilio in Trullo condemnatum, a Caesare Baronio ipso in quibusdam improbatum: a Iuelo, Whitakero, Reynoldo, Lubberto, Perkinso detectum, a Bilsono denique, Feyldo, Mortono, Hierarchicis ipsis conspu-tum, conspurcatum, explosum, exibilatum: non solum pro vero Apostolorum discipulo, sed etiam digno Apostolorum in historia sacra pertexenda successaneo amplecti necesse sit, ni fidem etiam nostram prodere velimus & prostituere? Atque vel ex hoc uno intellgere promptum, quàm Dowmamus vanus sit, quum patres saeculo posteriores credendos affirmat, quando de prioribus saeculis in materia facti, testimonium ferunt. Nam ut Carolum Bovinum, Athanasius, & Eusebius deficiant, quos pro Clementis constitutionibus testes producit: Cyrillus tamen Hierosolymitanus, Epiphanius & Chrysostomus non deficient. Cyrillus etenim Catechis. 18. citat librum quintum sub his verbis: ut scribit Clemens, ut multi narrant; & Chrysostomus Homilia 53. in Mattheum ita habet. Quomodo autem quidem sacerdotes ab hominibus ordinentur, manifeste in libro octavo Canonum Apostolorum Apostolorum dicitur. Epiphanius vero ita. Caeterum ad hoc afferunt fatè idem Audiani Apostolorum constitutionem quae apud multos in ambiguo est, sed non reprobata. Omnis enim regularis ordo in ipsa habetur, & nihil à fide adulteratum, neque à confessione, neque ab Ecclesiastica gubernatione & regula. —Decernunt enim in eadem constitutione Apostoli, &c. Nihil miri est, si Epiphanius contrà Aerium defendit Epiphanius, tanquam ab Apostolis constitutum: cum has Clementis constitutiones, tanquam ab Apostolis ipsis sancitas defendit: nihilque in eis quoad gubernationem Ecclesiae adulteratum esse dicat. Multa ad refutationem afferre non est opus: ipsa constitutio quam tuetur contra Audianos Epiphanius eiusmodi est: ut & Epiphanium refutare, & eandem explodere Carolus ipse Bovinus coactus sit. [Tantum (inquit) abest ut ea quae hoc capite legimus Apostoli statuerunt, ut etiam contraria horum ab ipsis praecepta videantur. —Ipsa constitutio se prodit, & tantùm non vocem emittens, clamat se novam esse. Ait enim aequinoctium fieri vigesima secunda Dystri-mensis, hoc est, Martij. Perspicuum est autem Christi tempore, aequinoctium fuisse vigesima quinta Martij. Quare nova est constitutio, fortasse edita post Concilium Nicenum in quo Paschae observatio, ad eam rationem redacta fuit, &c. Quid igitur est? Clemens iste, verus ille Apostolorum discipulis non est: neque hic liber Constitutionum antiquus, sed post Concilium Nicaenum editus: neque authenticam authoritatem ullam habet ad Episcopatum Hierarchicum comprobandum.
units.tr: § Whoever refuses to give credit to their testimonies deserves no credit himself? What do you think, reader? Should we not congratulate Downame, who has given us supplementary witnesses so excellent, so necessary and so worthy of belief, by which the defects of sacred history may be made good? Yet this Clement must be halted here, lest perhaps we be deceived by some wandering impostor. Who then is this Clement? Without doubt he means Clement of Rome, the true disciple of the Apostles. But there is only one genuine letter of his (says Eusebius), against all the things ascribed to Clement as spurious. And in that letter, who knows that Downame has written anything about the episcopate of Titus and Timothy? What then? Downame must mean either the Recognitions, or the Decretal Epistles, or the Constitutions of the Apostles, which are ascribed to Clement. And there is such a resemblance between the Constitutions of the Apostles and the Canons of the Apostles, which are also ascribed to Clement by Bellarmine, Baronius and others, that I believe Downame had chiefly these in view. Nor is it an obstacle that he admits that canon 85 of the Apostles, which confirms the constitutions of Clement, was condemned in the Trullan council. For why would he not embrace these constitutions, although they were corrupted by heretics (for the council condemns them for no other reason), and yet embrace the canons of the Apostles, which he confesses were corrupted by heretics? What then? Will this impostor, who is cried down on all sides by everyone, be a successor to Luke in recording the memory of the Acts of the Apostles? Indeed, a supplementer to the sacred letters of Paul, an author so worthy of faith that he deserves no faith, and whoever refuses to give him faith is to be rejected? Did I expect these things from Downame? Would I not have cried out at the most shameless impudence, had anyone other than Downame uttered such bawling? Has it come at last to this, that a notorious forger, forbidden by canon law, condemned by the Trullan council, disapproved in some points by Caesar Baronius himself, detected by Jewel, Whitaker, Reynolds, Lubbert and Perkins, and finally spat upon, defiled, exploded and hissed off by Bilson, Feild and Morton, and by the Hierarchicals themselves, must be embraced not only as a true disciple of the Apostles, but even as a worthy successor of the Apostles in weaving sacred history, unless we are willing to betray and prostitute our own faith as well? And from this one instance alone one may easily understand how empty Downame is, when he affirms that Fathers of later centuries are to be believed, when they bear witness about earlier centuries in a matter of fact. For, to leave out Athanasius and Eusebius, whom he produces as witnesses for Clement's constitutions, Cyril of Jerusalem, Epiphanius and Chrysostom will not fail us. For Cyril, in Catechesis 18, cites the fifth book in these words: as Clement writes, as many relate; and Chrysostom, in Homily 53 on Matthew, has this: How priests are ordained by men is clearly stated in the eighth book of the Canons of the Apostles. And Epiphanius says this: Moreover, the Audians bring forward for this purpose the Constitution of the Apostles, which is doubtful among many, but not rejected. For every regular order is contained in it, and nothing corrupted in the faith, nor in the confession, nor in ecclesiastical government and rule. For the Apostles decree in the same constitution, etc. It is no wonder if Epiphanius, in opposing Aerius, defends it as established by the Apostles, since he defends these constitutions of Clement as sanctioned by the Apostles themselves, and says that nothing in them concerning the government of the Church is corrupted. It is not necessary to bring many arguments against this: the very constitution which Epiphanius defends against the Audians is of such a kind that even Charles Bovinus himself was forced both to refute Epiphanius and to explode the same constitution. [So far is it (he says) that the things we read in this chapter were established by the Apostles, that their contrary precepts are even seen to be from them. The constitution itself betrays itself, and, scarcely uttering a voice, cries out that it is new. For it says that the equinox falls on the twenty-second of Dystrimensis, that is, of March. But it is clear that in Christ's time the equinox was on the twenty-fifth of March. Therefore the constitution is new, perhaps published after the Council of Nicaea, in which the observance of Easter was reduced to that rule, etc.] What then is this? That Clement is not the true disciple of the Apostles, nor is this book of Constitutions ancient, but was published after the Council of Nicaea, nor does it have any authentic authority to establish the Hierarchical episcopate.

units.la: 5 Tertius author suppositicius, Ignatius; de quo notum omnibus est, quantopere Hierarchici glorientur. Purissima Ecclesiae facies (inquit Scultingius) in Ignatio est: Ignatij epistolae (inquit Baronius) viva imago Ecclesiae, disciplinae, & traditionum sunt. Non Ecclesiae sed Synagogae Sathanae sunt, quae non conformant ad Ecclesiam tempore Ignatij. Hinc stomachantur nostri quòd harum Epistolarum authoritatem in dubium vocari videant. Ita Lous: Epistolas tuas sanctissimi Ignatii adulterinas esse contendunt. In idenim impudentiae diverticulum si non se r ceperint, adulterata penitus & turpissimis sordibus aspersa, eorum doctrina habeatur. Richardus Bancrottus ita: Aut ad merem Genevensem Ignatius loqui debet: aut si plus quam volunt urgeas, pauperculus antiquus pater iste, tanquam fictitius, & homo vanus, iure repetatur. His ut respondeatur, non ego hic disputabo pro nobis Ignatius sit: sive sit, sive non sit perinde est. Fictitium etenim authorem fuisse, absque impudentia affirmari potest: id quod in ullis argumentis liquere poterit.
units.tr: 5 The third supposititious author is Ignatius, in whose name everyone knows how greatly the hierarchists boast. Ignatius is the purest face of the Church (says Scultingius); the letters of Ignatius are a living image of the Church, its discipline and its traditions (says Baronius). Those who do not conform to the Church of Ignatius's time are not the Church but the synagogue of Satan. Hence our people are angered that they see the authority of these letters being called into doubt. So Lous: They contend that your letters of the most holy Ignatius are spurious. Unless they take refuge in this corner of shamelessness, their doctrine must be held to be utterly adulterated and smeared with the foulest filth. Richard Bancroft says this: Either Ignatius must speak according to the Geneva pattern, or, if you press more than they wish, this poor old father must rightly be disowned as a fabrication and a vain man. To answer these men, I will not here argue for us that Ignatius is genuine or not; whether he is or not makes no difference. For it can be asserted without shamelessness that the author was a fabrication, and this can become clear from several arguments.

units.la: Primo, in omnibus fere Epistolis satis copiosis (quod observarunt Magdeburgenses) occasio scribendi praetermittitur nec vel divinari licet, quare ad hanc aut illam Ecclesiam, potius quàm ad aliam, literas mittere Ignatius voluerit. Unde hoc? annon quia fingi occasiones ab interpolatore satis commodè non potuerant?
units.tr: First, in almost all the fairly lengthy Epistles (as the Magdeburg centuriators observed) the occasion for writing is passed over, and it cannot even be guessed why Ignatius wished to send letters to this church rather than to another. Whence this? Is it not because an interpolator could not conveniently have invented occasions?

units.la: Secundo
units.tr: Secondly

units.la: Secundò, refert Eusebius, scripsisse Ignatium a Smyrna & cum ultra Smyrnam esset, a Troade scripsisse : quod ( ut rursus Magdeburgenses ) itineris Ignatiani ratio & cursus non patitur. [ Expende (inquiunt) quàm longum iter fit, Antiochiâ ad littus Ægæi pelagi se recipere, ibique retrò sursum versus Septentrionem ascendere, & præcipuas civitates in littore sitas usque ad Troadem perlustrare : cum tamen iter ad Romam sit destinatum versus occasum. An decem illi Leopardi à quibus captivus ducebatur has illum ambages quaerere permittebant? aut per tot circuitus illi ancillatos fuisse verisimile est? aut fidem Christianam adeo illi diligebant,ut ad eandem terendam ad tot loca eum divertentem comitarentur? Humanius tractatus Paulus erat, quàm Ignatius quando Romam captivus abducebatur, qui tamen multò rectiori & breviori itinere tractatus est.]
units.tr: Secondly, Eusebius reports that Ignatius wrote from Smyrna, and when he was beyond Smyrna, from Troas; and the route and course of Ignatius's journey do not allow this (as again the Magdeburg centuriators say). [Consider, they say, how long a journey it is to go from Antioch to the shore of the Aegean Sea, and then to turn back northwards and travel through the chief cities on the coast as far as Troas, when the journey to Rome was directed towards the west. Could those ten leopards, by whom he was led as a prisoner, allow him these detours? Is it likely that he was waited on by servants through so many circuits? Or did they so love the Christian faith that they accompanied him, turning aside to so many places, in order to trample it underfoot? Paul was treated more humanely than Ignatius when he was led captive to Rome, yet he was conveyed by a much straighter and shorter route.]

units.la: Tertiò, ea authoritate Ignatius erat, ut eum magis imitari Iustinus & Irenæus, & Cyprianus ipse voluerit si modo illius Epistolæ illorum ætate extitissent, qui cum tamen usque adeo imitatus est, ut prope quibusdam cum Tertulliano Montanizare videatur. Atque nulla apud hos patres Ignatij Epistolarum imitatio, imò ne citatio quidem reperitur, donec ad constitutiones Apostolorum deventum est,quas post Concilium Nicænum confectas esse docuimus supra. Multas sententias collegit Carolus Bovinus, quæ in Epistolis Ignatij & in constitutionibus Apostolorum, penitus eædem reperiuntur. Quid igitur sentiendum? aut Ignatius ex Clemente, aut Clemens ex Ignatio has sententias desumpsit. Si Ignatius ex Clemente, ut Carolo Bovino placet, tum post Concilium Nicænum & non ante, scriptæ hæ Epistolæ Ignatij sunt. Si Clemens ex Ignatio, rationem expecto, cur primò hic author sententias Ignatij ita condensaret? Iustinus, Irenæus, Tertullianus, Cyprianus, Origenes, similiter non condensarent? Atqui certè à nemine horum, adeo frequenter citatum Ignatium fuisse constat : ego verò epistolas Ignatij à nemine unquam ante Concilium Nicænum, omninò citatas dico. Quod si citatus fuisset, non tamen inde sequeretur, epistolas hasce ab ipso Ignatio scriptas fuisse, quia citat Hermæ pastorem Irenæus, quem librum tamen à verò Herma quem Paulus meminit Roman. 16. scriptum non fuisse,sed sub persona Hermæ fictum agnoscunt omnes. Qui librum fictum citavit Irenæus, nonne Epistolas Ignatij veras multo magis citasset, si ante extitissent : præsertim cum ostendat Iohannes Reynoldus omnia undique testimonia etiam ex Ethnicis conquisivisse Irenæum : & Iustinum Martyrem & Clementis Epistolam citavisse. Respondebis eundem Reynoldum dicere Irenæum Ignatium citasse hisce verbis. Quidam è nojtris. At non Epistolam aliquam citare Irenæum dicit Reynoldus (quod & in aperto est) sed tantùm Ignatij dictum quoddam. Verba sic se habent. Quemadmodum quidam de nostris dixit, propter Martyrium in Deum adiudicatus ad bestias : quoniam frumentum sum Christi, & per dentes bestiarum molor,ut mundus panis Deo Deo inveniar. Cum Clementem citat, utitur hâc voce, scripsit: cum citat Iustinum: Bene inquit Iustinus in eo libro qui est ad Marcionem, &c. in hac autem citatione hoc tantum ait. Quidam è nostris dixit: adde quod nomina Clementis & Iustini ponat, cum quid ex eorum scriptis adfert: Ignatium verò circumscribit tantùm: quibus omnibus patet, non illius scriptam Epistolam aliquam, sed tantùm illius dictum quodpam, quod vulgo tum circumferebatur, eum allegasse. Quo suspectior Eusebius, qui Epistolas Ignatij nullo alio argumento confirmare potuit, quàm hac Irenæi citatione.
units.tr: Thirdly, Ignatius had such authority that Justin, Irenaeus and Cyprian would surely have wished to imitate him more, if his letters had existed in their time. Yet they imitated him so little that some seem, like Tertullian, to have become Montanists. And no imitation of Ignatius's letters, not even a citation of them, is found among these Fathers, until we come to the Apostolic Constitutions, which we have shown above were composed after the Council of Nicaea. Charles Bovinus has collected many sentences which are found entirely the same in the letters of Ignatius and in the Constitutions of the Apostles. What then must we think? Either Ignatius took these sentences from Clement, or Clement took them from Ignatius. If Ignatius took them from Clement, as Charles Bovinus is pleased to hold, then these letters of Ignatius were written after the Council of Nicaea and not before. If Clement took them from Ignatius, I want to know why this author would first have condensed the sayings of Ignatius in such a way; would Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Cyprian and Origen likewise not have condensed them? But surely it is established that Ignatius was cited by none of these men, though he was cited so often; and I say that the letters of Ignatius were never cited by anyone at all before the Council of Nicaea. But even if he had been cited, it would not follow that these letters were written by Ignatius himself, because Irenaeus cites Hermas as a pastor, yet all acknowledge that the book he cited was not written by the real Hermas whom Paul mentions in Romans 16, but was fabricated under Hermas's name. Would Irenaeus, who cited a fabricated book, not have cited the genuine letters of Ignatius much more, had they existed before? Especially since John Reynolds shows that Irenaeus sought out testimonies from every quarter, even from the heathen, and cited Justin Martyr and the letter of Clement. You will reply that the same Reynolds says Irenaeus cited Ignatius in these words, Quidam è nostris. But Reynolds does not say that Irenaeus cited any letter (which is also clear), only a certain saying of Ignatius. The words stand thus: As one of our people said, condemned to the beasts for martyrdom to God, "I am the wheat of Christ, and I am ground by the teeth of beasts, that I may be found pure bread for God." When he cites Clement, he uses the word wrote; when he cites Justin: Justin rightly says in that book which is against Marcion, etc.; but in this citation he says only One of our people said. Add that when he quotes something from their writings he gives the names of Clement and Justin, whereas he only refers to Ignatius without naming him. From all these things it is plain that he alleged not some written letter of his, but only a certain saying of his which was then commonly circulated. The more suspect is Eusebius, who could confirm the letters of Ignatius by no other argument than this citation of Irenaeus.

units.la: Quartò, septem tantum Epistolas scripsisse refert Eusebius, quod Hieronymus confirmat, in Catalogo virorum illustrium, at nos iam duodecim habemus. Quid de Epistola Mariæ ad Ignatium sentiendum: lectoris iudicio eum permittit Baronius, transfodit verò Suarez. An beata virgo aliquid scripserit (inquit) non constat: nam Epistola quædam ad Ignatium quæ nomine eius circumfertur, incerte authoritatis est: si constaret eam à beata virgine scriptam, nemo ut existimo dubitaret, quin inter Canonicas scripturas esset numeranda. Quid etiam de Epistola Polycarpi quæ unà cum Epistolis Ignatij extat sentiendum est? Ita Eusebius: Polycarpus dicit se ab Ignatio per Epistolam rogatum esse ut Epistolà ferret ad Philippenses: at nihil huiusmodi in Polycarpi Epistola quæ nunc extat. Non rogabo etiam quid de ipsis septem Epistolis Ignatij reliquis sentiendum sit: ut omittam probabile esse, eas esse fictitias, quemadmodum hæ sociæ Epistolæ Mariæ nempe & Polycarpi fictæ sunt: respondeo & eas antiquorum patrum citationibus ut nunc extant, non respondere.Theodoretus si quidem dialogo 3. affert testimonium ex Epistola Ignatij ad Smyrnenses, quod in hac nunc edita non reperitur. Idem Theodoretus dialog. 1. & Gelasius contra Eutychem, citat ex Epistola Ignatij ad Ephesios testimonium, quod in his nunc editis exemplaribus nusquam apparet.
units.tr: Fourthly, Eusebius reports that Ignatius wrote only seven letters, which Jerome confirms in his Catalogue of Illustrious Men; but we now have twelve. What must be thought of the letter of Mary to Ignatius? Baronius leaves that to the judgment of the reader, but Suarez runs it through: Whether the blessed Virgin wrote anything (he says) is not established; for a certain letter to Ignatius which circulates under her name is of uncertain authority; if it were established that it was written by the blessed Virgin, no one, I think, would doubt that it should be numbered among the canonical Scriptures. What also must be thought of the letter of Polycarp, which is found together with the letters of Ignatius? Thus Eusebius: Polycarp says that he was asked by Ignatius, through a letter, to carry a letter to the Philippians; but nothing of the kind is in the letter of Polycarp which now exists. I will not ask also what must be thought of the other seven letters of Ignatius themselves; to pass over the probability that they are fabricated, just as those companion letters of Mary and Polycarp are fabricated, I answer that they do not correspond to the citations of the ancient Fathers as they now stand. Theodoret, indeed, in his third dialogue, brings forward a testimony from the letter of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, which is not found in the edition now published. The same Theodoret, in his first dialogue, and Gelasius against Eutyches, cite a testimony from the letter of Ignatius to the Ephesians, which nowhere appears in the copies now published.

units.la: Postremò Hieronymus dialog.3. contra Pelagianos, testimonium citat ex Ignatij Epistolis,quod in his editis non habetur. Sed & scrupulus adhuc alius restat,in Ignatio non citando. De anno quo Christus baptizatus est dissentiunt à sese patres, Ignatius verò ab omnibus (inquit Baronius) Is anno 30. expleto baptizatum tradit: contra quam sententiam audacter insurgit Epiphanius? Hoc probabili argumento est, has Epistolas Ignatianas tum temporis non extitisse. Quid enim? Num tota antiquitas sese Ignatio opponerat? In re tantùm controversa, non Ignatium consuluissent? non citassent? sine mentione omni præterijssent? si contrà sentirent,nonne illius authoritatem refutassent?
units.tr: Last, Jerome in his third dialogue against the Pelagians cites a testimony from the letters of Ignatius which is not contained in the published editions. But there remains yet another difficulty, in not citing Ignatius. The Fathers disagree among themselves about the year in which Christ was baptized, but Ignatius agrees with all (says Baronius), placing his baptism at the completion of the thirtieth year. Against this opinion Epiphanius boldly rises up. This is a probable argument that these Ignatian letters did not exist at that time. For what? Did all antiquity oppose Ignatius? In a matter of controversy would they not have consulted Ignatius, cited him, or passed him by without any mention at all? And if they had held the contrary view, would they not have refuted his authority?

units.la: Quintò,phraseis harum Epistolarum tempori Ignatiano non conveniunt,frequens etenim apud eum, sacerdotis, altaris, offerendi, sacerdotijq; mentio est, quæ nomina in prima Ecclesia non fuisse observata fatetur ipse Bellarm. qui veteres longo tempore, Iudeorum causa,ab his abstinuisse dicit.
units.tr: Fifthly, the phrases of these letters do not agree with the Ignatian age, for there is frequent mention in him of priest, altar, offering and priesthood, which names, Bellarmine himself confesses, were not observed in the primitive Church, saying that the ancients for a long time abstained from them on account of the Jews.

units.la: Sextò, in Epistola ad Philippenses, cum esse socium eorum qui Christum occiderunt dicit, qui cum Iudæis Pascha celebrat: quo strepitu sorex se iste prodidit non Ignatium orientalem, sed hominem potiùs occidentalem, Romanumq; fuisse. Magna controversia de Pascha te inter Episcopos orientales & occidentales fuit: quorum illi Iohannis & Philippi exemplo freti, quartâ decimâ lunâ una cum Iudæis celebrandum Pascha censuerant: Orientales morem contrarium acriter tuebantur, qui post in Concilio Nicæno sancitus erat: sic ut post hoc Concilium scribens Epiphanius, ex Canone Apostolorum, quem citat, Orientales refutet. Quid igitur? contra Apostolorum Canonem, contra Orientales coepiscopos suos ivisse Ignatium,& in castra Occidentalium transfugisse verisimile est? Fac hoc verisimile, id tamen quomodo verisimile fuit, Victorem Romanum hanc Ignatij authoritatem prætermittere voluisse? cum orientalem contra Orientales citasse Ignatium præsertim tantæ authoritatisvirum, pro causa sua maximè fecit. Redolent certè ista Ignatij tempora illa, quæ Nicænum Concilium subsecuta sunt.
units.tr: Sixthly, in the Epistle to the Philippians, when he says that the man who celebrates the Passover with the Jews is a partner of those who killed Christ, that squeak has given the game away: this Ignatius was not an Oriental but rather a Westerner, a Roman. There was a great controversy over the Passover between the bishops of the East and of the West. The former, relying on the example of John and Philip, held that the Passover should be kept on the fourteenth day of the moon together with the Jews. The Orientals fiercely defended the opposite custom, which was later enacted at the Council of Nicaea. So Epiphanius, writing after this Council, refutes the Orientals from the Canon of the Apostles, which he cites. What then? Is it likely that Ignatius went against the Canon of the Apostles and against his fellow bishops of the East, and deserted to the camp of the Westerners? Grant that it is likely: how is it likely that Victor the Roman wished to pass over this authority of Ignatius? Citing an Oriental against the Orientals, and above all a man of such great authority as Ignatius, would have served his cause most of all. Certainly those times of Ignatius smell of the period that followed the Council of Nicaea.

units.la: Septimo, qui Sabbato ieiunat, cum Christi occisorem esse dicit Ignatius in Epistola ad Philippenses: at jejunium Sabbati nunquam interdictum fuit in Ecclesia Orientali, ante tempora Marcionis, qui Sabbato jejunavit in odium Dei creatoris omnium. Canone 65. Apostolorum hoc jejunium interdictum est: sed Cæsar Baronius ipse fatetur, non antè tempora Marcionis hunc Canonem inventum & insertum fuisse. Quid ni igitur dicendum, hanc Epistolam Ignatij non nisi post tempora Marcionis scriptam?
units.tr: Seventhly, the man who fasts on the Sabbath says that Ignatius, in the Epistle to the Philippians, calls him a murderer of Christ. But fasting on the Sabbath was never forbidden in the Eastern Church before the time of Marcion, who fasted on the Sabbath out of hatred for God the Creator of all things. Canon 65 of the Apostles forbids this fast, but Caesar Baronius himself admits that this canon was not invented and inserted until after the time of Marcion. Why, then, should we not say that this Epistle of Ignatius was written only after the time of Marcion?

units.la: Octavo, citat contra nos Dominamus, verba Ignatij in Epistola ad Philadelphienses: quibus insinuat separationem quorundam suo tempore ab Episcopo: contra quos ad unitatem cum Episcopo hortatur, a divisione vero ab Episcopo dehortatur. Ex his verisimile est, non nisi post Novati aut Donati tempora, has Epistolas Ignatij scriptas esse: quæ enim occasio tempore Ignatij horum quæso verborum fuit.
units.tr: Eighthly, Downame cites against us the words of Ignatius in the Epistle to the Philadelphians, in which he hints at the separation of certain men from the bishop in his own time. Against these he urges unity with the bishop, and he warns against division from the bishop. From this it is likely that these Epistles of Ignatius were written only after the times of Novatus or Donatus, for what occasion was there in the time of Ignatius for these words, I ask you?

units.la: Nonò, in Epistola ad Trullenses dicit se intelligere angelorum & Archangelorum ordines, multivarias diversitates, virtutum & dominationum differentias, sedium atq; potestatum distantias, thronorum magnificentias, Cherubim & Seraphim excellentis spiritus sublimatem: quæ Ignatij spiritum minimè sapiunt, imo ne tempora quidem redolent. Dicit Baronius Dionysium, hæc in re Ignatium citasse, quod falsum est: quod si citaret verò, suspitio augeretur: redolent hæc quidem Dionysij tempora, quæ Ignatio multò posteriora sunt. Apponi hic possunt quæ habet de Ignatio Socrates. Iam vero dicamus unde consuetudo hymnorum, qui in Ecclesia alternis dicantantur, initium cœperit. Ignatius Antiochiæ quæ est in Syria, tertius à Petro Apostolo Episcopus, qui cum Apostolis ipsis multum versatus est, visionem vidit Angelorum sanctam trinitatem hymnis alterna voce decantatis collaudantium dantium dantium: & formam canendi in ea visione expressam Ecclesiæ Antiochenæ tradidit. Vnde illa traditio in omnibus Ecclesiis recepta est: in quibus observandum contra Downnamum, quàm parum patres juniores de Ecclesiis antecedentibus in materia facti, idonei testes sint. Quàm traditionibus & relationibus à manu in manum tradidis fidendum, quàm parum denique, quæ passim inculcat de universâ Ecclesiæ praxi firma sint. Mihi (inquit) sufficit testimonium quod citavi, Eusebij tempore, qui intra ducentos ab Ignatio annos vixit, suspectum non fuisse. Nam si Eusebius & qui illius tempore vixerunt, nullam causam noverunt, cur Epistola Ignatij ad Ephesios suspecta esset: nullam ego causam nosco cur pro suspecta refutator eam habere debeat. Sufficit igitur quòd Socratis testimonium illius tempore suspectum non fuit? certe tam verum hymnos alternos in tota Ecclesiæ primæ praxi usurpatos fuisse (quod tamen est salsissimum) eosque per visionem ab angelis acceptos Ignatium tradidisse, quam verum est, Ignatium Episcopum Hierarchicum fuisse: eumque epistolam illam scripsisse, quæ nunc extat, ad Ephesios.
units.tr: Ninthly, in the Epistle to the Trallians he says that he understands the orders of angels and archangels, the manifold diversities, the differences of virtues and dominions, the distances of seats and powers, the magnificence of thrones, and the exalted sublimity of the Cherubim and Seraphim. These things hardly taste of the spirit of Ignatius; nay, they do not even smell of his times. Baronius says that Dionysius cited Ignatius on this matter, which is false; and if he had cited him, suspicion would only grow. These things smell rather of the times of Dionysius, which are much later than Ignatius. What Socrates says about Ignatius may be added here. Now let us say where the custom of hymns, sung in the Church by alternating voices, began. Ignatius, bishop of Antioch in Syria, third from the Apostle Peter, who had much to do with the Apostles themselves, saw a vision of angels singing the holy Trinity with hymns chanted in alternate voices, and he handed down to the Church of Antioch the form of singing expressed in that vision. From this tradition it was received in all the Churches. In this matter it must be observed, against Downame, how little the later Fathers are reliable witnesses about the earlier Churches as to matters of fact. How little must we trust traditions and reports handed down from hand to hand, and, in short, how little firm are the things he everywhere insists upon about the universal practice of the Church. For me (he says) it is enough that the testimony I cited was not regarded as suspect in the time of Eusebius, who lived within two hundred years of Ignatius. For if Eusebius and those who lived in his time knew of no reason why the Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians should be suspect, I for my part know of no reason why a refuter should count it as suspect. Is it therefore enough that the testimony of Socrates was not regarded as suspect in his time? Certainly it is as true that hymns sung alternately were used in the whole practice of the early Church (which is nevertheless most absurd), and that Ignatius handed them down after receiving them from angels in a vision, as it is true that Ignatius was a hierarchical bishop, and that he wrote that epistle which now exists, to the Ephesians.

units.la: Decimò, quum traditionem quadragesimæ, jejunij quartæ feriæ, ordinum minorum, Acoluthorum, exorcistarum &c. nobis ex Ignatio objiciunt pontificij, quid aliud habent quod respondeant nostri, quàm hæc longo post tempore introducta, satis solido argumento esse, has Ignatij epistolas supposititias esse? Vndecimò, qualia illa quæso sunt quæ in epistola ad Magnesianos reperiuntur? Non presbyter, non Diaconus, non laicus sine Episcopo debet aliquid facere, sicut Christus sine patre nihil facit. Num hæc aut spiritum, aut etiam tempora Ignatij redolent? Quàm etiam illud ἀκυρω, quod de honorando rege et episcopo verba faciens, episcopum præponit regi. Duodecimò, cum in citando Ignatio Downnamus tam multus sit, cur non rationes produxit, quæ fidem Ignatio afferere possint? Producit inquies: nam hæ epistolæ piæ & doctæ sunt inquit, & sufficiens probatio est, eas non esse fictitias quòd ab Eusebio memorentur. Negatur hanc probationem sufficientem esse: falli etenim potuit Eusebius de illis epistolis, æquè ac de illius hymnis Socrates, traditione tantùm. Collegerat quis fortè dicta Ignatij ante tempus Eusebij, eaque in formam epistolarum redegit: sed Ignatium ipsum epistolas scripsisse, non magis certum est ex Eusebij relatione, quàm certum est, epistolas Pauli ad Senecam, & Senecæ ad Paulum genuinas esse, quod memorentur ab Hieronymo in catalogo virorum illustrium, et tanquam genuinæ ab eodem approbentur. Accedo propius ad ipsum Eusebium: dicit ille, Ignatium septem epistolas scripsisse, quid tum? sic etiam dicit (ac non ille solum, sed universa prima Ecclesia) librum pastoris, verum Hermæ scriptum fuisse: quod tamen quàm falsum sit, iam omnes facilè internoscunt. Negatur secundò, has epistolas Ignatij quæ nunc extant, illas ipsas esse, quæ ab Eusebio commemorantur. At in epistola ad Ephesios inquis eadem verba reperiuntur quæ recitat Eusebius. Euseb. Quinq; has epistolas dolavit, & titulum & verba Eusebij imitari non potuerit? Extant inquis in epistola ad Ephesios eadem verba quae Eusebius recitat: at habuimus supra Theodoretum & Gelasium verba quaedam citasse ex epistola Ignatij ad Ephesios, quae in ista quae iam circumfertur, minime extant.
units.tr: Tenthly, when the Papists object to us from Ignatius the tradition of Lent, of the fast on Wednesday, of the minor orders, of Acolytes, of exorcists, and so on, what else do our people have to answer, except that these things were introduced long after, and that this is a sufficiently solid argument that these Epistles of Ignatius are spurious? Eleventhly, I ask you, what sort of things are those found in the Epistle to the Magnesians? Neither a presbyter, nor a deacon, nor a layman ought to do anything without the bishop, just as Christ does nothing without the Father. Do these words smell of the spirit or even of the times of Ignatius? Consider also that Greek word [ἀκυρω], which, when he is speaking about honouring the king and the bishop, places the bishop before the king. Twelfthly, since Downame is so lavish in citing Ignatius, why did he not produce the reasons that could bring credit to Ignatius? He produces them, you will say, for these Epistles are pious and learned, he says, and it is sufficient proof that they are not fictitious that Eusebius mentions them. It is denied that this proof is sufficient. For Eusebius could have been mistaken about those Epistles, just as Socrates was about his hymns, on mere tradition. Perhaps someone had collected the sayings of Ignatius before the time of Eusebius and reduced them into the form of epistles. But that Ignatius himself wrote the epistles is no more certain from the report of Eusebius than it is certain that the epistles of Paul to Seneca and of Seneca to Paul are genuine, although they are mentioned by Jerome in his catalogue of illustrious men and approved by him as genuine. Let me come closer to Eusebius himself: he says that Ignatius wrote seven epistles. So what? He also says (and not he alone, but the whole early Church) that the Book of the Shepherd was written by Hermas. Yet how false that is, everyone now easily perceives. It is denied, secondly, that these Epistles of Ignatius which now exist are the very ones mentioned by Eusebius. But, you say, in the Epistle to the Ephesians the same words are found that Eusebius recites. Did Eusebius recite these epistles? Could not someone who forged five of them have imitated both the title and the words of Eusebius? You say that the same words that Eusebius recites are found in the Epistle to the Ephesians. But above we noted that Theodoret and Gelasius cited certain words from the Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, which are by no means found in the one that now circulates.

units.la: 9 Decimo tertio & ultimo, doctorum virorum judicia, hac in re, a nobis sunt: fictitias etenim has Ignatij epistolas esse docent inter alios, Magdeburgenses Centur. 2. lib. 10. Gulielmus Whitakerus cont. 1. qu. 6. cap. 19. Sibrandus Lubbertus de princip. Christian. dogmat. lib. 7. cap. 10. & Gulielmus Perkins. in problem. quem ego quia unus de nobis est non citassem, nisi eum ante a Georgio Downamo citatum vidissem. Quid ipsi Hierarchici? Thomas Bilsonus in canonibus Apostolorum fidentior est, quam in Ignatio. Canones (inquit) qui dicuntur Apostolorum, antiquioris disciplinae documenta sane perveteta sunt. Pagina vero proxima ita habet de Ignatio. Ejusdem hujus vocis usum in epistolis illis, quae Ignatij feruntur, semel atque iterum invenio. Observa eandem notam inussisse Ignatio, quam canonibus, laudem vero vetustatis attribuisse Canonibus, quam Ignatij epistolis non attribuit. Quum dicit, Canones qui dicuntur Apostolorum, aperte innuit, eos ipsorum Apostolorum minime esse, sicuti alibi aperte docet: pari ratione quum dicit, epistolae quae feruntur Ignatij, eas Ignatij minime esse subinsinuat. Eadem ni fallor doctissimi Causaboni opinio est. Probandum illi erat, ad priscam Ecclesiae disciplinam demonstrandam potiora esse prioris saeculi, quam quarti aut quinti testimonia. Instat autem in Cypriano solo. Vel unicus (inquit) Christi Martyr sanctissimus Cyprianus, primitivae Ecclesiae mentem & disciplinam totam, melius nos docuerit, quam multi alij qui in quarto saeculo vixerunt. Cur omisit Ignatium ergo, si eum genuinum existimasset? nam & multo antiquior est, & multa de disciplina habet, sic ut Baronius, ecclesiasticae disciplinae faciem purissimam in eo lucere dicat. Iohannes Bridgesius Episcopus Oxoniensis, multo apertissimus est. Quicunque (inquit) in Ignatij nomine illas epistolas scripsit: non enim audeo (tam audacter ut fratres) affirmare, eas ipsius Ignatij esse. Richardus Stochius, ita in sua versione Whitakeriana. Authoritate Ignatij obrui veritas non debet, cujus fides exigua est, si tamen omnino vulla: non te latent quae doctorum hominum omnium de illis Ignatij epistolis judicia sint. Gratianus ipse non multum huic Ignatio favet: multa in his epistolis reperiuntur, quae illius temporibus doceri incredibile est, qualis ista stricta quadragesima observatio est: imo non nisi iam pridem hae epistolae impressae & publicatae sunt.
units.tr: 9 Thirteenthly and lastly, the judgements of learned men in this matter are on our side. For they teach that these Epistles of Ignatius are fictitious: among others, the Magdeburg Centuriators, Centuria 2, book 10; William Whitaker, Controversy 1, question 6, chapter 19; Sibrandus Lubbertus, On the Principles of Christian Doctrine, book 7, chapter 10; and William Perkins, in his Problems. I would not have cited him, since he is one of us, had I not first seen him cited by George Downame. What do the Hierarchicals themselves say? Thomas Bilson is more confident about the Canons of the Apostles than about Ignatius. The Canons (he says) which are called the Apostles' are indeed very ancient documents of an earlier discipline. But the next page says this about Ignatius: I find the use of this very word in those epistles which are attributed to Ignatius, once and again. Notice that he has stamped the same mark on Ignatius as on the canons, but he has not granted to the Ignatian epistles the praise of antiquity that he gave to the Canons. When he says "the Canons which are called the Apostles'," he clearly hints that they are not really the Apostles' own, as he teaches plainly elsewhere; by the same reasoning, when he says "the epistles which are attributed to Ignatius," he subtly suggests that they are not Ignatius's. I think the opinion of the most learned Casaubon is the same. He had to prove that the testimonies of the earlier century are more weighty than those of the fourth or fifth for demonstrating the early discipline of the Church. He insists, however, on Cyprian alone: The one and only most holy martyr of Christ, Cyprian, has taught us better the mind and the whole discipline of the early Church than many others who lived in the fourth century. Why then did he leave out Ignatius, if he thought him genuine? For Ignatius is much older and has much to say about discipline, so that Baronius says that the most pure face of ecclesiastical discipline shines forth in him. John Bridges, bishop of Oxford, is much more outspoken: Whoever wrote those epistles under the name of Ignatius, for I do not dare (as boldly as you brethren do) to affirm that they are Ignatius's own. Richard Stock, in his translation of Whitaker: The truth ought not to be overthrown by the authority of Ignatius, whose trustworthiness is slight, if indeed it is any at all. You are not unaware of the judgements of all learned men about those Epistles of Ignatius. Gratian himself does not greatly favour this Ignatius: many things are found in these epistles which it is incredible were taught in his times, such as this strict observance of Lent. Indeed, these epistles were not printed and published until quite recently.

units.la: 10 Quartus author fictitius qui ab Hierarchicis produci solet, Dyonisius Areopagita est. Iohannes siquidem Whitgiftus, interrogationes in baptismo ad infantes, in Ecclesia Anglicana hodie usurpatas, ita tuetur. Nova non sunt, neque nuper inventa, sed magnae antiquitatis. Nam Dyonisius Areopagita earum meminit, &c. Quam autem indignum dignum sit nos hoc fabulatore & circumforanco prægravari, videre est in Gulielmo Whitakero Cont. 1. quæst. 6. cap. 12. Sibrando Lubberto de princip. Christianorum dogmat. lib. 7. cap. 10. Gulielmo Perkin, : in problemat. Gulielmo Fulcone in responf. ad AngloRhemen. In Act. 17. Thom. Mortono Apolog. Catholic. q. 2. lib. 2. cap. 3. aliisque authoribus nostris, qui laruam huic Dyonisio egregiè detraxerunt.
units.tr: 10 The fourth fictitious author whom the Hierarchicals usually bring forward is Dionysius the Areopagite. John Whitgift defends in this way the questions put to infants at baptism, which are used today in the English Church: They are not new, nor recently invented, but of great antiquity. For Dionysius the Areopagite mentions them, etc. How unworthy it is that we should be burdened by this fabulist and charlatan can be seen in William Whitaker, Contra Duraeum, question 6, chapter 12; Sibrandus Lubbertus, On the Principles of Christian Doctrine, book 7, chapter 10; William Perkins, in his Problemata; William Fulke, in his Response to the Rhemists, on Acts 17; Thomas Morton, Catholic Apology, question 2, book 2, chapter 3; and our other authors, who have thoroughly stripped this Dionysius of his mask.

units.la: 11 Quintus author fictitius qui ab Hierarchicis produci solet, author epistolarum decretalium est, sub nomine Clementis, Anacleti, Aniceti, &c. Sed ecquis ullus Evangelicus, inquis, his epistolis decretalibus fidem adhibendam censebit? Quid ni, dummodo (ut est apud Comicum) obrem. Richardus etenim Bancroftus, in capite eo, quo nostros in patres contemptus exaggerat, hos etiam patres inter reliquos a nobis reijci & repudiari indignissimè fert. Quando antiquitas & legitimus usus nominis Archiepiscopi, ex authoritate Clementis, Anacleti & Anaceti probatur, horum authoritatum citationem ipsius infirmi citationem appellant: hos omnes authores sub pedibus proterunt, Clementes, Anacletus, Anicetus, tanquam circumforanei notis Thaziciis compertos ab eis dimittuntur. Vide lector cum quo hominum genere nobis lis est: certè cum eis, qui vel ipsis papistis quibusdam longè deteriores sunt. Cæsar etenim Baronius fatetur epistolas Clementis quas nunc habemus, easdem non esse cum eis quas Ruffinus transtulit: & fusè disputat Nicolaus Cusanus contra harum Clementis et Anacleti epistolarum ligitimationem: et Antonius Cautius denique jurisconsultus doctissimus, has epistolas decretales verè transfigit. Hos citans Richardus Fyldus Hierarchicus, Philistæos proprio gladio cadere (dicit) et se mutuis verberibus conficere. Omitto nomen Philistæorum, hoc tamen dico: dum ea quæ Philistæorum sunt Hierarchici satagunt, eos gladio proprio ad illum Philistæorum morem, non immeritò cadere. Primò etenim hic ipse Fyldus Hierarchicus, quasi gladio evaginato has decretales epistolas transverberat, ac proinde per ipsorum latus Richardum Bancroftum vulnerat. Deinde Thomas Bilsouus Hierarchicus has epistolas decretales fictitias esse docte disputat. Ad hæc, Thomas Mortonus Hierarchicus adversus decretales epistolas multa habet. Postremò, Iohannes Whitgiftus, citat ille quidem pro episcopatu et Archiepiscopatu comprobando Clementis epistolam: sed præ pudore aliud illi nomen indit, ex Polidoro Vergilio, Compendium scilicet Christianæ religionis, quin etiam hanc Clementis epistolam agnoscit fictitiam his verbis. Nemo negat quin epistolæ Clementis fictitiæ sint. Itane verò fictitiæ, & tamen ad comprobandum Archiepiscopatum pressæ? Certè Nicolai Cusani is candor erat, ut quanquam primatui Romanæ Ecclesiæ consultum pervellet: pet has epistolas decretales tamen, propterea quòd fictitiæ fuut, consuli eidem nollet. Quo nomine laude dignus & Matheus Sutcliuius Hierarchicus: qui de epistolis decretalibus Clementis, Anacleti, &c. Verba faciens & authoritas est. Matheus Sutclivius non magis animadvertisse videtur Egesippum quem nunc habemus adulterinum fuisse, atque ipse Downamus; non tamen eam fidem quam Downamus adhibendam esse censet. Incertum est (inquit) an Petro ex urbe fugienti apparuerit Christus, & ea dixerit quae narrat Egesippus. Ambrosius, Gregorius, & fortasse Athanasius fabulam ex Egesippo hauserunt, &c.
units.tr: 11 The fifth fictitious author whom the Hierarchicals usually bring forward is the author of the decretal letters, published under the names of Clement, Anacletus, Anicetus, and others. But, you say, what Evangelical will think that these decretal letters deserve any credence? Why not, provided that (as the comic poet has it) it is useful. Indeed Richard Bancroft, in the chapter in which he magnifies his contempt for our Fathers, most indignantly complains that these Fathers too are rejected and repudiated by us along with the rest. When the antiquity and lawful use of the name of Archbishop are proved by the authority of Clement, Anacletus and Anaclete, they call the citation of these authorities a citation of a weak man: they trample all these authors underfoot, Clements, Anacletus, Anicetus, and dismiss them as charlatans, detected by the Thasian marks. Let the reader see with what kind of men we have our quarrel: surely with those who are far worse than some of the very Papists themselves. Caesar Baronius indeed admits that the letters of Clement which we now have are not the same as those which Rufinus translated; and Nicholas of Cusa argues at length against the legitimacy of these letters of Clement and Anacletus; and Antonius Contius, a most learned jurist, finally pierces these decretal letters through as spurious. Richard Field, a Hierarchical, citing these men, says that the Philistines fall by their own sword and destroy themselves with mutual blows. I pass over the name of the Philistines, but I say this: while the Hierarchicals busy themselves with what belongs to the Philistines, they fall, not undeservedly, by their own sword in the manner of those Philistines. For first, this same Field, as a Hierarchical, as if with his sword drawn, runs these decretal letters through, and so wounds Richard Bancroft through their side. Then Thomas Bilson, a Hierarchical, learnedly argues that these decretal letters are fictitious. Besides, Thomas Morton, a Hierarchical, has much against the decretal letters. Lastly, John Whitgift, though he cites the letter of Clement to prove episcopacy and archiepiscopacy, out of shame gives it another name, taken from Polydore Vergil, a Compendium of the Christian Religion; indeed he even acknowledges this letter of Clement to be fictitious in these words: No one denies that the letters of Clement are fictitious. Are they really fictitious, and yet pressed into service to prove archiepiscopacy? Certainly Nicholas of Cusa had such candour that, although he wished well to the primacy of the Roman Church, he would not on account of these decretal letters defend it, because they are fictitious. Matthew Sutcliffe, a Hierarchical, also deserves praise on this account, who, speaking of the decretal letters of Clement, Anacletus, etc., says: and it is an authority. Matthew Sutcliffe does not seem to have noticed that the Eusebius-Egesippus we now have was a forgery, and Downame himself too; yet he does not think it deserves the credence that Downame gives it. It is uncertain (he says) whether Christ appeared to Peter as he was fleeing from the city and said the things that Hegesippus relates. Ambrose, Gregory, and perhaps Athanasius drew the fable from Hegesippus, etc.

units.la: Septimus author supositicius ab Hierarchicis productus Dorotheus est. Hujus vitam collegit Meredithus Hanmerus Hierarchicus: cui dubium non est, quae nunc Dorothei Synopsis extat, ab illo vero Dorotheo scriptam fuisse, quem multis laudibus ornat Eusebius lib. 7. cap. 31. & Democharcs institut. Christian. relig. & quem martyrio sub Iuliano coronatum Petrus de Natalibus asserit. lib. 6. de sanctis. Atque hunc Dorotheum opponit Bellarmino Matheus Sutclivius, ut probet non alium, sed Barnabam Ecclesiam Romanam primo fundasse. At etiamsi eum fictitium existimasset Sutclivius, melius tamen adversus Bellarminum eum ex parte amplexurum produceret potuit, quam adversus nos Downamus, eundem penitus reijcientes & repudiantes. Probat is Apostolos Iacobum ordinasse episcopum Hierosolimitanum ex Dorotheo in Synopsi, sed eum loco penultimo citans, ante solum Augustinum. Alibi vero magnificentiori sede collocatur: citatur etenim loco primo ante Hieronimum & reliquos omnes, ut probetur Timotheum episcopum Ephesi Hierar. fuisse: ante omnes inquam eos, quos authores fide dignos Downamus affirmat. Quam vero parum fide dignus Dorotheus ipse sit, probat fusissime & eruditissime, ut alios omittam, Iohannes Reinoldus. Sane inquit Dorotheus ipse quisquis fuerit, synopsin hanc nescio an majori imperitia an impudentia fecerit ac ediderit: inepte, quia sine judicio, ea, quae ipse stultissime somniavit putaverit esse vera: impudenter, quia ea quae ipse sibi opinionis errore affinxerat, tanquam verissima scriptis commendavit. En authorem Downami fide dignum: quem mirandum non est si Timotheum fecerit Ephesi episcopum, quum in alios tam liberalis fuerit, ut (citante Reinoldo) Caesarem Philip. 4. 22. commemoratum id est, Neronem imperatorem secerit episcopum Dirrachij, & Priscillam uxorem Aquilae donarit episcopatu Colophonis. Addit insuper Reinoldus Celarem Baronium, qui fatetur nullum fuisse talem Dorotheum Episcopum Tyri, sed authorem hujus operis esse alium recentiorem cujus errores notat passim in Annalibus: nec non Bellarminum, qui ait Synopsin hanc falso Dorotheo adscribi: eamque plenam esse narrationibus confictis et mendacibus affirmat. Inter 72. Discipulos numerat Eunuchum Reginae Aethiopum, quem a Philippo conversum constat post ascentionem Domini: & Iuniam Episcopum facit, quam tamen faeminam fuisse certum est: Haec ita cum sint, miror Thomam Mortonum Hierarchicum asseruisse, Sixtum Senensem, hunc Dorotheum tanquam verum & genuinum agnovisse. Octavus author superest, non fictitius ille quidem, alius tamen quàm qui ab Hierarchicis producitur: Ambrosius nempè ille, author commentariorum in epistola: squi in 1. Tim. 5. 1. de seniorum abrogatione conquerit ur. Multas paginas implet Downamus, Ambrosium Mediolanensem Archiepiscopum fuisse, ut probet verisimile nullo modo esse, Archiepiscopus qui esset, de seniorum laicorum abrogatione conquesturum. Quasi presbyterium lacerdotale, si libertatem avitam suam retenuerit, adaeque limitibus Archiepiscopatus Downamiani non officiat, ac presbyterium (ut illi quidem loqui placet) laicū. Sed hoc opus,ut inquit Iohannes Reinoldus, non est Ambrosii, sed alterius cujuspiam, sive Hilarij, ut putant Theologi Lovanienses sive Aug. sive fortassis alicujus qui Ambrosius nominaretur, non tamen esset Amb. episcopus Mediolanensis: aliòi vero sic objicitur, Ambros. in commentario in 1. Tim. 3 appellare Damasum domus dei rectorem. Respondet Reinold. Quisquis fuit qui illud scripsit, Ambrosius celebris episcopus Mediolanensis non fuit, cui falsò inscribuntur commentarij in Paulum, sicut Theologi vestri Lovanienses observerunt & testificati sunt: Praefat. in Bibl. Exc. f. Antverpæ: Plantino. & censur. In lib. quaest. vet. & nov. Testament. in appendice operum Augustini: Infert deinde verba illa de Damaso, Ambrosij Mediolanensis esse non posse. Quia bis autor ante Damasum mortuus sit, qua multiplici innotatione persuasi multi sunt (ut notant vestri Lovanienses) quòd liber quaestionum veteris et novi testamenti qui titulum Augustini fert, & hij Ambrosio ascripti, ab eodem authore scripti fuerint. Nam qui illum librum scripsit, scripsit anno 300. ut apparet ex quaest. 44. Haec semel atque iterum repetit Reinoldus in libro de Divortiis. Similiter Gulielm. Whitakerus. Respondeo hos commentarios non esse Ambrosij, ut multi suspicantur. Nequehaec nostra tantum sententia est, sed censores etiam Lovanienses idem sentiunt. Tribuunt enim illi hos commentarios ei, qui librum quaestionum veteris & novi testamenti scripsit qui habetur in appendice operum Augustini Tom. quarto. Et commentarios in Epistolas non esse Ambrosij, multorum opinio est. Infert deinde locum de Damaso corruptum esse. Secundum nostrum argumentum (inquit) sumitur a confessione adversariorum. Nam si idem author fuit horum commentariorum, qui fuit quaestionum veteris & novi testamenti, tum non potuit facere mentionem Damasi. Nam ille liber scriptus est, anno trecentisimo post Christum, quem admodum ex quaestione 44. apparet. at Damasus Papa factus est anno 370 post Christum. Haec quae de Ambrosio isto comperi, minimè retinenda duxi, sive ad causam nostram faciant sive non, quia ab initio mihimet propositui candide agere, iuxta illud. Inter bonos bene agere. Inuit Georgius Downamus de hoc authore dubitatum esse: subdit tamen non hoc dico, quasi hanc ejus authoritatem elevare vellem. Hoc ille supponens verba Ambrosij pro Senioribus minimè facere: at Cornelius Scultingius aliud videns aliud quoque Boquino respondet, Ait ille, Ambrosium autorem hujus commentarij in Epistolam ... Epistolam ad Timotheum, vide Westcapellium contra Seniores in Catechef. de sacramento ordinis, ubi agit de presbyteris sol. 197. Ad vitandos nempe Seniores Ambrosium hunc rejicit Scultingius: quomodo Bellarminus eodem pressus respondet. Eruditos homines satis habere cognitum hoc opus non esse Ambrosii neque cujusquam Catholici: Irridet hominis partialitatem Reinoldus, quia alibi hunc Ambrosium citat, ad confirmandam authoritatem Romani Pontificis. Neque vero ut Lovanienses suspicantur, Hilarius Luceferianus esse potest: cum ante exortos Luceferianos mortuus sit: neque quod Franciscus Lucas innuere videtur cum eum Ambrosiastrum appellat, quasi ipse sua scripta supponeret Ambrosio: cum etiam ante Ambrosium mortuus sit. Recte Richardus Fyldus, hos commentarios Ambrosio ascriptos dicit. non tamen ab ipso authore ascriptos fuisse constat: hoc vero & praestantissimo cuicunque authori contingere potest, ut ab aliis alteri ipsius opera ascribantur. Quod vero ante concilium Nicaenum viverit, id pondus ipsius testimonio de Senioribus abrogatis addit: quod demonstrabitur suo loco.
units.tr: The seventh supposititious author produced by the Hierarchicals is Dorotheus. Meredith Hanmer, a Hierarchical, has collected his life; but there is no doubt that the Synopsis of Dorotheus which now exists was written by that true Dorotheus whom Eusebius praises with many commendations (book 7, chapter 31), and whom Democharis, in his Institutes of the Christian Religion, and Peter de Natalibus, in book 6 of On the Saints, assert was crowned with martyrdom under Julian. And Matthew Sutcliffe sets this Dorotheus against Bellarmine, to prove that it was not some other man but Barnabas who first founded the Roman Church. But even if Sutcliffe had thought him fictitious, he could have produced him to better effect against Bellarmine, as partly accepted, than Downame does against us, rejecting and repudiating him altogether. Downame proves from Dorotheus in the Synopsis that the Apostles ordained James bishop of Jerusalem, but he cites him in the second-to-last place, just before Augustine alone. Elsewhere, however, he is placed in a more honourable seat: he is cited in the first place, before Jerome and all the rest, to prove that Timothy was bishop of Ephesus, as the Hierarchicals hold; before all of them, I say, whom Downame affirms to be trustworthy authors. How little trustworthy Dorotheus himself is, is proved most fully and learnedly, to pass over others, by John Reynolds. Indeed he says, whoever Dorotheus was, I do not know whether he made and published this Synopsis out of greater ignorance or greater impudence: foolishly, because without judgement, he thought those things true which he himself had most stupidly dreamed: impudently, because he commended to writing, as most true, things which he had invented through the error of his own opinion. Behold the author Downame considers trustworthy! It is no wonder if he made Timothy bishop of Ephesus, since he was so generous towards others that (as Reynolds cites) he made Caesar, mentioned in Philippians 4:22, namely the Emperor Nero, bishop of Dyrrhachium, and bestowed the bishopric of Colophon on Priscilla, the wife of Aquila. Reynolds adds further that Baronius admits there was no such Dorotheus, bishop of Tyre, but that the author of this work was another and more recent man, whose errors he notes here and there in the Annals; and also Bellarmine, who says that this Synopsis is falsely ascribed to Dorotheus, and affirms that it is full of invented and false narratives. He counts among the seventy-two disciples the eunuch of the Queen of the Ethiopians, who is known to have been converted by Philip after the Lord's ascension; and he makes Junia a bishop, although it is certain that she was a woman. These things being so, I wonder that Thomas Morton, a Hierarchical, asserted that Sixtus of Siena recognised this Dorotheus as true and genuine. There remains an eighth author, not indeed fictitious, but other than the one produced by the Hierarchicals: that Ambrose, namely, the author of the commentaries on the Epistle to Timothy, who in 1 Timothy 5:1 complains of the abrogation of the elders. Downame fills many pages to prove that Ambrose was archbishop of Milan, so as to show that it is in no way likely that an archbishop, whoever he was, would complain of the abrogation of lay elders. As if the priestly presbytery, if it retained its ancient freedom, would not obstruct the limits of Downame's archbishopric, or the presbytery (as he is pleased to call it) of the laity. But this work, as John Reynolds says, is not Ambrose's, but that of some other, either Hilary, as the Louvain theologians think, or Augustine, or perhaps someone who was called Ambrose but was not Ambrose, bishop of Milan. Against another objection, in his commentary on 1 Timothy 3, Ambrose calls Damasus the ruler of God's house, Reynolds replies: Whoever it was who wrote that, Ambrose the famous bishop of Milan was not the one to whom the commentaries on Paul are falsely ascribed, as your Louvain theologians have observed and testified, in the preface to the Antwerp Plantin edition of the Bibliotheca Exc. and in their censure of the book of Questions on the Old and New Testament, in the appendix to the works of Augustine. He then adduces those words about Damasus, saying they cannot be Ambrose's: because the author died twice before Damasus, which has persuaded many, by many indications (as your Louvain theologians note), that the book of Questions on the Old and New Testament, which bears the title of Augustine, and which is ascribed to these Ambrose, was written by the same author. For the man who wrote that book, wrote in the year 300, as appears from Question 44. Reynolds repeats this once and again in his book on Divorces. Likewise William Whitaker. I reply that these commentaries are not Ambrose's, as many suspect. Nor is this only our opinion, but the Louvain censors also think the same. For they attribute these commentaries to him who wrote the book of Questions on the Old and New Testament, which is found in the appendix to the works of Augustine, volume four. And that the commentaries on the Epistles are not Ambrose's is the opinion of many. He then goes on to say that the passage about Damasus has been corrupted. According to our argument (he says) it is taken from the admission of our opponents. For if the same author wrote these commentaries as wrote the Questions on the Old and New Testament, then he could not make mention of Damasus. For that book was written in the three-hundredth year after Christ, as appears from Question 44; but Pope Damasus was made pope in the year 370 after Christ. I have thought it not right to retain what I have learned about this Ambrose, whether it bears on our cause or not, because from the beginning I resolved to act candidly, in accordance with the saying: Among good men, to act well. Georgius Downame states that doubt has been raised about this author; he adds, however, I do not say this as if I wished to lower his authority. He, supposing that the words of Ambrose do not favour the Seniors at all; but Cornelius Scultingius, seeing otherwise, replies to Bochinus as well: He says that Ambrose is the author of this commentary on the Epistle ... the Epistle to Timothy. See Westcappel against the Seniors in the Catechesis on the sacrament of orders, where he treats of presbyters, page 197. Scultingius, clearly, rejects this Ambrose in order to avoid the Seniors, as Bellarmine, pressed by the same difficulty, replies. Reynolds mocks the partiality of this man, since elsewhere he cites this Ambrose in support of the authority of the Roman Pontiff. Nor can Hilary the Luciferian be the author, as the Louvain theologians suspect, since he died before the Luciferians arose; nor is it what Francis Lucas seems to hint, when he calls him Ambrosiaster, as if he himself were putting his writings under Ambrose's name, since he too died before Ambrose. Richard Field rightly says that these commentaries are ascribed to Ambrose; yet it is not established that they were ascribed by the author himself; and this can happen to any most excellent author, that his works are ascribed to another by others. That he lived before the Council of Nicaea, however, adds weight to his testimony about the abrogation of the elders, which will be shown in its place.

units.la: 15 Atque hij authores supposititij praecipui sunt, qui ab Hierarchicis produci solent: sunt & alij, sed eos brevitatis causa praetereo, haec pauca subjicientur in genere de hujusmodi scriptoribus admonentia. Primò, ne quis credat Bancrofto, Downamo, reliquisque Hierarchicis quando objiciunt non nisi ad quaerendum subterfugium nos hos patres tanquam fictitios repudiare. Norit quisquis potius commune hoc omnibus protestantibus, a papistis objectum improperium esse. Solenne (inquiunt) protestantium perfugium est, quo patrem sibi adversum conantur eludere, respondere, supposititium esse. Rhemens. annot. in Act. 17. Gretzer. de jur. prohibit. lib. 2. cap. 6. Posuanien: in thes. Campian. Rat. 5. Atque pro nobis purgandis faciunt quae respondent nostri ad hanc calumniam papistarum. Primò, mirandum non est inquit Sutclivius, antiqua quaedam minimè genuina esse. Legimus enim multas epistolas et scripta edita fuisse nomine Apostolorum & aliorum sanctorum virrum, quae tamen propter manifestas corruptelas & falsitates haereticorum, inter Apocryphas & dubiae fidei scripturas relata sunt. Regatu fratrum meorum (inquit Dyonisius Corinthiorum episcopus) scripsi epistolas, sed illas Apostoli diaboli, alia eximentes, alia interserentes, impleverant zizaniis. Instemus in constitutionibus Clementis supra commemoratis. Probat Thomas Mortonus inane esse de quaerendo subterfugio opprobrium ex Caesare Baronio cujus ista verba sunt. Constitutiones Clementis inter Apocrypha ab omnibus numerantur, & hoc responsum est honestum confugium. Tom. 2. q. 12. & 17. Secundò, respondet Mortonus ad hanc calumniam, si modo subterfugium sit, subterfugium non protestantibus proprium, sed Papistis commune esse. Idipsum et nobis respondere licet: nam et Hierarchici adversus Papistas dum scribunt, patres fictos saepè declinant. Quidni declinarent, sicut & jam nos? Non est Gretzere (inquit Mortonus,) quod acerbd acerbè feralis, si protestantes, quibus (in hoc verè Nasonibus,) fraus haec vestra suboluit, in respondendo ingeminare saepe cogantur, ILLVD SVPPOSITITIVM. Larvatiisti authores pueris terriculamento esse possunt, viris autem cordatis esse ludibrio debent.
units.tr: These are the chief forged authors whom the Hierarchicals usually bring forward. There are others, but I pass them over for brevity. A few general remarks about writers of this sort will be added. First, let no one believe Bancroft, Downame and the other Hierarchicals when they object that we reject these fathers as forged only to find an escape. Let whoever knows that this reproach, common to all Protestants, was thrown at them by the Papists. It is (they say) the customary refuge of Protestants, by which they try to evade an adversary father: they answer that he is supposititious. Rhemish annotations on Acts 17; Gretser, On Prohibited Books, bk 2, ch. 6; Posevin, in the theses of Campian, Ratio 5. What our men reply to this calumny of the Papists serves to clear us. First, it is no wonder, says Sutcliffe, that some ancient writings are not at all genuine. For we read that many letters and writings were published under the names of the Apostles and other holy men, which nevertheless, on account of manifest corruptions and falsehoods introduced by heretics, have been placed among the Apocrypha and among writings of doubtful faith. "At the request of my brothers" (says Dionysius, bishop of Corinth) "I wrote letters, but the apostles of the devil, removing some things and inserting others, have filled them with tares." Let us insist on the Constitutions of Clement mentioned above. Thomas Morton proves that it is empty to make a reproach of seeking an escape from the words of Caesar Baronius: The Constitutions of Clement are counted among the Apocrypha by all, and this answer is an honest refuge. Vol. 2, qq. 12 and 17. Second, Morton answers this calumny: if it is indeed an escape, it is not an escape peculiar to Protestants but common to the Papists. We may answer the same: the Hierarchicals too, when they write against the Papists, often shy away from the forged fathers. Why should they not shy away, as we now do? Gretser need not take it bitterly (says Morton) if Protestants, to whom (truly, in this, like Nasos) your fraud has been detected, are often compelled to repeat in their answers: THAT SUPPOSITITIOUS THING. Masked authors may be a terror to children, but they ought to be a laughing-stock to sensible men.

units.la: Secundò, male hij fictitij patres ab Hierarchicis producuntur: peccatum hoc etenim idem cum Zozymi, Caelestini, Bonifacij, Innocentij Romanorum Pontificum est: qui ad stabiliendam primatus Romani tyrannidem, supposititium ex concilio Nicaeno Canonem produxerunt. Multa in libris supra commemoratis adulterata esse, nec ipsi diffiteri possunt: quid ergò ea nobis praefertis? (inquit Sutclivius:) aut cur utimini testibus dubiis? cur instrumenta producitis falsa? num ex fonte erroris vos veritatem probaturos putatis? Respondet Saravia, de citatione Canonum Apostolorum agens. Quod ante me fecere plurimi insignis & rarae erudítionis viri mihi licere judicavi, & eos citavi, ut citari soleant. Ego non sum primus qui ex illis Canonibus citavi eos, qui cum ratione, & antiquitate, & aequitate consentiunt. Cur quaeso id in me magis Bezae displiceat, quàm in Petro Martyro, in Calvino, & aliis, quos auctores hujus mei facti habeo? Simili excusatione utitur Iohannes Whitgiftus in citandis Epistolis decretalibus. Nemo negat quin Epistolae Clementis fictitiae sint: neque eum aliter allego, aut Anacletum, aut alium quemvis hujusmodi, quàm quomodo Calvinus, Iuellus, & alij docti viri sciunt, ut in eorum scriptis manifestum est. Imò longe aliter; Petrus Martyr etenim, Calvinus, Iuellus, hos authores suppositicios adversus Papistas citant qui eorum authoritate exosculantur: Hierarchici verò adversus Reformatos Protestantes, qui eam refugiunt rejiciuntque: atque Petrus Martyr, Calvinus, Iuellus, pro veritate Ecclesiarum reformatarum eos allegant: Hierarchici verò, pro falsa disciplina Ecclesiae Papisticae asserenda & comprobanda.
units.tr: Second, these forged fathers are wrongly produced by the Hierarchicals. For this is the same sin committed by the Roman Pontiffs Zosimus, Celestine, Boniface and Innocent, who, to establish the tyranny of the Roman primacy, produced a canon supposedly from the Council of Nicaea that was forged. The Papists themselves cannot deny that many of the books mentioned above have been corrupted: why then do you set them before us? (says Sutcliffe) or why do you use doubtful witnesses? why do you produce false documents? Do you think you will prove the truth from a fountain of error? Saravia replies, speaking of the citation of the Canons of the Apostles: What many men of distinguished and rare learning did before me, I judged I might lawfully do: I cited them as they are customarily cited. I am not the first to cite from those Canons those things which agree with reason, antiquity and fairness. Why, I ask, should this displease Beza in me more than in Peter Martyr, Calvin and others, whom I have as authors of this my action? John Whitgift uses a similar excuse in citing the decretal epistles: No one denies that the Epistles of Clement are fictitious; nor do I cite them otherwise, or Anacletus or any other of that kind, than as Calvin, Jewel and other learned men know, as is plain in their writings. Indeed, the case is quite different. For Peter Martyr, Calvin and Jewel cite these supposititious authors against the Papists, who embrace them on their authority; but the Hierarchicals cite them against the Reformed Protestants, who shun and reject them. And Peter Martyr, Calvin and Jewel allege them in support of the truth of the reformed Churches, whereas the Hierarchicals allege them to assert and confirm the false discipline of the Papist Church.

units.la: Tertiò, perperam objicit Downamus ex Ignatio quem fictitium dicimus, Cartwrigh. & Traversium testimonia nonnunquam allegare: & Bancroftus, nosmet eorundem suppositititiorum patrum testimonijs saepe uti, quum pro nobis facere videntur: quorum tamen citationes in ipsis reprehendere solemus. Quid ni? quamdiu horum authoritatem non solùm recipitis ipsi, verùm et nobis invitis obtruditis. An prohibitum, turdum proprijs pennis transfigere, bovem loro proprio flagellare, hostem proprijs oppugnare vel artibus vel armis? Quid Mortonus objicientibus Papistis, protestantes eorum patrum supposititiorum testimonijs uti, quorum citationes in Catholicis reprehendunt? Non tamen Protestantes (inquit) in eodem crimine falsi vobiscum implicantur quià vos scripta supposititia objectando fidem falsam conciliare illis studetis: illi verò eadem vobis opponendo, (argumento ad hominem) vestram futilitatem redarguere voluerunt. Citat in margine Aristotelem, Elench. l. 2. ubi docet, contra Sophistam, artis esse, (non licere modò) argumentis etiamsi minimè bonis, ex illius tamen sententia bonis, errorem confutare. Veritas inquit Irenaeus ab omnibus bus accipit testimonium, & à domesticis quia amici sunt, & ab extraneis quia inimici. Illa enim est vera, & absque contradictione probatio, quae etiam ab adversariis ipsis, singula testimonia praefert.
units.tr: Third, Downame objects wrongly that Cartwright and Travers sometimes cite Ignatius, whom we call forged, and Bancroft that we ourselves often use the testimonies of these same supposititious fathers when they seem to favour us, though we are wont to censure their citations in the Catholics. Why not? As long as you not only accept their authority yourselves but thrust it upon us against our will. Is it forbidden to pierce a thrush with its own feathers, to flog an ox with its own strap, or to attack an enemy with his own arts or arms? What does Morton say to the Papists objecting that Protestants use the testimonies of supposititious fathers whose citations they condemn in Catholics? Yet Protestants (he says) are not involved with you in the same crime of forgery, because you, by objecting forged writings, seek to win false faith for them, whereas they, by setting the same against you (an argument ad hominem), wish to refute your triviality. He cites in the margin Aristotle, Sophistical Refutations, bk 2, where he teaches that against a sophist it is the art (not merely lawful) to refute error by arguments, even if they are not very good, yet good according to his opinion. Truth, says Irenaeus, receives testimony from all: from its own because they are friends, and from outsiders because they are enemies. For that is true and unassailable proof which the adversaries themselves put forward, each testimony.

units.la: Quartò, observandus usus est, quem ex patribus fictitijs deducit Reynoldus: Fidem illam putridis fulcris niti docet, quae universitate, Antiquitate, & consensu nituntur. Quid ita? Ratio inter reliquas multas haec una est, propter falsationes patrum, & difficultatem secernendi veros à salsis. Idem habet Sixtus Senensis, qui à Thoma Mortono Hierarchico comprobatur. Incertum est quid definiunt patres propter libros supposititios qui falso patribus adscribuntur? Atque haec de errato Hierarchico in patribus citandis secundo, quòd patres fictitij producantur.
units.tr: Fourth, the use Reynolds makes of the forged fathers deserves notice. He teaches that faith rests on rotten props, namely that which rests on universality, antiquity and consent. Why so? Among many other reasons, this one: because of the falsifications of the fathers and the difficulty of separating the true from the false. Sixtus of Siena has the same view, and he is approved by Thomas Morton, a Hierarchical. It is uncertain what the fathers define, because of the supposititious books that are falsely ascribed to the fathers. And this is the second error of the Hierarchicals in citing the fathers: that they produce forged fathers.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CAP. XIV.

units.la: Erratum tertium Hierarchicorum quòd patres antiquos tam longe neotericis anteponant ex scripturis corripitur.
units.tr: The third error of the Hierarchicals, in preferring the ancient Fathers so far above recent writers, is rebuked from Scripture.

units.la: TErtium est, quod antiquos patres Neotericis Ecclesiarū reformatarum doctoribus scriptoribusque anteponunt, nullam quidem ad causam aliam, quam poeta reddit: Fama miratrix seniforis aevi: quam ex Ecclesiaste, Iohannes Luellus noster, alicubi refellit, Ne dixeris, quid est cur dies priores fuerint meliores istis: nam non ex sapientia rogares super hoc. Eccles.7.10. Hoc Thomas Bilsonus sequutus si fuisset: non ita contra neotericos scriptores arguisset. [Quum multi doctrina & antiquitate praestantes viri, nihil ejusmodi suspicati sint, Chrysostomus, Hieronymus, Ambrosius, Theodoretus, Primasius, Oecumenius, Theophilactus--quis aequum putet, ut post quindenas annorum centurias, nova atque incognita regendae Ecclesiae formula hoc solo argumento excudatur, quod quibusdam Theologis recentioribus, verba Pauli ita accipi posse videantur?] Subdole interposita haec, hoc solo argumento: & praeter argumentum (quo utitur Bilsonus) ipsum: qui ex eo disputat locum Pauli non juxta sensum Theologorum recentiorum intelligendum: quia à patribus quindenis centuriis antiquioribus, non ita intellectus sit. Quae Bancroftus, adversus nostrum patrum fastidium virulentissimè profuderit, ac si sapientia mortua esset, antequam Genevensis disciplinae axiomata nata, superius à nobis allata sunt. Ita Georgius Downamus. [Cum de authoritate simpliciter quaestio habetur, quaenam major sit, dico cum philosopho Rhetor.lib.1.cap.15. cum testes duplicis generis sunt ... quidam veteres quidam novi, majoris fidei antiqui sunt.] Alibi ita: Optimus quem habent color est, novos quosdam scriptores idem cum eis sentire.
