Quòd si vero consideremus, duos aut tres primarios viros, presbyterium excogitasse, illudq; alijs commendasse, aliósq; eis absq; debito examine consensisse: rationem nullam habebimus, multa testimonia æstimare, vel primariorum authorum vel posteriorum disciplinæ presbyterialis fautorum, cum omnes in hac causa participes sint.] Rursus: Omnium argumentorum quæ proferent vis authoritate quorundam novorum innititur: quod arguendi genus est ad id excogitatum, ut imperiti in pristina sententia suâ retineantur. Postremò, Vel unius patris testimonium (in materia facti) rem affirmantis, plus ponderis apud nos habere debet, quam negatio disciplinariorum in toto orbe omnium.
units.tr: The third error is that they set the ancient Fathers above the recent teachers and writers of the reformed Churches, for no other reason than the one the poet gives: Fame is the admirer of an aged era. Our John Lewis (Luellus) refutes this somewhere from Ecclesiastes: Do not say, "Why were the former days better than these?" For you do not ask this wisely. Eccles. 7.10. If Thomas Bilson had followed this, he would not have argued so against recent writers. [Since many men outstanding in learning and antiquity, Chrysostom, Jerome, Ambrose, Theodoret, Primasius, Oecumenius, Theophylact, suspected nothing of the kind, who would think it fair that, after fifteen centuries, a new and unknown form of governing the Church should be hammered out on this one argument alone, namely that the words of Paul may seem to some more recent theologians to be capable of being so understood?] These points are slipped in covertly, and rest on this one argument; and apart from the argument itself (which Bilson uses), he argues that the passage of Paul is not to be understood according to the sense of the recent theologians, because it has not been so understood by the Fathers of the fifteen earlier centuries. Bancroft poured out a great deal of venom against our disdain for the Fathers, as if wisdom had died before the axioms of the Geneva discipline were born; these things were set forth above by us. So George Downame. [When the question is simply about authority, which is the greater, I say with the philosopher, in the Rhetoric, book 1, chapter 15: when there are two kinds of witnesses ... some ancient and some recent, the ancient are of greater trustworthiness.] Elsewhere he says: The best colour they have is that certain recent writers agree with them. But if we consider that two or three leading men devised the presbytery, and commended it to others, and that others assented to them without due examination, we shall have no reason to value many testimonies, whether of the leading authors or of the later supporters of presbyterial discipline, since all are parties in this cause. Again: The force of all the arguments they bring rests on the authority of certain new men; this is a kind of argument devised so that the unskilled may be kept in their former opinion. Lastly, the testimony of a single Father affirming a matter of fact ought to carry more weight with us than the denial of all the disciplinarians in the whole world.

units.la: Non ego hic singula limatius excutiam: videmus quàm deprimantur scriptores neoterici, extollantur vero patres: quàm firma causa Hierarchica fiat, quòd a patribus circumvalletur, quàm reformatorum infirma quod neotericos tantùm scriptores fautores habeat: quàm denique laudentur Hierarchici in eo quod patres eorumque consensum sequantur: condemnentur vero reformati, quòd scriptoribus recentioribus potiùs adhæreant. Quàm vero hæc omnia perperam fiant ut appareat, docebitur primò ex ipsis sacris, non ita leviter de scriptoribus recentioribus sentiendum, quasi patribus præponendi non essent: neque adeo de patribus magnificè censendum, quasi neotericis postponendi non viderentur. Primò, ab ipsius spiritus sancti testimonio disputo quod pro novitijs Ecclesiæ luminibus, antiquis patribus præferendis, multis quidem in locis loquitur: quum sub lege zona lumborum esset, jam in Christo pro conditione evangelicarum Ecclesiarum adumbrato, ad mamillas transfertur, ob fidei maiorem claritatem, gratiarumque uberiorem splendorem: quibus factum est, ut in prima Apostolica Ecclesia, vestes sanctorum ad omne opus bonum quam commodissimè agendum artissimè constringebantur: ab hac vero ecclesia prima cum recessum est, dico nullo loco, intermedia patrum tempora hoc habitu in Apocalypsi tota, unquam introducta esse. De his vero reformatis nuperis temporibus alio ratio est, in quibus, & non ante, hic habitus restitutus Ecclesiæ est uti constat aperte Ap. 15. 6. ubi quotquot judicia iræ Dei, vel alios imbuendo, vel ipsimet agendo, in papistis exerunt, angeli dicuntur aureis phialis donati & præcincti circa pectora zonis aureis.
units.tr: I shall not examine each point too finely here. We see how the recent writers are depressed and the Fathers exalted; how firm the Hierarchical cause becomes because it is fortified by the Fathers, how weak the reformed cause is because it has only recent writers as supporters; and finally how the Hierarchicals are praised for following the Fathers and their consensus, while the reformed are condemned for clinging rather to recent writers. That all these things are wrongly done will be shown, first, from the sacred writings themselves: that one must not think so lightly of recent writers, as if they were not to be preferred to the Fathers, nor think so highly of the Fathers, as if they did not seem to be to be set below the recent writers. First, I argue from the very testimony of the Holy Spirit, which in many places speaks of the new lights of the Church as to be preferred to the ancient Fathers. When under the law the girdle was on the loins, it was already foreshadowed in Christ, and under the condition of the evangelical Churches it is transferred to the breasts, for the greater clarity of faith and the richer brightness of grace. From this it came about that in the first apostolic Church the garments of the saints were girded very tightly, so that they might perform every good work as conveniently as possible. But from this first Church, when there was a departure from it, I say in no place, in the intervening times of the Fathers, was this dress ever introduced in the whole of the Apocalypse. Concerning these reformed men of recent times the case is different, for in them, and not before, this dress has been restored to the Church, as is plainly evident in Rev. 15.6, where all those who, either by teaching or by acting themselves, carry out the judgments of God's wrath upon the Papists, are said to be angels given golden bowls and girded about the breast with golden belts.

units.la: Secundò, Ecclesia reformata ab anno 1300. ad annum 1520. in Thyatira quasi in adumbratur Ap. 2. 18. quæ Epheso opponitur Ecclesiæ ad annum 300. decurrentis typo, quæ quasi θύαιρα dicta est, quòd indies in pejus ruit. Atque ultima opera hujus reformatæ nuper Ecclesiæ, tanquam majora primis commendat Christus, Apo. 2. 19. in antiqua vero ante Constantinum Ecclesia, opera posteriora tanquam peiora primis condemnat, atque adeo condemnat, ut primum amorem eam deseruisse contestatur, Ap, 2. 4. Quid igitur est? Wiclivius, Hussus, Hieronimus Pragensis, cæterique Ecclesiæ renascentis nostræ pastores, nonne aperte, patribus Constantini temporA præcedentibus præferuntur? per illos etenim factum est, ut Ecclesiæ illorum temporibus deficeret; at horum ministerio profecit Ecclesia: sic ut de ea dici possit. Iter justorum quasi lux, crescens quotidie magis magisque usque ad perfectam diem Pro. 4. 18.&c. Plantati in domo Lebove in atriis Dei nostri germina profundent: adhuc abundabunt in canicie, Pingues & virentes erunt, Psalm.92.15.
units.tr: Second, the reformed Church from the year 1300 to the year 1520 is, as it were, foreshadowed in Thyatira, Rev. 2.18, which is set over against the Church of the Ephesian type that runs down to the year 300, which is called, as it were, thyaira [θύαιρα], because it daily rushes towards the worse. And Christ commends the last works of this recently reformed Church as greater than the first, Rev. 2.19; but in the ancient Church before Constantine he condemns the later works as worse than the first, and indeed condemns them so far that he testifies they had forsaken their first love, Rev. 2.4. What then is the case? Are not Wycliffe, Hus, Jerome of Prague, and the other ministers of our renewed Church plainly preferred to the Fathers who preceded the times of Constantine? For through those men it came about that the Church failed in their times, but by the ministry of these the Church has made progress, so that of it can be said: The path of the righteous is like the light that shines ever more and more unto the perfect day, Prov. 4.18, etc. Those planted in the house of the Lord, in the courts of our God, shall bring forth fruit; they shall still be fat and flourishing in old age, Ps. 92.15.

units.la: Tertio, cultus divinus qualis in Ecclesia esse debet, mare vitreum & Chrystalinum vocatur, quia pellucidum & ab omni humano fermento purum Ap.4.6. Videamus igitur, quod de antiquo mari Patrum, & nostro reformato, spiritus sancti judicium est. Tempus quo patres maxime floruerunt, spatium tertij & quarti seculi erat, ut omnibus notum: rare autem tum temporis vitreum & Chrystallinum? Imo terrenum & versum in sanguinem, idque ob montem in idem mare projectum, per Episcopatus & Patriarchatus invectionem Ap. 8.8. At vero mare reformatae Ecclesiae & coeleste est, & Chrystallinum Ap.15.1. Quod igni mistum dicitur, id ex accidente est, imo ex culpa Episcoporum in Anglia, & Lutheranorum in Germania, qui purum divini numinis cultum, per pastores reformatos restitutum, fervenți contentionis igni commacularunt.
units.tr: Third, the divine worship such as ought to be in the Church is called a glassy and crystalline sea, because it is transparent and pure from every human leaven, Rev. 4.6. Let us therefore see what the Spirit's judgment is concerning the ancient sea of the Fathers and our reformed sea. The time in which the Fathers chiefly flourished was the space of the third and fourth centuries, as is known to all; but at that time was the sea glassy and crystalline? Rather it was earthly and turned into blood, and that because a mountain had been cast into the same sea, through the introduction of episcopacy and patriarchate, Rev. 8.8. But the sea of the reformed Church is heavenly and crystalline, Rev. 15.1. That it is said to be mingled with fire is an accident, or rather the fault of the bishops in England and of the Lutherans in Germany, who have defiled with the fervent fire of contention the pure worship of the divine majesty, restored through the reformed ministers.

units.la: Quarto Diocletiano & Maximiniano in Ecclesiam saeviente, caelum antiquae Ecclesiae sedes, abscessisse dicitur, tanquam liber complicatus, id est, ipsa Ecclesiae facies, miscere obnubilata fuit, Ap.6. 13. Hinc perspici licet quam strenue patres eorum temporum suas partes egerint, qui sua culpa, sede sua, pelli Ecclesiam passi sunt: quam Iohannis tempore in ipso caelo collocatam accepissent Ap.12.1. Neque vero per patres seculi sequentis, huic malo medicina adhibita est: tanta saltem, quanta per Pastores temporum reformatos. Non etenim tempore patrum (quantum ego advertere possum) in caelo ullibi a Iohanne collocatur ecclesia, ut nostra ecclesia reformata: nempe tum demum quum e solitudine sua per Evangelij restitutionem exire ecclesia incipit, & non ante in caelo visitur Apoc. 14. 1. & 15.
units.tr: Fourth, when the Emperors Diocletian and Maximian raged against the Church, the heaven of the ancient Church is said to have departed, as a book being rolled up, that is, the very face of the Church was darkened and became confused, Rev. 6.13. From this one may see how vigorously the Fathers of those times played their parts, who, through their own fault, suffered the Church to be driven from her seat, which John had seen placed in heaven itself, Rev. 12.1. Nor indeed in the Fathers of the following century was any remedy applied to this evil, at least not as great as that applied through the reformed ministers of our times. For in the time of the Fathers (so far as I can perceive) the Church is nowhere placed in heaven by John, as our reformed Church is; indeed, that Church only then comes out of her solitude, through the restoration of the Gospel, and is not seen in heaven before, Rev. 14.1 and 15.

units.la: Quinto, reformatio ecclesiae per pastores recentiores Apocalypseos capite decimo descripta, eam foelicitatem ecclesiae restituit, quae tempore patrum vix contigisse videatur. Forte illam foelicitatem eo in capite praedicari dices, quae comparationem tantum respiciat temporum papalium, non autem temporum quarti seculi, multo minus tertij, minime omnium secundi. Atq; ex historiae & visionis huiusce speciali modo aparere patet; non solum descendisse de caelo Christum ad consolandum ecclesiam suam adversus stellam cadentem, verum etiam adversus projectum montem, & tempestatem grandinis & nebulosam ecclesiae faciem, etiam, quae tempore patrum acciderunt. Utcunque sit, non eae laudes a Iohanne temporibus patrum attribuuntur vspiam quae hic ecclesiae reformatae. Nec patrum tempore de caelo descendisse Christum uspiam dicitur ut hic descendit v. 1. spiritualē praesentiam ecclesiae promittens. Quam caelum ecclesiae propē Constantinum nubulosum facit, dictum est supra, sol nempe cilicius factus est, & luna versa est in sanguinem: An non hic opus ut descenderet Christus, ut nusquam dicitur tempore patrum descendisse ut in ecclesia reformata. v. 1. circa caput iridem habens, serenitatis signum maximum: quo apparet nebulosum cælum semper mansisse tempore patrum: at non ante tempora reformatæ ecclesiæ nostræ serenasse omnia Christum, ut jam summâ clementiâ suâ serenavit. Atque nunc tandem facies Christi, ut sol splendere incipit v. 1. non ita de tertio aut quarto seculo usquam dicitur: ut sol Ecclesiæ Constantinum antecedentis cilicinus, lucem suam pristinam non ita recuperasse constat, ut jam nostra reformata Ecclesia recuperavit. Multa insuper patres pro veritate passi sunt: sed eorum constantia & patientia non ita à Spiritu sancto collaudatur, uti collaudatur pastorum ecclesiæ reformatæ: quorum gratia prodit Christus, pedes habens similes chalcolybano, & columnis igneis v. 1. obsignem constantiam Hussi, Hieronymi aliorumq; infinitorum qui in rogis Martyrij sui, tanquam in camino, instar chalcolybani, arserint invicti, & tanquam aurum, defæcati sunt. Atque nunc tandem liber apertus v. 2. apparet, tempore nempe ecclesiæ nostræ reformatæ: pastoribus recentioribus devorandus datur, quibus etiam mandatum jam novum rursus prophetandi datur, v. 20. Atqui in Ecclesia Constantinum proximè antecedente liber Ecclesiæ complicatus erat, ut supra ostensum: rogo igitur cur non ante apertus dicitur quam ad reformationis tempora, nisi quia scripturæ intelligentia non adeo perfectè patribus restituta fuerit, ut nunc pastoribus reformatæ ecclesiæ restituta. Postremo tempore Constantini commemorantur tonitrua & fulgura contentionum. Ap. 8. 5. si igitur tempore patrum ea puritas, lux, intelligentia Evangelij fuisset, qualis in ecclesia iam nostra reformata: cur non etiam eorum tempore aut paria aut similia commemorantur? Nunquam enim ante reformationem Evangelij aut voce ita magnâ vociferans introducitur Christus, ut nunc introducitur, v. 3. ad virtutem potentiamque Evangelij per pastores reformatos prædicati ostendendam: nunquam etiam ante reformata hæc nostra tempora introducuntur pastores tanquam Filij Tonitrus, immo tanquam ipsa tonitrua, ut nunc introducuntur, v. 3. tonitrua porro ejusmodi, quæ tanquam Echo ad vocem Angeli tantummodo respondeant: id est nihil loquentes, nihil docentes quod non divinitus edocti erant. Num ullo in loco laus similis tribuitur patribus? certè nullo: imo planè contrarium potius de eorum tempore dicitur, nempe quod instar tonitruum Evangelium efficaciter prædicantium tonitrua & fulgura contentionum quàm infestissimè tum resonarent. Apoc. 8. 5.
units.tr: Fifth, the reformation of the Church through the recent ministers, described in the tenth chapter of the Apocalypse, restores that happiness of the Church which seems hardly to have fallen to the lot of the times of the Fathers. Perhaps you will say that the happiness spoken of in that chapter regards only a comparison with the papal times, not with the times of the fourth century, much less the third, least of all the second. But from the history and the particular manner of this vision it plainly appears that Christ came down from heaven not only to comfort his Church against the falling star, but also against the mountain cast down, and the storm of hail and the clouded face of the Church, which happened also in the times of the Fathers. However that may be, those praises are not attributed by John anywhere to the times of the Fathers, which are attributed here to the reformed Church. Nor is it said anywhere that Christ came down from heaven in the time of the Fathers as he comes down here, promising in v. 1 the spiritual presence of the Church. That the heaven became clouded near the time of Constantine, as was said above, is clear: the sun was made sackcloth and the moon turned into blood. Was there not need here for Christ to come down? It is nowhere said that he came down in the time of the Fathers, as he has come down in the reformed Church. V. 1: having a rainbow about his head, the greatest sign of serenity, by which it appears that the heaven remained cloudy always in the time of the Fathers; but not before the times of our reformed Church did Christ make all things serene, as now in his supreme clemency he has made them serene. And now at last the face of Christ begins to shine as the sun, v. 1; this is nowhere said of the third or fourth century, so that it is evident the sun of the Church that preceded Constantine, made of sackcloth, did not recover its former light as our reformed Church has now recovered it. Moreover the Fathers suffered many things for the truth, but their constancy and patience are not so praised by the Holy Spirit as the constancy of the ministers of the reformed Church is praised, through whose grace Christ appears, having feet like chalcolibanum [χαλκολίβανον] and pillars of fire, v. 1. This refers to the steadfast constancy of Hus, Jerome, and other countless men who, on the pyres of their martyrdom, as in a furnace, burned like chalcolibanum, unconquered, and were refined like gold. And now at last the open book appears, v. 2, namely in the time of our reformed Church: it is given to be devoured by the recent ministers, to whom also a new commission to prophesy again is given, v. 20. But in the Church immediately preceding Constantine the book of the Church was rolled up, as shown above. I ask therefore why it is not said to have been opened before the times of the Reformation, unless because the understanding of Scripture was not so perfectly restored to the Fathers as it has now been restored to the ministers of the reformed Church. Lastly, in the time of Constantine thunders and lightnings of contentions are mentioned, Rev. 8.5. If therefore in the time of the Fathers there had been that purity, light, and understanding of the Gospel which there is now in our reformed Church, why are equal or similar things not mentioned in their time? For never before the reformation of the Gospel is Christ introduced crying out with so loud a voice as he is now introduced, v. 3, to show the power and strength of the Gospel preached through the reformed ministers. Nor before these our recent times are ministers introduced as sons of thunder, indeed as the thunders themselves, as they are now introduced, v. 3; and thunders of such a kind as merely answer, like an echo, to the voice of the angel, that is, speaking nothing and teaching nothing that they had not been taught by God. Is any similar praise anywhere given to the Fathers? Certainly nowhere. Rather the contrary is said of their time, namely that, like thunders proclaiming the Gospel effectively, they then resounded most hostilely with thunders and lightnings of contention. Rev. 8.5.

units.la: Sextò, datur ab Angelo reformatis scriptoribus calamus ad metiendum domum Dei, id est, ad progressum Ecclesiæ parifaciendum Ap. 11. 2. Hic calamus Eusebio, Sozomeno, Socrati, sæterisque antiquis historicis datus nusquam dicitur, sicut perperam antiquos historicos tam acriter obijciat nobis Downnamus, Bancroftus, Hierarchici reliqui: qui cum nostris reformatis nullo modo comparandi sunt. Mirum illis videtur, si quis veteribus historicis in materia facti fidem non adhibendam censeat: at mirandum potius fidem historicis recentioribus ab illis detrahi: nam vt tempore recentiores sunt, calamum tamen habuerunt cum, quo melius Ecclesiae progressus & immutationes observare potuerint, quàm ex antiquis ulli, quibus eiusmodi calamus nullus fuisse datus legitur.
units.tr: Sixthly, the Angel gives the reformed writers a reed to measure the house of God, that is, to measure the progress of the Church (Rev. 11:2). Nowhere is such a reed said to have been given to Eusebius, Sozomen, Socrates, or the other ancient historians, though Downame, Bancroft and the rest of the Hierarchists wrongly object the ancient historians to us so fiercely. Yet those men cannot be compared with our reformed writers at all. It seems strange to them if anyone thinks faith should not be given to the ancient historians in matters of fact; but it is rather to be wondered at that they take away faith from the more recent historians. For however much more recent they are in time, they had a reed with which they could observe the progress and changes of the Church better than any of the ancients, to whom no such reed is read to have been given.

units.la: Septimò, a tempore Constantini, quo patres n a imè floruerunt, recepit se Ecclesia in interius templi sacrarium Ap. 21. 2. & in solitudinem fugit Ap. 12. 6. 14. ad clangorem vero 7 tubæ ad annum 1558 & non ante templum palam apertrum est, imo sanctum ipsum sanctorum imo & arca ipsa fœderis patefacta Ap. 11. 19. Apocalypseos vero capite 15, 5. quiddam adhuc amplius adijcitur, operâ nempè reformatorum pastorum, apertum esse ipsius testimonij tabernaculum, id est, intima ipsa arcæ fœderis (in arca etenim testimonium condebatur) esse patefacta, et in propatulo collocata. Quinetiam dicitur, reformatorum doctorum ministerio templum repletum fuisse fumo v. 8: quo ostenditur horum sæculo, magis quam antè, patrum sæculo, præsentiam Dei in Ecclesia apparere.
units.tr: Seventhly, from the time of Constantine, when the Fathers flourished most, the Church withdrew into the inner sanctuary of the temple (Rev. 21:2) and fled into the wilderness (Rev. 12:6, 14). But at the sound of the seventh trumpet, up to the year 1558, the temple was not openly laid bare; indeed the holy of holies itself and the very ark of the covenant were not yet opened (Rev. 11:19). In Revelation chapter 15, verse 5, something still more is added: by the work of the reformed ministers the tabernacle of the testimony was opened, that is, the innermost part of the ark of the covenant (for the testimony was stored in the ark) was laid open and set out in the public view. It is also said that by the ministry of the reformed teachers the temple was filled with smoke (v. 8), by which it is shown that in this age the presence of God appears in the Church more than before, in the age of the Fathers.

units.la: Octavò, a tempore Constantini ac proinde a tempore quo maximè patres abundarunt, testes Dei, qui vetus & novum testamentum significant, prophetant induti sacco Apo. 11, 2. Hoc ostenditur a Constantini tempore corruptam indies & obscuratam scripturam fuisse, non ab hæreticis aut Arianis solùm sed a patribus etiam: nam si hij puritatem scripturæ retinuissent, non hæreticorum causâ, qui extranei & professi hostes erant, quasi in sacco prophetans scriptura inducerētur. Quid quòd ipsa prophetandi vox, ipsos veros tum temporis doctores respiciat? Quid igitur est? Non ita fideliter scripturas patres interpretati sunt: sed allegoriis & alienis expositionibus eam detorserunt: ad superstitiones tum invectas humanasque traditiones eas inflexerunt: sensum illis pro libidine affinxerunt, aut saltem eum non intelligere aut assequi potuerunt: quo factum est, ut aurea illarum vestis detracta sit patrum culpâ, & vestis lugubris impositâ. Hoc ita cum sit, quis patres sequetur, aut quis eorum authoritatem tanquam inconbitatam recipiet? imo quis potiùs scriptoribus reformatis non adhæcebit, qui vestem hanc lugubrem, in vestem lætitiæ commutarunt? Pro sacco etenim quo patres scripturas dedecorarunt; linum isti purum & splendidum eis restituerunt: inde est, quòd scripturæ interpretes qui in Ecclesiis reformatis jampridé floruerunt, Angeli dicantur, Lino puro & splendido amicti ap. 15. 6.
units.tr: Eighthly, from the time of Constantine, and therefore from the time when the Fathers most abounded, the witnesses of God, who signify the Old and New Testament, prophesy clothed in sackcloth (Rev. 11:2). This shows that from Constantine's time Scripture was daily corrupted and obscured, not only by heretics and Arians but by the Fathers too. For if the Fathers had kept the purity of Scripture, it would not have been brought forward as prophesying in sackcloth on account of the heretics, who were outsiders and avowed enemies. Moreover, the very word "prophesying" refers to the true teachers of that time. What then is the case? The Fathers did not interpret the Scriptures so faithfully; they twisted them with allegories and foreign expositions, bent them to the superstitions and human traditions then introduced, attached meanings to them at their pleasure, or at least could not understand or grasp their sense. The result was that their golden garment was stripped off through the Fathers' fault, and a mournful garment put on. Since this is so, who will follow the Fathers, or who will accept their authority as beyond question? Indeed, who would not rather cling to the reformed writers, who have changed this mournful garment into a garment of joy? For in place of the sackcloth in which the Fathers disgraced the Scriptures, these men have restored to them pure and shining linen. Hence the interpreters of Scripture who flourished long ago in the reformed Churches are called angels, clothed in pure and shining linen (Rev. 15:6).

units.la: 5 Nonò, doctrina patrum stepitus aquarum dicitur, Apocalypsis 14. 2. idque propter confusum & indistinctum sonum, qui non tam docet, quàm inutili murmure aures ferit, uti Tho. Brightmanno visum sum, qui fusam hujus interpretationis & dilucidam rationem reddit. Quid verò doctores reformati? Num & eorum doctrina talis? Imo doctrina Ecclesiarum reformatarum, voci suavissimæ & jucundissimæ comparatur, voci nempe citharæ dorum: & doctores recentiores nou solùm tauquam cytharædi introducuntur, verumetiam tanquam cytharædi qui cytharas Dei, id est, præstantissimas habeant Apo. 15: 2. 3.
units.tr: Ninthly, the doctrine of the Fathers is called the sound of many waters (Rev. 14:2), on account of its confused and indistinct sound, which does not so much teach as strike the ears with a useless murmur, as Thomas Brightman thought, who gives a full and clear account of this interpretation. But what of the reformed teachers? Is their doctrine also of this kind? Nay, the doctrine of the reformed Churches is compared to the sweetest and most pleasant voice, namely that of harpers playing on harps. And the recent teachers are introduced not only as harpers but as harpers who have the harps of God, that is, the most excellent ones (Rev. 15:2–3).

units.la: Decimò, Apo, 4. animalia & Seniores in Ecclesia prima visuntur, quæ tempore quarti & tertij cælli nusquam aparent: nusquam inquam ab Ecclesia prima usque ad Helveitca tempora animalium mentio ulla: tum demum & non ante testituuntur Ecclesiæ Apoc. 14, 3.
units.tr: Tenthly, the living creatures and the elders are seen in the early Church (Rev. 4), but they appear nowhere in the time of the third and fourth centuries. Nowhere, I say, from the early Church down to the times of the Helvetic Churches is there any mention of the living creatures; only then, and not before, are they restored to the Church (Rev. 14:3).

units.la: Vndecimò & ultimo, nulla ejusmodi spocialia elogia de antiquis patribus reperiuntur, qualia de Pastoribus recentioribus reformatis. Quàm honorificè etenim inducitur à Iohannes Wiclivius cum εὐαγγελιον sub nomine Angeli primi Ap. 14. 6. Hussus cum εὐαγγελιστης sub nomine Angeli secundi, Apo. 14. 8. Lutherus cum εὐαγγελιον sub nomine Angeli tertij Apo. 14. 9. Observandum, Evangelium quod primus Wiclivius promulgavit, evangelium æternum dici, quo occurritur objectoni novitatis, idque uon ad papistas solos, verùm & Hierarchicos etiam refutandos. Quid etenim si patres a disciplina reformata dissentiant: æterna tamen hæc est, quemadmodum & ipsa doctrina æterna: nam Wiclevium in disciplina contra Hierarchicam Anglicanam nobiscum sentire, suo loco demonstrabitur. Atq; hoc pro theologis recentioribus, antiquis patribus præferendis, ex ipsis sacris scripturis desumptum argumentum nostrum primum est,
units.tr: Eleventhly and lastly, no such special eulogies are found about the ancient Fathers as are found about the more recent reformed ministers. How honourably John Wycliffe is introduced with the gospel [εὐαγγέλιον] under the name of the first angel (Rev. 14:6); Hus with the evangelist [εὐαγγελιστής] under the name of the second angel (Rev. 14:8); Luther with the gospel [εὐαγγέλιον] under the name of the third angel (Rev. 14:9). It is to be observed that the gospel which Wycliffe first proclaimed is called the everlasting gospel, by which the objection of novelty is met; and this is to be refuted not only against the Papists alone but also against the Hierarchists. For even if the Fathers differ from reformed discipline, this gospel is nevertheless eternal, just as its doctrine is eternal; for that Wycliffe agreed with us against the Anglican Hierarchy in matters of discipline will be shown in its proper place. And so this is our first argument, drawn from the Holy Scriptures themselves, for preferring recent theologians to the ancient Fathers.

units.la: CAPIS. Hierarchicum erratum II. perstringitur a divina dis- pensationis modo.
units.tr: CHAPTER II. The Hierarchical error II is exposed from the manner of divine dispensation.

units.la: SEcundum a dispensationis divinæ ratione sumitur, quæ per vices scripturæ sacræ intelligentiam largiri solet: sic ut tempore progrediente, magis magisq; enitescere veritas & elucere soleat. Non male Tertullianus, plura seculis posterioribus quoad materiam patefieri debere existimauit: quòd verò quæ in scripturis docentur temporis progressu indies clarius reveletur: id ratio quæ ab illo adfertur docet. Nihil sine ætate est, omnia tempus expectant. Aspice ipsam creaturam paulatim ad fructum promoveri. Sic & justitia primò fuit in rudimentis naturæ: deinde per legem & prophetas promovit in infantiam, deinde per Evangelium efferbuit in juventutem. Certè ut olim per gradus patefactum evangelium est, & quo propiùs ad tempus Messiæ accessum, eo lux clarius aucta: ita quo propiùs ad illustrem Christi adventum ad ecclesiam Iudeorum omnium illustrissimam, Ap. 1. 7. nostra tempora appropinquant, eo majorem claritate communicare necesse est. Pro. 4. 18. Iter Ecclesiae [quasi lux solis quae magis magisque elucet usque ad perfectam diem:] qui igitur fieri potest, quin lux nostra luce patrum jam auctior sit, tam prope appropinquans ad Iudeorum restitutionem, quando pudebit ipsam lunam & sol ipse erubescet Isa 24. 23. Hinc citat Iuellus contra Hardingum, ad nostra tempora praeferenda, illud ex Glossa in Proem. Clement. Veritas pedetentim cognoscitur: & ex concilio Basil. Spiritus sanctus non illuminat omnes eodem tempore, sed quando vult. Iohannes vero Reynoldus in hac re multus est. Citat Aulum Gellium. lib. 12. c. 11. qui veritatem temporis filiam pronunciavit ex Sophocle, qui dixit diem omnia revelare: cui ita subjungit: Non multo secus ac Apostolus 1. Cor. 3. 13. Uniuscujusque opus manifestum fiet, dies etenim declarabit. Unde liceret mihi disputare, nostram sententiam esse veram etiamsi concederem tot antiquos scriptores contra sentire. Quamobrem etsi olim antequam veritas temporis filia latens gigneretur, multi fuerint in hoc errore, tamen hodie dum docti viri omnia excutiunt diligentius, lux ipsa patefacta est--quandoquidem videmus nostro seculo multa in lucem esse edita atque patefacta in quibus majores nostri sunt hallucinati, quod ne Papistae quidem inficiari possunt] Haec ille? Non igitur virorum doctorum suffragiis destituimur, ad os Bancrofto obthurandum: Quid? qui annis 1400. juniores sunt plus videre putandum est, quam sancti patres qui ad ipsa tempora Apostolorum tam prope accedebant? Quidni? cum primae & nascentis Ecclesiae antiquitas temporis potius defectum insinuet: nostrae autem jam provecta aetas perfectionem majorem adferat, persapientissima dispensatione divina ita ferente, ut per gradus veritas emergeret. Falsa igitur opinio est quae jam a plurimis tenetur: antiquitatem temporis, perfectionis notam esse: contra quam ita disputat Isidorus Pelusiota: [Si quid quod reprehensionem meretur Christi oraculis adjunctum esse perspicis, id ostende & tibi victoriam concedam. Sin autem cum hoc dicere nequeas, morem atque consuetudinem tanquam firmum aliquod praesidium retines, apparet te per speciosum consuetudinis praetextum, id quod utile est repudiare. Neque enim grave & scleratum est aliquid innovare, quum utilitas novitati adjuncta est. Non enim noxia & utilia vetustate perpenduntur: verum id explorandum est, an in antiquioribus rebus vitium inveniatur, ac contra, in recentioribus an virtus reperiatur.
units.tr: The second argument is drawn from the rationale of the divine dispensation, which usually grants the understanding of Holy Scripture by stages, so that as time goes on the truth tends to shine forth and become more evident. Tertullian was not wrong to think that many things concerning the subject matter would be revealed in later ages, and the reason he gives for this shows that what is taught in the Scriptures is made clearer day by day as time advances: Nothing is without its age; all things await their time. Look at creation itself, how it is gradually brought on towards fruit. So too righteousness was at first in the rudiments of nature; then through the law and the prophets it advanced to infancy; then through the Gospel it grew up into youth. Certainly, just as the gospel was once revealed by degrees, and as the light increased more brightly the nearer the approach of the time of the Messiah, so now, the nearer our times draw to the illustrious coming of Christ, the gospel to the most illustrious church of all the Jews (Rev. 1. 7), the more necessarily it must impart greater clarity (Prov. 4. 18: "the path of the Church is like the light of the sun, which shines more and more unto the perfect day"). How then can it be that our light, drawing so near to the restoration of the Jews, should not be brighter than the light of the fathers? Why should the moon be ashamed, and the sun itself blush? (Isa. 24. 23). Hence Jewel, against Harding, cites in support of preferring our own times that passage from the gloss on the Proemium of the Clementines: Truth is known little by little; and from the Council of Basel: The Holy Spirit does not enlighten all men at the same time, but when he wills. John Reynolds, however, is very full on this point. He cites Aulus Gellius (book 12, chapter 11), who, following Sophocles, called truth the daughter of time, since day reveals all things; and he adds: "Not much differently from the Apostle (1 Cor. 3. 13): The work of each man shall be made manifest, for the day shall declare it." Hence I might argue that our view is true even if I conceded that so many ancient writers thought otherwise. Therefore, although formerly, before truth, the daughter of time, was begotten out of hiding, many were in this error, yet today, while learned men examine all things more diligently, the light itself has been brought forth. For we see that in our century many things have been brought to light and made known in which our forefathers went astray, something the Papists themselves cannot deny. Thus he. We are not, then, deprived of the support of learned men, with which to stop the mouth of Bancroft: What? Should those who are 1400 years younger be thought to see more than the holy fathers, who lived so close to the times of the Apostles themselves? Why not? For the antiquity of the first and newly born Church rather suggests a lack of time, whereas the advanced age of our own times brings a greater perfection, the most wise divine dispensation so ordaining that truth should emerge by degrees. It is therefore a false opinion, now held by very many, that antiquity of time is a mark of perfection. Isidore of Pelusium argues against this view thus: "If you perceive that anything deserving censure has been added to the oracles of Christ, show it, and I will concede you the victory. But if you cannot say this, and you hold on to custom and usage as some firm defence, it is clear that under the specious pretext of custom you reject what is useful. For it is neither a grave nor a wicked thing to introduce something new when usefulness is joined to novelty. For things are not weighed as harmful or useful by their age; rather it must be examined whether a fault is found in older things, and, on the contrary, whether a virtue is found in more recent ones."

units.la: 2 In eandem sententiam Guilielmus Whitakerus. Non est quod patres antiquos nobis objiciant, cum nullam interpretationis suae rationem affirant. Non illi praeferendi sint quod antiqui fecerint si melior ratio recentium sit. Vides hic nullam authoritatem tempora patrum habere quod sint antiqua: nullum detrimentum tempora nostra pati, quod sint recentiora: sic ut alias res Bancrofium agere necesse sit, quum ab antiquitate patrum, & nostra recentissima temporis novitate disputet.
units.tr: 2. To the same effect William Whitaker: "There is no reason for them to object the ancient fathers to us, since they do not affirm any reason for their interpretation. The fathers should not be preferred to us merely because they did what the ancients did, if the recent interpreters have the better reason." You see here that the age of the fathers has no authority simply because they are ancient, and that our own times suffer no loss simply because they are more recent; so that Bancroft, when he argues from the antiquity of the fathers and the very recent novelty of our own times, must be dealing with other matters.

units.la: Accommodatissimè verò ad Ri. Bancrofti verba ipsa Iohannes Whitus Hierarchicus respondet ita. Quod adeo acriter adversus nos urgetur, verisimile est doctores antiquos uti otc Apostolorum temporibus propinquiores plus vidisse, quam nos qui tam longè remoti sumus, id Dominicus Bannes prorsus inficiatur 22. pag. 58. & 59. his verbis. Necessarium non est inquit quò à temporibus Apostolorum remotior ecclesia est, eò minus fidei perfectam in ea cognitionem esse: quia à temporibus Apostolorum non suerunt doctissimi viri in Ecclesia qui dexteritatem habuerunt, in rebus fidei intelligendis exponendisque. Non igitur eò majoribus tenebris involvimur nos, quo temporis respectu à Christo magis distamus; sed potius horum temporum posteriorum doctores, quum pij sint, & patrum vestigijs inhæreant, multò magis expressam intelligentiam in quibusdam quam illi habuerunt, assecuti sunt. Hinc videre est, eandem libertatem quam nos in patribus legendis adversarios sibi assumere, & rationi consonum putare, interdum judicia propria eis anteponere. Respondet etiam ille, ad ipsa verba Georg. Downami, qui in authoritatis contentione, patres scriptoribus recentioribus anteponendos supra dixit, quod illi antiquiores, hij verò recentiores sint. Ita enim habet. [Instituatur quæstionis statūs sicut à Icsuitis instituitur. Georg. de Valentia ita loquitur. Quæstio est, utrum hodie in controversijs fidei, plebs Christiana assentiri debeat potius Cypriano & Augustino, judicans quòd eorum opinio scripturis consentanea sit, quam Luthero & Calvino, idem de eorum opinione sentiens: non obstante quòd Lutherus & Calvinus quemadmodum & Cyprianus & Augustinus errare potuerunt, & in aliis etiamnum errarint? In hoc casu pronunciamus, quòd debeamus potius assentiri Cypriano & Augustino.] In quo loquitur absurdè, & contra quàm non Cyprianus & Augustinus solum, sed etiam doctores sui permittunt. Conveniunt etenim errare patres potuisse, & presentis temporis viros doctos in rebus multis plus intelligentiæ habere, quàm illi habeant, ac proinde in quibusdam salva reverentia eos rejici posse. Quod manifesto argumento est verum esse quod dicimus, nempe Lutherum, Calvinum, Centuriatores, in quibusdam potius credendos, quam Cyprianum & Augustinum. Ratio est quia quandoque meliroribus medijs abundant, ad veritatem eruendam. Subjungenda hisce sunt, quæ paulò ante idem Iohannes Whitus posuit.
units.tr: John White, the Hierarchical writer, replies very aptly to the very words of Richard Bancroft in this way: "That the ancient teachers are pressed so hard against us, is likely because those nearer to the times of the Apostles saw more than we, who are so far removed. Dominicus Banez utterly denies this (p. 58 and 59 of his work 22), in these words: 'It is not necessary that the further the Church is removed from the times of the Apostles, the less perfect knowledge of the faith it has; for since the times of the Apostles there have not been most learned men in the Church who had skill in understanding and explaining matters of faith.'" Therefore we are not plunged into greater darkness the further we stand from Christ in point of time; rather, the teachers of these later times, since they are godly and cling to the footsteps of the fathers, have attained, in some matters, a much more expressed understanding than those earlier men had. Hence one may see that our opponents claim for themselves the same freedom in reading the fathers that we do, and think it reasonable at times to prefer their own judgements to them. He also replies to the very words of George Downame, who, in the contention about authority, said above that the fathers are to be preferred to recent writers because the former are older and the latter more recent. For he says this: "Let the state of the question be set out as the Jesuits set it out. George of Valencia speaks thus: 'The question is whether, today, in controversies of faith, the Christian people ought rather to assent to Cyprian and Augustine, judging their opinion to be consonant with the Scriptures, than to Luther and Calvin, who think the same of their own opinion, although Luther and Calvin, like Cyprian and Augustine, could err, and have in other matters erred. In this case we pronounce that we ought rather to assent to Cyprian and Augustine.'" In this he speaks absurdly, and contrary to what not only Cyprian and Augustine but also his own teachers allow. For it is agreed that the fathers could err, and that learned men of the present time have in many matters more understanding than they had, and so in some matters they may be rejected with due reverence. This is a clear proof that what we say is true, namely that Luther, Calvin and the Centuriators are to be believed rather than Cyprian and Augustine in certain points. The reason is that sometimes they have better means at hand for bringing out the truth.

units.la: [Quanquam patres miserit Deus ad instruendam ecclesiam suam: non illa tamen eorum missio, aut alia fuit, vel majori authoritate manita, quam missio presentis temporis pastorum, qui eandē authoritatem docendi habent, & eodem à non errando privilegio gaudent: & in nulla re ab illis differunt, nisi sola antiquitate.] Annon vides egregie cum Baucroftum,tum Downamum, pro patribus præferentes unspurantes ab Hierarchico quodam suo refutatos?
units.tr: "Although God sent the fathers to instruct his Church, yet their mission was not different, nor backed by greater authority, than the mission of the ministers of the present time, who have the same authority of teaching and enjoy the same privilege of not erring; and they differ from them in nothing except antiquity alone." Do you not see how well both Bancroft and Downame, who prefer the fathers, have been refuted by a certain Hierarchical writer of theirs?

units.la: CAP. XVI. Hierarchicum erratum III. efficitur à præsentis temporis conditione.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI. The third error of the hierarchy is shown from the condition of the present time.

units.la: ARgumentum nostrum Tertium a præsentis temporis conditio‐ne sumitur. Quis enim neget tempus reformationis Heb. 9. 10. præferendum retroactis seculis illis, quorum imperfectio, ad majorem profectum perducitur: jam vero tempus hoc nostrum, respectu patrum, tempus reformationis est: multa corrigit quæ in scriptis patrum male tradita sunt, multa in lucem profert, quæ illos latebant, multos denique eorum errores emendat. Non est mihi hic necesse abire longius: Iohan. ipse Whitgiftus rem totam consicit; quid enim luculentius, clarius, disertius, quam hoc illius pro noli‐ testimonium? Doctrinam Evangelij (inquit) multo purius nostri, quam ab antiquis Episcopis factum est, profitentur. Fere omnes Græci cum epis‐ copi tum scriptores, & pars magna latinorum, liberio arbitro, operum meritis, invocatione sanctorum maculati sunt. Quid amplius desiderandum? Loquitur ille quidem de solis episcopis, & nihil sibi in animo propo‐nit, quàm ut episcopos modernos veteribus anteponeret: sed ra‐ tio quam afert omnibus hujuscè seculi nostri doctoribus & scripto‐ ribus communis est: qui si in doctrina Evangelij patribus præferendi sunt, cur non in disciplina etiam? Ita Paulus 2. Thess. 2. 7. Iam peragitur mysterium iniquitatis: tantùm qui nunc obstat, obstabit usque dum è medio sublatus fuerit, & tunc revelabitur iniquus ille, quem Dominus consumet spiritu oris sui, & illustri adventu suo abolebit. Habemus hic patrum tempora, ita cum nostris comparata, ut illa Antichristũ foverint atque promoverint: nostra verò Antichristum deleant & profligant. Neque enim obstiterunt Antichristo patres ut nostri obsisterunt, sed disciplinam adulterando, quanquam nescientes illi scalas fabricarunt quibus ascenderet: quod hic obstat apud Paulum, Imperatoris Romæ residentia est, quâ Constantinopolin translatâ, involat Antichristus in sellam, jam vacuam illam, quam illi præparassent. Non ita reformati, quos pro instrumentis suis elegit Deus ut ex spiritu oris sui, & illustri adventu suo deleretur. Atque oris mentio aperte Evangelij restituti prædicatores complectitur: de illustri adventu, cu‐ jus hic quoque mentio fit, dubitatio quidem magna subest, quid per illum intelligatur. De adventu ad iudicium interpretantur plurimi, à quibus ego non recederem, nisi pro certo haberem, longè ante judi‐ cium ultimum, Antichristum prorsus abolitum iri.
units.tr: Our third argument is drawn from the condition of the present time. For who would deny that the time of reformation (Heb. 9.10) is to be preferred to those past centuries whose imperfection is carried forward to greater progress? Indeed, this time of ours is a time of reformation compared with the Fathers. It corrects many things handed down wrongly in the Fathers' writings, brings to light many things that were hidden from them, and finally amends many of their errors. There is no need for me to go further here: John Whitgift himself settles the whole matter. For what is more lucid, clearer, or more explicit than his testimony on this point? Our people (he says) profess the doctrine of the Gospel far more purely than it was done by the ancient bishops. Almost all the Greeks, both bishops and writers, and a great part of the Latins, were stained by free will, the merits of works, and the invocation of saints. What more could be desired? He speaks indeed only of bishops, and intends nothing except to set modern bishops above the ancient ones. But the reason he gives is common to all the teachers and writers of this age of ours. If they are to be preferred to the Fathers in the doctrine of the Gospel, why not in discipline too? So Paul, 2 Thess. 2.7: The mystery of iniquity is already at work; only he who now restrains will restrain until he is taken out of the way, and then that lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord will consume with the breath of his mouth and abolish by the brightness of his coming. Here we have the times of the Fathers, which, compared with ours, so fostered and promoted Antichrist, whereas our times destroy and overthrow him. For the Fathers did not resist Antichrist as ours have resisted him. Rather, by corrupting discipline, though unknowingly, they built the ladders by which he would climb. What in Paul is the obstacle is the residence of the emperor at Rome. When this was transferred to Constantinople, Antichrist flew into the seat, now empty, which they had prepared for him. Not so the reformed, whom God chose as his instruments so that the Lord might be destroyed by the breath of his mouth. And the mention of the "mouth" clearly embraces the preachers of the restored Gospel. Concerning the "brightness of his coming," which is also mentioned here, there is indeed great doubt as to what is meant. Most interpret it as the coming to judgment, and I would not depart from them, unless I held for certain that Antichrist would be utterly abolished long before the final judgment.

units.la: Narrat siquidem Iohannes, primò sedem bestiæ demolitam iri, tum postea bestiam ipsam interituram, deinde Draconem id est Turcam periturum: quibus confectis, restituetur ecclesia Iudæorum & diutis‐simè forte etiam per nonnulla secula florebit, antequam redeat ad judicium Christus. Hoc ita cum sit, referendus quidem hic illustris adventu
units.tr: For John relates that first the seat of the beast would be demolished, then the beast itself would perish, and afterwards the Dragon, that is the Turk, would perish. When these things are accomplished, the church of the Jews will be restored, and perhaps will flourish for some centuries before Christ returns to judgment. This being so, the "brightness of his coming" is indeed to be referred here

units.la: Pa.472. test, quamdiu hostem pro amico habet? Ap. 9. 1. dicitur stella cecidisse, longè antequam tuba quinta clanxit, etsi tum primum illius casus cōspicuus factus sit. Ecce apertum Spiritus sancti testimonium, Antichristum in Episcopatu, & Archiepiscopatu, & Patriarchatu, tempore patrum extitisse, sed adeo latenter ut à patribus conspici minime potuerit, qui ad quintæ tubæ clangorem non pertigerunt. Ap. 13. 3. Admiratus est totus mundus post bestiam exortam & conspicuam factam: quid, hæc admiratio uno tum impetu cepit? minimè vero, sed fundamenta à patribus hujus admirationis jacta sunt, qui etsi non admirati sint post bestiam, ut quicquid ille præceperit, credendum & faciendum putarent, admirati tamen bestiam sunt; quum nimio splendore bestiæ occæcati, neque satis attendentes, quò tandem mali res evaderet, inflatius prædicabant Apostolicæ Cathedræ prærogativam. Hoc confitetur Richardus Feyldus, qui patres Petri cathedræ nimium addictos, diffiteri non potest. At obstare videtur Paulus 2. Thess. 2. 7. qui Antichristum tum retectum & revelatum fuisse dicit quando sedes imperialis, quæ ante obstabat, Constantinopolin ab urbe Romæ amota fuit. Respondeo hunc locum pro nobis facere: retectio etenim & revelatio Antichristi duplex est. Prima in suo fundamento, cujus respectu bestiam passim revelatam fuisse affirmat Iohannes a tempore Constantini: Secunda in illius fastigio, cujus initium, non ante clangorem quintæ tubæ post annum 600. revelatum dicit. Neutta vero actualem suis temporibus conspectum implicat, sed potentialem tantum. Prima revelatio in Hierarchia ecclesiastica a patribus qui tum vivebant actualiter animadversa minimè est: sic nec secunda in ipso papatu ab hominibus qui cum vivebant: quid tum? conspici tamen potuit & nostris jam sæculis conspicitur: postquam Calamus ab Angelo datus est, quo sano judicio præditi homines progressus Ecclesiæ observarunt, quem patres hoc calamo destituti metiri minime potuerunt, Apoc. 10. 1. Quis igitur dubitat, quin in quæstione Hierarchica, quæ revelationem Antichristi primam concernit, plus jam nostrates, quam patres unquam viderint? Consid erentur Irenæi illa, similia quibus & sanctus alicubi Augustinus habet. Omnis prophetia priusquam habet efficaciam, ænigmata & ambiguitas sunt hominibus: cum autem evenerit tempus, & evenit quod prophetatum est, tum prophetia habet liquidam & certam expositionem. Hinc Danieli, 12. 9. occlusæ sunt & obsignatæ hæ res usque ad tempus determinatum. Nullus hic tergiversandi locus: quo remotiores ab adimpletione earum rerum quæ prædicantur de Antichristo, patres fuerint, eo Antichristus illis ambiguus magis & ænigmaticus ut sit, necesse est: nostri autem reformati scriptores qui tempore illo determinato vivunt, quo res antè ad impletionem obsignatæ, jam recluduntur, in rebus Ancichristi discernendis ac proinde in quæstione de Hierarchiæ Antichristianitate determinādo non possunt non plus videre, quàm patres antiqui potuerunt.
units.tr: Pa.472. ... for how long does he hold the enemy as a friend? Rev. 9.1 says that a star had fallen long before the fifth trumpet sounded, although its fall became visible only then. Behold the clear testimony of the Holy Spirit: Antichrist existed in the episcopate, the archbishopric and the patriarchate in the time of the Fathers, but so hiddenly that he could not be seen by the Fathers, who did not reach the sound of the fifth trumpet. Rev. 13.3: The whole world marvelled after the beast had arisen and become visible. Did this marvelling begin in one stroke? By no means; rather, the foundations of this admiration were laid by the Fathers. Although they did not admire the beast so as to think that whatever it commanded must be believed and done, they nevertheless admired the beast. Blinded by the excessive splendour of the beast, and not sufficiently attending to where things would end, they preached the prerogative of the Apostolic See more inflatedly. Richard Field confesses this, and cannot deny that the Fathers were too devoted to the chair of Peter. But Paul, 2 Thess. 2.7, seems to stand in the way, for he says that Antichrist was then uncovered and revealed when the imperial seat, which had previously hindered him, was removed from the city of Rome. I answer that this passage favours us. For the uncovering and revelation of Antichrist is twofold. The first is in its foundation, with respect to which John affirms that the beast was revealed everywhere from the time of Constantine. The second is in its summit, whose beginning he says was revealed not before the sounding of the fifth trumpet, after the year 600. Neither, however, implies an actual sight in the writers' own times, but only a potential one. The first revelation in the ecclesiastical hierarchy was not actually noticed by the Fathers who then lived, nor was the second in the papacy itself noticed by the men who lived with it. So what? It could nevertheless be seen, and in our centuries it is seen, since the reed was given by the Angel, by which men endowed with sound judgment have observed the progress of the Church. The Fathers, lacking this reed, could not measure it, Rev. 10.1. Who therefore doubts that in the hierarchical question, which concerns the first revelation of Antichrist, our countrymen now see more than the Fathers ever did? Consider the words of Irenaeus, similar to those which holy Augustine also has somewhere: every prophecy, before it has its effect, is an enigma and an ambiguity to men; but when the time has come, and what was prophesied has happened, then the prophecy has a clear and certain explanation. Hence Dan. 12.9: these things were closed up and sealed until the appointed time. There is no room for evasion here. The further the Fathers were from the fulfilment of those things which are foretold of Antichrist, the more necessarily Antichrist must have been ambiguous and enigmatic to them. But our reformed writers, who live in that determined time when the things previously sealed until their fulfilment are now unsealed, cannot fail to see more in discerning the things of Antichrist, and therefore in determining the question of the Antichristianity of the hierarchy, than the ancient Fathers could.

units.la: CAP. XVIII. Hierarchicorum erratum arguitur quadrifariam, id est à recentiorum adiumentis, diligentia, modis, & medijs patrum melioribus.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII. The error of the Hierarchists is refuted in four ways, namely from the aids of more recent writers, from their diligence, their methods, and the means that the earlier Fathers used.

units.la: ARGumentum nostrum quintum, ab adjumentis illis sumitur quæ ab ipsis patribus recentiores reformatores sunt mutuati. Facile est inventis addere: jam verò Theologi recentiores, non suis solum viribus pollent, sed & patrum laboribus & lucubrationibus adjuvantur. Hic ego ad Thomam Mortonum quantumvis Hierarchicum provoco: cuius hæc positio est: [Nostræ ætatis Theologis ad veritatem eruendam plus præsidij adest, quam fuit antiquis:] præsidium verò illud intelligit quod recentiores ex patrum laboribus capiunt. Hinc clarè adducit ex ipsis pontificijs testimonia, quæ ego subjungenda puto: non solum quia à Mortono approbantur, sed etiam quia rationem insuper afferunt, qua recentiorum scriptorum dignitas, præ patrum authoritate clarior elucéscit. Ita Roffensis. Non obscurum cuiquam esse possit, multa esse tam ex scripturis aliis, quàm ex Evangelijs luculentius nunc excussa & intellecta perspicacius quam olim, nimirum quia veteribus adhuc non erat præfracta glacies, aut quia non sufficiebat eorum ætas, totum scripturarum pelagus ad amussim expendere. Ita Stella. Al sit ut ego condemne quod tot tantis scriptores simul affirmarunt, bene tamen scimus Pygmæos Gigantum humeris impositos plus quam ipsos Gigantes videre. Vtitur hac similitudine & Dominicus Bannes, prout à Iohanne Whito Hierarchico citatur. Hinc etenim probat, recentiores Theologos antiquis patribus intelligentiores esse, quia ut pueri Gigantum humeris impositi quandoquidem Gigantum proceritate altius elvantur mirum non est, si longiùs prospiciant quàm ipsi Gigantes aspicere possunt. Pergit verò Mortonus Salmoronem citans. Non omnibus omnia dedit Deus, ut quælibet ætas suis gaudeat veritatibus, quas prior ætas ignoravit, quælibet ætas antiquitati semper detulit: sed illud asserimus, quò iuniores eo perspicatiores esse doctores. Quid igitur est? patribus glacies præfacta non erat, ut iam nostris præfracta est: scripturæ immensum pelagus una patrum ætate pertransiri nō potuit: patres gigantes fuisse, recentiores vero pygmæos esse nulla ratione cu i potest: quod si vero hæc ita sint, recentiores patrum laboribus perfruentes, plus patribus videre consentaneum est: quælibet ætas mensuram suam habet, nostra vero & suam habet, & ætatum insuper antecedentium mensurâ fruitur. Ita relinquitur fœlicitatem nostrorum temporum, longè præferendam esse temporibus patrum, juxta illud Salvatoris, Ioh. 4. 37. In hoc enim est sermo veritatis quod alius est seminator & alius messor. Ego misi vos ad metiendum id in quo vos non laborastis: alij enim laboraverunt & vos ingressi estis in laborem illorum.
units.tr: Our fifth argument is drawn from those aids which the more recent reformers have borrowed from the Fathers themselves. It is easy to add to what has been discovered. Indeed, the more recent theologians are not only strong in their own abilities, but are also helped by the labours and studies of the Fathers. Here I appeal to Thomas Morton, however much of a Hierarchist he may be, whose position is this: [Theologians of our age have more help for bringing out the truth than the ancients had.] By that help he means what the more recent writers take from the labours of the Fathers. He clearly cites from the Papists themselves testimonies which I think should be added here, not only because Morton approves of them, but also because they give a further reason why the authority of recent writers shines more brightly than that of the Fathers. So Fisher of Rochester: It cannot be unclear to anyone that many things, from other Scriptures as well as from the Gospels, have now been examined more brightly and understood more sharply than formerly, namely because for the ancients the ice was not yet broken, or because their age was not long enough to weigh the whole sea of Scripture exactly. So Stella: Let it not be that I condemn what so many great writers have affirmed together; yet we well know that pygmies, placed on the shoulders of giants, see more than the giants themselves. Dominicus Bannes also uses this comparison, as it is cited by John White the Hierarchist. For from it he proves that recent theologians are more intelligent than the ancient Fathers, because, like boys lifted upon the shoulders of giants, they are raised higher by the height of the giants, so it is no wonder if they see further than the giants themselves can look. Morton goes on, citing Salmeron: God has not given all things to all, so that each age may rejoice in its own truths, which a previous age did not know; each age has always yielded to antiquity: but we assert this, that the younger teachers are the more perceptive. What follows, then? The ice was not broken for the Fathers as it is now broken for us; the immense sea of Scripture could not be crossed in the single age of the Fathers; the Fathers were giants, while the recent writers are in no way pygmies. But if these things are so, it is consistent that recent writers, enjoying the labours of the Fathers, should see more than the Fathers. Each age has its own measure, but our age has its own and also enjoys the measure of the ages that went before. So it follows that the happiness of our times is far to be preferred to the times of the Fathers, according to the saying of the Saviour, John 4:37: For in this is the saying true, that one sows and another reaps. I sent you to reap that on which you did not labour: others laboured, and you have entered into their labour.

units.la: Argumentum nostrum sextum à patrum securitate sumitur, recentiorum centiorum vero Theologorum diligentia. De priori, ita Augustinus, disputans in catholica Eccl. si., non se aliter intelligi arbitrabatur, tali quaestione nullus pulsabatur, vt is nondum litigantibus securius loquebatur. Hinc fatetur Bellarminus patres aliquando incautius, aliquando cautius locutos. De posteriore vero testatur Iohannes Reynoldus, qui hinc probat, aetatis praesentis Theologos, antiquis patribus praeferendos, in hodiernis quaestionis elucidandis: quia omnia jam quae quaestiones istas concernunt, diligentius excussa sunt quam olim suerunt. Quam praeposterus igitur Downamus: cui quum objiceretur praeferendos neotericos patribus esse, quia in quaestione disciplinaria ventilanda plus patribus defudarunt, ita respondet. Propter hunc ipsum respectum authoritas patrum praeferenda est, ob rationem quam reddit Philosophus. Pistotatoi de paliloi, adiaphthoroi gar, quum e contra neoterici scriptores, qui se nobis patres sequentibus opponunt in causa ista partes sunt, atque ita praejudicantur ut partiales. An quicquam unquam audivisti (lector) dictum absurdius? Hoc enim modo omnis opera in veritate eruenda: in quaestionibus Theologicis ventilandis, omnis diligentia ab ecclesia Dei tollitur: quorsum etenim operam impendetes? Nulla merces labori tuo alia debetur, Downami sententia, quam ut propter hunc ipsum respectum nunquam deinceps hac in causa credendus aut audiendus sis. At patres qui in quaestione disciplinaria ventilanda versati non sunt, juxta Aristotelem adiaphthori sunt: & tu hanc adiaphthorium in ecclesiam induces: quae judicem cum eo magis idoneum reddat, quo minus operae in veritate quaerenda posuit: constitue igitur in lite judicem, non jurisconsultum, is etenim operae multum posuit in jure edisendo: sed forensem aliquem qui studium in jure nullum collocavit: is etenim adiaphoros. Iterum, num adiaphoria in quaestionibus Theologicis probanda est illa, quae neutrarum partium est? concludis etenim qui hanc vel illam partem sequitur, partem jam esse, & pro partiali praejudicandum: cujus contrarium verum est. Ille etenim partialis, qui re incognita & inaudita, vel non satis perpensa, prae partium studio, in hanc vel illam partem rapitur: qui partem aliquam amplectitur, quam post longam disquisitionem, veram esse comperit (qui neotericorum scriptorum casus est) is pars quidem est, sed partialis non est, ac proinde tantum abest ut pro partiali repudiandus sit: ut o potius credendus magis, quo labore & opera sua manifestum indicium praebuit, se nulla alia causa quam ipso veritatis amore permotum fuisse. Sed non ego ineptus, si tam ineptam responsionem pluribus refutandam cucurrem?
units.tr: Our sixth argument is drawn from the security of the Fathers and the diligence of the recent theologians. Concerning the former, Augustine says, when disputing in the catholic Church, he did not think he was understood otherwise, and no one was pressed with such a question, so that he spoke more safely while no one was yet contending. Hence Bellarmine admits that the Fathers sometimes spoke less cautiously and sometimes more cautiously. Concerning the latter, John Reynolds bears witness, and from this proves that the theologians of the present age are to be preferred to the ancient Fathers in clarifying present questions, because everything that concerns those questions has now been examined more diligently than it once was. How absurd, then, is Downame! When it was objected to him that the recent writers are to be preferred to the Fathers because they have laboured more over the disciplinary question under debate, he answers thus: For this very reason the authority of the Fathers is to be preferred, on account of the reason the Philosopher gives: "The most trustworthy are the old, for they are unchanged" [πιστότατοι δὲ παλαιοί, ἀδιάφθοροι γάρ]. Whereas the recent writers, who set themselves against us who follow the Fathers, are parties in this cause, and so are prejudged as partisans. Have you ever heard anything more absurd, reader? For in this way all effort in searching out the truth, all diligence in examining theological questions, is removed from the Church of God. For why would anyone bestow effort? No other reward is owed to your labour, according to Downame's opinion, than that for this very reason you should never afterwards be believed or heard in this cause. But the Fathers, who have not been engaged in examining the disciplinary question, according to Aristotle are unchanged, and you would bring this unchanged state into the Church, which would make a judge the more suitable the less effort he has put into seeking the truth. So appoint as judge in a lawsuit not a jurist, for he has put much effort into studying law, but some outsider who has devoted no study to law: for he is unaffected. Again, is that indifference to be approved in theological questions which belongs to neither party? For you conclude that whoever follows this or that side is already a party, and is to be prejudged as partisan, when the opposite is true. For he is partisan who, with the matter unknown and unheard, or not weighed sufficiently, is swept into this or that side out of zeal for a party. But he who embraces a side which, after long inquiry, he has found to be true (which is the case of the recent writers), is indeed on a side, but is not partisan, and so far from being to be rejected as partisan, he is rather to be trusted all the more, since by his labour and effort he has given clear evidence that he was moved by no other cause than the love of truth itself. But am I not foolish, if I were to run through many pages refuting so foolish a reply?

units.la: 3 Argumentum nostrum septimum ab eo modo sumitur quem in scripturis inter retinendis antiqui patres sequuti sunt: certe enim Andradius patres linguam Hebraicam nescientes, allegoricas scripturarum interpretationes omni conatu statos esse dicit: praesentes autem <bl>secuti</bl> doctores verum Spiritus sancti sensum, cum ex prima verborum borum significatione, tum ex circumstantiarum ipsius textus consi-deratione, & aliorum in scripturis locorum collatione, fidelius exactiusque tradidisse. Citat haec Feildus & approbat: quo Bancroftus & Downamus discere potuerunt quam vanum sit, iudicia patrum, sententiis neotericorum scriptorum atque interpretum anteponere. Ne vero hoc a causa nostra alienum dicant, age, bellas illas lepidasq; patrum interpretationes proferamus, quas in causa disciplinaria produxerunt. Qui in quaestione de Hierarchiae Antichristianitate patrum sententias praevalere volunt: ij eorum de Antichristo interpretationes potiores esse tueri debent.
units.tr: 3 Our seventh argument is drawn from the method which the ancient Fathers followed in interpreting Scripture. For Andrades says that the Fathers, not knowing the Hebrew language, strove with every effort toward allegorical interpretations of Scripture, while the recent teachers, following the true sense of the Holy Spirit, have handed it down more faithfully and exactly, both from the primary meaning of the words and from the consideration of the circumstances of the text itself, and from the comparison of other passages of Scripture. Field cites and approves this; from it Bancroft and Downame could have learned how vain it is to set the judgments of the Fathers before the opinions of recent writers and interpreters. But lest they say this is foreign to our cause, come, let us bring forward those charming and witty interpretations of the Fathers which they produced in the disciplinary cause. Those who want the opinions of the Fathers to prevail in the question of the Antichristianity of the hierarchy must also defend their interpretations of Antichrist as the more important.

units.la: Probat Bellarminus Antichristum unum hominem futurum ex Iohan. 5. 43. Si alius venerit in nomine suo, & citat Chrysostomum, Cyrillum, Hieronymum, Irenaeum, Theodoretum: quibus nihil aliud habet Whitakerus quod respondeat quam quod nos jam de patribus respondemus: non est quod patres antiquos nobis obijciant: non tantum apud nos antiquitas valere debet aut nuda authoritas, quantum ratio. Omnes patres inquit Bellarminus, quae de Antiocho apud Danielem habentur, allegorice de Antichristo interpretantur. Quid ad hoc Whitakerus; constat patres antiquos hac in re non satis attentos fuisse, ideoque vim verbis saepe afferre & violentas expositiones confingere.
units.tr: Bellarmine proves that Antichrist will be one man, from John 5:43: If another shall come in his own name; and he cites Chrysostom, Cyril, Jerome, Irenaeus, Theodoret. Whitaker has nothing else to answer them except what we are now answering concerning the Fathers: There is no reason for them to object the ancient Fathers to us: antiquity or bare authority ought not to count for as much among us as reason does. All the Fathers, says Bellarmine, interpret allegorically of Antichrist what is found about Antiochus in Daniel. What does Whitaker say to this? It is certain that the ancient Fathers were not sufficiently attentive in this matter, and so often force the words and devise violent expositions.

units.la: Aequipollent certe ista verbis Cartwrighti, quae tantopere Bancroftus exagitat. Saepe textum violenter patres trahunt ad praesentem ecclesiarum suarum usum: probat Bellarminus, Antichristum non nisi tres annos cum medio regnaturum ex Irenaeo, Cyrillo Hierosolit. Chrysostomo, Theodoreto, Lactantio, Ambrosio, Hieronymo, Augustino, Gregorio, Damasceno, & Hyppolito qui ita Iohannem in Apocalypsi intellexerunt. An quicquam hic respondere Whitakerus potest quam quod a nobis responderi solitum: si nunc viverent hi patres, aliter sentirent: vixerunt illi antequam agnitus & mundo patefactus Antichristus est, non videbant quod postea eventurum esset: non mirum ergo si conjecturas suas secuti sunt; verum illi non in hac re una tantum, sed & in aliis multis erraverunt, &c. Probat Bellarminus Enoch & Eliam redituros & contra Antichristum praedicaturos ex consensu patrum, & producit Hilarium, Origenem, Chrysostomum Theodoretum, Augustinum, Primasium, Gregorium, Hyppolitum, Bedam, Arathum, quibus Whitakerus more nostro respondere coactus est. Patribus oppono Christum. Rursus, Necesse est, ut ad patres redeat, aut illi secum inde cum aperta scriptura minime constant. Simili modo respondet patribus de regno Antichristi per tres tantum annos & dimidium: neque nos urgendi sumus in hac causa patrum testimonijs, qui in multis rebus quae ad hanc quaestionem spectant hallucinati sunt & turpiter erraverunt, quia ante adventum Antichristi vixerunt. Probat Bellarminus Antichristum non ante finem mundi venturum, ex Irenaeo, Tertulliano, Augustino, Theodoreto, quos ita rejicit Whitakerus. Ego scio esse patres qui sic statuant: sed dico tamen hos patres communem erroris opinionem sequi & secum non constare. Probat Bellarminus Antichristum Hierosolymis Apoc. 5. 10. Et fecisti nos Deo nostro reges & sacerdotes, & regnabimus super terram. Atque hoc adeo clarum est, ut subeat mirari qua fronte Hierarchici hic patres sequi, hocque illorum testimonium pro superioritate episcopali citare audeant: Illud patrum de Timotheo non adeo clarum? cogita tamen donec ad illius disquisitionem veniatur quam hoc in loco crassissime patres hallucinati sunt, & in illo simpliciter hallucinari possit.
units.tr: Those words certainly amount to the same as those of Cartwright, which Bancroft so greatly harasses: "The Fathers often violently drag the text to the present usage of their churches." Bellarmine proves that Antichrist will reign only three years and a half, from Irenaeus, Cyril of Jerusalem, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Lactantius, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Gregory, Damascene, and Hippolytus, who understood John in the Apocalypse in this way. Can Whitaker answer anything here other than what we are accustomed to answer: If these Fathers were alive now, they would think otherwise: they lived before Antichrist was recognised and revealed to the world, they did not see what would happen afterwards; so it is no wonder if they followed their conjectures; but they erred not only in this matter but in many others, etc. Bellarmine proves that Enoch and Elijah will return and preach against Antichrist from the consent of the Fathers, and he produces Hilary, Origen, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Augustine, Primasius, Gregory, Hippolytus, Bede, Arethas, to whom Whitaker was forced to respond in our manner: I set Christ against the Fathers. Again: It is necessary that he return to the Fathers, or else they do not agree with plain Scripture. In a similar way he answers the Fathers about the reign of Antichrist for only three years and a half: Nor are we to be pressed in this cause with the testimonies of the Fathers, who in many matters that bear on this question have gone astray and erred shamefully, because they lived before the coming of Antichrist. Bellarmine proves that Antichrist will not come before the end of the world, from Irenaeus, Tertullian, Augustine, Theodoret, whom Whitaker rejects in this way: I know there are Fathers who hold this view: but I say that these Fathers follow a common opinion of error and do not agree among themselves. Bellarmine proves that Antichrist will be at Jerusalem from Revelation 5:10: And you have made us kings and priests to our God, and we shall reign upon the earth. And this is so clear that one is astonished with what brazenness the Hierarchists dare to follow the Fathers here and cite their testimony for episcopal superiority. Is that Father's testimony about Timothy not so clear? Yet consider, until we come to an examination of it, how very grossly the Fathers went astray in this passage, and how one could simply go astray in it.

units.la: § Argumentum nostrum octavum a medijs ducitur: non enim ea media scientiae habuerunt patres quibus hac aetas nostra abundat. Quid enim ego de linguarum cognitione dicerem nunc renovata, & expolitissima artium cultura ea introducta, quam nulla unquam aetas vidit? quid de collegiorum magnificentissima & extructione & dotatione, ex quibus tanquam ex equo Trojano prodierunt innumeri viri pietate & eruditione praestantes, qui tenebris aetatum superiorum dissipatis quasi iubare ardenti ecclesiam illustrant? quid ad extremum de arte Typographica quasi caelitus inventa ad annum 1440. qua factum, ut uno jam die plus imprimi, quam aetate patrum per totum annum describi poterit, quamque dono linguarum aliquatenus aequiparare Iohannes Foxus non dubitavit. Haec cognitionis renovandae amplificandaeque praeclara instrumenta Ap. 10. praedicta non dubito: nostrumque tempus illud esse devorandi libros & quasi de novo prophetandi quod patribus non illuxit: providebat siquidem sapientia divina ad debellandum Antichristum, haeresium omnium centrum, majoribus copijs opus jam fore, quam tempore patrum fuit. Disputat ita de patribus Bancroftus: potuerunt doctrinam contra haereses quascunque tuei patres, & veram ecclesiae disciplinam interposuerunt? Atqui mi Domine non adversus haereses aut tot aut tantas veritatem tutati patres sunt, adversus quot & quantas nostri: imo si patres, & nulli nisi patres hoc seculo vixissent, quo quoquo loco religio fuisset? promptum igitur Bancrofti ad instar disputare. Adversus haereses majores, virtute majori dimicant tam nostri, quam unquam patres dimicarunt: veram igitur disciplinam ecclesiae nonne melius patribus cognoscere potuerunt? Accidit doctorum hominum consensus, imo & ipsorum Hierarchicorum: citat etenim Iohannes Whitus Andradium defensorem concil. Trident. lib. 1. qui plura aetati nostrae revelasse Deum dicit, quam unquam patribus, & plura ad veritatem eruendam media largitum fuisse: citat Thomas Mortonus Salmeronem qui quo inniores eo perspicatiores doctores asserit. Citat deniq; Rich. Feildus Guidonem Bonderianum, qui omnia hoc seculo renovata dicit, literaturamque quasi denuo renatam, ut Christus in nobis de novo formari, & nos in illo de novo nasci pessimus. Adjicit ex Andradio Feildus ingratos esse eos qui seculum nostrum patrum seculo minime praeferunt: idque duplici nomine: primo in Deum, qui tam largiter dona sua in huius generationis filios effudit, secundo in homines qui tanta sua in tam fabrica succcessu & tam ingenti eccle-
units.tr: Our eighth argument is drawn from the means of knowledge. The Fathers did not have the resources that this age of ours abounds in. What should I say about the knowledge of languages, now revived, and the most refined cultivation of the arts, introduced in a way no age has ever seen? What of the magnificent construction and endowment of colleges, from which, as from the Trojan horse, have come forth countless men outstanding in piety and learning, who, having dispelled the darkness of earlier ages, illuminate the Church like a blazing torch? And finally, what of the art of printing, almost divinely invented around 1440, by which more can now be printed in a single day than could be copied in a whole year in the age of the Fathers, a gift which John Foxe did not hesitate to compare, in some measure, with the gift of tongues?
