I do not doubt that these splendid instruments for renewing and extending knowledge were foretold in Revelation 10, and that our time is the time of devouring books and of prophesying anew, which did not dawn on the Fathers. For divine wisdom foresaw that, to overcome Antichrist, the centre of all heresies, greater forces would now be needed than in the time of the Fathers. Bancroft argues thus about the Fathers: "Could the Fathers defend doctrine against whatever heresies, and set up the true discipline of the Church? Yet, my Lord, the Fathers did not defend the truth against so many or so great heresies as ours have done. Indeed, if only the Fathers, and none but the Fathers, had lived in this century, in what state would religion be in any place?" So one may easily argue in Bancroft's manner: "Our people fight against greater heresies with greater courage than the Fathers ever fought. Could they not then have known the true discipline of the Church better than the Fathers did?" There is agreement among learned men, indeed even among the Hierarchists themselves. John Whitgift cites Andradius, the defender of the Council of Trent, book 1, who says that God has revealed more to our age than ever to the Fathers, and has granted more means for bringing the truth to light. Thomas Morton cites Salmeron, who asserts that the more recent the teachers, the more perceptive they are. Finally, Richard Field cites Guido Bonderianus, who says that all things have been renewed in this century, and that letters have been reborn as if anew, so that Christ should be formed anew in us and we should be born anew in him. Field adds, from Andradius, that they are ungrateful who by no means prefer our century to the century of the Fathers, and this on two counts: first towards God, who has poured out his gifts so lavishly on the children of this generation; second towards men, who have laboured so greatly for the success of this undertaking and for the great benefit of the Church in searching out the truth.

units.la: De eccles. ... 47. p. 325. Apo. log. P. 2. ab 2 c. 20. In praefat. Testament. Syriac. siæ commodo, in veritate eruendâ elaborarunt. Idem scilicet quod Augustinus. Qui contempta veritate præsumit consuetudinem sequi, aut circa fratres invidus est & malignus quibus veritas revelatur, aut circa Deum ingratus cujus inspiratione ecclesia instruitur. Quidni igitur contemptus Hierarchicorum adversus scriptores novitios & major sit & majori cum ingratitudine conjunctus: quam qui nobis injustè objicitur contemptus patrum: utinam per omnia liceat lectorem putidissimas illas Bancrofti virulentias relegere quibus horrendum clamat, præferri modernos patribus: cuius tamen testimonia quæ ex Augustino profert, tam adversus contemptum συγχρονων, quam antiquorum agunt. [Ita intellexerit Ambrosius, ita Cyprianus, ita Gregorius, Augustini iudicio multum ponderis habuit.] inquit. O inceptias pro patribus præferendis, citat Augustinum, & ita citat, ut Ambrosium primo loco ponat, qui ipsa Augustini ætate vixerat. Certè antiquior Pater nobis Cavinus, aut forte etiam Theodorus Beza, quàm Augustino Ambrosius erat: quæ igitur habet Augustinus in citando Ambrosium, ea non Bancrofto pro patribus, sed nobis pro Calvino & Beza inserviunt: ea verò ista sunt. Beatum loquor Ambrosium cujus pro catholica fide gratiam, constantiam, labores & periculA, sive laboribus, sive sermonibus, & ipse sum expertus, & mecum non dubitat orbis prædicare totus. Hæc Calvino & Bezæ conveniunt optimè, quidni igitur pro notis adversus Bancroftum, quæ subjunxit Augustinus pro se adversus Iulianum? sic Bancroftus ipse Iulianus ille sit, cui tam virulenter reformatos assimulat: Quid nomen delanire niteris meum & Ambrosium (Calvinum) facis tacito eius nomine Manichæum (Puritanum.) Cernis nempè cum quibus tua maledicta sustinéas acriùs, cum quibus mihi sit causa communis: quum nulla consideratione sobrijs pulsare columnis, & expugnare conaris, cernis quàm tibi periculosum sit, tam horribile crimen objicere talibus, & quàm mihi gloriosum sit, quodlibet crimen audire cum talibus. Si cernis, cerne, & tandem tace: Pelagianam (Hierarchicam) linguam, tot linguis catholicis deprime, tot venerandis oribus proterva ora submitte. Rufus de catholicis fidei doctoribus & defensoribus verba faciens, non antiquis modo sed & ætati suæ contiguis (& contigui ætati nostræ, Calvinus, Beza, Martyr &c. fuerunt) ea habet quæ jam nobis dicere licet. Quod credunt, c edo: quod tenent, teneo: quod docent, doceo: quod prædicant, prædico. Istos cede, & me non cædes? acquiesce istis & quiescis à me, postremò, si mihi per eos amicus fieri non vis, saltem peto, ne per me illorum efficieris inimicus, sed quomodo non efficiaris si in isto errore permanseris?
units.tr: De eccles. ... 47. p. 325. Apo. log. P. 2. ab 2 c. 20. In praefat. Testament. Syriac. Indeed this is the same as what Augustine says: "Whoever, having despised the truth, presumes to follow custom, is either envious and malicious towards the brothers to whom the truth is revealed, or ungrateful towards God, by whose inspiration the Church is taught." Why, then, should the contempt of the Hierarchists for novel writers not be both greater and joined with greater ingratitude, than the contempt of the Fathers that is unjustly charged against us? I wish it were permitted to read through all those most foul virulences of Bancroft, with which he loudly declares that modern men are preferred to the Fathers. Yet the testimonies he brings from Augustine act against the contempt of [συγχρόνων] contemporaries just as much as against that of the ancients. ["Thus Ambrose understood, thus Cyprian, thus Gregory; Augustine's judgment gave it much weight."] He says: "Oh, what an absurd pretext for preferring the Fathers!" He cites Augustine, and cites him in such a way as to place Ambrose first, although Ambrose had lived in Augustine's own lifetime. Certainly Calvin, or perhaps even Theodore Beza, is for us an older father than Ambrose was for Augustine. So what Augustine says in citing Ambrose serves not Bancroft's cause for the Fathers but ours, for Calvin and Beza. And these are his words: "I speak of the blessed Ambrose, whose grace, constancy, labours and dangers for the Catholic faith, both in his labours and in his sermons, I myself have experienced, and the whole world with me does not doubt to proclaim." These words fit Calvin and Beza perfectly. Why then should they not also be used against Bancroft, in the words Augustine added in his own defence against Julian? Let Bancroft himself be that Julian, whom he so virulently compares with the reformed: "Why do you strive to disparage my name, and by silently naming Ambrose (Calvin) you make Manichaeus (the Puritan)? You see with whom your slanders are the more fiercely borne, with whom I have a common cause. When you attempt to batter and overthrow with no consideration the sober pillars, you see how dangerous it is for you to bring so horrible a charge against such men, and how glorious it is for me to hear any charge whatever together with such men. If you see, see, and at last be silent: press down the Pelagian (Hierarchical) tongue with so many Catholic tongues, and humble the insolent faces with so many venerable mouths." Rufus, speaking of the Catholic teachers and defenders of the faith, includes not only the ancients but also those close to his own time (and Calvin, Beza, Martyr and others were close to our time), and he says things which we may now say to them: "What they believe, I believe; what they hold, I hold; what they teach, I teach; what they preach, I preach. Will you yield to them, and will you not yield to me? Acquiesce in them, and you will be at rest from me. Finally, if you do not wish to become my friend through them, at least I ask that you do not become their enemy through me; but how will you not become so, if you remain in this error?"

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: Argumentum nonum à patrum incompetentia.
units.tr: The ninth argument, from the incompetence of the Fathers.

units.la: ARgumentum nostrum nonum à patrum incompetentia ea ducitur, in hac quæstione disciplinaria, quæ in scriptoribus recentioribus qui à causa nostra stant, non reperitur. Dicunt Iurisconsulti fidem testium diligenter examinandam esse, & prudenti iudici dispiciendum, quantum cuique fidei habendum sit. Rationem reddit Marcus Cicero. Multa sæpe homines dicunt, quæ à cupiditate aliqua & inimicitia, profecta videntur: itaque non sine causa in prudenti iudice id desideratur, ut expendat quæ à quoquo dicantur, inter affectus autem qui testem transversum agere solent amor potentissimus est: est autem quisque ut sibi proximus ita sibi amicissimus: hinc negant iurisconsulti (quod & ius canonicum) habendam esse cuiquam fidem in causa sua. Quid autem? patres qui adversus nos ab Hierarchicis producuntur episcopi ut plurimum erant: sic cum pro episcopatu loquuntur, in causa sua loquuntur: ecquis eos igitur credendos dicet? nos ab eis provocare prohibebit? Hierarchicis denique fidet, patres in sua causa loquentes venditantibus? Sic Christus ipse: Si pro meipso testimonium dicerem testimonium meum verum non esset Ioh.5.3. Ne Scipioni quidem in causa propria credendum dixit Cicero. Canonistæ ipsi (inquit Reynoldus) sic habent. Familiaris est hæc probatio, quum Papa alium Papam adducit in testem, & nonne pariter familiaris probatio, cum episcopus episcopum. Percurre scriptores nostros singulos: ad authoritates patrum Romanorum, à Bellarmino productas, ecquid habent quod respondent aliud, quam quod nos iam causamur, patres in causa sua audiendos non esse. Incipiam à Matheo Sutclivio Hierarchico qui adversus Damasum, Leonem, Gelasium, Gregorium, omnes sanctos patres ita excipit. Pontifices Romani ineptè in causa propria testaturi producuntur, nec enim Christus ipse Iesus, licet veritas esset & via, de seipso testimonium perhibebat. At inquit Bellarminus sanctissimi fuere. At (inquit) nonnunquam homines alioqui sancti in causa sua nimis sibi favere solent, & propterea minus idonei testes censentur: Rursus producit Bellarminus testimonium Gelasij: respondet: Ridiculum est postulare ut quisquam testibus domesticis & in propriis causa testantibus credet: Similiter Daniel Chamierus. Non sunt legitima Pontificorum Romanorum de suo ipsorum iure testimonia. Similiter Iohannes Iuellus, hominis authoritas in causa propria magna esse non potest. Dicit Imperator, nemo sibi debet ius dicere: & in ipsis decretis notatur. Papa non debet esse iudex in causa propria. Similiter Gulielmus Whitakerus, de Leone, Gelasio, Damaso, Gregorio, sanctis patribus, imo & ipso Victore habet. Quid iniquius esse potest, quàm eundem & reum & testem esse? Nemo in re sua aut ius aut testimonium dicit. Asicanus, inquit Cicero, qui suo cognomine declarat, tertiam partem orbis terrarum se subegisse, tamen si sua res ageretur testimo-
units.tr: Our ninth argument, from the incompetence of the Fathers, is drawn from this disciplinary question, which is not found among the more recent writers who stand on our side. The jurists say that the testimony of witnesses must be carefully examined, and that a prudent judge must consider how much credit each witness deserves. Marcus Cicero gives the reason: Men often say many things that seem to proceed from some desire or enmity. So it is not without cause that a prudent judge is required to weigh what each man says. Among the feelings that commonly pervert a witness, love is the most powerful. Each man is as dear to himself as he is near to himself. Hence the jurists (and the canon law) deny that anyone should be believed in his own cause. What then? The Fathers whom the Hierarchs bring forward against us were for the most part bishops. So when they speak on behalf of the episcopate, they speak in their own cause. Who, then, will say they are to be believed? Will he forbid us to appeal from them? Do the Hierarchs finally trust the Fathers when, speaking in their own cause, they peddle their wares? So Christ himself said: If I bear witness about myself, my witness is not true (Ioh.5.3.). Not even to Scipio is credit to be given in his own cause, said Cicero. The canonists themselves (says Reynolds) hold thus: this proof is familiar when the Pope brings in another Pope as a witness; and is not the proof equally familiar when a bishop brings in a bishop? Run through our writers one by one. Do they have any answer to the authorities of the Roman Fathers cited by Bellarmine, other than what we now allege, that the Fathers are not to be heard in their own cause? I will begin with Matthew Sutcliffe, the Hierarch, who dismisses Damasus, Leo, Gelasius, Gregory, and all the holy Fathers in this way: The Roman pontiffs are produced as witnesses in their own cause, foolishly; for not even Christ Jesus himself, although he was the truth and the way, bore witness concerning himself. But Bellarmine says, They were most holy. But (says Sutcliffe) men who are otherwise holy are often too partial to themselves in their own cause, and for that reason are judged less fit witnesses. Again, Bellarmine produces the testimony of Gelasius; Sutcliffe replies: It is ridiculous to demand that anyone should believe witnesses who are members of the household and who testify in their own cause. Similarly Daniel Chamier: The testimonies of the Roman pontiffs concerning their own right are not lawful. Similarly John Jewel: A man's authority cannot be great in his own cause. The Emperor says, No one ought to give judgment in his own case; and in the decretals themselves it is noted: The Pope ought not to be judge in his own cause. Similarly William Whitaker, concerning Leo, Gelasius, Damasus, Gregory, the holy Fathers, and even Victor, holds: What can be more unjust than for the same man to be both defendant and witness? No one speaks either law or testimony in his own affair. Cicero says of Asicanus, who by his surname declares that he has subdued a third part of the lands of the world, that if his own affair were being tried he would not give testimony. Now the affair of the Roman pontiffs is being tried; why then does Bellarmine bring us their testimonies?

units.la: Def.Apol. p.2.c.3. D.5. testimonium non dicit: Agitur nunc res Romanorum Pontificum: quorsum ergo nos horum testimonijs aggreditur Bellarminus? Imo sic ipsi Parisienses Sorbonistæ. De authoritatibus quæ ex scriptis Romanorum pontificum producuntur non est magnopere laborandum: quia Iohannes Gerson & alij doctores Parisienses, uno verbo respondent. Nemini in sua causa credendum. Hæc illi de antiquissimis episcopis Romæ, Clemente, Aniceto, Anacleto, &c. ex suppositione eorum epistolas decretales esse genuinas. Quod si autem privilegium aliquod pro Augustino, Ambrosio, Chrysostomo & reliquis præ ceteris patribus ostendi non potest: ridiculi sunt. Sutclivij judicio, Whitakeri censura iniqui Hierarchici qui eos de jure suo episcopali testantes inducunt: & ineptos & simplices eos esse par est, qui istiusmodi authoritatibus commoventur.
units.tr: Def.Apol. p.2.c.3. D.5. Indeed the Sorbonists of Paris themselves say the same: We need not labour greatly over the authorities drawn from the writings of the Roman pontiffs, because John Gerson and the other Parisian doctors answer in one word: no one is to be believed in his own cause. They say this about the most ancient bishops of Rome, Clement, Anacletus, Anicetus, and the rest, on the supposition that the decretal letters attributed to them are genuine. But if some privilege cannot be shown for Augustine, Ambrose, Chrysostom, and the rest above the other Fathers, they are ridiculous. By Sutcliffe's judgment, and by Whitaker's censure, the Hierarchs who bring forward these men testifying about their episcopal right are unjust; and those who are moved by such authorities must be foolish and simple.

units.la: Animadvertendum tamen est horum patrum testimonia, ubi occurrant, pro nobis quidem firmissima esse, ut quilibet adversus seipsos testificentur: consulatur hic Iohannes Reinoldus fuse disputans, cuilibet testi adversus se testimonium ferenti credendum esse. Probat ex digest. de testibus: b. Nullus. probat ex Paulo Burgensi. Nosse inquit debes in dialogis disputatoriis & iudiciariis, alternationibus contentiosis semper credi homini contra se etiam si non credatur pro se. Probat ex Paulo qui ex Epimenide alioqui, mendaci poeta, contra se tamen & Cretenses suos testimonium dicentem citans: probat denique ex Cornelio Tacito qui vel ipsum Neronem contra se testificantem credendum esse existimavit. Atqui postquam de patribus vidimus, eos minime in quæstione Hierarchica idoneos testes esse: videndum jam de præsentibus seculi doctoribus &c. adversus quos nihil habet quod excipiat Downamus quam quod in hac causa partes sunt. Ita cum testimonium aliquod profertur, respondere illi solemne. Aretius audiendus non est, est enim in hac causa pars. Sic de ceteris. Quum tu exceptionem novam, irrationabilem insuper & iniquissimam, & nunquam ante auditam audis: annon tecum miraris multum lector? Hac etenim exceptione tolluntur prorsus testimonia omnia, etiam testium integerrimorum. Ecquis etenim est qui testimonium ferre potest in causa aliqua, & non in ea causa pars esse? Nunquam in quæstionem venit, aut vitio vertum est, quod pars hnius vel illius causæ quis testis esset, sed quod partialis esset, præ partium scilicet studio, aut affectu alio: quod tantum abest ut probare Downamus potuerit de scriptoribus neotericis ut ne probare quidem tentaverit, argumento vllo alio quàm isto nullo, quòd partes sint: ac si inter patricipem & patrialem nihil interesset? vide Bright. P. 651. Atqui ut nullum aliud argumentum protulerit Downamus contra scriptores neotericos quam quod participes essent, subire tamen in mentem cuiquam potest: illud haud minus neotericis obijci posse, quod Hieronymo Bancroftus & Downamus obijciunt: nempe quod cum adversus superiorjatem Episcopi disputat αυτοφωνικως, non δογματικως locutus fit: hanc exceptionem alibi inquit Bannroftus vel ipsi agnoscunt: agnoscimus sanè, quemadmodum agnoscit Basilius qui quum Gregorius Nεocesariensis, filium & patrem hypostasi unum esse dixisset, excipit quod non dogmaticωs, sed eristicωs ista dixerit. Observandum hic est antigonisticus disputare nunquam in vitio poni, nisi quando eristicus disputatur, id est ut tu ipse Bancrofte interpretaris, quando æstu disputationis ultra limites quis provehitur ut aliquid proserat incommodè, quod sedato animo (qualis illorum esse solet qui dogmata tantum tradunt) non dixisset. Hoc absque si fuisset delererentur ex voluminibus patrum omnia eorum scripta polemica: reijcientur etiam disputationes theologicæ omnes quæ contra hæreticos scribi solent. His præmissis nego Hyeronimum præ æstu disputationis solo superioritatem episcopi inficiari: cum ministrorum paritatem tueatur, etiam in commentarijs & epistolis suis, ubi dogmaticos tantum scribit ac ne quidem polemicos disputat: affirmo è contra Epiphanium magnum illum Hierarchicorum patronum, quem etiam unicum pro episcopatus jure divino proferre possunt hujus labis affirmem fuisse. non etenim dogmaticos scribit quando contra Aerium disputat imo ne polimicos quidem, sed planè eristicos, & antagonisticos, idque vel Thomæ Bilsoni ipsius confessione: qui ita habet. Scio Epiphanium paulò vehementiorem hic videri. & in præstringendo Aerij errore, uti verbis durioribus, veluti stultitia plenis, nugis, errore, & lapsu gravissimo seducti à diabolo, &c. Atqui presbyter (inquit Downamus) Hieronymus cum esset pro presbyteri dignitate pugnavit antagonisticos: quod & omnes scriptores neoterici qui episcopis se opponunt, presbyteri enim sunt. Atqui argumenta duo suppetant neq; Hieronymum neque scriptores neotericos, quanquam presbyteri tantum sunt, pro presbyteri tamen dignitate eristicos contendere: sed solo amore veritatis disciplinam reformatam adamare. Primo, quia electione sua propria spontaneaque voluntate in presbyteri gradu subsident, cum episcopi esse possent si modo vellent. Annon Hieronymus episcopus esse potuerat, si id muneris effactasset? annon vitam monachalem Episcopali sponte præstulit? Ita Isidorus Pelusiota qui Hieraclem commendat quod episcopatum repudiasset: sponte monachus vivere elegit, cum episcopū agere potuisset, si episcopi munus tam approbasset, quam condemnasset. Ita Bernardus: episcopatum sæpe oblatum repudiavit & monachus vivere sponte elegit, quum episcopus imo & cardinalis evadere potuisset. De Hieronymo denique Zanchio narratur, eum tantum doctorem ordinarium & vixisse, & consenuisse, & expirasse: quum tamen superintendens esse potuerit: quam præsidentiam (quanquam multis modis Anglicana meliore) à fratribus sæpe illi oblatam constanter & fortiter repudiavit. Ita Calvinus & Beza & reliqui reformationis authores, episcopi esse potuerunt ipsi, si episcopatum licitum esse existimassent. Quamquam igitur presbyteri tantū scriptores recentiores sint: non tamen eristicos pro presbyterij dignitate contemcontendere putandi sunt, cum sponte presbyteri sint, & episcopi esse nolint. Secundo si cristicoos pro presbyterij dignitate adversus superiorem episcopum contenderint nuperi reformatores, eodem ambitionis æstro perciti, adversus Seniores etiam contenderent, ne in presbyterio pares una cum pastoribus essent. Rejicit Downamus scriptores neotericos tanquam testes incompetentes, non solum cum contra episcopum sed etiam cum pro senioribus scribunt? Nunquid aliqua ratione, certè nulla. nam si cristicoos scriberent, partialesq; essent, & in ambitionem nimiam incumberent presbyterialis suæ quam gerant dignitatis: ut cum Cæsare superiorem Episcopum non ferant, ita nec cum Pompeio ferrent pares seniores. Atque hæc sunt quæ pro scriptoribus præsentis sæculi antiquis patribus præferendis, dicenda habuimus.
units.tr: It must be noted, however, that where the testimonies of these Fathers occur against themselves, they are indeed most firm for us, so that anyone may bear witness against himself. Let John Reynolds be consulted here, who argues at length that credit must be given to any witness who testifies against himself. He proves it from the Digest, On Witnesses, the law "Nullus"; he proves it from Paul of Burgos: You must know, he says, that in disputations and judicial dialogues, in contentious exchanges, a man is always believed when he speaks against himself, even if he is not believed when he speaks for himself. He proves it from Paul, who, citing Epimenides (otherwise a lying poet) as one who testified against himself and against his own Cretans; and finally he proves it from Cornelius Tacitus, who thought that even Nero himself, when testifying against himself, was to be believed. But since we have seen concerning the Fathers that they are by no means competent witnesses in the Hierarchical question, we must now consider the present teachers of the age, etc. Against them Downame has nothing to object except that they are parties to this cause. Thus, when some testimony is brought forward, it is the customary answer: Aretius is not to be heard, for he is a party in this cause. And so on for the rest. When you hear this new exception, unreasonable besides and most unjust, and never heard before, do you not, reader, marvel greatly along with me? For by this exception all testimonies are utterly swept away, even those of the most upright witnesses. For who is there who can give testimony in some cause without being a party to that cause? It has never been called into question, nor has it ever been held against anyone, that a man was a party to this or that cause and so a witness; rather, it has been held against him that he was partial, that is, through zeal for his party or through some other feeling. Downame has been so far from being able to prove this against the more recent writers that he has not even attempted to prove it, using no argument at all except this one: that they are parties. As if there were no difference between a partisan and a party-man! See Bright, p. 651. And although Downame has brought forward no other argument against the more recent writers than that they are participants, yet it may well occur to anyone that the same charge can be levelled against the moderns as Bancroft and Downame level against Jerome: namely, that when he disputes against the superiority of the bishop, he spoke autophonikōs [αυτοφωνικως], not dogmatikōs [δογματικῶς]. Bancroft says elsewhere that this exception is acknowledged even by the Hierarchs themselves. We certainly acknowledge it, just as Basil acknowledges it, who, when Gregory of Neocaesarea had said that Son and Father are one in hypostasis, excuses him on the ground that he spoke these things not dogmatically but eristically [ἐριστικῶς]. It must be observed here that to dispute antagonistically is never counted a fault, except when one disputes eristically; that is, as you yourself, Bancroft, interpret it, when in the heat of disputation someone is carried beyond the limits and brings forward something inconvenient which he would not have said with a calm mind, such as is characteristic of those who only hand down doctrines. If this were allowed, all the polemical writings of the Fathers would be removed from their volumes, and all the theological disputations that are customarily written against heretics would be rejected as well. With this premise, I deny that Jerome, in the heat of disputation alone, denied the superiority of the bishop, since he defends the parity of ministers, not only in his commentaries but also in his letters, where he writes only dogmatically and does not even dispute polemically. On the contrary, I affirm that Epiphanius, that great patron of the Hierarchs, whom they can alone produce for the divine right of episcopacy, was guilty of this fault. For he does not write dogmatically when he disputes against Aerius; indeed, not even polemically, but plainly eristically and antagonistically, and this even by the confession of Thomas Bilson himself, who says: I know that Epiphanius seems rather vehement here, and in exposing the error of Aerius he uses harsher words, full of folly, trifles, error, and a most grievous lapse, led astray by the devil, etc. But Jerome, says Downame, was a presbyter, and when he fought for the dignity of the presbyter he did so antagonistically; and so do all the modern writers who oppose the bishops, for they are presbyters. Yet two arguments are available to show that neither Jerome nor the modern writers, although they are only presbyters, contend eristically for the dignity of the presbyter, but rather that they love the reformed discipline out of the love of truth alone. First, because by their own choice and free will they remain in the rank of presbyter, when they could be bishops if they only wished. Could not Jerome have been a bishop, had he sought that office? Did he not of his own accord prefer the monastic life to the episcopal? So Isidore of Pelusium commends Hieracles for rejecting the episcopate: He chose of his own accord to live as a monk, when he could have acted as a bishop, if he had approved the office of bishop as much as he condemned it. So too Bernard: he often refused the episcopate when it was offered to him, and chose freely to live as a monk, when he could have become not only a bishop but even a cardinal. Finally, of Jerome it is related by Zanchius that he lived, grew old, and died only as an ordinary teacher, though he could have been a superintendent, a presidency which his brethren often offered him, and which he constantly and bravely refused (though it was in many ways better than the English arrangement). So also Calvin, Beza, and the other authors of the Reformation could have been bishops themselves, if they had judged episcopacy lawful. Therefore, although the more recent writers are only presbyters, they are not to be thought to contend eristically for the dignity of the presbyterate, since they are presbyters of their own accord and are unwilling to be bishops. Second, if the recent reformers had contended eristically for the dignity of the presbyterate against the superior bishop, stirred by the same goad of ambition, they would also have contended against the elders, lest they be equals of the ministers in the presbytery. Does Downame reject the more recent writers as incompetent witnesses not only when they write against the bishop but also when they write for the elders? Surely for no reason, for there is none. For if they wrote eristically and were partial, and gave themselves over to excessive ambition for the dignity of the presbyterate that they hold, then just as they would not tolerate a superior bishop, as Caesar, so they would not tolerate the elders as equals, as Pompey. These are the things we have had to say in favour of preferring the ancient Fathers to the writers of the present age.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: Obiectio à patrum sanctitate desumpta, tollitur.
units.tr: An objection drawn from the holiness of the Fathers is answered.

units.la: HIs visis, reliquum est ut uni tandem obiectioni quæ sola superest respondeamus à patrum sanctitate desumpta. Ego nunquam credam, inquit Saravia, Ambrosium, Augustinum, reliquos sanctos patres Episcopatum tyrannicum gerere voluisse. Similiter Bilsonus: Quid de ea potestate dicemus, quam tot myriades doctissimorum & sanctissimorum antistitum & habuerunt & exercuerunt? Num dominatum illicitum & tyrannidem non ferendam putabimus? Num ecclesiam Christi universam, ab ejus primis incunabulis ad nostram usque tempestatem, non religione modò & conscientia, sed etiam intelligentia & sensu communi suo destitutam arbitrabimur, ut inter pastoralem authoritatem & tyrannicam dominationem, quid interesset non potuerit distinguere? & si quis eam notam omnibus Ecclesijs inurat: non eius amentiam potius detestandam, quam stultitiam argumentis refutandam judicabimus? Adjiciatur Cornelius Scultingius, eodem etenim cum illo, spiritu scribunt Hierarchici & loquuntur. Absit longè à pijs mentibus, ut veterem Ecclesiæ formam, & tot summæ pietatis & eruditionis Episcopos, Athanasios, Ambrosios, Augustinos, Chrysostomos, Basilios, Nazianzenos &c. accusare audeant tyrannis cum Puritanis.
units.tr: Having seen these points, it remains that we at last answer the one objection that is left, drawn from the holiness of the Fathers. "I will never believe," says Saravia, "that Ambrose, Augustine and the other holy Fathers wished to exercise a tyrannical episcopate." Bilson says much the same: "What shall we say of that power which so many myriads of most learned and most holy bishops both possessed and exercised? Shall we think that it is an unlawful dominion and a tyranny not to be endured? Shall we judge that the whole Church of Christ, from its earliest cradle down to our own time, was destitute not only of religion and conscience but also of understanding and common sense, so that it could not tell the difference between pastoral authority and tyrannical domination? And if anyone brands all the churches with that mark, shall we not rather judge his madness to be detested than his folly to be refuted by arguments?" Add Cornelius Scultingius, for these Hierarchical writers speak in the same spirit as he does. "Far from godly minds be it," they say, "that they should dare to accuse of tyranny, together with the Puritans, the ancient form of the Church and so many bishops of the highest piety and learning: Athanasius, Ambrose, Augustine, Chrysostom, Basil, Gregory Nazianzen, and the rest."

units.la: Primò, sanctos patres nos nunquam tyrannos diximus, ac ne Episcopos quidem Anglicanos: aliud enim est, per errorem tyrannicum Episcopatum gerere, aliud tyrannum esse. Tyrannus est, qui tyranice agit, imperium usurpat, quod novit esse non suum: quum de patribus, sicut & de hodiernis Anglicanis Episcopis verum sit: eos tyrannos quidem non esse, licet (quod ad materiam facti) quod tyrannorum erat, fecerint: sicut de Massilien sibus dictum olim, eas quidem insipientes non fuisse, eadem tamen fecisse quæ insipientes.
units.tr: First, we have never called the holy Fathers tyrants, nor even the Anglican bishops. For it is one thing to exercise a tyrannical episcopate through error, and another thing to be a tyrant. A tyrant is one who acts tyrannically and usurps a rule which he knows is not his own. Since this is true both of the Fathers and of the present-day Anglican bishops, they are not tyrants, although (as far as the substance of the deed goes) they have done what belongs to tyrants. Just as it was once said of the Massilians that, though they were not foolish, they did the same things that fools do.

units.la: Secundo, videat Bilsonus ne amentis sit, eo modo quo ille nos, amentiæ insimulare. Præmittit, si delegatio Timothei nos non confutet: amentes tamen nos esse, si universam Ecclesiæ praxim rejiciamus, Id est, etsi Scriptura Episcopum Hierarchicum minimè probat: approbavit tamen universa Ecclesia, quam rejicere amentia est. Forte. Nempè quomodo amens Paulus. Quando etenim ex scripturis locutus est, & ex scripturis solis, sobrius erat non amens Act. 26. 25. aut si amens, amens Deo. 2. Cor. 5. Eadem iam nostra causa est. Solo verbo Dei fidem nostram niti volumus, non ullâ humanâ praxi: sic Pauli vestigijs inhærentes, non nisi Deo amentes sumus: sed amens ipse Billonus potius, qui scripturis Episcopatum Hierarchicum condemnantibus minimè credit, juxta illa Chrysostomi. Si quis scripturas non credit, eum aversare velut furibundum & mente captum.
units.tr: Second, let Bilson take care lest he himself be mad, and be charged with madness in the very way he charges us. He puts forward the claim that, even if the commission given to Timothy does not refute us, we are nonetheless mad if we reject the whole practice of the Church; that is, even if Scripture by no means approves a Hierarchical bishop, the whole Church has approved him, and to reject it is madness. Perhaps so. Indeed, that is how Paul was mad. For when he spoke from the Scriptures, and from the Scriptures alone, he was sober and not mad (Acts 26:25); or if he was mad, he was mad for God (2 Cor. 5:13). Our cause is now the same. We wish our faith to rest on the Word of God alone, not on any human practice. Clinging to the footsteps of Paul, we are mad only for God. But Bilson himself is rather mad, for he does not believe Scripture, which condemns the Hierarchical episcopate, and so he fits the words of Chrysostom: "If anyone does not believe the Scriptures, shun him as one raving and out of his mind."

units.la: Tertio, inde à temporibus Apostolorum ad nostram usque tempestatem durasse Episcopum, falsum est.
units.tr: Third, the claim that the episcopate has lasted from the times of the Apostles down to our own time is false.

units.la: Quartò, Episcopatus quem patres gesserunt, non idem erat, cum nostro Hierarchico Anglicano, quod suo loco demonstrabitur.
units.tr: Fourth, the episcopate which the Fathers held was not the same as our Hierarchical Anglican episcopate, as will be shown in its place.

units.la: Quintò, de eruditione patrum vidimus: de sanctitate jam vidéamus. Sancti Patres, qui Episcopi fuerunt, dicitis. Quid? annon & sancti Reformati etiam, qui Episcopatum illicitum putant? Inspice Apocalyps. 20. 6. 20. 6. Beatus & sanctus qui habet partem in resurrectione prima (id est, in resurrectione Gentiū à Papatu: resurrectio etenim hic prima Gentium est à Papatu, secunda Iudæorum ab infidelitate) in hos enim secunda mors non habet potestatem, sed regnabunt cum Deo mille annis: scilicet ab an. 1300. ad annos dehinc septingentos. Rursus: v. 9. Ascenderunt super latitudinem terræ, & circumierunt castra sanctorum & urbem dilectam: quæ de Ecclesia reformata, ejusdemque civibus, nemo non intelligenda vidit: quod si igitur ex attributo sanctitatis aliquid concludi possit, sequeretur Episcopum non esse licitum, quia qui id putant, & beati & sancti sint. Quid & non sancti Episcopi etiam qui partem in hac resurrectione habent? quis negat? sentiendum tamen pro parte suâ quam in resurrectione à Papatu habent eos sanctos esse: sic quoad Episcopatum & disciplinam sancti non sunt, sed quoad doctrinam tantum: nam in disciplina qui resurgere à Papatu possint, qui disciplinam adhuc Papalem retinent? Atque juxta hanc proportionem de patrum etiam sanctitate judicandum. Quod nempè in doctrina integri fuerint, eousq; sancti: nō quoad eorū disciplinam corruptam, in qua Papatus fundamentum jactum est: in eo num sancti? Insistamus parumper in hoc ipso vigesimo, quod citavimus, Apocalypseos capite. Agitur v. 4. de statu ecclesiæ durante ligatione Satanæ, per mille annos, qui à tempore Constantini ad annum 1300. decurrebant. Per hoc intervallum sedere super thronos sancti dicuntur, & vivere & regnare cum Christo: sed quid? non adoraverunt bestiam neque imaginem ejus, nec acceperunt characterem ejus in frontibus suis, aut in manibus suis. Dictum hoc præcipuè fateor, est de sanctis qui in periodo horum millium annorum ultima vixerunt, sub ipso Papatu scilicet cui strenue & fortiter restiterunt. Sed ita arguo : fi illi in ultima periodo tantummodo vixerunt, & repugnarunt cum Christo, & sederunt super thronos qui bestiae restiterunt: tum etiam in periodo prima, qui huic Bestiae restiterunt etiam. Restiterunt vero Bestiae patres quoad doctrinae integritatem : non quoad corruptam disciplinam,quâ bestiae viam praemuniverunt: ergo ob doctrinam solummodo,non autem quoad disciplinam sanctitatis fuerint. Ain vero inquis patres, qui in prima periodo horum millium annorum vixerunt,quoad doctrinae integritatem bestiae restituisse? Certè, ob fidem etenim suam, Ecclesia per hoc interval-lum, super montem Sion cum agno stat, habens nomen ejus & patris ejus scriptum in frontibus suis, c. 14. 1. Deducunt haec nos ad 7. 3. nam & numerus obsignatorum à Constantino,idem cum his agni satellibus est, quadraginta quatuor millia: & character quo obsignavit in frontibus Constantinus,hic qualis fit describitur : nempe nomen Dei patris & Christi : quo fides justificans intelligitur, qua patris Dei favor in Christo per fiduciam filialem apprehenditur. Atque huc usque,quod ad ipsum fidei fundamentum bestiae restituerunt patres, doctrina tamen non usquè adeo aut pura, aut luculenta, qualis reformatorum doctorum est: id quod ex eodem loco liquet. Dum etenim progressum ecclesiae illo in loco prosequitur, comparat doctrinam patrum strepitui aquarum,qui confusus est: doctrinâ Waldensium, Wiclevi, Huffi,&c. voci tonitrui: doctrinâ vero ecclesiâ Lutheri,& Calvini téporib9 voci citharaedorum 14.2. Quid igitur est? Sancti fuerunt patres propter doctrinâ:non ita tamen quâ reformati sanctì,quia tantum interest inter doctrinâ,quantu inter aquarum strepitum,& vocè citharaedi. Respondebitur fortasse sanctos fuisse patres ob doctrinam quidem, sed non ob doctrinam solam, verum & ob disciplinam etiam. At probationem defidero : ea vero nulla adferri potest: imò in contrarium probatio nobis manifesta suppetit Apoc.8. 8.9. Postquam gradum Hierarchicorum à patribus invectorum, sub nomine montis ardentis mentionem Iohannes fecisset: descendit deinde ad affectum hujus montis, in tertia parte orbis,id est in Europa.Vbi Roma indies eo usque intumuit ambitione,donec mare versum in sanguinem esser, id est doctrina & disciplina adeo corrupta : ut & navis in hac tertia parte id est ordines superiores, & marina creatura reliqua: nautae & remiges,&c. id est,ordines inferiores clericorum moererentur. Videbis Lector: ut in hoc monte explicando, adstringit sese Spiritus sanctus ad nautas & remiges, id est ad ordines Ecclesiasticos: propterea quod haec tuba secunda, corruptionem tantum disciplinae concernat. Hinc ita disputo. Si patres in gradibus Hierarchicis suis,viam praemunierunt disciplinae adeo corruptae, ut ea posset ad umbilicum perdita, Ecclesiastici in Europa mercentur corrupto fungentes ministerio : ũ certè in disciplinafua minimè sancti fuerunt; sed utut salvari ipsi fuerint peccatum tamen in ea per se mortalem commiserunt.
units.tr: Fifth, we have seen concerning the learning of the Fathers; now let us look at their holiness. "The holy Fathers, who were bishops," you say. But what? Are not the Reformed also holy, who think the episcopate unlawful? Look at Revelation 20:6: "Blessed and holy is he who has part in the first resurrection" (that is, in the resurrection of the Gentiles from Popery; for this first resurrection is that of the Gentiles from Popery, and the second is that of the Jews from unbelief), "for over these the second death has no power, but they shall reign with God a thousand years": clearly from the year 1300 for the next seven hundred years. Again, at verse 9: "They went up over the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city." Everyone who has seen this has understood it to refer to the reformed Church and its citizens. So if anything could be concluded from the attribute of holiness, it would follow that the episcopate is not lawful, because those who think so are both blessed and holy. What then? Are not bishops also holy who have a share in this resurrection? Who denies it? Yet they are holy only in so far as they have a share in the resurrection from Popery; so they are holy as regards the episcopate and discipline, no, they are holy only as regards doctrine. For how can men rise from Popery in discipline when they still retain the Papal discipline? And by this same proportion we must judge the holiness of the Fathers too. They were holy so far as they were sound in doctrine, but not as regards their corrupt discipline, in which the foundation of Popery was laid. Are they holy in that? Let us linger a little on this twentieth chapter of the Apocalypse which we have cited. At verse 4 it speaks of the state of the Church during the binding of Satan for a thousand years, which ran from the time of Constantine to the year 1300. During this interval the saints are said to sit upon thrones, and to live and reign with Christ. But what? "They did not worship the beast or its image, nor did they receive its mark on their foreheads or on their hands." I confess that this is said chiefly of those saints who lived at the end of this period of a thousand years, under Popery itself, against which they resisted bravely and strongly. But I argue thus: if those men lived only in the last period and resisted the beast, and reigned with Christ and sat on the thrones, then those who resisted this beast also did so in the first period. Now the Fathers resisted the beast in the soundness of their doctrine, but not in their corrupt discipline, by which they paved the way for the beast. Therefore they were holy only because of their doctrine, and not in respect of their discipline. But you will say: did the Fathers who lived in the first period of those thousand years resist the beast in soundness of doctrine? Certainly, for by their faith the Church during this interval "stands with the Lamb on Mount Zion, having the name of him and of his Father written on its foreheads" (Rev. 14:1). These words lead us to Revelation 7:3. For the number of those sealed by Constantine is the same as that of the Lamb's attendants, the hundred and forty-four thousand; and the mark with which Constantine sealed their foreheads is described here as the name of God the Father and of Christ, by which justifying faith is understood, by which the favour of God the Father is apprehended in Christ through filial trust. So far, the Fathers restored the beast as regards the foundation of faith itself, but their doctrine was not so pure or so clear as that of the Reformed teachers. This is plain from the same passage. For when it follows the progress of the Church in that place, it compares the doctrine of the Fathers to the sound of waters, which is confused; the doctrine of the Waldenses, Wycliffe, Hus and others to the voice of thunder; and the doctrine of the Church in the times of Luther and Calvin to the voice of harpers (Rev. 14:2). What then is the result? The Fathers were holy because of their doctrine, but not in the way the Reformed are holy, since there is as much difference between their doctrine as there is between the noise of waters and the voice of a harper. It will perhaps be answered that the Fathers were holy because of their doctrine, but not because of doctrine alone; also because of their discipline. But I miss the proof of this, and none can be offered. On the contrary, a clear proof lies ready to hand, Revelation 8:8–9. After John had mentioned the rank of Hierarchical officers introduced by the Fathers, under the name of a burning mountain, he goes on to its effect in the third part of the earth, that is in Europe. There Rome swelled with ambition to such a degree that the sea was turned into blood, that is, doctrine and discipline were so corrupted that in this third part the ships, that is the higher orders, and the remaining sea creatures, the sailors and rowers and so on, that is the lower orders of the clergy, perished. You will see, reader, that in explaining this mountain the Holy Spirit confines himself to sailors and rowers, that is to the ecclesiastical orders, because this second trumpet concerns only the corruption of discipline. Hence I argue thus. If the Fathers, in their Hierarchical grades, paved the way for a discipline so corrupt that it could be destroyed to its very root, and the clergy in Europe are now perishing, serving a corrupt ministry, then certainly they were not holy in their discipline. But however much they themselves may have been saved, they nevertheless committed a sin in it which is mortal in itself.

units.la: Sed ut detur patres antiquos recentibus reformatis sanctiores suisse: non tamen sequitur eos in gradibus Hierarchicis, aut statuendis, aut exercendis, vel non peccasse vel non errasse: cum & sanctissimi quique cujusque aetatis a mundo initio, naevis suis non caruerunt. Neque haec nobis propria exceptio est: sed omnibus protestantibus, imò & ipsis etiam Hierarchicis communis: idque in hac ipsa causa ecclesiasticae disciplinae. Objicit Bellarminus sanctos Romanos episcopos: Quid aliud quàm hoc nostrer habet Whitakerus quod respondeat? Quanquam pij fuerunt inquit, semper tamen sui honoris & propriae dignitatis nimium studiosi fuerunt quod tum etiam apparuit, cum ecclesia in summis angustiis fuit. Iustat in Victore qui ecclesias Asiaticas propter observationem Paschatis diversam excommunicare conatus est; & annon Victor sanctus fuit, imo & Christi Martyr etiam? Pergit Whitakerus. Etiam illi episcopi qui martyres fuerunt aliquando tamen passi sunt. Cyprianus de suis temporibus sic scribit. Ambitio dormit in sinu sacerdotum. de jejun. & tent. Augustinus Romanae civitati jactantiam tribuit. Quaest.vet. & nov. Test. 101. Basilius episcoporum occidentalium deplorat. Epist. ad Euseb. Samosat. Concilium Africanum Romanos Episcopos primos saeculi in ecclesiam invexisse dicit. Henricus Paraeus episcopus Glocestrensis, in sua versione Reynoldiana, nonne ipsum Reynoldum approbat? Objicit Hartus more Hierarchico, Episcopi Romani fuerunt viri sancti. Respondet. Sancti quidem fuerunt, sed tamen homines, affectus suos habuerunt, & plus satis ambitione suae sedis intumuerunt: Apostoli sancti fuerunt, narrat tamen spiritus sanctus ad instructionem nostram, eos non solum superioritatem affectasse sed etiam pro eadem certasse, Matth.21.20. Luk.9.46. & 22.24. Quid ni de reliquis episcopis sanctis inter patres, nobis itidem respondere liceat. Innocentius, Leo, Gelasius, Vigilius, Pelagius, Gregorius majores Apostolis (inquit Reynoldus) non fuerunt: si nec Ambrosius, Chrisostomus, Augustinus, &c. Quid Damasus? nonne pater sanctus? Ambitione tamen laboravit (inquit Whitakerus) Quid Pelagius? nonne sanctus pater? Eum tamen in sua causa partialem non diffitetur Fyldus. Quid Leo? nonne sanctus pater? Is tamen ob privatum affectum in propria sede efferendi, fidei leviusculae, sapientum judicio est, inquit Bilsonus. Math. Sutclevius, multo acrius. Leo aperte & impudenter mentitur, & absque ratione contra veritatem pro Ecclesiae suae dignitate pugnat. Quid denique Gregorius magnus? nonne de sanctis patribus unus? Eum tamen tanquam sedis suae gratificantem idem rejicit Sutclev. His omnibus exemplis liberamur nos, si patres quantumvis sanctos, in causa Hierarchica rejiciamus: ut quos affectionibus humanis laborasse constat, ac ab ambitione minimè fuisse alienos. Venia tamen prae nostris episcopis Anglicanis digniores: quos lux oborta magis inexcusabiles reddidit. Meminerint igitur Cypriani illud citatum quidem à Iohanne Iuello adversus Pontificios: sed non minus
units.tr: But grant that the ancient Fathers were holier than the recent reformed. It does not follow that they neither sinned nor erred in establishing or exercising the hierarchical grades, since the holiest men of every age from the beginning of the world have not been free of their blemishes. Nor is this an exception peculiar to us. It is shared by all Protestants, and indeed by the Hierarchicals themselves, and it holds in this very matter of ecclesiastical discipline. Bellarmine objects to the holy Roman bishops. What else has our Whitaker to answer? "Although they were pious," he says, "they were always too zealous for their own honour and dignity. This also appeared when the Church was in its greatest distress." Take Victor, who tried to excommunicate the Asian churches because they observed Easter differently. Was Victor not holy, indeed even a martyr of Christ? Whitaker goes on: "Even those bishops who were martyrs sometimes nevertheless erred." Cyprian writes of his own times in this way: "Ambition sleeps in the bosom of priests" (on fasting and temptation). Augustine ascribes boastfulness to the Roman city (Questions on the Old and New Testament, 101). Basil laments the bishops of the West (letter to Eusebius of Samosata). The African Council says that the Roman bishops first introduced themselves into the Church of the age. Does Henry Parry, bishop of Gloucester, in his Reynolds translation, not himself approve of Reynolds? Hart objects in the Hierarchical manner: "The Roman bishops were holy men." He replies: "Holy indeed they were, but they were still men. They had their affections and swelled up more than enough with the ambition of their see. The apostles were holy, yet the Holy Spirit relates for our instruction that they not only aspired to superiority but also contended for it" (Matth. 21.20; Luk. 9.46; 22.24). Why may we not likewise answer in the same way about the other holy bishops among the Fathers? Innocent, Leo, Gelasius, Vigilius, Pelagius and Gregory, says Reynolds, were not greater than the apostles; nor were Ambrose, Chrysostom, Augustine, and so on. What of Damasus? Was he not a holy father? "Yet he laboured under ambition," says Whitaker. What of Pelagius? Was he not a holy father? Fulke does not deny that "he was nevertheless partial in his own cause." What of Leo? Was he not a holy father? Yet, says Bilson, "on account of a private affection for exalting his own see, he is of slight faith, in the judgment of the wise." Matthew Sutcliffe says it far more sharply: "Leo lies openly and shamelessly, and without reason he fights against the truth for the dignity of his own Church." Finally, what of Gregory the Great, is he not one of the holy Fathers? Yet Sutcliffe rejects him too, as one who "gratified his own see." We are freed by all these examples if we reject the Fathers, however holy, in the hierarchical cause, since it is established that they laboured under human affections and were by no means free of ambition. Yet they deserve more pardon than our English bishops, whom the dawning light has rendered all the more inexcusable. Let them therefore remember that saying of Cyprian, which John Jewel quoted against the Papists, though it touches the Hierarchicals no less than them:

units.la: De concil. p.118. de eccles.lib.4.cap 52. Cont Apol.c.1.p.414. de pont.Rom. p.176. Ibid.p.115. Collat. cum Harl.c.8. d.5. minus Hierarch. quam illos attingens. Ignosci potuit simpliciter erranti: post inspirationem vero & revelationem factam; qui in eo quod erravERAT, perfecte prudens & sciens, sine venia ignorantiae peccat. Praesumptione enim atque obstinatione superatur. Citat hanc sententiam Cypriani Augustinus de Baptis. lib. 4. & ex Augustino Tho. Bilsonus Hierarchicus. Simile illud est quod citat Iuellus ex Hilario. Illis, in eo quod nesciunt potest adhuc in tuto esse salus si credant: tibi vero jam omnia ad salutem clausa sunt qui negas quod jam ignorare non potes. Adjicit vero Iuellus loco priore, & Chrysostomum in Psal. 9. Qui in luce peccat imprudentior est. Ex furibus enim leges eos gravis puniunt, qui interdiu furantur.
units.tr: (De concil. p. 118; De eccles. lib. 4, cap. 52; Cont. Apol. c. 1, p. 414; De pont. Rom. p. 176; ibid. p. 115; Collat. cum Harl. c. 8, d. 5.) "Pardon could be granted to one who erred in simplicity; but after inspiration and revelation have been given, one who, knowing and fully aware, persists in the error he has made sins without the pardon of ignorance. For he is overcome by presumption and obstinacy." Augustine, in On Baptism, book 4, cites this saying of Cyprian, and Thomas Bilson the Hierarchical cites it from Augustine. Similar to it is what Jewel cites from Hilary: "For those who do not know what they do not know, salvation may still be safe if they believe; but for you, who deny what you can no longer fail to know, all things leading to salvation are already closed." Jewel adds to the former passage also Chrysostom on Psalm 9: "He who sins in the light is more imprudent. For the law punishes thieves more severely who steal by day."

units.la: Bilsonus vero sententiam alteram Cypriani addit. [Si quis praedecessorum nostrorum vel per ignorantiam vel per simplicitatem non teneret, quod Dominus authoritate & exemplo suo docuit: Deus illam simplicitatem condonabit, Nobis vero qui admoniti & edocti sumus nulla ejusmodi indulgentia relinquitur.] Objiciunt nobis Cypriani authoritatem Hierarchici: Sic & Cyprianum citarant adversus Augustinum Donatistae. Respondere igitur cum August. possumus. Quod in Cypriano naevus, in vobis fuligo est, nec inconvenit ratio. Nam illum inquit naevum in candore sanctae animae charitatis ubera conte-gerunt: hanc autem fuliginem in istorum tartarea foeditate vultus impacatus ostendit. Quid enim? annon vultus episcoporum Anglicanorum in suos fratres reformatos impacatus? Vtinam etiam & non implacabilis. Hoc respectu eorum multo minor forte inter patres & illorum saltem quosdam ab Hierarchicis citatos, quam rursus apud Vincentium Lyrinensem, inter Cyprianum, & Cyprianum venditantes Donatistas. O mira rerum conversio! Authores ejusdem opinionis Catholici, consectatores vero haeretici judicantur: absolvuntur magistri, condemnantur discipuli. Ita Ioh. Reynoldus noster. Qui scientium animas Deum ante judicium non visuras, in patribus & Armenis opinio est eadem, quae tamen in patribus non nisi error erat, jam in Armenis haeresis est. Quanto ingenio Origines & Tertullianus, quanta doctrina, quam singulari eloquentia fuerint omnes intelligunt: adeo ut alter Graecorum, alter Latinorum princeps habitus sit vel Vincentij Lyrinensis judicio c. 24. Atqui isti in errores multos inciderunt, qui vero pertinaciter eorum sententias defenderunt, haeretici habiti sunt, & Tertullianistae, & Origenistae appellati, ab his qui contra haereses scripserunt. Quod igitur monuit Saulem & Saulis sectatores David, omnesque filios virorum tum temporis potentum; utrum in eo persequendo quem Deus sibi asciverit, & gloria Dei oppugnanda, recte an secus facerent, serio cum animis suis cogitarent in cubili suo, & deinceps quiescerent, Psa. 4. 3. 5. id jam Episcopis Anglicanis faciendum; nam si Christi regni gloriam, virosque Dei oppugnare non desinant; non proderit velamentum patrum, sed tam illis inutile futurum est, eorum exemplo nuditatem suam tegere, quam Donatistis irritum Cypriani, Tertullianistis vanum Tertulliani Tertullani, Origenistis frivolum Origenis authoritatem venditare. Aliquid erat in eo quod objecerit Bellarminus, patres Africanos ex ignorantia deceptos esse,nos vero ex malitia peccare,si modo verum: totus enim Whitakerus in eo est,ut probet eos non errasse; aliàs concedit consequentiam, nempe ex malitia his diebus peccari, quando Patrum errores pertinaciter defenduntur; qua certe Hierarchici plurimi vereor ne obcæcati sint. Multum est in ipsa terra justitiæ transgredi,& majestatem Iehovæ contueri nolle Isa. 26. 10. Intelligo, in luce revelata, in ecclesia reformata, in veritate patefacta, errorem Hierarchicum pertinaciter tueri, & oculos claudere adversus maiestatem Dei in sua ipsius disciplina, circumcirca in Ecclesiis collucentem,leve (mihi crede) peccatum non est. Atque hæc de extraneo firmamento Hierarchico sexto,nempe patrum authoritate.
units.tr: Bilson, however, adds the other saying of Cyprian: [If any of our predecessors, through ignorance or simplicity, did not hold what the Lord taught by his authority and example, God will pardon that simplicity; but for us, who have been admonished and instructed, no indulgence of that kind is left.] The Hierarchicals bring Cyprian's authority against us. So the Donatists also cited him against Augustine, and we can answer them as Augustine did: "What is a spot in Cyprian is soot in you, and the reason is not out of place. For in him the breasts of charity covered that spot in the whiteness of a holy soul; but in you the restless countenance shows that soot in its Tartarean foulness." For is not the countenance of the English bishops restless towards their reformed brethren? Would that it were not also implacable. With regard to this, perhaps the difference is much smaller between the Fathers, or at least some of them cited by the Hierarchicals, than it is again between Vincent of Lérins's Cyprian and the Cyprian boasted of by the Donatists. O wondrous reversal of things! The authors of the same opinion are judged Catholic, while its followers are judged heretical: the masters are absolved, the disciples condemned. So says our John Reynolds: "The opinion that souls knowing do not see God before the judgment was held by the Fathers and by the Armenians alike; yet in the Fathers it was only an error, while among the Armenians it is now a heresy. All understand how great the talent, how great the learning, and how singular the eloquence of Origen and Tertullian were, so much so that the one was considered the chief of the Greeks and the other of the Latins, even by the judgment of Vincent of Lérins (c. 24). Yet these men fell into many errors, and those who stubbornly defended their opinions were held heretics and were called Tertullianists and Origenists by those who wrote against the heresies." Therefore, what David warned Saul and the followers of Saul, and all the sons of the mighty men of that time, namely to consider seriously in their own hearts, upon their beds, whether they acted rightly or otherwise in persecuting the one whom God had chosen for himself and in attacking the glory of God, and then to be still (Ps. 4.3, 5), this the English bishops must now do. For if they do not cease to attack the glory of Christ's kingdom and the men of God, the veil of the Fathers will not help them. It will be as useless to them as it is to cover their nakedness with the example of those men, as it would be for the Donatists to flaunt the empty authority of Cyprian, for the Tertullianists the vain authority of Tertullian, or for the Origenists the frivolous authority of Origen. There was something in what Bellarmine objected, that the African Fathers were deceived through ignorance, whereas we sin through malice, if indeed it is true. For Whitaker's whole argument is to prove that they did not err; otherwise he concedes the consequence, namely that in these days people sin through malice when the errors of the Fathers are stubbornly defended. I fear that many of the Hierarchicals are indeed blinded by this. "It is great to transgress in the very land of righteousness, and to be unwilling to behold the majesty of Jehovah" (Isa. 26.10). I understand that to stubbornly defend a Hierarchical error in the revealed light, in the reformed Church, in the truth now made plain, and to close one's eyes against the majesty of God shining round about in the Churches in his own discipline, is not a light sin, believe me. And so much for the sixth external prop of the Hierarchy, namely the authority of the Fathers.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: Argumentum septimum Hierarchicorum à conciliorum authoritate dissolvitur.
units.tr: The seventh argument of the Hierarchicals is refuted from the authority of councils.

units.la: SEptimum,Papisticum pariliter est ; nempè authoritas conciliorum ; de quâ sententiam Hierarchicorum ita ponit Richardus Bancroftus; Christus certo consilio semet Ecclesiæ suæ (loquitur autem de Synodis) obstrinxit: ut illius directione in rebus controversis adjuvantur fideles: cujus piæ determinationi in materijs quæstionarijs, filij illius obsequentes, sese submittere debent. Et quid ultra quis Papisticissimus dicere potuit? Supponit etenim concilia errare non posse, & eorum determinationes esse semper pias: & absurdè fidem illis necessariò adhibendam esse docet. Certè æquivolent ista (ut mihi videtur) illis Scultingij, qui ex Sess. 20. Concilij Basilienfis, decretis Synodalibus Conciliorum generalium, nervum regulæ ac disciplinæ ecclesiasticæ maximè niti contendit, indeque probat nervum disciplinæ Calvinianos non habere, quòd Puritani non ex generalibus Synodis, sed ex solis scripturis disciplinam hauriendam esse existiment. Respondeo verò primò, concilia authoritatem nullam habere,nisi nitantur sacra scripturâ quod docet fuisse adversus Papistas, Thomas Mortonus Hierarchicus. Iniqua (inquit Bellarminus) est conditio Protestantium, ut in Concilijs ex sola scriptura divina sententiæ ferantur,& non ex canonibus. Imò inquit ille æquissima quo citat Patres. [Ex scriptura qui vere loqui desiderat,sumere debet quod loquatur. Non eximatur dogma veritatis necessarium, quod ex scripturis non probatur. Extra scripturam sensus nullus sanctus, sicut olim nihil sanctum extra templum.] Origines.
units.tr: The seventh argument is equally Papist: namely, the authority of councils. Richard Bancroft sets out the Hierarchicals' view on this: Christ has bound himself by a certain decision to his Church (he is speaking of synods), so that the faithful are helped in controverted matters by its guidance, and his obedient sons ought to submit to its pious determination in questions of this kind. What more could the most thorough Papist have said? He assumes that councils cannot err and that their decisions are always pious, and he teaches that faith must necessarily be given to them, which is absurd. In my view these arguments are the same as those of Scultingius, who, drawing on the twentieth session of the Council of Basel and on the synodal decrees of general councils, maintains that the strength of the rule and discipline of the Church rests chiefly on these, and from this he concludes that the Calvinists have no strength of discipline, because the Puritans think discipline should be drawn not from general synods but from Scripture alone. I answer, first, that councils have no authority unless they rest on Holy Scripture. Thomas Morton, a Hierarchical, taught this against the Papists. The condition of the Protestants is unfair, says Bellarmine, in that judgments in councils are given from divine Scripture alone, and not from the canons. Nay, he says, it is most fair, and he cites the Fathers for it. [Whoever wishes to speak truly must take from Scripture what he says. No necessary dogma of truth that is not proved from Scripture should be admitted. Outside Scripture there is no holy sense, just as once there was nothing holy outside the temple.] Origen. [Finally, at the Council of Nicaea, Constantine put forward a copy of the Bible in the midst of them and said: Let us take the explanations of questions from the divinely inspired words.] From these things he finally concludes that Christian liberty is that alone which is accustomed to rest in the law of God alone; since this is the voice of God himself, it must be the soul of every council. You see, then, that the Hierarchical arguments drawn from councils are bodies without a soul, because they are deprived of the authority of Holy Scripture. John Jewel uses the same defence against Harding: Since God speaks most fully in the Scriptures, he says, to refer the matter to the decision of a council is nothing other than to ask whether men are willing to confirm the divine precept by their own authority or not. And against those iron chains of councils with which Saravia strives to bind us in discipline, just as Harding did in doctrine, he cites that saying of Clement of Alexandria: Since the Word himself has come to us from heaven, we need no longer go to the teaching of men; and also that saying of Chrysostom: It would be the height of absurdity for one who had been taught by God afterwards to hold communion with men.

units.la: [Postrem ò, in Concilio Nicæno, propositο in medio Bibliorum codice, ita Constantinus. Ex verbis divinitus inspiratis sumamus quæstionum explicationes.] Ex his tandem concludit, Christianam libertatem eam solam esse, quæ in sola Dei lege acquiescere solet: quę cum ipsius Dei vox sit: Concilij cujusque animam esse necesse est. Vides igitur & argumenta Hierarchica ex Concilijs desumpta, cadavera esse absq; anima, quòd ab authoritate sacræ scripturæ destituantur. Ioh. Iuellus eadem defensione utitur adversus Hardingum: Cum in Scripturis inquit plenissimè loquatur Deus, rem ad Concilij determinationem revocare, quid aliud est, quàm inquirere, utrū divinum præceptum authoritate sua confirmare necnè homines velint. Atque adversus illa chalybæa Conciliorum vincula, quibus nos in disciplina, vincire Saravia nititur, perinde ac Hardingus in doctrina, citat illa Clementis Alexandrini: Quoniam ipsum verbum ad nos venit de cœlo, non est nobis amplius eundum ad hominum doctrinam: necnon illa Chrysostomi: Fuisset extremæ absurditatis, eum, qui edoctus fuerat à Deo postea cum hominibus communicare.
units.tr: Secondly, just as Scripture is so perfect that it has no need of the authority of councils, so men are so imperfect that it is not safe to rest upon their authority. Richard Field, who argues at length, has seen this clearly: no infallibility can be sought from councils, councils have erred, and they can always err. He adds, from Thomas Waldensis, that it is safer to follow the consensus of the Fathers continued through many centuries than that of those who gather in one place, at one time, in one age. So if that consensus of the Fathers is weak, as has been shown above, much more weak is the consensus in a council. To Bancroft, who alleges Christ's promise made to the Church, Field replies thus: However Christ promised that he would be present with his Church, which will be fulfilled in the elect, he did not bind himself in such a way to any gathering of men assembled in council that they could in no way err. To the same Field, and to the other Hierarchicals who charge us with impudence because we oppose the authority of councils, he answers from Panormitanus and John Gerson: It is no impudence if a private person, even alone, withstands a council, provided he has on his side the authority of Holy Scripture (as the reformed hold).

units.la: Secundò, sicut ea scripturæ perfectio est, ut Conciliorum authoramento non sit opus, ita ea hominum imperfectio, ut eorum inniti authoritate non sit tutum. Hoc perspectum Richardo Feyldo, qui fusè disputat, nullam ex conciliis infallibilitatem peti posse, errasse concilia, etiam semper errare posse. Addit ex Thoma Waldensi, tutius esse, consensum patrum per multa secula continnatum sequi, quam eorum, qui uno tantum in loco, uno tempore, ætate una congregantur: sic ut iste consensus patrum infirmus si fuerit, ut supra demonstratum est, multò magis eorum consensus in concilio infirmus sit. Bancrofto verò, promissum Christi Ecclesiæ factum allegunti respondet ita: Vtcunque Ecclesiæ suæ se affuturum spopondit Christus, quod in electis adimplebitur: nulli tamen societati hominum in concilio quidem congregatæ se ita obstrinxit, ut errare minimè possint, Eidem, cæterisque Hierarchicis, impudentiam nobis objectantibus quòd conciliorum authoritati refragemur: respondet ex Pamormitano, & Iohanne Gersone: impudentiam nullam esse, si privatus quis, etsi solus, restiterit concilio, si authoritatem sacræ scripturæ (ut habent reformati) secum consentientem habeat.
units.tr: Secondly, just as Scripture is so perfect that it has no need of the authority of councils, so men are so imperfect that it is not safe to rest on their authority. Richard Field clearly saw this. He argues at length that no infallibility can be sought from councils: councils have erred, and they can always err. He adds, from Thomas Waldensis, that it is safer to follow the consent of the Fathers, maintained through many centuries, than that of those who gather in one place, at one time, in one age. So if the consensus of the Fathers, as shown above, is weak, the consensus of a council is much weaker still. To Bancroft, who alleges the promise Christ made to his Church, he replies: However Christ promised that he would be present with his Church, which will be fulfilled in the elect, he did not so bind himself to any society of men gathered in council that they could by no means err. To the same man and the other Hierarchists, who charge us with impudence for resisting the authority of councils, he replies from Panormitanus and John Gerson: There is no impudence if a private person, even alone, resists a council, provided he has on his side the authority of Holy Scripture (as the reformed have it).

units.la: Tertiò, respondens Hardingo Iohannes Iuellus regerit: Conciliis minimè protestantes defici, & ex hoc apparere nos Concilia non contemnere, quòd concilia convocare (re ita ferente) soleant. Quòd si verò contumeliam contemptus a Protestantibus hoc removeat: cur non & a nobis reformatis etiam? Synodos etenim convocare solemus, & Synodorum multarum authoritate, confirmata disciplina reformata est. Dixit olim Augustinus, Posteriora Concilia à prioribus sæpè (ad scripturæ normam scilicet) emendari. Quid si igitur, Synodus reformatæ disciplinæ, antiqua non nulla concilia corrigant? Neque tamen sequitur, (ut recte Reynoldus) quod inde infert Bellarminus, Inter antiqua concilia, concilia priora minoris authoritatis esse, quam posteriora, sed retinendum potius Isidori hoc dogma est: Quotiescunque in gestis conciliorum discors sententia invenitur, illius sententia concilij praelett, 34. tius teneatur cujus antiquior & prior extat authoritas. Iugulat hoc inquies Synodos vestras reformatas, de mutata disciplina. Nequaquam vero: cum seculis medijs de quibus loquitur Isidorus, hęc nostra tempora longe przcellant, ut supra demonstratum est: & Synodos antiquissimas quarum ille authoritatem praefert, adversus nostram disciplinam facere, probari non possit.
units.tr: Thirdly, answering Harding, John Jewel retorts: The Protestants are not lacking in councils, and it is clear from this that we do not despise councils, since we are accustomed to convene them when circumstances require. But if this removes the reproach of contempt from the Protestants, why not from us reformed as well? For we too are accustomed to convene synods, and by the authority of many synods our discipline has been reformed and confirmed. Augustine once said: Later councils have often been corrected by earlier ones (namely by the rule of Scripture). What if, then, a synod of reformed discipline corrects some ancient councils? Nor does it follow, as Reynolds rightly says, what Bellarmine infers from this, that among the ancient councils, the earlier are of less authority than the later. Rather, the dogma of Isidore is to be retained: Whenever a discordant opinion is found in the acts of councils, the opinion of that council is to be preferred whose authority is older and earlier. You will object that this overthrows our synods and our changed discipline. By no means. The middle ages of which Isidore speaks are far inferior to these our times, as shown above; and it cannot be proved that the most ancient synods, whose authority he prefers, are against our discipline.

units.la: 3 Quartò, Pudet me inquit Hadrianus Saravia, quum antiqua Concilia, Canones antiqui, à Calvino & Bezâ in re disciplinaria rupti & violati sint. Quos tu Canones antiquos memoras? Scripsit Iohannes Lydius Francofurtensis in librum Prateoli de Conciliis: is Pag.10. ita habet. Extat Tomo secundo conciliorum, Anonimi cujusdam qui vixit anno 1198. scriptum quoddam, quod appellatur Opusculum Tripartitum: ubi inveni sententiam memorabilem, quam hic adscribam: Concilia antiqua (inquit) & etiam posteriora vix inveniuntur. cap. 10. Verum hoc imprimis de conciliis primis, quę ante Nicenum celebrata sunt: quæ si extarent, major fortasse de Conciliis antiquissimis ruptis, conquerendi occasio penes reformatos esset, quàm è contrà. Sed extant nonnulla inquies: At de horum Canonibus conqueri non datur, cum de Episcopali superioritate, canones nullos ediderunt. Liceat igitur Guilielmi Whitakeri illa reponere: [Quo quodq; concilium antiquius eò sanctius & sincerius fuit, ut aqua quò propior fonti eò purior & dulcior. Paulatim irrepserunt pravæ opiniones. Ante Constantinum Magnum, provincialia tantum quædam concilia habemus, in quibus nihil de primatu Romani Pontificis sancitum est (sic nec de majoritate Episcopali.) At ego pluris ejusmodi unum concilium facio, quàm quodvis eorum, quæ postea secuta sunt. Nam sæviente persecutione, Episcopi de Ecclesia & religione magis soliciti erant, eâ verò sublata mox ambitio invasit ecclesiam.] Hinc illa querela Nazianzeni: [Equidem ut verè quod res est scribam, prorsus decrevi fugere omnem Conventum Episcoporum. Nullius enim Concilij bonum exitum unquam vidi. Concilia enim non minuunt mala sed augent potius.] Male tractatur hoc nomine à Bibliorum interpretibus nostris Nazianzenus: qui in omnium Conciliorum derogationem, hæc illius redundare putare videntur. Atque recte adfert ista Bilsonus, adversus omnium cujusque ætatis Conciliorum infallibilitatem, idque ratione additâ, quia major pars sæpe meliorem vincit. Eadem & Ioh. Iuellus habet adversus Haraingum: & Ioh. Whitus Hierarchicus. Thomas Bilsonus alibi, & Richardus Fyldus, ad turbulenta tempora sua hæc verba Nazianzeni restringunt: qui tamen de hoc tempore, haud minus quam reliqui cum justificant. De illis suis temporibus potiò adjicit Whitus ex Vincentio Lyrinensi adverl.profan.novitat.cap.4. Ecclesiam sæva contagione commaculatam esse. Quid igitur est? Concilia ante Nicænum pro se afferre Hierarchici nequeunt: quæ vero ex Concilijs Nicænum subsequentibus adferri solent testimonia, nullius momenti & ponderis sunt. Insistunt vero in his Concilijs quarti & quinti seculi præcipuè Hierarchici: cujus quidem prævaricationis, modestos puduisse oportuit. Quale etenim quæso hoc argumentum est? Concilia quædam quæ post invalescentem Episcoporum ambitionem, post corruptam disciplinam, post contentiones invectas, ad concilij cujusque exitum bonum impediendum, majoritatem Episcopalem approbant, ergo ea sancta & legitima est?
units.tr: 3 Fourthly, I am ashamed, says Adrian Saravia, that the ancient councils and ancient canons have been broken and violated by Calvin and Beza in matters of discipline. Which ancient canons do you mean? John Lydius of Frankfurt, writing on Prateolus's book on councils, says at p. 10: In the second volume of the councils there is an anonymous work, by someone who lived in 1198, called the Tripartite Little Work, in which I found a memorable saying, which I shall set down here: "The ancient councils" (it says) "and even the later ones are scarcely to be found." Ch. 10. But this holds above all of the first councils, celebrated before Nicaea. If these were extant, the reformed would perhaps have greater cause to complain of the broken ancient councils than the reverse. But, you will say, some are extant, and one cannot complain about their canons, since they issued no canons about episcopal superiority. Let me therefore quote William Whitaker: "The older any council is, the holier and purer it was, as water is purer and sweeter the closer it is to its source. Bad opinions crept in gradually. Before Constantine the Great we have only certain provincial councils, in which nothing was decreed about the primacy of the Roman Pontiff (nor about episcopal majority). But I value one such council more than any of those that followed later. For while persecution raged, bishops were more anxious about the Church and religion; but once persecution ceased, ambition soon invaded the Church." Hence the complaint of Nazianzen: "To write what is really the case, I have quite resolved to flee every gathering of bishops. For I have never seen a good outcome of any council. Councils do not lessen evils but rather increase them." Our Bible interpreters handle Nazianzen badly on this point, as they seem to think his words reflect on all councils. Bilson rightly adduces these words against the infallibility of the councils of every age, adding the reason that the greater part often overcomes the better. John Jewel has the same against Harding, and John White in his Hierarchicus does too. Thomas Bilson elsewhere, and Richard Field, restrict these words of Nazianzen to the turbulent times of his own day, though they justify them no less than the others do for this time. White, moreover, quotes from Vincent of Lérins (against profane novelties, ch. 4) that the Church was stained by a grievous contagion in their own times. What then? The Hierarchists cannot bring forward councils before Nicaea in their favour; and the testimonies they usually adduce from the councils after Nicaea are of no weight or value. Yet the Hierarchists especially insist on the councils of the fourth and fifth centuries, and in this prevarication the modest should have been ashamed. For what kind of argument, I ask, is this? Certain councils, held after the ambition of the bishops had grown strong, after discipline had been corrupted and contentions introduced, which hindered the good outcome of any council, approve episcopal majority: therefore they are holy and lawful?

units.la: 4 Sed de ipso Nicæno Concilio hæc accipere, absurdum & ridiculum Bancrofto videtur: à quo, quid non audit Tho. Cartwrightus; cum ab eo exemplar politeias ecclesiasticæ tutò peti posse differetur? Durum tamen inquies quod ibidem in Beza sigillat, Nicænum concilium, sedem meretricis qua super montes septem sedet, præparasse. Atqui ex canone hujus concilij sexto hoc liquidò constat, quo Romanus Episcopus Patriarcha constituitur, quæ illius prærogativa labem primam dedit: quum referente Ænea Sylvio, parvus ante respectus ad Romanam Ecclesiam habveretur. Quò minorem rationem habuit Bancroftus, concilium Nicænum magnificè prædicare, Coluviem verò Genevensem (ita enim appellat) in qua disciplina primo reformata fuit, præ eo contemnere: in concione etiam sua ad crucem Paulinam nobis monstri loco obijcere, quod regnum Christi hoc in concilio labefactatum sentiamus, in quo divina illius maiestas tam sincerè stabiliebatur.
units.tr: 4 But it seems absurd and ridiculous to Bancroft that these things should be taken of the Nicene Council itself. What does Thomas Cartwright not hear from him? Yet a copy of the ecclesiastical polity can safely be sought from him, though it is put off.
