You will say it is harsh that Beza there stamps the Nicene Council as having prepared the seat of the harlot who sits upon the seven mountains. Yet from the sixth canon of this council it is clear enough that the Roman bishop is constituted Patriarch, and that prerogative gave the first blemish, since, as Aeneas Silvius reports, the Roman Church was held in little regard before. Bancroft has all the less reason to praise the Nicene Council extravagantly and to despise the Geneva sewer (for so he calls it), where discipline was first reformed. In his sermon at Paul's Cross he also throws it in our faces as a monstrous thing that we think the kingdom of Christ was weakened in this council, in which the divine majesty of that kingdom was so sincerely established.

units.la: Primò, concilium Hierosolymitanum Niceno præponendum dicimus. Præsertim cum ab eo concilio alia (ut rectè Whitakerus) formam suam sumere debeant: id quod Mortonus Hierarchicus vel ipso Bellarmino probat. Sequitur vero Synodum Hierosolymitanum concilium Niczenum? illius morem imitatur? Qui id fieri potest? cum morem antiquum in stabilienda Hierarchia secuta sit Nicæna synodus: in concilio vero Hierosolymitano mori nihil datum sit (sicut nihil omnino dandum) sed ex scripturis ejsque solis sanctum sit. Probat hoc vel ex ipsis papistarum scriptoribus Thomas Mortonus ipse scriptor Hierarchicus. Act. 15. 15. Huic dicto Petri concordant verba Phophetarum sicut scriptum &c. Colligunt ex his verbis Caietanus, Montanus, Canus, Ferus, non ausos fuisse ipsos Apostolos quicquam à se definire, sed ex variis scripturarum locis disputationem primum instituisse, & ad postremum iuxta allegata earum testimonia rem totam definivisse. At nihil hujusmodi à Niceno concilio, in Hierarchia stabilienda observatum: mos humanus, non lex divina consessui huic se testante cynosuræ loco fuit: non dicunt scripturæ obtineant, sed τα αρχαια.
units.tr: First, we say that the Council of Jerusalem is to be placed before the Nicene. This is especially so since other councils ought to take their form from that one (as Whitaker rightly says), which Morton the Hierarchist proves even from Bellarmine himself. But does it follow that the Synod of Jerusalem imitated the Nicene council, or that council imitated its custom? How can that be, when the Nicene synod followed an ancient custom in establishing the hierarchy, whereas in the Council of Jerusalem nothing was given to custom (as nothing at all should be), but was made holy from the Scriptures and from them alone? Thomas Morton himself, a Hierarchist writer, proves this even from the papists' own writers. Acts 15:15: The words of the prophets agree with this saying of Peter, as it is written, etc. From these words Cajetan, Montanus, Canus and Ferus gather that the Apostles themselves did not dare to define anything on their own, but first instituted a disputation from various places of Scripture, and at last settled the whole matter according to the testimonies adduced from them. But nothing of this kind was observed by the Nicene Council in establishing the hierarchy. Human custom, not divine law, served that assembly as its guiding star, as it itself testifies. It does not say that Scripture prevails, but [τα αρχαια], the ancient things.

units.la: 5 Secundò, quod pro Hierarchia adfert Bancroftus ex concilio Niceno: id ab ipsa scriptura quasi nominatim condemnatur. Quanquam etenim respectu eorum quæ adversus hæresim Arianam fecerit, illius fumus instar suffitus ascendisse dicitur Ap. 8. 4. respectu tamen Hierarchiæ minimè leviter accusatur, quòd montem ardentem tem igni projecerit in Ecclesiam, Ap. 8. 8. & bestia cum ex mari id est corrupta doctrina ac disciplina ascendisse dicitur Ap. 12.1. id in relatione dicitur ad corruptas Nicæni concilij de disciplina sanctiones: nam quòd tum primo in fundamento suo bestia conspicua facta sit, supra demonstratum est. Quid quod tubæ Apoc. 8.6. in ipso Nicæno concilio clanxisse dicantur, vel saltem Angeli se præparasse ad clangendum quia ipsa tum mala, initio conspicua, & in eo quasi tubâ promulgata sunt?
units.tr: 5 Second, what Bancroft brings forward for the hierarchy from the Nicene Council is condemned almost by name in Scripture itself. For although, with respect to what it did against the Arian heresy, it is said to have gone up like the smoke of incense (Rev. 8:4), yet with respect to the hierarchy it is not lightly accused of having cast a burning mountain into the Church (Rev. 8:8). And when the beast is said to have risen out of the sea, that is, from corrupt doctrine and discipline (Rev. 12:1), this is said with reference to the corrupt decrees of the Nicene Council on discipline; for that the beast first became conspicuous in its foundation has been shown above. What of the trumpets of Revelation 8:6, which are said to have sounded in the Nicene Council itself, or at least the angels are said to have prepared themselves to sound, because those evils then first became conspicuous and were, as it were, proclaimed by that trumpet?

units.la: Tertiò, prunæ ardentes ex altari concilij Niceni in terram conjectæ fuisse dicuntur Ap. 8. 5. propterea quod turbas multas hoc concilium dederit in hominibus terrestribus, sic ut malum remedio creverit. At sic & ipsæ inquies scripturæ sacræ, ut nunc dierum Evangelium, per abusum hominum terrestrium turbas multas dare solet, absq; ullo peccato suo. At dispar est ratio: Concilium etenim Nicænum contentiosos Episcopos, facultate potentiaq; armavit ad nocendum: & per majoritatem quam eis concessit, eorum animus superbire, imò & ebullire cæpit, ad Ecclesiam perturbandam. Verum igitur & in Nicæno concilio est quod Nazianzenus de reliquis ejusdem seculi, dixit, nullum nempe eorum fœlicem exitum se vidisse, ut discant mortales fidem suam in scriptura solâ fundare, nullam autem hominum quamvis sanctorum congregatam multitudinem supra modum venerari.
units.tr: Third, burning coals are said to have been cast from the altar of the Nicene Council onto the earth (Rev. 8:5), because this council gave many disturbances among earthly men, so that the remedy grew into a disease. But you will say that the holy Scriptures themselves, as the Gospel nowadays, are wont to give many disturbances through the abuse of earthly men, without any fault of their own. But the case is not alike. The Nicene Council armed contentious bishops with power and authority for doing harm, and through the majority it granted them, their spirit began to swell with pride, indeed to boil over, to the disturbance of the Church. So there is in truth, even in the Nicene Council, what Nazianzen said of the rest of that century: that he had seen none of them having a happy end, so that mortals may learn to found their faith on Scripture alone, and to venerate no assembled multitude of men, however holy, beyond measure.

units.la: 6 Quartò, cur adeo mirum Bancrofto videtur, Nicænum concilium errare potuisse in suo Hierarchico canone? Quia piè statuit scilicet, de divina natura Christi contra Arianos. Quasi adeo rarum sit ut benè de quibusdam sentientes homines, in aliis tamen errent? Non ego canonem quem adversus Miletium habet, urgebo: licet eum nostri contra pontificios urgere passim soleant: solis eis instantijs contentus ero, quæ apud ipsos Hierarchicos reperiuntur. Citat enim Io. Whitgiftus Ambrosium, lib. 10. epist. 82. quod in concilio Necæno contra Bigamiam clericorum sancitum sit: & Hieronymum, quod idem librum Iudith inter sacras scripturas, commemoravit. Hæc si sunt vera, erroribus alijs, præterquam Hirarchicis laboravit hoc concilium: de quo insuper non est alienum à proposito considerare, quod habet Socrates: Visum erat Episcopis legem novam in Ecclesiam introducere, ut qui essent sacris initiati (sicut Episcopi, Presbyteri, & Diaconi) cum uxoribus, quas, cum erant laici in matrimonium duxissent, minimè dormirent. Restitum quidem huic decreto est à Paphnutio, sed à Paphnutio solo: & quanquam uxores non ademptæ, quibus dum erant laici nupserant: in hoc tamen aqua hæsit, ut post sacram initiationem uxores ducere pro hiberentur. His perpensis, quomodo quæso absque periculo, fides concilio tam prono ad errorem niti potest?
units.tr: 6 Fourth, why does it seem so strange to Bancroft that the Nicene Council could have erred in its hierarchical canon? Because, forsooth, it rightly decided about the divine nature of Christ against the Arians. As if it were so rare for men who think rightly about some matters to err in others! I will not press the canon which it has against Meletius, although our people commonly press it against the papists. I will be content with those instances alone which are found among the hierarchists themselves. John Whitgift cites Ambrose, book 10, letter 82, that at the Nicene Council it was decreed against the bigamy of clergy; and Jerome, that the same council recorded the book of Judith among the holy Scriptures. If these things are true, this council laboured under errors other than hierarchical ones. Besides, it is not irrelevant to my purpose to consider what Socrates has: It seemed good to the bishops to introduce a new law into the Church, that those who were initiated into the sacred offices (such as bishops, presbyters and deacons) should not sleep with the wives whom they had married while they were laymen. This decree was indeed resisted by Paphnutius, but by Paphnutius alone; and although wives were not taken away from those whom they had married while laymen, yet on this point it stuck fast, that after sacred initiation they were forbidden to take wives. Having weighed these things, how, I ask, can faith in a council so prone to error rest without danger?

units.la: Quintò, concilium Nicænum pro Hierarchia Anglicana nihil fecit: ascribitur etenim can. 9. Hierarchia mori antiquo: at Hierarchia Anglicana divino jure se tuetur. Sanare hoc vulnus videtur Downamus ex eo,quòd concilium Nicænum in his verbis mos antiquus obtineat, de Patriarchis tantummodo loquatur, quos in hoc canone d icit jure humano & positivo introductos. At contrà Lous. Synodus Nicæna Metropolitanos(nō Patriarchas modo)antiquissimos dicit.Contra Thomas Bilsonus. Primatus Meteopolitani ex consuetudine erat, ut testatur concilium Nicænum. Contra denique Iohannes Whitgiftus, qui fusè disputat & metropolitanum & patriarcham ab initio eosdem, & metropolitanum non patriarcham modo in Concilio Nicæno stabilitum,id quod probat productis in medium testimonijs varijs, nempè ex Iohanne Calvino, Flaccio Illyrico, Iohanne Foxo, & Francisco Villiero.
units.tr: Fifth, the Nicene Council did nothing for the English hierarchy. For it is ascribed (canon 9) to the ancient custom which shall prevail, whereas the English hierarchy defends itself by divine right. Downame seems to heal this wound by saying that the Nicene Council, in the words let the ancient custom prevail, speaks only of patriarchs, whom in this canon it says were introduced by human and positive law. But on the contrary Lous: The Nicene Synod calls the metropolitans (not only the patriarchs) most ancient. Against this, Thomas Bilson: The primacy of the metropolitan was by custom, as the Nicene Council attests. Finally, against them both is John Whitgift, who argues at length that both the metropolitan and the patriarch were established from the beginning, and the metropolitan, not only the patriarch, was established in the Nicene Council; he proves this by bringing forward various testimonies, namely from John Calvin, Flacius Illyricus, John Foxe and Francis Villiers.

units.la: 7 Sextò, nudam concilij Nicæni authoritatem nemimem adstringere,apud omnes nostrates Guilielmum Whitakerum, Ioh. Reynoldum, Tho.Bilsonum, Tho.Mortonum, Ioh.Iuellum cæterosque adversus papistas & Iesuitas exploratissimum dogma est. Probant ex Augustino. Nec ego Nicænum, nec tu debes Ariminensje,tanquam præjudicaturus proferre concilium. Nec ego huius authoritate, nec tu illius detineris. Scripturarum authoritatibus,utriusque communibus testibus,res cum re,causa cum causa,ratio cum ratione concertet, Quod de præjudicio dicit,habetur & apud Ambrosium etiam qui ne fidem quidem Nicænam urgendam putavit contra Arianos : nè videatur perversitas,non examinata,sed prejudicata damnari.
units.tr: 7 Sixth, that the bare authority of the Nicene Council binds no one is a most well-established doctrine among all our countrymen, namely William Whitaker, John Reynolds, Thomas Bilson, Thomas Morton, John Jewel and the others against the papists and Jesuits. They prove it from Augustine: Neither I should bring forward the Nicene Council, nor you the Council of Rimini, as though you were to prejudge the matter. Neither am I bound by its authority, nor are you by that one. Let the case contend with the case, the cause with the cause, and the reason with the reason, by the authority of the Scriptures, the common witnesses of both sides. What he says about prejudgment is also found in Ambrose, who thought that even the Nicene faith ought not to be urged against the Arians, lest it might seem that a perversity was condemned not examined but prejudged.

units.la: Septimò & ultimò, consideranda prudenti lectori est,annon verisimilia sint, quæ Iohannes Lydius Francofurtensis,de Nicænorum canonum (qui jam extant) incertitudine in medium profert. Canonum numerus incertus apud authores est: & mirum est exemplaria huius concilij, inter se tantum differre,ut nesciant cui sit fidendum. Dicit opusculum tripartitum c. 10. Antiqua concilia, & etiam posteriora, non inveniuntur. - Acta bujus Synodi etsi hodie græcè extent, tamen accuratissimè scripta,iniuria temporis, & Arianorum conatibus, cum Baronio, perijsse credo. Nam hæc quæ habemus nimis frigida sunt: nec sapiunt Athanasium, Hosium,Paphnutium, aliosque qui con illo interfuere. Hæc de fundamento Hierarchico septimo,nempe Conciliorum authoritate.
units.tr: Seventh and last, the prudent reader should consider whether the things which John Lydius of Frankfurt brings forward about the uncertainty of the Nicene canons (which now exist) are not probable. The number of the canons is uncertain among the authors, and it is remarkable that the copies of this council differ so much among themselves that they do not know which to trust. The little work in three parts, chapter 10, says that the ancient councils, and even the later ones, are not found. The Acts of this Synod, although they survive today in Greek, were, I believe, written most carefully, but have perished through the injury of time and the attempts of the Arians, along with Baronius. For those which we have are too frigid; they do not savour of Athanasius, Hosius, Paphnutius, and the others who took part in it. These are the points about the seventh hierarchical foundation, namely the authority of the councils.

units.la: CAP. XX. II.
units.tr: CHAP. XX. II.

units.la: Octavum Hierarchicum fundamentum nempe fides historiæ ecclesiasticæ tollitur.
units.tr: The eighth Hierarchical foundation, namely the trustworthiness of ecclesiastical history, is overthrown.

units.la: Sequitur octavum, similiter papisticum, nempe fides historiæ ecclesiasticæ: idem etenim sentiunt Hierarchici cum Cano: cujus hæc positio est. Illud pro certo accipiendum, quod omnium gravium & probatorum historicorum testimonio confirmatur. Richardus Feildus ita. Clarum est ex testimonijs antiquitatis, Petrum, Iacobum maiorem,& Iohannem, Iacobum Episcopum Hierosolymitarum ordinasse. Sic Anacletus tus Epistola secunda si quae ei fides adhibenda sit: sic Clemens Alexandrinus apud Eusebium, sic Hieronymus de viris illustribus. Hic ego cujusque aequi in ipso initio conscientiam appello. Fabulâ istâ nihil ineptius fingi potest: ut ipsa clamat, & suo loco demonstrabitur. Non est igitur quod Hierarchicorum vociferationibus commoveamur cum rem claram esse clamant, ex historicorum veterum consensu, Episcopos Hierarchicos in prima Ecclesia extitisse: cum eorum moderatissimo, ex eisdem clarum sit etiam Iacobum Apostolum Episcopum fuisse, idque ex ordinatione novâ: quo nihil potest dici salsius. Sed audiatur omnium vehementissimus Georgius Downamus.
units.tr: Next comes the eighth foundation, likewise Papistical, namely the trustworthiness of ecclesiastical history. The Hierarchists agree with Cano on this point, and his position is this: That must be accepted as certain which is confirmed by the testimony of all the weighty and approved historians. Richard Field writes thus: It is clear from the testimonies of antiquity that Peter, James the Greater, and John ordained James, Bishop of Jerusalem. So Anacletus, in his second Epistle, if any faith is to be given to it; so Clement of Alexandria, cited by Eusebius; so Jerome in his book On Illustrious Men. Here I appeal at the very outset to the conscience of every fair-minded reader. No fable more absurd could be invented, as the fable itself cries out, and it will be shown in its proper place. There is therefore no reason for us to be moved by the clamour of the Hierarchists when they cry out that it is plain, from the agreement of the ancient historians, that Hierarchical bishops existed in the primitive Church. Even by the most moderate of them, it is equally plain from the same sources that the Apostle James was also a bishop, and that from a new ordination, than which nothing can be said more insipid. But let us hear the most vehement of them all, George Downame.

units.la: [ Quaestio est (inquit) de materia facti, in qua fides patribus deneg anda non est. Nonne vnanimi consensu testatur omnis antiquitas, episcopos primitivae ecclesiae, reliquos ministris gradu superiores fuisse, & ecquis nostrum eum frontem gerit, ut id denegare audeat? ] Rursus [Communi consensu antiquissimorum & probatissimorum scriptorum probatur Titum & Timotheum episcopos fuisse: quorum refutatoris negatio si aequa lance ponderetur, nae ipsa vanitate vanior reperietur] Iterum [Neminem nisi episcopum ordinare potuisse, generalis omnium patrum consensus est: quorum vel unius authoritas, in materia facti, totam disciplinariorum rationem deprimere debet] Postremo [Acta Apostolorum quae post Lucae historiam perpetrata sunt, memoriae prodita sunt partim ab Hegesippo & Clemente, & aliis antiquis authoribus, qui testantur Paulum, Timotheum Ephesi, Titum Cretae Episcopos ordinasse, & quod ipse aliique Apostoli episcopos alios locis aliis instituerint. Quorum testimonia quicunque fidem adhibere abnuit: ipse fidem nullam meretur.] Videre hinc est, quaenam praecipua Hierarchicorum anchora sit: & quo argumento claram suam sententiam esse comprobare soleant: ex irrefragabili nempe antiquorum scriptorum in materia facti authoritate. Hanc cum perinde urgeant papistae in quaestione de Petri ad Romam adventu: perinde etiam illis respondere habemus, quod his respondet Gailm. Whitakerus. [Quod aliqui impudentiae nos accusant, quod rem tam certam & claram in quaestionem vocemus: ego non modo nihil clarum & certum video, sed omnia potius dubia & obscura.]
units.tr: [The question is (he says) one of matter of fact, in which faith is not to be denied to the Fathers. Does not all antiquity bear unanimous witness that the bishops of the primitive Church were superior in rank to the other ministers, and which of us bears such a brazen face that he dares to deny it?] Again [By the common consent of the most ancient and most approved writers it is proved that Titus and Timothy were bishops; if the denial of their opponent were weighed in an even balance, he would indeed be found emptier than emptiness itself.] Again [That no one but a bishop could ordain is the general consensus of all the Fathers; the authority of even one of them, in a matter of fact, ought to overthrow the whole argument of the disciplinarians.] Lastly [The Acts of the Apostles that were done after the history of Luke have been handed down to memory partly by Hegesippus and Clement and other ancient authors, who testify that Paul ordained Timothy at Ephesus and Titus at Crete as bishops, and that he and the other Apostles appointed bishops in various places. Whoever refuses to give faith to these testimonies deserves no faith himself.] From this one may see what the chief anchor of the Hierarchists is, and by what argument they are accustomed to prove that their opinion is clear: namely, by the irrefutable authority of the ancient writers in matters of fact. Since the Papists press this argument equally in the question of Peter's coming to Rome, we have equally to answer them with what William Whitaker answers to these men: [That some accuse us of impudence for calling into question a matter so certain and so clear: I do not merely see nothing clear and certain, but rather everything doubtful and obscure.]

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: Argumentum nostrum primum a sola scripturae Authentica authoritate.
units.tr: Our first argument, from the sole authentic authority of Scripture.

units.la: VEniamus ad argumenta. Argumentum nostrum primum à scripturae authoritate ducitur, quae sola in materiis facti, haud secus atque in rebus fidei, nos solos certos reddit. Perspectum commentario hoc, qui in Genesim librum historicum scribens de historia etiam sacra hoc affirmat. [ Solis scripturis reservata est haec authoritas,ut ideo id ita esse credamus, quia ita scripserunt.] Si solis scripturis haec authoritas reservetur, contumeliosior in scripturas Papistis ipsis Downnamus, qui hanc authoritatem patribus communem facit,dum credendum esse contendit Hierarchicos Episcopos in Ecclesijs primis fuisse,quia ita illi scripserunt. At parum forte fide dignus Cajetanus: sciendum igitur Tho. Mortonum hanc illius sententiam & citare & approbare: sic ut hac in re Hierarchicum ab Hierarchico confutatum habeamus. Ita Ioh. Turrecremata. [Nihil asserendum est de divinis,nisi quod divinarum scripturarum testimonio & ratione probari potest, ut Hieronymus & Augustinus scribunt.] Haec in materia facti adfert Whitakerus & approbat ita. [Recte. Utinam id ipsum omnes papistae perpetuò tenerent: facilius certè omnes controversiae inter nos dirimerentur.] Produxit Ioh. Reynoldus de Eusebio & historicis reliquis hoc testimonium Can.li.11.c.6. [Praeter authores sacros,nullus historicus certus esse potest, & idoneus ad faciendam certam in Theologia fidem,] quod adeo à se evidens & apparens esse dicit, ut suis probationibus confirmari opus non habeat. Tantum Flavij Vopisci in vita Aureliani,verum & lepidum dictum citat: qui historiam scribere aggrediens, eò se id consilentius facere dicit,quia in mentiendo comites habiturus erat: cum nullum historicum sciverit, qui non in aliquo mentitus sit. Quod si hoc autem (inquit Reynoldus) omnibus historicis acciderit, exceptis eis qui scripturas exararunt, qui per Spiritum Dei non hominis scripserunt: tum Eusebius quoque quanquam historicus bonus, eidem vitio subiectus esse potuit.] Approbat ista Henricus Parqus Episcopus Gloceftrensis in sue versione Reynoldiana. Onuphrius Patavinus,de Petri adventu ad Romam agens, usus est argumento negativo ex Actis Apostolorum. Huic ita occurrit Baronius, Argumentatio inquit, Nouatoribus peculiaris, qui in receptu habent, ut negent, quicquid in scripturis non habetur expressum. Sed Lucas multa praetermisit &c. Quorsum haec inquis? Nempe ut intelligatur communem protestantium opinionem hanc esse, historiam perfectam in sacris haberi, sic ut necessario credendum non sit, quod in eisdem non habetur traditum. Male igitur Causaubonus, & contrà reliquorum communem sententiam, cum ita Peronio postulanti ut antiquitas ad tempora usque Martini extenderetur, ita responderet. Hoc postulatum parum illis (reformatis) aequum videbitur, qui universam Ecclesiae primitiuae historiam, Actuum Apostolicorum divino illo quidem, sed tamen unico libello volunt contineri. Ab horum sententia longè abest aequissimus prudentissimusque Rex qui in epistola monitoria sua, quanti facerct patres etiam quarti aut quinti seculi ingenuè declarauit. Peius verò multò Downnamus, qui Egesippum,Clementem,& alios scriptores antiquos accersendos existimat, ut ita historia Lucae,ubi desijt,continueretur. At si non historiam perfectam liber Actorum continet, minime tamen ad patres quarti aut quinti seculi. Certè hac repudiata,incertas patrum narrationes consectari,non modo ridiculum,sed & impium esset. Atque certè miror Downamo non venisse in mentem, continuatorem sancti Lucæ Apostolum Iohannem potiorè esse, quàm patrum quenquam,quanquam maximè genuinum. Annon historia Apocalypsis est? Quid igitur sibi illa volunt, c. 4. v. 1. Ascende hûc & ostendam tibi quæ oportet fieri posthac? Annon historia perfecta etiam? Quid igitur illud sibi vult,c. 5.v. 1. quod hic liber intus & à tergo scriptus dicatur? Annon ostendunt hæc, hunc eundem plenè persecteque exaratum? Adde quod c.10.v.7. Pertingat hujus libri historia, usque ad consummationem mysterij Dei ,sicut annunciavit servis suis prophetis. At obscurior forte Apocalypsis, quàm ut loco historiæ servire possit. Quorsum igitur illa tam magnifica referatio sigillorum, quæ tantis laudibus piorum celebratur c.5.v.8. Quorsum mandatum, Ne obsignaveris verba prophetiæ libri hujus: tempus enim prope est,c.22.v. 10. Quorsum denique promissio? Beatus qui legit, & beati qui audiunt verba prophetiæ libri huius, & observant ea, quæ in ea scripta sunt : tempus enim prope est, c.1.v.3. Non igitur historiam tantam sacram habemus,sed & in sacris historiam perfectam; sic ut ad patres in materia facti divertere ad fidem faciendam in re aliqua Theologica controversa, loco sacrilegij sit. Num hæc mea sententia sola est? Annon Hierarchici prudentiores idem planè sentiunt? Audiatur primò Richardus Feyldus, Quis non plane videt, inquit,Evangelistas historiam de morte & vita Christi memoriæ tradentes, sanctum Lucam in Actis Apostolorum, Ecclesias ab Apostolis institutas narrantem, sanctum Iohannem revelationem quam vidit scribentem, intendisse,ut perfectam doctrinæ Christianæ summam plenamque fidei directionem tradrerint,de futuro rerum statu, usque ad consummationem seculi. Audiatur deinde Hadrianus Saravia. Quis, inquit, ecclesiæ status fuerit, & quam tradiderint rationem gubernandæ ecclesiæ Apostoli, nemo docere poterit: nisi ex sacris literis & Apostolorum temporibus. Audiatur postremo Matheus Sutclivius, quem ego Iohanni Whitgifto oppono. Contendit ille, Anabaptisticum esse in materia facti, à scriptura, negativè argumentari. At contrà Sutclivius: disputans etenim contra Petri ad Romam adventum, ita arguit. Probatur sententia nostra primò, quia nusquam ex scriptura probatur. Nihil eius scripsit in epistolis suis Petrus, nihil Paulus, nihil quires Apostolorum gestas diligenter & accuratè persequutus est Lucas. Rursus. Respondet Bellarminus, non valere argumentum ab authoritate negativè. Primo per argumentum ab authoritate sacræ scripturæ validè valet. Ex scripturis non probatur, ergò non est dogma fidei, Ita argumentatur Apostolus,ita etiam argumentantur Patres, idque necessariò sequitur, quia scriptura est canon fidei, & nihil est nunc necessariò credendum extrà scripturas. Ita conficitur,in materia facti, historicos nullos nisi sacros, aut fidem facere; aut ad fidem obligare.
units.tr: Let us come to the arguments. Our first argument is drawn from the authority of Scripture, which alone, in matters of fact just as in matters of faith, makes us certain. This is clear to anyone who considers the commentator who, writing on the book of Genesis as a historical work, affirms this of sacred history too: "This authority is reserved to the Scriptures alone, so that we believe a thing to be so because they have written it so." If this authority is reserved to the Scriptures alone, then Downham, who makes it common to the Fathers, is more insulting to the Scriptures, since he contends that the hierarchical bishops existed in the first churches because the Fathers wrote so. But Cajetan is perhaps not sufficiently trustworthy. We should know, then, that Thomas Morton both cites and approves that opinion of his, so that in this matter we have a hierarchical writer refuted by a hierarchical writer. So too John of Torquemada: "Nothing is to be asserted about divine things unless it can be proved by the testimony of the divine Scriptures and by reason, as Jerome and Augustine write." Whitaker brings forward this statement in matters of fact and approves it thus: "Rightly. Would that all the papists would always hold this same view: all controversies between us would certainly be settled more easily." John Reynolds produced this testimony from Eusebius and the other historians, Can. lib. 11, c. 6: "Apart from the sacred authors, no historian can be certain, or suitable for producing certain faith in theology," which he says is so evident and obvious in itself that it needs no confirmation by proofs. He cites only the saying of Flavius Vopiscus in the life of Aurelian, a true and witty remark: that when he set out to write history, he would do so more quietly, because he would have liars as companions, since he knew no historian who had not lied in something. "But if this (says Reynolds) has happened to all historians, except those who wrote the Scriptures, who wrote through the Spirit of God and not of man, then Eusebius too, although a good historian, could have been subject to the same fault." Henry Parry, bishop of Gloucester, approves these things in his translation of Reynolds. Onuphrius of Padua, treating of Peter's coming to Rome, used a negative argument from the Acts of the Apostles. Baronius meets this thus: The argument, he says, is peculiar to the Innovators, who hold as a rule that they deny whatever is not expressed in the Scriptures. But Luke omitted many things, etc. Why these things, you ask? Namely, so that it may be understood that the common opinion of the Protestants is this: that complete history is contained in the sacred books, so that it is not necessary to believe what is not handed down in them. Causaubon therefore wrongly, and contrary to the common opinion of the others, when Peronius demanded that antiquity be extended down to the times of Martin, replied thus: "This demand will seem little fair to those of the reformed persuasion, who want the whole history of the primitive Church to be contained in the Acts of the Apostles, a divine but nonetheless single little book. Far from their opinion is the most equitable and wisest King, who in his monitory letter openly declared how highly he esteemed the Fathers even of the fourth or fifth century." Much worse is Downham, who thinks that Hegesippus, Clement and other ancient writers must be called in, so that the history of Luke might be continued where it left off. But if the book of Acts does not contain a complete history, it by no means follows that we should turn to the Fathers of the fourth or fifth century. Certainly, to reject this and pursue the uncertain narratives of the Fathers would be not only ridiculous but also impious. And I am indeed surprised that it did not occur to Downham that the Apostle John, who continued the story of St Luke, is a better authority than any of the Fathers, however genuine. Is not the Apocalypse a history? What then do the words of ch. 4 v. 1 mean: "Come up here, and I will show you what must happen hereafter"? Is that not also a complete history? What then does it mean in ch. 5 v. 1 that this book is said to be written within and on the back? Do these things not show that this same book was written fully and completely? Add that in ch. 10 v. 7 the history of this book reaches to the consummation of the mystery of God, as he announced to his servants the prophets. But perhaps the Apocalypse is too obscure to serve in place of history. Why then that so magnificent unsealing of the seals, which the pious celebrate with such praise, ch. 5 v. 8? Why the command, "Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near," ch. 22 v. 10? Why finally the promise: Blessed is he who reads, and blessed are they who hear the words of the prophecy of this book and keep those things which are written in it, for the time is near, ch. 1 v. 3? Therefore we have not only so great a sacred history, but in the sacred books a complete history; so that to turn to the Fathers for proof in matters of fact, in order to establish the faith in some controverted theological point, is a kind of sacrilege. Is this my opinion alone? Do not the more prudent hierarchical writers think exactly the same? Let us hear first Richard Field: Who does not plainly see, he says, that the Evangelists, in handing down to memory the history of the death and life of Christ, and St Luke in the Acts of the Apostles, narrating the churches instituted by the Apostles, and St John writing the revelation he saw, intended to hand down the complete summary of Christian doctrine and the full direction of faith, concerning the future state of things, to the consummation of the age. Next let us hear Adrian Saravia: Who, he says, the state of the Church was, and what method of governing the Church the Apostles handed down, no one can teach except from the sacred letters and the times of the Apostles. Lastly let us hear Matthew Sutcliffe, whom I set against John Whitgift. Whitgift contends that it is Anabaptistic to argue negatively from Scripture in matters of fact. But on the contrary, Sutcliffe, disputing against Peter's coming to Rome, argues thus: Our opinion is proved first, because it is nowhere proved from Scripture. Peter wrote nothing of it in his epistles, Paul nothing, and Luke, who diligently and accurately pursued the deeds of the Apostles, nothing either. Again: Bellarmine replies that an argument from authority is not valid when negative. First, an argument from the authority of Holy Scripture is valid in itself. What is not proved from Scripture is not a dogma of faith. Thus the Apostle argues, and thus the Fathers also argue, and this necessarily follows, because Scripture is the canon of faith, and nothing now must necessarily be believed outside the Scriptures. Thus it is concluded that, in matters of fact, no historians except sacred ones either make faith or bind us to faith.

units.la: CAP. XXIIII. Secundum nostrum Argumentum à frivolis & incredibi- libus Historicorum additamentis.
units.tr: CHAP. XXIV. Our second argument, from the trifling and incredible additions of the historians.

units.la: ARgumentum nostrum secundum, à frivolis illis & incredibilibus additamentis derivatur, quæ historiæ sacræ, historici ecclesiastici pueriliter adjecerunt. Narrant Clemens, Eusebius, Dorotheus, Cephaм à Paulo Antiochiæ reprehensum, non fuisse Petrum Apostolum, sed alium ejusdem nominis qui fuit unus de 70. discipulis: quod nonne quæso aperte falsum? Narrat Clemens ex prædecessorum suorum relatione antiqua, & Eusebius rem memoria dignum iudicat: quod Iacobi carnifex ab eodem mirabiliter conversus sit: quod numnam quæso verisimile? Apud Eusebium, Philippus Apostolus & Philippus Evangelista ab antiquis confusi, ac si unus essent. Iohannes verò Apostolus, & Iohannes Senior divisi sunt ac si duo essent: quod nonne quæso puerile? Sed quoniam infinitum esset reliqua absque methodo persequi: insistam Cæsaris Baronij vestigijs, ad quem etiam brevitatis causa remitto lectorem. Consulat igitur Annales illos, in quibus in unum congesta videat, quæ puriliter tradiderunt Patres, de vitæ continentia in Maria virgine p. 63. de summo pontificatu Zachariæ, p. 64. de illius inter porticum & altare occisione p. 66. de Christi natali p.64. de baptismi anno p. 65. & 68. de Magis & eorum Angelo p. 65. de arbore se coram Christo incurvante, dum fugeret in Ægiptum p.66. de infantia Christi p. 67. de Iohan. Baptif. spelunca, locustis, monachatu p. 67. 68. de tribus Marijs confusis in unam p. 610. de lapide quo Stephanus lapidatus est, p. 615. de loco ubi natus Paulus p.618. de fonte Siloæ ad preces Esaiæ erumpente p. 625. de nominibus 70. discipulorum p. 625. de Iohanne spoliato syndone pag. 626. de interitu Iudæ p. 626. de columna ad quam Christus flagillatus p. 627. de palma p. 627. de spinea corona p. 627. de Calvaria à cranio Adami ibi sepulto denominata p. 627. de Golgotha quasi medio terræ p. 627. de terra Golgothæ miracula edente, & cruce non diminuta p.627. de anno passionis p. 628. de Christo resurgente, primùm conspecto à Maria p. 628. de persecutione Iosephi Aramatheę, & miraculo fontis Emauntis, quod Christus in eo lavasset pedes p. 628. de impressis vestigijs Christi in monte Oliveti p. 631. de gestis Pauli & Teclæ, multisq; alijs, quæ me pigot (præsertim lassum & defatigatum) commemorare. Hij nempe patres sunt, quibus fidem non adhibere impudentia extrema Downamo videtur: quum in hujusmodi fabulosis, aut saltem incertissimis (de quibus & Episcopatus Hierarchicus est) censere eis adhibendam fidem esse, res sacrilegij est. Quod si verò in his finem denegari illis posse dixerit, in Hierarchia non item: præterquam quod propositio illius generalis est; Impudentiæ nempe & audaciæ esse, patribus
units.tr: Our second argument is drawn from those trifling and incredible additions which the ecclesiastical historians have childishly attached to sacred history. Clement, Eusebius and Dorotheus relate that Cephas, rebuked by Paul at Antioch, was not the apostle Peter but another man of the same name, one of the seventy disciples. Surely, I ask you, this is plainly false? Clement relates it from the ancient tradition of his predecessors, and Eusebius judges it worth recording that the executioner of James was wonderfully converted by him. Surely, I ask you, this is probable? In Eusebius, the apostle Philip and the evangelist Philip were confused by the ancients as if they were one man, while John the apostle and John the Elder were divided as if they were two. Surely, I ask you, this is childish? But since it would be endless to pursue the rest without method, I shall follow in the footsteps of Caesar Baronius, to whom I also refer the reader for the sake of brevity. Let him consult those Annals, in which he will see gathered together what the Fathers have childishly handed down: on the perpetual virginity of Mary, p. 63; on the high priesthood of Zechariah, p. 64; on his being killed between the porch and the altar, p. 66; on Christ's birth, p. 64; on the year of baptism, pp. 65 and 68; on the Magi and their angel, p. 65; on the tree bowing before Christ as he fled into Egypt, p. 66; on the infancy of Christ, p. 67; on John the Baptist's cave, his locusts and his monastic life, pp. 67–68; on three Marys confused into one, p. 610; on the stone with which Stephen was stoned, p. 615; on the place where Paul was born, p. 618; on the fountain of Siloam breaking forth at the prayer of Isaiah, p. 625; on the names of the seventy disciples, p. 625; on John being stripped of his linen cloth, p. 626; on the death of Judas, p. 626; on the column to which Christ was bound for scourging, p. 627; on the palm, p. 627; on the crown of thorns, p. 627; on Calvary being named from the skull of Adam buried there, p. 627; on Golgotha as the middle of the earth, p. 627; on the earth of Golgotha working miracles and the cross not being diminished, p. 627; on the year of the Passion, p. 628; on Christ's resurrection, first seen by Mary, p. 628; on the persecution of Joseph of Arimathea, and the miracle of the spring at Emmaus, in which Christ had washed his feet, p. 628; on the footprints of Christ impressed on the Mount of Olives, p. 631; on the deeds of Paul and Thecla, and many others, which it irks me (especially as I am tired and worn out) to recall. These are the Fathers whom, Downame thinks, it is the utmost shamelessness not to trust; yet to judge that credence must be given to such fabulous, or at least most uncertain, matters (on which the hierarchical episcopate also depends) is a sacrilege. But if he says that an end can be set to these matters, this cannot be done in the Hierarchy: besides, his proposition is a general one, namely that it is shamelessness and audacity to be wary of the Fathers.

units.la: Eusèb.lib. 1. c.13. — L.2.c.9. — Lib.4.c.35. magnum profectò eorum esse classem intelliges, qui absque delectu percepe-rant aniles fabulas. Ita Franciscus Guicciardinus in Paralipomenis: Sæpè profundis tenebris res antiquæ demersæ iacent: quod si de Sylvestri ætate verum, de qua loquitur, quanto magis de antiquissimæ Ecclesiæ ultimis primordiis? Quid Eusebius ipse? Res ipsa hæc iam in exordio expetit ut mihi ignoscatur. Confiteor nimirum maius esse viribus nostris, absolutumque et incomprehensibile quod polliceamur ac profitemur. Nam et primi nos argumentum hoc jam aggressi, velut desertam quandam et invisitatam viam ingredi conamur: ubi nusquam nobis nuda eorum hominum vestigia deprehendere licet, qui eandem hanc sint ante nos viam ingressi, nisi exiguas duntaxat occasiones. Prodeat in medium Ioh. Reynoldus, Eusebium omnium Historicorum principem agnoscit alibi & merito: quis enim non agnosceret: quum cum tamen allegasset & commendasset Ioh. Hartus: respondet [Eusebium (ut historici cæteri) erroris subiectum esse. Quod eò citius persuasum esse debet, quod Papa Gelasius in Concilio 70, Episcoporum, ejus historiam ut improbatam condemnarit, Dist. 15. c. 3. Hanc reprobationem tanquam justam comprobat Canus, & rationes profert: nempe propter narrationem Epistolæ Christi ad Agbarum lib. 1. cap. 14. & illius ex Clemente Alexandrino multarum rerum transcriptionem lib. 1. cap. 1. & sic deinceps passim, cum & illa fabula & huius opera à Concilio improbata sint.] Richardus Fyldus initia Ecclesiæ adeo obscura sentit, ut approbet Lindani illud: Quædam officia in Primitiva Ecclesia fuisse, quæ iam ignota sunt. Loquitur de aliis fateor: sed de officio Seniorum verissimè hoc dici potest: quod in Ecclesia prima notum, deinde in desuetudinem abijt, ac si nunquam extitisset. Qui vero propter desuetudinem Seniores agnoscere non potuerunt: potuerunt è contra propter invectam Episcoporum alienam consuetudinem, persuasum habere, eiusmodi munus quod suis seculis invaluerat, in in prima Ecclesia extitisse. Concludo ex canone Toletano. Longinquitate sæpe fit temporis, ut non pateat conditio originis.
units.tr: You will understand that they form a great company, those who without discrimination have accepted old wives' tales. Thus Francesco Guicciardini in the Paralipomena: "Ancient things often lie sunk in deep darkness; if this is true of the age of Sylvester, of which he speaks, how much more true is it of the final beginnings of the most ancient Church?" What of Eusebius himself? This very matter, at the outset, asks that I be pardoned. I confess indeed that what we promise and profess is beyond our powers, and is absolute and incomprehensible. For we who have first undertaken this argument are attempting to enter a deserted and unvisited road, where we can find hardly any bare footprints of those men who entered this way before us, except a few slight traces. Let John Reynolds come forward. He elsewhere acknowledges Eusebius as the prince of all historians, and rightly, for who would not? Yet when John Hart had cited and commended him, Reynolds replies that Eusebius, like the other historians, is subject to error. This ought to be all the more readily believed because Pope Gelasius, in a council of seventy bishops, condemned his history as disapproved (Dist. 15, c. 3). Canus approves this rejection as just and offers reasons: namely, the account of Christ's letter to Abgar (book 1, ch. 14), and his transcription of many matters from Clement of Alexandria (book 1, ch. 1), and so on throughout, since both that fable and this work have been disapproved by the Council.] Richard Field holds the beginnings of the Church to be so obscure that he approves Lindanus's saying that some offices existed in the primitive Church which are now unknown. He speaks of others, I admit; but of the office of elders this can be said most truly: it was known in the first Church, then fell into disuse, as if it had never existed. Yet those who could not recognise the elders because of their disuse could, on the contrary, because of the foreign custom of the bishops that had been introduced, be persuaded that an office of this kind, which had prevailed in their own times, had existed in the first Church. I conclude with the canon of Toledo: "Through the length of time it often happens that the origin of a thing is not evident."

units.la: CAP. XXVII. Argumentum nostrum quintum, ab exili principio narrationum historicarum.
units.tr: CHAP. XXVII. Our fifth argument, from the slight beginnings of historical narratives.

units.la: QVod ita describit Tertullianus: Veritati nemo præscribere potest, non spatiū temporū, non patrocinia personarum, non privilegium nationum. Ex his enimferè consuetudo initium, ab aliqua ignorantia aut simplicitate sortita, in usum per successionem corroboratur; & ità adversus veritatem vindicatur. Multus est Downamus in exaggeranda Reformatorum impudentia, qui unanimi Historicorum consensui, fidem negari posse credunt. Cur non stomachatur in Tertullianum etiam? qui hujusmodi consensum veritati præscribere non posse putat; rat: Præsertim cum exordium ab ignorantia & simplicitate sortitæ consuetudines multæ, per usum successione corroboratum, unanimem consensum ipsum adeptæ sint. Ex hac Hypothesi disputamus adversus Downamum, verbis Sutclivij Hierarchici, qui ita Downamo gregali suo contradicit.
units.tr: So Tertullian describes it: "No one can prescribe against the truth: not the length of time, not the patronage of persons, not the privilege of nations. For custom, which generally takes its beginning from some ignorance or simplicity, is strengthened over time by use and succession, and so defends itself against the truth." Downame is very vehement in inveighing against the impudence of the Reformers, who believe that faith cannot be denied to the unanimous consensus of the historians. Why does he not rage against Tertullian too, who thinks that such a consensus cannot be prescribed against the truth? Especially since many customs, which took their start from ignorance and simplicity, and were strengthened by use through succession, have even obtained a unanimous consensus. On this hypothesis we dispute against Downame, in the words of Sutcliffe the hierarchist, who thus contradicts Downame, his like-minded colleague.

units.la: 1. Author huius narrationis de certamine Petri cum Simone Mago fuit Clemens nescio quis: Nec obstat quod hanc eandem narrationem postea aliquot authores fide digni habent: omnes enim ab uno fonte acceperunt: & solent nonnunquam fabulosa, apud bonos alioqui authores reperiri.
units.tr: 1. The author of this narrative about Peter's contest with Simon Magus was a certain Clement, I know not who. Nor is it an objection that several authors worthy of belief later report this same narrative; for they all took it from one source, and fabulous things are sometimes found even in otherwise good authors.

units.la: 2 Probat Hartus, monachos Apostolorum temporibus fuisse, quia Philo Iudæus de monachis scripsit, ut narrat Eusebius, l. 2. 17. Respondet Reynoldus non de monachis Christianis, sed de Essenis monachis Iudæis scripsisse Philonem: Eusebium vero hallucinatum fuisse quem Epiphanius, Hieronymus, Cassianus, aliique patres sequuti, in præcipitium acti sunt. Cur non exclamat Downamus in nostrorum impudentiam, quod unanimi patrum consensui, in materia facti, quod ad monachos, refragentur? Vide etenim quam omnia conveniant. Testatur unaminis consensus Historicorum, Episcopos Hierarchicos Apostolorum temporibus fuisse. Sic Downamus: Testatur Eusebius, & reliqui assentiuntur, monachos Apostolorum Temporibus fuisse, sub Caio imperatore, eo etenim tempore Philo vixit, qui de monachis Christianis scripsit: Sic Hartus: Ecqua in istis ratiocinijs differentia? Sed & productum quiddam de Hieronymo, hic minimè præterendum est. Notum est quàm tumidis buccis venditetur ab Hierarchicis locus ille Hieronymi, de Episcopis à Marco Alexandriæ electis, &c. Respondeti a nostris assolet, a Marco, exclusiuè intelligendum, quod a Bancrofto deridetur immeritò. Sed quid si inclusive intelligatur Hieronymus, sic ut sub Marco Episcopos floruisse putet? Nec etenim magis Hierarchicos hoc juvaret, atque Hartum adjuvit, quòd ex Philone & Eusebio, Monachos sub Marco (id enim verbis distinctis asserit) Alexandriæ floruisse dixerit. Qui monachos falso asseruit sub Marco Alexandriæ fuisse, nonne etiam Episcopos sub Marco fuisse Alexandriæ, opinari potuit falso? Certè vel hæc una secunda instantia aperte evincit: argumentum nullum duci posse ab unanimi Historicorum consensu in materia facti, quando de seculis antecedentibus, nominatim vero Apostolicis temporibus testificatur.
units.tr: 2. Hartus proves that monks existed in the times of the Apostles, because Philo the Jew wrote about monks, as Eusebius relates in book 2, chapter 17. Reynolds replies that Philo wrote not about Christian monks but about the Essene monks, who were Jews, and that Eusebius was mistaken, and that Epiphanius, Jerome, Cassian and the other Fathers who followed him were led headlong into error. Why does Downame not cry out at the impudence of our people, who resist the unanimous consensus of the Fathers on a matter of fact, concerning monks? For see how well everything agrees. The unanimous consensus of the historians testifies that hierarchical bishops existed in the times of the Apostles. Thus Downame: Eusebius testifies, and the rest agree, that monks existed in the times of the Apostles, under the emperor Caius; for at that time Philo lived, who wrote about Christian monks. Thus Hartus. Is there any difference in these arguments? But something produced from Jerome must by no means be passed over here. It is well known with what puffed-up cheeks the hierarchists boast of that passage of Jerome about bishops elected by Mark at Alexandria, and so on. Our people usually reply that "from Mark" must be understood exclusively, a reply which Bancroft undeservedly mocks. But what if Jerome is understood inclusively, so that he thinks bishops flourished under Mark? This would help the hierarchists no more than it helped Hartus, who, from Philo and Eusebius, said that monks flourished at Alexandria under Mark (for he asserts this in plain words). Whoever wrongly asserted that monks existed at Alexandria under Mark, could he not also wrongly suppose that bishops existed at Alexandria under Mark? Certainly this second instance clearly proves that no argument can be drawn from the unanimous consensus of historians on a matter of fact, when they testify about earlier centuries, and especially about the Apostolic times.

units.la: 3 Iustantia nostra tertia, de Petri Episcopatu erit: consentiunt etenim Patres omnes ne uno quidem contradicente, Petrum Apostolorum Romanæ Ecclesiæ fuisse Episcopum, De hoc ita Downamus: Petrum Romæ Episcopum fuisse, ne ipse refutator credit. Idipsum ni fallor (his etenim verbis insinuatur) & Downamus ipse credit: quo igitur evanuerunt soliti clamores illi de impudentia, audacia, novitate, superbia, quando patribus consentientibus in materia facti non adhibetur fides?
units.tr: 3. Our third instance concerns Peter's episcopate. For all the Fathers agree, without a single dissenter, that Peter was the Apostle and bishop of the Roman Church. On this Downame says: That Peter was bishop of Rome, not even the refuter himself believes. I think (for this is insinuated in these words) that Downame himself believes it too. Why then have those familiar outcries about impudence, audacity, novelty and pride vanished, when, with the Fathers agreeing on a matter of fact, no faith is given to them?

units.la: 4 Instantia tius teneatur cujus antiquior & prior extat authoritas. Iugulat hoc inquies Synodos vestras reformatas, de mutata disciplina. Nequaquam vero: cum seculis medijs de quibus loquitur Isidorus, hec nostra tempora longe precellant, ut supra demonstratum est: & Synodos antiquissimas quarum ille authoritatem praefert, adversus nostram disciplinam facere, probari non possit.
units.tr: 4. Instance: "That is to be held which has the older and prior authority." You will say that this overthrows your reformed synods and their changed discipline. By no means: for the middle ages, of which Isidore speaks, far surpass these our times, as was shown above; and it cannot be proved that the most ancient synods, whose authority he prefers, act against our discipline.

units.la: 3 Quartò, Pudet me inquit Hadrianus Saravia, quum antiqua Concilia, Canones antiqui, à Calvino & Bezâ in re disciplinaria rupti & violati sint. Quos tu Canones antiquos memoras? Scripsit Iohannes Lydius Francofurtensis in librum Prateoli de Conciliis: is Pag.10. ita habet. Extat Tomo secundo conciliorum, Anonimi cujusdam qui vixit anno 1198. scriptum quoddam, quod appellatur Opusculum Tripartitum: ubi inveni sententiam memorabilem, quam hic adscribam: Concilia antiqua (inquit) & etiam posteriora vix inveniuntur. cap. 10. Verum hoc imprimis de conciliis primis, quę ante Nicenum celebrata sunt: quae si extarent, major fortasse de Conciliis antiquissimis ruptis, conquerendi occasio penes reformatos esset, quàm è contrà. Sed extant nonnulla inquies: At de horum Canonibus conqueri non datur, cum de Episcopali superioritate, canones nullos ediderunt. Liceat igitur Guilielmi Whitakeri illa reponere: [Quo quoque concilium antiquius eò sanctius & sincerius fuit, ut aqua quò propior fonti eò purior & dulcior. Paulatim irrepserunt pravae opiniones. Ante Constantinum Magnum, provincialia tantum quaedam concilia habemus, in quibus nihil de primatu Romani Pontificis sancitum est (sic nec de majoritate Episcopali.) At ego pluris ejusmodi unum concilium facio, quàm quodvis eorum, quae postea secuta sunt. Nam saeviente persecutione, Episcopi de Ecclesia & religione magis soliciti erant, eâ verò sublata mox ambitio invasit ecclesiam.] Hinc illa quaerela Nazianzeni: [Equidem ut verè quod res est scribam, prorsus decrevi fugere omnem Conventum Episcoporum. Nullius enim Concilij bonum exitum unquam vidi. Concilia enim non minuunt mala sed augent potius.] Male tractatur hoc nomine à Bibliorum interpretibus nostris Nazianzenus: qui in omnium Conciliorum derogationem, haec illius redundare putare videntur. Atque recte adfert ista Bilsonus, adversus omnium cujusque aetatis Conciliorum infallibilitatem, idque ratione addita, quia major pars saepe melior rem vincit. Eadem & Ioh. Iuellus habet adversus Hardingum: & Ioh.Whitus Hierarchicus. Thomas Bilsonus alibi, & Richardus Fyldus, ad turbulenta tempora sua haec verba Nazianzeni restringunt: qui tamen de hoc tempore, haud minus quam reliqui cum justificant. De illis suis temporibus porrò adjicit Whitus ex Vincentio Lyrinensi adversl.profan.novitat.cap.4. Ecclesiam saeva contagione commaculatam esse. Quid igitur est? Concilia ante Nicaenum pro se adferre Hierarchici nequeunt: quae vero ex Concilijs Nicaenum subsequentibus adferri solent testimonia, nullius momenti & ponderis sunt. Insistunt vero in his Concilijs quarti & quinti seculi præcipuè Hierarchici: cuius quidem prævaricationis,modestos puduisse oportuit. Quale etenim quæso hoc argumentum est? Concilia quædam quæ post invalescentem Episcoporum ambitionem, post corruptam disciplinam,post contentiones invectas, ad concilij cuiusque exitum bonum impediendum,maioritatem Episcopalem approbant, ergo ea sancta & legitima est?
units.tr: 3. Fourthly, "I am ashamed," says Adrian Saravia, "that the ancient councils and ancient canons have been broken and violated by Calvin and Beza in matters of discipline." Which ancient canons do you mean? John Lydius of Frankfurt wrote on Prateolus' book on the councils, and at page 10 he has this: In the second volume of the councils there is a certain writing of an anonymous author who lived in the year 1198, called the Opusculum Tripartitum; there I found a memorable opinion, which I shall set down here: "Ancient councils" (he says) "and even later ones are scarcely to be found." Chapter 10. But this is said chiefly of the first councils, celebrated before Nicaea; if these were extant, there would perhaps be a greater occasion for the reformed to complain of the most ancient councils being broken than the contrary. But some are extant, you will say; yet there is no ground for complaint about their canons, since they issued no canons on episcopal superiority. Let me then set down those words of William Whitaker: [The earlier a council was, the holier and purer it was, as water is purer and sweeter the nearer it is to its spring. Bad opinions crept in gradually. Before Constantine the Great we have only certain provincial councils, in which nothing was enacted about the primacy of the Roman Pontiff (nor, likewise, about episcopal majority). But I value any one of these councils more than any of those that followed later. For while persecution raged, bishops were more anxious about the Church and religion; but once it was removed, ambition soon invaded the Church.] Hence that complaint of Nazianzen: [To write what is truly the case, I have firmly resolved to flee every assembly of bishops. For I never saw a good outcome from any council. Councils do not diminish evils but rather increase them.] Our interpreters of the Bible treat Nazianzen badly in this matter, for they seem to think that these words reflect on all councils. Bilson rightly adduces these things against the infallibility of councils of every age, adding this reason: because the greater part often overcomes the better. John Jewel has the same against Harding, and John White the hierarchist. Thomas Bilson elsewhere, and Richard Field, restrict the words of Nazianzen to their own turbulent times; yet they justify them for this time no less than the others. Moreover, about their own times White adds, from Vincent of Lerins, Against Profane Novelties chapter 4, that the Church was stained by a cruel contagion. What then is the case? The hierarchists cannot bring forward the councils before Nicaea in their favour, and the testimonies usually adduced from the councils following Nicaea are of no weight or importance. But the hierarchists insist chiefly on the councils of the fourth and fifth centuries; surely modesty should have made them ashamed of such prevarication. For what sort of argument, I ask, is this? Certain councils, which approve episcopal majority after the ambition of bishops had grown strong, after discipline was corrupted, and after contentions were introduced, which impeded the good outcome of every council; therefore that council is holy and lawful?

units.la: 4 Sed de ipso Niceno Concilio hæc accipere, absurdum & ridiculum Bancrofto videtur: à quo, quid non audit Tho. Cartwrightus; cum ab eo exemplar politeias ecclesiasticæ tutò peti posse dissimiliter. Durum tamen inquit quod ibidem in Beza sugillat, Niceænum concilium,sedem meretricis qua super montes septem sedet,præparasse. Atqui ex canone huius concilij sexto hoc liquido constat, quo Romanus Episcopus Patriarcha constituitur, quæ illius prærogativa labem primam dedit: quum referente Ænea Sylvio, parvus aute respectus ad Romanum Ecclesiam habebatur. Quo minorem rationem habuit Bancroftus, concilium Niceænum magnificè prædicare, Collatio em vero Genevensem (ita enim appellat) in qua disciplina primo reformata fuit, præ eo contemnere: in concione etiam sua ad crucem Paulinam nobis monstri loco obijcere, quod regnum Christi hoc in concilio labefactatum sententiamus, in quo divina illius maiestas tam sincerè stabiliebatur.
units.tr: 4. But to take these things about the Nicene Council itself seems absurd and ridiculous to Bancroft, by whom Thomas Cartwright is scarcely spared; yet from Cartwright a copy of the ecclesiastical polity may safely be sought, in a different sense. "Hard, however," he says, "is what Beza there also finds fault with, that the Nicene council prepared the seat of the harlot who sits on the seven hills." And yet from the sixth canon of this council it is clearly established that the Roman bishop is constituted patriarch, and that this prerogative first gave the blemish; since, as Aeneas Sylvius reports, little regard was had for the Roman Church. How much less regard Bancroft had, in magnificently extolling the Nicene council, while despising the Geneva conference (for so he calls it), in which discipline was first reformed, in comparison with it; and in his sermon at Paul's Cross throwing it at us as a monstrous thing that we judge the kingdom of Christ to have been shaken in this council, in which that divine majesty was so sincerely established.

units.la: Primò, concilium Hierofolymitanum Niceno præponendum dicimus. Præsertim cum ab eo concilio alia (ut rectè Whitakerus) formam suam sumere debeant: id quod Mortonus Hierarchicus vel ipso Bellarmino probat. Sequitur vero Synodum Hierosolymitanum concilium Niceunum? illius morem imitatur? Qui id fieri potest? cum morem antiquum in stabilienda Hierarchia secuta fit Nicæna synodus: in concilio vero Hierofolymitano mori nihil datum fit (sicut nihil e nomine dandum) sed ex scripturis ejsque solis sancitum fit. Probat hoc vel ex ipsis papistarum scriptoribus Thomas Mortonus ipse scriptor Hierarchicus. Act. 15. 15. Huic disto Petri confirmant verba Thoph. tarum sicut scriptum &c. Colligunt ex his verbis Cajetanus, Montanus, Canus, Ferus, non ausos fuisse ipsos Apostolos quicquam à se definire, sed ex variis scripturarum locis caspurationem primum instituisse, & ad postremum iuxta allegata carum cum testimonia rem totam definivisse. At nihil hujusmodi à Niceno concilio, in Hierarchia stabilienda observatum. mos humanus, non lex divina consessui huic se testante cynosurae loco fuit: non dicunt scripturae obtineant, sed ἐν ἀρχῇ.
units.tr: First, we say that the Council of Jerusalem must be placed before the Nicene. This is especially so since other councils, as Whitaker rightly says, ought to take their form from that council, a point Morton the Hierarchist proves even from Bellarmine himself. But does it follow that the Synod of Jerusalem imitates the Nicene council's custom? How could it? The Nicene synod followed an ancient custom in establishing the hierarchy, whereas at the Council of Jerusalem nothing was granted on the basis of custom (just as nothing is to be granted on the basis of a name), but everything was sanctioned from Scripture and from Scripture alone. Thomas Morton, the Hierarchist writer himself, proves this from the papist writers themselves. Acts 15.15: To this agree the words of the prophets, as it is written, and so on. From these words Cajetan, Montanus, Canus and Ferus infer that the apostles themselves did not dare to define anything on their own authority, but first instituted an inquiry from various places of Scripture and at last settled the whole matter according to the testimonies of Scripture alleged. But nothing of this kind was observed at the Nicene council in establishing the hierarchy. Human custom, not divine law, was the guiding star of that assembly, as it testifies of itself: they do not say "let the custom prevail" but "from the beginning" [ἐν ἀρχῇ].

units.la: § Secundò, quod pro Hierarchia adfert Bancroftus ex concilio Niceno: id ab ipsa scriptura quasi nominatim condemnatur. Quanquam etenim respectu corum quæ adversus hæresim Arianam secerunt, illius fumus instar suffitus ascendisse dicitur Ap. 8. 4. respectu tamen Hierarchiæ minimè leviter accusatur, quòd montem arden-
units.tr: Secondly, as to what Bancroft brings forward from the Nicene council in favour of the hierarchy, this is condemned by Scripture itself, almost by name. For although, with respect to what it did against the Arian heresy, its smoke is said to have ascended like the smoke of incense (Rev. 8.4), with respect to the hierarchy it is accused by no light charge, namely that it has cast a burning mountain

units.la: Ap. 8. 4. tem igni projecerit in Ecclesiam, Ap. 8. 8. & bestia cum ex mari id est corrupta doctrina ac disciplina ascendisse dicitur Ap. 12.1. id in relatione dicitur ad corruptas Nicæni concilij de disciplina sanctiones: nam quòd tum primo in fundamento suo bestia conspicua facta sit, supra demonstratum est. Quid quod tubæ Apoc. 8.6. in ipso Nicæno concilio clanxisse dicantur, vel saltem Angeli se præparasse ad clangendum quia ipsa tum mala, initio conspicua, & in eo quasi tubâ promulgata sunt?
units.tr: (Rev. 8.4) into the Church (Rev. 8.8), and that the beast has risen out of the sea, that is, out of corrupt doctrine and discipline (Rev. 12.1). This is said in reference to the corrupt decrees on discipline of the Nicene council; for that the beast first became visible in its foundation has been demonstrated above. What of the fact that the trumpets (Rev. 8.6) are said to have sounded at the Nicene council itself, or at least that the angels prepared themselves to sound, because those evils were then first made visible and, as it were, proclaimed by that council as by a trumpet?

units.la: Tertiò, prunæ ardentes ex altari concilij Niceni in terram conjectæ fuisse dicuntur Ap. 8. 5. propterea quod turbas multas hoc concilium dederit in hominibus terrestribus, sic ut malum remedio creverit. At sic & ipsæ inquies scripturæ sacræ, ut nunc dierum Evangelium, per abusum hominum terrestrium turbas multas dare solet, absq; ullo peccato suo. At dispar est ratio: Concilium etenim Nicænum contentiosos Episcopos, facultate potentiaq; armavit ad nocendum: & per majoritatem quam eis concessit, eorum animus superbire, imò & ebullire cæpit, ad Ecclesiam perturbandam. Verum igitur & in Nicæno concilio est quod Nazianzenus de reliquis ejusdem seculi, dixit, nullum nempe eorum fœlicem exitum se vidisse, ut discant mortales fidem suam in scriptură solâ fundare, nullam autem hominnum quamvis sanctorum congregatam multitudinem supra modum venerari.
units.tr: Thirdly, burning coals are said to have been cast from the altar of the Nicene council onto the earth (Rev. 8.5), because this council gave rise to many disturbances among earthly men, so that the remedy became the cause of greater evil. But, you will say, Holy Scripture itself does the same: as now in our day the Gospel is wont, through the abuse of earthly men, to give rise to many disturbances, without any fault of its own. But the case is different. The Nicene council armed contentious bishops with power and authority to do harm, and through the superiority it granted them their minds began to swell with pride, indeed to boil over, to the disturbance of the Church. Thus there is also at the Nicene council what Gregory of Nazianzus said of the rest of that same century: that he had seen none of them come to a happy end, so that mortals may learn to found their faith on Scripture alone, and never to venerate any multitude of men, however holy, beyond measure.

units.la: 6 Quartò, cur adeo mirum Bancrofto videtur, Nicænum concilium errare potuisse in suo Hierarchico canone? Quia piè statuit scilicet, de divina natura Christi contra Arianos. Quasi adeo rarum sit ut bene de quibusdam sentientes homines, in alijs tamen errent? Non ego canonem quem adversus Miletium habet, urgebo: licet eum nostri contra pontificios urgere passim soleant: solis eis instantijs contentus ero, quæ apud ipsos Hierarchicos reperiuntur. Citat enim Io. Whitgiftus Ambrosium, lib. 10. epist. 82. quod in concilio Necæno contra Bigamiam clericorum sancitum sit: & Hieronymum, quod idem librum Iudith inter sacras scripturas, commemoravit. Hæc si sunt vera, erroribus alijs, præterquam Hirarchicis laboravit hoc concilium: de quo insuper non est alienum à proposito considerare, quod habet Socrates: Visum erat Episcopis legem novam in Ecclesiam introducere, ut qui essent sacris initiati (sicut Episcopi, Presbyteri, & Diaconi) cum uxoribus, quas, cum erant laici in matrimonium duxissent, minimè dormirent. Restitum quidem huic decreto est à Paphnutio, sed à Paphnutio solo: & quanquam uxores non ademptæ, quibus dum erant laici nupserant: in hoc tamen aqua hæsit, ut post sacram initiationem uxores ducere pro hiberentur. His perpensis, quomodo quæso absque periculo, fides concilio tam prono ad errorem niti potest?
units.tr: Fourthly, why does it seem so strange to Bancroft that the Nicene council could err in its hierarchical canon? Because, forsooth, it rightly decided concerning the divine nature of Christ against the Arians. As if it were so rare for men who think rightly about some matters to err in others! I will not press the canon it has against Meletius, although our people commonly press it against the papists; I will be content with the arguments found among the hierarchists themselves. John Whitgift cites Ambrose, Epistle 82 of Book 10, that at the Nicene council it was decreed against the bigamy of clerics; and Jerome, who mentions that the same council counted the book of Judith among the sacred Scriptures. If these things are true, this council laboured under errors other than hierarchical ones. Moreover, it is not out of place to consider what Socrates reports: It seemed good to the bishops to introduce a new law into the Church, that those who were initiated into the sacred offices (namely bishops, presbyters and deacons) should not sleep with the wives whom they had married while they were laymen. This decree was indeed resisted by Paphnutius, but by Paphnutius alone; and although the wives to whom they had been married while laymen were not taken away, yet on this point the matter stuck, that after sacred initiation they were forbidden to take wives. With these things weighed, I ask, how without danger can faith be placed in a council so prone to error?

units.la: Quintò, concilium Nicænum pro Hierarchia Anglicana nihil fecit: ascribitur etenim can. 9. Hierarchia mori antiquo: at Hierarchia Anglicana divino jure se tuetur. Sanare hoc vulnus videtur Downamus ex eo,quòd concilium Nicænum in his verbis mos antiquus obtineat, de Patriarchis tantummodo loquatur, quos in hoc canone d icit jure humano & positivo introductos. At contrà Lous. Synodus Nicæna Metropolitanos (nō Patriarchas modo) antiquissimos dicit.Contra Thomas Bilsonus. Primatus Meteopolitani ex consuetudine erat, ut testatur concilium Nicaenum. Contra denique Iohannes Whitgiftus, qui fusè disputat & metropolitanum & patriarcham ab initio eosdem, & metropolitanum non patriarcham modo in Concilio Nicæno stabilitum,id quod probat productis in medium testimonijs variis, nempè ex Iohanne Calvino, Flaccio Illyrico, Iohanne Foxo, & Francisco Villiero.
units.tr: Fifthly, the Nicene council did nothing for the Anglican hierarchy. For it is ascribed (canon 9) to the hierarchy of the ancient custom, whereas the Anglican hierarchy defends itself by divine right. Downame seems to heal this wound by arguing that the Nicene council, in the words let the ancient custom prevail, speaks only of patriarchs, whom it says were introduced by human and positive law in this canon. On the contrary, Lou[s?] says: The Nicene Synod calls metropolitans (not patriarchs only) most ancient. Against this, Thomas Bilson: The primacy of the metropolitan was by custom, as the Nicene council attests. Finally, against both, John Whitgift, who at length disputes that metropolitan and patriarch alike were established from the beginning, and that the metropolitan, and not the patriarch only, was established at the Nicene council; he proves this by bringing forward various testimonies, namely from John Calvin, Flacius Illyricus, John Foxe and Francis Vallier.

units.la: 7 Sextò, nudam concilij Nicæni authoritatem nemimem adstringere, apud omnes nostrates Guilielmum Whitakerum, Ioh. Reynoldum, Tho.Bilsonum, Tho.Mortonum, Ioh.Iuellum cæterosque adversus papistas & Iesuitas exploratissimum dogma est. Probant ex Augustino. Nec ego Nicaenum, nec tu debes Ariminense, tanquam praejudicaturus proferre concilium. Nec ego huius authoritate, nec tu illius detineris. Scripturarum authoritatibus,utriusque communibus testibus,res cum re,causa cum causa,ratio cum ratione concertet, Quod de praejudicio dicit,habetur & apud Ambrosium etiam qui ne fidem quidem Nicænam urgendam putavit contra Arianos: nè videatur perversitas,non examinata,sed prejudicata damnari.
units.tr: Sixthly, that the bare authority of the Nicene council binds no one is the most well-established doctrine among all our people: William Whitaker, John Reynolds, Thomas Bilson, Thomas Morton, John Jewel and the others most skilled against the papists and Jesuits. They prove it from Augustine: Neither I am bound to bring forward the Nicene council, nor you the council of Rimini, as if to prejudge the case. Neither am I held by its authority, nor you by its. Let the matter contend with the matter, the cause with the cause, the reason with the reason, by the authority of the Scriptures, the common witnesses of both sides. What he says about prejudging is also found in Ambrose, who thought that even the Nicene faith ought not to be urged against the Arians, lest it seem that a case was condemned unexamined and prejudged.

units.la: Septimò & ultimò, considerandum prudenti lectori est,annon verisimilia sint, quæ Iohannes Lydius Francofurtensis,de Nicænorum canonum (qui jam extant) incertitudine in medium profert. Canonum numerus incertus apud authores est: & mirum est exemplaria huius concilij, inter se tantum differre,ut nesciant cui sit fidendum. Dicit opusculum tripartitum c. 10. Antiqua concilia, & etiam posteriora, non inveniuntur.--Acta huius Synodi etsi hodie graecè extent, tamen accuratissimè scripta, iniuria temporis, & Arianorum conatibus, cum Baronio, periisse credo. Nam hæc quæ habemus nimis frigida sunt: nec sapiunt Athanasium, Hosium, Paphnutium, aliosque qui con illo interfuere. Hæc de fundamento Hierarchico septimo,nempe Conciliorum authoritate.
units.tr: Seventhly and lastly, the prudent reader should consider whether those things are not probable which John Lydius of Frankfurt brings forward concerning the uncertainty of the Nicene canons (which now exist). The number of the canons is uncertain among authors, and it is remarkable that the copies of this council differ so much among themselves that one does not know which to trust. The little work in three parts, chapter 10, says that the ancient councils, and even the later ones, are not found. The acts of this synod, although they survive in Greek today, were, I believe with Baronius, written most accurately but perished through the injury of time and the efforts of the Arians. For what we have is far too cold; it does not savour of Athanasius, Hosius, Paphnutius and the others who were present with him. These are the points concerning the seventh foundation of the hierarchy, namely the authority of the councils.

units.la: CAP. XX. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX. II.

units.la: Octavum Hierarchicum fundamentum nempe fides historiae ecclesiasticae tollitur.
units.tr: The eighth Hierarchical foundation, namely the trustworthiness of ecclesiastical history, is overthrown.

units.la: Sequitur octavum, similiter papisticum, nempe fides historiae ecclesiasticae: idem etenim sentiunt Hierarchici cum Cano: cujus haec positio est. Illud pro certo accipiendum, quod omnium gravium & probatorum historicorum testimonio confirmatur. Richardus Feildus ita. Clarum est ex testimonijs antiquitatis, Petrum, Iacobum maiorem,& Iohannem, Iacobum Episcopum Hierosolymitarum ordinasse. Sic Anacletus tus Epistolæ secunda si quæ ei fides adhibenda sit: sic Clemens Alexandrinus apud Eusebium, sic Hieronymus de viris illustribus. Hic ego cujusque æqui in ipso initio conscientiam appello. Fabulâ istâ nihil ineptius fingi potest: vt ipsa clamat, & suo loco demonstrabitur. Non est igitur quod Hierarchicorum vociferationibus commoveamur cum rem claram esse clamant, ex historicorum veterum consensu, Episcopos Hierarchicos in prima Ecclesia extitisse: cum eorum moderatissimo, ex eisdem clarum sit etiam Iacobum Apostolum Episcopum fuisse, idque ex ordinatione novâ: quo nihil potest dici salsius. Sed audiatur omnium vehementissimus Georgius Downamus.
units.tr: The eighth foundation follows, likewise Papist: namely, the trustworthiness of ecclesiastical history. The Hierarchists agree here with Cano, whose position is this: "That must be accepted as certain which is confirmed by the testimony of all grave and approved historians." Richard Field says: "It is clear from the testimonies of antiquity that Peter, James the Greater, and John ordained James, Bishop of Jerusalem. So Anacletus in his second Epistle, if that writing deserves any credit; so Clement of Alexandria in Eusebius; so Jerome in De viris illustribus." Here I appeal to the conscience of every fair-minded reader at the very outset. No more absurd fable can be invented; as it cries out for itself, and will be shown in its proper place. There is therefore no reason for us to be moved by the clamours of the Hierarchists when they shout that it is plain, from the agreement of the ancient historians, that Hierarchical bishops existed in the primitive Church. Even by the more moderate of them, it is plain from the same sources that the Apostle James was also a bishop, and that on the basis of a new ordination; nothing can be said more foolish than this. But let us hear the most vehement of them all, George Downame.

units.la: [ Quæstio est (inquit) de materia facti, in qua fides patribus denegANDA non est. Nonne vna animi consensu testatur omnis antiquitas, episcopos primitivæ ecclesiæ, reliquis ministris gradu superiores fuisse, & ecquis nostrum eum frontem gerit, ut id denegare audeat?] Rursus [Communi consensu antiquissimorum & probatissimorum scriptorum probatur Titum & Timotheum episcopos fuisse: quorum refutatoris negatio si æqua lance ponderetur, næ ipsa vanitate vanior reperietur] Iterum [Neminem nisi episcopum ordinare potuisse, generalis omnium patrum consensus est: quorum vel unius authoritas, in materia facti, totam disciplinariorum rationem deprimere debet] Postremo [Acta Apostolorum quæ post Lucæ historiam perpetrata sunt, memoriæ prodita sunt partim ab Hegesippo & Clemente, & aliis antiquis authoribus, qui testantur Paulum, Timotheum Ephesi, Titum Cretæ Episcopos ordinasse, & quod ipse aliique Apostoli episcopos alios locis aliis instituerint. Quorum testimonia quicunque fidem adhibere abnuit: ipse fidem nullam meretur.] Videre hinc est, quænam præcipua Hierarchicorum anchora sit: & quo argumento claram suam sententiam esse comprobare soleant: ex irrefragabili nempè antiquorum scriptorum in materia facti authoritate. Hanc cum perinde urgeant papistæ in quæstione de Petri ad Romam adventu: perinde etiam illis respondere habemus, quod his respondet Guilm. Whitakerus. [Quod aliqui impudentiæ nos accusant, quòd rem tam certam & claram in quæstionem vocemus: ego non modo nihil clarum & certum video, sed omnia potius dubia & obscura.]
units.tr: [The question (he says) concerns a matter of fact, in which the Fathers are not to be denied credit.
