Does not all antiquity bear witness with one mind that the bishops of the primitive Church were superior in rank to the other ministers, and which of us bears so brazen a forehead as to dare to deny it?] Again: [By the common consent of the most ancient and most approved writers, it is proved that Titus and Timothy were bishops; and if the denial of the refuter were weighed in an even balance, it would be found more vain than vanity itself.] Again: [That no one but a bishop could ordain is the general consensus of all the Fathers; and the authority of even one of them, in a matter of fact, ought to overthrow the whole argument of the disciplinarians.] Finally: [The acts of the Apostles which were done after the history of Luke have been handed down to memory partly by Hegesippus and Clement, and other ancient authors, who testify that Paul ordained Timothy at Ephesus and Titus at Crete as bishops, and that he himself and the other Apostles appointed bishops in other places. Whoever refuses to give credit to these testimonies deserves no credit himself.] From this one may see what the chief anchor of the Hierarchists is, and by what argument they are accustomed to prove that their opinion is plain: namely, by the unassailable authority of the ancient writers in a matter of fact. Since the Papists press this same point in the question of Peter's coming to Rome, we have a similar answer to them, the one William Whitaker gave: [Since some accuse us of impudence in calling into question a matter so certain and clear, I do not merely see nothing clear and certain, but rather everything doubtful and obscure.]

units.la: CAP. XXIII. Argumentum nostrum primum a sola scripturæ Authentica authoritate.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII. Our first argument, drawn from the sole authentic authority of Scripture.

units.la: VEniamus ad argumenta. Argumentum nostrum primum à scripturæ authoritate ducitur, quæ sola in materiis facti, haud secus atque in rebus fidei, nos solos certos reddit. Perspectum commentario hoc, qui in Genesim librum historicum scribens de historia etiam sacra hoc affirmat. [Solis scripturis reservata est hæc authoritas,ut ideo id ita esse credamus, quia ita scripserunt.] Si solis scripturis hæc authoritas reservetur, contumeliosior in scripturas Papistis ipsis Downamus, qui hanc authoritatem patribus communem facit,dum credendum esse contendit Hierarchicos Episcopos in Ecclesijs primis fuisse,quia ita illi scripserunt. At parum forte fide dignus Cajetanus: sciendum igitur Tho. Mortonum hanc illius sententiam & citare & approbare: sic ut hac in re Hierarchicum ab Hierarchico confutatum habeamus. Ita Ioh. Turrecremata. [Nihil asserendum est de divinis,nisi quod divinarum scripturarum testimonio & ratione probari potest, ut Hieronymus & Augustinus scribunt.] Hæc in materia facti adfert Whitakerus & approbat ita. [Recte. Vtinam id ipsum omnes papistæ perpetuò tenerent: facilius certè omnes controversiæ inter nos dirimerentur.] Producit Ioh. Reynoldus de Eusebio & historicis reliquis hoc testimonium Can.li.11.c.6. [Præter authores sacros,nullus historicus certus esse potest, & idoneus ad faciendam certam in Theologia fidem,] quod adeo à se evidens & apparens esse dicit, ut suis probationibus confirmari opus non habeat. Tantùm Flavij Vopisci in vita Aureliani,verum & lepidum dictum citat: qui historiam scribere aggrediens, èo se id consilentius facere dicit,quia in mentiendo comites habiturus erat: cum nullum historicum sciverit, qui non in aliquo mentitus sit. Quod si hoc autem ( inquit Reynoldus) omnibus historicis acciderit, exceptis eis qui scripturas exararunt, qui per Spiritum Dei non hominis scripserunt: tum Eusebius quoque quanquam historicus bonus, eidem vitio subiectus esse potuit.] Approbat ista Henricus Parçus Episcopus Glocestrensis in suæ versione Reynoldiana. Onuphrius Patavinus,de Petri adventu ad Romam agens, visus est argumento negativo ex Actis Apostolorum. Huic ita occurrit Baronius, Argumentatio inquit, Nouatoribus peculiaris, qui in receptu habent, ut negent, quicquid in scripturis non habetur expressum. Sed Lucas multa prætermisit &c. Quorsum hæc inquis? Nempè ut intelligatur communem protestantium opinionem hanc esse, historiam perfectam in sacris haberi, sic ut necessariò credendum non sit, quod in eisdem non habetur traditum. Malè igitur Causaubonus, & contrà reliquorum communem sententiam, cum ita Peronio postulanti ut antiquitas ad tempora usque Martini extenderetur, ita responderet. Hoc postulatum parum illu (reformatis) æquum videbitur, qui vniversam Ecclesiæ primitiuæ historiam, Actuum Apostolicorum divino illo quidem, sed tamen vnico libello volunt contineri. Ab horum sententia longè abest æquissimus prudentissimusque Rex qui in epistola monitoria sua, quanti faceret patres etiam quarti aut quinti seculi ingenuè declaravit. Peius verò multò Downamus, qui Egesippum,Clementem,& alios scriptores antiquos accersendos existimat, ut ita historia Lucæ,ubi desijt,continueretur. At si non historiam perfectam liber Actorum continet, minime tamen ad patres quarti aut quinti seculi. Certè hac repudiata,incertas patrum narranarrationes consectari, non modo ridiculum, sed & impium esset. Atque certe miror Downamo non venisse in mentem, continuatorem sancti Lucæ Apostolum Iohannem potiorè esse, quàm patrum quenquam, quanquam maximè genuinum. Annon historia Apocalypsis est? Quid igitur sibi illa volunt, c. 4. v. 1. Ascende huc & ostendam tibi quæ oportet fieri posthac? Annon historia perfecta etiam? Quid igitur illud sibi vult, c. 5. v. 1. quod hic liber intus & à tergo scriptus dicatur? Annon ostendunt hæc, hunc eundem plenè perfectèque exaratum? Adde quod c.10.v.7. Pertingat hujus libri historia, usque ad consummationem mysterii Dei, sicut annunciavit servis suis prophetis. At obscurior fortè Apocalypsis, quàm ut loco historiæ servire possit. Quorsum igitur illa tam magnifica referatio sigillorum, quæ tantis laudibus piorum celebratur c.5.v.8. Quorsum mandatum, Ne obsignaveris verba prophetiæ libri hujus: tempus enim prope est, c.22.v.10. Quorsum denique promissio? Beatus qui legit, & beati qui audiunt verba prophetiæ libri huius, & observant ea, quæ in ea scripta sunt: tempus enim prope est, c.1.v.3. Non igitur historiam tantam sacram habemus, sed & in sacris historiam perfectam; sic ut ad patres in materia facti divertere ad fidem faciendam in re aliqua Theologica controversa, loco sacrilegii sit. Num hæc mea sententia sola est? Annon Hierarchici prudentiores idem plane sentiunt? Audiatur primò Richardus Feyldus, Quis nouplùm videt, inquit, Evangelistas historiam de morte & vita Christi memoriæ tradentes, sanctum Lucam in Actis Apostolorum, Ecclesias ab Apostolis institutas narrantem, sanctum Iohannem revelationem quam vidit scribentem, intendisse, ut perfectam doctrinæ Christianæ summam plenamque fidei directionem tradarent, de statu verum statu, usque ad consummationem seculi. Audiatur deinde Hadrianus Saravia. Quis, inquit, ecclesiæ status fuerit, & quam tradiderint rationem gubernandæ ecclesiæ Apostoli, nemo docere poterit: nisi ex sacris literis & Apostolorum temporibus. Audiatur postremo Matheus Sutclivius, quem ego Iohanni Whitgifto opponò. Contendit ille, Anabaptisticum esse in materia facti, à scriptura, negativè argumentari. At contrà Sutclivius: disputans etenim contra Petri ad Romam adventum, ita arguit. Probatur sententia nostra primò, quia nusquam ex scripturis probatur. Nihil eius scripsit in epistolis suis Petrus, nihil Paulus, nihil quires Apostolorum gestas diligenter & accuratè persequutus est Lucas. Rufus. Respondet Bellarminus, non valere argumentum ab authoritate sacræ scripturæ valide valet. Ex scripturis non probatur, ergo non est dogma fidei. Ita argumentatur Apostolus, ita etiam argumentantur Patres, ideòque necessariò sequitur, quia scriptura est canon fidei, & nihil est nunc necessariò credendum extra scripturas. Ita conficitur, in materia facti, historicos nullos nisi sacros, aut fidem facere; aut ad fidem obligare.
units.tr: Let us come to the arguments. Our first argument is drawn from the authority of Scripture, which alone makes us certain in matters of fact, no less than in matters of faith. This is clear to anyone who, writing a commentary on Genesis, says that this holds even of sacred history. This authority is reserved to Scripture alone, so that we believe a thing is so because they wrote that it is so. If this authority is reserved to Scripture alone, the Papists themselves treat Scripture more contemptuously than Downame does, who makes this authority common to the Fathers, while he contends that hierarchical bishops existed in the earliest churches because those writers said so. But Cajetan is perhaps scarcely worthy of trust. One should know, then, that Thomas Morton both cites and approves this opinion of his, so that in this matter we have a hierarchical man refuted by a hierarchical man. So too John of Torquemada: Nothing is to be asserted about divine things except what can be proved by the testimony of divine Scripture and by reason, as Jerome and Augustine write. Whitaker brings this forward in a matter of fact and approves it thus: Rightly. Would that all Papists always held this same view; certainly all controversies between us would be settled more easily. John Reynolds produces this testimony from Eusebius and the other historians (Can. lib. 11, c. 6): Apart from the sacred authors, no historian can be certain, or fit to make faith certain in theology, which he says is so evident and obvious to him that it needs no confirmation by proofs. He cites only the saying of Flavius Vopiscus in the life of Aurelian, a true and witty remark: Vopiscus, beginning to write history, says he will do so more quietly, because he would have lies as companions, since he has known no historian who has not lied in some point. But if this (says Reynolds) has happened to all historians, except those who wrote the Scriptures, who wrote by the Spirit of God and not of man, then Eusebius too, though a good historian, may have been subject to the same fault. Henry Parry, Bishop of Gloucester, approves these things in his version of Reynolds. Onuphrius of Padua, treating of Peter's coming to Rome, seemed to argue negatively from the Acts of the Apostles. Baronius meets this thus: The argument is peculiar to the Innovators, who hold as a principle that they deny whatever is not expressly found in the Scriptures. But Luke omitted many things, etc. What is the point of this, you ask? Namely, that it be understood that the common opinion of the Protestants is that a complete history is contained in the sacred books, so that it is not necessary to believe what is not handed down in them. Causaubon therefore spoke wrongly, and contrary to the common opinion of the rest, when Peiresc demanded that antiquity be extended down to the times of Martin, and answered thus: This demand will seem little fair to the reformed, who want the whole history of the primitive Church to be contained in the Acts of the Apostles, a divine but single little book. Far from their opinion is the most just and most prudent King, who in his monitory letter declared frankly how much he values even the Fathers of the fourth or fifth century. Far worse is Downame, who thinks that Hegesippus, Clement and other ancient writers must be summoned, so that the history of Luke might be continued where it left off. But if the book of Acts does not contain a complete history, it nonetheless does not point to the Fathers of the fourth or fifth century. Certainly, to reject this and pursue the uncertain narratives of the Fathers would be not only ridiculous but impious. And I am surprised that it did not occur to Downame that the Apostle John, the continuator of St Luke, carries more weight than any of the Fathers, however genuine. Is not the Apocalypse a history? What, then, do the words of c.4.v.1 mean: Come up hither, and I will show you what must be done hereafter? Is that not a complete history too? What does c.5.v.1 mean, that this book is said to be written within and on the back? Do not these things show that this book was written out fully and perfectly? Add c.10.v.7: the history of this book reaches to the consummation of the mystery of God, as he declared to his servants the prophets. But the Apocalypse is perhaps too obscure to serve in place of history. Why, then, that so magnificent unsealing of the seals, celebrated with such praise by the pious, c.5.v.8? Why the command, Seal not up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is at hand, c.22.v.10? Why finally the promise: Blessed is he who reads, and blessed are they who hear the words of the prophecy of this book and keep those things which are written in it, for the time is at hand, c.1.v.3? Therefore we have not only a great sacred history, but in the sacred books a complete history; so that to turn to the Fathers in a matter of fact, in order to establish the faith on some controverted theological point, is a sacrilege. Is this my opinion alone? Do not the more prudent Hierarchists think exactly the same? Let Richard Field be heard first: Who does not now see, he says, that the Evangelists, handing down to memory the history of the death and life of Christ, St Luke narrating in the Acts the churches instituted by the Apostles, and St John writing the revelation he saw, intended to deliver the complete sum of Christian doctrine and full direction of faith concerning the true state of the Church until the consummation of the age? Next let Adrian Saravia be heard: What the state of the Church was, and what plan of governing the Church the Apostles handed down, no one can teach except from the sacred letters and the times of the Apostles. Finally let Matthew Sutcliffe be heard, whom I set against John Whitgift. Whitgift contends that it is Anabaptistic to argue negatively from Scripture in matters of fact. But Sutcliffe, disputing against Peter's coming to Rome, argues on the contrary: Our opinion is proved first because it is nowhere proved from the Scriptures. Peter wrote nothing of it in his epistles, nor did Paul, nor did Luke, who diligently and accurately pursued the deeds of the Apostles. Again. Bellarmine replies that the argument from the authority of Scripture does not hold validly. It is not proved from Scripture, therefore it is not a dogma of faith. The Apostle argues thus, and the Fathers argue thus, and therefore it necessarily follows, since Scripture is the canon of faith, that nothing is now necessarily to be believed outside the Scriptures. Thus it is concluded that, in matters of fact, no historians except sacred ones either make faith or bind us to faith.

units.la: CAP. XXIIII. Secundum nostrum Argumentum à frivolis & incredibilibus Historicorum additamentis.
units.tr: CAP. XXIV. Our second argument, from the frivolous and incredible additions of the historians.

units.la: Argumentum nostrum secundum, à frivolis illis & incredibilibus additamentis derivatur, quæ historiæ sacræ, historici ecclesiastici pueriliter adjecerunt. Narrant Clemens, Eusebius, Dorotheus, Cephām à Paulo Antiochiæ reprehensū, non fuisse Petrum Apostolum, sed alium ejusdem nominis qui fuit unus de 70. discipulis: quod nonne quæso aperte falsum? Narrat Clemens ex prædecessorum suorum relatione antiqua, & Eusebius rem memoria dignum iudicat: quod Iacobi carnifex ab eodem mirabiliter conversus sit: quod numnam quæso verisimile? Apud Eusebium, Philippus Apostolus & Philippus Evangelista ab antiquis confusi, ac si unus essent. Iohannes vero Apostolus, & Iohannes Senior divisi sunt ac si duo essent: quod nonne quæso puerile? Sed quoniam infinitum esset reliqua absque methddo persequi: insistam Cæsaris Baronij vestigijs, ad quem etiam brevitatis causa remitto lectorem. Consulat igitur Annales illos, in quibus in unum congesta videat, quæ puerиliter tradiderunt Patres, de vitæ continentia in Maria virgine p. 63. de summo pontificatu Zachariæ, p. 64. de illius inter porticum & altare occisione p. 66. de Christi natali p.64. de baptismi anno p. 65. & 68. de Magis & eorum Angelo p. 65. de arbore se coram Christo uncurvante, dum fugeret in Ægiptum p. 66. de infantia Christi p. 67. de Iohan. Baptif. spelunca, locustis, monachatu p. 67. 68. de tribus Marijs confusis in unam p. 610. de lapide quo Stephanus lapidatus est, p. 615. de loco ubi natus Paulus p.618. de fonte Siloæ ad preces Esaiæ erumpente p. 625. de nominibus 70. discipulorum p. 625. de Iohanne spoliato syndone pag. 626. de interitu Iudæ p. 626. de columna ad quam Christus flagellatus p. 627. de palma p. 627. de spinea corona p. 627. de Calvaria à cranio Adami ibi sepulto denominata p. 627. de Golgotha quasi medio terræ p. 627. de terra Golgothæ miracula edente, & cruce non diminuta p. 627. de anno passionis p. 628. de Christo resurgente, primùm conspecto à Maria p. 628. de persecutione Iosephi Aramatheę, & miraculo fontis Emauntis, quod Christus in eo lavasset pedes p. 628. de impressis vestigijs Christi in monte Oliveti p. 631. de gestis Pauli & Teclæ, multisq; alijs, quæ mepiget (præsertim lassum & defatigatum) commemorare. Hij nempe patres sunt, quibus fidem non adhibere impudentia extrema Downamo videtur: quum in hujusmodi fabulosis, aut saltem incertissimis (de quibus & Episcopatus Hierarchicus est) censere eis adhibendam fidem esse, res sacrilegij est. Quod si verò in his finem denegari illis posse dixerit, in Hierarchia non item: præterquam quod propositio illius generalis est, Impudentiæ nempe & audaciæ esse, patribus
units.tr: Our second argument is drawn from those frivolous and incredible additions which the ecclesiastical historians have childishly attached to sacred history. Clement, Eusebius and Dorotheus relate that Cephas, rebuked by Paul at Antioch, was not the apostle Peter but another man of the same name, one of the seventy disciples. Is this, I ask, not plainly false? Clement relates, on the authority of an ancient tradition handed down by his predecessors, and Eusebius judges the story worth recording, that the executioner of James was wonderfully converted by him. Is this, I ask, at all likely? In Eusebius, the apostle Philip and the evangelist Philip are confused by the ancients as if they were one man, while John the apostle and the elder John are separated as if they were two. Is this, I ask, not childish? But since it would be endless to pursue the rest without method, I shall follow the footsteps of Caesar Baronius, to whom I also refer the reader for the sake of brevity. Let him consult those Annals, in which he will find gathered together what the Fathers childishly handed down: on the continence of life of the virgin Mary, p. 63; on the high priesthood of Zechariah, p. 64; on his killing between the porch and the altar, p. 66; on the birth of Christ, p. 64; on the year of the baptism, pp. 65 and 68; on the Magi and their angel, p. 65; on the tree that bowed itself before Christ as he fled into Egypt, p. 66; on the infancy of Christ, p. 67; on the cave of John the Baptist, the locusts, and his monastic life, pp. 67–68; on three Marys confused into one, p. 610; on the stone with which Stephen was stoned, p. 615; on the place where Paul was born, p. 618; on the fountain of Siloam bursting forth at the prayer of Isaiah, p. 625; on the names of the seventy disciples, p. 625; on John stripped of his linen cloth, p. 626; on the death of Judas, p. 626; on the column to which Christ was scourged, p. 627; on the palm, p. 627; on the crown of thorns, p. 627; on Calvary, named from the skull of Adam buried there, p. 627; on Golgotha as the middle of the earth, p. 627; on the earth of Golgotha working miracles, and the cross not diminished, p. 627; on the year of the passion, p. 628; on Christ's resurrection, first seen by Mary, p. 628; on the persecution of Joseph of Arimathea, and the miracle of the spring at Emmaus, in which Christ had washed his feet, p. 628; on the footprints of Christ impressed on the Mount of Olives, p. 631; on the deeds of Paul and Thecla, and many other things which I am loath to recount, especially as I am weary and worn out. These, surely, are the Fathers whom to refuse belief is, in Downame's view, the utmost impudence; yet to hold that belief must be given to them in such fabulous, or at least most uncertain, matters (on which the hierarchical episcopate also depends) is a sacrilege. But if he should say that credit may be denied to these, though not in the case of the Hierarchy, then, apart from the fact that his general proposition is that it is impudence and audacity to put no trust in the Fathers

units.la: Eusebius lib. 1. c.13.
units.tr: Eusebius, book 1, chapter 13.
Book 2, chapter 9.

units.la: Lib.4.c.35. patribus in materia facti minimè credere: regere mihi in promptu est, Sutclivij illud. Multa de Paulo & Tecla & aliis Apostolis & sanctis hominibus narrantur fabulosa, quibus nemo necessario tenetur credere---Si verum hoc— cur non & reliquis Clementis narrationibus fides adhibeatur? Apposita hæc responsio est: docet etenim ad allidendam Downamiani argumenti vim satis esse, quod multa alia apud historicos fabulosa sint, quibus si minimè credendum est, cur quæso in causa Hierarchiæ fides illis necessario, sub peccato impudentiæ, adjungenda?
units.tr: Book 4, chapter 35. in matters of fact at all: I have ready to hand the reply of Sutcliffe: "Many fabulous things are told about Paul and Thecla and the other apostles and holy men, which no one is necessarily bound to believe... If this is true, why should belief not also be given to the rest of Clement's narratives?" This reply is pertinent: it shows that, to break the force of Downame's argument, it is enough that many other fabulous things are found in the historians, which are rightly not to be believed. Why, I ask, in the question of the Hierarchy must belief in them be necessarily added, on pain of the sin of impudence?

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CAP. XXV.

units.la: Argumentum III. à fidei natura.
units.tr: Argument III, from the nature of faith.

units.la: Tertium nostrum argumentum a fidei natura sumitur, quæ certiora fundamenta requirit, quàm quæ ab historicis Ecclesiasticis aut solent, aut possint suppeditari. Meridithus Hanmerns Hierarchicus hanc de Historicis Ecclesiasticis censuram exercet. Cum in his historijs quædam reperissem quæ melius fuissent non fuisse scripta: venit mihi in mentem illud Augustini. Divinitatis solius est non errare. Certus sum memunem ita FATVVM, ut antiquitate & authoritate harum historiarum niti velit ac si scripturæ sacræ essent: fides quædam historica est, si in historiam aliquam incideris minus probatam, penes authorem sit fides. Quid igitur est? In quæstionibus Theologicis non tantum testimonia valent, ut fidem Christianam facere possint: quid igitur nobis in quæstione de Hierarchia cum historicis Ecclesiasticis negotij est: quum vel ipso Hierarchico teste fidem nullam nisi historicam quandam, & dubiam nobis ingenerare possunt. Indignatur absque causa R. Bancroftus, quod credere nolimus Episcopos Hierarchicos in Ecclesia prima extitisse: nos uno ictu abscindere dicit omnes scriptores Ecclesiasticos, qui nunc extant, quasi testes insufficientes earum rerum, quæ ante illorum tempora acciderunt. Quidni insufficientes quidem, utpote à quibus (vel ipso Hanmero teste) fides Christiana proficisci nequeat: non tamen penitus abscinduntur, quæ in causa Hierarchiæ repudiantur, cum constat alios fines aliosque usus varios, scriptam eorum historiam habere: quam ut de Episcopo Hierarchico testificentur. Ita Hadrianus Saravia. De Apostolis quod adfirt Beza credendum quantum verbo Dei & ex sacra historia probat: quæ ubi nos deficit ad Historias ecclesiasticas recurrere nemo prohibet: & quamvis scriptoribus illis humanitus quædam exciderunt, unde eorum scripta æqualem scriptis Apostolicis non possunt habere authoritatem: tamen tanquam fabulosa rejicienda non sunt.-- Qui à veritate quæ satis aliunde nota est discernere quæ fabulosa sunt nequeunt: historias cum fructu legendi non tenet rationem. Primò, si ad historias recurrendum non sit nisi ubi historia sacra deficit: in quæstionibus Theologicis nunquam ad historias recurrendum rendum omnino est, quia ad eas terminandas, historia sacra nusquam, nunquam, nullo modo deficit.
units.tr: Our third argument is drawn from the nature of faith, which requires firmer foundations than those that ecclesiastical historians usually do or can supply. Meredith Hanmer, the Hierarchist, passes this judgment on the ecclesiastical historians: When I had found certain things in these histories that would have been better left unwritten, the saying of Augustine came into my mind: "It belongs to God alone not to err." I am sure that no one has so trusted the antiquity and authority of these histories as if they were Scripture itself. Some measure of historical faith is owed to them; if you come upon some history that is less well attested, the responsibility for believing it rests with its author. What, then, is the upshot? In theological questions, testimonies alone do not carry enough weight to establish the Christian faith. So what business have we with the ecclesiastical historians in the question of the hierarchy, since, even on the testimony of the Hierarchist himself, they can produce only a certain historical and doubtful faith in us? R. Bancroft is indignant without cause that we will not believe that Hierarchical bishops existed in the primitive Church. He says we cut off at one stroke all the ecclesiastical writers who now survive, as if they were insufficient witnesses to events that happened before their time. Yes, they are indeed insufficient, since (even on Hanmer's own testimony) Christian faith cannot proceed from them. Yet those writers are not wholly cut off, even in the question of the hierarchy that we reject, since it is clear that their history was written with other aims and for various other uses, and it is not meant to bear witness to a Hierarchical bishop. So says Hadrianus Saravia: As for what Beza asserts about the Apostles, it is to be believed only so far as he proves it from the Word of God and sacred history. Where that fails us, no one forbids us to have recourse to ecclesiastical histories. Although certain things have fallen from those writers through human frailty, so that their writings cannot have authority equal to the Apostolic writings, they are still not to be rejected as fabulous. Those who cannot distinguish what is fabulous from the truth, which is sufficiently known from elsewhere, cannot profit from reading histories. First, if one must have recourse to histories only where sacred history fails, then in theological questions there is never any need to have recourse to histories at all, since sacred history never, at no time and in no way, fails to settle those matters.

units.la: Secundo, credendum tantum historiae sacrae Saravia dicit: non humanae, quia quaedam humanitas eisdem scriptoribus excidere solent.
units.tr: Second, Saravia says that only sacred history is to be believed, not human history, since some human frailty usually falls upon the same writers.

units.la: Tertiò, falli eum dicit in legendis Historicis, cui veritas aliunde nota non est, ut vera à fabulosis queat discernere. Ita ad Scripturas nos solas reduxit, simulque causam aperuit Hierarchici erroris. Nempe non posse ejusdem patronos, vera in historijs discernere à fabulosis, quia veritas disciplinae reformatae aliunde eis à sacris Scripturis nota non sit. Quod igitur Matheus Sutclivius de historiis adventus Petri ad Romam agens respondet Papistis, Ad testimonia patrum expedita est responsio, quae fama acceperunt, narrant, sed dubia & incerta: Quidni & Downamo respondere nobis licitum? Ad testimonia patrum expedita est responsio in materia facti ecclesiae primae, quae fama incerta acceperunt, narrant (si quid de Episcopo Hierarchico narrent) sed dubia & incerta. Haec dubia non patitur Whitakerus in quaestionibus Theologicis temerandis, locum aliquem habere: de sepulchris etenim Petri & Pauli quae Romae visuntur ita respondet, ad antiquorum historicorum & testimonia & monumenta.Nititur hoc totum fide humana, & ex historica veritate pendet: at fides & religio nostra certiori testimonio niti debet, nempe testimonio Spiritus Sancti.
units.tr: Third, he says that those who read historians whose truth is not known from elsewhere go wrong, since they cannot distinguish true from fabulous. In this way he has led us back to Scripture alone, and at the same time he has revealed the cause of the Hierarchical error. Namely, the defenders of that position cannot distinguish true things from fabulous things in the histories, because the truth of the reformed discipline is not known to them from elsewhere than the holy Scriptures. Therefore, just as Matthew Sutcliffe, discussing the histories of Peter's coming to Rome, answers the Papists: The reply to the testimonies of the Fathers is easy: they relate what they received by report, but the matter is doubtful and uncertain. Why should it not likewise be lawful for us to answer Downame? The reply to the testimonies of the Fathers is easy, concerning a matter of fact in the primitive Church: they relate what they received by uncertain report (if they relate anything about a Hierarchical bishop), but it is doubtful and uncertain. Whitaker does not allow that such doubt has any place in the profaning of theological questions. Thus he answers concerning the tombs of Peter and Paul that are shown at Rome, appealing to the testimonies and monuments of the ancient historians: All this rests on human faith and depends on historical truth; but our faith and religion ought to rest on a surer testimony, namely the testimony of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CAP. XXVI.

units.la: Argumentum IV, à rerum priscarum obscuritate.
units.tr: Argument IV, from the obscurity of early things.

units.la: ARgumentum nostrum quartum à rerum priscarum obscuritate sumitur. Ioh. Reynoldus Ecclesiae priscae sententiam ita cavillationibus & sophismatis obseptam dicit, ut similis sit Archimedis sepulchro, ad quod accedere Ciceroni non datum, nisi vepretis atque dumetis multis resectis: ad quod etiam cum accessit, nil nisi Epigramma exesis posterioribus partibus deprehendere potuit: ex quibus conjiceret monimentum illud Arichimedis esse. Idem nobis accidit in causa Hierarchiae, non solum Hierarchicorum dumetis obsepta, verumetiam temporis longinquitate in ipsis Historicis Ecclesiasticis propemodum exesa. Patet hoc, ex hoc ipso Io. Reynoldo, qui in hanc sententiam, & citat & approbat Iosephum Scaligerum. Cum delectu (inquit) Eusebij scripta legenda esse non dubitabit, quisquis illa attentius legit, quam ipse scripta veterum. Adjungit deinde: Veteres summi illi viri cum de incunabulis Christianismi scribunt, multa à veritate aliena pronunciarunt. Non abludit Caesar ipse Baronius, cujus ista verba sunt: Maior ex nostris quam ex haereticis superesset labor, cum liceat ingenue fateri, quod nulla res in Ecclesia ita hactenus negligi visa sit, ac Ecclesiasticorum rerum narratio– Quod si posteriores historias consulas magnam magnam profecto eorum esse classem intelliges, qui absque delectu perceperant aniles fabulas. Ita Franciscus Guicciardinus in Paralipomenis: Saepè profundis tenebris res antiquae demersae iacent: quod si de Sylvestri ætate verum, de qua loquitur, quanto magis de antiquissimæ Ecclesiæ ultimis primordiis? Quid Eusebius ipse? Res ipsa haec iam in exordio exposcit ut mihi ignoscatur. Confiteor namque maius esse viribus nostris, absolutumque & incomprehensibile quod polliceamur ac profitemur. Nam & primi nos argumentum hoc jam aggressi, velut desertam quandam & inustatam viam ingredi conamur—ubi nusquam nobis nuda eorum hominum vestigia deprehendere licet, qui eandem hanc sint ante nos viam ingressi, nisi exiguas duntaxat occasiones. Prodeat in medium Ioh. Reynoldus, Eusebium omnium Historicorum principem agnoscit alibi & merito: quis enim non agnosceret: quum eum tamen allegasset & commendasset Ioh. Hartus: respondet [Eusebium (ut historici caeteri) errori subiectum esse. Quod eò citius persuasum esse debet, quod Papa Gelasius in Concilio 70, Episcoporum, ejus historiam ut improbatam condemnarit, Dist.15. c. 3. Hanc reprobationem tanquam justam comprobat Canus, & rationes profert: nempe propter narrationem Epistolæ Christi ad Agbarum lib.1. cap.14. & illius ex Clemente Alexandrino multarum rerum transcriptionem lib.1.cap.1.& sic deinceps passim, cum & illa fabula & huius opera à Concilio improbata sint.] Richardus Fyldus initia Ecclesiæ adeo obscura sentit, ut approbet Lindani illud: Quædam officia in Primitiva Ecclesia fuisse, quæ iam ignota sunt. Loquitur de aliis fateor: sed de officio Seniorum verissime hoc dici potest: quod in Ecclesia prima notum, deinde in desuetudinem abijt, ac si nunquam extitisset. Qui vero propter desuetudinem Seniores agnoscere non potuerunt: potuerunt è contra propter invectam Episcoporum alienam consuetudinem, persuasum habere, eiusmodi munus quod suis seculis invaluerat, in in prima Ecclesia extitisse. Concludo ex canone Toletano. Longinquitate sæpe fit temporis, ut non pateat conditio originis.
units.tr: Our fourth argument is drawn from the obscurity of early things. John Reynolds says that the teaching of the early Church is so hemmed in with cavils and sophisms that it resembles the tomb of Archimedes, which Cicero could reach only after many brambles and thorns had been cut away, and even when he reached it he could make out nothing but an epigram, with the latter parts eaten away, from which he might conjecture that the monument was Archimedes'. The same thing has happened to us in the case of hierarchy: it is not only walled in by the thickets of the hierarchists, but is also almost eaten away in the ecclesiastical historians themselves by the lapse of time. This is clear from John Reynolds himself, who both cites and approves Joseph Scaliger to this effect: No one who reads Eusebius more attentively than he reads the writings of the ancients will doubt that he must be read with discrimination. He then adds: Those great men of old, when they write of the beginnings of Christianity, have pronounced many things foreign to the truth. Caesar Baronius, the cardinal, does not disagree, and his words are these: The labour would be greater for us than for the heretics, since it must be freely confessed that no matter in the Church has so far seemed so neglected as the narration of ecclesiastical affairs. But if you consult the later histories, you will understand that there is a large class of those who took in old wives' tales without discrimination. So Francesco Guicciardini in his Paralipomena: Often ancient affairs lie sunk in profound darkness. If this is true of the age of Sylvester, of which he speaks, how much more true is it of the last beginnings of the most ancient Church? What does Eusebius himself say? This very matter asks at the outset that I be pardoned. For I confess that what we promise and profess is beyond our powers and cannot be fully grasped. Since we are the first to take up this subject, we are trying to enter a deserted and untrodden road, where nowhere can we find the bare footprints of those men who entered this same way before us, except only a few slight traces. Let John Reynolds come forward: he acknowledges elsewhere, and rightly so (for who would not?), that Eusebius is the prince of all historians; yet when John Hart had cited and commended him, Reynolds replies that Eusebius, like the other historians, was subject to error. This ought to be all the more convincing because Pope Gelasius, in the Council of seventy bishops, condemned his history as disapproved (Dist. 15, c. 3). Canus approves this rejection as just and gives reasons: namely, on account of his account of the letter of Christ to Abgar (book 1, chapter 14), and his copying of many things from Clement of Alexandria (book 1, chapter 1), and so on throughout, since both that fable and his work were disapproved by the Council. Richard Field judges the beginnings of the Church so obscure that he approves Lindanus' statement: Some offices existed in the primitive Church which are now unknown. He speaks of other offices, I admit; but this can most truly be said of the office of elders: it was known in the first Church, and then fell into disuse as if it had never existed. Yet those who could not recognise elders because of their disuse could, on the contrary, because of the introduction of the bishops' alien custom, be persuaded that an office of this kind, which had prevailed in their own ages, had existed in the first Church. I conclude with the Canon of Toledo: It often happens through the length of time that the condition of the origin does not appear.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: Argumentum nostrum quintum, ab exilii principio narrationum historicarum.
units.tr: Our fifth argument, concerning the beginning of historical narratives.

units.la: QVod ita describit Tertullianus: Veritati nemo præscribere potest, non spatium temporis, non patrocinia personarum, non privilegium nationum. Ex his enim fere consuetudo initium, ab aliqua ignorantia aut simplicitate sortita, in usum per successionem corroboratur; & ita adversus veritatem vindicatur. Multus est Downamus in exaggeranda Reformatorum impudentia, qui unanimi Historicorum consensui, fidem negari posse credunt. Cur non stomachatur in Tertullianum etiam? qui hujusmodi consensum veritati præscribere non posse putat; tat: Praesertim cum exordium ab ignorantia & simplicitate sortitae consuetudines multae, per usum successione corroboratum, unanimem consensum ipsum adeptae sint. Ex hac Hypothesi disputamus adversus Downamum, verbis Sutclivij Hierarchici, qui ita Downamo gregali suo contradicit.
units.tr: Tertullian describes it thus: No one can prescribe against the truth: not the length of time, not the patronage of persons, not the privilege of nations. For custom generally takes its beginning from some ignorance or simplicity, and by succession is strengthened into practice; and so it is defended against the truth. Downame is very full in exaggerating the impudence of the Reformers, who believe that faith cannot be denied to the unanimous agreement of the historians. Why does he not rage against Tertullian as well, who thinks such agreement cannot be prescribed against the truth? Especially since many customs, having their origin in ignorance and simplicity and strengthened by use through succession, have obtained even unanimous consent. On this hypothesis we dispute against Downame, in the words of Sutcliffe the Hierarchist, who thus contradicts Downame, his fellow member of the flock.

units.la: 1. Author huius narrationis de certamine Petri cum Simone Mago fuit Clemens nescio quis: Nec obstat quod hanc eandem narrationem postea aliquot authores fide digni habeant: omnes enim ab uno fonte acceperunt: & solent nonnunquam fabulosa, apud bonos alioqui authores reperiri.
units.tr: 1. The author of this narrative about Peter's contest with Simon Magus was some Clement, I know not who. Nor does it count against this that several later authors who are trustworthy report the same narrative, for they all drew it from one source, and fabulous things are often found even in otherwise good authors.

units.la: 2 Probat Hartus, monachos Apostolorum temporibus fuisse, quia Philo Iudaeus de monachis scripsit, ut narrat Eusebius, l.2. 17. Respondet Reynoldus non de monachis Christianis, sed de Essenis monachis Iudaeis scripsisse Philonem: Eusebium vero hallucinatum fuisse quem Epiphanius, Hieronymus, Cassianus, aliique patres sequuti, in praecipitium acti sunt. Cur non exclamat Downamus in nostrorum impudentiam, quod unanimi patrum consensui, in materia facti, quod ad monachos, refragentur? Vide etenim quam omnia conveniant. Testatur unaminis consensus Historicorum, Episcopos Hierarchicos Apostolorum temporibus fuisse. Sic Downamus: Testatur Eusebius, & reliqui assentiuntur, monachos Apostolorum Temporibus fuisse, sub Caio imperatore, eo etenim tempore Philo vixit, qui de monachis Christianis scripsit: Sic Hartus: Ecqua in istis ratiocinijs differentia? Sed & productum quiddam de Hieronymo, hic minimè praeterendum est. Notum est quàm tumidis buccis venditetur ab Hierarchicis locus ille Hieronymi, de Episcopis à Marco Alexandriae electis, &c. Responderi a nostris assolet, a Marco, exclusiue intelligendum, quod a Bancrofto deridetur immeritò. Sed quid si inclusive intelligatur Hieronymus, sic ut sub Marco Episcopos floruisse putet? Nec etenim magis Hierarchicos hoc juvaret, atque Hartum adjuvit, quòd ex Philone & Eusebio, Monachos sub Marco (id enim verbis disertis asserit) Alexandriae floruisse dixerit. Qui monachos falso asserunt sub Marco Alexandriae fuisse, nonne etiam Episcopos sub Marco fuisse Alexandriae, opinari potuit falso? Certè vel hęc una secunda instantia aperte evincit: argumentum nullum duci posse ab unanimi Historicorum consensu in materia facti, quando de seculis antecedentibus, nominatim vero Apostolicis temporibus testificatur.
units.tr: 2. Hartus proves that there were monks in the time of the Apostles, because Philo the Jew wrote about monks, as Eusebius relates in book 2, chapter 17. Reynolds replies that Philo wrote not about Christian monks but about the Essene monks, who were Jews, and that Eusebius was mistaken, and that Epiphanius, Jerome, Cassian and the other Fathers who followed him were driven headlong into error. Why does Downame not cry out at the impudence of our side, that they resist the unanimous consent of the Fathers, in a matter of fact, concerning the monks? For see how all these things agree. The unanimous consent of the historians testifies that Hierarchical bishops existed in the time of the Apostles. So Downame: Eusebius testifies, and the rest agree, that monks existed in the time of the Apostles, under the emperor Caius; for at that time Philo lived, who wrote about Christian monks. So Hartus. Is there any difference in these arguments? But something adduced from Jerome must also not be passed over here. It is well known with what puffed-up cheeks the Hierarchists sell that passage of Jerome about the bishops appointed by Mark at Alexandria, and so on. Our side usually answers that "from Mark" must be understood exclusively, which Bancroft mocks undeservedly. But what if Jerome is understood inclusively, so that he thinks bishops flourished under Mark? This would help the Hierarchists no more than it helped Hartus, who, from Philo and Eusebius, said that monks flourished at Alexandria under Mark (for he asserts this in plain words). Those who falsely assert that monks existed at Alexandria under Mark: could not they also have falsely supposed that bishops existed at Alexandria under Mark? Certainly this one second instance clearly shows that no argument can be drawn from the unanimous consent of historians in a matter of fact, when they testify about earlier centuries, and especially the Apostolic times.

units.la: 3 Iustantia nostra tertia, de Petri Episcopatu erit: consentiunt etenim Patres omnes ne uno quidem contradicente, Petrum Apostolorum Romanae Ecclesiae fuisse Episcopum, De hoc ita Downamus: Petrum Romae Episcopum fuisse, ne ipse refutator credit. Idipsum ni fallor (his etenim verbis insinuatur) & Downamus ipse credit: quo igitur evanuerunt soliti clamores illi de impudentia, audacia, novitate, superbia, quando patribus consentientibus in materia facti non adhibetur fides?
units.tr: 3. Our third instance will concern the episcopate of Peter. For all the Fathers, not one dissenting, agree that Peter was the bishop of the Roman Church. On this Downame says: Peter was bishop of Rome, not even the refuter believes it. I think the same thing (for it is insinuated in these words), and Downame himself believes it. Why then have those customary clamours about impudence, audacity, novelty and pride vanished, when the Fathers agree in a matter of fact and faith is not given?

units.la: 4 Instantia
units.tr: 4 Instance

units.la: 4 Instanta nostra quarta de Petri adventu ad Romam erit: nam quod Petrus fuerit Romæ, patres omnes, omnes Historici uno ore testificantur. Hunc unanimem consensum Patrum in materia facti, non dubitant nostri scriptores omnes in dubium vocare. Matheus vero Sutclivius, de Hierarchicis unus, ut manifestè falsum confutat. Certe eo tempore, quo eum Romæ fuisse, affirmant Patres, Romæ non fuit, ut à nostris difertissime demonstratur: cessent igitur dehinc Downami clamores, impudentiæ esse, historicis omnibus in materia facti consentientibus fidem non adiungere.
units.tr: Our fourth instance concerns Peter's coming to Rome. For that Peter was at Rome, all the Fathers and all the historians testify with one voice. Our writers do not hesitate to call this unanimous consent of the Fathers in a matter of fact into doubt. Matthew Sutcliffe, one of the Hierarchists, refutes it as manifestly false. Certainly at the time when the Fathers affirm that he was at Rome, he was not at Rome, as is most clearly demonstrated by our side. Let the clamours of Downame cease henceforth, that it is impudence not to give credit to all the historians agreeing in a matter of fact.

units.la: 5 Instantia nostra quinta de loco erit, ubi Petrus epistolam suam primam scripserit: consentiunt etenim Patres omnes, eam per Babilonem intellexisse ipsam Romam. Hunc unanimem consensum rejiciunt nostri omnes: quid verò dico rejiciunt? falsi etiam convincunt: obtinebit tamen Downami positio, patribus semper credendum esse, quando in materia facti consentiunt?
units.tr: 5. Our fifth instance concerns the place where Peter wrote his first epistle. For all the Fathers agree that they understood Babylon to mean Rome itself. All our side reject this unanimous consent; or rather, what do I say, reject? They even convict it of falsehood. Will Downame's position nevertheless prevail, that the Fathers must always be believed when they agree in a matter of fact?

units.la: 6 Instantia nostra sexta & ultima de Marco Evangelista erit: consentiunt etenim patres omnes, Marcum à Petro commemoratum, non filium proprium, sed Evangelistam Marcum esse: unde etiam inferunt cum evangelium suum scripsisse Babyloniæ id est Romæ. Hoc ex Papio, authore uno, eoque simplici profectum suisse, probat Reynoldus Collat. cum Hart. cap. 8. D. 3. improbat verò rationibus multis, quod & ceteri scriptores omnes: quorum argumenta si ponderentur, cui quæso probabile fiet narrationem Hieronymi de Marco Ecclesiam Alexandrinam fundante veram & genuinam esse? Nam ut illum Ecclesiæ Alexandrinæ antistitem non negem: fundamentum tamen Hieronymi, quod à Petro primum Romæ deductus fuerit, & post ab eodem ad plantandam Alexandriæ Ecclesiam missus verum esse non potest. At præter istam narrationem, fundamentum nullum habemus aliud, Marcum unquam Alexandriæ fuisse: vides igitur quam in dubio sit, quod dixit Hieronymus, Episcopos à Marco Alexandriæ fuisse: quem ipsum Marcum Alexandriæ fuisse omnino, adhuc non satis constet. Syriacam Testamenti versionem, ut probat ex Bederiano Feyldus, ab Assyrijs & Persis accepimus: illi vero eam sibi à Marco Evangelista traditam dicunt. Hoc si verum sit, Marcum in Syria, potius quàm in Ægypto vixisse probabile est. Utcunque sit, de adventu Marci ad Alexandriam, hallucinatus Hieronymus est: quid ni igitur de Episcopis à Marco Alexandriæ florentibus hallucinari etiam potuit? Ita conficitur infirmum Downami argumentum esse ab unanimi consensu antiquorum in materia facti desumptum: quia ab autore uno, multæ historicæ narrationes falsò fictæ, in hunc consensum abierunt.
units.tr: 6. Our sixth and last instance concerns Mark the Evangelist. For all the Fathers agree that the Mark mentioned by Peter is not his own son but the Evangelist Mark, whence they also infer that he wrote his Gospel at Babylon, that is, at Rome. That this came from Papias alone, a single and simple author, Reynolds proves in his collation with Hart, chapter 8, division 3; and he disapproves on many grounds, as do all other writers. If their arguments are weighed, I ask, to whom will it become probable that Jerome's narrative of Mark founding the Church of Alexandria is true and genuine? For although I do not deny that he was the bishop of the Alexandrian Church, Jerome's foundation, that he was first brought to Rome by Peter and afterwards sent by him to plant the Church at Alexandria, cannot be true. Apart from that narrative we have no other ground for thinking that Mark was ever at Alexandria at all. You see then how doubtful is what Jerome said, that bishops at Alexandria were from Mark; whether Mark himself was ever at Alexandria is not sufficiently established. The Syriac version of the New Testament, as Feyldus proves from Bede, we received from the Assyrians and Persians, but they say it was handed down to them by Mark the Evangelist. If this is true, it is probable that Mark lived in Syria rather than in Egypt. However that may be, Jerome was mistaken about Mark's coming to Alexandria; why then could he not also have been mistaken about the bishops who flourished at Alexandria under Mark? Thus it is concluded that Downame's argument, drawn from the unanimous consent of the ancients in a matter of fact, is weak, because from a single author many falsely invented historical narratives passed into this consensus.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CAP. XXVII.

units.la: Argumentum VI. ab incertudine historia ecclesiastica.
units.tr: Argument VI, from the uncertainty of ecclesiastical history.

units.la: ARgumentum noftrum fextum, ab incertitudine hiftoriæ ecclefiaftaticæ ducitur, etiam in eis materijs faƈti, in quibus antiquis adjumentis maximè abundabant. Quùm objeciffet Refutator, Eufebium de Titi & Timothei Epifcopatu teftem parum idoneum effe, propterea quod annis 230. poft Timotheum & Titum vixerit : regeffit Downamus ita. Odiofum & infulfum eft, (ne quid gravius dicam) ut quifquam fentiat, voluiffe Eufebium ex proprio cerebro hoc teftificari, & non potius ex eorum relatione qui feculis fuperioribus vixerant, præfertim cum adjiciat in hiftorijs proditum eft. Vrget hoc ipfu Th.Bilfonus : Timotheus (utex hiftoriis, narrat Eufeb.lib.3. cap.4. primus fuit qui Ephefinæ Parœciæ, ficut & Titus Cretenfium Ecclefiarum Epifcopatum fortitus eft. Vrget deniq; hoc ipfum & Robertus Bellarminus.
units.tr: Our sixth argument is drawn from the uncertainty of ecclesiastical history, even in those matters of fact in which the ancient writers were most richly supplied with evidence. When the Refuter objected that Eusebius was an unreliable witness concerning the episcopate of Titus and Timothy, because he lived 230 years after Timothy and Titus, Downame replied as follows: It is odious and foolish (not to say worse) for anyone to think that Eusebius wished to bear this witness out of his own head, and did not rather draw it from the report of those who lived in earlier ages, especially since he adds that it is recorded in the histories. Th. Bilson presses this same point: Timothy (as Eusebius, book 3, chapter 4, relates from the histories) was the first to obtain the episcopate of the Ephesian parish, just as Titus obtained that of the churches of Crete. Robert Bellarmine too finally presses this same point.

units.la: Primo quid fi per Hiftoriâ, intellexerit Eufebius, nihil aliud quam fcriptû Pauli in Epiftolis ad Titum & Timotheum? tum aperte perperam Hiftoriam facrâ intellexit. Sed Hiftoriam aliam intellexit Eufebius (inquit Bilfonus) Quemadmodum Sedulius in 1. Tim. 1. cuius ista verba funt : Timotheus Epifcopus fuit Ephefi ut in libro hiftoriarum dicitur, Fac ita effe : nihil tamen ex Eufebio folidi concludi poteft, quum veteres citat, quia Eufebius parum attente veteres Hiftorias legit, inquit Iofephus Scaliger, quod ab Ioh.Reynoldo noftro comprobatur. Parum attente cum dicunt id etiam includunt, quod judicio caveret, hiftorias falfas a veris difcernendi. Id in Epifcopali Timothei & Titi majoritate Eufebio accidere potuiffe quis diffitebitur, qui illius infcitiam animadvertit, in alijs monumentis falfis non difcernendis? Exempli gratia. Abgari hiftoria quid ineptius, vel ipfius Gelafij teftimonio, Dift.15.c.3. Hanc tamen in Edeffæ archivis extitiffe, ad fuam ufque ætatem affirmat. Lib.3. cap.20. Citatur Sozomenus in textu Eufebij qui annis 100. poft Eufebium vixit. Vitiatur hic textus Eufebij inquis. Eô minus inquam neceffario Hiftoricis credendum, quò magis vitiari folent. Hiftoriam illam quam de iuvene & Iohanne ibi narrat, ex Clemente Alexandrino citat, refpondes. Eô rurfus inquam minus Eufebio credendum : quod ex talibus hiftoricis pendeat, qualis Clemens Alexandrinus eft, uti antea ex Cano conftitit, qui Dift.15.cap.320. recitat quæ opera Clementis Alexandrini improbantur. Lib.4. cap.36. Duos effe Iohannes Ephefinos probat, non folum ex hiftoria fed ex duobus monumentis Ephefi, quorum utrumque Iohannis effe dicitur.
units.tr: First, what if Eusebius meant by "histories" nothing other than the writings of Paul in his Epistles to Titus and Timothy? Then he plainly understood "sacred history" wrongly. But Eusebius understood another history, says Bilson, as Sedulius does on 1 Tim. 1, whose words are: Timothy was bishop of Ephesus, as is said in the book of histories. Grant that this is so: still nothing solid can be concluded from Eusebius, since he cites the ancients, because Eusebius read the ancient histories with little care, says Joseph Scaliger, which our John Reynolds also confirms. When they say with little care, they also include the lack of judgment to separate false histories from true. Who will deny that this could have happened to Eusebius in the episcopal succession of Timothy and Titus, when we notice his ignorance in failing to distinguish false monuments from others? For example: what is more absurd than the history of Abgarus, even by the testimony of Gelasius himself, Dist. 15, c. 3? Yet he affirms that it existed in the archives of Edessa down to his own age. Book 3, chapter 20: Eusebius's text is cited through Sozomen, who lived 100 years after Eusebius. You say this text of Eusebius is corrupted. I reply that it is therefore all the less necessary to believe historians, the more often they are corrupted. You answer that the story Eusebius there tells about the young man and John he takes from Clement of Alexandria. I reply again that Eusebius is to be believed the less for that, since he depends on historians of the sort Clement of Alexandria is, as was shown before from Cano, who in Dist. 15, c. 320 recites the works of Clement of Alexandria that are condemned. Book 4, chapter 36: Eusebius proves that there were two Johns of Ephesus, not only from history but from two monuments at Ephesus, each of which is said to be John's.

units.la: Qui ex hiftoria veteri duos Iohannes, Iohannem nempe Apoftolum, & Iohannem Seniorem, quorum ille Epiftolam Iohannis priorem, hic duas posteriores & Apocalypsim fcripfit, falfò afferuit : nonne etiam ex historia veteri asserere falso potuit, Timotheum Ephesi, Titum Cretæ Episcopos fuisse. In materia facti quis ex eis qui Eusebium antecesserunt Irenæo potior? Erravit ille tamen inquit Eusebius: quòd dixerat Papiam Apostolos vidisse, cujus contrarium ex scripto isto Papiæ probat. In hoc scripto, inducit Papiam non tam attendentem Lectioni Scripturarum, quàm relationibus Seniorum qui cum Apostolis conversati sunt. Quid hic fit? multa fabulosa, inquit habet tanquam ex viva relatione ad se relata. Notetur igitur quam vim illa Downami habeant, Eusebius non ex suo cerebro dixit, Timotheum Ephesi episcopum fuisse, sed ex prædecessorum relatione.
units.tr: If someone falsely asserted from ancient history that there were two Johns, namely the Apostle John and John the Elder, of whom the one wrote the first Epistle of John, and the other the two later Epistles and the Apocalypse, could he not also falsely assert from ancient history that Timothy was bishop of Ephesus and Titus bishop of Crete? In matters of fact, who among those who preceded Eusebius is more reliable than Irenaeus? Yet he erred, says Eusebius, in saying that Papias had seen the Apostles, which the Papias writing itself proves to be the opposite. In this writing Papias is introduced as attending not so much to the reading of the Scriptures as to the reports of the elders who had lived with the Apostles. What is the upshot? He has many fabulous things, which he says he received as if from a living report. Let it be noted, then, how little force that argument of Downame has: Eusebius did not say out of his own head that Timothy was bishop of Ephesus, but from the report of his predecessors.

units.la: Historia Petri Romæ crucifixi, quid incertius vel ipsius Math. Sutclivij judicio? Hanc tamen non solum ex scriptis Procli & Dionysij Corinthij, sed etiam ex Petri tumulo, qui usq; ad illius ætatem, ostendi Romæ solebat, probat Euebsius lib.2.c.25. Objicit hunc tumulum Bellarminus, & addit semper creditum fuisse, Petrum Romæ esse mortuum usq; ad Wiclephi tempora. Quid ad hoc Sutclivius? Quasi vero inquit, credula plebs non etiam nuper legendas de Georgio & Catherina & Tecla, & alijs suis commentitijs veras esse crediderunt? Audis Sutclivium, historicos ab Eusebio citatos, imò & historiam Eusebij ipsam, hac quidem in re cum nuperis legendis commentitijs comparantem. Iacobum Apostolum à Christo Salvatore & Apostolis Hierosolymorum episcopum constitutum fuisse, quid vanius? Ita tamen Eusebius lib.7.c.18. Sedem Jacobi Apostoli-- ad hoc usq; temporis servatam, fratres istic qui successione ordinaria subsecuti sunt, omnibus manifestè monstraunt. Miraculum Narcisci aquam in oleum vertentis, ad alendas lampidas in vigilia Paschatis, quam inepte fictum? Ita tamen Eusebius, lib.6.c.8. Apud quamplurimos illic fratres tam prolixo tempore inde ad nos usque exiguum aliquod illius miraculi documentum asservari ferunt. Ad extremum notetur censura Ioh. Bridgefij episcopi Oxoniensis de Irenæo. Irenæus inquit quanquam Apostolis propinquus (certè Eusebio longe propinquior) & ad Romam ex proposito peregrinatus fuerit, & ibi archiva scrutatus: in Petro tamen ab alijs decipi potuit, sicut in rebus alijs deceptus erat. Ita nihil solidi ex historicis concluditur, nec quidem dum veteribus historijs & monumentis adjuvantur: quid ni igitur ad scripturas solas confugiamus, ad exemplar Guilielmi Barloi, qui cum antiquitate, patribus, concilijs urgeretur, ita ab his omnibus ad scripturas provocat. Quod ad antiquitatem, eam judicem poscimus, sic ut ea sit ad quam provocat Ignatius. Quod ad historias: nullae illius potiores, quàm quae illius digito scribuntur, qui antiquus dierum est. Quod ad patres: nemo illo prior, quem vocat Iustinus patrem patrum, is est sanctus Paulus. Quod ad Concilia, nulla credantur quàm Synodus Apostolorum.
units.tr: What is more uncertain than the history of Peter being crucified at Rome, even by the judgment of Matthew Sutcliffe? Yet Eusebius proves this, book 2, chapter 25, not only from the writings of Proclus and Dionysius of Corinth, but also from Peter's tomb, which was shown at Rome down to their age. Bellarmine objects to this tomb, and adds that it was always believed that Peter died at Rome, down to the time of Wycliffe. What does Sutcliffe say to this? As if indeed, he says, the credulous common people did not also believe that the recently read legends about George and Catherine and Thecla, and other fabrications of their own, were true? You hear Sutcliffe, who compares the historians cited by Eusebius, and even Eusebius's own history, in this matter with the recent fabricated legends. That James the Apostle was appointed by Christ the Saviour and the Apostles as bishop of Jerusalem: what is more empty? Yet Eusebius says so, book 7, chapter 18: The see of the Apostle James, kept down to this time, shows plainly to all that the brothers who succeeded there in ordinary succession... The miracle of Narcissus turning water into oil, to feed the lamps on the vigil of Easter: how clumsily it is invented! Yet Eusebius, book 6, chapter 8: Among very many brothers there, they say, some small record of that miracle has been kept from that time right down to us. Finally, let us note the judgment of John Bridges, bishop of Oxford, on Irenaeus: Irenaeus, although he was near the Apostles (certainly far nearer than Eusebius), and although he deliberately travelled to Rome and searched the archives there, could nevertheless be deceived by others about Peter, just as he was deceived in other matters. Thus nothing solid is concluded from the historians, nor indeed while they are supported by ancient histories and monuments. Why then should we not flee to the Scriptures alone, following the example of William Barlow, who, when pressed with antiquity, the Fathers and the councils, appeals from all of these to the Scriptures? As for antiquity, we demand that it be judged by that standard to which Ignatius appeals. As for histories: none is more authoritative than those written by the finger of Him who is the Ancient of Days. As for the Fathers: no one is earlier than him whom Justin calls the father of fathers, namely Saint Paul. As for councils: none should be believed more than the Council of the Apostles.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII.

units.la: Argumentum VII. Ab historicorum in his rebus inscitia.
units.tr: Argument VII. From the ignorance of historians on these matters.

units.la: ARgumentum nostrum septimum, ab inscitia historicorum circa eas materias faćti quæ ecclesiæ gubernationem quàm proximè attingunt. Quàm illud falsum Ambrosij, initio laicos indiscriminatim & prædicasse & baptizasse, donec functiones ecclesiasticæ in ordinem redigerentur? Loquitur (inquit) Whitgiftus de eis qui vocationem nonnullam habuerant: sed consulantur ipsa verba Ambrosij, qui hunc morem cessasse dicit, quamprimùm homines vocari cæperant. Quàm frigida illa de Simeone fabula apud Eusebium? I.3.c.11. post Martyrium Iacobi, rumor est Apostolos & discipulos Domini qui tum in vita superstites erant, in unū undiq; cum cognatis Domini esse congregatos: & Simeonem Cleopæ filium, sede paræciæ Hierosolymitanæ dignum iudicasse? Tanquam rem certam narrat Eusebius ex Clem. Alexandrino, Iohanne Apostolum post reditum ab exilio, abijsse ad vicina gentium loca, ut partim constitueret Episcopos, partim totas ecclesias componeret, partim clerum eligeret ex his quos Spiritus sanctus indicasset. Credit hoc Bilsonus, & inde elicit, vocationem ministrorum per sortes, in Ecclesiæ primordijs in more fuisse: quo indicio, perspici licet ex iure Canonico, quod ex patribus multis probat, electionem ministrorum per sortes illicitam esse. Insto postremò in eis quæ ex Philone Iudæo produxit Eusebius Scribit Philo (inquit) quo pacto præsideant inter eos ij quibus ecclesiastica commissa sunt ministeria, diaconatus etiam, & quæ supra cunctos eminent Episcopatus præsidentia. Hæc & citat & approbat, imò & pro Episcopo Hierarchico urget Io. Bridgesius. Quâ fide? Consulatur etenim vel unus Ioh. Reynolds noster, satis ille supraq; ostendit Philonem Iudæum non fuisse Christianum, eumq; de Christianis hæc minimè scripsisse, sed tantummodò de Essæis Iudaicis. Atque certè tam verum est Episcopos Hierarchicos ab initio fuisse, atque Apostolos convenisse ad Simeonem ordinandum in episcopum, & Iohannem clericos elexisse per sortes, & Philonem denique Iudæum de Episcopis Christianis Hierarchicis scripsisse. Verum nempe est, quod habet Whitakerus, quos Eusebius Episcopos vocat in Ecclesia prima, non nisi singularum ecclesiarum pastores fuisse, & presbyteros fuisse ex more & consuetudine scripturarum Phil. 1.1. Neque desunt hujus veritatis vestigia quædam in ipso Eusebio: nam cum non loquitur a se sed veteres citat, apparet primò presbyteros tantum fuisse in aliorum scriptis ab ipso citatis, qui in suis Episcopi nominantur.
units.tr: My seventh argument is drawn from the ignorance of historians about those matters of fact which bear most closely on the government of the Church. How false is that claim of Ambrose's, that at first laymen indiscriminately both preached and baptized, until ecclesiastical functions were brought into order? "Whitgift speaks" (he says) "of those who had some kind of calling." But let the words of Ambrose himself be consulted, who says that this custom ceased as soon as men had begun to be called. How flimsy is that story about Simeon in Eusebius (3.11)? After the martyrdom of James, there is a rumour that the Apostles and the disciples of the Lord who were then still alive gathered together from every quarter with the relatives of the Lord, and that they judged Simeon, son of Clopas, worthy of the see of the Jerusalem congregation. Eusebius relates it as a certain fact, on the authority of Clement of Alexandria, that the Apostle John, after his return from exile, went off to the neighbouring regions of the nations, partly to appoint bishops, partly to set in order whole churches, partly to choose clergy from those whom the Holy Spirit had pointed out. Bilson believes this, and from it infers that the calling of ministers by lot was customary in the beginnings of the Church. From this one may see, by the canon law, which he proves from many Fathers, that the election of ministers by lot is unlawful. Finally, I press the passage Eusebius produced from the Jewish writer Philo: "Philo writes" (he says) "how those to whom the ecclesiastical ministries are committed preside among them, and also the deacons, and the presidency of the bishop, who rises above all others." Eusebius both cites this and approves it, and John Bridges even urges it on behalf of the hierarchical bishop. On what grounds? Let our own John Reynolds be consulted, at least: he has sufficiently shown, and more than sufficiently, that Philo the Jew was not a Christian and did not write these things about Christians, but only about the Jewish Essenes. And indeed it is as true that hierarchical bishops existed from the beginning, and that the Apostles met to ordain Simeon as bishop, and that John chose clerics by lot, and that Philo the Jew wrote about Christian hierarchical bishops, as it is that the bishops whom Eusebius calls bishops in the primitive Church were only the pastors of single congregations, and were elders by the custom and usage of the Scriptures (Phil. 1.1). Nor are some traces of this truth lacking in Eusebius himself. For when he does not speak on his own account but cites the ancients, it appears, first, that in the writings of others which he cites, only elders are mentioned, though in their own writings they are called bishops.

units.la: 2 Hoc ipsum Bellarminus ipse fatetur alibi: primos nempe Episcopos Romanos ex consuetudine illorum temporum fuisse presbyteros appellatos. Citat verò Eusebium lib.5.c.23. Vbi non ab Eusebio quidem ipso (expectandum etenim ab Episcopo qui annis 300. vixerat hoc non est) sed ab Irenaeo apud Eusebium, antiqui Episcopi etiam Romani, semel,bis,iterum, presbyteri appellantur. Qui ante Soterem presbyteri Ecclesiae praefuerant, Anicetum dicimus & Pium,& Hyginum,& Telesephorum,& Xystum,&c. presbyteri illi qui te praecesserunt &c. Polycarpus Aniceto non suasit: qui sibi presbyterorum quibus successerat consuetudinem servandam esse dicebat. Haec Eusebius dum Irenaei verba refert: quae ipse de Ecclesiae praesidibus,id est,sermone suo,Episcopis interpretatur. Similis locus est lib.3.c.36. ubi Papiae scripta recitat; Episcoporum mentio nulla,sed presbyterorum tantum. Quae aliquando à presbyteris didici. Vbi quisquam venit qui presbyterorum verba exquirebat. Quid Aristion,& Presbyter Iohannes discipuli Domini dixerint, &c. Haec itaque cum sint,non potest solidum pro Episcopis Hierarchicis, argumentum ab Eusebio sumi: ut qui Episcopos appellare soleat, qui in prima ecclesia presbyteri tantum & fuerunt,& appellabantur.
units.tr: Bellarmine himself admits this elsewhere: that the first Roman bishops were called elders, according to the custom of those times. He cites Eusebius, book 5, chapter 23, where, not from Eusebius himself (for one could not expect this from a bishop who lived about three hundred years later), but from Irenaeus, as quoted by Eusebius, the ancient Roman bishops also are called elders, once, twice, and again. "Those who had gone before Soter as elders presiding over the Church, we name Anicetus, and Pius, and Hyginus, and Telesphorus, and Xystus, etc. Those elders who went before you, etc. Polycarp did not persuade Anicetus; for he said that the custom of the elders to whom he had succeeded was to be kept." Eusebius says this while reporting the words of Irenaeus, which he himself interprets of the presidents of the Church, that is, in his own language, bishops. A similar passage is in book 3, chapter 36, where he recites the writings of Papias. There is no mention of bishops, but only of elders: "Things which I have at some time learned from the elders. When someone came who was searching out the words of the elders: what Aristion and the elder John, the disciples of the Lord, had said, etc." Since these things are so, no solid argument for hierarchical bishops can be drawn from Eusebius, since he is accustomed to call bishops those who in the primitive Church were only, and were called, elders.

units.la: CAP. XXIX.
units.tr: CHAP. XXIX.

units.la: Argumentum VIII. ab incerto medio historicorum ecclesiasticorum.
units.tr: Argument VIII, from the uncertain medium of the ecclesiastical historians.

units.la: ARgumentum nostrum octavum,ab incerto medio sumitur,quo usi Historici Ecclesiastici sunt, in eis materijs facti recensendis,quae aetatibus superioribus acciderunt,praedecessorum nempe suorum relatione. Credi vult Geo. Downamus ecclesiasticis historicis, quando testimonium ferunt de materijs facti in aetatibus superioribus: quoniam ex cerebro suo non finxerunt, sed relationes eorum qui praecesserunt secuti sint. Quam verò hoc postulatu iniquum sit, ostendit Tertullianus, Natura famae omnibus nota est. Vestrum est. Fama malum, quo non velocius ullum. An verò famae credat nisi inconsiderati? Quia sapiens non credit incerto. Quod ab uno aliquando principe exorta sit, necesse est exinde & in traduces linguarum & aurium serpat. Dicitur de Christo Esa.11.3. non judicabit secundum auditum aurium suarum: qui fit igitur,ut ex historicis Ecclesiasticis, secundum auditum aurium suarum loquentibus & scribentibus, hanc controversiam de re Hierarchia iudicari postulat? Rectè ipse historicus Socrates. Fabula inquit nunquam bis narratur quin duplo longior evadat. Exemplo vel ipse sit. Quam incredibile etenim quod narrat de miraculo Serapionis lib. 1.c.8. Hoc tamen suis ipsis auribus se audivisse testatur,imò à Ruffino accepisse. Objicit Bellarminus eodem fere modo quo Downamus,de rebus antiquis, errores non fingi quantum ad summam,quum celebres sunt,qualis traditio de Petri ad Romam adventu est. Respondet Franciscus Iunius id quod iam nos. Quam multi praepositae dant operam, hic memoriae nostrae ut res palam gestas obscurent
units.tr: Our eighth argument is drawn from an uncertain middle term, which the ecclesiastical historians used when they recorded matters of fact that happened in earlier ages, namely by relying on the reports of their predecessors. George Downame wants the ecclesiastical historians to be believed when they bear witness to matters of fact in earlier ages, since they did not invent these from their own brains but followed the accounts of those who had gone before. How unfair this demand is, Tertullian shows: The nature of rumour is known to all. It is yours. Rumour is an evil than which none is swifter. Would anyone believe rumour unless he were thoughtless? For a wise man does not believe the uncertain. Because it arose at some time from a single source, it necessarily creeps on from the tongues and ears of one transmitter to another. It is said of Christ, Isa. 11.3: he shall not judge according to the hearing of his ears. How is it, then, that Downame asks that this controversy about the matter of hierarchy be decided by ecclesiastical historians, who speak and write according to the hearing of their ears? The historian Socrates rightly says: A story, he says, is never told twice without becoming twice as long. Let Socrates himself serve as the example. How incredible is what he relates about the miracle of Serapion, Book 1, ch. 8! Yet he testifies that he heard it with his own ears, indeed that he received it from Rufinus. Bellarmine objects, in much the same way as Downame, that about ancient matters errors are not invented in the main point when they are well known, as is the tradition of Peter's coming to Rome. Francis Junius answers what we also say: How many people take pains to bury in a cloud of lies the things that were openly done in our memory

units.la: Lib.2. c.7. §.126. rent sepeliant q; mendaciorum nubes; Qui I sibi in republica historici partium singularum non arrogaverunt? Quid non arrogant ecclesiastici in religionis causâ? Nam etiam res una quae palam geritur suo tempore & loco, eadē clam eos solet esse, qui tempore & loco sunt longinquiores: ut nihil de eis dicam qui animis absunt quàm longissimè. Haec nostri adversus Papistas respondere coguntur: neque ut opinor cuiquam aequo displicent. Quòd si item narrationes eorum qui eodem seculo vivunt incertę sint: quanto magis historicorum Ecclesiasticorum quando de aetatibus antecedentibus testimonium ferunt?
units.tr: ......and to bury in a cloud of lies. Who among the historians have not claimed for themselves the side of particular parties in the commonwealth? What do ecclesiastical writers not claim in a matter of religion? For even one thing done openly at its own time and place is usually hidden from those who are more remote in time and place, not to mention those who are as far away as possible in their minds. Our side is compelled to answer these things against the Papists, and, I think, they do not displease anyone who is fair. But if the narratives of those who live in the same century are uncertain, how much more uncertain are those of the ecclesiastical historians when they bear witness about earlier ages?

units.la: 2 Audiatur Daniel Chamierus: num ille alio argumento fabulam de certamine Petri cum Simone Mago explodit, quàm hoc nostro! testimonia scilicet Egesippi, Arnobij, Damasi, Cyrilli, Epiphanij, Theodoreti, Ambrosij, Hieronymi, Sulpitij, Gregorij, Turonensis, Eusebij, Marini, Augustini, quos Bellarminus colligit, insufficientia esse, quòd multis seculis post eam rem gestam vixerint. Vide quantam historicorum cohortem profligat iste telo nostro: quod si in illo reprehenderit nullus, nec adeo in nos exęstuet Bancroftus, quod in causa Hierarchiae historicos repudiemus judices, quòd longè post primam Polyteiae Ecclesiasticae institutionem vixerint? Sed Hierarchici forte nostri in hoc certamine potiores. Prodeat igitur in scenam Iohannes Bridgesius Episcopus Oxoniensis: qui nunc ex eo lapsum Irenaeum in aetate Christi gravissimè dicit, propterea quòd relationes & traditiones antiquorum incautius veneratus esset? Prodeat deinde Mat. Sutclivius: qui de Petri ad Romam adventu agens, cum historicorum consensu confirmato, non dubitavit, hoc nostrum responsum tanquam murum aeneum papistis objicere. Historicis nempe istis fidem adhibendam non esse, quia nihil nisi audita referant, ut qui seculis posterioribus longè floruerint. Hic crebro inculcat. Audita & famâ recepta narrant, quae nihil probant praeter incertam famam. Irenaeus de Petro tantum quae famâ divulgata tradit. Eusebius nihil praeter auditum loquitur. Arnobius non aliter narrat, quàm alij à quibus ea prius acceperat. Epiphanius traditionem veterum memoriae prodit. Chrysostomus & Orosius audita tantum narrant. Antonius multas credit & narrat fabulas. Quid Damasius, Isidorus, & Audo de hac re scripserint, non multum refert: res enim vetustate obsoletas narrant. Omnes audita narrant nullus visa: quis autem credat testibus de auditu deponentibus? Egesippus & Chronici Eusebiani author, & Origenes apud Eusebium, & alij etiam patres communem famam sequuti sunt—sed nos testimonia certa & indubitata flagitamus. Iohannes Reynoldus è numero Hierarchicorum eximendus quidem est: non tamen illius judicium Hierarchicis contemnendum. Is autem id Eusebio accidere posse dicit, quod habet Thucidides lib. 3. A manu in manum de eis quę ante sua tempora gesta sunt famas sequuntur ἀκοαστῶς: absque ulla examinatione, & probatione. Hunc cum audis, & Henrici etiam Paraei Episcopi Glocestrensis sententiam audis qui hunc Iohannis Reynoldi transtulit.
units.tr: 2 Let Daniel Chamier be heard. Does he explode the fable of Peter's contest with Simon Magus by any other argument than this one of ours? Namely, that the testimonies of Hegesippus, Arnobius, Damasus, Cyril, Epiphanius, Theodoret, Ambrose, Jerome, Sulpicius, Gregory of Tours, Eusebius, Marinus and Augustine, whom Bellarmine collects, are insufficient because they lived many centuries after the event. See what a crowd of historians this man routs with our weapon! If no one has censured him for that, why should Bancroft fume against us because, in the cause of hierarchy, we reject the historians as judges, since they lived long after the first institution of the ecclesiastical polity? But perhaps our Hierarchists are the stronger in this contest. Let John Bridges, bishop of Oxford, come forward onto the stage: he who now says that Irenaeus went badly wrong about the age of Christ, most seriously, because he had too incautiously venerated the reports and traditions of the ancients? Then let Matthew Sutcliffe come forward, who, when treating of Peter's coming to Rome and confirming it by the agreement of the historians, did not hesitate to throw our answer at the Papists as a brazen wall. That is, that no faith is to be placed in those historians, because they report nothing but what they have heard, as men who flourished in later centuries. He repeatedly drives this home: They narrate what they have heard and received by report, which proves nothing but an uncertain rumour. Irenaeus transmits about Peter only what has been spread abroad by rumour. Eusebius says nothing but what he has heard. Arnobius narrates no differently than others from whom he had received it earlier. Epiphanius hands down the tradition of the men of old. Chrysostom and Orosius narrate only what they have heard. Antonius believes and narrates many fables. What Damasus, Isidore and Audo wrote about this matter does not matter much, for they narrate things made obsolete by age. All narrate what they have heard, none what they have seen; and who would believe witnesses who depose from hearsay? Hegesippus, the author of the Chronicle of Eusebius, Origen in Eusebius, and other Fathers too followed common report, but we demand certain and indubitable testimonies. John Reynolds is indeed to be exempted from the number of the Hierarchists, yet his judgment is not to be scorned by the Hierarchists. He says that what Thucydides records can happen to Eusebius: They follow reports of things done before their own time, passing from hand to hand, [ἀκοαστῶς] without any examination or proof. When you hear this man, you also hear the opinion of Henry Parry, bishop of Gloucester, who translated this of John Reynolds.

units.la: CAP XXX. Argumentum nostrum nonum ab Historicorum more loquendi.
units.tr: CAP XXX. Our ninth argument, from the way historians speak.

units.la: ARgumentum nostrum nonum & ultimum, ab historicorum more sumitur: nempe ut pro more sui temporis & loqui & sentire soleant: ad quam nostram responsionem mirum est, quantum Hierarchici excandescant. Bancroftus ita.
