Aut Patres nobis illorum sensu exponendi sunt, sicut pater omnium expositionum ejusmodi, illud psalmi exposuit: Angelis suis mandavit de te: aut dicent eos fuisse non nisi homines, quod& locuti sunt prout aetas in qua vixerant requirebat: quod falsè scripserint, & multi huiusmodi. Quasi non aliter sentiendum de eis esset, quam de hominibus scenae temporique servientibus, de palponibus qui hominibus placere student, de seductoribus, de viris denique ambitiosis. Rursus, Sozomenus & Volusianus, inquit Cartwrightus, scripserint non juxta id quod res erat, sed juxta consuetudinem & morem aetatis suae in qua scripserunt, quasi dicerent mentiebantur. Sequerentur ista si de industria contra scientiam atque conscientiam suam se seculo suo accomodassent: jam cum per errorem suae aetatis torrente arrepti fuerint, non magis mentiri, aut tempori servire dicendi patres sunt, atque ipse Bancroftus, qui errore simili occaecatus, eam ecclesiae regendae formam sub Apostolis extitisse putat qui nunc in Anglia viget. Ita ratiocinatur Bellarminus. Multis jam seculis soli Clerici primarij eligunt, quod tamen fieri non potuisset si jure divino omnes clerici electores fuissent. En ratiocinationem jam Hierarchicis familiarem: multis seculis & jam hodie Hierarchia recepta est: ergo contraria disciplina de jure divino minimè est. Luditur aequivocatione inquit Iunius. Nam aliud ex facto aliud ex jure possumus. Ex jure quidem divino fieri non potuit, sed ex facto potuit & revera factum est a Pontificijs, prout nullus ordo in rebus humanis institui potest, quin brevi adnascatur vitium improbitate hominum. Atqui si vitiosum a more praesentis nostrique seculi argumentari: cur non & a more seculi etiam in quo patres & historici floruerunt: cum tam illi erroribus suae aetatibus noxij fuerint, quemadmodum qui hodie vivunt. Exempla nonnulla inspiciamus.
units.tr: Our ninth and last argument is taken from the way historians speak, namely that they usually both speak and think according to the custom of their own time. It is remarkable how much the Hierarchicals fume at this answer of ours. Bancroft says: Either the Fathers must be expounded to us in their own sense, as the father of all such expositions expounded that verse of the psalm, "He hath given his angels charge over thee"; or they will say that they were nothing but men, and that they spoke as the age in which they lived required, and that they wrote falsely, and many such things. As if they were to be thought of no differently than men who serve the stage and the times, flatterers who strive to please men, seducers, and, in short, ambitious men. Again: Sozomen and Volusian, says Cartwright, wrote not according to what the thing was, but according to the custom and manner of the age in which they wrote, as if he were saying that they lied. These things would follow if they had deliberately accommodated themselves to their age against their knowledge and conscience. But since they were carried away by the stream of their age through error, the Fathers are no more to be called liars or time-servers than Bancroft himself, who, blinded by a similar error, thinks that the form of church government which now flourishes in England existed under the Apostles. Bellarmine reasons thus: For many ages now only the chief clergy have elected, which could not have happened if by divine right all the clergy had been electors. Here is an argument already familiar to the Hierarchicals: for many centuries, and even today, the Hierarchy has been received; therefore the contrary discipline is by no means of divine right. It is a play on words, says Junius. For we can speak of one thing as a matter of fact and of another as a matter of right. By right indeed it could not have happened by divine law, but as a matter of fact it could, and in truth it was done by the Papists, since no order can be instituted among human affairs without vice soon creeping in through the wickedness of men. But if it is a fallacy to argue from the custom of our present age, why not also from the custom of the age in which the Fathers and the historians flourished? For they were as liable to be harmed by the errors of their own times as those who live today. Let us look at some examples.

units.la: 2 Disputat Sanctus Chrysostomus more prorsus Bellarmini apud Tho.Bilsonum hom.14.in Act.1. [Quamnam dignitatem & qualem χειροτονίαν hij acceperint necessarium est intelligere. Num Diaconorum? At hoc in Ecclesijs (nunc) non est: sed ad praesbyteros pertinet ista dispensatio (videlicet viduis curandis) destinata. Quare hoc nomen (aut munus quod acceperunt isti septem) neq; Diaconorum plane & manifeste, neque presbyterorum fuisse existimo.] Spondit Downnamus, si locum vel unum ex scripturis aut patribus planum & manifestum pro disciplina reformata adducere possimus, se de tota causa cessurum. Intelligit vero ita planum & manifestum, qui nulla sophistica eludi possit, qualem pro ipsa deitate Christi contra Arianos, patres, aut Evangelici jam hodie in gravissimis fidei controversijs adducere nunquam potuerunt. Alioquin loci æquis omnibus plani & manifesti, quam plurimi adduci possunt: sicuti pro Diaconis tantum eleemosynarijs, 6.cap.libri Actorum, locum planum & manifestum esse dicimus. Chrysostomo planus & manifestus minime est. Quid ita? quia praxis ecclesiæ contraria est: ita enim ratiocinatur, non ita nunc est in ecclesia: quare ego contrarium existimo. Nonne potuit Bilsonum sophisma hujusmodi approbare? aut si hujus puduisse non oportuit, nonne tamen pudere debuit, diffiteri patres, ex pede præsenti antiquitatem metiri solitos? Certè si Chrysostomus hic ex more sui seculi arguat, adversus apertam scripturæ lucem: cum ex more sui seculi sensisse & scripsisse contra scripturam consequetur. Sed non Chrysostomus tantum hoc morbo laboravit. Ambrosius etenim in Ephes.4. ex more sui seculi & scripsit & sensit, quum per Apostolos intelligit Episcopos, per prophetas presbyteros, per Evangelistas Diaconos: nempe tales, quales suo tempore in Ecclesia extitisse viderat. An negari potest, ex more sui seculi hac interpretatione & sensisse & scripsisse Ambrosium? Certe non negat Iohannes Bridgesius cujus ista verba sunt. Applicat (inquit) hæc omnia munera (nempe quæ Ephes. 4. reperiuntur) ad morem Ecclesiæ, quæ fuit post tempora Apostolorum. Quinimo non negat Hadrianus Saravia, ingenuè etenim confitetur, Ambrosius applicat illa omnia munera ad statum Ecclesiæ sui temporis: quam proprie non disputo. 3 Disputat Whitgiftus nomen Archiepiscopi ante concilium Nicænum extitisse. Quid ita? quia Petrus Alexandrinus qui ante concilium Nicænum vixit, ab Epiphanio Archiepiscopus appellatur. Respondemus, loqui Epiphanium pro more sui seculi: quia Archiepiscopatus sedes suo tempore Alexandriæ fuit; ideo putavit & veteres etiam ejusdem urbis Episcopos, similes Archiepiscopos fuisse. Num fallimur? Consule igitur Eusebium: apud quem hic ipse Petrus, non Archiepiscopus, sed tantum Episcopus appellatur. Simili errore Eusebius ipse tenebatur, episcopos suæ ætatis videns: veteres Pastores similes episcopos fuisse credidit, qui tamen tantummodo presbyteri erant, ut supra ex parte demonstratum. Idem de cæteris sentiendum prorsus est: ut de quibus non absque causa Daniel Chamierus ita conqueratur. Solent plerumque vulgi consuetudines vitiosæ, etiam magnos interdum viros abripere, ut non contradicant, imò verò non aliter sentiant quàm plurimos vident credere. Instat in monachatu: de quo mirum apud priscos silentium: cum verò sub Constantini tempore vel paulo prius emergere cepisset: tum subitò Apostolica traditio evasit, sub Apostolorum temporibus vel ipsius iudicio floruit: ab ipsis deniq; Apostolis descendit: ut verum sit in hujusmodi moribus, quod olim à Patercolo dictum. Non ibi consistunt exempla unde cœperunt ceperunt: sed quamlibet in tenuem recepta tramitem, latissime evagandi sibi viam faciunt, & ubi semel à recto aberratum est in præceps pervenitur. Quæ nebula oculos Hierarchicos obsidet, ut in episcopis videre nequeant id fieri potuisse saltem, revera factum esse, quod vident in monachis & indignantur? Utcunque sit, responsionem nostram, locutos nempè patres esse ex sui seculi more, moremque præsentem illis nebulam offudisse, ut episcopos perinde ac monachos ab Apostolis descendisse crederent, ridere Hierarchici nequeunt: nisi & præcipuos scriptores nostros ridere velint, qui eâdem responsione adversus Papistas crebrò uti adiguntur.
units.tr: 2. Chrysostom, in his fourteenth homily on Acts 1, as quoted by Thomas Bilson, argues in exactly the manner of Bellarmine: [It is necessary to understand what dignity and what ordination [χειροτονίαν] they received. Was it that of deacons? But that does not exist in the churches now; that dispensation (namely, the care of widows) belongs to the elders. Therefore I judge that this name, or the office which those seven received, was neither plainly and manifestly that of deacons nor that of elders.] Downame promised that if we could bring forward a single passage from Scripture or the Fathers that is plain and manifest in favour of the reformed discipline, he would yield the whole cause. By "plain and manifest" he means such a passage as cannot be evaded by any sophistry, of the kind that neither the Fathers against the Arians, nor the Evangelicals today, have ever been able to bring forward in the most serious controversies of faith, even for the deity of Christ. Otherwise, very many passages can be cited which are plain and manifest to all fair-minded people, just as we say that the sixth chapter of the Acts is a plain and manifest passage for deacons who were only almoners. To Chrysostom it is by no means plain and manifest. Why so? Because the practice of the Church is contrary to it. For he reasons thus: It is not so now in the Church; therefore I judge the contrary. Could Bilson not have approved a sophism of this kind? Or if he should not have been ashamed of it, ought he not at least to have been ashamed to deny that the Fathers were accustomed to measure antiquity by the present foot? Certainly, if Chrysostom here argues according to the custom of his age, against the plain light of Scripture, it follows that he thought and wrote against Scripture according to the custom of his age. But Chrysostom was not the only one afflicted with this disease. Ambrose, in his commentary on Ephesians 4, both wrote and thought according to the custom of his age, when he understands by the Apostles bishops, by the prophets elders, and by the evangelists deacons: namely, such as he had seen existing in the Church in his own time. Can it be denied that Ambrose both thought and wrote in this interpretation according to the custom of his age? John Bridges certainly does not deny it, and these are his words: He applies all these offices (namely those found in Ephesians 4) to the custom of the Church which came after the times of the Apostles. Indeed Hadrian Saravia does not deny it either, for he frankly confesses: Ambrose applies all those offices to the state of the Church of his own time, which I do not properly dispute. 3. Whitgift argues that the name of archbishop existed before the Council of Nicaea. Why so? Because Peter of Alexandria, who lived before the Council of Nicaea, is called archbishop by Epiphanius. We reply that Epiphanius spoke according to the custom of his own age, because the archiepiscopal see was at Alexandria in his time; therefore he thought that the bishops of the same city in earlier times were similar archbishops. Are we mistaken? Consult Eusebius, then, in whose work this same Peter is called not archbishop but only bishop. Eusebius himself was under a similar error: seeing the bishops of his own age, he believed that the ancient ministers were similar bishops, although they were only elders, as has been shown in part above. The same must be thought of the rest, about whom Daniel Chamier complains not without reason: Bad customs of the common people usually carry away even great men at times, so that they do not contradict, indeed they do not think otherwise than they see most people believing. Consider monasticism: there is a remarkable silence about it among the ancients; but when it began to emerge under Constantine or a little earlier, suddenly it turned into apostolic tradition, and it flourished under the times of the Apostles or by their judgement, and finally it descended from the Apostles themselves. So it is true of customs of this kind what was once said by Paterculus: Examples do not stay where they began, but once received into even a slender track, they make for themselves a very wide path of wandering, and once one has strayed from the right way, one plunges headlong. What mist besieges the eyes of the Hierarchicals, so that they cannot see that what they see in the monks and are indignant about could at least have happened, and indeed did happen, among the bishops? However that may be, the Hierarchicals cannot laugh at our answer, namely that the Fathers spoke according to the custom of their own age, and that the custom of the present time has cast that mist over them, so that they believed bishops, just as much as monks, to have descended from the Apostles. Unless they also wish to laugh at our chief writers, who are constantly forced to use this same answer against the Papists.

units.la: 4 Obicit Bellarminus Chrysostomum & Oecumenium manus impositionem per presbyterium retulisse ad ordinationem episcoporum: id quod Downamus & reliqui Hierarchici jam hodie arguunt. Quid ad hæc Chamierus? Num responsionis nostræ puduit? Hoc illi sine dubio dixerunt (inquit) ex præjudicio temporis sui, vel potius annuentes presbyteros tum temporis, quod deinceps esset mutatum. Ad Epiphanium a Bellarmino similiter objectum, pro Episcopi maioritate eodem modo respondet. Epiphanius sui temporis consuetudinem tuetur satis frigidè. Similiter ad Hieronymum. Superest Hieronymus, quem manifestum est de suo loqui tempore. Ad patres a Bellarmino productos, qui dicunt Episcopos figuram gerere Apostolorum, presbyteros vero septuaginta discipulorum tantum ita respondet. Etsi consideretur omnes antiquos in ea comparatione consentire, non esse tamen judicium juris divini sed præsentis consuetudinis. Eandem responsionem in rebus aliis scriptores alij adhibere solent. Ecquam enim aliam responsionem habet Whitakerus ad Bernardum de primatu Papæ testantem, quam hanc? Vixit ætate admodum superstitiosa in qua Antichristus utrumque cornu erexerat: & fuit multis illius seculi erroribus infectus. Sic ad patres a Bellarmino prolatos de Antichristo. Dico hos patres communem opinionis errorem sequi. Similiter respondet ad testimonium Prosperi, de Romanæ sedis prærogativa. Prosper dixit Romam esse sedem Petri ex communi opinione. Quoties Matheus Sutclivius ipse Hierarchicus hac responsione usus, ad unanimem patrum consensum de adventu Petri ad urbem Romæ: nos supra ostendimus. Alibi ad Bernardum respondens, & ipsis verbis nostris utitur. Nec obstat quod Bernardus contra est. Ille enim loquitur secundum sui seculi mores, quando antiquata pristina disciplina esset. Hæc qui perpendit, minimè in nobis reprehendet, quod in hisce scriptoribus non potest non admittere. Neque enim ratio ulla est, ut qui temporibus eis vixerunt, in quibus antiquata per Episcoporum maioritatem disciplina fuit, pro eâdem audiantur: quam ut audiantur pro papatu etiam, qui sub papatu vixerunt. Vel ipsius Hadriani Saraviæ est, consuetudinem violentum tyrannum esse, quid miri igitur, si eadem abrepti antiqui patres fuerint? Atque hæc de fundamento Hierarchicorum extraneo octavo: fide nempè & authoritate Historicorum m.
units.tr: 4. Bellarmine objects that Chrysostom and Oecumenius referred the laying on of hands by the presbytery to the ordination of bishops, which Downame and the other Hierarchicals today also argue. What does Chamier say to this? Was he ashamed of our answer? They said this without doubt (he says) out of the prejudice of their own time, or rather agreeing that the elders at that time were such, which afterwards was changed. To what Bellarmine similarly objects from Epiphanius for the greater dignity of bishops, he replies in the same way: Epiphanius defends the custom of his own time quite coldly. Similarly with regard to Jerome: There remains Jerome, who is clearly speaking of his own time. To the Fathers produced by Bellarmine, who say that bishops bear the figure of the Apostles and elders only the figure of the seventy disciples, he replies thus: Even if all the ancients are considered to agree in that comparison, it is nevertheless not a judgement of divine law but of present custom. Other writers are accustomed to use the same answer in other matters. What other answer does Whitaker have to Bernard, who bears witness to the Pope's primacy, than this? He lived in an age exceedingly superstitious, in which Antichrist had raised up both horns, and he was infected with many errors of that age. So too with the Fathers produced by Bellarmine concerning Antichrist: I say that these Fathers followed the common error of opinion. He similarly replies to the testimony of Prosper concerning the prerogative of the Roman see: Prosper said that Rome is the see of Peter according to common opinion. How often Matthew Sutcliffe, himself a Hierarchical, has used this answer in reply to the unanimous consensus of the Fathers on Peter's coming to the city of Rome, we have shown above. Elsewhere, answering Bernard, he uses our very words: Nor does it stand in the way that Bernard is against it. For he speaks according to the customs of his age, when the former discipline had become obsolete. Whoever weighs these things will not blame us for admitting in these writers what we cannot help admitting. For there is no reason why those who lived in times when the discipline had become obsolete through the predominance of bishops should be heard in favour of that same thing, any more than those who lived under the papacy should be heard in its favour. Indeed it is Saravia's own view that custom is a violent tyrant; what wonder, then, if the ancient Fathers were carried away by it? And this is concerning the eighth argument, foreign to the Hierarchicals: namely the trust and authority of the historians.

units.la: CAP. XXXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXI.

units.la: Argumentum Hierarchicorum nonum à jure canonico.
units.tr: The ninth argument of the Hierarchists, from canon law.

units.la: SEquitur nonum, supra quàm reliqua papisticum, jus scilicet canonicum: pro quo ita Bancrofto declamare placet. Ingens latratus est adversus Ecclesiam Anglicanam, quod actu Parliamentario, quædam partes iuris Canonici retinende & ab Episcopis exercende sunt ad commodiorem Ecclesiæ gubernationem: ita ut vel ipsum nomen Iuris Canonici, odio omnium proximum sit, simplici factiosorum multitudine in eam opinionem inclinante, ipsum nomen legis talis, papisticum, illegitimum, & diabolicum esse, unde exclamare solet, crucifige, crucifige, tolle, nolumus eo regi, recipi nolumus. Quod de actu Parliamentario dicit, de eo sic habendum 25. Henric.8.c.19. [statuitur, omnes Canones in vigore solito retinendos, qui legibus & statutis regni Anglicani non sunt contrarij, quique regali prærogativæ non prejudicant.] Hinc author Abstracti, ministros in Anglia non prædicantes, pluralitatem beneficiorum, civilem iurisdictionem in Episcopis, & excommunicationem per Episcopum solum, cum nonnullis abusibus alijs jugulat: quia in jure Canonico sanctiones quædam reperiantur, adversus hæc purgameta, quæ neque regni Anglicani statutis, neq; regiæ prærogativæ adversantur. Violant igitur & ipsi jus Canonicum, pro quo tantopere decertant: imò quod multò magis est, statutum regni, actumq; Parliamentarium violant, cui parere & obedire oportuit. Nos interim quid? Observamus nempè, quod jubet Apostolus. Omnia probate, quod verum est tenete: imò observamus, quod ex hoc præcepto, in sancto Bernardo, Thomas Mortonus Hierarchicus ipse comprobat. [Nec dico præpositorum decreta à subditis dijudicanda esse, ubi nihil jubere deprehenduntur divinis contrarium institutis: sed necessariam esse dico prudentiam, qua advertatur, quid adversatur; & libertatem, qua ingenuè contemnatur] Quid verò? Quædam illæ partes quas meminit Bancroftus, totum iuris Canonici corpus continent: excepta papali jurisdictione, & doctrinâ fidei, & idolatriâ Romanæ Ecclesiæ? Quid igitur, disciplina Ecclesiastica Anglicana tota Canonica est? Ita: & disciplina Canonica tota in regimine Anglicano exercetur, sic ut nihil interest inter Episcopale consistorium Parisiense, & Anglicanum, quod ad canones, quod ad modum procedendi, quod ad instrumenta publica, quod ad officiarios, quod ad litigandi formulas, quod ad reliqua denique attinet, quæ in foro papali externo practicantur.
units.tr: The ninth argument follows, which the Papists press harder than the rest, namely canon law, and for it Bancroft is pleased to declaim thus: There is a great outcry against the Church of England because, by Act of Parliament, certain parts of canon law are to be retained and exercised by the bishops for the more convenient government of the Church. So much so that the very name of canon law is hated above all else, the simple crowd of factious people inclining to the opinion that the very name of such a law is papistical, illegitimate and devilish; whence they are wont to cry out, "Crucify, crucify, away with him, we will not have him to reign over us, we will not have him received." What he says about the Act of Parliament is to be understood as follows, from 25 Henry VIII, c. 19: [it is enacted that all canons are to be retained in their accustomed force, which are not contrary to the laws and statutes of the realm of England, and which do not prejudice the royal prerogative]. Hence the author of the Abstract throttles, along with some other abuses, the non-preaching ministers in England, the pluralities of benefices, civil jurisdiction in bishops, and excommunication by the bishop alone, because certain sanctions are found in canon law against these corruptions, which oppose neither the statutes of the realm of England nor the royal prerogative. They therefore themselves violate the canon law for which they contend so zealously; indeed, what is much worse, they violate the statute of the realm and the Act of Parliament, to which it was fitting that they submit and yield obedience. What then do we do? We observe, of course, what the Apostle commands: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good [1 Thess. 5]. Indeed we observe this precept, which Thomas Morton the Hierarchist himself approves from St Bernard. [I do not say that the decrees of superiors are to be judged by their subjects where they are found to command nothing contrary to divine institutions; but I say that prudence is necessary, by which one notices what is opposed, and freedom, by which one frankly rejects it.] But what then? Do those parts which Bancroft mentions comprise the whole body of canon law, except the papal jurisdiction, the doctrine of faith, and the idolatry of the Roman Church? If so, is the whole ecclesiastical discipline of England canonical? Yes: and the whole canonical discipline is exercised in the English government, so that there is no difference between the episcopal consistory of Paris and the English one, as regards the canons, the manner of proceeding, the public instruments, the officials, the forms of litigation, and, in short, all the rest that is practised in the external papal court.

units.la: CAP. XXXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXII.

units.la: Probatur sex argumentis indignum esse Ecclesiam Christi lege Antichristi regi.
units.tr: It is shown by six arguments that the Church of Christ is unworthily ruled by the law of Antichrist.

units.la: QVàm autem indignum sit ut Ecclesia Christi, jure Antichristi, hunc in modum regatur, hæ sequentes rationes planè faciunt.
units.tr: How unworthy it is that the Church of Christ should be governed in this way, by the law of Antichrist, the following reasons make plain.

units.la: 1 Primò, quod prædicitur de fumo ex Abysso surgente, post datas Papæ infernales claves; id à Thoma Brightmano, ad decretorum & decretalium spurcities extenditur in Ap. 9.2. Nec immeritò; clavis etenim non tantum doctrinam sed & disciplinam etiam continet: quorum posterior nonne per decreta & decretalia in atram noctem convertitur? Certè scripturas in desuetudinem venisse, quin & antiquum etiam jus Canonicum, post hæc scripta à Gratiano, Philippus Mornæus testis est. Per idem inquit tempus Gratianus decretalia consarcinat: non feliciùs quàm Pandectas Justinianus. Aventinus lib.4. nobis author est, ante Gratianum ius canonicum longè diversum fuisse. Etenim inquit, uti est in nostris Bibliothecis sincerum, duas continet partes: Prima, ista sunt universorum conciliorum, quæ quidem recepta esse constat: Altera, Constitutiones & epistolas maximorum Pontificum complectitur, ut quæque gesta fuerunt. Quod utinam ab hoc labore abstinuisset: & hoc interim Eugenius approbat & in omnibus universitatibus legi iubet, haud dubium quia sub unius pontificium iugum universum ecclesiam redigebat. Hic requiritur Petrus Damianus, Evangelium clauditur, & per ora Ecclesiastici ordinis forensia iudicia duxerunt. Huic malo ut medela procuretur, statutum à nostris in Anglia est ne quis juris canonici Doctor, in aliqua Academia crearetur. Quæ mens quæsò huj° statuti, nisi ut promotionis cuiusque spe præcisa, nullus in re tam vili, studia sua bonaque horas collocaret. Videsis igitur quam bonam operam ecclesiæ nostræ locet Bancroftus reliquique Hierarchici, qui iure eo eam regi volunt, quod putei fumum longè lateque usque ab initio diffudit, quod in gratiam Antichristi conlarcinatum erat, in ipsis medijs solis aerisque obnubilati tenebris: quod scripturas earumque studium sepelivit: à quo denique ingenuus quisque per ipsa regni nostri statuta, in suis studijs avocatur?
units.tr: (1) First, what is foretold of the smoke rising out of the Abyss, after the infernal keys were given to the Pope, Thomas Brightman extends to the filth of the decrees and decretals, in Rev. 9.2. And not unjustly: for the key contains not only doctrine but also discipline, and is the latter not turned into thick darkness by the decrees and decretals? That the Scriptures have fallen into disuse, and that even the ancient canon law was lost after the writings of Gratian, Philip Mornay is a witness: At the same time Gratian patched together the decretals, no more happily than Justinian his Pandects. Aventinus, in book 4, is our authority that before Gratian the canon law was very different. For, he says, as there is in our libraries a sound copy, it contains two parts: the first contains the decrees of all the councils, which are plainly accepted; the second contains the constitutions and letters of the greatest Popes, as each was done. Would that he had abstained from this labour! Meanwhile Eugenius approves this and orders it to be read in all universities, no doubt because it was bringing the whole Church under the yoke of one pontiff. Here Peter Damian is also appealed to: The Gospel is shut up, and forensic judgments have taken the place of the mouths of the ecclesiastical order. To remedy this evil, our countrymen in England have enacted that no one be created Doctor of canon law in any university. What, I ask, is the purpose of this statute, except that, with all hope of promotion cut off, no one should spend his studies and good hours on a thing so worthless? You see, then, what a good service Bancroft and the other hierarchs render to our Church, who want it governed by that law, which from the beginning has spread the smoke of the pit far and wide, which was compiled in favour of Antichrist, and which has been obscured by the very darkness of the middle ages, which has buried the Scriptures and the study of them, and from which, finally, every free-born person is called away from his studies by the very statutes of our kingdom.

units.la: 2 Secundo disputamus ab efficienti: quis etenim in regno Christi iuri Antichristi locus? Respondet Whitgiftus ita. Quantum de iure Canonico adversatur scripturis, Antichristianum & diabolicum est: sed quidam in eodem Canones apprimè boni & utiles qui bene recepti possunt. Bonas leges mutuari licet à Turcis & Paganis idololatris: & cur non à papistis etiam? Ante dixi non ipsum rei adinventorem ponderandum esse: si bonum & legitimum sit, eo uti licet, quicunque adinventor fuerit. Primò, falsum est, mutuari leges licere à papistis perinde ac à Turcis: domesticus etenim hostis & dissimulatus aperto nocentior: & conformitas cum papistis (utcunque reclamet Richardus Hookerus) scandalo infirmis
units.tr: (2) Second, we argue from the efficient cause: what place has the law of Antichrist in the kingdom of Christ? Whitgift answers thus: Insofar as the canon law is opposed to the Scriptures, it is antichristian and diabolical; but there are in the same some very good and useful canons which can well be received. It is permitted to borrow good laws from the Turks and pagan idolaters: and why not from the papists too? I said before that the originator of a thing is not to be weighed: if it is good and lawful, it may be used, whoever the originator may be. First, it is false that it is lawful to borrow laws from the papists just as from the Turks: for a domestic enemy, and one who is disguised, is more harmful than an open one; and conformity with the papists (however much Richard Hooker protests) is fuller of scandal to the weak

units.la: Lib.4.s.7. infirmis plenior : & non adversus Turcam ac adversus papam, fertur Spiritus sanctus per Apocalypsim : sed in Bestiam magis quàm in Draconem invehitur. Secundo : non opus habet Ecclesia Dei ut vel à Turcis vel a papistis mutuetur leges : sufficit scriptura, sufficiunt regni nostri politica statuta : si non sufficiant, libertas penes Ecclesiam est, a sese leges condere : sic ut hæc circumcursatio in Ægyptum non video quomodo excusari possit : præsertim cum indignissimum sit ut Christus opem Antichristi hostis sui imploraret : ac si absque istius sordidissimis inventis, suam ecclesiam gubernare nequeat. Tertiò, si lex regis os regis sit, loquitur in disciplina nostra, tamdiu papa; quamdiu illius iura legesque exercentur : sic ut non videam quomodo magis (rebus sic stantibus) Antichristo gratificari valeamus, quam illius ius Canonicum Christi Ecclesiæ imponendo. Respondet D. Cousinus, ius Canonicum exequi nos non tanquam ius papæ, sed tanquam ius proprium nostrumque. At inquam quo iure, ius illius ius nostrum sit : absque non dico necessitate, sed & utilitate ulla?
units.tr: Book 4, s. 7. ...fuller of scandal to the weak: and the Holy Spirit is not sent against the Turk but against the pope, as the Apocalypse shows; it is aimed at the Beast rather than at the Dragon. Second, the Church of God has no need to borrow laws either from the Turks or from the papists: Scripture is sufficient, the political statutes of our kingdom are sufficient; if they should not suffice, the Church has the freedom to make laws for itself. So I do not see how this running about to Egypt can be excused, especially since it is most unworthy that Christ should implore the help of his enemy Antichrist, as if he could not govern his Church without the most filthy inventions of that one. Third, if the law is the mouth of the king, then, in our discipline, the pope speaks for as long as his rights and laws are practised; so that I do not see how, things standing thus, we could more agreeably gratify Antichrist than by imposing his canon law upon the Church of Christ. D. Cousin answers: We enforce canon law not as the right of the pope, but as our own and proper right. But I ask, by what right is his right our right, without any necessity, I do not say, but even any usefulness?

units.la: 3 Tertio, disputamus a materia. Quantum in iure Canonico adversatur scripturis, Antichristianum & diabolicum est: qui fit igitur ut ius Canonicum practicetur, in multis rebus, quæ scripturæ cõtrariantur?Quenā hæ sunt roges?quasi facilè enumerari nõ possint? Ipsa Canonica sive potius papalis Hierarchia, Canonici sive potius papales Ecclesiastici gradus, Canonica sive potius papalis Episcopi iurisdictio : procurationes papisticæ, dispensationes papisticæ, pluralitates papisticæ, nonresidentiæ papisticæ, ceremoniæ papisticæ, excommunicationes papisticæ, ordinationes papisticæ, absolutiones papisticæ, degradationes papisticæ, visitationes papisticæ, oblationes papisticæ, curiæ de facultatibus : sententiam reliquam exhauriat qui vult, me quidem & pudet & piget, hæc carcinomata contrectare. Rectè Budæus. Ius canonicum iuri diuino derogare non potest, iuxta Clementinā. Lex superioris per inferiorē tolli nō potest : in his singulis autē,legē divinâ superiore tollit Anglia,ius Canonicū practicādo.
units.tr: (3) Third, we argue from the matter. Insofar as canon law is opposed to Scripture, it is antichristian and diabolical; how comes it, then, that canon law is practised in many things which are contrary to Scripture? Why should I ask for these? As if they could not easily be enumerated! The canonical, or rather papal, hierarchy itself; the canonical, or rather papal, ecclesiastical grades; the canonical, or rather papal, jurisdiction of the bishop; papistical proctorships, papistical dispensations, papistical pluralities, papistical non-residences, papistical ceremonies, papistical excommunications, papistical ordinations, papistical absolutions, papistical degradations, papistical visitations, papistical oblations, the courts of faculties. Let whoever wishes exhaust the rest of the list; as for me, I am both ashamed and loath to handle these cancers. Budé rightly says: Canon law cannot derogate from divine law, according to the Clementines. The law of the superior cannot be removed by the inferior. But in each of these matters England, by practising canon law, removes the higher divine law.

units.la: 4 Quarto disputamus à forma: in hac etenim juris Canonici praxi mutavit Anglia formam regiminis Ecclesiastici Aristocraticam per presbyterium, in Hierarchicam per Episcopum: idque ut iuri Canonico locus sit. Ita etenim disputat Thomas Bilsonus: excludendi à consistoriis seniores sunt, & à negotiorum Ecclesiasticorum tractatione penitus arcendi. Quid ita? Quia rudes in iure Canonico sunt, & antiquarum constitutionum prorsus ignari. Primo si arcendi à negotiis publicis sunt, qui legum publicarum ignari,cur immiscent se Episcopi rebus civilibus? cū iuris communis ignari sint : quod etiam difficilius cognitu est quam ius Canonicum? Secundo juris Canonici num Episcopi quæso ipsi tam gnari sunt? Si ita: pulchrè statuto Anglicano satisfecerunt, quod ut quisque abstraheret ab hujus Canonici juris studio, DOCTOREM creari juris Canonici precisè prohibuit. At officiales circa se Episcopi habent, respondet Bilsonus, qui juris Canonici periti sunt, & res Ecclesiæ Episcopi nomine administrant, At inquam hoc modo duplicatur peccatum: nam & nostri isti officiales sunt contra verbum Dei ab Antichristo introducti: & peccaret Episcopus si per alios in verbo Dei institutos, officium præstaret: nam officium nullum in verbo Dei demandatur, sine mandato illud ipsum per se exequendi. Tertiò nihil refert si juris Canonici ignari seniores sint: sciunt Canonem illum quem quasi regulam sufficientem commendat Palus. Gal. 6.
units.tr: (4) Fourth, we argue from the form. In this practice of canon law England changed the Aristocratic form of ecclesiastical government, through the presbytery, into the Hierarchical form, through the bishop; and this so that there might be room for canon law. Thomas Bilson argues thus: The elders are to be excluded from the consistories and wholly kept away from the handling of ecclesiastical business. Why so? Because they are untrained in canon law and entirely ignorant of the ancient constitutions. First, if they are to be kept away from public business because they are ignorant of public laws, why do the bishops meddle in civil affairs, when they are ignorant of the common law, which is also harder to know than canon law? Second, are the bishops themselves, I ask, so skilled in canon law? If so, they have satisfied the English statute beautifully, which, in order to withdraw everyone from the study of this canon law, absolutely forbade the creation of a Doctor of canon law. But bishops have officials about them, Bilson replies, who are skilled in canon law and administer the affairs of the Church in the bishop's name. But I say that in this way the sin is doubled: for these officials of ours too are introduced by Antichrist, against the Word of God; and a bishop would sin if he performed his office through others who were instituted in the Word of God, for no office is committed in the Word of God without a command to perform it oneself. Third, it matters nothing whether the elders are ignorant of canon law: they know that canon which Palus commends as a sufficient rule. Gal. 6.

units.la: 5 Quinto disputamus à fine: nullam etenim ob causam aliam pro jure Canonico tanquam pro aris decertant Hierarchici: quàm ut majoritatem suam corroborent, propter quam, presbyter nullus apud nos admittetur, qui non juramento se obstrinxerit, ad Canonicam obedientiam Episcopo præstandam: & ad otium, luxum, auaritiamque suam explendam; ut qui rei tenentur Canonicarum fraudum illarum, quas ita ex Guilielmo Budeo recenset Reynoldus. Vbi boni æquique & benignitatis sinus solebat esse, ibi litium officina capturarumque improbarum. Inde illa formularum aucupia & rituum pontificiorum cautiones, ad circumscribendam familiam domini concinnatæ. Inde multarum compendii præsulibus enata, acceptorum paginas luculenter augentia. Inde itidem sacrilegæ nundinæ earum rerum quæ in commercio humano sine piaculo esse non possunt. Mitto nunc tesseras non modo venialos, sed etiam venales impunitatem scelerum & solutionum sacrarum legum sordida benignitate largientes. Canones melioribus annis factos ut eis velut regulis vita Clericorum dirigeretur, & velut patrum præscriptis posteri formarentur, iam in amusses plumbeas evasisse quis non videt?——Canones pontificis ex usu Ecclesiæ, Antistitum flexibiles plumbei & cerei facti sunt: ut jamdiu instituta majora, & sanctiones pontificiæ non moribus regendis usui esse, sed argentariæ factitandæ authoritatem accommodare videantur.
units.tr: (5) Fifth, we argue from the end: the hierarchs fight for canon law as for their altars for no other reason than to strengthen their majority, on account of which no elder is admitted among us who has not bound himself by oath to render canonical obedience to the bishop, and to satisfy his own idleness, luxury and greed; so that those who are held guilty of those canonical frauds, which Reynolds lists from William Budé, are such as these: Where there used to be the bosom of goodness, fairness and kindness, there is now a workshop of lawsuits and of wicked captures. Hence those hunts for formulas and the precautions of papal ceremonies, contrived to circumvent the household of the lord. Hence arose for the bishops many sources of profit, brilliantly swelling the pages of receipts. Hence likewise the sacrilegious markets of those things which in human commerce cannot be without sin. I pass over now the tokens, which grant impunity for crimes and the release from sacred laws, not only cheap but even for sale, with a filthy kindness. The canons made in better years, so that by them, as by rules, the life of the clergy might be directed, and so that posterity might be formed by the prescriptions of the fathers, who does not see that they have now turned into leaden rulers? ... The canons of the pope, according to the custom of the Church, have become flexible and waxen leaden things in the hands of the bishops: so that the greater institutions and papal sanctions now seem to serve not to govern morals, but to lend authority to the making of money.

units.la: Sextò disputamus ab effectis. Thomas Bilsonus ità. Quæ leges Papæ superstitionem & tyrannidem alebant vel augebant, jampridem, gratia Deo sit, è medio sublatæ sunt. Alias verò, quæ veteris Ecclesiæ disciplinam sapere videntur, si quæritis dissolvere, optarem equidem ut novas antea ab omnibus examinandas proponere quam veteres configere velitis, ne populum perinde legibus solutum, ac presbyteros vestros faciatis. Facilius est evertere Ecclesiam aut Rempublicam, quam erigere: Destruere, quàm ædificare, nisi easdem leges rursus recipiatis, audacter dico, nepotes vestros, ad quartam usque progeniem, nec pacem nec ordinem in Ecclesiis vestris habituros. Vt omittantur cætera, & ad sua loca differantur: satis audax quidem Bilsonus, sed cautus tamen: quintam progeniem meminit, ut haberet quod responderet ad Ecclesias reformatas, quæ eum falsi ad hunc usque diem argunt. At qui probabile fiat, eas pacem & ordinem, abrogato jure Canonico, non habituras, quoad progeniem quartam, quam ad hunc usq; diem habuerunt: nisi propter eorum, in exequenda quam acceperant (summo Dei beneficio) disciplinâ, negligen-
units.tr: Sixthly, we argue from effects. Thomas Bilson says this: Those laws which nourished or increased the superstition and tyranny of the Pope have long since, thanks be to God, been removed from the midst. But as for the others, which seem to savour of the discipline of the ancient Church, if you seek to dissolve them, I would indeed wish that you first propose new ones for everyone to examine, rather than tear up the old ones, lest you make the people as released from laws as your presbyters. It is easier to overthrow a Church or a commonwealth than to raise it up; to destroy than to build. Unless you receive those same laws again, I boldly say that your descendants, down to the fourth generation, will have neither peace nor order in your Churches. Let the rest be left aside and deferred to their proper places. Bilson is indeed bold enough, but cautious too: he mentions the fifth generation, so that he would have something to answer to the reformed Churches, which have convicted him of falsehood to this day. But how probable is it that, with canon law abrogated, they will have no peace or order down to the fourth generation, which they have had until today, unless through their own neglig-
