units.la: De perpet. gubernat. c. 14. p. 539. negligentiam,ejusdem commeritum exterminium patiantur? Cornelius Scultingius eadem cum Bilsono prorsus habet, quae proponere visum,ut có melius pateat, quo ista criminatio tendat. Citat ex Leone: Universa pacis tranquillitas non aliter poterit custodiri, nisi sua Canonibus inviolata reverentia servetur. Nihil tentandum in injuriam Canonum, sufficiant limites, quos sanctissimorum patrum decreta posuerunt. Deinde ita subinfert: Haec testimonia solida confutant Calvinistas, qui ex solis scripturis disciplinam pati velint: non ex vetustis paternis constitutionibus. Quid igitur est? Solius scripturae authoritas quae sola in disciplinae essentialib9 regula est, hoc ariete impetitur: juris vero Canonici necessitas adversus eam ita asseritur, ac si ex eâ violatâ quam invexit Synodus, disciplinâ, incommoda maiora & plura oriantur, quàm ex illâ, quam Deus ipse in verbo suo sanxerat. Sed (ut Bilsoni verbis utar) Deo gratia sit, qui ad hunc usque diem luculentam experientiâ demonstravit, rem multò secus esse. Quid ego de Germania dicerem? de Geneva? de Comitatu Palatinatus? Non etenim confusio ea, ea rerum perturbatio, non rerum divinarum ignoratio ea, non ea rerum sacrarum profanatio: non in moribus turpitudo ea, ea in Canonibus corruptela, in his Ecclesiis, quae in Anglia reperitur: ut discant mortales, quanto sit satius, verbo Dei, quàm jure Antichristi, Ecclesiam gubernari. Sed effectus regiminis nostri per jus Canonicum, separatim excutiantur.
units.tr: De perpet. gubernat. c. 14. p. 539. negligence, so that they suffer a destruction deserved by it, in carrying out the discipline they received (by the highest benefit of God)? Cornelius Scultingius holds exactly the same as Bilson, which I thought worth setting out, so that it may more clearly appear where this accusation tends. He cites from Leo: The whole tranquillity of peace cannot be preserved unless reverence for the Canons is kept inviolate. Nothing is to be attempted to the injury of the Canons; let the limits be enough which the decrees of the most holy fathers have set. Then he adds: These solid testimonies refute the Calvinists, who wish to be governed by Scripture alone, not by the ancient paternal constitutions. What then is the case? The authority of Scripture alone, which is the sole rule in the essentials of discipline, is attacked with this battering-ram; while the necessity of canon law is so asserted against it, as if greater and more numerous evils arose from the violation of the discipline introduced by the Synod than from that which God himself had ordained in his word. But (to use Bilson's words) thanks be to God, who has shown by clear experience until this day that the matter stands very differently. What should I say of Germany? Of Geneva? Of the Palatinate? For there is no such confusion, no such disorder of affairs, no such ignorance of divine things, no such profanation of sacred things; no such turpitude in morals, no such corruption in the Canons, as in those Churches which are found in England; so that mortals may learn how much better it is for the Church to be governed by the word of God than by the law of Antichrist. But let the effects of our government under canon law be examined separately.

units.la: Primò, Canones illi fecerunt, qui disciplinam a Christo Iesu institutam exulare primò jusserant: & jus Canonicum hodie etiamnum eandem in exilio detinet. Primum ut probetur, non opus est abire longiùs: hac ipsa in pagina, in qua declamat pro jure Canonico Thomas Bilsonus, ita ex prima presbyterorum exclusione sive oppressione habet. In ea opinione estis ut universam Christi Ecclesiam ad opprimendos presbyteros, & mutandam Apostolicam regendae Ecclesiae formam conspirasse existimetis: cum revera conciliorum Canones & Christianorum principum constitutiones, moderando ac terminando eas omnes controversias quae in presbyteriis antea tractari solebant, effecerint, ut nec tanta eorum utilitas esset, nec tantus eis honos haberetur. Proinde soli Episcopo, nec consciis, nec consultis presbyteris legum etiam executionem mandarunt, &c. En hic Episcopatus Hierarchici incunabula, en diem natalem. Non ita regebatur Ecclesia Apostolorum temporibus, uti nunc regitur, vel ipso Bilsono confitente. Apostolorum temporibus presbyteria erant, & in presbyteriis regalia Ecclesiae tractabantur: non tum solus Episcopus quicquam agebat, ut nunc agit omnia: major erat honos presbyterorum Apostolicis saeculis: postquam Episcopatus Hierarchicus caput extulerat, longè minor. Nonne habemus confitentem rerum? Sed hanc mutationem regiminis utilitas extorsit. Imò vel ipso confitente, ambitio: hinc etenim factum fuisse ais, quod Canonum executio soli Episcopo demandata sit, quòd majores Curiae minorum decuriarum judicijs, decreta sua submittere nollent. Mitto multas quae hic latent inepti-as, tias, quæ suis locis tractabuntur: num Apostoli rogo ita superbi, ut decreta sua nollent nisi ab Episcopis administrari? Si decreta Apostolorum quæ sancita sunt, Episcopum quasi custodem solum non invexerint: cur posteriorum temporum Canones, presbyteros excluderent: quos Apostolicorum Canonum executionem parem omnes habuisse ex eo constat, quod Act. 15. non Episcopo alicui uni, sed Ecclesiis singulis Concilij Hierosolymitani Canones & custodiendi & exequendi traditi sunt. Atque consideretur contradictio. Rogo cur non in consistorijs presbyteriorum communi suffragio res jam quæq; decernenda, perinde ac in Synodo Hierosolymitana Actorum 15? Num Episcopi majores Apostolis? negotia illius Synodi permiserunt Apostoli liberis suffragijs presbyterorum: non ita jam Episcopi. Quis non manifestam spiritus discrepantiam videt? Hæc forma inquiunt mutata est postea. Non rogo quo iure, alius isti disquisitioni locus erit: tantum hoc tempore interrogo de tempore, quando hęc mutatio facta est? Respondet Cæsar Baronius, mutata est hæc forma ab ipsis Apostolis, quando dicebatur Episcopo Timotheo: Ne cito manus impone. Noli recipere accusationem, &c. sic ut sine causa conquerantur presbyteri de oppressione, quod non libertate jam gaudeant ea, sub Episcopis, qua in Synodo Hierosolymitana sub Apostolis potiebantur. Imo inquit Bilsonus res secus habet: antiqua presbyterorum quam olim habuerunt libertas, duravit usque ad multiplicatos Canones: tum primùm eorum honos diminuebatur, quia tum cœpit eorum utilitas minor esse: sic ut nullam de oppressione conquerendi causam habeant. Nullam Bilsone, quando ea libertate spoliantur, quam ab Apostolis habuerunt acceptam? Sed causa erat jam utilitas eorum minor. At inquam hæc utilitas eorum minor facta est: imo ne ubique superbia quidem intolerabili dici potest, Apostolis Episcopos præferendos sic ut eorum authoritas minorè invexerit necessitate presbyterorum: quâ Apost. non invexit. Hoc vidit Baronius, sic ut nullo modo querelæ justæ presbyterorum de oppressione, occurri posse statuatur: nisi hæc eorum libertas, adempta eis ab ipsis Apostolis statuatur.
units.tr: First, those Canons made it so that the discipline instituted by Christ Jesus was first ordered into exile, and canon law still today keeps it in exile. To prove the first point we need not go far: on this very page, in which Thomas Bilson declaims for canon law, he thus speaks about the first exclusion or oppression of the presbyters: You are of the opinion that the whole Church of Christ conspired to oppress the presbyters and to change the Apostolic form of governing the Church; whereas in truth the Canons of the councils and the constitutions of Christian princes, by moderating and ending all those controversies which used to be treated in the presbyteries, have brought it about that their usefulness is not so great, nor is such honour given to them. Accordingly they entrusted the execution of the laws solely to the bishop, neither informing nor consulting the presbyters, etc. Here we have the cradle and birthday of hierarchical episcopacy. The Church was not governed in the times of the Apostles as it is now governed, as Bilson himself confesses. In the times of the Apostles there were presbyteries, and the royal affairs of the Church were handled in the presbyteries; the bishop did not then act alone in anything, as he now acts in everything. The honour of the presbyters was greater in Apostolic ages; after hierarchical episcopacy raised its head, it became much less. Do we not have the man confessing the facts? But the advantage of this change of government forced it. Indeed, by Bilson's own confession, it was ambition: for you say that this came about because the execution of the Canons was entrusted to the bishop alone, since the greater courts were unwilling to submit their decrees to the judgements of the lesser divisions. I pass over the many foolish trifles that lie hidden here, which will be treated in their places. Tell me, did the Apostles really become so proud that they would not have their decrees administered except by bishops? If the decrees of the Apostles, which were enacted, did not introduce the bishop as sole guardian, why should the Canons of later times exclude the presbyters, whom we know all had an equal share in the execution of the Apostolic Canons? This is clear from Acts 15, where the Canons of the Council of Jerusalem were handed over to be both observed and executed not to any one bishop but to the individual Churches. And let the contradiction be considered. I ask why in the consistories of the presbyteries matters are not decided by common vote, just as in the Synod of Jerusalem in Acts 15? Did the Apostles allow the affairs of that Synod to be settled by the free votes of the presbyters? Bishops now do not do so. Who does not see the manifest discrepancy of spirit? They say this form was changed afterwards. I do not ask by what right; that question will have another place. For now I ask only about the time: when was this change made? Caesar Baronius answers that this form was changed by the Apostles themselves, when it was said to Timothy the bishop: Lay hands on no one hastily. Do not receive an accusation, etc. So the presbyters complain of oppression without cause, since they no longer enjoy under bishops the liberty they had under the Apostles in the Synod of Jerusalem. Nay, says Bilson, the matter stands otherwise: the ancient liberty the presbyters once had lasted until the Canons multiplied; only then did their honour begin to diminish, because only then did their usefulness begin to be less; so they have no cause to complain of oppression. No cause, Bilson, when they are stripped of that liberty which they had received from the Apostles? But the cause was already their lesser usefulness. But I say: this usefulness of theirs became less? Indeed, it cannot even be called intolerable pride everywhere to prefer bishops to Apostles, so that their authority introduced a lesser necessity for presbyters, which the Apostles did not introduce. Baronius saw this, so that it is decided that the just complaints of the presbyters about oppression can in no way be met, unless this liberty of theirs is held to have been taken from them by the Apostles themselves.

units.la: 8 Secundò, jus Canonicum tyrannidem in Ecclesia fovet. Ita Hadrianus Saravia: Minor injuria & tyrannis in consistoriis Episcoporum timenda est, quàm in Genevensi presbyterio: quia hæc magis libera est à legibus: Episcopi verò legibus (nempe juri Canonico) ita sunt astricti, ut nihil eorum arbitrio relictum sit. Miraberis forte Lector, tam futilia, ingenio tanto excidere potuisse: certè valde mirandum est, ingenium tantum non advertisse & legibus presbyterium Genevense subjectum esse, etsi juri illi Canonico subjectum non sit, sic ut eorum arbitrio nihil sit relictum: & nihil consistorium Episcopale prohiberi à tyrannide, quòd sit subjectum juri Canonico; sed ad tyrannidem jure isto armari potius. Idem & Thomas Bilsonus causatur; dum invehit in eos qui Episcopos vehementius insectantur, ac si tyrannidem in fratres sibi usurparent. Plures leges (praeter jus Canonicum intelligit) nobis habere non expedit, meliores vol is ferre non licet : qui ex presbyteri-orum nutu & arbitrio pendere,quam legum praescripto mallet vivere, nisi insinuum opinor esse neminem. Abrogatis ijs quandocunque velitis, consistoriis vestris negotium facessite, & videte quantum interfit inter constantem Canonum aequitatem, & factiosam presbyterorum temeritatem. Ecce insanos vocat Ecclesiarum reformatorum cives omnes, qui Presbyteris se subjiciunt, juri Canonico non subjectis : & gubernationem in eisdem Ecclesiis presbyterialem, factiosam temeritatem vocat,quia juri Canonico non subjiciuntur : eam denique laudem juri tribuit Canonico,ac si nulla constans aequitas reperiri posset, ubi illud abrogatur. Quid homini facias tam more Bacchidum insigniter debacchanti ? Ad rem quod attinet, respondemus duo. Primò, presbyteria reformata nihil suo nutu & arbitrio agunt, neque a legibus libera sunt : regunt etenim ex verbo Dei, & ex Canonibus Ecclesiasticis, de quibus Cornelius Scultingius ita: Disciplinae Canones etiam in initio in suis Synodis volunt Calvinistae praelegi, & proponi : in quo sunt similes Catholicorum. Secundo, non sequitur tyrannidem nullam metuendam esse in consistorijs Episcoporum, quia juri Canonico subjiciuntur : sed conficitur prorsus contrarium. Cum enim jus Canonicum potestatem Episcopis tyrannicam plane tribuat, & Canones multis modis in ipsam plebem tyrannicos praescribat : qui fieri potest, quin promoveat, tanto abest ut impediat tyrannidem? Num tyrannus a tyrannide per legem tyrannicam cohiberi quaeso potest ? annon e contra lege tyrannica confirmatur tyrannus? Ego Episcopos Anglicanos tyrannos non dicerem : ut pro quibus intercedere Christum reor, Ignosce mi pater, non norunt quid faciunt: quod tamen est tyrannorum faciunt, quamdiu tyrannicam gubernationem (quae in jure Canonico praestat) usque exercere volunt.
units.tr: 8 Secondly, canon law fosters tyranny in the Church. Thus Hadrian Saravia: A lesser wrong and tyranny is to be feared in the consistories of bishops than in the presbytery of Geneva, because the latter is more free from laws; but bishops are so bound by laws (namely canon law) that nothing is left to their judgement. The reader may perhaps wonder that such trifles could fall from so great a mind; certainly it is very wonderful that such a mind did not notice that the presbytery of Geneva is subject to laws, even though it is not subject to that canon law, so that nothing is left to its judgement; and that a episcopal consistory is not restrained from tyranny by being subject to canon law, but is rather armed for tyranny by that law. Thomas Bilson makes the same complaint, when he attacks those who most vehemently assail bishops, as if they usurped tyranny over their brethren. It is not expedient for us to have more laws (he means besides canon law), nor is it lawful to bring in better ones; he would rather live at the nod and judgement of the presbyters than by the prescription of laws, unless I think there is no one who is not insane. Abrogate them whenever you like, labour at your consistories, and see how much difference there is between the constant equity of the Canons and the factious rashness of the presbyters. Behold, he calls all the citizens of the reformed Churches who submit themselves to presbyters, which are not subject to canon law, insane; and the presbyterial government in those same Churches he calls factious rashness, because they are not subject to canon law; finally he attributes to canon law such praise as if no constant equity could be found where it is abrogated. What can you do with a man so notably raving in the manner of the Bacchantes? As to the matter, we reply to two points. First, reformed presbyteries do nothing at their own nod and judgement, nor are they free from laws: they govern by the word of God and by ecclesiastical Canons, about which Cornelius Scultingius says: The Calvinists wish the canons of discipline to be read aloud and set forth at the beginning of their synods, in which they are like the Catholics. Second, it does not follow that no tyranny is to be feared in the consistories of bishops because they are subject to canon law; the exact opposite follows. For since canon law plainly grants bishops tyrannical power, and prescribes Canons that are in many ways tyrannical even towards the common people, how can it be that it does not promote tyranny? Far from preventing tyranny, it does promote it. Can a tyrant, I ask, be restrained from tyranny by a tyrannical law? Is not the tyrant rather confirmed by a tyrannical law? I would not call the English bishops tyrants, for whom I think Christ interceded: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do; yet they do what tyrants do, as long as they wish to go on exercising the tyrannical government which canon law provides.

units.la: 9 Tertiò, Canonum jurisque Canonici observatio Anglicana, libertatem Christianam ab Ecclesiis Christi adimit: in Canonibus Ecclesiasticis, tum rescindendis, tum condendis, prout utilitas Ecclesiarum postularit. Ita Hadrianus Saravia: Quod nunquam in Apostolos, vix in Timotheum ipsi& similes fidos Christi servos cadere potuit, ut sua abuterentur potestate, proclive fuit, & est aliis Episcopis, quos Deus non tanta munivit gratia. Idcirco prudenti consilio legibus adstricti fuere sequentium saeculorum Episcopi: ne sua potestate abuterentur. Quas leges ex conciliorum & patrum monumentis quivis petere possunt. Haec eo adferuntur, ut ordinatio per solum Episcopum inviolata semper permaneat, juxta antiquos Canones: quibus adstringi aequum omnes putat, etsi Timotheus hujusmodi Canonibus opus non habuit, ob insignem qua munitus erat gratiam. Revocandum hic in memoriam est, quod habet Lous. Disputat ille exactam regiminis Ecclesiastici formam pro nova Ecclesia in verbo praescriptam non esse, ut olim in veteri Synagoga: quia spiritu prudentiae Deus novam Eccle-siam
units.tr: 9 Thirdly, the English observance of the canons and of canon law takes Christian liberty away from the churches of Christ, since the church canons may be annulled or enacted as the advantage of the churches requires. Thus Hadrianus Saravia: That it could hardly ever happen to the Apostles, or scarcely to Timothy and similar faithful servants of Christ, to abuse their power, but it is easy, and remains so, for other bishops whom God has not endowed with such great grace. For this reason the bishops of later centuries were bound by wise counsel to laws, so that they would not abuse their power. Anyone can seek these laws from the records of councils and fathers. These things are brought forward so that ordination by the bishop alone may always remain inviolate, according to the ancient canons, which he thinks everyone ought fairly to be bound by, although Timothy had no need of such canons, because of the outstanding grace with which he was endowed. Here we must recall what Lous holds. He argues that an exact form of ecclesiastical government is not prescribed in the Word for the new Church, as it was once in the old synagogue, because God in the spirit of prudence so fully furnished the new Church that it does not require so great a mass of prescriptions. He adduces this to prove that the churches, instructed by the spirit of prudence, may change the essentials of discipline as circumstances require.

units.la: Cmt. Bez., c.24.p.289
units.tr: Comment. Bez., c. 24, p. 289

units.la: Quaeinmonit Eccles.p.86. siam tam plane instruxit, ut tantam non requirat prescripti onum molem. Hec adfert ut probet, penes Ecclesiam spiritu prudentiae instructam esse disciplinae essentialia, prout res tulerit, immutare. Non abludit Remonstrator, pro mutabilitate etenim disciplinae disputans ita habet. Deus nobis usum Christianae libertatis, & spiritus doni E clesiae dedit: ut eisdem disciplinetur, quod ad eas materias, quae in verbo non continentur. Supponis autem formam regiminis Ecclesiastici in verbo minime contineri Ob gratiarum defectum astringit Episcopos antiquis Canonibus Hadrianus Saravia: ob gratiarum abundantiam, ne verbo Dei quidem, astrictam esse Ecclesiam dicit Lous & Remonstrator, in disciplinae forma. Nullam tu hic opinionum differentiam adnotas? Sic autem disputamus nos. Si verbo Dei in essentialibus disciplinae non adstringamur: tum juri Canonico in circumstantialibus multo minus. Si dona spiritus habeat Ecclesia, ad novam formam disciplinae condendam: tum Dona spiritus multo magis habet, ad novos Canones condendos de accidentalibus disciplinae: quod si habeat, jus Canonicum abrogare Ecclesiae licet. Ad Saraviam vero quod attinet, non ille quem tetigit gratiarum defectus Canonibus antiquis abrogandis obstabit: quum gratiam tantam, imo & majorem habeat praesens Ecclesia, quam antiqua habuit ad Canones, pro se regenda, de novo, condendos: sic ut illis jam veteribus eam adstringi non sit opus. Magis ergo opus habeat Ecclesia ut Canonibus pluribus adiuvetur quam Timotheus: Dico Canones qui in scripturis habetur sufficere, ut presens ecclesia(rescissis antiquis, minus huic tempori accommodis) Canones de suo condat: iuxta illa ipsius Bilsoni. In Synodis, timor domini & institutio Apostolorum ad omnia sufficit. Non fert Bancroftus ista. Quum non absque violentia, hoc in nostra persona, sarcasmo laevit. Si legi ulli Ecclesiasticae obedientiam concedimus: illa sanciatur a nobismetipsis: apage omnes veteres & constitutiones antiquas? At leges nos nullas condimus absque luce scripturae praeunte, a nobismetipsis: & quae in scripturis conduntur Canones, a nobismetipsis proficisci dici non possunt: Hanc vero regulam sequentes, nosmetipsos legem condere quis vetabit? Quid, rejectis veteribus constitutionibus? Quid & veteres constitutiones refigere apud Bancroftum, nefas? Sic quidem videtur: idque non solum hoc loco: sed & alibi: cap. etenim 2. p. 16. quasi indignum facinus objicit Genevae, quod jus Canonicum abrogavit: Dixine igitur in initio absque causa iuris Canonici observationem Anglicanam libertatem Ecclesiis Christi adimere?
units.tr: Quaeinmonit Eccles., p. 86. ...so fully furnished it. The Remonstrant does not differ, for arguing for the changeability of discipline he says: God has given us the use of Christian liberty and the gift of the Spirit to the church, so that it may order itself in those matters which are not contained in the Word. But you assume that the form of ecclesiastical government is in no way contained in the Word. Hadrianus Saravia binds bishops to the ancient canons on account of a lack of grace; Lous and the Remonstrant say that the church is not bound, even by the Word of God, in the form of discipline, on account of an abundance of grace. Do you not note here a difference of opinion? But we argue thus. If we are not bound by the Word of God in the essentials of discipline, then much less are we bound by canon law in matters of circumstance. If the church has the gifts of the Spirit to frame a new form of discipline, then it has much more the gifts of the Spirit to enact new canons concerning the accidentals of discipline; and if it has these, the church may abrogate canon law. As for Saravia, the lack of grace which he mentions will not stand in the way of abrogating the ancient canons, since the present church has as much grace, indeed greater grace, than the ancient church had to frame new canons for governing itself, so that there is no need for it to be bound to those old ones. The church therefore needs more canons to help it than Timothy did. I say that the canons contained in the Scriptures are enough for the present church to make its own canons (the ancient ones being rejected as less suited to this age), in accordance with those words of Bilson himself: In synods, the fear of the Lord and the teaching of the Apostles are sufficient for all things. Bancroft does not bear these things. He strikes at them with sarcasm, not without violence towards us: If we grant obedience to any ecclesiastical law, let it be sanctioned by ourselves: away with all the old decrees and ancient constitutions? But we enact no laws from ourselves, without the light of Scripture going before; and the canons which are framed in Scripture cannot be said to proceed from ourselves. Who will forbid us, following this rule, to enact laws ourselves? What, with the old constitutions rejected? Is it an outrage, in Bancroft's view, even to unseal the old constitutions again? So he seems to think, and not only in this place but elsewhere too: in chapter 2, page 16, he objects to Geneva, as though it were an unworthy deed, that it abrogated canon law. Did I not say at the start that the English observance of canon law takes away liberty from the churches of Christ, without cause?

units.la: 10 A Cornelio etenim Scultingio papistisq; reliquis, (quantum ego quidem consequor) Bancroftus nihil differt. Fontes legum Ecclesiasticarum inveniuntur in scriptura: Deinde in canonibus Apostolorum & aliorum sequentium Conciliorum. Rursus: Niceni patres mansuras in finem mundi leges Ecclesiasticorum Canonum condiderunt. Quare dicant & scribant Puritani non ex patribus sed solis scripturis hauriendam esse disciplinam. plinam. Hos porro deinceps confutat, argumento de immutabilitate antiquorum Canonum Bancroftiana, ex Leone epist. 53. Nihil contra sacrorum Canonum constituta agendum. Epist. 54. Providendum ne paternarum regulæ sectionum violentur. Epist. 62. Tanta est apud me Nicenorum canonum reverentia, ut ea quæ sunt à sanctis patribus constituta non patiar nec permisserim aliqua novitate violari. Rectè quidem his verbis postremis seipsum Leo interpretatur: non ob novitatis studiū, refigenda antiqua statuta sunt: quæ tamen studio pietatis, vel causæ commodioris utilitatis refigenda esse, vel ipse confitetur alibi. Sicut quædam sunt quæ nulla possunt ratione convelli, ita multa sunt quæ pro necessitate temporum, ac consideratione ætatum oporteant temperari. Similiter Gregorius: Regulæ patrum traditæ sunt, prout res postulare videbatur, temporis, loci, personarum, reiq; ipsius habita ratione. Hæc cum in ius Canonicum relata sint: ius Canonicum licitè abrogari posse, vel ex ipso iure Canonico patet. Stupenda igitur Scultingij vox, Canones Nicænos ad finem seculi manere oportet: Canones ipsi Apostolorum Act. 15. æterni non erant, sed pro circumstantiarum varietate mutabiles: imò causa cessante, cessare ipsi non solum potuerunt, sed ut habet Lyranus, debuerunt: & Canones tamen juris Canonici æterni & immutabiles?
units.tr: 10 Indeed, Bancroft (so far as I can make out) differs nothing from Cornelius Schultingius and the other Papists. The sources of ecclesiastical laws are found in Scripture; then in the canons of the Apostles and of the councils that followed. Again: The Nicene fathers enacted ecclesiastical canons which would remain until the end of the world. Let the Puritans therefore say and write that discipline is to be drawn not from the fathers but from Scripture alone. He then refutes these men with Bancroft's argument from the immutability of the ancient canons, taken from Leo's letter 53: Nothing is to be done against the decrees of the sacred canons. Letter 54: Care must be taken that the rules of the fathers are not violated. Letter 62: I have such reverence for the Nicene canons that I will not allow those things which have been established by the holy fathers to be violated by any novelty. Leo rightly interprets himself by these last words: the ancient statutes are not to be unsealed out of a desire for novelty; yet he himself admits elsewhere that some of them must be unsealed out of zeal for piety, or for a more convenient advantage. Just as there are some things which can be overthrown by no reason, so there are many things which must be tempered for the necessity of the times and in consideration of the ages. Similarly Gregory: The rules of the fathers were handed down as the matter seemed to require, having regard to time, place, persons and the matter itself. Since these things have been carried into canon law, it is clear even from canon law itself that canon law may lawfully be abrogated. Astonishing, then, is the saying of Schultingius: The Nicene canons ought to remain until the end of the age. The canons of the Apostles themselves, Acts 15, were not eternal, but changeable according to the variety of circumstances; indeed, when the cause ceased, they could not only cease but, as Lyranus holds, ought to have ceased. And yet the canons of canon law are eternal and immutable?

units.la: 11. Quartò, iure Canonico condemnati sancti martyres, Mariæ temporibus, in agro Ferrario, exusti rogis sacrificabantur: nonne igitur meretur ius ipsum Canonicum, eodem loco, eodemque modo ut sacrificaretur? At non nostro jure Canonico condemnati illi erant, sed papali. Quoad processum juridicum plane nostro: sed missum hoc fiat: nostro iam quot, & quanti, degradati, depositi, bonis omnibus exuti, miseriis & calamitatibus obruti, quibus mori fuisset fatius? Appositum hic Chrysostomi exemplum per Canonem quendam Arianorum, Constantinopoli exauthorati. Ita Socrates: Cum diceret Iohannes hunc canonem non ad Ecclesiam illorum, sed ad Ecclesiam Arianorum pertinere (nam qui Antiochiæ ad fidem consubstantialis tollendam convenerant, præ odio versus Athanasium recepto, hunc canonem ediderant) reiecto illius responsio, contra eum sententiam pronunciarunt: illud neutiquam animis complexi, quòd qui hoc canone usi fuissent, etiam Athanasium abdicaverant. Viva hic imago processus juridici Episcopalis, adversus fideles verbi ministros abdicatos. Cur nobis a Canone Papistico provocare non licet, perinde ac Chrysostomo ab Ariano? Cur Canon Papisticus ad Ecclesiam nostram pertinet, magis quàm Arianus ad Ecclesiam etiam Orthodoxam? Indignum facinus moliti tum Episcopi sunt, quum propter violationem Canonis Ariani abdicarunt Chrisostomum: & indignum nihil ab Episcopis Anglicanis committitur, quum propter violationem Canonis Papistici, fideles præcones Evangelij tantos, tam multos, tam misere tractatos, ab Ecclesijs amovent?
units.tr: 11. Fourthly, by canon law holy martyrs were condemned in Mary's time and, burnt, were sacrificed on the pyres in Smithfield. Ought not canon law itself therefore to be sacrificed in the same place and in the same way? But those men were condemned not by our canon law but by the papal law. As to the judicial process it is plainly ours; but let that pass. Think how many, and how great, were degraded, deposed, stripped of all their goods, overwhelmed with miseries and calamities, for whom it would have been better to die. Chrysostom's example is apt here, deposed by a canon of the Arians at Constantinople. So Socrates: When John said that this canon pertained not to their church but to the church of the Arians (for those who had gathered at Antioch to abolish the faith of consubstantiality, out of hatred towards Athanasius, had issued this canon), they rejected his answer and pronounced sentence against him, not at all considering in their minds that those who had used this canon had also deposed Athanasius. Here is a living picture of the episcopal judicial process against faithful ministers of the Word who have been deposed. Why are we not permitted to appeal from a Papist canon, just as Chrysostom did from an Arian? Why does a Papist canon pertain to our church more than an Arian canon pertains to the Orthodox church? The bishops at that time committed an unworthy deed when, on account of the violation of an Arian canon, they deposed Chrysostom; and is nothing unworthy committed by the English bishops when, on account of the violation of a Papist canon, they remove from the churches so many faithful heralds of the Gospel, so miserably treated?

units.la: 12. Quinto, gravamina à iure Canonico in ipsum gregem quanta redunredundant? In mentem veniat, quantos clamores excitare Hierarchici solent in Seniores: quia Ecclesiae onerosi futuri essent, si admitterentur: obliti interim quantum onus per jus Canonicum invehatur, in alendo Episcopo pomposo domino, in alendis Canonicis, Cantoribus, Officialibus, Notarijs, Advocatis, Apparitoribus, reliquaque cohorte, de quibus merito illud ex poeta repetere possis. Nos merces sumus & fruges consumere nati. Mitto curiarum fraudulentas expilationes, quae a totis provincijs exiguntur: vel hoc quam onerosum, quod longo itinere ad ecclesiam suam Cathedralem, saepe remotam per viginti aut triginta millia passuum, contendendum cuiquam sit qui litem habet adversus suos, idque non sineingenti opum suarum iactura. Aequitatem vero Mosaicae legis, qua in portis cuiusque civitatis, quaeque lites iudicabantur, reformatae Ecclesiae imitantes, toto hoc onere suos levarunt, in quibus per presbyteria sua, lites quaeque (ut vult Cyprianus) terminantur, ubi primo ortae sunt. Quid quod litium dilatio, ad civium incommodum, vel a mane usque ad vesperam Deo displiceat. Exod. 18? Iam vero inter legem civilem ab omnibus nationibus velut aequissimam in usu receptam, & ius Canonicum ab omnibus ecclesijs reformatis explosum hoc interest: quod non vltra annos tres ad ultimum in iure civili lis prorogetur, sed quibus expletis, cessat mox actio: jure vero Canonico terminus nullus, nullus finis litigandi est: ut taceam artes, quibus ad emungenda litigantium marsupia, protelationes, & dilationes hij Davi comminiscantur: sic ut non paucis acciderit, ut nè per totam quidem vitam, litis exitum videre possint. Atque hoc argumentum nostrum ab effectis quintum est.
units.tr: 12. Fifthly, how great are the burdens that canon law brings upon the flock itself? Let it come to mind how loudly the hierarchs are wont to cry out against the elders, because they would be burdensome to the church if they were admitted; forgetting meanwhile how great a burden is brought in by canon law, in maintaining a pompous lord bishop, in maintaining canons, cantors, officials, notaries, advocates, apparitors, and the rest of that crowd, of whom you may fittingly repeat that line of the poet: We are born to consume goods and fruits. I pass over the fraudulent plundering of the courts, which is exacted from whole provinces; or how burdensome it is that anyone who has a suit against his own people must travel a long journey to his cathedral church, often distant twenty or thirty thousand paces, and that not without great loss of his resources. But the reformed churches, imitating the equity of the Mosaic law, by which suits were judged at the gates of each city, have relieved their people of this whole burden; in their presbyteries all suits are settled (as Cyprian wishes) where they first arose. What of the delay of lawsuits, which, to the inconvenience of the citizens, is displeasing to God from morning until evening? Exod. 18? Indeed, between the civil law, received in use by all nations as most equitable, and canon law, rejected by all the reformed churches, there is this difference: in civil law a lawsuit is not deferred beyond three years at the most, and when these have run out, the action soon ceases; but in canon law there is no limit, no end to litigation. I say nothing of the tricks by which those Davuses devise delays and postponements to squeeze the purses of litigants, so that for many it has happened that they could not see the outcome of a suit even for their whole lives. And this is our fifth argument, drawn from its effects.

units.la: 13 Sexto & ultimo, disputamus a nostrorum testimonijs. Num jure Canonico regi ecclesiam Martinus Lutherus voluit qui & ius canonicum igni comburendum curavit in aperto foro Wittemburgensi, & (quod in eo Cornelius Scultingius abhominatur) Decretalia excretalia appellare consuevit? Num jure Canonico regi ecclesi-am voluit Calvinus qui Institut. lib. 4.c.10. jus canonicum, evanidum vocat disciplinae spectrum, quo nomine, apud eundem Sultingium vapulat? Num jure canonico regi ecclesiam vult Philippus Mornaeus, qui hoc ipsum deplorat, quod unquam consarcinatum suerit? Num jure denique canonico regi ecclesiam voluit Guilielmus Whitakerus; qui ita de eo loquitur. Ius Canonicum Decretale & Pontificium, apud nos nullam vim habere debet, quia Antichristianum est, & ab omni pietate & religione omnino abhorret. Porrò ut a nostris dissonant Hierarchici, ita argumentis Scultingianis atque Papisticis viam muniunt, ut colligere cuiquam promptum, ex verbis istis. Gravissima, maximique momenti quaestio est, disciplinae ex iure canonico: faciens contra Anonymum puritanum Rupellensem, qui scribens contra Calvino-Papistas, ius canonicum in disciplina penitus rejicit. Atque haec contra jus Canonicum argumenta nostra sunt: iam Hierarchici audiendi.
units.tr: 13 Sixthly and lastly, we argue from the testimony of our own people. Did Martin Luther want the Church governed by canon law, he who had the canon law burned in the open marketplace at Wittenberg and was accustomed to call the Decretals "excretals" (a jest that Cornelius Scultingius abhors)? Did Calvin want the Church governed by canon law, he who in Institutes book 4, chapter 10, calls canon law a "faded specter of discipline," for which name Scultingius lashes him in the same place? Does Philip Mornay want the Church governed by canon law, he who laments that it was ever patched together? Did finally William Whitaker want the Church governed by canon law? He speaks of it thus: "The Decretal and Pontifical canon law ought to have no force among us, because it is antichristian and wholly abhorrent from all piety and religion." Moreover, just as the Hierarchists differ from our people, so they pave the way for the arguments of Scultingius and the Papists, so that anyone can easily gather this from those words: "The question of discipline drawn from canon law is most grave and of the greatest moment." This runs against the anonymous Rochelle Puritan, who, writing against the Calvino-Papists, utterly rejects canon law in discipline. These are our arguments against canon law; now the Hierarchists must be heard.

units.la: CAP. XXXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIII.

units.la: Argumenta Hierarchica pro iure Canonico refutantur.
units.tr: The Hierarchical arguments for canon law are refuted.

units.la: PRimò objiciunt, nos juris canonici abrogationem postulando, nihil aliud quærere quam immunitatem, & a legibus plane omnibus solutioneu: sic enim nos loquentes inducit R. Bancroftus. Exclamant de iure canonico, crucifige, crucifige, tolle, illo regi nolumus, nolumus recipi. Quasi dicerent, exleges sumus, regulas & ordinationes detestamur, quod bonum videtur in oculis nostris id faciemus. Primò, videat Bancroftus ne ad Pharaonem quam proximè accedat, populo Dei, id tum quærenti quod iam nos, (ut excusso humano jugo, libere Deo secundum illius voluntatem in verbo suo patefactam serviamus) haud absimiliter (ut mihi quidem videtur) immunitatis desiderium objicienti. Exod. 5. 4. Quare abstrahitis populum hunc ab operibus suis, abite ad onera vestra. & v. 8. desides sunt, idcirco clamant, abeamus, sacrificemus Deo nostro & v. 9. Aggravetur hæc servitus super homines istos, & operentur in ea, neque attendant verbis falsis. Secundo, an exleges nos, qui verbo Dei & nos & Ecclesiam regi cupimus: annon Hierarchici exleges potius, qui perinde faciunt, quod ad regimen Ecclesiæ, quod illi exleges in Psalmo, 2. 5. Disrumpamus lora istorum: & proiiciamus à nobis densos funes istorum? Tertio, legat quis Synodum Middelburgensem anno 1581. Dordracensem anno 1574. Generalem Synodum Belgij, Germaniæ, & Galliæ anno 1478. Concilia Ecclesiarum reformatarum Franciæ anno 1559. 61. 62. 63. Synodum Lugdunensem anno 1563. Synodum Palatinensem anno. Synodum Ecclesiarum Belgicarum, habitam Embdæ anno 1571. &c. num is reformatos pronunciabit exleges qui non solum leges sibi condunt, sed & leges eas, quæ summam severitatem spirant; tantum abest, ut immunitatem sibi quærere videantur?
units.tr: First, they object that in demanding the abrogation of canon law we seek nothing but immunity, freedom from all laws whatever; this is how Bancroft speaks of us. They cry out against canon law, "Crucify, crucify, away with it! We will not have that king; we will not be ruled by him." As if they said: we are lawless, we detest rules and ordinances, and whatever seems good in our eyes, that we will do. First, let Bancroft take care that he does not come too close to Pharaoh, who objected in much the same way (as it seems to me) to the people of God when they sought, as we now do, to shake off the human yoke and serve God freely according to his will revealed in his word, and so sought immunity. Exod. 5. 4. Why do you take the people away from their works? Get you to your burdens. And v. 8: They are idle, therefore they cry, Let us go and sacrifice to our God. And v. 9: Let heavier work be laid upon these men, that they may labour in it, and let them not regard lying words. Second, are we the lawless ones, who desire to be ruled by the word of God, both ourselves and the Church? Or are not the Hierarchical men rather the lawless, who do the very thing against the government of the Church that the lawless ones in Psalm 2 do: Let us break their bands asunder, and cast away their cords from us? Third, let anyone read the Synod of Middelburg of 1581, the Synod of Dort of 1574, the general synod of Belgium, Germany and France of 1478, the councils of the reformed churches of France of 1559, 1561, 1562 and 1563, the Synod of Lyons of 1563, the Palatine synod in the year..., the synod of the Dutch churches held at Emden in 1571, and so on. Will he then pronounce the reformed lawless, when they not only make laws for themselves but also laws that breathe the utmost severity? So far are they from seeming to seek immunity for themselves.

units.la: 2 Objiciunt secundo factiosum novitatis studium, & inde declarant, quanta incommoda sequantur, ex veterum legum mutatione: quibus cum alibi à me abundè responsum sit, non est quod hoc loco expectet multa lector. Salicâ lege fune ad collum suspenso prodire debet qui legem novam suadet; & apud Æginetas ratum est, ut qui novæ legis condendæ occasionem dat, invisus omnibus & execrabilis maneret: Disputat Aristoteles mutare leges esse infirmas facere leges: politic. lib. 2. c. 8. Disputat Tholossanus lib. 10. c. 5. ex Cleonis sententia apud Thucydidem. Melius agi cum civitatibus, quæ malis legibus constanter utuntur, quàm qui pro bonis mutant: quia non tantum proderit qui corrigere perget, quantum nocebit assuefactio superioribus non parendi, Disputat Bodinus denique de Repub. lib. 4. c. 3. & 4. [ipsam vetustatis speciem tam charam cuique esse, ut lex antiqua sine magistratibus facilè se tueri possit: legum verò novitas vix ulla præmiorum spe, aut metu pœnarum, aut magistratuum officijs, consistere possit.] re possit.] Hæc quanquam meram spirent prudentiam carnalem, quæ spiritui inimica, est: reformationem tamen disciplinæ in Anglia, non levibus remoris, impediverunt. Primò autem, nullas leges Ecclesiastici condunt, sed Canones potius, ut erudite Duarenus adnotavit: qui pro varietate locorum, & temporum, variari debent: ut supra ex ipso iure Canonico demonstratum. Secundò, magna pars Hierarchicorum, Whitgiftus, Hookerus, Sutclivius, Bridgesius &c. formam ipsam regiminis Ecclesiastici, & in essentialibus mutabilem contendunt: jus tamen Canonicum id est papisticum apud nos mutare nefas? Tertiò, præcipit Deus ut statuta sua observentur, non patrum, quamquam antiquissima Ezec. 20. 18, 30. & relata est in ipsum corpus iuris Canonici sententia ista Augustini & Cypriani: Quælibet consuetudo quantumvis vetusta, quantumvis vulgata, veritati omnino est postponenda, & usus qui veritati est contrarius, est abolendus. Ita nuper Benignus Milletotus. Imprudens imò temerarius conatus indicatur, mutare velle quod in longo consensu omnium, constans & fixum habetur. Ac sanè non temerè faciendæ mutationes, ne legis authoritas vilescat, quæ tempore præsertim & longa consuetudine confirmatur. At cum evidens & certa utilitas, imò necessitas animos excitat ad veritatem ex densissimis longi ac diuturni erroris tenebris eruendam: sanè sine metu, sine temporis aut diuturnæ consuetudinis respectu, tenemur eum aperte profiteri. Hoc exigit veritas cui nemo præscribere potest, non spatium temporum, non patrocinia personarum, non privilegium nationum. 3 Tertiò, obijcit Bancroftus ita. Viretus videns quanquam sero, quanta incommoda disciplinæ nostræ accrescerent ex iuris Canonici abrogatione ita habet. Pulchram in ecclesia reformationem arbitrati sunt, omnes Canones & decreta abolere una cum statutis quæ antiqui patres & Doctores ordinarunt, ad rectam in Ecclesia disciplinam conservandam. Quod maximè Viretum urebat illud erat, quod hoc modo principes à iugo disciplinæ colla sua eximissent. Atque hoc est, quo puritani iam nostri ringuntur: quod in actu parliamentario providetur, ne quid juris Canonici valeret quod legibus huius regni, aut regali prærogativæ contrarium sit. Non etiam cogitare possumus quin intima eorum corda Viretus denudarit. Primò conqueri Viretus potuit de antiquorum canonum (quos ille putavit vtiles) abrogatione: ut interim jure Canonico ecclesiam regi nollet, ut noluisse certum est. Secundò intima cordis nostri denudare Viretus quomodo potuit: cum ipso dicente in tantum ab eo dissideamus, ut pro iure canonico retinendo contenderit ille, nos pro eodem abrogando laboremus. Tertiò, notum toti mundo est, juris Canonici abrogationem exposcere reformatos: primò quia regali prærogativæ Iesu Christi qui rex est regum, deinde verò quia regali prærogativæ terrenorum regum & principum contrarium est: sic ut istâ Bancrofti calumniâ nihil putidius, sicut nihil virulentius cogitari possit. 4 Quartò, obijcit Bancroftus. Si quid in iure canonico occurrat quod ipsis ipsis usui esse possit: inde illud ferri contentisunt, & sibi ipsis laudem adscribere eam, quae veris authoritatibus debetur. Cartwrightus, ceteraque fraternitas, in essentiali disciplinae delineatione sua, plusquam septem ex octo partes ex iure Canonico, antiquisque constitutionibus, delibarunt. Primò notetur hoc testimonium de disciplinae reformatae antiquitate. Delineationem essentialem disciplinae, quam exaravit Thomas Cartwrightus non ille ex canonico iure hausit, sed ex solo Dei verbo: quòd autem plus quam septem illius ex octo partes in veteribus constitutionibus reperiatur: nec adeo episcopale regimen antiquum est, ut præ vobis fertis: nec disciplina reformata adeò nova, ut saepè declamitare soletis. Secundò, Gratianus (inquit D. Mornæus) decretum consarcinat ex Canonibus & decretis antiquis, quae quidem ipsa pluribus locis ad temporis corruptelam accommodat: quanquam multa nobis vestigiis relinquit, quorum ope, aliquam Ecclesiae & doctrinam & praxim, investigare sedulò quaerentibus datur. Hæc vestigia in doctrina indagare nostri solent, easque citare adversus pontificios, etsi doctrinam juris Canonici alioqui detestentur: quid ni igitur & reformatis liceat, ea in disciplina contra Hierarchicos allegare, etiamsi disciplinam alioqui canonicam nec immeritò condemnent. Consulatur vel unus ille Hierarchicus Thomas Bilsonus: omnium corruptissimum in citandis patribus Gratianum affirmat: qui tamen Gratianum urgere contra Rhemistas neutiquam cessat. Quàm verò frivolè hinc deducitur, iure Canonico regendam Ecclesiam concedere nos oportere, quòd quædam nonnunquam ex eodem allegare soleamus? Scultingianum hoc argumentum esto: id est, ineptum & puerile: sic etenim ille, eodem prorsus modo. Optimè iudicat Bucerus ut & Zepperus suprà, conciliorum canones & quae Gratianus congessit ex conciliis variis & sanctorum patrum rescriptis a dist. 23. ad dist. 96. legenda esse de munere Episcopali. Rectè sentit Gratianum plurima dignissima lectu & in Ecclesiis restitutum necessaria continere, quae sancti patres ex ipso spiritus sancti canone, de sacris ministeriis desumpta perquam commodè explicarunt, quae adversantur Anonymo libro Rupellensi qui docuit in negotio disciplinae solas scripturas consulendas, nec esse ullo modo ad ius canonicum recurrendum. Quod ad Zepperum, in meo exemplari nihil aliud quàm quaedam ex Gratiano citat: quod ad Bucerum, additamenta sunt cerebri Sultingiani, quaecunque; hinc legis, praeterquam illa de lectione Gratiani à distinct. 23. ad 96. Distinctio verò 23. hunc in modum auspicatur. Breviter quae inter Ecclesiastica officia sit differentia monstravimus. Quid igitur? legi non vult Gratianum Bucerus in eis canonibus, quia differentiam Episcopi superiorem continent: sed in eis tantum qui illius tanquam paterni pastoris conversationem depingunt, quales illi sunt qui à dist. 23. usque ad distinct. 96. decurrunt. Atque haec de fundamento extraneo Hierarchicorum nono: Iuris nempè Canonici practicatione.
units.tr: 2 Secondly, they object to the factious zeal for novelty, and from this they declare how great the inconveniences are that follow from changing the old laws. I have already answered these fully elsewhere, so the reader need not expect much on this point here. Under the Salic law, one who proposes a new law ought to come forth with a rope hung about his neck; and among the Aeginetans it was settled that whoever gave occasion for enacting a new law would remain hated and detested by all. Aristotle argues that changing laws makes laws weak (Politics, book 2, chapter 8). Tholosanus argues (book 10, chapter 5) from the opinion of Cleon in Thucydides: It is better to deal with states that constantly use bad laws than with those who change good ones for others; for he who keeps on correcting will do no more good than the habit of disobeying superiors will do harm. Finally, Bodin argues in his work on the Republic (book 4, chapters 3 and 4) [that the very appearance of antiquity is so dear to everyone that an old law can easily maintain itself without magistrates, whereas the novelty of laws can scarcely stand by any hope of rewards, or fear of penalties, or the offices of magistrates]. Although these arguments breathe nothing but carnal prudence, which is hostile to the Spirit, they have not, however, prevented the reformation of discipline in England, though not by slight hindrances. But first, they do not make laws for the Church at all, but rather canons, as Duaren has learnedly observed; and these must vary according to the variety of places and times, as has been shown above from canon law itself. Secondly, a great part of the Hierarchical writers, Whitgift, Hooker, Sutcliffe, Bridges and others, maintain that the very form of ecclesiastical government is changeable even in essentials; yet is it wicked for us to change, among us, the canon law, that is, the Papist law? Thirdly, God commands that his statutes be kept, not those of the fathers, however ancient (Ezek. 20. 18, 30). And that saying of Augustine and Cyprian has been carried into the very body of canon law: Whatever custom, however old, however widespread, is altogether to be set aside before the truth, and a practice contrary to the truth is to be abolished. So recently Benignus Millet: It is shown to be a rash and even reckless attempt to wish to change what is held firm and settled by long consensus of all. Indeed, changes are not to be made rashly, lest the authority of the law, which is confirmed especially by time and long custom, grow cheap. But when evident and certain usefulness, indeed necessity, stirs men's minds to draw out the truth from the thickest darkness of long and lasting error, then surely, without fear, and without regard to time or long custom, we are bound to profess it openly. This truth demands it, and no one can prescribe against it: not the length of times, not the patronage of persons, not the privilege of nations. 3 Thirdly, Bancroft objects as follows. Viretus, seeing, though late, how great the inconveniences for our discipline would grow from the abrogation of canon law, says this: they thought it a fine reformation in the Church to abolish all canons and decrees together with the statutes which the ancient fathers and doctors ordained for preserving right discipline in the Church. What troubled Viretus most was that in this way princes would free their necks from the yoke of discipline. And this is what our Puritans are now striving for, which is provided for in an act of Parliament, that nothing of canon law shall have force which is contrary to the laws of this realm or to the royal prerogative. Nor can we think otherwise than that Viretus has laid bare their inmost hearts. First, Viretus could complain of the abrogation of the ancient canons (which he thought useful), so that meanwhile he would not want the Church governed by canon law, as it is certain he did not want. Secondly, how could Viretus lay bare the inmost heart of our people, when by his own saying we differ so much from him that he strove to retain canon law while we labour to abrogate the same? Thirdly, it is known to the whole world that the reformed demand the abrogation of canon law, first because it is contrary to the royal prerogative of Jesus Christ, who is King of kings, and then because it is contrary to the royal prerogative of earthly kings and princes. So nothing more putrid than this calumny of Bancroft's, and nothing more virulent, can be imagined. 4 Fourthly, Bancroft objects: If anything in canon law occurs which may be of use to them, they contend that it is to be brought in, and they ascribe to themselves the praise that is due to true authorities. Cartwright and the rest of his brotherhood, in their outline of essential discipline, have drawn from canon law and ancient constitutions more than seven parts in eight. First, let this testimony be noted concerning the antiquity of reformed discipline. The essential outline of discipline which Thomas Cartwright drew up he did not draw from canon law, but from the word of God alone. That more than seven of its eight parts are found in the ancient constitutions is not so great a matter: the episcopal government is not so ancient as you pretend, nor is reformed discipline so new as you often rant. Secondly, Gratian (says Mornay) patches together his decree from canons and ancient decrees, which he himself in many places adapts to the corruption of the times; yet he leaves us many traces, by whose help it is given to those who seek diligently to investigate some doctrine and practice of the Church. We are accustomed to track down these traces in doctrine, and to cite them against the Papists, even though we otherwise detest the doctrine of canon law. Why, then, should it not be lawful for the reformed also to allege these things in discipline against the Hierarchical men, even though they otherwise rightly condemn the canonical discipline? Let even that Hierarchical man Thomas Bilson be consulted: he affirms that Gratian is the most corrupt of all in citing the fathers, yet he never ceases to press Gratian against the Rhemists. How frivolous, moreover, is the conclusion drawn from this, that we ought to concede that the Church be governed by canon law, because we are wont sometimes to allege something from it! Let this argument be Sultingian: that is, inept and childish. For he argues in exactly the same way: Bucer judges very well, as also Zepperus above, that the canons of the councils and what Gratian has gathered from various councils and the rescripts of the holy fathers, from distinction 23 to distinction 96, are to be read concerning the episcopal office. He rightly holds that Gratian contains many things most worthy to be read and necessary to be restored in the Churches, which the holy fathers, drawn from the very canon of the Holy Spirit concerning the sacred ministries, have explained most aptly; these things are opposed to the anonymous Rochelle book, which taught that in the matter of discipline only the Scriptures are to be consulted, and that in no way must one have recourse to canon law. As for Zepperus, in my copy he cites nothing but certain things from Gratian. As for Bucer, the additions are whatever figments of Sultingius's brain they are; you may read them, except those concerning the reading of Gratian from distinction 23 to 96. Now distinction 23 begins in this manner: We have briefly shown what the difference is between ecclesiastical offices. What then? Bucer does not wish Gratian to be read in those canons because they contain the difference of the superior bishop, but only in those which depict the conduct of that bishop as a kind of father and shepherd, such as those that run from distinction 23 to distinction 96. And so much concerning the ninth foreign foundation of the Hierarchical men: namely, the practice of canon law.

units.la: CAP. XXXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIV.

units.la: Argumentum X. Hierarchicum, a Scholastica Theologia.
units.tr: Argument X. The hierarchical argument, from Scholastic theology.

units.la: SEquitur decimum, maximè omnium Papisticum: Scholastica nempè Theologia, iuris Canonici germana soror, sicut à Lombardo, Gratiani ex pellice, germano fratre conscripta primò est. Hujus compilationem haud secus atque juris Canonici deplorat Mornæus: præsertim cum scripturis reiectis, unus Gratianus consulii indè cœptus sit, uuus in scholis prælegi Lombardus: sic ut hæresis censeretur, Thelogiæ fontem, in sacris veteris atque novi testamenti scripturis penitius investigare. Hinc dixit Canus, hæresim Lutheri, Melanthonis, & Wiclephi, cæterorumque qui eos secuti sunt ex scholasticorum contemptu fluxisse: quod ut verum sit, nihil tamen hinc labis religioni nostræ accrescere defendit Reynoldus, quia a scriptutis & patrib9 ad scholasticos descendere nihil aliud sit, quam si quis a rege & a concilio regis, ad servos ipsius viliores provocet. Quò maior Hierarchicorum culpa est, qui disciplinam in verbo descriptam deserentes, eam nobis obtrudunt, cuius fundamenta nulla alia sunt, quam quæ ex fætidis scholasticæ Theologiæ lacunis hauriri possunt, imò & solent etiam. Quod etenim Reynoldus adversus Hartum, id iam nobis adversus Hierarchicos dicere fas est. Scripturæ dicis causa prætenduntur: Canonistæ revera & scholastici, duæ illæ columnæ sunt, quibus papismus (& ipsa papistica Hierarchia Anglicana) ut olim Dagonis domus sustentatur. Cernere hoc in Georgio Downamo est: qui nonne & statum quæstionis terminis scholasticis explicat, & Hierarchiæ fundamentam in trita vulgataque scholasticorum distinctione collocat? Sic enim habet. Clavis est duplex: ordinis, & jurisdictionis. Jurisdictionis est duplex, in foro interno, & in foro externo. Clavis ordinis communis est & par in omnibus, clavis iurisdictionis in foro interno, presbyteris competit: iurisdictio vero in foro externo Episcopis solis propria est. Hæc medulla est mysterij Hierarchici, hoc fundamentum Episcopalis majoritatis, hoc robur denique eorum omnium, quæ in disputationibus Hierarchicorum proferri solent, ad regimen suum Ecclesiasticum statuminandum. Quàm verò indignum sit, tueri Evangelicos ejusmodi regimen, cuius fontes a scholasticis hnnc in modum repetuntur; ostendunt ista quæ sequuntur argumenta.
units.tr: The tenth argument, the most Papistical of all, follows: Scholastic theology, the true sister of Canon law, which was first composed by Lombard, the son of Gratian's concubine and his brother by blood. Mornaeus laments its compilation no less than that of Canon law. Since the Scriptures were rejected, Gratian alone was consulted from then on, and Lombard alone was lectured on in the schools, so that it came to be considered heresy to investigate the fountain of theology deeply in the sacred Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments. Hence Canus said that the heresy of Luther, Melanchthon and Wycliffe, and of the others who followed them, arose from contempt for the Scholastics. Although this may be true, Reynolds maintains that nothing of stain thereby attaches to our religion, because to go down from the Scriptures and the Fathers to the Scholastics is nothing other than to appeal from the king and the king's council to his lowest servants. All the more blameworthy, then, are the hierarchists, who, abandoning the discipline described in the Word, thrust upon us one whose foundations are none other than those that can be drawn, and indeed commonly are drawn, from the foul pools of Scholastic theology. What Reynolds said against Hart, we may now rightly say against the hierarchists: The Scriptures are put forward for show; the canonists and the Scholastics are in truth those two pillars on which Papism (and the Papistical hierarchy of England itself) is supported, as the house of Dagon once was. This is seen in George Downame, who explains the state of the question in Scholastic terms, and who places the foundation of the hierarchy in the worn and common Scholastic distinction. For he says: There is a twofold key: of order and of jurisdiction. Jurisdiction is twofold, in the internal forum and in the external forum. The key of order is common and equal in all; the key of jurisdiction in the internal forum belongs to presbyters; but jurisdiction in the external forum belongs to bishops alone. This is the marrow of the hierarchical mystery, this the foundation of episcopal majesty, this finally the strength of all those things that are usually brought forward in the disputations of the hierarchists to prop up their ecclesiastical government. How unworthy it is for Evangelicals to defend such a government, whose sources are thus drawn from the Scholastics, the following arguments show.

units.la: Primò, consideretur circumstantia temporis, quando hæc distinctio Hierarchica; & circumstantia personarum, à quibus excogitata est. Nonne enata est in medijs papatus tenebris? nonne genita a locustis? Certè, Theologiam scholasticam, partem illam fumi Apocalyptici statuit Brightmannus, quo sol & aer obnubilatur: idque fortè non immerito. Accede etenim ad lucem scripturæ, eâ claves ex æquo tribuuntur omnibus, uti à nostris contra papistas abundè probatum batum est. Quæ igitur Theologia eas diuidit in claves ordinis pares, & claves jurisdictionis impares: nonne fumum affundit clarissimæ scripturarum luci, & claves cœlestes, in abyssi claves vertit? Quod vero harum clavum fabri & fabricatores, Scholasticos intelligo, locustæ Apocalypticæ fuerint: ex constanti ætatum subsequentium omnium, & testimonio & calculo constat. Accusat etenim eos tanquam curiosos Iohannes Gerson, Bonaventuram vero laudat, quòd scholas ab ista curiositate, ad solas scripturas revocare annisus sit. Nicolaus Beroaldus Doctor Sorbonicus de scholasticis conqueritur ita. Sophisticis nugis arcanæ cœlestesque literæ jamdiu nimium depravatæ sunt & obruptæ. Non enim studiosorum ingenia exacuunt captiunculæ istæ, & tricæ spinosæ, ut plerisque persuasum est, sed mentis succum omnem exhauriunt, adeoque à studio pietatis abduxere nonnullos recentiores, ut plerisque ex eis qui vulgò Theologi vocantur, ne Evangelium quidem totum adhuc Pauli epistolas, Christiani scilicet dogmatis, Orthodoxæque fidei fundamenta, legere edissereque vacaverit. Robertus Gallus ita, qui floruit anno 1290. Fui videns in spiritu, & ecce vir circumibat, panem delicatum portans in humeris cum vino optimo, dependebantque panis & vinum per latera ejus, ipse verò tenebat manibus lapidem oblongum durissimum, dentibus rodens illum, ut famescens circa panem agere solet, nihil autè agebat; & ex lapide egrediebantur duo capita serpentina, & instruebat me spiritus domini dicens. Lapis hic quæstiones inutiles & curiosæ sint, in quibus famescentes laborant animarum substantialia relinquentes. Et dixi quid ergo capita illo dicuntur? & dixit. Nomen uni vana gloria: alteri, dissipatio religionis.
units.tr: First, consider the circumstances of time when this hierarchical distinction was devised, and the circumstances of the persons by whom it was thought out. Was it not born in the midst of the darkness of the Papacy? Was it not brought forth by locusts? Certainly Brightman judged Scholastic theology to be that part of the Apocalyptic smoke by which the sun and the air are darkened, and perhaps not without reason. For come to the light of Scripture, where the keys are given equally to all, as our people have amply proved against the Papists. Which theology, then, divides them into unequal keys of jurisdiction and equal keys of order? Does it not pour smoke over the most clear light of the Scriptures, and turn the heavenly keys into the keys of the abyss? That the makers and fabricators of these keys, by which I mean the Scholastics, were the locusts of the Apocalypse, is established by the consistent testimony and reckoning of all the following ages. John Gerson accuses them of being over-curious, but praises Bonaventure because he strove to recall the schools from this curiosity to the Scriptures alone. Nicholas Beroaldus, a doctor of the Sorbonne, complains of the Scholastics in this way: The secret and heavenly letters have long since been far too much corrupted and broken by sophistical trifles. For those little captious quibbles and thorny tricks do not sharpen the wits of students, as most people have been persuaded, but drain every juice of the mind, and so have drawn some of the more recent writers away from the pursuit of piety, so that most of those who are commonly called theologians have not had leisure even to read or explain the whole Gospel, or Paul's Epistles, which are the foundations of Christian doctrine and of orthodox faith. Robert Gallus says this, who flourished in the year 1290: I saw in spirit, and behold a man was walking about, carrying on his shoulders delicate bread with the best wine, and the bread and wine hung down by his sides; he himself held in his hands a very hard, oblong stone, gnawing it with his teeth, as hungry men are wont to do about bread, yet he accomplished nothing; and from the stone there came forth two serpent's heads. And the Spirit of the Lord instructed me, saying: This stone is useless and curious questions, over which the hungry labour, leaving aside the substance of souls. And I said: What then are the heads called? And he said: The name of one is vainglory, of the other, dissipation of religion. Nicholas Clemangis applies to Scholastic theology that saying of Paul: They languish about questions and quarrels, etc. And he compares it to the fruits of the Dead Sea, which outwardly have a beautiful appearance but within are smoke and ashes. John Jewel adds, following Erasmus, against the Scholastics, that they were so ignorant of the Scriptures, yet so puffed up with natural learning, that they brought forth monsters of impudence, and so absurd that they seem to have written them for pigs, not for men. Thomas More proposed that the Scholastics be mocked, and not undeservedly, says Thomas Morton the hierarchist. That saying about the Scholastics was approved: How wretched it is to draw the foundations of religion from these sophists? On which the expurgatory index says: Let it be deleted. Calvin called the Scholastics sophists, who know how to disclose their own frauds; on account of this, the Jesuit Salmeron calls Calvin a great scoundrel, but Morton defends Calvin and adds something of his own: I will prove that your school has long been a sort of marketplace of sophisms and most foolish tricks. From this it can be seen with what much better right the reformed discipline is ordered, since it draws its foundations from Scripture alone, together with Bonaventure, Gerson and Beroaldus, than the hierarchical discipline, which has been drawn and tasted from the curiosity of the schools according to Gerson, from the sophistical trifles of the schools according to Beroaldus, from the serpent's head and the hard stone of the Scholastics according to Gallus, and finally from the marketplace of sophisms according to Morton. Bancroft compares our arguments to the fruits of Sodom; but if Nicholas Clemangis is right, this calumny ought to return home to where it first set out. How wretched, says Ramus, it is to draw the foundation of religion from the sophists themselves; therefore the cause of George Downame is wretched, whose foundations are drawn from them. Those who, in Erasmus's judgement, wrote for pigs in the cause of discipline, should not they be sent off to the hog-pen along with the pigs themselves?

units.la: 3 Nicolaus Clemangis, ad scholasticam Theologiam accommodat illud Pauli; Languent circa quæstiones & pugnas, &c. Et comparat eam fructibus lacus Asphaltitis, qui foris speciem pulchram habent, sed intus fumum & cinerem. Adjicit Iohannes Iuellus ex Erasmo contra Scholasticos, eos adeo scripturæ ignaros fuisse, naturali verò scientia tumidos, ut portenta genuerint impudentia, & adeo sfusulsa, ut videantur suibus ea scripsisse, non hominibus. Thomas Morus Scholasticos deridendos proposuit, nec immerito inquit Thomas Mortonus Hierarchicus. Approbata ista de scholasticis vox fuit. Quam miserabile est de istis sophistis fundamenta religionis repetere? de quo index expurgatorius, Deleatur. Calvinus Scholasticos Sophistas vocavit, qui suas norunt fraudes detegere: propter quod, Calvinum magnum nebulonem Salmeron Iesuita appellat: defendit vero Calvinum Mortonus & insuper addit de suo. Probabo scholam vestram iamdiu emporium quoddam sophismatum, & stropharum ineptissimarum extitisse. Videre hinc licet, quanto potiori jure disciplina reformata sit, quæ cum Bonaventura, & Gersone, & Beroaldo ex sola scriptura fundamenta sua repetit: quàm Hirerarchica, quæ ex curiositate Scholæ juxta Gersonem, & sophisticis scholarum nugis, juxta Beroaldum, serpentino capite, & lapide durissimo scholasticarum juxta Gallum, ex emporio denique sophismatum juxta Mortonum, hausta & delibata est. Argumenta nostra fructibus Sodomæ comparat Bancroftus, sed si Nicolaus Clemangis verus, domum redeat oportet calumnia hæc, unde primò progressa est. Quàm miserabile est inquit Ramus ab ipsis sophistis fundamentum religionis repetere: miserabilis ergo Georg. Downami causa est, cujus hinc fundamenta petuntur. Qui suibus, Erasmi judicio, scripserunt, in causa disciplinæ, nonne cum suibus ipsis ad haram amandandi sunt?
units.tr: 3 Nicholas Clemangis applies to scholastic theology that saying of Paul: They languish about questions and quarrels, etc. He compares it to the fruit of the Dead Sea, which looks fair on the outside but is smoke and ash within. John Jewel adds, following Erasmus, against the Schoolmen, that they were so ignorant of Scripture, yet so puffed up with natural learning, that they produced monstrous impudence, and were so crude that they seem to have written those things for swine, not for men. Thomas More proposed that the Schoolmen should be ridiculed, and, not undeservedly, says Thomas Morton the Hierarchist. That opinion about the Schoolmen was approved. How wretched it is to derive the foundations of religion from these sophists? On this the expurgatory index says: Let it be deleted. Calvin called the Schoolmen sophists, who knew how to expose their own frauds; for this reason the Jesuit Salmeron calls Calvin a great rogue. But Morton defends Calvin and adds something of his own: I will prove that your school has long been a kind of market of sophisms and most foolish tricks. From this one may see with how much better right the reformed discipline is ordered, which, together with Bonaventure, Gerson and Beroaldus, derives its foundations from Scripture alone, than the hierarchical discipline, which has been drawn from the curiosity of the School (according to Gerson), from the scholastic trifles of the sophists (according to Beroaldus), from the serpent's head and the hardest stone of the Schools (according to Gallus), and finally from the market of sophisms (according to Morton), and has been drawn and tasted from them. Bancroft compares our arguments to the fruit of Sodom; but if Nicholas Clemangis is right, this calumny ought to return home to where it first set out. How wretched it is, says Ramus, to derive the foundation of religion from the sophists themselves. Therefore the cause of George Downame is wretched, since his foundations are sought from here. Those who, in the judgement of Erasmus, wrote for swine, in a matter of discipline, ought they not to be sent to the pigsty together with the swine themselves?

units.la: 4 Sicut suspecta disciplina Hierarchica esse debet, quòd illius fundamenta ex scholasticis repetuntur: ita quòd illius firmamenta etiam scholastica sunt. Ita Aventinus de Lombardo, & scholasticis, apud Dominum Morneum. Lombardus sacrosanctæ philosophiæ veritatem, fontemque purissimum, sicut plus millies à Iacobo Fabro & Iodoco Clitoveo præeptoribus meis accepi atque audivi, cæno quæstionum, & rivulis opinionum conturbavit, id quod & usus rerum, nisi cæci sumus, satis superque docet. Ita Iohannes Reynoldus: Illotis pedibus sanctuarium Domini ingressi sunt, unde philosophiâ Theologiam polluerunt, naturali rationis lumini plus nimium addicti. Post, sophisticam & dialecticam eis objicit, quo nomine eos cavere jubemur, 1. Tim. 6. 20. Nam oppositionem illam scientiæ, quæ est à Paulo condemnata, in scholasticis exuberare dicit. Perspici hinc licet, quid de oppositione Hierarchica sentiendum: sanctam etenim disciplinam cæno scholastico infecerunt, qui haud minus in causa disciplinæ, quam in causa doctrinæ illotis pedibus sanctuarium Domini ingressi sunt. Quod igitur de Nerone primo persecutore Christianorum: id nos de scholasticis distinctionis Hierarchicæ Downamianæ inventoribus primis dicere possumus. [Tali dedicatore damnationis nostræ gloriamur.] Porro tela Hierarchica omnia, ex horum ipsorum armamentario depromuntur: ex lumine scilicet naturali, ex philosophicis ratiocinijs, imò sophisticis argumentationibus: ut dijudicare cuivis facile, qui eorum scripta legit, altercationes præsertim logicales illas, quæ apud Downamum, atque Remonstratorem scatent. Non placet hæc subtilitas Iohanni Iuello, qui hos patres producit, Verba philosophorum excludit simplex veritas piscatorum. Ambrof. de Incarnat. cap. 9. Non in dialectica complacuit Deo salvum facere populum suum. Regnum Dei in simplicitate fidei est, non in contentione sermonis. Ambrof. de fid. lib. 1. cap. 3. Sapientes huius seculi (vivida Hierarchici scriptoris descriptio) videntes absque Grammatica & peritia philosophica consurgere muros Evangelij, velut cum irrisione quadam dicunt: perfacile hoc posse destrui caliditate sermonum, per astutas fallacias, & argumenta dialectica. Origen. in Cantic. Homil. 4. Citatur in hanc rem à Gratiano Hieronymus. Vino inebriantur qui sacras scripturas male intelligunt atque pervertunt: sicera, qui aluntur seculari sapientia & dialecticorum tendiculis. Recognoscant istinc insignia sua Hierarchici?
units.tr: 4 Just as the hierarchical discipline ought to be held suspect because its foundations are taken from the Schoolmen, so too its supports are scholastic. Thus Aventinus of Lombard and the Schoolmen, as quoted by Mr. Morney: Lombard muddied the truth of the most sacred philosophy and its purest fountain with the mire of questions and the streams of opinions, as I have received and heard more than a thousand times from my teachers James Lefèvre and Josse Clichtove; and the practice of affairs, unless we are blind, teaches this sufficiently and more than enough. Thus John Reynolds: They entered the sanctuary of the Lord with unwashed feet, whence they polluted theology with philosophy, being far too much devoted to the natural light of reason. Afterwards he objects to them sophistry and dialectic, from which we are commanded to beware, 1 Tim. 6.20. For he says that that opposition of knowledge, which was condemned by Paul, abounds in the Schoolmen. From this one may see what is to be thought of the hierarchical opposition: for they have infected holy discipline with scholastic mire, who entered the sanctuary of the Lord with unwashed feet no less in the matter of discipline than in the matter of doctrine. So what was said of Nero, the first persecutor of Christians, we may say of the first inventors of the hierarchical distinction of Downame's kind. [We glory in such a patron of our condemnation.] Further, all the hierarchical weapons are drawn from this very armoury of theirs: namely from the natural light, from philosophical reasonings, indeed from sophistical arguments, as anyone who reads their writings may easily judge, especially those logical wranglings which swarm in Downame and the Remonstrant. This subtlety did not please John Jewel, who cites these Fathers: The simple truth of fishermen excludes the words of philosophers. Ambrose, On the Incarnation, ch. 9: It did not please God to save his people by dialectic. The kingdom of God is in simplicity of faith, not in contention of words. Ambrose, On the Faith, bk. 1, ch. 3: The wise men of this age (a lively description by the hierarchical writer), seeing the walls of the Gospel rising up without grammar and philosophical skill, say with a kind of mockery that it can very easily be destroyed by the cunning of words, by subtle fallacies and dialectical arguments. Origen, On the Song of Songs, Homily 4. Jerome, cited on this point by Gratian: They are drunk with wine who misunderstand and pervert the sacred Scriptures; they are drunk with strong drink who are fed by worldly wisdom and the snares of the dialecticians. Do the hierarchists recognise their own marks in this?

units.la: 5 Tertiò, quæ Paulus de litigio verborum vitando monuit, 1. Tim. 6. 4. ea in scholasticis exuberare, non absq; causa docet Reynoldus: quos Hierarchici imitari non erubescunt. Num voces istæ ordinum & Iurisdictionis in sacris literis occurrunt usquam? aut etiam in scriptis patrum, aut in probato scriptore ullo ante tempora scholasticorum, de quibus tamen à scholasticis mutuatis tanta jam litigia excitant? Rectè Thomas Bilsonus: Scitis eos omnia confundere posse verborum æquivocationibus, si ludere & nugari libeat: sed omnibus Doctoribus litigium verborum interdixit Paulus.
units.tr: 5. Thirdly, the admonition of Paul to avoid "strife of words" (1 Tim. 6:4) is, as Reynolds rightly teaches, something the schoolmen overflow with, and not without reason; and the Hierarchists are not ashamed to imitate them. Do these terms of "orders" and "jurisdiction" occur anywhere in Holy Scripture? Or in the writings of the Fathers, or in any approved writer before the time of the schoolmen? Yet they have borrowed them from the schoolmen and now stir up such great disputes over them. Thomas Bilson rightly says: You know that they can confuse everything with equivocations of words, if they like to play and trifle; but Paul forbade all teachers the strife of words.

units.la: 6. Quartò, in discipulis scholasticorum reprehendit Reynoldus, quod argumentis veris constricti, excogitata distinctione aliqua evadere solent: quod vilis & degeneris ingenij, Ludovici vivis judicio, indicium est, quum qui sunt ingenui, potius respiciant quam id sit verum quod defendant: quàm quo modo possit defendi, veritatem quam victoriam pluris æstimantes. Iam verò quis non videt, ad eludendam argumentorum nostrorum vim; hanc distinctionem, seu ut verius dicam, divulsionem Iurisdictionis, & Ordinis, scholasticorum, ab Hierarchicis usurpatam? De cujus falsitate nihil ego jam dicam: alius erit ea de re dicendi locus: de vindicanda solius scripturæ authoritate jam laboro: sic ut huic loco satius sit, si ostendero hanc distinctionem esse explodendam quod in scripturis non reperiatur: quòd si etenim legitima responsio hæc nostra non sit; malè Pontificijs scriptores nostri responderunt, qui hoc argumento eorum frivolas distinctiones passim profligare solent. Ad distinctionem de dominio Papæ in principes, directè & indirectè, quid respondet Bilsonus? Nihil hoc aliud est, quam paupercolum subterfugium, à vobis excogitatum, ut Dei mandatum prævaricemini. Ad eandem distinctionem ita Saravia: Apage distinctionem sophisticam ad eludendam vim argumenti inventam.
