Cùm dixisset Hardingus, datam quidem fuisse Math. 16. extraordinariam potestatem omnibus, ordinariam verò uni tantum: hoc Iuello respondendum videbatur. Non refert quid dicit, præsertim cùm absque ulla ratione aut authoritate præterquam sua loquatur. Quis ex antiquis Doctoribus & patribus hanc distinctionem vidit? Rursus distinguenti Hardingo, Christum Ecclesiæ quoad internum influxum, Papam quoad externum regimen caput esse, respondet, Ex ipso solummodo loqueris, aliam authoritatem aut scripturarum aut doctorum nullam affers? Succeditur Petro inquit Bellarm. quia erat ordinarius pastor, non ceteris quia erant legati: Quid ad hæc Math. Sutclivius. Hoc nempe inquit sufficere putat. Hæc distinctio merum est somnium, absque scriptura, absque ullo antiquitatis testimonio, nemo in commentarijs, &c. Ad distinctionem papisticam, Papam ut Papam errare non posse, ut privatam personam posse, respondet Whitakerus. Facilè possunt Adversarij per hanc rimulam ineptæ distinctionis evadere: ideo hoc subterfugium excogitarunt. Distinguenti Bellarmino inter caput Ecclesiæ principale & ministeriale, respondet: Nullo hæc distinctio scripturæ nititur fundamento, ideoque merito explodenda est ex scholis Theologicis. Staplerono distinguenti inter fundamentum ἀλλο & ἱπερ respondet: Si semel ea lex & consuetudo obtinuerit in theologia, ut liberum sit cuivis distinctiones comminisci; nihil in omni religione fixum, certumque permanebit. Quis enim non eo modo quidvis labefactare poterit? Explorandae igitur distinctiones diligentius & dijudicandae sunt: eaque magni æstimanda Regula est, nullas in Theologia probandas distinctiones esse, nisi quae apertis scripturarum locis nituntur. Nam ut in philosophia distinctiones absurdae repudiantur quas ratio refellit: sic putare oportet nullam theologicam distinctionem, nisi quam vere nativam, atque ex ipsis scripturis desumptam esse constiterit.
units.tr: 6. Fourthly, Reynolds rebukes the schoolmen's disciples for this: when they are pressed by true arguments, they usually escape by devising some distinction. By the judgement of Ludovicus Vives this is a sign of a base and degenerate mind, since men of good birth look rather to whether what they defend is true than to how it can be defended, valuing victory above truth. Now who does not see that the Hierarchists have adopted this distinction, or rather, to speak more truthfully, this severing of jurisdiction from order, from the schoolmen, in order to evade the force of our arguments? I shall say nothing now of its falsehood; there will be another place to speak of that. I am now labouring to vindicate the authority of Scripture alone, so that for the purposes of this place it will be enough if I show that this distinction must be rejected because it is not found in Scripture. For if this answer of ours is not valid, then our writers have answered the Papists badly, those who commonly use this very argument to overthrow their flimsy distinctions. Against the distinction concerning the Pope's dominion over princes, directly and indirectly, what does Bilson reply? This is nothing but a wretched subterfuge, devised by you so that you may transgress the command of God. Against the same distinction Saravia says: Away with that sophistical distinction, invented to evade the force of an argument! When Harding had said that Matthew 16 gave an extraordinary power to all, but an ordinary power to one only, Jewel thought this must be answered thus: It does not matter what he says, especially since he speaks without any reason or authority other than his own. Which of the ancient teachers and Fathers saw this distinction? Again, when Harding distinguished, saying that Christ is head of the Church as to inward influence, and the Pope as to outward government, Jewel replies: You speak from yourself alone; do you bring forward no other authority, either of Scripture or of teachers? Bellarmine says that Peter was succeeded because he was an ordinary minister, not the others because they were legates. What does Mathew Sutcliffe say to this? He thinks this is sufficient, as he puts it. This distinction is pure dream, with no Scripture, no testimony of antiquity, no one in the commentaries, and so on. Against the Papist distinction, that the Pope as Pope cannot err but as a private person can, Whitaker replies. The adversaries can easily escape by this little crack of a foolish distinction; that is why they have devised this subterfuge. To Bellarmine, distinguishing between the principal and the ministerial head of the Church, Whitaker answers: This distinction rests on no foundation of Scripture, and therefore deservedly should be driven out of the theological schools. To Stapleton, distinguishing between the foundation (alio) and the foundation (hyper), he answers: If once such a law and custom prevails in theology, that anyone is free to invent distinctions, nothing in any religion will remain fixed and certain. For who could not in this way overthrow anything whatever? Distinctions must therefore be examined more carefully and judged more strictly; and this is the great rule to be esteemed: no distinctions are to be accepted in theology except those that rest on plain passages of Scripture. For just as in philosophy absurd distinctions are rejected when reason refutes them, so one must hold that no theological distinction is to be accepted unless it is shown to be truly native and drawn from the Scriptures themselves.

units.la: 7 Bellarmino distinguenti inter Petrum ut Apostolum, & Petrum ut ordinarium pastorem respondet. Quis insomniorum & distinctionum modus? Non quidvis fingere licet. Distinctionis ludibrium istud est. Rursus: Cum claves Math. 18. promittantur omnibus, quid Iesuita nunc sibi reservavit quo se in posterum tueatur: distinctionem, quae ut cetera deficiant nunquam deerit. Quis enim causam perderet, quam distinctione tam parabili possit defendere? Alibi. Quid ergo statuit de jurisdictione Episcoporum? Estne divinian humani juris. Hic nunc iterum distinctionem adhibet: sed male pereant distinctiones sophisticae, quae falsitatis & haeresis tuendae causa excogitantur. Ita Hadrianus Saravia ipse. Inanis & sophistica est omnis distinctio & fallaciae plena, quam quis scriptis sive sacris sive prophanis inducit, non ab illis desumit. Regula iuris est, non esse distinguendum ubi lex non distinguit. Ad eundem sensum Tho. Mortonus Hierarchicus: In uno genere artificii sophistici, videlicet distinguendi nimia subtilitate insistam: quae dum scholastici discipulos suos, ex errorum latebris explicare videri volunt, multo magis eos intricarunt. Cum tamen haec immota lex distinguendi esse debeat. NON EST DISTINGVENDVM VBI LEX NON DISTINGVIT. Haec ita cum sint, non est quòd Hierarchiam nostram magis quàm papalem quis admiretur: cum eodem, inter ordinem communem, &c jurisdictionem quibusdam reservatam distinctionis fundamento nititur: adversus quam si nihil aliud afferre possemus, sufficeret tamen, quod à scholasticis locis inventa sit, quòd non ante Ægyptiacas papatus tenebras prodierat: quòd sopisticen sapiat, quod novitatem, litigiumq; verborum inferat: quod denique in lege, in scriptura, ejusdemq; apertis locis nullis reperiatur. Atque haec de fundamento extraneo Hierarchicorum decimo: Scholasticae nempe Theologiae imitatione.
units.tr: 7. To Bellarmine, distinguishing between Peter as apostle and Peter as ordinary minister, he replies: What kind of dreams and distinctions is this? One may not invent whatever one likes. This distinction is a mockery. Again: Since the keys are promised to all in Matthew 18, what has the Jesuit now reserved for himself to fall back on in future? A distinction, which will never be lacking when everything else fails. For who would lose a cause that he could defend with a distinction so easily made? Elsewhere: What then does he decide about the jurisdiction of bishops? Is it of divine or of human right? Here again he brings in a distinction; but let sophistical distinctions perish, which are devised for the sake of defending falsehood and heresy. So says Adrian Saravia himself: Every distinction is empty and sophistical and full of fallacy, when anyone brings it in from his own writings, whether sacred or profane, and does not take it from them. The rule of law is: one must not distinguish where the law does not distinguish. To the same effect Thomas Morton, a Hierarchist himself: I shall dwell on one kind of sophistical craft, namely, distinguishing with excessive subtlety; for while the schoolmen wish to appear to explain their disciples out of the hiding-places of error, they have entangled them far more. Yet this rule of distinguishing ought to stand unshaken. ONE SHOULD NOT DISTINGUISH WHERE THE LAW DOES NOT DISTINGUISH. Since these things are so, no one should be surprised that our Hierarchy is not more admired than the papal one, since it rests on the same foundation of distinction, between the common order and jurisdiction reserved to certain men. Against it, even if we could bring nothing else, it would be enough that it was devised by the schoolmen, and did not come forth before the Egyptian darkness of the papacy; that it smells of sophistry; that it introduces novelty and strife of words; and finally that it is found nowhere in the law, in Scripture, or in its plain passages. And this is enough on the foreign foundation of the Hierarchists' tenth point: namely, imitation of scholastic theology.

units.la: CAP. XXXV.
units.tr: CAP. XXXV.

units.la: Argumentum XI. Hierarchicum à multitudine.
units.tr: The Eleventh Hierarchical Argument, from Multitude.

units.la: SEquitur undecimum, à papistis etiam mutuatum, nempè a Multitudine: quam pluribus modis urgere Hierarchici solent. Primò, æquum esse nuper censuerunt, ut pauciores reformati cum essent (sub Iacobi Regis auspicijs) pluribus cederent, præsertim cum ex ipsis plurimi authoritate pollerent, vel in Ecclesia, vel in republica Anglicana. At coincidit haec objectio cum papistica illa, quacum luctatur Iohannes Whitus Hierarchicus, qui pro nobis respondet ita. Non est absurdum neque impossibile, hominem privatum & in optima quaque Ecclesia errorem dispi cere: qua causa ecclesiam judicare potest, & praeferendum illius judicium est, ut quidem papistae ipsi minime negant. Eos vero recensent alibi. Citat Panormitanum de Elect. Extravagat. cap. signif. In rebus fidem concernentibus, judicium unius privati hominis praeferendum est Papae & toti concilio, si ille moveatur melioribus rationibus, & authoritatibus novi & veteris testamenti. Citat Iohannem Gerson de Exa. doct. p.1. considerat 5. Examen doctrinarum de fide non solum ad Papam, & concilium pertinet: sed ad quemcunque etiam in sacra scriptura sufficienter expertum: quia idoneus judex quisque est in eo quod novit. Rursus: Quidam Laicus in scripturis adeo excellenter doctus esse potest, ut illius assertio magis credenda sit, quam definitiva sententia Papae: nam Evangelium magis credendum est, quam Papa. Igitur si talis Laicus, quanquam privatus, veritatem docet, quae in Evangelio continetur, & Papa illud nescit, vel scire non vult: evidens est, quod illius judicium sit praeferendum. Citat deniq; Tractat. Interdict. Theolog. venet. prop. 23. Non salvat Christianum quod Pontifex dicit praeceptum suum esse iustum, sed oportet illud examinare, atque se iuxta regulam superius datam dirigere. Rursus. [Quia Iesuita adeo pro sua multitudine contendit, consideret quod scriptura iubeat, ut omnes examinent ea quae docentur, 1. Thess. 5.21. 1. Ioh. 4.1. cos etiam laudans qui ipsam doctrinam Apostolorum examinarent, Act. 17.11. mandansque a falsis prophetis cavere, Math. 7.15. & 24.4. Esa. 8.20. Ierem. 23.16. Rom. 16.17. & scrutari scripturas. Iof. 18, Ioh. 5.39. & sensus exercitatos habere, bona a malo discernendo, Hebr. 5.14. quae omnia frustra essent, si per lectionem ad certitudinem aliquam pervenire nequiremus, vel eam assecuti tenere adversus multitudinem: sed semper obligaremur rem ad eos referre, qui suspecti sunt, quorumque iudicium illud est, quod examinari debet. Rursus: [Vnus Michaias veritatem defendebat contra 4co. Prophetas, 1. Reg. 22. Vnus Paphnutius totum concilium Nicaenum direxit. Nicephor. lib. 8. c. 19. Christus & Apostoli toti Synagogae Iudaeorum restiterunt, & Elihu juvenis unus seniores 3. increpavit, Iob. 32.6.] Citat Chrisostomus Homil. 3. in Act. & Hieronymum in Noah. c. 2. quod Laicus temere Doctoribus Ecclesiae credere non debeat, sed eorum doctrinas examinare: praesertim cum populi aures sacerdotum cordibus saepe sanctiores sint, ut habet Hieronymus epist. ad Pammach. adversus errores Ioh. Hierosolym. Annon ex his abunde constat, non obligari Reformatos, ut multitudinem sequantur Hierarchicorum quanquam doctores in Ecclesia sint, & ad gubernacula sedeant?
units.tr: Next comes the eleventh argument, borrowed from the Papists as well, namely from multitude, which the Hierarchists are accustomed to press in several ways. First, they have lately held it fair that, since the reformed were fewer (under the auspices of King James), they should yield to the greater number, especially since many of their own side carried weight, either in the Church or in the English commonwealth. But this objection coincides with that Papist one with which John White the Hierarchist wrestles, and he answers us thus: It is neither absurd nor impossible for a private man, even in the best church, to discern an error; for which reason the church can judge, and its judgment is to be preferred, as the Papists themselves by no means deny. He cites those men elsewhere. He cites Panormitanus, on the Extravagantes of Elections, chapter "significasti": In matters concerning faith, the judgment of one private man is to be preferred to the Pope and the whole council, if he is moved by better reasons and by authorities of the New and Old Testament. He cites John Gerson, On the Examination of Doctrines, part 1, consideration 5: The examination of doctrines of faith pertains not only to the Pope and the council, but to anyone sufficiently experienced in Holy Scripture, since every person is a competent judge in what he knows. Again: A certain layman may be so excellently learned in the Scriptures that his assertion is to be believed more than the definitive sentence of the Pope; for the Gospel is to be believed more than the Pope. Therefore if such a layman, though private, teaches the truth contained in the Gospel, and the Pope either does not know it or does not wish to know it, it is evident that his judgment is to be preferred. Lastly he cites the Theological Tract on Interdicts, Venice, proposition 23: It does not save a Christian that the Pontiff says his command is just; rather it is necessary to examine it and to direct oneself according to the rule given above. Again: [Since the Jesuit so insists on his multitude, let him consider what Scripture commands, that all should examine the things that are taught: 1 Thess. 5.21; 1 John 4.1; praising also those who examined the very doctrine of the Apostles, Acts 17.11; and commanding us to beware of false prophets, Matt. 7.15 and 24.4; Isa. 8.20; Jer. 23.16; Rom. 16.17; and to search the Scriptures, Josh. 18; John 5.39; and to have senses trained to discern good from evil, Heb. 5.14. All these would be in vain if we could not by reading attain some certainty, or, having attained it, hold it against the multitude; but we would always be bound to refer the matter to those who are suspect, whose judgment is precisely what ought to be examined.] Again: [Micaiah alone defended the truth against 400 prophets, 1 Kings 22. Paphnutius alone directed the whole Council of Nicaea (Nicephorus, book 8, chapter 19). Christ and the Apostles resisted the whole synagogue of the Jews, and Elihu, a young man, rebuked the three elders, Job 32.6.] He cites Chrysostom, Homily 3 on Acts, and Jerome on Noah, chapter 2, that a layman should not rashly believe the teachers of the Church but should examine their doctrines, especially since the ears of the people are often more holy than the hearts of priests, as Jerome says in his letter to Pammachius against the errors of John of Jerusalem. Does it not sufficiently follow from these things that the Reformed are not bound to follow the multitude of the Hierarchists, although they are teachers in the Church and sit at the helm?

units.la: 2 Secunda objectio multitudinis ita ab Hadriano Saravia ponitur, Mos totius orbis & omnium temporum Ecclesiarum potior esse debet eo, qui est exigui populi & parvi temporis. Rufus: Si consensus in aliqua re Doctorum pondus habet, longe gravius illud esse debet quod omnium Ecclesiarum omnium locorum & temporum secum confinxit adfert: quam hujus nostri patremi saeculi paucorum. Atqui consensum superiorum temporum firmum in Theologia argumentum non esse, nos supra demonstravimus: in praesentiarum latis erit Hadriano Saraviae Hierarchico, Matthaei Sutclivij Hierarchici responsum opponere. Con-
units.tr: 2. The second objection from multitude is set forth thus by Hadrian Saravia: The custom of the whole world and of the Churches of all times ought to carry more weight than that of a small people and a short time. Again: If the consent of the teachers has weight in any matter, that agreement which the Churches of all places and times have gathered together ought to weigh far more heavily than that of a few men of this our present age. But we have already shown above that the consensus of earlier times is not a firm argument in theology. For the present it will suffice to set against Hadrian Saravia the Hierarchist the reply of Matthew Sutcliffe, also a Hierarchist. Con-

units.la: sensus cum Ecclesijs antiquis, est nota (Ecclesiae, ac proinde veritatis,) observantia cum fuerit: nam patres sibi invicem in multis adversantur, & haeretici consensum patrum sequenumero allegarunt, Ariani Origenem, Eutychiani Cyrillum, Cyprianum & alios patres. Deinde a scriptoris ipsis saepe dissentiunt patres: & quod de Arianis dicit Socrates, lib. 1. cap. 6. hoc nonnulli fecere patres: Explicandis scripturis saepe everterunt. At inquit Bellarminus, Theodosius patrum qui ante sua scripserunt tempora prolatis sententiis haereticos compescuit. Esto. Nam & nos secundum scripturas plurimum patribus tribuimus: in consensu vero cum patribus tanto minus est praesidij quam in consensu cum scripturis, quanto his illi minores sunt. Non tamen quae-
units.tr: sensus with the ancient Churches is a mark of the Church, and therefore of truth, only when it is observance; for the Fathers often oppose one another in many things, and heretics have frequently cited the consensus of the Fathers: the Arians cited Origen, the Eutychians Cyril, Cyprian and other Fathers. Moreover, the Fathers often dissent even from the writers themselves; and what Socrates says of the Arians, book 1, chapter 6, some Fathers also did: they often overturned the Scriptures in their explanations. But, says Bellarmine, Theodosius repressed heretics by means of sentences of the Fathers who wrote before his time. Granted. For we too attribute very much to the Fathers according to the Scriptures; but in agreement with the Fathers there is so much less support than in agreement with the Scriptures, as the Fathers are less than the Scriptures. Yet not

units.la: cunque scripserunt patres, ea vel Theodosius probavit, vel nos probanda censemus. Nec tantum sibi deferri postulant patres: pro quo citat Ambrosium. Nolo nobis credatur, scriptura recitetur. Et ad Gratianum: Facessat notas sententiae. Paulum interrogemus. Origenes sensibus & enarrationibus suis, sine scripturis testibus nullam postulat adhiberi fidem: solifa; Canonici scripturis deberi sine ulla recusatione consensum dicit Augustinus: & ad Hieronymum libertatem probandi vel improbandi, si quid a patribus recte aut secus dicatur, relinqui debere putat. Non Thomas quidem Aquinas necessario credendum censet patribus in materia fidei.
units.tr: whatever the Fathers wrote did Theodosius approve, nor do we think it all to be approved. Nor do the Fathers demand so much deference for themselves: on this point he cites Ambrose: "I do not wish that I be believed; let Scripture be read." And to Gratian: "Let the opinion of men cease; let us question Paul." Origen, in his senses and explanations, demands that no faith be given without the witnesses of Scripture; Augustine says that agreement is owed without any refusal to the canonical Scriptures alone, and he thinks that to Jerome there should be left the liberty of proving or disproving whatever is said rightly or otherwise by the Fathers. Not even Thomas Aquinas thinks the Fathers are necessarily to be believed in matters of faith.

units.la: Objectio multitudinis tertia ita ponitur a Georgio Downamo. Res evidens est multo maiorem partem Ecclesiarum Europaearum, per Episcopos gubernatam esse: Probat ex inductione multarum Ecclesiarum, quarum plurimae Lutheranae sunt, quarum longum catalogum concificit: atque hos Episcopos habere dicit quia superintendentes habent.
units.tr: The third objection from multitude is set forth by George Downame thus: It is clear that by far the greater part of the Churches of Europe is governed by bishops: He proves this by an enumeration of many Churches, most of which are Lutheran, and of which he makes a long catalogue; and he says these have bishops because they have superintendents.

units.la: Cum arguments multitudinis solo, nobis hoc tempore negotium est, quod ab Ecclesijs Lutheranis praecipue ductum minime valere, docet illa responsio Whitakeri, adversus papistas multitudinem obiicientes disputantis.Citat primo Augustinum.Si justus es noli numerare sed appende: stateram affer aequam non dolosam. Noli mirari turbas hominum incedentes mas latas. Multi sunt, & quis numerat? pauci autem per viam angustam incedunt. Profer inquam stateram, appende. Vide contra panca grana, quantam paleam leves.
units.tr: Only the argument from multitude remains for us to deal with at this time, which the reply of Whitaker, disputing against the Papists who object multitude, shows to be of little worth when drawn chiefly from the Lutheran Churches. He cites first Augustine: If you are just, do not count but weigh: bring a fair and not a deceitful balance. Do not wonder at the crowds of men walking on the broad way. They are many, and who counts them? But few walk by the narrow way. Bring, I say, the balance and weigh. See how light a little chaff is against a few grains.

units.la: Sequitur Chrysostomus: Quoniam precor utilitas est multum esse facum potius, quam paucos lapides preciosos? Non in numeri multitudine, sed invitutis probitate multitudo confusit. Elias unus erat, sed totus mundus non erat dignus qui reponderetur ipsi. Sequitur Gregorius Nazianzenus: Vbinam illi sunt qui multitudine Ecclesiam definiant & gregem exiguam aspernantur? 8. Obiectio quarta similiter Downami est, qui plures protestantes doctos, & Ecclesias reformatas, Episcoporum regimen approbare quàm impugnare dicit. Quod usq; adeo amplificat alibi, ut dicat, plures Ecclesias ab uno Episcopo in Anglia regi,regimine Hierarchico quam quæ sunt in toto Christiano orbe disciplinam reformatam profitentes, De Gallia iactat, in ea eruditissimos ad recipiendum Hierarchicum regimen paratos esse, cujus verisimilitudinem confirmat exemplo Scotiæ, ubi licet disciplina Genevensis longo tempore invaleret: cum tamen res ad suffragia relata esset, non ultra quinque inventi sunt, qui pro disciplina reformata starent. Quod si hæc omnia ita essent, respondere tamen cum Iuello non erubescimus. Veritas neque à multis neque à paucis pendet. Liberius quondam Constantio imperatori objicienti, Hoc orbis terrarum comprobavit, quanta tu es pars oblis terrarum qui pacem orbis dissolvis? respondit, Non, si ego solus sim, ideirtò minor est ratio fidei. Thomas Mortonus Hierarchicus approbat illud Cani quod habet Loc. Theolog. lib. 5. c. 5. Nos numero sententiam non metimur. Thomas Bilsonus ipse ita: Veritas numero non æstimatur, vel unus qui veritatem habet, sufficienter munitur adversus totum mundum. Citat in hanc sententiam Panormitanum alibi: quem etiam ad eandem sententiam confirmandam, Matthæus ipse Scutelivius & citat & approbat. Citat etiam Chrysostomum, qui queritur omnia esse confusa, quòd velut in theatris multitudo quærebatur non probata multitudo. Ad popul. Antioch. Homil. 26 deinde conludit. Multitudo nota Ecclesiæ (ac proinde veritatis) non est: quia Ecclesia sæpe in pauis consistit, deinde quia multitudo malorum & iniquorum major est: Postremò fuisti religio majora occupavit spatia quàm vera. Atque hæc de fundamento extraneo Hierarchicorum undecimo: nempè multitudine. CAP. XXXVI. Argumentum Hierarchicum XII. ab unitate. SEquitur duodecimum, papisticum item, nempè Vnitas: hinc etenim disciplinam reformatam, fictitium humani cerebri inventum esse concludit Bancroftus: quòd nos disciplinarij inter nos invicem non concordemus. Idem reliqui acclamant, D. Consinus præsertim, qui frivolas quasdam contradictionum species, ex nostratium scriptis colligit, quibus se totam disciplinæ causam satis superq; jugulasse putat. Multùm etiam in hoc labore desudat Bancroftus à capite Surveg, sui nono usque ad vigesimum: sed quorsum? Contra etenim Hadrianus Saravia: Diversitas de re quapiam, sive de eadem controversia, rei veritatem non tollit. Et Thomas Mortonus Hierarchicus: Si consensum in quaulibet doctrina velis, veteris Christianismi patrocinium perdis. Sed ut procedatur ordine: Primò, nihil aliud hoc argumento objiciunt nobis Hierarchici, quàm quod Pagani Christianis, Atheis Dei servis, papistæ protestantibus in universum objiciunt. Objiciebant etenim Christianis Pagani olim: religionem Christianam veram non esse, quòd Christiani circa nonnulla illius capita discordarent: quam objectionem frivolam esse ostendit Clemens Alexandrinus Stromat. lib. Origines contra Celsum lib.3. Lactantius lib.4.cap. ult. Augustinus de Civitat. Dei lib.16.c.2. de temp.serm.98. Et Isidorus Pelusiota epist.90. Ego ex Origine tantum pro præsenti nonnulli delibabo. Objicit Celsus, ut modo Bancroftus: Scinduntur Christiani, singulis suas factiones sibi parentibus, & ut in multitudinem dissonâ, aliis alios redarguentibus: nec jam quicquam præter nomen e commune superest, si tamen hoc præ pudore commune relinquitur, reliqua verò aliorum alii instituta sunt. Respondet Origines: Neminem sapientiam, aut medicinam, aut philosophiam, nedum fidem Christianam repudiaturum, quod medici & philosophi, inter se dissentiunt. Quid ni addam ego, & disciplinam reformatam etiam, si modo scriptores disciplinarij in nonnullis à se discreparent? Objectioni Atheorum respondet Chrysostomus. Gentilis dicit, vellem fieri Christianus, sed nescio cui adhaeream: multæ sunt inter vos pugnæ, nescio quod dogma eligam. Singuli dicunt, & verum dico: cui accedam, nescio, cum utrique scripturas prætexant. Respon leo illi, hoc multum pro nobis. Nam si diceremus nos rationibus credere, merito turbareris, sed cum scripturas accipimus, ac illæ sunt simplices, & veræ, facile tibi fuerit indagare. Annon idem fundamentum disciplinæ, scriptura scilicet, à reformatis recipitur? fundamentum hoc cum apud omnes unanimiter recipiatur, dissensiones reliquæ, infirmitatis quidem humanæ, non causæ tamen falsæ indicia sunt. Postremò objectio hæc de dissentionibus communis papistis: probare etenim nituntur illi religionem protestantium veram esse non posse, quod tantæ inter protestantes pugnæ & rixæ, imò & sectæ reperiantur. Respondet huic objectioni, & eam frivolam esse ostendunt, Iohannes Iuellus defens. Apol. p.3.c.3. D. 1. Guilielm. Whitakerus cont. 2. q. 5.c.8. Mattheus Sutclivius de eccles. lib.1.p.109. Thomas Mortonus Apol.sol. 1.lib.2. a capite primo ad caput decimum sextum. Richardus Feyldus de Eccles.lib.13.cap.42. & Iohannes Whitus Hierarchicus de Eccles.sect.33.34.35. & Digress.21.
units.tr: Chrysostom follows: For what is the advantage of there being many worthless things rather than a few precious stones? The crowd is confused not by the number of people but by the lack of goodness. Elijah was one man, yet the whole world was not worthy that he should be weighed against it. Gregory Nazianzen follows: Where are those who define the Church by its multitude and despise the little flock? 8. The fourth objection is likewise Downame's, who says that more learned Protestants and reformed Churches approve the government by bishops than oppose it. He pushes this so far elsewhere that he says more churches in England are ruled by one bishop under the hierarchical government than there are churches throughout the whole Christian world that profess the reformed discipline. He boasts that in France the most learned men are ready to accept the hierarchical government, and he confirms the likelihood of this by the example of Scotland, where, although the Genevan discipline had prevailed for a long time, when the matter was put to a vote no more than five men were found to stand for the reformed discipline. But even if all this were so, we are not ashamed to answer with Jewel: Truth depends neither on many nor on few. When the emperor Constantius once objected to Liberius, "This is the judgment of the whole world; how much a part of the world are you, who would dissolve the world's peace?", Liberius replied, "Even if I were alone, the reasoning of faith would not therefore be less." Thomas Morton the hierarchist approves that saying of Cano's in Loc. Theolog. lib. 5, c. 5: We do not measure opinion by number. Thomas Bilson himself says: Truth is not valued by number; one man who has the truth is sufficiently defended against the whole world. Elsewhere he cites Panormitanus to the same effect, and Matthew Sutcliffe himself both cites and approves him in confirming the same opinion. He also cites Chrysostom, who complains that everything is confused because, as in the theatres, a crowd was sought, not an approved crowd (To the People of Antioch, Homily 26). Then he concludes: The multitude is not a mark of the Church (and therefore not of truth), because the Church often stands in few; and again, because the multitude of the wicked and the unrighteous is greater. Lastly, false religion has occupied larger spaces than true. And this is the eleventh foundation of the hierarchists, which is alien to them, namely multitude. CHAP. XXXVI. The twelfth hierarchical argument, from unity. Next comes the twelfth argument, likewise a Papist one, namely unity. From this Bancroft concludes that the reformed discipline is a fictitious invention of the human brain, because we disciplinarians do not agree among ourselves. The rest cry out the same, especially D. Cosin, who gathers some trivial kinds of contradiction from the writings of our countrymen, by which he thinks he has quite cut the throat of the whole cause of discipline. Bancroft also sweats hard over this labour, from the ninth to the twentieth chapter of his Survey; but to what end? For Hadrian Saravia answers against him: Diversity of opinion about some matter, or about the same controversy, does not remove the truth of the thing. And Thomas Morton the hierarchist: If you want agreement in any doctrine whatever, you lose the defence of the old Christianity. But let us proceed in order. First, the hierarchists object to us in this argument nothing other than what the pagans in general object to Christians, atheists to the servants of God, and Papists to Protestants. For the pagans of old objected to the Christians that the Christian religion was not true because Christians disagreed about some of its articles. That this objection is trivial is shown by Clement of Alexandria in the Stromata, by Origen against Celsus, book 3, by Lactantius, book 4, last chapter, by Augustine in The City of God, book 16, chapter 2, and in the sermon On Time, no. 98, and by Isidore of Pelusium, letter 90. For the present I shall pick out only a few things from Origen. Celsus objects, just as Bancroft does now: The Christians are split, each man creating his own factions for himself, and, being in disagreement like a crowd, they refute one another; nothing remains common except the name, if even this is left in common out of shame, while the rest of their institutions are different one from another. Origen replies: No one would reject wisdom, or medicine, or philosophy, much less the Christian faith, because physicians and philosophers disagree among themselves. Why should I not add: nor the reformed discipline either, if the disciplinarian writers differ from one another on some points? Chrysostom answers the objection of the atheists: The Gentile says, "I would like to become a Christian, but I do not know which to cling to: there are many quarrels among you, and I do not know which dogma to choose. Each one speaks, and speaks the truth; I do not know which to join, since each of them pretends to Scripture." Answer him: this is much in our favour. For if we said that we believed on the basis of reasoning, you would rightly be disturbed; but since we accept the Scriptures, and these are simple and true, it will be easy for you to investigate. Is not the same foundation of discipline, namely Scripture, received by the reformed too? Since this foundation is received unanimously by all, the remaining disagreements are signs of human weakness, not of a false cause. Lastly, this objection about dissensions is common to the Papists: for they strive to prove that the religion of the Protestants cannot be true because such great quarrels and brawls, indeed even sects, are found among the Protestants. Jewel answers this objection and shows it to be trivial (Defence of the Apology, p. 3, c. 3, D. 1); so does William Whitaker (Against Cartwright? Contra 2, q. 5, c. 8); so does Matthew Sutcliffe (On the Church, book 1, p. 109); so does Thomas Morton (Apology, sol. 1, book 2, from chapter 1 to chapter 16); so does Richard Field (On the Church, book 3, chap. 42); and John White the hierarchist (On the Church, sections 33, 34, 35, and Digression 21).

units.la: 2 Secundò, frivolum est ab Vnitate Hierarchicorum argumentum: nisi pro vero supponatur, veritatem semper penes se habere eos, qui inter se unitatem colunt. Hoc autem aperte falsum esse ostendunt scriptores nostri supra nominati, instantijs multis, inter quos Guilielmus Whitakerus Thomam Aquinatem approbat, qui in Ephes.4.lect. 1. unitatem duplicem esse ait, unam bonam, aliam malam: & bonam in textu describi ab Apostolo quando ait. Soliciti estote servare unitatem Spiritus. Hinc illa Thomæ Mortoni thesis. Veritas unionis censenda non est, ubi non obtinet unio veritatis. Non igitur vera est unitas illa quam iactant Hierarchici Anglicani: sed illi papisticæ similis potius quam describit Flaccius Illyricus, in libro de dissidijs papistarum:
units.tr: 2 Secondly, the hierarchists' argument from unity is trivial, unless it is assumed as true that those who cultivate unity among themselves always have the truth in their possession. Our writers named above show by many instances that this is plainly false, among them William Whitaker, who approves Thomas Aquinas, who in Ephesians 4, lect. 1, says that unity is twofold, one good and one bad; and that the good is described by the Apostle in the text when he says: Be eager to keep the unity of the Spirit. Hence that thesis of Thomas Morton: The unity of truth is not to be counted as truth where the unity of truth does not hold. Therefore the unity that the English hierarchists boast of is not true unity, but rather resembles the Papist unity, which Flacius Illyricus describes in his book on the divisions of the Papists:

units.la: pag.802. quem ego non citassem, nisi prius a Guilielmo Whitakero, & Iohanne Whito Hierarchico productum vidissem. Prima Unitas falsa, Satanica est, inquiunt isti, quae ad commodum proprium, nempe ne regnum ejus destruatur, concordiam inter suos alit. De qua in proverbio dicitur. Vnus corvus alteri oculum non effodit. Hujus nulla suspitio in reformatos cadit, qui pro disciplina humili, & minime sibi fructuosa contendunt: cadit vero quam magna in Hierarchicos: quia verisimile non est, quin conjunctis viribus certare velint, ne regnum illud, quod sunt assecuti Ecclesiasticum in honoribus, divitiis, otio, luxu, & externa pompa positum, destruatur. Secunda falsa Unitas (inquiunt) est Ethnica, quando homines etsi contrarium videant, quiescunt tamen qui offendere nolint, aut se aliqua contentione (quae molestiam gignere solet) implicare. Quam vero vereor, ne in Anglia non pauci, moderatorum hominum nomen affectantes, hoc modo quiescant, ut qui Comitij Calderini sententiam sectentur, qui amicis ad Missam cum trahentibus, respondit olim. Eamus sane ad communes errores, quandoquidem ita vultis. Tertia falsa Unitas (inquiunt) est bellua, quando homines nihil intelligunt, sed opinionem communem sequuntur, ut se a veritatis indaganda officio laboreque, prorsus liberent & expediant. Hanc unitatem Hierarchicam in Anglia reperiri quisquis nescit, ipsam Angliam nescit, ipsaque adeo Episcoporum in Anglia artes, qui modis omnibus quibus datur, cognitionem disciplinae populo praeripiunt, ut a se solis (quod nunc faciunt) ut plurimum pendeant. Quarta falsa Unitas (inquiunt) est Iscariotica, quando homines honoribus & praemijs corrupti idem sentiunt: quam apud Hierarchicorum nullos vigere qui putat, parum ille reputat secum, quam multi ignorantiam in causa disciplinaria affectant, sic ut ne librum quidem de disciplina scriptum inspicere velint; quamque non pauci extant, qui temporis voci velificantur, ne promotiones quas affectant Ecclesiasticas manibus sibi extorqueri patiantur. Quarta falsa unitas (inquiunt) est tyrannica, quando terroribus prohibentur homines aliter sentire: cuius suspitio in Hierarchicis, inde ingens est, quod carceribus, multis, depauperationibus, aliisque molestiis infinitis satagant Episcopi, effectum dare, ne quis contra eorum regimen mussitet, aut pro disciplina reformata, vocem paulo liberiorem emittat. Sexta falsa Unitas Herodiana est (inquiunt) quando homines alioqui inter se dissentientes, adversus tamen hostem communem conspirant. Hujus unitatis suspicionem redolet in Anglia illud, quod feruntur qui alienas opiniones in rebus aliis disseminant, modo regimen Episcopale agnoscant: quum gratiam nullam nanscisci possint, in aliis omnibus doctrinae capitibus consentientes, qui hoc impugnant. Septima & ultima falsa Vanitas est (inquiunt) Vulpium Sampsonis: quando homines in cauda concordant, id est, in summa erroris sui, licet in eiusdem propugnatione, alij alio respiciant, faciesq; adversas gerant. Certe in summa Episcopalis regiminis mire conspirant Hierarchici in Anglia omnes: qui tamen ejusdem defensione mere variant, ut demonstrabitur paulò post.
units.tr: p. 802. I would not have cited him had I not first seen him quoted by William Whitaker and by John White the hierarchist. The first unity is false and Satanic, they say, which fosters concord among its own people for its own advantage, namely so that its kingdom is not destroyed. Of this a proverb is said: One crow does not gouge out the eye of another. No suspicion of this falls on the reformed, who contend for a humble discipline that brings them no profit; but it falls heavily on the hierarchists, because it is not unlikely that they wish to strive with combined strength lest that ecclesiastical kingdom they have attained, which consists in honours, riches, leisure, luxury, and outward pomp, be destroyed. The second false unity (they say) is heathen, when men, though they see the contrary, nevertheless keep quiet so as not to offend, or not to entangle themselves in any contention, which usually brings trouble. But I fear that in England not a few, who aspire to the name of moderate men, keep quiet in this way, like those who followed the opinion of Calderinus of the Comitia, who once answered friends who were dragging him to Mass: Let us go then to the common errors, since you wish it so. The third false unity (they say) is brutish, when men understand nothing but follow common opinion, so that they completely free and release themselves from the duty and labour of inquiring after the truth. Whoever does not know that this hierarchical unity is found in England does not know England itself, nor the arts of the bishops in England, who by every means available snatch from the people the knowledge of discipline, so that they depend mostly on themselves alone (which is what they now do). The fourth false unity (they say) is Judas-like, when men corrupted by honours and rewards think the same. Whoever thinks this flourishes among none of the hierarchists reckons little how many affect ignorance in the disciplinary cause, so that they do not even wish to look at a book written about discipline; and there are not a few who sail with the wind of the times, so as not to let the ecclesiastical promotions they aspire to be wrung from their hands. The fourth false unity (they say) is tyrannical, when men are forbidden by terror to think otherwise. The suspicion of this in the hierarchists is great, because the bishops busy themselves with prisons, many fines, impoverishment, and countless other annoyances, to make sure that no one murmurs against their government or utters a voice a little too free for the reformed discipline. The sixth false unity is Herodian (they say) when men who otherwise dissent from one another nevertheless conspire against a common enemy. The suspicion of this unity is suggested in England by the report that men who spread other people's opinions on other matters, provided they acknowledge episcopal government, are men who, since they cannot obtain any favour, agree with them in all other heads of doctrine, yet oppose this one. The seventh and last false unity is the foxes of Samson (they say): when men agree in the tail, that is, in the sum of their error, although in its defence they look different ways and make faces against one another. Certainly the hierarchists in England all conspire wonderfully in the sum of episcopal government, yet in its defence they vary greatly, as will be shown a little later.

units.la: 3 Tertiò, argumentum ab Vnitate Hierarchicum nihil valet, nisi pro certo supponatur, veritatem penes eos esse non posse, qui in omnibus non consentiunt, sed de nonnullis controversantur. Atqui hoc instantia plurimis, ab unoquoque seculo ductis Iohannes Whitus Hierarchicus refellit, cuius haec the sis generalis est. Ecclesiam Dei, per omnes aetates contentionibus turbatam fuisse. Dissentiebat inter se, Paulus & Barnabas inquit Act. 15.39. addo ego & in re disciplinaria dissensisse etiam: quid igitur, disciplina ab ejusdem exercitata, repudianda quaeso est? Pergit enumerare contentiones inter homines alioquin piissimos, & veritatis amantissimos: nempe inter Politianum & Victorem Cypriunum & Cornelium, Cyrillum & Theodoretum, Chrysostomum & Ephiphanium, Nazianzenum & patres Constantinopolitanos, Hieronymum & Rufinum, Paulinum & Ailsium, Leonem & Concilium Chalcedonense. Illam quam adfert Sozomeni vocem praeterire non possum. Contentionem, nempe doctrinam, id scandali generasse, ut plurimi a Christiana fide amplectendi abstererentur. Quid igitur? Etsi dissensio in aliquib. religionis falsitate minus probat, scandali tamen fecunda: praesertim cum (ut habet Whitakerus) probabile sit veritate eos deseruisse qui deseruerunt unitatem. Atque sane scandali crimine reformatorum dissentionem ego liberare nequeo: dico tamen scandalum tale datum non esse quale accipiunt Hierarchici: quia tanta eorum dissensio non est, quantam illi videri eam volunt, nempe ut vel probabilitatem quidem inferat, disciplinam reformatam humani cerebri figmentum esse.
units.tr: 3 Thirdly, the argument from unity that the Hierarchists use is worth nothing unless it is taken as certain that the truth cannot be with those who do not agree on everything but dispute about some points. Yet John Whitgift, a Hierarchist, refutes this by an objection drawn from very many ages, and his general thesis is this: the Church of God has been troubled by contentions in every age. Paul and Barnabas disagreed with each other, he says, Acts 15.39. I add that they also disagreed about discipline. Why, then, should discipline exercised by them be rejected? He goes on to list contentions among men otherwise most pious and most devoted to the truth, namely between Polycarp and Victor, Cyprian and Cornelius, Cyril and Theodoret, Chrysostom and Epiphanius, Gregory Nazianzen and the Constantinopolitan fathers, Jerome and Rufinus, Paulinus and Alypius, Leo and the Council of Chalcedon. I cannot pass over the words of Sozomen that he cites: the contention, namely over doctrine, produced such a scandal that very many were driven away from embracing the Christian faith. What then? Even if dissension over some falsehood in religion proves less, it is still fruitful of scandal, especially since (as Whitaker holds) it is probable that they have departed from the truth who have departed from unity. Indeed I cannot free the dissension of the reformed from the charge of scandal. Yet I say that the scandal given is not of the kind the Hierarchists take it to be, because their dissension is not so great as they want it to appear, namely great enough to suggest even a probability that reformed discipline is a figment of the human brain.

units.la: 4 Quartò igitur, quenam illa quaeso discordia nostra est? Primò instant Hierarchici, in dissensione, circa disciplinae reformatae fundamenta. Aequiparat enim Richardus Bancroftus disciplinarios ipsis papistis, qui ab initio primatum papae asserebant tantum hominum iure, immo ficto quodam Nicaeno Canone, in concilio Africano: post vero scripturas excogitarunt, & ad suum sensum pertraxerunt. Similiter ipse Calvinus inquit: agens etenim cum Tigurinis illo anno 1553. scripturam nullam pro disciplina Genevensi citavit: post vero quam multi scripturarum loci ad eam probandam detori sunt, & etiamnum hodie detorquentur? Quam putida calumnia haec? Annon tute confiteris, Calvinum in commentariis suis locos eos scripturae citasse qui nunc citantur, qui ante annum 1553 conscripti sunt, priusquam cum Tigurinis egisset? Annon quo incepit Calvinus ad reformandam disciplinam manum admovere, fuit 1537? a quo nominari tempus nullum poterit quando jure humano ac non divino ad instar papistarum, disciplinam reformatam Calvinus asseruerit. Revera Hierarchia ipsa, huius fraudis papisticae affinis est, cuius immerito disciplinam reformatam Bancroftus insimulat.
units.tr: 4 Fourthly, then, what is this discord of ours, I ask? First, the Hierarchists press the dissension over the foundations of reformed discipline. For Richard Bancroft equates the advocates of discipline with the papists themselves, who from the beginning asserted the primacy of the pope only by human right, indeed by a certain forged canon of Nicaea at the African council; afterwards they devised Scriptures and drew them to their own sense. Calvin likewise says: for when he dealt with the Zurich men in that year 1553, he cited no Scripture for the Geneva discipline; but afterwards how many passages of Scripture have been twisted to prove it, and are still twisted today? How rotten is this slander! Do you not yourself confess that Calvin, in his commentaries written before 1553, before he had dealt with the Zurich men, cited those very passages of Scripture that are cited now? Was it not in 1537 that Calvin began to lay his hand to reforming discipline? From that date no time can be named when Calvin asserted reformed discipline by human right and not by divine right, in the manner of the papists. Indeed the Hierarchy itself is akin to this papistical fraud, of which Bancroft wrongly accuses reformed discipline.

units.la: 5 De primatu papae Romani ita D. Mornaeus. Gelsius vellicavit nem si imitandam ratus, primatui deinceps tuando, non Nicaenum Syodumve Leo, non antiquam consuetudinem ut caeteri, sed vel illud Iud, Tu es Petrus amplectitur. Non hoc inquit Synodicis constitutionibus sed voce Evangelij &c. Carolus Sapiens author fuit Alano Chartiano ut scriberet libellum, cui titulus, Somnium Vicidarij ante 100 annos Lutetiae excusum. In eo scribitur. A Constantino, primo Christiano imperatore, Ecclesiam & Episcopum Romanum, ex consuetudine prioritatem obtinuisse: quam interim postea ex lege divina sibi deberi, falso persuadri voluerint. Docet hoc posterius testimonium papatum iure humano erectum primo, ius sibi divinum tandem usurpasse; anterius vero ipsam occasionem huiusce vsurpationis indicat, conflictum nempe Romanae Ecclesiae cum Constantinopolitana. Nam cum statutis Synodicis aequalitatem Constantinopolitana obtinuisset, non satis firmum praesidium iam erat, pro tutando Romano primatu per Synodos: ideo jus divinum urgendum sibi censuerant Romani Pontifices, aut de primatu cadendum. Et nonne quaeso similis progressus Hierarchiae Anglicanae idque ob causam similem? Episcopi etenim sub Henrico octavo, & Edwardo sexto, exta omnem aliam contradictionis positi, episcopatum iure humano afferebant tantummodo, ut suo loco demonstrabitur. Quando vero sub Elizabetha, Episcopatus in quaestionem vocatus esset: iam ex Apostolica constitutione vindicabatur: quia ius humanum infirmius esse videbatur. Ne principem tamen prorsus alienarent, ex Apostolica institutione Episcopum afferebant quidem, ut nec temere mutandus persuaderetur: sed tamen ex institutione Apostolica mutabili si ita magistratui commodum videretur. Quanquam non tam altos radices dogma egisse videtur, ex oratione Francisci Knolli in parliamento, qui Episcopos fundamentum suum de jure humano, tum deseruisse & dereliquisse affirmabat. Surrexerunt postea, Thomas Bilsonus, Richardus Bancroftus, Hadrianus Saravia & alij, qui cum periculum animadvertissent, quod hoc de mutabilitate Episcopatus dogma parere posset: non arbitrio principum suspendendum, sed jure divino immutabili communiendum existimarunt. Vehementissimus in hac persuasione altius infigenda erat Richardus Bancroftus Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis, coram quo, in ipsius palatio Lambethiano, cum Georgius Downamus pro Episcopali majoritate concionaretur, & iuris divini meminit; & distinctionem inter ius divinum quod immutabile, & jus Apostolicum quod mutabile, non sub sua sed sub aliorum persona propositit. Quid vero fit? Regia majestas (cui Deus benedicat) sententiam suam in contrarium divulgat: reliquisse nempe cum libertatem principibus, disciplinam Ecclesiae, ad formam reipublicae (prout ipsis visum fuerit) immutare. Iam Downamus in defensione concionis suae Lambethianae; non sub aliorum persona ut ante, sed in persona sua, pro disciplinae mutabilitate, omnibus remotis ambagibus pugnat. Hic verus progressus Hierarchiae Anglicanae est: ex quo iudicare cuivis facile, quinam suum fundamentum, ad exemplar papistarum immutarunt, Hierarchici vel reformati. Certe ego cum hanc historiam perlustro, non possum non de praxi dogmatis illius Nicolai Cusani cogitare, cum scripturas interpretandas esse dixit, juxta currentem praxim Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: 5 Concerning the primacy of the Roman pope, Mornay speaks thus: Gelasius, thinking it fit to imitate, thereafter in defending the primacy, did not embrace the Nicene or any synod, nor Leo, nor ancient custom like the others, but that saying (to that text) Thou art Peter. He says, "This is not by synodical constitutions but by the voice of the Gospel," etc. Charles the Wise was the author who induced Alain Chartier to write a little book entitled The Dream of the Garden, printed at Paris a hundred years ago. In it it is written: From Constantine, the first Christian emperor, the Church and the Roman bishop obtained precedence by custom; which afterwards they wanted to be persuaded was due to them by divine law. This latter testimony teaches that the papacy was first set up by human right and at last usurped a divine right for itself; the former indicates the very occasion of this usurpation, namely the conflict between the Roman Church and the Constantinopolitan. For when the Constantinopolitan church had obtained equality by synodical decrees, there was no longer a sufficiently firm bulwark for defending the Roman primacy through synods. Therefore the Roman pontiffs judged that they must press divine right, or give up the primacy. And is not the progress of the English Hierarchy, for a similar cause, similar, I ask? For bishops under Henry VIII and Edward VI, opposed to every other contradiction, asserted episcopacy only by human right, as will be shown in its place. But when under Elizabeth episcopacy was called into question, it was then defended by apostolic constitution, because human right seemed too weak. Yet, lest they alienate the prince altogether, they did indeed assert episcopacy by apostolic institution, so that it might be persuaded that it should not be changed rashly; but nevertheless by apostolic institution changeable if this seemed convenient to the magistrate. Although the doctrine does not seem to have struck very deep roots, as is clear from the speech of Francis Knollys in Parliament, who affirmed that the bishops had then abandoned and forsaken their foundation in human right. Afterwards there rose up Thomas Bilson, Richard Bancroft, Hadrian Saravia and others, who, seeing the danger that this doctrine of the changeability of episcopacy could bring, judged that it must not be left to the will of princes but must be fortified by an unchangeable divine right. Richard Bancroft, Archbishop of Canterbury, was most vehement in fixing this persuasion more deeply; in his presence, in his palace at Lambeth, when George Downame preached for episcopal majority and mentioned divine right, he put forward the distinction between divine right, which is unchangeable, and apostolic right, which is changeable, not in his own person but in the person of others. And what happened? His Royal Majesty (may God bless him) published his opinion to the contrary, namely that he left princes free to change the discipline of the Church to the form of the commonwealth, as seemed good to them. Now Downame, in defence of his Lambeth sermon, fights, not in the person of others as before but in his own person, for the changeability of discipline, with all ambiguity removed. This is the true progress of the English Hierarchy, from which it is easy for anyone to judge which of them, the Hierarchists or the reformed, have changed their foundation on the model of the papists. Certainly when I go through this history I cannot help thinking of the doctrine of Nicholas of Cusa, who said that Scriptures were to be interpreted according to the prevailing practice of the Church.

units.la: 6 Objiciunt secundo Hierarchici, vestigia priorum, reformatos posteriores deseruisse. Nulli vel mediocriter eruditi tanta acerbitate & ferocia (inquit Bilsonus) unquam exarserunt, quam hodie apud nos reformatores isti (vt se perhibent) ad unum omnes inflammati sunt. Qui hæc legit suspicari forte poterit modum excessisse reformatos Anglicanos: sed sese explicante Bilsonũ audiat. Qui Calvino successerunt, non in eadem moderatione successerunt (intelligit Bezam) alioquin primæ purissimæque Ecclesiæ nunquam hanc labem aspergerent, ac si humanum Episcopum, hoc est, non à Deo institutum, sed ab hominibus excogitatum invexisset: cum Calvinus veterem Episcoporum œconomiam diuinam esse fateatur, & sacro Canoni consentaneam. Itane verò? veterem Episcopum divinum censuit Calvinus, quem Beza humanum putat? Gravius hoc, quam Sutclivius. Puritani ideo in Politeia Ecclesiæ errarunt, quod nimis Calvino adhæserint, quæque ille dubitans dixit, ea nulla dubitatione nec examinatione impudenter affirmaverunt: puritani errarunt (inquit Bilsonus) quòd Calvini vestigia deseruerint: immò inde errarunt (inquit Sutclivius) quòd Calvino nimis adhæserint. Quid igitur? eadem tutatus Calvinus est quæ nos? Eadem inquit, sed dubitanter. Dubitanter verò, qui tam constanter, tot tantaque pro disciplina reformanda Genevæ passus est? Hæc Bancroftus commemorat, qui tantum abest ut dubitationem Calvino affigeret, ut è contra inflexibilem potius contumaciam, cum subdola vafritie conjunctam eidem impingeret. Nec tamen destituitur colore quodam vel ipse Bancroftus. Quisnam ille quæso inquis? Hic nempè, Calvinus primò tantum contendebat disciplinam suam fuisse legitimam, neque alias Ecclesias ad eandem obligabat. Ita jam habemus omnia, quæ de Calvino objici solent: videamus dehinc probationes. Primò concessiones illius quasdam introducunt. Anno 1437. Ad Cardinalem Sadoletum scribens (inquit Bancroftus) paratum se ostendit Episcopali Hierarchiæ obtemperare, si modo veritatem Episcopi amplecti vellent. In colloquio Wormatiensi & Ratisbonensi, Episcopalem functionem stare posse putabit, si ad Evangelium amplexandum Episcopi reduci possint. In Epistola ad Regem Poloniæ Archiepiscopatum appellavit honorem moderatum. Addit Saravia (quod & reliqui) quum ad veterem amicum factum Episcopum scriberet: non eum exhortasse ut Episcopatum deponeret, sed tantum instruxisse, quomodo sise in eodem gereret. Vtinam epistolarum quas citant numerum adjecissent: editionem secundam epistolarum Calvini verti, nullam epistolam ad Sadoletum reperi vel ad amicum factum Episcopum. In verbis quæ à Bancrofto citantur ad Sadoletum, Hierarchiam interpretatur regimen sacerdotale, in quo fraternam societatem servari vult: quæ Episcopatui Hierarchico Anglicano parum conveniunt. In verbis Saraviæ, quæ citat ex epistola ad veterem amicum factum Episcopum: notet hæc lector.
units.tr: 6 Secondly, the Hierarchists object that the later reformed have abandoned the footsteps of the earlier. No men of even moderate learning (says Bilson) ever flared up with such bitterness and ferocity as these reformers (as they call themselves) now among us are all inflamed. Whoever reads this may perhaps suspect that the English reformed have gone beyond the mark; but let him hear Bilson explaining himself. Those who succeeded Calvin did not succeed with the same moderation (he means Beza), otherwise the first and purest Church would never have sullied itself with this stain, as if they had introduced a human bishop, that is, not instituted by God but devised by men, since Calvin confesses that the ancient economy of bishops is divine and agreeable to the sacred canon. Is that really so? Did Calvin judge the ancient bishop to be divine, which Beza thinks human? This is more serious than what Sutcliffe says. The Puritans erred in the Polity of the Church because they clung too closely to Calvin, and shamelessly affirmed without any doubt or examination what he had said in doubt. The Puritans erred (says Bilson) because they forsook the footsteps of Calvin; indeed they erred from this (says Sutcliffe) because they clung too closely to Calvin. What then? Did Calvin defend the same things as we do? The same, he says, but with doubt. But how can one who suffered so constantly, and so much and so greatly, for reforming discipline at Geneva be called doubtful? Bancroft recalls these things, but he is so far from attaching doubt to Calvin that he rather charges him with an inflexible obstinacy joined with sly craftiness. Yet Bancroft himself is not without some colour. What is it, I ask, you say? Namely this: Calvin at first only contended that his discipline was lawful, and did not bind other churches to it. So now we have everything that is usually objected against Calvin; let us next see the proofs. First, they bring forward certain concessions of his. In 1537, writing to Cardinal Sadoleto (says Bancroft), he showed himself ready to obey the episcopal hierarchy, if only the bishops would embrace the truth. In the colloquy at Worms and at Regensburg he thought the episcopal function could stand, if bishops could be brought back to embracing the Gospel. In an epistle to the King of Poland he called the archbishopric a moderate honour. Saravia adds (as do the others) that when writing to a former friend who had become a bishop, he did not exhort him to lay down his episcopate, but only instructed him how to conduct himself in it. I wish they had added the number of the epistles they cite. In the second edition of Calvin's letters that I have read, I found no letter to Sadoleto, nor to a friend who had become a bishop. In the words that Bancroft cites to Sadoleto, the hierarchy is taken to mean a sacerdotal government, in which he wants fraternal fellowship kept; these hardly agree with the Anglican hierarchical episcopacy. As for the words of Saravia, which he cites from the letter to his former friend who had become a bishop, let the reader take note of them.

units.la: Equidem si me interroges quo te loco & ordine habeam: quidvis potius esse te quàm Episcopum respondebo, in quo, ne obscurissimam quidem lineam extare conspicor, quæ Episcopum, aliquâ saltem ex parte, figuret. Hæccine quæso illius Episcopatum approbantis sunt: annon penitus damnantis potius? In epistola ad Regem Poloniæ, verbis proximè præcedentibus ostendit, quo sensu veteris Archiepiscopi honorem moderatum vocat: quæ ista sunt. Vetus Ecclesia Patriarchas instituit, & Episcopos Provinciales. Quemadmodum si hodie illustrissimo Poloniæ regno unus præesset Archiepiscopus, non qui dominaretur in reliquos vel jus ab illis ereptum sibi arrogaret, sed qui ordinis causa in Synodis primum teneret locum, & sanctam inter collegas suos & fratres unitatem faceret. Quid hæc ad Episcopum Anglicanum? imò hæc Episcopum Anglicanum prorsus jugulant, tanquam honorem immoderatum sibi arrogantem: quando hac præsidentiâ, in ordinis conservandi gratiam, non contentus est, quem Calvinus solum moderatum existimat.
units.tr: Indeed, if you ask me what place and rank I give you, I would answer that you are anything rather than a bishop, since I can see not even the faintest line in you that would portray a bishop, at least in some part. Are these, I ask, the words of a man who approves of his episcopacy, or rather of one who utterly condemns it? In his letter to the King of Poland, in the words immediately preceding, he shows in what sense he calls the honour of the old archbishop moderate. The words are these: The ancient Church instituted patriarchs and provincial bishops, just as if today the most illustrious kingdom of Poland had one archbishop presiding over it, not one who would lord it over the rest or claim for himself a right snatched from them, but one who, for the sake of order, would hold the first place in synods and would make a holy unity among his colleagues and brethren. What has this to do with the Anglican bishop? Indeed these words utterly cut the throat of the Anglican bishop, as one who arrogates to himself immoderate honour, since he is not content with this presidency, held for the sake of preserving order, which Calvin alone thinks moderate.

units.la: 7 Secundò, confessiones quasdam ex Calvino introducunt Hierarchici, de veteribus Episcopis, quibus Episcopatum Hierarchicum Anglicanum, eum approbasse dicunt. Vrget illa Bilsonus de Concilio Nicæno Institut. lib. 4. c. 4. Si rem intueamur, invenīemus veteres Episcopos, non aliam regendæ Ecclesiæ formam voluisse fingere ab ea quam Deus verbo suo præscripsit. Hinc concludit, agnovisse Calvinum Episcopi superioritatem (de qua eum locutum probat ex sect. 2.) verbo divino consentaneam esse. Sed de eo quod sibi in animo veteres patres proposuerunt loquitur Calvinus, ut hæc verba demonstrant, voluisse fingere: id quod explicat his verbis. Si quæ imperfectio in eorum constitutionibus reperiatur: conati tamen sunt studio sincero, institutionem divinam, à qua non multum aberrarunt. Paulò ante. Ea ratione usi sunt, ut facile videas nihil ferè hac parte habuisse à verbo Dei alienum. Citantur ista à Bancrofro, sed quorsum? Non multum aberrarunt, aberrarunt igitur nonnihil. nihil ferè à verbo Dei alienum: ergo aliquid à verbo Dei alienum habuerunt. Sed quid hæc ad Episcopum Anglicanum? Audiatur Whitakerus, illius etenim verba mallem quàm mea. Objicit Bellarminus ipsis Hierarchichorum nostrorum verbis. [In singulis Ecclesijs Episcopi singuli constituebantur, id Calvinus concedit. Rursus in provincijs singuli Metropolitani; & hoc Calvinus fatetur. Item in majoribus urbibus Primates seu Patriarchæ: & hoc Calvinus fatetur.] Respondet Whitakerus [Primo dat quidem Calvinus fuisse in singulis Ecclesijs Episcopos singulos, in provincijs Archiepiscopos & Patriarchos, sed nullum his Calvinus aut Episcopis aut Archiepiscopis principatum vel dominatum in fratres reliquos tribuit. Secundo Calvinus nostrique omnes, hanc Metropolitanorum & primatuum Hierarchiam, non à Christo vel Apostolis institutam, sed Ecclesiæ authoritate introductam esse scribunt. Si volunt ex Calvino aut nostrorum scriptis papatum (ego Episcopatum) astruere: dent primò non divino, sed humano jure niti, aut nihil agunt. Tertiò alios fuisse Episcopos
units.tr: 7 Secondly, the Hierarchists bring forward certain statements of Calvin about the ancient bishops, from which they say he approved the Anglican hierarchical episcopacy. Bilson presses this point from the Council of Nicaea, Institutes book 4, chapter 4: If we look at the matter, we will find that the ancient bishops did not wish to devise any other form of governing the Church than that which God prescribed in his word. From this he concludes that Calvin acknowledged the superiority of a bishop (which he proves Calvin spoke of from section 2) to be consistent with the divine word. But Calvin is speaking of what the ancient fathers had in mind, as these words show: wished to devise. He explains this in the following words: If there is any imperfection in their constitutions, yet they strove with sincere zeal toward the divine institution, from which they did not much stray. A little before: They used such a method that you can easily see they had almost nothing in this regard alien to the word of God. These are quoted by Bancroft, but to what end? Did not much stray: they therefore strayed somewhat. Almost nothing alien to the word of God: therefore they had something alien to the word of God. But what has this to do with the Anglican bishop? Let Whitaker be heard, for I would rather use his words than mine. Bellarmine objects using the very words of our Hierarchists. [In each church single bishops were appointed; Calvin grants this. Again, in the provinces single metropolitans; Calvin confesses this. Likewise in the greater cities primates or patriarchs; Calvin confesses this.] Whitaker replies: [First, Calvin indeed grants that there were single bishops in each church, and archbishops and patriarchs in the provinces; but Calvin attributes to these bishops or archbishops no principality or dominion over the other brethren. Second, Calvin and all of ours write that this hierarchy of metropolitans and primates was not instituted by Christ or the apostles, but introduced by the authority of the Church. If they wish to establish from Calvin or from our writers' books a papacy (I say episcopacy), let them first grant that it rests on human, not divine, right, or they accomplish nothing. Thirdly, other bishops]

units.la: De Triplic. epist. p. 53.
units.tr: De Triplic. epist. p. 53.

units.la: c. 13. p. 326. copos in Concilio presbyterorum respondet Calvinus, quales in Senatu Consules erant. Caetum enim convocabant, de negotijs conserebant, sententias rogabant, monebant, hortabantur, consulebant, actionem regebant, jus sibi nullum in fratres arrogabant, non cogebant privatâ authoritate alios cedere, nihil denique agebant nisi communi Consilio. Hinc ergo concludere, esse aliquem, qui non modo gradu, existimatione, & dignitate, sed authoritate etiam & potestate reliquis superior sit, qui eos cogat, & in illos jurisdictionem exerceat, à ratione omninò alienum est. At Bellarminus (Hierarchicis etiam) Episcopos esse inter presbyteros vult, non quasi Consules in Senatu, sed quasi Reges & Principes in caetu Consiliariorum. Ita cum tam multa sint dissimilia, nullum hoc est ex Calvino argumentum. Haec ille, quae ego exscribenda duxi quia multum interest, quo brachio telum quodq; vibratur. Subscribit vero Bilsonus ipse: postquam etenim sibi ista objecisset ex Calvino: Calvinum apertè hac parte deserit, & eum sibi contrarium esse confitetur: dicit enim se illius judicio non accedere, &c.
units.tr: c. 13. p. 326. bishops in the council of presbyters, Calvin replies, were like the consuls in the Senate. For they summoned the assembly, conferred on business, asked for opinions, admonished, exhorted, advised, directed the proceedings, claimed for themselves no right over their brethren, did not compel others to yield by private authority, and in short did nothing except by common counsel. To conclude from this that there is someone who is superior to the rest not only in rank, esteem and dignity but also in authority and power, who compels them and exercises jurisdiction over them, is wholly foreign to reason. But Bellarmine (even for the Hierarchists) wants bishops to be among the presbyters not as consuls in the Senate, but as kings and princes in an assembly of councillors. Thus, since there are so many dissimilarities, this is no argument from Calvin. I have thought it worth copying out these things, because it matters greatly with what arm each weapon is hurled. Bilson himself, indeed, subscribes to this: for after he had put these objections to himself from Calvin, he abandons Calvin on this point and confesses that he is opposed to him, for he says that he does not accede to his judgement, etc.

units.la: 8 Quin ipse Downamus, hac ex parte Calvinum nominatim reliquosque à se differre fatetur, ut qui Decanum non Episcopum his dictis descripserit. Alibi postquam loca Calvini superius citata proposuisset p. 142. ita habet p. 145. Calvinus in eo à nobis dissentit, quòd Episcopum velit esse praesidentem tantummodo in caetu presbyterorum, sicut Romae Consul in Senatu erat. Cum igitur in essentia ipsa authoritatis Episcopalis ab Hierarchicis Calvinus dissentiat: si quis pudor supersit, nullum dehinc pro Episcopatu Anglicano ex Calvino argumentum depromtum audiemus. Obstruitur etiam os Richardo Bancroft o, virulenter Cartwrightum exagitanti, quod dixerat, Calvinum horrescere voluisse ad nomen Archiepiscopi, & tremere ad officium Episcopi Anglicani: cum nihil haberet quo hanc calumniam statuminaret, quàm haec loca ex Calvino, quae allata sunt: quae Archiepiscopum Episcopumque Anglicanum jugulare vidimus, si addantur (quae ille subdolè praetermisit) haec quae sequuntur, de consulari tantummodo Episcopi veteris praesidentia. Vbi igitur amplificationes illae Si cum b. see nostris Calvinum compares, eum Episcoporum praecipuum patronum fautoremque putares. [Rursus, hinc perspici potest quanta inter Calvinum, & nostrum Spiritum differentia est: quantumque intersit inter illorum intemperiem & hujus modestiam, illorum superbiam, hujus humilitatem, illorum temeritatem, ignorantiam & vertiginem, illius sobrietatem, eruditionem & judicium. Sed dici forte potest, vtcunque se Calvinus in hac causa gesserit; alterius tamen Bezae sententiae est. Revera est: sed ad maiorem suam indies infamiam.] Ita Georgius Downamus, Beza à Calvini moderatione desiit, modestior tamen erga Episcopos nostros Bezâ, quàm hij nostri disciplinarij plerumque esse solent. Quàm vellent mundo persuaderi Calvinum esse suum? quàm libenter si, non suum, sui tamen similiorem, quàm aut Beza aut Cartwrightus est? et quoniam Bezæ existimatio magna est: quàm vellent eum propius ad se accedere, quàm reformatos Anglicanos: quos ob omnibus reliêtos vellent. Sed ex superioribus liquet, idem sensisse Calvinum quod Beza, nosque nihil contra Episcopos in medium afferre, quod ab vtrisque non dictum sit prius.
units.tr: 8 Indeed Downame himself confesses that on this point he differs by name from Calvin and from the others, since he described the dean, not the bishop, in these terms. Elsewhere, after setting out the passages of Calvin cited above, he says at p. 145: "Calvin differs from us in this, that he wants the bishop to be only the president in an assembly of presbyters, just as the consul was in the Senate at Rome. Therefore, since Calvin dissents from the Hierarchists on the very essence of episcopal authority, if any shame remains, we shall hear no further argument for the Anglican episcopacy drawn from Calvin." Richard Bancroft too is silenced, who virulently harried Cartwright for saying that Calvin wished to shudder at the name of archbishop and tremble at the office of Anglican bishop. He had nothing to prop up this calumny except these passages from Calvin that were cited, which we have seen cut the throat of the Anglican archbishop and bishop, if one adds (as he craftily passed over) what follows, concerning only the consular presidency of the ancient bishop. Where, then, are those amplifications: If you compared Calvin with our bishops, you would think him the chief patron and supporter of bishops? [Again, from this it can be seen how great is the difference between Calvin and our spirit, and how much lies between the intemperance of those men and the modesty of this one, their pride and his humility, their rashness, ignorance and giddiness, his soberness, learning and judgement.] But it may perhaps be said that, however Calvin conducted himself in this cause, he nevertheless held the view of another man, Beza. Indeed he did, but to his own greater infamy with each passing day. So Georgius Downame: Beza departed from Calvin's moderation, yet he is more modest towards our bishops than our disciplinarians usually are. How they would wish to persuade the world that Calvin is theirs! How gladly would they have him, if not theirs, at least more like them than Beza or Cartwright is! And since Beza's reputation is great, how they would wish him to come nearer to themselves than the reformed Anglicans, whom they would wish abandoned by all! But from what has gone before, it is clear that Calvin thought the same as Beza, and that we bring forward nothing against bishops that was not said before by both of them.

units.la: 9 Tertiò obijciunt Hierarchici,quòd quaedâ adjecerimus, nonnulla etiam correxerimus,imò contraria invexerimus eis quae primò consulta erant. Exempli gratia, ita Bancroftus de reformatis Anglicanis. Anno 1574. Admonitio Parliamento exhibita est, quasi perfectam disciplinae ideam continens. Duobus annis post, alt vivit in ea quaedam Cartwrightus, praesertim in eo, quod populo plusquam oportuit videtur tributum. Anno 1584. nova disciplinae descriptio prodiit ipso Parliamenti tempore. Haec autem ipsa descriptio à Traversio correcta & alterata rursus est: & altera Parliamento anno 1585. in lucem edita. Post, haec ipsa Correctio anno 1589. in cœtu Coventriensi examinata fuit: semper enim aliquid desiderabatur, aut hoc aut illud semper displicebat. Neque in materia solum progressus nostros exagitant: sed & in vehementia zeli etiam, unde Thomas Bilsonus: Nulli unquam tantâ acerbitate & ferocia exarserunt, quanta hodie apud nos isti inflammati sunt. At inquam in ipso Evangelio confirmando similes progressus observari possunt: quos tantum abest quòd condemnet spiritus sanctus in Thyatira Ecclesiae primò reformatae typo, ut vehementer etiam collaudet Apoc. 2.19. Ultima tua maiora sunt primis. Cartwrightus vehementior Beza, Beza Calvino: fac ita esse, annon inter tres Angelos quorum ministerio Evangelium restitutum est, alter alterò vehementior Apoc.14. sic ut Lutherus, Wiclephe, atque Husso posterior, tanquam vehementissimus omnium introducatur? Quòd vero ad progressus in cognitione attinet, ferre non potest in Cartwrighto Bancroftus, ut pij sub Edwardo sexto id non viderint, quod videmus jam nos: quasi illi in crepusculo vixerint, nos in luce meridiana. Quid igitur? Profectum omnem tollit? Sic quidem videtur: contra quod Saravia. Primi Ecclesiarum reformatores non potuerunt videre omnia. Contrà etiam Iuellus, qui pro luce ex tenebris papisticis paulatim emergente, citat Ambrosium. Constat dilubium eodem numero quo cumulatum est, esse diminutum. De Noa & Arca c.17. contra Io. Reynoldus. Caecus ille in Evangelio à Christo sanatus (Mar.8.22.) vidit primum homines, sed instar arborum ambulantes: dein suum nuper prospicit Deus in reddenda luce animarum, ex tenebris papisticis Lutherus principio ad sacramenta conversus videbat non esse septe, putabat tamen plura esse quàm duo: post in Catechismo majori, re diligentius expensa, duo tantum statuit. In negotio Caenae, primo videbatur illi, licet panis inesset, tamen corpus domini unâ etiâ per consubstantiationem adesse, sed paulo ante mortem agens cum Philippo Melanchthone, fatebatur in negotio caenae nimium esse actum. Hinc oppositè pro nostrorum hominum vel additionibus vel alterationibus Ri. Feyl-
units.tr: 9 Thirdly, the Hierarchists object that we have added some things, corrected some, and indeed introduced things contrary to what had first been agreed. For example, Bancroft says this of the Anglican reformed: In 1574 an admonition was presented to Parliament, containing as it were a complete idea of discipline. Two years later, Cartwright lived in it, particularly in what seemed to give the people more than was fitting. In 1584 a new description of discipline appeared at the very time of Parliament. This same description was corrected and altered again by Travers, and another was published in Parliament in 1585. Afterwards, this very correction was examined in the Coventry assembly in 1589, for something was always lacking, and this or that always displeased. Nor do they harass our progress only in matter, but also in the vehemence of zeal, whence Thomas Bilson: Never did men blaze up with such bitterness and ferocity as those inflamed today are among us. But I say that in the very confirmation of the Gospel similar progress can be observed, which is so far from the Holy Spirit condemning it in the church of Thyatira, the first reformed type, that he even warmly praises it: Rev. 2.19. Your last works are greater than the first. Cartwright is more vehement than Beza, Beza than Calvin. Grant that it is so: is it not the case that among the three angels by whose ministry the Gospel was restored, one is more vehement than another (Rev. 14), so that Luther, Wycliffe and, later, Hus are presented as the most vehement of all? As for progress in knowledge, Bancroft cannot bear that in Cartwright the pious under Edward VI did not see what we now see: as if they lived in twilight, we in midday light. What then? Does he remove all progress? So it seems. Against this, Saravia: The first reformers of the churches could not see everything. Against it also Jewel, who, citing Ambrose for the light gradually emerging from papistical darkness, says: It is agreed that the deluge was diminished by the same number by which it was increased. On Noah and the Ark, chapter 17. Against this John Reynolds: That blind man healed by Christ in the Gospel (Mark 8.22) first saw men, but like trees walking; then God looks more clearly on giving light to souls out of papistical darkness. Luther, turning first to the sacraments, saw that there were not seven, yet thought there were more than two; afterwards, in the Larger Catechism, having weighed the matter more carefully, he established only two. In the matter of the Supper, at first it seemed to him that although bread was present, nevertheless the body of the Lord was present along with it by consubstantiation; but shortly before his death, dealing with Philip Melanchthon, he confessed that in the matter of the Supper too much had been done. Hence, on the contrary, against the additions or alterations of our men, Ri. Feyl-

units.la: {C.4.p.65. &66.} dus Hierarchus.
