Quòd Lutherus gradatim progressus est,& in scriptis posterioribus quædam rejecerit, quæ prius probarat,non adeo mirum videri debet, quàm adversarij videri volunt.. Augustinus scripsit librum retractationum,& prævisionem fidei quam primo in prædestinatione statuisset,post improbavit: unde illius adversarij, quasi non patribus solum, sed & sibi ipsi etiam eum contrarium accusabant. Ambrosius de seipso profitetur,quod multa docuisset, quæ secunda recognitione opus habebant. Quantumlibet quisque prosecerit inquit,nemo est,qui non habeat opus doceri quamdiu vivit. Thomas Aquinas, corrigit & alternat multa in Summa sua, quæ ante scripserat.] Nullum igitur hoc Bancrofti argumentum est adversus reformatos,quòd quædam addiderint in disciplina, quædam etiam correxerint & alterarint.
units.tr: {C.4.p.65. &66.} the Hierarch. That Luther progressed gradually, and in his later writings rejected some things he had earlier approved, ought not to seem as strange as his opponents want it to. Augustine wrote a book of Retractions, and later repudiated the foreknowledge of faith which he had first set down in his treatment of predestination; so his adversaries accused him of contradicting not only the Fathers but himself. Ambrose confesses of himself that he had taught many things which needed a second revision. "However far anyone has advanced," he says, "there is no one who does not need to be taught for as long as he lives." Thomas Aquinas corrects and changes many things in his Summa which he had written earlier. Therefore this argument of Bancroft's against the reformed is no argument at all: that they have added some things in discipline, and also corrected and altered some things.

units.la: 10. Quarto,objicit Ri.Bancroftus,dubitasse Reformatos Anglicanos de quibusdam, etiam longe postquam petitiones suas pro invehenda disciplina Parliamento exhibuissent. Venio nunc ad miraculum quod pollicitus vobis sum: sic enim de eo sentio. Cartwrightus & alij nuper ejus in carcere socij in Chamera Stellata, juramento pressi, confessi sunt, quædam esse in forma disciplinæ suæ, de quibus adhuc resolvi non possunt. Eadem vero hæc esse colligit, quæ in chartula quadam in Musæo Guilielmi Feyldi deprehensa est. An Doctor necessarius sit, in unaquaque Ecclesiæ, an viduæ necessariò habendæ? an suspensio necessariò exercenda? an seniores debeant esse perpetui? an majori parti suffragiorum semper standum sit? an patrimi necessarij? At quodnam inquam in his miraculum? Miraculum potius viros tam benè de Ecclesia meritos, carceribus inclusos, in camera stellata judicatos, adeò duriter denique tractatos, ut non chartulas quidem in musæis tutas à lictorum unguibus servare potuerint. At nonne horrendum,inquit, Parliamento & totius regni statui hos temerarios adeò abuti? Quo casu hoc regnum fuisset si tam temerarij in concedendo Parliamentarij fuissent, atque illi in petendo fuerant? Quo casu? Augæi quasi stabulum quoddam innumerorum abusuum expurgassent: & pristinam Ecclesiæ primæ faciem (quod ad disciplinæ essentialia) ad singularem Iesu Christi gloriam, ineffabile piorum gaudium, commodum denique totius regni, revexissent. Hæc enim indubitata, sine his dubitatis consistere possunt: sic ut nihil Bancrofto iniquius sit; qui nihil de disciplina postulandum censet, quamdiu de omnibus circumstantialibus minime liquet. Ita Clemens Alexandrinus: Si appositus est fructus verus & maturus, & alius verò quàm proximè similis, non propter similitudinem abstinendum est ab utroq: & quomodo si una est vis regia, & aliæ multæ ex quibus quædam etiam ferunt in præcipitium, non dubitabit quispiam in viam ingredi ob dissensionem sed quæret regiam: ita non est propter dissensiones à veritate discedendum, sed diligentius & exactius inquirendum. Hæc Thomas Mortonus & citans & approbans, R. Bancrofto validissimè contradicit: Non est à maturis fructibus propter immaturas abstinendum: ast Bancroftus à rectis &
units.tr: 10. Fourthly, Dr Bancroft objects that the Anglican reformers had doubts about certain matters, even long after they had presented their petitions to Parliament for introducing discipline. I now come to the wonder I promised you, for so I judge it. Cartwright and others, lately his fellow prisoners, pressed by oath in the Star Chamber, confessed that there are some things in the form of their discipline about which they still cannot make up their minds. And he infers that these are the same things which were found in a certain little paper in the museum of William Field. Is a teacher necessary in every congregation? Must widows necessarily be maintained? Must suspension necessarily be exercised? Ought the elders to be perpetual? Must the greater part of the votes always prevail? Are deacons necessary? But what, I ask, is the wonder in this? The wonder is rather that men so well deserving of the Church, shut up in prisons, judged in the Star Chamber, and at last treated so harshly that they could not even keep their little papers safe in the museum from the claws of the officers. But is it not horrible, he says, that these rash men should so abuse Parliament and the state of the whole realm? In what case would this kingdom have been, if they had been as rash in granting as they were in demanding? In what case? They would have cleansed the Augean stable of countless abuses, and restored the ancient face of the primitive Church (as far as the essentials of discipline are concerned) to the singular glory of Jesus Christ, to the unspeakable joy of the godly, and finally to the benefit of the whole realm. For these matters, which are certain, can stand without those which are doubtful; so that nothing is more unjust than Bancroft, who thinks nothing should be demanded regarding discipline as long as nothing is clear about all the circumstantial matters. So Clement of Alexandria: If a true and ripe fruit is set before us, and another which is very nearly similar but not ripe, we must not abstain from both on account of the similarity; and just as, if there is one royal road and many others, some of which even lead to a precipice, no one will hesitate to enter upon a path because of disagreement, but will seek the royal road: so we must not depart from the truth because of disagreements, but must inquire more diligently and exactly. Thomas Morton, both quoting and approving these words, contradicts R. Bancroft most strongly: One must not abstain from ripe fruits on account of unripe ones: but Bancroft thinks one must abstain from the right and ripe essential parts of discipline [see the next unit]

units.la: Scromat. l. 7
units.tr: Scromat. l. 7

units.la: Apol p. 1. l. 2. c. 10. & maturis disciplinæ partibus essentialibus abstinendum putat: quamdiu quædam circumstantiales nondum matura deliberatione adhuc satis concoctæ. Non deterreri debemus, quo minus in viam ingrediamur, etsi de via regia & recta controvertatur, sed potius ad rectam diligentius inquirendam propter dissensiones excitari: parum apud se Bancroftus consideravit quòd Paulus in partem contrariam jubet. Phil. 3. 15. 16. Quotquot adulti sumus hoc sentiamus: quod si quid aliter sentitis hoc quoque Deus revelabit vobis: attamen in eo ad quod pervenimus eadem incedamus regula, & idem sapiamus.
units.tr: Apol p. 1. l. 2. c. 10. as long as some circumstantial matters have not yet been sufficiently digested by mature deliberation. We ought not to be deterred from entering upon the way, even if there is controversy about the royal and right road; rather we should be stirred up by the disagreements to inquire more diligently into the right way. Bancroft has considered little that Paul bids the opposite: Phil. 3. 15. 16. As many of us as are mature, let us think this: and if you think otherwise in anything, God will reveal this to you also: nevertheless, let us walk by the same rule to which we have attained, and think the same.

units.la: 11. Quintò, duo disciplinariorum genera adnoto (inquit Downnamus) qui nobis in hac controversia opponuntur. Unum est secta quædam nova, non ita perinde inter nos exorta, qui nuper inventam parochialem disciplinam inducere student, quæ propius ad Brownistarum, quàm ullius bene ordinatæ Ecclesiæ praxin accedunt. Alterum genus, gravium & Doctorum Theologorum est, quales Calvinus & Beza fuerunt, qui pro ea tantum disciplina stant quæ Genevæ exercetur. Hæc discordia quæ putatur, à Mat. Sutcliffio, enucleatius ponitur ita: Genevenses unum tantum consistorium in 17. Parochijs habent: juxta quam consuetudinem Danæus, uno tantum presbyterio contentus est, in quaque civitate uni: Thomas Cartwrightus vero ejusdemque sectatores tenent: quòd presbyterium collocari debeat in singulis parœcijs. Exaggeratur verò à R. Bancrofto ita: In Scotia tota tantum 52. presbyteria sunt in præcipuis civitatibus constituta: quarum vnaquæque 24. parochias sub se continet, quæ nullo suo presbyterio reguntur. In inferiori Germania, quæque parœciæ sua presbyteria habent, sed alsque potestate in rebus grandioribus, puta in excommunicatione, quæ nulli particulari Ecclesiæ concessa est sine consilio & assensu generalis consistorij in magna urbe, & in Pagis & oppidulis, Colloquij sive classis. Genevæ quatuor aut quinque parœciæ sunt, & in territorio circiter 20. quæ uno tantum presbyterio reguntur, quod in urbe est. Scitum illud Sophoclis, qui interrogatus ab amico, cur fœminarum personas quasi semper bonas repræsentare solitus esset, cum Euripides eas tanquam semper malas repræsentavit, respondit: quia ego fœminas repræsento quales esse debent, Euripides, quales esse solent. Quibusdam mutatis dici quid simile potest, de diversitate ista, quæ inter veteres disciplinarios, atque novos (ut loquitur Downnamus) reperitur. Illi siquidem presbyteria sua formant, ut commodè formari solent & possunt: hi ut præcisè formari debent, juxta formam illam quæ in verbo patefacta est. Atque sane ea perfecta idea est, ut singulæ Ecclesiæ sua singula presbyteria habeant, atque ad hanc ut quam proximè accedatur, omni conatu eniten-dum est: sic ut perfectiores Ecclesiæ eæ esse debeant quæ huic centro propiores, imperfectiores verò quæ ab eodè remotius distant. Atqui gradus perfectionis & imperfectionis diversitatem quidem inferunt: contrarietatem non item: quum neque Scotia neque Geneva, neque inferior Germania unquam docuerit, non deberi in singulis Ecclesijs singula presbyteria constituti (ut docent Hierarchici) ut-cumque. cumque rebus suis sic stantibus & poscentibus, eam prævisam rationem forte sequi nequeant.
units.tr: 11. Fifthly, I note two kinds of advocates of discipline (says Downame) who are opposed to us in this controversy. One is a certain new sect, not so long arisen among us, who are eager to introduce the parish discipline recently devised, which comes closer to the practice of the Brownists than to that of any well-ordered Church. The other kind is that of grave and learned theologians, such as Calvin and Beza were, who stand only for that discipline which is practised at Geneva. This supposed discord is set out more clearly by Matthew Sutcliffe thus: The Genevans have only one consistory in 17 parishes; following this custom, Danaeus is content with only one presbytery in each city; but Thomas Cartwright and his followers hold that a presbytery ought to be set up in each parish. R. Bancroft exaggerates it thus: In the whole of Scotland there are only 52 presbyteries established in the principal cities, and each of these has 24 parishes under it, which are governed by no presbytery of their own. In Lower Germany each parish has its own presbytery, but without power in greater matters, for instance excommunication, which is granted to no particular Church without the counsel and assent of the general consistory in the great city, and in the villages and small towns, of the colloquy or classis. At Geneva there are four or five parishes, and in the territory about 20, which are governed by only one presbytery, which is in the city. There is that witty saying of Sophocles, who, when asked by a friend why he was accustomed to portray women always as good, while Euripides portrayed them always as bad, replied: "Because I portray women as they ought to be, Euripides as they commonly are." With a few changes something similar can be said about this difference which is found between the old advocates of discipline and the new (as Downame calls them). The former shape their presbyteries as they are usually and conveniently shaped and can be shaped; the latter as they must be shaped precisely, according to that form which is revealed in the Word. And indeed that is the perfect idea: that each Church should have its own single presbytery, and every effort must be made to come as near as possible to this; so that those Churches should be more perfect which are nearer this centre, and those more imperfect which are further removed from it. But degrees of perfection and imperfection imply a difference, indeed, but not a contradiction; since neither Scotland, nor Geneva, nor Lower Germany has ever taught that a single presbytery ought not to be set up in each Church (as the Hierarchs teach), however things stand with their affairs, and whatever their circumstances demand, they may not be able to follow that ideal plan.

units.la: Secundò, dico singulas Ecclesias & Genevæ, & in Germania inferiori, singula sua presbyreria habere. At absque potestate omni in rebus grandioribus ut in excommunicatione. Falsum. Nulla una Ecclesia altera superior est, sed omnes pares sunt: sic ut Diocesana, de qua tantopere barriunt, superioritas, merum somnium sit. Consistorium grande in urbe, colloquium & classis ruri, Synodus generalis locum tenent: in qua omnes Ecclesiæ par jus habent; non enim aut consistoria aut classes istæ ex alienis constant, sed ex singularum Ecclesiarum membris, quæ ex æquo ad ea mittuntur, & ex quibus ea ex æquo constant. Quemadmodum igitur inter Hierarchicos, cum Episcopi in Synodum conveniunt, & generali consensu statuta decernunt, quæ omnes obligant, pares tamen remanent: ita fit inter reformatos: minimè paritatem Ecclesiarum diminuit, quòd communi consilio & voluntaria combinatione id fiat, ut consensus in excommunicatione consistorij & classis requiratur. Potestas excommunicationis Ecclesiæ nulli adimitur, in ea decernitur per presbyterium, & in eadem cum consensu totius gregis exercetur. Quid hic simile regimini Anglicano? Verum si ad amussim ista exacte omnia non respondeant, respondeo cum Saravia: Ego tantus non sum, ut cujusquam Ecclesiæ defensionem in me susciperem.
units.tr: Secondly, I say that each Church both at Geneva and in Lower Germany has its own presbytery, but without any power in greater matters such as excommunication. False. No single Church is superior to another, but all are equal; so that the superiority of the diocesan, about which they bellow so much, is a mere dream. The great consistory in the city, the colloquy and classis in the country, and the general synod take the place of the: in which all Churches have equal right; for these consistories and classes do not consist of outsiders, but of members of the individual Churches, who are sent to them on equal terms and from whom they are constituted on equal terms. Therefore, just as among the Hierarchs, when bishops meet in synod and decree by general consent decisions which bind all, yet remain equal, so it is among the reformed: the equality of the Churches is in no way diminished because this is done by common counsel and voluntary combination, so that the consent of the consistory and classis is required in excommunication. The power of excommunication is taken from no Church; it is decreed in it through the presbytery, and in it is exercised with the consent of the whole flock. What here is like the Anglican government? But if all these things do not correspond exactly, I answer with Saravia: I am not so great that I should take upon myself the defence of any Church whatever.

units.la: CAP. XXXVII.
units.tr: CAP. XXXVII.

units.la: Obiectiones Hierarchicorum retorquentur.
units.tr: The objections of the Hierarchs are turned back.

units.la: QUam frivolæ sint de contradictionibus nostris objectiones Hierarchicæ videmus: jam retorquenda criminatio est quæ in Hierarchicis tam vera & justa, quam falsa in nobis injustaq; reperitur. Extat historia apud Socratem hujusmodi. Quum Valens contra Orthodoxos in dies singulos graviora supplicia excogitaret, Themistius, oratione coram eo habita, ita eum mitigare conatus est. Admonebat vero ne quæ ipsum caperet admiratio, de Christianorum dissensione: eam enim perexiguâ esse, si cum multitudine & turba opinionum quæ sunt apud gentiles philosophos comparetur. Deniq; velle Deum tam diversa & dispari ratione suam gloriam illustrare, quo singuli ejus maiestatem propterea magis revereantur, quòd non sit cuiquam in promptu accuratè cognoscere. His verbis inquit Socrates, imperator cœpit mitius agere. Accomoda verò ad propositum nostrum hæc: si quæ etenim leviusculæ in reformatis diversitates occurrunt, humanam potius infirmitatem, quàm causæ improbitatem demonstrant: Deo ita disponente, ut notum faceret, disciplinam suam rem abstrusiorem esse, quàm ut à quoquam accuratè intelligi queat. Dissensiones verò Hierarchicæ ut numero plures, ita & specie ejusmodi sunt, ut causæ ipsius improbitatem, non tantum probabiliter suadeant, sed & certò etiam demonstrent. Quasdam contradictiones tradiciones esse quæ hoc efficiunt, concedit Fyldus, qui etiam eas in duo genera dispertitur: [Primum, quando ipsa fundamenta incerta sunt: secundum, quando ipsæ assertiones ex incertis fundamentis ducte in sese contradictionem implicant. De primo sic habet. Divisiones quæ in Catholica Ecclesia oriuntur, a malitia Satanæ proficiscuntur, & in doctrina ipsa fundamentum non habent. Si probare vult Bellarminus, doctrinam nostram à se divisionem gignere: demonstrare debet, illius fundamenta & principia incerta esse, & ejusmodi, ut errorem, contrarietatem, & judicij incertitudinem pariant, quod neque facit nec facere potest: nam fundamentum totius doctrinæ nostræ verbum Dei est. De secundo ita disserit: Sed dicit Bellarminus, de not. Eccles. lib. 4. cap. 10. ipsum Lutherum testari (lib. de vit. monastici) contrarietatem & contradictionem notam esse falsitatis: quum ipsius scripta igitur posteriora primis contraria sint, tota ipsius doctrina vel ipsius judicio falsa est. Sciant qui hæc adversus Lutherum disputant, non sentire Lutherum, quòd tota cujuspiam doctrina falsa probatur ex eo quòd quædam retractat & corrigit: sed quod assertiones inde appareant falsæ, quod contradictionem implicent, & fundentur super dubias, incertas, & perplexas disputationes, & sic se mutuò perimunt, ex quo genere omnes præcipuæ partes Romanæ doctrinæ sunt.]
units.tr: How frivolous the Hierarchical objections to our supposed contradictions are, we can see. Now the charge should be turned back on them: it is found in the Hierarchs, as true and just as it is false and unjust when made against us. There is a story of this kind in Socrates. When Valens was devising ever harsher punishments against the Orthodox day by day, Themistius, in a speech delivered before him, tried to soften him in this way. He warned him not to be amazed at the disagreement among Christians: for it was very small if compared with the multitude and crowd of opinions found among the Gentile philosophers. Finally, God willed to display his glory through such diverse and unlike means, so that each man might revere his majesty all the more, because it is not in anyone's power to know it accurately. Socrates says that the emperor began to act more mildly after these words. Apply these words to our purpose: if any slight differences occur among the reformed, they show human weakness rather than the wickedness of the cause, God so arranging it that his discipline should be a matter too abstruse for anyone to understand accurately. The disagreements of the Hierarchs, however, are not only more numerous but of such a kind that they prove the wickedness of their cause not merely probably but also with certainty. Fulke concedes that certain contradictions, which are traditions, bring this about, and he divides them into two kinds: [First, when the foundations themselves are uncertain; second, when the assertions, drawn from uncertain foundations, entangle themselves in contradiction. On the first he writes thus. The divisions which arise in the Catholic Church proceed from the malice of Satan, and have no foundation in doctrine itself. If Bellarmine wishes to prove that our doctrine produces division, he ought to show that its foundations and principles are uncertain, and of such a kind as to bring forth error, contrariety, and uncertainty of judgment; this he neither does nor can do, for the foundation of all our doctrine is the Word of God. On the second he argues thus: But Bellarmine says, in his book on the marks of the Church, book 4, chapter 10, that Luther himself testifies (in his book on monastic vows) that contrariety and contradiction are marks of falsehood: since his later writings are contrary to his earlier ones, his whole doctrine is false, or false by his own judgment. Let those who argue this against Luther know that Luther does not hold that the whole doctrine of anyone is proved false because he retracts and corrects some things; rather, that assertions appear false because they involve contradiction, and are founded on doubtful, uncertain and perplexed disputations, and so destroy each other, a class into which all the principal parts of Roman doctrine fall.]

units.la: 2. Ita Matheus Sutclivius. Præcipua disciplinæ reformatæ fundamenta aut firmamenta adeò inter se invicem contraria sunt, ut tanquam Caducei fratres ex serpentinis dentibus sati se mutuò destruant. Omnes eorum contrarietates persequi, longum tractatum postularet, unde hæc conclusio sequitur: quòd veritas cum una sit, hæc eorum disciplina ex tam contrariis partibus, consarcinata, veritatem sapere nequeat. Licetne nobis eodem modo argumentari? Disciplina Hierarchica super incertos sensus hominum fundatur, disciplina reformata super Dei verbum solum: illaque in firmamentis assertiones gignit, quæ mutuò se perimunt, hæc non item: sequitur igitur disciplinam Hierarchicam falsam esse, reformatam verò veram. Hoc quàm verè asseratur, videndum primò, quàm inter sese digladientur Hierarchici, dum statuere nituntur fundamentum in genere disciplinæ Hierarchicæ suæ. Scripturam solam disciplinæ fundamentum esse concordamus nos, Hierarchici discordant: nulla etenim certa disciplina, aut absoluta disciplinæ forma in verbo præscribitur inquit Lous: contrà nobiscum stat Saravia. Certa forma disciplinæ est, quâ homines mutare nō possunt. De verbi isti ex solo verbo interpretatione concordamus nos, discordant Hierarchici: vide de triplic. 73. Visus Ecclesiæ quod ad disciplinam scripturæ interpres est: Downnam contra. Scripturæ ex scriptura interpretari solemne nobis & usitatum semper fuit. Patres fidè non facere concordamus nos: discordant Hierarchici. Contra reformatos in disciplina credendos patres dicunt, quos non esse credendos contra papistas strenuè contendunt: de iure divino in quo libet officio Ecclesiastico concordam° nos, discordat Hierarchi-
units.tr: 2. So Matthew Sutcliffe. The principal foundations or supports of the reformed discipline are so mutually contrary that, like the brothers of the caduceus sprung from serpent's teeth, they destroy each other. To pursue all their contrarieties would require a long treatise, whence this conclusion follows: since truth is one, this discipline of theirs, patched together from such contrary parts, cannot taste of the truth. May we argue in the same way? The Hierarchical discipline is founded on the uncertain opinions of men, the reformed discipline on the Word of God alone; and the former produces assertions in its foundations which destroy each other, the latter does not. It follows, therefore, that the Hierarchical discipline is false, and the reformed true. We must first see how far this is rightly asserted, by observing how the Hierarchs fight among themselves while they strive to establish the foundation of their Hierarchical discipline. We agree that Scripture alone is the foundation of discipline; the Hierarchs disagree. For no certain discipline, or fixed form of discipline, is prescribed in the Word, says Lous; against us stands Saravia. There is a certain form of discipline which men cannot change. We agree that the interpretation of the Word is from the Word alone; the Hierarchs disagree; see the De triplici... 73. The judgment of the Church is the interpreter of Scripture for discipline: Downame, on the contrary. To interpret Scripture from Scripture has always been our customary and usual practice. We agree that the Fathers are not to be trusted; the Hierarchs disagree. On the contrary, the Fathers are said to be to be trusted by the reformed in discipline, whom they vigorously contend are not to be trusted against the Papists. We agree about the divine right of any ecclesiastical office; the Hierarchs disagree.

units.la: Querimon. Eccles. p. 67. 68. In præf. Hierarchici: iure etenim divino disciplinam Hierarchicam tuentur alij, alij iure humano tantum, inter quos Iuellus ita. Ut Episcopus in Episcopum authoritatem habeat, neque à Paulo, neque à Petro, neque ab ullo divini verbi jure est, sed tantummodo ex antiqua consuetudine. De jure divino & Apostolico concordamus nos, discordant Hierarchici. Downamus Episcopi authoritatem non iure divino, sed Apostolico tuetur: Barlous & reliqui, & ἀποστολικῆ κτίσει, & πνευματικῇ θέσει, quam trium personarum decretum appellant. De disciplinae immutabilitate super verbum fundatae concordamus nos, discordant Hierarchici. Downamus & alij Episcopalem majoritatem mutabilem contendunt, alij tuentur immutabilem, sic ut Bilsonus libri sui hunc titulum fecerit, De perpetua Ecclesiae gubernatione. Quod si igitur Fyldus verus, doctrinam nostram contradictionem nullam gignere, quòd super verbum fundatam esse statuamus: papisticam gignere, quia non super verbum solum, sed incerta hominum judicia: quod si verus etiam Matheus Sutclivius, veram illam disciplinam non esse, cujus fundamenta incerta & contraria: tum vera recte disciplina reformata, Hierarchica verò falsa est.
units.tr: Querimonia Ecclesiae, p. 67, 68; in the preface. The Hierarchs: for some defend the Hierarchical discipline by divine right, others only by human right, among whom Jewel says thus: That a bishop should have authority over a bishop is not by the right of the divine Word, neither from Paul nor from Peter nor from anyone, but only from ancient custom. We agree about divine and apostolic right; the Hierarchs disagree. Downame defends the authority of bishops not by divine right but by apostolic right, as do Barlow and the rest, by apostolic creation [ἀποστολικῆ κτίσει] and spiritual placing [πνευματικῇ θέσει], which they call the decree of the three persons. We agree about the immutability of discipline founded upon the Word; the Hierarchs disagree. Downame and others contend that the episcopal majority is mutable, while others defend it as immutable, so that Bilson made this title of his book, On the perpetual government of the Church. If, therefore, Fulke is right that our doctrine produces no contradiction because we hold it to be founded on the Word, then the Papist doctrine produces it, because it is founded not on the Word alone but on the uncertain judgments of men; and if Matthew Sutcliffe is also right that a discipline whose foundations are uncertain and contrary is not true, then the reformed discipline is rightly true, and the Hierarchical discipline false.

units.la: 3 Sequitur contradictio Hierarchica in fundamentis speciálibus; intelligo loca scripturae illa ex quibus fundamenta petuntur, quae appellare Sutclivius videtur firmamenta. Primum, Thomas Bilsonus praecipuum Hierarchiae fundamentum in Timothei Episcopatu ponit, quem quasi perpetuum mandari vult, 1. Tim. 6.14. subjungens, quod si hic locus deficiat, jure humano, non divino Episcopatus tenendus sit. Atqui fundamentum istud funditus subvertitur à Georgio Downamo, qui contendit hunc locum, non de officio Timothei id est Episcopatu intelligendum, sed tantum de sola authoritate Timothei; quod idem est ac si dixisset, scriptam hanc epistolam Timotheo esse, non qua erat Episcopus, sed qua erat gubernator in genere, authoritate Ecclesiastica praeditus.
units.tr: 3. A Hierarchical contradiction follows in their particular foundations; I mean those passages of Scripture from which the foundations are sought, which Sutcliffe seems to call supports. First, Thomas Bilson places the chief foundation of the Hierarchy in the episcopate of Timothy, whom he wishes to be regarded as a perpetual commission, citing 1 Tim. 6.14, adding that if this passage fails, the episcopate is to be held by human right, not divine. But that foundation is utterly overthrown by George Downame, who contends that this passage is to be understood not of the office of Timothy, that is, the episcopate, but only of Timothy's authority alone; which is the same as if he had said that this letter was written to Timothy not as he was a bishop, but as he was a governor in general, endowed with ecclesiastical authority.

units.la: 4 Secundò, cum Georgius Downamus, pro Episcopali majoritate Lambethi concionaturus esset, in consecratione Bathoniensis, & Welensis Episcopi, quem quaeso textum elegit? Illum nempe de Angelo septem Ecclesiarum Apocalyptico, quem propriè Episcopum esse vult, qualis jam noster Anglicanus. At non est omnino, pro nihilo, quod nuper Bilsonus dixit: nam si jure tantum humano tenendus Episcopatus sit, si non illo ad Timotheum loco confirmetur: sequitur profectò nec hoc ex hoc textu de Angelo Asiano, neque ex alio sacrae scripturae loco ullo, jus illius divinum comprobari posse. Sed praestat audire Ha. Saraviam ita disputantem. Ignoscat mihi lector si rursus hic septem Ecclesiarum Asiae Episcopos citavero: illae Ecclesiae habuerint presbyteria sua, in quibus perpetuò septem illi Angeli praefuerint: in quibus non tantum ordine fuisse primos, sed gradu & authoritate, reprehensiones & objurgationes Dominicae lucè e vrius demonstrant. Faciùt haec pro Downamo inquies. Imò non faciunt: audi etenim quomodo hunc gradum & authoritatem in sequentibus explicat. In hoc coetu inquit Beza, fuit ordine primus, non potestate superior. Dominus Beza in presbyterorum coetu, admittit ordine primum, non potestate. Veretur enim ne veritati aut æquitati rerum, quæ communibus suffragijs decidendæ sunt, authoritas primi præiudicium adferat. Sed metus ille vanus est, quum in omni conventu, ubi suffragijs res est finienda, cessat ubiq; præsidis potestas, quæcunq; alias illa sit. Episcopis & Archiepiscopis in Synodis & capitulis quibus præsident, acturis de re in arbitrio posita conventus, eorum potestas sit, suffragijs res terminatur. Consulis fuit apud Romanos non parvum imperium: tamen in senatu consulebat, non imperabat. Age: hic noster præses nullius potestatis in illo cœtu presbyterorum, quomodo sine potestate aliqua præcipua præter eam quæ est ordinis, moderator esse potest actionum quæ illic tractabuntur? --- Ignoscat ingenij mei imbecillitati Dominus Beza si moderatorem & præsidem alicuius cœtus intelligere nequeam, etiam ubi pluralitas suffragiorum, non præsidis valeret authoritas, sine exorta quadam supra cæteros authoritate. Quid igitur est? Non ordinis tantum prioritatem, sed authoritatem etiam in cœtu presbyterorum Angelo Asiano tribuit Saravia, sed quam? Num Anglicanam, quæ authoritas regis est in cœtu consiliariorum? nihil minus, sed consulis tantum in Senatu, quæ consulat non imperet, actiones dirigat, non à se concludat: quæ suffragia numeret non tantum ponderet. Respondit nuper Clemens octavus Cardinali Peronio, se suffragia Cardinalium in re Veneta sibi consulentium ponderaturum non numeraturum: eandem potestatem arrogant sibi in presbyteros Episcopi Anglicani. Quid ita? Quia exortem illis auihoritatem tribuit Hieronymus. Puerile. Exortem etenim Hieronymi authoritatem habet Episcopus inquit Saravia, quando authoritatem habet moderandi cœtum, qui communibus suffragijs rem quampiam terminant. Ita Downamo contradicit Saravia, ejus judicio textus Downami nihil fecit pro Episcopo Anglicano. Attribuit Saravia Angelo Asiano extra cœtum, potestatem in presbyteros quandam. At dum potestatem in ipso cœtu Downamianam impugnat, nonne in precipuo Episcopalis majoritatis Anglicæ capite illi contradicit? Et quam tu ex illis verbis Angeli Asiani extrà cœtum authoritatem elicere poteris, quàm redarguendi? quæ Anglicani Episcopi numnam authoritatem omnem comprehendit?
units.tr: 4. Secondly, when George Downame was to preach at Lambeth for the episcopal majority, at the consecration of the bishops of Bath and Wells, what text, I ask, did he choose? That one, namely, about the angel of the seven churches in the Apocalypse, whom he wishes to be a bishop properly so called, as our Anglican bishops now are. But what Bilson recently said is not altogether for nothing: for if the episcopate is to be held by human right alone, if it is not confirmed by that passage to Timothy, it certainly follows that neither from this text about the Asian angel, nor from any other passage of Holy Scripture, can its divine right be proved. But it is better to hear Saravia arguing thus. Let the reader forgive me if I cite again here the bishops of the seven churches of Asia: those churches had their presbyteries, in which those seven angels presided continually; in which they were first not only in order but in rank and authority, as the Lord's reprimands and rebukes clearly demonstrate. You will say that this favours Downame. Indeed it does not: for hear how he explains this rank and authority in what follows. In this assembly, says Beza, he was first in order, not superior in power. Lord Beza, in the assembly of presbyters, admits him first in order, not in power. For he fears lest the authority of the first should prejudice the truth or the fairness of matters which are to be settled by common votes. But that fear is vain, since in every gathering where a matter is to be decided by votes, the power of the president ceases, whatever it otherwise is. Bishops and archbishops in synods and chapters, over which they preside, when the assembly is about to act on a matter left to its judgment, their power is only that the matter is ended by votes. The consul among the Romans held no small power; yet in the senate he consulted, he did not command, he directed the proceedings, he did not conclude them of his own accord, he counted the votes rather than weighing them. Come now: this president of ours has no power in that assembly of presbyters; how can he be a moderator of the actions which are to be treated there without some principal power beyond that which belongs to his order? --- Let Lord Beza forgive the weakness of my wit if I cannot understand how a moderator and president of any assembly, even where the plurality of votes is decisive, can have authority without some authority arising above the rest. What then is the case? Saravia grants the Asian angel not merely precedence of order but authority also in the assembly of presbyters; but of what kind? Is it the English kind, which is the authority of a king in a council of counsellors? Nothing less: but rather the authority of a consul in the senate, who advises rather than commands, directs the proceedings, does not conclude them by himself, counts the votes rather than weighing them. Clement VIII lately replied to Cardinal Perron that he would weigh the votes of the cardinals giving him counsel in the Venetian matter, not count them: the English bishops claim for themselves the same power over the presbyters. Why so? Because Jerome grants them an authority that is outside the assembly. A childish argument. For the bishop has an authority beyond that of Jerome, says Saravia, when he has authority to moderate the assembly which settles some matter by common votes. Thus Saravia contradicts Downame; in his judgment the passage cited by Downame does nothing for the English bishop. Saravia attributes to the Asian angel, outside the assembly, a certain power over the presbyters. But while he attacks the power that Downame ascribes within the assembly itself, does he not contradict him on the principal point of the English episcopal majority? And what authority, outside the assembly, could you derive from those words about the Asian angel, and how could it be proved? Does it comprehend all the authority of the English bishop at all?

units.la: 5. Accedamus ad fundamentum Hierarchiæ speciale tertium. Guilielmus Barlous Episcopus Roffensis electus a regia majestate erat, ut coram accersitis a Scotia ministris (inter quos præsens Andreas Melvinus erat) concionaretur, ad eos, ut Hierarchiam Anglicanam amplecterentur, convertendos. In hac corona, propter regiam nobilitatem præsentiam, Doctorum confluentiam, negotij magnitudinem, omnium deniq; cujusq; generis expectationem celeberrima, quem ille ad episcopatum Hierarchicum comprobandum, textum alium elegit, quàm Act. 20. 28? Posuit vos Episcopos. At haccine manu jugulatos senserunt sese ministri Scoticani? Consulatur vel unus G. Dowuamus: qui hos Episcopos hoc in loco commemoratos minimè Hierarchicos, sed tantum presbyteros, juxta nominis communitatem tum usitatam fuisse profitetur. Ita in hoc tertio fundamento contradictio reperitur, qua se mutuò perimunt Hierarchici. Nam ut Barloi sententiam perimit Downamus dum illius Episcopos in presbyteros mutat: ita & Downami sententiam perimit Barlous: dum illius Angelum Ephesinum presbyterio illo spoliat,1 Act. 20.28. ex cujus subjectione Episcopatum Hierarchicum Ephesi, potissimum comprobavit.
units.tr: 5. Let us come to the third special foundation of the Hierarchy. William Barlow, Bishop of Rochester, was appointed by the royal majesty to preach before the ministers summoned from Scotland (among whom Andrew Melville was present), in order to convert them to embrace the English Hierarchy. In that assembly, most celebrated for the royal presence, the gathering of doctors, the importance of the business and, in short, the expectation of every kind of person, which text did he choose to prove the hierarchical episcopate, other than Acts 20:28, "He has made you bishops." But did the Scottish ministers feel themselves slain by this hand? Let one consult George Downame, who professes that these bishops mentioned in that place were by no means hierarchical, but only elders, according to the common usage of the name at that time. Thus in this third foundation a contradiction is found, by which the hierarchists mutually destroy each other. For as Downame destroys Barlow's view while he changes Barlow's bishops into elders, so Barlow destroys Downame's view while he strips Downame's Ephesian angel of that presbytery, from whose subjection he chiefly proved the hierarchical episcopate at Ephesus.

units.la: 6. Inter fundamenta, seu firmamenta fundamentalia, recensendæ illæ Hierarchicorum responsiones sunt, quas fundamentis nostris opponere solent: in quibus ingens contradictio reperitur. Primò, contra unius Episcopi regimen citare solemus ex Math. 28.17. Dic Ecclesiæ: Ecclesia etenim plures designat non unum. Respondet Bilsonus, non de tribunali Ecclesiastico, sed de civili tantummodò (ut Erastus) hæc verba interpretanda esse, cui accedit Ri. Fyldus. At contra insurgit Hierarchicorum totus cœtus reliquus, qui de consistorio Ecclesiastico Christum hic verba facere dicunt. Ita Lancelotus Andreas Episcopus Cicestrensis: De exteriori foro Mat. 18. agitur: exterioris fori jurisdictio illo non alio loco fundata est. Audis? Nihili ergo fundamentum Bilsoni in 1.Tim.1.4. Nihili fundamentum Downami ex Angelo Apocalyptico; Nihil deniq; fundamentum Barloi, ex Episcopis Ephesinis. Dixerat Bilsonus, in Episcopatu Timothei fundari Episcopalem jurisdictionem & non alibi: ergo jurisdictionem in foro exteriori lege divinâ Episcopus unus nullam habet: nam jurisdictio fori exterioris inquit Andreas in nullo alio scriptura loco fundatur quam Math. 18. Atque certe res magni momenti est, quod alios Hierarchicos omnes dissipat qui fundamentum jurisdictionis Ecclesiasticæ in aliis scripturæ locis quærunt: majoris tamen quòd hoc in loco, in quo unico jurisdictio Ecclesiastica in foro exteriori fundatur, non uni alicui, sed toti Ecclesiæ datam dicit. Non uni inquit hic datur ne Petro quidem, quia unus quilibet peccare potest, & qui peccat quanquam Petrus quanquam in Ecclesia præsit; judicio Ecclesiæ subiectus est. Datur inquit Ecclesiæ potestas hanc jurisdictionem usurpandi, non uni quanquam ut Petrus præstantissimo, nec si usurparet, ratihabitio promissa, quia dicitur ut pluribus, quoscunq; ligaveritis, non tanquam uni, quoscunq; ligaveris. Videsne quam fortiter muri Ierichuntici Episcopales ab imo funditus diruuntur?
units.tr: 6. Among the fundamental foundations, or fundamental supports, we must count those answers of the hierarchists which they are accustomed to set against our foundations, and in which a huge contradiction is found. First, against the government of a single bishop we are accustomed to cite "Tell the Church" from Matthew 28:17. For "Church" designates many, not one. Bilson replies that these words must be interpreted not of an ecclesiastical tribunal but only of the civil one (as Erastus does), and Richard Field agrees with him. But against them rises the whole remaining band of hierarchists, who say that Christ here speaks of the ecclesiastical consistory. So Lancelot Andrewes, bishop of Chichester: "It is about the external forum in Matthew 18, and the jurisdiction of the external forum is founded in no other place." Do you hear? Nothing, then, is the foundation of Bilson in 1 Timothy 1:4. Nothing is the foundation of Downame from the Apocalyptic angel; and finally nothing is the foundation of Barlow from the Ephesian bishops. Bilson had said that episcopal jurisdiction is founded in the episcopate of Timothy and nowhere else; therefore one bishop has, by divine law, no jurisdiction in the external forum. "For the jurisdiction of the external forum," says Andrewes, "is founded in no other place of Scripture than Matthew 18." And certainly this is a matter of great moment, since it scatters all the other hierarchists who seek the foundation of ecclesiastical jurisdiction in other places of Scripture. Yet it is of greater weight that in this one place, where ecclesiastical jurisdiction in the external forum is founded, he says it is given not to any one person but to the whole Church. "Here it is given to no one," he says, "not even to Peter, because any one man can sin, and he who sins, although Peter presides in the Church, is subject to the judgment of the Church. The power is given," he says, "to the Church to exercise this jurisdiction, not to one, though he be the most excellent like Peter; nor, even if he should exercise it, would ratification be promised, because it is said to many, 'Whatever you shall bind,' not to one, 'Whatever you shall bind.'" Do you see how bravely the episcopal walls of Jericho are thrown down from the foundations?

units.la: 6. Secundo citamus pro paritate Ecclesiarum Math. 16.19. Vbi promittuntur claves (atque ita jurisdictio in foro exteriori) uni Petro, personam cuiuscunque singularis non vnius tantum chathedralis Ecclesiæ, tum gerenti: ut illius vnitas & in omnibus Ecclesijs æqualitas designetur. Respondet Bancroftus, vnus Episcopus repræsentare totam Ecclesiam potest, atque ita claves exercere vnus: perinde ac Petrus quum unus tantum esset, nomine Ecclesiæ, hic clavium promissionem recepit. Sophisma egregium. Nam cum Episcopus vnus jurisdictionem exercet,
units.tr: 6. Second, for the parity of churches we cite Matthew 16:19, where the keys (and so jurisdiction in the external forum) are promised to Peter, bearing the person not of a single chair church, but of any one at all, so that its unity and equality in all churches may be designated. Bancroft replies that one bishop can represent the whole Church and so exercise the keys alone, just as Peter, when he was alone, received the promise of the keys here in the name of the Church. An outstanding sophism! For when one bishop exercises jurisdiction,

units.la: {y} Tortura tertio pag. 41. exercet,vnus homo eam exercet;exercet etiam Episcopus iurisdictionem quandam singularem suam: atqui inquit Lancelotus Episcopus Cicestrensis, neque Petrus hic clavium promissionem recipit ut vnus homo, nec potestatem aliquam suam hic recipit, sed alienam. Verba sunt ista. Tibi, est ibi quidem singulari numero positum: sed etsi numerus est singularis, singularis ibi tamen persona Petri non est. Petro ibi promissae claves, non tamen ut Petro huic homini, quim Petro personam Ecclesiae gerenti: quando authoritatem Ecclesiae recipit hic Petrus, non suam.
units.tr: {y} Torture, third part, p. 41. exercises it, one man exercises it; and the bishop also exercises some jurisdiction of his own, singular. But, says Lancelot Andrewes, bishop of Chichester, neither does Peter here receive the promise of the keys as one man, nor does he receive any power of his own here, but another's. His words are these: "'To you' is indeed put here in the singular number; but although the number is singular, the person of Peter is not singular there. The keys were promised to Peter there, yet not as to this man Peter, but as to Peter bearing the person of the Church, since Peter here receives the authority of the Church, not his own."

units.la: 7 Tertio, contra Episcopi in suos fratres authoritatem, citamus Mat.20,21. Reges gentium dominantur in eos, vos autem non sic. Respondet Whitgiftus, non legitimam potestatem hic ministris interdici sed tantum tyrannicam. Atqui huic glossemati reclamat ipse Hierarchicus Matheus Sutclivius: qui adversus papae potestatem disputans, non tantum tyrannicam potestatem ministris hic interdictam esse dicit, sed & regiam etiam & legitimam: nam regalis potestas inquit inter gentes, cuius specialem mentionem hic Christus facit, legitima potestas erat.
units.tr: 7. Third, against the authority of a bishop over his brethren, we cite Matthew 20:25, "The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, but you shall not be so." Whitgift replies that what is forbidden to the ministers here is not lawful power but only tyrannical power. But his gloss is contradicted by the hierarchist Matthew Sutcliffe himself, who, disputing against the power of the Pope, says that not only tyrannical power but also royal and lawful power is forbidden to ministers here: "for royal power," he says, "which Christ mentions specifically here among the Gentiles, was lawful power."

units.la: 8 Quarto, citamus contra unius episcopi regimen 1. Cor. 5,4. ubi non ab uno episcopo, sed a pluribus, non in cathedrali Ecclesia aliqua longè remota, sed in praesentia & cum consensu ipsius ecclesiae in qua delinquitur excommunicandus incestuosus legitur. Respondet Bilsonus, nullum consensum Corinthiacae ecclesiae hic intersuisse: sed illi tantum relictum fuisse, ut mandatum Apostoli exequerentur, qui ipse solus & absens excommunicavit, sicut nunc in Anglia episcopus. Nam Apostolum hoc tempore episcopalem authoritatem in suis manibus retenuisse certum est, inquit. Atqui hoc adeo absonum absurdumque Hadriano Saraviae videtur, ut in contrariam partem peccet: statum nempe huius ecclesiae Corinthiacae fuisse hoc tempore Democraticum, adeoque multitudinem totam hic excommunicasse priusquam Pastor aliquis fuisset constitutus. Lancelotus vero Andreas Episcopus Cicestrensis, pastorem Corinthi fuisse constitutum credit, & normam ecclesiae stabilitam: qui tamen non ab uno Apostolo nedum episcopo, sed ab ipsa ecclesia excommunicatum incestum dicit. Probat ille non uni alicui puta Petro clavium potestatem mat:16, 19, promissam fuisse a praxi ecclesiae Corinthiacae, sub his verbis. Quaero iam de praxi censurae huius. Reperio 1. Cor: 5. Iubet ibi deduci in praxin, potentiam hanc Apostolus, in nomine Christi cum spiritu suo. Forte autem minus ibi caute locutus: illum credo dicere debuit, vel in nomine vel cum spiritu Petri saltem. Neutrum vero Paulus ibi dicit: qui congregatis illic potestatem censurae denunciandae facit,
units.tr: 8. Fourth, against the government of a single bishop we cite 1 Corinthians 5:4, where an incestuous man is read as to be excommunicated not by one bishop but by several, not in some cathedral church far removed, but in the presence and with the consent of the very congregation in which the offence was committed. Bilson replies that the Corinthian congregation had no consent here, but only that the command of the Apostle was left to them to carry out, since he alone and absent excommunicated, just as now in England the bishop does. "For it is certain," he says, "that the Apostle at this time retained episcopal authority in his own hands." But this seems to Adrian Saravia so absurd and so inept that he errs on the opposite side: he maintains that the state of this Corinthian church at this time was democratic, and so the whole multitude excommunicated here before any minister had been appointed. But Lancelot Andrewes, bishop of Chichester, believes that a minister was established at Corinth and a stable rule of the church, yet he says the incestuous man was excommunicated not by one Apostle, let alone one bishop, but by the church itself. He proves that the power of the keys promised not to one person, namely Peter, in Matthew 16:19, was practised by the Corinthian church, in these words: "I now ask about the practice of this censure. I find in 1 Corinthians 5 that the Apostle orders this power to be put into practice there, in the name of Christ, with his spirit. But perhaps he spoke there less cautiously: he ought to have said, I believe, either 'in the name' or 'with the spirit' of Peter at least. Paul says neither there; he who gathers them there gives them the power of announcing the censure."

units.la: 6 Citamus postremò contra unius Episcopi regimen 1. Timo. 4,14, ubi non per unum sed per manus presbyterij Timotheus ordinatus dicitur. Respondet Bilson° & Downam°. Si non per presbyterium, efficium presbyteratus intelligatur, in quo Tymotheus ordinatus est, presbyterium tamen ministrorum hic intelligi (juxta patres) non Seniorum, [?]ui in verbo non laborant. Fac ita esse: evertitur hic tamen dogma Hierarchicum, ordinationem esse solus episcopi: & ita episcopi ut eidem presbyteri minimè sese immiscere debeant. Quid enim ? Hoc presbyteriun nonne constabit ex presbyteris? episcopi etenim nulli fuerunt cum Tymotheus ordinabatur: ipse etenim Timotheus atque Titus primi ab Apostolis delegati episcopi fuerunt, uti disertè affirmat Bilsonus, & quantum ego asse qui possum Hierarchici reliqui omnes. Atqui 2: Tym: 1,6. ordinatum Timotheum dicit Paulus manibus suis. Quasi qui suas dicit, reliquorum excluderet? subordinata non pugnant: impositu manus Paulus ut præses, reliqui ut presbyterij partes. Quid quod Downamus Timothei ordinationem istam per manus Pauli separet ab illa priori per manus presbyterij? nam tum presbyterum, hic verò ordinatione nova episcopum creatum putat. Et quando rogo Evangelista creabatur? Evangelistæ respondet Saravia, usitato more, non ordinabantur omninò, sed immediatè ipsis Apostolis adiungebatur. At ut hoc pro præsenti commissum fiat, cum Evangelista Tymotheus fuerit, libenter a Downamo scirem, quorsum ordinatione nova in episcopum sanctus Tymotheus ordinaretur? Ut potestatem inquit acciperet imponendi manus quam Evangelista non habuerunt ut in Philippo cernere est Act. 8. 12. At superior gradus includit omnes inferiores inquit Saravia, non contra, sic ut qui Evangelista sit, is episcopi authoritatem ut haberet necesse est. Hac ratione eo res redit ut tendum sit, Tymotheum cum ordinabatur neque in presbyterum neque in episcopum, sed tantum in Evangelistam ordinatum fuisse: quia Evangelista superior gradus cum sit, & presbyteri & episcopi authoritatem secum apportavit: sic ut nullo usui inserviat ordinatio Tymothei, sive in presbyterum sive in episcopum.
units.tr: 6. Finally, against the government of a single bishop we cite 1 Timothy 4:14, where Timothy is said to have been ordained not by one man but "by the hands of the presbytery." Bilson and Downame reply: "If 'presbytery' is understood as the office of the presbyterate in which Timothy was ordained, nevertheless the presbytery here is understood (according to the Fathers) to be of ministers, not of elders who do not labour in the word." Grant that it is so: the hierarchical dogma is nonetheless overturned, that ordination belongs to the bishop alone, and so the presbyters themselves must not meddle in it. For what then? Will this presbytery not consist of presbyters? There were no bishops at all when Timothy was ordained, for Timothy and Titus were the first bishops sent out by the Apostles, as Bilson clearly affirms, and as far as I can judge, all the rest of the hierarchists too. Yet in 2 Timothy 1:6 Paul says that he ordained Timothy with his own hands. As if the one who says "his own" excluded the others? Subordinate things do not conflict: Paul laid on hands as president, the others as part of the presbytery. What is more, Downame separates that ordination of Timothy by the hands of Paul from that earlier one by the hands of the presbytery; for he thinks that by the first he was made a presbyter, but by the new ordination a bishop. And when, I ask, was the evangelist created? Saravia replies that in the customary manner evangelists were not ordained at all, but were attached directly to the Apostles themselves. But that this may be granted for the present, since Timothy was an evangelist, I would gladly learn from Downame why holy Timothy was ordained a bishop by a new ordination. "That he might receive," he says, "the power of laying on hands, which evangelists did not have, as can be seen in Philip, Acts 8:12." "But a higher rank includes all the lower ones," says Saravia, "not the reverse; so that whoever is an evangelist must necessarily have the authority of a bishop." By this reasoning the matter comes to this, that when Timothy was ordained he was ordained neither as a presbyter nor as a bishop, but only as an evangelist; because the evangelist, being a higher rank, brought with him the authority of both presbyter and bishop; so that Timothy's ordination serves no purpose at all, whether into the presbytery or into the episcopate.

units.la: 10. Atque ita in fundamentis, sive suis statuendis, siue nostris convellendis, Hierarchicorum quàm repugnatissimæ contradictiones reperiuntur: reliquum erat ut de eorum contradictionibus, aliquid diceretur, quæ in eorum assertionibus reperiuntur, quas super sua fundamenta extruere, & ædificare solent. Sed ingenuè fateor cum ad hoc opus me accingerem, lassitudinem me invasisse. Videbam has contradictiones innumeras esse, videbam commodius eas suis proprijs in locis tractari posse, & hinc mihi lectoriq; parcendum putavi, hàc sanctâ præsertim sponsione interpositâ, me totâ causâ casurum, ni assertiones Hierarchichas, ipsam Hierarchiæ essentiam intimam concernentes, super incertas & contrarias disputationes fundatas esse comprobavero: Facile esset ostendere inquit Feyldus omnem doctrinam Papisticam, incertitudinum & contradictionum massam esse, quod indicio est aberrare eos qui eam profitentur, adeo ut nec viam reftam, imò ne semetipsos quidem invenire poterint. Si doctrina Papistica omnis hujusmodi sit, tum & doctrina Hierarchica etiam, nam Papistica tota ea est & Papisticis fundamentis super ædificata. Quidni igitur eam cerebri humani figmentum esse vel ex hisce suis contradictionibus conclu-dam dam Tertullianum secuturus? Nihil interest illis licet diversa tractantibus, dum ad unius veritatis expugnationem conspirent. Mentior, si non a regulis suis etiam varient, inter se, dum unusquisque proinde suo arbitrio modulatur quae accepit, quemadmodum de suo arbitrio ea composuit ille qui tradidit. Agnoscit naturam suam & originis suae morem profectus rei. Atque haec de fundamento extraneo Hierarchicorum duodecimo nempe Unitate.
units.tr: 10. And so, in establishing their foundations and in overthrowing ours, the contradictions of the Hierarchists are found to be most flagrant. It remained to say something about their contradictions, which are found in their assertions, the assertions on which they are accustomed to build and raise their structure. But I frankly confess that, when I was girding myself to this work, weariness came over me. I saw that these contradictions were innumerable, and I saw that they could be treated more conveniently in their own proper places. I thought that both I and the reader should be spared on this point, especially since I have given a solemn pledge that I will lose the whole cause unless I prove that the Hierarchical assertions, which concern the very inner essence of Hierarchy, are founded on uncertain and conflicting disputations. It would be easy to show, says Feyld, that the whole Papistical doctrine is a mass of uncertainties and contradictions, which is evidence that those who profess it go astray, so that they can find neither the right way nor even themselves. If all Papistical doctrine is of this kind, then Hierarchical doctrine too is of this kind, for it is wholly Papistical and built upon Papistical foundations. Why then should I not conclude from these contradictions that it is a figment of the human brain, following Tertullian? It makes no difference to them, though they treat the matter differently, so long as they conspire to overthrow the one truth. I lie if they do not also vary among themselves from their own rules, since each one shapes what he has received according to his own judgement, just as the one who handed it down composed it by his own judgement. The progress of the thing acknowledges its own nature and the manner of its origin. And so much for the Hierarchists' foreign foundation, namely the twelfth, Unity.

units.la: CAP. XXXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXVIII.

units.la: Argumentum Hierarchicum XIII. ab externa prosperitate.
units.tr: The Thirteenth Hierarchical Argument, from outward prosperity.

units.la: DEcimum tertium & ultimum sequitur, nempe externa prosperitas: quam cum pro Ecclesiae ac proinde veritatis nota objiceret Bellarminus, responsum ei abunde est, à Guil. Whitakero cont. 2. q. 5. cap. 16. Mat. Sutclivio, de eccles. lib. 1. cap. 6. pag. 115. Tho. Mortono Apologet. Cathol. p. 1. lib. 2. cap. 35. 36. 37. Andrea Willeto deniq; Synops. cont. 2. quaest. 4. Tuentur vero hij omnes (id quod ipsi etiam Anglo Rhemenses confitentur) hominum aut nationum prosperos successus nullum signum aut testimonium esse verioris aut purioris religionis. Quo major Hierarchicorum culpa: de quibus vere Brightmannus. Ni videantur quid turpiter veritati praeferre, praesentem suam felicitatem editis libris & pro concionibus inflatius praedicant, ut videre licet ex multorum scriptis quae praeteritis his annis prodierunt. Atque certe vere admiranda gentis Anglicanae his temporibus superioribus, ab Evangelio restituto prosperitas, quam non immerito reponit adversus Bellarmiuum, Hierarchicus Mortonus noster. In uno Angliae regno inquit tanquam in amplissimo theatro, ipsa felicitas temporalis omnis virtutis suae insignia exhibait & quodammodo ostentavit. De magna vero Elizabetha (cujus memoria in benedictione est) citat ex Osorio Praefatione lib. de Re. & ex Biraro lib. Hist. Genes, 23. illius prudentia & virtute, regnum Angliae majori felicitate administratum quam ullum aliud, vel retroactis seculis, vel patrum, nostrave memoria. At quod ille certe Bellarmino reponit, eorum infelicitatem objicienti qui à papismo emersi sunt: id male nobis obganniunt, qui cum Claudio Espencaeo apud Willetum existimamus scripturam praedicere magnam fore ipsius Antichristi foelicitatem sic ut regimen, Anglicanum Antichristianum esse queat, quantumvis ingenti prosperitate perfruatur. Secundo, prosperitatem regni nostri soli divinae benignitati, nulli nostrae dignitati tribuendam dico: addo etiam & patientiae ut in vestra ecclesiae nostrae Laodicea videre est. Quid enim? Cum sese Amen in hanc Ecclesiam & principium creaturae Dei se exhibuisse dicit, Apoc. 5. 14. nonne ejusdem felicitatem, suae ipsius & veritati & potentiae eique soli vendicat? Nec immerito. Quid enim praeter solam potentiam suam, in nostra ecclesia vere Laodicaena, movere
units.tr: The thirteenth and last argument follows, namely outward prosperity. When Bellarmine put this forward as a mark of the Church, and therefore of truth, he was answered at length by William Whitaker (Cont. 2, q. 5, cap. 16), Matthew Sutcliffe (De Eccles. lib. 1, cap. 6, p. 115), Thomas Morton (Apologia Catholica, p. 1, lib. 2, cap. 35-37), and finally Andrew Willet (Synopsis, cont. 2, quaest. 4). All of these maintain (as the Rhemish translators themselves admit about the English) that the prosperous success of men or nations is no sign or evidence of a truer or purer religion. The fault of the Hierarchicals is all the greater, and Brightman speaks truly of them: Unless they seem shamefully to prefer something to the truth, they boast of their present happiness in their published books and in their sermons with more puffed-up language, as may be seen from the writings of many who have appeared in these past years. Certainly the prosperity of the English nation in these recent times, since the restoration of the Gospel, is truly admirable, and our Hierarchical Morton rightly sets it against Bellarmine. In the single kingdom of England, he says, as in the most spacious theatre, temporal happiness itself has displayed and in a way exhibited all the signs of its virtue. Concerning the great Elizabeth (whose memory is blessed), he cites from Osorius, in the preface of his book De Re..., and from Birarus, in his Historia Genesis (23), that under her prudence and virtue the kingdom of England was governed with greater happiness than any other, either in past ages or in the memory of our fathers and of ourselves. But what he rightly answers to Bellarmine, who objects to the unhappiness of those who have emerged from popery, is badly flung at us by those who, with Claude d'Espence (as cited by Willet), think that Scripture predicts a great happiness for Antichrist himself, so that the Anglican government could be Antichristian even though it enjoys enormous prosperity. Second, I say that the prosperity of our kingdom is to be attributed to divine kindness alone, and not to our merit; I add also to their patience, as can be seen in your Laodicea, our Church. For what? When he says that he has shown himself as the Amen and the beginning of the creation of God (Apoc. 5.14), does he not claim its happiness for himself alone, for his own truth and power? And rightly so. For what, besides their own power alone, could move them in our church, which is truly Laodicean, or what else do they think must be forced upon us, beyond Scripture alone, to settle the disciplinary controversy, unseasonably and (not to say) improperly?

units.la: ycre extant vel preter solam scripturam saltem ad controversiam disciplinariam terminandam, importunè sanè ne dicam improbè, nobis obtrudenda putant.
units.tr: What, besides their own power alone, could move them in our church, which is truly Laodicean, or what else do they think must be forced upon us, beyond Scripture alone, to settle the disciplinary controversy, unseasonably and (not to say) improperly?

units.la: CAP. XXXIX. De falsorum principiorum fundamento Hierarchicorum, for- mam disciplinae in verbo non contineri: ac primo de eorum vitiis in statu quaestionis explicando, quatuor diremtio- nibus sc. excessibus calumnijs & contradictionibus.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIX. Concerning the foundation of the false principles of the Hierarchists, namely that the form of discipline is not contained in the Word; and first, an explanation of their faults in stating the question, namely four divisions, that is, excesses, calumnies and contradictions.

units.la: DE falsis principijs Hierarchicis diximus: jam ad falsorum principiorum fundamentum salsissimum deveniendum. Ne etenim absque colore, scriptuam solam in negotijs disciplinae consulendam negare videantur: affirmant constanter certam disciplinae formam in eis minimè contineri. Ita Iohannes Whitgiftus. [ forma disciplinae non nominatim aut particulatim in scriptura expressa est. Rursus. Nullum genus regiminis in verbo expressum est aut inde necessariò concludi potest. Rursus. Nullum vnum certum aut persectum genus regiminis in scripturis Ecclesiae Dei aut praescribitur aut mandatur. Postremò. Nullum certum genus regiminis quasi perpetuum praescriptum est. Ita Cousinus Whitgifti Cancellarius. Omnes Ecclesiae eodem modo disciplinatae non sunt: neque necesse est ut sint: quandoquidem probari non potest, quod aliqua certa & exacta particularis forma disciplinae à verbo Dei nobis commendata sit. Ita Lous. Nulla certa disciplina in verbo praescripta est. Non certa disciplina, sed certae regulae tanquam cynosura, habentur in scripturis: principia tantum communia disciplinae in scripturis reperiuntur: non aliqua absoluta forma. Ita Richardus Hookerus. Negamus necessarium esse ut una aliqua completa forma politeias Ecclesiasticae in scripturis habeatur: sed generalia axiomata tantum quibus variae regiminum formae consonare possunt. Ita Iohannes Bridgesius. Deus non expressit ecclesiasticam gubernationem, aut ita saltem expressit ut ad eandem nos obligarit. ] Ne taedio sim omitto caeteros: praesertim cum ex istis liqueat, quaenam Hierarchicorum sententia sit: scripturam nempe solam, disciplinae fundamentum esse non posse: cum de forma regiminis Ecclesiastici nihil statuerit, sed eam reliquerit Magistratus arbitrio, & Ecclesiae cuiusque seculi discretioni. Hoc delirium priusquam refutatum eo, operæpretium erit adnotare, quaenam eorum peccata sint, in ipso statu quæstionis constituendo.
units.tr: We have spoken of the false Hierarchical principles; now we must come to the very salt-less foundation of those false principles. For lest they seem to deny, without any pretence, that Scripture alone is to be consulted in matters of discipline, they constantly affirm that no fixed form of discipline is contained in it. Thus John Whitgift: "No form of discipline is expressed in Scripture by name or in particular." Again. "No kind of government is expressed in the Word, nor can it be necessarily concluded from it." Again. "No one certain or perfect kind of government is either prescribed or commanded in the Scriptures of the Church of God." Lastly. "No certain kind of government is prescribed as if it were perpetual." So Cousin, Chancellor of Whitgift. "Not all Churches are disciplined in the same way, nor is it necessary that they should be, since it cannot be proved that any certain and exact particular form of discipline has been commended to us by the Word of God." So Lous. "No certain discipline is prescribed in the Word. Certain rules, like a guiding star, are found in Scripture, not a certain discipline; only common principles of discipline are found in Scripture, not any absolute form." So Richard Hooker. "We deny that it is necessary that one complete form of ecclesiastical polity be found in Scripture, but only general axioms to which various forms of government may agree." So John Bridges. "God has not expressed ecclesiastical government, or at least has not so expressed it that he has bound us to it." I omit the others, not to weary the reader; especially since from these it is clear what the opinion of the Hierarchists is: namely that Scripture alone cannot be the foundation of discipline, since it has laid down nothing about the form of ecclesiastical government, but has left it to the judgement of the magistrate and to the discretion of each age's Church. Before we refute this madness, it will be worth noting what their faults are, in the very setting out of the question itself.

units.la: 2 Primò igitur ut sententia haec consistat, incidùtur in plures planè Cyclopicas diremptiones, quarum ingenuü scriptorem puderet. Qualis etenim haec quaeso dolus est? Doctrinam meam contra papistas per solas scripturas tueri possum: disciplinam verò contra puritanos non item. Quid agam? Scripturae nempe sufficientiam contra papistas defendam
units.tr: 2. First, then, so that this opinion may stand, they fall into several plainly Cyclopean divisions, of which an honest writer would be ashamed. For what sort of trickery, I ask, is this? I can defend my doctrine against the Papists by Scripture alone, but I cannot do the same for discipline against the Puritans. What am I to do? I will defend the sufficiency of Scripture against the Papists in the cause of doctrine, but in order that the Puritan may not prevail, I will deny its sufficiency in his discipline.

units.la: {y} marks not assigned in printed text. in causa doctrinæ: sed ne prævaleat puritanus, in disciplina ejus sufficientiam pernegabo. Atqui simplicior & honestior multò vel ipse papista Cornelius Scultingius: qui contra Traversium disciplinam in verbo contineri negat, quia doctrina in verbo non continetur: nam hæ inquit gemellæ sorores sunt. Vident igitur papistæ, disciplinam pariter atque doctrinam, aut in verbo contineri aut non contineri: ut doctrina in verbo magis contineatur, quam disciplina; quis unquam ante dixit? Tertullianus forte, respondebis, cujus ista verba sunt. Lege fidei manente, cætera jam disciplinæ & conversationis admittunt novitatem correctionis. Citantur ista à Iohanne Whitgifto, ut probetur, doctrinam quidem in verbo perfectè contineri: formam verò disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ non item: sed perperam. Loquitur etenim Tertullianus de conversatione privatâ, non de publica disciplina Ecclesiastica. Quid si de ista loqueretur? Nonne pudet Montanistam revocare? Scripsit hæc etenim Tertullianus, postquam dogmate Montani imbutus per adventum paracleti, perfectiorem morum normam, quam quæ in scripturis prodita est patefactam esse censuisset. Atque hæc Hierarchicorum astuta diremptio prima est, inter doctrinam & disciplinam, ac si illa perfectè haberetur in verbo, ista non item.
units.tr: {y} marks not assigned in printed text. Yet even the Papist Cornelius Scultingius, who argues against Travers that discipline is not contained in the Word, is simpler and more honest: because doctrine is not contained in the Word either; for these, he says, are twin sisters. So the Papists see that discipline and doctrine alike are either contained in the Word or not contained in it. Who ever before said that doctrine is more fully contained in the Word than discipline? Tertullian, perhaps, you will reply, whose words these are: While the rule of faith remains, the other matters of discipline and conduct admit of the novelty of correction. These words are cited by John Whitgift to prove that doctrine is indeed perfectly contained in the Word, but the form of ecclesiastical discipline is not, and he does so wrongly. For Tertullian speaks of private conduct, not of public ecclesiastical discipline. But what if he spoke of that? Are we not ashamed to recall a Montanist? For Tertullian wrote these things after he had been imbued with the teaching of Montanus, and had judged that, through the coming of the Paraclete, a more perfect rule of conduct had been revealed than the one handed down in Scripture. So this is the first crafty division of the Hierarchists: between doctrine and discipline, as if the former were perfectly contained in the Word and the latter were not.

units.la: 3 Sequitur secunda. Numnam doctrina quæso sola perfectè in verbo continetur? Quid igitur de moribus statuendum? certe perfectam morum normam in verbo contineri existimavit Augustinus: dixit enim, In scripturis haberi quicquid vel ad fidem vel ad bonos mores pertinet. Quid ad hæc Hierarchici? Verum est inquit Remonstrator in directione particulari cujusque ecclesiæ membri, non autem in directione generali totius ecclesiæ in politeia sua. Bene est: concidit iam distinctio, & diremptio illa prima, qua dicebatur doctrinam tantum fidei (ut loquitur Hookerus) perfectè in verbo contineri: jam etenim fateri cogitur Remonstrator & morum etiam normam perfectam exactè in sacris reperiri. Nihil tamen hinc vos lucramini dicis: nam etsi ethicam persectè scripturis contineri concedit, ad vitam privatam dirigendam: diffitetur tamen politicam aliquam morum disciplinam in eadem tradi, ad totam Ecclesiam informandam. Diffitetur sanè, sed insanuit: minoris namque momenti ethica est, quam politeia ecclesiastica, periculosius in ista quam in illa peccatur: & opus ecclesia tota habet ut in ista dirigatur, perinde ac in illa quisque privatus: sic ut si illam perfectè descripserit in verbo Christus, & hanc descripsit etiam. Atque hæc astuta Hierarchicorum diremptio secunda est, inter ethicam morum atq; politicam directionem.
units.tr: 3. The second division follows. Is doctrine alone, I ask, perfectly contained in the Word? What then is to be said about morals? Certainly Augustine thought that a perfect rule of morals is contained in the Word; for he said, "In the Scriptures is found whatever pertains either to faith or to good morals." What do the Hierarchists reply to this? "It is true," says the Remonstrator, "for the particular direction of each member of the Church, but not for the general direction of the whole Church in its polity." Very well: the first division, by which it was said that only doctrine of faith (as Hooker puts it) is perfectly contained in the Word, now collapses; for the Remonstrator is forced to confess that the perfect rule of morals too is exactly found in the sacred books. Yet you say you gain nothing from this: for although he concedes that ethics is perfectly contained in Scripture for directing private life, he denies that any political discipline of morals is handed down in the same for informing the whole Church. He denies it indeed, but he is out of his mind; for ethics is of less importance than ecclesiastical polity, and one sins more dangerously in the latter than in the former; and the whole Church needs to be directed in its polity just as each private person is directed in his ethics. So if Christ has perfectly described the one in the Word, he has described the other too. This is the second crafty division of the Hierarchists: between the ethics of morals and political direction.

units.la: 4 Sequitur tertia. Numnam moralis disciplina ethica in verbo tantum reperitur, ut de politeia ecclesiastica nihil interim statuatur? quid igitur dicendum de pastoribus, de verbi prædicatione, & de sacramentorum administratione? Respondet Mat.Sutclivius ita. Dixtmus quantum Christus instituit ut observetur, qualia hæc sunt, ut sint pastores qui doceant, & ut quoddam regimen sit, & hujusmodi disciplina similis milis diligenter observari debet. Ita Io. Whitgiftus. Quod ad materiam disciplinae, verbum nempe & Sacramenta, praescribuntur in scripturis, & immutabilia sunt: quod ad formam autem regiminis attinet, ea nec praescripta in verbo est, nec immutabilis. Postremò ita D. Cousinns. Quod ad essentiales partes externae politeiae & gubernationis ecclesiae quae consistit in verae verbi Dei praedicatione, & debita sacramentorum administratione, & in virtute promovenda & impietate extirpanda, & ecclesia in pace & ordine conservanda, nulla inter nos opinionum differentia est. Bene est: concidit jam diremptio superior secunda: non ethica tantum pro moribus disciplina in verbo traditur: sed & aliqua etiam politica Ecclesiastica, ut hi diserte confitentur. Nihil tamen hinc vos lucramini dicis: cum etsi confitentur politicam ecclesiae docentem perfectè in verbo tradi: politicam tamen regentem, de qua tota quaestio est reperiri in sacris diffitentur. Diffitentur sanè sed delirant. Nam cum politeia Ecclesiastica docendo regat, & regendo doceat: quinam haec dirémptio consistere potest, ut quatenus docet habeatur in verbo, quâ autem regit non habeatur? Deinde essentialia ejusdem sunt inquit Cousinus, Virtutis promotio, vitiorum extirpatio, pacis ecclesiae conservatio Atqui inquam hi regiminis Ecclesiastici fructus sunt: & finem in verbo haberi qui dicit, & formam etiam, in eodem haberi ut confiteatur necesse est, unâ cum omnibus mediis, quibus ad finem attingi solet. Quod dicit Sutclivius, haberi in verbo ut sit regimen, quale autem hoc regimen sit non haberi, aut quales personae quibus administratur: idem est ac si diceret: authoritatem esse apud regem Angliae constituere ut regnum regatur: non autem ordinare aut regiminis formam, aut officiarios, per quos hoc regimen exerceretur. Atque haec dirémptio Hierarchicorum tertia est: ac si disciplina regens perinde ac docens in verbo Dei non reperiatur.
units.tr: 4. The third follows. Is moral discipline, which is ethics, found only in the Word, so that meanwhile nothing is settled about ecclesiastical polity? What then must be said about ministers, about the preaching of the Word, and about the administration of the sacraments? Matthew Sutcliffe answers thus: We have said what Christ has instituted to be observed: such things as that there should be ministers who teach, and that there should be some government, and that a discipline of this kind should be diligently observed. So John Whitgift: As to the matter of discipline, namely the Word and the sacraments, these are prescribed in Scripture and are unchangeable; but as to the form of government, this is neither prescribed in the Word nor unchangeable. Lastly, thus Cousin: As to the essential external parts of the polity and government of the Church, which consist in the true preaching of the Word of God and the due administration of the sacraments, and in promoting virtue and rooting out impiety, and in keeping the Church in peace and order, there is no difference of opinion among us. Very well: the previous second division now collapses, for discipline is delivered in the Word not only as ethics for morals but also in some measure as ecclesiastical politics, as these men openly confess. Yet you say you gain nothing from this, since, though they confess that the teaching side of ecclesiastical polity is perfectly handed down in the Word, they deny that the governing side, which is the whole question, is found in the sacred books. They deny it indeed, but they are mad. For since ecclesiastical polity governs by teaching and teaches by governing, what division can stand, by which it is held to be in the Word so far as it teaches, but not so far as it governs? Next, its essentials, says Cousin, are the promotion of virtue, the extirpation of vices, and the preservation of the peace of the Church. Yet I say that these are the fruits of ecclesiastical government; and whoever says that the end is found in the Word must also confess that the form is found in it too, together with all the means by which the end is usually attained. What Sutcliffe says, that it is found in the Word that there should be government, but not what kind of government this is, or what persons administer it, is the same as if one said: it is the authority of the King of England to establish that the kingdom be governed, but not to ordain either the form of government or the officials through whom this government would be exercised. This is the third division of the Hierarchists: as if governing discipline, just like teaching discipline, were not found in the Word of God.

units.la: § Sequitur quarta. Numnam de regimine ecclesiastico omnino nihil habetur in verbo? Quid igitur de Episcopis fiet?
