Immò inquit Richardus Hookerus, quanquam necesse non est ut scriptura ex propositio unam aliquam particularem formam ecclesiasticae politeias praescriberet: tamen quod ad modum gubernandi in genere, praecepta quae scriptura tradit pauca non sunt, & exempla sunt plurima quae imitanda omnibus ecclesiae gubernatoribus, etiam in particularibus proponit: imò quae principalis momenti sunt in ipsa particulari politeias ecclesiasticae formae (quanquam non ea quam illi imaginantur, sed quam nos contra eos defendimus) in his ipsis scripturis continentur. Bene est, per gradus tandem quanquam inviti ad nostras partes pertrahuntur. Satis cum pudore (dicit Remonstrator) adiguntur tandem confiteri Puritani, omnia politeias Ecclesiasticae in verbo Dei non contineri. Immò nihil nos adacti diximus: omnia verò id est particulares omnes circumstantias individuales (de quibus tu loqueris) in verbo Dei expressas esse non diximus unquam. Vester Hic pudor est. Satis enim cum pudore confiteri compellimini, modum gubernationis ecclesiasticae, quod ad genus, in scripturis reperiri, imò & particularem politeias formam in eisdem tradi, quinimò in hac particulari forma quæ principalia sunt in verbo haberi: quo quisquam nostrum plus unquam desideravit? Atque hæ extortæ confessiones Hierarchicorum sunt, in ipso statu quæstionis explicando. Primù, doctrina tantum habetur in verbo, non disciplina, tum disciplina ethica, sed non Ecclesiastica, tum ecclesiastica docens sed non regens, postremò regens quoad ea, quæ principalis momenti sunt, quod idem planè est quod nos ipsi dicimus.
units.tr: § The fourth follows. Is there really nothing at all about church government in the Word? What then will become of the bishops? Indeed, says Richard Hooker, although Scripture is not necessarily obliged to prescribe for us one particular form of ecclesiastical polity, yet as regards the manner of governing in general, the precepts which Scripture delivers are not few, and it sets before all governors of the Church very many examples to imitate, even in particulars: indeed, the things of principal importance in the particular form of ecclesiastical polity itself (though not that which they imagine, but that which we defend against them) are contained in these very Scriptures. Good: they are being drawn over to our side at last, step by step, though unwillingly. With considerable shame (says the Remonstrant) the Puritans are at last compelled to confess that not everything about ecclesiastical polity is contained in the Word of God. Indeed we have said nothing of the kind under compulsion; but that all things, that is, all particular individual circumstances (of which you speak), are expressed in the Word of God, we never said. This shame is yours. For you are compelled to confess, with considerable shame, that the mode of ecclesiastical government, as regards the genus, is found in Scripture; indeed that a particular form of polity is also delivered in them; and moreover that in this particular form the principal matters are found in the Word. What more has any of us ever desired? And these are the confessions extracted from the Hierarchs in explaining the very state of the question. First, doctrine only is found in the Word, not discipline; then ethical discipline, but not ecclesiastical; then ecclesiastical discipline as teaching, but not as ruling; and lastly ruling as regards those things which are of principal importance, which is exactly what we ourselves say.

units.la: 6 Secundo notentur excessus in quos rapti Hierarchici sunt: dum hanc sententiam absurdissimam suam nitantur stabilire. Gabriel Powellus in ipso limine, hoc tanquam præcipuam erroris puritanici causam ponit, quod Christum putent fuisse legislatorem. Hic citat Canonem Concilij Tridentini illum, quo anathema eis denunciatur qui Christum legislatorem negant; quo odium opinioni nostræ conflaret, quam cum papistis adversus Evangelicos affirmat conspirare. Puduit hujus excessus Collinsium Cantabridgiensem quendam, qui in sua concione ad crucem Paulinam, Powellum excusare conatur, ac si id tantum voluisset, Christum non fuisse legislatorem tantummodò. Sed negat Powellus verbis apertis Christum fuisse legislatorem omnino, in quo delirio solus non est. Ira enim Mat. Sutclivius. Ut Christus sit externus legislator, durum sonat in Christianorum auribus. Alibi post, Ut politeiæ suæ existimationem concilient, sobrie & graviter disputare solent, Christum Iesum quod ad externam politeiam Ecclesiæ legislatorem esse, & quod in externis rebus Ecclesiasticis, nullis alijs legibus gubernari nos oportet quam quas ille tulit, quæ res, ut ante dixi, mira. In libro vero de presbyterio, per totum undecimum caput contendit, Christum & Mosem, Evangelium & legem ita opponi, ut Christus minime legislator sit, sicut Moyses, Evangelium fidem tantum requirat, leges autem proponat nullas, sicut lex proponere solet. De externa autem politeia Ecclesiæ apertissimus est in hæc verba. Ego inquit nulla ratione Christum Deum & hominem quoad externam ecclesiæ politeiam, legislatorem certe posse dici demonstrabo. En quo Hierarchicos hoc dogma transversus rapuit? Potius etenim Christus legislator negandus est, quàm ut de ecclesiastica politeia leges ullas sanxisse confitendum. Sed ô miseros. Ipse etenim Powellus postquam Christum legislatorem negasset; leges tamen plurimas de Adiaphoris ab ipso Christo sancitas recenset: & Mat. Sutclivius eo ipso in capite in quo Christum in externis legislatorem pei negavit, ita disciplinam suam definit. Dicimus disciplinam ecclesiasticam esse in hac quæstione, externum ordinem, partim in verbo, partim verò à Christiano magistratu & præcipuis Ecclesiæ ministris (si desit magistratus) juxta verbi regulas præscriptum. Hæc ille, qui nuper dixerat Christum nullo modo legislatorem fuisse, in externa præsertim politeia Ecclesiæ, jam partim saltè legislatorē, esse vult: quidni ad plenū et iam, sicut non partim rex est, partim non, sed absolutissimæ perfectissimæq; potestatis. Atque hæc absurda illa sunt: in quæ incidunt Hierarchici, dum hanc suam sententiam morosius tuentur: politeiam nempe ecclesiasticam in verbo Dei non contineri.
units.tr: 6 Secondly, let us note the excesses into which the Hierarchs are carried while they strive to establish this most absurd opinion of theirs. Gabriel Powell, at the very threshold, sets this down as the chief cause of the Puritan error: that they think Christ was the lawgiver. Here he cites that canon of the Council of Trent by which anathema is pronounced on those who deny Christ to be lawgiver, so as to kindle hatred against our opinion, which he asserts conspires with the Papists against the Evangelicals. A certain Collins of Cambridge was ashamed of this excess; in his sermon at St Paul's Cross he tries to excuse Powell, as if he had meant only this: that Christ was not merely a lawgiver. But Powell in plain words denies that Christ was a lawgiver at all, and in this madness he is not alone. For Matthew Sutcliffe says: That Christ should be an external lawgiver sounds harsh in the ears of Christians. Elsewhere, afterwards: In order to win credit for their polity, they are wont to dispute soberly and gravely that Christ Jesus is the lawgiver as regards the external polity of the Church, and that in external ecclesiastical matters we ought to be governed by no other laws than those he enacted; which thing, as I said before, is strange. In his book on the presbytery, throughout the whole eleventh chapter, he contends that Christ and Moses, the Gospel and the Law, are so opposed that Christ is by no means a lawgiver as Moses was; the Gospel requires faith only and proposes no laws, as the law is wont to do. But concerning the external polity of the Church he is most explicit in these words: I, he says, will show that by no reasoning can Christ, God and man, be rightly called the lawgiver as regards the external polity of the Church. See where this dogma has carried the Hierarchs headlong! Indeed Christ must rather be denied to be lawgiver than be confessed to have enacted any laws concerning ecclesiastical polity. But oh, wretched men! For Powell himself, after he had denied Christ to be lawgiver, nevertheless recounts very many laws about adiaphora enacted by Christ himself; and Sutcliffe, in that very chapter in which he denied that Christ was a lawgiver in external matters, defines his discipline thus: We say that ecclesiastical discipline in this question is external order, prescribed partly in the Word, but partly by the Christian magistrate and the chief ministers of the Church (if the magistrate be lacking), according to the rules of the Word. He says these things, he who lately said that Christ was in no way a lawgiver, especially in the external polity of the Church; now he wants him to be a lawgiver partly at least. Why not wholly and entirely? A king is not partly king and partly not, but holds power that is most absolute and perfect. And these are the absurdities into which the Hierarchs fall while they defend their opinion more stubbornly: namely, that ecclesiastical polity is not contained in the Word of God.

units.la: 7 Tertium eorum vitium in statu quæstionis explicando, eorum calumnias continet, quibus hunc ipsum statum à nobis positum, aut subdolè invertunt aut malitiosè exagitant. Statum quæstionis ex Lamberto Danæo repetere libet. Distinguendum est inquit de disciplinæ partibus: quædam esse in ea essentialia omnino, quædam accidentalia. Essentialia sunt omnia quæ de electione & munere personarum ecclesiasticarum hic traduntur. Accidentalia sunt quæ ad particularem earum rerum modum seruandum, formamque aliquam constituendam & cuiusque populi commoditatis rationem habendam pertinent, veluti quoties episcopo sit in hebdomade concionandum, quibus diebus, qua hora, quo loco, & cætera, quæ sunt huiusmodi. Rursus. In disciplina ecclesiastica distinguamus ea quæ sunt fundamentalia ab accessoriis & levioribus. Fundamentalia sunt hæc ut legitimæ vocationes personarum retineantur, veluti pastores, presbyteri, Diaconi, & ut ij legitime electi suo munere fungantur, vel deponantur & removeantur. Accessoria dico quæ ut hæc fiant & ob eventum in ecclesia quoque, pro tempore, personis, & locis statui possunt. Accessoria incolumi manente disciplina in ecclesia variari possunt: maneat autem semper disciplinæ fundamentum & pars præcipua. Hunc statum quæstionis dilucidè satis & perspicuè positum, dolosè primum invertunt isti. Richardus siquidem Hookerus, & remonstrator, & alij, cum disciplinam in verbo non contineri probant, eò sermonem deflectunt, quòd ceremoniæ ecclesiæ, ut loquitur Hookerus, & circumstantiæ individuales ut loquitur Remonstrator, in verbo expresso non habeantur. Ita larvas sibi fingunt quibuscum luctentur: & fucum lectori faciunt, ac si accidentalia & accessoria in verbo expresso haberi putemus, quod nemini nostrum in mentem unquam venit.
units.tr: 7 Thirdly, the third of their faults in explaining the state of the question consists in their calumnies, by which they either subtly invert or maliciously harass the very state of the question which we have laid down. I think it fitting to take the state of the question from Lambert Danaeus. One must distinguish he says, concerning the parts of discipline: some are wholly essential, some accidental. The essential things are all those which are here handed down concerning the election and office of ecclesiastical persons. The accidental things are those which pertain to keeping the particular mode of those matters, establishing some form, and taking account of the convenience of each people: such as how often the bishop is to preach in the week, on which days, at what hour, in what place, and the like, which are of this kind. Again: In ecclesiastical discipline let us distinguish those things which are fundamental from the accessory and lesser ones. The fundamental things are these: that the lawful callings of persons be retained, such as ministers, elders, and deacons, and that those lawfully elected discharge their office, or be deposed and removed. I call accessory those things which may be arranged so that these things are done, and which, according to the occasion in the Church, may be set up by time, persons, and places. The accessory things can be varied while discipline remains intact in the Church; but the foundation and principal part of discipline must always remain. This state of the question, set forth clearly and plainly enough, these men first invert by guile. For Richard Hooker, the Remonstrant, and others, when they prove that discipline is not contained in the Word, turn the discussion to this: that the ceremonies of the Church, as Hooker puts it, and the individual circumstances, as the Remonstrant puts it, are not found in the express Word. Thus they fashion for themselves phantoms to wrestle with, and make a show for the reader, as if we thought accidental and accessory things were found in the express Word, which never came into the mind of any of us.

units.la: 8 Secundò, Mat. Sutclivius distinctionem nostram agnoscit inter substantialia & circumstantialia, sed in ea id vitio dat quod non planum faciamus quid per substantiam quid per circumstantiam intelligimus, sed sub generali nube verborum subterfugium quærimus. Sed hoc ipsius vitium est; dicit disciplinam partim tantum describtam in verbo, partim non, quid autem illud sit quod describitur, quid, quod non describitur omnino non narrat: sicut & Richar. Hookerus præcipua disciplinæ in verbo contineri affirmat, quæ autem hæc præcipua sint, non dicit. At perspicuè a nobis sæpe traditum quid per substantialia disciplinæ intelligimus: insto tantum in confessione Gallica, quæ ita scrupulo huic medetur. Credimus veram ecclesiam gubernari debere ea politeia sive disciplina quam Dominus noster Iesus Christus sanxit, ita videlicet ut in ea sint Pastores, Presbyteri, & Diaconi, &c.
units.tr: 8 Secondly, Matthew Sutcliffe acknowledges our distinction between substantial and circumstantial things, but finds fault with it on the ground that we do not make plain what we mean by substance and what by circumstance, but seek a refuge under a general cloud of words. But this fault is his own: he says discipline is partly described in the Word and partly not, but what it is that is described, and what is not described at all, he does not tell us; just as Richard Hooker also affirms that the principal parts of discipline are contained in the Word, but does not say what these principal parts are. We, however, have often set forth clearly what we understand by the substantial parts of discipline. I insist only on the French Confession, which meets this scruple so well: We believe that the true Church ought to be governed by that polity or discipline which our Lord Jesus Christ established, namely that there be in it Pastors, Elders, and Deacons, etc.

units.la: 2 Tertio, male nos substantiam aut essentiam in externis somniare dicit Sutclivius. Præsertim cum Turriano objecit Sadeel, quod substantiam & essentialem formam, in externa forma ecclesiæ inesse voluerit.
units.tr: 2 Thirdly, Sutcliffe says that we dream of substance or essence in external things, especially since Sadeel objected to Turrianus that he had wished the substance and essential form to be present in the external form of the Church.

units.la: Tractat. de disciplin. c. 1.
units.tr: Tractat. de disciplin. c. 1.

units.la: Tractat. de disciplin. c. 14. p. 152. luerit non indicat locum: & mihi jam Sadeelem versare non vacat: hoc satis est,quod hoc ipso in loco, accidentium quandam essentiam esse vel ipsemet fateatur. Quid? annon de disciplinae substantialibus & essentialibus & Whitgiftus & Cousinus multa habent? Had. Saravia ita. Quamvis ecclesiastica gubernatio recepto evangelio, nonnihil (quantum per verbum Dei licet) ad reipublicae statum inflectenda sit: cavendum tamen est, ne ipsius tollatur substantia. Similiter Geor.Donnamus,se episcoporum vocationem,tantum quod substantiam, defensurum, suo ipso defensionis suae initio profitetur. Atque hoc vitium Hierarchicorum in statu quaestionis tertium est.
units.tr: Tractat. de disciplin. c. 14. p. 152. ...has not indicated the place, and I have no time now to go through Sadeel. It is enough that in this very place he himself admits that discipline has some accidental essence. Well? Do not Whitgift and Cousin have much to say about the substantial and essential parts of discipline? Hadrian Saravia says: Although ecclesiastical government, once the gospel is received, may and should be bent somewhat towards the state of the commonwealth (as far as the Word of God allows), yet care must be taken that its substance is not taken away. Likewise Georg Donnamus, at the very start of his defence, declares that he will defend the calling of bishops only as far as it is substance. And this is the third fault of the Hierarchists in setting out the state of the question.

units.la: 9 Quartum eorum contradictiones immanes continet. Stant etenim ex parte una,Whitgiftus,Sutclivius, Hookerus: Stant ex adversa,Bilsonus,Bancroftus,Saravia: quorum illi priores disciplinam in verbo non contineri,immutabiliter saltem: hi vero & in verbo contineri & perpetuum tanquam immutabilem mandari asseverant. Hadrianu tantu Saraviā citabo,qui cum Beza objecisset, disciplinae lege s haud minus ac doctrinae in scriptura haberi,quas figere aut refigere non liceat, respondit. In quos haec dicit Dominus Beza? ignosce mihi, quod antea dixi hic repeto, ipsum & hic ςυμφωνῶν. Concedit igitur, ut doctrinam ita & disciplinam perfecte verbo contineri. Atque haec de statu quaestionis satis. Dimicandnm jam adversus priorem Hierarchicorum gregem est, & disciplinam perfecte in verbo Dei contineri comprobandum.
units.tr: 9 The fourth fault contains monstrous contradictions. On one side stand Whitgift, Sutcliffe and Hooker; on the other stand Bilson, Bancroft and Saravia. The former say that discipline is not contained in the Word, at least not unchangeably; the latter assert that it is both contained in the Word and commanded as perpetual and unchangeable. I will cite only Hadrian Saravia, who, when Beza had objected that the laws of discipline are no less than the doctrine in Scripture, which may not be fixed or refixed, replied: To whom does the Lord Beza say these things? Forgive me, what I said before I repeat here, that he himself here too agrees [συμφωνῶν]. He therefore concedes that discipline, like doctrine, is perfectly contained in Scripture. And so much for the state of the question. We must now fight against the former flock of the Hierarchists and prove that discipline is perfectly contained in the Word of God.

units.la: CAP. XL.
units.tr: CHAP. XL.

units.la: Contrarium nostrum fundamentum, certam scilicet disciplinae formam in verbo praescribi undecem argumentis probatur.
units.tr: That our contrary foundation, namely that a certain form of discipline is prescribed in the Word, is proved by eleven arguments.

units.la: ARgumentum nostrum primum à sacrarum scripturarū apertis testimonijs sumitur, 1.Cor.4.17. Misi vobis Timotheum qui vobis in memoriam revocabit quae sunt viae meae in Christo sicut ubique in omnibus ecclesijs doceo: Vias nominat, non viam: ac proinde disciplinam comprehendit quae perinde ac doctrina,in omnibus ecclesijs uniformiter ab ipso Christo sancita est: quum & ea ipsa,via in Christo appelletur.1.Tim.3.15. Haec tibi scribo ut noris quomodo tibi versandum sit in domo Dei. Definitio haec politeiae est, ut sit ordo, quo quisq; dirigitur,quomodo illi in domo Dei versandum sit;haec scripta in hac epistola dicitur: certa igitur disciplinae forma in hac Epistola reperitur,quam mutare nefas. Id liquet aperte ex locis huius epistolae aliis 1.Tim. 5.21. Obtestor in conspectu Dei Domini nostri Iesu Christi & electorum Angelorum ut haec serves absque eo ut unum alteri praeferas. De judicijs ecclesiasticis ante egerat & de ordinationibus: certa igitur forma regiminis praescripta in verbo est, quae absque peccato violari nequit.1.Tim.6.13.14. Contestor te coram Deo qui vivificat omnia & Iesu Christo qui testatum fecit coram Pontio Pilato praeclaram illam confessionem, sessionem, ut serves hoc mandatum incontaminatus & irreprehensus usque ad illustrem illum adventum Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Mandata reddit Beza numero plurali, quàm benè aut secus, penes unumquemque judicium esto: frivola certè Richardi Hookeri tergiversatio est, qui τὴν ἐντολὴν non τὰς ἐντολὰς nominari dicit, ut non omnia mandata hic intelligantur sed præcipuum mandatum illud de quo verbis similibus Timotheum admonet, 2. Tim. 4. 1. Obtestor te coram Deo & Domino Iesu Christo, qui judicaturus est vivos & mortuos in illustri illo suo adventu & regno suo. Prædica sermonem, &c. At in contestatione simili priori 1. Tim. 5. 21. mandata nominavit numero plurali; & mandatum hoc in loco, quanquam numeri singularis sit, totam tamen eam officii rationem continet, quæ de politeia hâc in Epistola, præscripta est, sicut Lous ipse admonet: nam epilogus hoc Epiphonema est, quo epistola tota rata habetur, & quasi sigillo Apostolico confirmatur, & divina authoritate communitur usque quò Dominus Christus ad judicandum venerit: pueriliter igitur confugit Hookerus ad epistolam secundam, ut hanc ratificationem epistolæ primæ ad mandatum tantummodò de verbo prædicando restringat: quam omnia mandata de politeia comprehendere, Bilsonus, Saravia, Downnamus, & reliqui quod sciam Hierarchici omnes confitentur. Imò hunc locum imprimis urgent pro divino Episcopi Hierarchici jure: quoniam hanc epistolam Timotheo ut Episcopo scriptam fuisse opinantur. Diluetur hæc offucia loco suo: interim observetur hæc inter Hookerum & reliquos gregales suos contradictio: utpote præqua levis sit, aut potius nulla, quam nobis objicit, de viduarum necessitate. Mandatum inquit de viduis 1. Tim. 5. 9. Vos ipsi abrogatis: non igitur vel ex vestro judicio, ad perpetuitatem mandatorum omnium hæc Pauli contestatio extendenda est. Respondeo, qui mandatum de viduis fundamentale putant, ij viduas semper retinendas censent: qui viduas abrogari posse putant, ij viduas non fundamentales, sed accessorias muneri diaconatus censent, ut in Danęo videre est. Quid igitur? Nulli dubitant quin hæc Pauli contestatio ad omnia politeias mandata se porrigat quæ quidem fundamentalia sunt: scrupulus qui hæret hic tantum est: an mandatum de viduis fundamentale necne sit, vel accessorium.
units.tr: My first argument is taken from the plain testimonies of Holy Scripture. 1 Cor. 4.17: I have sent you Timothy, who will remind you of my ways in Christ, just as I teach everywhere in all the churches. He names ways, not a way, and so he includes discipline, which, like doctrine, has been sanctioned uniformly in all the churches by Christ himself, since that same thing is called a way in Christ. 1 Tim. 3.15: I write these things to you so that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God. This is the definition of polity: it is the order by which each person is directed as to how he must behave in the house of God, and this is what is set down in this epistle. A certain form of discipline is therefore found in this epistle, and it is wrong to change it. This is clear from other passages of the same epistle. 1 Tim. 5.21: I charge you before God, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the elect angels, to keep these things without preferring one to another. He had earlier dealt with ecclesiastical judgments and with ordinations. A certain form of government is therefore prescribed in the Word, and it cannot be violated without sin. 1 Tim. 6.13-14: I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and before Jesus Christ, who witnessed before Pontius Pilate that noble confession, that you keep this commandment unstained and blameless until the glorious appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ. Beza renders "commandment" in the plural. Whether he is right or wrong, let each judge for himself. Richard Hooker's evasion is certainly frivolous. He says that τὴν ἐντολήν [the commandment] is named, not τὰς ἐντολάς [the commandments], so that not all commandments are meant here, but that particular commandment about which he warns Timothy in similar words at 2 Tim. 4.1: I charge you before God and the Lord Jesus Christ, who will judge the living and the dead at his glorious appearing and in his kingdom. Preach the word, etc. But in the earlier, similar charge (1 Tim. 5.21) he named commandments in the plural; and this commandment in the present place, although singular, nevertheless contains that whole account of duty which is prescribed in this epistle concerning polity, as Lous himself reminds us. For the epilogue is an epiphonema by which the whole epistle is held valid, as it were sealed with the apostolic seal and secured by divine authority until the Lord Christ comes to judge. Hooker therefore childishly takes refuge in the second epistle, so as to restrict this ratification of the first epistle to the command about preaching the word alone. Yet Bilson, Saravia, Downame, and all the other Hierarchical writers, so far as I know, confess that all the commandments concerning polity are included. Indeed they press this passage above all for the divine right of the Hierarchical bishop, since they think this epistle was written to Timothy as a bishop. This pretence will be refuted in its place. Meanwhile let it be noted how Hooker contradicts his fellow soldiers here. The objection he raises against us about the necessity of widows is so slight, or rather nothing at all. "The command about widows, 1 Tim. 5.9," he says, "you yourselves abrogate; therefore this contestation of Paul's need not be extended to the perpetual validity of all commandments, not even by your judgment." I reply: those who think the command about widows is fundamental hold that widows must always be retained; those who think widows can be abrogated consider them not fundamental but accessory to the office of deacon, as may be seen in Danaeus. What then? No one doubts that this contestation of Paul extends to all the commandments of polity that are indeed fundamental. The only scruple that remains is whether the command about widows is fundamental or accessory.

units.la: 2. Argumentum nostrum secundum à scripturæ perfectione ducitur, de qua ita Irenæus: Hæretici cum ex scripturis arguuntur, in accusationem convertuntur ipsarum scripturarum, quasi non possit inveniri in his veritas ab his qui nesciunt traditionem. Hoc cum papistæ facerent, scripturas imperfectas asserentes egregie eorum perfectio & ad omnia sufficiencia, à Iuello, Whitakero, Lubberto, Reynoldo, Bilsono, Sutclivio, Mortono, aliisque defensa atque propugnata est. At nihil ad Politeiam Ecclesiæ (inquis) quæcunq; ab his allata sunt, sed ad fidei doctrinam tantum. Imò rationes eorum generales sunt, & mores includunt, non duntaxat fidem: citant omnes 2. Tim. 3. 16. ubi vir Dei, id est rector & gubernator Ecclesiæ, in omnibus per scripturas perfectus redditur. Revocetur in memoriam vox illa Richardi Hookeri: Verbum Dei respectu finis ad quem à Deo ordinatur, perfectum, exactum, & absolutum est: perfectam igitur exactam absolutamq; quoad fundamentalia Politeias formam continet: nam omne quòd ordinetur ad hunc inter ceteros finem ut Politeiam describat, non est à quoquam dubitatum. Confiteris etenim ipse præcipua Politeias in verbo contineri, quid ni ergo & substantia Politeias tota? Quod si nihil de Politeia tetigisset verbum, aliquid esset: jam vero cum de Politeia agere instituit, aut totam illius substantiam continet aut imperfecta est. Disciplina partim inquit Sutclivius in verbo Dei descripta est, partim Ecclesiæ arbitrio relicta. Quid sibi hoc partim vult? nonne apponitur pleno? nonne plane papisticum est? nonne scripturam imperfectionis arguit pro more papistarum? Non igitur adversus papistas solum, sed etiam adversus Hierarchicos, hę patrum voces militant; quas à Tho.Bilsono, Ioh.Reynoldo, alijsq; nostris productas habemus. Ita Ireneus; Scripturæ perfectæ sunt quippè à verbo Dei & spiritu eius dictatæ. Ita Tertullianus; Adoro plenitudinem scripturæ. Ita Athanasius: Sufficiant per se divinitus inspiratæ literæ ad veritatis indicationem. Ita Cyrillus: Omne verbum quod ad Deum pertinet in duobus testamentis inquiri & determinari potest. Ita Vincentius Lyrinensis: Canon scripturæ perfectus est & sufficiens, imò plusquam sufficiens ad omnia. Citat Optatum Io.Reynoldus, qui verbum Dei testamento comparat; apud quem videre est quantę sit blasphemiæ testamentum Dei, cuiuscunque imperfectionis arguere. Ita conficitur, cùm scriptura perfecta sit in omnibus de quibus agit, & cum de Politeia tractet: eam, aut certam disciplinę formam prescripsisse, aut imperfectionis merito arguendam esse.
units.tr: My second argument is drawn from the perfection of Scripture, of which Irenaeus speaks thus: When heretics are refuted from the Scriptures, they turn the accusation against the Scriptures themselves, as if the truth could not be found in them by those who do not know the tradition. When the Papists did this, asserting that the Scriptures are imperfect, their perfection and sufficiency for all things was splendidly defended and championed by Jewel, Whitaker, Lubbert, Reynolds, Bilson, Sutcliffe, Morton, and others. But you say that what they brought forward has nothing to do with the polity of the Church, only with the doctrine of faith. Indeed their arguments are general and include morals, not faith alone. All of them cite 2 Tim. 3.16, where the man of God, that is, the ruler and governor of the Church, is made perfect in all things through the Scriptures. Let us recall that saying of Richard Hooker: The Word of God, with respect to the end for which it is ordained by God, is perfect, exact, and absolute. Therefore it contains a perfect, exact and absolute form of polity as far as its fundamentals are concerned, for that it is ordained, among its other ends, to describe polity, no one has doubted. For you yourself confess that the chief points of polity are contained in the Word. Why then should the whole substance of polity not be contained in it? If the Word had said nothing about polity, that would be one thing; but now that it undertakes to treat of polity, it either contains its whole substance or it is imperfect. Discipline is partly, says Sutcliffe, described in the Word of God, partly left to the judgment of the Church. What does this "partly" mean? Is it not added to what is full? Is it not plainly Papist? Does it not argue that Scripture is imperfect, in the manner of the Papists? Therefore these sayings of the Fathers fight not only against the Papists but also against the Hierarchical writers, which we have from Thomas Bilson, John Reynolds and our other writers. Thus Irenaeus: The Scriptures are perfect, since they were dictated by the Word of God and his Spirit. Thus Tertullian: I adore the fullness of Scripture. Thus Athanasius: The divinely inspired letters are sufficient in themselves for the indication of truth. Thus Cyril: Every word that pertains to God can be sought out and determined in the two testaments. Thus Vincent of Lérins: The canon of Scripture is perfect and sufficient, indeed more than sufficient, for all things. John Reynolds cites Optatus, who compares the Word of God to a testament, where one may see how great a blasphemy it is to charge the testament of God with any imperfection. It follows, then, that since Scripture is perfect in all the matters it treats, and since it treats of polity, it has either prescribed a certain form of discipline or it must rightly be charged with imperfection.

units.la: 3. Argumentum nostrum tertium ab imperfectione sumitur fundamentorum aliorum omnium quando à verbo Dei discesseris. Nullum certum fundamentum Polieteia Ecclesiastica quæso habebit? Quod si vero aliquod habeat, verbum ut habeat necesse est. Richardus Hookerus ita: Possibile non est ut aliqua Politeia Ecclesiastica bona sit, nisi Deus ejusdem author sit. Æmuli sint necesse est, quæ Dei non sunt, habet Tertullianus. Quid igitur? nobiscum coalescit Hookerus? Minime verò. Politeiam siquidem Ecclesiasticam sicut & civilem à Deo ita esse vult, quâ lumen rationis à Deo est: de quo ita Ciceronem loquentem inducit. Ille (Deus) hujus legis inventor, disceptator, lator est. Atqui inquam Politeia Ecclesiastica inter res supernaturales est, uti ante demonstravimus, quando eam regnum Iesu Christi esse, comprobavimus, quod est cælestę, & spirituale, & minime de hoc mundo. In rebus autem supernaturalibus, sapientia humana locum non habet Col.2.23. sed ipsa Politeia Ecclesiastica, inter reliquos Ecclesiæ cultus, mare purum esse debet absque omni mixtura humanæ adjnventionis Ap.4.6. Ita Thomas Aquinas: Theologia non supponit sua principia ab aliqua sapientia humana, sed tantum à sapientia
units.tr: My third argument is taken from the imperfection of all other foundations once you have departed from the Word of God. What certain foundation, I ask, will ecclesiastical polity have? But if it has any, it must necessarily have it from the Word. Richard Hooker says: It is not possible that any ecclesiastical polity should be good unless God is its author. Those things which are not of God must necessarily be rivals, as Tertullian has it. What then? Does Hooker agree with us? By no means. For he wants ecclesiastical polity, like civil polity, to be from God only insofar as it comes from the light of reason, and of this he introduces Cicero speaking thus: (God) is the discoverer, arbiter and proposer of this law. But I say that ecclesiastical polity is among supernatural things, as we showed earlier when we proved that it is the kingdom of Jesus Christ, which is heavenly, spiritual, and not at all of this world. In supernatural things, however, human wisdom has no place (Col. 2.23). Ecclesiastical polity itself, among the other worship of the Church, ought to be a pure sea, without any mixture of human invention (Rev. 4.6). Thus Thomas Aquinas: Theology does not take its principles from any human wisdom, but only from

units.la: Cōt. Apol.p. 2.p.256 & p.4.pag.581 Lib2.c.47. Lib.de Cam L.cōt.Gent. In Lev l.5. Adversf. profan.trad. novu. Collat. cum Hart.p.397 398. Lib.3.f.2. De habit. mulier. pientia divina, à qua sicut summa sapientia omnis nostra cognitio ordinari debet. Hujus scientiae cognitio non est per naturalem rationem sed per revelationem & ideo de aliis judicat omnibus. Quorsum igitur tractatus ille Hookeri longus, de rationis commendatione, ad Politeiam Ecclesiasticam dirigendam? Imò quorsum illa commendatio conciliorum & Canonum etiam, quos ex Iure Canonico cap. Violatores 25 q. 1. ex instinctu spiritus sancti conditos fuisse asseverat? Instinctus siquidem spiritus Sancti absque verbo somniandus nullus est, uti ane demonstratum: neque concilia, aut scripta patrum ita scientiâ verbi Dei, aut spiritus gratia munita sunt, quin labi, & errare possint, perinde ac concilium illud, cui David ipse praefuit 1. Chron. 13.9,10. cum 15.13. Sic fundamentum certum absque verbo pro Politeia Ecclesiastica nullum est: quod unicum certum principium esse, in rebus singulis supernaturalibus, & ipsi quoque sancti patres constituerunt. Rejicit siquidem testimonia & Optati & Ambrosii Augustinus: atque posthac d: verbo subinfert: Ipse dominus Iesus discipulos testimonijs legum & prophetarum confirmandos esse iudicavit. Haec sunt causae nostrae documenta, h.e. fundamenta. Ambrosius in hunc modum: Ad illum doctorem propheta contendit, qui solus est magister verus. Quomodo enim potest homo quasi verum docere quod nescit, cum ipse sit mendax. Ita sequitur, aut certam disciplinae formam in verbo reperiri, aut Ecclesiam deficì ab illo certo fundamento, quo in rebus reliquis supernaturalibus singulis adiuvatur.
units.tr: Cōt. Apol.p. 2.p.256 & p.4.pag.581 Lib2.c.47. Lib.de Cam L.cōt.Gent. In Lev l.5. Adversf. profan.trad. novu. Collat. cum Hart.p.397 398. Lib.3.f.2. De habit. mulier. the wisdom of God, from which, as the highest wisdom, all our knowledge must be ordered. The knowledge of this science is not by natural reason but by revelation, and therefore it judges all other things. To what end, then, that long treatise of Hooker's on the commendation of reason, for directing the Ecclesiastical Polity? Indeed, to what end also that commendation of councils and canons, which he asserts were established by the instinct of the Holy Spirit, citing the Canon Law, Violatores, 25 q. 1? For no instinct of the Holy Spirit is to be dreamed of apart from the Word, as has been shown. Nor are councils or the writings of the Fathers so fortified by knowledge of God's Word, or by the grace of the Spirit, that they cannot slip and err, just as that council over which David himself presided (1 Chron. 13.9, 10, with 15.13). So there is no certain foundation for the Ecclesiastical Polity apart from the Word, and the Fathers themselves established this as the one certain principle in every supernatural matter. Augustine rejects the testimonies of both Optatus and Ambrose; and afterwards he adds in words: The Lord Jesus himself judged that his disciples were to be confirmed by the testimonies of the law and the prophets. These are the proofs of our cause, that is, its foundations. Ambrose, in this manner: The prophet contends with that teacher who alone is the true master. For how can a man teach as true what he does not know, since he himself is a liar? It follows, then, that either a certain form of discipline is to be found in the Word, or the Church is cut off from that sure foundation by which, in all other supernatural matters, it is helped.

units.la: 4. Argumentum nostrum quartum, à differentia sumitur quae est inter Politeiam civilem & Ecclesiasticam: quae objectioni cuidam respondere potest, quae adversus superiora ab Hierarchicis adfertur. Respondebunt etenim forte fundamentum certum in verbo Politeiam Ecclesiasticam habere, quo ad generalia, perinde ac Politeia civilis: etiamsi speciatim & nominatim nulla aliqua certa illis illius forma constituatur. Hoc si sit verum, nulla erit differentia inter Politeiam civilem & Ecclesiasticam quae jam permagna est. Nam distinguntur res Iehovae à negotijs regis 2. Cronic. 19. 11. & Iohan. 18. regnum Christi distinguit à regnis mundi, ut haec mundana, illud caelestae & spirituale statuatur. Hinc arguo dupliciter. Primò, in omni re supernaturali, illius substantia speciatim in verbo revelatur, circumstantiae verò individuales tantummodo per generalia principia diriguntur: ergò cum in hoc differat Ecclesiastica Politeia à civili, quòd haec res naturalis sit, illa spiritualis & caelestis: quoad substantiam ut in verbo revelentur necesse est. Secundò, quemadmodum in Politeia civili, supremus magistratus ejus certam formam constituit, qua de causa negotium regis dicitur in Chron.19. 11. ita in Ecclesiastica, Christus certam illius formam sanxit, quia ejusdem ille rex supremus est, Ioh. 8.36. Hinc certum ad hoc usque diem axioma invaluit, discrimen hoc esse inter civilem & Ecclesiasticam Politeiam: quòd haec una & certa sit utpote in verbo definita: illa vero hominum minum arbitrio varia & diversa. Ita Hadrianus Saravia: Nulli genti Deus unquam ullam certam ac perpetuam imperij formam dedit quam pro ratione loci ac temporum mutari non liceat, Sed huius regiminis de quo differrimus diversa est ratio: quoniam cum proximè à Deo est profecta,eam pro arbitrio suo homines mutare non possunt. Sed quid ego urgeo Saraviam? contra Matthaeus ipse Sutclivius, quamquam huius veritatis impugnator acerrimus: quum tamen adversus papistas disputat, ad eam ipsam confugere compellitur. Fundamentum Bellarmini pro papatu & gubernatione monarchica hoc est, quod monarchia optimum reipublicae regimen sit, & eadem sit reipublicae & Ecclesiae gubernandae ratio. Adversus hoc fundamentum Bellarmini contrarium ille extruit:diversum nempe esse reipublicae & Ecclesiae administrandae rationem & formam. Rationes multas adfert, quarum ego duas tantum recensebo. Prima, quia Ecclesia corpus mysticum & spirituale est, respublica verò corpus politicum. Secunda, quia una certa à Christo Ecclesiae gubernandae ratio praescribitur, at reipublicae formae possunt esse variae. Ad scribam ipsa verba. Sicut unus est Ecclesiae summus pastor & princeps Iesus Christus qui eadem omnibus ubiq; hominibus leges & praecepta dat: sic una est Ecclesiae vera & essentialis forma. At rerum publicarum ut variij sunt magistratus, sic variae reperiuntur formae: nam haec à rege, illa ab optimatibus, alia à potentioribus & locupletioribus è populo regitur: omnesq; istae formae bonae sunt. At secus fit in Ecclesia. Nam ut unus est summus Ecclesiae rex: ita una est fidei formula, unaq; Ecclesiasticae Politeiae ratio, à qua qui discedunt, in labem gubernationis Ecclesiae incidunt, & Christi leges transgrediuntur.
units.tr: 4. Our fourth argument is drawn from the difference between the civil and the Ecclesiastical Polity, which can answer an objection that the Hierarchicals bring against what has been said above. For they will perhaps reply that the Ecclesiastical Polity has a sure foundation in the Word as regards general matters, just as the civil polity does, even though no particular and definite form of it is laid down in that Word. If this were true, there would be no difference between the civil and the Ecclesiastical Polity, and yet the difference is very great. For the affairs of Jehovah are distinguished from the business of the king (2 Chron. 19.11), and the kingdom of Christ is distinguished from the kingdoms of the world, so that the latter is worldly, while the former is established as heavenly and spiritual (John 18). I argue in two ways. First, in every supernatural matter its substance is revealed in detail in the Word, while the individual circumstances are only directed by general principles. Therefore, since the Ecclesiastical Polity differs from the civil in this respect, that the civil is a natural thing while the ecclesiastical is spiritual and heavenly, it is necessary that its substance be revealed in the Word. Second, just as in the civil polity the supreme magistrate establishes its definite form (for which reason the business of the king is spoken of in Chron. 19.11), so in the Ecclesiastical polity Christ has sanctioned its definite form, because he is its supreme King (John 8.36). Hence the certain axiom has prevailed to this day, that this is the difference between the civil and the Ecclesiastical Polity: that the latter is one and certain, being defined in the Word, whereas the former is various and diverse according to the arbitrary judgement of men. So Hadrian Saravia: God has never given any nation a certain and perpetual form of government which may not be changed according to the circumstances of place and time. But this government of which we are speaking has a different reason: since it has proceeded most immediately from God, men cannot change it at their own pleasure. But why do I press Saravia? Matthew Sutcliffe himself, though a most bitter opponent of this truth, is nevertheless compelled to take refuge in it when he disputes against the Papists. The foundation of Bellarmine for the papacy and for monarchical government is that monarchy is the best form of government of a commonwealth, and that the same method must govern both the commonwealth and the Church. Against this foundation of Bellarmine, Sutcliffe builds the contrary: namely, that the method and form of governing a commonwealth and of administering the Church are different. He brings many reasons, of which I shall recount only two. The first is that the Church is a mystical and spiritual body, whereas the commonwealth is a political body. The second is that Christ has prescribed one certain method of governing the Church, whereas the forms of commonwealths may be various. Let me set down his very words: Just as Jesus Christ is the one supreme pastor and prince of the Church, who gives the same laws and precepts to all men everywhere, so there is one true and essential form of the Church. But as the magistrates of commonwealths are various, so the forms are various: for one is ruled by a king, another by the nobles, another by the more powerful and wealthy from among the people; and all these forms are good. But it is otherwise in the Church. For as there is one supreme King of the Church, so there is one formula of faith and one method of Ecclesiastical Polity, and those who depart from it fall into the ruin of the government of the Church and transgress the laws of Christ.

units.la: 5. Argumentum nostrum quintum à comparatione Politeiae Iudaicae sumitur: à comparatione inquam non ut Whitgiftus calumniatur convectione. Neque enim Politeiam Iudaicam convehit, qui hoc argumento utitur: nullo modo verisimile esse, minus exactam Politeiam Ecclesiae sanxisse Christum, quam sanxit Moses, quem cum Mose comparat Paulus, tanquam adaeq; fidelem in Domo Dei. Heb.3.2.3.5. Respondet Ioh. Bridgesius: De interno domus Dei regimine tantum loqui Paulum non de externo. Similiter Mat. Sutclivius huic argumento hoc tantum respondet: Christi regnum in Ecclesia non esse in rebus externis, sed in conscientiarum regimine & dominio collocandum. Remonstrator, hanc comparationem inter Christum & Mosen in eo versari dicit, quod Christus instructionem adaeque claram in fide ac moribus reliquerit, atque ipse Moses, imo multo clariorem. Atqui comparatio in genere statuitur de fidelitate in exstruenda & gubernanda domo Dei absque ulla restrictione: id quod Ri.Hookerus videns, respondet comparationem institui inter utriusq; fidelitatem circa eas res quas in commisso habebant: iam verò Deum non mandasse Christo dicit, ut fortoam Ecclesiasticae Politeiae sanciret pro Ecclesia Christiana, uti Mosi mandavit, formam Politeiae constituere pro Iudaica. At minus Christi authoritati quae accepit à patre haec responsio
units.tr: 5. Our fifth argument is drawn from the comparison with the Jewish Polity: a comparison, I say, not, as Whitgift slanders, a conveyance. For he who uses this argument does not convey the Jewish Polity; the argument is this: it is in no way likely that Christ established a less exact polity for the Church than Moses established, whom Paul compares with Christ as equally faithful in the house of God (Heb. 3.2, 3, 5). John Bridges replies: Paul speaks only of the internal government of the house of God, not of the external. Likewise Matthew Sutcliffe answers this argument only with this: The kingdom of Christ in the Church is not to be located in external matters, but in the governance and dominion of consciences. The Remonstrant says that this comparison between Christ and Moses consists in this: that Christ left instruction in faith and morals equally clear, and Moses himself, indeed far clearer. Yet the comparison is set up in general terms concerning faithfulness in building and governing the house of God, without any restriction. Richard Hooker, seeing this, replies that the comparison is instituted between the faithfulness of each with regard to those things which they had been entrusted with. And he says that God did not command Christ to establish, for the Christian Church, a form of Ecclesiastical Polity, as he commanded Moses to establish a form of polity for the Jews. But this answer agrees ill with the authority that Christ received from the Father.

units.la: {1} responsio spōsio cōvenit: Mat. 28.18. Omnis potestas mihi data est in cœlo & terra Isa.9.6. Impositus est principatus humeris ejus. Isa.22. 22. Imponam clavem Davidis humeris eius — & suspendent de eo totam gloriam domus paternæ ejus etiam omnia vasa parvi pretij, tum vasa craterum, tum vasa lagenarum. Notentur hæc ultima: ostendunt enim & minima etiam negotia quæque tradita in commissio fuisse Christo: claves saltem, id est iurisdictionem Ecclesiasticam: quam eum ordinare videmus, Mat. 16.19. Atqui inquiunt non tantum in commisso datum Christo ac Mosi fuisse hinc liquet: quod Moses Politeiam Civilem exactè descripserit, quod Christus non fecit. Quid hoc ad rem; comparatio enim instituitur à Paulo inter Christum & Mosem, quoad Domum Dei non quoad rempublicam, sicut magistratus Politicus Christus non erat, sed spiritualis duntaxat Ecclesiæ suæ rex. Sed ipsa dictandi ratio inquit hoc discrimen subinsinuat: occasionaliter etenim dictantur ab Apostolis quæ Politeiam concernant, non more legali sanctiuntur, quemadmodum processit Moses. At merè papisticum hoc argumentum est. Ita enim arguunt apud Ri. Fyldum. Scriptura non est perfecta quia scripta est iuxta particulares occasiones quæ offerebantur, non autem ex proposito, ut perfectam regulam fidei contineret. Atq; sane peræque imperfectionem fidei arguit occasionalis ista scriptio, ac imperfectionem politeias: sed utcunq; occasionaliter epistolæ Apostolorum scriptæ fuerint, inquit Fyldus: divina providentia tamen perfectam fidei normam continent, sic & Politeias Ecclesiasticæ etiam. Arguit tertiò Hookerus, leges Mosaicas Iudaicam tantum gentem concernere: & ideo comparationem nullam inferri posse, tam exactæ Politeias pro omnibus Ecclesijs Christianis, quæ multæ imò pæne innumeræ sunt. Tetigit antè hanc rationem Lous: Mosi possibile erat, inquit, uni genti formam certam Politeiæ præscribere: at Christo non ita facile fuit omnibus gentibus legem certam figere. O quantum inane! Cur non unam certam regiminis formam omnium gentium Ecclesijs præfigere tam possibile fuit, quoad substantialia: quam unam certam doctrinam de fide & moribus: imò unam certam disciplinam docentem, quoad munus pastorale, & sacramentorum administrationem, quod omnes confitentur? Arguit Hookerus quartò, non adeo exactam Politeias Ecclesiasticæ formam ab ipso Mose delineatam fuisse, quin multi casus inciderint, qui absque speciali revelatione determinari non potuerint, qua speciali revelatione jam caret Ecclesia Levit. 24. 12. Num. 15.24. Num.9. Num.27.&c. Nihil hinc adversus nos concluditur: casus multos in Politeia novos incidere solere confitemur, qui iuxtà analogiam præceptorum fundamentalium aut regulas scripturæ generales determinari debent, sic ut eis non obstantibus, certa quædam quoad fundamentalia disciplinæ forma jam in verbo continueretur, perinde ac apud Iudæos olim continebatur, quanquam novi multi individuales casus inciderint vel ipso fatente Io.Whitgifto.Ne res quidem minima, inquit, quæ in Ecclesia agenda erat, in lege Mosis omittebatur.
units.tr: {1} This answer agrees ill with the promise: Matt. 28.18, All power is given to me in heaven and on earth. Isa. 9.6, The government is laid upon his shoulders. Isa. 22.22, I will lay the key of David upon his shoulder, and they shall hang upon him all the glory of his father's house, all the vessels of small account, whether vessels of cups or vessels of flagons. Let these last words be noted: for they show that even the smallest matters committed to him were entrusted to Christ, at least the keys, that is, Ecclesiastical jurisdiction, which we see him ordain (Matt. 16.19). But they say that it is clear from this that more than what was committed to Christ was given to Moses, because Moses described the civil polity exactly, which Christ did not do. What does this matter to the point? For the comparison is instituted by Paul between Christ and Moses as regards the house of God, not as regards the commonwealth, just as Christ was not a political magistrate but only the spiritual King of his Church. But the very manner of speaking suggests this distinction: for the Apostles dictate what concerns the polity occasionally, and they do not sanction it by legal enactment, as Moses proceeded. But this argument is purely Papistical. For so they argue in the words of Richard Fulke: Scripture is not perfect, because it was written according to particular occasions which presented themselves, and not with a plan to contain a perfect rule of faith. Indeed, this occasional writing argues the imperfection of faith just as much as the imperfection of the polity; but, however occasionally the Epistles of the Apostles were written, says Fulke, yet by divine providence they contain a perfect norm of faith; so too for the Ecclesiastical polities. Thirdly, Hooker argues that the Mosaic laws concern only the Jewish nation, and therefore no comparison can be drawn with a polity so exact for all Christian churches, which are many, indeed almost innumerable. Lous touched on this reason before: It was possible for Moses, he says, to prescribe a certain form of polity for one nation; but it was not so easy for Christ to fix a certain law for all nations. O how empty! Why was it not as possible to prescribe one certain form of government for the Churches of all nations, as far as the essentials go, as it is to have one certain doctrine of faith and morals, or indeed one certain discipline teaching the pastoral office and the administration of the sacraments, which all men confess? Hooker argues in the fourth place that the form of the Ecclesiastical Polity was not delineated so exactly by Moses himself that many cases did not arise which could not be determined without special revelation, and which special revelation the Church now lacks (Lev. 24.12; Num. 15.24; Num. 9; Num. 27, etc.). Nothing is concluded from this against us. We confess that many new cases tend to arise in the polity, which ought to be determined according to the analogy of the fundamental precepts or the general rules of Scripture, so that, these notwithstanding, a certain form of discipline, as to fundamentals, is already contained in the Word, just as it was once contained among the Jews, although many new individual cases have arisen, as even John Whitgift admits: Not even the smallest matter, he says, that had to be done in the Church was omitted in the law of Moses.

units.la: Quid igitur? ipsa fundamentalia Ecclesiastici regiminis in lege Christi omittebantur? Libertas nostra, respondet Whirgiftus, liberationem postulat à tam exiêtis legum normâ: imo libertatem à Christo partam, à servitute Iudaica, pedibus proculcant, inquit Lous, qui certam formam Politeiae in verbo contineri affirunt. Non opus est multis. In legibus Mosaicis duo sunt, multitudo & directio: multitudo onus erat, directio beneficium: hinc sequitur libertatem nostram à servitute Iudaica in eo versari, quòd à multitudine observationum Mosaicarum liberamur: directio beneficium cum sit, tam exactam nostram Politeiam iam habemus, quam quae apud Iudaeos erat; aut Ecclesia nostra deficit & illâ Iudaicâ inferior est. Hinc comparationi huic acquiescit Hn. Saravia. Quum etenim urgeret D. Beza certam esse à Christo sub Evangelio constitutam regiminis Ecclesiastici formam quemadmodum olim à Mose fuerat, respondet ille: Meam sententiam confirmat quisquis ita scribit & loquitur: & facile idem sentiremus, si eandem gubernationis formam quâ Apostoli usi sunt retentam fuisse Genevae, & in aliis Ecclesiis Galliae & inferioris Germaniae observari, doceri possit. Imo quid ipse Matheus Sutclivius. Contemptim quidem loquitur ille in tractatu suo de disciplina de hoc argumento nostro, à Mosis & Christi comparatione desumpto c. 12. p. 152. in libro vero de presbyterio c. 11. ulterius progreditur: contendit etenim Christum legislatorem non esse ut Moses erat, in externis praesertim, sed Mediatorem tantum. Sed adversus Bellarminum disputans, novus homo emergit. Quid Bellarminus? eodem nempe fundamento nititur, quo Hierarchici, non esse scilicet eandem rationem novi testamenti, quae veteris, legi Mosis non licuisse addere, Evangelio licere. Quid ita? Audi eam ipsam Hierarchicorum cantilenam. Quia Deus in lege omnia determinavit in speciali, in novo autem testamento latae sunt leges communissimae, quae specialiter per Apostolos & eorum successores pro locorum & temporum diversitate determinandae essent. Quid ad haec Sutclivius. Recipe defensionem plane nostram iisque totidem verbis. Haec ne ipsa adversus Christum contumeliosa est. Cur enim ille perfectiorem non dat legem quam Moses, praesertim cum Mosi longè praestet? Praeterea repugnat perfectioni Evangelij. Nam si omnia specialiter in lege praecepta sunt, & nihil fere in Evangelio ut ipse subindicat, tunc erit lex Mosis Evangelio praestantior: quod tamen nec verum est, nec à Bellarmino conceditur. At intelligit ista de fide tantum & sacramentis Sutclius. Etiam loquitur generatim, & Politeiam includit, ut demonstrant sequentia. Postremo haec responsio Bellarmini falsa est: nam non magis licet Evangelij legem addere, quam legi Mosis. Nec obstat quòd à conciliis & pijs principibus aliquae leges de rebus Ecclesiasticis additae sunt: Illae enim non sunt additiones ad legem Dei, nec in conscientia obligabant, nisi quatenus aliquid de lege Dei participabant. Ita conficitur, certam quandam Politeiae formam quoad substantialia in Evangelio contineri, quia in lege continebatur.
units.tr: What then? Were the fundamentals of ecclesiastical government themselves left out of Christ's law? Our liberty, Whitgift replies, demands release from so strict a rule of laws. Indeed, they trample underfoot the liberty won by Christ from Jewish servitude, says Lous, those who affirm that a certain form of polity is contained in the Word. Many words are not needed. In the Mosaic laws there are two things, multitude and direction: the multitude was a burden, the direction a benefit. It follows that our liberty from Jewish servitude consists in this, that we are freed from the multitude of Mosaic observances. Since direction is a benefit, we now have a polity as exact as the one the Jews had; otherwise our Church is lacking and inferior to that Jewish one. Sir Saravia accepts this comparison. For when Dr Beza insisted that a certain form of ecclesiastical government was established by Christ under the Gospel, just as it had once been by Moses, Saravia replies: Whoever writes and speaks in this way confirms my opinion, and we would easily agree with it too, if it could be shown that the same form of government which the Apostles used was kept at Geneva and is observed in the other Churches of France and Lower Germany. Indeed, what does Matthew Sutcliffe himself say? He speaks disparagingly in his treatise on discipline, in chapter 12, page 152, where he takes this argument from the comparison of Moses and Christ; but in his book on the presbytery, chapter 11, he goes further. He contends that Christ was not a lawgiver as Moses was, especially in external matters, but only a Mediator. But disputing against Bellarmine, a new man emerges. What does Bellarmine say? He rests on the same ground as the hierarchists, namely that the New Testament does not stand in the same relation as the Old, so that it was not allowed to add to the law of Moses but is allowed to add to the Gospel. Why so? Hear that very song of the hierarchists: Because God determined everything in the law in particular, but in the New Testament the laws given are most general, which were to be determined in particular by the Apostles and their successors according to the diversity of places and times. What does Sutcliffe answer to this? Take up our defence, quite plainly, and in just these words: This is even insulting to Christ. For why would he not give a more perfect law than Moses, especially since he is far superior to Moses? Moreover, it contradicts the perfection of the Gospel. For if everything is prescribed in particular in the law, and almost nothing in the Gospel, as he himself hints, then the law of Moses will be superior to the Gospel; yet this is neither true nor conceded by Bellarmine. But Sutcliffe understands these words only of faith and the sacraments. Yet he speaks generally and includes polity, as the following shows: Finally, this answer of Bellarmine is false: for it is no more permitted to add to the law of the Gospel than to the law of Moses. Nor does it count against this that some laws concerning ecclesiastical matters have been added by councils and pious princes: for those are not additions to the law of God, nor did they bind the conscience except insofar as they shared in something of the law of God. Thus it is concluded that a certain form of polity, as to its essentials, is contained in the Gospel, because it was contained in the law.

units.la: 6 Argumentum nostrum sextum à subjecto politeias Ecclesiasticae ducitur, ecclesia nempe, quæ vineæ, domui, civitati, corpori deniq; assimilatur, sic ut illius custodes, politeia, œconomi, partes deniq; essentiales in verbo Dei ut ordinentur necesse est. Respondet ad ista attributa conjunctim Hookerus: ea non implicare certam immutabilemque formam disciplinæ, quia vel nobis ipsis fatentibus, quædam in politeia ecclesiastica sunt minoris momenti, quæ alterationem pati possunt. Quàm jejunè? Quomodo etenim sequitur, custodes vineæ, politeiam essentialem civitatis, œconomos comus, partes essentiales corporis mutari posse, quod quædam minoris momenti, vineæ, civitatis, domus negotia, & habitus externus corporis nonnunquam immutari possint? Videamus de singulis separatim. Primò vinea Domini dicitur ecclesia, quam ab ipso Deo per politeiam excultam legimus, Isa. 5. 2. 3. 4. præcipuè verò Cant 8. 4. Vinea est Salomoni in loco ferace, locat vineam suam custodibus, quisque affert pro fructu eius mille nos siclos argenti. Vineæ, quæ mea est, apud me permaneant, &c. Quum anno 1606. eligerentur à rege, qui pro disciplina Anglicana, coram ministris tum præsentibus, concionarentur: demandatum Iohanni Kingo erat, qui nunc est Episcopus Londinensis, ut contra Seniores & presbyterium declamitaret. Textum verò sumpsit ille hunc ipsum ex Canticis locum: & nullam vineæ certam gubernationis formam à Solomone Vineæ domino constitutam esse, asseveravit. Num hoc in textu reperit? imò nonne textu ipso hoc Glossema confutatur? Vera etenim Francisci Iani expositio (cui ille nihil respondet.) Ne rex quidem ipse ut vineam haberet sit cissimum, eam aut i si posset colere, aut totum illius fructum perciperet, sed colendam aliis locat, & aliquid eis de proventu tenetur attribuere: ego vero inquit sponsus neque aliis colendam loco, neque mihi quicquam de ea detrahi sinam, adeo sum illius Zelotypus, sed oculi mei semper versantur in ea, & fructus illius nè tantillum quidem alienari sino, aut aliena voluntate administrari. Vide igitur huius hominis oscitantiam, qui nec textum quidem suum intellexit. Salomonem etenim ver. 4. suam vineam locantem aliis, intelligit Christum suam Ecclesiam custodibus locantem: cum contra manifesta hic antithesis inter Salomonem atque Christum instituatur, sic ut Salomon quidem vineam suam locat aliis, permittens eam alienæ voluntate administrari: Christus verò Ecclesiam non elocat, sed ipse per se eam colit, permittens nemini voluntate sua rem administrare: sed pro speciali ipsius amore & Zelotypia, curam illius in seipsam suscipiens. Non igitur vel Zelotypia in suam vineam specialis, vel potestas in eandem Christi elocata nemini, vel fructuum denique reservatio permittet, ut Politeiæ ejusdem constitutionem arbitrio hominum reliquisse videatur: præsertim cum Politeia Ecclesiæ, medium illud sit, quo fructus proventusque ubertim affluunt, quas sibi soli reservasse hic Christus affirmatur.
units.tr: 6. Our sixth argument is drawn from the subject of ecclesiastical polity, namely the Church, which is compared to a vineyard, a house, a city, and finally a body, so that its keepers, its polity, its stewards, and finally its essential parts must necessarily be ordained in the Word of God. Hooker answers these attributes all together: they do not imply a certain and unchangeable form of discipline, because, as we ourselves concede, some things in ecclesiastical polity are of lesser importance and may undergo alteration. How feebly! For how does it follow that the keepers of a vineyard, the essential polity of a city, the stewards of a house, and the essential parts of a body can be changed, merely because some things of lesser importance, such as the affairs of a vineyard, a city, or a house, and the external habit of a body, can sometimes be changed? Let us look at each separately. First, the vineyard of the Lord is called the Church, which we read was tended by God himself through polity, Isaiah 5:2, 3, 4, and especially Song of Songs 8:4: Solomon has a vineyard in a fruitful place; he lets out the vineyard to keepers, and each brings for its fruit a thousand shekels of silver. My vineyard, which is mine, let it remain with me, etc. When in the year 1606 certain men were chosen by the king to preach on behalf of English discipline before the ministers then present, John King, who is now Bishop of London, was commissioned to declaim against the elders and the presbytery. He took this very passage from the Song of Songs as his text, and asserted that no fixed form of government was established for the vineyard by Solomon, its lord. Does he find this in the text? Rather, is this gloss not refuted by the text itself? For the true exposition of Francis Junius (to which he makes no reply) is this: not even the king himself, who had a vineyard, wished to tend it or could tend it, or would receive all its fruit; he lets it out to others to be tended and is bound to assign them some part of the yield. But I, says the bridegroom, will neither let it out to others to be tended nor allow anything to be taken from it for myself; so jealous am I of it, but my eyes are always upon it, and I will not allow its fruit to be alienated even in the least, nor administered by another's will. See then the carelessness of this man, who did not even understand his own text. For he takes Solomon, letting out his vineyard to others in verse 4, to mean Christ letting out his Church to keepers; whereas a clear antithesis is set up here between Solomon and Christ: Solomon lets out his vineyard to others, allowing it to be administered by another's will; but Christ does not let out his Church, but tends it himself, allowing no one to administer it by his own will, and taking its care upon himself out of his special love and jealousy for it. Therefore neither his special jealousy for his own vineyard, nor the power over it that Christ has let out to no one, nor finally the reservation of its fruits, will allow it to seem that he has left the constitution of its polity to the decision of men, especially since the polity of the Church is that means by which fruits and yields flow in abundance, and which Christ here is declared to have reserved to himself alone.

units.la: 2 Secundo, civitas Ecclesia dicitur regis magni: & civitatis anima (inquit Hookerus ex persona nostra) Politeia est. Adjicit in margine
units.tr: 2. Second, the Church is called the city of the great King, and the soul of the city is polity, says Hooker, speaking in our person. In the margin he adds

units.la: Ex persona nostra Guilielmi Traversij verba: Nisi reipublicæ suæ statum omnem Christus constituerit, magistratus ordinarit, singulorum munera potestatemque descripserit, quæ judiciorum forià ratio habenda, quomodo civium finiendæ lites: non solum minus Ecclesiæ Christianæ providit, quam Moses olim Iudaicæ, sed quam à Lycurgo, Salomone, Numa, civitatibus suis prospectum fuit. Ponit ista odiose Hookerus, sed cur non refellit? Certe refelli ista non possunt, id quod etiam in Cornelio Scultingio videre est, qui licet thesim Traversianam sibi refutandam suscepisset, & disciplinam in verbo non perfectè contineri asseruisset: ad hoc tamen illius argumentum, respondet omnino nihil. Tertiò, Ecclesia domus Dei est, 1. Tim. 3. 15. Heb. 3. 3. 4. & quænam domus benè constituta ordine caret quo gubernatur? In domo quisquam œconomios constituit præter patremfamilias? Numerus, gradus, ordo, habitus, servorum Salomonis, tot illius sapientiæ testimonia erant: quomodo ergo verisimile fiat, Christum majorem Salomone, non eam certam domus suæ gubernandæ rationem reliquisse, in qua quasi in speculo, sapientia, cura, & illius providentia erga Ecclesiam suâ reluceret. Hæc Hookerus ex persona nostra: quibus tamen ne verbum quidem respondet. Respondet Remonstrator plurima in quaque domo œconomi arbitrio discretionique relinqui solere: quod ipsum causam non attingit. Quæstio etenim nostra non de rebus minoris momenti est: nam circumstantias individuales Ecclesiæ arbitrio relictas esse confitemur: sed de ipso domus Dei regimine, imò de œconomis ipsis, quorum designationem domus œconomis relictam esse quis unquam audivit? Luc. 12. 12. Quisnam est dispensator fidelis & prudens quem constituit dominus ejus super familiam suam, ut det portionem eius in tempore suo. Ecce rectores domus, ipse dominus constituit. Quo etiam pertinet calamus ille Apoc. 11. Datus Angelo ad metiendam domum Dei: ostendit etenim non absque calamo relictam esse Ecclesiam Dei, vel quoad regimen: nam de mensuratione regiminis adversus Antichristi tyrannidem, peraeque ac adversus hæresim de mensuratione ipsius fidei, agit hoc in loco vates. Sic nempè decuerat, nè domus posterior, priori cederet: de qua singula in Dei verbo descripta fuisse, testatur David, 1. Chron. 28. 12. 13. 19. Tunc tradidit Salomoni filio suo structuram domus, & omnium quæ erant penes eum per spiritum de atrys Iehovæ, etiam pro distributionibus sacerdotum & Levitarum & pro omni opere ad ministerium domus Iehovæ. ——Hæc omnia descripta à manu Iehovæ incumbere mihi instruxit me; omnia opera huius structuræ. Quid multis? Concedit hic pedib. in sententiam nostram adversariorum omnium acerrimus, Matheus ipse Sutclivius: sic etenim adversus Bellarm. scribit: Dubium non est quin universam domum suam & omnes ejus ministros Christus perfectè constituerit & descripserit. Quare cum Pontifex nullum suæ iurisdictionis mandatum ostendere possit, ipsa nulla est. Neque enim ulla maior est nullitas: quàm quæ ex defectu iuris est. Nonne & ministros regentes perfectè à Christo institutos asserit, contra Pseudoregentem regentem disputans? Nonne nullitatem jurisdictionis (puta in Episcopis) ponit, ubi nullum in verbo mandatum extat? Postremò, corpori assimilatur Ecclesia, quod & concedit Richardus Hookerus, sed nihil tamen pro certa regiminis forma facere contendit: quia Politeia, tantum hujus corporis vestitus & ornatus est, qui immutari & variari sine piaculo ullo potest. At officia Ecclesiastica pastores, nempè, Seniores, & Diaconos, pro quibus contendimus, non vestitum hujus corporis sed membra vocat, Rom.12.5. sic ut Christus ea omnia in verbo formare instar figuli censendus sit: quamadmodum in corpore naturali, formare & figurare singula ejus membra, creator Deus dicitur.
units.tr: The words of William Travers, spoken in our person: Unless Christ has established the whole state of his commonwealth, ordained the magistrates, and described the duties and powers of individuals, what plan is to be had for the courts of judgment, and how are citizens' disputes to be settled? Then he has provided for the Christian Church less than Moses once provided for the Jewish one, and less than Lycurgus, Solomon and Numa provided for their cities. Hooker sets this down invidiously, but why does he not refute it? Surely these things cannot be refuted, as may also be seen in Cornelius Schultingius, who, although he had undertaken to refute Travers's thesis for himself, and had asserted that discipline is not perfectly contained in the Word, nevertheless makes no reply at all to this argument of his. Third, the Church is the house of God, 1 Timothy 3:15, Hebrews 3:3, 4. And what house that is well ordered lacks the order by which it is governed? Does anyone appoint stewards in a house except the head of the household? The number, grades, order and habits of Solomon's servants were so many witnesses of his wisdom: how then does it become probable that Christ, greater than Solomon, left no certain plan for governing his house, in which his wisdom, care and providence toward the Church would shine forth as in a mirror? Hooker says this in our person, yet he does not answer a single word to these things. The Remonstrant replies that in every household many things are customarily left to the steward's judgment and discretion; but this does not touch the cause at all. For our question is not about matters of lesser importance: we concede that individual circumstances are left to the judgment of the Church. The question is about the very government of the house of God, indeed about the stewards themselves, whose appointment has ever been heard of as left to the steward of a house? Luke 12:42: Who then is the faithful and wise steward, whom his lord shall set over his household, to give them their portion of food in due season? Behold, the lord himself appoints the rulers of the house. To this also pertains that reed in Revelation 11: given to the angel to measure the house of God; for it shows that the Church of God was not left without a measuring reed, even as to its government: for the prophet in this place deals with the measuring of the government against the tyranny of Antichrist, just as he deals with the measuring of the faith itself against heresy. This was indeed fitting, lest the later house should yield to the earlier, each detail of which, David testifies, was described in the Word of God, 1 Chronicles 28:12, 13, 19. Then he gave to Solomon his son the pattern of the house, and of all that was with him by the Spirit, of the courts of Jehovah, and for the divisions of the priests and Levites, and for all the work of the ministry of the house of Jehovah. All these things, written by the hand of Jehovah, he made me understand, all the works of this pattern. Why say more? Matthew Sutcliffe himself, the most fierce of all our adversaries, concedes our view here with both feet: for he writes thus against Bellarmine: There is no doubt that Christ has perfectly constituted and described his whole house and all its ministers. Therefore, since the Pope can show no commission for his jurisdiction, it is null. For there is no greater nullity than that which arises from a defect of right. Does he not also assert, disputing against the pseudo-ruling elder, that the ruling ministers were perfectly instituted by Christ? Does he not place a nullity of jurisdiction (namely in bishops) where no commission is found in the Word? Lastly, the Church is compared to a body, which Richard Hooker also concedes, but he nevertheless contends that this does nothing for a fixed form of government, because polity is only the clothing and ornament of this body, which can be changed and varied without any sacrilege. But the ecclesiastical offices, namely the pastors, the elders and the deacons, for which we contend, he calls not the clothing of this body but its members, Romans 12:5. So Christ must be regarded as forming all these in the Word as a potter does, just as in a natural body God the Creator is said to form and shape each of its members.

units.la: 8 Argumentum nostrum septimum, ab officio principis & capitis ecclesiae Iesu Christi derivatur: nonne etenim regis est sancire leges ut regnu quâ optimè suu gubernetur? Quid aliud sonat ab Isaia illa.97.Iustitia & iudicio Christu regnu suu stabilire? Quid aliud, illa Pauli, 1. Cor.12.4. Christu ut Dominu & administrationes pro regenda Ecclesia sua instituisse? Quid aliud denique; illa Iacobi 4.12. Unus est legislator, nempè Deus? Respondet Lous. Quod de uno legislatore dicitur id de legislatore primario est intelligendum: aliter, legislatores secundarios esse nemo inficiabitur, nisi qui ipsum magistratum sustulerit. Respondeo, eandem esse hanc distinctionem de legislatore primario & secundario quae illa Bellarmini & Stapletoni est, de capite & fundamento ecclesiae primario & secundario. Num magistratum quaeso tollunt scriptores nostri qui distinctionem hanc exhibilant? Manere potest in negotijs suis legislator magistratus, ut Deus interim in negotijs Iehovae, 2. Chron.19.11 legislator solus agnoscatur. Atque cum blasphemare papistas dicunt nostri, cum papam secundarium quasi caput sub Christo substituant: ita parum a blasphemia absunt Hierarchici, cum sub Christo primario legislatore, praelatos Ecclesiae quasi legislatores supponunt secundarios: in negotijs politeias illius, quae quidè essentialia sunt. Sed cautior forte Matheus Sutclivius, inter quem & Lounm, ista notabilis contradictio est. Primarium siquidem legislatorem agnoscit Christum Lous, in politeia ecclesiae suae constituenda, quem nec regem omnino, nec legislatorem Matheus Sutclivius ferre potest. Ita enim habet. In isto homine personato (adversarium intelligit, contra quem scribit) quis ferret Christum Redemptorem, in novum, in rebus externis legislatorem converti? Rursus, Christus leges nullas Ecclesiasticas tulit. Iterum, Ego nulla ratione Christum externae ecclesiae politeiae legislatorem dici posse demonstrato. Postremò. Christus quoad externam ecclesiae politeiam dicendus non est rex & legislator. Miraris haec tam falsa iuxta ac impia tanto Theologo excidisse? Non habent extrema pudorem. Non ex sensu suo sobriè scripsit ista Sutclivius, sed studio contradicendi abreptus, suasque partes defendendi: quod vel hinc constat, quod contra Bellarminu disputans, ut imminueret potestatem papae quam illi attribuit in legibus ferendis, contrarium prorsus ponit. Sic enim scribit. Sicut unus legislator, ita una essentialis ecclesiæ gubernatio, reipublicæ verò forma varia. Rursus. Nullæ ecclesiæ gubernationis leges, certæ & immutabiles nisi à Christo: nam is ecclesiæ legislator est, isque solus.
units.tr: 8 Our seventh argument is derived from the office of the prince and head of the Church, Jesus Christ. Is it not the king's task to enact laws by which his kingdom may be best governed? What else does that saying of Isaiah (9.7) mean, that Christ establishes his kingdom with justice and judgement? What else does Paul's saying (1 Cor. 12.4) mean, that Christ as Lord instituted administrations for ruling his Church? And what else does James's saying (4.12) mean: "There is one lawgiver, namely God"? Lous replies: What is said of one lawgiver must be understood of the primary lawgiver. Otherwise no one will deny that there are secondary lawgivers, unless he would abolish the magistracy itself. I answer that this distinction between a primary and a secondary lawgiver is the same as that of Bellarmine and Stapleton between a primary and a secondary head and foundation of the Church. I ask, do our writers who set out this distinction abolish the magistracy? The magistrate may remain a lawgiver in his own affairs, just as God is still acknowledged as the sole lawgiver in the affairs of Jehovah (2 Chron. 19.11). And just as our people say the Papists blaspheme when they set up a secondary pope, as it were a head under Christ, so the Hierarchists are scarcely free from blasphemy when, under Christ the primary lawgiver, they posit the prelates of the Church as secondary lawgivers, in matters of its polity, which are indeed essential. But Matthew Sutcliffe is perhaps more cautious, and between him and Lous there is a notable contradiction. For Lous acknowledges Christ as the primary lawgiver in constituting the polity of his Church, whereas Matthew Sutcliffe cannot bear Christ as king or lawgiver at all. For he says: In that masked man (he means the adversary against whom he writes), who would bear that Christ the Redeemer has been turned into a lawgiver in external matters? Again: Christ enacted no ecclesiastical laws. Again: I show that by no reasoning can Christ be called the lawgiver of the external polity of the Church. Lastly: Christ, as regards the external polity of the Church, is not to be called king and lawgiver. Are you surprised that such false and impious statements fell from so great a theologian? They have no shame. Sutcliffe did not write these things soberly from his own judgement, but was carried away by the urge to contradict and to defend his own side.
