This is clear even from this: when disputing against Bellarmine, in order to diminish the power the pope claims in enacting laws, he puts forward the exact opposite. For he writes: As there is one lawgiver, so there is one essential government of the Church, but the form of the commonwealth is various. And again: There are no laws of church government that are certain and unchangeable except those from Christ, for he is the lawgiver of the Church, and he alone.

units.la: 9 Argumentum nostrum octavum, à materia essentialium illorum ducitur, quæ perfectè a Christo in verbo suo instituta asseveramus: quæ à D. Theodoro Beza ita posita sunt. Ecclesiastica inquit administrationis essentialia, duabus præcipue in rebus, posita sunt: nempè in ipsis perpetuis muneribus sacris, & in eorundem accurata & distincta descriptione, ad quam eorum usus est referendus. Ad hoc respondens Hadrianus Saravia ea præclara esse testatur, & nihil contra suam sententiam tacere. Nec mirum. Nam cum Apostolus hanc vocationem suam licitam probet, quod non ab hominibus sed à Deo ipsius Apostolatus esset. Gal. 1.1. hoc supponit pro fundamento, omnes licitas vocationes à Deo esse, quæ verò ab hominibus sunt, & aliunde instituuntur eas esse illicitas. Notum hoc ipsis Pharisæis & Scribis: illicitum etenim ministerium Iohannis hinc probant quod authoritatem in verbo Dei nullam haberet: atque Iohannes, supponens eos verum præsumsisse, in verbo fundari ministerium suum docet Ioh. 1: 23. Falsò ratiocinati sunt Scribæ & Pharisei, dicit Whitgiftus: & nos ex responso Iohannis inconsequenter arguimus, respondet Remonstrator: sed rationem nullam adferunt, sicut nec adferre possunt. Quæ etenim ratio deprimere illa Christi poterit. Math. 21.25. in quibus supponens ministerium quodvis illicitum esse quod est ab hominibus institutum: ministerium Iohannis idcirco licitum docet, quod esset à cælo, id est, à Deo, in suo verbo stabilitum. Hinc pertinent illa Pauli Heb.5.5. Nemo (ne ipse Christus quidem Filius Dei) honorem sibi in ecclesia sumit, nisi qui vocatus est, ut Aaron: fuit autem ministerium Aaronis in verbo constitutum. Deridet hanc rationem nostram in tractatu suo de disciplina Matheus Sutclivius: adversus verò Bellarminum disputans pro more suo approbat. Sic enim scribit. Imò nec Christus Iesus, licet Filius Dei pontificatum suum assumpsit nisi missus: nec ecclesiæ administrationem suscepit, nisi à patre Ecclesiæ præpositus. Quod si ergo nec Christus Iesus sine patris mandato suum assumsit pontificatum: temerè faciunt qui ecclesiæ pontificatum generalem assumunt sine mandato. In ecclesia enim Dei nemo sibi honorem sumit, nisi qui missus est quemadmodum Aaron: Proferant ergo pontifices Romani mandatum Domini: ostendant missionem suam: doceant se à Domino ecclesiæ universali præpositos. Quid cessant? quid tacent? cur tergi versantur? Eodè in capite post. Refellitur inquit pontificum Romanorum principatus, quia non est ex Christi institutione. Postremò, ideo pontificium authoritatem illicitam probat, quia dici illi potest ex Roberto Gallo. Quis posuit idolum hoc in sede mea, ut imperaret gregi meo? & ad illum accommodari possit Tertullianum illud. Qui estis? quomodo & unde venistis? quid in meo agitis non meis? Quin & noster hac quidem in re Remonstrator est. Non negamus, inquit, quin omnes legitimæ vocationes authoritatem habeant ex verbo Dei, est etsi non totidem verbis. Quod vero dicit non totidem verbis, id hujus sententiae mentem non mutat. Sic est alibi. Directa authoritas, vel immediata est ex ipsi Dei voce, vel mediata per directam consequentiam ex verbo collecta: sic omnis vocatio ex verbo deducibilis est.
units.tr: 9 Our eighth argument is derived from the matter of those essentials, which we maintain were perfectly instituted by Christ in his Word, and which have been set down by the venerable Theodore Beza in these words: The essentials of ecclesiastical administration, he says, rest chiefly on two things: namely, on the perpetual sacred offices themselves, and on the careful and distinct description of them, to which their use is to be referred. In reply, Hadrian Saravia testifies that these are excellent points and that he passes over nothing contrary to his own opinion. This is no surprise. For when the Apostle proves that his calling is lawful, because his apostleship was from God and not from men (Gal. 1.1), he assumes as a foundation that all lawful callings are from God, and that those which are from men and instituted otherwise are unlawful. The Pharisees and scribes knew this well: they argued that John's ministry was unlawful because it had no authority in the Word of God. And John, assuming that they had rightly presumed this, teaches that his ministry is grounded in the Word (John 1.23). The scribes and Pharisees reasoned falsely, says Whitgift; and from John's answer we argue inconsequentially, replies the Remonstrant. But they bring forward no reasoning, nor can they. What reasoning could overturn that of Christ (Matt. 21.25)? There, assuming that any ministry is unlawful which is instituted by men, he teaches that John's ministry was therefore lawful, because it was from heaven, that is, from God, established in his Word. To this belong Paul's words (Heb. 5.4): No one (not even Christ himself, the Son of God) takes honour to himself in the Church, unless he is called, as Aaron was. Aaron's ministry was established in the Word. Matthew Sutcliffe mocks this argument of ours in his treatise on discipline, but when disputing against Bellarmine he approves it in his own manner. For he writes thus: Indeed, neither did Christ Jesus, although the Son of God, assume his priesthood unless he was sent, nor did he undertake the administration of the Church unless he was set over it by the Father of the Church. If therefore Christ Jesus did not assume his priesthood without the Father's command, those who assume the general priesthood of the Church without a command act rashly. For in the Church of God no one takes honour to himself, unless he is sent as Aaron was. Let the Roman pontiffs therefore produce the Lord's command; let them show their mission; let them teach that they have been set over the universal Church by the Lord. Why do they hesitate? Why are they silent? Why do they turn their backs? In the same chapter, afterwards: The principate of the Roman pontiffs, he says, is refuted, because it is not from the institution of Christ. Lastly: He proves the pontifical authority to be unlawful because it may be said to them, in the words of Robert Gallus: "Who set this idol in my seat, to rule my flock?" and that saying of Tertullian may be applied to them: "Who are you? How and whence did you come? What are you doing in my domain, which is not yours?" Indeed our own Remonstrant is on this point of the same mind: We do not deny, he says, that all lawful callings have their authority from the Word of God, though not in so many words. That he says "not in so many words" does not change the sense of his view. He says elsewhere: A direct authority, or an immediate one, is from the very voice of God, or a mediate one, derived by direct consequence from the collected Word. Thus every calling can be deduced from the Word.

units.la: 10 Argumentum nostrum nonum à regiminis ecclesiastici fine vsq; ducitur. Eiusdem etenim est & finem & media ad finem constituere: sicut finem regiminis praecisè in verbo Christus sanxerit, & politeiam etiam ecclesiae quae est eiusdem finis medium, ut sanxerit, censendus est. Finis vero politeias, ecclesiae salus atque aedificatio est: & quis putarit, absque certis mediis omnibus, eisque certò constitutis, ecclesiam orbam Christum Iesum reliquisse? Quid quod politeia, vti cetera media omnia, non nisi gratiarum suppeditatione, & caelesti benedictione ad finem suum valent? Gratiam suppeditare alicui officio ecclesiastico, homo non potest: ergo nec officium aliquod constituere. Certè pro varietate gratiarum, varietatem administrationum in verbo constitutam videamus: & officia Ecclesiastica ipsa, dona sunt Eph.4.12.1. Cor. 12, 5. Rom.12. 5.6: sic ut de Christi & potentia & liberalitate derogetur plurimum, si penes hominem sit, ac non penes Christum solum eadem constituere. Quod ad benedictionem vero, uti cum benedixit Moses tabernaculo, quando omnia structa vidisset iuxta formam illam quae ei in monte ostensa est, Exod:39.43. ita tum & non aliter benedicit regimini Ecclesiastico Christus, quando omnia ad amussim verbi sui compos ita & ordinata videt. Nulla ab illo aurora expectanda quando verbum illius non asseritur Is: 8: 20. imo humanis inventis adeò non favet, ut minetur eis, qui ambulant in flamma ignis sui, & in scintillis, quas sibimetipsis succenderint. E manu mea accidet hoc vobis: in dolore iacebitis. Isa.50.11. Quid opus est multis? opus habent stellae ecclesiarum ut ut Christi manu teneantur & protegatur, Ap.1.16. nonne igitur opus est, ut omnes ab ipsius manu fabricentur? Stellae certè erraticae sunt Iud.13. officia quaecunq; ecclesiastica, quae non opera manus Christi, sed opera manuum humanarum sunt. An rarum in scripturis humana inventa condemnata audire, vel hoc solo nomine. Opera sunt manuum tuarum? Psa.135,15. Isa.28. 317. & 37. 19. Ier. 16.&c.
units.tr: 10 Our ninth argument is drawn from the end of ecclesiastical government. For it belongs to the same authority to set both the end and the means to the end. Just as Christ has sanctioned the end of government precisely in his Word, so the polity of the Church, which is a means to that same end, must be judged to have been sanctioned by him as well. But the end of the polity is the salvation and edification of the Church, and who would think that Christ Jesus left the Church bereft, without all the means, and those means certainly fixed? Moreover, like all other means, the polity attains its end only through the supply of grace and heavenly blessing. A man cannot supply grace to any ecclesiastical office, and therefore cannot appoint any office. Let us certainly see the variety of administrations established in the Word in accordance with the variety of graces, and the ecclesiastical offices themselves are gifts (Eph. 4.12; 1 Cor. 12.5; Rom. 12.5–6). So it would greatly detract from the power and the generosity of Christ if the same things were established by man rather than by Christ alone. As for blessing, just as Moses blessed the tabernacle when he had seen everything built according to the pattern shown him on the mountain (Exod. 39.43), so Christ in the same way and no otherwise blesses ecclesiastical government when he sees everything ordered exactly according to his Word. No dawn is to be expected from him when his Word is not upheld (Isa. 8.20). Indeed he so little favours human inventions that he threatens those who walk in the flame of their own fire, and in the sparks which they themselves have kindled. This shall come to you from my hand: you shall lie down in sorrow (Isa. 50.11). Why say more? The stars of the Churches need to be held and protected in the hand of Christ (Rev. 1.16); is it not therefore necessary that all of them be made by his hand? Certainly every ecclesiastical office that is not the work of Christ's hand but the work of human hands is a wandering star (Jude 13). Is it rare in the Scriptures to hear human inventions condemned on this ground alone? They are the works of your hands (Ps. 135.15; Isa. 28.17 and 37.19; Jer. 16, etc.).

units.la: 11. Argumentum nostrum decimum ab officio nostro ducitur, fide nempè & obedientiâ erga disciplinam. Quae etenim fides absq; verbo Rom.10. 17. quae obedientia nisi mandato? Respondet Remonstrator, fidem & obedientiam erga politeiam ecclesiasticam esse posse perinde ac civilem, etsi certa illius forma in verbo Dei non prescribitur: respectu nempè principiorum illorum generalium, quae in scriptura de eadem reperiuntur. At primò, res supernaturalis cum politeia ecclesiastica sit, quo nomine à civili distat: speciatim in verbo nisi prescribatur, languet erga eandem obedientia, vacillat fides. Secundò, fac generalibus principiis tantum politeias ecclesiasticae fidem dari, obedientiam praestari posse: & arctiori tamen vinculo ligamur nos ad uramutramque, si non generaliter,sed speciatim in verbo mandetur: quod à Christo præstermissum fuisse verisimile non est: Ratio apud Richardum Hookerum extat,in nostra persona,ab illo,ita posita. Quamdiu persuadentur homines de ordine aliquo, quòd ab hominibus solis fit, de prudentia sua præsumunt, putantque non mode parem sed meliorem etiam sese adinvenire posse. Inde est,quod institutà humana tam promptam & alacrem obedientiam elicere nequeant: atque ea est,quando ad Deum confientia respicit, quasi ad illius ordinis authorem. Hoc illud fuit quod Mosis leges de Politeia Ecclesiastica commendavit, cui simile quiddam à Paganis legislatoribus nonnulli prætendebant: falso quidem, prudenter tamen vim hujusce persuasionis discernentes. Itaque ad majorem obedientiam expediens erat, ut Deus ipse Politeias ecclesiasticæ author esset. Huic vero nihil respondet Hookerus: quia frivola? fiat judicium ex consequentibus. Ex dogmate nostro certa quædam ubique τυπῶς & in disciplina perinde ac in doctrina pax & unitas conservatur: ex dogmate vero Hierarchico Anabaptisticis confusionibus via aperitur, mutationibus politicis fenestra aperitur: funestis denique ecclesiarum dilacerationibus causa præbetur, sicut in Anglia hodie apparet. Rursus ex dogmate nostro consolatio cuique politeias administrato suppeditatur, ut qui jam cum Ieremia dicere possit: Non me intrusi coram te: ex dogmate vero Hierarchico conscientiæ confusio,qualis illa fuit sacerdotum Ieroboami: cum consciï effent se proprias implevisse manus,& absque ulla vocatione diivinâ semetipsos confecrasse. Postremò ex dogmate nostro proficiscitur ergo politeias administros reverentia, cum plebi quotidie ob oculos versabitur, Qui vos spernit me spernit. Murmuratio vestra non est adversus nos,sed adversus Iehovam: ex dogmate vero Hierarchico contemptus,qualis in Malachia denunciatur: nam sordida semper in domo Dei institutio humana visa est. 11 Argumentum nostrum undecimum & ultimum à testimonio sanctorum sumitur,qui in ecclesia quoque seculo floruerunt. Ita Cyprianus. Legat hoc unum verbum & in hoc mandato meditetur Christiane religio & invenient ex hac scriptura omnium doctrinarum regulas emanasse,& hinc nasci & huc reverti, quicquid ecclesiastica continet disciplina,& in omnibus veritum esse & sibi quicquid dilectio non confirmat. Responderet det Remonstrator. Per disciplinam intelligi hic doctrinam quemadmodum verbis paulo antecedentibus f. 8. Non me latet te docente ad sacandas corruptionem mearum putredines prodesse—sit disciplinæ tuæ Evangelio tuo mediante infusum. Hinc insultat Demonstratori,tanquam lectori Cypriani inepto aut collectionem aliorum sequenti, ne lecto quidem à sese Cypriano. Sed inepti simus Cypriani lectorem ipse Remonstrator est,id quod proximè antecedentia verba demonstrant. Loquere magister bene libenter te audio & cum adversariis mihi: etiam in plagis & doloribus intelligo disciplinam: nec me latet, &c. Quid igitur est? Per sal disciplinam hæc non (quod ille ineptissime somniat) intelligit doctrinam. nam Cyprianus, sed disciplinam correctionis. In testimonio vero nostro perspiciet quivis, doctrinarum regulam & disciplinam ecclesiasticam, quasi res diversas seiunctim poni, & utramque ex aequo a scriptura derivari. Sic & alibi in negotiis disciplinae ad scripturam a Cypriano revocamur. Hinc fit ii nata & disciplinae violationes nascuntur: dum ad veritatis originem non creditur, nec caput quaeritur, nec magistri caelestis doctrina servatur. Innuunt ista doctrinam de disciplina tractatam esse, scripturam disciplinae caput esse, ut errata in disciplina corrigantur. Quid quod doctrinam de disciplina eam speciatim nominat, quae episcopatus Anglicani nervos exsecat? Dicit enim in uno loco unam cathedram post pastoribus omnibus aequalem attributam esse, sicut testatur Ri. Fyldus, & Guil. Whitakerus qui in hunc sensum Cyprianum interpretantur. Citatur a Demonstratore testimonium istud Tertulliani. Nobis nihil ex nostro arbitrio inducere licet: sed nec eligere quod aliquis arbitrio suo induxerit: Apostolos Domini habeamus authores qui nec ipsi quicquam a suo arbitrio quod inducerent elegerunt, sed acceptam a Christo disciplinam fideliter nationibus assignarunt. Non autem puto Demonstratorem existimasse disciplinam ecclesiasticam hic specialiter nominatam fuisse, quo nomine immerito apud Remonstratorem vapulat: sed sermonis Tertulliani generalitate innixum fuisse: qua nihil de nostro abitrio in disciplina eligendum dicit, sive doctrinam contineat illa, sive ecclesiae disciplinam. Ita Augustinus. Sive de Christo, sive de ecclesia, sive de quacunque alia re quae pertinet ad fidem vitamque nostram, non dico si nos sed si Angelus de caelo vobis annuntiaverit praeterquam quod in scripturis legalibus & Evangelicis accepistis, anathema sit. Johannes Reynoldus dum hanc sententiam Augustini adversus Hartum urget, insistit in eo praecipue, quod non dicat contra quam, sed praeterquam, ut non solum quae contra verbum illicita Augustinus sentiat, sed etiam quae vel praeter scripturam fiunt. Non igitur solum (quod vult Hookerus) quae in politeia ecclesiastica contra Dei verbum sunt, Pauli & Augustini judicio prohibentur, sed etiam quae praeter verbum geruntur: nam cum ecclesiam Augustinus speciatim nominet, vitamque nostram: quis putarit ecclesiae disciplinam quae ad mores dirigendos est destinata, eum excepisse? Sequitur Damasus, quem citat & approbat Richardus Fyldus, qui Chorepiscopos ideo extirpandos confirmat, quod in verbo, eorum ordo authoritatem nullam habeat. Qui ita arguit, nomine omnia officia ecclesiastica etiam regent a in verbo ita posita putat ut alia inducere illicitum sit, praeterquam ea quae in verbo sanciuntur? Verba sunt: eorum institutio omni authoritate caret, ipsi sunt qui & presbyteri. Non amplius quam duos ordines inter discipulos Domini esse cognovimus id est duodecim Apostolorum, & septuaginta discipulorum: unde iste tertius processerit penitus ignoramus. Et quod ratione caret extirpari necesse est. Referuntur in ius Canonicum ista: in quibus ut quaedam erroris sunt proxima, hoc tamen sanum est: quod necesse putetur ut officia omnia ecclesiastica extirpentur, quae carent authoritate ritate & ratione ex scripturis.
units.tr: 11. Our tenth argument is drawn from our duty, namely faith and obedience towards discipline. For what faith is there without the word (Rom. 10.17), and what obedience without a command? The Remonstrant replies that faith and obedience towards the ecclesiastical polity can exist just as they do towards the civil polity, even though its particular form is not prescribed in the word of God, but only with respect to those general principles which Scripture contains about it. But first, since the ecclesiastical polity is supernatural, it differs from the civil in this respect: unless it is prescribed particularly in the word, obedience towards it grows weak and faith wavers. Second, suppose that faith and obedience can be given to an ecclesiastical polity by general principles alone; we are nonetheless bound to both by a tighter bond if they are commanded in the word not generally but particularly. It is not likely that Christ passed this over. Richard Hooker gives the reasoning, put in our person by him as follows: As long as men are persuaded of some order that is made by men alone, they presume upon their own wisdom, and think that they can devise not only an equal but a better one. Hence it is that they cannot elicit so prompt and willing an obedience to human institutions; and that obedience is found when the conscience looks to God as the author of that order. This is what commended Moses' laws concerning the ecclesiastical polity, and something similar was claimed by some pagan lawgivers: falsely indeed, yet they rightly discerned the force of this persuasion. Thus it was fitting for greater obedience that God himself should be the author of the ecclesiastical polity. Hooker makes no reply to this; he calls it trivial. Let judgment be made from the consequences. By our doctrine a certain order is preserved everywhere in a fixed pattern [τυπῶς], and peace and unity in discipline just as in doctrine. By the hierarchical doctrine, however, a way is opened to Anabaptist confusions, a window is opened to political changes, and finally cause is given for the deadly tearing of the churches, as appears today in England. Again, by our doctrine comfort is supplied to each man who administers the polity, so that he can now say with Jeremiah: I have not thrust myself in before you. By the hierarchical doctrine there is confusion of conscience, such as that of the priests of Jeroboam, who, being aware that they had filled their own hands and consecrated themselves without any divine calling. Lastly, from our doctrine there proceeds reverence for the administrators of the polity, since the people will daily have before their eyes: He who despises you despises me. Your murmuring is not against us but against Jehovah. By the hierarchical doctrine there is contempt, such as is announced in Malachi; for human institution has always seemed sordid in the house of God. 11. Our eleventh and last argument is taken from the testimony of the saints who also flourished in the Church in the ages. Thus Cyprian: Let the Christian religion read this one word and meditate on this command, and they will find that the rules of all doctrines have sprung from this Scripture, and that whatever ecclesiastical discipline contains arises from it and returns to it, and that everything is to be feared which love does not confirm. Let the Remonstrant reply. Here discipline is understood as doctrine, as in the words a little before, f. 8: "I am not unaware that, under your teaching, it profits to cure the putrefactions of my corruptions... may your discipline be infused through your Gospel." Hence he mocks the Demonstrator as an inept reader of Cyprian, or as one following another's collection, without even having read Cyprian himself. But the inept reader of Cyprian is the Remonstrant himself, as the words immediately preceding demonstrate: Speak, master, I gladly hear you, and with my adversaries too; even in blows and pains I understand discipline; nor am I unaware, etc. What then is it? By discipline here he does not understand doctrine (as that man most ineptly dreams), but the discipline of correction. In our testimony anyone will see that the rule of doctrine and ecclesiastical discipline are set down as separate things, as if distinct, and that both are derived equally from Scripture. So too elsewhere we are recalled by Cyprian to Scripture in matters of discipline: Hence come the violations of discipline that arise, while men do not believe in the origin of truth, do not seek its head, and do not keep the teaching of the heavenly Master. These words imply that doctrine concerning discipline has been treated, that Scripture is the head of discipline, so that errors in discipline may be corrected. What of the fact that he names specifically as doctrine of discipline that which cuts the sinews of the English episcopate? For he says that in one place one chair was assigned, equal for all the ministers after the apostles, as Richard Fulke testifies, and William Whitaker, who interpret Cyprian in this sense. The Demonstrator cites this testimony of Tertullian: We may bring in nothing by our own choice, nor choose what anyone has introduced by his own choice. Let us have the Lord's apostles as authors, who did not themselves choose anything of their own will to introduce, but faithfully handed on to the nations the discipline received from Christ. I do not think, however, that the Demonstrator supposed that ecclesiastical discipline was specially named here, for which he is undeservedly beaten by the Remonstrant; rather he relied on the generality of Tertullian's words, in which he says that nothing is to be chosen from our own judgment in discipline, whether that discipline contains doctrine or the discipline of the Church. Thus Augustine: Whether concerning Christ, or concerning the Church, or concerning any other matter which pertains to our faith and life, I do not say if we, but if an angel from heaven should announce to you anything other than what you have received in the legal and Evangelical Scriptures, let him be anathema. John Reynolds, when he presses this sentence of Augustine against Hart, insists chiefly on the fact that it does not say contrary to which but other than which, so that Augustine judges not only what is unlawful as contrary to the word, but also what is done apart from Scripture. Therefore it is not only (as Hooker wishes) what is against God's word in the ecclesiastical polity that is forbidden by the judgment of Paul and Augustine, but also what is done beside the word. For since Augustine names the Church specifically, and our life: who would think that the discipline of the Church, which is designed to direct morals, was excepted? Damasus follows, whom Richard Fulke cites and approves, who confirms that country bishops (chorepiscopi) must be rooted out because their order has no authority in the word. Does he who argues thus think that all ecclesiastical offices, even those regulated by name, have been so set down in the word that it is unlawful to introduce any besides those which the word sanctions? The words are: "Their institution lacks all authority; they are the ones who are also presbyters. We know that there were no more than two orders among the disciples of the Lord, that is, of the twelve apostles and the seventy disciples; whence this third arose we are utterly ignorant. And what lacks reason must necessarily be rooted out." These things are cited into the canon law; and although some of them border on error, this much is sound: that it is thought necessary that all ecclesiastical offices which lack authority and reason from the Scriptures be rooted out.

units.la: Hoc si effectum datum in Anglia, vbi quęso Episcopi Anglicani futuri essent: qui per scripturas ijdem cum presbyteris sunt (ut de Chorepiscopis loquitur Damasus & jus Canonicum) & omni ex sacris desumpta ratione carent. Ita Nazianzenus. Nemo sapiat supra quam oportet sapere, nevè lege justior, luce splendidior, canone rectior, praecepto officiosior videri velit? Loquitur ita de disciplina Ecclesiastica Nazianzenus, sicut ipse Thomas Bilsonus attestatur: qui haec adfert, nè in controversijs disciplinaris quisquam nostrum, vlla zeli religionisve specie, vltra praeceptum, legem, canonem verbi divini nosmet abripi patiamur. Qui ita loquuntur, nonne legem in verbo Dei, nonne praeceptum, nonne Canonem, nonne lucem, de disciplina ecclesiastica, tradita esse confitentur? Ita Chrysostomus. Qui non utitur sacra scriptura sed ascendit aliunde, id est, non concessa via, hic non pastor est, sed fur & latro. Impugnat primum Papae hoc testimonio Iohanues Iuellus, eo quod a Christo in verbo suo non instituatur. Sed ratio haec nonne & Episcopos Anglicanos & quodvis praeterea officium ecclesiasticum ex Ecclesia exturbat, quod in Dei verbo perinde ac papatus ipse non instituitur? Ita Leo. Exortes sunt mysterij divini qui a Petri soliditate recesserunt. Rursus. Petri forma cunctis ecclesiae Rectoribus proposita est. Erravit quidem in hypothesi huius formę Leo: quod tamen exemplar Apostolicae disciplinae ligare, & formam quandam disciplinae ab eisdem propositam innuit, in eo quidem certè sapit, vel Matheo Sutclivio assentiente: qui hinc pontificis primatum iugulat, quod a Petri soliditate recesserit, imò a forma illius quam longissimè recesserit: id quod de Anglicano Episcopatu, & omni alio ecclesiastico officio ab hominibus introducto verissimè aptissimeq; dicitur. Ita Iohannes Gerson. [Nulla potest lingua satis exprimere, quantum malū, quantum periculum, quantam confusionem, sacrae scripturae contemptus (quae proculdubio sufficiens est, pro ecclesiae gubernatione, alias Christus imperfectus legislator esset) & humanorum inventorum affectatio in ecclesiam invexit. Ad huius rei evidentiam consideretur cleri status, cui sapientia cœlestis dispensari debuit: sed cum meretricē illa, sapientia humana adulterium commiserunt illi: sic ut status ecclesiae merè bestialis & monstrosus evaserit: infra cœlum, supra vero terra, subest spiritus, dominatur caro &c. non erubescunt tamen quidam dicere, humanis inventionibus melius ecclesiam gubernari, quam lege divina, & lege Evangelij Christi, quae assertio blasphema est. Evangelica etenim doctrina, ecclesiae terminos dilatavit, & ad coelum sublimavit: quam Hagarae filij sapientiam illam quaerentes, quae de terra est, ad sterquilinium usque dejecerunt.] Citat ista & approbat Richardus Fyldus Hierarchicus: quae & sententiam nostram de certa disciplinae forma in verbo Dei perfectè tradita manifestè confirmant: & politeiam Anglicanam iugulant, imò miseriam quę & humanam sapientiam in disciplina ecclesiastica, deformantem sequi solet;& in regnum Anglicanum per Hierarchiam Episcopalem humanam jam (pro dolor) invecta est, adeo graphicè depingunt, ut nihil supra. Alibi de negotijs disciplinarijs loquens adversus papam, ita habet. Superest ut aliqua sit relicta inobliquabilis & indeviabilis regula ab optimo legislatore Christo, secundum quam possit abusus huiusmodi potestatis reprimi, dirigi, atque moderari. Haec autem regula est ecclesia & generale concilium. In hac Hadrianus Saravia ità. Rectè à Gersone notatum suit ab optimo legislatore Christo in ecclesiam regulam inobliqualem relictam esse: sed sacræ scripturæ sint illa regula &c. In hac sententia fuerunt ij qui Petro Ahaco attestante, in concilio Constantiensi, & longè ante ordinem Cardinalium tollendum putarunt, quod nec a Christo, nec ab Apostolis institutus esset, sicut olim de statu Corepiscoporum factum erat. Citatur a D. Mornæo & approbatur Bucæus, cuius ista de certa disciplinæ forma in verbo tradita, sententia est. Navis nobis disciplinæ socialis ac civilis à servatore relicta est ecclesiæ conditore, quæ continuo ministerio, instrumento gubernaculo instructa fuit ab ipso, aut eius auspicijs. Statim etiam à puppi pollicitus est, ad exoptatam loci rectores perlaturum, si clavem certam tenere, si nusquam non spiritui afflaturo pandere ecclesiæ porrexisset: (sacras utique scripturas à spiritu sancto profectas contulisset.) Accedant Hierarchici. Thomas Bilsonus ita. Hijs quæ dixi non est consequens ut politeiam ecclesiasticam, quam nubisunque libeat, ex ingenio nostro fingamus, quin potius dant ea est opera ut externam administrationem in ecclesia regenda eam observemus quam Dominus noster ipse docuit. Quem verò etiam in externa forma ecclesiæ gubernandæ Dominus ab initio sanxit, obscurum esse non poterit, si sacras literas consulamus. Ita Richardus Bancroftus. Conclusio mea ædificatur, supra unam de Demonstrativis propositionibus Iohannis Valli. Illud regimen ecclesiæ cuius origo ignota est nullam habet authoritatē à verbo Dei sed illicitum est. Postremè ita Hadrianus Saravia. Non ignoramus ab Apostolis perfectam ecclesiæ formam traditam: & quid sit de hac re nostra sententia, jam diximus. Unde nos intulimus & consequens esse diximus ut illa omnia manēs in ecclesia, per quæ ædificatur nēpè verbi Dei prædicatio, sacramentorum administratio, cum ea regiminis forma quæ fuit ab initio sub Apostolis, nec ostenditur vel mutata, vel inhibita posteris. His omnibus argumentis, constat unam quandam certam regiminis Ecclesiastici formam à Christo, in verbo, traditam & institutam esse.
units.tr: If this were put into effect in England, where, I ask, would the Anglican bishops be? By the testimony of Scripture they are the same as presbyters (as Damasus and the canon law say of the chorepiscopi), and they have no basis in anything taken from the sacred writings. So Nazianzen: Let no one think more highly than he ought to think, nor wish to be seen as more just than the law, brighter than the light, more upright than the canon, or more dutiful than the precept. Nazianzen speaks in this way about church discipline, as Thomas Bilson himself attests. Bilson quotes him, so that none of us in disputes about discipline should allow himself to be carried away, under any appearance of zeal or religion, beyond the precept, the law, or the canon of the divine Word. Do not those who speak in this way concede that the law, the precept, and the canon of church discipline are delivered in the Word of God, and that this is the light? So Chrysostom: He who does not use Holy Scripture but climbs up some other way, that is, by a route not granted, is not a minister but a thief and a robber. John Jewel first attacks the Pope with this testimony, on the ground that the papacy is not instituted by Christ in his Word. But does not the same argument also cast out of the Church the Anglican bishops and every other ecclesiastical office, since they too are not instituted in the Word of God, just as the papacy itself is not? So Leo: They are cut off from the divine mystery who have departed from the firmness of Peter. And again: The pattern of Peter is set before all the rulers of the Church. Leo was indeed mistaken in his hypothesis about this pattern; yet in insisting that the example of apostolic discipline binds us, and in implying a certain form of discipline set forth by the apostles, he is surely right, with Matthew Sutcliffe agreeing. Sutcliffe uses this to overthrow the primacy of the pontiff: that he has departed from the firmness of Peter, indeed has departed as far as possible from his form. What is said here of the papacy is most truly and most aptly said of the Anglican episcopate and of every other ecclesiastical office introduced by men. So John Gerson: [No language can adequately express how much evil, how much danger, how much confusion the contempt of Holy Scripture (which is without doubt sufficient for the government of the Church; otherwise Christ would have been an imperfect lawgiver) and the pursuit of human inventions have brought into the Church. To see the evidence of this, let us consider the state of the clergy, to whom heavenly wisdom ought to have been dispensed; but when they committed adultery with that harlot, human wisdom, the condition of the Church became purely bestial and monstrous: below heaven, but above the earth, the spirit lies under, the flesh rules, and so on. Yet some are not ashamed to say that the Church is governed better by human inventions than by the divine law and the law of the Gospel of Christ, which assertion is blasphemous. For evangelical doctrine has enlarged the bounds of the Church and raised it up to heaven; those who sought that wisdom of the sons of Hagar, which is of the earth, have cast it down even to the dunghill.] Richard Field, in his book Of the Church, cites and approves these words, and they clearly confirm our view that a certain form of discipline has been perfectly delivered in the Word of God, and they overthrow the Anglican polity. Indeed they depict so vividly the misery that usually follows when human wisdom deforms church discipline, and that (alas!) has now been introduced into the English realm through the episcopal hierarchy, that nothing could be more graphic. Speaking elsewhere of disciplinary matters against the Pope, Field says: It remains that some unbending and unerring rule was left by Christ, the best lawgiver, by which the abuse of this kind of power could be restrained, directed, and moderated. This rule, however, is the Church and a general council. On this Adrian Saravia says: Gerson rightly noted that an unbending rule was left by Christ, the best lawgiver, in the Church; but the rule is Holy Scripture, etc. To this opinion belonged those who, as Pierre d'Ailly attests at the Council of Constance, and long before the order of cardinals, thought that it should be abolished, because it had been instituted neither by Christ nor by the apostles, just as the state of the chorepiscopi had once been abolished. Mornay cites and Buceus approves this opinion, whose view of a fixed form of discipline delivered in the Word is as follows: The ship of social and civil discipline has been left to us by the Saviour, the founder of the Church, which he equipped from the start with a continuous ministry, with instruments and a helm, either by himself or under his auspices. He promised, right from the stern, that he would bring it to the desired harbour of its rulers, if he had extended to the Church a sure key to hold, and a means to open it to the Spirit who blows everywhere: (that is, he would have bestowed the sacred Scriptures, which proceed from the Holy Spirit). Let the hierarchists come forward. Thomas Bilson says: It does not follow from what I have said that we should devise for ourselves an ecclesiastical polity as we please, as if from our own wit; rather, we should take care to observe the external administration of the Church, as our Lord himself taught it. And what the Lord from the beginning ordained concerning the external form of governing the Church cannot be obscure, if we consult the sacred letters. So Richard Bancroft. My conclusion is built upon one of the demonstrative propositions of John Vallis: That government of the Church whose origin is unknown has no authority from the Word of God, but is unlawful. Lastly, Adrian Saravia: We do not deny that a perfect form of the Church was handed down by the apostles; and what our view is on this matter we have already said. Hence we have inferred, and said it follows, that all those things by which the Church is built up, namely the preaching of the Word of God and the administration of the sacraments, together with that form of government which existed from the beginning under the apostles, are neither shown to have been changed nor forbidden to posterity. From all these arguments it is established that a certain fixed form of ecclesiastical government was delivered and instituted by Christ in the Word.

units.la: CAP. XLI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLI.

units.la: Argumenta Hierarchica dissolvuntur.
units.tr: The Hierarchical arguments are overthrown.

units.la: SVperest ut adversa Hierarchicorum argumenta dissolvamus. Prima objectio est à circumstantijs Politeias: hoc etenim perpetuum apud Whitgiftum, Hookerum, Sutclivium, reliquosq; Sophisma est: non esse certam Politeias formam in verbo speciatim positam: quia ceremoniæ & ejusdem circumstantiæ speciatim in scripturis non describantur. Primò, insulsum hoc argumentum est? quid enim? Nulla erit Ethices & bonorum operum certa in scripiuris tradita regula, quia operum bonorum circumstantiæ non nisi regulis generalibus diriguntur? Disciplinæ docentis quod ad verbi prædicationem & sacramentorum administrationem, certam formam speciatim in verbo traditam esse confitentur ipsi: cujus tamen circumstantias non nisi generaliter tradi in aperto & confesso est. Postremò certam formam Politeias Ecclesiasticæ à Mose Iudæis in verbo definitam fuisse non inficiantur: in ecclesia tamen Iudæorum concessum est, inquit Hookerus, horum sacrificiorum, Synagogarum ædi-ficationem, pulpitorum & cathedrarum erectionem: id est, circumstantias ejusdem Politeias, Ecclesiæ arbitrio relictas fuisse. Non igitur sequitur sub-stantiam Politeias Ecclesiasticæ in verbo traditam minime jam esse, quia eiusdem circumstantiæ non traduntur. Secundò, statum quæstionis invertunt, idque nobis affingunt, quod ne in mentem venit unquam. Verba Hookeri ista sunt. Distinctio illorum de substantia & circum-stantijs, quamquam vera, eorum proposito non satisfacit: nam sive res maioris momenti sint, sive minoris, si eas Deus in verbo ut perpetuas mandavit: nulla ratio est quæ alterum earum genus, magis altero, mutare liceat. His in verbis impingit nobis Hookerus, ac si circumstantias Politeias perinde ac substantiam, in verbo mandatas in perpetuum existimaremus, quod quisquamnè de nostris affirmavit quæso, imò vel somniavit unquam?
units.tr: It remains for us to dissolve the arguments of the Hierarchicals against us. The first objection is drawn from the circumstances of the polity. This is a fallacy that runs constantly through Whitgift, Hooker, Sutcliffe and the rest: there is no fixed form of polity laid down in the Word, because the ceremonies and their particular circumstances are not described in Scripture. First, is this argument not foolish? For what follows? There would be no fixed rule of ethics and good works delivered in Scripture, because the circumstances of good works are directed only by general rules. They themselves confess that for the teaching of the Word, the preaching of the Word and the administration of the sacraments there is a fixed form laid down in the Word in particular, yet it is openly and admittedly the case that its circumstances are handed down only in general terms. Last, they do not deny that Moses prescribed a fixed form of ecclesiastical polity for the Jews in the Word: yet in the Jewish Church, says Hooker, it was granted that the offering of these sacrifices, the building of synagogues, and the erection of pulpits and chairs, that is, the circumstances of that same polity, were left to the discretion of the Church. It does not follow, therefore, that the substance of the ecclesiastical polity delivered in the Word is by no means now in force, because its circumstances are not handed down. Second, they reverse the state of the question, and attribute to us something that has never even entered our minds. Hooker's words are these: That distinction of theirs between substance and circumstances, though true, does not serve their purpose; for whether the matters be of greater or of lesser importance, if God has commanded them in the Word as perpetual, there is no reason why it should be lawful to change one kind more than the other. In these words Hooker assails us as if we thought that the circumstances of the polity, like its substance, were commanded in the Word for ever. I ask you, did any of our people ever affirm this, or indeed ever even dream of it?

units.la: Tertiò, circa distinctionem hanc de circumstantijs & substantia egregie cavillantur. Eam veram esse agnoscit Hookerus, sed non ita Matheus Sutclivius, qui eam exagitat ut ineptam & imperitam: addit insuper nos quasdam circumstantias perinde atque substantiam perpetuas stabilire. Sed expedita responsio est. Quædam circumstantiæ individuales sunt, & has intelligimus; cum mutabiles & minimè in verbo speciatim delineatas Politeias circumstantias dicimus: Quædam vero circumstantiæ generales sunt, & has non absque causa & speciatim in verbo descriptas, & immutabiles affirmamus: cujusmodi sunt in circumstantia loci, prædicatio verbi, sacramentorum administratio, administrorum electio in loco publico: & in circumstantia temporis, quòd non alio tempore administer aut pastor eligendus sit, quam in locum defuncti, aut quando sedes aliàs vacat.
units.tr: Third, they carp cleverly at this distinction between circumstances and substance. Hooker acknowledges that it is true, but Matthew Sutcliffe does not agree, and attacks it as inept and unskilled; he adds moreover that we establish certain circumstances as perpetual just as we do the substance. But the answer is easy. Some circumstances are individual, and it is these we mean when we call the circumstances of the polity changeable and not particularly outlined in the Word. Other circumstances are general, and these we affirm, not without cause and as particularly described in the Word, to be unchangeable. Such are, in regard to place, the preaching of the Word, the administration of the sacraments, and the choosing of ministers in a public place; and, in regard to time, that a minister is to be chosen at no other time than in the place of one who has died, or when the office is otherwise vacant.

units.la: 2 Objectio Hierarchicorum secunda sequitur, ab Ecclesiæ authoritate desumpta, quæ authoritatem nullam haberet in ferendis legibus de Politeia Ecclesiastica, si modo certa ejusdem forma in verbo descripta haberetur. Ita M. Sutclivius: Si Christus, inquit, legislator externæ Politeiæ esset, legesq; Ecclesiæ tulisset, non magis Ecclesiæ & Syno-do leges scribere & promulgare liceret, quàm populo & subditis sibi leges cōdere præter sui principis & magistratus voluntatē. Ita pagina precedenti: Si quæ in externis rebus Christus mandaverit & Apostoli insserint pro legib. habenda sunt, nulla alia authoritate, nulla legislatione opus esset. Nam si in novo Testamento reperiantur, ut Christi verbum valebunt: ut stultè quis faceret, si novum Testamentum lege confirmaret. Valet enim suo jure multo magis quam humanae ullae leges: & conscientias astringit, quas humanae leges & ab homine latae non ligant. Respondeo primò hoc argumentum papisticum esse, ad scripturae imperfectionem comprobandā, non in causis disciplinae tantùmodo, sed etiam in causis fidei. Quid enim? Annon certa fidei forma in verbo traditur, & tamen in causis fidei Ecclesiae & Synodi adversus haereses cujuscunq; temporis leges tulerunt? Hoc inde fit, inquiunt papistae, quia scriptura in tradenda fidei formâ imperfecta est. Nam in consequentia hujus argumenti cum Sutclivio conspirant, ut in Cornelio Scultingio videre est, qui pari modo argumentatur. Si necesse est quasdam regulas novas quotidie sic casibus exigentibus adjici: cur falsò docent puritani contra Calvinopapistas, ex solis scripturis hauriendam disciplinam esse, easque solas sufficere. Secundò, Perduellis non in Ecclesiam solam, verumetiam in ipsum magistratum Sutclivius est: nam si certa rei forma in verbo descripta omnem legislationem authoritatem abscindit: magistratus in causis fidei authoritatem leges ferendi nullum habet, cum fidei forma perfectè in scriptura traditur, quae suo valore valet. Tertio, argumento huic Sutcliviano, ita respondit Richardus Hookerus: Quanquam frustra esset leges condere, quas scriptura prius condidit, quia in mandatis Dei, nihil reliqui est, quàm ut executioni mandentur: tamen pro eis quae mandantur in scripturis, in officio Ecclesiae est, providere legibus, nè licentia aut segnitie hominum, mandata Dei non adimpleantur. Exempli gratiâ, Nehem. 10.34.35.36. Instituimus nobis praecepta --- ut scriptum est in lege. Instituimus nos allaturos primitias terrae nostrae. Primò patet hinc, in reformatione disciplinae nihil tentandum praeter id quod scriptum est: secundo legislationi locum esse, ubi certa forma disciplinae ante à Deo praescripta est, ut forma ea observetur diligentius & collapsa restituatur.
units.tr: The second objection of the Hierarchicals follows, drawn from the authority of the Church, which would have no authority to enact laws concerning the ecclesiastical polity if a fixed form of it were described in the Word. So Matthew Sutcliffe: If Christ, he says, were the lawgiver of the external polity, and had enacted laws for the Church, it would be no more lawful for the Church and the Synod to write and publish laws than for the people and subjects to make laws for themselves apart from the will of their prince and magistrate. So on the preceding page: If the things Christ has commanded in external matters, and the Apostles have inserted, are to be held as laws, no other authority and no other legislation would be needed. For if they are found in the New Testament, they will have the force of Christ's word; and it would be foolish for anyone to confirm the New Testament by a law. For it has its own right far more than any human laws, and binds consciences, which human laws enacted by man do not bind. I reply, first, that this argument is Papist, aimed at proving Scripture imperfect, not only in matters of discipline but also in matters of faith. For what? Is not a fixed form of faith delivered in the Word, and yet have the Church and the Synods not enacted laws in matters of faith against heresies of every age? This follows, say the Papists, because Scripture is imperfect in delivering the form of faith. For in the consequence of this argument they agree with Sutcliffe, as one may see in Cornelius Schultingius, who argues in the same way: If it is necessary that certain new rules be added every day as cases require, why do the Puritans falsely teach against the Calvino-papists that discipline is to be drawn from Scripture alone, and that Scripture alone is sufficient? Second, Sutcliffe is an enemy not only of the Church but of the magistrate himself. For if a fixed form of a thing described in the Word cuts off all legislative authority, then the magistrate has no authority to enact laws in matters of faith, since the form of faith is delivered perfectly in Scripture, which is valid by its own worth. Third, Richard Hooker answered this argument of Sutcliffe's as follows: Although it would be vain to make laws which Scripture has already made, because in the commandments of God nothing remains but that they be put into execution, nevertheless, for those things which are commanded in Scripture, it is the office of the Church to provide laws, lest through the license or sloth of men the commandments of God go unfulfilled. For example, Nehemiah 10:34, 35, 36: We have ordained for ourselves the ordinances ... as it is written in the law. We have ordained that we would bring the firstfruits of our land. First, it is plain from this that in the reformation of discipline nothing is to be attempted beyond what is written. Second, there is room for legislation where a fixed form of discipline has already been prescribed by God, so that this form may be observed more diligently and restored when it has fallen into ruin.

units.la: 3. Tertia objectio Hierarchicorum, oppositione nititur ea, quae est inter legem & Evangelium, ubi Matheus Sutclivius ita: Qui Christum externae Politeiae Ecclesiae legislatorē esse volunt, illud de novā Christi & persectori legislatione, pontificiorum dogma, longo intervallo revocant: Evangelium novam legem appellant: mori loquendi in scripturis usitato repugnant. Christus nunquam legislator appellatur, imò Mosi legislatori opponitur: & illius dogmata non lex sed verbum dicuntur. Apostoli doctrinam de lege & Evangelio opponunt: legemq; & Evangelium ubiq; opposita esse videas, ut illa opera, hac fidem tantum requirat, quae non in faciendo, sed in credendo tantum versatur. Respondeo primò, non legislationem Christi in externis tantum, sed & in internis & in externis haec argumentatio tollit: quod nonne quaeso blasphemum? Quomodo etenim Christus Ecclesiae rex, si non legislator, erit? Secundò, putidum est, quod de papistici dogmatis revocatione objicit: id quod verba ipsa Calvini Calvini obstendunt, quæ producit ex institut. lib. 2. c. 8. f. 2. Appellat, inquit, Sutclivius pernitiosissimum dogma, Christum tulisse legem Evangelicam. Certè pontificio sensu: quasi Christus Math. 5 non veterem legem exponeret, sed novam eamque perfectiorem de juramentis, homicidio, adulterio, diligendis inimicis induceret, quam illi Evangelicam vocant. Tertiò, non minus putidum est, quæ subinfert de oppositione legis & Evangelij: nam de fœderis differentiâ in hominibus præcipuè justificandis ea omnia intelliguntur. Iam verò quomodo sequitur, nullam in Evangelio legislationem Iesu Christi reperiri: quia conditio fœderis legalis, & fœderis Evangelici in hominibus justificandis, adversa planè & opposita est? Annon Rom. 3. Evangelium lex fidei appellatur? non igitur repugnat naturæ Evangelij ut Christus in eo leges ferat. Respondet Sutclivius: agimus de lege proprie accepta quid quid mandatur aut vetatur? Et quomodo agit de lege Paulus? Cur non improprius illius sensus qui sit exponis? Cum Evangelium, inquit, promissi in Christo gratis nitatur, lex verò in vetando & mandando consistat: qui potest Evangelium dici lex cum nihil vetet aut imperet? At qui non nobiscum jam, sed cum Apostolo litigas, qui Evangelium appellat legem. At non simpliciter legem appellat, sed cum oppositione fidei. Nempe quia fidem mandat fideique fructus, infidelitatem verò ejusdemque fructus vetat quod ni ita sit, dicas nobis rationem cur Evangelicum legem fidei appellarit, aut cur Ioh. 3. 23. fides mandatum esse dicatur.
units.tr: 3. The third objection of the Hierarchicals rests on the opposition that exists between the law and the Gospel, where Matthew Sutcliffe says: Those who want Christ to be the lawgiver of the external polity of the Church recall from a long distance that dogma of the Papists about a new legislation of Christ the perfecter: they call the Gospel a new law, which is contrary to the manner of speaking used in Scripture. Christ is never called a lawgiver; rather he is set against Moses the lawgiver, and his teachings are called not law but word. The Apostles set the doctrine of law against that of Gospel; and you see that law and Gospel are everywhere opposed, in that the one requires works, the other faith only, which lies not in doing but only in believing. I reply, first, that this argument removes the legislation of Christ not only in external but also in internal matters: is this not, I ask you, blasphemous? For how will Christ be King of the Church if he is not lawgiver? Second, it is foul what he objects about the revocation of the Papist dogma; the very words of Calvin show this, which he quotes from the Institutes, book 2, chapter 8, section 2: Sutcliffe, he says, calls it a most pernicious dogma that Christ brought the Gospel law. Certainly in the Papist sense: as if Christ in Matthew 5 were not expounding the old law, but introducing a new and more perfect one concerning oaths, murder, adultery and loving enemies, which they call the Evangelical law. Third, it is no less foul what he adds about the opposition between law and Gospel; for all of that is understood of the difference of covenants, chiefly in the justification of men. Now, how does it follow that no legislation of Jesus Christ is found in the Gospel, just because the condition of the legal covenant and of the Gospel covenant in justifying men is plainly adverse and opposed? Does not Romans 3 call the Gospel the law of faith? It is therefore not contrary to the nature of the Gospel that Christ should enact laws in it. Sutcliffe replies: we are speaking of law properly taken, which is whatever is commanded or forbidden. And how does Paul speak of law? Why not explain the improper sense of it? Since the Gospel, he says, rests freely on the promise in Christ, but law consists in forbidding and commanding, how can the Gospel be called law when it forbids or commands nothing? But you are no longer disputing with us, but with the Apostle, who calls the Gospel law. Yet he does not call it law simply, but with the opposition of faith. Clearly because it commands faith and the fruits of faith, and forbids unbelief and its fruits; for if this were not so, tell us the reason why he called the Evangelical law the law of faith, or why John 3:23 says that faith is called a commandment.

units.la: 4. Quarta objectio Hierarchicorum, à legis moralis consideratione ducitur: ita enim rursus Matheus Sutclivius argumentatur. Si Christus de externa Ecclesiæ Politeia leges tulit, tum lex moralis non esset perfecta ut Ps. 19. & 119 dicitur: sed nova quædam lex moralis introduceretur: nova etiam esset ἀνομία præter legis moralis transgressionem, aliaque bona opera præter legis moralis obedientiam. Nonne miraris Lector quid huic homini mali acciderit? Num rectè sapit? Cui ignotum præcepta de Politeia Ecclesiastica, ad legis moralis præceptum secundum pertinere, & in eodem contineri? Num aliam legem moralem tulit Moses, quando cerram Politeias Ecclesiasticæ formam Iudæis prescripsit? & ἀνομία nulla est in legibus Ecclesiasticis sub Evangelio transgrediendis? Cur igitur pro peccatoribus Puritani habentur? Cur pro disciplina sua ita exagitantur ab Hierarchicis reformatæ Ecclesiæ? Cur in Consistorijs Anglicanis pro legum Ecclesiasticarum transgressione quotidie homines puniuntur? Supersunt objectiones aliæ duæ: omnes nempe damnatos esse qui disciplinam in verbo descriptam non amplectuntur, si aliqua præscripta essent: & Ecclesias quæ eandem repudiant, Ecclesias veras minimè esse: sed eis jam antè à nobis satisfactum est. Ita certam esse regiminis Ecclesiastici formam in verbo præscriptam demonstravimus, & contraria Hierarchicorum argumenta singula irrita fecimus.
units.tr: 4. The fourth objection of the Hierarchists is drawn from the consideration of the moral law. Matthew Sutcliffe argues this way again: If Christ enacted laws concerning the external polity of the Church, then the moral law would not be perfect, as is said in Ps. 19 and 119. Instead some new moral law would be introduced. There would also be a new lawlessness beyond the transgression of the moral law, and other good works beyond obedience to the moral law. Does not the reader wonder what harm has befallen this man? Is he thinking straight? Is it unknown to him that the precepts about ecclesiastical polity belong to, and are contained in, the second precept of the moral law? Did Moses give another moral law when he prescribed to the Jews the fixed form of ecclesiastical polity? And is there no lawlessness in transgressing the ecclesiastical laws under the Gospel? Why then are the Puritans held to be sinners? Why are they so harassed by the Hierarchists of the reformed Church for their discipline? Why in the Anglican consistories are people punished every day for transgressing the ecclesiastical laws? Two other objections remain: namely, that all are condemned who do not embrace the discipline described in the Word, if any prescriptions were laid down; and that Churches which reject it are not true Churches at all. But we have already satisfied them on these points. Thus we have demonstrated that a fixed form of church government is prescribed in the Word, and we have rendered each of the Hierarchists' contrary arguments null.

units.la: CAP. XLII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLII.

units.la: Politeia Ecclesiastica quoad substantiam immutabilis est, quod exemplis demonstratur.
units.tr: The ecclesiastical polity is immutable in substance, as examples show.

units.la: QVod si autem Politeia Ecclesiastica quoad substantiam in verbo prœscripta habeatur: sequitur eandem quoad substantiam immutabilem esse, sic ut de eadem diminuere, vel eidem addere illicitum sit. Imò non sequitur inquiunt Hierarchicorum plurimi: ubi primò excipiunt adversus factum Apostolorum in disciplina exercenda: deinde adversus eorundem doctrinam in disciplina præscribenda: quorum neutrum legem perpetuam dictare volunt, quæ immutari nequeat. De primo, sic Io. Bridgesius, Episcopus Oxoniensis. Num unumquodque exemplum primitivæ Ecclesiæ præceptum aut mandatum faciunt? Rursus: Forte rerum nonnullarum in primitiva Ecclesia exemplum aliquod ostendere possunt, sed nec ipsum generale, nec eiusdem perpetuam regulam aliquam, quæ omnes Ecclesias & ætates omnes ad illud exemplum astringat. Ita Io. Whitgiftus: Ex facto aut exemplo legem facere iniquum est. Hoc argumentum à facto nihil valet. Nunquam licet, inquit Zwinglius, neque in divinis, neque in profanis à facto ad jus argumentari. Rursus, Non solum infirmum sed & periculosum etiam argumentandi genus est, arguere. Apostoli fecerunt, ergo & nos facere oportet, vel Apostoli non fecerunt, ergo nobis non licet facere. Zwinglius vir insignis, inprimis Anabaptistas hoc modo arguentes reprehendit, & dicit argumentum à facto ad jus, vel à non facto ad non ius nunquam valere, nisi illud exemplum super aliquam legem vel regulam fundetur. Postremò, Tho. Bilsonus, arguentibus pro libertate populi in electionibus, ab exemplo electionis Diaconorum ita respondet: Exempla multum distant à præceptis. Ex facto singulari regula generalis non potest constitui sine maxima & manifestissima ratione, quæ conclusionem cohærentem & necessarium esse demonstret. His ut respondeatur, agendum est primo, in genere de exemplorum vi & valore: deinde speciatim de obligatione facti Apostolorum, & Ecclesiarum quæ sub illis floruerunt.
units.tr: But if the ecclesiastical polity is held to be prescribed in the Word as to its substance, it follows that it is immutable as to its substance, so that it is unlawful either to take anything from it or to add anything to it. Indeed, most of the Hierarchists say, it does not follow. They first make an exception against the practice of the Apostles in exercising discipline, and then against their doctrine in prescribing discipline. Neither of these, they hold, dictates a perpetual law that cannot be changed. On the first point, John Bridges, Bishop of Oxford, says: Do they make every example of the primitive Church a precept or command? Again: Perhaps they can show some example of certain things in the primitive Church, but neither the example itself as a general rule, nor any perpetual rule drawn from it, that binds all Churches and all ages to that example. So John Whitgift: It is unfair to make a law from a fact or an example. An argument from fact is worth nothing. It is never permitted, says Zwingli, to argue from fact to right, either in divine or in human matters. Again: It is not only a weak but also a dangerous kind of argument: the Apostles did it, therefore we ought to do it; or the Apostles did not do it, therefore we may not do it. Zwingli, a distinguished man, rebukes especially the Anabaptists who argue in this way, and says that an argument from fact to right, or from non-fact to non-right, never holds unless that example rests upon some law or rule. Lastly, Thomas Bilson, answering those who argue for the people's liberty in elections from the example of the election of deacons, replies: Examples differ greatly from precepts. A general rule cannot be constituted from a single fact without a very great and most manifest reason, which shows the conclusion to be coherent and necessary. To answer these objections we must first treat, in general, of the force and value of examples, and then, specifically, of the obligation of the Apostles' deeds and of the Churches that flourished under them.

units.la: 2 Primo igitur cum exempla particularia nobis in scripturis ut typi sive ἐντύπωματα proponuntur ut similia vel imitemur vel devitemus, tum eadem pro lege communi habenda sunt: uti manifestò liquet ex 1. Cor. 10. 11. Phil. 4. 8. 9. 10. Heb. 11. per totum. Heb. 12. 3. Iob. 13. 15. Iud. 7. Exemplum ego præbui vobis, inquit Christus, Ioh. 13. 15. ut prout ego feci vobis & vos faciatis. De exemplo vero sanctorum Heb. 12. 3. habetur illud, nebulam esse qua dirigamur, per allusionem ad nebulam illam quæ Israelitis in deserto præivit, ut recta via ad terram Canaan ducerentur. Iam vero intentio spiritus Sancti in Actis Apostolorum perscribendis, eorum exempla eandem vim obtinere docet: quorsum enim liber de actis Apostolorum scriptus, nisi ut tum eorum acta nobis essent, & quasi nebulæ quibus in via recta, Quid igitur? ipsa fundamentalia Ecclesiastici regiminis in lege Christi omittebantur? Libertas nostra, respondet Whitgiftus, liberationem postulat à tam exiêtis legum normâ: imo libertatem à Christo partam, à servitute Iudaica, pedibus proculcant, inquit Lous, qui certam formam Politeias in verbo contineri asserunt. Non opus est multis. In legibus Mosaicis duo sunt, multitudo & directio: multitudo onus erat, directio beneficium: hinc sequitur libertatem nostram à servitute Iudaica in eo versari, quòd à multitudine observationum Mosaicarum liberamur: directio beneficium cum sit, tam exactam normam Politeias iam habemus, quam quæ apud Iudæos erat; aut Ecclesia nostra deficit & illâ Iudaicâ inferior est. Hinc comparationi huic acquiescit Ha. Saravia. Quum etenim urgeret D. Beza certum esse à Christo sub Evangelio constitutam regiminis Ecclesiastici formam quemadmodum olim à Mose fuerat, respondet ille: Meam sententiam confirmat quisquis ita scribit & loquitur: & facile idem sentiremus, si eandem gubernationis formam quâ Apostoli usi sunt retentam fuisse Genevæ, & in aliis Ecclesiis Galliæ & inferioris Germaniæ observari, doceri possit. Imo quid ipse Matheus Sutclivius. Contemptim quidem loquitur ille in tractatu suo de disciplina, de hoc argumento nostro, à Mosis & Christi comparatione desumpto c. 12. p. 152. in libro verò de presbyterio c. 11. ulterius progreditur: contendit etenim Christum legislatorem non esse ut Moses erat, in externis præsertim, sed Mediatorem tantum. Sed adversus Bellarminum disputans, novus homo emergit. Quid Bellarminus? eodem nempe fundamento nititur, quo Hierarchici, non esse scilicet eandem rationem novi testamenti, quæ veteris, legi Mosis non licuisse addere, Evangelio licere. Quid ita? Audi eam ipsam Hierarchicorum cantilenam. Quia Deus in lege omnia determinavit in speciali, in novo autem testamento latæ sunt leges communissimæ, quæ specialiter per Apostolos & eorum successores pro locorum & temporum diversitate determinandæ essent. Quid ad hæc Sutclivius. Accipe defensionem plane nostram idque totidem verbis. Hæc responsio adversus Christum contumeliosa est. Cur enim ille perfectiorem non daret legem quam Moses, præsertim cum Mosi longè præstaret? Præterea repugnat perfectioni Evangelij. Nam si omnia fere iuxta in lege præcepta sunt, & nihil fere in Evangelio ut ipse subindicat, tunc erit lex Mosis Evangelio præstantior: quod tamen nec verum est, nec à Bellarmino conceditur. At intelligit ista de fide tantum & sacramentis Sutclius. Etiam loquitur generatim, & Politeiam includit, ut demonstrant sequentia. Postremò hæc responsio Bellarmini falsa est: nam nôn magis licet Evangelij legi addere, quam legi Mosis. Nec obstat quòd à concilijs & pijs principibus aliquæ leges de rebus Ecclesiasticis additæ sunt: Illæ enim non sunt additiones ad legem Dei, nec in conscientia obligabant, nisi quatenus aliquid de lege Dei participabant. Ita conficitur, certam quandam Politeias formam quoad substantialia in Evangelio contineri, quia in lege continebatur.
units.tr: 2 First, then, since particular examples in Scripture are set before us as types or figures [ἐντύπωματα], to be imitated or avoided, they must be held as a common law. This is plain from 1 Cor. 10:11; Phil. 4:8, 9, 10; Heb. 11 throughout; Heb. 12:3; John 13:15; Jude 7. Christ says, John 13:15: I have given you an example, that you should do just as I have done to you. As for the example of the saints, Heb. 12:3 teaches that they are a cloud by which we are guided, alluding to the cloud that went before the Israelites in the wilderness so that they might be led by the straight way to the land of Canaan. Now the intention of the Holy Spirit in recording the Acts of the Apostles shows that their examples have the same force. For why was the book of the Acts of the Apostles written, unless that their deeds might be before us, and be as clouds by which we are led in the straight way? What then? Were the fundamental elements of ecclesiastical government left out of Christ's law? Our liberty, answers Whitgift, demands liberation from so strict a rule of laws. Indeed, those who assert that a certain form of polity is contained in the Word, says Lous, trample under foot the liberty won by Christ from Jewish servitude. There is no need for many words. In the Mosaic laws there are two things, multitude and direction. The multitude was a burden, the direction a benefit. From this it follows that our liberty from Jewish servitude consists in being freed from the multitude of Mosaic observances. Since direction is a benefit, we now have as exact a norm of polity as the Jews had; otherwise our Church is deficient and inferior to that Jewish one. Hence Hadrian Saravia also accepts this comparison. For when Beza urged that it is certain that a form of ecclesiastical government was established under the Gospel by Christ, just as it once was by Moses, Saravia replies: Whoever writes and speaks thus confirms my opinion, and we would easily think the same, if it could be shown that the same form of government which the Apostles used was retained at Geneva and observed in the other Churches of France and Lower Germany. Indeed, what of Matthew Sutcliffe himself? In his treatise on discipline, c. 12, p. 152, he speaks contemptuously of this argument of ours drawn from the comparison of Moses and Christ; but in his book on the presbytery, c. 11, he goes further, contending that Christ is not a lawgiver as Moses was, especially in external matters, but only a Mediator. Yet when he disputes against Bellarmine, a different man emerges. What of Bellarmine? He rests on the same foundation as the Hierarchists, namely that the reason of the New Testament is not the same as that of the Old: it was not permitted to add to the law of Moses, but it is permitted to add to the Gospel. Why so? Hear the very refrain of the Hierarchists: Because God determined everything in the law in particular, but in the New Testament the most general laws were enacted, which were to be determined in particular by the Apostles and their successors according to the diversity of places and times. What does Sutcliffe reply to this? Take his defence, which is quite our own, and in these very words: This answer is insulting to Christ. For why would he give a less perfect law than Moses, especially since he far surpasses Moses? Moreover it contradicts the perfection of the Gospel. For if almost everything is commanded in the law, and almost nothing in the Gospel, as he himself hints, then the law of Moses will be more excellent than the Gospel; which is neither true nor conceded by Bellarmine. But Sutcliffe understands these things only of faith and the sacraments. Yet he speaks generally and includes polity, as the following shows: Finally, Bellarmine's answer is false: for it is no more lawful to add to the law of the Gospel than to the law of Moses. Nor does it stand in the way that some laws concerning ecclesiastical matters have been added by councils and pious princes. For those are not additions to the law of God, nor did they bind the conscience, except insofar as they shared in something of the law of God. Thus it is concluded that a certain form of polity, as to its essentials, is contained in the Gospel, because it was contained in the law.

units.la: 6 Argumentum nostrum sextum à subjecto politeias Eccl. siasticæ ducitur, ecclesia nempe, quæ vineæ, domui, civitati, corpori denique; assimilatur, sic ut illius custodes, politeia, œconomi, partes denique; essentiales in verbo Dei ut ordinentur necesse est. Respondet ad ista attributa conjunctim Hookerus: ea non implicare certam immutabilemque formam disciplinæ, quia vel nobis ipsis fatentibus, quædam in politeia ecclesiastica sunt minoris momenti, quæ alterationem pati possunt. Quàm jejunè? Quomodo etenim sequitur, custodes vineæ, politeiam essentialem civitatis, œconomos communs, partes essentiales corporis mutari posse, quod quædam minoris momenti, vineæ, civitatis, domus negotia, & habitus externus corporis nonnunquam immutari possint? Videamus de singulis separatim. Primò vinea Domini dicitur ecclesia, quam ab ipso Deo per politeiam excultam legimus, Isa. 5. 2. 3. 4. præcipuè verò Cant 8. 4. Vinea est Salomoni in loco fer-race, locat vineam suam custodibus, quisque affert pro fructu eius mille nos siclos argenti. Vineæ, quæ mea est, apud me permaneant, &c. Quum anno 1606. relegerentur à rege, qui pro disciplina Anglicana, coram ministris tum præsentibus, concionarentur: demandatum Iohanni Kingo erat, qui nunc est Episcopus Londinensis, ut contra Seniores & presbyterium declamitaret. Textum verò sumi sit ille hunc ipsum ex Canticis locum: & nullam vineæ certam gubernationis formam à Solomone Vineæ domino constitutam esse, asseveravit. Num hoc in textu reperit? imò nomine textu ipso hoc Gl sema confutatur? Vera etenim Francisci Iunij expositio (cui ille nihil respondet.) Ne rex quidem ipse ut vineam haberet sit ciffimum, eam aut i si potest colere, aut totum illius fructum percipere, sed colendam alis locat, & aliquid eis de proventu tenetur attribuere: ego vero inquit sponsus neque alijs colendam loco, neque mihi quicquam de ei detrahi sinam, adeo sum illius Zelotypus, sed oculi mei semper versantur in ea, & fructus illius nè tantillum quidem alienari sino, aut aliena voluntate administrari. Vide igitur huius hominis ofcitantiam, qui nec textum quidem suum intellexit. Salomonem etenim ver. 4. suam vineam locantem alijs, intelligit Christum suam Ecclesiam custodibus locantem: cum contra manifesta hic antithesis inter Salomonem atque Christum instituatur, sic ut Salomon quidem in vineam suam elocat alijs, permittens eam alienæ voluntate administrari: Christus vero Ecclesiam non elocat, sed ipse per sese eam colit, permittens nemini voluntate sua rem administrare: sed pro speciali ipsius amore & Zelotypia, curâm Illius in seipsam suscipiens. Non igitur vel Zelotypia in suam vineam specialis, vel potestas in eandem Christi elocata nemini, vel fructuum denique reservatio permittet, ut Politeiæ ejusdem constitutionem arbitrio hominum reliquisse videatur: præsertim cum Politeia Ecclesiæ, medium illud sit, quo fructus proventusque ubertim affluunt, quas sibi soli reservasse hic Christus affirmatur.
units.tr: 6 Our sixth argument is drawn from the subject of ecclesiastical polity: the Church, which is compared to a vineyard, a house, a city, and finally a body. Its guardians, the polity, its stewards, and finally its parts must therefore necessarily be ordained as essentials in the Word of God. Hooker answers these attributes together, saying that they do not imply a certain and unchangeable form of discipline, because, as we ourselves admit, some things in ecclesiastical polity are of lesser importance and can undergo alteration. How feeble this is! For how does it follow that the guardians of a vineyard, the essential polity of a city, the common stewards, and the essential parts of a body can be changed, because some lesser things, the business of a vineyard, a city, or a house, and the external habit of a body, can sometimes be changed? Let us look at each separately. First, the vineyard of the Lord is called the Church, which we read was cultivated by God himself through polity, Isa. 5:2–4, and especially Cant 8. 4: Solomon has a vineyard in a fertile place; he lets his vineyard to keepers, each of whom brings for its fruit a thousand shekels of silver. My vineyard, which is mine, remains with me, etc. When in 1606 the king was preaching in favour of the English discipline before the ministers then present, John King, who is now Bishop of London, was commissioned to declaim against the seniors and the presbytery. He took his text from this very passage of the Song, and asserted that no fixed form of government had been established by Solomon, the lord of the vineyard. Does he find this in the text? Rather, this gloss is refuted by the text itself. For the true exposition is that of Francis Junius, to which he makes no reply: Not even the king himself is so fortunate as to have a vineyard; either he cannot cultivate it himself or enjoy all its fruit, but leases it to others to cultivate and is bound to assign them some part of the produce. But I, says the bridegroom, will neither let it to others to cultivate nor allow anything to be taken from it for myself. So jealous am I of it. But my eyes are always upon it, and I do not allow its fruit to be alienated even a little, or administered by another's will. See, then, the carelessness of this man, who did not even understand his own text. For he takes Solomon, who in v. 4 lets his vineyard to others, to mean Christ letting his Church to custodians. Yet here a clear antithesis is set up between Solomon and Christ: Solomon indeed lets his vineyard to others, permitting it to be administered by another's will; but Christ does not let out the Church, but himself tends it by himself, permitting no one to administer the thing by his own will, and, out of his special love and jealousy, taking its care upon himself. Therefore neither a special jealousy for his own vineyard, nor a power of Christ entrusted to no one over it, nor finally the reservation of its fruits, will allow us to think that the constitution of its polity has been left to human judgment. This is especially so since the polity of the Church is the very means by which fruits and revenues flow in abundance, and these Christ is affirmed to have reserved for himself alone.

units.la: 2 Secundo, civitas Ecclesia dicitur regis magni: & civitatis anima (inquit Hookerus ex persona nostra) Politeia est. Adjicit in margine
units.tr: 2 Secondly, the Church is called the city of the great King, and the soul of the city (says Hooker, speaking in our person) is the polity. In the margin he adds

units.la: Guilielmi Traversij verba: Nisi reipublicæ suæ statum omnem Christus constituerit, magistratus ordinarit, singulorum munera potestatemque descripserit, quæ judiciorum forica ratio habenda, quomodo civium finiendæ lites: non solum minus Ecclesiæ Christianæ providit, quam Moses olim Judaicæ, sed quam à Lycurgo, Salomone, Numa, civitatibus suis prospectum fuit. Ponit ista odiose Hookerus, sed cur non refellit? Certe refelli ista non possunt, id quod etiam in Cornelio Scultingio videre est, qui licet thesim Traversianam sibi refutandam suscepisset, & disciplinam in verbo non perfectè contineri asseruisset: ad hoc tamen illius argumentum, respondet omnino nihil. Tertiò, Ecclesia domus Dei est, 1. Tim. 3. 15. Heb. 3. 3. 4. & quænam domus benè constituta ordine caret quo gubernatur? In domo quisquam œconomios constituit præter patrem familias? Numerus, gradus, ordo, habitus, servorum Salomonis, tot illius sapientiæ testimonia erant: quomodo ergo verisimile fiat, Christum majorem Salomone, non eam certam domus suæ gubernandæ rationem reliquisse, in qua quasi in speculo, sapientia, cura, & illius providentia erga Ecclesiam suâ reluceret. Hæc Hookerus ex persona nostra: quibus tamen ne verbum quidem respondet. Respondet Remonstrator plurima in quaque domo œconomi arbitrio discretionique relinqui solere: quod ipsum causam non attingit. Quæstio etenim nostra non de rebus minoris momenti est: nam circumstantias individuales Ecclesiæ arbitrio relictas esse confitemur: sed de ipso domus Dei regimine, imò de œconomis ipsis, quorum designationem domus œconomis relictam esse quis unquam audivit? Luc. 12. 12. Quisnam est dispensator fidelis & prudens quem constituit dominus ejus super familiam suam, ut det portionem eius in tempore suo. Ecce rectores domus, ipse dominus constituit. Quo etiam pertinet calamus ille Apoc. 11. Datus Angelo ad metiendam domum Dei: ostendit etenim non absque calamo relictam esse Ecclesiam Dei, vel quoad regimen: nam de mensuratione regiminis adversus Antichristi tyrannidem, pereaeque ac adversus hæresim de mensuratione ipsius fidei, agit hoc in loco vates. Sic nempè decuerat, nè domus posterior, priori cederet: de qua singulis in Dei verbo descripta fuisse, testatur David, 1. Chron. 28. 12. 13. 19. Tunc tradidit Salomoni filio suo structuram domus, & omnium quæ erant penes eum per spiritum de atrys Iehovæ, etiam pro distributionibus sacerdotum & Levitarum & pro omni opere ad ministerium domus Iehovæ. ——Hæc omnia descripta à manu Iehovæ incumbere mihi instruxit me; omnia opera huius structuræ. Quid multis? Concedit hic pedib. in sententiam nostram adversariorum omnium acerrimus, Matheus ipse Sutclivius: sic etenim adversus Bellarm. scribit: Dubium non est quin universam domum suam & omnes ejus ministros Christus perfectè constituerit & descripserit. Quare cum Pontifex nullum suæ iurisdictionis mandatum ostendere possit, ipsa nulla est. Neque enim ulla maior est nullitas: quàm quæ ex defectu iuris est. Nonne & ministros regentes perfectè à Christo institutos asserit, contra Pseudoregentem regentem disputans? Nonne nullitatem jurisdictionis (puta in Episcopis) ponit,ubi nullum in verbo mandatum extat?
