Postremò, corpori assimilatur Ecclesia,quod & concedit Richardus Hookerus, sed nihil tamen pro certa regiminis forma facere contendit: quia Politeia, tantum hujus corporis vestitus & ornatus est, qui immutari & variari sine piaculo ullo potest. At officia Ecclesiastica pastores,nempè,Seniores,& Diaconos,pro quibus contendimus, non vestitum hujus corporis sed membra vocat, Rom.12.5. sic ut Christus ea omnia in verbo formare instar figuli censendus sit: quamadmodum in corpore naturali,formare & figurare singula ejus membra,creator Deus dicitur.
units.tr: the words of William Travers: Unless Christ had established the whole state of his commonwealth, ordained the magistracy, and described the duties and powers of each, together with the method of judgment to be observed and the manner of settling citizens' disputes, he would have provided less for the Christian Church than Moses once provided for the Jewish nation, and less than Lycurgus, Solomon and Numa provided for their cities. Hooker puts these points as a reproach, but why does he not refute them? Certainly they cannot be refuted, as may be seen also in Cornelius Scultingius, who, although he undertook to refute Travers' thesis and asserted that discipline is not fully contained in the Word, nevertheless makes no reply at all to his argument. Thirdly, the Church is the house of God (1 Tim. 3. 15; Heb. 3. 3, 4). And what well-ordered house lacks the rule by which it is governed? Does anyone in a household appoint a steward apart from the father of the family? The number, grades, order and conduct of Solomon's servants were so many testimonies to his wisdom. How, then, can it be likely that Christ, greater than Solomon, left no sure plan for governing his house, in which his wisdom, care and providence toward the Church might shine forth as in a mirror? Hooker says this in our person, yet his opponents do not answer a single word to these points. The Remonstrant replies that in every household much is usually left to the steward's discretion and judgment. But that does not touch the cause. For our question does not concern matters of minor importance: we confess that the individual circumstances of the Church are left to its judgment. The question is about the very government of God's house, and indeed about the stewards themselves, whose appointment, left to the household, has anyone ever heard of? Luke 12. 42: Who then is the faithful and wise steward whom his lord shall set over his household, to give them their portion in due season? Behold, the lord himself appoints the rulers of the house. To this also pertains that reed in Rev. 11: A reed was given to the angel to measure the house of God. It shows that the Church of God has not been left without a measuring line, even as to its government: for the prophet in this place deals with the measuring of government against the tyranny of Antichrist, just as he deals with the measuring of the faith itself against heresy. Surely it was fitting that the later house should not yield to the former, and David testifies that the pattern of it was described to each detail in God's Word (1 Chron. 28. 12, 13, 19): Then he gave to his son Solomon the plan of the house, and of all that was with him by the Spirit, for the courts of Jehovah, and for the divisions of the priests and Levites, and for all the work of the ministry of the house of Jehovah. ... All these things were described by the hand of Jehovah, who made me understand, all the works of this structure. Why say more? Even Matthew Sutcliffe, the most bitter of all our adversaries, concedes our position on this point with his whole foot. For he writes thus against Bellarmine: There is no doubt that Christ has perfectly established and described his whole house and all its ministers. Therefore, since the Pope can show no mandate for his jurisdiction, his jurisdiction is null. For there is no greater nullity than that which arises from a lack of right. Does not Sutcliffe also assert that the ruling ministers were perfectly instituted by Christ, when he disputes against the false ruling minister? Does he not posit a nullity of jurisdiction (namely in bishops) where no mandate exists in the Word? Lastly, the Church is compared to a body, which Richard Hooker also concedes, but he nevertheless contends that this is no support for a fixed form of government, because the polity is only the clothing and ornament of this body, which can be changed and varied without any sin. But the ecclesiastical offices, namely ministers, elders and deacons, for which we contend, he calls not the clothing of this body but its members (Rom. 12. 5). So Christ must be deemed to have formed all these in the Word as a potter does, just as in a natural body God the Creator is said to form and shape each of its members.

units.la: 8 Argumentum nostrum septimum, ab officio principis & capitis ecclesiae Iesu Christi derivatur: nonne etenim regis est sancire leges ut regnū quā optimè suū gubernetur? Quid aliud sonat ab Isaia illa.9 7.Iusticia & iudicio Christū regnū suū stabilire?Quidaliud,illa Pauli, 1. Cor.12.4.Christū ut Dominū & Iministrationes pro regenda Ecclesia sua instituisse?Quid aliud deniq; illa Iacobi 4.12.Vnus est legislator,nēpè Deus? Respondet Lous. Quod de uno legislatore dicitur id de legislatore primario est intelligendum: aliter, legislatores secundarios esse nemo inficiabitur,nisi qui ipsum magistratum sustulerit. Respondeo, eandem esse hanc distinctionem de legislatore primario & secundario quae illa Bellarmini & Stapletoni est, de capite & fundamento ecclesiae primario & secundario. Num magistratum quaeso tollunt scriptores nostri qui distinctionem hanc exhibilant? Manere potest in negotijs suis legislator magistratus, ut Deus interim in negotijs Iehovae, 2. Chron.19.11 legislator solus agnoscatur. Atque cum blasphemare papistas dicunt nostri,cum papam secundarium quasi caput sub Christo substituant: ita parum a blasphemia absunt Hierarchici,cum sub Christo primario legislatore, praelatos Ecclesiae quasi legislatores supponunt secundarios: in negotijs politeias illius, quae quidē essentialia sunt. Sed cautior forte Matheus Sutclivius, inter quem & Lounum,ista notabilis contradictio est. Primarium siquidem legislatorem agnoscit Christum Lous, in politeia ecclesiae suae constituenda,quem nec regem omninò,nec legislatorem Matheus Sutclivius ferre potest. Ita enim habet. In isto homine personato (adversarium intelligit,contra quem scribit) quis ferret Christum Redemptorem, in novum, in rebus externis legislatorem conversi? Rursus, Christus leges nullas Ecclesiasticas tulit. Iterum, Ego nulla ratione Christum externe ecclesiae politeiae legislatorem dici posse demonstrato. Postremò. Christus quoad externam ecclesiae politeiam dicendus non est rex & legislator. Miraris haec tam salsa iuxta ac impia tanto Theologo excidisse? Non habent extrema pudorem. Non ex sensu suo sobrie scripsit ista Sutclivius,sed studio contradicendi abreptus, suasque partes defendendi: quod vel hinc constat,quod contra Bellarminū disputans, ut imminueret potestatem papae quam illi attribuit in legibus ferendis, contrarium prorsus ponit. Sic enim scribit. Sicut unus legislator, ita una essentialis ecclesiæ gubernatio, reipublicæ verò forma varia. Rursus. Nullæ ecclesiæ gubernationis leges, certæ & immutabiles nisi à Christo: nam is ecclesiæ legislator est, isque solus.
units.tr: 8 Our seventh argument is derived from the office of the prince and head of the Church, Jesus Christ. Is it not the king's task to enact laws so that his kingdom may be governed as well as possible? What else does that saying of Isaiah 9:7 mean: Christ establishes his kingdom with justice and judgment? What else does that of Paul, 1 Cor. 12:4, mean: Christ as Lord has instituted administrations for governing his Church? And what else, finally, does that of James 4:12 mean: There is one lawgiver, namely God? Lous replies: What is said of the one lawgiver must be understood of the primary lawgiver; otherwise no one will deny that there are secondary lawgivers, unless he abolishes the magistracy itself. I reply that this distinction between a primary and a secondary lawgiver is the same as that of Bellarmine and Stapleton between the primary and secondary head and foundation of the Church. Do our writers, who set out this distinction, I ask, abolish the magistracy? The magistrate can remain a lawgiver in his own affairs, just as God in the affairs of Jehovah (2 Chron. 19:11) is acknowledged as the sole lawgiver. And just as our men say that the Papists blaspheme when they substitute the Pope as a secondary head under Christ, so the Hierarchists are scarcely free from blasphemy when, under Christ the primary lawgiver, they posit the prelates of the Church as secondary lawgivers, in matters of his polity, which are indeed essential. But perhaps Matthew Sutcliffe is more cautious, and between him and Lous there is a notable contradiction. For Lous acknowledges Christ as the primary lawgiver in establishing the polity of his Church, whom Matthew Sutcliffe cannot bear to call king at all, nor lawgiver. For he writes thus: In this masked man (he means the adversary against whom he writes) who could endure Christ the Redeemer turned into a new lawgiver in external matters? Again: Christ enacted no ecclesiastical laws. Again: I demonstrate that Christ can in no way be called the external lawgiver of the Church's polity. Lastly: As regards the external polity of the Church, Christ is not to be called king and lawgiver. Are you surprised that such things, as foolish as they are impious, have escaped so great a theologian? They have no shame. Sutcliffe did not write these things soberly from his own judgment, but, carried away by a zeal for contradicting, and by the wish to defend his own side. This is clear from the fact that, disputing against Bellarmine in order to diminish the power the latter attributes to the Pope in enacting laws, he asserts the exact opposite. For he writes: Just as there is one lawgiver, so there is one essential government of the Church, while the form of the commonwealth is various. And again: There are no laws of Church government that are fixed and unchangeable except from Christ; for he is the lawgiver of the Church, and he alone.

units.la: 9 Argumentum nostrum octavum, à materia essentialium illorum ducitur, quæ perfectè à Christo in verbo suo instituta asseveramus: quæ à D. Theodoro Beza ita posita sunt. Ecclesiastica inquit administrationis essentialia, duabus præcipue in rebus, posita sunt: nempè in ipsis perpetuis muneribus sacris, & in eorundem accurata & distincta descriptione, ad quam eorum usus est referendus. Ad hoc respondens Hadrianus Saravia ea præclara esse testatur, & nihil contra suam sententiam facere. Nec mirum. Nam cum Apostolus hanc vocationem suam licitam probet, quod non ab hominibus sed à Deo ipsius Apostolatus esset. Gal. 1. 1. hoc supponit pro fundamento, omnes licitas vocationes à Deo esse, quæ verò ab hominibus sunt, & aliunde instituuntur eas esse illicitas. Notum hoc ipsis Pharisæis & Scribis: illicitum etenim ministerium Iohannis hinc probant quod authoritatem in verbo Dei nullam haberet: atque Iohannes, supponens eos verum præsumsisse, in verbo fundari ministerium suum docet Ioh. 1: 23. Falsò ratiocinati sunt Scribæ & Pharisei, dicit Whitgiftus: & nos ex responso Iohannis inconsequenter arguimus, respondet Remonstrator: sed rationem nullam adferunt, sicut nec adferre possunt. Quæ etenim ratio deprimere illa Christi poterit. Math. 21. 25. in quibus supponens ministerium quodvis illicitum esse quod est ab hominibus institutum: ministerium Iohannis idcirco licitum docet, quod esset à cælo, id est, à Deo, in suo verbo stabilitur. Hinc pertinent illa Pauli Heb. 5. 5. Nemo (ne ipse Christus quidem Filius Dei) honorem sibi in ecclesia sumit, nisi qui vocatus est, ut Aaron: fuit autem ministerium Aaronis in verbo constitutum. Deridet hanc rationem nostram in tractatu suo de disciplina Matheus Sutclivius: adversus verò Bellarmi num disputans pro more suo approbat. Sic enim scribit. Imò nec Christus Iesus, licet Filius Dei pontificatum suum assumpsit nisi missus: nec ecclesiæ administrationem suscepit, nisi à patre Ecclesiæ præpositus. Quod si ergo nec Christus Iesus sine patris mandato suum assumsit pontificatum: temerè faciunt qui ecclesiæ pontificatum generalem assumunt sine mandato. In ecclesia enim Dei nemo sibi honorem sumit, nisi qui missus est quemadmodum Aaron: Proferant ergo pontifices Romani mandatum Domini: ostendant missionem suam: doceant se à Domino ecclesiæ universalis præpositos. Quid cessant? quid tacent? cur tergi versantur? Eodē in capite post. Refellitur inquit pontificum Romanorum principatus, quia non est ex Christi institutione. Postremò, ideo pontificium authoritatem illicitam probat, quia dici illi potest ex Roberto Gallo. Quis posuit idolum hoc in sede mea, ut imperaret gregi meo? & ad illum accommodari possit Tertullianii illud. Qui estis? quomodo & unde venistis? quid in meo agitis non meis? Quin & noster hac quidem in re Remonstrator est. Non negamus quin omnes legitimæ vocationes authoritatem habeant ex verbo Dei, etsi eli non totidem verbis. Quod vero dicit non totidem verbis, id hujus Remonstrat. sententiae mentem non mutat. Sic est alibi. Directa authoritas, vel c.2.p. 24. immediata est ex ipsi Dei voce, vel mediata per directam consequentiam ex p.22. verbo collecta: sic omnis vocatio ex verbo deducibilis est.
units.tr: 9 Our eighth argument is drawn from the matter of those essentials, which we affirm were perfectly instituted by Christ in his Word, and which Theodore Beza has set out thus: The essentials of ecclesiastical administration, he says, are placed chiefly in two things: namely in the perpetual sacred offices themselves, and in their exact and distinct description, to which their use is to be referred. Replying to this, Adrian Saravia testifies that these points are excellent and do nothing against his opinion. No wonder. For when the Apostle proves his calling lawful, because his apostleship was from God and not from men (Gal. 1:1), he presupposes as a foundation that all lawful callings are from God, and that those which are from men and are instituted otherwise are unlawful. This was known to the Pharisees and Scribes themselves: they argued from this that the ministry of John was unlawful, because it had no authority in the Word of God. And John, supposing that they had rightly presumed this, teaches that his ministry is grounded in the Word (John 1:23). The Scribes and Pharisees reasoned falsely, says Whitgift; and we argue from John's reply inconsequentially, answers the Remonstrant. But they bring no reason, as indeed they cannot. For what reasoning can overturn that of Christ (Matt. 21:25)? In that passage, presupposing that any ministry is unlawful which is instituted by men, he teaches that the ministry of John was lawful for this reason: that it was from heaven, that is from God, and is established in his Word. To this pertains that saying of Paul, Heb. 5:4: No one (not even Christ himself, the Son of God) takes the honour to himself in the Church, unless he is called, as Aaron was. Now the ministry of Aaron was established in the Word. Matthew Sutcliffe mocks this argument of ours in his treatise on discipline; yet when disputing against Bellarmine he approves it, as is his way. For he writes thus: Indeed Christ Jesus, although the Son of God, did not assume his priesthood unless he was sent, nor did he take up the administration of the Church unless he was set over it by the Father of the Church. If therefore Christ Jesus did not assume his priesthood without the Father's command, those who take up the general priesthood of the Church without a command act rashly. For in the Church of God no one takes the honour to himself unless he is sent, as Aaron was. Let the Roman pontiffs therefore produce the mandate of the Lord; let them show their commission; let them teach that they have been set over the universal Church by the Lord. Why do they hesitate? Why are they silent? Why do they twist and turn? In the same chapter, later: The principate of the Roman pontiffs is refuted, because it is not from the institution of Christ. Lastly: He proves the Pontifical authority illicit because it can be said to him, in the words of Robert Gallus: Who placed this idol in my seat, to rule my flock? and that saying of Tertullian may be applied to him: Who are you? How and whence did you come? What are you doing in what is mine, not yours? Indeed our Remonstrant is in agreement with us on this point. We do not deny that all lawful callings have their authority from the Word of God, even if not in so many words. As for his saying "not in so many words," this does not change the meaning of this Remonstrant's opinion. It is the same elsewhere: Direct authority, or immediate authority, is from the very voice of God; or it is mediate, through a direct consequence drawn from the Word, as explained on p. 22. Thus every calling is deducible from the Word.

units.la: 10 Argumentum nostrum nonum à regiminis ecclesiastici fine vsq; ducitur. Eiusdem etenim est & finem & media ad finem constituere: sicut finem regiminis praefaife in verbo Christus sanxerit, & politeiam etiam ecclesiae quae est eiusdem finis medium, ut fancivegit, censendus est. Finis vero politeias, ecclesiae salus atque aedificatio est: & quis putarit, absque certis mediis omnibus, eisque certo constitutis, ecclesiam orbam Christum Iesum reliquisse? Quid quod politeia, vti caetera media omnia, non nisi gratiarum suppeditatione, & coelesti benedictione ad finem suum valent? Gratiam suppeditare alicui officio ecclesiastico, homo non potest: ergo nec officium aliquod constituere. Certe pro varietate gratiarum,varietatem administrationum in verbo constitutam videamus: & officia Ecclesiastica ipsa, dona sunt Eph.4.12.1. Cor: 12, 5. Rom.12. 5.6: sic ut de Christi & potentia & liberalitate derogetur plurimum, si penes hominem sit, ac non penes Christum solum eadem constituere. Quod ad benedictionem vero, uti tum benedixit Moses tabernaculo, quando omnia structa vidisset iuxta formam illam quae ei in monte ostensa est, Exod:39.43. ita tum & non aliter benedicit regimini Ecclesiastico Christus, quando omnia ad amussim verbi sui compositas & ordinata videt. Nulla ab illo aurora expectanda quando verbum illius non asseritur Ii: 8: 20. imo humanis inventis adeo non favet, vt minetur eis, qui ambulant in flamma ignis fui, & in scintillis, quas sibimetipsis succenderint. E manu mea accidet hoc vobis: in dolore iacebitis. Isa.50.11. Quid opus est multis? opus habent stellae ecclesiarum ut ut Christi manu teneantur & protegantur, Ap.1.16. nõne igitur opus est,ut omnes ab ipsius manu fabricentur? Stellae certe erraticae sunt Iud.13. officia quaecunq; ecclesiastica,quae non opera manus Christi, sed opera manuum humanarum sunt. An rarum in scripturis humana inventa condemnata audire, vel hoc solo nomine. Opera sint manuum tuarum? Psa.135,15. Isa.28.317. & 37.19. Ier.16.&c.
units.tr: 10 Our ninth argument is drawn from the end of ecclesiastical government. It belongs to the same authority to set both the end and the means to that end. Just as Christ in the Word has laid down the end of government, so the constitution of the Church, which is a means to that same end, must be regarded as having been ordained by him. The end of a constitution is the salvation and edification of the Church. Who would think that Christ Jesus left the Church without certain and fixed means for all things? Moreover, like all other means, a constitution attains its end only by the supply of grace and heavenly blessing. A man cannot supply grace to any ecclesiastical office, and therefore he cannot establish any office. Surely we see that the variety of administrations is appointed in the Word according to the variety of gifts, and the ecclesiastical offices themselves are gifts (Eph. 4.12; 1 Cor. 12.5; Rom. 12.5, 6). So much would be taken away from the power and generosity of Christ if these things were left to man and not to Christ alone. As for the blessing, just as Moses blessed the tabernacle when he saw everything built according to the pattern shown him on the mountain (Exod. 39.43), so Christ blesses ecclesiastical government in no other way than when he sees all things composed and ordered according to the exact measure of his Word. We should expect no dawn from him when his Word is not upheld. Indeed, he so little favours human inventions that he threatens those who walk in the flame of their own fire and in the sparks they have kindled for themselves: This shall come to you from my hand: you shall lie down in sorrow (Isa. 50.11). Why say more? The stars of the Churches need to be held and protected by the hand of Christ (Rev. 1.16); is it not therefore necessary that all of them be made by his hand? Surely every ecclesiastical office that is not the work of Christ's hand but of human hands is a wandering star (Jude 13). Is it rare in Scripture to hear human inventions condemned, even by this name alone? Are they the works of your hands? (Ps. 135.15; Isa. 28.317; 37.19; Jer. 16, etc.)

units.la: 11. Argumentum nostrum decimum ab officio nostro ducitur, fide nempe & obedientia erga disciplinam.Quae etenim fides absq; verbo Rom.10.17. quae obedientia nisi mandato? Respondet Remonstrator,fidem & obedientiam erga politeiam ecclesiasticam esse posse perinde ac civilem,etsi certa illius forma in verbo Dei non praescribitur: respectu nempe principiorum illorum generalium, quae in scriptura de eadem reperiuntur. At primo, res supernaturalis cum politeia ecclesiastica sit,quo nomine a civili distat: speciatim in verbo nisi praescribatur,languet erga eandem obedientia,vacillat fides. Secundo,sic generalibus principiis tantum politeias ecclesiasticae fidem dari, obedientiam praestari posse: & arctiori tamen vinculo ligamur nos ad utramque, si non generaliter, sed speciatim in verbo mandetur: quod à Christo praetermissum fuisse verisimile non est: Ratio apud Richardum Hookerum extat, in nostra persona, ab illo, ita posita. Quamdiu persuadentur homines de ordine aliquo, quòd ab hominibus solis sit, de prudentia sua praesumunt, putantque non modo parem sed meliorem etiam sese adinvenire posse. Inde est, quod instituta humana tam promptam & alacrem obedientiam elicere nequeant: atque ea est, quando ad Deum conscientia respicit, quasi ad illius ordinis authorem. Hoc illud fuit quod Moses leges de Politeia Ecclesiastica commendavit, cui simile quiddam à Paganis legislatoribus nonnulli praetendebant: falso quidem, prudenter tamen vim hujusce persuasionis discernentes. Itaque ad majorem obedientiam expediens erat, ut Deus ipse Politeias ecclesiasticae author esset. Huic vero nihil respondet Hookerus: quia frivola? fiat judicium ex consequentibus. Ex dogmate nostro certa quaedam ubique ἀπλανῶς & in disciplina perinde ac in doctrina pax & unitas conservatur: ex dogmate vero Hierarchico Anabaptisticis confusionibus via struitur, mutationibus politicis fenestra aperitur: funestis denique ecclesiarum dilacerationibus causa praebetur, sicut in Anglia hodie apparet. Rursus ex dogmate nostro consolatio cuique politeias administro suppeditatur, ut qui jam cum Ieremia dicere possit: Non me intrusi coram te: ex dogmate vero Hierarchico conscientiae confusio, qualis illa fuit sacerdotum Ieroboami: cum conscii essent se proprias implevisse manus, & absque ulla vocatione diivnâ semetipsos consecrasse. Postremò ex dogmate nostro proficiscitur erga politeias administros reverentia, cum plebi quotidie ob oculos versabitur, Qui vos spernit me spernit. Murmuratio vestra non est adversus nos, sed adversus Iehovam: ex dogmate vero Hierarchico contemptus, qualis in Malachia denunciatur: nam sordida semper in domo Dei institutio humana visa est.
units.tr: 11. Our tenth argument is drawn from our office, namely faith and obedience towards discipline. For what faith is there without the word (Rom. 10.17), and what obedience without a command? The Remonstrator replies that faith and obedience towards an ecclesiastical polity can exist just as they do towards a civil one, even though its particular form is not prescribed in the word of God, but only with respect to those general principles which Scripture contains about it. But first, since the supernatural matter is the ecclesiastical polity, it differs from the civil one in this respect: unless it is prescribed in the word, and particularly so, obedience towards it grows faint and faith wavers. Second, although faith in and obedience to an ecclesiastical polity could thus be given and rendered by general principles alone, we are bound to both by a tighter tie if the matter is commanded in the word not generally but particularly. It is not likely that Christ overlooked this. Richard Hooker's reasoning, set out in our person, is as follows: As long as men are persuaded that some order comes from men alone, they presume on their own wisdom, and think that they can devise not merely an equal but even a better one. Hence it is that human institutions cannot draw forth such prompt and eager obedience; and that obedience is given when conscience looks to God, as to the author of that order. This is what Moses commended in the laws concerning the ecclesiastical polity, and something similar was claimed by some pagan lawgivers, falsely indeed, yet prudently discerning the force of such persuasion. Therefore, for greater obedience, it was expedient that God himself should be the author of the ecclesiastical polity. Hooker makes no reply to this; is it because it is trifling? Let judgment be made from the consequences. From our doctrine a certain peace and unity is preserved everywhere unerringly [ἀπλανῶς], and in discipline just as in doctrine. From the hierarchical doctrine, however, a way is built for Anabaptist confusions, a window is opened to political changes, and finally a cause is given for the deadly tearing apart of churches, as is evident today in England. Again, from our doctrine comfort is supplied to each administrator of the polity, so that he can already say with Jeremiah: I have not thrust myself in before you. From the hierarchical doctrine comes confusion of conscience, such as that of the priests of Jeroboam, who, aware that they had filled their own hands and consecrated themselves without any divine calling. Lastly, from our doctrine there arises reverence towards the administrators of the polity, since it will be daily before the eyes of the people: He who despises you despises me. Your murmuring is not against us, but against Jehovah. From the hierarchical doctrine comes contempt, such as is denounced in Malachi, for human institution has always seemed sordid in the house of God.

units.la: 11 Argumentum nostrum undecimum & ultimum à testimonio sanctorum sumitur, qui in ecclesia quoque seculo floruerunt. Ita Cyprianus. Legat hoc unum verbum & in hoc mandato meditetur Christianae religio & inveniet ex hac scriptura omnium doctrinarum regulas emanasse, & binc nasci & huc reverti, quicquid ecclesiastica continet disciplina, & in omnibus irritum esse & frivolum quicquid dilectio non confirmat. Respondet Remonstrator. Per disciplinam intelligi hic doctrinam quemadmodum verbis paulo antecedentibus f. 8. Non me latet te docente ad siccandas corruptionem mearum putredines profuisse — sal disciplinae tuae Evangelio tuo mediante infusum. Hinc insultat Demonstratori, tanquam lectori Cypriani inepto aut collectionem aliorum sequenti, ne lecto quidem à sese Cypriano. Sed ineptissimus Cypriani lector ipse Remonstrator est, id quod proximè antecedentia verba demonstrant. Loquere magister bone libenter te audio & cum adversariis mihi: etiam in plagis & doloribus intelligo disciplinam: nec me latet, &c. Quid igitur est? Per sal disciplinae hic non (quod ille ineptissimè somniat) intelligit doctrinam
units.tr: 11. Our eleventh and last argument is drawn from the testimony of the saints, who flourished in the Church also in this age. So Cyprian: Let the Christian religion read this one word and meditate on this command, and it will find that the rules of all doctrines have sprung from this Scripture, and that whatever ecclesiastical discipline contains arises from it and returns to it, and that whatever love does not confirm is in every case void and worthless. The Remonstrator replies: By discipline is meant here doctrine, as in the words a little before, f. 8: "I am not unaware that, as you taught me, it has helped to dry up the putrefactions of my corruption"... "the salt of your discipline infused through your Gospel". From this he mocks the Demonstrator, as if he were a reader of Cyprian who was foolish, or who followed another's collection, not having even read Cyprian himself. But the most foolish reader of Cyprian is the Remonstrator himself, as the words immediately preceding show: Speak, good master, I gladly hear you, and with my adversaries too; even in blows and pains I understand discipline; nor am I unaware, etc. What then is the case? By "the salt of discipline" he does not mean (as the Remonstrator foolishly dreams) doctrine, but the discipline of correction.

units.la: L.3.p.166. nam Cyprianus, sed disciplinam correctionis. In testimonio vero nostro perspiciet quivis, doctrinarum regulam & disciplinam ecclesiasticam, quasi res diversas sejunctim poni, & utrasque ex æquo à scriptura derivari. Sic & alibi in negotijs disciplinæ ad scripturam à Cypriano revocamur. Hinc sci sumta & disciplinæ violationes nascuntur: dum ad veritatis originem non creditur, nec caput quaeritur, nec magistri cœlestis doctrina servatur. Innuunt ista doctrinam de disciplina tractatam esse, scripturam disciplinæ caput esse, ut errata in disciplina corrigantur. Quid quod doctrinam de disciplina eam speciatim nominat, quæ episcopatus Anglicani nervos exsecat? Dicit enim in uno puto unam cathedram post pastoribus omnibus æqualem attributam esse, sicut testatur Ri. Fyldus, & Guil. Whitakerus qui in hunc sensum Cyprianum interpretantur. Citatur à Demonstratore testimonium istud Tertulliani. Nobis nihil ex nostro arbitrio inducere licet: sed nec eligere quod aliquis arbitrio suo induxerit: Apostolos Domini habeamus authores qui nec ipsi quicquam à suo arbitrio quod inducerent elegerunt, sed acceptam à Christo disciplinam fideliter nationibus assignarunt. Non autem puto Demonstratorem existimasse disciplinam ecclesiasticam hic speciali-ter nominatam fuisse, quo nomine immeritò apud Remonstratorem vapulat: sed sermonis Tertulliani generalitate innixum suisse: quâ nihil de nostro arbitrio in disciplina eligendum dicit, sive doctrinam contineat illa, sive ecclesiæ disciplinam. Ita Augustinus. Sive de Christo, sive de ecclesia, sive de quacunque alia re quæ pertinet ad fidem vitamque nostram, non dico si nos sed si Angelus de cœlo vobis annunciaverit præterquam quod in scripturis legalibus & Evangelicis accepistis, anathema sit. Johannes Reynoldus dum hanc sententiam Augustini adversus Hartum urget, insistit in eo præcipuè, quod non dicat contrà quàm, sed præterquam, ut non solum quæ contra verbum illicita Augustinus sentiat, sed etiam quæ vel præter scripturam fiunt. Non igitur solum (quod vult Hookerus) quæ in politeia ecclesiastica contra Dei verbum sunt, Pauli & Augustini judicio prohibentur, sed etiam quæ præter verbum geruntur: nam cum ecclesiam Augustinus speciatim nominet, vitamque nostram: quis putarit ecclesiæ disciplinam quæ ad mores dirigendos est destinata, eum excepisse? Sequitur Damasus, quem citat & approbat Richardus Fyldus, qui Chorepiscopos ideo extirpandos confirmat, quod in verbo, eorum ordo authoritatem nullam habeat. Qui ita arguit, nomine omnia officia ecclesiastica etiam regent a in verbo ita posita putat ut alia inducere illicitum sit, præterquam ea quæ in verbo sanciuntur? Verba sunt: eorum institutio omni authoritate caret, idem sunt qui & presbyteri. Non amplius quam duos ordines inter discipulos Domini esse cognovimus id est duodecim Apostolorum, & septuaginta discipulorum: unde iste tertius processerit penitus ignoramus. Et quod ratione caret extirpari necesse est. Referuntur in ius Canonicum ista: in quibus ut quædam erroris sunt proxima, hoc tamen sanum est: quod necesse putetur ut officia omnia ecclesiastica extirpentur, quæ carent authoritate
units.tr: L.3.p.166. For in our testimony anyone will see that the rule of doctrine and ecclesiastical discipline are set down separately as different things, and that both are equally derived from Scripture. So also elsewhere, in matters of discipline, we are recalled by Cyprian to Scripture: Hence both the violations of discipline arise, while there is no belief in the origin of the truth, nor is the head sought, nor is the doctrine of the heavenly Master kept. These words imply that doctrine has been treated about discipline, that Scripture is the head of discipline, so that errors in discipline may be corrected. What of the fact that he names by name the doctrine of discipline that cuts the sinews of the English episcopate? For he says: in one fen, one chair has been assigned to all pastors equally after the apostles, as Richard Field and William Whitaker attest, who interpret Cyprian in this sense. The Demonstrator cites this testimony of Tertullian: It is not allowed to us to bring in anything at our own discretion, nor to choose what someone has brought in at his discretion. We have the apostles of the Lord as authors, who themselves chose nothing at their own discretion to bring in, but faithfully handed down to the nations the discipline received from Christ. Yet I do not think the Demonstrator supposed that ecclesiastical discipline was specially named here, for which reason he is rightly and unjustly lashed by the Remonstrator; rather he relied on the generality of Tertullian's words, by which he says that nothing is to be chosen at our own discretion in discipline, whether that discipline contains doctrine or the discipline of the Church. So Augustine: Whether concerning Christ, or concerning the Church, or concerning any other matter that pertains to our faith and life, I say not "if we", but "if an angel from heaven should announce to you anything besides what you have received in the legal and evangelical Scriptures", let him be anathema. John Reynolds, while urging this saying of Augustine against Hart, insists chiefly on the fact that he does not say contrary to but besides [praeterquam], so that Augustine condemns not only what is unlawful and contrary to the word, but also what is done beside Scripture. Therefore, as Hooker wishes, it is not only what is against the word of God in the ecclesiastical polity that is forbidden by the judgment of Paul and Augustine, but also what is done beside the word. For since Augustine names the Church expressly, and our life too, who would think that he excepted the discipline of the Church, which is destined to direct morals? There follows Damasus, whom Richard Field cites and approves, who confirms that country bishops ought to be rooted out because their order has no authority in the word. He who argues thus, does he think that all ecclesiastical offices, even those regulated by name, are placed in the word in such a way that it is unlawful to introduce others, except those which the word sanctions? The words are: their institution is destitute of all authority; they are the same as presbyters. We know that there were no more than two orders among the disciples of the Lord, that is the twelve apostles and the seventy disciples; whence this third arose we are wholly ignorant. And what lacks reason must necessarily be rooted out. These things are cited in canon law; and although some of them are very close to error, this at least is sound: that it is thought necessary that all ecclesiastical offices which lack authority be rooted out.
