units.la: Hoc si effectum datum in Anglia, vbi quæso Episcopi Anglicani futuri essent: qui per scripturas ijdem cum presbyteris sunt (ut de Chorepiscopis loquitur Damasus & jus Canonicum) & omni ex sacris desumpta ratione carent. Ita Nazianzenus. Nemo sapiat supra quam oportet sapere, neve lege justior, luce splendidior, canone rectior, precepto officiosior videri velit? Loquitur ita de disciplina Ecclesiastica Nazianzenus, sicut ipse Thomas Bilsonus attestatur: qui hæc adfert, ne in controversijs disciplinaris quisquam nostrum, vlla zeli religionisve specie, vltra præceptum, legem, canonem verbi divini nosmet abripi patiamur. Qui ita loquuntur, nonne legem in verbo Dei, nonne præceptum, nonne Canonem, nonne lucem, de disciplina ecclesiastica, tradita esse confitentur? Ita Chrysostomus. Qui non utitur sacra scriptura sed ascendit aliunde, id est, non concessa via, hic non pastor est, sed fur & latro. Impugnat primum Papæ hoc testimonio Iohanues Iuellus, eo quòd à Christo in verbo suo non instituatur. Sed ratio hæc nonne & Episcopos Anglicanos & quodvis præterea officium ecclesiasticum ex Ecclesia exturbat, quod in Dei verbo perinde ac papatus ipse non instituitur? Ita Leo. Exortes sunt mysterij divini qui a Petri soliditate recesserunt. Rursus. Petri forma cunctis ecclesiæ Rectoribus proposita est. Erravit quidem in hypothesi huius formæ Leo: quod tamen exemplar Apostolicæ disciplinæ ligare, & formam quandam disciplinæ ab eisdem propositam innuit, in eo quidem certè sapit, vel Matheo Sutclivio assentiente: qui hinc pontificis primatum iugulat, quod a Petri soliditate recesserit, imò à forma illius quam longissimè recesserit: id quod de Anglicano Episcopatu, & omni alio ecclesiastico officio ab hominibus introducto verissimè aptissimeq; dicitur. Ita Iohannes Gerson. [Nulla potest lingua satis exprimere, quantum malū, quantum periculum, quantam confusionem, sacræ scripturæ contemptus (quæ procul dubio sufficiens est, pro ecclesiæ gubernatione, alias Christus imperfectus legislator esset) & humanorum inventorum affectatio in ecclesiam invexit. Ad huius rei evidentiam consideretur cleri status, cui sapientia cælestis disponsari debuit: sed cum meretrice illa, sapientia humana adulterium commiserunt illi: sic ut status ecclesiæ merè bestialis & monstrosus evaserit: infra cœlum, supra vero terra, subest spiritus, dominatur caro &c. non erubescunt tamen quidam dicere, humanis inventionibus melius ecclesiam gubernari, quam lege divina, & lege Evangelij Christi, quæ assertio blasphema est. Evangelica etenim doctrina, ecclesiæ terminos dilatavit, & ad cœlum sublimavit: quam Hagaræ filij sapientiam illam quærentes, quæ de terra est, ad sterquilinium usque dejecerunt.] Citat ista & approbat Richardus Fyldus Hierarchicus: quæ & sententiam nostram de certa disciplinæ forma in verbo Dei perfectè tradita manifestè confirmant: & politeiam Anglicanam iugulant, imò miseriam quæ & humanam sapientiam in disciplinâ ecclesiasticâ, deformantem
units.tr: If this were put into effect in England, where, I ask, would the English bishops be? They are, by Scripture, the same as presbyters (as Damasus speaks of chorepiscopi, and so does canon law), and they lack every reason drawn from the sacred writings. So Nazianzen: "Let no one think more highly than he ought to think, or wish to seem more just than the law, brighter than the light, more correct than the canon, more dutiful than the precept?" Nazianzen speaks thus about ecclesiastical discipline, as Thomas Bilson himself attests, who cites this: "In controversies about discipline let none of us, under any pretext of zeal or religion, allow himself to be carried beyond the precept, the law, the canon of the divine Word." Do not those who speak thus confess that the law, the precept, the canon and the light concerning ecclesiastical discipline have been handed down in the Word of God? So Chrysostom: "He who does not use Holy Scripture but climbs up by some other way, that is, not by the permitted way, is not a minister but a thief and a robber." John Jewel first attacks the Pope with this testimony, on the ground that it is not instituted by Christ in his word. But does not this argument also cast out of the Church the English bishops and any other ecclesiastical office whatever, which are no more instituted in the Word of God than the papacy itself? So Leo: "They are strangers to the divine mystery who have departed from the firmness of Peter." And again: "The form of Peter is set before all the rulers of the Church." Leo indeed erred in his application of this form, but in indicating that it binds us to the pattern of apostolic discipline, and that a certain form of discipline was laid down by them, he surely showed wisdom, with the agreement of Matthew Sutcliffe, who on this ground demolishes the primacy of the Pontiff: "because he has departed from the firmness of Peter, indeed he has departed as far as possible from his form." This is said most truly and most aptly of the English episcopate and of every other ecclesiastical office introduced by men. So John Gerson: [No tongue can sufficiently express how much evil, how much danger, how much confusion the contempt of Holy Scripture (which is undoubtedly sufficient for the government of the Church, for otherwise Christ would be an imperfect lawgiver) and the pursuit of human inventions have brought into the Church. To see the evidence of this, let the state of the clergy be considered, to whom heavenly wisdom ought to have been betrothed; but they have committed adultery with that harlot, human wisdom, so that the state of the Church has become altogether bestial and monstrous: below heaven, but above the earth, the spirit lies beneath, the flesh rules, and so on. Yet some are not ashamed to say that the Church is governed better by human inventions than by the divine law and the law of the Gospel of Christ, which assertion is blasphemous. For evangelical teaching has enlarged the bounds of the Church and raised it to heaven; those sons of Hagar who seek that wisdom which is of the earth have cast it down even to the dunghill.] Richard Field, in his Of the Church, cites and approves these words, and they plainly confirm our view that a definite form of discipline has been perfectly delivered in the Word of God; they also overthrow the English polity, indeed they depict so vividly the wretchedness which, like the human wisdom that deforms discipline in the Church,

units.la: Serm. in die circumcis. p. 3. mensid. 1. sequi solet;& in regnum Anglicanum per Hierarchiam Episcopalem humanam jam (pro dolor) invecta est, adeo graphicè depingunt, ut nihil supra. Alibi de negotiis disciplinaris loquens adversus papam, ita habet. Superest ut aliqua sit relicta inolliquabilis & indeviabilis regula ab optimo legislatore Christo, secundum quam possit abusus huiusmodi potestatis reprimi, dirigi, atque moderari. Haec autem regula est ecclesia & generale concilium. In hac Hadrianus Saravia ita. Rectè à Gersone notatum fuit ab optimo legislatore Christo in ecclesiam regulam inolliquabilem Gretserus relictam esse: sed sacrae scripturae sint illa regula &c. In hac sententia fuerunt ij qui Petro Aliaco attestante, in concilio Constantiensi, & longè ante ordinem Cardinalium tollendum putarunt, quod nec a Christo, nec ab Apostolis institutus esset, sicut olim de statu Corepiscoporum factum erat. Citatur a D. Mornaeo & approbatur Budaeus, cuius ista de certa disciplinae forma in verbo tradita, sententia est. Navis nobis disciplinae socialis ac civilis à Servatore relicta est ecclesiae conditore, quae continuo ministerio, instrumento gubernaculi, instructa fuit ab ipso, aut eius auspicijs. Statim etiam à puppi pollicitus est, ad exoptatum locum rectores perlaturum, si clavem certum tenere, si nusquam non spiritui afflaturo pandere ecclesia porrexisset: (sacras utique scripturas à Spiritu sancto profectas contulisset.) Accedant Hierarchici. Thomas Bilsonus ita. Hijs quae dixi non est consequens ut politiam ecclesiasticam, quam nobiscunque libeat, ex ingenio nostro fingamus, quin potius danda est opera ut externam administrationem in ecclesia regenda eam observemus quam Dominus noster ipse docuit. Quam verò postiam in externa forma ecclesiae gubernandae Dominus ab initio sanxit, obscurum esse non poterit, si sacras literas consulamus. Ita Richardus Bancroftus. Conclusio mea aedificabitur, supra unam de Demonstrativis propositionibus Johannis Vitalli. Illud regimen ecclesiae cuius origo ignota est nullam habet authoritatem à verbo Dei sed illicitum est. Postremo ita Hadrianus Saravia. Non ignoramus ab Apostolis perfectam ecclesiae formam traditam: & quid sit de hac re nostra sententia, jam diximus. Unde nos intulimus & consequens esse diximus ut illa omnia manerent in ecclesia, per quae aedificatum inter verbi Dei praedicatio, sacramentorum administratio, cum ea regiminis forma quae fuit ab initio sub Apostolis, nec ostenditur vel mutata, vel inhibita posteris. His omnibus argumentis, constat unam quandam certam regiminis Ecclesiastici formam à Christo, in verbo, traditam & institutam esse.
units.tr: ...usually follows, and which has now (alas) been introduced into the English kingdom through the episcopal hierarchy, that nothing could be added. Speaking elsewhere of matters of discipline, against the Pope, he says: "It remains that some unbreakable and unerring rule has been left by Christ, the best of lawgivers, by which the abuse of such power may be restrained, directed and moderated. This rule is the Church and a general council." Adrian Saravia, on this point: "It was rightly noted by Gerson that an unbreakable rule was left to the Church by Christ, the best of lawgivers; but let the sacred Scriptures be that rule, etc." Among those who held this view, as Pierre d'Ailly testifies, at the Council of Constance, and long before, were those who thought that the order of cardinals, which was not instituted by Christ or the apostles, should be abolished, as had once been done with the status of the chorepiscopi. Mornay cites it and Budé approves it; his opinion on a definite form of discipline delivered in the Word is this: "The ship of social and civil discipline has been left to us by the Saviour, the founder of the Church; it was equipped from the start by him, or under his auspices, with a continuous ministry and the instrument of the helm. He promised too, straight from the stern, that he would bring the rulers to the desired place, if the Church would hold the key firmly and open itself to the breath of the Spirit wherever it blows" (that is, if it had embraced the Holy Scriptures, which proceed from the Holy Spirit). Let the advocates of the hierarchy come forward. Thomas Bilson: "It does not follow from what I have said that we should invent for ourselves an ecclesiastical polity as we please; rather, we must take care to observe in the external administration of the Church that which our Lord himself taught. What polity the Lord ordained from the beginning for the external form of governing the Church cannot be unclear, if we consult the sacred letters." So Richard Bancroft: "My conclusion is built upon one of the demonstrative propositions of John Vitelli: that form of church government whose origin is unknown has no authority from the Word of God, but is unlawful." Lastly, Adrian Saravia: "We are not unaware that a perfect form of the Church was handed down by the apostles; and what our opinion on this matter is, we have already said. Hence we have concluded, and said it follows, that all those things should remain in the Church by which the preaching of the Word of God and the administration of the sacraments are built up, together with that form of government which existed from the beginning under the apostles, and it is not shown to have been either changed or forbidden to posterity." From all these arguments it is established that a certain definite form of ecclesiastical government has been handed down and instituted by Christ in the Word.

units.la: CAP. XLI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLI.

units.la: Argumenta Hierarchica dissolvuntur.
units.tr: The Hierarchical arguments are refuted.

units.la: Svperest ut adversa Hierarchicorum argumenta dissolvamus. Prima objectio est à circumstantijs Politeias: hoc etenim perpetuum apud Whitgiftum, Hookerum, Sutclivium, reliquosq; Sophisma est: non esse certam Politeias formam in verbo speciatim.
units.tr: It remains for us to dissolve the arguments of the Hierarchists. The first objection is drawn from the circumstances of the polity. This is a fallacy that runs constantly through Whitgift, Hooker, Sutcliffe and the rest: that there is no particular fixed form of polity in the Word.

units.la: Quid igitur? ipsa fundamentalia Ecclesiastici regiminis in lege Christi omittebantur? Libertas nostra, respondet Whitgiftus, liberationem postulat à tam exiētā legum normā: imo libertatem à Christo partam, à servitute Iudaica, pedibus proculcant, inquit Lous, qui certam formam Politicas in verbo contineri affirmant. Non opus est multis. In legibus Mosaicis duo sunt, multitudo & directio: multitudo onus erat, directio beneficium: hinc sequitur libertatem nostram à servitute Iudaica in eo versari, quòd à multitudine observationum Mosaicarum liberamur: directio beneficium cum sit, tam exactam normam Politicas iam habemus, quam quæ apud Iudæos erat; aut Ecclesia nostra deficit & illā Iudaicā inferior est. Hinc comparationi huic acquiescit Hn. Saravia. Quum etenim urgeret D. Beza certam esse à Christo sub Evangelio constitutam regiminis Ecclesiastici formam quemadmodum olim à Mose fuerat, respondet ille: Meam sententiam confirmat quisquis ita scribit & loquitur: & facile idem sentiremus, si eandem gubernationis formam quā Apostoli usi sunt retentam fuisse Genevæ, & in aliis Ecclesiis Galliæ & inferioris Germaniæ observari, doceri possit. Imo quid ipse Matheus Sutclivius. Contemptim quidem loquitur ille in tractatu suo de disciplina de hoc argumento nostro, à Mosis & Christi comparatione desumpto c.12. p.152. in libro vero de presbyterio c.11. ulterius progreditur: contendit etenim Christum legislatorem non esse ut Moses erat, in externis præsertim, sed Mediatorem tantum. Sed adversus Bellarminum disputans, novus homo emergit. Quid Bellarminus? eodem nempe fundamento nititur, quo Hierarchici, non esse scilicet eandem rationem novi testamenti, quæ veteris, legi Mosis non licuisse addere, Evangelio licere. Quid ita? Audi eam ipsam Hierarchicorum cantilenam. Quia Deus in lege omnia determinavit in speciali, in novo autem testamento latæ sunt leges communissimæ, quæ specialiter per Apostolos & eorum successores pro locorum & temporum diversitate determinandæ essent. Quid ad hæc Sutclivius. Recipe defensionem plane nostram iisque totidem verbis. Hæc ne ipsa adversus Christum contumeliosa est. Cur enim ille perfectiorem non dedit legem quam Moses, præsertim cum Mosi longè præstaret? Præterea repugnat perfectioni Evangelii. Nam si omnia specialiter in lege præcepta sunt, & nihil fere in Evangelio ut ipse subindicat, tunc erit lex Mosis Evangelio præstantior: quod tamen nec verum est, nec à Bellarmino conceditur. At intelligit ista de fide tantum & sacramentis Sutclius. Etiam loquitur generatim, & Politeiam includit, ut demonstrant sequentia. Postremò hæc responsio Bellarmini falsa est: nam non magis licet Evangelii legi addere, quam legi Mosis. Nec obstat quòd à concilijs & pijs principibus aliquæ leges de rebus Ecclesiasticis additæ sunt: Illæ enim non sunt additiones ad legem Dei, nec in conscientia obligabant, nisi quatenus aliquid de lege Dei participabant. Ita conficitur, certam quandam Politicas formam quoad substantialia in Evangelio contineri, quia in lege continebatur. 6 Argumentum nostrum sextum à subiecto politicas Ecclesiasticæ ducitur, ecclesia nempe, quae vineae, domui, civitati, corpori deniq; assimilatur, sic ut illius custodes, politeia, oeconomi, partes deniq; essentiales in verbo Dei ut ordinentur necesse est. Respondet ad ista attributa conjunctim Hookerus: ea non implicare certam immutabilemque formam disciplinae, quia vel nobis ipsis fatentibus, quaedam in politeia ecclesiastica sunt minoris momenti, quae alterationem pati possunt. Quàm jejunè? Quomodo enim sequitur, custodes vineae, politeiam essentialem civitatis, oeconomos comus, partes essentiales corporis mutari posse, quod quaedam minoris momenti, vineae, civitatis, domus negotia, & habitus externus corporis nonnunquam immutari possint? Videamus de singulis separatim. Primò vinea Domini dicitur ecclesia, quam ab ipso Deo per politeiam excultam legimus, Isa. 5. 2. 3. 4. praecipuè verò Cant 8. 4. Vinea est Salomoni in loco fertile, locat vineam suam custodibus, quisque affert pro fructu eius mille nos siclos argenti. Vineae, quae mea est, apud me permanent, &c. Quum anno 1606. relige-rentur à rege, qui pro disciplina Anglicana, coram ministris tum praesentibus, concionarentur: demandatum Iohanni Kingo erat, qui nunc est Episcopus Londinensis, ut contra Seniores & presbyterium declamitaret. Textum verò sumpsit ille hunc ipsum ex Canticis locum: & nullam vineae certam gubernationis formam à Solomone Vineae domino constitutam esse, asseveravit. Num hoc in textu reperit? imò nonne textu ipso hoc Gl ssema confutatur? Vera etenim Francisci Lamp expositio (cui ille nihil respondet.) Ne rex quidem ipse ut vineam habeat sus carissimam, eam aut i se potest colere, aut totum illius fructum percipere, sed colendam aliis locat, & aliquid eis de proventu tenetur attribuere: ego vero inquit sponsus neque aliis colendam loco, neque mihi quicquam de ei detrahi sinum, adeo sum illius Zelotypus, sed oculi mei semper versantur in ea, & fructus illius nè tantillum quidem alienari sino, aut aliena voluntate administrari. Vide igitur huius hominis oscitantiam, qui nec textum quidem suum intellexit. Salomonem etenim ver. 4. suam vineam locantem alijs, intelligit Christum suam Ecclesiam custodibus locantem: cum contra manifesta hic antithesis inter Salomonem atque Christum instituatur, sic ut Salomon quidem vineam suam locat alijs, permittens eam aliena voluntate administrari: Christus vero Ecclesiam non locat, sed ipse per sese eam colit, permittens nemini voluntate sua rem administrare: sed pro speciali ipsius amore & Zelotypia, curam Illius in seipsam suscipiens. Non igitur vel Zelotypia in suam vineam specialis, vel potestas in eandem Christi locata nemini, vel fructuum denique reservatio permittet, ut Politeiae ejusdem constitutionem arbitrio hominum reliquisse videatur: praesertim cum Politeia Ecclesiae, medium illud sit quo fructus proventusque ubertim affluunt, quas sibi soli reservasse hic Christus affirmatur.
units.tr: What then? Were the fundamental principles of ecclesiastical government left out of the law of Christ? "Our liberty," answers Whitgift, "demands freedom from so strict a rule of laws." Nay, says Lous, "those who maintain that a fixed form of polity is contained in the Word trample underfoot the liberty won for us by Christ from Jewish bondage." There is no need for many words. In the Mosaic laws there are two things, multitude and direction. The multitude was a burden, the direction a benefit. It follows that our liberty from Jewish bondage consists in this, that we are freed from the multitude of Mosaic observances. Since direction is a benefit, we now have as exact a rule of polity as the one the Jews had, or else our Church is lacking and inferior to that Jewish one. Hence Hadrian Saravia agrees with this comparison. When Dr Beza urged that a fixed form of ecclesiastical government had been established by Christ under the Gospel, just as it had once been established by Moses, Saravia replied: "Whoever writes and speaks in this way confirms my opinion, and we would easily agree with it, if it could be shown that the same form of government which the Apostles used was retained at Geneva and is observed in the other churches of France and Lower Germany." Nay, what does Matthew Sutcliffe himself say? He speaks contemptuously of this argument of ours, drawn from the comparison of Moses and Christ, in his treatise on discipline, chapter 12, page 152. But in his book on the presbytery, chapter 11, he goes further. He contends that Christ was not a lawgiver as Moses was, especially in external matters, but only a Mediator. Yet when he disputes against Bellarmine, he emerges as a new man. What does Bellarmine say? He rests on the same foundation as the Hierarchists, namely that the New Testament does not have the same reason as the Old: it was not lawful to add to the law of Moses, but it is lawful to add to the Gospel. Why so? Hear that very song of the Hierarchists: "Because God determined everything in the law in particular, but in the New Testament the laws were given in the most general terms, which were to be determined in particular by the Apostles and their successors according to the diversity of places and times." What does Sutcliffe reply to this? Take up our defence, which is entirely ours, in these very words: "Is this not itself insulting to Christ? For why did he not give a more perfect law than Moses, especially since he far surpassed Moses? Moreover, it contradicts the perfection of the Gospel. For if everything is commanded in particular in the law, and almost nothing in the Gospel, as he himself hints, then the law of Moses will be more excellent than the Gospel, which is not true, nor is it granted by Bellarmine." But Sutcliffe understands these words only of faith and the sacraments. Yet he speaks generally, and includes polity, as the following shows: "Finally, this answer of Bellarmine is false: for it is no more lawful to add to the Gospel than to the law of Moses. Nor is it an obstacle that some laws concerning ecclesiastical matters have been added by councils and godly princes. For these are not additions to the law of God, nor did they bind the conscience except insofar as they shared in something of the law of God." Thus it is established that a certain fixed polity, as to its essentials, is contained in the Gospel, because it was contained in the law. 6 Our sixth argument is drawn from the subject of ecclesiastical polity, namely the Church, which is compared to a vineyard, a house, a city, and finally a body. Thus its keepers, its polity, its stewards and finally its essential parts must necessarily be ordained in the Word of God. Hooker answers these attributes together: they do not imply a fixed and unchangeable form of discipline, because, as we ourselves admit, some things in ecclesiastical polity are of minor importance and can undergo alteration. How feebly! For how does it follow that the keepers of a vineyard, the essential polity of a city, and the stewards of a house, and the essential parts of a body, can be changed, merely because certain things of minor importance, such as the affairs of a vineyard, a city or a house, and the external habit of the body, can sometimes be changed? Let us look at each separately. First, the vineyard of the Lord is the Church, which we read was cultivated by God himself through polity, Isaiah 5:2-4, and especially Song of Songs 8:4: "Solomon has a vineyard in a fertile place; he leases the vineyard to keepers, each one bringing for its fruit a thousand shekels of silver. My vineyard, which is mine, remains with me," etc. In the year 1606, when the king was addressing ministers, who were then present, in favour of the English discipline, the task was given to John King, who is now Bishop of London, to declaim against the elders and the presbytery. He took as his text this very passage from the Song of Songs, and he asserted that no fixed form of government had been established for the vineyard by Solomon, its lord. Does he find this in the text? Rather, is this gloss not refuted by the text itself? For the true exposition is that of Francis Lamp, to which he makes no reply: "Not even the king himself, who has a most dear vineyard, can cultivate it himself or receive all its fruit, but he leases it to others to cultivate, and is bound to assign them some of its produce. But I, says the bridegroom, neither leave it to others to cultivate, nor allow anything of it to be taken from me, so jealous am I of it; my eyes are always upon it, and I do not allow even the smallest part of its fruit to be alienated or administered by another's will." See, then, the carelessness of this man, who did not even understand his own text. For in verse 4 he takes Solomon, leasing his vineyard to others, to mean Christ leasing his Church to keepers. Yet a clear antithesis is set up here between Solomon and Christ: Solomon leases his vineyard to others, permitting it to be administered by another's will; but Christ does not lease the Church, he cultivates it himself, permitting no one to administer the matter according to his own will, but taking up its care himself out of his special love and jealousy for it. Therefore neither a special jealousy for his own vineyard, nor a power over it which Christ has leased to no one, nor finally a reservation of its fruits, would allow it to seem that he has left the constitution of that polity to the judgment of men. Especially since the polity of the Church is the means by which the fruits and produce flow in abundance, which Christ is said to have reserved for himself alone.

units.la: 2 Secundo, civitas Ecclesia dicitur regis magni: & civitatis anima (inquit Hookerus ex persona nostra) Politeia est. Adjicit in margine
units.tr: 2 Second, the Church is called the city of the great King, and the soul of the city (says Hooker, speaking in our person) is the polity. He adds in the margin

units.la: Guilielmi Traversij verba: Nisi reipublicæ suæ statum omnem Christus constituerit, magistratus ordinarit, singulorum munera potestatemque descripserit, quæ judiciorum forum ratio habenda, quomodo civium finiendæ lites: non solum minus Ecclesiæ Christianæ providit, quam Moses olim Iudaicæ, sed quam à Lycurgo, Salomone, Numa, civitatibus suis prospectum fuit. Ponit ista odiose Hookerus, sed cur non refellit? Certè refelli ista non possunt, id quod etiam in Cornelio Scultingio videre est, qui licet thesim Traversianam sibi refutandam suscepisset, & disciplinam in verbo non perfectè contineri asseruisset: ad hoc tamen illius argumentum, respondet omnino nihil. Tertiò, Ecclesia domus Dei est, 1. Tim. 3. 15. Heb. 3. 3. 4. & quænam domus benè constituta ordine caret quo gubernatur? In domo quisquam œconomios constituit præter patremfamilias? Numerus, gradus, ordo, habitus, servorum Salomonis, tot illius sapientiæ testimonia erant: quomodo ergo verisimile fiat, Christum majorem Salomone, non eam certam domus suæ gubernandæ rationem reliquisse, in qua quasi in speculo, sapientia, cura, & illius providentia erga Ecclesiam suâ reluceret. Hæc Hookerus ex persona nostra: quibus tamen ne verbum quidem respondet. Respondet Remonstrator plurima in quaque domo œconomi arbitrio discretionique relinqui solere: quod ipsum causam non attingit. Quæstio etenim nostra non de rebus minoris momenti est: nam circumstantias individuales Ecclesiæ arbitrio relictas esse confitemur: sed de ipso domus Dei regimine, imò de œconomis ipsis, quorum designationem domus œconomis relictam esse quis unquam audivit? Luc. 12. 12. Quisnam est dispensator fidelis & prudens quem constituit dominus ejus super familiam suam, ut det portionem eius in tempore suo. Ecce rectores domus, ipse dominus constituit. Quo etiam pertinet calamus ille Apoc. 11. Datus Angelo ad metiendam domum Dei: ostendit etenim non absque calamo relictam esse Ecclesiam Dei, vel quoad regimen: nam de mensuratione regiminis adversus Antichristi tyrannidem, peræque ac adversus hæresim de mensuratione ipsius fidei, agit hoc in loco vates. Sic nempè decuerat, nè domus posterior, priori cederet: de qua singuls in Dei verbo descripta fuisse, testatur David, 1. Chron. 28. 12. 13. 19. Tunc tradidit Salomoni filio suo structuram domus, & omnium quæ erant penes eum per spiritum de atrys Iehovæ, etiam pro distributionibus sacerdotum & Levitarum & pro omni opere ad ministerium domus Iehovæ. ——Hæc omnia descripta à manu Iehovæ incumbere mihi instruxit me; omnia opera huius structuræ. Quid multis? Concedit hic pedib. in sententiam nostram adversariorum omnium acerrimus, Matheus ipse Sutclivius: sic etenim adversus Bellarm. scribit: Dubium non est quin universam domum suam & omnes ejus ministros Christus perfectè constituerit & descripserit. Quare cum Pontifex nullum suæ iurisdictionis mandatum ostendere possit, ipsa nulla est. Neque enim ulla maior est nullitas: quàm quæ ex defectu iuris est. Nonne & ministros regentes perfectè à Christo institutos asserit, contra Pseudoregentem regentem disputans? Nonne nullitatem jurisdictionis (puta in Episcopis) ponit,ubi nullum in verbo mandatum extat? Postremò, corpori assimilatur Ecclesia,quod & concedit Richardus Hookerus, sed nihil tamen pro certa regiminis forma facere contendit: quia Politeia, tantum hujus corporis vestitus & ornatus est, qui immutari & variari sine piaculo ullo potest. At officia Ecclesiastica pastores,nempe, Seniores,& Diaconos,pro quibus contendimus, non vestitum hujus corporis sed membra vocat, Rom.12.5. sic ut Christus ea omnia in verbo formare instar figuli censendus sit: quemadmodum in corpore naturali,formare & figurare singula ejus membra,creator Deus dicitur.
units.tr: the words of William Traver: Unless Christ himself has established the whole state of his commonwealth, ordained the magistrates, and described the duties and powers of each, and what method of judgment is to be observed, and how the disputes of citizens are to be settled, then he has provided less for the Christian Church than Moses once provided for the Jewish one, and less than Lycurgus, Solomon and Numa provided for their cities. Hooker sets this down spitefully, but why does he not refute it? Certainly these things cannot be refuted, as may be seen also in Cornelius Schultingius, who, although he undertook to refute Travers's thesis for himself and asserted that discipline is not fully contained in the Word, nevertheless makes absolutely no reply to this argument of his. Third, the Church is the house of God, 1 Tim. 3:15, Heb. 3:3-4. And what well-ordered house lacks the order by which it is governed? Does anyone appoint stewards in a house except the master of the family? The number, grades, order and habits of Solomon's servants were so many witnesses to his wisdom. How then is it likely that Christ, greater than Solomon, left no certain rule for governing his house, in which his wisdom, care and providence toward the Church would shine forth as in a mirror? Hooker says this in our person, yet he does not answer it with a single word. The Remonstrant replies that in every house a great deal is usually left to the judgment and discretion of the steward. That very answer does not touch the cause. For our question is not about matters of minor importance: we admit that the individual circumstances of the Church have been left to its judgment. Our question is about the very government of God's house, indeed about the stewards themselves. Who has ever heard that the appointment of the stewards of a house was left to the steward? Luke 12:42: "Who then is the faithful and wise steward whom the lord has set over his household, to give them their portion of food in due season?" Behold, the rulers of the house: the Lord himself appointed them. To this also pertains that reed in Revelation 11: "Given to the angel to measure the house of God." For it shows that the Church of God was not left without a measuring reed, even as to its government. For the prophet in this place deals with the measuring of government against the tyranny of Antichrist, just as he deals with the measuring of the faith itself against heresy. So it was fitting, lest the later house should yield to the former. That each part of it was described in God's Word is attested by David, 1 Chronicles 28:12-13, 19: "Then he gave to Solomon his son the pattern of the house, and of all that was in him by the Spirit, of the courts of Jehovah, and of the divisions of the priests and Levites, and of all the work for the service of the house of Jehovah. ... All these things were described by the hand of Jehovah, who instructed me, all the works of this pattern." Why say more? Matthew Sutcliffe himself, the most bitter of all our adversaries, concedes to our view with both feet. For thus he writes against Bellarmine: "There is no doubt but that Christ has perfectly established and described his whole house and all its ministers. Therefore, since the Pope can show no mandate of his jurisdiction, it is null. For there is no greater nullity than that which comes from a lack of right." Does he not also assert that the ruling ministers were perfectly instituted by Christ, when he disputes against the false ruling elder? Does he not also set down the nullity of jurisdiction (namely in bishops), where no mandate exists in the Word? Finally, the Church is compared to a body, which Richard Hooker also concedes, but he nevertheless contends that this does nothing for a fixed form of government, because polity is only the clothing and ornament of this body, which can be changed and varied without any sin. But the ecclesiastical offices, namely the pastors, that is the elders and deacons, for which we contend, he calls not the clothing of this body but its members, Rom. 12:5. So Christ is to be regarded as having formed all of them in the Word, like a potter, just as in a natural body God the Creator is said to form and shape its individual members.

units.la: 8 Argumentum nostrum septimum, ab officio principis & capitis ecclesiæ Iesu Christi derivatur: nonne etenim regis est sancire leges ut regnū quā optimè suū gubernetur? Quid aliud sonat ab Isaia illa.9 7.Iusticia & iudicio Christū regnū suū stabilire?Quidaliud,illa Pauli, 1. Cor.12.4.Christū ut Dominū & ministrationes pro regenda Ecclesia sua instituisse?Quid aliud deniq; illa Iacobi 4.12.Vnus est legislator, nēpē Deus? Respondet Lous. Quod de uno legislatore dicitur id de legislatore primario est intelligendum: aliter, legislatores secundarios esse nemo inficiabitur,nisi qui ipsum magistratum sustulerit. Respondeo, eandem esse hanc distinctionem de legislatore primario & secundario quae illa Bellarmini & Stapletoni est, de capite & fundamento ecclesiæ primario & secundario. Num magistratum quaeso tollunt scriptores nostri qui distinctionem hanc exsibilant? Manere potest in negotijs suis legislator magistratus, ut Deus interim in negotijs Iehovæ, 2. Chron. 19.11 legislator solus agnoscatur. Atque cum blasphemare papistas dicunt nostri,cum papam secundarium quasi caput sub Christo substituant: ita parum a blasphemia absunt Hierarchici,cum sub Christo primario legislatore, prælatos Ecclesiæ quasi legislatores supponunt secundarios: in negotijs politeias illius, quæ quidē essentialia sunt. Sed cautior fortè Matheus Sutclivius, inter quem & Lounm,ista notabilis contradictio est. Primarium siquidem legislatorem agnoscit Christum Lous, in politeia ecclesiæ suæ constituenda,quem nec regem omninò,nec legislatorem Matheus Sutclivius ferre potest. Ita enim habet. In isto homine personato (adversarium intelligit,contra quem scribit) quis ferret Christum Redemptorem, in novum, in rebus externis legislatorem converti? Rursus, Christus leges nullas Ecclesiasticas tulit. Iterum, Ego nulla ratione Christum externæ ecclesiæ politeiæ legislatorem dici posse demonstrato. Postremò. Christus quoad externam ecclesiæ politeiam dicendus non est rex & legislator. Miraris hæc tam salsa iuxta ac impia tanto Theologo excidisse? Non habent extrema pudorem. Non ex sensu suo sobrie scripsit ista Sutclivius,sed studio contradicendi abreptus, suasque partes defendendi: quod vel hinc constat,quod contra Bellarmi nū disputans, ut imminueret potestatem papæ quam illi attribuit in legibus ferendis, contrarium prorsus ponit. Sic enim scribit. Sicut unus legislator, ita una essentialis ecclesiae gubernatio, reipublicae verò forma varia. Rursus. Nullae ecclesiae gubernationis leges, certae & immutabiles nisi à Christo: nam is ecclesiae legislator est, isque solus.
units.tr: 8 Our seventh argument is derived from the office of the prince and head of the Church, Jesus Christ. Is it not the task of a king to enact laws so that his kingdom may be governed as well as possible? What else does that saying of Isaiah 9.7 mean, Christ establishes his kingdom with justice and judgement? What else does that of Paul, 1 Cor. 12.4, mean, Christ as Lord instituted ministries for governing his Church? And finally, what else does that of James 4.12 mean, There is one lawgiver, namely God? Lous replies: What is said of one lawgiver must be understood of the primary lawgiver; otherwise no one will deny that there are secondary lawgivers, unless he has abolished the magistracy itself. I answer that this distinction between a primary and a secondary lawgiver is the same as that of Bellarmine and Stapleton between the primary and secondary head and foundation of the Church. Do our writers, I ask, who scoff at this distinction, abolish the magistrate? The magistrate may remain a lawgiver in his own affairs, just as God meanwhile is acknowledged as the sole lawgiver in the affairs of Jehovah, 2 Chron. 19.11. And just as our men say the Papists blaspheme when they set up the pope as a secondary head under Christ, so the Hierarchists are not far from blasphemy when they set up the prelates of the Church as secondary lawgivers under Christ the primary lawgiver, in the affairs of his polity, which are indeed essential. But Matthew Sutcliffe is perhaps more cautious, and between him and Lous there is a notable contradiction. For Lous acknowledges Christ as the primary lawgiver in constituting the polity of his Church, whereas Matthew Sutcliffe cannot bear him as king at all, nor as lawgiver. For he says: In that personated man (he means the adversary against whom he writes), who would tolerate Christ the Redeemer being turned into a lawgiver in external matters? Again: Christ enacted no ecclesiastical laws. Again: I can demonstrate by no reasoning that Christ can be called the lawgiver of the external polity of the Church. Lastly: Christ is not to be called king and lawgiver with regard to the external polity of the Church. Are you surprised that such things, as false as they are impious, fell from so great a theologian? They have no shame at the extremes. Sutcliffe did not write these things soberly from his own judgement; he was carried away by the urge to contradict and to defend his own side. This is evident even from the fact that when disputing against Bellarmine, in order to diminish the power the pope claimed for himself in enacting laws, he asserts the exact opposite. For he writes thus: As there is one lawgiver, so there is one essential government of the Church, but the form of the commonwealth is various. And again: There are no laws of church government that are certain and unchangeable except those from Christ; for he is the lawgiver of the Church, and he alone.

units.la: 9 Argumentum nostrum octavum, à materia essentialium illorum ducitur, quae perfectè a Christo in verbo suo instituta asseveramus: quae à D.Theodoro Beza ita posita sunt. Ecclesiastica inquit administrationis essentialia, duabus praecipue in rebus, posita sunt: nempè in ipsis perpetuis muneribus sacris, & in eorundem accurata & distincta descriptione, ad quam eorum usus est referendus. Ad hoc respondens Hadrianus Saravia ea praeclara esse testatur, & nihil contra suam sententiam tacere. Nec mirum. Nam cum Apostolus hanc vocationem suam licitam probet, quod non ab hominibus sed à Deo ipsius Apostolatus esset. Gal. 1.1. hoc supponit pro fundamento, omnes licitas vocationes à Deo esse, quae verò ab hominibus sunt, & aliunde instituuntur eas esse illicitas. Notum hoc ipsis Pharisaeis & Scribis: illicitum etenim ministerium Iohannis hinc probant quod authoritatem in verbo Dei nullam haberet: atque Iohannes, supponens eos verum praesumsisse, in verbo fundari ministerium suum docet Ioh. 1: 23. Falsò ratiocinati sunt Scribae & Pharisei, dicit Whitgiftus: & nos ex responso Iohannis inconsequenter arguimus, respondet Remonstrator: sed rationem nullam adferunt, sicut nec adferre possunt. Quae etenim ratio deprimere illa Christi poterit. Math. 21.25. in quibus supponens ministerium quodvis illicitum esse quod est ab hominibus institutum: ministerium Iohannis idcirco licitum docet, quod esset à caelo, id est, à Deo, in suo verbo stabilitum. Hinc pertinent illa Pauli Heb. 5.5. Nemo (ne ipse Christus quidem Filius Dei) honorem sibi in ecclesia sumit, nisi qui vocatus est, ut Aaron: fuit autem ministerium Aaronis in verbo constitutum. Deridet hanc rationem nostram in tractatu suo de disciplina Matheus Sutclivius: adversus verò Bellarminum disputans pro more suo approbat. Sic enim scribit. Imò nec Christus Iesus, licet Filius Dei pontificatum suum assumpsit nisi missus: nec ecclesiae administrationem suscepit, nisi à patre Ecclesiae praepositus. Quod si ergo nec Christus Iesus sine patris mandato suum assumsit pontificatum: temerè faciunt qui ecclesiae pontificatum generalem assumunt sine mandato. In ecclesia enim Dei nemo sibi honorem sumit, nisi qui missus est quemadmodum Aaron: Proferant ergo pontifices Romani mandatum Domini: ostendant missionem suam: doceant se à Domino ecclesiae universali praepositos. Quid cessant? quid tacent? cur tergi versantur? Eodé in capite post. Refellitur inquit pontificum Romanorum principatus, quia non est ex Christi institutione. Postremò, ideo pontificium authoritatem illicitam probat, quia dici illi potest ex Roberto Gallo. Quis posuit idolum hoc in sede mea, ut imperuret gregi meo? & ad illum accommodari possit Tertullianii illud. Qui estis? quomodo & unde venistis? quid in meo agitis non meis? Quin & noster hac quidem in re Remonstrator est. Non negamus quin omnes legitimae vocationes authoritatem habeant ex verbo Dei, etsi est non totidem verbis. Quod vero dicit non totidem verbis, id hujus sententiae mentem non mutat. Sic est alibi. Directa authoritas, vel immediata est ex ipsi Dei voce, vel mediata per directam consequentiam ex verbo collecta: sic omnis vocatio ex verbo deducibilis est.
units.tr: 9 Our eighth argument is drawn from the matter of those essentials, which we affirm were perfectly instituted by Christ in his Word; as D. Theodore Beza sets them out: The essentials of ecclesiastical administration, he says, rest chiefly on two things: namely, on the perpetual sacred offices themselves, and on their accurate and distinct description, to which their use is to be referred. Replying to this, Adrian Saravia testifies that these are excellent points and that he says nothing against his own opinion. This is no surprise. For when the Apostle proves his calling lawful, because his apostleship was from God and not from men, Gal. 1.1, he assumes as a foundation that all lawful callings are from God, and that those which come from men and are instituted otherwise are unlawful. The Pharisees and Scribes themselves knew this well: they proved the ministry of John unlawful because it had no authority in God's Word; and John, supposing they had reasoned rightly, teaches that his ministry is grounded in the Word, John 1.23. The Scribes and Pharisees reasoned falsely, says Whitgift; and we argue inconsequently from John's answer, replies the Remonstrator. But they bring no reason, and indeed they cannot. For what reason could overturn that answer of Christ, Matt. 21.25? In it, assuming that every ministry instituted by men is unlawful, he teaches that John's ministry was lawful for this reason: that it was from heaven, that is, from God, established in his Word. To this belong those words of Paul, Heb. 5.5: No one (not even Christ himself, the Son of God) takes honour to himself in the Church, unless he is called, as Aaron was. Aaron's ministry, however, was established in the Word. Matthew Sutcliffe mocks this argument of ours in his treatise on discipline; yet when disputing against Bellarmine he approves it in his own way. For he writes thus: Indeed neither did Christ Jesus, although he was the Son of God, assume his priesthood unless he was sent, nor did he undertake the administration of the Church unless he was appointed by the Father of the Church. If therefore Christ Jesus did not assume his priesthood without the Father's command, those who take up the general priesthood of the Church without a command act rashly. For in the Church of God no one takes honour to himself unless he is sent, as Aaron was. Let the Roman pontiffs therefore produce the command of the Lord; let them show their mission; let them teach that they have been placed over the universal Church by the Lord. Why do they hesitate? Why are they silent? Why do they turn their backs? In the same chapter, later: The principate of the Roman pontiffs is refuted, he says, because it is not from the institution of Christ. Finally, he proves the papal authority unlawful because the words of Robert Gallus can be said to it: Who placed this idol in my seat, to rule over my flock? and that saying of Tertullian can be applied to it: Who are you? How and whence did you come? What are you doing in my affairs, which are not yours? Indeed our own Remonstrator agrees with this on the point: We do not deny that all lawful callings have their authority from the Word of God, though it is not in so many words. That he says "not in so many words" does not change the sense of this opinion. So elsewhere: Direct authority, or immediate authority, is from the very voice of God, or mediate through a direct consequence drawn from the Word: thus every calling can be deduced from the Word.

units.la: 10 Argumentum nostrum nonum à regiminis ecclesiastici fine vsq; ducitur. Eiusdem etenim est & finem & media ad finem constituere: sicut finem regiminis precisè in verbo Christus sanxerit, & politeiam etiam ecclesiae quae est eiusdem finis medium, ut sanciverit, censendus est. Finis vero politeias, ecclesiae salus atque aedificatio est: & quis putarit, absque certis medijs omnibus, eisque certò constitutis, ecclesiam orbam Christum Iesum reliquisse? Quid quod politeia, vt cetera media omnia, non nisi gratiarum suppeditatione, & coelesti benedictione ad finem suum valent? Gratiam suppeditare alicui officio ecclesiastico, homo non potest: ergo nec officium aliquod constituere. Certè pro varietate gratiarum, varietatem administrationum in verbo constitutam videamus: & officia Ecclesiastica ipsa, dona sunt Eph.4.12.1. Cer: 12, 5. Rom.12. 5.6: sic ut de Christi & potentia & liberalitate derogetur plurimum, si penes hominem sit, ac non penes Christum solum eadem constituere. Quod ad benedictionem vero, uti tum benedixit Moses tabernaculo, quando omnia structa vidisset iuxta formam illam quae ei in monte ostensa est, Exod:39.43. ita tum & non aliter benedicit regimini Ecclesiastico Christus, quando omnia ad amussim verbi sui composita & ordinata videt. Nulla ab illo aurora expectanda quando verbum illius non asseritur Is: 8: 20. imo humanis inventis adeo non favet, vt minetur eis, qui ambulant in flamma ignis sui, & in scintillis, quas sibimetipsis succenderint. E manu mea accidet hoc vobis: in dolore iacebitis. Isa.50.11. Quid opus est multis? opus habent stellae ecclesiarum ut ut Christi manu teneantur & protegatur, Ap.1.16. nõne igitur opus est, ut omnes ab ipsius manu fabricentur? Stellae certè erraticae sunt Iud.13. officia quaecunq; ecclesiastica, quae non opera manus Christi, sed opera manuum humanarum sunt. An rarum in scripturis, humana inventa condemnata audire, vel hoc solo nomine. Opera sint manuum tuarum? Psa.135,15. Isa.28. 317. & 37. 19. Ier. 16.&c.
units.tr: 10 Our ninth argument is drawn from the end of ecclesiastical government. For it belongs to the same authority to establish both the end and the means to the end. Just as Christ has sanctioned the end of government precisely in the Word, so he is to be judged to have sanctioned the polity of the Church as well, which is a means to that same end. Now the end of polity is the salvation and building up of the Church; and who would think that Christ left the Church without certain means, and these all fixed? Moreover, polity, like all other means, avails for its end only through the supply of grace and heavenly blessing. A man cannot supply grace to any ecclesiastical office; therefore neither can he establish any office. Let us certainly see that, along with the variety of graces, a variety of administrations was instituted in the Word; and the ecclesiastical offices themselves are gifts, Eph. 4.12; 1 Cor. 12.5; Rom. 12.5, 6. So much would be taken from the power and generosity of Christ if it lay with man, and not with Christ alone, to establish these. As for blessing: just as Moses blessed the tabernacle when he had seen everything built according to the pattern shown to him on the mountain, Exod. 39.43, so Christ likewise blesses ecclesiastical government in no other way than when he sees everything composed and ordered according to the exact rule of his Word. No dawn is to be expected from him when his Word is not upheld, Isa. 8.20; indeed he is so far from favouring human inventions that he threatens those who walk in the flame of their own fire and in the sparks which they have kindled for themselves. This will come to you from my hand: you shall lie down in sorrow. Isa. 50.11. Why say more? The stars of the Churches must be held and protected in the hand of Christ, Rev. 1.16; is it not therefore necessary that all of them be made by his hand? Certainly any ecclesiastical offices that are not the work of Christ's hand, but works of human hands, are wandering stars, Jude 13. Is it rare in the Scriptures to hear human inventions condemned, even on this ground alone? Are they the works of your hands? Ps. 135.15; Isa. 28.17 and 37.19; Jer. 16, etc.

units.la: 11. Argumentum nostrum decimum ab officio nostro ducitur, fide nempe & obedientiâ erga disciplinam. Quae etenim fides absq; verbo Rom.10. 17. quae obedientia nisi mandato? Respondet Remonstrator, fidem & obedientiam erga politeiam ecclesiasticam esse posse perinde ac civilem, etsi certa illius forma in verbo Dei non prescribitur: respectu nempe principiorum illorum generalium, quae in scriptura de eadem reperiuntur. At primò, res supernaturalis cum politeia ecclesiastica sit, quo nomine à civili distat: speciatim in verbo nisi prescribatur, languet erga eandem obedientia, vacillat fides. Secundò, fac generalibus principiis tantum politeias ecclesiasticae fidem dari, obedientiam praestari posse: & arctiori tamen vinculo ligamur nos ad utramque, si non generaliter, sed speciatim in verbo mandetur: quod à Christo prætermissum fuisse verisimile non est: Ratio apud Richardum Hookerum extat, in nostra persona, ab illo, ita posita. Quamdiu persuadentur homines de ordine aliquo, quòd ab hominibus solis sit, de prudentia sua præsumunt, putantque non modo parem sed meliorem etiam sese adinvenire posse. Inde est, quod instituta humana tam promptam & alacrem obedientiam elicere nequeant: atque ea est, quando ad Deum conscientia respicit, quasi ad illius ordinis authorem. Hoc illud fuit quod Mosis leges de Politeia Ecclesiastica commendavit, cui simile quiddam à Paganis legislatoribus nonnulli prætendebant: falso quidem, prudenter tamen vim hujusce persuasionis discernentes. Itaque ad majorem obedientiam expediens erat, ut Deus ipse Politeias ecclesiasticæ author esset. Huic verò nihil respondet Hookerus: quia frivola? fiat judicium ex consequentibus. Ex dogmate nostro certa quædam ubique sυντἇξια & in disciplina perinde ac in doctrina pax & unitas conservatur: ex dogmate verò Hierarchico Anabaptisticis confusionibus via astruitur, mutationibus politicis fenestra aperitur: funestis denique ecclesiarum dilacerationibus causa præbetur, sicut in Anglia hodie apparet. Rursus ex dogmate nostro consolatio cuique politeias administro suppeditatur, ut qui jam cum Ieremia dicere possit: Non me intrusi coram te: ex dogmate verò Hierarchico conscientiæ confusio, qualis illa fuit sacerdotum Ieroboami: cum conscij essent se proprias implevisse manus, & absque ulla vocatione diivnâ semetipsos consecrasse. Postremò ex dogmate nostro proficiscitur erga politeias administros reverentia, cum plebi quotidie ob oculos versabitur, Qui vos spernit me spernit. Murmuratio vestra non est adversus nos, sed adversus Iehovam: ex dogmate verò Hierarchico contemptus, qualis in Malachia denunciatur: nam sordida semper in domo Dei institutio humana visa est.
units.tr: 11. Our tenth argument is drawn from our duty, namely faith and obedience towards discipline. For what faith is there without the word (Rom. 10.17), and what obedience without a command? The Remonstrator replies that faith and obedience towards the ecclesiastical polity can exist just as they do towards the civil one, even though its particular form is not prescribed in the word of God, namely with respect to those general principles which Scripture contains about it. But first, since the ecclesiastical polity is a supernatural thing, and in this it differs from the civil, obedience towards it grows weak and faith wavers, unless it is prescribed specifically in the word. Secondly, grant that faith and obedience towards an ecclesiastical polity can be given on the basis of general principles alone. Yet we are bound to both by a tighter bond if they are commanded specifically in the word and not merely in general, and it is not likely that Christ passed this over. The reasoning is found in Richard Hooker, who puts it in our person thus: As long as men are persuaded of some order that comes from men alone, they presume on their own wisdom and think they can devise an order equal or even better. Hence it is that human institutions cannot draw forth so prompt and eager an obedience; whereas they do so when the conscience looks to God as the author of that order. This is what commended Moses' laws concerning the ecclesiastical polity, and something similar was claimed by some pagan lawgivers, falsely indeed, but they wisely discerned the force of this persuasion. Therefore, for greater obedience, it was expedient that God himself should be the author of the ecclesiastical polity. Hooker makes no reply to this, perhaps because it is trivial? Let judgment be made from the consequences. From our doctrine a certain harmony is preserved everywhere, and peace and unity in discipline as much as in doctrine. From the hierarchical doctrine, however, a way is opened to Anabaptistical confusions, a window is opened to political changes, and finally a cause is given for the deadly rending of churches, as is evident in England today. Again, from our doctrine comfort is supplied to each administrator of the polity, so that he can already say with Jeremiah: I have not thrust myself in before you. But from the hierarchical doctrine comes confusion of conscience, such as that of the priests of Jeroboam, who, being aware that they had filled their own hands and consecrated themselves without any divine calling. Lastly, from our doctrine arises reverence towards the administrators of the polity, since the people will have before their eyes every day: He who despises you despises me, and your murmuring is not against us but against Jehovah. From the hierarchical doctrine comes contempt, such as is denounced in Malachi; for human institution has always appeared as something base in the house of God.

units.la: 11 Argumentum nostrum undecimum & ultimum à testimonio sanctorum sumitur, qui in ecclesia quoque seculo floruerunt. Ita Cyprianus. Legat hoc unum verbum & in hoc mandato meditetur Christiana religio & inveniet ex hac scriptura omnium doctrinarum regulas emanasse, & hinc nasci & huc reverti, quicquid ecclesiastica continet disciplina, & in omnibus irritum esse & frivolum quicquid dilectio non confirmat. Respondet Remonstrator. Per disciplinam intelligi hic doctrinam quemadmodum verbis paulo antecedentibus f. 8. Non me latet te docente ad siccandas corruptionem meorum putredines prodesse — sal disciplinæ tuæ Evangelio tuo mediante infusum. Hinc insultat Demonstratori, tanquam lectori Cypriani inepto aut collectionem aliorum sequenti, ne lecto quidem à sese Cypriano. Sed ineptissimus Cypriani lector ipse Remonstrator est, id quod proximè antecedentia verba demonstrant. Loquere magister bone libenter te audio & cum adversariis mihi: etiam in plagis & doloribus intelligo disciplinam: nec me latet, &c. Quid igitur est? Per sal disciplinæ hic non (quod ille ineptissime somniat) intelligit doctrinam nam Cyprianus, sed disciplinam correctionis. In testimonio vero nostro perspiciet quivis, doctrinarum regulam & disciplinam ecclesiasticam, quasi res diversas sejunctim poni, & utramque ex æquo à scriptura derivari. Sic & alibi in negotiis disciplinæ ad scripturam à Cypriano revocamur. Hinc sæpe ista & disciplinæ violationes nascuntur: dum ad veritatis originem non creditur, nec caput quæritur, nec magistri cœlestis doctrina servatur. Innuunt ista doctrinam de disciplina tractatam esse, scripturam disciplinæ caput esse, ut errata in disciplina corrigantur. Quid quod doctrinam de disciplina eam speciatim nominat, quæ episcopatus Anglicani nervos exsecat? Dicit enim in uno pastore unam cathedram post pastoribus omnibus æqualem attributam esse, sicut testatur Ri. Fyldus, & Guil. Whitakerus qui in hunc sensum Cyprianum interpretantur. Citatur à Demonstratore testimonium istud Tertulliani. Nobis nihil ex nostro arbitrio inducere licet: sed nec eligere quod aliquis arbitrio suo induxerit: Apostolos Domini habeamus authores qui nec ipsi quicquam à suo arbitrio quod inducerent elegerunt, sed acceptam à Christo disciplinam fideliter nationibus assignarunt. Non autem puto Demonstratorem existimasse disciplinam ecclesiasticam hic specialiter nominatam fuisse, quo nomine immerito apud Remonstratorem vapulat: sed sermonis Tertulliani generalitate innixum suisse: quâ nihil de nostro arbitrio in disciplina eligendum dicit, sive doctrinam contineat illa, sive ecclesiæ disciplinam. Ita Augustinus. Sive de Christo, sive de ecclesia, sive de quacunque alia re quæ pertinet ad fidem vitamque nostram, non dico si nos sed si Angelus de cœlo vobis annuntiaverit præterquam quod in scripturis legitimis & Evangelicis accepistis, anathema sit. Iohannes Reynoldus dum hanc sententiam Augustini adversus Hartum urget, insistit in eo præcipuè, quod non dicat contrà quàm, sed præterquam, ut non solum quæ contra verbum illicita Augustinus sentiat, sed etiam quæ vel præter scripturam fiunt. Non igitur solum (quod vult Hookerus) quæ in politeia ecclesiastica contra Dei verbum sunt, Pauli & Augustini judicio prohibentur, sed etiam quæ præter verbum geruntur: nam cum ecclesiam Augustinus speciatim nominet, vitamque nostram: quis putarit ecclesiæ disciplinam quæ ad mores dirigendos est destinata, eum excepisse? Sequitur Damasus, quem citat & approbat Richardus Fyldus, qui Chorepiscopos ideo extirpandos confirmat, quod in verbo, eorum ordo authoritatem nullam habeat. Qui ita arguit, nomine omnia officia ecclesiastica etiam regent a in verbo ita posita putat ut alia inducere illicitum sit, præterquam ea quæ in verbo sanciuntur? verba sunt: eorum institutio omni authoritate caret, idem sunt qui & presbyteri. Non amplius quam duos ordines inter discipulos Domini esse cognovimus id est duodecim Apostolorum, & septuaginta discipulorum: unde iste tertius processerit penitus ignoramus. Et quod ratione caret extirpari necesse est. Referuntur in ius Canonicum ista: in quibus ut quædam erroris sunt proxima, hoc tamen sanum est: quod necesse putetur ut officia omnia ecclesiastica extirpentur, quæ carent authoritate
units.tr: 11. Our eleventh and last argument is taken from the testimony of the saints, who also flourished in the Church in this age. Thus Cyprian: Let the Christian religion read this one word and meditate on this commandment, and it will find that from this Scripture the rules of all doctrines have flowed, and that from here they are born and to here they return, whatever ecclesiastical discipline contains; and that whatever love does not confirm is void and frivolous in all things. The Remonstrator replies: by discipline is meant here doctrine, as shown by the words a little before, in f. 8: I am not unaware that, by your teaching, the salt of your discipline, infused through your Gospel, serves to dry up the putrefactions of my corruption. Hence he insults the Demonstrator as if he were an inept reader of Cyprian, or one who follows another's collection, not even having read Cyprian himself. But the most inept reader of Cyprian is the Remonstrator himself, as the words immediately before show: Speak on, good master, I gladly hear you, and I hear you with my adversaries; I understand discipline even in blows and pains; nor am I unaware, etc. What then is the case? By the salt of discipline he does not mean doctrine, as he most ineptly dreams, but the discipline of correction. In our testimony anyone will see that the rule of doctrine and ecclesiastical discipline are set apart as separate things, and that both are equally derived from Scripture. So also elsewhere, in matters of discipline, we are recalled to Scripture by Cyprian: Hence these violations of discipline often arise, when men do not believe in the origin of truth, do not seek the head, and do not keep the teaching of the heavenly Master. These words imply that doctrine concerning discipline is being treated, that Scripture is the head of discipline, so that errors in discipline may be corrected. What of the fact that he names specifically the doctrine of discipline which cuts the sinews of the Anglican episcopate? For he says: in one shepherd, one chair is assigned, equal among all the shepherds, as Richard Fulke testifies, and William Whitaker, who interpret Cyprian in this sense. The Demonstrator cites the following testimony of Tertullian: We may bring in nothing of our own choice, nor may we choose what anyone has brought in by his own choice. We have the Apostles of the Lord as authors, who themselves chose nothing of their own will to bring in, but faithfully handed down to the nations the discipline received from Christ. I do not think, however, that the Demonstrator supposed that ecclesiastical discipline was specifically named here, for which he is undeservedly beaten by the Remonstrator; rather he relied on the generality of Tertullian's language, by which he says that nothing of our own choice is to be chosen in discipline, whether that discipline contains doctrine or the discipline of the Church. So also Augustine: Whether concerning Christ, or concerning the Church, or concerning any other matter that pertains to our faith and life, I do not say if we, but if an angel from heaven should announce to you anything other than what you have received in the legitimate and Evangelical Scriptures, let him be anathema. John Reynolds, while pressing this saying of Augustine against Hart, insists chiefly on the fact that he does not say contrary to but other than, so that Augustine judges not only those things that are unlawful against the word, but also those that are done apart from Scripture. Therefore not only (as Hooker wishes) those things in the ecclesiastical polity that are against the word of God are prohibited by the judgment of Paul and Augustine, but also those that are done beyond the word. For since Augustine names the Church specifically, and our life, who would think that he excepted the discipline of the Church, which is destined to direct morals? There follows Damasus, whom Richard Fulke cites and approves, who maintains that chorepiscopi must be rooted out because their order has no authority in the word. Does he who argues thus think that all ecclesiastical offices, even those of the regents, are so set down in the word that it is unlawful to introduce anything other than what is sanctioned in the word? These are his words: their institution is devoid of all authority; they are the same as the elders. We know that there were no more than two orders among the disciples of the Lord, that is, the twelve Apostles and the seventy disciples; from where that third order came we are wholly ignorant. And what lacks reason must necessarily be rooted out. These things are cited into the canon law; and although some of them come near to error, this at least is sound: that it is thought necessary that all ecclesiastical offices which lack authority and reason from the Scriptures be rooted out.
