units.la: Hoc si effectum datum in Anglia, vbi quæso Episcopi Anglicani futuri essent: qui per scripturas ijdem cum presbyteris sunt (ut de Chorepiscopis loquitur Damasus & jus Canonicum) & omni ex sacris desumpta ratione carent. Ita Nazianzenus. Nemo sapiat supra quam oportet sapere, neve lege justior, luce splendidior, canone rectior, præcepto officiosior videri velit? Loquitur ita de disciplina Ecclesiastica Nazianzenus, sicut ipse Thomas Bilsonus attestatur: qui hæc adfert, nè in controversijs disciplinaris quisquam nostrum, vlla zeli religionisve specie, vltra præceptum, legem, canonem verbi divini nosmet abripi patiamur. Qui ita loquuntur, nonne legem in verbo Dei, nonne præceptum, nonne Canonem, nonne lucem, de disciplina ecclesiastica, tradita esse confitentur? Ita Chrysostomus. Qui non utitur sacra scriptura sed ascendit aliunde, id est, non concessa via, hic non pastor est, sed fur & latro. Impugnat primum Papæ hoc testimonio Iohanues Iuellus, eo quod à Christo in verbo suo non instituatur. Sed ratio hæc nonne & Episcopos Anglicanos & quodvis præterea officium ecclesiasticum ex Ecclesia exturbat, quod in Dei verbo perinde ac papatus ipse non instituitur? Ita Leo. Exortes sunt mysterij divini qui a Petri soliditate recesserunt. Rursus. Petri forma cunctis ecclesiæ Rectoribus proposita est. Erravit quidem in hypothesi huius formæ Leo: quod tamen exemplar Apostolicæ disciplinæ ligare, & formam quandam disciplinæ ab eisdem propositam innuit, in eo quidem certè sapit, vel Matheo Sutcliffo assentiente: qui hinc pontificis primatum jugulat, quod a Petri soliditate recesserit, imò à forma illius quam longissimè recesserit: id quod de Anglicano Episcopatu, & omni alio ecclesiastico officio ab hominibus introducto verissimè aptissimeque dicitur. Ita Iohannes Gerson. [Nulla potest lingua satis exprimere, quantum malū, quantum periculum, quantam confusionem, sacræ scripturæ contemptus (quæ proculdubio sufficiens est, pro ecclesiæ gubernatione, alias Christus imperfectus legislator esset) & humanorum inventorum affectatio in ecclesiam invexit. Ad huius rei evidentiam consideretur cleri status, cui sapientia cælestis disponsari debuit: sed cum meretrice illa, sapientia humana adulterium commiserunt illi: sic ut status ecclesiæ merè bestialis & monstrosus evaserit: infra cœlum, supra terra, subest spiritus, dominatur caro &c. non erubescunt tamen quidam dicere, humanis inventionibus melius ecclesiam gubernari, quam lege divina, & lege Evangelij Christi, quæ assertio blasphema est. Evangelica etenim doctrina, ecclesiæ terminos dilatavit, & ad cœlum sublimavit: quam Hagaræ filij sapientiam illam quærentes, quæ de terra est, ad sterquilinium usque dejecerunt.] Citat ista & approbat Richardus Fyldus Hierarchicus: quæ & sententiam nostram de certa disciplinæ forma in verbo Dei perfectè tradita manifestè confirmant: & politeiam Anglicanam jugulant, imò miseriam quæ & humanam sapientiam in disciplinâ ecclesiasticâ, deformantem sequi solet;& in regnum Anglicanum per Hierarchiam Episcopalem humanam jam (pro dolor) invecta est, adeo graphicè depingunt, ut nihil supra. Alibi de negotijs disciplinarijs loquens adversus papam, ita habet. Superest ut aliqua sit relicta inobliquabilis & indeviabilis regula ab optimo legislatore Christo, secundum quam possit abusus huiusmodi potestatis reprimi, dirigi, atque moderari. Haec autem regula est ecclesia & generale concilium. In hac Hadrianus Saravia ita. Rectè à Gerfone notatum fuit ab optimo legislatore Christo in ecclesiam regulam inobliquabilem esse: sed sacræ scripturæ sint illa regula &c. In hac sententia fuerunt ij qui Petro Aliaco attestante, in concilio Constantiensi, & jam ante ordinem Cardinalium tollendum putarunt, quod nec a Christo, nec ab Apostolis institutus esset, sicut olim de statu Corepiscoporum factum erat. Citatur a D. Mornaeo & approbatur Budaeus, cuius ista de certa disciplinæ forma in verbo tradita, sententia est. Navis nobis disciplinæ socialis ac civilis à servatore relicta est ecclesiæ conditore, quæ continuo ministerio, instrumento gubernaculi instructa fuit ab ipso, aut eius auspicijs. Platonem etiam à puppi potius est, ad exoptatum locum rectores perlaturum, si clavem certum tenere, si nusquam non spiritui afflaturo pandere ecclesia porrexisset: (sacras utique scripturas à spiritu sancto profectas contulisset.) Accedant Hierarchici. Thomas Bilsonus ita. Hijs quæ dixi non est consequens ut politiam ecclesiasticam, quam nolisicunque libeat, ex ingenio nostro fingamus, quin potius dandæ est opera ut externam administrationem in ecclesia regenda eam observemus quam Dominus noster ipse docuit. Quem verò Dominus ab initio sanxit, obscurum esse non poterit, si sacras literas consulamus. Ita Richardus Bancroftus. Conclusio mea ædificatur, supra unam de Demonstrativis propositionibus Johannis Vallii. Illud regimen ecclesiæ cuius origo ignota est nullam habet authoritatem à verbo Dei sed illicitum est. Postremo ita Hadrianus Saravia. Non ignoramus ab Apostolis perfectam ecclesiæ formam traditam: & quid sit de hac re nostra sententia, jam diximus. Unde nos intulimus & consequens esse diximus ut illa omnia mandata in ecclesia, per quæ ædificatur verbi Dei prædicatio, sacramentorum administratio, cum ea regiminis forma quæ fuit ab initio sub Apostolis, nec ostenditur vel mutata, vel inhibita posteris. His omnibus argumentis, constat unam quandam certam regiminis Ecclesiastici formam à Christo, in verbo, traditam & institutam esse.
units.tr: If this were put into effect in England, where, I ask, would the Anglican bishops be? They are, by the Scriptures, the same as presbyters (as Damasus speaks of chorepiscopi, and the canon law does too), and they have no rationale drawn from the sacred writings. So Nazianzen: Let no one think himself wiser than he ought to be, nor wish to seem more just than the law, brighter than the light, more upright than the canon, or more dutiful than the precept. Nazianzen speaks in this way about ecclesiastical discipline, as Thomas Bilson himself attests, who cites these words: Let us not allow any of us, in controversies about discipline, under any pretence of zeal or religion, to be carried away beyond the precept, the law, the canon of the divine Word. Do not those who speak this way confess that the law, the precept, the canon and the light concerning ecclesiastical discipline have been handed down in the Word of God? So Chrysostom: He who does not use Holy Scripture but climbs up by some other way, that is, by a path not granted, is not a minister but a thief and a robber. John Jewel first attacks the Pope with this testimony, on the ground that the Pope is not instituted by Christ in his Word. But does this argument not also cast out the Anglican bishops, and every other ecclesiastical office, from the Church, since they too are not instituted in the Word of God, just as the papacy itself is not? So Leo: They are strangers to the divine mystery who have departed from the firmness of Peter. Again: The form of Peter is set before all the rectors of the Church. Leo indeed erred in his hypothesis about this form; yet in that he binds the pattern of apostolic discipline and implies a certain form of discipline set forth by the same apostles, he certainly speaks wisely, with the agreement of Matthew Sutcliffe, who from this overthrows the primacy of the bishop of Rome: because he has departed from the firmness of Peter, indeed he has departed very far from his form. This is most truly and aptly said of the Anglican episcopate and of every other ecclesiastical office introduced by men. So John Gerson: [No tongue can sufficiently express how much evil, how much danger, how much confusion the contempt of Holy Scripture (which is undoubtedly sufficient for the government of the Church; otherwise Christ would be an imperfect lawgiver) and the pursuit of human inventions have brought into the Church. To see this clearly, let the state of the clergy be considered, to whom heavenly wisdom ought to have been betrothed; but they have committed adultery with that harlot, human wisdom, so that the state of the Church has become purely bestial and monstrous: beneath heaven, above earth, the spirit is subject, the flesh rules, and so on. Yet some are not ashamed to say that the Church is governed better by human inventions than by the divine law and the law of the Gospel of Christ, which assertion is blasphemous. For evangelical doctrine has enlarged the bounds of the Church and raised it up to heaven; but the sons of Hagar, seeking that wisdom which is of the earth, have cast it down even to the dunghill.] Richard Field, in his Of the Church, cites and approves these words; they also clearly confirm our opinion that a certain form of discipline has been perfectly delivered in the Word of God, and they overthrow the Anglican polity. Indeed they depict so vividly the misery which human wisdom, deforming ecclesiastical discipline, is wont to bring, and which (alas) has already been carried by the Episcopal hierarchy into the English kingdom, that nothing could be more graphic. Speaking elsewhere about disciplinary matters against the Pope, he says: It remains that some unbending and unerring rule should have been left by Christ, the best lawgiver, by which the abuse of such power might be checked, directed and governed. This rule, however, is the Church and a general council. On this Hadrianus Saravia says: Gerson rightly noted that Christ, the best lawgiver, left an unbending rule in the Church; but the holy Scriptures are that rule, etc. To this opinion belonged those who, as Pierre d'Ailly testifies, at the Council of Constance and already before, thought the order of Cardinals should be abolished, because it had been instituted neither by Christ nor by the Apostles, just as the state of the chorepiscopi had once been abolished. Budaeus, cited and approved by D. Mornay, holds this opinion of a certain form of discipline delivered in the Word: The ship of social and civil discipline has been left to us by the Saviour, the founder of the Church, and it was furnished from the beginning with a continuous ministry, a steering instrument, by himself or under his auspices. Plato would have brought the rulers to the desired place more from the stern, if the Church had offered a sure key to hold, and an opening to the Spirit blowing everywhere (namely, if it had consulted the holy Scriptures, which proceed from the Holy Spirit). Let the Hierarchists come forward. Thomas Bilson says: It does not follow from what I have said that we should invent an ecclesiastical polity from our own wit as we please; rather we must take care to observe in governing the Church that external administration which our Lord himself taught. And what the Lord ordained from the beginning cannot be obscure, if we consult the sacred letters. So Richard Bancroft. My conclusion is built upon one of the demonstrative propositions of John Vaux: That government of the Church whose origin is unknown has no authority from the Word of God, but is unlawful. Finally, Hadrianus Saravia says: We are not ignorant that the perfect form of the Church was handed down by the Apostles; and we have already stated our opinion on this matter. Hence we have inferred, and said it follows, that all those things in the Church by which the preaching of the Word of God and the administration of the sacraments are built up should remain, together with that form of government which existed from the beginning under the Apostles; nor is it shown to have been changed or forbidden to posterity. From all these arguments it is established that a certain fixed form of ecclesiastical government has been delivered and instituted by Christ in the Word.

units.la: CAP. XLI.
units.tr: CHAP. XLI.

units.la: Argumenta Hierarchica dissolvuntur.
units.tr: The Hierarchical arguments are dissolved.

units.la: SVperest ut adversa Hierarchicorum argumenta dissolvamus. Prima objectio est à circumstantijs Politeias: hoc etenim perpetuum apud Whitgiftum, Hookerum, Sutclivium, reliquosq; Sophisma est: non esse certam Politeias formam in verbo speciatim posita:
units.tr: It remains for us to dissolve the opposing arguments of the Hierarchists. The first objection is drawn from the circumstances of the polity. This is the constant sophism of Whitgift, Hooker, Sutcliffe and the rest: that no certain form of polity is laid down in the Word by name,

units.la: {a} De Auferibil. papa confud. II. positam: quia ceremoniæ & ejusdem circumstantiæ speciatim in scripturis non describantur. Primò, insulsum hoc argumentum est? quid enim? Nulla erit Ethices & bonorum operum certa in scripturis tradita regula, quia operum bonorum circumstantiæ non nisi regulis generalibus diriguntur? Disciplinæ docentis quod ad verbi prædicationem & sacramentorum administrationem, certam formam speciatim in verbo traditam esse confitentur ipsi: cujus tamen circumstantias non nisi generaliter tradi in aperto & confesso est. Postremò certam formam Politeiæ Ecclesiasticæ à Mose Iudæis in verbo definitam fuisse non inficiantur: in ecclesia tamen Iudæorum concessum est, inquit Hookerus, horum sacrificiorum, Synagogarum ædificationem, pulpitorum & cathedrarum erectionem: id est, circumstantias ejusdem Politeiæ, Ecclesiæ arbitrio relictas fuisse. Non igitur sequitur substantiam Politeiæ Ecclesiasticæ in verbo traditam minime jam esse, quia eiusdem circumstantiæ non traduntur. Secundò, statum quæstionis invertunt, idque nobis affingunt, quod ne in mentem venit unquam. Verba Hookeri ista sunt. Distinctio illorum de substantia & circumstantiis, quamquam vera, eorum proposito non satisfacit: nam sive res maioris momenti sint, sive minoris, si eas Deus in verbo ut perpetuas mandavit: nulla ratio est quæ alterum earum genus, magis altero, mutare liceat. His in verbis impingit nobis Hookerus, ac si circumstantias Politeias perinde ac substantiam, in verbo mandatas in perpetuum existimaremus, quod quisquamnè de nostris affirmavit quæso, imò vel somniavit unquam?
units.tr: {a} as set out in the book on the removable papacy, Book II, because the ceremonies and their particular circumstances are not described by name in the Scriptures. First, this argument is silly. For what? Will there be no certain rule of ethics and good works handed down in the Scriptures, because the circumstances of good works are governed only by general rules? In the teaching discipline, they themselves confess that a certain form has been laid down in the Word by name for the preaching of the Word and the administration of the sacraments, yet it is openly and admittedly the case that its circumstances are handed down only in general terms. Last, they do not deny that Moses prescribed a certain form of ecclesiastical polity for the Jews in the Word. Yet in the Jewish church, says Hooker, it was allowed that the offering of these sacrifices, the building of synagogues, and the erection of pulpits and seats were left to the discretion of the Church: that is, the circumstances of that same polity were left to the Church's judgment. It does not follow, therefore, that the substance of the ecclesiastical polity handed down in the Word is no longer in force, because its circumstances are not handed down. Second, they invert the state of the question and attribute to us what has never even entered our minds. Hooker's words are these: That distinction of theirs between substance and circumstances, though true, does not serve their purpose: for whether the matters are of greater or lesser weight, if God has commanded them in the Word as perpetual, there is no reason why one kind should be changed any more than the other. In these words Hooker charges us as if we held the circumstances of the polity, no less than its substance, to be commanded in the Word for ever. Which of our people, I ask you, has ever affirmed this, or indeed even dreamed of it?

units.la: Tertiò, circa distinctionem hanc de circumstantiis & substantia egregie cavillantur. Eam veram esse agnoscit Hookerus, sed non ita Matheus Sutclivius, qui eam exagitat ut ineptam & imperitam: addit insuper nos quasdam circumstantias perinde atque substantiam perpetuas stabilire. Sed expedita responsio est. Quædam circumstantiæ individuales sunt, & has intelligimus; cum mutabiles & minimè in verbo speciatim delineatas Politeias circumstantias dicimus: Quædam verò circumstantiæ generales sunt, & has non absque causa & speciatim in verbo descriptas, & immutabiles affirmamus: cujusmodi sunt in circumstantia loci, prædicatio verbi, sacramentorum administratio, administrorum electio in loco publico: & in circumstantia temporis, quòd non alio tempore administer aut pastor eligendus sit, quam in locum defuncti, aut quando sedes aliàs vacat.
units.tr: Third, they carp cleverly at this distinction between circumstances and substance. Hooker acknowledges it to be true, but Matthew Sutcliffe does not, who assails it as inept and unskilled; he adds moreover that we establish some circumstances as perpetual in the same way as the substance. But the reply is ready to hand. Some circumstances are individual, and it is these we mean when we call the circumstances of the polity changeable and not laid down in the Word by name. Other circumstances are general, and these, not without reason, we affirm to be described in the Word by name and to be unchangeable. Such are, in respect of place, the preaching of the Word, the administration of the sacraments, and the choice of ministers in a public place; and, in respect of time, that a minister is to be chosen at no other time than in the place of one who has died, or when the see is otherwise vacant.

units.la: 2 Objectio Hierarchicorum secunda sequitur, ab Ecclesiæ authoritate desumpta, quæ authoritatem nullam haberet in ferendis legibus de Politeia Ecclesiastica, si modo certa ejusdem forma in verbo descripta haberetur. Ita M. Sutclivius: Si Christus, inquit, legislator externæ Politeiæ esset, legesque Ecclesiæ tulisset, non magis Ecclesiæ & Synodo leges scribere & promulgare liceret, quam populo & subditis sibi leges condere præter sui principis & magistratus voluntatē. Ita pagina precedenti: Si qua in externis rebus Christus mandaverit & Apostoli iusserint pro legib. habenda sunt, nulla alia authoritate, nulla legislatione opus esset. Nam si in novo Testamento reperiantur, ut Christi verbum valebunt: ut stultè quis faceret, si novum Testamentum lege confirmaret. Valet enim suo jure multo magis quàm humanae ullae leges: & conscientias astringit, quas humanae leges & ab homine latae non ligant. Respondeo primò hoc argumentum papisticum esse, ad scripturae imperfectionem comprobandam, non in causis disciplinae tantùmodo, sed etiam in causis fidei. Quid enim? Annon certa fidei forma in verbo traditur, & tamen in causis fidei Ecclesiae & Synodi adversus haereses cujuscunq; temporis leges tulerunt? Hoc inde fit, inquiunt papistae, quia scriptura in tradenda fidei formâ imperfecta est. Nam in consequentia hujus argumenti cum Sutclivio conspirant, ut in Cornelio Sculingio videre est, qui pari modo argumentatur. Si necesse est quasdam regulas novas quotidie sic casibus exigentibus adjici: cur falsò docent puritani contra Calvino-papistas, ex solis scripturis hauriendam disciplinam esse, easque solas sufficere. Secundò, Perduellis non in Ecclesiam solam, verùmetiam in ipsum magistratum Sutclivius est: nam si certa rei forma in verbo descripta omnem legislationum authoritatem abscindit: magistratus in causis fidei authoritatem leges ferendi nullum habet, cum fidei forma perfectè in scriptura traditur, quae suo valore valet. Tertio, argumento huic Sutclivliano, ita respondit Richardus Hookerus: Quanquam frustra esset leges condere, quas scriptura prius condidit, quia in mandatis Dei, nihil relinqui est, quàm ut executioni mandentur: tamen pro eis quae mandantur in scripturis, in officio Ecclesiae est, providere legibus, ne licentia aut segnitie hominum, mandata Dei non adimpleantur. Exempli gratiâ, Nehem 10.34.35.36. Instituimus nobis praecepta — ut scriptum est in lege. Instituimus nos alaturos primitias terrae nostrae. Primò patet hinc, in reformatione disciplinae nihil tentandum praeter id quod scriptum est: secundo legislationi locum esse, ubi certa forma disciplinae antè à Deo praescripta est, ut forma ea observetur diligentius & collapsa restituatur.
units.tr: The second objection of the Hierarchists follows, taken from the authority of the Church, which would have no authority to enact laws concerning the ecclesiastical polity, if indeed a certain form of it were described in the Word. So Matthew Sutcliffe: If Christ, he says, were the legislator of the external polity, and had enacted laws for the Church, it would be no more lawful for the Church and Synod to write and promulgate laws than for a people and subjects to make laws for themselves apart from the will of their prince and magistrate. So in the preceding page: If Christ has commanded anything in external matters, and the Apostles have ordered it, it must be held as law; no other authority and no further legislation would be needed. For if they are found in the New Testament, they will have the force of Christ's word; it would be foolish for anyone to confirm the New Testament by law. For it has force by its own right far more than any human laws, and it binds consciences, which human laws enacted by man do not bind. I reply, first, that this argument is Papist, aimed at proving the imperfection of Scripture, not only in matters of discipline but also in matters of faith. For what? Is not a certain form of the faith handed down in the Word, and yet have the Church and Synods nonetheless enacted laws in matters of faith against heresies of every age? This follows, the Papists say, because Scripture is imperfect in handing down the form of faith. For in the consequence of this argument they agree with Sutcliffe, as may be seen in Cornelius Schlingen, who argues in the same way: If it is necessary that certain new rules be added every day as cases require, why do the Puritans falsely teach against the Calvinist-Papists that discipline is to be drawn from Scripture alone, and that Scripture alone suffices? Second, Sutcliffe is a traitor not only to the Church but to the magistrate himself: for if a certain form of a thing described in the Word cuts off all authority of legislation, the magistrate has no authority to enact laws in matters of faith, since the form of faith is delivered perfectly in Scripture, which holds its force by its own value. Third, Richard Hooker answers this Sutcliffian argument as follows: Although it would be vain to enact laws which Scripture has already enacted, since in God's commandments nothing is left but that they be put into execution, nevertheless, for those things which are commanded in Scripture, it is the Church's office to provide laws, lest through the licence or sloth of men the commandments of God go unfulfilled. For example, Nehemiah 10:34–36: We bound ourselves to the precepts... as it is written in the law. We bound ourselves to bring the firstfruits of our land. From this it is clear, first, that in the reform of discipline nothing is to be attempted beyond what is written; second, that there is room for legislation where a certain form of discipline has been prescribed by God beforehand, so that this form may be observed more diligently and what has fallen may be restored.

units.la: 3. Tertia objectio Hierarchicorum, oppositione nititur ea, quae est inter legem & Evangelium, ubi Matheus Sutclivius ita: Qui Christum externae Politeiae Ecclesiae legislatorem esse volunt, illud de nova Christi & perfectiori legislatione, pontificiorum dogma, longo intervallo revocant: Evangelium novam legem appellant: mori loquendi in scripturis usitato repugnant. Christus nunquam legislator appellatur, imò Mosi legislatori opponitur: & illius dogmata non lex sed verbum dicuntur. Apostoli doctrinam de lege & Evangelio opponunt: legem & Evangelium ubique opposita esse videas, ut illa operâ, hac fidem tantum requirat, quae non in faciendo, sed in credendo tantùm versatur. Respondeo primò, non legislationem Christi in externis tantùm, sed & in internis & in externis haec argumentatio tollit: quod nonne quaeso blasphemum? Quomodo etenim Christus Ecclesiae rex, si non legislator, erit? Secundò, putidum est, quod de papistici dogmatis revocatione objicit: id quod verba ipsa
units.tr: The third objection of the Hierarchists rests on the opposition that exists between law and Gospel, where Matthew Sutcliffe says: Those who want Christ to be the legislator of the external polity of the Church bring back, from a long way off, that papist dogma of a new and more perfect legislation of Christ: they call the Gospel a new law, which goes against the manner of speaking in use in Scripture. Christ is never called a legislator; rather he is set against Moses the legislator, and his doctrines are called not law but word. The Apostles set the doctrine of the law against that of the Gospel: you may see the law and the Gospel everywhere set in opposition, so that the one requires works, the other faith only, which consists not in doing but only in believing. I reply, first, that this argument removes Christ's legislation not only in external but also in internal matters, and in both: which is surely blasphemous? For how will Christ be King of the Church if he is not its legislator? Second, what he objects about the recall of the papist dogma is foolish, which the words themselves...

units.la: CAP. XLII. Politeia Ecclesiastica quoad substantiam immutabilis est, quod exemplis demonstratur.
units.tr: CAP. XLII. The ecclesiastical polity is immutable in substance, as is shown by examples.

units.la: {a}Quod si autem Politeia Ecclesiastica quoad substantiam in verbo praescripta habeatur: sequitur eandem quoad substantiam immutabilem esse, sic ut de eadem diminuere, vel eidem addere illicitum sit. Imo non sequitur inquiunt Hierarchicorum plurimi: ubi primo excipiunt adversus factum Apostolorum in disciplina exercenda: deinde adversus eorundem doctrinam in disciplina praescribenda: quorum neutrum legem perpetuam dictare volunt, quae immutari nequeat. De primo, sic Io. Bridgesius, Episcopus Oxoniensis. Num unumquodque exemplum primitivae Ecclesiae praeceptum aut mandatum faciunt? Rursus: Forte rerum nonnullarum in primitiva Ecclesia exemplum aliquod ostendere possunt, sed nec ipsum generale, nec eiusdem perpetuam regulam aliquam, quae omnes Ecclesias & aetates omnes ad illud exemplum astringat. Ita Io. Whitgiftus: Ex facto aut exemplo legem facere iniquum est. Hoc argumentum a facto nihil valet. Nunquam licet, inquit Zwinglius, neque in divinis, neque in profanis a facto ad jus argumentari. Rursus, Non solum infirmum sed & periculosum etiam argumentandi genus est, arguere. Apostoli fecerunt, ergo & nos facere oportet, vel Apostoli non fecerunt, ergo nobis non licet facere. Zwinglius vir insignitér doctus inprimis Anabaptistas hoc modo arguentes reprehendit, & dicit argumentum a facto ad jus, vel a non facto ad non ius nunquam valere, nisi illud exemplum super aliquam legem vel regulam fundetur. Postremo, Tho. Bilsonus, arguentibus pro libertate populi in electionibus, ab exemplo electionis Diaconorum ita respondet: Exempla multum distant a praeceptis. Ex facto singulari regula generalis non potest constitui sine maxima & manifestissima ratione, quae conclusionem cohaerentem & necessarium esse demonstret. His ut respondeatur, agendum est primo, in genere de exemplorum vi & valore: deinde speciatim de obligatione facti Apostolorum, & Ecclesiarum quae sub illis floruerunt.
units.tr: {a}But if the ecclesiastical polity is held to be prescribed in the Word as to its substance, it follows that it is immutable as to substance, so that it is unlawful either to diminish from it or to add to it. Yet most of the hierarchists say that this does not follow. They make two exceptions: first, against the deed of the Apostles in exercising discipline; second, against the Apostles' teaching in prescribing discipline. Neither of these, they say, is meant to lay down a perpetual law that cannot be changed. On the first point, John Bridges, Bishop of Oxford, says: Do they make every example of the primitive Church into a precept or command? Again: Perhaps they can point to some example of certain matters in the primitive Church, but neither the example itself is general, nor is there any perpetual rule drawn from it that binds all churches and all ages to that example. So John Whitgift: It is wrong to make a law from a deed or an example. This argument from a deed is worth nothing. It is never lawful, says Zwingli, to argue from a deed to a right, either in divine or in human matters. Again: It is not only a weak but also a dangerous kind of argument: the Apostles did it, therefore we ought to do it; or the Apostles did not do it, therefore we are not allowed to do it. Zwingli, a man distinguished in learning, rebukes especially the Anabaptists who argue in this way, and says that an argument from a deed to a right, or from a non-deed to a non-right, never holds unless that example is founded on some law or rule. Lastly, Thomas Bilson, answering those who argue for the people's liberty in elections from the example of the election of deacons, replies: Examples differ much from precepts. A general rule cannot be established from a single deed without a very great and very manifest reason, which shows the conclusion to be coherent and necessary. To answer these points, we must first discuss in general the force and value of examples, and then specifically the obligation of the deed of the Apostles and of the churches that flourished under them.

units.la: 2. Primo igitur cum exempla particularia nobis in scripturis ut {b}sive imitanda proponuntur ut similia vel imitemur vel devitemus, tum eadem pro lege communi habenda sunt: uti manifesto liquet ex 1. Cor. 10. 11. Phil. 4. 8. 9. 10. Heb. 11. per totum. Heb. 12. 3. Joh. 13. 15. Iud. 7. Exemplum ego praebui vobis, inquit Christus, Ioh. 13. 15. ut prout ego feci vobis & vos faciatis. De exemplo vero sanctorum Heb. 12. 3. habetur illud, nebulam esse qua dirigamur, per allusionem ad nebulam illam quae Israelitis in deserto praevivit, ut recta via ad terram Canaan ducerentur. Iam vero intentio spiritus Sancti in Actis Apostolorum perscribendis, eorum exempla eandem vim obtinere docet: quorsum enim liber de actis Apostolorum scriptus, nisi ut eorum acta nobis essent, & quasi nebulae quibus in via recta duceremur? Disputat Bellarminus Christum se submisisse Caesari & Pilato de facto,non de jure: cui respondet Whitakerus, quidis sponte,tamen in exemplum trahendum,ut cum lavit pedes discipulorum & passus est. Habeat hoc sibi Iohannes Whitgiftus qui argumentum a facto Apostolorum ad jus non valere arbitratur, ad morem Bellarmini,qui eodem fundamento nititur. Quid si verbis totidem non dicatur, fecerunt hoc Apostoli in regenda Ecclesia, ut vos faceretis, prout illi fecerunt: sic nec totidem verbis de submissione Christi dicitur, ut nos eandem imitaremur: contendunt tamen nostri illius exemplum jus inferre, per intentionem spiritus Sancti, qui illud exarandum curavit,ut nos eandem exprimeremus: id quod de gestis Apostolorum in Ecclesiae Politeia exercendâ jam dicere licet. Nonne eorum facta in Politeia Ecclesiastica, perinde à Deo,perinde recta & honesta fuerunt,atque illa submissio Christi ad Pilatum?
units.tr: 2. First, then, when particular examples in Scripture are set before us for imitation, so that we should either imitate or avoid similar things, those examples must be held as a common law. This is plain from 1 Cor. 10:11; Phil. 4:8–10; Heb. 11 throughout; Heb. 12:3; John 13:15; Jude 7. I have given you an example, says Christ, John 13:15, that you should do as I have done to you. As for the example of the saints, Heb. 12:3 speaks of a cloud by which we are guided, alluding to the cloud that went before the Israelites in the wilderness so that they might be led by the straight way to the land of Canaan. Now the intention of the Holy Spirit in writing the Acts of the Apostles shows that their examples have the same force: for why was the book of the Acts of the Apostles written, except that their deeds should be before us, and like a cloud by which we might be led along the straight way? Bellarmine argues that Christ submitted to Caesar and Pilate in deed, not in right. Whitaker answers him: Christ indeed did this voluntarily, yet it is to be drawn into an example, just as when he washed the disciples' feet and suffered. Let John Whitgift, who thinks that an argument from the deed of the Apostles to right is invalid, keep this answer for himself, since he follows Bellarmine's custom, which rests on the same foundation. And if it is not said in so many words, "The Apostles did this in governing the Church, so that you should do as they did," neither is it said in so many words of Christ's submission that we should imitate it. Yet our side contends that his example implies a right, through the intention of the Holy Spirit, who took care that it be written down so that we might express the same thing. This may now be said of the deeds of the Apostles in exercising the polity of the Church. Were not their deeds in the ecclesiastical polity as much from God, as right and honourable, as that submission of Christ to Pilate?

units.la: 3 Secundo, quae facta fuisse legimus ab hominibus quâ sancti & Christiani, ea facienda sunt ab omnibus, qui sancti & Christiani haberi volunt,quae vero facta sunt ab aliquibus quâ ministri, prophetae, vel magistratus fuerunt, ea imitanda sunt, non quidem ab omnibus, ab ijs tamen qui ad eadem munera vocati sunt.Hinc argumentatur à particulari exemplo Eliae, Iacob.5.17. à speciali exemplo Abrahami Paulus,Rom.4.24. Absurdum igitur illud Whitgifti & Bilsoni argumentum ab exemplo particulari non valere,nisi forte absurde Iaccobum & Paulum argumentatos fuisse,censendum sit. Ita de Pauli argumento Petrus Martyr: Hoc etiam praeterea hinc elicitur, quoties aut dogma nobis aliquod constituendum aut praeceptum aliquod Dei explicandum est, opportunè fieri,si probatio ab exemplis petatur. Nam in locis scrupulosis & exilibus,probatio ab exemplis magnam perspicuitatem adhibet,in illis enim mens & sensus conjunguntur,&c.
units.tr: 3. Second, deeds that we read were done by men as saints and Christians must be done by all who wish to be considered saints and Christians; but deeds done by some as ministers, prophets, or magistrates are to be imitated, not indeed by all, but by those who are called to the same offices. From this, James argues from the particular example of Elijah (James 5:17), and Paul argues from the special example of Abraham (Rom. 4:24). Therefore that argument of Whitgift and Bilson, that an argument from a particular example is invalid, must be judged absurd, unless perhaps James and Paul argued absurdly. Peter Martyr says this about Paul's argument: Moreover, it is further drawn from this, that whenever we must establish some doctrine or explain some precept of God, it is fitting to seek proof from examples. For in obscure and abstruse places, proof from examples brings great clarity, for in these the mind and the senses are joined together, etc.

units.la: 4. Tertiò,exempla quae ordinarie & communiter facta sunt, ea ordinarie imitanda: quae verò ex speciali causa, in ea demum causa praestanda sunt. patet hoc ex Luc.4.25.26.27. ubi probat Christus in causa simili,miracula sibi absque vocatione Nazarethae faciend\u00e6 non esse,sicut alijs in locis ad quos à Deo vocabatur,à particulari facto & exemplo Eliae Prophetae & Elizaei,qui ad eos solos profecti sunt, ad quos a Deo mittebantur. Huc referendum argumentum illud in casu simili necessitatis, quo probat Christus, ob necessarium corporis pastum,licere discipulis in die Sabbathi spicas vellere, a particulari facto & exemplo Davidis,qui in casu simili,simile fecit,Math. 12.4.
units.tr: 4. Third, examples that were done ordinarily and commonly are to be imitated ordinarily; but those done from a special cause are to be performed only in that same special cause. This is clear from Luke 4:25–27, where Christ proves, in a similar case, that he should not perform miracles at Nazareth without a calling, as in other places to which he was sent by God, by the particular deed and example of the prophets Elijah and Elisha, who went only to those to whom they were sent by God. To this belongs the argument in a similar case of necessity, by which Christ proves that the disciples were allowed, because of the necessity of bodily food, to pluck ears of corn on the Sabbath, from the particular deed and example of David, who in a similar case did a similar thing (Matt. 12:4).

units.la: 5. Patet ex hoc responsio ad argumentum Bilsonianum, quo probat factum Apostolorum in Diaconorum electione nos non ligare quia quiddam in eo speciale erat, quod minimè ligat. Quid enim? Quod populi consensus requirebatur id ordinarie factum erat,idcirco ordinariè imitandum. Quod populus in electione illa praevit id non ordinarie gestum est, sed ex causa speciali,Graecarum scilicet viduarum murmure,adversus Hebraeas.Haec istius electionis circumstantia tantum tum fuit, eaque specialis & occasionalis, sic ut nisi redeat similis, a nobis exprimenda non est.
units.tr: 5. From this there is an answer to the Bilsonian argument, by which he proves that the deed of the Apostles in electing deacons does not bind us, because there was something special in it that does not bind at all. For what? The consent of the people was required, and that was done ordinarily, therefore it is to be imitated ordinarily. That the people went before in that election was not done ordinarily, but from a special cause, namely the murmuring of the Greek widows against the Hebrew women. This circumstance of that election was then only, and it was special and occasional, so that, unless a similar case returns, it is not to be expressed by us.

units.la: 5. Quartò, quæ ex vocatione & donis extraordinarijs præstita sunt, ab eis tantummodo (quoad specialem agendi rationem) imitanda sunt, qui eadem vocatione & eisdem donis ornantur. Patet hoc ex Luc. 9. 54. 55. ubi Apostoli reprehenduntur, quia in igne cœlitus devocando, Eliæ exemplum imitari vellent. Quò major hodie Episcoporum Anglicanorum culpa est, quum Apostolorum authoritatem in reliquos ministros, semper in Ecclesia retinendam putant, & ipsi etiamnum retinent. Quid enim? Apostoli nonne extraordinarij fuerunt, ipsi verò ordinarij tantum? Num extraordinarijs donis Apostolorum ornantur, sine quibus ipsorum potestas extraordinaria cómode exerceri nequit? Nesciunt igitur quo spiritu sunt, quum extraordinariam Apostolorum authoritatem in collegas suos affectent: perinde ac Apostoli ipsi, quum factum Eliæ extraordinarium imitari voluerunt. Atque hæc de exemplorum obligatione in genere.
units.tr: 5. Fourth, things done from an extraordinary calling and gifts are to be imitated (as to the special manner of acting) only by those who are endowed with the same calling and the same gifts. This is clear from Luke 9:54–55, where the Apostles are rebuked because they wished to imitate the example of Elijah in calling down fire from heaven. How much greater is the fault of the Anglican bishops today, who think that the authority of the Apostles over the other ministers must always be retained in the Church, and who still retain it themselves! For what? Were not the Apostles extraordinary, while these men are only ordinary? Are they endowed with the extraordinary gifts of the Apostles, without which their extraordinary power cannot conveniently be exercised? They therefore do not know what spirit they are of, when they claim for themselves the extraordinary authority of the Apostles over their colleagues, just as the Apostles themselves did when they wished to imitate the extraordinary deed of Elijah. And so much on the obligation of examples in general.

units.la: 6. Dicendum jam est de exemplis & factis Apostolorum speciatim, quæ in causis Politeiæ obligare in perpetuum his rationibus demonstratur. Primò, etsi doctrinam Apostolorum Lucæ liber contineat, inscribitur tamen, non, liber doctrinæ, sed liber actorum Apostolorum: quò patet intentionem spiritus sancti hanc esse, nos ad acta Apostolorum remittere tanquam ad speculum, in quo intueri liceat, quid facto opus sit. Atque cum inter profanam atq; sacram historiam hoc interfit, quòd ad cognitionem illa scripta sit, hæc porrò etiam ad admonitionem, 1. Cor. 10. 11. sequitur historiam Actorum hanc admonitoriam quoque esse, & sic obligatoriam ad acta similia in casibus similibus, a nobis exprimenda. Secundò, ita transit Lucas, c. 1. v. 1. ab historia Evangelij, ad historiam Apostolorum, ut in unum quasi volumen hos libros compingeret: unde sequitur perfectâ directione destitutam fuisse Ecclesiam si hoc libro destitueretur: eundemq; usum & necessitatem hujus libri jam esse, qualis historiæ Evangelicæ est.
units.tr: 6. We must now speak of the examples and deeds of the Apostles specifically, which are shown to bind in perpetuity in matters of the polity, for these reasons. First, although the book of Luke contains the teaching of the Apostles, it is nevertheless entitled not the book of doctrine but the book of the Acts of the Apostles. This shows that the intention of the Holy Spirit is for us to refer to the Acts of the Apostles as to a mirror, in which we may see what must be done. And since this differs between profane and sacred history, that the former was written for knowledge while the latter is also written for admonition (1 Cor. 10:11), it follows that the history of the Acts is also admonitory, and so binding for us to express similar deeds in similar cases. Second, Luke passes from the history of the Gospel to the history of the Apostles in such a way as to join these books together as if into one volume. Whence it follows that the Church would have been left without perfect direction if it were deprived of this book, and that this book now has the same use and necessity as the history of the Gospel.

units.la: 7. Tertiò, dicitur cap. 1. v. 3. locutum fuisse Christum de regno suo, id est, de Politeia Ecclesiæ suæ: quod in ipso limine ponitur, pro actorum postmodum memorandorum authoramento: quo intelligatur, à Christo profectum pro regula fuisse, quicquid ab illis in regni & Politeias Christi fundatione actum est. Evanescit hâc luce, quod nobis pro nebula offundit Whitgiftus ex Huldrico Zwinglio, factum Apostolorum non inferre jus. Addit etenim Zwinglius nisi alias regula illius facti habeatur: jam vero regula factorum Apostolorum habetur in hoc, quod à Christo profectum dicitur, quod ab illis gestum est in regno suo, ac proinde in Politeia Ecclesiastica constituenda. Quod enim hic locutus est Apostolis Christus de regno suo, ejusdem generis est atque illud Marc. 13. 37. Quod vobis dico, id dico omnibus. Sumatur exemplum à mandato baptismi, quod non nisi Apostolis datum à domino est: quodsi igitur quod dictum est illis dictum non sit omnibus, qui eorum successores sunt, mandato baptizandi deficiuntur Ecclesiarum administri ad diem usque hunc.
units.tr: 7. Thirdly, at ch. 1 v. 3 it is said that Christ spoke to them about his kingdom, that is, about the polity of his Church. This is placed at the very threshold as the warrant for the acts recorded afterwards, so that whatever was done in founding Christ's kingdom and polity is understood to have proceeded from Christ and to serve as a rule. This light dispels what Whitgift, following Huldrych Zwingli, casts over us as a fog, namely that a deed of the Apostles does not establish a right. Zwingli adds: "unless some other rule for that deed is had." But the rule for the deeds of the Apostles is had in this: what was done by them in his kingdom is said to have proceeded from Christ, and so is to be applied in constituting the ecclesiastical polity. For when Christ here spoke to the Apostles about his kingdom, it is of the same kind as Mark 13.37: What I say to you, I say to all. Take as an example the command to baptize, which the Lord gave only to the Apostles. If what was said to them was not said to all who are their successors, the ministers of the Churches are without the command to baptize down to this day.

units.la: Quartò, ad facta & exempla Apostolorum imitanda saepissime revocamur. 2. Tim. 3. 10. Tu vero assecutus es doctrinam meam & vitae meae rationem. 1 Cor. 4. 17. Ille vobis revocabit in memoriam vias meas, sicut doceo in singulis Ecclesiis. Phil. 4. 9. Quae de me audivistis, & in me vidistis ea facite.
units.tr: Fourthly, we are very often called back to imitate the deeds and examples of the Apostles. 2 Tim. 3.10: "But you have followed my teaching and my manner of life." 1 Cor. 4.17: "He will bring to your remembrance my ways, as I teach in every Church." Phil. 4.9: "The things you have heard and seen in me, do these."

units.la: 8. Quintò, impositionem manuum necessariam ex Calvino lib. Inst. 4. c. 3. §. 16. asserunt ipsi Hierarchici, cujus fundamentum ecquid quaeso aliud est praeterquam praxis Apostolorum? Imò impositio manuum super presbyteros eorumque ordinatio solis episcopis reservata, quae episcopatus apex est, hoc ipso fundamento nititur, facto nempe particulari episcoporum: Ita enim Bilsonus, Downamus, Saravia argumentantur. Actor. 8. Philippus Samariae manus non imponit, sed Petrus & Iohannes soli, ergo soli jam episcopi qui solum Apostolorum successores sunt jus manus imponendi habent. Mutuati nempe sunt haec argumenta ab Isidoro cujus haec in jure Canonico verba extant. Pontificatus apicem non tenent presbyteri, quia nec charisma ite frontem signant, nec paracletum spiritum dant, quod solis deberi episcopis lectio Actuum Apostolorum demonstrat. Atque certè tam vere sequitur ex hoc facto Apostolorum chrysma episcopis solis deberi, quod vult Isidorus: atque impositionem manuum, quod volunt Hierarchici: utcunque sit, à facto particulari Apostolorum pendet ista ratiocinatio, quam facessere Whitgiftus, Bridgesius, & alibi Bilsonus jubet.
units.tr: 8. Fifthly, the Hierarchists themselves assert from Calvin, Institutes 4.3.16, that the laying on of hands is necessary. What, I ask, is its foundation other than the practice of the Apostles? Indeed the laying on of hands upon elders and their ordination, reserved to bishops alone (which is the summit of the episcopate), rests on this very foundation, namely a particular deed of the Apostles. So Bilson, Downame and Saravia argue. Acts 8: Philip did not lay on hands in Samaria, but Peter and John alone did; therefore bishops alone, who are the sole successors of the Apostles, now have the right to lay on hands. They borrowed these arguments from Isidore, whose words are found in the canon law: "Elders do not hold the summit of the pontificate, since they do not sign the forehead with the chrism nor give the Paraclete Spirit, which the reading of the Acts of the Apostles shows is owed to bishops alone." Certainly it follows as truly from this deed of the Apostles that the chrism is owed to bishops alone, as Isidore wants, and that the laying on of hands is owed to them, as the Hierarchists want. However that may be, this reasoning depends on a particular deed of the Apostles, and it is what Whitgift, Bridges, and Bilson elsewhere bid us to dismiss.

units.la: Sextò, observatio Sabbathi necessario ligat: ex traditione, Ecclesiaeque authoritate inquiunt Romanenses & Rhemenses: imò ex exemplo Christi & Apostolorum inquiunt nostri, imprimis Barlous Episcopus Lincolnensis. Quodsi vero in controversia Sabbathi, adversus papistas à solo exemplo argumentantur ipsi Hierarchici, indigna ludificatio est, adversus puritanos, in controversia Politeiae Ecclesiasticae, Apostolicam praxim ludificari, ac si obligandi vim haberet nullam, nulla exinde argumenta solida depromi possint.
units.tr: Sixthly, observance of the Sabbath binds necessarily. The Romanists and Rhemists say this from tradition and the authority of the Church; indeed our own people say it from the example of Christ and the Apostles, above all Barlow, Bishop of Lincoln. But if, in the controversy about the Sabbath against the papists, the Hierarchists themselves argue from example alone, it is an unworthy mockery, when against the Puritans in the controversy over ecclesiastical polity, to make a joke of Apostolic practice as if it had no binding force and no solid arguments could be drawn from it.

units.la: 6. Septimò, exemplum & praxis hominum Apostolis longe inferiorum, vim argumentandi solidam suppeditant, Hierarchicorum judicio: & nonne igitur exemplum Apostolorum multò magis? In praesentiarum insto in Bilsono solo. Quibusdam, inquit, Metropolitanorum institutio à Timotheo & Tito duci videtur, quod si cui non probetur, ego illi minimè repugno; mihi autem antiqua manifesta & perpetua primae Ecclesiae consuetudo in eligendis Metropolitanis, certissimo quidem argumento est, hunc morem aut ab Apostolis eorumque discipulis receptum & posteris traditum fuisse: aut tantam necessitatis rationem in prima Ecclesiae administratione habuisse, ut totus deinceps orbis Christianus eundem semper retinuerit. En, qui nuper dixerat exemplum Apostolorum in Diaconorum electione non valere: jam exemplum Ecclesiæ Apostolos sequentis in Metropolitanis valere affirmat, ut sint perpetui. Retractandum certe, aut hoc aut illud est: nam si exemplum sequentis Ecclesiæ pro perpetuitate Metrapolitanorum Argumentum certissimum suppeditet: Argumentum certissimum multo magis exhibet exemplum ipsorum Apostolorum, Ecclesiæque illius primæ, quæ sub illis floruerint. Consideretur interim quo res Hierarchica redijt. Per eos enim qui certam politeiæ normam in verbo præscriptam negant, stat: ut scripturas deinceps pro Episcopatus authoritate allegare nequeant: per eos autem qui ab exemplo Apostolorum argumentari non licere profitentur, ut nec praxim Ecclesiæ subsequentis citare possint: nam si ab exemplo Apostolorum arguere non licet, certè ab exemplo ecclesiæ sequentis multo minus.
units.tr: 6. Seventhly, the example and practice of men far inferior to the Apostles supply a solid force of argument, by the Hierarchists' own judgment. Does not the example of the Apostles then much more? For the present I press Bilson alone: "To some," he says, "the institution of Metropolitans seems to be derived from Timothy and Titus. If this does not please anyone, I by no means oppose him. But to me the ancient, manifest and perpetual custom of the primitive Church in electing Metropolitans is a most certain argument that this custom was either received from the Apostles and their disciples and handed down to posterity, or had such a reason of necessity in the early administration of the Church that the whole Christian world afterwards always kept it." See, he who lately said that the example of the Apostles in the election of deacons did not hold, now affirms that the example of the Church following the Apostles holds for Metropolitans, so that they are perpetual. One or the other must certainly be retracted. For if the example of the following Church supplies a most certain argument for the perpetuity of Metropolitans, the example of the Apostles themselves, and of that primitive Church which flourished under them, supplies a much more certain argument. Let us consider meanwhile where the hierarchical cause has come. For by those who deny a certain norm of polity prescribed in the Word, it follows that they can no longer cite Scripture for the authority of the episcopate. And by those who profess that it is not lawful to argue from the example of the Apostles, it follows that they cannot even cite the practice of the succeeding Church. For if it is not lawful to argue from the example of the Apostles, certainly it is much less lawful to argue from the example of the succeeding Church.

units.la: 8. Octavò, exemplum & factum Apostolorum obligare, communis semper sapientum opinio fuit. Ita Franciscus Duarenus: De ratione & forma ordinandi ministros Ecclesiæ, nullum in sacra scriptura præceptum extare arbitror, sed ritus ab Apostolis observatus, quorum exemplum vice cuiusdam præcepti nobis esse debet, ex aliquot scriptorum summorum locis, cognosci poterit. Dixerat in Concilio Basiliensi, Ludovicus Romanus Protonotarius, non esse argumentum sumendum ex gestis Apostolorum, ut quorum exempla miranda essent magis quam imitanda. Quid ad hoc coetus Basiliensis? Fuit eius oratio, inquit Æneas Sylvius, eo molestior, quo plures erant suis contacti verbis: maximeque in eo sibi est reclamatum, quod dixerat Apostolos non esse imitandos: id enim quasi blasphemum omnes impugnarunt. Otthuinus Geratius adjicit in margine: Ludovicus nec multa nec valde bona adduxit: nimirū quum ex malo corio nemo bonos consuere queat calceos. Respondet verò Ludovicus Atrebatensis, concilij hujus præses, ad hunc modū: Licet Ludovicus Apostolorū exemplū nobis interdixerit, ego illorū potissimū in Actibus sisto. Quid enim est quod magis sequi nos deceat, quam Ecclesiæ primæ doctrinam atque consuetudinem? Nihil prohibet imitari Apostolos, quia cum omnia ad nostram doctrinam scripta sint: apparet Apostolos voluisse, nobis exemplum dare. Videmus hujus concilij quodnam hac de re judicium fuerit: annon pudet Hierarchicos, Hierarchiam suam statuminare in eo quod vel ipsis papistis blasphemum est. A papistis accedamus ad nostros: qui quoties à factis Apostolorum contra papistas argumentantur? Deficeret me dies si instarem in singulis: & molestus essem in re à se satis aperta: sufficiat igitur Guilielmus Whitakerus: consule librum de Concil. d. 26. ubi videas quomodo ex facto Apostolorum contra Bellarminum disputat. Imò Hierarchici ipsi hac in re pro nobis adversus vel se vel suos pugnant. Hadrianus Saravia (quem ad finem nil refert) praxin Apostolicam in gubernatione Ecclesiæ, adversus D. Bezam semper esse retinendam multis contendit: Quoniam ea ab ipsis Apostolis abrogata minime est: abrogassent autem si eam perpetuam esse nollent. Non enim ignorarunt, homines plus moveri exemplis quàm præceptis.
units.tr: 8. Eighthly, that the example and deed of the Apostles binds has always been the common opinion of the wise. Thus Francis Duaren: "I think there is no precept in Holy Scripture concerning the manner and form of ordaining ministers of the Church, but the rite observed by the Apostles, whose example ought to stand for a kind of precept for us, may be learned from several passages of the greatest writers." At the Council of Basel, Louis of Rome, protonotary, had said that no argument should be drawn from the deeds of the Apostles, since their examples were to be admired rather than imitated. What did the Council of Basel make of this? "His speech was," says Aeneas Sylvius, "the more troublesome, the more people were touched by his words. And especially they cried out against him because he had said the Apostles were not to be imitated; for they all attacked this as if it were blasphemous." Otthuinus Geratius adds in the margin: "Louis brought forward neither many nor very good points: since no one can sew good shoes from bad leather." Louis of Arras, president of this council, replied as follows: "Although Louis has forbidden us the example of the Apostles, I set before us especially theirs in the Acts. For what is more fitting for us to follow than the doctrine and custom of the primitive Church? Nothing prevents us from imitating the Apostles, since all things have been written for our teaching: it is clear that the Apostles wished to give us an example." We see what judgment this council made on this matter. Are the Hierarchists not ashamed to prop up their hierarchy on what is blasphemous even to the papists themselves? Let us turn from the papists to our own people. How often do they argue from the deeds of the Apostles against the papists? The day would fail me if I pressed each instance, and I would be tedious on a matter already sufficiently clear. Let William Whitaker suffice: consult his book on the Councils, disp. 26, where you may see how he disputes against Bellarmine from the deed of the Apostles. Indeed, in this matter the Hierarchists themselves fight for us against themselves or their own people. Hadrian Saravia (whose ending matters little here) strongly contends against Beza that the apostolic practice in governing the Church is always to be retained: "since it was by no means abrogated by the Apostles themselves; and they would have abrogated it if they did not wish it to be perpetual. For they were not unaware that men are moved more by examples than by precepts."

units.la: Cont. Bez. t. 14. p. 139 sis : ut si quid necessarium esset posteris tradi, exempli proprij abrogationem testari necessarium fuisset. Demonstratio Mathei Sutclivij pro Episcopi authoritate tertia, à voce & usu Apostolorum est : ut ipse titulus capitis indicat : putat igitur satis solida argumenta ab ipso exemplo Apostolorum desumi posse. Thomas Bilsonus ita pro episcopatu differit. Erudite illud à Tertulliano notatur. Constabit id esse ab Apostolis traditum, quod apud Ecclesias Apostolorum fuerit sacrosanctum: & ab Augustino. Quod universa tenet Ecclesia, nec concilijs institutum, sed semper retentum est, non nisi authoritate Apostolica traditum rectissime creditur. Iam vero in Ecclesijs Episcopus fuit, etiam antequam concilia de his statuere cepisset: idcirco hic mos retractandus non est. Ita & morem & factum Ecclesiarum Apostolicarum, non Apostolorum solum, obligare in perpetuum Bilsonus credit. Duo haec patrum testimonia postquam citasset Georgius Downamus, adjungit Cartwrightum, qui dicit etiam exemplum Apostolorum sine mandato necessitatem trahere. Ita pro Episcopo suo, vel ex solo exemplo Apostolorum, Ecclesiarumque, pugnare Downamus non veretur : quam sibi constanter viderit ipse : parum etenim haec ratiocinatio ex facto Apostolorum obligante, illi congruere mihi quidem videtur, qui Politeiam Ecclesiasticam mutabilem esse vult. Atque ita confectum est, etiam facta Apostolorum in Ecclesiae Politeia, sive constituenda sive exercenda, necessitatem inferre, ut ea immutabilis sit.
units.tr: Against Beza, vol. 14, p. 139: "…so that if anything necessary were to be handed down to posterity, it would have been necessary to attest the abrogation of its own example." Mathew Sutcliffe's demonstration, the third for the authority of a bishop, from the voice and practice of the Apostles, is as the title of the chapter itself indicates. He thinks that solid arguments can therefore be drawn from the example of the Apostles themselves. Thomas Bilson argues thus for the episcopate: "It is learnedly noted by Tertullian that what is shown to have been handed down by the Apostles is what was held sacrosanct in the Churches of the Apostles; and by Augustine: what the whole Church holds, not instituted by councils but always retained, is rightly believed to have been handed down by apostolic authority. Now in the Churches there was a bishop even before councils began to decide on these matters; therefore this custom is not to be retracted." Thus Bilson believes that the custom and the deed of the apostolic Churches, not of the Apostles alone, bind for ever. After George Downame had cited these two testimonies of the Fathers, he adds Cartwright, who says that even the example of the Apostles, without a command, brings necessity. Thus Downame does not hesitate to fight for his bishop even from the example of the Apostles and Churches alone, how consistently he himself saw. For this reasoning, that a deed of the Apostles binds, seems to me to agree poorly with one who wants the ecclesiastical polity to be mutable. And so it is concluded that the deeds of the Apostles, in constituting or in exercising the polity of the Church, also bring necessity, so that it is immutable.
