units.la: Disciplinae immutabilitas à doctrina Apostolorum probatur: & primo refutantur duae Hierarchicorum exceptiones sibi invicem contrariae.
units.tr: The immutability of discipline is proved from the doctrine of the Apostles, and first the two mutually contradictory objections of the hierarchists are refuted.

units.la: DIcendum jam est de doctrina Apostolorum quam de Politeia Ecclesiastica tradiderunt: quae quò minus ejusdem immutabilitatem inferre videatur, negatur à quibusdam eam obligare omnino; ab alijs, obligare eam quidem concedidur, non tamen in perpetuum. Ita exceptiones duae adversus doctrinae Apostolicae de Politeia immutabilitatem sunt: quam sibi invicem contrariae quis non videt? Posterior enim priorem tollit: quum eam obligare dicit, quod à prima non conceditur. Haec vero prima a Matheo Sutclivio prosecta est, qui Christum in externis legislatorem non esse postquam posuisset, ita ex nostra persona objicit. At Christus, inquiunt illi Mat. 18. de vitandis scandalis & monendis fratribus mandata dedit: dicunt etiam Paulum quaedam praecepta Corinthijs, alia Timotheo & Tito dedisse, & quod Christus rex appelletur, & magis fidelis in Dei familia quam Moses, dicatur, libenter usurpant. Atqui facilis est responsio, Christi regnum in Ecclesia, non esse in rebus externis, sed in conscientiarum dominio & regimine collocandum: Christiique & Apostolorum quae feruntur leges, in rebus rebus externis Christianam nunquam sustulerant libertatem: nam & in casu iuris, licet non appellato fratre ad Ecclesiam rem deferre: & passim cessavit ablutio pedum, & osculatio prima Christianorum. Nonnunquam etiam occurrunt tempora, cum Episcopi & Diaconi haberi non possunt. Ad regulas Pauli 1.Tim. 3. non sunt omnia exactè exigenda, ut nulli eligendi sunt Episcopi aut Diaconi nisi qui illis quasi ad amussim respondeant. Satis est si omnem adhibuerimus curam, ut quam prope possimus accedamus. Dicimus igitur leges morales acuratè servandas, Ecclesiasticas Apostolorum constitutiones quatenus tempora & mores patiuntur, ut nulla vis auferatur Christianæ libertati. Hæc ille: quæ cujus notæ meritique sunt, consequentiis hisce incnstrabo.
units.tr: It must now be said concerning the doctrine of the Apostles, which they handed down about the ecclesiastical polity. To make it seem less likely that this doctrine implies the immutability of that polity, some deny that it binds at all, while others concede that it binds but not forever. So there are two objections against the immutability of the Apostolic doctrine about polity. Who does not see that they contradict each other? For the latter destroys the former, since it says that the doctrine binds, which the first does not grant. The first objection was put forward by Matthew Sutcliffe, who, after he had asserted that Christ is not a lawgiver in external matters, raises it in our name as follows: "But Christ, they say, gave commands in Matthew 18 about avoiding scandals and admonishing brothers. They also say that Paul gave certain precepts to the Corinthians and others to Timothy and Titus, and they gladly use the fact that Christ is called King, and that he is said to be more faithful in God's household than Moses. But the answer is easy: Christ's kingdom in the Church is not to be placed in external matters but in the dominion and rule of consciences. And the laws that are said to be Christ's and the Apostles' never took away Christian liberty in external matters. For even in a case of law, one may bring the matter to the Church without calling in a brother; and the washing of feet and the first kiss of the Christians have passed away everywhere. Sometimes too there are times when bishops and deacons cannot be had. The rules of Paul in 1 Timothy 3 need not all be demanded exactly, so that no bishops or deacons may be chosen except those who correspond to them as if by a plumb line. It is enough if we use every care to come as near as we can. We say, therefore, that the moral laws are to be kept exactly, and the ecclesiastical constitutions of the Apostles as far as times and customs allow, so that no force is taken away from Christian liberty." So he says. What these statements are worth, and what they deserve, I shall show by the following consequences.

units.la: 1. Primò, ad papismum accedere illa dico: Christum non vult esse in Politeia Ecclesiastica legislatorem. Quid igitur de mandatis Christi sentiendum quæ de rebus Ecclesiasticis dedit. Illæ quæ feruntur leges, inquit, id est, ex opinione Puritanorum, leges quidem meo judicio non sunt sed constitutiones tantum Ecclesiasticæ, quæ à legibus moralibus longissimè discernuntur. Cur igitur non retunde loquitur cum Papistis? non sunt præcepta sed consilia tantum: idem sensus subest: nam permissam putat libertatem esse vel servare vel non servare, prout mores & tempora ferunt.
units.tr: 1. First, I say that these statements come close to Popery: they hold that Christ does not wish to be a lawgiver in the ecclesiastical polity. What then should we think of the commands of Christ which he gave about church matters? "Those laws that are handed down," he says, "that is, according to the opinion of the Puritans, are not laws in my judgment, but only ecclesiastical constitutions, which are very far distinguished from moral laws." Why then does he not speak sharply with the Papists? "They are not precepts but only counsels": the same sense underlies it, for he thinks that liberty is granted to keep them or not to keep them, as customs and times bring.

units.la: 2. Secundò, olent etiam Adiaphorismum idque quidem ante hoc tempus inauditum: non enim solum præcepta Politeias, præcepta de rebus indifferentibus esse statuit, quæ indifferentes non sunt: sed etiam ipsa præcepta indifferentia facit, quod quisquamnè quæso ante audivit unquam? Semper etenim in Ecclesia Dei judicatum est, res indifferentes ipsas præceptas non esse, quæ vero de earum usu præcepta traduntur, ea & immutabilia esse & necessario observanda, qualia sunt illa quæ 1.Cor.14.40. ab Apostolo proponuntur. Qualis hic igitur Mathei Sutclivij Adiaphorismus est? Primò, quanquam præcepta Politeias, de ipsis rebus sint, & non tantummodo de rerum usu: Politeiam tamen rem indifferentem esse vult. Secundò, quanquam præcepta de indifferentibus necessario observanda sint ac indifferentia non sint: facit tamen ille præcepta Politeias, ipsa inquam præcepta, indifferentia, & necessariò observanda esse negat. Tertiò, quod in usu solum rerum indifferentium locum habet, nempè ut dirigantur prout expedit: hoc ille ad ipsum præceptum trahit ac si ob morum & temporum occasiones præceptū ipsum, alterari, violari, tolli possunt.
units.tr: 2. Second, he also smells of Adiaphorism, and indeed of a kind unheard of before this time. For he does not only hold that the precepts of the polity are precepts about indifferent things, which are not indifferent; he even makes the precepts themselves indifferent. Who, I ask, has ever heard of such a thing before? For it has always been judged in the Church of God that the things themselves are not made the subject of precepts, but the precepts that are handed down about their use are both unchangeable and to be observed necessarily, such as those that the Apostle sets forth in 1 Corinthians 14:40. What sort of Adiaphorism, then, is this of Matthew Sutcliffe? First, although the precepts of the polity concern the things themselves and not merely their use, he nevertheless wants the polity to be a thing indifferent. Second, although precepts about indifferent things must be observed necessarily and are not indifferent, he nevertheless makes the precepts of the polity indifferent, and denies that these precepts themselves must be observed necessarily. Third, what has a place only in the use of indifferent things, namely that they be directed as expedient, he transfers to the precept itself, as if, because of the occasions of customs and times, the precept itself could be altered, violated, or removed.

units.la: 3. Tertiò favent etiam libertinismo: affectant enim libertatem à præceptis Christi & Apostolorum: de qua porro Lous ita. Libertatem à Christo partam procurant, qui disciplinam veram certam & immutabilem ex verbo statuunt. Atqui inquam libertas à Christo parta libera est, ergo ipsius præcepta servitus Iacob. 1. 25. & 2. 12. non datur ulli ab ipsius præceptis liberari: miserrima etenim peccato servitus ejusmodi libertas est: quam dum inducere in ecclesiā Hierarchici isti volunt, nonnè quæso offendunt in illud 1.Petri 2.16, Ut liberi, ac
units.tr: 3. Third, they also favour libertinism: they aim at liberty from the precepts of Christ and the Apostles. Of this Lous says: "They procure the liberty won by Christ who establish a true, certain and unchangeable discipline from the Word." But, I say, liberty won by Christ is free, therefore no one is set free from his precepts, which is the servitude of James 1:25 and 2:12. For liberty of that kind is a most wretched servitude to sin. When these hierarchists want to bring it into the Church, do they not, I ask, offend against "that saying of 1 Peter 2:16, As free, and

units.la: nov non veluti malitiæ velamen habentes libertatem sed servi Dei, id est, præceptis ejus servientes ac proinde ad nullam ab eisdem libertatem suspirantes? Quarto hypocrisin fovent cum tyrannide immani conjunctam, qualis et illa Saulis fuit: qui etsi legis violationem in sanguine effundendo absque pœna dimiserit: legem tamen suam, eamque incommodè nimis latam, adeo rigidè persequitur; ut Ionathan ipse quanquam optimè meritus, ob parum mellis degustati ad mortem condemnandus sit. 1. Sam. 14. 44. Imò in Saulina disobedientia Hierarchici sunt, quæ proximo capite commemoratur: præcepta Christi & Apostolorum de politeia Ecclesiastica à tergo rejiciunt, & libertatem ab eodem sibi assumunt: quum interim qui ad libertatem Christianam provocant ab humanis inventis qualis permittitur, imò mandatur. 1. Cor. 7. 22. 23. (puta à cononibus de crucis signo, de superpelliceo, & hujusmodi nugamentis, superstitiosis quidem & in cultu Dei illicitis, sed fac indifferentibus) habentur pro ridiculis; quid dixi? pro ridiculis haberi eos? imo degradantur, excommunicantur, & bonis omnibus exuuntur. Hoc nimirum reliqui erat ad mensuram Hierarchiæ implendam, ut quæ libertatem imo libertinismum potius à Christi præceptis de Politeia sibi assumpsisset: ullam Christianam libertatem à præceptis suis, id est, humanis interdiceret: ut quæ jugum Christi excussisset ipsa (ô Domine quousque) jugum suum aliorum cervicibus sanè intollerandum imponeret.
units.tr: not using liberty as a cover for malice, but as servants of God," that is, serving his precepts, and therefore not longing for any liberty from them? Fourth, they foster hypocrisy joined with monstrous tyranny, like that of Saul, who, although he let go the violation of the law without punishment in the shedding of blood, yet pursues his own law, and one brought in too harshly, so rigidly that Jonathan himself, although he had deserved very well, is condemned to death for tasting a little honey (1 Sam. 14:44). Indeed, the hierarchists are guilty of the disobedience of Saul, which was mentioned in the previous chapter: they cast behind their backs the precepts of Christ and the Apostles about the ecclesiastical polity, and assume liberty from them for themselves; meanwhile those who appeal to Christian liberty from human inventions, which is granted and even commanded (1 Cor. 7:22, 23), (for example, from the ceremonies of the surplice, the sign of the cross, and such trifles, superstitious indeed and unlawful in the worship of God, but granted to be indifferent), are regarded as ridiculous. Why do I say "regarded as ridiculous"? They are even degraded, excommunicated, and stripped of all their goods. This was surely all that was left to fill up the measure of the hierarchy: that the power which had taken to itself liberty, or rather libertinism, from the precepts of Christ about the polity, should forbid any Christian liberty from its precepts, that is, from human ones; and that the one who had shaken off the yoke of Christ should itself (O Lord, how long?) lay its own yoke upon the necks of others, truly intolerable.

units.la: 4. Quintò & ultimo rebellionis cuiusdam speciem habent. Quid enim aliud spirant, quam legem Christi de privata admonitione violari posse absq; peccato, quum leges Pauli ad Timoth. de episcopis eligendis nec ita rigide exigendas dicit? Licet non appellato fratre rem ad ecclesiam deferre: id est, licet audacter contra mandatum Christi ire? & leges Pauli ad Timotheum non prohibent, quin probanda sit quæ in Anglia jam dominatur ministrorum caterva, (si tamen ministri qui ne Latinè quidem sciunt, certè qui verbum Dei prædicare non possunt, sed meri muti canes sunt, perdentes gregem cui præsunt, & humanarum animarum sanguine sat facti [i.e. guss?] Quanquam admonendus es (lector) multò levius cum quam res postulat, in priore rebellione describenda locutum esse. Licet, inquit, non appellato fratre eum ad ecclesiam deferre. Sed hoc parum est, pro eo quod in Anglia geritur: ubi non tantùm absque ulla privata admonitione, ad consistoria Episcoporum deferuntur homines, verumetiam excommunicantur. Atque hæc ad exceptionem Hierarchicorum primam, quod doctrina Christi & Apostolorum de politeia ecclesiastica, immutabiles nullas leges habeat, imò ne leges quidem obligatorias, sed præcepta tantum nescio quæ indifferentia.
units.tr: 4. Fifth and last, they have a kind of rebellion. For what else do they breathe, than that the law of Christ about private admonition may be violated without sin, since they say that the laws of Paul to Timothy about choosing bishops are not to be exacted so rigidly? "Although the matter may be brought to the Church without calling a brother," that is, although one may boldly act against the command of Christ? And the laws of Paul to Timothy do not forbid that the band of ministers which now rules in England should be approved (if indeed they are ministers who do not even know Latin, and certainly cannot preach the Word of God, but are mere dumb dogs, destroying the flock over which they preside, and sated with the blood of human souls [i.e. guss?]). Yet you must be warned, reader, that in describing the earlier rebellion he spoke far more mildly than the matter requires. "Although," he says, "one may bring him to the Church without calling a brother." But this is little, compared with what is done in England: there men are not only brought before the consistories of the bishops without any private admonition, but are also excommunicated. And this is the answer to the first objection of the hierarchists, that the doctrine of Christ and the Apostles about the ecclesiastical polity has no unchangeable laws, indeed not even binding laws, but only certain indifferent precepts.

units.la: §. Accedendum jam est ad exceptionem secundam, quæ obligare quidem præcepta fatetur quæ de politeia ecclesiastica in verbo Dei reperiuntur, sed tamen in perpetuum minimè obligare dicit: Quædam præcepta divina sunt, quæ perpetua tamen non sunt. Certè, sed recte Saravia. Praecepta de politeia ecclesiastica perpetua sunt, etsi quaedam divina non sunt perpetua. Quo minus hoc obtineat, in duas hominum opiniones, sese haec exceptio secunda distringit: quarum prima invaliditatem ipsius praecepti, secunda invaliditatem praecipientis objicit. Prima a Richardo Hookero ponitur ita, ubi de politeiis ecclesiasticis mutabilitate disserit. Leges, quamquam a Deo ipso ordinatae, et quamquam finis ad quem ordinatae fuerunt permanent; cessare tamen possunt, si per alterationem personarum aut temporum insufficientes reperiantur ad finem illum assequendum: quo respectu, cur praesumere nobis non licet? inclamare Deum pro ea mutatione et alteratione, quam ipsa rerum conditio necessariam facit? In hoc casu non praesumunt homines, Dei ordinationem mutare: sed ordinationi Dei cedunt, quae ipsa requirit ut immutetur. Haec medulla est eorum, quae fuse disputat, pro politeiis ecclesiasticae mutatione, quando pro conditione rerum et temporis reperitur invalida ad finem suum obtinendum. Atqui negamus cum summa Dei sapientia et providentia stare posse, ut politeiam ecclesiasticam instituerit, quae ulla rerum, personarum, temporumve conditione, fieri possit invalida aut insufficiens ad finem suum (ad quem ab eo est ordinata,) assequendum. Fac autem invalidam et insufficientem evadere eam posse. Quis legem validiorem feret? quis politeiam ecclesiasticam magis sufficientem instituet? Num caro et sanguis? At ipse concedis, meliorari ab hominibus non posse, quae a Deo instituta sunt: meliorantur veri, si melior, validior, magis sufficiens, quoquo tempore, politeia ecclesiae ab hominibus institui possit, atque ea est, quae ab ipso Deo est instituta. Ego sane quomodo cohaereant ista non video: sed est et aliud scisci tandum. Quis judicium feret, quando cum pro rerum conditione leges politeiae ecclesiasticae invalidae a Deo latae sunt? Quis item si invalidae sint, judicabit, utrum humana politeia sit validior ea, quae est a Deo lata? Ad postremum, fieri potest, ut dividantur sententiae, quis judicabit, quae nam ex illis politeiis quae ab hominibus proponuntur, maxime valida et sufficiens sit? Vide quantis praesumptionibus haec assertio scateat, in quibus tamen hominem meminem praesumere dicis. Nonne praesument hodie Episcopi Anglicani, quando disciplinam reformatam naso suspendunt: ac si invalidissima esset ad pacem ecclesiae, salutem ecclesiae, aedificationem ecclesiae, aut conservandam aut promovendam? Audi O Deus noster (inquit Nehemias) nos esse contemptui, et converte probrum eorum in caput eorum: ut quod in Anglia bene jam Deus coepit opus politeias reformatae, quod vel a vulpe dirui potuisse Tobiae isti existimant, felicissime procedat; probro in Hierarchiae suae caput converso, sub qua omnia indies in deterius prolabuntur, retroque collapsa feruntur. Non est igitur Hookere, non est mihi credo, praesumptio levis, sed Samballiticum contemptum spirans, quando praesumit judicare caro, invalidas Dei leges esse, quae de sua politeia tulit: praesertim cum pollicitus fuerit, se vel puerum Isa. 11. 8. id est pauperulum quendam ministrum, et regimen, humano quidem iudicio, invalidissimum, ipsos leones, tigrides, pardos, ursos denique & Basiliscos, in ordinem redacturum.
units.tr: §. We must now come to the second objection, which admits that the precepts found in the Word of God about the ecclesiastical polity do bind, but says that they by no means bind forever: "Some divine precepts are such that they are not perpetual." Certainly, but Saravia rightly says: "The precepts about the ecclesiastical polity are perpetual, even if some divine precepts are not perpetual." That this may not hold, this second objection divides itself into two opinions of men: the first objects to the invalidity of the precept itself, the second to the invalidity of the one who gives it. The first is put forward by Richard Hooker, where he discusses the mutability of ecclesiastical polities, thus: "Laws, although ordained by God himself, and although the end for which they were ordained remains, can nevertheless cease, if through a change of persons or times they are found insufficient to attain that end. In this respect, why is it not lawful for us to presume? To cry out to God for that change and alteration which the very condition of things makes necessary? In this case men do not presume to change the ordinance of God, but yield to the ordinance of God, which itself requires that it be changed." This is the marrow of what he argues at length, in favour of changing ecclesiastical polities, when by the condition of things and times they are found invalid for attaining their end. But we deny that it can stand with the supreme wisdom and providence of God that he should have instituted an ecclesiastical polity which, by any condition of things, persons, or times, could become invalid or insufficient for attaining its end (for which it was ordained by him). But grant that it could become invalid and insufficient. Who will bring a more valid law? Who will institute an ecclesiastical polity more sufficient? Flesh and blood? But you yourself concede: "What has been instituted by God cannot be bettered by men; but if a better, more valid, more sufficient polity of the Church can be instituted by men at any time, then that is improved, and it is the one which has been instituted by God himself." I certainly do not see how these things cohere; but there is also another question to be settled. Who will give judgment, when laws of the ecclesiastical polity have been given by God and are invalid because of the condition of things? Who likewise, if they are invalid, will judge whether a human polity is more valid than the one which was given by God? Finally, it may happen that opinions differ: who will judge which of those polities that are proposed by men is most valid and sufficient? See how full of presumptions this assertion is, while yet you say that no man presumes. Do not the English bishops presume today, when they turn up their noses at the reformed discipline, as if it were most invalid either for preserving or for promoting the peace of the Church, the salvation of the Church, or the building up of the Church? "Hear, O our God," says Nehemiah, "for we are despised, and turn their reproach upon their own head": so that the work of the reformed polity, which God has already happily begun in England, which these Tobiahs think could have been overthrown even by a fox, may proceed most happily, the reproach being turned upon the head of their hierarchy, under which everything daily slides into worse and is carried backward in collapse. It is not therefore, Hooker, it is not, I believe, a light presumption, but a Sanballatic contempt breathing, when flesh presumes to judge that the laws of God, which he gave about his own polity, are invalid, especially since he promised that he would bring into order even a boy (Isa. 11:8), that is, some poor little minister, and a government most invalid by human judgment, even lions, tigers, leopards, bears, and finally basilisks.

units.la: 6 At inquit Hookerus Præsto est exemplum, quum lex divina mutata est idque licitè ab hominibus, quando inualida reperta fuit, ad suum finem obtinendum. Iltud quidem exemplum, ego vel maximè audire aveo. Lex inquit de furto immutata est, quando illius pœna augmentata est, propterea quod restitutio quadrupli non erit sufficiens ad furtum cohibendum.
units.tr: 6 But Hooker says: "There is an example at hand of when the divine law has been changed, and lawfully so by men, when it was found to be too weak to attain its end." I am most eager to hear that example. "The law about theft," he says, "was changed when its penalty was increased, because restitution of fourfold would not be sufficient to restrain theft."

units.la: At quid hæc ad rem? Augmentatio inquit, est mutatio quædam: sed non de hujusmodi mutatione jam agitur: probandum etenim tibi sumpsisti cessare posse politeiam ecclesiæ, & aliam ab hominibus surrogari, quando inualida reperitur ad finem suum assequendum. Secundo negò hanc pœnæ augmentationem, ipsius legis mutationem ullam esse, cujus, si non litera, sententia tamen, hanc ipsam pœnæ augmentationem re ita ferente intendebat. Æquitas, inquit concilium Basiliense, in sinu principis habitare semper debet, quæ relictâ legis litera, rationem illius sequitur: Sic Thomas Aquinas, ordinatur æquitas, ut quando litera legis deficit, illius intentio seruetur, prout æqualitas iustitiæ & bonum publicum potest, ut ita: fulurint. Hoc ita cum sit, violaretur lex de furto si relictâ litera, illius intentio non spectetur, quæ est ut furtum supprimatur. Non igitur mutatio hujus legis, pœnæ hujus literalis multiplicatio est: sed æqua illius administratio, uti ipsę legis intentio (pro illa quam continet æquitate) postulat. Tertio contrarium hinc probari, præberique exemplum, quid hominibus faciendum sit: quando lex divina aliqua minus valida videatur. Probat Hookerus cessationem politeias ecclesiasticæ, ab exemplo, quo lex aliqua augmentatur, ecquid absurdius? Abolitio etenim legis, & ejusdem augmentatio contraria sunt: tantum abest ut aboleat legem, qui eandem augmentat, ut ex adverso eam firmet atque roboret: tantum igitur abest, ut probet propositum hæc instantia, ut potius contrarium docet: nempe cum politeia ecclesiastica invalida reperitur, non statim ab hominibus abolendam, sed augmentandam potius, & modis omnibus muniendam esse. Quarto, nulla hic ab Hookero proportio seruatur in circumstantijs. Mutabilem illè politeiam Ecclesiasticam esse vult, pro locorum & temporum & personarum conditione: at non pro locorum & temporum & personarum conditione hæc lege de furto mutatio fuit: neque mutatur substantia, sed circumstantia pœnæ: sic nihil hinc concluditur, nisi hoc tantum: quum propter exuberantem hominum malitiam sanctiones & pœnæ ecclesiasticæ minus validè videntur, diligentius & rigidius exercendas eas esse: & magistratus porro authoritate, pænisque civilibus validius muniendas. Atque hæc ad exceptionem Hierarchicorum secundam: leges nempè de politeia ecclesiastica immutabiles non esse, quia fieri potest, ut invalidè reperiantur ad finem suum assequendum.
units.tr: But what has this to do with the matter? "An increase," he says, "is a certain kind of change." But that is not the kind of change we are now discussing. You took it upon yourself to prove that the polity of the Church may cease and be replaced by another devised by men, "when it is found too weak to attain its end." Second, I deny that this increase of the penalty was any change of the law at all. If not its wording, then its meaning, which the law intended, and the circumstances required, was this very increase of the penalty. "Equity," says the Council of Basel, "ought always to dwell in the bosom of the prince, which, leaving the letter of the law, follows its reason." So Thomas Aquinas: "Equity is ordained so that, when the letter of the law fails, its intention is preserved, so far as the equality of justice and the public good allow." Since this is so, the law about theft would be violated if, leaving the letter aside, its intention were not regarded, which is that theft be suppressed. Therefore the change of this law is not a multiplication of this literal penalty, but a fair administration of it, as the intention of the law itself (by the equity it contains) requires. Third, the contrary is proved from this, and an example is given of what men ought to do when a divine law seems rather weak. Hooker proves the cessation of ecclesiastical polity from the example of a law which is increased. What could be more absurd? For the abolition of a law and its increase are opposites. He who increases a law is so far from abolishing it that, on the contrary, he confirms and strengthens it. So this instance is so far from proving the proposition that it rather teaches the opposite: namely that when ecclesiastical polity is found weak, it is not to be abolished at once by men, but rather increased and fortified in every way. Fourth, Hooker here observes no proportion in the circumstances. He wants the ecclesiastical polity to be changeable according to the condition of places, times and persons. But the change in the law about theft was not made according to the condition of places, times and persons. Nor is its substance changed, only the circumstance of the penalty. So nothing follows from this except this alone: that since, because of the overflowing wickedness of men, the ecclesiastical sanctions and penalties seem less valid, they ought to be exercised more diligently and rigorously, and the magistrate should further strengthen them with authority and with civil penalties. And this is enough for the second objection of the Hierarchists, namely that laws concerning ecclesiastical polity are not immutable, because they may be found too weak to attain their end.

units.la: 7 Sequitur opinio Hierarchicorum nonnullorum secunda: quæ non ex invaliditate præcepti, sed præcipientis potius pugnat. Hanc tuetur Georgius Downamus, qui distinguens inter jus divinum quod immutabile esse vult, & jus Apostolicum quod mutabile: Politeiam Ecclesiasticam, speciatim Hierarchicum Episcopatum, non iure divino immutabili, sed iure Apostolico mutabili pendere affirmat. Primò, in hac distinctione advertenda illius novitas est, & reprehendenda: præsertim cum novitatem nobis ubique obijciat.
units.tr: 7 There follows a second opinion of some Hierarchists, which contends not against the invalidity of the precept but rather against the authority of the one who commands. It is upheld by George Downame, who, distinguishing between divine law, which he wants to be unchangeable, and apostolic law, which is changeable, affirms that the ecclesiastical polity, specifically the hierarchical episcopate, depends not on unchangeable divine law but on changeable apostolic law. First, the novelty of this distinction is to be noted and rebuked, especially since he is always throwing novelty in our faces.

units.la: Turpe est doctori cum culpa redarguit ipsum.
units.tr: It is shameful for a teacher to rebuke another when he is himself at fault.

units.la: Quod si autem novam esse inficietur, proferat Patrem, proferat Scholasticum, proferat Canonistam, proferat Papistam, proferat Protestantem, proferat Hierarchicum, qui ea ante usus sit. Secundò, in hac distinctione advertatur quòd Episcopatum Hierarchicum ex jure divino esse non vult: id quod diserte plures affirmant, ut lib. 1. p. 2. lib. 3. p. & lib. 4. o. Iam hoc pro nobis satis est. Si etenim ex jure divino non sit, ex jure humano est: inter jus divinum & jus humanum nullum datur medium. Patet hoc ex ipsis sacris, in quibus vocatio aut à Deo est, aut ab hominibus Gal. 1: 1, & ministerium Ecclesiasticum unumquodque aut a cælo aut ab hominibus Math. 21,25. ministri denique ipsi quoad ortum aut cæli aut terræ stellæ sunt. Ap: 12. 1 cum Ap.9: 1. Ap: 13: 2. Concordat jus Canonicum, consentit Isidorus: Omnes (inquit) leges aut divinæ sunt aut humanæ: membra itaque dividentia, non jus divinum & Apostolicum, sed divinum & humanum, sunt. Quod ad jus Apostolicum attinet, illud revera divinum est: distinctum à divino vult Downamus, tum esse humanum ut confiteatur necesse est.
units.tr: But if he denies that it is new, let him produce a Father, a Schoolman, a canonist, a Papist, a Protestant, or a Hierarchist who used it before. Secondly, let it be noted in this distinction that he does not want the hierarchical episcopacy to be from divine right, which many state plainly, as in lib. 1. p. 2. lib. 3. p. and lib. 4. o. Now this is enough for us. For if it is not from divine right, it is from human right, since there is no middle ground between divine right and human right. This is clear from the Scriptures themselves, in which a calling is either from God, or from men (Gal. 1.1), and the ecclesiastical ministry is each thing either from heaven or from men (Matth. 21.25); finally, the ministers themselves, as to their origin, are stars either of heaven or of earth (Apoc. 12.1 with Apoc. 9.1, Apoc. 13.2). Canon law agrees, and Isidore concurs: All laws (he says) are either divine or human. So the dividing members are not divine and apostolic law, but divine and human law. As for apostolic law, it is really divine. Downame wants it to be distinct from divine law, but he must confess that it is human.

units.la: 8 Dixi nuper hanc distinctionem inter jus divinum & Apostolicum in nullo authore reperiri: certè sensu Downamiano, ut jus Apostolicum medium quoddam jus sit quod nec sit divinum nec humanum. Alias reperitur apud Bellarminum a quo forte locum alium accepit Downamus: qui cœlibatum sacerdotum non jure divino, sed Apostolico jure niti vult, & ita esse dispensabile. Iam verò per jus Apostolicum, Bellarminus jus humanum intelligit: probè intelligens, inter jus divinum & humanum, nullum jus medium intervenire. Verba hæc sunt. Beatus Thomas in 2. 2. q. 88. art. 1. diserte docet votum continentiæ esse annexum ordinibus sacris, ex solo ecclesiæ decreto, ac proinde dispensabile esse. Idem docet Caietanus in opusculo Tom. 1. Tractat. 27. & Sotus lib. 7. de Iustitia q: 6. art. 1. vbi etiam docent, quod ego verissimum puto, decretum hoc quo votum est annexum ordinibus non quidem proprie divinum esse: sed tamen esse Apostolicum, & in tota ecclesia à temporibus Apostolorum longo tempore esse observatum. Nunc probandum est non jure divino, sed humano duntaxat (adverte, appellat nunc jus humanum, quod primis hujus capitis verbis, jus Apostolicum appellaverat) prohibitum esse sacerdotum coniugium, & proinde in hac dispensari posse. Observanda sunt in Soto & Bellarmino parentibus primis distinctionis hujusce Downamianæ inter jus divinum & Apostolicum hæc tria. Primò, in jure tantum humano mutabilitátem & difpensabilitátem reperiri,sic ut Episcopatus Hierarchicus cum Downami judicio mutabilis sit,ex jure humano tantum esse consequetur. Secundò, jus illud Apostolicum, quod juri divino opponitur,merè jus humanum esse,& nullo modo divinum: sic ut Episcopatus Hierarchicus Downami judicio merè sit humanus. Tertiò, per Apostolicum intelligi apud authores, inventum humanum,antiquo tempore observatum: sic ut cum Hieronymus,Episcopum vocet traditionem Apostolicam nihil aliud intelligat,quàm ordinem humanum quidem, sed tempore antiquissimo observatum, quod ipsissimam esse Hieronymi mentem,suo loco demonstrabitur.
units.tr: 8 I said recently that this distinction between divine and apostolic law is found in no author, at least not in the Downamian sense, that apostolic law is some middle law which is neither divine nor human. Elsewhere it is found in Bellarmine, from whom Downame perhaps took the other point: that the celibacy of priests rests not on divine law but on apostolic law, and so is dispensable. Now indeed by apostolic law Bellarmine understands human law, clearly recognising that no middle law intervenes between divine and human law. His words are these: "Blessed Thomas, in 2.2 q. 88 art. 1, expressly teaches that the vow of continence is attached to sacred orders by the decree of the Church alone, and therefore is dispensable." Cajetan teaches the same in the opusculum, Tom. 1, Tract. 27, and Soto in book 7 de Iustitia q. 6 art. 1, where they also teach (which I think most true) that this decree by which the vow is attached to the orders is not properly divine, but nevertheless is apostolic, and has been observed for a long time throughout the whole Church since the times of the Apostles. It must now be proved that the marriage of priests is forbidden not by divine law but by human law alone (note that he now calls human law what in the first words of this chapter he had called apostolic law), and therefore can be dispensed with. In Soto and Bellarmine, the first parents of this Downamian distinction between divine and apostolic law, three things are to be observed. First, mutability and dispensability are found only in human law, so that if the hierarchical episcopate is mutable in Downame's judgement, it would follow that it is from human law alone. Second, that apostolic law, which is opposed to divine law, is merely human law and in no way divine, so that the hierarchical episcopate, in Downame's judgement, is merely human. Third, that by "apostolic" the authors understand a human invention observed from very ancient times. So when Jerome calls episcopacy an apostolic tradition, he means nothing other than an order which is human indeed, but observed from the most ancient times. That this is Jerome's very mind will be shown in its place.

units.la: 9 Tertio,ut hanc distinctionem Georgius Downamus, mala fide ex mutilato sensu ab ipsius authoribus,Dominico à Soto,& Roberto Bellarmino interpolavit: ita mala mente & ad malum finem,eandem jam pessimè immutatam mundo propinat. Mala ipsius mens hinc apparet,quod in concione suâ Lambethianâ, quæ coram Ri. Bancrofto Archiepiscopo habita est,qui Episcopatum immutabilem haberi voluit: non aufns est Downamus hanc distinctionem à se proponere, sed sub persona aliorum. Sic enim habet in notâ marginali. Differentia à quibusdam fit inter eaque sunt divini, & ea quæ sunt Apostolici juris, quorum prima ipsorum sensu immutabilia sunt, posteriora non item. Qui hoc modo loquitur (illorum sensu) annon sensum suum,sententiam propriam aliam esse subinsinuat? Quid vero in ipso concionis textu, iuxta hanc notam marginalem reperitur? Certè quod alienam illius mentem ab hac distinctione,apertè demonstrat. Sic enim fatus tum temporis est. Parva quidem differentia est,ut ego Apostolicam institutionem intelligo: quia quod Apostoli in sua Apostolica functione fecerunt, id fecerunt per directionem spiritus sancti, sic ut vere de suis ordinationibus dicere potuerint. Visum est spiritui sancto & nobis. Act.15.25. Adde quod concionis illius p.73. ordinationem Apostolicam allegat. 1.Cor.9.14. Vt probet ministrorum alimoniam ex iure divino esse, quod nonne quæso implicat jus Apostolicum esse jus divinum? At ante defensionem hujus concionis mutatæ sunt vices: prodiit interim liber regius in quo notum facit Rex, disciplinam Ecclesiæ, suo judicio, ad arbitrium pr ncipis, flexibilem & mutabilem esse: dehinc jam in personam suam suscipit Downamus, quod ante in concione sua, sub persona tantummodo aliorum proposuerat: Hierarchiam nempè & politiam Ecclesiæ, non ex divino immutabili iure, sed ex Apostolico mutabili esse.
units.tr: 9 Third, just as Georgius Downame, in bad faith, distorted this distinction from its authors, Dominic à Soto and Robert Bellarmine, by a mutilated sense, so with a bad mind and for a bad end he now serves the same distinction to the world, wickedly altered. His bad mind appears from this: in his Lambeth sermon, preached before the Most Reverend Richard Bancroft, Archbishop, who wished the episcopate to be held immutable, Downame did not dare to put this distinction forward himself, but put it in the mouths of others. For thus he has it in a marginal note: "A difference is made by some, and those things are of divine right and those of apostolic right; of which the former are immutable in their sense, the latter not so." Does not he who speaks in this way (in their sense) hint that his own sense and opinion is different? What indeed is found in the text of the sermon itself, according to this marginal note? Certainly it plainly shows that his mind was alien to this distinction. For thus he spoke at that time: "The difference is small, as I understand apostolic institution, because what the Apostles did in their apostolic office, they did by the direction of the Holy Spirit, so that they could truly say of their ordinations: It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us (Acts 15:25)." Add that on page 73 of that sermon he cites the apostolic ordinance (1 Cor. 9:14) "to prove that the maintenance of ministers is from divine right." Does this not, I ask, imply that apostolic law is divine law? But before the defence of this sermon the roles were changed. Meanwhile a royal book appeared, in which the King made known that the discipline of the Church, in his judgement, is "flexible and mutable at the will of the prince." Then Downame took upon himself in his own person what before in his sermon he had proposed only under the persons of others: namely that the hierarchy and polity of the Church is not from immutable divine right but from mutable apostolic right.

units.la: 10 A mala ipsius mente, accedamus ad malum finem. Eô siquidem libentius hanc distinctionem amplestitur Downamus,quod eadem ludificari posse videt authoritates eorum, qui Episcopatum Hierarchicum de jure divino esse negant. Quid enim? Negant inquit de jure divino immutabili esse, hoc & ego nego: interim non negant esse de iure Apostolico mutabili, quo sensu, inter alios,ipse Hieronymus interpretandus. Nam quum alibi dicit Episcopum non esse ex dispositione Dominica
units.tr: 10 From his bad intention, let us come to his bad purpose. Downame embraces this distinction all the more readily because he sees that it can make a mockery of the authorities of those who deny that the hierarchical episcopate is of divine right. For what does he say? They deny, he says, that it is of immutable divine right; I deny this too. Meanwhile they do not deny that it is of mutable apostolic right, in which sense Jerome, among others, must be interpreted. For when he says elsewhere that a bishop is not by the Lord's appointment

units.la: Lib.3.p.26 minica, hoc tantum vult, non esse ex iure divino immutabili. Alibi Episcopum traditionem Apostolicam appellat: id est, Episcopus est ex iure mutabili Apostolico: sic ut Hieronimus idem plane nobiscum sentiat. Imo non sentit, quod ut appareat, observentur paululum haec tria ιεραρχικα Hierarchica. Hadrianus Saravia de hoc loco Hieronymi agens, Haec tantum in eo sibi displicere dicit, quod negat Episcopum ex Dominica dispensatione esse: alias nihil mali in eo est, quod Episcopum dicit esse ex consuetudine: quia ex consuetudine & ex verbo simul Episcopus est: quo sensu Augustinus intelligendus est, cum Episcopi honorem ex usu Ecclesiae esse affirmat. En subterfuginm primum: quando patres dicunt Episcopum esse ex usu & ex consuetudine: non intelligunt ex consuetudine sola, sed ex consuetudine & verbo simul: At inquam patres, Hyeronimus praesertim, consuetudinem & Dominicam dispositionem opponunt, sic ut ex verbo & consuetudine etiam Episcopum Hierarchicum esse minime omnium senserint: sed ex consuetudine sola absque verbo. Imo non ita est, inquit Downamus, sentit etenim Hieronimus mecum, Hieronimus non magis Arianus est quam ipse ego sum: negat quidem Episcopum esse ex Dominica dispositione, sed idem quod ego sentit, nempe hoc tantum, quod non sit ex iure divino immutabili, quod mea ipsissima defensio est. En subterfugium secundum: quod evertitur a Saravia: intelligit inquit Hieronymus Episcopum non esse ex institutione iureque divino, itaque dicendum est, Hieronymum hac in re plane Arianum esse. Accersendus iam Bellarminus est. Hieronymus, inquit, Episcopum quoad ordinis potestatem superiorem presbyteris facit iure divino, ut patet ex epistola ad Evagrium ubi sic ait. Quid facit Episcopus excepta ordinatione quod non facit presbyter? at iure divino agnoscere non videtur discrimen inter iurisdictionem Episcopi & presbyteri: tamen agnoscit hoc discrimen, tanquam legitime imo necessario ad schismata vitanda ab Apostolis introductum. Agit de hoc ipso Hieronymi loco ibi Bellarminus: en igitur subterfugium tertium. Dicendum quidem cum Saravia est, sentire Hieronymum, Episcopum non esse ex iure divino, sed Apostolico tantum, id est humano (sic etenim Apostolicum interpretari Bellarminum docuimus nuper:) sed non generaliter tamen interpretandum est, sed de jurisdictione tantum, non autem de potestate ordinationis. Sed si potestas tantum ordinationis, jure divino tribuatur Episcopo, auferatur ab eo autem jure divino in presbyteros omnis jurisdictio, quae humano tantum jure nititur Hieronymi judicio, cecidit plane splendor omnis Episcopalis: imo cecidit etiam absoleta distinctio illa inter ordinem, & jurisdictionem, ac si in ista impares ministri essent qui in primo pares sunt.
units.tr: Lib.3.p.26 Dominical appointment: he means only that it is not of immutable divine right. Elsewhere he calls the episcopate an apostolic tradition, that is, the episcopate is of mutable apostolic right, so that Jerome plainly agrees with us. Indeed he does not agree, as will appear if these three hierarchical [ιεραρχικά] points are observed a little more closely. Adrian Saravia, treating this passage of Jerome, says that he is displeased only in this, that he denies the episcopate to be from the Lord's dispensation; otherwise there is nothing wrong in his saying that the episcopate is from custom, since the bishop is from custom and from the word at once. In this sense Augustine must be understood when he affirms that the honour of bishops is from the usage of the Church. Here is the first evasion: when the Fathers say that the episcopate is from usage and custom, they do not mean from custom alone, but from custom and the word together. But I say that the Fathers, Jerome above all, set custom against the Dominical appointment, so that they never thought the hierarchical episcopate to be from the word and custom together, but from custom alone, without the word. Not so, however, says Downame, for Jerome thinks with me. Jerome is no more an Arian than I am. He indeed denies that the episcopate is from the Dominical appointment, but he holds the same as I do, namely only that it is not of immutable divine right, which is my very own defence. Here is the second evasion, which Saravia overthrows: Jerome, he says, understands that the episcopate is not from divine institution and right, and so it must be said that Jerome is plainly an Arian in this matter. Now Bellarmine must be summoned. Jerome, he says, makes the bishop superior to presbyters by divine right as regards the power of ordination, as is clear from his letter to Evagrius, where he says thus: "What does a bishop do, apart from ordination, that a presbyter does not do?" Yet he does not seem to acknowledge by divine right any distinction between the jurisdiction of bishop and presbyter; nevertheless he acknowledges this distinction as introduced by the Apostles, rightly and indeed necessarily, to avoid schisms. Bellarmine there treats of this very passage of Jerome: here, then, is the third evasion. It must indeed be said with Saravia that Jerome thinks the episcopate is not of divine right but only of apostolic right, that is, human (for we lately showed that Bellarmine teaches the word apostolic to be so understood), but it must not be interpreted generally; it applies only to jurisdiction, not to the power of ordination. But if only the power of ordination is granted to the bishop by divine right, while all jurisdiction over presbyters, which rests on human right alone in Jerome's judgment, is taken away from him, then all episcopal splendour has plainly fallen, and indeed that old distinction between order and jurisdiction has fallen too, as if in the latter the ministers were unequal who are equal in the former.

units.la: 11 Quarto, in hac Downami distinctione reprehendendum illud est, quod quae jure divino sanciuntur, ea omnia immutabilia esse supponit Lancelotus Perusinus ita. Ius divinum est quod continetur in lege & in Evangelio atque immutabile semper permanet. Respicit in his Perusinus ad illa prima verba Gratiani. Humanum genus duobus regitur, naturali turali videlicet iure & moribus. Ius naturale est quod in lege & Evangelio continetur, quo quisque iubetur aliis facere, quod sibi vult fieri. Male autem Gratianum Perusinus interpretatur, si modo Thomam Aquinatem audire placet. Non intelligendus est Gratianus (inquit) quasi omnia quae sunt in lege & in Evangelio sint de lege naturae & sic immutabilia: sed quod quae sunt de lege naturae & immutabilia sunt ibi plenarie tradantur, & ex instantia Gratiani patet, qua quisque iubetur aliis facere quod sibi vult fieri. Annon Perusianum & Downnamianum dogma confodiunt ista? Non omnia (inquit Aquinas) immutabilia sunt, quae iuris divini: quod patet in ceremonialibus Mosaicis, & in mandatis aliis mutabilibus Math. 10.5.14. & 12, 19, & 15, 20, & 19,21. Iob. 13,14,15, &c. At haec mandata mutabilia (respondebunt forte) jus divinum non secum traxerunt: mandata quidem a Deo sunt, sed absque juris ullius divini positione. Absurde. Omne siquidem mandatum divinum hanc vim habet ut juste fieri possit, quod mandatur: si ita, tum jus divinum mandatum omne divinum ponit: Ius (inquit Isidorus) est dictum, quia justum est: ergo quicquid ex divino mandato iuste fieri potest, jus etiam divinum habet, absque quo iuste fieri nequivisset. Ad eundem sensum Aquinas. Ius divinum est (inquit) quod divinitus promulgatur. Ad eundem Sibrandus Lubertus. Ius inquit dicitur a iussu per Apocopem. Quid igitur est? Cum omnia mandata divina ex jure divino sint, & illorum multa mutabilia sint: male in istac distinctione supponit Downnamus, omnia immutabilia esse, quae de jure divino sunt.
units.tr: 11 Fourthly, in this distinction of Downame, what must be censured is that Lancelot of Perugia supposes everything sanctioned by divine right to be immutable, thus: Divine right is what is contained in the law and in the Gospel, and always remains immutable. In these words Perugia refers to the opening words of Gratian: The human race is governed by two things, namely natural right and customs. Natural right is what is contained in the law and the Gospel, by which each is commanded to do to others what he wishes done to himself. But Perugia interprets Gratian badly, if we may be allowed to hear Thomas Aquinas. Gratian (he says) is not to be understood as if all things that are in the law and in the Gospel were of the natural law and so immutable; rather, those things that are of the natural law and immutable are there delivered fully, and the example of Gratian, by which each is commanded to do to others what he wishes done to himself, makes this plain. Do not these words pierce through the dogma of Perugia and Downame? Not all things (says Aquinas) that are of divine right are immutable; this is clear in the Mosaic ceremonies and in other mutable commands (Matt. 10.5, 14; and 12.19; and 15.20; and 19.21; John 13, 14, 15, etc.). But perhaps they will reply that these mutable commands did not bring divine right with them: they are indeed from God, but without any positing of any divine right. Absurd. For every divine command has this force, that what is commanded can be done justly; if so, then every divine command posits divine right. Right (says Isidore) is so called because it is just; therefore whatever can be justly done by divine command also has divine right, without which it could not have been done justly. To the same effect Aquinas: Divine right is (he says) what is promulgated by God. To the same effect Sibrandus Lubbertus: Right, he says, is so called from "iussu" by apocope. What follows, then? Since all divine commands are of divine right, and many of them are mutable, Downame is wrong in supposing in this distinction that everything that is of divine right is immutable.

units.la: 12 Quinto, in distinctione hac Downami, peccatur in eo, quod quae divini juris sunt, & immutabilia sunt, ea statuit adeo necessaria, ut nulla ecclesia absque eis esse possit. Hinc ista infert. Quanquam teneo vocationem episcoporum, respectu primae institutionis, Apostolicam esse ac proinde divinam ordinationem: tamen non eam divini juris esse teneo: quasi generaliter, perpetuo, immutabiliter, necessaria, ac si nulla ecclesia vera esse possit, quae eadem caruerit. Rursus, Non ita teneo functionem episcoporum Diocesanorum ita divini juris esse, quasi generaliter, perpetuo, & immutabiliter necessaria esset ad esse Ecclesiae, & nullum aliud regimen admitti possit. Eadem rursus repetit, p. 140. Quae divino igitur jure perpetua & immutabilia sunt: ea ad esse ecclesiae pertinere vult, sic ut nulla ecclesia vera carere eisdem queat. Atqui hocin theoremate transfugit aperte in Separistarum castra: adversus quos demonstravimus alibi, ecclesiam veram esse posse, etsi quibusdam careat, quae perpetuo & immutabiliter quasi necessaria, mandata e Domino injunctaque ecclesiae sunt. Atque disciplina quidem ecclesiastica, etsi perpetuo & immutabiliter necessaria sit: tamen non ad esse ecclesiae simpliciter, sed tantum ad bene esse pertinet. Neque mirari hoc fas est: quum Sacramenta perpetuo & immutabiliter quasi necessaria injuncta sint: quibus tamen ecclesia in deserto caruit, sicut supra ex D. Beza est adnotatum. At qui necessaria dici possunt, inquies si eis ecclesia carere potest, & tamen Dei ecclesia esse? Respondeo, quum non sunt res indifferentes, quia ecclesia ea absque peccato mutare non potest, aut carere voluntario: peccat igitur ecclesia, quae ea non habet. Peccat sanè, ut in Anglicana ecclesia videre jam est, quae veram Christi politeiam ecclesiasticam respuit: sed peccatum istud ejusmodi non est, ut ipsam ecclesiae esse destruat: quamdiu in ea fidei puritas in doctrina conservatur.
units.tr: 12 Fifthly, in this distinction of Downame there is a fault in this, that he holds those things which are of divine right and immutable to be so necessary that no Church can exist without them. Hence he infers this: Although I hold the calling of bishops, with respect to its first institution, to be Apostolic and therefore a divine ordinance, yet I do not hold it to be of divine right in such a way as to be generally, perpetually and immutably necessary, as if no Church could be a true Church that lacked it. Again: I do not so hold the function of diocesan bishops to be of divine right, as if it were generally, perpetually and immutably necessary to the being of the Church, and no other government could be admitted. He repeats the same again on p. 140. He therefore wishes those things which are perpetual and immutable by divine right to pertain to the being of the Church, so that no true Church can lack them. Yet in this theorem he openly goes over to the camp of the Separatists, against whom we have shown elsewhere that a Church can be a true Church even though it lacks some things which were commanded by the Lord and enjoined on the Church as perpetually and immutably necessary. Indeed ecclesiastical discipline, although it is perpetually and immutably necessary, pertains not to the being of the Church simply, but only to its well-being. Nor is it right to wonder at this, since the sacraments were enjoined as perpetually and immutably necessary, yet the Church has gone without them in the wilderness, as was noted above from Beza. But perhaps you will ask: how can things be called necessary if the Church can lack them and still be the Church of God? I reply: since they are not indifferent things, because the Church cannot change them without sin, or go without them voluntarily, the Church which does not have them sins. It sins indeed, as can now be seen in the English Church, which rejects the true ecclesiastical polity of Christ; but this sin is not of such a kind as to destroy the very being of the Church, so long as the purity of faith is preserved in it in doctrine.

units.la: 13. Sextò & ultimo, distinctio ista Downami est absque differentia, quoniam membra coincidunt: nam & quae Apostolici juris à Downamo dicuntur, eadem revera & juris etiam divini sunt. Differentia quidē quaedā est inter mandata divina, quòd Deus quaedā immediate per seipsum, quaedam mediatè per Apostolos tradidit: sed haec differentia nihil prohibet, quin utraque adaeque immutabilia sint, & ex jure divino ligent. Vidit hoc Downami gregalis Thomas Bellius scriptor Hierarchicus, ejus verba haec sunt: Res dupliciter, inquit, dici possunt esse jure divino. Primò, quia sunt à Deo immediate: Secundo, quia sunt mediate ab illis, qui à sancto Dei spiritu ita diriguntur ut errare nequeant: quo sensu superioritas Episcoporum in reliquos ministros de jure divino esse dicitur sive ordinatio divina. Similis Guilielmi Barloi Episcopi Lincolniensis sententia est. Agit de loco Hieronymi, ubi negat Episcopum esse ex institutione dominica. Distinguit verò fere sensu Downamiano inter divinum praeceptum & consilium Apostolicum ex 1.Corint. 7.6. & dicit Hieronymi mentem esse, Episcopum quidem non esse ex ullo scripto mandato Christi, vel ab ulla expressa ejusdem regula: sed ex consilio, traditione, γνώμη ἀγεάφη, & institutione Apostolica. Hanc mentem Hieronymi & Georgius Downamus fingit, quam etiam approbat, sed Barlous non item: Non ita Hieronymus transfire debet, inquit, ac si functio Episcopalis non esset directe ipsa domini institutio. Non etenim spiritus per Apostolos solùm, qui eum magna mensura acceperunt, sed etiam per Christum ipsum, qui eum sine mensura accepit, hanc superioritatem ordinavit. Pergit deinde probare per immediatum Christi institutum, regimen Episcopale ordinandum esse, qui idem immutabile contra Downamum statuit. Non tamen putat mutabile futurum (quod Downamus) si mediato tantum Apostolico jure niteretur. Nam & non scriptas illas διαταξεις Apostolorum quas memorat ex 1. Cor. 11.34. & permissiones Apostolorum illas, absque expresso Christi mandato quas memorat ex 1. Cor.7.6. & 25. juris divini esse vult, quid ita? Quia, inquit, licet haec mandavit Paulus absque expresso mandato Christi: non tamen mandavit absque certo & infallibili spiritu Christi, sicut ait ver.40. Scio me habere spiritum Christi. Propter hunc spiritum Christi, quae absque immediato mandato scripto; & speciali revelatione sibi sacta mandaret, 1.Cor.8.9.13. & 10.25.29. & 11.4.14.23.25.] ea ad postremum hoc vinculo ligat, 1.Cor.14.37. Si quis se Prophetam putat & spiritualem, cogitet, quae ad vos scribo, quod Dei mandata sint. Ecce, quae mediata ab Apostolis praecipiuntur, ipsa Dei mandata sunt, haud secus ac ea quae immediato praecepto nituntur: quidni igitur perinde ex jure divino etiam?
units.tr: 13. Sixthly and lastly, Downame's distinction makes no real difference, since the two members coincide. For those things which Downame calls of apostolic right are in fact also of divine right. There is indeed a difference between divine commands, in that God delivered some things immediately through himself and others mediately through the Apostles. But this difference does not prevent both kinds from being equally unchangeable and binding by divine right. Thomas Bell, Downame's fellow-follower and the writer on hierarchy, saw this. His words are these: Things may be said to be of divine right in two ways, he says. First, because they are from God immediately. Second, because they are from those whom the Holy Spirit of God so directs that they cannot err. In this sense the superiority of bishops over the other ministers is said to be of divine right, or a divine ordinance. The opinion of William Barlow, Bishop of Lincoln, is similar. He discusses the passage of Jerome where Jerome denies that a bishop is by the Lord's institution. He distinguishes, almost in Downame's sense, between a divine precept and an apostolic counsel, citing 1 Cor. 7.6, and he says that Jerome's meaning is that a bishop is indeed not from any written command of Christ or any express rule of his, but from counsel, tradition, an unwritten judgment [γνώμη ἄγραφος], and apostolic institution. Georgius Downame imagines this to be Jerome's meaning and approves it, but Barlow does not: Jerome ought not to be read as if the episcopal office were not directly the Lord's own institution. For he ordained this superiority not only through the Apostles, who received the Spirit in large measure, but through Christ himself, who received the Spirit without measure. He goes on to prove, from Christ's immediate institution, that episcopal government must be ordained, and against Downame he holds it to be unchangeable. Yet he does not think it would be changeable (as Downame does) if it rested only on apostolic right, mediately given. For he holds that those unwritten ordinances of the Apostles which he cites from 1 Cor. 11.34, and those permissions of the Apostles, given without an express command of Christ, which he cites from 1 Cor. 7.6 and 25, are also of divine right. Why so? Because, he says, although Paul enjoined these without an express command of Christ, yet he did not enjoin them without the certain and infallible Spirit of Christ, as he says in verse 40: I think that I have the Spirit of Christ. By this Spirit of Christ he enjoined those things which were without an immediate written command and a special revelation made to him, 1 Cor. 8.9.13, 10.25.29, 11.4.14.23.25. Finally he binds them with this bond, 1 Cor. 14.37: If anyone thinks himself a prophet or spiritual, let him acknowledge that the things I write to you are the commandments of God. Behold, the things enjoined mediately by the Apostles are themselves the commandments of God, no less than those which rest on an immediate precept. Why then should they not likewise be of divine right?

units.la: 14. Accedit Guilielmus Whitakerus,qui Bellarmino locum Hieronymi unà cum Downnamo quoad verba interpretanti, ac si Episcopum sentiret, non quidem ex jure divino esse, sed ex jure Apostolico tamen,respondet ita.Bellarminus secum pugnat & Hieronymum facit loqui pugnantia. Nam si Hieronymus putavit jurisdictionem illam Episcopi non esse iuris divini,quomodo tum fuit illud discrimen ab Apostolis introductum? Et quomodo Hieronymus ex Apostolorum scriptis non esse discrimen aliquod probare potuit? Certè quod Apostoli ut necessarium sanxerint atque introduxerunt iuris divini vim obtinet. Hadrianus Saravia de Hieronymo respondens, ait eum errasse cum diceret, Apostolorum tempore introductum fuisse ab Apostolis Episcopum, sed non ex dominica dispositione,quis ex hoc sequeretur, Apostolos contra domini institutionem fecisse,quod falsum est: cum constet Apostolos nihil ordinasse, quod non esset à domino institutum, quaecunque causa ordinandi fuerit. Ex quibus juxta-positis ego quatuor colligo. Primò, contra Downnamum, Apostolicas ordinationes esse iura divina, quia Apostoli nihil instituerant, nisi ex divino iure, ut Whitakerus, nisi ex domini institutione ut Saravia. Secundò, quicquid inducitur in Ecclesiam,quod Politeiam Ecclesiasticam, non ex iure divino, ut Whitakerus,non ex domini institutione, ut Saravia ; id contra domini institutionem esse ideo& illicitum: etiamsi ab Apostolis ipsis hoc factum esset. Tertiò,Hierarchicorum responsionem,Hieronymum sentire Episcopum introductum ipso tempore Apostolorum contra schismata vanam esse & frivolam, quia Apostoli nihil induxerunt nisi ex iure & instituto divino : at vero Hieronymi sententia est (quocunque demum tempore introductus Episcopus fuit:) eum non ex dominica dispositione,non ex jure divino,non ex domini instituto fuisse introductum. Quartò, si Hieronymus dixisset, Episcopum introductum fuisse non quidem ex divino iure, sed tamen Apostolico, pugnantia locutus est: idem enim est ut si dixisset, non ex divino iure, & tamen ex divino iure. Atque Bellarminus pugnantia loquitur, inquit Whitakerus, cum Episcopum non iure divino iuxta Hieronymum,sed Apostolico inductum dicit: sic & pugnantia Georgius Downnamus, idque non in uno loco: Quaecunque functio est Apostolicae institutionis, divina ordinatio censenda est. Probat ex Beza : Si ab Apostolis profectum esset, non vereor,id totū divinae institutioni ascribere. Rursus: Sive primò ordinata a Christo ,sive ab Apostolis instituta ea functio suit: eius author Christus est, sive immediate iuxta primum, sive mediatè iuxta secundum. Atque ea Apostolicae institutionis esse dicuntur, quae Christus instituit per Apostolos. Huc referenda,quae supra allata sunt ex responsione ad praefat. p. 2. & ex libro 4.p.139. 140. ubi dicit Episcopum divinae ordinationis esse, quia Aostolicae institutionis. Quid hic habet Downnamus quod respondeat? Divinam ordinationem non inferre divinum ius? Apage ineptias: nam ordinatio jussum quoddam est,& omne jussum importat jus, ut inos supra demonstravimus.
units.tr: 14. William Whitaker also agrees. He answers Bellarmine, who, along with Downame, interprets the words of Jerome as if he held that the episcopal office is not of divine right but nevertheless of apostolic right. Whitaker replies as follows. Bellarmine contradicts himself and makes Jerome speak contradictory things. For if Jerome thought that this jurisdiction of the bishop was not of divine right, how then was that distinction introduced by the Apostles? And how could Jerome prove from the writings of the Apostles that there was no such distinction? Surely what the Apostles decreed and introduced as necessary has the force of divine right. Adrian Saravia, responding about Jerome, says that he erred when he said that a bishop was introduced by the Apostles in the Apostles' own time, but not by the Lord's appointment. From this it would follow that the Apostles acted against the Lord's institution, which is false, since it is established that the Apostles ordained nothing which was not instituted by the Lord, whatever the reason for ordaining it was. From these juxtaposed statements I draw four conclusions. First, against Downame, apostolic ordinances are rights of God, because the Apostles instituted nothing except from divine right, as Whitaker says, except from the Lord's institution, as Saravia says. Second, whatever is introduced into the Church that belongs to the ecclesiastical polity, if not from divine right, as Whitaker says, if not from the Lord's institution, as Saravia says, is therefore contrary to the Lord's institution and unlawful, even if it was done by the Apostles themselves. Third, the reply of the hierarchists, that Jerome thinks the bishop was introduced in the very time of the Apostles against schisms, is empty and frivolous. For the Apostles introduced nothing except by divine right and divine institution; but Jerome's opinion is (whenever the bishop was introduced) that he was introduced not by the Lord's appointment, not by divine right, not by the Lord's institution. Fourth, if Jerome had said that the bishop was introduced not indeed by divine right but nevertheless by apostolic right, he would have spoken contradictory things. For this is the same as saying not by divine right, and yet by divine right. And Bellarmine speaks contradictory things, says Whitaker, when he says that the bishop was introduced not by divine right according to Jerome, but by apostolic right. So too Georgius Downame speaks contradictory things, and not in one place only: Whatever office is of apostolic institution is to be regarded as a divine ordinance. He proves this from Beza: If it proceeded from the Apostles, I do not hesitate to ascribe it wholly to divine institution. Again: Whether that office was first ordained by Christ or instituted by the Apostles, Christ is its author, either immediately according to the first, or mediately according to the second. And those things are said to be of apostolic institution which Christ instituted through the Apostles. To this belongs what was cited above from the reply to the preface, p. 2, and from book 4, pp. 139–140, where he says that the bishop is of divine ordinance because he is of apostolic institution. What does Downame have to answer here? That a divine ordinance does not imply divine right? Away with such nonsense! For an ordinance is a kind of command, and every command implies a right, as we demonstrated above.

units.la: CAP. XLIV. Argumenta nostra pro disciplina immutabilitate à doctrina Apostolorum.
units.tr: CAP. XLIV. Our arguments for the immutability of church discipline from the teaching of the Apostles.

units.la: ITa tria illa fundamenta dejecimus & solo æquavimus, quibus Hierarchici freti, Politeiam Ecclesiasticam, mutabilem esse statuunt: ad argumenta jam nostra, accedendum nobis est. Primò, ab officio Christi disputamus, quod ejus ἀνωνλίσματα durant in perpetuum. Quid Sacerdotij? Vnica oblatione consecravit in perpetuum eos qui sanctificantur, Heb. 10.14. Quid Prophetiæ? Fides semel tradita est sanctis, Iud.3. Si de Sacerdotio & prophetia rectè dicitur ea semel operata fuisse, quæ in perpetuum durent: Cur non & de regali etiam dicetur ossicio, illud semel Politeiam Ecclesiasticam instituisse, quæ etiam duraret in perpetuum? Heb.12.26.27. Adhuc semel ego cancutium non solum terram se etiam cælum. Porro illud adhuc semel, declarat instabilium rerum amotionem, ut mancant quæ sunt stabilia. Deducit hinc Apostolus nos regnum assecutos stabile, quod verti non possit, ergo & media etiam stabilia, quibus ad hoc regnum provehimur: in quibus est Politeia Ecclesiastica. Atque de Politeia Iudaica cur vaticinetur Propheta eam abolitam iri? & ex propheta concludit Apostolus, semel tantum abolitionem istiusmodi fore, non deinceps: certum mihi quidem videtur, & Politeiam Ecclesiasticam sub Evangelio stabilem hic fieri absque ulla concussione: ex mente Apostoli, una ista & nulla deinceps abolitio futura est, nulla inquam: mutatio semel facta est, ceremoniarum & Politeias Iudaicæ: sed semel tantum non deinceps, mutatio istiusmodi contigit.
units.tr: So we have overthrown and levelled to the ground those three foundations on which the hierarchists rely when they declare the ecclesiastical polity to be changeable. We must now come to our own arguments. First, we argue from the office of Christ, that his offices [ἀξιώματα] endure for ever. What of the priesthood? By one offering he has perfected for ever those who are sanctified (Heb. 10.14). What of the prophetic office? The faith has once for all been delivered to the saints (Jude 3). If it is rightly said of the priesthood and of prophecy that they were once performed and yet endure for ever, why should it not also be said of the kingly office that he once instituted the ecclesiastical polity, which would also endure for ever? (Heb. 12.26–27): Yet once more I shake not only the earth but also the heaven. Now this "yet once more" signifies the removal of things that are shaken, so that the things that are unshaken may remain. From this the Apostle infers that we have obtained a kingdom that is stable and cannot be overturned; therefore also the means by which we are advanced to this kingdom are stable, and among them is the ecclesiastical polity. And why does the prophet foretell that the Jewish polity would be abolished? From the prophet the Apostle concludes that such an abolition would happen only once, and not thereafter. It seems certain to me that the ecclesiastical polity under the Gospel is made stable here, without any shaking. In the mind of the Apostle, this one abolition is to be the only one in future, none after it. I say none: the change of the ceremonies and of the Jewish polity has been made once; but a change of this kind happens only once, not again.

units.la: Pertinet huc quod 1. Cor.15.24. regnum suum externum non ante finale Judicium deponit Christus: tum mediate regnare cessabit, Ecclesiam gubernare. Ergo regnum ipsius externum, illiusque extetna media (in quibus Politeia Ecclesiastica est) ad diem judicij, prout in verbo posita & descripta sunt, stabilia & fixa permanebunt.
units.tr: To this belongs what is said in 1 Cor. 15.24: Christ does not lay down his external kingdom before the final judgment. Then he will cease to reign mediately, to govern the Church. Therefore his external kingdom, and its external means (among which is the ecclesiastical polity), will remain stable and fixed until the day of judgment, as they are set forth and described in the Word.

units.la: 2 Secundo, nota quâ partes verbi mutabiles, ab immutabilibus secerni solent, ipsius finis vel mutabilitas est vel immutabilitas: ita, cum finis ad quem ordinatur Politeia Ecclesiastica immutabilis & perpetuus sit, eadem perpetua etiam ut sit necesse est. Viderunt hoc Iuristæ, quorum placitum, apud Iohannem Bertachium, istud est, Ius idem est ubi juris eadem ratio est. Alias res igitur agit Sutclivius, quum formam regiminis Ecclesiastici ex eo probat mutabilem esse, quod mutata sit Politeia Iudaica, mutata regiminis forma quæ fuit sub Christo & Apostolis mutatum etiam præceptum de suffocato & sanguine. Hæc etenim omnia si mutabilia, nihil mirum, propter causas mutabiles, ad fines mutabiles, ordinata fuerunt: & cessante causa cessant effectus ut rectè respondet ad horum postremum Nicolaus Lyranus: Quod ad regimen sub Christo & Apostolis, extraordinarium utrumque tis : ut si quid necessarium esset posteris tradi, exempli proprij abrogationem testari necessarium fuisset. Demonstratio Mathei Sutclivij pro Episcopi authoritate tertia, à voce & usu Apostolorum est : ut ipse titulus capitis indicat : putat igitur satis solida argumenta ab ipso exemplo Apostolorum desumi posse. Thomas Bilsonus ita pro episcopatu differit. Erudite illud à Tertulliano notatur. Constabit id esse ab Apostolis traditum, quod apud Ecclesias Apostolorum fuerit sacrosanctum: & ab Augustino. Quod universa tenet Ecclesia, nec concilijs institutum, sed semper retentum est, non nisi authoritate Apostolica traditum rectissime creditur. Iam vero in Ecclesijs Episcopus fuit, etiam antequam concilia de his statuere cæpisset: idcirco hic mos retractandus non est. Ita & morem & factum Ecclesiarum Apostolicarum, non Apostolorum solum, obligare in perpetuum Bilsonus credit. Duo hæc patrum testimonia postquam citasset Georgius Downamus, adjungit Cartwrightum, qui dicit etiam exemplum Apostolorum sine mandato necessitatem trahere. Ita pro Episcopo suo, vel ex solo exemplo Apostolorum, Ecclesiarumque, pugnare Downamus non veretur : quam sibi constanter videreit ipse : parum etenim hæc ratiocinatio ex facto Apostolorum obligante, illi congruere mihi quidem videtur, qui Politeiam Ecclesiasticam mutabilem esse vult. Atque ita confectum est, etiam facta Apostolorum in Ecclesiæ Politeia, sive constituenda sive exercenda, necessitatem inferre, ut ea immutabilis sit.
units.tr: Secondly, note that the mutable parts of the Word are customarily distinguished from the immutable by their end: if the end is changeable or unchangeable, so is the means. Since the end to which the ecclesiastical polity is ordained is immutable and perpetual, the means must necessarily also be perpetual. The jurists have seen this; their maxim, as cited by John Bertachius, is this: The law is the same where the reason of the law is the same. Sutcliffe, however, argues otherwise when he proves from the fact that the Jewish polity was changed that the form of ecclesiastical government is changeable, since the form of government that existed under Christ and the Apostles was changed, and the precept about what is strangled and blood was also changed. For if all these things are changeable, it is no wonder: they were ordained for changeable causes and changeable ends, and when the cause ceases, the effects cease too. Nicholas of Lyra rightly answers this objection: the government under Christ and the Apostles was extraordinary in both respects, so that if anything were necessary to be handed down to posterity, the abrogation of their own example would have needed to be stated. Matthew Sutcliffe's third demonstration for the authority of bishops is drawn from the voice and practice of the Apostles, as the very title of the chapter indicates; he thinks that solid arguments can be derived from the very example of the Apostles. Thomas Bilson argues for episcopacy thus: This has been well noted by Tertullian: it will be established that that was handed down by the Apostles which was held sacrosanct in the churches of the Apostles; and by Augustine: what the whole Church holds, and which was not instituted by councils but has always been retained, is rightly believed to have been handed down by apostolic authority. Now in the churches there was a bishop even before councils began to decree concerning these matters; therefore this custom is not to be called into question. Thus Bilson believes that the custom and practice of the apostolic churches, not only of the Apostles, binds for ever. After George Downame had cited these two testimonies of the Fathers, he adds Cartwright, who says that even the example of the Apostles, without a command, carries necessity. Downame does not hesitate to fight thus for his bishop, on the example of the Apostles and the churches alone; he seems to himself to be consistent in doing so. Yet such reasoning, that an apostolic fact binds, seems to me hardly consistent with one who wants the ecclesiastical polity to be changeable. And so it is established that the deeds of the Apostles, whether in constituting or in exercising the polity of the Church, bring necessity, so that it is immutable.

units.la: CAP. XLIII. Disciplinæ immutabilitas à doctrina Apostolorum probatur: & primo refutantur duæ Hierarchicorum exceptiones sibi invicem contrariæ.
units.tr: CAP. XLIII. The immutability of discipline is proved from the doctrine of the Apostles, and first two mutually contrary objections of the Hierarchists are refuted.

units.la: Dicendum jam est de doctrina Apostolorum quam de Politeia Ecclesiastica tradiderunt: quæ quò minus ejusdem immutabilitatem inferre videatur, negatur à quibusdam eam obligare omnino; ab alijs, obligare eam quidem conceditur, non tamen in perpetuum. Ita exceptiones duæ adversus doctrinæ Apostolicæ de Politeia immutabilitatem sunt: quam sibi invicem contrariæ quis non videt? Posterior enim priorem tollit: quum eam obligare dicit, quod à prima non conceditur. Hæc vero prima a Matheo Sutclivio prosecta est, qui Christum in externis legislatorem non esse postquam posuisset, ita ex nostra persona objicit. At Christus, inquiunt illi Mat. 18. de vitandis scandalis & monendis fratribus mandata dedit: dicunt etiam Paulum quædam præcepta Corinthijs, alia Timotheo & Tito dedisse, & quòd Christus rex appelletur, & magis fidelis in Dei familia quam Moses, dicatur, libenter usurpant. Atqui facilis est responsio, Christi regnum in Ecclesia, non esse in rebus externis, sed in conscientiarum dominio & regimine collocandum: Christique & Apostolorum quæ feruntur leges, in rebus rebus externis Christianam nunquam sustulerant libertatem: nam & in casu iuris, licet non appellato fratre ad Ecclesiam rem deferre: & passim cessavit ablutio pedum, & osculatio prima Christianorum. Nonnunquam etiam occurrunt tempora, cum Episcopi & Diaconi haberi non possunt. Ad regulas Pauli 1. Tim. 3. non sunt omnia exactè exigenda, ut nulli eligendi sunt Episcopi aut Diaconi nisi qui illis quasi ad amussim respondeant. Satis est si omnem adhibuerimus curam, ut quam prope possimus accedamus. Dicimus igitur leges morales acuratè servandas, Ecclesiasticas Apostolorum constitutiones quatenus tempora & mores patiuntur, ut nulla vis auferatur Christianæ libertati. Hæc ille: quæ cujus notæ meritisque sunt, consequentiis hisce incnstrabo.
units.tr: Now I must speak of the doctrine of the Apostles which they handed down concerning the ecclesiastical polity. To weaken the inference of its immutability, some deny that it binds at all, while others grant that it binds but not forever. So there are two objections against the immutability of the Apostolic doctrine on polity, and who does not see that they are contrary to each other? The second destroys the first, since it says the doctrine binds, which the first does not grant. The first of these was put forward by Matthew Sutcliffe, who, after stating that Christ is not a lawgiver in external matters, objects in our name as follows: But Christ, they say, in Matt. 18 gave commands about avoiding offences and admonishing brethren. They also say that Paul gave certain precepts to the Corinthians and others to Timothy and Titus, and they gladly use the fact that Christ is called King and that he is said to be more faithful in God's house than Moses. But the answer is easy. The kingdom of Christ in the Church is to be located not in external matters but in the dominion and rule over consciences. The laws that are recorded as Christ's and the Apostles' never took away Christian liberty in external matters: for even in a case of law one may bring the matter before the Church without the brother having been named; and the washing of feet and the first kiss of Christians have passed away in many places. Sometimes, too, times come when bishops and deacons cannot be had. Not everything is to be exacted exactly by the rules of Paul in 1 Tim. 3, so that no bishops or deacons may be chosen except those who correspond to them as if by a plumb-line. It is enough if we take all care to come as near to them as we can.
