We say, therefore, that the moral laws are to be kept exactly, but the ecclesiastical constitutions of the Apostles are to be kept so far as times and customs allow, so that no force is taken away from Christian liberty. So he. I shall examine these statements, whatever their character and worth, by the following consequences.

units.la: 1. Primò, ad papismum accedere illa dico: Christum non vult esse in Politeia Ecclesiastica legislatorem. Quid igitur de mandatis Christi sentiendum quæ de rebus Ecclesiasticis dedit. Illæ quæ feruntur leges, inquit, id est, ex opinione Puritanorum, leges quidem meo judicio non sunt sed constitutiones tantum Ecclesiasticæ, quæ à legibus moralibus longissimè sicernuntur. Cur igitur non retunde loquitur cum Papistis? non sunt præcepta sed consilia tantum: idem sensus subest: nam permissam putat libertatem esse vel servare vel non servare, prout mores & tempora ferunt.
units.tr: 1. First, I say that these statements come close to Popery: that Christ does not wish to be the lawgiver in the ecclesiastical polity. What then are we to think of the commands of Christ which he gave about ecclesiastical matters? Those laws that are put forth, he says, that is, according to the opinion of the Puritans, are not laws in my judgement but only ecclesiastical constitutions, which are sharply distinguished from moral laws. Why then does he not rebuke the Papists plainly? They are not precepts but only counsels. The same sense underlies both: for he thinks it is a permitted liberty either to keep or not to keep them, as customs and times may dictate.

units.la: 2. Secundò, olent etiam Adiaphorismum idque quidem ante hoc tempus inauditum: non enim solum præcepta Politeias, præcepta de rebus indifferentibus esse statuit, quæ indifferentes non sunt: sed etiam ipsa præcepta indifferentia facit, quod quisquamnè quæso ante audivit unquam? Semper etenim in Ecclesia Dei judicatum est, res indifferentes ipsas præceptas non esse, quæ vero de earum usu præcepta traduntur, ea & immutabilia esse & necessario observanda, qualia sunt illa quæ 1. Cor. 14. 40. ab Apostolo proponuntur. Qualis hic igitur Mathei Sutclivij Adiaphorismus est? Primò, quanquam præcepta Politeias, de ipsis rebus sint, & non tantummodo de rerum usu: Politeiam tamen rem indifferentem esse vult. Secundò, quanquam præcepta de indifferentibus necessario observanda sint ac indifferentia non sint: facit tamen ille præcepta Politeias, ipsa inquam præcepta, indifferentia, & necessariò observanda esse negat. Tertiò, quod in usu solum rerum indifferentium locum habet, nempè ut dirigantur prout expedit: hoc ille ad ipsum præceptum trahit ac si ob morum & temporum occasiones præceptū ipsum, alterari, violari, tolli possunt.
units.tr: 2. Second, he also smacks of an Adiaphorism, and one hitherto unheard of: for he does not only state that the precepts of the polity are precepts about indifferent things, when they are not indifferent, but he also makes the precepts themselves indifferent. Who, I ask, has ever heard of such a thing? For it has always been judged in the Church of God that the indifferent things themselves are not commanded, but that the precepts laid down about their use are both unchangeable and to be necessarily observed, such as those which the Apostle sets forth in 1 Cor. 14:40. What sort of Adiaphorism, then, is this of Matthew Sutcliffe's? First, although the precepts of the polity concern the things themselves and not merely their use, he nevertheless wills that the polity is an indifferent thing. Second, although precepts about indifferent things must be necessarily observed, and indifferent things are not indifferent, he nevertheless makes the precepts of the polity, the precepts themselves I say, indifferent, and denies that they are to be necessarily observed. Third, what holds good only in the use of indifferent things, namely that they be directed as is expedient, he drags over to the precept itself, as if the precept itself could be altered, violated or abolished on account of the occasions of customs and times.

units.la: 3. Tertiò favent etiam libertinismo: affectant enim libertatem à præceptis Christi & Apostolorum: de qua porro Lous ita. Libertatem à Christo partam proculcant, qui disciplinam veram certam & immutabilem ex verbo statuunt. Atqui inquam libertas à Christo parta libera est, ergo ipsius præcepta servitus Iacob. 1. 25. & 2. 12. non datur ulli ab ipsius præceptis liberari: miserrima etenim peccato servitus ejusmodi libertas est: quam dum inducere in ecclesiā Hierarchici isti volunt, nonnè quæso offendunt in illud 1. Petri 2. 16, Ut liberi, et non
units.tr: 3. Third, they also favour libertinism: for they aim at liberty from the precepts of Christ and the Apostles. Of this Lous says: They trample underfoot the liberty won by Christ, who establish a true, certain and unchangeable discipline from the word. Yet, I say, the liberty won by Christ is free, therefore there is no liberty from his precepts; the slavery of James 1:25 and 2:12 is not something from which anyone can be freed from his precepts. For liberty of that kind is the most wretched slavery to sin. When these Hierarchists wish to introduce it into the Church, do they not, I ask, offend against the words of 1 Pet. 2:16, As free, and not

units.la: Querimonia ecclef. p. 62 non veluti malitiæ velamen habentes libertatem sed servi Dei, id est, præceptis ejus servientes ac proinde ad nullam ab eisdem libertatem suspirantes? Quarto hypocrisin fovent cum tyrannide immani conjunctam, qualis et illa Saulis fuit: qui etsi legis violationem in sanguine effundendo absque pœna dimiserit: legem tamen suam, eamque incommodè nimis latam, adeo rigidè persequitur; ut Ionathan ipse quanquam optimè meritus, ob parum mellis degustati ad mortem condemnandus sit. 1. Sam. 14. 44. Imò in Saulina disobedientia Hierarchici sunt, quæ proximo capite commemoratur: præcepta Christi & Apostolorum de politeia Ecclesiastica à tergo rejiciunt, & libertatem ab eodem sibi assumunt: quum interim qui ad libertatem Christianam provocant ab humanis inventis qualis permittitur, imò mandatur. 1. Cor. 7. 22. 23. (puta à cononibus de crucis signo, de superpelliceo, & hujusmodi nugamentis, superstitiosis quidem & in cultu Dei illicitis, sed fac indifferentibus) habentur pro ridiculis; quid dixi? pro ridiculis haberi eos? imo degradantur, excommunicantur, & bonis omnibus exuuntur. Hoc nimirum reliqui erat ad mensuram Hierarchiæ implendam, ut quæ libertatem imo libertinismum potius à Christi præceptis de Politeia sibi assumpsisset: ullam Christianam libertatem à præceptis suis, id est, humanis interdiceret: ut quæ jugum Christi excussisset ipsa (ô Domine quousque) jugum suum aliorum cervicibus sanè intollerandum imponeret.
units.tr: Complaint of the Church, p. 62 using liberty as a cloak for wickedness, but as servants of God, that is, serving his precepts, and therefore not longing for any liberty from them? Fourth, they foster hypocrisy joined with monstrous tyranny, like that of Saul: who, although he let a breach of the law in shedding blood go unpunished, nevertheless pursues his own law, and one too unreasonably broad, so rigidly that Jonathan himself, although most deserving, is to be condemned to death for tasting a little honey (1 Sam. 14:44). Indeed the Hierarchists are guilty of Sauline disobedience, which was mentioned in the previous chapter: they cast behind their backs the precepts of Christ and the Apostles on the polity, and assume a liberty from them for themselves; meanwhile those who appeal to Christian liberty from human inventions, which is permitted or even commanded (1 Cor. 7:22, 23), (I mean, for example, from the ministers' objections to the sign of the cross, the surplice, and suchlike trifles, superstitious indeed and unlawful in the worship of God, but suppose them indifferent), are regarded as ridiculous. Why do I say regarded as ridiculous? Rather they are degraded, excommunicated and stripped of all their goods. This, surely, was all that remained to fill up the measure of Hierarchy: that the one who had assumed for himself a liberty, or rather a libertinism, from the precepts of Christ about polity should forbid any Christian liberty from his precepts, that is, from human ones; that the one who had cast off the yoke of Christ should itself (O Lord, how long?) impose its own yoke, truly intolerable, on the necks of others.

units.la: 4. Quintò & ultimo rebellionis cuiusdam speciem habent. Quid enim aliud spirant, quam legem Christi de privata admonitione violari posse absq; peccato, quum leges Pauli ad Timoth. de episcopis eligendis nec ita rigide exigendas dicit? Licet non appellato fratre rem ad ecclesiam deferre: id est, licet audacter contra mandatum Christi ire? & leges Pauli ad Timotheum non prohibent, quin probanda sit quæ in Anglia jam dominatur ministrorum caterva, (si tamen ministri) qui ne latine quidem sciunt, certè qui verbum Dei prædicare non possunt, sed meri muti canes sunt, perdentes gregem cui præsunt, & humanarum animarum sanguine sat facti pigues? Quanquam admonendus es (lector) multo levius eum quam res postulat, in priore rebellione describenda locutum esse. Licet, inquit, non appellato fratre eum ad ecclesiam deferre. Sed hoc parum est, pro eo quod in Anglia geritur: ubi non tantùm absque ulla privata admonitione, ad consistoria Episcoporum deferuntur homines, verumetiam excommunicantur. Atque hæc ad exceptionem Hierarchicorum primam, quod doctrina Christi & Apostolorum de politeia ecclesiastica, immutabiles nullas leges habeat, imò ne leges quidem obligatorias, sed præcepta tantum nescio quæ indifferentia.
units.tr: 4. Fifth and last, they have a kind of rebellion. For what else do they breathe than that the law of Christ concerning private admonition may be violated without sin, since they say that the laws of Paul to Timothy about choosing bishops are not to be exacted so rigidly? Is it lawful, even without naming the brother, to bring the matter before the Church? That is, is it lawful to go boldly against the command of Christ? And do not the laws of Paul to Timothy forbid that we should approve the company of ministers now ruling in England (if indeed they are ministers), who do not even know Latin, and certainly cannot preach the Word of God, but are mere dumb dogs, destroying the flock over which they preside, and fattened on the blood of human souls? Yet, reader, you must be warned that he has spoken much more lightly than the matter requires in describing the earlier rebellion. It is permitted, he says, even without naming the brother, to bring the matter before the Church. But this is little compared with what is done in England, where men are not only brought before the bishops' consistories without any private admonition, but are even excommunicated. And so much for the first objection of the Hierarchists, that the doctrine of Christ and the Apostles on ecclesiastical polity has no unchangeable laws, nay not even binding laws, but only certain indifferent precepts.

units.la: 5. Accedendum jam est ad exceptionem secundam, quæ obligare quidem præcepta fatetur quæ de politeia ecclesiastica in verbo Dei reperiuntur, sed tamen in perpetuum minimè obligare dicit: Quaedam præcepta divina sunt, quæ perpetua tamen non sunt. Certè, sed recte
units.tr: 5. We must now come to the second objection, which grants that the precepts found in the word of God about the ecclesiastical polity do bind, but says that they do not bind forever: Some divine precepts are such that they are not perpetual. Certainly, but rightly

units.la: 2. Exceptio Saravia. Præcepta de politeia ecclesiastica perpetua sunt, etsi quædam divina non sunt perpetua. Quò minùs hoc obtineat, in duas hominum opiniones, sese hæc exceptio secunda diffringit: quarum prima invaliditatem ipsius præcepti, secunda invaliditatem præcipientis obicit. Prima à Richardo Hookero ponitur ita, ubi de politeiæ ecclesiasticæ mutabilitate disserit. Leges, quanquam à Deo ipso ordinatæ, & quamquam finis ad quem ordinatæ fuerunt permanent; cessare tamen possunt, si per alterationem personarum aut temporum insufficientes reperiantur ad finem illum assequendum: quo respectu, cur præsumere nobis non licet? inclamare Deum pro ea mutatione & alteratione, quam ipsa rerum conditio necessariam facit? In hoc casu non præsumunt homines, Dei ordinationem mutare: sed ordinationi Dei cedunt, quæ ipsa requirit ut immutetur. Hæc medulla est eorum, quæ fusè disputat, pro politeiæ ecclesiasticæ mutatione, quando pro conditione rerum & temporis reperitur invalida ad finem suum obtinendum. Atqui negamus cum summâ Dei sapientiâ & providentia stare posse, ut politeiam ecclesiasticam instituerit, quæ ullâ rerum, personarum, temporumve conditione, fieri possit invalida aut insufficiens ad finem suum (ad quem ab eo est ordinata,) assequendum. Fac autem invalidam & insufficientem evadere eam posse. Quis legem validiorem feret? quis politeiam ecclesiasticam magis sufficientem instituet? Num caro & sanguis? At ipse concedis, meliorari ab hominibus non posse, quæ à Deo instituta sunt: meliorantur verò, si melior, validior, magis sufficiens, quoquo tempore, politeia ecclesiæ ab hominibus institui possit, atque ea est, quæ ab ipso Deo est instituta. Ego sanè quomodo cohæreant ista non video: sed est & aliud scifcitandum. Quis judicium feret, quando cum pro rerum conditione leges politeiæ ecclesiasticæ invalidæ à Deo latæ sunt? Quis item si invalidæ sint, judicabit, utrum humana politeia sit validior eâ, quæ est à Deo lata? Ad postremum, fieri potest, ut dividantur sententiæ, quis judicabit, quæ nam ex illis politeiis quæ ab hominibus proponuntur, maximè valida & sufficiens sit? Vide quantis præsumptionibus hæc assertio scateat, in quibus tamen hominem meminem præsumere dicis. Nonne præsument hodie Episcopi Anglicani, quando disciplinam reformatam naso suspendunt: ac si invalidissima esset ad pacem ecclesiæ, salutem ecclesiç, ædificationem ecclesiæ, aut confervandam aut promovendam? Audi O Deus noster (inquit Nehemias) nos esse contemptui, & converte probrum eorum in caput eorum: ut quod in Anglia bene jam Deus cepit opus politeias reformatæ, quod vel à vulpe dirui potuisse Tobiæ isti existimant, felicissimè procedat; probro in Hierarchiæ suæ caput converso, sub quâ omnia indies in deterius prolabuntur, retroque collapsa feruntur. Non est igitur Hookere, non est mihi credé, præsumptio levis, sed Samballiticum contemptum spirans, quando præsumit judicare caro, invalidas Dei leges esse, quæ de sua politeia tulit: præsertim cum pollicitus fuerit, se vel puerum Isa. 11. 8. id est pauperulum quendam ministrum, & regimen, humano quidem judicio,invalidissimum,ipsos leones,tigrides,pardos,ursos denique& Basilicos,in ordinem redacturum.
units.tr: 2. The exception of Saravia: The precepts concerning the ecclesiastical polity are perpetual, even if some divine precepts are not perpetual. That this may not hold, this second exception splits into two opinions of men: the first objects to the invalidity of the precept itself, the second to the invalidity of the one who prescribes it. The first is put forward by Richard Hooker, where he discusses the mutability of the ecclesiastical polity: Laws, although ordained by God himself, and although the end for which they were ordained remains, can nevertheless cease, if through a change of persons or times they are found insufficient to attain that end. In this respect, why are we not permitted to presume? To call on God for that change and alteration which the very condition of things makes necessary? In such a case men do not presume to alter God's ordinance, but yield to God's ordinance, which itself requires that it be changed. This is the substance of what he argues at length, in favour of altering the ecclesiastical polity when, by the condition of things and of the times, it is found invalid for attaining its end. But we deny that it can stand with the supreme wisdom and providence of God that he should have instituted an ecclesiastical polity which, by any condition of things, persons or times, could become invalid or insufficient for attaining its end (for which he ordained it). Yet suppose it could become invalid and insufficient. Who will enact a more valid law? Who will institute an ecclesiastical polity more adequate? Flesh and blood? But you yourself concede that what has been instituted by God cannot be improved by men; yet it is improved if a better, more valid, more adequate polity of the Church can at any time be instituted by men, and that is the one which has been instituted by God himself. I certainly do not see how these statements cohere; but there is also another question to be asked. Who will pass judgement when the laws of the ecclesiastical polity have been enacted by God as invalid, given the condition of things? Who likewise, if they are invalid, will judge whether a human polity is more valid than the one enacted by God? Finally, it may happen that opinions diverge: who will judge which of those polities proposed by men is most valid and sufficient? See how full of presumptions this assertion is, while you say that no man presumes anything! Do not the English bishops presume today, when they turn up their noses at the reformed discipline, as though it were most invalid for preserving or promoting the peace of the Church, its welfare and its edification? Hear us, O our God (says Nehemiah), for we are despised, and turn their reproach upon their own head; so that the work of reforming the polity, which God has already well begun in England, and which those Tobiahs think could have been overthrown even by a fox, may proceed most happily, with the reproach turned upon the head of their hierarchy, under which everything daily slides for the worse and is carried headlong backwards. It is therefore not a light presumption, Hooker, believe me, but a spirit of Sanballatic contempt, when flesh presumes to judge that the laws of God, which he has enacted concerning his own polity, are invalid; especially since he has promised that he would bring into order, even a child (Isa. 11. 8), that is, some poor little minister, and a government which, by human judgement, is most feeble: indeed the lions, the tigers, the leopards, the bears, and finally the basilisks themselves.

units.la: 6 At inquit Hookerus Præsto est exemplum,quum lex divina mutata est idque licitè ab hominibus,quando invalida reperta fuit,ad suum finem obtinendum. Istud quidem exemplum,ego vel maximè audire aveo. Lex inquit de furto immutata est,quando illius pœna augmentata est,propterea quod restitutio quadrupli non erit sufficiens ad furtum cohibendum. At quid hæc ad rem? Augmentatio inquit, est mutatio quædam: sed non de hujusmodi mutatione jam agitur: probandum etenim tibi sumpsisti cessare posse politeiam ecclesiæ, & aliam ab hominibus surrogari, quando invalida reperitur ad finem suum assequendum. Secundo nego hanc pœnæ augmentationem,ipsius legis mutationem ullam esse,cujus,si non litera,sententia tamen,hanc ipsam pœnæ augmentationem re ita ferente intendebat. Æquitas, inquit concilium Basiliense, in sinu principis habitare semper debet,quæ relictâ legis litera, rationem illius sequitur: Sic Thomas Aquinas,ordinatur æquitas,ut quando litera legis deficit,illius intentio servetur, prout æqualitas justitiæ & bonum publicum postulat. Tertio contrarium hinc probari,pręberique exemplum,quid hominibus faciendum sit: quando lex divina aliqua minus valida videatur. Probat Hookerus cessationem politeiæ ecclesiasticæ, ab exemplo, quo lex aliqua augmentatur, ecquid absurdius? Abolitio etenim legis,& ejusdem augmentatio contraria sunt: tantum abest ut aboleat legem, qui eandem augmentat, ut ex adverso eam firmet atque roboret: tantum igitur abest,ut probet propositum hæc instantia,ut potius contrarium doceat: nempe cum politeia ecclesiastica invalida reperitur,non statim ab hominibus abolendam, sed augmentandam potius, & modis omnibus muniendam esse.
units.tr: 6. But, says Hooker: There is at hand an example, when a divine law has been changed, and that lawfully by men, when it was found invalid for attaining its end. I, indeed, most gladly want to hear this example. The law concerning theft, he says, was changed when its penalty was increased, because restitution of fourfold would not be sufficient to restrain theft. But what has this to do with the matter? An increase, he says, is a certain change; but it is not of this kind of change that the question now is: for you have undertaken to prove that the polity of the Church can cease, and another be substituted by men, when it is found invalid for attaining its end. Second, I deny that this increase of the penalty is any change of the law at all, since the law, if not in its letter, yet in its meaning, intended this very increase of the penalty, as the matter itself bears out. Equity, says the Council of Basel, ought always to dwell in the bosom of the prince; it leaves the letter of the law and follows its reason. So Thomas Aquinas: equity is so ordered that, when the letter of the law fails, its intention is preserved, as the equality of justice and the public good require. Third, the opposite is proved from this, and an example is given of what men ought to do when a divine law seems somewhat less valid. Hooker proves the cessation of the ecclesiastical polity from the example of a law being increased: what could be more absurd? For the abolition of a law and its increase are contrary things: he who increases a law is so far from abolishing it that, on the contrary, he confirms and strengthens it. So far, then, is this instance from proving his proposition that it rather teaches the contrary: namely, that when the ecclesiastical polity is found invalid, it is not to be abolished at once by men, but rather to be increased and fortified in every way.

units.la: Quarto, nulla hic ab Hookero proportio servatur in circumstantiis. Mutabilem illè politeiam Ecclesiasticam esse vult, pro locorum & temporum & personarum conditione: at non pro locorum & temporum & personarum conditione hæc legis de furto mutatio fuit: neque mutatur substantia,sed circumstantia pœnæ:sic nihil hinc concluditur, nisi hoc tantum: quum propter exuberantem hominum malitiam sanctiones & pœnæ ecclesiasticæ minus validè videntur,diligentius & rigidius exercendas eas esse: & magistratus porro authoritate,pœnisque civilibus validius muniendas. Atque hæc ad exceptionem Hierarchicorum secundam: leges nempè de politeia ecclesiastica immutabiles non esse,quia fieri potest, ut invalidè reperiantur ad finem suum assequendum.
units.tr: Fourth, Hooker observes no proportion in the circumstances. He wants the ecclesiastical polity to be mutable according to the condition of places, times and persons; but this change in the law of theft was not made according to the condition of places, times and persons; nor is the substance changed, but only the circumstance of the penalty. So nothing follows from it except this alone: that, because of the excessive wickedness of men, the ecclesiastical sanctions and penalties seem less effective, and they are to be exercised more diligently and more rigorously, and moreover are to be fortified more strongly by the authority and civil penalties of the magistrate. And so much for the second exception of the Hierarchists: that laws concerning the ecclesiastical polity are not immutable, because it may happen that they are found invalid for attaining their end.

units.la: 7 Seguitur opinio Hierarchicorum nonnullorum secunda: quæ non ex invaliditate præcepti, sed præcipientis potius pugnat. Hanc cuetur Georgius Downamus, qui distinguens inter jus divinum quod immutabile esse vult, & jus Apostolicum quod mutabile: Politeiam Ecclesiasticam, speciatim Hierarchicum Episcopatum, non iure divino immutabili, sed iure Apostolico mutabili pendere affirmat. Primò, in hac distinctione advertenda illius novitas est, & reprehendenda: præ-fertim cum novitatem nobis ubique obijciat.
units.tr: 7. There follows the second opinion of certain Hierarchists, which contends not against the invalidity of the precept but rather against the one who prescribes it. George Downame defends this, who, distinguishing between divine law, which he wants to be immutable, and apostolic law, which is mutable, affirms that the ecclesiastical polity, specifically the hierarchical episcopate, depends not on immutable divine law but on mutable apostolic law. First, in this distinction its novelty is to be noted and reproved, especially since he throws novelty in our face everywhere.

units.la: Turpe est doctori cum culpa redarguit ipsum.
units.tr: It is shameful for a teacher to be refuted by his own fault.

units.la: Quod si autem novam esse inficietur, proferat Patrem, proferat Scholasticum, proferat Canonistam, proferat Papistam, proferat Protestantem, proferat Hierarchicum, qui ea ante visus sit. Secundò, in hac distinctione advertatur quòd Episcopatum Hierarchicum ex jure divino esse non vult: id quod diserte plures affirmant, ut lib. 1. p. 2. lib. 3. p. & lib. 4. o. Iam hoc pro nobis satis est. Si etenim ex jure divino non sit, ex jure humano est: inter jus divinum & jus humanum nullum datur medium. Patet hoc ex ipsis sacris, in quibus vocatio aut à Deo est, aut ab hominibus Gal. 1: 1, & ministerium Ecclesiasticum vnumquodque aut a cælo aut ab hominibus Math. 21,25. ministri denique ipsi quoad ortum aut cœli aut terræ stellæ sunt. Ap: 12. 1 cum Ap.9: 1. Ap: 13: 2. Concordat jus Canonicum, consentit Isidorus: Omnes (inquit) leges aut divinæ sunt aut humanæ: membra itaque dividentia, non jus divinum & Apostolicum, sed divinum & humanum, sunt. Quod ad jus Apostolicum attinet, illud revera divinum est: distinctum à divino vult Downamus, tum esse humanum ut confiteatur necesse est.
units.tr: But if he denies that it is new, let him produce a Father, a Schoolman, a Canonist, a Papist, a Protestant, or a Hierarchical writer who had seen it before. Secondly, let it be noted in this distinction that he does not want the Hierarchical episcopate to be from divine right, which many assert in so many words, as in book 1, part 2, book 3, part [ ] and book 4, [ ]. Now this is quite enough for us. For if it is not from divine right, it is from human right, since there is no middle ground between divine right and human right. This is plain from the sacred writings, where a calling is either from God or from men (Gal. 1:1), and where each ecclesiastical ministry is either from heaven or from men (Matt. 21:25); and the ministers themselves, as to their origin, are stars of heaven or of earth (Rev. 12:1 with Rev. 9:1, Rev. 13:2). Canon law agrees, and Isidore concurs: All laws (he says) are either divine or human. The dividing members are therefore not divine right and Apostolic right, but divine and human. As for Apostolic right, that is truly divine; and if Downame wants it distinguished from divine right, he must admit that it is human, as he is bound to do.

units.la: 8 Dixi nuper hanc distinctionem inter jus divinum & Apostolicum in nullo authore reperiri: certè sensu Downamiano, ut jus Apostolicum medium quoddam jus sit quod nec sit divinum nec humanum. Alias reperitur apud Bellarminum a quo forte locum aliquem accepit Downamus: qui cœlibatum sacerdotum non jure divino, sed Apostolico jure niti vult, & ita esse dispensabile. Iam verò per jus Apostolicum, Bellarminus jus humanum intelligit: probè intelligens, inter jus divinum & humanum, nullum jus medium intervenire. Verba hæc sunt. Beatus Thomas in 2. 2. q. 88. art. 11. diserte docet votum continentiæ esse annexum ordinibus sacris, ex solo ecclesiæ decreto, ac proinde dispensabile esse. Idem docet Caietanus in opuscul: Tom. 1. Tractat. 27. & Sotus lib. 7. de Iustitia q: 6. art. 1. vbi etiam docent, quod ego verissimum puto, decretum hoc quo votum est annexum ordinibus non quidem proprie divinum esse: sed tamen esse Apostolicum, & in tota ecclesia à temporibus Apostolorum longo tempore esse observatum. Nunc probandum est non jure divino, sed humano duntaxat (adverte, appellat nunc jus humanum, quod primis hujus capitis verbis, jus Apostolicum appellaverat) prohibitum esse sacerdotum coniugium, & proinde in hac dispensari posse. Observanda sunt in Soto & Bellarmino parentibus primis distinctionis hujusce Downamianæ inter jus divinum & Apostolicum hæc tria. Primò, in jure tantum humaminica, hoc tantum vult, non esse ex iure divino immutabili. Alibi Episcopum traditionem Apostolicam appellat: id est, Episcopus est ex iure mutabili Apostolico: sic ut Hieronimus idem plane nobiscum sentiat. Imo non sentit, quod ut appareat, observentur paululum haec tria ἱερarchica. Hadrianus Saravia de hoc loco Hieronymi agens, Haec tantum in eo sibi displicere dicit, quod negat Episcopum ex Dominica dispensatione esse: alias nihil mali in eo est, quod Episcopum dicit esse ex consuetudine: quia ex consuetudine & ex verbo simul Episcopus est: quo sensu Augustinus intelligendus est, cum Episcopi honorem ex usu Ecclesiae esse affirmat. En subterfuginm primum: quando patres dicunt Episcopum esse ex usu & ex consuetudine: non intelligunt ex consuetudine sola, sed ex consuetudine & verbo simul: At inquam patres, Hyeronimus praesertim, consuetudinem & Dominicam dispositionem opponunt, sic ut ex verbo & consuetudine etiam Episcopum Hierarchicum esse minime omnium senserint: sed ex consuetudine sola absque verbo. Imo non ita est, inquit Downamus, sentit etenim Hieronimus mecum, Hieronimus non magis Aerianus est quam ipse ego sum: negat quidem Episcopum esse ex Dominica dispositione, sed idem quod ego sensit, nempe hoc tantum, quod non sit ex iure divino immutabili, quod mea ipsissima defensio est. En subterfugium secundum: quod evertitur à Saravia: intelligit inquit Hieronymus Episcopum non esse ex institutione iureque divino, itaque dicendum est, Hieronymum hac in re plane Aerianum esse. Accersendus iam Bellarminus est. Hieronymus, inquit, Episcopum quoad ordinis potestatem superiorem presbyteris facit iure divino, ut patet ex epistola ad Evagrium ubi sic ait. Quid facit Episcopus excepta ordinatione quod non facit presbyter? at iure divino agnoscere non videtur discrimen inter iurisdictionem Episcopi & presbyteri: tamen agnoscit hoc discrimen, tanquam legitime imo necessario ad schismata vitanda ab Apostolis introductum. Agit de hoc ipso Hieronymi loco ibi Bellarminus: en igitur subterfugium tertium. Dicendum quidem cum Saravia est, sentire Hieronymum, Episcopum non esse ex jure divino, sed Apostolico tantum, id est humano (sic etenim Apostolicum interpretari Bellarminum docuimus nuper:) sed non generaliter tamen interpretandus est, sed de jurisdictione tantum, non autem de potestate ordinationis. Sed si potestas tantum ordinationis, jure divino tribuatur Episcopo, auferatur ab eo autem jure divino in presbyteros omnis jurisdictio, quae humano tantum jure nititur Hieronymi judicio, cecidit plane splendor omnis Episcopalis: imo cecidit etiam absoleta distinctio illa inter ordinem, & jurisdictionem, ac si in ista impares ministri essent qui in primo pares sunt.
units.tr: 8 I said a little while ago that this distinction between divine and Apostolic right is found in no author, at least in Downame's sense, in which Apostolic right is some middle kind of right that is neither divine nor human. Elsewhere, however, it is found in Bellarmine, from whom Downame perhaps took some passage, since he wants the celibacy of priests to rest not on divine right but on Apostolic right, and so to be dispensable. Now Bellarmine understands by Apostolic right human right, understanding well that no middle right lies between divine and human right. His words are these: Blessed Thomas, in 2.2, q. 88, art. 11, clearly teaches that the vow of continence is annexed to the sacred orders by the decree of the Church alone, and therefore can be dispensed. Caietan teaches the same in his Opuscula, vol. 1, treatise 27, and Soto in book 7 of On Justice, q. 6, art. 1, where they also teach, which I think most true, that this decree by which the vow is annexed to the orders is not indeed properly divine, but is nevertheless Apostolic, and has been observed for a long time throughout the whole Church from the times of the Apostles. It must now be proved that the marriage of priests is forbidden not by divine right but by human right alone (note that he now calls it human right, which in the first words of this chapter he had called Apostolic right), and so it can be dispensed. In Soto and Bellarmine, the originators of this Downamite distinction between divine and Apostolic right, three things must be observed. First, he means only that it is not from immutable divine right. Elsewhere he calls the episcopate an Apostolic tradition, that is, the episcopate is from mutable Apostolic right; so that Jerome thinks entirely as we do. Indeed he does not think so, which will appear if these three points are observed a little more closely. Adrian Saravia, treating of this passage of Jerome, says that this alone displeases him in it, that he denies the episcopate to be from the Lord's appointment; otherwise there is nothing wrong in his saying that the episcopate is from custom, because the episcopate is from custom and from the Word together; and in this sense Augustine must be understood when he affirms that the honour of the episcopate is from the usage of the Church. Here is the first evasion: when the Fathers say that the episcopate is from usage and custom, they do not mean from custom alone but from custom and the Word together. But I say that the Fathers, Jerome especially, set custom against the Lord's disposition, so that they least of all thought the Hierarchical episcopate to be from the Word and custom together, but from custom alone without the Word. On the contrary, it is not so, says Downame, for Jerome thinks with me; Jerome is no more an Arian than I am. He indeed denies that the episcopate is from the Lord's disposition, but he thought the same as I do, namely only this, that it is not from immutable divine right, which is my very own defence. Here is the second evasion, which Saravia overturns: Jerome, he says, understands the episcopate not to be from divine institution and right, so it must be said that Jerome in this matter is plainly an Arian. Now Bellarmine must be summoned. Jerome, he says, makes the episcopate superior to presbyters, as regards the power of ordination, by divine right, as is plain from his letter to Evagrius, where he says: What does a bishop do, apart from ordination, that a presbyter does not do? Yet he does not seem to recognise, by divine right, any difference between the jurisdiction of a bishop and of a presbyter; still he recognises this difference as introduced by the Apostles, lawfully and indeed necessarily to avoid schisms. Bellarmine discusses this very passage of Jerome there: here is the third evasion. It must indeed be said with Saravia that Jerome thought the episcopate was not from divine right but from Apostolic right only, that is, human right (for we have lately shown that Bellarmine so interprets Apostolic right); but it must not be interpreted generally, only of jurisdiction and not of the power of ordination. But if the power of ordination alone is granted to the bishop by divine right, while all jurisdiction over presbyters, which rests on human right only, is taken from him by Jerome's judgment, then all the splendour of the episcopate has plainly fallen; indeed, the obsolete distinction between order and jurisdiction has also fallen, as if in the latter the ministers were unequal who are equal in the former.

units.la: ii Quarto, in hac Downami distinctione reprehendendum illud est, quod quae jure divino sanciuntur, ea omnia immutabilia esse supponit Lancelotus Perusinus ita. Ius divinum est quod continetur in lege & in Evangelio atque immutabile semper permanet. Respicit in his Perusinus ad illa prima verba Gratiani. Humanum genus duobus regitur, naturali
units.tr: Fourthly, in this distinction of Downame there is to be reproved the assumption that whatever is enacted by divine right is therefore immutable. Lancelot Perusinus says this: Divine right is what is contained in the law and in the Gospel and always remains immutable. In these words Perusinus refers to the first words of Gratian: The human race is governed by two things, natural

units.la: Instit. tit. 2 Dist. 1. turali videlicet iure & moribus. Ius naturale est quod in lege & Evangelio continetur, quo quisque iubetur aliis facere, quod sibi vult fieri. Male autem Gratianum Perusinus interpretatur, si modo Thomam Aquinatem audire placet. Non intelligendus est Gratianus (inquit) quasi omnia quae sunt in lege & in Evangelio sint de lege naturae & sic immutabilia: sed quod quae sunt de lege naturae & immutabilia sunt ibi plenarie tradantur, & ex instantia Gratiani patet, qua quisque iubetur aliis facere quod sibi vult fieri. Annon Perusianum & Downnamianum dogma confodiunt ista? Non omnia (inquit Aquinas) immutabilia sunt, quae iuris divini: quod patet in ceremonialibus Mosaicis, & in mandatis aliis mutabilibus Math. 10.5.14. & 12, 19, & 15, 20, & 19, 21. Iob. 13,14,15, &c. At haec mandata mutabilia (respondebunt forte) jus divinum non secum traxerunt: mandata quidem à Deo sunt, sed absque juris ullius divini positione. Absurde. Omne siquidem mandatum divinum hanc vim habet ut juste fieri possit, quod mandatur: si ita, tum jus divinum mandatum omne divinum ponit: Ius (inquit Isidorus) est dictum, quia justum est: ergo quicquid ex divino mandato iuste fieri potest, jus etiam divinum habet, absque quo iuste fieri nequivisset. Ad eundem sensum Aquinas. Ius divinum est (inquit) quod divinitus promulgatur. Ad eundem Sibrandus Lubertus. Ius inquit dicitur à iussu per Apocopem. Quid igitur est? Cum omnia mandata divina ex jure divino sint, & illorum multa mutabilia sint: male in istac distinctione supponit Downnamus, omnia immutabilia esse, quae de jure divino sunt.
units.tr: Institutes, title 2, distinction 1: that is, by natural right and by customs. Natural right is what is contained in the law and the Gospel, by which each is commanded to do to others what he wishes done to himself. But Perusinus interprets Gratian badly, if we are willing to listen to Thomas Aquinas. Gratian (he says) is not to be understood as if all things that are in the law and in the Gospel are of the natural law and so immutable; but what are of the natural law and immutable are there fully set out, and the example of Gratian makes this plain, by which each is commanded to do to others what he wishes done to himself. Do not these things pierce the dogma of Perusinus and Downame? Not all things (says Aquinas) that are of divine right are immutable; this is plain in the Mosaic ceremonies and in other mutable commands, Matt. 10:5; 14; 12:19; 15:20; 19:21; John 13, 14, 15, etc. But these mutable commands, they will perhaps reply, did not bring divine right with them: they are indeed from God, but without the establishing of any divine right. This is absurd. For every divine command has this force, that what is commanded can be done justly; if so, then every divine command establishes divine right. Right (says Isidore) is so called because it is just; therefore whatever can be done justly by divine command also has divine right, without which it could not have been done justly. Aquinas is to the same effect: Divine right is what is promulgated by God. Sibrandus Lubbertus to the same effect: Right, he says, is called from command (iussus) by apocope. What then is the result? Since all divine commands are of divine right, and many of them are mutable, Downame is wrong in supposing in this distinction that all things that are of divine right are immutable.

units.la: 12 Quinto, in distinctione hac Downami, peccatur in eo, quod quae divini juris sunt, & immutabilia sunt, ea statuit adeo necessaria, ut nulla ecclesia absque eis esse possit. Hinc ista infert. Quanquam teneo vocationem episcoporum, respectu primae institutionis, Apostolicam esse ac proinde divinam ordinationem: tamen non eam divini juris esse teneo: quasi generaliter, perpetuo, immutabiliter necessaria, ac si nulla ecclesia vera esse possit, quae eadem caruerit. Rursus, Non ita teneo functionem episcoporum Diocesanorum ita divini juris esse, quasi generaliter, perpetuo, & immutabiliter necessaria esset ad esse Ecclesiae, & nullum aliud regimen admitti possit. Eadem rursus repetit, p. 140. Quae divino igitur jure perpetua & immutabilia sunt: ea ad esse ecclesiae pertinere vult, sic ut nulla ecclesia vera carere eisdem queat. Atqui hocin theoremate transfugit aperte in Separistarum castra: adversus quos demonstravimus alibi, ecclesiam veram esse posse, etsi quibusdam careat, quae perpetuo & immutabiliter quasi necessaria, mandata è Domino injunctaque ecclesiae sunt. Atque disciplina quidem ecclesiastica, etsi perpetuo & immutabiliter necessaria sit: tamen non ad esse ecclesiae simplic iter, sed tantum ad bene esse pertinet. Neque mirari hoc fas est: quum Sacramenta perpetuo & immutabiliter quasi necessaria injuncta sint: quibus tamen ecclesia in deserto caruit, sicut supra ex D. Beza est adnotatum. At qui necessaria dici possunt, inquies si eis ecclesia carere potest, & tamen Dei ecclesia esse? Respondeo, quum non sunt res indifferentes, quia ecclesia ea absque peccato mutare non potest, aut carere voluntario: peccat igitur ecclesia, quæ ea non habet. Peccat sanè, ut in Anglicana ecclesia videre jam est, quæ veram Christi politeiam ecclesiasticam respuit: sed peccatum istud ejusmodi non est, ut ipsam ecclesiæ esse destruat: quamdiu in ea fidei puritas in doctrina conservatur.
units.tr: 12. Fifthly, Downame's distinction goes wrong in this respect: he holds that whatever is of divine right and immutable is so necessary that no church can exist without it. From this he infers: Although I hold the calling of bishops, with respect to its first institution, to be apostolic and therefore a divine ordinance, I do not hold it to be of divine right, as though it were generally, perpetually and immutably necessary, so that no church could be a true church that lacked it. Again: I do not so hold the office of diocesan bishops to be of divine right, as though it were generally, perpetually and immutably necessary to the being of the Church, and no other government could be admitted. He repeats the same thing on p. 140. So he wants whatever is perpetual and immutable by divine right to pertain to the being of the Church, so that no true church can lack it. Yet in this theorem he plainly goes over to the camp of the Separatists, against whom we have shown elsewhere that a church may be true even though it lacks some things that were commanded by the Lord and enjoined on the church as perpetually and immutably necessary. Ecclesiastical discipline, though it is perpetually and immutably necessary, pertains not simply to the being of the Church but only to its well-being. Nor should this seem strange, since the sacraments were enjoined as perpetually and immutably necessary, and yet the Church lacked them in the wilderness, as was noted above from Beza. But you will object: how can things be called necessary if the Church can lack them and yet be the Church of God? I answer: they are not indifferent things, because the Church cannot change them or do without them voluntarily without sin; so the Church that does not have them sins. It sins indeed, as can now be seen in the English Church, which rejects the true ecclesiastical polity of Christ. But this sin is not of such a kind as to destroy the being of the Church, so long as the purity of faith in doctrine is preserved in it.

units.la: 13. Sextò & ultimo, distinctio ista Downami est absque differentia, quoniam membra coincidunt: nam & quæ Apostolici juris à Downamo dicuntur, eadem revera & juris etiam divini sunt. Differentia quidē quædā est inter mandata divina, quòd Deus quædā immediate per seipsum, quædam mediatè per Apostolos tradidit: sed hæc differentia nihil prohibet, quin utraque adæque immutabilia sint, & ex jure divino ligent. Vidit hoc Downami gregalis Thomas Bellius scriptor Hierarchicus, ejus verba hæc sunt: Res duplicitèr, inquit, dici possunt esse jure divino. Primò, quia sunt à Deo immediate: Secundò, quia sunt mediate ab illis, qui à sancto Dei spiritu ita diriguntur ut errare nequeant: quo sensu superioritas Episcoporum in reliquos ministros de jure divino esse dicitur sive ordinatio divina. Similis Guilielmi Barloi Episcopi Lincolniensis sententia est. Agit de loco Hieronymi, ubi negat Episcopum esse ex institutione dominica. Distinguit verò fere sensu Downamiano inter divinum præceptum & consilium Apostolicum ex 1. Corint. 7. 6. & dicit Hieronymi mentem esse, Episcopum quidem non esse ex ullo scripto mandato Christi, vel ab ulla expressa ejusdem regula: sed ex consilio, traditione, χωρία ἀχεάφη, & institutione Apostolica. Hanc mentem Hieronymi & Georgius Downamus fingit, quam etiam approbat, sed Barlous non item: Non ita Hieronymus transfire debet, inquit, ac si functio Episcopalis non esset directè ipsa domini institutio. Non etenim spiritus per Apostolos solùm, qui eum magna mensura acceperunt, sed etiam per Christum ipsum, qui eum sine mensura accepit, hanc superioritatem ordinavit. Pergit deinde probare per immediatum Christi institutum, regimen Episcopale ordinandum esse, qui idem immutabile contra Downamum statuit. Non tamen putat mutabile futurum (quod Downamus) si mediato tantum Apostolico jure niteretur. Nam & non scriptas illas διατάξεις Apostolorum quas memorat ex 1. Cor. 11. 34. & permissiones Apostolorum illas, absque expresso Christi mandato quas memorat ex 1. Cor. 7. 6. & 25. juris divini esse vult, quid ita? Quia, inquit, licet hæc mandavit Paulus absque expresso mandato Christi: non tamen mandavit absque certo & infallibili spiritu Christi, sicut ait ver. 40. Scio me habere spiritum Christi. Propter hunc spiritum Christi, quæ absque immediato mandato scripto; & speciali revelatione sibi facta mandaret, 1. Cor. 8. 9. 13. & 10. 25. 29. & 11. 4. 14. 23. 25.] ea ad postremum hoc vinculo ligat, 1. Cor. 14. 37. Si quis se Prophetam putat & spiritualem, cogitet, quæ ad vos scribo, quod Dei mandata sunt. Ecce, quæ mediata ab Apostolis præcipiuntur, ipsius Dei mandata sunt, haud secus ac ea quæ immediato præcepto nituntur: quidni igitur perinde ex jure divino etiam?
units.tr: 13. Sixthly and lastly, Downame's distinction is without difference, since the members coincide: for those things which Downame calls of apostolic right are in fact also of divine right. There is indeed some difference between divine commands, in that God delivered some immediately through himself and some mediately through the apostles; but this difference does not prevent both from being equally immutable and binding by divine right. Thomas Bell, Downame's fellow-follower and a hierarchical writer, saw this; his words are these: Things can be said to be of divine right in two ways. First, because they are from God immediately; second, because they are from those who are so directed by the Holy Spirit of God that they cannot err. In this sense the superiority of bishops over the other ministers is said to be of divine right, or a divine ordinance. The opinion of William Barlow, Bishop of Lincoln, is similar. He treats the passage of Jerome where Jerome denies that a bishop is by the Lord's institution. He distinguishes, almost in Downame's sense, between a divine precept and an apostolic counsel, from 1 Corinthians 7:6, and says that Jerome's meaning is that a bishop is not indeed from any written command of Christ or any express rule of his, but from counsel, tradition, unwritten [ἄγραφα], and apostolic institution. Downame imagines this to be Jerome's meaning and also approves it, but Barlow does not: Jerome ought not to be so passed over, he says, as if the episcopal office were not directly the Lord's own institution. For it was not only through the apostles, who received the Spirit in great measure, but through Christ himself, who gave the Spirit without measure, that this superiority was ordained. He goes on to prove from Christ's immediate institution that the episcopal government must be ordained, and he holds this to be immutable, against Downame. Yet he does not think it would be mutable (as Downame does) if it rested only on apostolic right mediately. For he holds that those unwritten ordinances [διατάξεις] of the apostles which he mentions from 1 Corinthians 11:34, and those permissions of the apostles, without an express command of Christ which he mentions from 1 Corinthians 7:6 and 25, are also of divine right. Why so? Because, he says, although Paul gave these without an express command of Christ, yet he did not give them without the certain and infallible Spirit of Christ, as he says in verse 40: I think that I have the Spirit of Christ. Because of this Spirit of Christ, the things which he commanded without an immediate written command and a special revelation made to him (1 Cor. 8:9, 13; 10:25, 29; 11:4, 14, 23, 25) he binds finally with this bond, 1 Corinthians 14:37: If anyone thinks himself a prophet or spiritual, let him acknowledge that the things I write to you are the commands of God. Behold: those things which are commanded mediately by the apostles are the very commands of God, no less than those which rest on an immediate precept. Why then should they not likewise be of divine right?

units.la: 14. Accedit Guilielmus Whitakerus, qui Bellarmino locum Hieronymi unà cum Downamo quoad verba interpretanti, ac si Episcopum sentiret, non quidem ex jure divino esse, sed ex jure Apostolico tamen, respondet ita. Bellarminus secum pugnat & Hieronymum facit loquipugnantia. Nam si Hieronymus putavit jurisdictionem illam Episcopi non esse iuris divini, quomodo tum fuit illud discrimen ab Apostolis introductum? Et quomodo Hieronymus ex Apostolorum scriptis non esse discrimen aliquod probare potuit? Certè quod Apostoli ut necessarium sanxerint atque introduxerint iuris divini vim obtinet. Hadrianus Saravia de Hieronymo respondens, ait eum errasse cum diceret, Apostolorum tempore introductum fuisse ab Apostolis Episcopum, sed non ex dominica dispositione, quis ex hoc sequeretur, Apostolos contra domini institutionem fecisse, quod falsum est: cum constet Apostolos nihil ordinasse, quod non esset à domino institutum, quaecunque causa ordinandi fuerit. Ex quibus juxta-positis ego quatuor colligo. Primò, contra Downamum, Apostolicas ordinationes esse iura divina, quia Apostoli nihil instituerant, nisi ex divino iure, ut Whitakerus, nisi ex domini institutione ut Saravia. Secundò, quicquid inducitur in Ecclesiam, quod Politeiam Ecclesiasticam, non ex iure divino, ut Whitakerus, non ex domini institutione, ut Saravia; id contra domini institutionem esse ideoque illicitum: etiamsi ab Apostolis ipsis hoc factum esset. Tertiò, Hierarchicorum responsionem, Hieronymum sentire Episcopum introductum ipso tempore Apostolorum contra schismata vanam esse & frivolam, quia Apostoli nihil induxerunt nisi ex iure & instituto divino: at vero Hieronymi sententia est (quocunque demum tempore introductus Episcopus fuit:) eum non ex dominica dispositione, non ex jure divino, non ex domini instituto fuisse introductum. Quartò, si Hieronymus dixisset, Episcopum introductum fuisse non quidem ex divino iure, sed tamen Apostolico, pugnantia locutus est: idem enim est ut si dixisset, non ex divino iure, & tamen ex divino iure. Atque Bellarminus pugnantia loquitur, inquit Whitakerus, cum Episcopum non iure divino iuxta Hieronymum, sed Apostolico inductum dicit: sic & pugnantia Georgius Downamus, idque non in uno loco: Quaecunque functio est Apostolicae institutionis, divina ordinatio censenda est. Probat ex Beza: Si ab Apostolis profectum esset, non vereor, id totum divinae institutioni ascribere. Rursus: Sive primò ordinata a Christo, sive ab Apostolis instituta ea functio fuit: eius author Christus est, sive immediate iuxta primum, sive mediatè iuxta secundum. Atque ea Apostolicae institutionis esse dicuntur, quae Christus instituit per Apostolos. Huc referenda, quae supra allata sunt ex respons. ad praefat. p. 2. & ex libro 4. p. 139. 140. ubi dicit Episcopum divinae ordinationis esse, quia Apostolicae institutionis. Quid hic habet Downamus quod respondeat? Divinam ordinationem non inferre divinum ius? Apage ineptias: nam ordinatio jussum quoddam est, & omne jussum importat jus, ut inos supra demonstravimus.
units.tr: 14. William Whitaker also agrees. When Bellarmine, along with Downame, interprets Jerome's words as if he meant that the bishop is not of divine right but nonetheless of apostolic right, Whitaker replies thus: Bellarmine contradicts himself and makes Jerome say contradictory things. For if Jerome thought that jurisdiction of that kind was not of divine right, how then was that distinction introduced by the apostles? And how could Jerome prove from the writings of the apostles that there was no such distinction? Surely what the apostles decreed and introduced as necessary has the force of divine right. Adrian Saravia, answering concerning Jerome, says that he erred when he said that a bishop was introduced by the apostles in apostolic times, but not by the Lord's appointment. What would follow from this? That the apostles acted against the Lord's institution, which is false, since it is established that the apostles ordained nothing that was not instituted by the Lord, whatever the cause of ordaining was. From these juxtaposed opinions I draw four conclusions. First, against Downame: apostolic ordinances are divine rights, because the apostles instituted nothing except by divine right, as Whitaker says, except by the Lord's institution, as Saravia says. Second, whatever is introduced into the Church that is not of divine right, as Whitaker says, not by the Lord's institution, as Saravia says, is against the Lord's institution and therefore unlawful, even if it had been done by the apostles themselves. Third, the hierarchical reply, that Jerome thinks the bishop was introduced in the very time of the apostles against schisms, is empty and frivolous, because the apostles introduced nothing except by divine right and divine institution. But Jerome's opinion is (whatever time the bishop was introduced) that he was introduced not by the Lord's disposition, not by divine right, not by the Lord's institution. Fourth, if Jerome had said that the bishop was introduced not indeed by divine right but nonetheless by apostolic right, he would have spoken contradictions: for it is the same as if he had said, not by divine right, and yet by divine right. And Bellarmine speaks contradictions, says Whitaker, when he says that the bishop was introduced not by divine right, according to Jerome, but by apostolic right. So too Georgius Downame contradicts himself, and not in only one place: Whatever office is of apostolic institution is to be regarded as a divine ordinance. He proves this from Beza: If it proceeded from the apostles, I do not fear to ascribe the whole of it to divine institution. Again: Whether that office was first ordained by Christ or instituted by the apostles, Christ is its author: either immediately, according to the first case, or mediately, according to the second. And those things are said to be of apostolic institution which Christ instituted through the apostles. To this belong the things cited above from the answer to the preface, p. 2, and from book 4, pp. 139–140, where he says the bishop is of divine ordinance because of apostolic institution. What has Downame to answer here? That a divine ordinance does not imply divine right? Away with such foolishness! For an ordinance is a kind of command, and every command implies right, as we have shown above.

units.la: CAP. XLIV.
units.tr: CHAP. XLIV.

units.la: Argumenta nostra pro disciplina immutabilitate à doctrina Apostolorum.
units.tr: Our arguments for the immutability of church discipline, from the doctrine of the Apostles.

units.la: Ta tria illa fundamenta dejecimus & solo æquavimus, quibusHierarchici freti, Politeiam Ecclesiasticam, mutabilem esse statuunt: ad argumenta jam nostra, accedendum nobis est. Primò, ab officio Christi disputamus, quod ejus ἀρχιερωσύνη durant in perpetuum. Quid Sacerdotij? Vnica oblatione consecravit in perpetuum eos qui sanctificantur, Heb. 10.14. Quid Prophetiæ? Fides semel tradita est sanctis, Iud.3. Si de Sacerdotio & prophetia recte dicitur ea semel operata fuisse, quæ in perpetuum durent: Cur non & de regali etiam dicetur ossicio, illud semel Politeiam Ecclesiasticam instituisse, quæ etiam duraret in perpetuum?Heb.12.16.27. Adhuc semel ego cancutiam non solum terram sed etiam cœlum. Porro illud adhuc semel, declarat institutorum rerum amotionem, ut maneant quæ sunt stabilia. Deducit hinc Apostolus nos regnum affectutos stabile, quod verti non possit, ergo & media etiam stabilia, quibus ad hoc regnum provehimur: in quibus est Politeia Ecclesiastica. Atque de Politeia Iudaica cur vaticinetur Prophetæam abolitam iri? & ex propheta concludit Apostolus, semel tantum abolitionem istiusmodi fore, non deinceps: certum mihi quidem videtur, & Politeiam Ecclesiasticam sub Evangelio stabilem hic fieri absque ulla concussione: ex mente Apostoli, una ista & nulla deinceps abolitio futura est, nulla inquam: mutatio semel facta est, ceremoniarum & Politeias Iudaicæ: sed semel tantum non deinceps, mutatio istiusmodi contigit.
units.tr: We have overthrown those three foundations and levelled them to the ground, and the Hierarchists, relying on them, hold that the ecclesiastical polity is mutable. Now we must come to our own arguments. First, we argue from the office of Christ, that his high priesthood [ἀρχιερωσύνη] endures for ever. What of the priesthood? By one offering he has perfected for ever those who are sanctified, Heb. 10.14. What of the prophetic office? The faith has been once for all delivered to the saints, Jude 3. If it is rightly said of the priesthood and the prophetic office that they were accomplished once and for all and endure for ever, why should it not also be said of the kingly office that he once instituted the ecclesiastical polity, which would also endure for ever? Heb. 12.26–27: Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also heaven. Now this "yet once more" declares the removal of things that have been made, so that the things that are stable may remain. From this the Apostle infers that we have received a kingdom that is stable and cannot be shaken, and therefore also the stable means by which we are advanced to this kingdom, among which is the ecclesiastical polity. And why does he prophesy that the Jewish polity will be abolished? From the prophet the Apostle concludes that such an abolition will happen only once, and not thereafter. It seems certain to me that the ecclesiastical polity under the Gospel is here made stable without any shaking. According to the mind of the Apostle, this one abolition is future, and no other, none at all, I say: the change of the ceremonies and polity of Judaism has been made once, but only once, not thereafter; a change of this kind has happened.

units.la: Pertinet huc quod 1. Cor.15.24. regnum suum externum non ante finale iudicium deponit Christus: tum mediate regnare cessabit, Ecclesiam gubernare. Ergo regnum ipsius externum, illiusque extetna media (in quibus Politeia Ecclesiastica est) ad diem judicij, prout in verbo posita & descripta sunt, stabilia & fixa permanebunt.
units.tr: To this belongs 1 Cor. 15.24: Christ does not lay down his external kingdom before the final judgment; then he will cease to reign mediately, to govern the Church. Therefore his external kingdom and its external means (among which is the ecclesiastical polity), as they are set down and described in the Word, will remain stable and fixed until the day of judgment.

units.la: 2 Secundo, nota quâ partes verbi mutabiles, ab immutabilibus secerni solent, ipsius finis vel mutabilitas est vel immutabilitas: ita, cum finis ad quem ordinatur Politeia Ecclesiastica immutabilis & perpetuus sit, eadem perpetua etiam ut sit necesse est. Viderunt hoc Iuristæ, quorum placitum, apud Iohannem Bertachium, istud est, Ius idem est ubi juris eadem ratio est. Alias res igitur agit Sutclivius, quum formam regiminis Ecclesiastici ex eo probat mutabilem esse, quod mutata sit Politeia Iudaica, mutata regiminis forma quæ fuit sub Christo & Apostolis mutatum etiam præceptum de suffocato & sanguine. Hæc etenim omnia si mutabilia, nihil mirum, propter causas mutabiles, ad fines mutabiles, ordinata fuerunt: & cessante causa cessant effectus ut recte respondet ad horum postremum Nicolaus Lyranus: Quod ad regimen sub Christo et Apostolis, extraordinarium utrumque
units.tr: Secondly, it is customary to separate the mutable parts of the Word from the immutable ones by noting their end: if the end itself is either mutable or immutable, then the means ordained to it must be likewise. Since the end to which the ecclesiastical polity is ordained is immutable and perpetual, the polity itself must of necessity be perpetual too. The lawyers have seen this, and their rule, as given by John Bertachius, is this: The law is the same where the reason of the law is the same. Sutcliffe argues otherwise when he proves that the form of ecclesiastical government is mutable because the Jewish polity has been changed, and the form of government that existed under Christ and the Apostles has been changed, and the command about what is strangled and blood has also been changed. If all these things are mutable, it is no wonder, since they were ordained for mutable causes and mutable ends, and when the cause ceases the effects cease too. Nicholas of Lyra answers the last of these rightly: As for the governance under Christ and the Apostles, each was extraordinary

units.la: Bbb utrumque erat: at forma Politeias institutæ ordinaria est, ad ordinarium finem: longe igitur diversa horum ratio est. Imò inquit Downnamus, Timothei functio ordinaria est, & tamen non perpetua.
units.tr: each was so; but the form of the polity that was instituted is ordinary, for an ordinary end. The reasoning in the two cases is therefore wholly different. "Indeed," says Downame, "the office of Timothy is ordinary, and yet not perpetual."

units.la: 3. Non dicimus omnia ordinaria perpetua esse simpliciter, perpetua tamen durante fine omnia esse, vel ipse Richardus Hookerus agnoscit. De legibus positivis nunquam additur, inquit, quamdiu perpetuandæ sunt: quod si nullibi exprimatur, directio nulla de earum vel perpetuitate, vel mutabilitate superest, præter considerationem naturæ & qualitatis eorundem. Natura autem cuiusque legis iudicari debet, ex fine ad quem ordinatur, & ex aptitudine præceptorum ad eundem finem inducendum. Si ratio igitur cur leges instituantur sciri possit, & apparet eadem perpetuæ necessitatis esse: tum eæ ipsæ perpetuæ sunt, nisi forte validæ esse cessent, ad illum propositum, ad quod erant ab initio institutæ.] Hoc postremum nuper à nobis exactum est: remanet igitur Hookeri iudicio, leges Politeias Ecclesiæ immutabiles esse, qua rationem & finem (uti manifesto constat) perpetuum habent. Ita Georgius Carletonus. Qui putant officia Timothei & Titi extraordinaria & temporaria fuisse eorum usum & finem minime consi derant: qui neque extraordinarij sunt, neque ad tempus perdurantes, sed plane ordinarij & perpetui. Finium & usuum necessitas, similem probat necessitatem in gubernatoribus ipsis: ita regimen Episcoporum ab Apostolis institutum est, ut ad finem usque mundi duraret. Imò quid si Georgius Downnamus ipse, qui Carletono, in perpetuitate Episcopatus, ex professo adversatur: alicubi tamen adactus sit, hanc ipsam ob causam, eorum perpetuam durationem contra seipsum confiteri? Ecce etenim insignes contradictiones. Episcopi semper retinendi, non necessitate absolutâ, necessitate tamen expedientiæ, quæ ad finem & usum suum exp etit ut semper in Ecclesia maneant, eorumq; functio semper est utilis. Rursus: Episcopi semper retinendi, quia ut inquit Hieronymus, salus Ecclesiæ in eorum superioritate consistit. Rursus: Causæ Episcoporum nempe pax & salus Ecclesiæ, semper omnibus temporibus eædem sunt, ergo semper remanere debent, id quod Hieronymus sentit.] Citantur ista a me ut ostendatur, quibus & quantis contradictionibus Hierarchiæ defensio icatet: & una liqueat ex ipsorum adversariorum confessione Politeiam Ecclesiæ immutabilem esse, quia usum & finem immutabilem habet. Errant quidem in hypothesi Carletonus & Downnamus, Episcopale regimen illud ipsum esse, quod est in verbo institutum: thesis tamen verissima est, regimen ab Apostolis institutum perpetuum esse, quia ad finem & usum Ecclesiæ perpetuum ordinatur.
units.tr: Thirdly, we do not say that all ordinary things are perpetual without qualification, but that all of them are perpetual while their end endures; even Richard Hooker acknowledges this. Concerning positive laws, he says, it is never added how long they are to last; but if this is nowhere expressed, no direction remains concerning their perpetuity or mutability, apart from a consideration of their nature and quality. Now the nature of each law ought to be judged from the end to which it is ordained, and from the fitness of its precepts to bring about that end. If therefore the reason why laws are instituted can be known, and it appears that the need for them is perpetual, then they themselves are perpetual, unless perhaps they cease to be valid for that purpose for which they were instituted from the beginning. This last point has just been established by us. It therefore remains, by Hooker's judgment, that the laws of the ecclesiastical polity are immutable, since they have a perpetual reason and end (as is clearly evident). So too George Carleton: Those who think the offices of Timothy and Titus were extraordinary and temporary have quite failed to consider their use and end; for they are neither extraordinary nor lasting only for a time, but plainly ordinary and perpetual. The necessity of the ends and uses proves a similar necessity in the governors themselves: thus the government of bishops was instituted by the Apostles so that it would last until the end of the world. What if George Downame himself, who professedly opposes Carleton on the perpetuity of the episcopate, has nevertheless been forced somewhere, for this very reason, to confess against himself that their perpetual duration is necessary? Here indeed are remarkable contradictions: Bishops are always to be retained, not by absolute necessity, but yet by the necessity of expediency, which, with respect to its end and use, requires that they always remain in the Church, and their function is always useful. Again: Bishops are always to be retained, because, as Jerome says, the safety of the Church consists in their pre-eminence. Again: The causes of bishops, namely peace and the safety of the Church, are always the same at all times; therefore they must always remain, which is what Jerome thinks. I cite these things so that it may be shown with what and how many contradictions the defence of the hierarchy is beset, and so that it may be plain, from the confession of its own opponents, that the ecclesiastical polity is immutable because it has an immutable use and end. Carleton and Downame indeed err in their hypothesis that the episcopal government is itself that which is instituted in the Word; but the thesis is most true: the government instituted by the Apostles is perpetual, because it is ordained to the end and use of the Church, which is perpetual.

units.la: 4. Tertiò, quanquam Politeia Ecclesiastica (inquit Hookerus) mutabilis à se se sit, mutari tamen minime oportet, si in scripturis, illius mutatio nullibi reperiatur: leges etenim mutationis capaces non sunt, si qui eas tulit illorum mutationem prohibeat. Bene est: at ipse legislator Christus (inquam) suam Politeiam immutabilem esse iussit. 1. Tim. 6. 13. 14. Denuncio tibi coram Deo qui vivificat omnia, & Iesu Christi—ut serves hoc
units.tr: Fourthly, although the ecclesiastical polity (says Hooker) is mutable in its own nature, it ought by no means to be changed, if no change of it is to be found anywhere in the Scriptures; for laws capable of change are not changed if the one who enacted them forbids their change. Well said. But the very lawgiver, Christ, I say, has commanded that his polity be immutable. 1 Tim. 6.13–14: I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and before Jesus Christ, that you keep this

units.la: Lib.4. p 145. 147. Lib.3 f.10. De Iuris diff. c.4.p.41. lib.3.p.57. 58. lib.3 p 64. bb.3.p.130 & 131. ib.3.f.11. p.155. hoc mandatum incontaminatus & irreprehensus, usque ad illustrem illum adventum Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Quidni hic liceat acclamare cum Augustino in causa simili? Quem non terreret tam vehemens contestatio? Dari cervicis igitur merito dixeris Hierarchicos illos, qui in Politeias quidem mutabilitate, supra ipsam meretricem Romanam, frontes suos perfricuerunt. Sic etenim Cornelius Scultingius: Calvinus seniorum concilium perpetuum vult: Musculus non, qui electionem & formam gubernationis ab Apostolis usurpatam nunc propter magistratum minimè utilem esse censet, nos contra sacerdotum concilium cum Episcopo semper necessarium dicimus. Idipsum quò minus Hierarchici nonnulli dicant de Ecclesiae Politeia, elusiones huius loci varias excogitarunt. Prima est Richardi Hookeri: Haec verba non important perpetuam praeceptorum Apostolicorum observationem: sed usque ad adventum Christi: non important tanquam in quo ista observari oportet, sed potius tempus illud, ad quod observationis praemium reservatur. Sed hoc putidum glossema colorem in se nullum habet: & ab Hierarchicis omnibus respuitur, qui notari ipsum tempus concedunt, in quo hoc mandatum Apostoli est observandum.
units.tr: (Lib. 4, pp. 145, 147; Lib. 3, f. 10; De Iuris diff. c. 4, p. 41; lib. 3, p. 57, 58; lib. 3, p. 64; bb. 3, p. 130, 131; ib. 3, f. 11, p. 155) commandment without spot or reproach, until the glorious appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ. Why may I not here cry out with Augustine in a similar case? Who would not be terrified by so vehement an adjuration? Those Hierarchists may rightly be called brazen-faced, who, in the matter of the polity's mutability, have rubbed their foreheads raw beyond even the Roman harlot herself. So Cornelius Scultingius: Calvin wants a perpetual council of elders; Musculus does not, who thinks that the election and form of government used by the Apostles is now of little use on account of the magistrate; we, on the other hand, say that a council of priests together with a bishop is always necessary. Because some Hierarchists do not want to say the same thing about the polity of the Church, they have devised various evasions of this passage. The first is that of Richard Hooker: These words do not imply a perpetual observance of the Apostolic precepts, but only until the coming of Christ; they do not imply that these things are to be observed in that time, but rather that the time is that to which the reward of observance is reserved. But this foolish gloss has no colour at all, and it is rejected by all the Hierarchists, who concede that the time is indicated in which this command of the Apostle is to be observed.

units.la: 5 Secunda est Georgij Downami, qui distinguens inter potestatem & formam atque modum potestatis: Apostolum hic loqui affirmat, non de forma & modo potestatis, gubernandi, ordinandi, iurisdictionem exercendi ut ea perpetua in Ecclesia esset. Haec dum explicat infert haec porismata. Primò. [Quanquam potestas Timothei hoc in loco immutabilis statuatur, non tamen officium illud, per quod hanc potestatem exercuit. Secundò, officium Timothei, Episcopi officium fuit, sed scribit haec Paulus ad Timotheum, ut authoritatem & potestatem gubernandi in genere habentem. Tertiò, Episcopi Timothei successores tantummodo sunt: sed scribuntur haec verba, etsi primariò quidem Episcopis legitimis Timothei successoribus: secundariò tamen omnibus, qui similiter authoritatem habituri essent, quanquam non sint successores. Quartò, ij non successores quibus haec scribuntur, presbyteri sunt: qui mutatâ Politeiâ, & in casu necessitatis, authoritatem ordinandi & jurisdictionem exercendi habent. Quintò, quanquam Politeia legitime mutari possit, sic ut quandoque authoritas Timothei penes presbyteros esse possit, quanquam illius successores non sint: actualiter tamen Politeia Ecclesiae, nunquam in tanto mutabitur, sed perdurabunt alicubi Episcopi usque ad adventum Christi, sic ut etsi non solis, semper tamen existentibus Timothei successoribus haec verba scripta fuerint.] Haec medulla est eorum, quae Downamus excogitavit, quò minus forma Politeias Ecclesiasticae, quam ille in regimine Episcopali ponit, hoc in loco immutabilis sanciri videatur.
units.tr: The second is that of George Downame, who, distinguishing between the power and the form and mode of the power, affirms: The Apostle here speaks not of the form and mode of the power, of governing, ordaining, and exercising jurisdiction, so that these would be perpetual in the Church. While explaining this, he draws the following corollaries. First, [although the power of Timothy is here declared immutable, that office by which he exercised this power is not so]. Secondly, the office of Timothy was the office of a bishop, but Paul writes these things to Timothy as one having authority and power of governing in general. Thirdly, the successors of Timothy are only bishops, but these words are written, though primarily indeed to the lawful successors of Timothy, yet secondarily to all who would have similar authority, even though they are not successors. Fourthly, those to whom these things are written, who are not successors, are elders, who, when the polity has been changed and in a case of necessity, have authority to ordain and to exercise jurisdiction. Fifthly, although the polity can lawfully be changed, so that at some time the authority of Timothy may rest with the elders, even though they are not his successors; nevertheless, in actual fact, the polity of the Church will never be changed to such an extent, but bishops will last somewhere until the coming of Christ, so that, although not only bishops, yet always bishops who are successors of Timothy exist, these words have been written.] This is the substance of what Downame has devised, so that the form of the ecclesiastical polity, which he places in episcopal government, may not seem to be fixed as immutable by this passage.

units.la: 6. Examinemus verò paulisper. Primò futile est quod garrit, Paulum hic locutum de potestate non de forma potestatis. Quomodo probatur? aut unde liquet magis de una quam de altera hic Paulum loqui? Imo ratio supperit manifesta loqui hic Paulum, de singulis mandatis, quæ in hac epistola præcedunt, & in Epistola præcedenti: non modo de potestate egit, verum de forma modoq;etiam. Epiphonema etenim hæc verba continent, quo authoritas toti libro comparatur: perinde ac Apocal.22.18. Testor cuivis audienti verba Prophetiæ hujus, si quis adjecerit ad hæc, imponet ei Deus plagas scriptas in libro isto. Et si quis abstulerit aliquid auferet Deus partem ejus——ex iis quæ scripta sunt in libro isto. Mos igitur spiritus Sancti observandus: solet enim in hujusmodi sanctionibus scriptorum suorum authoritatem roborare. Locus utrobique idem est, in calce libri, forma loquendi eadem: Denuncio, inquit Paulus,Testor, inquit Iohannes: materia denique eadem est: nam servare mandatum hujus libri incontaminatum & irreprehensum idem est ac si dixisset, (Iohannes) sine additione vel diminutione. Secundò, imperitè officium appellat formam & modum authoritatis, quod authoritatis cujusque vel causa potius vel subjectum est: nam unde authoritas nisi ab officio? & quodnam legitimæ potestatis subjectum, nisi officium legitimum? Tertiò, nefanda Downami officij & potestatis divulsio est, ut officium quidem oboleri & mutari possit, potestas non item. Quàm hoc absurdum etiam, quòd authoritatem unius officij, in officium aliud transferri legitimè idque ad hominibus posse putat: quòd cuiusque confusionis Anabaptisticæ, fenestram aperit. Hinc etenim fiet ut authoritas pastoris sit penes Diaconum, authoritas Diaconi transferri possit in Seniorem: & Senior authoritatem Pastoris vel Diaconi habeat, si id magistratui visum fuerit. Evigila Downame, ut transmigrationis huiusce tuæ commenta videas. Nam cum Episcopum aboleri posse putes, remanente interim Episcopi propria authoritate, accidens somnias absque subiecto: & cum Episcopi authoritatem ad presbyterorum ordinem transferri posse statuis: quid aliud quàm μετεμψύχωσιν & transubstantiationis imaginem quandam renovas?
units.tr: 6. Let us examine this a little more closely. First, it is pointless for him to chatter that Paul here speaks of the power and not of the form of power. How is this proved? Or on what ground is it clear that Paul speaks here of one rather than the other? Indeed, the reasoning clearly shows that Paul is speaking here of the individual commands that precede in this epistle and in the previous one. He has dealt not only with the power but also with its form and manner. These words are an epiphonema, by which the authority of the whole book is set beside the commands: just as in Apoc. 22.18: I testify to everyone who hears the words of this prophecy: if anyone adds to these things, God will lay upon him the plagues written in this book. And if anyone takes away anything, God will take away his part... from those things which are written in this book. The manner of the Holy Spirit is therefore to be observed, for in such sanctions He is accustomed to confirm the authority of His writings. The place is the same in both, at the end of the book, and the form of speaking is the same: I declare, says Paul; I testify, says John. Finally, the matter is the same as well, for to keep the command of this book unpolluted and blameless is the same as if John had said: without addition or subtraction. Second, he unskilfully calls office the form and manner of authority, when office is rather the cause or subject of each authority. For whence does authority come, if not from office? And what is the subject of lawful power, if not a lawful office? Third, Downame's divorce of office from power is monstrous, so that the office may indeed be abolished and changed, but the power may not. How absurd also is his opinion that the authority of one office may be transferred lawfully to another office, and that this may be done by men! This opens a window to every Anabaptist confusion. For from this it will follow that the authority of the minister belongs to the deacon, that the authority of the deacon can be transferred to the elder, and that the elder holds the authority of the minister or deacon if this seems good to the magistrate. Wake up, Downame, and see the inventions of this transmigration of yours! For when you think the bishop can be abolished while the bishop's own authority remains, you dream of an accident without a subject; and when you establish that the authority of the bishop can be transferred to the order of presbyters, what else do you revive but a kind of metempsychosis [μετεμψύχωσιν] and an image of transubstantiation? Fourth, it is wickedly said that the office of bishop can be abolished by the magistrate, if it was instituted by divine ordinance, as Downame wishes. For by the same reasoning the magistrate could abolish the office of minister and deacon as well. Yet those offices cannot be abolished; therefore the office of the hierarchical bishop can be.
