I myself do not think a stronger argument, or a fuller confession from an adversary, could be desired: that the office of bishop, just like that of minister and deacon, was in no way instituted by Christ. Fifth, it is absurdly said by some that Paul does not write to Timothy's successors in writing to Timothy here. For when a single individual is taken, in whom some law is established, that individual certainly represents all his successors, but only his successors. For example, when God wished to fix the law of nature, He spoke to the first herb, the first plant, the first individual tree; He spoke to all herbs, plants and trees succeeding in the same kind, but not to others that were not successors within the same kind. Hence James 3.12: Can the fig tree, my brethren, bear olives, or a vine figs? Does Paul write here to Timothy for the elders? Very well. Are the elders therefore the lawful successors of Paul and Timothy? And can Timothy's power be transferred to the elders through the magistrate, and that lawfully? There was therefore no episcopal power of Timothy which was not properly the same as the power of the elder; for if God had instituted it otherwise, the magistrate could not have made the elder capable of episcopal power. Sixth and last, if Paul wrote these things not about Timothy's episcopal office but about Timothy's authority in general, then he did not write these things to Timothy as bishop, but only to Timothy as one who holds authority in general. But if he did not write these things to Timothy as bishop, then no divine right can be brought forward for bishops; for the words of the whole preceding epistle contain this authority, as said above. Thus Downame has clearly gone over into our camp, and with his own hands he tears down what he had built elsewhere against us, when he said: this epistle to Timothy is a type of the episcopal function. He also wounds his own side, above all Thomas Bilson, who admits that no divine right can be brought forward for bishops if these words were not written to Timothy as bishop. Has not Downame laboured splendidly, who undermines from its foundations the one basis for the divine right of the episcopal function?

units.la: 7 Quartò, nefariè dicitur officium Episcopi à magistratu aboleri posse, si modo divinâ ordinatione (quod vult Downamus) institutum fuerit. Pari etenim ratione & officium Pastoris & Diaconi abolere magistratus poterit. Non possunt vero ista officia aboleri. tamen Episcopi Hierarchici officium potest: non argumentum ego quidem fortius, aut pleniorem ab adversario confessionem desideratem: Episcopi officium ,perinde ac Pastoris at Diaconi, à Christo miuimè institutum esse. Quintò, ineptè dicitur quibusdam Timothei non successoribus, in Timorheo hic Paulum scribere: nam cum unum individuum sumitur, in quo lex aliqua stabilitur, repræsentat quidem individuum illud successores omnes, sed successores tantum. Exempli gratia: cum legem naturæ figere Deus voluisset, quod primæ herbæ, primæ plantæ, primæ arbori individuali dixit Deus: id ad omnes herbas,plantas,arbores in eodem genere succedentes dixit: sed non ad alias quæ in eodem genere successorum non essent; unde Iac.3.12. Nunquid potest fratres mei ficus olcas edere, aut vites ficus? Scribit hic in Timotheo presbyteris Paulus? bene est. Presbyteri igitur Pauli Timothei legitimi successores sunt? Et transferri potest Timothei potestas in presbyteros per magistratum, idque legitime? Nulla igitur Episcopalis Timothei potestas fuit, quae non eadem presbyteri proprie: si alias Deus instituisset, Episcopalis potestatis presbyterum capacé magistratus reddere non potuisset. Sexto & ultimo, si scripserit haec Paulus, non de Timothei officio Episcopali, sed de authoritate Timothei in genere: tum non haec scripsit Timotheo ut Episcopo, sed tantum Timotheo ut authoritatem in genere habenti: at si haec non scripsit Timotheo ut Episcopo tum nullum jus divinum proEpiscopis proferri potest: totius etenim Epistolae praecedentis haec verba authoramentum continent, ut ante dictum. Ita plane in castra nostra transijt Downamus: planeque suis manibus dejicit, quae contra nos alibi aedificarat: quando dixit, Hanc epistolam ad Timotheum, Episcopalis functionis typum esse. Vulnerat etiam suos, inprimis Thomam Bilsonum: qui nullum jus divinum proferri pro Episcopis posse fatetur: si haec verba scripta non fuerint Timotheo ut Episcopo. Annon pulchrè laboravit Downamus, qui hoc unicum, pro jure divino functionis Episcopalis fundamentum imis sedibus subruit?
units.tr: 7 Fourthly, it is wrongly said that the office of bishop can be abolished by the magistrate, if it was indeed instituted by divine ordinance (as Downame wishes). By the same reasoning the magistrate could abolish the office of minister and the office of deacon. Yet those offices cannot be abolished. The office of the hierarchical bishop, however, can be. I for my part find no stronger argument, nor a fuller confession from an opponent, than this: the office of bishop, just like that of minister and deacon, was by no means instituted by Christ. Fifthly, some who are not successors of Timothy foolishly say that Paul here writes to Timothy. For when a single individual is taken, in whom some law is established, that individual certainly represents all his successors, but only his successors. For example, when God wished to fix the law of nature, he said to the first herb, the first plant and the first tree that they should each bring forth after their kind; he said this to all herbs, plants and trees succeeding in the same kind, but not to others that were not successors within that kind. Hence James 3.12: "Can the fig tree, my brethren, bear olive berries, or a vine figs?" Does Paul here write to Timothy about elders? Very well. Then are the elders the lawful successors of Paul and Timothy? And can Timothy's power be transferred to the elders by the magistrate, and that lawfully? There was therefore no episcopal power in Timothy that was not, in the same way, the power of an elder; otherwise, if God had instituted something different, the magistrate could not have made an elder capable of episcopal power. Sixthly and lastly, if Paul wrote these things not about Timothy's episcopal office but about Timothy's authority in general, then he did not write these things to Timothy as a bishop, but only to Timothy as one who holds authority in general. But if he did not write these things to Timothy as a bishop, then no divine right can be produced in favour of bishops; for the words of the whole preceding Epistle contain this authority, as said before. Thus Downame has plainly passed over into our camp, and with his own hands he tears down what he had built elsewhere against us, when he says that this Epistle to Timothy is a type of the episcopal function. He also wounds his own side, above all Thomas Bilson, who admits that no divine right can be produced for bishops if these words were not written to Timothy as a bishop. Has Downame not laboured well, who by this one thing undermines to its foundations the sole basis for the divine right of the episcopal function?

units.la: 8 Quintò, videamus quid viri docti de hac re senserint. Ita Io.Gerson: Maior fuit Ecclesia primitiva autho itas, quoad predicta, quam nunc est. Non enim est in potestate Papae, aut Concilij aut Ecclesiae, immutare traditiones datas ab Evangelistis & à Paulo, ut quidam delirant. Delirium igitur Gersonis judicio, assertio haec de Politeias Ecclesiasticae mutabilitate Hierarchica est: praesertim cum ea Apostolica & Paulina traditio sit. Ita Franciscus Zabraella: Si Papa vult destruere illud quod Apostoli docuerunt convincitur errare. Non potest ad Doctrinam solam restringi hoc: disputat etenim & in eo opere de negotijs Ecclesiasticae disciplinae. Ita Ioh. Budaeus: Sacrosanctos canones meliorib us annis factos, ut eis velut regulis vita clericorum dirigeretur, & velut patrum proscriptis posteri formarentur, in amusses plumbeas iam ebasisse quis non videt? Quales olim fuerunt Canones plumbei, ut nobis non structuram operum tenore aequabili dirigant, sed extructorū commodo & libidine flexibiles, structurae accommodentur. Indignatus hic est Canones antiquos in amusses plumbeas evasisse: nos Canonem sacrum pro homium commodo & libidine in canones plumbeos, ab Hierarchicis coversos jam esse, non indignabimur? Hoc fieri, cum Politeia Ecclesiae ad magistratus arbitrium, flexibilis & mutabilis statuitur: ex nostris scriptoribus omnibus constat, Bilsono inprimis & Reynoldo: quam ad verbum Dei solum revocat, tanquam ad Lydium lapidem: ab inventis vero humanis abducit, tanquam à regula Lesbia. Hiero. Zanchium ad hoc propositum in Politeia Ecclesiastica reformanda huc citat & approbat Haid. Saravia. Verba ista sunt: Sunt igitur ad formam veteris & Apostolicae Ecclesiae, omnes Ecclesiae reformandae: & omnia tam cultus, & quidem judicio, invalidissimum, ipsos leones, tigrides, pardos, ursos denique & Basiliscos, in ordinem reduſturum.
units.tr: 8 Fifthly, let us see what learned men have thought about this matter. Thus John Gerson: The authority of the primitive Church was greater, as to the aforesaid matters, than it is now. For it is not in the power of the Pope, or of a Council, or of the Church, to change the traditions given by the Evangelists and by Paul, as some rave. Therefore, in Gerson's judgment, the assertion that the hierarchical polity of the Church is changeable is a delirium, especially since it is an apostolic and Pauline tradition. Thus Francis Zabraella: If the Pope wishes to destroy what the Apostles taught, he is convicted of error. This cannot be restricted to doctrine alone; for he also discusses, in that same work, matters of ecclesiastical discipline. Thus John Budaeus: Who does not see that the most sacred canons, made in better years, by which the life of the clergy was to be directed, and by which posterity was to be formed as by the rules of the Fathers, have turned into leaden rules? What were the leaden canons of old, which do not direct the structure of works by an even standard, but bend to the convenience and whim of the builders, so that the structure is adapted to them? He here is indignant that the ancient canons have turned into leaden rules; shall we not be indignant that the sacred canon, for the convenience and whim of men, has now been turned by the hierarchists into leaden canons? This happens when the polity of the Church is made flexible and changeable at the discretion of the magistrate. It is clear from all our writers, above all Bilson and Reynolds, that they recall it to the Word of God alone, as to the Lydian stone, and lead it away from human inventions, as from a Lesbian rule. Haddon Saravia cites and approves Zanchius here for this purpose, in reforming the ecclesiastical polity. His words are: Therefore all churches are to be reformed according to the form of the old and apostolic Church, and all forms of worship, and indeed, in my judgment, most powerless, would bring back to order lions, tigers, leopards, bears, and even basilisks.

units.la: 6 At inquit Hookerus Præsto est exemplum, quum lex divina mutata est idque licitè ab hominibus, quando invalida reperta fuit, ad suum finem obtinendum. Istud quidem exemplum, ego vel maximè audire aveo. Lex inquit de furto immutata est, quando illius pœna augmentata est, propterea quod restitutio quadrupli non erit sufficiens ad furtum cohibendum.
units.tr: 6 But Hooker says: There is an example at hand, when a divine law has been changed, and lawfully so by men, when it was found to be invalid, in order to attain its end. That example, I for one am most eager to hear. The law about theft, he says, was changed when its penalty was increased, because restitution of fourfold would not be sufficient to restrain theft.

units.la: At quid hæc ad rem? Augmentatio inquit, est mutatio quædam: sed non de hujusmodi mutatione jam agitur: probandum etenim tibi sumpsisti cessare posse politeiam ecclesiæ, & aliam ab hominibus surrogari, quando invalida reperitur ad finem suum assequendum. Secundo nego hanc pœnæ augmentationem, ipsius legis mutationem ullam esse, cujus, fi non litera, sententia tamen, hanc ipsam pœnæ augmentationem re ita ferente intendebat. Æquitas, inquit concilium Basilienfe, in finem principis habitare semper debet, quæ relicta legis litera, rationem illius sequitur: Sic Thomas Aquinas, ordinatur æquitas, ut quando litera legis deficit, cit, illius intentio ferv etur, prout æqualitas justitiæ & bonum publicum potiarit. Hoc ita cum fit, violaretur lex de furto fi relicta litera, illius intentio non spectetur, quæ est ut furtum fuppriatur. Non igitur mutatio hujus legis, pœnæ hujus literalis multiplicatio est: sed æqua illius administratio, uti ipse legis intentio (pro illa quam continet æquitate) postulat. Tertio contrarium hinc probari, præberique exemplum, quid hominibus faciendum fit: quando lex divina aliqua minus valida videatur. Probat Hookerus cessationem politeias ecclefiastice, ab exemplo, quo lex aliqua augmentatur, ecquid abfurdius? Abolitio etenim legis, & ejusdem augmentatio contraria sunt: tantum abest ut aboleat legem, qui eandem augmentat, ut ex adverso eam firmet atque roboret: tantum igitur abest, ut probet propositum hæc instantia, ut potius contrarium docet: nempe cum politeia ecclefiaftica invalida reperitur, non statim ab hominibus abolendam, sed augmentandam potius, & modis omnibus muniendam esse. Quarto, nulla hic ab Hookero proportio fervatur in circumstantijs. Mutabilem illè politeiam Ecclesiasticam esse vult, pro locorum & temporum & personarum conditione: at non pro locorum & temporum & personarum conditione hæc legis de furto mutatio fuit: neque mutatur substantia, sed circumstantia pœnæ: sic nihil hinc concluditur, nisi hoc tantum: quum propter exuberantem hominum malitiam sanctiones & pœnæ ecclesiastice minus valide videntur, diligentius & rigidius exercendas eas esse: & magistratus porro authoritate, pœnisque civilibus validius muniendas. Atque hæc ad exceptionem Hierarchicorum fecundam: leges nempe de politeia ecclefiastica immutabiles non esse, quia fieri potest, ut invalidè reperiantur ad finem suum assequendum.
units.tr: But what has this to do with the matter? Augmentation, he says, is a kind of change: but it is not of this kind of change that we are now speaking. For you have undertaken to prove that the polity of the Church can cease, and another be substituted by men, when it is found invalid to attain its end. Secondly, I deny that this increase of the penalty is any change of the law itself, whose intention, if not its letter, was aiming at this very increase of the penalty, as the circumstances required. Equity, says the Council of Basel, must always dwell in the aim of the prince, which, leaving the letter of the law, follows its reason. So Thomas Aquinas: Equity is ordained so that, when the letter of the law fails, its intention is observed, as far as the equality of justice and the public good prevail. Since this is so, the law about theft would be violated if, the letter being set aside, its intention were not regarded, which is that theft be suppressed. Therefore the increase of this penalty is not a change of this law, but a fair administration of it, as the intention of the law itself (by the equity it contains) demands. Thirdly, the contrary is proved from this, and an example is given of what must be done by men when a divine law seems rather weak. Hooker proves the cessation of the ecclesiastical polity from an example in which some law is increased. What could be more absurd? For abolition of a law and its augmentation are contrary: he who augments a law is so far from abolishing it that, on the contrary, he confirms and strengthens it. So this instance is so far from proving his proposition that it rather teaches the opposite: namely, that when the ecclesiastical polity is found weak, it is not to be abolished by men at once, but rather to be augmented and fortified in every way. Fourthly, Hooker observes no proportion in the circumstances. He wants the ecclesiastical polity to be changeable according to the condition of places, times and persons; but this change of the law about theft was not made according to the condition of places, times and persons, nor is the substance changed, but only the circumstance of the penalty. So nothing follows from this except only this: that, because of the excessive wickedness of men, the ecclesiastical sanctions and penalties seem too weak, and they are to be exercised more diligently and rigorously, and further fortified by the authority and civil penalties of the magistrate. And so much for the second exception of the hierarchists: that laws concerning the ecclesiastical polity are not unchangeable, because it may happen that they are found invalid to attain their end.

units.la: 7 Sequitur opinio Hierarchicorum nonnullorum fecunda: quæ non ex invaliditate præcepti, sed præcipientis potius pugnat. Hanc tuetur cuetur Georgius Downamus, qui distinguens inter jus divinum quod immutabile esse vult, & jus Apostolicum quod mutabile: Politeiam Ecclesiasticam, speciatim Hierarchicum Episcopatum, non iure divino immutabili, sed iure Apostolico mutabili pendere affirmat. Primo, in hac distinctione advertenda illius novitas est, & reprehendenda: praesertim cum novitatem nobis ubique objiciat.
units.tr: 7 There follows a second opinion of certain Hierarchicals, which contends not against the weakness of the precept but rather against the authority of the one who commands it. George Downame defends this view. Distinguishing between divine law, which he holds to be unchangeable, and apostolic law, which he holds to be changeable, he affirms that the ecclesiastical polity, and specifically the hierarchical episcopate, depends not on unchangeable divine law but on changeable apostolic law. First, the novelty of this distinction is to be noted and censured, especially since he throws novelty in our faces everywhere.

units.la: Turpe est doctori cum culpa redarguit ipsum.
units.tr: It is shameful for a teacher to be refuted by his own fault.

units.la: Quod si autem novam esse inficietur, proferat Patrem, proferat Scholasticum, proferat Canonistam, proferat Papistam, proferat Protestantem, proferat Hierarchicum, qui ea ante visus sit. Secundo, in hac distinctione advertatur quod Episcopatum Hierarchicum ex jure divino esse non vult: id quod diserte plures affirmant, ut lib. 1. p. 2. lib. 3. p. & lib. 4. o. Iam hoc pro nobis satis est. Si etenim ex jure divino non sit, ex jure humano est: inter jus divinum & jus humanum nullum datur medium. Patet hoc ex ipsis sacris, in quibus vocatio aut a Deo est, aut ab hominibus Gal. 1:1, & ministerium Ecclesiasticum unumquodque aut a coelo aut ab hominibus Math. 21,25. ministri denique ipsi quoad ortum aut coeli aut terrae stellae sunt. Ap: 12. 1 cum Ap.9: 1. Ap: 13:2. Concordat jus Canonicum, consentit Isidorus: Omnes (inquit) leges aut divinae sunt aut humanae: membra itaque dividentia, non jus divinum & Apostolicum, sed divinum & humanum, sunt. Quod ad jus Apostolicum attinet, illud revera divinum est: distinctum a divino vult Downamus, tum esse humanum ut confiteatur necesse est.
units.tr: But if he denies that it is new, let him produce a Father, let him produce a Schoolman, let him produce a Canonist, let him produce a Papist, let him produce a Protestant, let him produce a Hierarchical, who held it before. Second, let it be noted that in this distinction he does not want the Hierarchical episcopate to be from divine law, a point which several writers state plainly, as in book 1, page 2, book 3, page … and book 4, page …. Now this is enough for us. For if it is not from divine law, it is from human law, since there is no middle ground between divine law and human law. This is plain from the sacred writings, in which a calling is either from God or from men (Gal. 1:1), and every ecclesiastical ministry is either from heaven or from men (Matt. 21:25). Finally, the ministers themselves, as to their origin, are stars either of heaven or of earth (Rev. 12:1 with Rev. 9:1, Rev. 13:2). Canon law agrees, and Isidore concurs: All laws (he says) are either divine or human. So the dividing members are not divine and apostolic law but divine and human law. As for apostolic law, it is truly divine; Downame wants it distinguished from divine law, yet he must confess that it is human.

units.la: 8 Dixi nuper hanc distinctionem inter jus divinum & Apostolicum in nullo authore reperiri: certe sensu Downamiano, ut jus Apostolicum medium quoddam jus sit quod nec sit divinum nec humanum. Alias reperitur apud Bellarminum a quo forte locum aliquem accepit Downamus: qui coelibatum sacerdotum non jure divino, sed Apostolico jure niti vult, & ita esse dispensabile. Iam vero per jus Apostolicum, Bellarminus jus humanum intelligit: probe intelligens, inter jus divinum & humanum, nullum jus medium intervenire. Verba haec sunt. Beatus Thomas in 2. 2. q. 88. art. 11. diserte docet votum continentiae esse annexum ordinibus sacris, ex solo ecclesiae decreto, ac proinde dispensabile esse. Idem docet Caietanus in opuscul: Tom. 1. Tractat. 27. & Sotus lib. 7. de Iustitia q: 6. art. 1. vbi etiam docent, quod ego verissimum puto, decretum hoc quo votum est annexum ordinibus non quidem proprie divinum esse: sed tamen esse Apostolicum, & in tota ecclesia a temporibus Apostolorum longo tempore esse observatum. Nunc probandum est non jure divino, sed humano duntaxat (adverte, appellat nunc jus humanum, quod primis hujus capitis verbis, jus Apostolicum appellaverat) probibitum esse sacerdotum coniugium, & proinde in hac dispensari posse. Observanda sunt in Soto & Bellarmino parentibus primis distinctionis hujusce Downamianae inter jus divinum & Apostolicum haec tria. Primo, in jure tantum humaminica, boc tantum vult, non esse ex iure divino immutabili. Alibi Episcopum traditionem Apostolicam appellat: id est, Episcopus est ex iure mutabili Apostolico: sic ut Hieronimus idem plane nobiscum sentiat. Imò non sentit, quod ut appareat, observentur paululum haec tria ἱεραρχικά Hierarchica. Hadrianus Saravia de hoc loco Hieronymi agens, Haec tantum in eo sibi displicere dicit, quòd negat Episcopum ex Dominica dispensatione esse: alias nihil mali in eo est, quod Episcopum dicit esse ex consuetudine: quia ex consuetudine & ex verbo simul Episcopus est: quo sensu Augustinus intelligendus est, cum Episcopi honorem ex usu Ecclesiae esse affirmat. En subterfuginm primum: quando patres dicunt Episcopum esse ex usu & ex consuetudine: non intelligunt ex consuetudine sola, sed ex consuetudine & verbo simul: At inquam patres, Hyeronimus praesertim, consuetudinem & Dominicam dispositionem opponuut, sic ut ex verbo & consuetudine etiam Episcopum Hierarchicum esse minimè omnium senserint: sed ex consuetudine sola absque verbo. Imò non ita est, inquit Downamus, sentit etenim Hieronimus mecum, Hieronimus non magis Aerianus est quàm ipse ego sum: negat quidem Episcopum esse ex Dominica dispositione, sed idem quod ego sensit, nempe hoc tantum, quod non sit ex iure divino immutabili, quod mea ipsissima defensio est. En subterfugium secundum: quod evertitur à Saravia: intelligit inquit Hieronymus Episcopum non esse ex institutione iureque divino, itaque dicendum est, Hieronymum hac in re plane Aerianum esse. Accersendus iam Bellarminus est. Hieronymus, inquit, Episcopum quoad ordinis potestatem superiorem presbyteris facit iure divino, ut patet ex epistola ad Evagrium ubi sic ait. Quid facit Episcopus excepta ordinatione quod non facit presbyter? at iure divino agnoscere non videtur discrimen inter iurisdictionem Episcopi & presbyteri: tamen agnoscit hoc discrimen, tanquam legitimè imò necessario ad schismata vitanda ab Apostolis introductum. Agit de hoc ipso Hieronymi loco ibi Bellarminus: en igitur subterfugium tertium. Dicendum quidem cum Saravia est, sentire Hieronymum, Episcopum non esse ex jure divino, sed Apostolico tantum, id est humano (sic etenim Apostolicum interpretari Bellarminum docuimus nuper:) sed non generaliter tamen interpretandus est, sed de jurisdictione tantum, non autem de potestate ordinationis. Sed si potestas tantum ordinationis, jure divino tribuatur Episcopo, auferatur ab eo autem jure divino in presbyteros omnis jurisdictio, quae humano tantum jure nititur Hieronymi judicio, cecidit planè splendor omnis Episcopalis: imò cecidit etiam absoleta distinctio illa inter ordinem, & jurisdictionem, ac si in ista impares ministri essent qui in primo pares sunt.
units.tr: 8 I said recently that this distinction between divine and apostolic law is found in no author, at least in Downame's sense, in which apostolic law would be some middle kind of law that is neither divine nor human. Elsewhere, however, it is found in Bellarmine, from whom Downame perhaps took some passage. Bellarmine holds that the celibacy of priests rests not on divine law but on apostolic law, and so can be dispensed with. Now by apostolic law Bellarmine means human law, clearly understanding that no middle law lies between divine and human law. His words are these: Blessed Thomas, in 2.2, q. 88, art. 11, plainly teaches that the vow of continence is attached to the sacred orders by the decree of the Church alone, and therefore can be dispensed with. Cajetan teaches the same in his Opuscula, vol. 1, treatise 27, and Soto in book 7 of On Justice, q. 6, art. 1, where they also teach, which I think most true, that this decree by which the vow is attached to the orders is indeed not properly divine, but is nevertheless apostolic, and has been observed throughout the whole Church for a long time since the Apostles. Now it must be proved that the prohibition of priests' marriage rests not on divine law but on human law alone (note: he now calls human law what in the first words of this chapter he had called apostolic law), and therefore that it can be dispensed with. In Soto and Bellarmine, the first parents of this Downamian distinction between divine and apostolic law, three things are to be observed. First, in calling it merely human law, they mean only that it is not from unchangeable divine law. Elsewhere Bellarmine calls the episcopate an apostolic tradition, that is, the episcopate is from changeable apostolic law; so Jerome thinks quite the same as we do. Indeed he does not think so, as will appear if these three Hierarchical points are observed a little. Adrian Saravia, treating this passage of Jerome, says: He is displeased only in this, that he denies the episcopate to be from the Lord's appointment; otherwise there is nothing wrong in his saying that the episcopate is from custom, because the episcopate is from custom and from the word together; in this sense Augustine must be understood when he affirms that the honour of bishops is from the usage of the Church. Here is the first subterfuge: when the Fathers say that the episcopate is from usage and custom, they do not mean from custom alone, but from custom and the word together. But I say that the Fathers, Jerome especially, set custom against the Lord's disposition, so that they did not at all think the hierarchical episcopate to be from the word and custom together, but from custom alone without the word. Not so, says Downame, for Jerome thinks with me. Jerome is no more an Arian than I am. He indeed denies that the episcopate is from the Lord's disposition, but he thinks just what I think, namely only this, that it is not from unchangeable divine law, which is my very own defence. Here is the second subterfuge, which Saravia overturns: Jerome, he says, understands the episcopate not to be from institution and divine right; therefore it must be said that Jerome in this matter is plainly an Arian. Now Bellarmine must be summoned. Jerome, he says, makes the bishop superior to presbyters, as to the power of order, by divine right, as appears from the letter to Evagrius, where he says: What does a bishop do, apart from ordination, that a presbyter does not? Yet by divine right he does not seem to acknowledge a difference between the jurisdiction of bishop and presbyter; still he acknowledges this difference, as introduced legitimately, and indeed necessarily, by the Apostles to avoid schisms. Bellarmine there treats this very passage of Jerome. Here, then, is the third subterfuge. It must indeed be said with Saravia that Jerome thinks the episcopate is not from divine law but only from apostolic law, that is, human law (for we have recently shown that Bellarmine interprets apostolic law in this way), but it is not to be interpreted in general, only as regards jurisdiction, not as regards the power of ordination. But if only the power of ordination is granted to the bishop by divine law, while all jurisdiction over presbyters rests, by Jerome's judgment, on human law alone, then all the splendour of the episcopate has plainly fallen; indeed that obsolete distinction between order and jurisdiction has fallen too, as if the ministers were unequal in the second when they are equal in the first.

units.la: II. Quartò, in hac Downami distinctione reprehendendum illud est, quod quae jure divino sanciuntur, ea omnia immutabilia esse supponit Lancelotus Perusinus ita. Ius divinum est quod continetur in lege & in Evangelio atque immutabile semper permanet. Respicit in his Perusinus ad illa prima verba Gratiani. Humanum genus duobus regitur, naturali
units.tr: II. Fourth, in this distinction of Downame's, the following must be censured: he assumes that everything ordained by divine law is unchangeable. Lancelot of Perugia does the same, saying: Divine law is that which is contained in the Law and in the Gospel, and always remains unchangeable. In these words Perugia has in view the opening words of Gratian: The human race is governed by two things, natural

units.la: Institut. tit. 2 Dist. 2. non sunt res indifferentes, quia ecclesia ea absque peccato mutare non potest, aut carere voluntario: peccat igitur ecclesia, quae ea non habet. Peccat sane, ut in Anglicana ecclesia videre jam est, quae veram Christi politeiam ecclesiasticam respuit: sed peccatum istud ejusmodi non est, ut ipsam ecclesiae esse destruat: quamdiu in ea fidei puritas in doctrina conservatur.
units.tr: Institutes, title 2, distinction 2. These are not indifferent things, because the Church cannot change them without sin, nor can it lack them by its own choice; so the Church sins if it does not have them. Certainly it sins, as can now be seen in the English Church, which rejects the true ecclesiastical polity of Christ; but this sin is not of such a kind as to destroy the Church itself, as long as the purity of faith is preserved in doctrine.

units.la: 13. Sextò & ultimo, distinctio ista Downami est absque differentia, quoniam membra coincidunt: nam & quae Apostolici juris à Downamo dicuntur, eadem revera & juris etiam divini sunt. Differentia quidem quaedam est inter mandata divina, quòd Deus quaedam immediate per seipsum, quaedam mediatè per Apostolos tradidit: sed haec differentia nihil prohibet, quin utraque adaeque immutabilia sint, & ex jure divino ligent. Vidit hoc Downami gregalis Thomas Bellius scriptor Hierarchicus, ejus verba haec sunt: Res dupliciter, inquit, dici possunt esse jure divino. Primò, quia sunt à Deo immediate: Secundò, quia sunt mediate ab illis, qui à sancto Dei spiritu ita diriguntur ut errare nequeant: quo sensu superioritas Episcoporum in reliquos ministros de jure divino esse dicitur sive ordinatio divina Similis Guilielmi Barloi Episcopi Lincolnensis sententia est. Agit de loco Hieronymi, ubi negat Episcopum esse ex institutione dominica. Distinguit vero fere sensu Downamiano inter divinum praeceptum & consilium Apostolicum ex 1. Corint. 7. 6. & dicit Hieronymi mentem esse, Episcopum quidem non esse ex ullo scripto mandato Christi, vel ab ulla expressa ejusdem regula: sed ex consilio, traditione, μορία ἀρχαΐον, & institutione Apostolica. Hanc mentem Hieronymi & Georgius Downamus fingit, quam etiam approbat, sed Barlous non item: Non ita Hieronymus transfire debet, inquit, ac si functio Episcopalis non esset directe ipsa domini institutio. Non etenim spiritus per Apostolos solum, qui eum magna mensura acceperunt, sed etiam per Christum ipsum, qui eum sine mensura accepit, hanc superioritatem ordinavit. Pergit deinde probare per immediatum Christi institutum, regimen Episcopale ordinandum esse, qui idem immutabile contra Downamum statuit. Non tamen putat mutabile futurum (quod Downamus) si mediato tantum Apostolico jure niteretur. Nam & non scriptas illas διαταξεις Apostolorum quas memorat ex 1. Cor. 11. 34. & permissiones Apostolorum illas, absque expresso Christi mandato quas memorat ex 1. Cor. 7. 6. & 25. juris divini esse vult, quid ita? Quia, inquit, licet haec mandavit Paulus absque expresso mandato Christi: non tamen mandavit absque certo & infallibili spiritu Christi, sicut ait ver. 40. Scio me habere spiritum Christi. Propter hunc spiritum Christi, quae absque immediato mandato scripto; & speciali revelatione sibi facta mandaret, 1. Cor. 8. 9. 13. & 10. 25. 29. & 11. 4. 14. 23. 25.] ea ad postremum hoc vinculo ligat, 1. Cor. 14. 37. Si quis se Prophetam putat & spiritualem, cogitet, quae ad vos scribo, quod Dei mandata sunt. Ecce, quae mediata ab Apostolis praecipiuntur, ipsa Dei mandata sunt, haud secus ac ea quae immediato praecepto nituntur: quidni igitur perinde ex jure divino etiam?
units.tr: 13. Sixth and last, Downame's distinction is without difference, since its members coincide: for those things which Downame calls of apostolic law are in truth also of divine law. There is indeed some difference between divine commands, in that God delivered some things immediately through himself and some mediately through the Apostles; but this difference does not prevent both from being equally unchangeable and binding by divine law. Downame's companion Thomas Bell, a Hierarchical writer, saw this. His words are: Things can be said to be by divine law in two ways. First, because they are immediately from God; second, because they are mediately from those who are so directed by the holy Spirit of God that they cannot err; in this sense the superiority of bishops over other ministers is said to be by divine law, or divine ordinance. The view of William Barlow, Bishop of Lincoln, is similar. He treats the passage of Jerome where he denies that the episcopate is from the Lord's institution. He distinguishes, in a sense almost like Downame's, between divine precept and apostolic counsel, from 1 Cor. 7:6, and says that Jerome's mind is that the episcopate is not from any written command of Christ, or from any express rule of his, but from counsel, tradition, [ancient custom], and apostolic institution. Downame imagines this to be Jerome's mind and approves it, but Barlow does not: Jerome ought not to pass over it so, as if the episcopal function were not directly the institution of the Lord himself. For it was ordained that this superiority should be given not only by the Spirit through the Apostles, who received it in large measure, but by Christ himself, who received it without measure. He goes on to prove by Christ's immediate institution that episcopal government must be ordained, and he holds that it is unchangeable, against Downame. Nor does he think it will be changeable (as Downame does) if it rests only on mediate apostolic law. For he holds that those unwritten ordinances of the Apostles which he mentions from 1 Cor. 11:34, and those permissions of the Apostles, without an express command of Christ which he mentions from 1 Cor. 7:6 and 25, are also of divine law. Why so? Because, he says, although Paul gave these commands without an express command of Christ, he did not give them without the certain and infallible Spirit of Christ, as he says in verse 40: I think I have the Spirit of Christ. On account of this Spirit of Christ, the things which he commanded without an immediate written command and a special revelation made to him (1 Cor. 8:9, 13; 10:25, 29; 11:4, 14, 23, 25) he binds at last with this bond, 1 Cor. 14:37: If anyone thinks himself a prophet or spiritual, let him acknowledge that the things I write to you are the commandments of God. Behold, the things commanded mediately by the Apostles are themselves the commandments of God, no less than those which rest on an immediate precept. Why then should they not be equally of divine law?

units.la: 14. Accedit Guilielmus Whitakerus,qui Bellarmino locum Hieronymi unà cum Downnamo quoad verba interpretanti, ac si Episcopum sentiret, non quidem ex jure divino esse, sed ex jure Apostolico tamen,respondet ita. Bellarminus secum pugnat & Hieronymum facit loqui pugnantia. Nam si Hieronymus putavit jurisdictionem illam Episcopi non esse iuris divini,quomodo tum fuit illud discrimen ab Apostolis introductum? Et quomodo Hieronymus ex Apostolorum scriptis non esse discrimen aliquod probare potuit? Certè quod Apostoli ut necessarium sanxerint atque introduxerunt iuris divini vim obtinet. Hadrianus Saravia de Hieronymo respondens, ait eum errasse cum diceret, Apostolorum tempore introductum fuisse ab Apostolis Episcopum, sed non ex dominica dispositione,quia ex hoc sequeretur, Apostolos contra domini institutionem fecisse,quod falsum est: cum constet Apostolos nihil ordinasse, quod non esset à domino institutum, quæcunque causa ordinandi fuerit. Ex quibus juxta-positis ego quatuor colligo. Primò, contra Downnamum, Apostolicas ordinationes esse iura divina, quia Apostoli nihil instituerant, nisi ex divino iure, ut Whitakerus, nisi ex domini institutione ut Saravia. Secundò, quicquid inducitur in Ecclesiam,quod Politeiam Ecclesiasticam, non ex iure divino, ut Whitakerus,non ex domini institutione, ut Saravia; id contra domini institutionem esse ideoʒ illicitum: etiamsi ab Apostolis ipsis hoc factum esset. Tertiò,Hierarchicorum responsionem,Hieronymum sentire Episcopum introductum ipso tempore Apostolorum contra schismata vanam esse & frivolam, quia Apostoli nihil induxerunt nisi ex iure & instituto divino : at vero Hieronymi sententia est (quocunque demum tempore introductus Episcopus fuit:) eum non ex dominica dispositione,non ex jure divino,non ex domini instituto fuisse introductum. Quartò, si Hieronymus dixisset, Episcopum introductum fuisse non quidem ex divino iure, sed tamen Apostolico, pugnantia locutus est: idem enim est ut si dixisset, non ex divino iure, & tamen ex divino iure. Atque Bellarminus pugnantia loquitur, inquit Whitakerus, cum Episcopum non iure divino iuxta Hieronymum,sed Apostolico inductum dicit: sic & pugnantia Georgius Downnamus, idque non in uno loco: Quæcunque functio est Apostolicæ institutionis, divina ordinatio censenda est. Probat ex Beza : Si ab Apostolis profectum esset, non vereor,id totū divinæ institutioni ascribere. Rursus: Sive primò ordinata a Christo ,sive ab Apostolis instituta ea functio fuit: eius author Christus est, sive immediate iuxta primum, sive mediatè iuxta secundum. Atque ea Apostolicæ institutionis esse dicuntur, quæ Christus instituit per Apostolos. Huc referenda,quæ supra allata sunt ex respons. ad præfat. p. 2. & ex libro 4.p.139. 140. ubi dicit Episcopum divinæ ordinationis esse, quia Aostolicæ institutionis. Quid hic habet Downnamus quod respondeat? Divinam ordinationem non inferre divinum ius? Apage ineptias: nam ordinatio jussum quoddam est,& omne jussum importat jus, ut inos suprà demonstravimus.
units.tr: 14. Next comes William Whitaker, who, agreeing with Downame that the words of Jerome, if taken as meaning that the bishop was not indeed of divine right but nevertheless of apostolic right, reply as follows. Bellarmine contradicts himself and makes Jerome say contradictory things. For if Jerome thought that that jurisdiction of the bishop was not of divine right, how then was that distinction introduced by the apostles? And how could Jerome prove from the writings of the apostles that there was no such distinction? Certainly what the apostles ordained and introduced as necessary has the force of divine right. Hadrian Saravia, answering Jerome, says that he erred when he said that the bishop was introduced by the apostles in the time of the apostles, but not by divine disposition, because from this it would follow that the apostles acted against the Lord's institution, which is false: since it is clear that the apostles ordained nothing that was not instituted by the Lord, whatever the reason for ordaining it was. From these statements set side by side I draw four conclusions. First, against Downame, the apostolic ordinances are divine rights, because the apostles instituted nothing except from divine right, as Whitaker says, except from the Lord's institution, as Saravia says. Second, whatever is introduced into the Church that is not from divine right, as Whitaker says, not from the Lord's institution, as Saravia says, is contrary to the Lord's institution and therefore unlawful, even if it had been done by the apostles themselves. Third, the answer of the hierarchists, that Jerome holds the bishop was introduced in the very time of the apostles against schisms, is empty and frivolous, because the apostles introduced nothing except from divine right and divine institution. But Jerome's view is that, whenever the bishop was in fact introduced, he was introduced not by divine disposition, not by divine right, not by the Lord's institution. Fourth, if Jerome had said that the bishop was introduced not indeed by divine right but nevertheless by apostolic right, he would have spoken contradictions, for it is the same as if he had said, not by divine right, and yet by divine right. "And Bellarmine speaks contradictions," says Whitaker, "when he says that the bishop was introduced, according to Jerome, not by divine right but by apostolic right." So Georgius Downame also speaks contradictions, and not in one place only: Whatever function is of apostolic institution is to be regarded as a divine ordinance. He proves this from Beza: If it proceeded from the apostles, I do not hesitate to ascribe the whole of it to divine institution. Again: Whether that function was first ordained by Christ or instituted by the apostles, Christ is its author, either immediately, according to the first case, or mediately, according to the second. And those are said to be of apostolic institution which Christ instituted through the apostles. To this should be referred what was cited above from the answer to the preface, p. 2, and from book 4, pp. 139 and 140, where he says that the bishop is of divine ordinance because it is of apostolic institution. What has Downame here to answer? That divine ordinance does not imply divine right? Away with such absurdities! For an ordinance is a kind of command, and every command implies a right, as we have shown above.

units.la: CAP. XLIV. Argumenta nostra pro disciplina immutabilitate à doctrina Apostolorum.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLIV. Our arguments for the immutability of discipline from the doctrine of the Apostles.

units.la: Ita tria illa fundamenta dejecimus & solo æquavimus, quibus Hierarchici freti, Politeiam Ecclesiasticam, mutabilem esse statuunt: ad argumenta jam nostra, accedendum nobis est. Primò, ab officio Christi disputamus, quod ejus [illegible, ~10 letters] durant in perpetuum. Quid Sacerdotij? Unica oblatione consecravit in perpetuum eos qui sanctificantur, Heb. 10.14. Quid Prophetiæ? Fides semel tradita est sanctis, Iud.3. Si de Sacerdotio & prophetia rectè dicitur ea semel operata fuisse, quæ in perpetuum durent: Cur non & de regali etiam dicetur ossicio, illud semel Politeiam Ecclesiasticam instituisse, quæ etiam duraret in perpetuum? Heb. 12.26.27. Adhuc semel ego concutiam non solum terram sed etiam cœlum. Porro illud adhuc semel, declarat instabilium rerum emotionem, ut maneant quæ sunt stabilia. Deducit hinc Apostolus nos regnum assecutos stabile, quod verti non possit, ergo & media etiam stabilia, quibus ad hoc regnum provehimur: in quibus est Politeia Ecclesiastica. Atque de Politeia Iudaica cur vaticinetur Propheta eam abolitam iri? & ex propheta concludit Apostolus, semel tantum abolitionem istiusmodi fore, non deinceps: certum mihi quidem videtur, & Politeiam Ecclesiasticam sub Evangelio stabilem hic fieri absque ulla concussione: ex mente Apostoli, una ista & nulla deinceps abolitio futura est, nulla inquam: mutatio semel facta est, ceremoniarum & Politeias Iudaicæ: sed semel tantum non deinceps, mutatio istiusmodi contigit.
units.tr: So we have overthrown those three foundations and levelled them to the ground, the foundations on which the Hierarchists rely when they declare the ecclesiastical polity mutable. Now we must turn to our own arguments. First, we argue from the office of Christ, that his [illegible] endure for ever. What of the priesthood? "With one offering he has perfected for ever those who are sanctified," Heb. 10.14. What of prophecy? "The faith was once delivered to the saints," Jude 3. If it is rightly said of priesthood and prophecy that the things which endure for ever were done once for all, why should it not also be said of the kingly office that he once established the ecclesiastical polity, which would also endure for ever? Heb. 12.26-27: "Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also heaven. Now this 'yet once more' signifies the removal of things that are shaken, so that the things that are unshaken may remain." From this the Apostle infers that we have obtained a stable kingdom which cannot be overturned, and therefore also the stable means by which we are advanced to this kingdom, among which is the ecclesiastical polity. And why does the prophet foretell that the Jewish polity will be abolished? From the prophet the Apostle concludes that such an abolition will happen only once, not afterwards. It seems certain to me that the ecclesiastical polity under the Gospel is here made stable, without any shaking. According to the mind of the Apostle, there will be this one abolition and no abolition after it, none, I say. A change of the ceremonies and polity of Judaism has been made once, but only once, and no such change has happened since.

units.la: Pertinet huc quod 1. Cor. 15.24. regnum suum externum non ante finale Judicium deponit Christus: tum mediate regnare cessabit, Ecclesiam gubernare. Ergo regnum ipsius externum, illiusque extetna media (in quibus Politeia Ecclesiastica est) ad diem judicij, prout in verbo posita & descripta sunt, stabilia & fixa permanebunt.
units.tr: Relevant here is 1 Cor. 15.24: Christ does not lay down his external kingdom before the final judgment. Then he will cease to reign mediately and to govern the Church. Therefore his external kingdom, and its external means (among which is the ecclesiastical polity), will remain stable and fixed until the day of judgment, as they are posited and described in the Word.

units.la: 2 Secundo, nota quâ partes verbi mutabiles, ab immutabilibus secerni solent, ipsius finis vel mutabilitas est vel immutabilitas: ita, cum finis ad quem ordinatur Politeia Ecclesiastica immutabilis & perpetuus sit, eadem perpetua etiam ut sit necesse est. Viderunt hoc Iuristæ, quorum placitum, apud Iohannem Bertachium, istud est, Ius idem est ubi juris eadem ratio est. Alias res igitur agit Sutclivius, quum formam regiminis Ecclesiastici ex eo probat mutabilem esse, quod mutata sit Politeia Iudaica, mutata regiminis forma quæ fuit sub Christo & Apostolis mutatum etiam præceptum de suffocato & sanguine. Hæc etenim omnia si mutabilia, nihil mirum, propter causas mutabiles, ad fines mutabiles, ordinata fuerunt: & cessante causa cessant effectus ut rectè respondet ad horum postremum Nicolaus Lyranus: Quod ad regimen sub Christo & Apostolis, extraordinarium utrumque utrumque erat: at forma Politeias institutæ ordinariæ est, ad ordinarium finem: longe igitur diversa horum ratio est. Imò inquit Downamus, Timothei functio ordinaria est, & tamen non perpetua.
units.tr: Second, note that the parts of the Word which are mutable are usually distinguished from the immutable by their end: either the end itself is mutable or it is immutable. So since the end for which the ecclesiastical polity is ordained is immutable and perpetual, the polity itself must necessarily be perpetual too. The lawyers saw this; their maxim, as cited by John Bertachius, is: "The law is the same where the reason of the law is the same." Sutcliffe argues differently when he proves the form of Church government mutable because the Jewish polity was changed, the form of government that existed under Christ and the Apostles was changed, and the precept about what is strangled and about blood was changed. If all these things are mutable, it is no wonder, since they were ordained for mutable causes and to mutable ends; and when the cause ceases, the effects cease. Nicholas of Lyra rightly answers the last of these: "As for the government under Christ and the Apostles, both were extraordinary. But the form of the polity instituted is ordinary, for an ordinary end. So their reason is far different. Indeed, says Downame, the office of Timothy is ordinary, and yet not perpetual."

units.la: 3. Non dicimus omnia ordinaria perpetua esse simpliciter, perpetua tamen durante fine omnia esse, vel ipse Richardus Hookerus agnoscit. De legibus positivis nunquam additur, inquit, quamdiu perpetuandæ sunt: quod si nullibi exprimatur, directio nulla de earum vel perpetuitate, vel mutabilitate superest, præter considerationem naturæ & qualitatis earundem. Natura autem cuiusque legis iudicari debet, ex fine ad quem ordinatur, & ex aptitudine præceptorum ad eundem finem inducendum. Si ratio igitur cur leges instituantur sciri possit, & apparet eadem perpetuæ necessitatis esse: tum ea ipsæ perpetuæ sunt, nisi forte validæ esse cessent, ad illum propositum, ad quod erant ab initio institutæ.] Hoc postremum nuper à nobis exactum est: remanet igitur Hookeri iudicio, leges Politeias Ecclesiæ immutabiles esse, qua rationem & finem (uti manifesto constat) perpetuum habent. Ita Georgius Carletonus. Qui putant officia Timothei & Titi extraordinaria & temporaria fuisse eorum usum & finem minime consilerant: qui neque extraordinarij sunt, neque ad tempus perdurantes, sed plane ordinarij & perpetui. Finium & usuum necessitas, similem probat necessitatem in gubernatoribus ipsis: ita regimen Episcorum ab Apostolis institutum est, ut ad finem usque mundi duraret. Imò quid si Georgius Downamus ipse, qui Carletono, in perpetuitate Episcopatus, ex professo adversatur: alicubi tamen adactus sit, hanc ipsam ob causam, eorum perpetuam durationem contra seipsum confiteri? Ecce etenim insignes contradictiones. Episcopi semper retinendi, non necessitate absolutâ, necessitate tamen expedientiæ, quæ ad finem & usum suum exposcit ut semper in Ecclesia maneant, eorumq; functio semper est utilis. Rursus: Episcopi semper retinendi, quia ut inquit Hieronymus, salus Ecclesiæ in eorum superioritate consistit. Rursus: Causæ Episcoporum nempe pax & salus Ecclesiæ, semper omnibus temporibus eædem sunt, ergo semper remanere debent, id quod Hieronymus sentit.] Citantur ista a me ut ostendatur, quibus & quantis contradictionibus Hierarchiæ defensio icatet: & una liqueat ex ipsorum adversariorum confessione Politeiam Ecclesiæ immutabilem esse, quia usum & finem immutabilem habet. Errant quidem in hypothesi Carletonus & Downamus, Episcopale regimen illud ipsum esse, quod est in verbo institutum: thesis tamen verissima est, regimen ab Apostolis institutum perpetuum esse, quia ad finem & usum Ecclesiæ perpetuum ordinatur.
units.tr: Third, we do not say that all ordinary things are perpetual absolutely, but that all are perpetual while their end endures, and even Richard Hooker acknowledges this. "Concerning positive laws it is never added how long they are to be perpetuated. But if this is nowhere expressed, there remains no direction about their perpetuity or mutability, beyond consideration of their nature and quality. The nature of any law, however, ought to be judged from the end for which it is ordained, and from the fitness of its precepts to bring about that end. If therefore the reason why laws are instituted can be known, and it appears that this reason is of perpetual necessity, then those laws themselves are perpetual, unless perhaps they cease to be valid for that purpose for which they were instituted from the beginning." We have lately pressed this last point. Therefore, by Hooker's judgment, the laws of the ecclesiastical polity remain immutable, since their reason and end (as is clearly evident) are perpetual. So too George Carleton: "Those who think the offices of Timothy and Titus were extraordinary and temporary do not consider their use and end. These offices are neither extraordinary nor lasting only for a time, but plainly ordinary and perpetual." The necessity of ends and uses proves a similar necessity in the governors themselves. Thus the government of bishops was instituted by the Apostles so that it would last to the end of the world. Indeed, what if George Downame himself, who professedly opposes Carleton on the perpetuity of episcopacy, has nonetheless been driven somewhere, for this very reason, to confess against himself their perpetual duration? Behold, indeed, his remarkable contradictions: "Bishops are always to be retained, not by absolute necessity but by the necessity of expediency, which, for its end and use, requires that they always remain in the Church; and their function is always useful." Again: "Bishops are always to be retained, because, as Jerome says, the safety of the Church consists in their superiority." Again: "The causes of bishops, namely peace and the safety of the Church, are always the same in all times; therefore they must always remain, which is what Jerome thinks." I cite these so that it may be shown with what and how great contradictions the defence of the hierarchy is beset, and so that it may be plain, from the confession of their own adversaries, that the ecclesiastical polity is immutable, because it has an immutable use and end. Carleton and Downame indeed err in their hypothesis, in holding that episcopal government itself is what is instituted in the Word. Yet the thesis is most true: the government instituted by the Apostles is perpetual, because it is ordained for the end and use of the Church, which is perpetual.

units.la: 4. Tertiò, quanquam Politeia Ecclesiastica (inquit Hookerus) mutabilis à se se sit, mutari tamen minime oportet, si in scripturis, illius mutatio nullibi reperiatur: leges etenim mutationis capaces non sunt, si qui eas tulit illorum mutationem prohibeat. Bene est: at ipse legislator Christus (inquam) suam Politeiam immutabilem esse iussit. 1. Tim. 6. 13. 14 Denuncio tibi coram Deo qui vivificat omnia, & Iesu Christi— ut servec hoc hoc mandatum incontaminatus & irreprehensus, usque ad illustrem illum adventum Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Quidni hic liceat acclamare cum Augustino in causa simili? Quem non terreret tam vehemens contestatio? Duri cervicis igitur merito dixeris Hierarchicos illos, qui in Politeias quidem mutabilitate, supra ipsam meretricem Romanam, frontes suos perfricuerunt. Sic etenim Cornelius Scultingius: Calvinus seniorum concilium perpetuum vult: Musculus non, qui electionem & formam gubernationis ab Apostolis usurpatam nunc propter magistratum minimè utilera esse censet, nos contrà sacerdotum concilium cum Episcopo semper necessarium dicimus. Idipsum quò minus Hierarchici nonnulli dicant de Ecclesiae Politeia, elusiones huius loci varias excogitarunt. Prima est Richardi Hookeri: Haec verba non important perpetuam praeceptorum Apostolicorum observationem: sed usque ad adventum Christi: non important tanquam in quo ista observari oportet, sed potius tempus illud, ad quod observationis praemium reservatur. Sed hoc putidum glossema colorem in se nullum habet: & ab Hierarchicis omnibus respuitur, qui notari ipsum tempus concedunt, in quo hoc mandatum Apostoli est observandum.
units.tr: Fourth, thirdly: "Although the ecclesiastical polity," says Hooker, "is mutable in itself, it ought by no means to be changed if its change is nowhere found in the Scriptures. For laws are not capable of mutation if the one who gave them forbids their change." Well and good. But Christ himself, the lawgiver (I say), commanded that his polity be immutable. 1 Tim. 6.13-14: "I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and before Christ Jesus ... that you keep this commandment without spot and blameless, until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ." Why should I not here cry out with Augustine in a similar case? "Who would not be terrified by so vehement a protestation?" One might rightly call those Hierarchists stiff-necked, who in the matter of changing the polity have rubbed their foreheads harder even than the Roman harlot herself. Thus Cornelius Scultingius: "Calvin wants a perpetual council of elders; Musculus does not, who judges that the election and form of government taken up by the Apostles is now by no means useful on account of the magistrate. We, on the contrary, say that a council of priests with a bishop is always necessary." That some of the Hierarchists do not say the same about the polity of the Church, they have devised various evasions of this passage. The first is that of Richard Hooker: "These words do not imply a perpetual observance of the Apostolic precepts, but only until the coming of Christ. They do not imply that in which these things must be observed, but rather that time to which the reward of observance is reserved." But this stinking gloss has no colour in itself, and it is rejected by all the Hierarchists, who concede that the time itself is indicated in which this commandment of the Apostle is to be observed.

units.la: 5 Secunda est Georgij Downami, qui distinguens inter potestatem & formam atque modum potestatis: Apostolum hic loqui affirmat, non de forma & modo potestatis, gubernandi, ordinandi, iurisdictionem exercendi ut ea perpetua in Ecclesia esset. Haec dum explicat infert haec porismata. Primò. [Quanquam potestas Timothei hoc in loco immutabilis statuatur, non tamen officium illud, per quod hanc potestatem exercuit. Secundò, officium Timothei, Episcopi officium fuit, sed scribit haec Paulus ad Timotheum, ut authoritatem & potestatem gubernandi in genere habentem. Tertiò, Episcopi Timothei successores tantummodo sunt: sed scribuntur haec verba, etsi primariò quidem Episcopis legitimis Timothei successoribus: secundariò tamen omnibus, qui similiter authoritatem habituri essent, quanquam non sint successores. Quartò, ij non successores quibus haec scribuntur, presbyteri sunt: qui mutatâ Politeiâ, & in casu necessitatis, authoritatem ordinandi & jurisdictionem exercendi habent. Quintò, quanquam Politeia legitimè mutari possit, sic ut quandoque authoritas Timothei penes presbyteros esse possit, quanquam illius successores non sint: actualiter tamen Politeia Ecclesiae, nunquam in tanto mutabitur, sed perdurabunt alicubi Episcopi usque ad adventum Christi, sic ut etsi non solis, semper tamen existentibus Timothei successoribus haec verba scripta fuerint.] Haec medulla est orum, quae Downamus excogitavit, quò minus forma Politeias Ecclesiasticae, quam ille in regimine Episcopali ponit, hoc in loco immutabilis sanciri videatur.
units.tr: Fifth, the second evasion is that of George Downame, who, distinguishing between the power and the form and manner of the power, affirms: "The Apostle here speaks not of the form and manner of the power, of governing, ordaining and exercising jurisdiction, so that this would be perpetual in the Church." While explaining this, he draws these corollaries. (1) "Although the power of Timothy is here set down as immutable, the office by which he exercised this power is not so. (2) The office of Timothy was the office of a bishop, but Paul writes these things to Timothy as one who has authority and power of governing in general. (3) Timothy's successors are only bishops; but these words are written, though primarily to the legitimate successors of Timothy as bishops, yet secondarily to all who would likewise have authority, though they are not successors. (4) Those to whom these things are written, who are not successors, are elders, who, when the polity is changed and in case of necessity, have authority to ordain and to exercise jurisdiction. (5) Although the polity may legitimately be changed, so that at some time the authority of Timothy may rest with the elders, although they are not his successors, yet actually the polity of the Church will never be changed to such an extent. Bishops will endure somewhere until the coming of Christ, so that, although not only (Timothy's successors), yet always, these words have been written with those successors existing." This is the marrow of what Downame has devised, by which the form of the ecclesiastical polity, which he places in episcopal government, is made to seem immutable in this passage.

units.la: 6. Examinemus verò paulisper. Primò futile est quod garrit, Paulum hic locutum de potestate non de forma potestatis. Quomodo probatur? aut unde liquet magis de una quam de altera hic Paulum loqui? Imo ratio suppetit manifesta loqui hic Paulum, de singulis mandatis, quæ in hac epistola præcedunt, & in Epistola præcedenti: non modo de potestate egit, verùm de forma modoq;etiam. Epiphonema etenim hæc verba continent, quo authoritas toti libro comparatur: perinde ac Apocal.22.18. Testor cuivis audienti verba Prophetiæ hujus, si quis adjecerit ad hæc, imponet ei Deus plagas scriptas in libro isto. Et si quis abstulerit aliquid auferet Deus partem ejus——ex iis quæ scripta sunt in libro isto. Mos igitur spiritus Sancti observandus: solet enim in hujusmodi sanctionibus scriptorum suorum authoritatem roborare. Locus utrobique idem est, in calce libri, forma loquendi eadem: Denuncio, inquit Paulus, Testor, inquit Iohannes: materia denique eadem est: nam servare mandatum hujus libri incontaminatum & irreprehensum idem est ac si dixisset, (Iohannes) sine additione vel dimunitione. Secundò, imperitè officium appellat formam & modum authoritatis, quod authoritatis cujusque vel causa potius vel subjectum est: nam unde authoritas nisi ab officio? & quodnam legitimæ potestatis subjectum, nisi officium legitimum? Tertiò, nefanda Downami officij & potestatis divulsio est, ut officium quidem oboleri & mutari possit, potestas non item. Quàm hoc absurdum etiam, quòd authoritatem unius officij, in officium aliud transferri legitimè idque ad hominibus posse putat: quòd cuiusque confusionis Anabaptisticæ, fenestram aperit. Hinc etenim fiet ut authoritas pastoris sit penes Diaconum, authoritas Diaconi transferri possit in Seniorem: & Senior authoritatem Pastoris vel Diaconi habeat, si id magistratui visum fuerit. Evigila Downame, ut transmigrationis huiusce tuæ commenta videas. Nam cum Episcopum aboleri posse putes, remanente interim Episcopi propria authoritate, accidens somnias absque subiecto: & cum Episcopi authoritatem ad presbyterorum ordinem transferri posse statuis: quid aliud quàm μετεμψύχωσιν & transubstantiationis imaginem quandam renovas?
units.tr: 6. Let us examine this a little more closely. First, his chatter that Paul spoke here about the power and not about its form is futile. How is this proved? Or on what basis is it clear that Paul speaks here of one rather than the other? Indeed, there is a plain reason to think Paul is speaking here of the individual commands that precede in this epistle and in the earlier one: he has dealt not only with the power but also with its form and manner. For these words form an epiphonema, by which authority is ascribed to the whole book, just as in Rev. 22.18: I testify to everyone who hears the words of this prophecy: if anyone adds to these, God will lay upon him the plagues written in this book. And if anyone takes away anything, God will take away his part from those things which are written in this book. The manner of the Holy Spirit is therefore to be observed, for in such sanctions he is accustomed to confirm the authority of his writings. The place is the same in both, at the end of the book, and the form of speech is the same: I declare, says Paul; I testify, says John. Finally, the matter too is the same, for keeping the command of this book uncorrupted and blameless is the same as if John had said: without addition or subtraction. Second, he unskilfully calls the office the form and manner of authority, when it is rather the cause or subject of any authority. For whence does authority come except from office? And what is the subject of lawful power except a lawful office? Third, Downame's separation of office and power is an abominable one, so that the office can indeed be abolished and altered, but the power cannot. How absurd it is also that he thinks the authority of one office can be transferred lawfully to another office, and that this can be done by men. This opens a window for every kind of Anabaptist confusion. For it will follow that the authority of the minister lies with the deacon, that the authority of the deacon can be transferred to the elder, and that the elder will have the authority of minister or deacon if the magistrate sees fit. Wake up, Downame, and see the inventions of this transmigration of yours! For since you think the bishop can be abolished while the bishop's own authority remains, you dream of an accident without a subject; and since you lay down that the authority of the bishop can be transferred to the order of presbyters, what else do you renew but metempsychosis [μετεμψύχωσις] and some image of transubstantiation?

units.la: 7 Quartò, nefariè dicitur officium Episcopi à magistratu aboleri posse, si modo divinâ ordinatione (quod vult Downamus) institutum fuerit. Pari etenim ratione & officium Pastoris & Diaconi abolere magistratus poterit. Non possunt verò ista officia aboleri: tamen Episcopi Hierarchici officium potest: non argumentum ego quidem fortius, aut pleniorem ab adversario confessionem desideratem: Episcopi officium, perinde ac Pastoris at Diaconi, à Christo miuimè institutum esse. Quintò, ineptè dicitur quibusdam Timothei non successoribus, in Timorheo hic Paulum scribere: nam cum unum individuum sumitur, in quo lex aliqua stabilitur, repræsentat quidem individuum illud successores omnes, sed successores tantum. Exempli gratia: cum legem naturæ figere Deus voluisset, qnod primæ herbæ, primæ plantæ, primæ arbori individuali dixit Deus: id ad omnes herbas,plantas,arbores in eodem genere succedentes dixit: sed non ad alias quæ in eodem genere successorum non essent; unde Iac.3.12. Nunquid potest fratres mei ficus oleas edere, aut vites ficus? Scribit hic in Timotheo presbyteris Paulus? Bene est. Presbyteri igitur Pauli Timothei legitimi successores sunt? Et transferri potest Timothei potestas in presbyteros per magistratum, idque legitime? Nulla igitur Episcopalis Timothei potestas fuit, quae non eadem presbyteri proprie: si alias Deus instituisset, Episcopalis potestatis presbyterum capacé magistratus reddere non potuisset. Sexto & ultimo, si scripserit haec Paulus, non de Timothei officio Episcopali, sed de authoritate Timothei in genere: tum non haec scripsit Timotheo ut Episcopo, sed tantum Timotheo ut authoritatem in genere habenti: at si haec non scripsit Timotheo ut Episcopo tum nullum jus divinum pro Episcopis proferri potest: totius etenim Epistolae praecedentis haec verba authoramentum continent, ut ante dictum. Ita plane in castra nostra transijt Downamus: planeque suis manibus dejicit, quae contra nos alibi aedificarat: quando dixit, Hanc epistolam ad Timotheum, Episcopalis functionis typum esse. Vulnerat etiam suos, inprimis Thomam Bilsonum: qui nullum jus divinum proferri pro Episcopis posse fatetur: si haec verba scripta non fuerint Timotheo ut Episcopo. Annon pulchrè laboravit Downamus, qui hoc unicum, pro jure divino functionis Episcopalis fundamentum imis sedibus subruit?
units.tr: 7. Fourth, it is wrongly said that the magistrate can abolish the office of bishop, provided it was instituted by divine ordinance (as Downame wants). For by the same reasoning the magistrate could abolish the office of minister and of deacon. Yet those offices cannot be abolished, whereas the office of the hierarchical bishop can. I certainly know of no stronger argument, nor a fuller confession to be desired from an opponent: the office of bishop, just like that of minister and deacon, was by no means instituted by Christ. Fifth, it is absurd to say to some who are not Timothy's successors that Paul here writes to Timothy. For when one individual is taken, in whom some law is established, that individual certainly stands for all his successors, but only for his successors. For example, when God wished to fix the law of nature, he spoke to the first herb, the first plant, the first individual tree: he spoke to all herbs, plants and trees succeeding in the same kind, but not to those which were not successors within that kind. Hence Jas. 3.12: Can a fig tree, my brothers, bear olives, or a vine figs? Does Paul here write to the presbyters in the person of Timothy? Very well. Are the presbyters therefore the lawful successors of Paul's Timothy? And can Timothy's power be transferred to the presbyters by the magistrate, and that lawfully? There was therefore no episcopal power of Timothy that was not properly the same as that of a presbyter. If God had instituted otherwise, the magistrate could not have made a presbyter capable of episcopal power. Sixth and last, if Paul wrote these things not about Timothy's episcopal office but about Timothy's authority in general, then he did not write these things to Timothy as a bishop, but only to Timothy as one having authority in general. But if he did not write these things to Timothy as a bishop, then no divine right can be brought forward for bishops. For the words of the whole preceding epistle contain this authorisation, as said before. So Downame has plainly crossed over into our camp, and with his own hands he knocks down what he had built elsewhere against us, when he said that this epistle to Timothy is a type of the episcopal function. He also wounds his own side, above all Thomas Bilson, who confesses that no divine right can be brought forward for bishops if these words were not written to Timothy as a bishop. Has not Downame worked beautifully, who undermines from its lowest foundations this one foundation of the divine right of the episcopal function?

units.la: 8 Quintò, videamus quid viri docti de hac re senserint. Ita Io. Gerson: Maior fuit Ecclesiae primitivae authoritas, quoad praedicta, quam nunc est. Non enim est in potestate Papae, aut Concilij aut Ecclesiae, immutare traditiones datas ab Evangelistis & a Paulo, ut quidam delirant. Delirium igitur Gersonis judicio, assertio haec de Politeia Ecclesiasticae mutabilitate Hierarchica est: praesertim cum ea Apostolica & Paulina traditio sit. Ita Franciscus Zabraella: Si Papa vult destruere illud quod Apostoli docuerunt, convincitur errare. Non potest ad Doctrinam solam restringi hoc: disputat etenim & in eo opere de negotijs Ecclesiasticae disciplinae. Ita Ioh. Budaeus. Sacrosanctos canones melioribus annis factos, ut eis velut regulis vita clericorum dirigeretur, & velut patrum prescriptis posteri formarentur, in amusses plumbeas iam evasisse quis non videt? Quales olim fuerunt Canones plumbei, ut nobis non structuram operum tenore aequabili dirigant, sed extructorum commodo & libidine flexibiles, structurae accommodentur. Indignatus hic est Canones antiquos in amusses plumbeas evasisse: nos Canonem sacrum pro hominum commodo & libidine in canones plumbeos, ab Hierarchicis coversos jam esse, non indignabimur? Hoc fieri, cum Politeia Ecclesiae ad magistratus arbitrium, flexibilis & mutabilis statuitur: ex nostris scriptoribus omnibus constat, Bilsono inprimis & Reynoldo: quam ad verbum Dei solum revocat, tanquam ad Lydium lapidem: ab inventis vero humanis abducit, tanquam a regula Lesbia. Hiero. Zanchium ad hoc propositum in Politeia Ecclesiastica reformanda huc citat & approbat Had. Saravia. Verba ista sunt: Sunt igitur ad formam veteris & Apostolicae Ecclesiae, omnes Ecclesiae reformandae: & omnia tam cultus, & disciplina disciplina, quàm dogmata, non ad Lesbiam regulam humani judicij, sed lapidem Lydium divini verbi examinanda. Verumenimverò, est quod Geor. Downnamum, hujus regulæ Lesbiæ pudeat: sicut & pudere ipsum necesse est: nisi ipsa præcipua Episcopalis functionis fundamenta subvertere velit. Quid enim? Annon præcipuum ejusdem sustentaculum apud Bilsonum & Saraviam istud est: oportere Apostolorum superioritatem in ministros in Episcopis perdurare, in Ecclesijs omnium seculorum: quia eo hoc regimine in pagis opus habent, quod habuerunt Ecclesiæ quum Apostoli vixerunt? Tolle hoc fulcrum & Episcopalis functionis necessitas cadit: idq; vel ipsius Downami judicio, cujus in concione pro Episcopis, p.79. hęc verba sunt: Multo magis necessarium est, ut omnium ætatum Ecclesiæ Episcopos habeant, quam Ecclesiæ primæ, quando Apostoli in vivis fuerunt. Hoc verò fundamentum vacillare quis non videt, si Episcopalis functio statuatur mutabilis ad arbitrium magistratus? In eadem concione dixit: Functionem & authoritatem Timothei & Titi esse ordinariam & necessariam: non solum ad bene esse sed etiam ad ipsum esse ecclesiæ. Quid apertius? Imo, inquit, in defensione hoc tantum volui, functionem hanc esse ordinariam authoritatem necessariam. Dixit in concione Episcopos esse necessariò retinendos: quod in Defensione ita eludit: intellexi esse necessariò retinendos, non necessitate absoluta, sed necessitate expedientiæ. Quam miseræ hæ quæso tergiversationes sunt? Quàm etiam contradictoriæ? Functio non est necessaria, sed authoritas tantum: functio est necessaria necessitate expedientiæ, non necessitate absolutâ. Quasi quisquam nostrum Politeiam necessitate absoluta necessariam unquam dixerit? at quod necessitate expedientiæ necessarium est, non sit perpetuò retinendum? Sit ipse judex: Ex singularitate, ordinatione, & jurisdictione Episcoporum tria beneficia pendere dicit, Unitatem, perpetuationem, & ὁμοξίαν Ecclesiæ: & nonne quæso perpetuum est, quod hęc perpetuanda continet? Ecclesiarum, inquit, Provincialium & Nationalium Metropolitani Episcopi rectores sunt, & rectores esse debent. Quid sibi hoc DEBENT vult? Quod debet fieri, annon perpetuò faciendum? Simile est quod dicit, superioritatem in ordinatione & jurisdictione, quam Timotheus & Titus habuerunt, non cum illis mori: sed in successoribus continuari DEBUISSE. Rursus? Præscripta officia Timotheo, perfici & peragi DEBENT ab ipsis & eorum successoribus, usque ad adventum Christi. Atque quoniam in mentionem huius loci ad Timotheum rursus incidimus: adnotentur insignes contradictionis istæ. Vidimus nuper, quomodo statuerit, hunc locum non de functione Episcopali, sed tantum de authoritate functionis intelligendum: item, quanquam primario Episcopis loquatur, secundario tamen presbyteris, qui etsi Timothei successores non legitimi: tamen mutata Politeiæ forma, jurisdictionem Timothei sibi demandatam exercere possunt. Libetne audire quomodo in ista Downamus ruat alibi? In ultimo non potest, inquit, authoritas & potestas Timothei illiusve executio mandari Presbyteris. Rursus: harum rerum cura ad Presbyteros non pertinet. In secundo, præcepta
units.tr: 8. Fifth, let us see what learned men have thought about this matter. Thus John Gerson: The authority of the early Church was greater, as to the things mentioned, than it is now. For it is not in the power of the Pope, or of a council, or of the Church, to change the traditions handed down by the Evangelists and by Paul, as some rave. Therefore, in Gerson's judgement, this assertion that the polity of the Church is changeable is a hierarchical delirium, especially since it is an apostolic and Pauline tradition. Thus Francis Zabarella: If the Pope wishes to destroy what the Apostles taught, he is convicted of error. This cannot be restricted to doctrine alone, for he also discusses in that work matters of ecclesiastical discipline. Thus John Budaeus: Who does not see that the most sacred canons made in better times, so that the life of the clergy might be guided by them as by rules, and that posterity might be formed by the precepts of the fathers as by a model, have turned into leaden rules? Such were the leaden canons of old, which do not guide the construction of works with an even tenor, but bend to the convenience and whim of the builders and adapt themselves to the structure. Budaeus is indignant that the ancient canons have turned into leaden rules. Shall we not be indignant that the sacred canon has already been turned, for the convenience and whim of men, into leaden canons by the hierarchical party? This happens when the polity of the Church is established as flexible and changeable at the will of the magistrate. It is agreed by all our writers, above all by Bilson and Reynolds, that it recalls the polity of the Church to the word of God alone, as to the Lydian stone, and draws it away from human inventions, as from the Lesbian rule. Hadrian Saravia cites and approves Jerome Zanchius for this purpose of reforming the ecclesiastical polity. His words are: Therefore all the churches are to be reformed according to the form of the old and apostolic Church, and all things, both worship and discipline and doctrines, are to be examined not by the Lesbian rule of human judgement, but by the Lydian stone of the divine word. Truly, there is good reason why Downame should be ashamed of this Lesbian rule, just as he must be ashamed, unless he wishes to overturn the chief foundations of the episcopal function itself. For what? Is not the chief prop of this in Bilson and Saravia that the superiority of the Apostles over the ministers must endure in bishops in the churches of every age, because in that form of government the churches of our time need what the churches had when the Apostles were alive? Remove this support, and the necessity of the episcopal function falls, and that by the very judgement of Downame himself, in whose sermon for bishops, p. 79, these words stand: It is much more necessary that the churches of all ages should have bishops than the first churches, when the Apostles were alive. Yet who does not see that this foundation wavers, if the episcopal function is established as changeable at the will of the magistrate? In the same sermon he said: The function and authority of Timothy and Titus is ordinary and necessary, not only for the well-being but also for the very being of the church. What could be plainer? Indeed, he says, in the defence I wanted only this: that this function is an ordinary and necessary authority. He said in the sermon that bishops are to be retained of necessity; in the Defence he evades this thus: I understood that they are to be retained of necessity, not of absolute necessity but of the necessity of expediency. How wretched, I ask, are these shifts! How contradictory too! The function is not necessary, but only the authority; the function is necessary by the necessity of expediency, not by absolute necessity. As if any of us has ever called the polity necessary by absolute necessity! Or what is necessary by the necessity of expediency is not to be retained perpetually? Let him be his own judge: He says that three benefits depend on the singularity, ordination and jurisdiction of bishops: the unity, the perpetuation and the homoiousia of the Church.
