And is not that which contains the things to be perpetuated surely itself perpetual? The metropolitan bishops, he says, are and ought to be the rulers of the provincial and national churches. What is the force of this OUGHT? What ought to be done, ought it not to be done perpetually? It is similar when he says that the superiority in ordination and jurisdiction which Timothy and Titus had ought not to have died with them, but ought to have been continued in successors. Again: The offices prescribed to Timothy ought to be carried out and completed by them and their successors until the coming of Christ. And since we have again come upon this place about Timothy, let these striking contradictions be noted. We have just seen how he has determined that this passage is to be understood not of the episcopal function but only of the authority of the function; likewise, that although it speaks primarily to bishops, it speaks secondarily to presbyters, who, though not lawful successors of Timothy, can nevertheless exercise the jurisdiction committed to Timothy once the form of polity has been changed. Would you like to hear how Downame collapses elsewhere in these matters? In the last place, he says, the authority and power of Timothy, or the execution of it, cannot be committed to presbyters. Again: the care of these matters does not pertain to the presbyters. In the second place, the precepts (which in the epistle to Timothy are to endure as until the coming of Christ)

units.la: p. 79. lib.4 p.100 & 147. lib.3 p.57. Serm. p.32. bb.3.p.3. Serm. p.75. 79. Defens.lib.3 p.72. & lib.4 p.84. 98 100. Lib.4.p.77 lib.3 p.72. 72. & lib.4 p.79. Ibid. [praecepta quae in Epistola ad Timotheum tanquam ad adventum Christi duratura dantur, Episcopis tantummodo dantur & eorum successoribus. Rursus: Praecepta 1. Tim. 5. 19. 22. perpetuae directiones non sunt, non ad Christianos, non ad alios ministros, sed ad Episcopos solos. In primo: Epistolae ad Titum & Timotheum scriptae, typi & exemplaria sunt Episcopalis functionis: scriptaeq; ex proposito sunt, ad informandos Episcopos, quomodo functionem suam exercere debeant usque ad finem saeculi.] Quoties in hisce, Politeias Ecclesiasticae (quam in regimine Episcopali ponit Downamus) perpetuitas asseritur, usque ad adventum Christi, usque ad finem saeculi? Idem asserit, in citandis testimonijs patrum, & quae non solum de Episcopalis regiminis facto verumetiam de iure testari dicit, quod illi perpetuum esse volunt, in citando Hieronymo praesertim, cuius judicium hoc esse dicit: quod Episcopus ad vitanda schismata semper retinendus sit. Postremo, idem facile colligere licet ex testimonijs accommodandis, quae pro Episcopali functione, ex alijs scripturis profert: Locos etenim Phil. 2. 29. Heb. 13. 17. Populum Anglicanum ad honorandos Episcopos etiamnum hodie obligare dicit. At si ad hunc diem ligent, ligant etiam Anglicani populi posteros in perpetuum. Affine illud est quod ex 1. Tim. 5. 17. affert: Quod si quis minister duplici honore reverentiae & sustentationis honorandus est, idque jure divino: tum Episcopi ministri praecipui multo magis. Certe, si Episcopi ministri praecipui sint, tum & perpetui etiam multo magis quam presbyteri erunt: praesertim cum sensu Downamiano, Episcopi illi sint, qui Ecclesiarum Pastores sunt: Presbyteri tantum sunt Episcoporum delegati, quod delegatus perpetuus erit, delegans non item? Miror suam vanitatem Hierarchicos non videre? Planum etenim est Episcopos a Christo institutos non esse ut Pastores, & ministros praecipuos: si modo ut Presbyteri, quos a Christo institutos omnes fatentur, perpetui non sint. Episcopi, inquit Downamus, stellae illae sunt quos Christus sua dextra tenet Apoc. 1. 20. sunt praecipui domus Dei oeconomi, sunt ἡγούμενοι illi quos Paulus memorat, Heb. 13. 17. at stellae oeconomi, duces, iique praecipui aut soli, authoritate humana quavis removeri a coelo, a domo, ab acie possunt? Atque haec adversus Politeias Ecclesiasticae mutabilitatem dicta sunt in genere quidem, ita tamen ut primam immutationis partem praecipue feriant, quae est per Diminutionem & Ablationem.
units.tr: p. 79. lib.4 p.100 & 147. lib.3 p.57. Serm. p.32. bb.3.p.3. Serm. p.75. 79. Defens.lib.3 p.72. & lib.4 p.84. 98 100. Lib.4.p.77 lib.3 p.72. 72. & lib.4 p.79. Ibid. [The precepts given in the Epistle to Timothy as lasting until the coming of Christ are given only to bishops and their successors. Again: The precepts of 1 Tim. 5. 19. 22. are not perpetual directions; they are addressed not to Christians or to other ministers, but to bishops alone. In the first place: The Epistles to Titus and to Timothy are types and examples of the episcopal function, and they were written deliberately to instruct bishops how they ought to exercise their function until the end of the age.] How often, in these passages, is the perpetuity of the ecclesiastical polity (which Downame places in episcopal government) asserted: until the coming of Christ, until the end of the age? He asserts the same thing when he cites the testimonies of the Fathers, and says that they bear witness not only to the fact of episcopal government but also to its right, which they wish to be perpetual; he does so especially when he cites Jerome, whose judgment he says is this: that a bishop is always to be retained in order to avoid schisms. Finally, the same can easily be gathered from the testimonies which he brings forward from other Scriptures in support of the episcopal function. For he says that the passages Phil. 2. 29. and Heb. 13. 17. still today bind the English people to honour bishops. But if they bind us to this day, they also bind the English people's descendants for ever. Akin to this is what he adduces from 1 Tim. 5. 17.: If any minister is to be honoured with a double honour of reverence and maintenance, and this by divine right, then the bishops, as the chief ministers, are much more so. Certainly, if the bishops are the chief ministers, then they will be perpetual also, and much more so than the presbyters; especially since, in Downame's sense, the bishops are those who are the pastors of the churches, while the presbyters are only delegates of the bishops. Does a delegate last for ever, while the one who delegates does not? I marvel that the hierarchs do not see their own vanity. For it is plain that bishops were not instituted by Christ as pastors and chief ministers, if indeed they are not perpetual as presbyters, whom everyone admits were instituted by Christ. Bishops, says Downame, are those stars which Christ holds in his right hand, Rev. 1. 20.; they are the chief stewards of God's house, they are those leaders [ἡγούμενοι] whom Paul mentions, Heb. 13. 17. But can stars, stewards, and leaders, or those chief or sole leaders, be removed from heaven, from the house, or from the battle line by any human authority whatever? And these things have been said against the mutability of the ecclesiastical polity in general, yet in such a way that they chiefly strike at the first part of change, which is by Diminution and Ablation.

units.la: CAPVT. XLV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLV.

units.la: Non licet addere essentialibus disciplinae.
units.tr: It is not lawful to add to the essentials of discipline.

units.la: Vpereft, ut nonnihil adjiciatur, de mutationis specie altera, nempe Additione: ubi quaeritur, an ad Politeias essentialia addere quid Ecclesiae liceat? nominatim vero, an licitum sit novuum aliquod officium Ecclesiasticum excogitare, & in Ecclesia collocare, quod non est verbo speciatim institutum? Negamus nos, aiunt Hierarchicorum chicorum nonnulli, de quibus M.Sutclivius est, cujus ista verba sunt: Haec inter nos quæstio est, utrum talem regiminis formam præscripserit pro Ecclesia Christus: ut in substantiâ (ut loquitur) nihil sit addendum, &c. aiunt illi, nos negamus. Geo.Downamus, Patriarchas jure humano licitè in Eccl:siam veterem introductos fuisse affirmat. Ha.Saravia eos jure divino niti quodammodo putat: ait enim Ecclesiam habuisse potestatem eos præficiendi, qualem habuit Paulus, quum Titum & Timotheum in gradu celsiori supra presbyteros collocavit. Et eadem sententia est: Nulla quidem jam in Ecclesia ministeria Ecclesiastica, quam quæ Apostoli ab initio instituerunt: licere tamen Ecclesiæ, nova ministeria & officia addere, prout occasio, & Ecclesiæ utilitas postulare videbitur. Ita Io. Bridgesius nunc Episcopus Oxoniensis: c Si putatis Ecclesiam Dei adeò necessario devinctam esse officijs eis, quæ Christus & Apostoli instituerunt, ut quædam ex illis omittere, quædam vero alia inducere nequeat, valdè erratis. Roborat verò alibi sententiam hanc suam, testimonijs Mar.Chemnitij, Nic.Hemengij, & Hier. Zanchij. Chemnitij judicium his verbis ab illo ponitur. [Non est in verbo Dei mandatum, qui, quot, aut quales, ordines in Ecclesia esse debent. Paulo post: Hæ ordinationes temporibus Apostolorum liberæ erant, ratione habitâ ordinis, decentiæ, & ædificationis. Testimonium quod adfert ex Nicolao Hemingio istud est: Sicut Christus ascendens in altum dona dedit hominibus, Apostolos, Prophetas, Evangelistas, Pastores & Doctores: ita potestatem Ecclesiæ suæ dedit, ad ædificationem. Hac potestate ordinat ministros Ecclesiæ ad commodum suum ut omnia ordine fiant, ad incrementum corporis Christi. Hinc pura Ecclesia tempora Apostolorum sequens, quosdam Episcopos quosdam verò Patriarchas ordinavit. Postremus verò Hier. Zanchius ita apud illum loquitur: Scimus Deum nostrum, Deum esse ordinis, non confusionis: & ordine servari, ἀταξία verò perdi Ecclesiam. Hanc ad causam liberum Ecclesiis reliquit, ut plures ordines adderent: modo id ad ædificationem fit. Quòd igitur tempore succedente, quidam collegis suis præfectus fuerit (Episcopum intelligit) id minimè improbandum judicamus.] Ita, quæ sit Hierarchicorum sententia vidimus: argumenta jam nostra in partem contrariam proponenda sunt, quibus manifesta illius falsitas redarguitur.
units.tr: It remains to add something about the other kind of change, namely Addition. Here the question is whether the Church may add anything to the essentials of the polity, and in particular whether it is lawful to devise some new ecclesiastical office and place it in the Church, when the Word has not specifically instituted it. Some of the Hierarchists deny this, says Mr Sutcliffe, whose words these are: This is the question between us, whether Christ prescribed such a form of government for the Church that nothing may be added in its substance (as they put it), etc. They say, we deny it. George Downame affirms that Patriarchs were lawfully introduced into the ancient Church by human law. Ha. Saravia thinks they rest in some way on divine law, for he says the Church had the power to set over them such as Paul had when he placed Titus and Timothy in a higher rank above the elders. He holds the same view when he writes: Indeed there are now no ecclesiastical ministries in the Church except those the Apostles instituted from the beginning; yet it is lawful for the Church to add new ministries and offices, as occasion and the usefulness of the Church shall seem to require. So John Bridges, now Bishop of Oxford: If you think the Church of God is so necessarily bound to those offices which Christ and the Apostles instituted that it cannot omit some of them or introduce others, you are greatly mistaken. He further confirms this opinion of his by the testimonies of Martin Chemnitz, Nicholas Hemming and Hieronymus Zanchius. Chemnitz's judgment is quoted by him in these words: There is no command in the Word of God as to how many or what kinds of orders there ought to be in the Church. A little later: These arrangements were free in the times of the Apostles, with regard to order, decency and edification. The testimony he brings from Nicholas Hemming is this: As Christ, ascending on high, gave gifts to men, Apostles, Prophets, Evangelists, Pastors and Teachers, so he gave his Church the power to build it up. By this power the Church orders its ministers for its own benefit, so that all things are done in order, for the increase of the body of Christ. Hence the pure Church, following the times of the Apostles, ordained some bishops and some patriarchs. The last, Hieronymus Zanchius, speaks thus in his work: We know that our God is a God of order, not of confusion, and that the Church is preserved by order, but destroyed by disorder [ἀταξία]. For this reason he left it free to the Churches to add more orders, provided this is done for edification. Therefore we judge that it is in no way to be condemned that, as time went on, someone was set over his colleagues (he means a bishop). Thus we have seen what the view of the Hierarchists is. Our arguments must now be put forward on the other side, by which its manifest falsity is refuted.

units.la: Primò, hæc sententia scripturam imperfectionis arguit, ut in Chemnitio videre est: qui hoc illi fundamentum substruit, nullam esse ordinum Ecclesiasticorum in verbo Dei perfectam salicem determinationem. Quod nos supra refutavimus. Sapiunt itaque papismum Hierarchici, idemq; cum C. Scultingio sentiunt. Nullam legimus, inquit, functionum Ecclesiasticarum determinatam explicationem, vel à Christo in Evangelio, vel ab Apostolis in sacris literis expressam. Quid vero? In hoc tamen superare Hierarchicos videtur: quod etsi non in verbo expressa sit, statutam tamen ab Apostolis perfectam hujusmodi determinationem putat. Sic enim loquitur pagina præcedente. Omnis officia
units.tr: First, this opinion argues that Scripture is imperfect, as may be seen in Chemnitz, who lays this foundation for it: that there is no complete and solid determination of ecclesiastical orders in the Word of God. We have already refuted this above. The Hierarchists therefore savour of Papistry, and agree with C. Scultingius, who says: We read of no determinate explanation of ecclesiastical functions, either given by Christ in the Gospel or expressed by the Apostles in the sacred writings. But in this the Hierarchists seem to go further, in that, although such a determination is not expressed in the Word, they nevertheless think the Apostles established a perfect one of this kind. For he speaks so on the preceding page: All offices

units.la: Trad. de disc. cipl. c.1. p.8
units.tr: Trad. de disc. cipl. c.1. p.8

units.la: Lib.2. p.38 officiis quæ ad externam politeiam & gubernationem ecclesiæ pertinent ab Apostolis fuisse constituta credendum est: etiamsi de eis nec Christus quicquam præcepisse, nec Apostoli ordinasse legantur. Quid, quod hæc perpetua putet: quæ ab Hierarchis putantur libera?
units.tr: Lib.2. p.38 offices which pertain to the external polity and government of the Church must be believed to have been established by the Apostles, even though no command of Christ about them is read, nor any ordinance of the Apostles. What is more, he thinks these offices are perpetual, which the Hierarchs think are free?

units.la: Secundò, bonis intentionibus hæc sententia patrocinatur: liberum etenim relinquit Ecclesiæ addere officia, modo id fiat ad ædificationem: id est, modò intentione bonâ hoc fiat, ad finem ecclesiæ utilem. Instamus in re, quæ ad politeiam Ecclesiasticam attinet. Annon Davidis intentio bona fuit, quando in animo habuit, domum Deo ædificare? Immò optima: sic enim vel ipse Deus. Dixit Iehova Davidi patri meo: eò quod fuit tibi in animo ædificare Domum nomini meo, bene fecisti quòd fuisti eo animo, 1.Reg.8.18. Nunquid itaque videre lubet, quàm ingrata sit Deo, additio ista in politeia ecclesiastica, quanquam à bono animo progrediatur, & nihil sibi proponat aliud, quam gloriam Dei & ecclesiæ ædificationem? Advertantur igitur verba Nathanis: generali etenim ratione utitur, qua omnes jam similes additiones tanquam gladio percutiuntur. 1.Chron.17.6. Quocunque itabam in toto Israele, an quicquam locutus sum ulli Iudicum Israelis, quare non ædificatis mihi domum cedrinam? Nunc ergo, &c. Habetur hîc Enthymema nostrum totidem verbis. Nullam in verbo Deus de officio ecclesiastico addito mentionem fecit: ergò est illicitum. Quid ergo? Ecclesiæ authoritas in legibus ecclesiasticis ferendis nulla quæso est? Annon quod utile videtur sancire potest? Potest quidem in politeias accidentalibus: in substantialibus, quæ jam in verbo expressa sunt non potest, quocunque prætextu, expedientiæ vel utilitatis: Licet enim cum Guil.Whitakero nostro ratiocinari: Quomodo non expedit, uti eâ (politeia) quam Christus instituit? Nosnè Christo melius scimus quid ecclesiæ expedit? Non patiuntur certè septem oculi Christi, Apo.5. 6. ut videre jam homines possint officium aliquod ecclesiasticum, ecclesiæ utile atque expediens, quod ille non vidit: neque patitur domus quam sibi sapientissimè ædificavit excisis columnis suis septem, Pro. 9.1. ut columnam quasi octavam, intelligo officium Ecclesiasticum novum jam addere opus sit.
units.tr: Second, this opinion is defended by good intentions, for it leaves it free to the Church to add offices, provided this is done for edification, that is, provided it is done with a good intention and for a useful end of the Church. Let us press the point, which concerns the ecclesiastical polity. Was not David's intention good when he purposed to build a house for God? Indeed it was most excellent, as God himself declares: The LORD said to David my father: Because it was in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well that it was in your heart (1 Kings 8:18). Does it therefore please us to see how unwelcome to God is this addition to the ecclesiastical polity, although it proceeds from a good mind and proposes nothing to itself but the glory of God and the edification of the Church? Let the words of Nathan then be noted, for he uses a general argument by which all such additions are struck down as with a sword: Wherever I walked in all Israel, did I speak a word to any of the judges of Israel, asking why they did not build me a house of cedar? Now therefore, etc. (1 Chron. 17:6). Our enthymeme is found here in just these words: God made no mention in his Word of an added ecclesiastical office; therefore it is unlawful. What then? Has the Church, I ask, no authority to enact ecclesiastical laws? May it not sanction what seems useful? It may indeed in accidental matters of the polity; but in essentials, which are already expressed in the Word, it cannot, under any pretext of expediency or usefulness. For we may reason with our own William Whitaker: How is it not expedient to use that polity which Christ instituted? Do we know better than Christ what is useful for the Church? Certainly the seven eyes of Christ (Rev. 5:6) do not allow men to see some ecclesiastical office useful and expedient for the Church which he did not see; nor does the house which he wisely built, with its seven pillars hewn out (Prov. 9:1), allow that, as it were, an eighth pillar, that is, a new ecclesiastical office, should now be added.

units.la: 2 Tertio, contemptum planè verbi hæc Hierarchica sapit: quum addi officia nequeant, nisi ea dedecorentur, quæ Christus in verbo suo instituta jampridem sunt: sic ut peccatum Ieroboamicum hæc additio planè sit: cui hoc tanquam audax facinus impingitur, quod sacerdotes instituisset qui non fuerunt ex filiis Levi: id est, ex eorum genere & numero, quos Deus ipse ordinasset, 1.Reg.12.31. Adversus hoc peccatum cum contestatur Rex Abijah, ostendit planè, & ea tantum officia usurpanda ab ecclesiis esse, quæ Deus instituit: & omnia alia removenda quæ ad similitudinem politeias papisticæ adjuncta ab hominibus sunt. Sic enim fatur, 2.Chron.13.9. Annon depulistis sacerdotes Iehovæ filios Aharonis & Levitas? & fecistis vobis sacerdotes ut populi reliquarum regionum? — Nos autem habemus Iehovam Deum nostrum, quem
units.tr: Third, this Hierarchical doctrine plainly savours of contempt for the Word, since offices cannot be added without dishonouring those things which Christ has long since instituted in his Word. So this addition is plainly a sin like that of Jeroboam, against which the charge is brought that he had made priests who were not of the sons of Levi, that is, not of the kind and number which God himself had appointed (1 Kings 12:31). Against this sin King Abijah protests, and he plainly shows that the churches must use only those offices which God instituted, and must remove all others which men have added in imitation of the Papistic polity. For he speaks thus: Have you not driven out the priests of the LORD, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites? And have you made for yourselves priests like the peoples of other lands? But we have the LORD our God, whom

units.la: Ccc quem non dereliquimus: sacerdotes autem ministrantes Iehovæ sunt, filij Aaronis, & Leviæ sunt in opere suo.--- Observamus enim observationem Iehovæ Dei nostri: vos autem dereliquistis eum. Ecce, officia Ecclesiastica à Deo instituta, observatio quædam illius est, quæ perpetuo observanda est: non observatur autem sed derelinquitur, quando alia ossicia superinducuntur ab hominibus, quæ nationibus populorum (puta papistis) similia sunt.
units.tr: whom we have not forsaken; and the priests who minister to the LORD are the sons of Aaron, and the Levites are in their work. For we keep the charge of the LORD our God; but you have forsaken him. Behold, the ecclesiastical offices instituted by God are a kind of observance of him, which must be kept perpetually. But they are not kept; rather they are forsaken, when other offices are superinduced by men which are like the customs of the nations (namely the Papists).

units.la: 3 Quartò, violat Hierarchica assertio ista, sanctionem illam de verbo Dei, specialem: quæ prohibet ne quid illi adjiciatur. Deut.4.2. Ne addite ad verbum illud quod ego præcipio vobis neque detrahite de eo, ut servetis præcepta Iehovæ Dei vestri, quæ ego præcipio vobis, Deut.12.31. Ne facito sic Iehovæ Deo tuo.--- Vnamquamque rem quam ego præcipio vobis eam observantes facite: nè addito ei, neque detrahito ex ea. Pro.30. 5. Totus sermo Dei purgatissimus est,--- ne adjicito ad verba ejus, ut non corripiat te, & efficiaris mendax. Ad hæc R. Hookerus, respondet hoc tantum. Verum est de verbo Dei: falsa constructione sensus, & verborum ipsorum falsificatione scienter eniti ut aliquid videatur divinum quod divinum non est, vel non videatur quod est, manifestè abuti & falsificare divinam evidentiam est, quæ injuria vel illata hominibus, merito gravissima iudicatur. Quod utinam observarent illi qui politeiam Ecclesiasticam in verbo scriptam esse dicunt quæ scripta non est: annon etenim hoc Dei præceptis addere est? ac si numero plura essent, quam revera sunt? Quid igitur? Solamnè hic illam additionem prohiberi censet Hookerus, quæ se divinam præ se fert? non autem illam quæ se profitetur esse humanam? Sic quidem videtur: sed ut hoc vinculo exempti sit Hierarchici Anglicani, quando suas additiones profitentur humanas esse non divinas. Quid vero ego nomino Hierarchicos Anglicanos? tota gens pontificia excusetur, si modo hoc verum sit: dicere enim possunt, prohibita solum ea additia est, quæ se divinam esse iactat; nos verò traditiones nostras, minimè dicimus divinas esse, imò apertè profitemur eas in verbo non esse scriptas, sed mera Ecclesiæ authoritate introductas. At in loco Deuteronomij posteriori, additiones eæ prohibentur, quæ similes gentium superstitionibus sunt, quæ nunquam pro divinis venditabantur: & in loco proverbiorum, mendacij est omne quod adjicitur verbo Dei humanum: quia cum sermo Dei purgatissimus sit, mendax esse oportet, quicquid ab homine mendaci adjicitur: omnis etenim homo mendax, solus autem Deus verus. Rom.3.4.
units.tr: Fourth, this Hierarchical assertion violates that special prohibition in the Word of God which forbids anything to be added to it: Deut. 4:2: You shall not add to the word which I command you, neither shall you take from it, that you may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you. Deut. 12:31: You shall not do so to the LORD your God. Whatever thing I command you, take care to observe it; you shall not add to it nor take from it. Prov. 30:5: Every word of God is pure. Do not add to his words, lest he rebuke you and you be found a liar. To these R. Hooker replies only this: It is true of the Word of God: to strive knowingly, by a false construction of the sense and a falsifying of the words themselves, to make something appear divine which is not divine, or not to appear what it is, is manifestly to abuse and falsify the divine evidence, an injury which, if done to men, is rightly judged most grievous. Would that those who say the ecclesiastical polity is written in the Word would observe this, when it is not written there! Is not this, in fact, adding to God's precepts, as if there were more of them in number than there really are? What then? Does Hooker think only that addition is forbidden which claims to be divine, and not that which professes to be human? So it seems; but this is a way out only for the English Hierarchists, when they profess their additions to be human, not divine. Why do I name only the English Hierarchists? Let the whole Papist nation be excused, if this is true: for they can say, Only that addition is forbidden which boasts itself to be divine; but we do not at all say that our traditions are divine; indeed we openly profess that they are not written in the Word, but introduced by the mere authority of the Church. Yet in the later passage of Deuteronomy, the additions forbidden are those which resemble the superstitions of the nations, which were never put forward as divine; and in the passage of Proverbs, every human addition to the Word of God is a lie, because the word of God is most pure, so whatever is added by a lying man must be false, for every man is a liar, but God alone is true (Rom. 3:4).

units.la: 4 Huc pertinet quod habet Apostolus, 1.Cor.3.12. ubi quodcunq; humanum, super fundamentum scripturarum (ut loquitur Agur purgatissimum) superædificatur; lignum est, fœnum est, stipula est. Tantum itaq; abest ut excusentur additiones quæ præ se ferunt humanas se esse, non divinas: ut hoc nomine (tanquam impudentiores) graventur potius; ut quæ scripturas imperfectionis coarguant, quæ perfectæ sunt, se vero venditant, quæ præter verbi fundamentum, sunt mendaces. Hoc sensu hoc mandatu interpretatur Ambrosius. Nihil inquit, vel vel rationis gratia adjungere debemus mandato. Nihil quod vel bonum videtur addendum, sed simplex & pura mandati forma servanda est. Addenda de proprio, semiplenum Dei intellexit esse mandatum. Docet nos igitur praesentis series lectionis, neque detrahere aliquid debere divinis mandatis, neque addere. Accedo ad Whitgiftum, qui multa excogitat quidem, ut haec prohibitio additionis ab Hierarchicis avertatur: ista tamen elusio Hookeriana ne quidem illi in mentem venit. Addunt verbo inquit primo, qui docent contra verbum; secundo, qui aliquid necessarium faciunt ad salutem quod in verbo non continetur; tertio, qui meriti opinionem fovent, in eis quae praeter verbum invenerunt; Quarto, qui tanquam illegitimum prohibent, quod per verbum Dei legitimum est. Respondet Cartwrightus, omissum illud esse, quod praecipue Moses intendit, videlicet, ut ne quid fiat, magis minusve quam quod verbo Dei praecipitur. Replicat Whitgiftus, hoc in suis distributionibus contineri: atque non continetur: obtineat etenim hoc praeceptum, & non tantum peccat qui contra verbum facit, sed etiam qui praeter: non tantum quin meriti opinionem fovet in eis quae praeter verbum facit, sed qui praeter verbum facit omnino, sive meriti opinionem foveat sive non; non tantum qui rem addit tanquam necessariam ad salutem, sed qui rem addit omnino sive necessariam dicat sive non: sic ut huius prohibitionis modo aperte Hierarchici illaqueantur: cum in politeia addunt praeter verbum, etsi id minime necessarium ad salutem fateantur.
units.tr: 4 To this belongs the Apostle's saying in 1 Cor. 3.12, where whatever is human is built upon the foundation of Scripture (as Agur, speaking of the purest word, puts it): it is wood, hay, and stubble. So far is it from the case that additions which profess to be human and not divine are excused, that they are rather to be burdened the more on this account, as being more shameless: they are the additions which, while they are imperfect, expose the Scriptures as imperfect, and which, while they claim to be complete, are false, since they lie outside the foundation of the Word. Ambrose interprets this command in this sense: "We ought to add nothing to the command, not even for the sake of reason. Nothing should be added that seems good, but the simple and pure form of the command must be kept. He who adds from his own resources understood the command of God to be half-finished. The sequence of the present reading therefore teaches us that we must neither take anything away from the divine commands nor add anything." I come now to Whitgift, who devises many arguments to turn away this prohibition of addition from the Hierarchicals; yet that evasion of Hooker's has not even occurred to him. "They add to the Word," he says, "first, those who teach against the Word; second, those who make something necessary to salvation which is not contained in the Word; third, those who foster the opinion of merit in the things they have devised apart from the Word; fourth, those who forbid as unlawful what is lawful by the Word of God." Cartwright replies that the thing Moses chiefly intends has been left out, namely that nothing be done more or less than what is commanded by the Word of God. Whitgift retorts that this is contained in his distinctions: "and yet it is not contained. For this precept holds, and not only does he sin who acts against the Word, but also he who acts beside it: not only he who fosters the opinion of merit in the things he does beside the Word, but he who acts beside the Word at all, whether he fosters the opinion of merit or not; not only he who adds a thing as necessary to salvation, but he who adds a thing at all, whether he call it necessary or not." Thus the Hierarchicals are plainly ensnared by the very manner of this prohibition, since in the polity they add beside the Word, even though they confess that it is by no means necessary to salvation.

units.la: § Atque quoniam Whitgifti, Hookeri, Zanchij, reliquorumque Hierarchicorum hoc commune fundamentum est, licitas esse in politeia ecclesiastica additiones, dummodo non sint contra verbum: videamus quid respondeant nostri ad papistas, quando traditinnes suas hoc ipso fundamento statuminant. R. Bellarminus ad hoc mandatum Mosis respondens, tria adfert praecipua. Primo, prohiberi tantum additionem ad opus praeceptum non ad secundum numerum praeceptorum: secundo, prohiberi tantum additionem corrumpentem: tertio, prohiberi tantum additionem legum contrariarum. Quid ad haec M. Sutclivius Hierarchicus? Respondet ad primum: additiones pontificias esse ad opera praecepta: quod ex hoc probat Gui. Whitakerus, quia multo plura praeceperunt quam Dominus. Atqui idem jam Hierarchicis respondere nobis licet: multoplura officia induxerunt, aut induci posse affirmant, quum quae Deus praecepit: peccant igitur adversus hoc mandatum Mosis. Respondet Sutclivius ad secundum, leges pontificias esse corrumpentes additiones: quod & in additionibus Hierarchicis verum est: officia etenim nova quae inducunt, vel induci posse affirmant, politeiam a Deo institutam corrumpunt, adulterant, imo & eliminant etiam, ut in officijs Seniorum & Diaconorum videre est. Respondet ad tertium Sutclivius. Quasi vero nullae essent novae leges nisi contrariae? & non ea esset legis perfectio, ut omnes alias leges --- excluderet? praeterea haec interpretatio verbis Mosis adversatur: ipse etenim diserte loquitur & dicit Deut.12. Hoc tantum facito Domino; nihil addas aut minuas. Non opus hic alijs verbis est : excludit non leges contrarias modo, sed & quascunque, imo opus quodcunque, quod vel praeter mandatum Dei sit. Defendit idipsum Gui. Whitakerus, non solum prohiberi hoc Mosis praecepto, quae contra, sed etiam quae praeter verbum sunt : nec mirum ; verum enim est quod ex Baldo Iurisconsulto Perkinsius, & ni fallor, Iuellus etiam noster adfert. Quod praeter legem est, id etiam, & contra legem. Adjiciatur colophonis loco, illa Iohannis contestatio, quae similis superioribus est. Apoc. 22. 18. Enimvero una testor cuivis audienti verba prophetiae huius : si quis addiderit ad haec, imponet ei Deus plagas scriptas in libro isto & si quis abstulerit aliquid ex verbis libri prophetae huius, auferet Deus partem bu-ius e libro vitae, &c. Quaero, annon de officijs ecclesiasticis egerat in Apocalypsi Iohannes ? Videant igitur quae vel adjiciendum eis putant, quae ille tanquam sola legitima posuit, Apoc. 4. vel detrahendum existimant de eis comminationibus quas adversus illegitima detonavit: in quibus mihi quidem certum est, Episcopatum Hierarchicum unum esse. Ap. 8. 8.
units.tr: § And since this common foundation of Whitgift, Hooker, Zanchius and the rest of the Hierarchicals is that additions in the ecclesiastical polity are lawful, provided they are not against the Word, let us see what our people answer to the Papists, when they establish their traditions on this very foundation. R. Bellarmine, responding to this command of Moses, brings forward three main points. "First, only addition to the work commanded is forbidden, not addition to the number of the commands; second, only corrupting addition is forbidden; third, only addition of laws contrary to the others is forbidden." What does M. Sutcliffe, the Hierarchical, reply to these? To the first he answers that "the papal additions are to commanded works," which Whitaker proves from this, that they have commanded far more than the Lord did. Yet we too may now make the same reply to the Hierarchicals: they have introduced, or affirm that they can introduce, many more duties than those God has commanded; they therefore sin against this command of Moses. Sutcliffe answers to the second that "the papal laws are corrupting additions"; and this is true also of the Hierarchical additions. For the new offices which they introduce, or affirm can be introduced, corrupt and adulterate the polity instituted by God, and even eliminate it, as may be seen in the offices of elders and deacons. Sutcliffe answers to the third: "As if there were no new laws except contrary ones? And would not that be the perfection of the law, which excluded all other laws? Moreover, this interpretation opposes the words of Moses: for he speaks plainly and says in Deut. 12: 'Do only this for the Lord; add nothing or take away.' There is no need here for other words." It excludes not only contrary laws, but any laws whatever, indeed any work whatever which is beside the command of God. Whitaker defends the same point, that not only what is against the word but also what is beside the word is forbidden by this precept of Moses; and this is no wonder, for it is true, as Perkins and, unless I am mistaken, our own Jewel also cite from the jurist Baldus: "What is beside the law is also against the law." Let the testimony of John, similar to those above, be added as a colophon: Apoc. 22.18. "For I testify to everyone who hears the words of this prophecy: if anyone adds to these, God will impose on him the plagues written in this book; and if anyone takes away anything from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his part from the book of life, etc." I ask: did John not treat of ecclesiastical offices in the Apocalypse? Let them see, then, what they think must be added to those offices which he laid down as the only lawful ones (Apoc. 4), or what they think must be taken away from those threats which he thundered against unlawful ones; in which I am certainly sure that the Hierarchical episcopate is the one meant (Apoc. 8.8).

units.la: 6 Quinto, nullum officium ecclesiasticum addi potest, nisi ab homine; quodcunque autem in ecclesia excogitatur ab hominibus, illicitum illud est. Patet hoc ex Mat. 21. 25. ubi supponit Christus ministerium Iohannis illicitum esse, si modo e terra fuerit : patet ex Ap. 13. 12. ubi hoc nomine condemnatur papatus quod ortum ex terra habeat: patet denique ex Gal. 1. 1. ubi concedit Paulus Apostolatum suum illicitum fuisse, si fuisset ab hominibus.
units.tr: 6 Fifthly, no ecclesiastical office can be added except by man; but whatever is devised in the Church by men is unlawful. This is clear from Matt. 21.25, where Christ presupposes that the ministry of John would have been unlawful if it had been from men; it is clear from Rev. 13.12, where the papacy is condemned on this ground, that it has its origin from the earth; and it is clear finally from Gal. 1.1, where Paul concedes that his apostleship would have been unlawful had it been from men.

units.la: Sexto, si ecclesia potest (ut sub nostra persona posse dicit. C. Scultingius) novos gradus & officia ecclesiastica adjicere & invenire : potest etiam tollere & diminuere jam instituta: ejusdem enim potestatis est abolere & instituere. Sed absurdum est posse ecclesiam ordinem aliquem a Christo vel Apostolis institutum tollere; ergo. Huic argumento respondens Scultingius, primo negat in officijs quae nunc in ecclesia sunt superaddi quicquam, quia a Christo aut ab Apostolis instituta omnia sunt: Negat deinde eandem esse addendi & tollendi rationem: quia illud axioma, eiusdem est addere cuius est tollere, tenet tantum in eis quae a seipso instituta sunt : & instituta absolute atque propria authoritate: unde si daretur ecclesiam instituisse, non tamen tollere potest, aeque ac instituere : quia in instituendo ministeriali tantum authoritate utitur, principalis author est Spiritus sanctus. Hanc ob causam non potest abolere sola, quod non constituit sola. Io. Whitgiftus idem primo respondet quod Scul-tingius, nulla officia quae iam in ecclesia Anglicana sunt addita esse, sed ab Apostolis instituta, deinde cum majorem huius syllogismi, tum minorem adioritur. [Major tua (inquit) falsa est, posse ecclesiam tollere si modo addere possit. Addere etenim homo potest ministerijs, & non peccare adversus Dei mandatum, quia adjumenta esse possunt ministerijs, divinitus institutis, quum tollere aliquod ministerium nequeat absque manifesta mandati divini violatione. Insuper, praeter ea minis-teria instructa a Deo & necessaria omnibus temporibus, addi possunt aliqua quæ expediunt quibusdam temporibus, & tamen ecclesia quę habet authoritatem ista addere, authoritatem non habet ita tollere. Minor etiam tua ambigua est, ecclesiam non posse aliquod ministerium à Deo institutum tollere: non potest quidem homo ministeria ea tollere quæ Deus ut perpetua instituit; sed tollere potest ea quę solum ad tempus instituta sunt prout occasio requirit.] Respondeo: Nulla ecclesia authoritatem habet nè ministerialem quidem instituendi in substantialibus politeias suæ, quodsi haberet, haberet etiam parem tollendi, idque in officijs quæ non à seipso sed à Deo sunt instituta.
units.tr: Sixthly, if the Church can (as Scultingius, speaking in our person, says it can) devise and introduce new grades and ecclesiastical offices, it can also remove and diminish those already instituted; for it belongs to the same power to abolish as to institute. But it is absurd that the Church should be able to remove any order instituted by Christ or the Apostles; therefore... Scultingius, replying to this argument, first denies that anything is added to the offices now in the Church, because all of them were instituted by Christ or the Apostles. He then denies that the reasoning for adding and for removing is the same: "for that axiom, that the power to add belongs to the one who has the power to remove, holds only in those things which were instituted by oneself, and instituted absolutely and by one's own authority. Hence, even if one granted that the Church had instituted, it could not remove as it could institute, because in instituting it uses only a ministerial authority; the principal author is the Holy Spirit. For this reason it cannot abolish alone what it did not establish alone." John Whitgift likewise first answers as Scultingius does, "that no offices which are now in the English Church have been added, but were instituted by the Apostles"; then he attacks both the major and the minor premise of this syllogism. "Your major premise (he says) is false, that the Church can remove if it can add. For man can add to ministries and not sin against the command of God, because they can be aids to ministries divinely instituted, whereas he cannot remove any ministry without a manifest violation of the divine command. Moreover, besides those ministries which were ordained by God and are necessary in all times, some can be added which are expedient for certain times; and yet the Church which has authority to add these does not have authority to remove them in this way. Your minor premise is also ambiguous, that the Church cannot remove any ministry instituted by God: man indeed cannot remove those ministries which God instituted as perpetual; but he can remove those which were instituted only for a time, as occasion requires." I reply: no church has authority, not even ministerial authority, to institute in the substantials of its polity; and if it had it, it would also have an equal authority to remove, and that in offices which were instituted not by itself but by God.

units.la: 7 Primò, Moses & Iohannes, addere & detrahere paria faciunt: utrumque ex æquo prohibetur, utrumque ex æquo punitur: ubi igitur imparitates istæ sunt quas Whitgiftus excogitavit: certè hęc authoritas divina eas omnes in ventum disspulit. Secundo, patet vel ex ratione dialecticâ, authoritatem habere eum tollendi, qui authoritatem addendi habet: tollere etenim & addere cum contraria sint, & neutrum insit à natura: in idem subiectum incidunt; sic ut authoritatem tollendi habeat, qui habet addendi, perinde ac authoritatem habet abrogandi leges qui instituendi, condemnand qui absolvendi, ligandi qui solvendi, & sic in ceteris. Tertiò, patet ex ratione Theologica: nam addere institutis divinis perinde de authoriate & majestate jubentis detrahit, atque de eisdem tollere, pariliter igitur illicitum est. Patet hoc in igne addito per Nadab & Abihu, & in altari Damasceno addito pro Ahazam, & in additionibus Pharisęorum, quas Christus Dominus condemnat. Locum hic habent etiam quæ adversus additamentum pulcritudinis in mulieribus antiqui patres disputarunt. Sic a Cyprianus. Opus Dei est omne quod nascitur, diaboli quodcunque mutatur, intelligit vero mutationem per additionem. Sic Augustinus. b Injuriam facit pictori, qui addere ad illius picturam vult. Postremo sic Tertullianus. c Displi it illis nimirum plastica Dei; in ipsis redarguunt, reprehendunt artificem omnium; reprehendunt enim, quum emendant, quum adjicient, &c. Eadem sunt quæ in libro de habitu mulierum habet: ex quibus hæc citat Ri. Hookerus. d Æmuli sint necesse est, quæ Dei non sunt: aut igitur mentem Tertulliani non observat aut additiones omnes, æmulos appellat Dei, quia non ab ipso profectæ sunt. Utcunque sit certum est, per totum librum tertium, tollere & addere paria eum fecisse, & utrumque pariter licere, aut non licere.
units.tr: 7 First, Moses and John treat adding and subtracting as equal: both are forbidden equally, and both are punished equally. Where then are the inequalities that Whitgift has devised? Surely this divine authority has scattered them all to the wind. Second, it is clear even from dialectical reasoning that whoever has authority to add also has authority to remove. For to remove and to add are contraries, and neither belongs to a thing by its nature; they fall upon the same subject. Thus whoever has authority to add has authority to remove, just as whoever has authority to enact laws has authority to repeal them, whoever has authority to acquit has authority to condemn, and whoever has authority to loose has authority to bind, and so on in other cases. Third, it is clear from theological reasoning: adding to divine institutions takes away from the authority and majesty of the one who commands just as much as removing from them does, so the two are equally unlawful. This is shown by the fire added by Nadab and Abihu, by the Damascene altar added for King Ahaz, and by the additions of the Pharisees, which Christ the Lord condemns. The arguments that the ancient Fathers advanced against the adding of beauty in women also apply here. Thus Cyprian: a Everything that is born is the work of God; whatever is changed is the work of the devil; he means by "change" addition. Thus Augustine: b He wrongs the painter who wants to add to his picture. Lastly, thus Tertullian: c Those are displeasing to God's craftsmanship; in these things they find fault with the maker of all things; for they find fault when they correct, when they add, and so on. These are the same points that he makes in his book on the dress of women, and from these Richard Hooker cites the following: d Those things which are not God's must necessarily be his rivals. Either Hooker has not observed Tertullian's meaning, or Tertullian calls all additions rivals of God, because they did not proceed from him. However that may be, it is certain that throughout the third book he holds that adding and removing are equal, and that both are equally lawful or both unlawful.

units.la: 8 Quartò, quum dicit Whitgiftus, addere posse hominem ad ministeria Dei, quæ ipsis adminiculo esse possint, principium petit: nulla etenim ministeria addita ab hominibus, ministeria à Deo instituta adjuvare possunt: sed eis nocent potius & incommodant, id quod hac ipsa die, cuivis oculato videre licet. Atque par est tollendi ratio: adæque etenim papista dicere potest, de oblatione calicis, eam usui esse, & commodæ sacramenti administrationi inservire. Quinto, quum homini licere dicit, tollere ministeria ea quæ ad tempus tantum à Deo instituta
units.tr: 8 Fourth, when Whitgift says that man can add to the ministries of God those things which may serve as aids to them, he begs the question. For no ministries added by men can aid the ministries instituted by God; rather they harm them and hinder them, as anyone with eyes can see on this very day. And the reasoning for removal is parallel. For a Papist could just as well say, concerning the offering of the cup, that it is useful and serves the convenient administration of the sacrament. Fifth, when he says that a man may remove those ministries which God instituted only for a time,

units.la: a Hb. de habit. virg. Serm. de temp. 247.
units.tr: a Hom. on the dress of virgins; Sermon on the times, 247.

units.la: b Lib. de cult. fœminar. c. 5.
units.tr: b Book on the cultivation of women, ch. 5.

units.la: c Lib. 3. f. 2. p. 135. tuta sunt,multipliciter peccat. Primo sibi ipsi contradicit, nam paulo ante hanc differentiam posuit, quod addere homo possit ad ministeria a Deo instituta,& ipsius praeceptum non violare,sed non tolere,absque manifesta mandati divini violatione. Secundo, vagatur extra quaestionem quae de praesenti politeia ecclesiastica est,sub Evangelio,in qua quum nulla jam officia sint ad tempus tantum instituta, quorsum haec instantia,de ablatione ministeriorum quae minime petua sunt? Tertio,falsum est quod dicit; nam omnes in mundo homines munus Apostolorum & Evangelistarum & Prophetarum minime tollere potuerunt: etsi ea instituerit Deus, ut ad tempus tantum durarent aliquantulum futurum.
units.tr: c Book 3, f. 2, p. 135. ...were instituted only for a time, he sins in many ways. First, he contradicts himself, for a little earlier he made this distinction: that a man may add to the ministries instituted by God without violating his precept, but may not remove them without a manifest violation of the divine command. Second, he wanders outside the question, which concerns the present ecclesiastical polity under the Gospel. In this polity, since no offices are any longer instituted only for a time, why this objection about the removal of ministries that are by no means permanent? Third, what he says is false; for all men in the world have been unable to remove the office of the Apostles, Evangelists and Prophets, even though God instituted them to last only for a while.

units.la: 9 Septimo,ecclesia non potest nova & distincta dona impartiri novis officijs & dignitatibus,sicut Christum dona distincta dedisse legimus officijs eis,quae sunt ab ipso instituta 1. Cor.12.28. Ephes. 4.11. Hoc enim solius Christi est: ergo etiam non potest novas dignitates ordinare. Propono hoc argumentum rursus verbis Scultingianis: cujus responsio partim cum Whitgiftiana coincidit,partim ea sanior est. Respondent utrique,nulla jam esse nova ministeria, sed gradus tantum unius ejusdemque ministerij: de quo agetur suo loco. Concedit vero Scultingius,distincta dona cuique ministerio annexa esse : quod Whitgiftus non concedit,cujus ista verba sunt: Necessarium non est ut qui officium aliquod instituunt, dona etiam darent eidem officio competentia: nam tum nemo hominum officium aliquod instituere posset. Satis igitur est, ut obligat ad officium a se institutum, viros eos,quos Deum idoneos fecisse videt. Respondeo, si officium intelligat ecclesiasticum, verum est neminem hominem ejusmodi aliquod instituere posse : si de civili officio intelligit,extra oleas vagatur: ratio etenim longe diversa est. Civilis namque politeia res humana est, ac proinde potest magistratus invenire qui jam idonei sunt: aut potest etiam viros idoneos ipse reddere,externis adminiculis suppeditatis. At politeia ecclesiae res est divina, supernaturalis, spiritualis & caelestis : sic ut neminem idoneum reperire ecclesia possit ad officium aliquod novum: quia Christus officijs a seipso iustitutis sua dona largitur tantummodo,non eis,quae in ipsius contumeliam ab hominibus excogitantur. Porro, non nisi humana adjumenta conferre homo potest : at in officijs ecclesiasticis humana adjumenta non desiderantur: arma etenim hujus politeias carnalia non sunt. Ita fit, ut nihil nisi idolum quidem in ecclesiam introducere homo possit : officium vero aliquod ecclesiasticum necessarijs donis ornatum,non possit.
units.tr: 9 Seventh, the Church cannot bestow new and distinct gifts on new offices and dignities. We read that Christ gave distinct gifts to the offices that he himself instituted (1 Cor. 12.28; Eph. 4.11). For this belongs to Christ alone; therefore the Church also cannot ordain new dignities. I propose this argument again in the words of Scultingius, whose answer partly coincides with Whitgift's and partly is sounder. Both reply that there are now no new ministries, but only grades of one and the same ministry, which will be discussed in its proper place. Scultingius, however, concedes that distinct gifts are attached to each ministry, which Whitgift does not concede. Whitgift's words are these: It is not necessary that those who institute some office should also give to that office the gifts suited to it; for then no man could institute any office. It is enough, therefore, that they whom he sees God to have made fit are bound to the office he has instituted. I reply: if he means an ecclesiastical office, it is true that no man can institute such an office; if he means a civil office, he wanders beyond the mark, for the reasoning is entirely different. Civil polity is a human affair, and therefore the magistrate can find men who are already fit, or can himself make men fit by supplying external aids. But the polity of the Church is a divine, supernatural, spiritual and heavenly thing, so that the Church can find no one fit for any new office, because Christ bestows his gifts only on the offices instituted by himself, not on those that men devise to his dishonour. Moreover, man can supply only human aids, whereas in ecclesiastical offices human aids are not required, for the weapons of this polity are not carnal. So it comes about that man can introduce into the Church nothing but an idol, and cannot furnish an ecclesiastical office with the necessary gifts.

units.la: 10 Octavo,non patiuntur ecclesiae attributa,ut officium aliquod novum homo in eadem institutere possit. Quid enim? Regnum Iesu Christi ecclesia est: & in regno alieno quanquam humano, peregrinus audit,officiarium aliquem novum imponere & ordinare? Domus Dei est;& in domo alterius oeconomos quis instituere praesumit,praeter eos qui sunt ab ipso patrefamilias ordinati; Postremo, ecclesia corpus Christi est: & membrum corpori adjici à quoquam potest, ut interim monstrum non existat?
units.tr: 10 Eighth, the attributes of the Church do not allow a man to institute a new office in it. For what? The Church is the kingdom of Jesus Christ; does a stranger presume to impose and appoint some new officer in another's kingdom, even a merely human one? The Church is the house of God; does anyone presume to appoint stewards in another's house, apart from those whom the father of the family himself has ordained? Lastly, the Church is the body of Christ; can anyone add a member to the body without a monster coming into existence?

units.la: 11 Nonò, audiantur sententiæ sapientum. Ita Cyprianus, ut citatur à R.Feyldo, Vnus Deus, unus Christus, una ecclesia, una cathedra, voce dominica supra Petrum fundata. Nullum aliud altare erigi, nullum aliud sacerdotium institui potest, præter altare & sacerdotium illud quod jam est institutum. Quicunque alibi colligit, spargit. Sacerdotium cuius hic mentio est, non ad papam solum, sed ad omnes ministros pertinere ostendit contra Bellarminum Feyldus: nonne igitur aperte proclamat Cyprianus, nullos alios ministros institui in ecclesia posse, præter eos qui jam instituti sunt? Neque ad sacerdotium tantum docens restringi hæc verba possunt, ut sic de officijs ecclesiasticis, quæ ad regimen ecclesiæ pertinent, loqui Cyprianus non videatur: agit etenim contra schismaticos, contra quos & docentia & regentia sacerdotia, hoc argumento ita communit, ut intra ecclesiam tantummodo, non autem extra apud schismaticos, ea reperiri posse existimentur. Atqui inquies vel ex hac confessione liquet, non adversus nova sacerdotia intra ecclesiam Cyprianum loqui, sed de eis tantum quæ contra ecclesiam per schismaticos invehuntur. Quasi homogenea extra ecclesiam si illicita sint, quia præter sacerdotium instituta sint: tum heterogenea intra ecclesiam non sint illicita magis, quia eò magis præter sacerdotium à Deo institutum sunt, quo alterius generis sunt, ab eo quod est à Deo institutum. Quid quod, novum sacerdotium erigere, & novum altare erigere paria faciat Cyprianus? novum autem altare, tam intra ecclesiam, quam extra ecclesiam illicitum est. Alibi Christum, unicum Episcopatus radicem, facit Cyprianus, vel Gul. Whitakero nostro interpretante: at radix alius statuitur præter Christum, quando authoritas tribuitur hominibus ut novum aliquem Episcopatum invehere & instituere possint. Citatur Damasus a R. Feyldo: is enim Chorepiscopos illicitos putat, quia eorum origo non est ex scripturis sacris: & omnes pariter officiarios ecclesiasticos novos condemnat, qui ab hominibus superadduntur. Citatur enim Durandus, ab eodem R. Feyldo & approbatur: asserit is inferiores ordines, proprie ordines non esse, sed cultus divini solemnitates tantum: quia ab ecclesia introducti videntur, quæ ordines proprie dictos instituere nequit. Postremò, Archiepiscopi Bituriensis in Synodo Parisina ista quædam verba ferunt. Ecclesiasticus ordo penitus est confusus quia multi falcem mittunt in messem alienam: ut ecclesia Dei jam monstrum dici possit. Sicut enim in corpore naturali contingit, quod monstrum dicitur, cum membrum unum alterius officium habet, sic in corpore spirituali scilicet ecclesia, non utique literati & prudentes fratres videlicet maiores & minores officium specialiter nobis commissum occupant: sed iniustè, cum nemo debeat sibi honorem assumere, nisi qui a Domino sicut Aaron vocatur. Omnia hic pro nobis loquitur. Additio officij ecclesiastici additio membri est, quæ corpus ecclesiæ monstrosum reddit. Quæ officia ecclesiæ adduntur, loqui? Imo ratio suppetit manifesta loqui hic Paulum, de singulis mandatis, quae in hac epistola praecedunt, & in Epistola praecedenti: non modo de potestate egit, verum de forma modoq;etiam. Epiphonema etenim haec verba continent, quo authoritas toti libro comparatur: perinde ac Apocal.22.18. Testor cuivis audienti verba Prophetiae hujus, si quis adjecerit ad haec, imponet ei Deus plagas scriptas in libro isto. Et si quis abstulerit aliquid auferet Deus partem ejus——ex iis quae scripta sunt in libro isto. Mos igitur spiritus Sancti observandus: solet enim in hujusmodi sanctionibus scriptorum suorum authoritatem roborare. Locus utrobique idem est, in calce libri, forma loquendi eadem: Denuncio, inquit Paulus, Testor, inquit Iohannes: materia denique eadem est: nam servare mandatum hujus libri incontaminatum & irreprehensum idem est ac si dixisset, (Iohannes) sine additione vel dimunitione. Secundo, imperite officium appellat formam & modum authoritatis, quod authoritatis cujusque vel causa potius vel subjectum est: nam unde authoritas nisi ab officio? & quodnam legitimae potestatis subjectum, nisi officium legitimum? Tertio, nefanda Downami officij & potestatis divulsio est, ut officium quidem oboleri & mutari possit, potestas non item. Quam hoc absurdum etiam, quod authoritatem unius officij, in officium aliud transferri legitime idque ad hominibus posse putat: quod cuiusque confusionis Anabaptisticae, fenestram aperit. Hinc etenim fiet ut authoritas pastoris sit penes Diaconum, authoritas Diaconi transferri possit in Seniorem: & Senior authoritatem Pastoris vel Diaconi habeat, si id magistratui visum fuerit. Evigila Downame, ut transmigrationis huiusce tuae commenta videas. Nam cum Episcopum aboleri posse putes, remanente interim Episcopi propria authoritate, accidens somnias absque subiecto: & cum Episcopi authoritatem ad presbyterorum ordinem transferri posse statuis: quid aliud quam μετεμψύχωσιν & transubstantiationis imaginem quandam renovas?
units.tr: 11 Ninth, let us hear the opinions of the wise. Thus Cyprian, as cited by R. Feyld: One God, one Christ, one Church, one chair, founded by the Lord's word upon Peter. No other altar can be raised, no other priesthood instituted, besides that altar and priesthood which already exist. Whoever gathers elsewhere, scatters. Feyld, against Bellarmine, shows that the priesthood of which he speaks pertains not to the pope alone but to all ministers. Does not Cyprian then plainly proclaim that no other ministers can be instituted in the Church besides those already instituted? Nor can these words be restricted to the priesthood alone, as though Cyprian did not seem to speak of ecclesiastical offices that pertain to the government of the Church. For he is contending against the schismatics, and against them he so fortifies both teaching and ruling priesthoods with this argument that they are thought to be found only within the Church, and not outside it among the schismatics. But you will object that even from this admission it is clear that Cyprian is not speaking against new priesthoods within the Church, but only against those that the schismatics bring in against the Church. As if, when homogeneous things outside the Church are unlawful because they are instituted besides the priesthood, then heterogeneous things within the Church were not unlawful all the more, because they are all the more besides the priesthood instituted by God, the more they differ in kind from what God has instituted. What more? Does Cyprian make raising a new priesthood and raising a new altar equivalent? Yet a new altar is unlawful both within the Church and outside it. Elsewhere Cyprian makes Christ the one root of the episcopate, as our Gulielmus Whitaker interprets it; but another root is set up beside Christ when authority is granted to men to introduce and institute some new episcopate. Damasus is cited by R. Feyld. For he thinks that chorepiscopi are unlawful, because their origin is not from the holy Scriptures, and he condemns all in the same way who are added as new ecclesiastical officers by men. For Durandus is cited by the same R. Feyld and approved: he asserts that the lower orders are not properly orders at all, but only solemnities of divine worship, because they seem to have been introduced by the Church, which cannot institute orders properly so called. Lastly, the Archbishop of Bourges in the Synod of Paris brings forward these words: The ecclesiastical order has been utterly confused, because many put their sickle into another's harvest, so that the Church of God can now be called a monster. For as in the natural body what is called a monster occurs when one limb has the office of another, so in the spiritual body, that is the Church, not indeed learned and prudent brethren, namely the greater and the lesser, occupy the office specially committed to us, but unjustly, since no one ought to assume honour for himself unless he is called by the Lord, as Aaron was. Everything here speaks on our side. The addition of an ecclesiastical office is the addition of a member, which makes the body of the Church monstrous. Does Paul speak here of the offices that are being added? Indeed, the reasoning makes it plain that he speaks here of the individual commands that precede in this epistle and in the preceding epistle; he treats not only of the power but of the form and manner too. For these words contain a kind of epiphonema, by which authority is given to the whole book, just as in Revelation 22.18: I testify to everyone who hears the words of this prophecy: if anyone adds to these things, God will lay upon him the plagues written in this book. And if anyone takes away anything, God will take away his part—from those things which are written in this book. The manner of the Holy Spirit is therefore to be observed, for in such sanctions he is accustomed to strengthen the authority of his writings. The place is the same in both, at the end of the book, and the form of speaking is the same: I announce, says Paul; I testify, says John. Lastly, the matter is the same: to keep the command of this book uncorrupted and blameless is the same as if he had said, without addition or subtraction. Second, Paul unskilfully calls the office the form and manner of authority, when it is rather the cause or subject of each authority; for whence is authority, if not from the office? And what is the subject of lawful power, if not a lawful office? Third, Downame's separation of office and power is a monstrous one, as if the office could be abolished and changed, but the power could not. How absurd also is his opinion that the authority of one office may be transferred lawfully to another office, and that this can be done by men, which opens a window to every Anabaptist confusion. For from this it would follow that the authority of the minister would rest with the deacon, that the authority of the deacon could be transferred to the elder, and that the elder would have the authority of minister or deacon if it seemed good to the magistrate. Wake up, Downame, and see the inventions of this transmigration of yours. For when you think the bishop can be abolished while the bishop's own authority remains, you dream of an accident without a subject; and when you declare that the authority of the bishop can be transferred to the order of presbyters, what else do you revive but a kind of metempsychosis and an image of transubstantiation?

units.la: Quarto, nefarie dicitur officium Episcopi a magistratu aboleri posse, si modo divina ordinatione (quod vult Downamus) institutum fuerit. Pari etenim ratione & officium Pastoris & Diaconi abolere magistratus poterit. Non possunt vero ista officia aboleri: tamen Episcopi Hierarchici officium poterit: non argumentum ego quidem fortius, aut pleniorem ab adversario confessionem desideratem: Episcopi officium, perinde ac Pastoris at Diaconi, a Christo miuime institutum esse. Quinto, inepte dicitur quibusdam Timothei non successoribus, in Timotheo hic Paulum scribere: nam cum unum individuum sumitur, in quo lex aliqua stabilitur, repraesentat quidem individuum illud successores omnes, sed successores tantum. Exempli gratia: cum legem naturae figere Deus voluisset, quod primae herbae, primae plantae, primae arbori individuali dixit Deus: id ad omnes herbas, plantas, arbores in eodem genere succedentes dixit: sed non ad alias quae in eodem genere successorum non essent; unde Iac.3.12. Nunquid potest fratres mei ficus olcas edere, aut vites ficus? Scribit hic in Timotheo presbyteris Paulus? bene est. Presbyteri igitur Pauli Timothei legitimi successores sunt? Et transferri potest Timothei potestas in presbyteros per magistratum, idque legitime? Nulla igitur Episcopalis Timothei potestas fuit, quae non eadem presbyteri proprie: si alias Deus instituisset, Episcopalis potestatis presbyterum capace magistratus reddere non potuisset. Sexto & ultimo, si scripserit haec Paulus, non de Timothei officio Episcopali, sed de authoritate Timothei in genere: tum non haec scripsit Timotheo ut Episcopo, sed tantum Timotheo ut authoritatem in genere habenti: at si haec non scripsit Timotheo ut Episcopo tum nullum jus divinum pro Episcopis proferri potest: totius etenim Epistolae praecedentis haec verba authoramentum continent, ut ante dictum. Ita plane in castra nostra transijt Downnamus: planeque suis manibus dejicit, quae contra nos alibi aedificarat: quando dixit, Hanc epistolam ad Timotheum, Episcopalis functionis typum esse. Vulnerat etiam suos, inprimis Thomam Bilsonum: qui nullum jus divinum proferri pro Episcopis posse fatetur: si haec verba scripta non fuerint Timotheo ut Episcopo. Annon pulchre laboravit Downnamus, qui hoc unicum, pro jure divino functionis Episcopalis fundamentum imis sedibus subruit?
units.tr: Fourthly, it is wickedly said that the office of bishop can be abolished by the magistrate, if it was instituted by divine ordinance (as Downame wants). By the same reasoning, the magistrate could also abolish the office of minister and of deacon. Yet those offices cannot be abolished, while the office of the hierarchical bishop could be. I for my part would not want a stronger argument or a fuller confession from the opponent: that the office of bishop, like that of minister and deacon, was by no means instituted by Christ. Fifthly, some foolishly say, not successors of Timothy, that Paul is writing here to Timothy in the person of the elders. When a single individual is taken in whom some law is established, that individual certainly represents all his successors, but only successors. For example, when God wished to fix the law of nature, he said to the first herb, the first plant, the first individual tree what he meant for all herbs, plants and trees succeeding in the same kind, but not for others that were not successors in that kind. Hence James 3:12: "Can the fig tree, my brethren, bear olive berries, or a vine figs?" Does Paul write here to elders in the person of Timothy? Very well. Are the elders therefore the lawful successors of Timothy? And can Timothy's power be transferred to the elders by the magistrate, and that lawfully? There was therefore no episcopal power of Timothy that was not properly the same as that of an elder. If God had instituted otherwise, the magistrate could not have made an elder capable of episcopal power. Sixthly and lastly, if Paul wrote these things not about Timothy's episcopal office but about Timothy's authority in general, then he did not write them to Timothy as bishop, but only to Timothy as one holding authority in general. But if he did not write them to Timothy as bishop, then no divine right can be put forward for bishops, for these words, as said before, contain the authority of the whole preceding epistle. So plainly Downame has crossed over into our camp, and with his own hands throws down what he had built elsewhere against us, when he said that this epistle to Timothy is a type of the episcopal function. He also wounds his own side, above all Thomas Bilson, who admits that no divine right can be put forward for bishops if these words were not written to Timothy as bishop. Has not Downame worked hard to good effect, when he undermines to its lowest foundations this single foundation of the divine right of the episcopal function?

units.la: 8 Quinto, videamus quid viri docti de hac re senserint. Ita Io. Gerson: Maior fuit Ecclesiae primitivae authoritas, quoad praedicta, quam nunc est. Non enim est in potestate Papae, aut Concilij aut Ecclesiae, immutare traditiones datas ab Evangelistis & a Paulo, ut quidam delirant. Delirium igitur Gersonis judicio, assertio haec de Politeiae Ecclesiasticae mutabilitate Hierarchica est: praesertim cum ea Apostolica & Paulina traditio sit. Ita Franciscus Zabraella: Si Papa vult destruere illud quod Apostoli docuerunt convincitur errare. Non potest ad Doctrinam solam restringi hoc: disputat etenim & in eo opere de negotijs Ecclesiasticae disciplinae. Ita Ioh. Budaeus. Sacrosanctos canones melioribus annis factos, ut eis velut regulis vita clericorum dirigeretur, & velut patrum proscriptis posteri formarentur, in amusses plumbeas iam evasisse quis non videt? Quales olim fuerunt Canones plumbei, ut nobis non structuram operum tenore aequabili dirigant, sed extructorum commodo & libidine flexibiles, structurae accommodentur. Indignatus hic est Canones antiquos in amusses plumbeas evasisse: nos Canonem sacrum pro homiuum commodo & libidine in canones plumbeos, ab Hierarchicis coversos jam esse, non indignabimur? Hoc fieri, cum Politeia Ecclesiae ad magistratus arbitrium, flexibilis & mutabilis statuitur: ex nostris scriptoribus omnibus constat, Bilsono inprimis & Reynoldo: quam ad verbum Dei solum revocat, tanquam ad Lydium lapidem: ab inventis vero humanis abducit, tanquam a regula Lesbia. Hiero. Zanchium ad hoc propositum in Politeia Ecclesiastica reformanda huc citat & approbat Had.Saravia. Verba ista sunt: Sunt igitur ad formam veteris & Apostolicae Ecclesiae, omnes Ecclesiae reformandae: & omnia tam cultus, & disciplina
units.tr: 8 Fifthly, let us see what learned men have thought about this matter. Thus John Gerson: The authority of the primitive Church was greater, as to the matters mentioned, than it is now. For it is not in the power of the Pope, or of a council, or of the Church, to change the traditions handed down by the Evangelists and by Paul, as some rave. Therefore, in Gerson's judgement, the assertion that the polity of the Church is changeable by hierarchical authority is raving, especially since that polity is an apostolic and Pauline tradition. Thus Francis Zabarella: If the Pope wishes to destroy what the Apostles taught, he is convicted of error. This cannot be restricted to doctrine alone, for in that work he also discusses matters of ecclesiastical discipline. Thus John Budaeus: Who does not see that the most sacred canons, made in better times, so that the life of the clergy might be directed by them as by rules, and posterity formed by them as by the precepts of the fathers, have by now turned into leaden rules? Such once were the leaden canons, which do not direct the structure of works by an even course, but bend to the convenience and whim of the builders, so that the structure is adapted to them. He is indignant that the ancient canons have turned into leaden rules. Shall we not be indignant that the sacred canon, for the convenience and whim of men, has already been turned by the hierarchical party into leaden canons? This happens when the polity of the Church is established as flexible and changeable at the will of the magistrate. It is clear from all our writers, above all Bilson and Reynolds, that the polity is recalled solely to the Word of God, as to the Lydian stone, and drawn away from human inventions, as from the Lesbian rule. Hadrian Saravia cites and approves Jerome Zanchius for this very purpose, of reforming the polity of the Church. His words are these: Therefore all the churches are to be reformed according to the form of the ancient and Apostolic Church, and all things, both worship and discipline

units.la: De Triplic. ISic. p. 104 disciplina, quàm dogmata, non ad Lesbiam regulam humani judicij, sed lapidem Lydium divini verbi examinanda. Verumenimverò, est quod Geor. ipsum Downamum, hujus regulæ Lesbiæ pudeat: sicut & pudere necesse est: nisi ipsa præcipua Episcopalis functionis fundamenta subvertere velit. Quid enim? Annon præcipuum ejusdem sustentaculû apud Bilsonum & Saraviam istud est: oportere Apostolorum superioritatem in ministros in Episcopis perdurare, in Ecclesijs omnium seculorum: quia eo hoc regimine in pagis opus habent, quod habuerunt Ecclesiæ quum Apostoli vixerunt? Tolle hoc fulcrum & Episcopalis functionis necessitas cadit: idq; vel ipsius Downami judicio, cujus in concione pro Episcopis, p. 79. hæc verba sunt: Multo magis necessarium est, ut omnium ætatum Ecclesiæ Episcopos habeant, quam Ecclesiæ primæ, quando Apostoli in vivis fuerunt. Hoc verò fundamentum vacillare quis non videt, si Episcopalis functio statuatur mutabilis ad arbitrium magistratus? In eadem concione dixit: Functionem & authoritatem Timothei & Titi esse ordinariam & necessariam: non solum ad bene esse sed etiam ad ipsum esse ecclesiæ. Quid apertius? Imo, inquit, in defensione hoc tantum volui, functionem hanc esse ordinariam authoritatem necessariam. Dixit in concione Episcopos esse necessariò retinendos: quod in Defensione ita eludit: intellexi esse necessariò retinendos, non necessitate absoluta, sed necessitate expedientiæ. Quam miseræ hæ quæso tergiversationes sunt? Quàm etiam contradictoriæ? Functio non est necessaria, sed authoritas tantum: functio est necessaria necessitate expedientiæ, non necessitate absolutâ. Quasi quisquam nostrum Politeiam necessitate absoluta necessariam unquam dixerit? at quod necessitate expedientiæ necessarium est, non sit perpetuò retinendum? Sit ipse judex: Ex singularitate, ordinatione, & iurisdictione Episcoporum tria beneficia pendere dicit, Vnitatem, perpetuationem, & ⟨συνοχὴν⟩ Ecclesiæ: & nonne quæso perpetuum est, quod hæc perpetuanda continet? Ecclesiarum, inquit, Provincialium & Nationalium Metropolitani Episcopi rectores sunt, & rectores esse debent. Quid sibi hoc DEBENT vult? Quod debet fieri, annon perpetuò faciendum? Simile est quod dicit, superioritatem in ordinatione & iurisdictione, quam Timotheus & Titus habuerunt, non cum illis mori: sed in successoribus continuari DEBVISSE. Rursus? Præscripta officia Timotheo, perfici & peragi DEBENT ab ipsis & eorum successoribus, usque ad adventum Christi. Atque quoniam in mentionem huius loci ad Timotheum rursus incidimus: adnotentur insignes contradictionis istæ. Vidimus nuper, quomodo statuerit, hunc locum non de functione Episcopali, sed tantum de authoritate functionis intelligendum: item, quanquam primario Episcopis loquatur, secundario tamen presbyteris, qui etsi Timothei successores non legitimi, tamen mutata Politeiæ forma, iurisdictionem Timothei sibi demandatam exercere possunt. Libetne audire quomodo in ista Downamus ruat alibi? In ultimo non potest, inquit, authoritas & potestas Timothei illiusve executio mandari Presbyteris. Rursus: harum rerum cura ad Presbyteros non pertinet. In secundo,
units.tr: De Triplic. ISic. p. 104 discipline, rather than doctrines, to be examined not by the Lesbian rule of human judgement but by the Lydian stone of the divine Word. Yet there is reason why Geo. Downame himself should be ashamed of this Lesbian rule, as he must be, unless he wishes to overturn the chief foundations of the episcopal function. For what? Is not the chief prop of it, among Bilson and Saravia, this: that the superiority of the Apostles over the ministers must remain in bishops, in the churches of all ages, because in villages they need the same government the churches had while the Apostles lived? Remove this prop and the necessity of the episcopal function falls, and this by Downame's own judgement, in whose sermon for bishops, p. 79, these words stand: It is much more necessary that the churches of all ages have bishops than the first church, when the Apostles were alive. But who does not see that this foundation totters, if the episcopal function is established as changeable at the will of the magistrate? In the same sermon he said: The function and authority of Timothy and Titus is ordinary and necessary, not only for the well-being but for the very being of the church. What could be plainer? Nay, he says, in the defence I wished only this, that this function is an ordinary and necessary authority. He said in the sermon that bishops are to be retained necessarily, which in the Defence he evades thus: I understood that they are to be retained necessarily, not by absolute necessity but by the necessity of expediency. What wretched evasions, I ask, are these? How contradictory too! The function is not necessary, but only the authority; the function is necessary by the necessity of expediency, not by absolute necessity. As if any of us ever called the polity necessary by absolute necessity! But what is necessary by the necessity of expediency, must it not be retained perpetually? Let him be his own judge: From the singularity, ordination and jurisdiction of bishops, he says, three benefits depend: unity, perpetuation and the cohesion of the Church. And is not what these things are to perpetuate surely perpetual, I ask? Metropolitan bishops, he says, are, and ought to be, the rulers of the provincial and national churches. What does this OUGHT TO BE mean? What ought to be done, must it not be done perpetually? Similar is what he says: The superiority in ordination and jurisdiction which Timothy and Titus had ought not to have died with them, but ought to have continued in their successors. Again: The duties prescribed to Timothy ought to be performed and carried out by them and their successors until the coming of Christ. And since we have again come upon Timothy in mentioning this place, let these notable contradictions be noted. We saw lately how he has laid down that this place is to be understood not of the episcopal function but only of the authority of the function; likewise, although it speaks primarily to bishops, yet secondarily to elders, who, although not lawful successors of Timothy, can nevertheless, the form of the polity having been changed, exercise the jurisdiction committed to Timothy. Do you wish to hear how Downame elsewhere collapses on this point? In the last place, he says, the authority and power of Timothy, or its execution, cannot be committed to elders. Again: The care of these matters does not pertain to elders. In the second,
