lib.3.p.71. 72. & lib.4 p.70. Ibid. [præcepta quæ in Epistola ad Timotheum tanquam ad adventum Christi duratura dantur, Episcopis tantummodo dantur & eorum successoribus. Rursus: Præcepta 1.Tim.5.19.22. perpetuæ directiones non sunt, non ad Christianos, non ad alios ministros, sed ad Episcopos solos. In primo: Epistolæ ad Titum & Timotheum scriptæ, typi & exemplaria sunt Episcopalis functionis: scriptæq; ex proposito sunt, ad informandos Episcopos, quomodo functionem suam exercere debeant usque ad finem sæculi.] Quoties in hisce, Politeias Ecclesiasticæ (quam in regimine Episcopali ponit Downnamus) perpetuitas asseritur, usqve ad adventum Christi, usque ad finem sæculi? Idem asserit, in citandis testimonijs patrum, & quæ non solum de Episcopalis regiminis facto verumetiam de iure testari dicit, quod illi perpetuum esse volunt, in citando Hieronymo præsertim, cuius judicium hoc esse dicit: quòd Episcopus ad vitanda schismata semper retinendus sit. Postremò, idem facile colligere licet ex testimonijs accommodandis, quæ pro Episcopali functione, ex alijs scripturis profert: Locos etenim Phil. 2.29. Heb.13.17. Populum Anglicanum ad honorandos Episcopos etiamnum hodie obligare dicit. At si ad hunc diem ligent, ligant etiam Anglicani populi posteros in perpetuum. Affine illud est quod ex 1. Tim. 5.17. affert: Quod si quis minister duplici honore reverentiæ & sustentationis honorandus est, idque jure divino: tum Episcopi ministri præcipui multo magis. Certè, si Episcopi ministri præcipui sint, tum & perpetui etiam multo magis quam presbyteri erunt: præsertim cum sensu Downnamiano, Episcopi illi sint, qui Ecclesiarum Pastores sunt: Presbyteri tantum sunt Episcoporum delegati, quod delegatus perpetuus erit, delegans non item? Miror suam vanitatem Hierarchicos non videre? Planum etenim est Episcopos à Christo institutos non esse ut Pastores, & ministros præcipuos: si modo ut Presbyteri, quos à Christo institutos omnes fatentur, perpetui non sint. Episcopi, inquit Downnamus, stellæ illæ sunt quos Christus sua dextra tenet Apoc. 1.20. sunt præcipui domus Dei œconomi, sunt ἡγούμενοι illi quos Paulus memorat, Heb.13.17. at stellæ œconomi, duces, iisque præcipui aut soli, authoritate humanâ quâvis removeri à cœlo, à domo, ab acie possunt? Atque hæc adversus Politeias Ecclesiasticæ mutabilitatem dicta sunt in genere quidem, ita tamen ut primam immutationis partem præcipuè feriant, quæ est per Diminutionem & Ablationem.]
units.tr: Ibid. [Precepts which in the Epistle to Timothy are given as if they were to last until the coming of Christ are given only to bishops and their successors. Again: The precepts in 1 Tim. 5.19, 22 are not perpetual directions, not for Christians, not for other ministers, but for bishops alone. In the first place: The epistles written to Titus and Timothy are types and patterns of the episcopal function, and were written on purpose to instruct bishops how they ought to exercise their office until the end of the age.] How often in these passages is the perpetuity of the ecclesiastical polity (which Downame places in episcopal government) asserted, until the coming of Christ, until the end of the age? He asserts the same in citing the testimonies of the Fathers, which he says bear witness not only to the fact of episcopal government but also to its right, and which they wish to be perpetual; he does so especially in citing Jerome, whose judgment he says this is: that a bishop is always to be retained in order to avoid schisms. Finally, the same can easily be gathered from the proof-texts which he brings from other Scriptures in support of the episcopal function: for he says that the passages Phil. 2.29 and Heb. 13.17 still bind the English people today to honour bishops. But if they bind to this day, they bind the English people's posterity as well, forever. Akin to this is what he brings from 1 Tim. 5.17: If any minister is to be honoured with double honour of reverence and maintenance, and that by divine right, then the chief ministers, the bishops, much more so. Certainly, if bishops are the chief ministers, then they will also be perpetual, much more than the elders are, especially since, in Downame's sense, the bishops are those who are the pastors of the churches, while the elders are merely delegates of the bishops. Will the delegate be perpetual, and the one who delegates not? I marvel that the hierarchists do not see their own vanity. For it is plain that bishops were not instituted by Christ as pastors and chief ministers, if at least they are not perpetual as elders are, whom everyone confesses were instituted by Christ. Bishops, says Downame, are those stars which Christ holds in his right hand, Rev. 1.20; they are the chief stewards of God's house; they are the leaders [ἡγούμενοι] whom Paul mentions, Heb. 13.17. But can stars, stewards and leaders, and those chief or only ones, be removed from heaven, from the house, from the ranks, by any human authority? And these things have been said against the mutability of the ecclesiastical polity in general, yet in such a way that they chiefly strike at the first part of the change, which is by diminution and removal.]

units.la: CAPVT. XLV. Non licet addere essentialibus disciplinæ.
units.tr: CHAPTER 45. It is not lawful to add to the essentials of discipline.

units.la: Vperest, ut nonnihil adjiciatur, de mutationis specie altera, nempe Additione: ubi quæritur, an ad Politeias essentialia addere quid Ecclesiæ liceat? nominatim verò, an licitum sit novuum aliquod officium Ecclesiasticum excogitare, & in Ecclesia collocare, quod non est verbo speciatim institutum? Negamus nos, aiunt Hierarchicorum officia quae ad externam politeiam & gubernationem ecclesiae pertinent ab Apostolis fuisse constituta credendum est: etiamsi de eis nec Christus quicquam praecepisse, nec Apostoli ordinasse legantur. Quid, quod haec perpetua putet: quae ab Hierarchis putantur libera?
units.tr: It remains to say something about the other kind of change, namely addition. The question is whether the Church may add anything to the essentials of the polity, and in particular whether it is lawful to devise some new ecclesiastical office and install it in the Church, when the Word has not specifically instituted it. Our opponents answer, "No." They say that the offices of the Hierarchics, which pertain to the external polity and government of the Church, must be believed to have been established by the Apostles, even though neither Christ is read to have commanded anything about them nor the Apostles to have ordained them. Why, then, do they think these offices perpetual, when the Hierarchics regard them as optional?

units.la: Secundò, bonis intentionibus haec sententia patrocinatur: liberum etenim reliquit Ecclesiae addere officia, modo id fiat ad aedificationem: id est, modo intentione bona hoc fiat, ad finem ecclesiae utilem. Instamus in re, quae ad politeiam Ecclesiasticam attinet. Annon Davidis intentio bona fuit, quando in animo habuit, domum Deo aedificare? Immò optima: sic enim vel ipse Deus. Dixit Iehova Davidi patri meo: eò quod fuit tibi in animo aedificare Domum nomini meo, bene fecisti quòd fuisti eo animo, 1. Reg. 8. 18. Nunquid itaque videre lubet, quàm ingrata sit Deo, additio ista in politeia ecclesiastica, quanquam à bono animo progrediatur, & nihil sibi proponat aliud, quam gloriam Dei & ecclesiae aedificationem? Advertantur igitur verba Nathanis: generali etenim ratione utitur, qua omnes jam similes additiones tanquam gladio percutiuntur. 1. Chron. 17. 6. Quocunque itabam in toto Israele, an quicquam locutus sum ulli Iudicum Israelis, quare non aedificatis mihi domum cedrinam? Nunc ergo, &c. Habetur hic Enthymema nostrum totidem verbis. Nullam in verbo Deus de officio ecclesiastico addito mentionem fecit: ergò est illicitum. Quid ergo? Ecclesiae authoritas in legibus ecclesiasticis ferendis nulla quaeso est? Annon quod utile videtur sancire potest? Potest quidem in politeias accidentalibus: in substantialibus, quae jam in verbo expressa sunt non potest, quocunque praetextu, expedientię vel utilitatis: Licet enim cum Guil. Whitakero nostro ratiocinari: Quomodo non expedit, uti eâ (politeia) quam Christus instituit? Nosne Christo melius scimus quid ecclesiae expedit? Non patiuntur certè septem oculi Christi, Apoc. 5. 6. ut videre jam homines possint officium aliquod ecclesiasticum, ecclesiae utile atque expediens, quod ille non vidit: neque patitur domus quam sibi sapientissimè aedificavit, excisis columnis suis septem, Pro. 9. 1. ut columnam quasi octavam, intelligo officium Ecclesiasticum novum jam addere opus sit.
units.tr: Secondly, this opinion pleads good intentions. It leaves the Church free to add offices, provided this is done for edification, that is, provided it is done with a good intention and for a purpose useful to the Church. Let us press the point on the matter that concerns the ecclesiastical polity. Was not David's intention good when he resolved to build a house for God? Indeed it was most excellent, for God himself said so: Jehovah said to David my father: because it was in your mind to build a house for my name, you did well that you had that mind, 1 Kings 8.18. Do we therefore wish to see how displeasing to God this addition in the ecclesiastical polity is, even though it proceeds from a good mind and proposes to itself nothing but the glory of God and the edification of the Church? Let us attend, then, to the words of Nathan. He uses a general argument by which all such additions are struck down as with a sword: 1 Chron. 17.6, Wherever I walked in all Israel, did I speak a word to any of the judges of Israel, asking why you have not built me a house of cedar? Now therefore, etc. Here is our enthymeme in so many words: God made no mention in his Word of an added ecclesiastical office; therefore it is unlawful. What then? Has the Church no authority at all, I ask, to enact ecclesiastical laws? May it not sanction whatever seems useful? It may indeed do so in the accidental matters of the polity; but in the substantial matters, which are already expressed in the Word, it may not, under any pretext of expediency or usefulness. For we may reason with our Whitaker: How is it not expedient to use that polity which Christ instituted? Do we know better than Christ what is expedient for the Church? Certainly the seven eyes of Christ, Rev. 5.6, do not allow men to see some ecclesiastical office, useful and expedient for the Church, which he did not see. Nor does the house which he most wisely built for himself, having hewn out its seven pillars, Prov. 9.1, allow that there is now need to add, as it were an eighth pillar, a new ecclesiastical office.

units.la: 2 Tertio, contemptum planè verbi haec Hierarchica sapit: quum addi officia nequeant, nisi ea dedecorentur, quae Christus in verbo suo instituta jampridem sunt: sic ut peccatum Ieroboamicum haec additio planè sit: cui hoc tanquam audax facinus impingitur, quod sacerdotes instituisset qui non fuerunt ex filijs Levi: id est, ex eorum genere & numero, quos Deus ipse ordinasset, 1. Reg. 12. 31. Adversus hoc peccatum cum contestatur Rex Abijah, ostendit planè, & ea tantum officia usurpanda ab ecclesijs esse, quae Deus instituit: & omnia alia removenda quae ad similitudinem politeias papisticae adjuncta ab hominibus sunt. Sic enim fatur, 2. Chron. 13. 9. Annon depulistis sacerdotes Iehovae filios Aharonis & Levitas? & fecistis vobis sacerdotes ut populi reliquarum regionum? — Nos autem habemus Iehovam Deum nostrum, vel rationis gratia adjungere debemus mandato. Nihil quod vel bonum videtur addendum, sed simplex & pura mandati forma servanda est. Addendo de proprio, semiplenum Dei intellexit esse mandatum. Docet nos igitur praesentis series lectionis, neque detrahere aliquid debere divinis mandatis, neque addere. Accedo ad Whitgiftum, qui multa excogitat quidem, ut haec prohibitio additionis ab Hierarchicis avertatur: ista tamen elusio Hookeriana ne quidem illi in mentem venit. Addunt verbo inquit primo, qui docent contra verbum; secundo, qui aliquid necessarium faciunt ad salutem quod in verbo non continetur; tertio, qui meriti opinionem fovent, in eis quae praeter verbum invenerunt; Quarto, qui tanquam illegitimum prohibent, quod per verbum Dei legitimum est. Respondet Cartwrightus, omissum illud esse, quod praecipue Moses intendit, videlicet, ut ne quid fiat, magis minusve quam quod verbo Dei praecipitur. Replicat Whitgiftus, hoc in suis distributionibus contineri: atque non continetur: obtineat etenim hoc praeceptum, & non tantum peccat qui contra verbum facit, sed etiam qui praeter: non tantum quin meriti opinionem fovet in eis quae praeter verbum facit, sed qui praeter verbum facit omnino, sive meriti opinionem fovcat sive non; non tantum qui rem addit tanquam necessariam ad salutem, sed qui rem addit omnino sive necessariam dicat sive non: sic ut huius prohibitionis modo aperte Hierarchici illaqueantur: cum in politeia addunt praeter verbum, etsi id minime necessarium ad salutem fateantur.
units.tr: Thirdly, this Hierarchical doctrine smacks plainly of contempt for the Word. Offices cannot be added without dishonouring those things which Christ has long since instituted in his Word. So this addition is plainly the sin of Jeroboam, against which the charge is brought as a bold deed, that he made priests who were not of the sons of Levi, that is, not of the kind and number which God himself had ordained, 1 Kings 12.31. Against this sin King Abijah protests when he shows plainly that the churches ought to use only those offices which God instituted, and that all others added by men in imitation of the Papistical polity are to be removed. For he speaks thus, 2 Chron. 13.9: Have you not cast out the priests of Jehovah, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites, and made for yourselves priests like the peoples of other lands? But we have Jehovah our God, and we ought to add nothing to his command, not even for the sake of reason. Nothing that seems even good is to be added, but the simple and pure form of the command must be kept. By adding something of one's own, one understood the command to be only half complete. The lesson of this passage, then, is that we must neither take anything away from the divine commands nor add to them. I come to Whitgift, who devises many arguments indeed to turn aside this prohibition of addition from the Hierarchics; yet that Hookerian evasion did not even occur to him. He says: First, those add to the Word who teach against the Word; second, those who make something necessary to salvation which is not contained in the Word; third, those who foster the opinion of merit in those things which they have devised beyond the Word; fourth, those who forbid as unlawful what is lawful through the Word of God. Cartwright replies that the point Moses especially intends is omitted, namely that nothing be done more or less than what is commanded by the Word of God. Whitgift retorts that this is contained in his distributions; but it is not contained. For this precept stands, and not only does he sin who acts against the Word, but also he who acts beyond it; not only he who fosters the opinion of merit in things done beyond the Word, but he who does something beyond the Word altogether, whether or not he fosters the opinion of merit; not only he who adds a thing as necessary to salvation, but he who adds a thing altogether, whether or not he calls it necessary. So the Hierarchics are plainly caught in the snare of this prohibition in the mode described, since in the polity they add beyond the Word, even though they admit that the addition is in no way necessary to salvation.

units.la: 5 Atque quoniam Whitgifti, Hookeri, Zanchij, reliquorumque Hierarchicorum hoc commune fundamentum est, licitas esse in politeia ecclesiastica additiones, dummodo non sint contra verbum: videamus quid respondeant nostri ad papistas, quando traditinnes suas hoc ipso fundamento statuminant. R. Bellarminus ad hoc mandatum Mosis respondens, tria adfert praecipua. Primo, prohiberi tantum additionem ad opus praeceptum non ad secundum numerum praeceptorum; secundo, prohiberi tantum additionem corrumpentem; tertio, prohiberi tantum additionem legum contrariarum. Quid ad haec M. Sutclivius Hierarchicus? Respondet ad primum: additiones pontificias esse ad opera praecepta: quod ex hoc probat Gui. Whitakerus, quia multo plura praeceperunt quam Dominus. Atqui idem jam Hierarchicis respondere nobis licet: multoplura officia induxerunt, aut induci posse affirmant, quum quae Deus praecepit: peccant igitur adversus hoc mandatum Mosis. Respondet Sutclivius ad secundum, leges pontificias esse corrumpentes additiones: quod & in additionibus Hierarchicis verum est: officia etenim nova quae inducunt, vel induci posse affirmant, politeiam a Deo institutam corrumpunt, adulterant, imo & eliminant etiam, ut in officijs Seniorum & Diaconorum videre est. Respondet ad tertium Sutclivius. Quasi vero nullae essent novae leges nisi contrariae? & non ea esset legis perfectio, ut omnes alias leges -- excluderet? praeterea haec interpretatio verbis Mosis adversatur: ipse etenim diserte loquitur & dicit Deut.12. Hoc tantum facito Domino; nihil addas aut minuas. Non opus est ic aliis verbis est. aliqua quæ expediunt quibusdam temporibus, & tamen ecclesia quę habet authoritatem ista addere , authoritatem non habet ita tollere. Minor etiam tua ambigua est,ecclesiam non posse aliquod ministerium à Deo institutum tollere: non potest quidem homo ministeria ea tollere quæ Deus ut perpetua instituit; sed tollere potest ea quę solum ad tempus instituta sunt prout occasio requirit.] Respondeo: Nulla ecclesia authoritatem habet nè ministerialem quidem instituendi in substantialibus politeias suæ, quodsi haberet, haberet etiam parem tollendi,idque in officijs quæ non à seipso sed à Deo sunt instituta.
units.tr: 5 Since this common foundation of Whitgift, Hooker, Zanchius and the other Hierarchics is that additions in the ecclesiastical polity are lawful, provided they are not against the Word, let us see how our men answer the Papists, when the Papists establish their traditions on this very foundation. Robert Bellarmine, answering this command of Moses, brings forward three main points. First, only addition to the work commanded is forbidden, not addition to the number of the commandments; second, only corrupting addition is forbidden; third, only addition of contrary laws is forbidden. What does the Hierarchic Master Sutcliffe reply to these? To the first, he replies that the Papistical additions are to the works commanded; William Whitaker proves this from the fact that they have commanded far more than the Lord did. Yet we too may now answer the Hierarchics in the same way: they have introduced, or affirm that it can be introduced, many more offices than those which God commanded, and so they sin against this command of Moses. Sutcliffe replies to the second, that the Papistical laws are corrupting additions; and this is true also of the Hierarchical additions. For the new offices which they introduce, or affirm can be introduced, corrupt and adulterate the polity instituted by God, and indeed even eliminate it, as can be seen in the offices of elders and deacons. Sutcliffe replies to the third: As if there were no new laws except contrary ones? Would not that be the perfection of a law, that it should exclude all other laws? Moreover, this interpretation is opposed to the words of Moses: he himself speaks plainly and says, Deut. 12, "Only do this for the Lord; add nothing and take nothing away." There is no need for other words. Some things are expedient at certain times, and yet the Church, which has authority to add these, does not have authority to remove them in this way. Your minor premise, too, is ambiguous: that the Church cannot remove any ministry instituted by God. Man indeed cannot remove those ministries which God instituted as perpetual; but he can remove those which were instituted only for a time, as occasion requires. I reply: no Church has authority, not even ministerial authority, to institute anything in the substantial matters of its polity. And if it had such authority, it would also have equal authority to remove, and that in the case of offices which were instituted not by itself but by God.

units.la: 7 Primò, Moses & Iohannes,addere & detrahere paria faciunt: utrumque ex æquo prohibetur,utrumque ex æquo punitur: ubi igitur imparitates istæ sunt quas Whitgiftus excogitavit: certè hęc authoritas divina eas omnes in ventum disputit. Secundo,patet vel ex ratione dialectica,authoritatem habere eum tollendi,qui authoritatem addendi habet: tollere etenim & addere cum contraria sint,& neutrum insit à natura: in idem subiectum incidunt; sic ut authoritatem tollendi habeat,qui habet addendi,perinde ac authoritatem habet abrogandi leges qui instituendi, condemnand qui absolvendi, ligandi qui solvendi,& sic in cæteris. Tertiò,patet ex ratione Theologica : nam addere institutis divinis perinde de authoriate & majestate jubentis detrahit,atque de eisdem tollere, pariliter igitur illicitum est. Patet hoc in igne addito per Nadab & Abihu, & in altari Damasceno addito pro Ahazam,& in additionibus Pharisęorum,quas Christus Dominus condemnat. Locum hic habent etiam quæ adversus additamentum pulcritudinis in mulieribns antiqui patres disputarunt. Sic a Cyprianus, Opus Dei est omne quod nascitur, diaboli quodcunque mutatur,intelligit vero mutationem per additionem. Sic Augustinus. b Injuriam facit pictori, qui addere ad illius picturam vult. Postremo sic Tertullianus. c Displicent illis nimirum plastica Dei: in ipsis redarguunt, reprehendunt artificem omnium; reprehendunt enim, quum emendant, quum adjiciunt,&c. Eadem sunt quæ in libro de habitu mulierum habet: ex quibus hæc citat Ri. Hookerus. d Æmuli sint necesse est, quæ Dei non sunt: aut igitur mentem Tertulliani non observat aut additiones omnes,æmulos appellat Dei,quia non ab ipso profectæ sunt. Vtcunque sit certum est,per totum librum tertium, tollere & addere paria eum fecisse,& utrumque pariter licere, aut non licere.
units.tr: 7 First, Moses and John make addition and subtraction equal: each is equally forbidden and equally punished. Where, then, are the inequalities that Whitgift has invented? Surely this divine authority dismisses them all as empty talk. Second, it is clear even from dialectical reasoning that whoever has the authority to add also has the authority to take away, since to take away and to add are contraries, and neither belongs to a thing by nature. They fall on the same subject. So whoever has the power of adding has the power of removing, just as whoever has the power of repealing laws has the power of enacting them, whoever has the power of condemning has the power of acquitting, whoever has the power of binding has the power of loosing, and so on in other cases. Third, it is clear from theological reasoning: adding to God's institutions takes away from the authority and majesty of the one who commands, just as taking away from them does, and so it is equally unlawful. This is shown by the fire added by Nadab and Abihu, by the altar of Damascus added in the time of Ahaz, and by the additions of the Pharisees, which Christ the Lord condemns. What the ancient Fathers argued against adding beauty to women also applies here. Thus Cyprian says: Whatever is born is the work of God; whatever is changed is the work of the devil, and by "change" he means change by addition. So too Augustine: He wrongs the painter who wants to add to his picture. Finally, so Tertullian: Of course they find fault with God's creations; in them they accuse and reprove the Maker of all things, for they reprove when they correct, when they add, and so on. These are the same points he makes in his book on women's dress, from which Richard Hooker quotes these words: They must necessarily be rivals of God, those things which are not of God. Either Hooker does not observe Tertullian's meaning, or Tertullian calls all additions rivals of God because they did not come from him. However that may be, it is certain that throughout the third book Parker has treated addition and subtraction as the same, and holds that both are equally lawful or equally unlawful.

units.la: 8 Quartò, quum dicit Whitgiftus,addere posse hominem ad ministeria Dei,quæ ipsis adminiculo esse possint, principium petit: nulla enim ministeria addita ab hominibus, ministeria à Deo instituta adjuvare possunt: sed eis nocent potius & incommodant, id quod hac ipsa die, cuivis oculato videre licet. Atque par est tollendi ratio : adæque etenim papista dicere potest,de oblatione calicis,eam usui esse, & commodæ sacramenti administrationi inservire. Quinto, quum hominini licere dicit,tollere ministeria ea quæ ad tempus tantum à Deo instituta
units.tr: 8 Fourth, when Whitgift says that a man may add to the ministries of God things that could serve as aids to them, he begs the question. For no ministries added by men can help the ministries instituted by God; rather they harm and hinder them, as anyone with eyes can see even today. The argument for subtraction is equally valid, for a papist could just as well say that the cup in the Lord's Supper is useful and serves the proper administration of the sacrament. Fifth, when he says that a man may take away ministries that God instituted only for a time,

units.la: a Hb. de habit. virg. b Serm. de temp. 247. c Lib. de cult. fœminar. c.5. d Lib.3. f.2. p.135. corpus Christi est: & membrum corpori adjici à quoquam potest, ut interim monstrum non existat?
units.tr: a Hebrew, on the virgins' dress. b Sermon on the time, 247. c Book on women's adornment, ch. 5. d Book 3, f. 2, p. 135. is the body of Christ, and can anyone add a member to the body so that there is no monster?

units.la: 11 Nonò,audiantur sententiæ sapientum. Ita Cyprianus, ut citatur à R.Feyldo ,Vnus Deus,unus Christus,una ecclesia, una cathedra,voce dominica supra Petrum fundata.Nullum aliud altare erigi,nullum aliud sacerdotium institui præter altare & sacerdotium illud quod jam est institutum. Quicunque alibi colligit,spargit. Sacerdotium cuius hic mentio est,non ad papam solum,sed ad omnes ministros pertinere ostendit contra Bellarminum Feyldus: nonne igitur aperte proclamat Cyprianus, nullos alios ministros institui in ecclesia posse, præter eos qui jam instituti sunt?Neque ad sacerdotium tantum docens restringi hæc verba possunt, ut sic de officijs ecclesiasticis, quæ ad regimen ecclesiæ pertinent, loqui Cyprianus non videatur: agit etenim contra schismaticos,contra quos & docentia & regentia sacerdotia, hoc argumento ita communit, ut intra ecclesiam tantummodo, non autem extra apud schismaticos,ea reperiri posse existimentur.Atqui inquies vel ex hac confessione liquet,non adversus nova sacerdotia intra ecclesiam Cyprianum loqui, sed de eis tantum quæ contra ecclesiam per schismaticos invehuntur. Quasi homogenea extra ecclesiam si illicita sint,quia præter sacerdotium instituta sint: tum heterogenea intra ecclesiam non sint illicita magis, quia eò magis præter sacerdotium à Deo institutum sunt,quo alterius generis sunt,ab eo quod est à Deo institutum.Quid quod,novum sacerdotium erigere,& novum altare erigere paria faciat Cyprianus ? novum autem altare, tam intra ecclesiam,quam extra ecclesiam illicitum est. Alibi Christum, unicum Episcopatus radicem,facit Cyprianus, vel Gui. Whitakero nostro interpretante:at radix alius statuitur præter Christum,quando authoritas tribuitur hominibus ut novum aliquem Episcopatum invehere & instituere possint. Citatur Damasus a R. Feyldo : is enim Chorepiscopos illicitos putat,quia eorum origo non est ex scripturis sacris: & sacerdotes pariter officiarios ecclesiasticos novos condemnat, qui ab hominibus superadduntur. Citatur enim Durandus, ab eodem R. Feyldo & approbatur : asserit is inferiores ordines, proprië ordines non esse, sed cultus divini solemnitates tantum: quia ab ecclesia introducti videntur,quæ ordines proprië dictos instituere nequit. Pofstremò, Archiepiscopi Bituriensis in Synodo Parisina ista quædam verba ferunt. Ecclesiasticus ordo penitus est confusus quia multi falcem mittunt in messem alienam : ut ecclesia Dei jam monstruum dici possit. Sicut enim in corpore naturali contingit,quod monstrum dicitur, cum membrum unum alterius officium habet,sic in corpore spirituali sciliect ecclesia, non utique literati & prudentes fratres videlicet maiores & minores officium specialiter nobis commissum occupant : sed iniustè,eum nemo debeat sibi honorem assumere,nisi qui a Domino sicut Aaron vocatur. Omnia hic pro nobis loquitur. Additio officij ecclesiastici additio membri est, quæ corpus ecclesiæ monstrosum reddit. Quæ officia ecclesiæ adduntur, humanitus inventū fuisse, ut verba illa planum faciunt quæ habentur in 2. Chron. 29. 25. Ex præcepto Davidis & Gadis videntis regis & Nathanis Prophetæ: nam à Iehova præceptum illud erat per Prophetas ejus. Fieri potest ut libentius audiri velint (inquit Hookerus) quando reges Israelis commendant, qui sine expresso Dei verbo nihil in Politeia Ecclesiæ tentare voluerunt. Itaque sanè: libentur etiam & audire abs te volumus, quomodo non omnes additiones eorum exemplum jugulat, quæ præsertim fiunt ad politeias Ecclesiasticæ substantialia, inprimis verò ad officia Ecclesiastica ea quæ à Deo ipso sunt instituta. Habeas interim, non nostram commendationem valere quicquam: commendantur illi à spiritu sancto: quorsum quæso, nisi ut nos eorum vestigijs ambulemus, atque ita à spiritu nostro nolmetipsos abstineamus. Non temerè hujus verbi memini: nam ut peccatum est Mal. 2. 16. spiritum nostrum non continere, à multiplicatione uxorum, ultra Dei institutum, qui spiritus satis habuit plures uxores hominibus dandi si voluisset: ita similiter peccatum est, spiritum nostrum non continere à multiplicando officia Ecclesiæ ultra præscriptam ab ipso Deo Politeiam: præsertim cum spiritus abundantiam habuerit ad providendum quæ officia Ecclesiæ profutura erant, & ad eadem quæ præviderat instituendum. Quoniam igitur Deo ita visum, versentur semper ante oculos, David, Solomon, Iehosaphat, Iosias, Nehemias, qui hoc nomine commendantur, quòd nihil verbo Dei addiderint, nihil detraxerint, sed in Politeia Ecclesiastica, spiritum suum ad verbi normam exactissime strictissimeq; conformarunt. 2. Chron. 29. 12, 13. 2. Chron. 13. 9, 10. 11. 2. Chron. 29. 25 Neh. 10. 29.
units.tr: 11 Ninth, let us hear the opinions of the wise. Thus Cyprian, as quoted by R. Feyld: One God, one Christ, one Church, one chair, founded upon the Lord's word over Peter. No other altar may be erected, and no other priesthood instituted, besides that altar and priesthood which already exists. Whoever gathers elsewhere, scatters. Feyld, against Bellarmine, shows that the priesthood of which he speaks pertains not only to the pope but to all ministers. Does not Cyprian then plainly declare that no other ministers may be instituted in the Church besides those already instituted? Nor can these words be restricted to the priesthood alone, so as to make Cyprian seem not to be speaking of ecclesiastical offices that pertain to the government of the Church. He is arguing against schismatics, and he argues so firmly that both teaching and ruling priesthoods are to be found within the Church only, and not outside it among the schismatics. But you will say that even from this statement it is clear that Cyprian is not speaking against new priesthoods within the Church, but only against those brought in by the schismatics against the Church. As if, forsooth, things of the same kind outside the Church are unlawful because they are instituted besides the priesthood, yet things of a different kind within the Church are not unlawful, and indeed are all the more beside the priesthood instituted by God, the more they differ in kind from what God has instituted. What about this: does Cyprian make the erection of a new priesthood and the erection of a new altar equally wrong? A new altar is unlawful both within the Church and outside it. Elsewhere Cyprian makes Christ the sole root of the episcopate, as our Whitaker interprets it. But another root is set up beside Christ when men are given authority to introduce and institute some new episcopate. Damasus is cited by R. Feyld. He holds that chorepiscopi are unlawful because their origin is not from holy Scripture, and he likewise condemns new ecclesiastical officers, the ministers that men add. For Durand is cited by the same R. Feyld and approved: he asserts that the lower orders are not properly orders at all, but only solemnities of divine worship, because they seem to have been introduced by the Church, which cannot institute orders properly so called. Finally, the Archbishop of Bourges in the Synod of Paris brings forward certain words: The ecclesiastical order is utterly confused, because many put their sickle into another's harvest, so that the Church of God may now be called a monster. For as in the natural body what is called a monster happens when one member has the office of another, so in the spiritual body, that is the Church, learned and prudent brothers, that is, the greater and lesser, do not occupy the office specially committed to us, but unjustly, since no one ought to assume honour for himself unless he is called by the Lord, as Aaron was. He speaks entirely for us here. The addition of an ecclesiastical office is the addition of a member, which makes the body of the Church monstrous. That the offices of the Church were added by human invention is made plain by the words in 2 Chron. 29:25: By the command of David and of Gad the king's seer and of Nathan the prophet; for that command was from the LORD through his prophets. Hooker says: "It may be that they wish to be heard more willingly when they commend the kings of Israel, who without an express word of God would attempt nothing in the polity of the Church." So indeed we gladly want you also to tell us how not all of their additions are refuted by their example, especially those made to the essential parts of the Church's polity, and above all to those ecclesiastical offices which were instituted by God himself. Be assured meanwhile that our commendation counts for nothing: they are commended by the Holy Spirit. To what end, I ask, except that we should walk in their footsteps and so abstain from our own spirit? I do not recall this word carelessly. As it is a sin (Mal. 2:16) not to restrain our spirit from multiplying wives beyond God's ordinance, though that Spirit had enough to give more wives to men had he wished, so it is likewise a sin not to restrain our spirit from multiplying the offices of the Church beyond the polity prescribed by God himself, especially since the Spirit had abundance to foresee which offices would benefit the Church and to institute those very offices which he had foreseen. Since it has pleased God thus, let David, Solomon, Jehoshaphat, Josiah and Nehemiah stand always before our eyes, who are commended for this: that they added nothing to the word of God and took nothing from it, but in the polity of the Church conformed their spirit most exactly and strictly to the rule of the Word. 2 Chron. 29:12–13; 2 Chron. 13:9–11; 2 Chron. 29:25; Neh. 10:29.

units.la: 3. Quintò & ultimò arguit à testimonio Theodori Bezæ Richardus Bancroftus, verbis istis: [Impugnantur à Puritanis Archiepiscopi & Episcopi, ex hoc principio Cartwrightiano, quòd quodvis augmentum authoritatis ministro additum, illius ministerium adeo immutat, ut novum ministerium fiat: in quo perpetuum eis ab ipso Beza silentium imponitur. Is de loco Hieronimi tractans adversus Saraviam, in quo dicitur Episcopos ordinis causa constitutos suisse, affirmat: Mutatio fuit non in re ipsa, idest, in ipso ordine sed in ordinis modo.] Paulo post adhuc amplius: [distinguendum est inter rei naturam, & id quod eidem accidentaliter adhæret, quia eo in aliud commutato & sublato, res ipsa permanet. Hinc eò tandem dilabitur & affirmare non dubitat, hujusmodi authoritatis augmentum, ordinis & modi alterationem, de essentia ministerij non esse, sed accidentale quiddam, quod pro circumstantiis locorum & temporum mutari possit, Atque hoc exemplo utitur: Ut unus quispiam judicio cæterorum compresbyterorum delectus, presbyterio præsidi esset & permaneret, id certe reprehendi nec potest nec debet. Imò in effectu concedit Archiepiscopi institutionem verbo Dei consentaneam esse, ex illa generali & verissima Apostolica regula. Ut omnia ordine fiant.] Hæc Bancroftus. Primò
units.tr: 3. Fifthly and lastly, Richard Bancroft argues from the testimony of Theodore Beza, in these words: [The Puritans attack the archbishops and bishops on this principle of Cartwright's: that any increase of authority added to a minister so changes his ministry that it becomes a new ministry. In this matter Beza himself imposes silence upon them. Treating a passage of Jerome against Saravia, where it is said that bishops were established for the sake of order, he affirms: "The change was not in the thing itself, that is, in the order itself, but in the mode of the order."] A little later, still further: [One must distinguish between the nature of a thing and what adheres to it accidentally, since when that is changed and removed the thing itself remains. Hence he does not hesitate to slide finally to the point of affirming that such an increase of authority and alteration of order and mode is not of the essence of the ministry, but something accidental, which may be changed according to the circumstances of places and times. And he uses this example: That one man, chosen by the judgement of the other fellow-presbyters, should preside over and remain in the presbytery, that certainly can neither be blamed nor ought to be blamed. Indeed, in effect he concedes that the institution of archbishops is consistent with the word of God, by that general and most true apostolic rule: Let all things be done in order.] So Bancroft. First,

units.la: p.152. p.153. p.141.152. P.153. P.143. P.118. mò fuut qui D. Bezam minus commodè locutum dolent, saltem qui siluisse hæc de re optant: sic nec ora adversariorum ista sua liberaliori concessione aperuisset: nec negotium fecisset suis calumnias eas refutandi: quin ex horum verborum nonnullis speciem aliquam mutuari videntur. Sed fac satis commode locutum fuisse: non tamen silentium uobis imposuit, uti Bancroftus gloriatur.
units.tr: p.152. p.153. p.141.152. P.153. P.143. P.118. Indeed there are some who regret that Beza spoke less becomingly, or at least wish he had kept silent on this matter. Had he not made that generous concession, the mouths of his opponents would not have been opened, and he would not have had the trouble of refuting their slanders; indeed, some of them seem to borrow a pretext from a few of his words. But grant that he spoke quite becomingly: even so, he did not impose silence on you, as Bancroftus boasts.

units.la: 4. Secundò etenim respondemus, falsum esse aut Cartwrightum aut reformatos alios asseraisse unquam, quamcunque auctionem authoritatis ministerii statim aliud inferre. Novimus etenim & veteres Episcopos, & modernos Germaniæ Superintendentes, authoritatis quandam augmentationem in eo accepisse, quòd perpetui Synodorum præsides & moderatores constituti sint: quum tamen ordinem nullum adipiscantur, qui non eis, cum reliquis collegis suis communis sit. Tertio, affermat Bancroftus, concludere nos, Archiepiscopos & Episcopos novum ministerium adeoq; illicitum evasisse, nunquam à Christo aut ab Apostolis institutum, quòd authoritatis suæ incrementum à conciliis acceperint. Hoc iterum falsum. Sententia etenim nostra est, authoritatem nullam Archiepiscopalem aut Episcopalem à Christo aut Apostolis iustitutam esse, quæ incrementum à conciliis &c. recipere posset. Interim quod das libenter accipimus, nempè Archiepiscopos & Episcopos incrementum authoritatis a conciliis accepisse: utpote ex quo aperte constat contra Downamum Archiepiscopos & Episcopos temporis successu non eosdem esse sed auctiores multò, quam qui primitus ab ipsis instituti finguntur. Non itaq; nobis silentium imposuit Beza: sed silentium Downamo imposuit Bancroftus. Quo etenim ore ille assertionem dehinc suam tueri poterit, nullam mutationem Episcopalis authoritatis factam fuisse per annos 300, post vero, diminutam quidem fuisse (non auctam) partim accessione magistratus, partim Dioceseon multiplicatione: quo factum est, ut neque ita libera neque ita larga authoritas Episcopalis fuerit, ac ab initio fuit.
units.tr: 4. Secondly, we reply that it is false that Cartwright or the other Reformed ever asserted that any increase in the authority of the ministry immediately implies something else. For we know that both the ancient bishops and the modern superintendents of Germany received a certain increase of authority in this, that they were appointed as perpetual presidents and moderators of synods; yet they obtain no rank that is not common to them along with their other colleagues. Thirdly, Bancroftus affirms that we conclude that archbishops and bishops have become a new ministry, and so an unlawful one, never instituted by Christ or the apostles, because they received an increase of their authority from councils. This again is false. For our view is that no archiepiscopal or episcopal authority was instituted by Christ or the apostles which could receive an increase from councils, etc. Meanwhile, what you concede we gladly accept, namely that archbishops and bishops received an increase of authority from councils; for it is clear from this that, contrary to Downame, archbishops and bishops are not the same as they were over time but are far greater than those who are feigned to have been first instituted by them. So Beza did not impose silence on us; rather, Bancroftus imposed silence on Downame. For with what face will he henceforth defend his assertion that no change was made in episcopal authority for three hundred years, and afterwards it was indeed diminished (not increased), partly by the addition of the magistrate and partly by the multiplication of dioceses; so that episcopal authority has been neither as free nor as large as it was from the beginning.

units.la: 5 Quartò, quod D. Beza de Episcopo apud Hieronymum introducto dicit, per mutationem, non in ordine ipso, sed in modo tantum ordinis accidentali: id judicio comprebyterorum ex Hieronymi sententia fuisse factum dicit. In quo silentium nonne quæso imposuit Hierarchicis, qui & ipsi sentiunt, & Hieronimum sentire dicunt, Episcopalem authoritatem non jure humano tantum sed ipso etiam jure divino niti? Quintò, quod D. Beza de veteribus Episcopis dicit, eos non ordine ipso, sed ordinis tantum modo accidentali à cæteris collegis distare, id maximè Hierarchicis, in duobus præcipuis capibus contravenit. Primò etenim hinc clarum est, veteres Episcopos nò fuisse tales quales nunc Anglia fovet; sed quales Superintendentes Germanici sunt, qui à se nihil agunt, sed presbyterorum consessum tantum moderantur, dum illi consilio consensuque communi omnia determinant. Secundò hinc clarum est Episcopos veteres & presbyteros unius ejusdemque ordinis fuisse: quomodo itaque hæc sententia Bezæ pro Hierarchicis facere potest, qui Episcopum à Presbitero in ipso ordine differre dicunt, qui Episcopatum & Presbyteratum duos esse ordines asserunt, qui denique differentiam inter Episcopum & Presbyterum ipso jure divino non in ordinis modo solùm, sed in ordine ipso consistere affirmant. Sextò quando loquitur D. Beza de ordine, non intelligit ordinem specialem, id est officium aliquod Ecclesiasticum, sed intelligit tantum ordinem præsidendi generaliter sumptum. Dicit ordinem requirere ut unus in cætu Ecclesiastico præsideat reliquis. Quomodo hoc probat? Tantum ex 1. Cor. 14.40. Omnia fiant ordine. Nullum igitur præceptum Ecclesiasticum somniat, uti somniant Hierarchici, qui in Epistola ad Timotheum cautum esse dicunt, ut esset in Ecclesia, certus quidam Episcopalis ordo & officium qui reliquos ministros regat.
units.tr: 5. Fourthly, what Beza says about the bishop introduced by Jerome, that the change was made not in the order itself but only in the accidental mode of the order, and that this was done by the judgment of the fellow elders according to Jerome's opinion: in this, I ask, has he not imposed silence on the hierarchists, who both themselves hold, and say that Jerome holds, that episcopal authority rests not only on human law but also on divine law itself? Fifthly, what Beza says of the ancient bishops, that they differed from their other colleagues not in the order itself but only in the accidental mode of the order, this especially runs counter to the hierarchists in two principal points. First, it is clear from this that the ancient bishops were not such as England now fosters, but such as the German superintendents are, who do nothing on their own but only moderate the assembly of elders, while those determine everything by common counsel and consent. Secondly, it is clear from this that the ancient bishops and the elders were of one and the same order. How, then, can this opinion of Beza favour the hierarchists, who say that a bishop differs from a presbyter in the order itself, who assert that episcopate and presbyterate are two orders, and who finally affirm that the difference between bishop and presbyter by divine law consists not only in the mode of the order but in the order itself? Sixthly, when Beza speaks of order, he does not mean a special order, that is, some ecclesiastical office, but only the order of presiding taken in general. He says that order requires that one person in an ecclesiastical assembly preside over the rest. How does he prove this? Only from 1 Cor. 14.40: Let all things be done decently and in order. He therefore dreams up no ecclesiastical precept, as the hierarchists dream, who say in the Epistle to Timothy that provision is made that there be in the Church a certain episcopal order and office which rules the other ministers.

units.la: 6. Septimò, quid aliud est ordinis ille modus accidentalis apud Bezam, qui ordinis essentiam minimè mutat? Certè nihil aliud quam perpetuitas præsidentiæ, quæ ante per vices mutata fuit, nova præsidis electione adhibita in unoquoque conventu. Huc tendunt illa p. 153. Accidentale fuit ut unus quispiam, judicio cæterorum compresbyterorum delectus, presbytero πρωτος esset, & permaneret, adverte, permaneret. Hæc dum Anglicè vertit Bancroftus, ita habet, presbyterio πρωτῷ esset. id est, præsidens vel prælatus. Prælatus verò? Imo de Prælato Anglicano minimè somnium somniavit Beza: hoc tantum vult. Quando Episcopus judicio cæterorum compresbyterorum delectus erat, præsidentia ipsa in essentia mutata non fuit, neque major ulla huius novi Episcopi authoritas erat, quam quæ veterum & antecedentium præsidum fuerat: tum enim in ordine ipso, ac non in ordinis modo solum, mutatio facta fuisset. Hoc tantum discrimen de novo introductum est in ordinis modo: ante multi per vices præsidere solebant, nunc unus tantum præsidebat: antè præses non permanebat sed in singulis conventibus mutabatur: jam vero permanebat & non mutabatur. Hic ille mos est, de quo dicit D. Beza, reprehendi nec potest nec debet, in quibus justificat ille quidem Superintendentem Germanicum, sed nullo modo Episcopum Archiepiscopumve Anglicanum.
units.tr: 6. Seventhly, what else is that accidental mode of order in Beza, which does not in the least change the essence of the order? Certainly nothing other than the perpetuity of the presidency, which was formerly exercised by turns, a new election of a president being held at each meeting. To this point those words on p. 153 tend: It was accidental that one person, chosen by the judgment of the other fellow elders, should be first [πρῶτος] among the elders, and remain so. Note the word remain. When Bancroftus translates this into English, it reads: should be first [πρωτῷ] in the presbytery, that is, presiding or prelate. But a prelate? Indeed Beza never dreamed of an Anglican prelate at all; he means only this. When a bishop was chosen by the judgment of the other fellow elders, the presidency itself was not changed in essence, nor was there any greater authority in this new bishop than what the earlier and former presidents had possessed; for then the change would have been made in the order itself, and not merely in the mode of the order. This only difference was newly introduced in the mode of the order: before, several men used to preside by turns, now only one presided; before, the president did not remain but was changed at each meeting; now he remained and was not changed. This is the custom of which Beza says it neither can nor should be censured, by which he indeed justifies the German superintendent, but in no way an English bishop or archbishop.

units.la: 7. Quod incrementum authoritatis, inquit Bancroftus, Cartwrightus putat essentiale, id Beza appellat accidentale, non in ordine ipso, sed in ordinis modo tantum. Duplex in his latet Sophisma. Primo, loquitur Bancroftus de ordine speciali Ecclesiastico, Beza non de ordine aliquo Ecclesiastico speciali, sed tantum de ordine præsidentiæ generali. Torquetur igitur cum ad hoc trahitur, ac si dixisset, non mutari ministerij Ecclesiastici essentiam, quando ipsius authoritas augetur: hoc tantum vult, non mutatur generalis ordo ab Apostolo præscriptus 1.Cor.14.40. qui in omni conventu Ecclesiastico per alicujus præsidentiam observandus est, quando ejus modus mutatur per potestatem aut vicissitudinem. Secundo, loquitur Bancroftus de augmento authoritatis in Ecclesiæ ministris ac si Beza hic augmentum in Episcopis & archiepiscopis reprehendi nec posse nec debere dixisset, aut ipsum ordinem in essentia mutari negasset. At nihil horum habet Beza: nec ille de augmento authoritatis loquitur omnino: imo Episcopum quando primo introducebatur, non majorem authoritatem habuisse putat, quam habuerunt antecedentes praesides: addo etiam, ideo Episcopi introductionem nihil mutasse de re ipsa putat, quia ipsa authoritas augmentata minime fuit, sed eadem semper permanebat. Hoc si factum fuisset, mutationem in ipsa essentia factam fuisse existimasset: nunc quia hoc factum non est, sed tantum mutata sit eadem authoritas praesidendi in perpetuum, quae ante non erat perpetua: ideo non in ordinis essentia sed in ordinis modo tantum hanc mutationem fuisse factam dicit. Atque ita jam tandem absolvimus juvante Deo, quod de principiis Politeias Ecclesiasticae dicendum erat. Vidimus scripturam solam Poletias Ecclesiae principium esse. Vidimus, papistica juxta ac falsa esse principia alia sive fundamenta sive firmamenta, quae praeter scripturam pro Hierarchia afferri & produci solent. Vidimus certam Politeias formam quoad substantialia, in verbo Dei praescriptam esse. Vidimus hanc formam immutabilem esse, sic ut vel de eadem detrahere, vel eidem addere nefas sit. Sequeretur forte, ut Episcopatum Hierarchicum ex eo illicitum demonstrarem, quod omnium aetatum consensu jure humano additum & superinductum in Ecclesiam sit: sed quia partim ex superioribus patet & quia hic liber plus justo jam intumuit, alius huic disputationi locus necessario nobis quaerendus est.
units.tr: 7. What Cartwright thinks an essential increase of authority, says Bancroftus, Beza calls accidental, not in the order itself, but only in the mode of the order. There is a double sophism lying hidden in this. First, Bancroftus speaks of a special ecclesiastical order, whereas Beza speaks not of any special ecclesiastical order but only of the general order of presiding. Therefore he is twisted when he is dragged into this, as if he had said that the essence of the ministry is not changed when its authority is increased. He means only this: the general order prescribed by the apostle in 1 Cor. 14.40, which is to be observed in every ecclesiastical assembly through the presidency of someone, is not changed when its mode is altered by power or by rotation. Secondly, Bancroftus speaks of an increase of authority in the ministers of the Church as if Beza had said here that an increase in bishops and archbishops neither can nor should be censured, or had denied that the order itself changes in essence. But Beza has none of these things: nor does he speak of an increase of authority at all. Indeed, he thinks that a bishop, when first introduced, had no greater authority than the earlier presidents had; I add that he thinks the introduction of the bishop changed nothing in the thing itself, because the authority itself was not increased at all, but remained always the same. If that had been done, he would have judged that a change had been made in the essence itself. Now, because this has not been done, but only the same authority of presiding has been made perpetual, which before was not perpetual, therefore he says that this change was made not in the essence of the order but only in the mode of the order. And so, with God's help, we have at last completed what had to be said about the principles of the ecclesiastical polity. We have seen that Scripture alone is the principle of the polity of the Church. We have seen that the other principles or foundations, or supports, which are usually brought forward and produced for the hierarchy besides Scripture, are Papistical as well as false. We have seen that a certain form of polity as regards its essentials is prescribed in the Word of God. We have seen that this form is unchangeable, so that it is wrong either to take anything away from it or to add anything to it. Perhaps it would follow that I should demonstrate the hierarchical episcopate to be unlawful on the ground that it has been added and superinduced upon the Church by human law with the consent of all ages; but because this is partly clear from what has gone before, and because this book has already swelled beyond what is right, another place for this disputation must necessarily be sought by us.

units.la: Finis Libri Secundi.
units.tr: End of the Second Book.
